records.title: [CHEAT SHEET] Chat Vs Cowork
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/AIWS Asset Hub/AI Workflow/[CHEAT SHEET] Chat Vs Cowork - AIWS Asset Hub · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: In this Cheat Sheet, find out whether you should use Claude Chat or Claude Cowork for a task. The One-Line Framework Chat is for thinking. Cowork is for doing.
records.content:
In this Cheat Sheet, find out whether you should use Claude Chat or Claude Cowork for a task.

The One-Line Framework

Chat is for thinking. Cowork is for doing.

That's it. That's the whole mental model.

If you're exploring ideas, asking questions, brainstorming directions — stay in Chat. It's cheap, fast, and built for back-and-forth.

If you need something done — a file created, a workflow executed, a task completed — move to Cowork. It's built to act on your world, not just talk about it.

The mistake everyone makes: using Cowork to brainstorm (expensive thinking) or using Chat to try to get work done (frustrating limitations).

What Chat Does Best

Chat is your whiteboard. You sketch, erase, rethink.

Brainstorming & Ideation — Explore 10 directions before committing to one. Chat is where you figure out what you want done before you spend tokens doing it.

Artifacts — Live previews of code, documents, diagrams right in the conversation. See what something looks like before you commit to building it for real.

Projects — Upload files as persistent context across conversations. Chat remembers what you've shared across sessions.

Web Search — Built-in, fast, cited. Chat can search the internet natively. Cowork can't do this without extra setup.

Low Token Cost — Conversations are cheap. A brainstorming session costs pennies. Exploration should be cheap — that's how you get to good ideas.

Quick Q&A — "What's the best way to structure a newsletter?" doesn't need an agent. It needs an answer.

Think of Chat like talking to a brilliant advisor. You wouldn't hand them a mop — you'd ask them what to think about, then go do the work.

What Cowork Does Best

Cowork is your workshop. You build, ship, deliver.

File Operations — Read, write, create, organize actual files on your computer. The output isn't trapped in a chat window — it's a real file you can open, edit, send.

Background Tasks — Start a task, walk away, come back to finished work. Cowork can grind while you take calls.

Multi-Step Workflows — Input goes in one end, finished work comes out the other. No babysitting each step.

Connectors — Notion, Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Figma, Vercel. Cowork works where you work. Output lands in your tools, not in a chat thread.

Browser Automation — Fill forms, navigate sites, extract data. Cowork can do the clicking for you.

Sub-Agents — Spawn parallel workstreams for big jobs. One command can kick off five different tasks running at the same time.

Think of Cowork like a capable team member sitting at your computer. They can open apps, create files, push buttons — not just give you advice.

The Decision Tree

Not sure where to start? Follow the flow:

┌──────────────────────────┐
│  Do I know exactly what  │
│     I want done?         │
└─────┬──────────┬─────────┘
     YES         NO
      │           │
      │           ▼
      │      ┌─────────┐
      │      │  CHAT   │
      │      │ Figure  │
      │      │ it out  │
      │      └─────────┘
      ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│  Does it need to create  │
│    or modify files?      │
└─────┬──────────┬─────────┘
     YES         NO
      │           │
      │           ▼
      │      ┌─────────┐
      │      │  CHAT   │
      │      │ Quick   │
      │      │  Q&A    │
      │      └─────────┘
      ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│  Will it take more than  │
│   3 back-and-forths?     │
└─────┬──────────┬─────────┘
     YES         NO
      │           │
      │           ▼
      │      ┌─────────┐
      │      │  CHAT   │
      │      │ handles │
      │      │   it    │
      │      └─────────┘
      ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│  Have I done this exact  │
│     task before?         │
└─────┬──────────┬─────────┘
     YES         NO
      │           │
      ▼           ▼
┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
│  COWORK  │ │  COWORK  │
│ Make it  │ │ Do it    │
│ a Skill  │ │  once    │
└──────────┘ └──────────┘

The through-line: if you're still figuring out WHAT to do, stay in Chat.

If you know what needs to get DONE, move to Cowork.

The Token Reality

This isn't about being cheap — it's about putting your spend where it creates value.

  • Chat: ~$0.01–0.05 per conversation turn. Cheap to explore. You can brainstorm 20 directions for the cost of a gumball.

  • Cowork: ~$0.10–0.50+ per task depending on complexity. Worth every penny when it actually does something — creates files, connects tools, runs workflows.

The expensive mistake: Using Cowork to think out loud. Every "hmm, what should my newsletter be about?" in Cowork costs 510x what it would in Chat, and Cowork isn't even better at it.

The frustrating mistake: Using Chat to try to get work done. "Save this to Notion" — Chat can't. "Organize my files" — Chat can't. You'll go back and forth 8 times before realizing you need Cowork.

Rule of thumb: If you're still in the "what should I..." phase, you're in Chat territory. If you're in the "now do this..." phase, that's Cowork.

The Explore → Execute → Codify Loop

This is the progression that separates casual AI users from people who actually compress their workweek.

Step 1: Explore in Chat

Use Chat to figure out the best approach. Test prompts. Refine your thinking. Use Artifacts to preview what the output might look like.

  • "What's the best structure for a client proposal?"

  • "Show me three different hook styles for a newsletter."

  • "How should I organize my meeting notes?"

Chat is where ideas are cheap and iteration is instant. Don't skip this step — it's what makes the next step fast.

Step 2: Execute in Cowork

Take your refined approach to Cowork. Test if it can actually do the full workflow end-to-end. Push the boundaries.

  • "Generate a client proposal from this meeting transcript and save it to my proposals folder."

  • "Write my newsletter using my voice training and push it to Notion."

  • "Read my last 3 meeting recordings and create follow-up action items for each."

This is where you discover what Cowork can really do — and where you'll have your "holy shit" moments.

Step 3: Codify as a Skill

Once Cowork proves it can do the work, save that workflow as a SKILL.md. Now you (or anyone on your team) can run it with one sentence.

  • "Run my proposal skill on this transcript."

  • "Run my newsletter skill."

  • "Run my meeting follow-up skill."

No more explaining. No more prompt engineering. One sentence, done.

Every task you accomplish in Cowork is a candidate for a Skill. Every Skill makes you faster the next time. This is how one person operates like a team.

When to Graduate a Workflow to a Skill

Not everything needs to be a Skill. But when you spot these signals, it's time:

  • Signal 1: You've done this task in Cowork more than twice. If you've typed similar instructions three times, you're wasting keystrokes. A Skill turns those instructions into a single sentence.

  • Signal 2: The steps are predictable. Same type of input leads to same type of output. Meeting transcript → proposal. Voice memo → social post. If the pattern is stable, codify it.

  • Signal 3: Someone else could benefit from running it. If a teammate, VA, or new hire would need to do this task, a Skill means they can run it on day one without training.

  • Signal 4: You're re-explaining the same context to Cowork. Every time you start a new session, you re-describe your voice, your format preferences, your folder structure. A Skill carries all of that context so you don't have to.

If you're copy-pasting prompts, it should be a Skill.

The Loop

When in doubt: start in Chat, graduate to Cowork, codify as a Skill.

Three times marks a pattern. Codify it.

records.content:
Prompt writing is the art of unbundling language.

In life, “tasks” are really just bundled terms for lots of smaller actions tied together.

For example, the task of “doing the dishes” is a bundled term for lots of smaller tasks (or “variables”) such as:

  • Emptying the dishwasher

  • Putting the dirty plates, cups, pots, and pans in the sink

  • Scrubbing the food off of each plate, cup, pot, and pan

  • Putting dishwasher-safe plates and cups in the dishwasher

  • Hand-washing the remaining pots, pans, and non-dishwasher safe items

  • Scrubbing the countertops and stove with a soapy sponge

  • Cleaning and drying the countertops and stove with a wet, and then dry, paper towel

Notice how by saying, “Just do the dishes!” isn’t very clear instruction.

It only becomes clear when you break the larger task (and bundled term) down into smaller variables.

And you need to do the same thing when prompting AI.

So, here’s a simple framework for “unbundling” any task into a long-form written AI prompt.

Prompt Writing Template

The goal of this first section is to provide AI context on 3 things:

  • (What) Specialization: What “speciality” would you like this AI (prompt) to have? This helps give AI direction when infinite knowledge is available. This is “what” you would like AI to help you do.

  • (How) Instruction: What “tangibly” would you like AI to do for you? In what order or presentation style? This tells AI what you would like to receive back. This is “how” you would like AI to do whatever it is you’re asking it to do.

  • (Why) Context: What “uniquely” would you like AI to do for you? This tells AI the specific type or way you would like it to accomplish its task. This is “why” you would like, whatever you’re asking to be done, done a certain way.

For example:

You are a Positioning Consultant, specifically for freelance writers who want to niche down as ghostwriters.

I am going to give you the industry I would like to be a ghostwriter within, and the service I want to specialize in, and I would like you to present back to me:

  • Positioning Upgrade #1: A list of 30 even more specific niches within that industry where I could find potential clients and consider reaching out to (with niche-specific messaging).

  • Positioning Upgrade #2: A constellation and list of 20 tangentially related industries or niches that aren’t exactly the same, but “close enough” that a lot of my skills could also be translated there as well.

  • Positioning Upgrade #3: And a short-form bio (160 characters or less, so it fits on X/Twitter) that positions me as a specialist in that industry, providing the specific service I want to offer.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on some context for each of these pieces I am looking for your help with.

~

Instruction

In the introduction, you will have prompted AI to:

  • Specialize in a skill

  • Instruct on a task

  • And give context to how you would like it to perform that task

Next, you must clarify the Instructions.

Quite literally, this is where you must repeat “what” you want AI to help you do, and then set the foundation for “how” you would like AI to perform that task.

The “how” is the most important part of the prompt (and where prompts truly become Intellectual Property) because anyone can ask AI to do “something.” What makes your prompt unique is that you are asking AI to do something in a particular way. This is no different than hiring an employee who has a specialized skill set. You aren’t just hiring them for a role—you’re hiring them to perform a role in a specific, unique, differentiated, and valuable way.

The same logic applies to prompting AI.

For Example:

There are 5 formats that work best for thought leadership short-form social content.

  • Format #1: Paragraph Style

  • Format #2: What, How, Why

  • Format #3: Listicle

  • Format #4: Old vs New

  • Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

I’m going to walk you through each format, describe what makes it unique, and then give you several examples of what a great short-form social post executing each format looks like—so you understand how to replicate.

~

Context

It’s not enough to tell AI to “do something.” You must also tell it “how” you would like it done—and the more specific you can be, the better.

But in order to tell AI “how” to do something effectively, it needs more than just high-level instruction.

It needs context.

Specifically, AI needs…

  • Rules: Clearly defined rules or explanation for why this particular task needs to be done in the specific way you are explaining.

  • Positive Attributes: Qualities that tangibly and objectively define what would classify as a “good” output. (Example: It’s not enough to say, “Write 3 really great social posts.” You must define the Positive Attributes that make for “great social posts,” according to you, as clearly as possible.)

  • Reinforcement Examples: Very specific examples that reinforce the rules and positive attributes of the individual task.

Now, a mistake a lot of Prompt Writers make is they do not include examples that perfectly match the rules & positive attributes. The reason this is a mistake is because now AI doesn’t have the ability to create pattern recognition. Instead, it’s forced to “use its own intuition”—which leads to low-quality outputs and sporadic thinking.

For Example:

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is a declarative perspective, opinion, or way of seeing the world distilled down into a single paragraph. Imagine this is the short paragraph in a book that so perfectly summarizes the topic at hand that readers can’t help but highlight it.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

  • Concise language and making statements in the most economical way possible (avoid lots of tiny words that make a sentence sound convoluted).

  • Alternating of long and short sentences to add emphasis, rhythm, and flow into the writing.

  • Some sort of strong opinion, polarizing point of view, declarative statement, or at least a perspective that isn’t “hedging” but takes a stance and stands by it.

  • Lightly poetic language. This should be subtle and barely perceptible to the average reader, but small uses of alliteration, repetition, or the use of literary mechanisms like a Polyptoton (same word, two different parts of speech), or an Antithesis (an obvious observation, followed by a non-obvious observation).

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #1: Paragraph Style short-form posts.

Example #1:

If you’re debating between going to that “networking event” and working, choose the work. When the work works out, the people will still be there to take your call. But if you never do the work, no amount of networking will get it done for you. They wont take your call either.

Example #2:

Success in life comes down to accepting how the world is and finding ways to make things work to your benefit. Failure in life occurs when you wish things were different, and wait for the world to adjust to you (it never happens).

Example #3:

One key to a good relationship is to simply accept all the things that annoy you about the other person. Acknowledge them, laugh about them, surrender to them, and once you do, it's so much easier to really love them. But until then, their quirks will just irritate you.

~

Final Delivery

Lastly, at the end of the prompt, you want to crystallize the delivery instructions.

Things you can consider to include here are:

  • Repeating objective constraints

  • Stating what you are going to provide AI

  • Stating what you would like AI to return back to you

  • Describing the final output you want to make sure gets delivered

For example:

I am now going to give you the topic, and I would like you to give me a day’s worth of short-form thought leadership social content.

Each post must read like a standalone Tweet, without any formatting labels or headers, and must fit within the 280 character constraint of X/Twitter.

~

Iteration

It’s very rare to write a prompt that delivers a perfect output on the first try.

Instead, you should view prompt writing as an iterative game—and one that benefits from conversing with AI itself.

  • Run the prompt

  • Evaluate the output

  • Identify mistakes

  • Share those mistakes with AI and ask why they happened

  • And ask what you should change in the prompt so those mistakes don’t happen again

Repeat this process several times to stress-test your prompt and ensure you can recreate positive outputs over and over again.

records.content:
The million-dollar question: “WHAT SHOULD I NAME MY PRODUCT?!”

The short answer is, as long as it’s tangible, it’s probably a good name.

Here are 20 naming conventions you can use to get the creative juices flowing:

  1. [Number] for [Number]

    • Example: “Ship 30 for 30.”

    • Why It Works: We anchor the user to a specific quantity and a defined timeframe. Clear, immediate, and tangible outcome: “I’ll achieve X in Y days.”

  2. [Topic/Skill] OS

    • Example: “LinkedOS.”

    • Why It Works: Positions your product as an “Operating System,” implying a structured, foundational system the user can install and run.

  3. The [Adjective] [Blueprint/Playbook/Toolkit]

    • Example: “The Ultimate Ghostwriter’s Blueprint.”

    • Why It Works: “Blueprint,” “Playbook,” “Toolkit,” etc., all sound like physical artifacts. Adding an adjective (e.g., “Ultimate,” “Rapid,” “Essential”) emphasizes its completeness.

  4. [Topic/Skill] in a Box

    • Example: “Podcasting in a Box.”

    • Why It Works: Conjures the image of an all-inclusive “kit” that contains everything you need to solve a specific problem.

  5. The [Number]-Day [Challenge/Accelerator]

    • Example: “The 14-Day YouTube Accelerator.”

    • Why It Works: Creates built-in urgency, a definitive time commitment, and a sense of community involvement (“challenge”) or speed (“accelerator”).

  6. The [Topic] Roadmap

    • Example: “The Ghostwriting Roadmap.”

    • Why It Works: “Roadmap” implies step-by-step direction, with tangible checkpoints along the way.

  7. The [Topic] Toolkit

    • Example: “The Freelance Pricing Toolkit.”

    • Why It Works: “Toolkit” suggests practical, hands-on resources or templates a user can “pick up” and apply.

  8. The [Topic] Vault

    • Example: “The Content Growth Vault.”

    • Why It Works: Suggests a hidden repository of resources, templates, or guides that feel exclusive and valuable.

  9. The [Topic] Launch Pad

    • Example: “The Low-Ticket Launchpad.”

    • Why It Works: Communicates that your program will “launch” users toward a goal—quick momentum and a clear starting point.

  10. [Number] Steps to [Outcome]

    • Example: “7 Steps to Your First $1,000 Ghostwriting Client.”

    • Why It Works: Highlights an exact pathway with a finite number of steps, making the product feel concise and doable.

  11. The [Topic] Playbook

    • Example: “The LinkedIn Leads Playbook.”

    • Why It Works: “Playbook” indicates a strategic, tactical document—like a sports team’s key plays that can be followed for consistent results.

  12. The [Topic] Bootcamp

    • Example: “The 30-Day Content Writing Bootcamp.”

    • Why It Works: Implies hands-on, rigorous training with tangible milestones—no fluff, just direct, action-focused learning.

  13. The [Topic] Sprint

    • Example: “The Blog Launch Sprint.”

    • Why It Works: Connotes speed and intensity over a short period—perfect for someone who wants quick wins.

  14. The [Topic] Command Center

    • Example: “The Social Media Command Center.”

    • Why It Works: A “command center” sounds like a centralized control hub, giving the impression of powerful oversight and organization.

  15. The [Topic] Protocol

    • Example: “The Ghostwriting Client Acquisition Protocol.”

    • Why It Works: “Protocol” suggests a tested, formalized procedure, giving the product a sense of authority and rigor.

  16. The [Topic] Lab

    • Example: “The Email Marketing Lab.”

    • Why It Works: Implies experimentation and discovery—users expect hands-on exercises, templates, and the freedom to test ideas.

  17. The [Topic] Method

    • Example: “The 5-Figure Freelancer Method.”

    • Why It Works: “Method” implies a replicable system—highly useful for establishing credibility (e.g., “I have a method, not just random tips.”).

  18. The [Topic] Starter Pack

    • Example: “The Instagram Growth Starter Pack.”

    • Why It Works: Positions your offer as a curated “starter kit” of resources, checklists, or tools for immediate set-up and quick wins.

  19. The [Topic] Accelerator

    • Example: “The Ghostwriter Accelerator.”

    • Why It Works: Suggests rapid progress or fast-track success toward a specific outcome, with the connotation of leveling up quickly.

  20. The [Topic] Workbook

    • Example: “The Content Repurposing Workbook.”

    • Why It Works: A “workbook” is inherently tangible—people envision step-by-step exercises, worksheets, and fill-in-the-blank templates they can literally (or digitally) write in.

records.content:
Use this cheat sheet to:

  • Create a free lead magnet asset to attract your ideal customer

  • Build a "next step" offer to give to your leads (after they consume your free lead magnet)

  • Softly sell your lead magnet and offer on social media

This is Social Selling 101:

Step 1: Create A Lead Magnet Asset

  • [ ] Pick one painful micro-problem your audience hits before your main offer (e.g., "Welcome email only gets 1% click-through").

  • [ ] Write a 2–5 page PDF: clean, legible pages (large headings, short bullets, one font pair, your 3 colors).

    • Title with outcome ("Fix Your Activation Email: 5 Steps to +40% Clicks")

    • Problem → Why it happens → Step-by-step fix (3–5 steps)

    • 1 real example or mini-case

    • Soft CTA to work with you

  • [ ] Build a simple landing page:

    • Clear Headline — problem solved in one line

    • Targeted Subhead — who it's for + credibility

    • Key Outcomes — 3–5 bullets of benefits

    • Simple Form — name + email fields

    • Thank-you Page — next step: find the PDF in your inbox

  • [ ] Add the opt-in link to: bio, Featured (first card), pinned post, and inside 1–2 relevant posts per month.

Step 2: Create a “Next Step” Offer - Digital Product or Service

  • [ ] Write your core, “next step” offer in one sentence: who it's for, outcome, timeline, price range (services or digital product).

  • [ ] Add booking link to Featured, bio, email signature, and welcome email.

  • [ ] Publish one offer post/month (problem → stakes → your method → proof → invite).

  • [ ] Track monthly: connection acceptance rate, comment count, average saves, profile visits, opt-in conversion %, discovery calls booked.

  • [ ] Fix the lowest metric first (e.g., low profile visits → strengthen hooks; low opt-ins → sharpen landing headline and bullets).

Step 3: Promote On Social

  • [ ] Rotate CTAs:

    • Direct: "Full breakdown is in my free guide—grab it here."

    • Benefits: "If activation is stuck, this 5-step PDF will unstick it."

    • Social proof: "This process added +18% in 21 days—details in the guide."

    • Conversation: "Comment 'guide' and I'll DM it."

  • [ ] Add one CTA per post (keep it soft, specific, and relevant to the topic).

  • [ ] Respond to commenters with a thanks + 1 helpful line + ask a relevant question (no links unless invited).

  • [ ] Warm DM script after value exchange in the comments:

    • Acknowledge context ("Saw your comment on [X]")

    • Ask goal/problem ("What's the target you're aiming for?")

    • Offer help ("I've got a 5-step checklist—want it?")

    • If they engage, offer a 15-minute audit (clear agenda and outcome, not a pitch call).

    • On call, offer your "next step" service/digital product as the next step to solving their problem

records.content:
This is a sequence of AI Prompts you can use (in ChatGPT, Claude, Bard, doesn’t matter) to train AI on brainstorming potential low-ticket digital product ideas.

Just copy/paste these prompts into your favorite AI platform and walk through the steps.

Step 1: Identify your niche-within-a-niche.

First, if you have absolutely no clue where to start, here’s a simple prompt to get your wheels spinning.

All you have to do is copy/paste this prompt and then give AI your general industry, and it will spit back all sorts of different ideas and options to choose from.

Here’s the prompt:

I am working on creating a low-ticket digital product (priced at $350, text and video course), but first I need some help picking a specific niche-within-a-niche.

Here is a training on how this exercise works, and why it's so important.

~

One of the challenges people have when it comes to creating digital products (and identifying meaningful problems to solve) is they start their brainstorming in a giant mega-category. 

Things like:

- Healthcare
- Technology
- Productivity
- Financial Services
- Health & Wellness
- Etc.

But it’s worth recognizing these mega-categories are HUGE. 

And trying to pinpoint “a problem” (or even a list of problems) inside one of these mega-categories is very, very challenging. 

Why?

Because inside each mega-category are:

- Different kinds of people
- Each of whom are faced with different problems
- Looking to achieve different goals

Take “healthcare” for example.

Inside “healthcare” we could be talking about/to:

- Doctors
- Physical therapists
- Healthcare executives
- Healthcare startup founders
- Healthcare insurance providers
- Etc.

And each of these different “audiences” have VERY different problems.

Which means the first step is to niche down. 

Ideally:

- Mega-Category →
- Niche →
- Niche-Within-Niche

It’s a game of specificity.

### How To Niche Down

So, let’s make this as actionable as possible.

How do you niche down?

- **By Industry: Take the mega-category and pick a sub-category within it.** For example: “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy.”
- **By Demographic: Take the mega-category, pick a sub-category, and then pick a specific demographic.** For example: “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy” → “Physical Therapy For Remote Workers”
- **By Physical Location: Take the mega-category, pick a sub-category, and then pick a specific physical location or geography.** For example: “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy” → “Physical Therapists In Chicago.”
- **By Digital Platform: Take the mega-category, pick a sub-category, and then pick a specific digital location or platform.** For example: “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy” → “Physical Therapists On LinkedIn.”
- **By Price: Take the mega-category, pick a sub-category, and then pick a price range or socioeconomic status.** For example: “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy” → “Physical Therapy For Single Mothers On Food Stamps.”
- **By Distribution: Take the mega-category, pick a sub-category, and then pick a specific form of delivery.** For example: “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy” → “Physical Therapy On Zoom.”

The point is, you will come up with WAY higher-quality digital product ideas if you go through this exercise and get more specific, first.

Whereas if you stay broad, all your ideas are going to be vague.

~

I am going to tell you the industry (mega-category) I'm in, and I would like you to give me:

- 10 profitable niche options within that industry
- And then for each of the 10 profitable niche options, give me 6 "niche-within-niche" options based on the 6 provided in the training:

- By industry
- By demographic
- By physical location
- By digital platform
- By price
- By distribution

Are you ready to begin? If so, I'll tell you my industry.

Step 2: Identify 10 Biggest Problems

Once you have some sort of niche-within-niche, it’s time to brainstorm the 10 Biggest Problems people in this niche have.

Note: Here I combine the “10 Biggest Problems” and “Most Valuable Problem To Solve” together in this prompt—so that AI not only recommends 10 problems you can solve within your niche-within-niche, but also tells you which 1 (based on my checklist for creating digital products) would be most valuable to solve.

Here’s the prompt—just don’t forget to plug in your niche-within-niche at the beginning!

My niche-within-niche is: 

Next, to create a profitable low-ticket digital product, I want to create a list of the 10 Biggest Problems within this specific niche.

I would like this list of 10 biggest problems to be problems that in some way help the target customer in this niche-within-niche:

- Make more money
- Save money (or stop losing money)
- Save a lot of time
- Or unlock some form of status or industry recognition

I would also like these 10 biggest problems to be things that, if you were consulting me on how to start a business and laugh a profitable low-ticket product in this niche-within-niche, would be the 10 most lucrative problems to solve.

At the end, I would like you to also recommend the most valuable problem out of the 10 you think I should create a product to solve, specifically by running through the following checklist:

- Is a problem that can be OBJECTIVELY measured (meaning you can “prove” that you’ve solved it for the customer).
- Is a problem that requires more than just “an answer” in order to solve (meaning some kind of implementation).
- But most importantly, is a problem that is in some way correlated to either MAKING MONEY, NOT LOSING MONEY, SAVING A TON OF TIME, or UNLOCKING STATUS.

Step 3: Identify 10 Most Desirable Outcomes

Lastly, because you’re going to want to use these later in your marketing, it’s worth taking your 10 Biggest Problems and using AI to help you build a list of the most desirable outcomes your target customer has.

Here’s the prompt—and don’t forget to provide your own 10 Biggest Problems at the end of the prompt!

Now, for each of these 10 Biggest Problems, I would like you to write next to each one the Most Desirable Outcome our target customer in this niche-within-niche would have and how their life would be different if each of these problems got solved. Use as tangible and objective language as possible, and please write each Desirable Outcome as an "I" statement, pretending you are the target customer.

For example:

- **Problem #1: Distractions** → “If I wasn’t distracted, I would be so much more productive.”
- **Problem #2: Over-Editing** → “If I wasn’t constantly over-editing, I would save myself hundreds of hours and publish way more often.”
- **Problem #3: Perfectionism** → “If I wasn’t such a perfectionist, I would get out of my own way, publish more, and maybe even live my dream of being a full-time writer.”
- **Problem #4: Procrastination** → “If I stopped procrastinating, I would finally start making progress toward my writing goals.”
- **Problem #5: Self-Confidence** → “If I had self-confidence, I would finally share the stories and insights and frameworks I think are valuable but have been afraid to write and publish.”
- **Problem #6: Generating Ideas** → “If I had a reliable system for generating ideas, I wouldn’t feel so reliant on my intuition and so easily talk myself out of writing anytime I was struggling to come up with things to say.”
- **Problem #7: Imposter Syndrome** → “If I didn’t have Imposter Syndrome, I would stop comparing myself to other people, publish more often, and just generally feel happier and more fulfilled with my path in life.”
- **Problem #8: Writing Consistently** → “If I was writing consistently, my audience would grow faster, my library would grow faster, and I would achieve my goals as a writer way faster.”
- **Problem #9: Choosing A Platform** → “If I knew which platform to write on, I could finally start my journey of writing online.”
- **Problem #10: Finding Time To Write** → “If I had more time to write, I would be able to write consistently, grow my audience and library faster, and feel like I was on the path to achieving my goals.”

records.title: [PROMPT] The Micro-Niche Generator
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/AIWS Asset Hub/Digital Products/[PROMPT] The Micro-Niche Generator - AIWS Asset Hub · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: The mistake most people make when coming up with a product idea(s) is trying to solve a problem in a mega-category. Mega-categories are broad topics: - AI - Fi
records.content:
The mistake most people make when coming up with a product idea(s) is trying to solve a problem in a mega-category.

Mega-categories are broad topics:

  • AI

  • Fitness

  • Marketing

While it’s possible to innovate here, it’s rare.

These categories are huge. 90% of the leaders in these niches almost always started with a specific problem first, then expanded once they dominated the smaller space.

Nike didn't start trying to dominate all of "fitness" or "sportswear." They started super specific: Affordable, high-quality shoes for runners. And over time, they expanded into the billion-dollar global brand we know today.

Here's how:

  • Mega-Category → Fitness

  • Niche → Runners

  • Niche-Within-Niche → Affordable Shoes

It’s simple, but it takes practice.

Let’s break it down.

6 Ways To Niche Down From Any Mega-Category

There are lots of ways you can niche down further, but I’ve found these 6 to be the best. When someone has a problem to solve, they filter potential solutions through these lenses:

  • "Who serves people like me?" (Demographics)

  • "Who works in my industry?" (Industry)

  • "Who's in my area?" (Location)

  • "What's in my budget?" (Price)

  • "Who specializes in the platform I use?" (Platform)

  • "Who sells the way I prefer to buy?" (Distribution)

This is how the human brain naturally segments and searches for solutions.

Every other niching method (company size, problem type, etc.) ultimately falls under one of these six umbrellas. By choosing one of these proven pathways, you're aligning with how customers already think, making it easier for them to find you and easier for you to position yourself as the perfect fit.

Here’s how it works:

Step 1: Take Your Mega-Category And Pick A Sub-Category Within It.

For example:

  • “Healthcare” → “Sports”

  • “Healthcare” → "Addiction Recovery"

  • “Healthcare” → “Physical Therapy.”

And so on.

Step 2: Apply One Of The 6 Ways To Niche Down From A Sub-Category Even Further.

Pick a specific demographic, location, platform, price, or method of distribution to find your niche within a niche.

Expanding on the Physical Therapy example above, your niche-within-niche could look like this:

  • By Industry: "Sports Physical Therapy"

  • By Demographic: “Physical Therapy For Remote Workers”

  • By Location: “Physical Therapists In Chicago.”

  • By Platform: “Physical Therapists On LinkedIn.”

  • By Price: “Physical Therapy For Single Mothers On Food Stamps.”

  • By Distribution: “Physical Therapy On Zoom.”

See how much more specific (and valuable) each gets?

This two-step process takes you from competing with millions of businesses to maybe competing with hundreds or dozens. When supply goes down and demand is more targeted—prices go up! Which is why it’s way easier to make more money solving specific problems. It’s the law of supply and demand.

Let’s look at another example.

Example: Ship 30 For 30

When we started Ship 30 for 30, we could have said "we help ALL writers."

Instead, we got specific:

  • Mega-Category: Writing

  • Niche: Internet Writing

  • Niche-Within-Niche: Internet Writing for Beginners

That specificity is what allowed us to create something that truly resonated with our audience.

The point is, you will come up with WAY higher-quality digital product ideas if you go through this exercise and get more specific, first.

Whereas if you stay broad, all your ideas are going to be vague.

Now it’s your turn.

Pick A Mega-Category You're Interested In And Try The 6 Ways To Niche-Down ChatGPT Prompt.

This prompt gives you a giant list of niches to choose from.

Simply replace any copy within the curly brackets (e.g. {Mega-Category or Industry}) with your own details:

I am working on creating a digital product, but first I need some help picking a specific niche-within-a-niche.

One of the challenges people have when creating digital products is they start brainstorming in giant mega-categories like Healthcare, Technology, Productivity, etc.

But these mega-categories are HUGE, with different kinds of people who face different problems and want to achieve different goals.

The first step is to niche down: 

Mega-Category → Niche → Niche-Within-Niche

Here are 6 ways to niche down:
- By Industry: Take the mega-category and pick a sub-category
- By Demographic: Pick a specific demographic within the niche
- By Physical Location: Pick a specific geography 
- By Digital Platform: Pick a specific platform
- By Price: Pick a price range or socioeconomic status
- By Distribution: Pick a specific form of delivery

I am going to tell you the industry (mega-category) I'm in, and I would like you to give me:

- 10 profitable niche options within that industry
- For each niche, give me 6 "niche-within-niche" options using the 6 methods above

Are you ready? 

My category is: {Mega-Category or Industry}

After you run the initial prompt, you can dial in your niche exploration even further by brainstorming more niches with the prompt below:

Great, let's lock in on {Insert A Sub-Category}.

Can you give me 10 more {Industry, Demographic, etc.} niche-within-niches?

Then There Are 3 Filters To Help You Choose Your Niche:

  • Filter #1: Personal Experience. Pick something you've actually dealt with or lived through. If you've never struggled with time management as a freelancer or worked with Sport Dog, don't create a product about it. The best products come from problems you've personally solved.

  • Filter #2: The "Friend Test". Would your friends immediately think of you when this niche comes up? If people already ask you for advice in this area, that's a strong signal you're on the right track.

  • Filter #3: Who Do You Know? Choose a niche where you can easily find and talk to 10-20 people. If you can't name specific people in this group or don't know where they hang out online, pick a different niche.

Bottom line:

Pick the niche where you're already the person people come to for help—even informally.

This is your biggest clue that you can create something valuable there.

records.title: [PROMPT] Services Outreach
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/AIWS Asset Hub/Services/[PROMPT] Services Outreach - AIWS Asset Hub · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Before you use the prompt, please watch the video above. You are an Outreach Specialist for ghostwriters who are pitching clients on their ghostwriting services
records.content:
Before you use the prompt, please watch the video above.

You are an Outreach Specialist for ghostwriters who are pitching clients on their ghostwriting services.

I am going to pull leads I would like to pitch my ghostwriting services to.

I’m going to give you:

- Their name
- Their company name

And I’d like you to look the person up on X, LinkedIn, Instagram, YouTube, and Google, and present back to me a brief summary of the lead filling in the following variables:

But I want you to organize each variable in a very specific way, so let’s go through each one.

~

Variable #1: Social Profiles

First, I’d like you to present to me a bulleted list of the lead’s prominent social profiles with links next to each one, so that I have them easily accessible.

The list should be presented in the following format, with coinciding links:

**Social Profiles:**

- LinkedIn: Link to the lead’s LinkedIn profile
- Twitter/X: Link to the lead’s Twitter/X profile
- Instagram: Link to the lead’s Instagram profile
- YouTube: Link to the lead’s YouTube profile
- Personal Website: Link to the lead’s personal website
- Newsletter: Link to the landing page or specific domain of the lead’s personal newsletter
- Company: Link to the lead’s primary business
- (Optional) Company #2: Link to the lead’s secondary business, if they have one
- Company Newsletter: Link to the landing page or specific domain of the lead’s company’s newsletter

~

Variable #2: Lead Summary Bio

Next, I would like you to write a detailed summary bio about the lead. This should inform me at a high-level about who they are, what they currently do, and what they’ve done in the past—so that I have appropriate context on their experiences going into pitching them.

The information I care most about:

- Where are they based?
- What is their primary business today and what is their official job title/role?
- What meaningful businesses have they been part of, worked for, or started/sold in the past?
- Have they appeared in the news at all?
- Have they won any awards, or been part of any meaningful social/status events?

~

Variable #3: Biggest Problems

Next, I would like you to audit the lead’s social profiles, personal website, and company website.

Here’s how I would like you to audit and identify the Biggest Problems I (the ghostwriter) could help them solve.

I specialize in 2 different services:

- Social Ghostwriting
- Newsletter Ghostwriting

When auditing the lead’s social content, go beyond frequency. Identify specific missed opportunities like: repeating the same ideas, overly technical posts with no narrative or story, low engagement despite frequent posting, no clear CTA or direction toward a lead funnel, or weak alignment with their audience’s pain points.

My Social Ghostwriting service is built to help founders:

- Build authority in their niche
- Generate inbound interest
- Save time by outsourcing ideation and writing
- Translate complex thinking into compelling content

In the DM and Email scripts for Social Ghostwriting, call out the #1 most obvious missed opportunity in their content strategy. Use that as the hook. Write casually, but ensure the script ties back to tangible outcomes (audience growth, lead gen, or positioning). Try to lightly match their tone/style, based on their current social content.

So first, I would like you to audit their social profiles and give them a score out of 3, based on the following criteria, along with a short paragraph description summary of why you gave the lead the score you did.

- Score of 0 = The person has not posted anything new in the last 30 days or more.
- Score of 1 = The person has posted at least 1 new piece of content in the last 15 days.
- Score of 2 = The person has posted 7 new pieces of content in the past 14 days.
- Score 3 = The person has posted 1 new piece of content every day for the past 14 days.

Second, I would like you to audit whether or not the lead is actively and strategically driving any of their social traffic to an email opt-in landing page or newsletter, and give them a score out of 3, based on the following criteria: 

- Score of 0 = The person has no link in their bio, and does not link to any external site in any of their content or in the comments of their content over the past 30 days.
- Score of 1 = The person has a link in their bio to a personal or company website.
- Score of 2 = The person has a link in their bio to a dedicated landing page to join a newsletter, and they have linked to this newsletter landing page at least 5 times in the past 30 days in their content or in the comments of their content.
- Score of 3 = The person has a link in their bio to a dedicated landing page to join a newsletter, or a landing page of a free-value opt-in, and they have linked to this landing page at least 15 times in the past 30 days in their content or in the comments of their content.

Third, I would like you to audit their personal website and company website looking for a newsletter, and give them a score out of 3, based on the following criteria (and if they have both a personal newsletter and a company newsletter, please audit and score both individually):

- Score of 0 = The person has no personal newsletter and/or no company newsletter
- Score of 1 = The person has a personal newsletter and/or the company has a newsletter, but it has a very weak offer (meaning all it says near the opt-in box is something like “Subscribe to our newsletter!” or “Subscribe to receive updates,” etc.)
- Score of 2 = The person has a personal newsletter and/or the company has a newsletter, and it has some sort of clear “offer” for why you should subscribe and what you can (tangibly) expect to receive in exchange.
- Score of 3 = The person has a personal newsletter and/or the company has a newsletter, and it has its own dedicated landing page with a specific offer (explanation for why you should subscribe), along with detailed descriptions of what you can expect in terms of content, frequency of newsletters, testimonials, etc. It’s very clear their newsletter/opt-in is working well.

~

Variable #4: Outreach Scripts

Based on the information you’ve gathered about the lead, I would like you to take my 2 ghostwriting services (Social Ghostwriting and Newsletter Ghostwriting) and generate 2 different outreach scripts for each—based on the biggest problems you’ve identified that coincide with each respective service. 

The 2 scripts are:

- DM script
- Email script

But there are rules I’d like you to follow for each script, so let me walk you through them.

DM Script Rules

Your DM script should adhere to the following rules:

- It should be broken up into 3 different messages, so that it resembles how a human types/texts, and it should be written as conversationally and casually as possible. Do not use big words, formal sounding language, or even perfect grammar/sentence structure. Intentionally make it sound like a friend quickly texting a friend.
- But these messages should not be written as if the other person is responding. They are going to be sent in succession, so they should “read” as if they are one big message—it’s just more effective to break them up into pieces.
- The first message should be a “hook” statement or question centered around the biggest problem—ideally something that immediately makes the person realize they have a problem. (Example: If their biggest problem is they have a weak offer for their newsletter, or their newsletter just says, “Subscribe to get updates,” maybe the first message hook can be: “Hey, random question but Is your newsletter broken?” This makes the person suddenly aware of a problem and missed opportunity.)
- The second message should be a very, very casual explanation of what I do and how I could be of service. (Example: “I’m asking because I'm actually a social ghostwriter, so this is what I specialize in and know this problem pretty well.)
- The third message should be some sort of CTA, prompting the lead to want to ask for help / accept help. (Example: “Happy to show you how to fix this, if you want” or “I actually took it upon myself to ghostwrite a sample post for you, if you want to take a look?”)

Email Script Rules

Your Email script should adhere to the following rules:

- It should be as short and concise as possible. The ideal outreach email is 5 sentences or less.
- It should be written as conversationally and casually as possible. Do not use big words, formal sounding language, or even perfect grammar/sentence structure. Intentionally make it sound like a friend emailing a friend. (This means never using phrases like, “I hope this finds you well.”)
- It should follow the same rules as the DM script, except in the second message (which in the email could be the “second sentence”) expand for another 1-2 sentences on how I would recommend solving this specific problem for the person.

Here’s an example so you know exactly how to present the DM & Email scripts (notice how casually they’re written):

**DM Script:**

1. Hey {Name}, noticed there's no newsletter linked on your profiles.
2. FYI, I help entrepreneurs run their newsletters so I know this space pretty well.
3. Any interest? At a minimum, happy to share some of the tactics I see working best these days.

**Email Script:**

Subject: tried subscribing but it’s broken

Hey {Name},

I noticed there's no newsletter or email opt-in on any of your social platforms. 

Seems like a pretty big missed opportunity!

Would you be open to a chat? I think I can help. 

~

I am going to give you the lead’s name and company name, and I’d like you to present back to me a report with the above variables I have asked you for, in order.

Are you ready?

records.title: [CHEAT SHEET] Headline Mastery
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/AIWS Asset Hub/Social Content/[CHEAT SHEET] Headline Mastery - AIWS Asset Hub · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Every time you sit down to write a headline, use this cheat sheet to make sure you are nailing all the fundamental pieces of writing an irresistible headline! ⚡
records.content:
Every time you sit down to write a headline, use this cheat sheet to make sure you are nailing all the fundamental pieces of writing an irresistible headline!

⚡Make The Topic More Specific

The most important part of your headline is the WHAT (the topic).

For example:

  • Are you writing about how to make money?

  • Or are you writing about how to save money?

  • Or are you writing about how to steal money?

  • Or are you writing about how to lose money?

The more specific you can be (right away in the headline) about WHAT you’re saying, the better.

⚡Make The Audience More Specific

Next, WHO is this topic for?

  • Are you writing about how millennials can make money?

  • Or are you writing about how college students can make money?

  • Or are you writing about how single moms can make money?

  • Or are you writing about how retired government officials can make money?

You can increase the voltage of your headlines by naming the audience directly in the headline.

And again: the more specific, the better.

⚡Twist The Knife: Make The Outcome More Specific

Finally, WHY should the reader read this piece?

What’s the negative outcome you are going to help them avoid, or the positive outcome you are going to help them unlock?

  • Are you writing about how college students can make money so they can pay off their student loans?

  • Or are you writing about how college students can make money so they don’t have to go to college in the first place?

  • Or are you writing about how college students can make money, invest in the stock market, and retire early?

  • Or are you writing about how college students can make money, start their own small business, and be their own boss?

A mediocre headline just tells you what it’s about.

A pretty good headline tells you what it’s about and who it’s for.

But an irresistible headline tells you what it’s about, who it’s for, and why it matters.

records.title: [CHEAT SHEET] LinkedIn Brand Builder
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/AIWS Asset Hub/Social Content/[CHEAT SHEET] LinkedIn Brand Builder - AIWS Asset Hub · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Hey there! This LinkedIn Brand Builder Cheat Sheet is designed to launch (or relaunch) your personal brand on LinkedIn. To help you do this, this cheatsheet is
records.content:
Hey there!

This LinkedIn Brand Builder Cheat Sheet is designed to launch (or relaunch) your personal brand on LinkedIn.

To help you do this, this cheatsheet is split into 3 sections:

  • Build Your Brand. Use this to position yourself in your niche, write your About section, and more.

  • Attract Your Audience. The exact action steps you need to build a loyal readership/attract the right customers on LinkedIn.

  • Leverage The Algorithm. How to write posts that get views and help build your audience.

Let's dive in!

Build Your Brand

  • Write your 1-line position: "I help [specific audience] solve [specific problem] so they can [specific result]."

  • List your last 2–5 years of experience: 5 jobs/roles, 5 wins, 5 paid problems you solved, 5 skills, 5 "odd" experiences. Circle overlaps.

  • Pick a category name you can own (short, specific, memorable): e.g., "Onboarding Email Surgeon" vs "Email Marketer."

  • Write 3 headline variations (≤220 chars). Include audience + mechanism + result. Choose the clearest one.

  • Write a 300-word About:

    1. Who you help

    2. The painful problem in their words

    3. Your method in plain English

    4. 2–3 proof points (metrics, logos, outcomes)

    5. CTA (DM, booking link, newsletter)

  • Design a banner with: big promise (10–15 words), 1 proof metric (e.g., "$3.2M pipeline generated"), and a soft CTA ("DM 'audit'" or "Join newsletter").

  • Upload a recent headshot (neutral background, face ~60–70% of frame, natural light, eye contact).

  • Turn Creator Mode ON and choose 5 relevant topics.

  • Verify your account (ID or work email).

  • Add 20–25 Skills across four buckets: Core Expertise, Adjacent Skills, Industry Keywords, Outcome Skills (order top 5 to match headline).

  • Featured: add 3 items — lead magnet, strongest case study, "start here" post.

  • Choose 3 brand colors (HEX), 2 fonts, and 1 image style (e.g., clean, high-contrast photos). Use them everywhere (posts, carousels, PDFs).

Attract Your Audience

  • Define 5 audience archetypes (role + stage + top problem). Example: "Seed-stage SaaS founder stuck at <$1M ARR; activation issues."

  • Make a list of 50 accounts your buyers already follow (investors, operators, tool founders, analysts).

  • Make a list of 25 adjacent creators your buyers also follow (not direct competitors).

  • Post 3–5×/week on set days (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri). Aim for: 2 short posts (50–120 words), 1 long post (200–450 words), 1 visual (carousel or infographic) every 1–2 weeks.

  • Comment 3–5×/day on posts your buyers see. Add 1 concrete example, a number, or a clarifying question (never "Great post").

  • Send 5–10 personalized connection requests/day (reference a post or specific challenge).

  • Welcome DM each new connection: quick thanks + 2–3 links to your most useful posts for their role/problem.

  • Check Who viewed your profile daily; connect or DM if relevant.

  • Define 3–5 content pillars your audience must master (e.g., Acquisition, Activation, Retention).

  • For each pillar, generate 10 ideas using these angles: Tips, Stats, Steps, Lessons, Benefits, Reasons, Mistakes, Examples, Questions, Personal story (that's 30–50 ideas).

  • Expand winning ideas across audience segments (beginner vs advanced, founder vs marketer, SMB vs enterprise).

  • Publish one "authority asset"/week (a small curated swipe: subject lines, onboarding emails, demo offers, hook lines). Add 3 bullet insights (what to copy, what to avoid, where it applies).

Leverage The Algorithm

  • Draft 5 hook options for every post before you write:

    • Question (provokes curiosity)

    • Bold statement (counterintuitive)

    • Specific number/stat

    • Short story opener

    • Mistake/lesson framing

  • Keep first 200 characters cliffhanger-worthy (earn the "See more").

  • Use short paragraphs (1–2 sentences), white space, and clear section lines; avoid walls of text.

  • Carousels (6–10 slides):

    • Big Promise — What you'll achieve quickly

    • Stakes — Problems if you don't act

    • Framework — Clear steps to follow

    • Example — Real-world application

    • Checklist — Common mistakes to avoid

    • Quick Win — One tool to try now

    • Call to Action — Next step or question

  • Infographics: one page that explains a process or compares options (e.g., "Activation checklist: 9 items").

  • Short video (30–60s): Hook (≤3s) → 3 points → CTA; add captions.

  • Images: rotate concepts — behind-the-scenes, "whiteboard" sketch, before/after, milestone, counterexample.

  • Post native content: put external links in the first comment or use your profile/Featured.

  • End with one engagement trigger: a question, a request for examples, or "Want the checklist? Comment 'checklist'."

  • Reply to every comment within 24 hours; ask a follow-up to continue the thread.

  • Maintain a predictable cadence/windows each week (teach the feed when to expect you).

  • Track per-post: saves, comments, profile visits, follows, and link clicks (if used).

  • Each week, clone your winner three ways: new hook, new audience segment, new format (text → carousel → video).

records.content:
There are 6 big Data Points you should focus on when reviewing your social content metrics.

  • Views

  • Likes

  • Comments

  • Shares

  • Peer Approval

  • Followers

And in this Cheat Sheet, we're going to give you a quick overview of each one (and what to look out for).

Let's dive in!

Data Point #1: Views

Views are the most talked about metric (right up there with follower count), but the truth is, views aren’t really all that important.

(We have accumulated over a billion views on our own content, and we can tell you… views are somewhat overrated).

Still, Views can be a helpful metric in understanding “which way the wind is blowing,” and whether or not readers would be interested in hearing more from you on a given topic.

That being said, views are super helpful. That’s the whole name of the game with the content you produce. You want to get reach as many people as possible, so pay attention to this metric!

But if you’re writing niche content, content that is designed to resonate with a specific audience, then pay attention to this metric too. If you get more views on a particular piece of niche content, pay attention to why and try to double down on this next format/hook/topic in the future.

Data Point #2: Likes

Likes are the next metric, and they’re important because they are the first metric that requires the reader to take some sort of action.

A View can happen passively (just someone scrolling through their feed).

But a Like is a signal of true engagement—and a better indicator of where your reader’s interests lie.

The same applies to Likes. As it is a more “active” metric than views, if you get more likes on a piece of content than normal then you know the topic is resonating for the audience it’s targeted at.

Data Point #3: Comments

Comments are the most important metric, and the strongest signal for what readers want to hear about from you.

Posts that get a lot of comments should be reflected on and analyzed.

  • Why did this topic prompt so much engagement?

  • What are readers commenting?

  • What questions do they have?

  • Etc.

You can use this to guide future pieces of content.

Data Point #4: Shares

Shares are like public bookmarks.

They are a signal of something people want to publicly associate themselves with—which is rare, and doesn’t happen with the vast majority of posts.

So when you see a post get a lot of Shares, it’s worth questioning why (and how you could potentially repeat that topic again and again in the future).

Data Point #5: Peer Approval

Lastly, it’s always worth putting the performance of a post in the context of what people you respect think.

A post might get very little public engagement, but if someone you really respects likes, comments, or sends you a message separately saying how great/helpful that post was… that’s a strong signal!

(For example: if you had a post that got 37 views and only 1 Like, you might think that post was terrible or that topic wasn’t resonating with readers. But if the 1 Like was from Jeff Bezos, how would that change your perception of the topic?)

Bonus Data Point #6: Followers

Everybody wants more followers.

But this misses an important point:

It’s not the number of followers that matter, it’s the quality of those followers that counts.

Because would you rather have:

  • 100,000 followers who are disengaged, mostly bots, and only found you because of one viral post not even remotely linked to your topic…

  • Or 1,000 followers who hang on your every post, want to throw money at you, and are always asking for more?

Exactly.

All Signal Is Good Signal

The big takeaway here should be that all signal is good signal.

Too often, writers will see 1 or 2 posts get very little engagement and then get discouraged and give up. How sad! We have posts flop every single day. It’s part of writing in the digital age where algorithms rule the world. But that doesn’t mean the writing is bad, or someone out there didn’t find value in what you wrote.

All signal is good signal—and oftentimes you can learn more about what your target readers want from posts that flop than the ones that go viral.

records.description: Lean Writing is all about testing small ideas, and then doubling-down on the ones that “work”—to increase the likelihood the next thing you write is something y
records.content:
Lean Writing is all about testing small ideas, and then doubling-down on the ones that “work”—to increase the likelihood the next thing you write is something you already know readers want to read.

And to make the process even easier for you, use this cheat sheet!

🔎 List 3 Main Points

Whatever it is you want to write about, share 3 Main Points (these are your big ideas).

Just 3.

For example, let’s say you’re writing about how to have an effective morning routine as a writer. Your 3 main points might be:

  • Wake up on the first alarm.

  • Read a page out of the thesaurus, first thing.

  • Take a 5-minute cold shower and then dive into your hardest writing for the day.

The “signal” you’re looking for is a) whether readers read and engage with this sort of piece, and b) which one of your Main Points they find most interesting. For example: the “read a page out of the thesaurus” idea is different and unique—and so readers will likely comment, “I’ve never tried that before, thanks!”

That’s a signal.

🔎 Double-Down On 1 Main Point. Share 3 More

Next, take your strongest signal and double-down on it.

Let’s say a bunch of readers commented, “Wow, I’ve never tried reading the thesaurus in the morning!” That signal is telling you something about that insight is interesting to people. So, write about that in more detail and depth. And now share 3 more “big ideas” relevant to that 1 proven idea.

For example, maybe you can write about the 3 biggest benefits you receive from reading a page out of the thesaurus first thing, every morning:

  • Benefit #1: It broadens your vocabulary.

  • Benefit #2: It warms your brain up for the day.

  • Benefit #3: It makes your writing more descriptive.

Then, the “signal” you’re looking for is which one of these ideas readers find most interesting.

And if no readers engage, then the big ideas you were sharing weren’t different/unique enough—and so you start back from the beginning and try again! But that’s OK. Because you have an infinite number of tries, and can play the game of Digital Writing over and over again, learning as you go.

🔎 Combine Your Highest Signal Data Points Into High-Value Assets

Once you start to gather signal on multiple ideas, you can start to expand them, combine them, and really begin building a high-value library of content.

For example: let’s say you were writing about how to build an effective routine as a writer. In the beginning, it might be hard to know how to write about that topic for longer than 300 words. But as you start small, and gather data, the answers reveal themselves—and you know (based on data) which “ideas” readers find most interesting:

  • Reading a page from the thesaurus each morning

  • Morning writing with bulletproof coffee & fasting

  • Take a shot of tequila before doing any hard editing

  • Etc.

Over time, the more of these “proven data points” you gather, the easier it becomes to write things you KNOW are going to resonate with readers—because the data says so!

And the more of these proven data points you stack on top of each other, the more “value” you can pack into any given asset.

Eventually, all these proven data points become the outline of not just your Digital Writing (Atomic Essays, Tweets, Twitter Threads, LinkedIn posts, Medium articles, etc.), but email courses, digital products, books, courses, and anything else you want to create in your niche.
