records.content:
Since you’re here, reading this right now, that means you’re part of our AI Writing Skool.

And if you’re part of our AI Writing Skool, that means you’re investing in your own education. You’re here to learn.

So if you’re investing in your own education, and you’re here to learn, then let me share with you a little secret about “learning.”

Bad students explain why it won’t work for them. Good students tell you how they’re going to make it work.

After mentoring 15,000+ writers across our various writing programs, I can tell you I’ve witnessed this first-hand.

We have lots of people join AI Writing Skool, or our Premium Ghostwriting Academy, and day one insist none of our frameworks will work for them.

  • “My niche is too saturated for this.”

  • “My target reader won’t read if I do this.”

  • “My target client won’t respond/buy if I do this.”

  • “My writing is more creative than what you’re telling me to do.”

  • Etc.

And when this happens, there are only two outcomes.

  • The student, shortly thereafter, quits.

  • Or, the student proceeds to keep doing things “their way,” failing to see any results.

I have yet to see someone come into one of our writing programs, tell me all of our frameworks don’t and will not work for them, and then go on to achieve miraculous outcomes doing something completely different. 15,000+ writers. Haven’t seen it once.

Meanwhile, do you know what Matthew Brown told me on his very first PGA call?

He told me, “My goal is to be your biggest success story.”

And guess what… he is!

He started at roughly the same level most people start at—he just also put in the work most people are unwilling to do. He showed up to every call and asked questions. He did all the homework. He asked for help whenever he got stuck. He was determined to make PGA work for him.

And today, his ghostwriting agency does $50k/mo+ in revenue—and he recently texted me saying he just crossed $1,000,000 in lifetime revenue.

Not once did I ever hear him say his niche was too saturated. Not once did I ever hear him “blame” external trends, industries, markets, customers, etc. Not once did I ever hear him say, “If this doesn’t work, then…”. He was determined to make it work from the very beginning. (And by the way, when I see someone truly exemplify this quality, I go out of my way to help them. I can’t tell you how many writers I have gone above and beyond for to personally mentor, outside of the boundaries of our writing programs. But I only do this for people who I see are as invested in their own success as they expect me to be.)

Anyways, Matthew got so much value out of PGA and our working together, that he tripled-down and continued to invest in his own education

(Meanwhile, lots of people join one of our writing programs, don’t do anything, then say “writing online is a trend and I missed the boat” or “ghostwriting is too saturated and doesn’t work anymore” and then give up.)

My point is, education only works if you’re willing to go on the journey to make it work for you.

I wrote a comprehensive piece about How To Be A Good Student here if you want further explanation.

Now, I’d like to give you one last reframe…

Let’s pretend you invest in your own education, and you buy some other person’s course or community or whatever, and it sucks. It’s just a mediocre product with sub-par information.

Did you just waste your money?

Again, it completely depends on your mindset, and whether you’re going to find a way to make that experience work FOR you or AGAINST you.

A few years ago, I spent a bunch of money on a course that sucked.

I won’t say who, because it doesn’t matter. But the point is, my first impulse was, “This wasn’t worth the money.”

Until I did some reflecting. And eventually I asked myself, “OK, this investment in my own education, on the surface, was a bad one. But how can I still find a way to make it worthwhile?

How can I MAKE this work for me?”

And that’s when I realized: the product “sucking” was a benefit in and of itself.

Because this person, whose product I had just purchased, had a very successful business—doing more revenue than we were doing at the time. And all of a sudden I started to realize that I didn’t just spend a bunch of money to learn what to do… I had just spent a bunch of money to learn what NOT to do.

So, I went through the whole product, and as I went, I made a list of everything I wished they had done differently. I made a list of everything I wanted as a customer, but didn’t get.

And then do you know what we did?

We went and built a similar product, except way better. It was called Category Newsletter Creator.

And that product became our biggest digital product drop ever, generating $650,000 in 10 days.

You can watch me engineer the entire email marketing sequence for that product here by the way.

I think about this experience often because I very easily could have “blamed” this other creator/business owner, insisted their education product “sucked,” and then give myself permission to not take any action or accountability.

Which is what most people do.

But instead, I MADE IT WORK FOR ME.

And that sub-par product inspired our most-successful digital product drop ever.

So yea, I “wasted” a bunch of money buying that sub-par product—only to make that experience work for me, and go on to generate a 100x return.

records.title: Niches Aren’t Saturated If You’re Skilled
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Mindset Fundamentals/Niches Aren’t Saturated If You’re Skilled - Digital Mindset Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: To a beginner, every niche in the world is spoken for. To a beginner, every niche in the world has “too much competition.” To a beginner, every niche in the wor
records.content:
To a beginner, every niche in the world is spoken for.

To a beginner, every niche in the world has “too much competition.”

To a beginner, every niche in the world is “too small” or “not lucrative enough.”

None of these are facts. They are just how you see the world when you lack skills.

And the more skills you acquire, it’s not that any of these things change. It’s that YOU change. The more skills you build, the more opportunities you recognize and the more equipped you feel to capitalize on them. Again, the niche doesn’t change. The competition doesn’t change. YOU changed—and the way you perceive all of these opportunities changes with you.

As a beginner, you also lack the experience to understand how deep each niche goes.

This is because you haven’t “gone deep” in a niche yet. If you had, you would know just how hard it is to capitalize on a single, teeny-tiny niche, well. I’ve been writing about “digital writing” for 10+ years. Thousands and thousands of Tweets and articles and YouTube videos and entire books written on this one subject. And every year that goes by, I realize how much MORE I can write about, how many MORE people I can help, how many MORE frameworks I can build, and so on.

Going deep in a niche is what teaches you that you can’t “do everything.” You can’t have 20 niches. Or, I suppose you can, you just won’t be successful in any of them. Because you can’t go deep in 20 niches. And you can’t help people in any meaningful way across 20 niches all at once.

If you want proof, just examine your own consumption habits.

Do you follow the same person for:

  • Stock pics

  • Relationship advice

  • Airbnb rental instructions

  • And health & wellness regimens?

Of course not.

You follow one person for one thing.

And another person for another thing.

That’s because, intuitively, you understand that within each “domain of expertise,” you want to listen and learn from someone who lives and breathes that one thing. What you don’t want is to listen and learn from someone who just sort-of-understands lots of things at the surface.

So, it’s not that you can’t have 20 niches.

It’s that you can’t capitalize, and do justice, and meaningfully help people across 20 different niches all at once.

The only way to go deep is to pick one.

When someone doesn’t find instant success in a niche, they think the niche is the problem.

And it’s not.

Every single niche on planet earth has potential. Lots and lots of potential. As I like to say often in our writing programs, if the niche had no potential then the niche wouldn’t exist. The mere fact it exists means there is potential (and lots of money floating around inside it—it’s just going to other people who are, currently, more skilled than you).

But this isn’t how you see the world as a beginner. Instead, what beginners do is they pick a niche, they start, and then they run into a little bit of friction. And that friction is uncomfortable, because it’s revealing a skill gap. (It’s like playing a video game and getting stuck on Level 2.) And what most beginners do to solve this problem is they decide to change niches. Which is a mistake. Because guess what? When you hop over to another niche, you’re going to start all over again, and then get stuck exactly where you were before—just inside a different niche.

Conversely, if you’re skilled, you could enter any niche you want and very quickly jump up the levels of success.

The other big reason so many people struggle to niche down is because they are afraid of wasting time.

Which creates an ironic sort of vicious cycle:

  • “I’m afraid if I pick the wrong niche then I’ll waste time.”

  • “But in worrying about picking the perfect niche, and not picking a niche and just getting started, I’m already wasting time.”

This fear is completely self-inflicted, and I can prove it with a silly example.

Would you like me, Nicolas Cole, to help you with your niche, your writing, your digital products, your monetization strategy, and your business—100% for free? You would, wouldn’t you?

OK, but I thought you just said if you pick the wrong niche, you’ll waste time, meaning the skills you build in one niche don’t translate to the next niche?

So if I’m not in your exact niche, why would you accept my help? I thought the skills didn’t translate?

Exactly.

You want my help not because I am in your exact niche, but because on some level you assume the underlying skills translate across every niche.

Which is why there’s no such thing as “picking the wrong niche and wasting time.”

  • When you pick a niche, you allow yourself to get started

  • As soon as you start, you begin to learn and improve (aka: build skills)

  • The deeper you go inside a niche, the more timeless skills you develop

  • Which means, if you ever want to pivot and change niches at some point in the future, you can. Except then, you’ll be significantly more equipped (because you’ve already “leveled-up” and gone deep in a previous niche).

So, stop overthinking it.

You aren’t choosing your “forever niche.”

You’re choosing your “first niche”—which is what allows you to get started building skills that will serve you forever.

records.title: Simplicity Is Velocity
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Mindset Fundamentals/Simplicity Is Velocity - Digital Mindset Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: The simpler your life is, the faster you will make progress. The simpler your business is, the faster it will scale. Complexity is the enemy of progress. Just i
records.content:
The simpler your life is, the faster you will make progress.

The simpler your business is, the faster it will scale.

Complexity is the enemy of progress.

Just imagine you have a pitcher of water.

And you want to pour the water from the pitcher into a glass.

Which is faster?

  • Pouring the water from the pitcher directly into the glass?

  • Or pouring the water from the pitcher, into a super-fancy osmosis machine that spins and twirls and mixes up the water in a complex network of tiny tubes… which then, at the very end, falls into the glass?

Obviously, the first one.

And yet, people LOVE to overcomplicate their goals, their lives, and their businesses.

Because on some level, they think, the more complex something is, the better it is. It’s more advanced. It’s more robust. It’s more high-tech. Etc.

But this image is a terrific example of what you should be doing instead:

This is what the SpaceX Raptor engine looked like at the very beginning (far left), compared to its most recent version (far right). It started, as most complicated things do, as a very complex engine. But the goal was not to make it “more complex.” The goal was to make it LESS complex.

That’s because Simplicity Is Velocity.

  • The simpler something is…

  • The fewer parts it requires…

  • The cheaper it is to execute…

  • The faster you can produce it…

I call this “unbundling.”

Anything you want to do, create, write, execute, is likely a bundled term inside your brain.

  • “I want to write a book.”

  • “I want to create a digital product.”

  • “I want to start a weekly newsletter.”

  • “I want to create a paid community.”

  • Etc.

A bundled term is a broad word or phrase that summarizes lots of smaller skills. And at face-value these bundled terms seem simple. But it’s actually the opposite. The more bundled a term, the more complex it is (the complexity is just hiding inside its bundled-ness). It’s not until we “unbundle” that bundled term that we realize, hang on a second, there’s actually a lot more here to figure out!

For example, let’s unbundle “I want to write a book.”

OK, what are the sub-skills or sub-tasks involved in writing a book?

Is writing a book as “simple” as just… sitting down… and writing a book?

Of course not!

  • You need to pick a topic.

  • You need to pick a target audience.

  • You need to pick a problem to help that target audience solve, and an outcome you want to help them unlock.

  • You need to come up with a title.

  • You need to come up with a subtitle.

  • You need to outline your book.

  • You need to outline each chapter of your book.

  • Etc.

(If we fully unbundled “I want to write a book,” we’d end up with a list of 100+ sub-skills or sub-tasks!)

But wait… there’s more!

Inside each of THOSE sub-skills or sub-tasks, chances are, we can (and should) unbundle even further.

For example: “You need to pick a topic.”

  • What kind of topic?

  • How niche is too niche?

  • What makes for a good topic vs bad topic?

  • How do you identify profitable topics (more likely to sell)?

  • How do you make your topic both specific and universal?

  • Etc.

It’s not until you start to unbundle these broad goals into sub-skills, and then unbundle each sub-skill into sub-sub-skills that you realize: we need to simplify!

So now imagine how funny you sound (or anyone—it’s not just you, everyone does this) when you say, “I want to do EVERYTHING!”

  • You want to write a book.

  • But you also want to build a digital product.

  • But you also want to start a newsletter.

  • But you also want to start a writing services business.

  • But you also want to get into Airbnb rentals.

  • But you also want to day-trade crypto.

  • But you also want to help your friend build their website.

  • Etc.

You “think” each of these is just “a bullet.” And you think each of these goals or pursuits is just one simple thing.

They’re not.

They are incredibly complex, bundled terms, that “look” simple and easy on the surface.

And it’s not until you go through the unbundling process that you realize how much effort and focus it takes to execute one thing well. Just one.

Which is why, Simplicity Is Velocity.

The more things you try to do at once, the more complexity you create, the slower you will move, the less progress you’ll make.

The fewer things you try to do at once, the less complexity you create, the faster you will move, the more progress you’ll make.

The choice is yours.

records.title: The Grass Is Always Greener
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Mindset Fundamentals/The Grass Is Always Greener - Digital Mindset Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: When I was building my ghostwriting agency back in 2018, I thought, “Service businesses suck—I should build a digital product business.” Then, in 2021, when we
records.content:
When I was building my ghostwriting agency back in 2018, I thought, “Service businesses suck—I should build a digital product business.”

Then, in 2021, when we started building our digital product business, I thought, “Digital product businesses are kinda boring—I should build a SaaS business.”

Then, in 2022, when we started building our SaaS business, Typeshare, I thought, “SaaS is really hard, we should build a paid newsletter business.”

Then, in 2023, when we started our paid newsletter, Write With AI, I thought, “Paid newsletter businesses kinda suck—I should build a monthly paid community.”

Then, in 2026, do you know where we ultimately circled back to? We thought, “We should start a ghostwriting agency!” (Which is right back where I started.)

The grass is always greener.

Every business has potential. And every business model can work.

The reason you’re stuck, or not making progress, or not as successful as you want to be, very rarely has to do with the business type or model itself.

Yes, every business model has its own pros and cons. Yes, some business models “scale faster” versus “have more defensibility” vs “are more profitable” etc.

But, by and large, every business type has potential. And every business model can work.

Every business is scalable.

The problem isn’t the business type or model, it’s that you lack some combination of skills in order to make that business type and model work.

When I was building my ghostwriting agency in 2018, I thought agencies weren’t scalable. Genuinely. I thought service-based businesses just weren’t something that had the potential to be as big as, say, SaaS.

But many of the biggest companies in the world as service-based businesses and agencies!

  • There are $1B+ advertising agencies

  • There are $1B+ management consulting firms

  • There are $1B+ blue-collar professional service franchises

  • There are $1B+ service-based food companies

  • Etc.

The problem was never the fact that “agencies couldn’t scale.”

The problem was that, at the time, I lacked the skills in order to scale an agency.

(Contrast that with today, when I have significantly more skills, and now our new ghostwriting agency, Velocity, is growing faster than my original ghostwriting agency did. Why? Because I/we have more skills!)

It’s a mistake to look over the fence at what someone else is doing and think, “That’s what I should do too.”

Sure, allow yourself to be inspired.

Sure, study other business types in other industries and see what you can steal for yourself.

Sure, pay attention to the ways in which the world is changing and adapt with the times.

But, generally speaking, you should internalize the fact that changing businesses, business models, and niches is almost always the mistake.

And you will make significantly more progress, and unlock higher and higher levels of success, when you just stay focused on one business for a long period of time.

records.title: You Can’t Steer A Stationary Ship
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Mindset Fundamentals/You Can’t Steer A Stationary Ship - Digital Mindset Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: In my early-20s, I had a mentor in Chicago who used to say to me, “Cole… you can’t steer a stationary ship.” It was a mantra to take action. And it wasn’t just
records.content:
In my early-20s, I had a mentor in Chicago who used to say to me, “Cole… you can’t steer a stationary ship.”

It was a mantra to take action.

And it wasn’t just me who heard him use this metaphor. When I’d shadow him to meetings, he’d say the same words to hot-shot startup founders and C-level executives of publicly traded companies. It was his way of cutting to the heart of the issue—which is that most people overthink.

They don’t want to take action. What they want to do is come up with “the perfect plan.”

But what happens to your perfect plan when the ship leaves the harbor and, suddenly, there’s a storm?

As Mike Tyson so poetically put it: “Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face.”

Or what about the popular proverb: “If you want to make God laugh, tell him your plans.”

The truth is, life doesn’t go according to plan. Ever.

  • You make a plan…

  • You take the first step on your plan…

  • Something happens: an unforeseen obstacle…

  • Now you have to change plans.

This is just how it goes, in every area of life.

Which means the name of the game is not to “make the perfect plan.”

The game is to START—and make up your plan as you go along, based on what’s happening to you and around you.

And my mentor cleverly summarized this idea by saying, “You can’t steer a stationary ship.” As long as your ship is in the harbor, you’re trying to make the perfect plan. And as long as you’re “planning” instead of executing, you’re failing.

(Another way he’d remind me of this lesson was by telling me: “Cole, whenever someone gives you an opportunity, just say Yes. Figure out how you’re going to do it later.”)

But this is scary!

Right?

  • What happens if you take the wrong first step?

  • What happens if you say Yes to an opportunity and can’t deliver?

  • What happens if you sign yourself up for a journey you aren’t equipped to handle?

  • Etc.

All valid questions.

But they all lead back to the same answer, which is: then you turn around and start over again.

Which is, in itself, “a change of plans.” And you only know now how your plans need to change BECAUSE YOU TOOK ACTION.

Unfortunately, this is not what people do.

Instead, their life looks something like this:

  • [11 Years & Counting] You make a plan…

  • [Not There Yet] You take the first step on your plan…

  • [Not There Yet] Something happens: an unforeseen obstacle…

  • [Not There Yet] Now you have to change plans.

Which, as you should be able to see in this silly little example, is a guaranteed recipe for failure. As long as you stay “planning” and not taking action, your ship hasn’t left the harbor. Which means you’re stuck. Which means you can’t learn. Which means you can’t improve. Which means you don’t actually know where or what to do next.

But the most successful people in life (and I don’t mean billionaires—I just mean happy people doing things they enjoy on a regular basis) live their lives like this:

  • [11 Seconds] You make a plan…

  • [2 Minutes] You take the first step on your plan…

  • [5 Minutes] Something happens: an unforeseen obstacle…

  • [11 Years & Counting] Now you have to change plans.

They START, and then live their lives in a perpetual state of steering and adjusting their ship based on what’s happening, what they’re learning, and wherever they want to sail to next.

Let me give you an example from my own life.

I have built 4 different multi-seven-figure writing-related businesses:

  • Digital Press: My first business, a ghostwriting agency.

  • Ship 30 for 30: The internet’s fastest-growing writing challenge.

  • Category Pirates: A paid newsletter on Substack & consulting business.

  • Premium Ghostwriting Academy: The internet’s largest training program for freelance writers.

Not to mention all the other 6-figure businesses I’ve built: Write With AI, Typeshare, and an entire suite of digital products.

But do you know what my very first “Internet business” was?

Do you know what my very first digital product was, way back in 2014?

It was a fitness eBook called Skinny to Shredded, giving readers my bodybuilding workouts and meal plans. This eBook series is how I earned my first $10,000 on the Internet.

Now, imagine if instead of just “starting somewhere,” I had spent all that time trying to create the perfect plan. (Which, by the way, I did that too. I wasted an obscene amount of time trying to map my entire life out. It never worked.)

I would have never learned!

  • I would have never learned how to create digital products.

  • I would have never learned how to accept payments on the Internet.

  • I would have never learned how to write viral Quora answers, linking to my products (my first taste of “passive revenue”).

  • I would have never learned how to setup my first website (the same domain I use today!).

  • Etc.

I would have deprived myself of the opportunity to START.

And guess what?

After I published this eBook series, and made $10,000 over the course of about a year, I ultimately decided I didn’t really want to build a life around being a fitness influencer. I wanted to be a writer. That’s what my college degree was in, Fiction Writing, and deep down I knew I wanted to be an author and earn a living by writing.

So, I started.

I learned.

Change of plans.

And that first product didn’t “slow me down.” It wasn’t a “waste of time.” Quite the opposite. It allowed me to figure out what I actually wanted to do with my life, faster. It helped me realize I wasn’t as passionate about fitness as I’d thought, faster. It helped me become a writer, and start living my dream, faster.

And I lost nothing.

I mean, look… I’m still telling you this story over a decade later.

The other side of this advice is: don’t be afraid to burn the boats.

When you know what direction you want to move next, don’t half-ass it.

Don’t try to keep one foot “in the old world” while the other foot tries to take a step forward. It won’t work. And even if it does, even if you are able to manage both, this refusal to commit will very quickly become your core bottleneck. You have to be willing to give up what you currently have in order to unlock the next thing you want even more.

Let me tell you about a life-changing moment when I had to do this.

At the start of 2021, I started Ship 30 for 30 with Dickie Bush. It was slow to start. But within a few months, it very quickly became a fast-growing business.

The problem was, it was new. And new is unpredictable. At the time, I was still ghostwriting inside my former agency, Digital Press. And Dickie was still working full-time at Blackrock as a hedge-fund trader. So both of us had a hard time rationalizing quitting our “predictable income streams.”

  • But then Ship 30 started growing…

  • Then we started making thousands of dollars per month, each…

  • Then tens of thousands of dollars per month, each…

  • Until eventually, about 8 months after starting Ship 30 for 30, Dickie and I were both earning ~5x our “full-time jobs.”

Around the 9-month mark, I decided, it was time to burn the boats.

I called up Dickie and I said, “Look, we have enough data now. We have 9 months of non-stop growth. And we are on pace to out-earn our full-time jobs by a factor of 10 by the end of the year. And if we want to take this thing to the next level, then we need to go all-in.”

He got off that call, rang his boss, and put in his month’s notice.

And I got off that call, rang the co-founder of my ghostwriting agency, and told him I was done. And to really drive the point home, and show you just how far I went to “burn the boats,” I gave my co-founder the whole business: the brand, the entity, the existing roster of clients, everything. I sold him the whole thing for $1.

I burned the boats. Everyone in my life told me I was insane.

And then the very next month, Ship 30 made me more money in 30 days than my ghostwriting agency had all year.

This is what’s required. In order to get the next thing you want, you often have to leave behind the thing that no longer serves you.

records.title: Your Relationship With Money
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Mindset Fundamentals/Your Relationship With Money - Digital Mindset Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Dictates How Much Money You Make The way you view money is not the way business owners view money. Fundamentally, this is why so many people struggle to get sta
records.content:
Dictates How Much Money You Make

The way you view money is not the way business owners view money.

Fundamentally, this is why so many people struggle to get started selling digital products or services on the Internet. Because, as a consumer, they can’t really fathom how or why someone else would pay hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of dollars for something—because “they” would never do that (or don’t have the means to do that).

But just because YOU see money that way… doesn’t mean everybody else sees money the same way.

Your relationship with money dictates how much money you make.

I’ll give you an example Dickie and I talk about all the time.

Back in 2021, Ship 30 for 30 started growing very quickly. Within 6 months we were on-pace to doing $1M in revenue for the year. All of a sudden we needed to start thinking about how to build the infrastructure for this new writing program of ours to scale beyond its current limits.

And one of the core problems we realized we needed to solve was email automation.

  • We needed to start a newsletter.

  • We needed to setup tags for subscribers inside that newsletter, so we could track readers from “click to close.”

  • And we needed to setup automations to send onboarding emails when someone bought Ship 30 for 30.

All pretty straight-forward stuff. But stuff we didn’t know how to do, at the time.

So, one day, Dickie found this online course called Mastering ConvertKit from a guy who taught email automation.

Dickie called me up and said, “I think the information in this course would give me everything I need to know in order to set all of this up. But it’s pretty expensive. It’s $1,000.”

(Keep in mind, at the exact moment we were having this conversation, Ship 30 had just done ~$20,000 in a single month, almost $10,000 directly to each of us.)

Now, was $1,000 “a lot of money?”

Well, to Dickie, who was 24 years old at the time, yes, $1,000 was “a lot of money.”

But in the context of our business, was $1,000 actually a lot of money? Not really. We had plenty of cash to reinvest in the business.

Anyways, long-story-longer, I told Dickie to buy the course. He spent the $1,000—and that investment in ourselves is how Ship 30 tripled in size, and went on to generate millions of dollars in revenue.

In fact, our story was so compelling, that an old podcast episode of us re-telling the story is the entire VSL for that course’s landing page today. You can watch it here.

The more you invest in yourself, the more you will increase your earning potential.

Fundamentally, money is a reflection of skills.

  • The more skills you have, and the more valuable the skills, the more money you make.

  • The fewer skills you have, and the less valuable the skills, the less money you make.

Which means, if at any point in your life you aren’t earning the amount of money you want to earn for yourself, the question isn’t, “How do I earn more money????”

The question is, “What skills do I need to build to earn more money?”

For example, what’s the difference between all the freelance writers on Upwork struggling to charge $10 per hour, and all the ghostwriters inside our Premium Ghostwriting Academy charging $5,000 per project?

Skills.

  • If your only skill is “writing,” you will make a little bit of money.

  • But if you can write and setup email automations, you will make more money.

  • And if you can write, and setup email automations, and help clients better monetize their lists, you will make more money.

  • And if you can write, and setup email automations, and help clients better monetize their lists, and manage difficult clients/personalities, you will make more money.

  • And if you can write, and setup email automations, and help clients better monetize their lists, and manage difficult clients/personalities, and keep every project organized and over-communicate every step of the way, you will make more money.

Making more money just means “building more skills.”

And the only way to build more skills is to either:

  • Spend the time (doing it & practicing yourself)

  • Spend the money (paying someone else to help you improve, or learn a new way of doing things)

You’re going to spend a resource either way (Time or Money).

records.title: A Niche Library Compounds In Value
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Niche Fundamentals/A Niche Library Compounds In Value - Digital Niche Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Let me leave you with this. The library of content you build in a niche is the mega-asset that compounds in value over time. One of my favorite examples of this
records.content:
Let me leave you with this.

The library of content you build in a niche is the mega-asset that compounds in value over time.

One of my favorite examples of this is Ryan Holiday.

His niche is Stoicism.

Ask 100 people who know Ryan Holiday what is niche is, and all 100 people will tell you, “Stoicism.” (I know, because I do this exercise frequently in our writing programs and everyone says the same word. “Stoicism.” That’s how you know you’ve won: you’ve become synonymous with a topic.)

But Ryan Holiday’s “personal brand” is not his most valuable asset.

It’s his library of content.

  • He tweets about Stoicism (and has a huge library of short-form content).

  • He writes articles & newsletters about Stoicism (and has a huge library of long-term content).

  • He has a podcast about Stoicism (and has a huge library of audio content).

  • He has a YouTube channel about Stoicism (and has a huge library of video content).

  • He has written a handful of different books about Stoicism.

  • Etc.

So, what is the “value” of this massive library?

Well, there are a few different ways of thinking about this:

First, there is tremendous value to Ryan Holiday. Every day that he writes about Stoicism, he makes the job of “writing about Stoicism” easier for himself tomorrow. I would bet, since he’s been doing this for 10+ years, that today he rarely creates very much net-new content for his social platforms or newsletter. It’s probably just remixed versions of things he’s written in the past. This is massively valuable. It means every day that goes by, his library becomes more powerful—capable of being re-used over and over and over again.

Second, there is tremendous future-value. When a new content platform or opportunity presents itself, does Ryan Holiday have to go create a whole bunch of new content? Of course not! He has a giant library to pull from—which means all he has to do is copy/paste “winning” content from his library over to whatever new platform comes out, or new opportunity presents itself. This means his library has future-value, because it can be reused over and over and over again to capitalize on future opportunities.

Third, there is tremendous “attention” value. He has created so much content on the topic of Stoicism online that whenever someone new gets introduced to Stoicism as a topic, what’s the likelihood they will discover Ryan Holiday’s work? It’s very high. His “web” of content is huge, and it spans multiple platforms. Which means, every day that goes by, he doesn’t have to work as hard to find new readers. The web attracts readers for him, passively, on autopilot.

Fourth, there is tremendous monetization value. Why does Ryan Holiday get 7-figure book deals? Is it because he’s a “great writer?” Nope. The ONLY reason he gets millions of dollars to write books about Stoicism is because the publisher knows those books are going to get plugged into his “Stoicism machine.” Which means the larger his library of Stoicism-related content grows, the more and more and more he can monetize Stoicism-related books and products.

Fifth, and this is the most “advanced” one… imagine one day a venture-backed meditation app decided they wanted to double-down on Stoicism-themed meditations. And they wanted to incorporate media into their app, content, and customer-acquisition strategy. And since they just raised $100M, they have cash to spend to acquire a creator. How much might they be willing to spend to buy the largest “library” of Stoicism-related content (with high-authority and quality)? The answer is tens of millions of dollars.

Building a library, in a niche, is your path to financial freedom.

As they say, “the riches are in the niches.”

That’s because, when you become synonymous with a topic, you can monetize that topic for years—even decades.

records.title: Become Known For A Niche You Own
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Niche Fundamentals/Become Known For A Niche You Own - Digital Niche Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Your goal is not to build an audience, broadly. Your goal is not to become Internet-famous, broadly. Your goal is not to generate lots of attention, broadly. Mo
records.content:
Your goal is not to build an audience, broadly.

Your goal is not to become Internet-famous, broadly.

Your goal is not to generate lots of attention, broadly.

Most people don’t understand what “personal branding” actually means.

  • The way you build an effective personal brand is NOT by becoming known, broadly.

  • Building a personal brand is about becoming known for a niche you own.

Let me tell you a quick story about how I learned this lesson, first-hand.

Back in 2014, I started writing on Quora.

I was 24 years old, and didn’t really “know very much.” I was young. I had just graduated from college a year prior. I was working as an entry-level copywriter at an advertising agency (the lowest-paid and least important person at the company). And, generally speaking, I didn’t have very much “value” to contribute via writing.

So, I wrote about the only thing I felt even moderately knowledgeable about at the time, which was personal development and work ethic.

Because at 24 years old, I was living a bit of an unconventional life. I wasn’t “successful” yet, but I had gotten very good at building good habits. I was 100% sober. I was obsessed with bodybuilding, and went to the gym every single day. I was disciplined with my meals (I used to bring Tupperware containers to work and each every 2.5 hours). And because I couldn’t afford Internet in my studio apartment, I spent a lot of time reading—specifically reading books about personal development.

So, when I started writing on Quora, that’s what I wrote about.

And a lot of my answers went viral! Mega, mega viral.

By the end of 2014, Quora’s team let me know that, at the time, I was the most-read writer on the entire platform (out of 200 million users). And, in hindsight, it made sense why. I was, quite literally, writing about the biggest, broadest topic on planet earth: personal development.

I didn’t really have a niche.

As a result, two things happened:

  • I generated tens of millions (and eventually, hundreds of millions of views) on my writing.

  • And, I made $0.

Yup, you heard me right.

All those views and I made no money. Nada. Zilch.

It wasn’t until I picked my first niche, which was bodybuilding, that I started to make money.

I wrote a viral answer about my fitness transformation.

That answer made me realize, “Hey, maybe I can get more specific here and just focus on sharing bodybuilding and fitness knowledge.”

And that niche is how I wrote my first eBook, which is how I made my first $10,000.

Then, as time went on, I started to realize I was more passionate about a different niche: Digital Writing.

Much smaller topic (especially at the time).

But it was something I enjoyed more, and it was a topic I thought, maybe, I could monetize.

Guess what happened?

  • The more I wrote about Digital Writing, the less views I got (smaller topic).

  • But the more money I made.

In fact, back in 2014/2015, I was generating more views than I am today.

And I have hundreds of thousands of followers today!

But I was generating “more views” back then because I was writing about bigger, broader topics. Which appeal to “more people,” but don’t resonate with as much depth. And what I ended up learning is that “attention for attention’s sake” is cool… but it doesn’t pay the rent.

It wasn’t until I picked a niche (and a small niche at that) that I started to make money from my writing.

Your success online, and the strength of your personal brand, sits in the context of your niche.

This is the goal.

Your goal is not followers, views, or any other vanity metric.

Your goal is to create a library of content, in a niche, over such a long time horizon that “you” and “the topic” become synonymous.

  • When people hear Stoicism, they think of Ryan Holiday.

  • When people hear Business Advice, they think of Alex Hormozi.

  • When people hear Buying Boring Businesses, they think of Codie Sanchez.

  • When people hear Digital Writing, they think of me.

  • Etc.

Personal branding is association with a topic.

And the more “you” associate with “a specific topic,” the more (and more easily) you will be able to monetize that topic.

records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Niche Fundamentals/Identifying Your Information Advantage - Digital Niche Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
So, what should your first niche be?

Well, it should be a topic area that meets the following criteria:

  1. It’s something you’re intrinsically interested in (meaning you actively enjoy continuing to learn about it)

  2. It’s something you have some level of experience in (meaning “you know things” about this industry/niche/topic the “average person” does not)

  3. It’s something you could see yourself writing about for a reasonable amount of time (meaning it’s not a shiny-object topic you only want to write about once)

This criteria can be summarized into, what I like to call, your Information Advantage.

What is an Information Advantage?

An Information Advantage is what you know about a topic, industry, or type of experience that “the average person” doesn’t.

For example, my first job out of college was working at an advertising agency. I worked there for 4 years. Did I become the CEO of the agency? No. Did I become an award-winning Creative Director? No. But simply because I’ve “worked in advertising,” that means I know more than “the average person” about advertising and advertising agencies!

This is an Information Advantage.

And Information Advantages exist everywhere.

  • Hobbies create Information Advantages. You being interested in something inherently means you know more than “the average person” about that thing.

  • Unique experiences create Information Advantages. You experiencing something “most people don’t” inherently means you know more than “the average person” about that thing.

  • Groups and communities create Information Advantages. You being part of a group or community, of any kind, inherently means you are surrounded by group-specific information that makes you more educated about “the topic of that group” than “the average person.”

  • Jobs create Information Advantages. You working a job, any job, inherently means you know more than “the average person” about that industry, and that job.

  • Etc.

The problem is, most people take their Information Advantage for granted.

And the primary reason why is because most people don’t realize the things they know are not common knowledge. “What they know” seems to obvious to them… they can’t wrap their head around the fact that someone else, someone “less experienced” than them (at this one specific thing) would find value in what they have to say or share. So they don’t even bother.

Which is a giant missed opportunity!

Your fastest-path to “success” is to pick a niche where you have an existing Information Advantage.

Why?

Because you already know valuable things! All you have to do is learn the fundamentals of writing online, and monetizing your knowledge online, and you can capitalize on that Information Advantage in a niche.

Unfortunately, this is not what most people do.

Instead, the #1 mistake people make is they don’t pick a niche based on an existing Information Advantage. They pick a niche based on what’s popular (or what they perceive to be popular, or “more lucrative”). Or, they pick a niche they’re just starting to get interested in, but don’t really know very much about yet.

To be clear: you can pick whatever niche you want. And picking “something” is better than picking nothing.

But when you pick a niche where you don’t have an existing Information Advantage, now you have to solve for two things at once:

  • You have to learn about the niche, and acquire an Information Advantage

  • And you also have to learn how to write about that niche, and monetize that niche.

It’s more work.

Which means it’ll take you longer to see progress.

Which means you’re more likely to get frustrated and give up!

So, don’t pick a niche just because it “seems popular” or “seems lucrative.”

This is a horrible way of making the decision.

Instead, pick a niche based on an existing Information Advantage.

Then, get to work learning how to “go deep,” write about, and successfully monetize your existing Information Advantage.

This is your fastest-path to success—regardless of what the niche itself is.

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Digital Niche Fundamentals: A proven system to identify your Information Advantage and become known for a niche you own.

This idea of “niching down” or “finding your niche” has to be one of the most misunderstood ideas in all of marketing. It’s something everyone struggles with (maybe yourself included!). It’s the thing people are most likely to overthink. And, it’s a simple marketing idea that a lot of people get wrong, which is the following:

  • “If I pick a niche, I’ll get too specific—and I’ll limit my opportunity.”

  • “So I won’t pick a niche, so I can stay broad—which will increase my opportunity.”

And this is fundamentally wrong.

Niching down does not limit your opportunity.

It expands it.

Conversely, “not niching down” and staying broad is what, ironically, ends up limiting your opportunity. Because when you say you do “everything” for “everyone,” then no one knows what your value is. Whereas if you say, “I specialize in this one thing,” suddenly everyone assumes you can translate that value across industries and help them, too.

This is a very simple but very difficult concept for people to understand.

Which is why we are dedicating an entire mini-course to it!

So, let’s help you niche down.

We hope you enjoy these Digital Niche Fundamentals.

records.title: Your First Niche
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Niche Fundamentals/Your First Niche - Digital Niche Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Of course, whenever I walk writers through the concept of “niching down,” they immediately hit me with all kinds of objections & faulty beliefs: - “What if I pi
records.content:
Of course, whenever I walk writers through the concept of “niching down,” they immediately hit me with all kinds of objections & faulty beliefs:

  • “What if I pick the wrong niche?!”

  • “What if I want to change niches later?!”

  • “What if my niche is too small/saturated?!”

  • “What if my niche gets destroyed by AI?!”

  • Etc. etc. etc.

It’s important to realize that all of these internal objections are faulty beliefs, and all of these faulty beliefs are self-inflicted and wrong. These are not facts. These are narratives you have created to give yourself permission to postpone taking action.

You are not picking your forever niche. You are picking your FIRST niche.

Now, let’s walk through the logic (slowly) why this is so important.

First, you literally cannot improve something that is not in motion. So what’s the first thing we need to solve for? We need to get you taking action! Which fundamentally means picking “something.” (This is not a trick. It’s just first-principles thinking. Before you can improve something, you have to pick something. Which means there’s no wrong answer. The only wrong answer is not picking anything at all.)

Second, once you pick “something,” you now have a vehicle to build skills inside. It doesn’t matter what your first niche is. It could be parenting. It could be digital marketing. It could be microplastics and food safety. IT DOES NOT MATTER. What matters is you pick “something” so you now have a vehicle to build inside and practice. And all the skills you will build are transferrable to any other niche you want at any point in the future.

Third, you must stick with a niche for longer than 3 days to learn how to “go deep.” Every time you pivot niches, you deprive yourself of the most important learning of all, which is how deep you can go inside a niche. Going deep takes work. It requires you to build all kinds of skills. And again, those skills are all transferrable to any niche you want to capitalize on at any point in the future. But you should mentally ballpark sticking with a niche for at LEAST a year. (Again, this is not wasted time. It’s the most valuable time you can spend, because now you’re learning.)

Fourth, you should use this first niche as an opportunity to build your first monetization vehicle. Every ****niche can be profitable. Every niche has opportunity. If there was no opportunity, and no money available in your niche, your niche would not exist. The mere fact it exists means there is opportunity and money floating around inside it. So, if you are “struggling to monetize your niche,” it’s not because the niche itself is broken or too competitive or too saturated, etc. It’s because you don’t have the required monetization skills yet. How do you build those skills? You need to commit to building those skills. Which means committing to a niche. Which means picking “something” and getting going. (See how all these things work together?)

Fifth, once you go deep in 1 niche, and successfully monetize 1 niche, you now have the skills to capitalize on any niche you want—forever. This is the step most people never get to (because they allow all their faulty beliefs to keep them from taking action and/or giving up too soon). But once you know how to provide real value to readers in 1 niche, and once you learn about different digital business models and how to monetize the value you provide, you can leverage those skills over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again.

But you will not get “there” until you pick a niche to start with.

Which is why you have to pick something.

And that means learning how to ride the Genius-Idiot Rollercoaster.

Everyone rides it, so let me tell you how it works:

  • When things are going well, you feel like you’re a genius.

  • And when things are going not-so-well, you feel like you’re an idiot.

Neither extreme is true.

In life and business, there will always be ups and there will always be downs. And the biggest mistake you can make is marrying your self-worth to either extreme. When you’re up, you think, “This is so easy! I’m so smart! I should pursue more ideas! I can do everything!” And when you’re down, you think, “This is so hard. I’m such an idiot. Why did I even pick this idea to begin with? I can’t do anything.”

But neither extreme is an accurate representation of reality.

These are just temporary snapshots of outlier scenarios.

“Reality” is what’s between these two extremes.

It’s the baseline you return back to.

  • And when you’re up, returning back to baseline feels like a loss.

  • And when you’re down, returning back to baseline feels like a win.

It’s the same baseline.

The only thing that has changed is the context that surrounds it.

So, keep this in mind when you pick your first niche.

Because here’s what’s going to happen:

  • You’re going pick something

  • You’re going to take 1 step forward

  • If you get lucky, and that step forward somehow leads to something successful (like the very first thing you write goes viral and gets a ton of views), you’re going to think, “I’m a genius!”

  • More likely, that step forward will lead to a mediocre outcome (shocker: the first thing you write isn’t magically the most beloved, treasured piece of writing ever), and you’re going to think, “I’m an idiot. Why did I even pick this stupid niche?”

And neither extreme is true.

Whatever happens, the path forward is still the same.

Doesn’t matter if you accidentally hit a home run, or publish something that gets 11 views.

Either way, tomorrow’s task is to write and publish something again.

records.title: Your Niche Constellation
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Niche Fundamentals/Your Niche Constellation - Digital Niche Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
Let’s talk about why niching down does not limit your opportunity.

And, if anything, expands it.

Every niche has a “constellation” that surrounds it.

For example, if my niche is “Digital Writing,” does that mean I can ONLY write about “writing on social platforms?”

Of course not.

  • I can also write about self-publishing in the digital age.

  • I can also write about ghostwriting, and providing writing services, in the digital age.

  • I can also write about different ways to monetize writing in the digital age.

  • I can also write about how to market your writing (and products/services) in the digital age.

  • Etc.

BUT, I only have the opportunity to write about all these other tangentially-related topics BECAUSE I have a clear niche that I am associated with: Digital Writing.

If someone follows me for Digital Writing, they don’t mind (and trust me) to write about other tangentially-related topics.

But if I don’t have a clear niche, then no one would follow or know “what to listen to me about” to begin with.

And your “niche constellation” is way bigger than you realize.

Take any topic on earth.

Let’s take “pregnancy” as a topic.

First, we need to “go deep” on pregnancy as a topic itself—and you can do this by generating ideas in the following categories:

  • Demographic: You could write about pregnancy for high net-worth mothers. You could also write about pregnancy for black women vs white women vs asian women, and different problems or scenarios each demographic might run into. You could also write about pregnancy for women later in life (age 35+). Etc.

  • Experience Level: You could write about pregnancy for first-time moms. You could also write about pregnancy for moms who already have one young child (completely different pregnancy experience). You could also write about pregnancy for moms who already have 2+ young kids. Etc.

  • Location: You could write about pregnancy and local resources in Chicago. Or pregnancy and local resources in Denver. Etc.

  • Price: You could write about pregnancy on a budget. You could also write about pregnancy if “money is no object” and what’s worth spending money on to have the best possible experience. You could also write about pregnancy bargains, shopping tips, how to get the most out of the things you buy, how to not waste money, etc.

  • Problem: You could write about pregnancy issues women run into when they’re considered high-risk. You could also write about what foods or supplements cause problems during pregnancy. You could also write about different pregnancy problems and how to resolve them with homemade remedies (since you can’t take most medications). Etc.

  • Outcomes: You could write about how to stay fit and not gain unnecessary weight during pregnancy. You could also write about how to maintain a healthy relationship with your significant other during pregnancy and hormone changes. You could also write about how to step into your new sense of identity as a mother during pregnancy. Etc.

That’s already soooooooo many topics! And sooooooo much opportunity within your niche.

But wait… there’s more!

We can start to see the scope and scale of the constellation that surrounds this niche when we consider the following ways you could tailor this topic to different tangentially-related industries.

If your niche is “pregnancy,” you could also write about:

  • Fertility & IVF clinics

  • Prenatal vitamins & supplements

  • OB-GYN practices

  • Midwifery & doula services

  • Maternity clothing

  • Baby gear (strollers, car seats, cribs)

  • Nursery furniture & decor

  • Breast pumps & lactation support

  • Baby food & formula

  • Diapers & wipes

  • Childbirth education classes

  • Postpartum recovery products

  • Pelvic floor physical therapy

  • Prenatal yoga & fitness

  • Maternity & newborn photography

  • Baby registries & gift services

  • Genetic testing & screening

  • Ultrasound & imaging centers

  • Pediatrics

  • Pregnancy & parenting apps

  • Sleep training & baby sleep consulting

  • Stretch mark & skincare products

  • Mental health (perinatal/postpartum depression)

  • Nutrition & dietitian services

  • Surrogacy agencies

  • Adoption services

  • Egg & sperm freezing/banking

  • Maternity & family health insurance

  • Life insurance & estate planning for new parents

  • Maternity leave & employment law

  • Car safety & vehicle upgrades (family vehicles)

  • Home childproofing

  • Cord blood banking

  • Chiropractic care (prenatal)

  • Massage therapy

  • Acupuncture & alternative medicine

  • Babymoon & family travel

  • Maternity & nursing-friendly hospitality

  • Subscription boxes (mom & baby)

  • Baby naming services & resources

  • Childcare & daycare

  • Nanny placement agencies

  • Parenting books & courses

  • Toys & early childhood development

  • CPR & infant safety training

  • Family meal delivery & meal prep

  • Mommy-and-me classes & community groups

  • Pregnancy-safe beauty & cosmetics

  • Fertility & cycle-tracking wearables

That is, quite literally, unlimited opportunity!

But you only get the opportunity to write about “all these tangentially-related topics” by niching down, first.

“Pregnancy” as a niche is what creates the center of this entire constellation.

But you should be able to see how, if you had no niche, and you just said, “I write about whatever I want to write about!” then the constellation is no longer clear.

And no one knows why they should follow you or read your writing.
