records.content:
Here’s your niche content strategy.

Are you ready?

(It’s so simple that you just might miss it…)

Your niche content strategy is to write lots of content about that topic—for a year.

That’s it.

  • It doesn’t matter what social platform(s) you pick.

  • It doesn’t matter what “order” you write about the topics.

  • It doesn’t matter whether each thing you write performs well or not-so-well.

  • It doesn’t matter if you write more short-form versus long-form, text versus video, etc.

It doesn’t matter.

The ONLY thing that matters is you build a library of content in a niche.

And “providing value” in your niche comes down to 3 things:

  • Answering the reader’s questions: If you answer your target reader’s questions, within this niche/topic of interest, that is “valuable.”

  • Helping the reader solve problems: If you help your target reader, within this niche/topic of interest, solve tangible problems, that is “valuable.”

  • Helping the reader achieve outcomes: And if you help your target reader, within this niche/topic of interest, learn how to achieve tangible outcomes, that is “valuable.”

Everything else is secondary.

Writing quality, style, etc., is secondary. Grammar is secondary. Virality is secondary.

Nothing else really matters except those 3 things: answering questions, solving problems, achieving outcomes.

And the easiest way to do this is by using my 10 Magical Ways (to write about & expand anything) framework:

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

Whatever niche you’re in, these are tangible things you can give the reader that “guarantee value.”

  • When you give the reader tips for how to solve a problem, or unlock an outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader stats that prove how to solve a problem (or why they have this problem to begin with), or unlock an outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader steps to solve a problem, or unlock an outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader lessons or takeaways from when you solved their exact same problem, or lessons learned achieving their exact same desired outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader benefits of solving a problem, or unlocking an outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader reasons they need to solve this problem, or reasons why they should care about unlocking a specific outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you point out mistakes people make when trying to solve a problem, or unlock a certain outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader examples of people with this exact problem, or examples of how other people unlocked this desired outcome, that’s valuable.

  • When you give the reader questions they should ask (themselves or someone else) when trying to solve a problem, or unlock an outcome, that’s valuable.

  • And when you share a personal story about a time you were faced with the exact same problem, or a time when you achieved their desired outcome, that’s valuable.

So, this is your content strategy.

You pick a niche (an area of interest / topic).

You commit to writing within that niche for 1+ years (so you can “go deep” and build all the underlying skills required in order to capitalize on any niche).

You build your Niche Constellation, so you can really see how much opportunity you have and how many sub-topics you have the freedom to write about.

And then you “provide value” to the reader by using the 10 Magical Ways to always give your target reader something tangible related to your chosen topic of interest/niche.

See?

Easy!

records.title: Don’t Chase Virality. Build A Library
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Don’t Chase Virality. Build A Library - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Before we get into the “the writing,” there’s a high-level frame I’d like to give you first. Virality doesn’t matter. It’s nice. It’s fun. It’s feel-good-dopami
records.content:
Before we get into the “the writing,” there’s a high-level frame I’d like to give you first.

Virality doesn’t matter.

It’s nice. It’s fun. It’s feel-good-dopamine.

But virality is not what ultimately “moves the needle” and makes you or your writing successful.

In fact, fun little story for you, but the most viral thing I’ve ever written happened way back in 2014. I wrote a Quora answer that landed on the front page of Reddit, and accumulated millions of views across Quora, Reddit, and various major publications that republished the viral story. It was the definition of “a home run.”

To this day (over a decade later), I have not written anything “more viral” than that.

So, imagine if “virality” had been my goal.

I would have FAILED!

Virality happens once. A library lives forever.

One of the fundamental ideas I try to educate people on is the value difference between short-term virality and a long-term library.

Virality is a short-term event.

  • You write something.

  • For whatever reason, it “hits.”

  • The algorithm runs with it.

  • You might get 24-48 hours of 100x distribution.

  • You might get 24-48 hours of rapid follower growth.

  • And then it stops.

  • And you’re right back where you started.

Obviously, these moments are fun. The human brain wasn’t built to be able to comprehend a million people all reading and liking and commenting on something you write from the comfort of your apartment, house, or local coffee shop—so when it happens, the surge of notifications is intoxicating.

It just doesn’t last.

A library is a long-term asset.

Forget “daily performance” or how viral anything you write/create goes.

  • When you write lots of things within a niche/topic…

  • You create a “web” of content in that niche/topic on the Internet…

  • The more you write, the larger your web grows…

  • The larger your web grows, the more easily people interested in your niche/topic can find you…

  • The easier it is for people to find you, the more you grow your dense, niche-specific audience…

  • The more dense, and the more niche-specific your audience, the more likely those readers are to buy something from you…

  • The more money you make.

For example, I have been writing about “digital writing” for over a decade.

My “web” on this topic is huge. Thousands and thousands and thousands of pieces of content—from articles to YouTube videos, Tweets to books. All on the same overarching topic: “Here’s how to write in the digital age.”

As a result, every single day, new people become interested in that topic. And every single day, some percentage of those people inevitably come across “me.”

  • They see how long I’ve been writing about this topic for (and assume I must be “pretty good at it”).

  • Which causes them to go further down my rabbit hole.

  • Which gives them the confidence to buy one of my books.

  • Which gives them the confidence to join one of our writing programs.

  • Which gives them the confidence to stick around inside of our ecosystem.

(I might even be describing the very path YOU took to get here, reading and consuming this, right now!)

More importantly, a library is an asset you can use forever.

When a new platform comes out, what do you think I do?

Do you think I sit down and tell myself, “OK Cole… now you need to create new content for this new platform.”

Of course not.

I just take my entire library, and start copy/pasting it over to the new platform.

  • When Instagram Threads came out in 2023, this is what we did. You can take a look here. 100% of the content on this platform are things I wrote years ago.

  • When Substack launched “Notes” in 2024, I did the same thing. You can take a look here. 100% of the short-form content on this platform are things I wrote years ago.

This is what’s possible when you get out of a “chasing virality” mindset and focus on building a library, in a niche, that compounds in value over time.

You can reuse your library across platforms.

You can remix your library into different forms of media (a Tweet can be a short-form video script, which can become a hook for a long-form article, etc.).

And most importantly, your library lives on the Internet forever—passively bringing new readers into your ecosystem, on autopilot, 24/7.

Virality is irrelevant.

All that matters is you build a library, in a niche you care about, for a decade.

records.title: Hooks & Headlines
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Hooks & Headlines - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: The fundamental pieces that make a great “hook” also make for a great: - Headline - Subject line - Opening sentence - First sentence of a new section - Etc. Any
records.content:
The fundamental pieces that make a great “hook” also make for a great:

  • Headline

  • Subject line

  • Opening sentence

  • First sentence of a new section

  • Etc.

Anytime you are writing something (whether it’s an asset, or a new section within an asset), you want to ask yourself how you can do 2 things:

  1. GRAB the reader’s attention

  2. And tell them, very clearly, where the piece is going

If your hook, or headline, or subject line, etc., accomplishes that goal, then congratulations—you’ve written a great “hook!”

But, to make this tangible, let’s first talk about headlines.

What is a headline?

A “headline” is:

  • The title of an article

  • The title of a blog post

  • The title of a newsletter (different from the subject line)

  • Anything with a title! (Many of these rules apply to book titles, for example)

And when writing a headline, there are really 5 pieces to consider.

I call this: The Perfect Headline Framework

  1. The Number: If you are using the listicle format, then you want to tell the reader “how many” things you’re giving them. This number helps them understand what they’re signing themselves up for. (A lower number means “this won’t take very long” whereas a higher number means “this will be very comprehensive.”)

  2. The What: Next, what literally are you giving the reader? This goes back to The 10 Magical Ways. Are you giving them Tips? Steps? Stats? Mistakes? Lessons? Reasons? Questions? Etc. And the 10 Magical Ways are just the tip of the iceberg. This decision is, quite literally, what are you giving the reader. Podcast episodes to listen to? Books to read? Places to visit? Etc. (And paired with The Number, you should see how this works: 6 mistakes, 5 podcast episodes, 7 must-read books, etc.)

  3. The Who: Next, who is this piece for? The easiest way to attract your target reader is to literally name them in the headline. “7 must-read books FOR aspiring writers” or “7 must-read books FOR first-time managers,” etc. When you name the archetype of person you’re trying to attract, they “see themselves” in your writing… and click! Because they know it’s for them.

  4. The Why: Next, why should the reader give you their time, energy, and attention? (And this is also true for products: why should the reader give you their hard-earned money?) The Why is the outcome of reading. “7 must-read books TO BECOME A PROFESSIONAL WRITER & STORYTELLER.” You don’t care about the 7 must-read books. You care about the 7 must-read books in order to do/accomplish something. That’s the Why.

  5. Twist The Knife: Lastly, when in doubt, give the reader more. If they give you their time, energy, attention, what else can you promise them? What additional benefits can you help them achieve/experience? What additional problems can you help them avoid? For example, “7 must-read books to become a professional writer & storyteller—and stop postponing your dream.” This is a copywriting technique called “twisting the knife.”

But you can also apply many of these same tactics at the sentence-level.

A headline is a “title.”

Whereas a “hook” is usually the word people use when talking about some kind of “opening sentence.”

Here are 6 easy ways to do that:

1. Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.

Plant your flag in the ground.

Pick one side of an argument and help the reader decide if your writing is (or isn’t) something they are interested in. No hedging. State what you believe to be true or false.

  • Becoming successful doesn’t just “happen.”

  • Going to the gym isn’t a hobby, it’s a lifestyle.

  • The wealthiest people have the simplest investments.

Reader’s read things with a “declarative” point of view.

2. Open with a thought-provoking question.

Get in the reader’s head with a curiosity inducing question.

  • Is there such a thing as eternal happiness?

  • What keeps amateurs from ever making it to pro status?

  • Did you know the average Millennial has less than $10,000 in savings?

Ask the question that your target reader is already asking themselves and they will want to know the answer you have for them.

3. Open with a controversial opinion.

Find a point of view in your industry and offer a counter-point to the accepted narrative.

Challenge the status quo. No need to be outlandish. Just make sure you’re ready to back it up.

For example:

  • ChatGPT is overhyped.

  • It’s impossible to be both rich and happy.

  • Intelligence isn’t something you’re born with.

Claim the opposite of conventional wisdom to interrupt the reader’s thinking, and get their attention.

4. Open with a moment in time.

Ground the reader in a specific date, time, scene, or setting.

  • My fear of cafeteria trays began in 8th grade.

  • At 5:46 AM pacific time, September 11th, 2001, America changed forever.

  • In 1982, David Ogilvy wrote a memo to his ad agency employees titled “How to write.”

Plant the reader firmly in the middle of a story to capture their imagination and pull them forward.

5. Open with a vulnerable statement.

Relate to the reader on an emotional level.

  • I’ve never been a very social person.

  • For 27 years, I’ve struggled with alcoholism.

  • For the first 10 years of my career, I was a terrible employee.

Bring the reader in by sharing your personal experience—we all want to relate to other people.

6. Open with a weird, unique insight.

Similar to the question opener, look for interesting stats or facts that make the reader say, “What?!”

  • California is not the largest state in the US. Alaska is.

  • Crows are one of the most intelligent animals on planet earth.

  • My wife can boil a dozen eggs in 7 minutes or less.

Find a little known stat in your industry and then open with it to grab attention.

records.title: Intangible vs Tangible
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Intangible vs Tangible - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Over the past decade, I have created a lot of different writing frameworks for myself—and I have gone on to share those frameworks with tens of thousands of wri
records.content:
Over the past decade, I have created a lot of different writing frameworks for myself—and I have gone on to share those frameworks with tens of thousands of writers.

But I can confidently say that this one, the one I’m about to share with you here, has had the biggest impact on my writing.

*And to be clear, this is not just a “copywriting” technique. This applies to all writing. In fact, I’d argue it’s this technique that makes for the most valuable non-fiction writing, period.

Here’s a secret about writing non-fiction, and creating digital products, that took me a very long time to learn.

Readers and customers always value “tangible” things more than “intangible” things.

  • Tangible: A “tangible” thing is some sort of object, experience, or visceral feeling/identity. You can hold it. You can measure it. You know when it’s happening.

  • Intangible: An “intangible” thing is… the opposite! It’s amorphous. It’s an idea. It’s an explanation. You can’t collect it, hold it, measure it, or viscerally experience it.

Which means the whole secret to creating compelling ideas & products in the digital world is to find ways to make IDEAS feel like Tangible Objects.

So, how do you do that?

Things that are Tangible

I come back to this list often:

  • Numbers: Numbers are tangible. $5. 37 minutes. 62 years old. Etc. Anything with a number implies a measurable amount, making it tangible.

  • Objects: Objects are tangible. Blueprint. Checklist. Template. Prompt. Guide. System. Cheat Sheet. Etc. Anything that is framed in the context of being an object implies it is an asset, and assets are always perceived to be more valuable than ideas.

  • Identity: Identities are tangible. First-Time Mom. HR Specialist. Crypto Copywriter. Retired Lawyer. Etc. Any identity, job title, or “named achievement” is tangible—because you either have that title, or you don’t.

  • Milestone: Milestones are tangible. You learn how to paint a lion in watercolor. You successfully make a putt from 15 feet. You can dunk. You can play Fur Elise on the piano. You graduate college. Etc. These are all milestones, and milestones are tangible because there is a clearly defined moment when “it happens.”

Weak writing speaks in Intangibles.

Basically, just take the above list and think of the opposite:

  • No Number: “I’ll help you lose some weight.” That is significantly weaker than “I’ll help you lose 15 pounds by summer.”

  • No Object: “Here’s how to create great content.” That is significantly weaker than “Here’s my viral content system & analytics dashboard template.”

  • No Identity: “Here’s how to get promoted.” That is significantly weaker than “Here’s how to get promoted to VP of Sales.”

  • Milestone: “I’ll teach you how to play the piano like a pro.” That is significantly weaker than “I’ll teach you how to play Fur Elise in 6 weeks.”

Weak writing speaks in Intangibles.

Strong writing speaks in Tangibles.

records.title: Lean Writing
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Lean Writing - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Lean Writing is the idea that every single thing you write can be expanded or compressed into 10+ other versions. - A tweet can be the outline of an Atomic Essa
records.content:
Lean Writing is the idea that every single thing you write can be expanded or compressed into 10+ other versions.

  • A tweet can be the outline of an Atomic Essay

  • An Atomic Essay can be expanded into an article or newsletter

  • 3-5 articles or newsletters can be stitched together into a book chapter

  • 10-20 articles or newsletters on a topic can be stitched together into a self-published book

  • A book can be broken apart into 100+ tweets

  • An article or newsletter can be read aloud as a YouTube video

  • A tweet or a thread can be read as an Instagram Reel, TikTok, or YouTube Short

  • Etc. etc. etc.

One of the biggest mistakes writers and content creators make is they think, when they write about something “once,” that’s it. They can never use it again.

In reality, it’s the complete opposite.

Write Once, Publish Everywhere, Remix Forever

Again, this speaks to the value of taking a library-first approach to your niche and your writing.

When you focus on building a library, in a niche, that library can be expanded, compressed, and remixed a thousand different times across a dozen different platforms inside a dozen different forms of media. Tweets can become videos. Videos can become newsletters. Newsletters can become books. And so on.

Which is why the value of your library compounds over time.

The larger your library in a niche grows, the more content you have to “play with” and republish, the EASIER your life gets as time goes on.

Lean Writing is also a form of data analysis.

In the “legacy writing” world, back in Hemingway’s day, it took a long time to get feedback on your writing.

  • You had to spend 2 years writing a book.

  • Then wait 18-24 months for it to get edited and published.

  • Then another few months for the magazine reviews to come in.

  • Until finally, ~4 years later, in a low-lit pub, Hemingway hear’s someone say, “Hemingway’s new novel sucked!” and he gets his first data point of feedback.

But the “digital writing” world doesn’t have these same constraints!

In the digital world, you can write an idea, publish it on a social platform, and start gathering data immediately.

  • Data in the form of Views

  • Data in the form of Likes

  • Data in the form of Comments

  • Data in the form of Shares

And all of this data, no matter how small, gives you a sense of what’s working and what’s not.

Lean Writing just means paying attention to that data, and then making decisions to double-down on ideas that are clearly resonating.

  • Write 10 things

  • Which one “performed” the best?

  • Write about that topic 10 more times (expand it, compress it, remix it, etc.)

  • Which one “performed” the best?

  • Write about that new topic 10 more times (expand it, compress it, remix it, etc.)

  • Which one “performed” the best?

  • Etc. etc. etc.

All successful writers & creators do this intuitively.

Which means you might as well do it consciously.

“But Cole?! What if I have no followers?! What if I have no audience?! What if I’m gathering no data?!”

You are—you’re just taking it for granted.

You think what you’re looking for is some massive outlier. You write 10 things, and 1 of them gets a million views. That’s wrong. That’s not what’s going to happen.

Instead, your data is going to look something like this:

  • You wrote 10 Tweets

  • 9 of them got <100 views

  • 1 of them got >100 views

Pop quiz: which topic should you consider doubling-down on and writing about some more?

(The last one. Because, even though it’s small, it is “the outlier.”)

Do you have to stick with this topic forever? No.

Do you have to double-down on a topic you don’t actually want to write about again? No.

The data is simply giving you options—specifically, data-backed options.

  • You should probably write more about things that are clearly resonating with people.

  • And you should probably write less about things that are clearly not resonating with people.

It’s that simple.

Here’s a Lean Writing example from Dickie so you can see how this works:

And here’s how he expanded his initial tweet into an Atomic Essay:

(Do you see how the “bulleted list” from his Tweet became the outline for his Atomic Essay—and all he did was “expand” each point? That’s Lean Writing!)

records.title: Personal Stories As Examples
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Personal Stories As Examples - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: One of the biggest objections I hear from writers/creators is how they: - Want some sort of external outcome (views, followers, newsletter subscribers, clients,
records.content:
One of the biggest objections I hear from writers/creators is how they:

  • Want some sort of external outcome (views, followers, newsletter subscribers, clients, customers, etc.)

  • But don’t want to “be sales-y” or “be promotional”

And to be honest, it’s not just writers/creators.

I ran into this constantly when I was building my ghostwriting agency back in 2017-2020. I would get on the phone with founders, CEOs, venture capitalists, really smart and successful people, and they would say to me, “I want XYZ to happen… but I don’t want to be promotional.”

OK, first of all… you can’t generate an external outcome without telling people about it.

And second…. you can tell people about things without being “promotional.”

Let me tell you the secret.

It’s 2 words.

For Example

After those 2 words, “For example…” you can say anything you want.

  • You can promote your book

  • You can promote your product

  • You can promote your company

  • You can promote yourself

It’s a license to promote.

But because it’s being framed as “an example,” as long as you bring the example back to the reader’s interests, they don’t view it as being promotional at all.

Watch.

I’ll do it right now.

How do I know this tactic is so effective?

Well, for example, back in 2016 I started writing a daily column for Inc Magazine. And they had this rule that you weren’t allowed to promote other people’s companies just for the sake of it. There had to be a purpose. But I was starting to become an entrepreneur, and I had friends who were entrepreneurs (who really wanted to get mentioned in Inc Magazine!). So, what did I do? I used this technique, and would write about my own ghostwriting services, as well as my friends’ companies, not “promoting” them—just using them as examples in the piece. And, in that context, Inc Magazine had no problem. Because I wasn’t being promotional. I was just… using an example! (This is how I ended up getting dozens and dozens of my friends mentioned in Inc Magazine by the way.)

There.

I just “promoted” my old Inc Magazine column to you.

  • Do you feel sold to?

  • Do you hate me?

  • Do you feel like I was being too “promotional?”

Of course not.

You just feel like I told you a story, and used something of “mine” as “an example.”

By the way, this is a core strategy we teach inside our beginner writing program, Ship 30 for 30. We encourage writers to identify a topic and write for a specific reader in their niche, and then use their own experiences (or products, or companies) as “the example”—allowing them to promote themselves without promoting themselves.

See? I just did it again here. (I did the slightly more advanced version, which is instead of saying “For example” I just said, “By the way.” But it’s the same mechanism.)

And you can do this over, and over, and over again. All the way down the page.

And as long as you use “the example” to illustrate a larger point that is valuable and helpful to the reader, the reader does not care. In fact, the only reason you’re even aware of what I’m doing here is because I’m literally telling you what I’m doing as I’m doing it.

The average reader won’t even know.

They’ll just think, “Oh, that’s an interesting example,” and keep reading.

And some percentage of those readers, once exposed to your example, will click and decide to go down the rabbit hole—exploring “the thing” you just subtly told them about.

records.title: Prep The Page
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Prep The Page - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: This writing technique is much better explained via video, so please watch the above to learn my “Prep The Page” approach! (This is how you solve Writer’s Block
records.content:
This writing technique is much better explained via video, so please watch the above to learn my “Prep The Page” approach!

(This is how you solve Writer’s Block forever—and remove the fear that comes from staring at the blank page.)

Bulleted-List Thinking

Everything is a list.

  • When you are giving the reader “tips” for how to do something better, what are you doing? You’re listing out “Tips.”

  • When you are telling the reader “questions” they should ask themselves before making a decision, what are you doing? You’re listing out “Questions.”

  • When you are describing a setting, a character, an object, what are you doing? You’re listing out “Attributes.”

  • What am I doing here, right now? I’m LISTING out examples of lists!

Writing is a game of lists.

It doesn’t matter if you’re writing an article for Buzzfeed or you’re writing a short story for the New Yorker. Lists are everywhere.

Which means “thinking in lists” is a core skill to build as a writer.

And I want to emphasize that when I say “lists,” I do not just mean writing a “listicle” with numbered points.

  1. First point.

  2. Second point.

  3. Third point.

  4. Etc.

But lists also show up in prose all the time. For example, have you ever read the novel, The Things They Carried? It’s about a platoon of American soldiers fighting on the ground in the Vietnam War. I have the book here on my desk, so let me share a quick excerpt:

~

“The things they carried were determined to some extent by superstition. Lieutenant Cross carried his good-luck pebble. Dave Jensen carried a rabbit’s foot. Normal Bowker, otherwise a very gentle person, carried a thumb that had been presented to him as a gift by Mitchell Sanders.”

~

What is the author, Tim O’Brien, doing here in the above excerpt?

He is LISTING meaningful objects each character carried with them.

(For what it’s worth, The Things They Carried has sold over 2 million copies, and was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1991.)

Lists are one of the foundational skills of great writing.

For a few reasons (watch, I’m about to list out the reasons for you!):

  • Reason #1: Lists of examples and details gives the reader “more,” which makes your writing more vivid, which gives the reader more value. When trying to learn a new idea, which would you prefer: for the writer to only give you 1 example, or 10 examples? Exactly. More examples = better. Or, in fiction, which would you prefer: for the writer to only give you 1 description of a character, a setting, a meaningful object, or 10 descriptions… each one helping you see in your mind’s eye what’s happening on the page with more and more clarity? Exactly. More descriptions = better.

  • Reason #2: Lists are the easiest container for organizing your thoughts (as a writer), and the easiest container to consume ideas (as a reader). This is fundamentally why “listicles” are the most popular content format on the Internet—by a wide margin. Because they are a container that guarantees organization (it’s a list!), making them easy to write, and easy to read.

  • Reason #3: Most importantly, “thinking in lists” forces clarity of ideas and the sequencing of those ideas. This is something that took me a VERY LONG TIME to understand about writing non-fiction. You don’t need to write 3,000 words or 30,000 words to “figure out what you’re trying to say.” You can clarify your thinking, and the sequencing of your ideas, with a simple bulleted list.

Before you write anything, you should be able to summarize the main points in a bulleted list.

For example, let’s say I wanted to write an article or newsletter about “how to attract your first 5,000 readers on LinkedIn.”

Do I need to actually write the piece to figure out what I want to say?

Of course not.

All I need to do is make a quick bulleted list of the main points—the core ideas I would want to share with the reader.

Which would be:

  1. Identify your niche

  2. Optimize your profile for that niche

  3. Commit to writing/publishing daily for a year

  4. Spend 15-30 minutes each morning commenting on other people’s posts (to fuel engagement)

  5. Each week, review your highest-performing topics and, the following week, consider doubling-down on your “winners” (and cutting your “losers”)

The above list of 5 ideas is, quite literally, the “value” of my article or newsletter.

So before you write anything, create a bulleted list of your “main ideas.”

If you can’t say what you’re trying to say in a simple bulleted list of your main ideas, then that means you don’t know what your main ideas are.

And I promise, no amount of “writing more words/prose” is going to clarify your thinking. It’s just going to compound the problem. Oftentimes, writers think, “If I had more words, then I’d be able to say what I’m trying to say!” But that’s a mistake.

The tighter and clearer your bulleted list of main ideas, the tighter and clearer the prose will be when you expand it.

The more loose and unclear your list of main ideas, the more loose and unclear the prose will be when you expand it.

records.title: Questions As Ideas
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Questions As Ideas - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: One of the biggest mistakes writers make when they sit down to write is they try to come up with “ideas.” But the problem with “coming with ideas” is you’re ess
records.content:
One of the biggest mistakes writers make when they sit down to write is they try to come up with “ideas.”

But the problem with “coming with ideas” is you’re essentially asking yourself to identify something specific inside of an infinite canvas. You have no anchor. No starting place. Which is why it often feels so difficult to “come up with ideas.” (This is the first symptom of what people eventually determine to be Writer’s Block.)

So, what’s the solution?

Questions As Ideas

The best ideas are actually answers to questions.

This is something I learned first-hand writing on Quora way back in 2014. Quora is a question/answer social site, and every single piece of content in your feed starts with a question.

“Writing,” then, is really just an exercise in answering your target reader’s questions.

If I asked you to start talking, you would probably freeze and not know what to say.

But if I asked you a question, and you knew the answer to the question, you would start talking without even thinking about it.

And this is true for every niche:

  • If you are in the “fitness” niche, then what questions do your target readers have about fitness?

  • If you are in the “parenting” niche, then what questions do your target readers have about parenting?

  • If you are in the “dating” niche, then what questions do your target readers have about parenting?

This is the secret to writing well and providing value within a niche.

Forget coming up with ideas.

Just answer questions.

(Not literally on Quora. I mean, you can. But I mean just start by identifying a question your target reader might have—and then write something that answers that question for them.)

For example, my niche is Digital Writing.

What questions do my target readers have about digital writing?

  • “What’s the best social platform to write on?”

  • “How do I know which social platform is best for my niche?”

  • “Does Medium still have good distribution? If I’m just starting out, should I start there?”

  • “When should I build an email list and start launching digital products?”

  • Etc. etc. etc.

It’s very easy to write when you know what question you’re answering in your writing.

(And conversely, it’s very hard to write when you don’t know what question you’re answering in your writing.)

And this idea of Questions-As-Ideas creates a flywheel.

Information Advantage + Time In Niche = Infinite Questions

Something a lot of writers ask me is, “Cole, how do I know whether or not my writing is providing value?”

This is actually a very easy question to answer.

  • When you have an Information Advantage in an industry or topic or interest, you inherently know “more” than the average person.

  • The reason you know “more” is because you have had more experiences, more exposure to the nuances of that industry/topic.

  • The more exposure you get to an industry/topic, the more questions you have—because you’re learning, and you are figuring out “what you don’t know you don’t know.”

  • The more you learn, the more your Information Advantage in a niche grows.

  • The more your Information Advantage grows in a niche, the more you become aware of what questions other people have—because you used to have those very same questions yourself.

  • And since you are aware of the questions people have, and now you know the answers (because you’ve spent more and more time in this particular niche), you now know what questions to answer to “provide value.”

See how this works?

This is why I don’t have an editor for any of my writing. I also don’t need to ask people, “Did you find that valuable?” I already know. And I know what the value is because I have such a large Information Advantage in the niche of Digital Writing—because I’ve spent 10+ years writing about this topic, almost exclusively.

Which means I have become “aware” of Infinite Questions to answer.

(Because I used to have all the same questions!)

“But Cole?! What if I don’t know what questions my target reader has?”

If you honestly can’t think of a single question your target reader has, that means you’ve made 1 of 2 mistakes:

  • Mistake #1: You’ve chosen a niche or topic because you think it’s popular and will be your fast-track to success, but you actually know nothing about it (no Information Advantage).

  • Mistake #2: You gave up after 3 seconds (try harder).

Every single experience in life gives you some sort of Information Advantage. And fundamentally, that means there was a “before” and an “after” moment. So, how you come up with Questions As Ideas is just by asking yourself, “What didn’t I know before… that I know now?”

And if you honestly, genuinely can’t identify a single question. Then just ask Claude or ChatGPT for some help.

records.title: Subjective vs Objective
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Subjective vs Objective - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Another way of thinking about Tangible vs Intangible language is to stress-test through this lens: “Is this Subjective? Or is this Objective?” - Subjective = Op
records.content:
Another way of thinking about Tangible vs Intangible language is to stress-test through this lens:

“Is this Subjective? Or is this Objective?”

  • Subjective = Open to interpretation. It’s intangible. Ask 10 different people what they think you mean, and you will get 10 different answers.

  • Objective = No interpretation. The language is so clear and tangible, that if you ask 10 different people what they think you mean, all 10 people will say the same thing back to you.

This is an incredibly simple, but incredibly difficult thing for people to recognize in their writing.

And I think it’s because so many people do this incorrectly, that when you “look around,” you’re surrounded by Intangible, Subjective language. And so you think, “That’s what I should do, too!”

But that’s wrong.

Your goal should be to speak in Tangible, Objective language.

Let’s do some rewrite examples to show you.

The same rules that determine Tangible vs Intangible language also apply to Subjective vs Objective language.

For example:

  • Subjective = “I will help you live a happy, healthy, wealthy life.” If you ask 10 different people how they define a happy, healthy, wealthy life, you will get 10 different answers. Because they are subjective. There is lots of room for interpretation.

  • Objective = “I will help you sleep 8 hours per night, eat <2,000 calories per day, and have $500,000 saved before you turn 50.” If you ask 10 different people what they think you mean, all 10 of them will say these exact things back to you. Because they are objective. There is no room for interpretation.

~

Here’s another one:

  • Subjective = “I’ll show you how to date.”

  • Objective = “I’ll give you 10 low-pressure conversation starters you can use at bars and restaurants to spark up conversations with men ages 22-30.”

~

One more:

  • Subjective = “I’ll help you up-level your marketing skills as an independent musician.”

  • Objective = “I’ll help you get your first 10,000 followers on TikTok and your first 1,000,000 views on a short viral music video.”

~

Once these two writing rules clicked for me—Tangible vs Intangible, Objective vs Subjective—the quality of my writing, ALL OF MY WRITING, improved dramatically.

And remember: thinking, and writing in this way, is a skill.

It takes practice!

records.title: The 10 Magical Ways
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/The 10 Magical Ways - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: All non-fiction writing can be reverse-engineered into a small handful of “things” readers value. I call these The 10 Magical Ways (To Write & Expand Anything):
records.content:
All non-fiction writing can be reverse-engineered into a small handful of “things” readers value.

I call these The 10 Magical Ways (To Write & Expand Anything):

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

Once you train your brain to recognize these pieces, you will see them everywhere.

AND, anytime you find yourself “stuck” on what to say next, all you have to do is pick one of these 10 Magical Ways… and give the reader that!

Why The 10 Magical Ways “guarantees value.”

What is “value?”

This is another one of those things that took me a long time to understand.

In non-fiction, people only care about 1 thing: getting an answer to their question.

That’s it.

And I can prove it with a simple example. Can you think of a time you were on Reddit, or some social platform, and you found yourself reading or consuming something despite the fact that there was something “wrong” with it? For example: maybe you were watching a video but the footage wasn’t that great. Or you were reading a post from someone but it was littered with grammatical errors. It didn’t matter. You still consumed it anyways.

The reason is because, in non-fiction, as long as the content educates you in some way (aka: answers a question you have), you will tolerate all kinds of “mistakes” if it means getting the answer you desire.

So, let’s go back to our question.

What is “value?”

Well, value is just identifying the different things you can give a reader to educate them—aka: answer their question.

For example, let’s pretend you are writing about real estate, and your target reader has the question, “How should I buy my first rental property?”

You guarantee value by looking at the list of 10 Magical Ways and asking yourself which of those “things” would sufficiently answer their question.

If the reader is asking “How To,” what could we give them that would be value?

  • Tips: We could give them tips to buy their first rental property correctly.

  • Stats: We could give them some stats about how to identify lucrative areas to buy rental properties that produce positive cash-flow.

  • Steps: We could give them steps to buy their first rental property.

  • Lessons: We could give them some hard lessons learned.

  • Benefits: We could educate them on the benefits of buying a certain type of rental property.

  • Reasons: We could give them reasons why they should buy one type of property and turn it into a rental, and reasons why they shouldn’t buy another type of property (because it wouldn’t make for a very good rental).

  • Mistakes: We could give them mistakes to avoid when trying to buy their first rental property.

  • Examples: We could give them examples of what to look for when identifying rental properties, or examples of other comparable rental properties in their desired area.

  • Questions: We could give them questions to ask their real estate agent, or the seller, when trying to determine whether they should buy this rental property.

  • Personal Stories: We could tell them a personal story about how you bought your first rental property, and things you learned in the process.

The point is: “value” is just you, answering your target reader’s question, and giving them something “valuable” (The 10 Magical Ways) in the process.

This is how you guarantee you’re providing value.

(And you should repeat this little thought exercise every time you sit down to write. You’re always answering your target reader’s questions!)

records.title: Visual Formatting
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Visual Formatting - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
Visual Formatting is incredibly important.

Formatting is what dictates whether or not people read your work. That’s because, when a reader is presented with something poorly formatted, they automatically come to the conclusion “this must not be very good.” Why? Because it doesn’t look professional, accessible, or skimmable.

Conversely, even if the writing is mediocre, a reader might still give it their attention if its formatted well. Why? Because it “looks” professional, accessible, and skimmable.

Visual Formatting are cues that tell the reader, “This is well-organized and worth your time.”

The big cues being:

  • Headers and clear section dividers

  • Cleanly formatted sections with prose that alternates between long & short paragraphs and sentences

  • Lists/bulleted lists

These are the easiest upgrades to make in your writing, and have the highest likelihood of capturing and keeping your target reader’s attention.

Here’s how:

Step 1: Start every section with a single-sentence opener.

If you want to instantly 10x the likelihood of readers being interested and curious to "keep reading," open your piece (and every subsequent section) with a single sentence.

There's something about seeing a sentence by itself that makes the reader think, "Well that was easy to read." And before they can even decide whether or not they want to keep reading, their eyes have already started skimming the next paragraph.

There are 6 specific types of single-sentence openers—all of which particularly well for "hooking" the reader's interest.

  • Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.

  • Open with a thought-provoking question.

  • Open with a controversial opinion.

  • Open with a moment in time.

  • Open with a vulnerable statement.

  • Open with a weird, unique insight.

Here's how you put this into action.

Let's say you have already written a big paragraph at the start of your piece. We can immediately 10x the quality of that intro section (and increase the likelihood the reader will get past that first sentence) just by making sure the "opener" is 1 single sentence.

Here's an example text:

The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question: "How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard? Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary? What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?" Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

That's a long paragraph!

In fact, as a reader, chances are you didn't even read the above paragraph all the way through. You probably saw "a big block of text" and decided to just skim right past it to the next bolded sentence. That's because, as readers, we almost can't help ourselves. We're always looking for the "next" milestone.

So, here's how we immediately 10x the quality of that opening paragraph.

Notice the difference:

The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question:

"How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard? Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary? What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?" Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

Wowza!

First of all, there's something nice and clean about the fact that the piece starts with just 1 simple sentence, yes? Can you feel it in your body? Do you feel how it isn't as much of a "mental lift?" This isn't an accident. Single-sentence openers feel easy. And readers love what feels easy.

Second, what type of single-sentence opener is this?

It's 1 strong, declarative statement: "The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question."

Boom.

The reader knows what this piece is about. The reader knows where we're going. And the reader can hear the conviction: "Sounds like you know what you're talking about!"

Which is what gives them the confidence to want to read the next sentence.

Step 2: Always look for opportunities to turn long paragraphs into bulleted lists.

  • If you are listing anything, ever, it should become a bulleted list.

  • If you are rambling off a dozen quick examples, it should become a bulleted list.

  • If you are making a series of distinct points to drive home a point, it should become a list.

Here's why:

Your #1 job as a writer is to always be asking, "How do I make this easier for the reader to fly through?" Which means (contrary to popular belief) abandoning the belief that your reader is supposed to sit there and drool over, appreciate, and gasp at each and every word—as if your adjective choice is a beautiful as Mona Lisa herself. Give it up. Let go of that dream. It doesn't matter. Whether the reader thinks you are "brilliant" or not is the wrong goal.

Your goal is for them to consume your work, and to not waste any of their time.

Period.

If you are successful, they'll come back for more.

If you are not successful, they'll say to themselves, "Wow that writer sure did waste a lot of my time" and never come back.

So, use bulleted lists when you see an opportunity to save them time!

Here's our opening paragraph again (including the single-sentence opener):

The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question:

"How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard? Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary? What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?" Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

But notice: that second paragraph is a listing out of a lot of questions. The content is fine, it's the formatting that could use some work.

So, here's an easy fix (and take note of how much easier it is to skim through):

The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question:

  • "How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard?"

  • "Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary?"

  • "What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?"

Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

Wowza!

Do you see how the above section looks like a nice neat sandwich now?

Single-sentence opener.

Quick bulleted list.

Closing sentence.

In all of 3 seconds, you can "consume" that entire introduction without almost any mental effort.

Now, how much "heavier" does this section feel if we go back to the original block of text?

The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question: "How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard? Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary? What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?" Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

Brutal.

In fact, you probably didn't read more than 2 words before your brain yelled: "NOPE!"

Step 3: Where are your subheads?

Subheads are bolded sentences throughout a piece that help the reader know "where" they are in your line of thinking.

Just like this module you’re reading here!

Because this module is organized into "Steps," and each Step is bolded, you can now skim and jump around the piece to find the section you're looking for (both during and after). As a reader, this is a terrific signal that what you're reading as been carefully constructed for your benefit—opposed to reading a long-winded, poorly formatted opinion article in The New Yorker that was clearly not written for your benefit, but for the benefit of the author: "Look what a professional writer I am!"

Some writers like to start their writing process by first listing out their Main Points in bolded subheads and then "coloring inside the lines" afterwards. (This is what I do.)

However, if you've already gotten into the writing and want to add subheads after the fact, the easiest way to use this formatting trick is to split your essay or piece equally into chunks. For example, if you are writing an Atomic Essay and it's ~300 words, then every 100 words should be a bolded subhead (splitting the piece equally into thirds).

For a few reasons:

  • Splitting the page evenly (visually) creates a sense of symmetry for the reader. It LOOKS easy and fun to read.

  • Splitting the page also gives the reader big, bolded "milestones" they can look forward to each time they scroll. If you split the page evenly down, then the reader won't be able to scroll more than twice without their eye "seeing" the next bolded subhead—encouraging them to keep reading (because they know the next section is "right around the corner").

  • Splitting the page also gives you clarity as to where you are taking the reader. Think of these subheads as the major mile markers helping remind you that you only have 100 words to talk about X, before you take a turn down a different street and have another 100 words to talk about Y, and so on.

Subheads bring clarity.

In the example text, the next sentence is a great opportunity for a subhead.

We already have a solid, formatted introduction.

And this next sentence is almost exactly 1/3rd down the page.

Time for a subhead!

For example:

The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question:

  • "How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard?"

  • "Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary?"

  • "What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?"

Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

(Bolding here to show, but you would make this an H1 or H3 subhead): But how you make the answer stick is by telling the reader a story.

For example, let's say the reader's question is, "What's it like to be an entrepreneur?" One way of answering this question would be to provide the reader with the formal definition of entrepreneurship. Be professional, right? "Entrepreneurship is the activity of setting up a business or businesses, taking on financial risks in the hope of profit." But how likely is the reader to remember what you've just told them? More importantly, how likely are they to be impacted and transformed by your words? They're not.

Wowza!

Can you see how your eye immediately gravitates to that subhead sandwiched in the middle of all the other text?

In fact, the way you probably "read" the above section goes like this:

  • Skim the subhead first (because it's bolded and easiest to see)

  • Then make a subconscious decision to either keep reading linearly or skim what came before it.

  • You look at the following paragraph and see a massive block of text. NOPE!

  • Instead, you decide to skim the first section because it's formatted well and easy to fly through.

This is what we mean when we say readers do not read linearly on the Internet.

They jump around.

They look for the next-easiest section to fly through.

Next time you click on an essay or article online, notice your own behavior. Chances are, you scroll and click around until you find the section that LOOKS most appealing to you.

So, how do we clean up the paragraph following the subhead?

Step 4: Use the 1/3/1 writing rhythm.

The last step to formatting is to go through each section and look for opportunities to use the classic 1/3/1 writing rhythm (or some variation of it):

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/2/5/2/1

  • Etc.

The key to immediately injecting rhythm and skimmability into your writing is to alternate length of sentences and sections—ideally opening and closing each section with a single sentence. These are your "doors," the things that get the reader INTO a given section (so make sure your doors slide open).

Like this:

[1] The reason people read is because they want an answer to their question:

  • [3] "How do I grow tomatoes in my backyard?"

  • "Are there techniques I can use to negotiate a better salary?"

  • "What is life like for teenagers who want to learn wizardry at Hogwarts?"

[1] Which means your job as a writer is a) to be conscious of what (specific) question you are answering for the reader, and b) give them the answer.

(H1 or H3) But how you make the answer stick is by telling the reader a story.

[1] For example, let's say the reader's question is, "What's it like to be an entrepreneur?"

[5] One way of answering this question would be to provide the reader with the formal definition of entrepreneurship. Be professional, right? "Entrepreneurship is the activity of setting up a business or businesses, taking on financial risks in the hope of profit." But how likely is the reader to remember what you've just told them? More importantly, how likely are they to be impacted and transformed by your words?

[1] They're not.

Wowza!

See how much easier that next section is to read just by breaking it up using this proven writing rhythm?

Open with 1 clear sentence.

Build the point over the next 4 sentences.

Close the point with 1 conclusion sentence.

You can use the 1/3/1, 1/4/1, 1/5/1, etc., writing rhythm all the way down the page and the reader won't have any idea what you're doing.

They'll just think, "Wow! This piece is formatted so beautifully! And the writing just flows!"

Only a trained eye (which you now have) will notice what's happening.

Conclusion: The key to formatting is to always think about reducing friction for the reader.

There are no right or wrong answers.

These are a few approaches that work well, but a better framework to internalize is to always be asking yourself, "How can I make this easier for the reader?"

  • If it would be easier to read in a bulleted list, do that.

  • If it would be easier to read in a step-by-step formatted guide, do that.

  • If it would be easier to read in a series of small, rapid-fire sections, do that.

Your North Star is what will be easiest and most enjoyable for the READER.

Not what "you" think would be cool, for you.

Remember, the reader is the main character here. And in order to be an effective writer, you must be in service to them.

records.title: Writing Rhythms
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Digital Writing Fundamentals/Writing Rhythms - Digital Writing Fundamentals · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: The key to injecting rhythm (and skimmability) into your writing is to alternate length of sentences and sections—ideally opening and closing each section with
records.content:
The key to injecting rhythm (and skimmability) into your writing is to alternate length of sentences and sections—ideally opening and closing each section with a single sentence.

For example:

  1. Start with one declarative sentence

  2. Follow it with three sentences that explain or build on the idea.

  3. End with another declarative sentence that wraps it up neatly.

Simple, right?

The 1/3/1 structure is all about pacing.

You give your reader an easy entry point, build on that with just enough info, and close with something impactful. Then, you repeat the process all the way down the page. It’s like a song, where each beat hits just right, pulling the reader through.

Your reader won’t even realize it, but they’ll keep reading because the flow just feels good.

Even “The Atlantic” could help their online readers by making posts easier to skim with the 1/3 /1 structure. See the difference?

The Easiest Place To Start

(1) If you're wondering where to apply the 1/3/1 rhythm first, look at your intros.

(3) The start of any piece sets the tone for how easy it will be for your reader to follow along. There's something about seeing a sentence by itself that makes the reader think, "Well that was easy to read." And before they can even decide whether or not they want to keep reading, their eyes have already started skimming the next paragraph.

(1) Scroll up and look at the intro for this post.

You can use the 1/3/1 writing rhythm all the way down the page and the reader won't have any idea what you're doing.

They'll just think:

  • "Wow!”

  • “The writing just flows!"

  • “This piece is formatted so beautifully!”

Only a trained eye (which you now have) will notice what's happening.

The key to formatting is to always think about reducing friction for the reader.

These are a few approaches that work well, but a better framework to internalize is to always be asking yourself, "How can I make this easier for the reader?"

  • If it would be easier to read in a bulleted list, do that.

  • If it would be easier to read in a step-by-step formatted guide, do that.

  • If it would be easier to read in a series of small, rapid-fire sections, do that.

Your North Star is what will be easiest and most enjoyable for the READER.

And there are all kinds of Writing Rhythms!

I really only have 2 rules:

  1. “Start” each section with a single-sentence opener and closer. These are your bookends. And strong, single-sentence openers and closers make sections much more accessible and memorable.

  2. Expand the middle. Meaning if you want to say more, or add more, don’t add it to your first sentence/opener or your last sentence/closer. Add to “the middle.”)

  3. Mirror the cascade up or down. If you expand the middle, whatever “pattern” you use to expand the middle should be mirrored (as close as possible) as you go into the closing sentence. So, for example, if you expand the middle with 1/5/1, but then decide you want to add a bit more (1/2/5) then you should aim to “mirror” that as you head into the end of the section (1/2/5/2/1). This creates a cascade and feeling of ascension/descension.

With that in mind, you can create all kinds of writing rhythms!

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/6/1

  • 1/7/1

  • 1/2/5/2/1

  • 1/2/3/5/3/2/1

  • 1/2/5/2/1/1

  • 1/1/3/7/3/2/1

  • Etc.

You have all kinds of options.

As long as the “rhythm” follows the 3 rules listed above.

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Module 1 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product.

In these modules, I’m going to show you how to:

  • Find your 1st Digital Product idea inside your social analytics

  • Create social content to validate your best Digital Product ideas

  • Outline the winning idea into a Digital Product

  • Gather feedback on your Digital Product Outline

  • Create your first Digital Product

  • Design your first Digital Product

  • Launch your first Digital Product

  • And ultimately… make your first $1 online!

So, we’re going to cover a lot!

But… let’s start simple.

In this module, we’re just going to focus on Finding Your 1st Digital Product Idea.

Let’s dive in!

The Mindset Of Creating Your First Digital Product

Here's the big idea we want to present to you:

Your first digital product (say, an eBook) does not need to be some "masterpiece."

In fact, your digital product might only be 10 or 20 pages.

It's not how long the digital product is, or how many words you've written, that determines its value. All that matters is that your digital product answers a valuable question to your target reader/customer.

Remember: the person buying your product isn't buying "a bunch of words" or even "a PDF."

What they're buying is an answer to a question they have.

"A digital product? Is my audience even big enough to create a digital product?"

The answer is: YES!

Here's the thing: most creators think they need to have a giant audience before they can create their first digital product. But this is a myth.

In fact, we launched our first digital products when we had less than 1,000 followers.

  • Cole created his first eBook in 2015 with just a couple hundred followers on Quora—and that eBook generated over $5,000 in revenue in the first few months.

  • And Dickie launched the very first cohort of Ship 30 for 30 back when he had less than 1,000 followers on Twitter—and Ship 30 for 30 has since grown into a cohort-based course helping thousands of writers each year.

Contrary to popular belief, you do NOT need a "huge" social media audience to launch your first digital product.

All you need is to know what, specifically, your audience cares about.

And then give them that.

Find Digital Product Ideas (In Your Analytics)

Now, the mistake most creators make is they sit down, stare out the window, and ask themselves, "Hmmm... what sort of digital product should I create?"

This is the wrong way of going about it.

Instead, you want to use data to determine where there are opportunities for you to create things people clearly want:

  • What topics are readers engaging with most from you?

  • What topics are prompting the most questions and comments?

  • What topics are receiving the most Likes and Views?

  • What topics do you notice work well, consistently, over and over again?

The answers to the above should give you some pretty good signal as to what sort of digital product would be worth creating.

So, here's an easy 2-step process you can use to spot these opportunities.

Step 1: Examine your analytics in Typeshare.

Open your Analytics dashboard (in Typeshare, or your preferred publishing/analytics platform) and sort by All Time.

Then sort by Replies (comments).

The reason it's good to sort by Replies is because the most valuable digital products answer people's questions. So you want to look for topics that trigger people to ask questions, or at least comment and engage. This is usually an early signal of a topic that's worth exploring more in-depth.

(And if you don't have content attracting many comments yet, then sort by Likes and use that as your next-best metric of interest.)

Step 2: Pull 3 high-performing topics.

As you sort through your analytics, pull out 3 topics you are interested in and would like to write more about—AND the data also says are interesting to readers.

This is key.

It's not very effective for you to just create what you want to create (and ignore the wants & needs of your audience). And similarly, it's also not effective (or fun) to force yourself to create something the data says is working, but you don't really have any interest in creating.

The goal is to find topics that do both: work for readers, and work for you.

So, looking at the above screenshot as an example, all of these topics are technically “proven.”

Which means the “works for readers” part is taken care of. Now, it’s about picking topics YOU are interested in, and would be willing to expand into a digital product (aka: what are you most curious about?).

So, the 3 high-performing topics I might pick would be:

  • “Over the past 10 years, I have read over 500 business books. 99% were 1 idea stretched across 300 pages. They should have been blog posts. Save yourself the time and just read these 10.”

  • “The first-time founder playbook.”

  • “In 2021, I published 4 books. In 2022, I plan on publishing 8. Here's the 5-step framework I use to write 60,000+ words in 30 hours or less (2,000 words per hour).”

Again, these are all proven topics in the sense that they performed well on social platforms.

But why I would choose to double-down on them should have more to do with the fact that I’m INTERESTED and CURIOUS in spending more time writing about these topics.

Because let’s face it: writing, and creating digital products, can be hard work.

Which means the only way you’re going to stay consistent is if you pick things you ENJOY working on.

And in the next module, I’m going to show you how to double-down on the high-performing topics you pick.

Hey there!

And welcome to Module 2 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product.

In this module, I’m going to show you how to further validate your high-performing topics—so you can see (objectively) which one has the highest likelihood of being a revenue-generating digital product.

Let’s dive in!

Lean Writing 101

Now, it's one thing to have a great idea.

But it's entirely another to put that idea to the test out in public.

Before you start creating your first digital product, it's worth testing your 3 high-performing topics on social—and seeing which ones continue to perform well with your readers.

This is what we like to call “Lean Writing.”

Meaning:

Before you take the time to create a digital product, start to finish, it's a good idea to do a temperature check and see if that topic is even something people would be interested in.

Dickie did this with the very first cohort of Ship 30 for 30.

Before taking the time to build out the idea of Ship 30 for 30, Dickie tweeted the idea to get a sense for whether this digital product was "valuable enough" and worth creating.

And sure enough, a handful of people responded.

Which, in hindsight, was a very small signal.

But sometimes all you need is a small signal to know you're working in the right direction.

Action Step: Take your 3 ideas, and write about them MORE online.

Describe your idea for your digital product, what questions you plan on answering, what problems you plan on solving, etc., and ask your audience if that would be helpful to them.

Or, simply say: "I want to create an eBook that explains {X}. What questions should I be sure to answer?"

Or, just write about those topics more… and see what happens.

The point is: you want to find ways to test your 3 ideas out in the open, first.

Then pay close attention to:

  • The questions people ask as a result.

  • The response you get ("I would love this!" or "I don't think this is the right idea.").

  • How many people engage and respond (relative to your audience).

  • And how excited you get about sharing this idea (make sure it's something you want to create, too!).

After testing these 3 ideas out in small ways, 1 of them will most likely emerge as the "winner."

And that's the topic you should expand into your first Digital Product!

Pro Tip: We always like paying attention to comments/questions the most.

To be clear, we’re not necessarily advocating for you to chase views or “attention.”

Sure, views can be a helpful high-level metric.

But remember: the riches are in the niches.

  • The more specific the niche/topic…

  • The more you will be able to help those people…

  • The more you will be able to charge (because you’re being so specific!).

And we’ve always found the best signal, as to which niche topic would be best to monetize, is comments.

Anytime people start asking you QUESTIONS, you know you’ve got a great niche topic on your hands.

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Module 3 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product.

In this module, I’m going to show you how to take a winning niche topic and EXPAND it into a Digital Product Outline.

Let’s dive in!

Digital Products 101

Once you’ve chosen a niche topic (based on data—and what’s resonating most with readers), it’s time to get to work!

Reminder: This might not be "your best idea ever," but that's fine. Your goal here is to create your FIRST digital product—and build the skill that allows you to create an infinite number of digital products, well into the future.

So…

What Is A "Digital Product?"

It’s very simple:

  • It’s a “packaged asset”…

  • That solves a specific problem…

  • For a specific person…

  • In a specific way.

And that “packaged asset” could be an entire text & video course, or it could be something as simple as a 20-page eBook.

Like… my first Digital Product!

Check this out:

These were my first 2 Digital Products: short eBooks (roughly 20 pages) that shared my workout routines and meal plans.

I created these in 2014, 24 years old and just a year out of college. (I was FAR from a “bodybuilding expert.”)

But this is how I made my first $5,000 online.

So, no… your 1st Digital Product does NOT:

  • Need to be high-production

  • Need to be 18 hours long

  • Even need to be a text & video course

It can literally be a 20-page eBook.

As long as it solves 1 specific problem, for 1 specific person, in 1 specific way.

The Big Mistake

Unfortunately, this isn’t what most people do.

Everyone begins their digital product journey thinking they want to create "something for everyone."

As a result, they end up creating something for no one.

(This is why most people's first digital product doesn't sell very well. It's not because the idea or the product itself was bad. The product didn't sell because the customer didn't know it was for them!)

How To Outline Your Digital Product (8 Questions)

When creating a “How To” digital product, you need to take the reader by the hand and guide them FROM where they are TO where you want them to end up.

So, let's create a quick outline you can fill in.

Write your answers to these questions down.

  1. Who is this for, specifically?

  2. What problem of theirs are you solving?

  3. What benefit gets unlocked when this problem gets solved?

  4. How "expensive" is this problem, and how are you providing the solution for a fraction of the normal cost?

  5. What myths keep people from solving this problem in their lives?

  6. What was the moment in your own life when you first experienced/became aware of this problem—and how did you overcome it?

  7. What 3rd-party examples, case studies, or stories can you point to that prove it's possible to overcome this problem (and if they do, what amazing things happen)?

  8. What 3-7 action steps/framework are you going to walk the reader through to help them solve this problem in an actionable, highly effective way?

If you can answer the above 8 questions, you essentially have 80% of the work done.

You know exactly what you are going to create, for who, what problem it solves, and why it matters.

So, go through this exercise… write your answers down somewhere… and then proceed to the next module!

Hey there!

And welcome to Module 4 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product.

In this module, I’m going to show you how to validate (aka: stress-test) the outline of your Digital Product… BEFORE you go through all the effort of expanding & building it.

DON’T SKIP THIS STEP!

(I know, I know… you think, “I’ve got it! I know what I want to build!” But we’ve had to learn this lesson the hard way. Just take our word for it, and do the exercise.)

Let’s dive in!

How To Stress-Test Your Digital Product Outline

Now, before you actually start assembling your Digital Product, it's worth doing one more pass to make sure you are going to create something people actually need.

Which means it's time to do some prospective reader/customer interviews.

Reach Out To Your Target Readers/Customers

If you want to create a Digital Product for digital writers, go DM 5-10 digital writers on X or LinkedIn or Instagram or wherever and ask for their feedback.

If you want to create a Digital Product for fintech entrepreneurs, go try to talk to 5-10 fintech entrepreneurs.

If you want to create a Digital Product for yoga instructors, go find 5-10 yoga instructors and see if you can pick their brain for 20-30 minutes.

The vast majority of creators skip this research step of the process—and as a result, end up creating something people sort-of want, but don't really need. HOWEVER, if you can make the time to go talk to your ideal readers/customers FIRST, they will 100% tell you exactly what problems they need help solving—and give you plenty of ideas for how you can make your Superniche Product insanely valuable to them.

Here’s how…

Step 1: Look for anyone who has commented on any of your content in the past week.

This means they’re probably up to at LEAST respond to your DM.

Send them this message:

Hey! I noticed you commented on my post last week about {topic}. Out of curiosity, what are you working on these days? I’m actually working on a product right now on {topic} specifically to help {specific person} solve {specific problem}. Let me know if you want to take a look! Happy to share what I’ve got so far—and if you have any follow-up questions on {Topic}, just let me know. Happy to help.

Step 2: Look for anyone who is a “peer” and frequently writes/creates about a similar topic.

By “peer” I don’t mean reaching out to someone with a gazillion followers.

I mean people who are roughly at the same level of followers as you are.

Send them this message:

Hey! Just wanted to send you a quick note. I read your content on {Topic} all the time. It’s really great. I’m actually working on a digital product on a similar topic. Any chance you’d be interested in taking a look? I’d really respect getting your quick opinion on it, if you don’t mind.

Go back and forth via DMs/email, or ask to jump on a Zoom call together!

I promise, you’ll learn sooooooo much if you take the time to do this BEFORE building the product.

Also, I’ve found a lot of people feel “weird” about this step—almost like they’re doing something wrong reaching out to people online.

And I hate to break it to you, but that’s 1000% a faulty belief.

People are way more willing to help you out than you realize.

All you have to do is ask!

Creating Your Digital Product 101

The time has come.
