  • You have outlined your Digital Product by answering the 8 key questions.

  • And you have stress-tested your Digital Product by interviewing and talking to 5-10 ideal readers/customers, making sure the information you are providing solves an important problem in their lives.

Now it's time to start assembling your Digital Product!

Note: You can create your eBook in Microsoft Word, Google Docs, Notion, etc.

For the actual creation of your digital product/eBook, use whichever platform is most comfortable for you.

The only thing that matters is being able to export your content as a PDF at the very end.

(This is possible in Microsoft Word, Google Docs, and Notion.)

Naming Your Digital Product (eBook)

To come up with your Main Title & Subtitle, use the 1 + 1 + 1 Product Creation Framework.

  • 1 Product (what’s the topic?)

  • For 1 Audience

  • Solving 1 Problem

For example:

  • [1 Product] The First-Time Founder Playbook

  • [For 1 Audience] The First-Time Founder Playbook For First-Time SaaS Startup Founders

  • [Solving 1 Problem] The First-Time Founder Playbook For First-Time SaaS Startup Founders: 20 Proven Strategies To Turn Your Side-Hustle Into A 7-Figure Software Business

If you’ve done it right, the 1 Product and 1 Audience parts of the framework should be your Main Title, and your 1 Problem should be your subtitle.

Here’s another example just to make sure you’ve got it. Let’s use this Twitter Thread that got a lot of engagement explaining a 5-step framework to write 60,000 words in 30 hours or less.

  • [1 Product] 60,000 Word Book In 30 hours Or Less

  • [For 1 Audience] How First-Time Authors Can Write A 60,000 Word Book In 30 hours Or Less

  • [Solving 1 Problem] How First-Time Authors Can Write A 60,000 Word Book In 30 hours Or Less: 5 Templates To Demolish Writer’s Block And Hit Publish

If you notice, things like frameworks, templates, and step-by-step guides make for the easiest Digital Products to start with.

That’s because customers can very easily rationalize buying something that moves them from “here” to “there,” or something that promises to save them hours (or even years) of frustrating trial-by-fire.

10 Proven Sections Of Any Digital Product

Next, it’s time to “expand” your outline into a Digital Product—aka, in this case, an eBook.

When creating a “How To” digital product, you need to take the reader by the hand and guide them FROM where they are TO where you want them to end up.

Now, your Digital Product can be as long or as short as you'd like, so long as you effectively help the reader/customer solve an important and urgent problem in their life.

But to make this easy for you, here is a template you can use to think about how to assemble the MOST VALUABLE digital product you can. Almost every great “How To” digital product on the Internet uses some variation of this outline, so please feel free to use this as your North Star and color in the lines.

And remember: it’s totally fine to steal someone else’s format, just make sure you plug your own unique content inside!

[Section 1]: Dear WHO

  • You, You, You: List of 5+ “who you might be” profiles

  • Stuck In Struggle City: List of 5+ biggest problems your target audience faces today

  • Blame Game: Give the audience something else to blame (other than themselves)

  • 3 Big Myths: The advice most people give to solve this problem

  • The Unlikely Answer: Your counterintuitive but proven answer

  • Benefits Of The Road Less Traveled: List 5+ rewards they unlock. “Here’s why”

  • Future, Reimagined: What their life looks like “on the other side”

  • Call To Adventure: “Are you ready to transform?”

[Section 2]: I Was Once Where You Are

  • Origin Story: When were you stuck in Struggle City?

  • Bad Advice: What did other “experts” tell you to do?

  • Quicksand: What are 5+ bad outcomes the bad advice led you to?

  • Dark Night Of The Soul: What was the low point? When did you think of giving up?

  • The Moment Of Change: When did you turn the corner? What happened? Who did you meet? What action did you take? What caused the shift?

  • Success Story: What did you do, and what did you achieve? This is what makes you a credible source of information.

  • I Did, You Can Too: Reverse engineer what you overcame & accomplished into a series of steps, templates, frameworks, etc., for the reader—and tease what the rest of the product will teach them.

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Module 6 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product.

In this module, I’m going to show you how to design your digital product and make it look professional.

Specifically:

  • Resources to increase the perceived value of your digital product

  • Different kinds of “proven designs” for digital products

  • And different recommendations depending on your budget

Let’s dive in!

4 Proven Product Design Styles

Design matters—but we want to be clear about something.

Design has to come second to the content itself.

Anyone can get a professional cover designed for their eBook. Anyone can hire a graphic designer to make their stuff "pop."

But what matters is if a customer buys, opens your digital product, and then finds it so valuable they have to tell 5 of their friends about it.

So while we want to emphasize the importance of design, just remember: design comes second to the content.

That said, here are 4 proven digital product design styles to give you a sense of the different execution styles out there.

1. Minimalist

Nobody does minimalist digital product design better than Jack Butcher.

Here is the product design for his courses, Build Once, Sell Twice.

It's a black background with white font & visual.

Doesn't get much easier than that!

Or here is entrepreneur Ryan Breslow's book, Fundraising.

Pretty simple!

So, no need to overthink it.

If you don't have an "eye" for design, or you are on a budget, this is your best bet. Pick 1-2 colors, pick a font, and create it yourself (or ask a cheap graphic designer on Fiverr to help you).

The beauty of minimalist design is it sort of leaves the reader wondering, "Well if the cover is this simple... what's inside?"

2. Operating System

Another design technique is treating your eBook look like a physical product—even though it's not.

People do this all the time for eBooks, courses, even services like consulting.

They create a graphic image that makes it "look" like a software bundle you'd buy at Best Buy, which sends the signal "Woah! There's a lot here!"

Justin Welsh does this masterfully for both his core products, The LinkedIn OS and The Content OS.

(He literally calls them "Operating Systems" so using the Operating System design approach makes sense.)

3. Stock Photo Professional

If you're just starting out and you want the lowest-barrier-to-entry option, your best bet is to use some stock photography.

Michael Mcgilll, who is a Ship 30 for 30 alumni and Captain's Table member, did this beautifully with his IT Leadership Blueprint product.

If you have the skills to do this yourself, go for it.

Otherwise, it's very feasible to find a graphic designer on Fiverr who would be willing to help you.

This option is very cost-effective, however still allows you to launch something that looks professional and ready to be purchased.

4. Original Cover

This is the most expensive option (since it usually requires you to collaborate with a talented designer), however it's also the one that leads to the most creativity.

If you have a very specific idea for a cover, and you want someone to help bring that cover idea to life with you, then you'll need to spend anywhere from $500 to $5,000 hiring a designer. If you have the budget, this can be a terrific way of making yourself "look" like you have a ton of resources behind you—even if it's just you and your laptop!

I did this for his book, The Art & Business of Online Writing.

I wanted the cover to look like a Medium article (since the book was all about how to write online), so I went and hired a designer from Penguin Random House who also freelanced on the side. The cover cost about $2,000, but the book has since sold more than 25,000 copies and generated more than $150,000 in revenue.

One could argue having a unique and differentiated cover played a meaningful role in that outcome!

Start wherever you feel most comfortable!

If you want to invest in hiring a designer to work with you to bring your idea to life, go for it.

Or, if you want to create your first digital product yourself and create the cover inside a program like Keynote, Sketch, or Photoshop, you can do that too.

The important part is: don't let this piece of the puzzle hold you back.

You can always upgrade the cover later if you want. Just focus on creating something that is "good enough" and represents your idea & the content inside that you're giving readers/customers.

Product Design Resources

OK, now that you have some product design directions in mind, here are some resources you can use to bring your idea to life. Here are your options, from free to most expensive.

1. FREE

If you have the talent and skills to create your own cover, go for it.

Chances are, your first Digital Product doesn't need to be all fancy shmancy. You just need to get something out into the world, and see the project through to completion so that you can learn, adjust, and improve for your next Digital Product.

Some great tools you can use here are:

  • Sketch

  • Keynote

  • Canva

2. Low Cost ($20 - $200)

If you want to invest a little bit in your Digital Product design, you have a few options that won't break the bank.

Use a cheap cover design system: This website indigitalcover.com gives you access to a fairly rudimentary editor (for $29) that allows you to work from a template, adjust background colors and font, and export. Doesn't get much easier than this.

Use a cost-efficient freelancer: There are TONS of graphic designers on Fiverr who charge as low as $10 or $20 per hour, and can easily help you create a basic cover and/or social media promo image for your Digital Product.

Here's an outreach template you can use to reach out to dozens of them and find one that's a good fit for your project:

Hey there, I'm looking for someone to design an eBook cover for me. I have a few ideas in mind, and looking for this to be a quick, one-off project. If I gave you a bit of direction, would you be able to create something for me in a few hours of work?

3. High Cost ($500 - $5,000)

There isn't much of a middle ground when it comes to design.

You have programs and freelancers on the low-end of the spectrum and the high-end of the spectrum, and not very much in-between.

Fiverr is a great resource for finding designers, as is asking around the Ship 30 for 30 community.

Here are 2 Shippers we know do terrific work:

  • Laura Evans-Hill

  • Brody Luebkeman

If you want to go outside the Ship 30 for 30 community, you can also look for freelance designers who have experience working at large publishing houses.

I recommend using I Need A Book Cover—which is a very cool “directory” website where you can find professional book cover designers who have worked at publishing houses (or currently work there, but want to freelance on the side). I have used this website for years.

And here's an outreach template you can use:

Hey there, I'm looking for a designer with experience creating unique book covers and digital product promo materials. I have a budget for this project, and found your work online and really loved it. Would you be willing to chat? Would love to learn more about your process, any ideas you might have, and cost for something like this. Thanks!

records.description: Hey there! And welcome to Module 7 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product. In this module, I’m going to show you how to LAUNCH your digital pro
records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Module 7 of 0 to $1: How To Create Your First Digital Product.

In this module, I’m going to show you how to LAUNCH your digital product online—and set yourself up for success.

Specifically:

  • Where & how to “host” your digital product for sale

  • Some best practices for launching your digital product to your audience

  • And some evergreen strategies to keep sales rolling in even after the launch

Let’s dive in!

The Mindset Of Launching Your Digital Product

It's launch time!

If you have stayed consistent writing online, then you're in a terrific position to launch and share your first Digital Product with your audience.

You have been giving people tons of free value, learning about your audience's questions, wants, needs, curiosities, and interests, and now it's time to help them take the next step on their learning journey.

This is the most important thing to understand about creating, launching, and monetizing digital products:

You are in the business of helping other people solve problems in their life.

That's the game.

Objectively speaking, how much money you are able to earn for yourself as a digital writer, creator, educator, and entrepreneur is directly correlated to the difficulty of problem you are able to help someone else solve in their life.

  • If you solve a mediocre, simple, low urgency, low pain point problem, then you will likely earn mediocre income from your efforts.

  • However, if you can solve complex, high-urgency, high pain point problems for people, then you will likely earn high levels of income from your efforts.

This is how the world works—and what makes some exchanges "more valuable" than others.

So, if your first digital product doesn't sell well, or if your audience doesn't seem enthralled with what you've created, don't beat yourself up. Don't stress over it. And don't start convincing yourself, "Nobody likes what I have to say. I'll never make any money from my craft online."

No, it just means you haven't found the real pain point yet!

And the more you get to know your audience, the more time you spend talking to them, listening, learning, and really truly understanding what they're going through and how you can help, the more likely you are to be the one who can provide them with a highly urgent, highly valuable solution.

(Which will pay you dividends in return.)

So, are you ready to put your first Digital Product to the test?

Let's go!

Digital Product Launch Checklist

To get you prepped to launch, here is a quick checklist for you to use to make sure you've checked all your boxes.

  1. Upload your product to Gumroad

  2. [Optional] Upload your product to your personal website

  3. Create & Edit your Gumroad Product Page

  4. Twitter Launch Post

  5. Medium (Keyword) Launch Post

  6. Quora (Question) Launch Post

  7. Website Launch Post

Once you get the first two steps set up, the rest is best practice stuff you should look to incorporate into all your digital product launches.Let's walk through each step so you know exactly how to bring your Superniche Product to market.

Step 1: Upload Your Product To Gumroad

We love Gumroad—because it's one of the easiest creator-friendly platforms to quickly and easily upload digital products and immediately start selling them.

Head over to Gumroad.com and create your account.

Once you've created your account, you'll want to click into Settings and connect your bank account information so that you can receive payments.

  • If you already have a business bank account, you'll enter your LLC and bank account info.

  • If you don't, you can receive payments as an individual and route payments to your primary bank account.

Both work.

You can also connect a PayPal account to receive payments via PayPal as well.

Payments on Gumroad are processed via credit card and then direct deposited into your bank account.

2. (Optional) Upload your product to your own personal website

If you'd like, you can also upload your digital product to your own website.

This is easiest if you are using a site hosted on Squarespace, Wix, or WordPress.

If you already have this set up, you are likely processing payments via Stripe, PayPal, and/or some other credit card processing platform.

If you do not have your own website, don't worry.

Especially for your first digital product, you do not need to have a personal website. There's no real difference in terms of selling digital products and monetizing via Gumroad opposed to your own website. And before you go make the investment of creating your own website, you're better off selling your products on Gumroad while you start building that new stream of revenue.

3. Gumroad Product Page

Once your product is hosted on Gumroad, it will have its own unique landing page (which you can edit, add images to, etc.). Here's what one of my Digital Products looks like: How To Market A Love Story.

The big things you want to make sure you have here are:

Superniche Product Description/Summary.

The first part of your product description should be a "teaser" for what your product is all about. A few good things to include are:

  • What's the industry and why does it matter (any stats you can include here?)

  • What problem are you solving & why is it urgent and important for the reader?

  • What is your 30-second bio, and why are you the right person to be educating on this subject?

"In This eBook, You Will Learn"

The second part of your product description should be 100% about what the reader is going to "get" in exchange for reading.

  • What walkthrough guide(s) are you going to give them?

  • What templates are they going to be able to immediately put into practice?

  • What mental shifts are you going to facilitate for them—and what will those mental shifts lead to (outcomes)?

Price

How much should you charge for your Digital Product?

There is no 1 right answer here. My suggestion is to not sell it for anything less than $7.99.

$8 to $15 is what most people sell short eBooks, ultimate guides, and beginner digital products for.

Depending on the problem you're solving for the reader though, you can also charge $20, or $30, or $50, or even $100 for your digital product. However, if you're going to charge $50 or $100, then the reader is going to need to know how to extract 10x that value from your product.

4. Twitter Launch Post

The next step is to "announce" your digital product to your social audience.

Now, here's the thing: don't put too much weight on the big day of your product launch.

The name of the game here isn't to sell 100 copies of your Digital Product in the first 5 hours. If that happens, great. But the real goal is for you to have a digital product that pays you dividends over the next few years. Selling 1 copy per day, or a few copies per week, every week, for the next 10 years is a much better outcome.

Here's an example of how I launched my Digital Product, How To Market A Love Story, on Twitter/X.

Short and simple.

And here's a template for you to use (you want to link to the product in the second tweet, not the first tweet):

Tweet #1:

It's here! Over the past X months, I've been hard at work creating an [ULTIMATE GUIDE] to X topic. My goal is to help you: • Solve pain point #1 • Solve pain point #2 • Solve pain point #3 Link below!

Tweet #2:

If you grab a copy, I'd love to hear what you think, what questions you have after reading that you'd like me to answer further, etc. DM me directly—would love to hear from you. [Link to Gumroad Product Page]

5. Medium (Keyword) Launch Post

This is a little digital marketing trick I want to share with you.

Medium has terrific SEO as a site—because it's one giant publication with millions of users, tens of thousands of writers, and tens of millions of page views.

To help "own" the keywords associated with your Digital Product, write an article on Medium with the name of your Superniche Product in the title.

The article can be an excerpt from your product, a general summary, a quick list of the most interesting points included, etc. All that matters is that you have a high-quality article on Medium with the same name as your Digital Product (as well as a link inside the article to your Gumroad product page so readers can click over and purchase a copy).

For example, here's a link to my Medium article that has the exact same title as my Digital Product.

6. Quora (Question) Launch Post

Once you've done the above on Medium, you can copy/paste the same content from your Medium article over to Quora.

Quora is another terrific platform (with billions of page views) because every Question on Quora also ranks on Google.

So another little digital marketing trick you can do here is ask a question on Quora (from your own account) that has the same keywords as the name of your Digital Product.

For example, what I did for my Digital Product launch is I asked the question, "How Do You Market A Love Story?" on Quora—and then copy/pasted my Medium article as the Answer to that question. (And yes, you can “ask yourself” questions, and then answer them.)

7. Website Launch Post

Finally, if you have your own website, you can also do the same as the above by creating a blog post on your site with the same name as your Digital Product.

This means you now have multiple assets online all ranking for your name, as well as the name of your Digital Product.

Now, you're probably not going to sell a ton of copies this way (because most people probably aren't going to Google searching for the name of your product), however the reason it's a good best practice is because as your Digital Product picks up traction, it's good to already own any search traffic around those keywords, as well as continuing to own the keyword of your name.

If and when people search your name into Google, you want your social platforms and your Digital Products to come up.

Like Justin Welsh here:

And that's it!

This is everything you need to bring your first digital product to the Internet.

Now, it's time to have a strategy to continue driving attention to your Digital Products as you continue your digital writing journey.

Evergreen Marketing Templates

The best part about building a library of Digital Products (especially for different audiences) is that you can continue to drive traffic to them over and over again.

Ideally, what you want is to have some sort of Superniche Product for each of the different Content Buckets you consistently write about online.

For example:

  • Content Bucket = Digital Writing

  • Superniche Product = A Beginner's Guide To Writing On Twitter

  • Content Bucket = Self-Publishing

  • Superniche Product = How To Self-Publish Your First Book

  • Content Bucket = Solopreneurship

  • Superniche Product = 7 Steps To Make Your First $1 As A Solopreneur

And so on.

This way, every time you write & create content in a given Content Bucket, you can always mention to readers, "Oh, and by the way, I also have this product here for you—if you'd like."

And this is how you continue to collect dividends from your online writing for years into the future.

So, here are a few CTA (Call To Action) templates you can use:

Tweet CTA

At the end of any relevant Twitter Thread or even individual Tweet that's getting traction, you can reply to your post with a final Tweet that drives people to your Superniche Product.

For example:

If you enjoyed this Thread and want to keep going down the rabbit hole on X topic, I encourage you to grab a copy of [NAME OF DIGITAL PRODUCT]. Inside you'll find X frameworks for solving Y. Enjoy!

Organic Atomic Essay CTA

If you are continuing to write Atomic Essays and want to casually mention that you have your own relevant product related to the topic you're writing about, here's an easy way to let readers know.

For example:

I write often about the topic of X. This year, I even put together an [ULTIMATE GUIDE] on the subject where I explain [PROBLEM, SOLUTION, OUTCOME]. (If you want to check it out, you can find the link in my bio.) But what I want to share with you here is...

Medium/Quora CTA

If you are writing articles on Medium or answering Questions on Quora, you should be linking to your Digital Product every chance you can—so long as it's relevant to the thing you're writing about.You can either do this organically inside the article (like the example above), or you can include a CTA at the end.

For example:

Did you enjoy this article? I am passionate about explaining X topic, and have even written an eBook on the subject. Click here to grab your copy of [NAME OF DIGITAL PRODUCT]. And feel free to DM me with any questions you have! I'd love to hear from you.

LinkedIn CTA

LinkedIn is similar to Twitter/X in that you want to link to your Digital Products in the comments/reply to your post—not in the main post itself. So, make a post on LinkedIn aimed at driving attention, and then in the comments direct people to your Digital Product.

For example:

If you want to accelerate your learning on X topic, here's a resource I put together to get you started: [link to Digital Product page]

Ongoing Strategy

Again, the best thing you can do for yourself as a digital writer/creator is build a library of relevant Digital Products you can point to every time you write about your core 3-5 content areas.

The more often you can direct readers to relevant resources, the more likely they are to buy.

Which is how you start monetizing your free content online (by driving readers of your free content to your paid content).

Congrats On Making Your First $1 Online!

If you execute all of these modules in order, you should make your first $1 online!

This is everything you need to get started.

Which means all that’s left is “execution risk.”

Meaning, your biggest bottleneck is no longer “information.” It’s literally just getting yourself to do it.

But trust the process!

Because who knows… if you stick with it, you might just go on the same journey we’ve gone on building digital products ourselves:

We started at $0, just like everyone else.

And about 4 years later, we’ve since generated over $10,000,000 in digital product sales.

But it all started with a simple eBook.

So, what are you waiting for?!

GO HIT PUBLISH & MAKE THAT FIRST $1!

records.description: Hey there! Welcome to Module 1 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as bo
records.content:
Hey there!

Welcome to Module 1 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as books, ebooks, and even audiobooks on Amazon (as well as other book publishing platforms).

And in this module, I’m going to give you a crash course on how this model works.

Specifically:

  • How to think of your newsletter as the V1 of all future book projects.

  • How to write and “group” newsletters together by topic to create multiple book projects.

  • And the nuances of this model so you can squeeze as much juice out of your content as possible.

My goal here is to get you started on the right foot.

Let’s dive in!

Category Pirates Case Study

This is a publishing (or should I say “republishing”) model I created when I started building Category Pirates in 2021.

And it’s a model I continue to be excited about, and use with my own projects as well.

High-level, the model goes like this:

  • Write newsletters (free or paid)

  • Group “similar” content together (into different piles)

  • Once a pile gets big enough, clean it up & republish as a book on Amazon (eBook, print, and/or audiobook)

  • Repeat forever

This model is how we double, triple, and quadruple monetized the Category Pirates newsletter—and added another $150,000+ per year in revenue, just from Amazon book sales.

It was incredibly effective.

So, let me walk you through how we did this step-by-step, and then I’ll address some of the big questions/objections I hear from people—before diving into “How To” do this yourself!

Category Pirates: 1 long-form newsletter per week

I wrote the Category Pirates weekly newsletter from 2021-2023, until I eventually exited the business.

(The other 2 partners bought me out, so I could focus exclusively on building Ship 30 for 30 and Premium Ghostwriting Academy.)

And in the beginning, our goal was for each newsletter to be around 800-1200 words.

But as time went on, and as we gathered more feedback from our readers, we learned that they actually wanted more. Despite conventional wisdom saying “nobody reads anymore” and “people prefer shorter newsletters,” that turned out to be wrong—at least, for us. So we started writing 2,000 word newsletters. Then 3,000 words. Then 5,000 words. Eventually, some of our newsletters ended up being upwards of 10,000 words.

They were getting so long, and so in-depth, that the term “newsletter” was no longer fitting.

So, we started calling them “mini-books.”

Mini-Book Republishing Model

But as time went on, we started to realize we were creating SO much content, and such GREAT content, that it was a shame readers only saw it in their inbox once and then never saw it again.

(Sure, they could dig through the archives, but you know what I mean.)

So, I came up with an idea:

What if, instead of “just” publishing this content as a weekly newsletter… we republished that same content as a mini-book on Amazon?

All we had to do was:

  • Choose a “repeatable” cover design

  • And create a process for formatting & uploading the content

Not very hard! (As I’m going to show you here shortly.)

So, that’s what we did…

Each “newsletter” that was longer than 5,000 words, we would republish as a “mini-book” on Amazon.

  • Sometimes, a single newsletter would be ~7,000 words and not need any more content, and we would just copy/paste on Amazon.

  • Other times, we’d write multiple shorter newsletters on a related topic—and then group them together (so they would amount to 5,000-10,000 words total) and then republish it on Amazon.

And this opened up a second revenue stream for us.

Now, did these mini-books sell like crazy on Amazon?

Not really.

Most of them only sold 1-3 copies per month, each.

But every once in a while, a mini-book would find a whole new audience—like Become Known For A Niche You Own—and end up selling a ton of copies.

That 1 mini-book ended up adding another $25,000+ in revenue to the business.

Big-Book Republishing Model

The mini-book republishing model was the gateway.

Once we realized we could double-monetize the content through mini-books on Amazon, we also realized we could take it a step further:

  • We could group similar mini-books together

  • And then republish the content again as a Big Book (print, eBook, and audiobook)

For example:

Most people don’t know (or don’t realize) that these 3 “Big Books” we published are actually just compilations of “Mini-Books” grouped by topic—which are just long-form newsletters (or multiple newsletters) stitched together.

It’s the same content.

And yet, republishing this newsletter/mini-book content allowed us to monetize a THIRD way—and added another $100,000+ in revenue to the business.

Questions/Objections

Now, whenever I walk people through this republishing model, I always get a handful of questions.

Which are really more like objections as to why “this doesn’t work” or “there’s no way this is true.”

Well, buckle up… because it does work, and everything I’m telling you is true.

“But Cole?! If I republish the same content on Amazon, won’t my readers get mad?”

No.

We originally thought this too, and the exact opposite happened.

Readers LOVED being able to have a print copy on their desk. And they LOVED being able to have newsletters grouped by topic in an eBook they could read on their Kindle/phone/iPad.

So much so, that they didn’t mind paying for the Category Pirates paid newsletter… and then paying AGAIN to buy the same content in a different medium (print/eBook/audiobook).

This is 100% a faulty belief.

(And if you still don’t believe me, just observe your own buying behavior. For example: if you love Star Wars, you had no problem buying the movie on VHS, then again on DVD, then again on Amazon Prime, etc.)

“But Cole?! Isn’t this against the rules? I thought republishing content was illegal?????”

No.

It’s YOUR content. You can do whatever you want with it. (This is the big benefit of not trying to get a book deal and signing away all the rights to a traditional publisher, by the way!)

The nuance here has to do with Amazon.

On Amazon there are 2 different ways you can publish a book:

  • “Broad” = Not exclusive to Amazon

  • KDP Exclusive = Free to read for any of Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP)’s subscribers, but the content can’t exist anywhere else on the Internet

The only rule here is you can’t execute this model AND be exclusive with KDP.

Which is fine.

You just don’t “check that box” when you upload your book, and you’re good.

“But Cole?! Don’t I need to know what sort of book I want to publish before I start writing my newsletter?”

No.

This is the part everyone misunderstands.

There is TREMENDOUS benefit in using your newsletter to write, explore, and test ideas…. FIRST.

Then, as time goes on, and as you notice which topics are resonating most with your target readers—which ones get the most engagement, attract the most comments or questions, etc.—that will give you signal as to which “book” you should strive to create.

When you see topics performing well, you should write about them more.

And as you write about a certain topic more, you will inherently end up “writing a book.”

It’s that easy.

“But Cole?! If I’m going to write a book, I would want it to be my masterpiece! This just seems like a shortcut to putting out a cheap product.”

If I hadn’t told you this is what we did, you wouldn’t have known.

And that’s the point.

Everybody who says, “I want my book to be my masterpiece” is really just being clever about how they procrastinate.

The truth is, using this model actually makes the writing process 100x easier.

Because:

  • You’re removing the pressure of “writing a masterpiece.”

  • You’re taking a more iterative approach by writing newsletter-first.

  • And your book is really just a compilation of content your readers already love—increasing the likelihood of its success.

As a recovering perfectionist myself, this model has helped me TREMENDOUSLY.

“But Cole?! What if I have a Paid Newsletter? Can I still use this model?”

Yes. Category Pirates is a paid newsletter.

And yes, even if your newsletter is FREE you can also still execute this model.

Repurposing Newsletters Into Book Chapters

There are 2 different ways you can leverage this publishing model:

  • First, you can think of any individual long-form newsletter as a “mini-book” in and of itself—which you can publish as a stand-alone “mini-book” on Amazon.

  • Second, you can think of each individual newsletter or “mini-book” as a chapter in a longer book—and all you have to do is string them together.

After publishing 50+ mini-books to Amazon, as well as 4 Big Books (each a compilation of newsletters/mini-books), I can tell you that the second option is better.

We had a couple mini-books perform well as standalones on Amazon, but 98% of the profit we generated came from our Big Books.

So, if I were you, I would think of newsletters as “book chapters” or “pieces of a book chapter,” and then group similar ideas together to create a Big Book instead.

It’s more work, but a bigger payoff.

It’s easier for me to explain how to do this live than in screenshots, so please watch the following Loom walkthrough above.

records.title: Module 2: Creating Your Book ISBN With Bowker

records.description: Hey there! Welcome to Module 2 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as books
records.content:
Hey there!

Welcome to Module 2 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as books, ebooks, and even audiobooks on Amazon (as well as other book publishing platforms).

And in this module, I’m going to show you how to begin the republishing process by first buying an ISBN for your book.

Let’s dive right in!

How ISBNs Work 101

An ISBN is that long number you see on the barcode of a book.

The formal definition is:

“An ISBN, or International Standard Book Number, is a 13-digit number that uniquely identifies a book or book-like product. ISBNs are used to identify a book's edition, publisher, language, and other information. They are also used by retailers, libraries, and distributors to search for books.” — Source

You need an ISBN for each book, and each different version of that book.

  • A unique ISBN for the print version

  • A unique ISBN for the eBook version

  • A unique ISBN for the audiobook version

  • A unique ISBN for an “updated” version you publish (in the future)

  • Etc.

The reason is because this is how publishers, booksellers, libraries, internet retailers, and other supply chain participants track orders, listings, and sales.

And if you are at all interested in building your own 1-Person Publishing Empire, you want to OWN your ISBNs.

Amazon’s Alternative

Now, if you don’t want to buy an ISBN for your own book (I don’t know why you wouldn’t just take 5 minutes and do this), Amazon also offers to issue you an ISBN for whatever book(s) you upload to their platform.

I WOULD NOT DO THIS.

If you take Amazon’s free ISBN, that ISBN can only be used on Amazon and cannot be re-used across other platforms—which means you can’t also publish your books on Apple Books, Kobo, Google Books, etc.

Not a huge deal since Amazon is the biggest platform out there, but it does limit your freedom and flexibility.

So I would encourage you to just learn how this works and buy all ISBNs yourself.

(This also makes your 1-Person Publishing Empire… more valuable!)

How To Buy ISBNs On Bowker

If you live in the United States, the only way to buy an ISBN is through a company called Bowker.

(Talk about a monopoly.)

If you live outside of the United States, each country has its own ISBN issuer/company. Just Google where you live and “how to buy an ISBN for my book” and you’ll find the right provider.

But for the sake of the walkthrough, I’m going to use Bowker as the example.

Step 1: Create An Account

You can do this here: https://www.myidentifiers.com

Then, once you’re logged in…

Step 2: Click “Buy ISBNs”

If you plan on using this model and repeating this process more than once, I’d recommend buying 10 ISBNs at once.

You get a meaningful price discount when you buy 10 at a time—opposed to 1.

*NOTE: Bowker’s website is incredibly outdated, and the checkout process can be a little janky.

After you click “Add To Cart,” you’ll be presented with this screen.

I would recommend adding EAN Barcodes to your cart as well—because you’re going to need to buy them later, so you might as well just do it now.

Proceed to Checkout and complete your purchase:

Step 3: My Account → My Identifiers

Next, if you go into your Account and click “My Identifiers,” you will see all of the ISBNs you just bought.

(It may take a few minutes to load if you just completed the purchase.)

As you can see above, these are all my different book titles—each one, and each format, assigned a different ISBN.

So, when you’re ready to add an ISBN to your book, select “Assign Title.”

Let Me Show You!

I’m going to show you how to do this while I execute this strategy in front of you.

I recently wrote a long-form newsletter called The Perfect Book Title:

It’s long, definitely as long as a book chapter.

Why not republish it on Amazon as a mini-book?

So…. that’s what I’m going to do! And I’m going to walk through all the steps with you here, so you can see exactly how this model works:

Step 4: Assign Title

Select an available ISBN from your list and begin filling in the information:

First section:

  • Book Title = Main Title

  • Subtitle = The Book’s Subtitle

  • “Describe Your Book” = optional, can add this later once you’ve written the book’s description.

  • Medium = eBook (or print, or audio, depending on which format you’re choosing for this ISBN)

  • Format = Digital Online (if eBook)

  • eBook File Type = EPUB (this is the ideal format, and also the format I’m going to show you how to export)

  • First Genre = Pick something relevant

  • Second Genre = Pick something relevant

Second section:

  • Individual = Your First & Last Name (or pen name)

  • Biography = You can add later, or copy/paste in a short bio

  • Function = Author

Third section:

  • Publisher = Your Name *(NOTE: If you go so far as to create an LLC for your 1-Person Publishing Empire (not required, but you can), you’ll end up creating a “Publisher” name inside Bowker. No need to worry about this yet though.)

  • Publication Date = The day you plan on the book going live on Amazon

  • Title Status = Active Record

  • Target Audience = Almost always Adult Education, but pick whatever is most relevant for your book

  • Set Dollar Amount = Choose the price of your book

*NOTE: The price is actually the most important part, because the price you select here needs to match up to the price you set on Amazon. So make sure these are the same.

Then hit Submit!

Now You’re Ready!!!

See? That wasn’t so hard.

Your book (and that individual format) has now been assigned an ISBN, which you can use to list your book for sale on Amazon.

Which means, it’s time to move on to the next step… formatting your book using Reedsy.

(Bonus!) Pricing Your Book/eBook/Audiobook

We could talk about pricing for 5 straight hours.

But I’m going to spare you that lecture—and just give you the need-to-know information.

Audiobook Pricing

The first thing you should know is that, on Amazon, you don’t really set the price of your audiobook.

Amazon forces you to price within a “range.”

And the price is entirely based on the length of the audiobook:

  • Under 1 hour: Under $7

  • 1–3 hours: $7–$10

  • 3–5 hours: $10–$20

  • 5–10 hours: $15–$25

  • 10–20 hours: $20–$30

  • Over 20 hours: $25–$35

So longer audiobooks = cost more = drive more revenue.

If you want more info, here’s a great article on audiobook pricing.

eBook Pricing

Now there are some nuances when it comes to pricing your eBook.

On Amazon, you have 2 pricing choices here:

  • If your eBook is priced between $2.99 and $9.99, you receive 70% of each product sold.

  • However, if you want to “undercut” the market and price your eBook below $2.99, OR you want to charge a “premium” above the market and price your eBook above $9.99, then you receive 35% of each product sold.

Here’s why:

Basically, Amazon knows that a lot of writers price their eBooks cheap ($2.99 or less) to try to incentivize impulse purchases, take advantage of giveaways and promotions, etc. And because they know so many writers do this, they say, “That’s fine—but then we take 65% of each sale.” So even if you “sell more copies” by pricing your eBook lower, net-net you end up making less money.

Which is why I would encourage you to price your eBook somewhere between $7 and $9.99.

This is the sweet spot.

Self-Publishing company, Scribe, has an amazing walkthrough guide on this topic here.

And they break the decision down like this:

  • Maximize copies: $0.99 – $3.99

  • Middle ground: $4.99 – $6.99

  • Maximize perceived value: $7.99 – $9.99

In addition, they also share this interesting data point: “There is no difference in sales between $7.99 and $9.99. And perhaps most shocking, books at $0.99 sell less than books priced at $3.99.”

I have spent a LOT of time reading, researching, and experimenting with pricing, and my default eBook price is always in the $6.99 - $9.99 range.

So I’d recommend just going with that.

(And if your follow-up question is: “But Cole?! Does page/word count matter when it comes to eBook pricing?!” Not really. Become Known For A Niche You Own, our most successful Category Pirates mini-book on Amazon, is 60 pages. And it’s priced at $7.99.)

Print Book Pricing

The easiest way to think about Print Books is just 2x-3x whatever the price of your eBook.

The truth is, eBooks are a better “product” than Print Books is pretty much every way imaginable:

  • Delivered Instantly: You can start reading 5 seconds after you buy it.

  • No Marginal Cost: Amazon has no printing cost, which means higher royalties for you.

  • Weighs 0 lbs: Unlike print books, you can carry 1,000+ eBooks in your pocket at all times.

  • Lasts Forever: eBooks can’t get lost, get worn out, or burn in a fire like Print Books can.

  • Etc.

Which means the people who buy a Print version of your book were going to buy no matter what.

Your Print Book is almost more like a “collectors edition,” because they want it for more than utility:

  • They want it in their hands.

  • They want it on their desk.

  • They want to annotate and mark it up.

  • They want to show it off on their coffee table.

So, what’s the takeaway?

Your eBook is for the person who just “wants to buy the information.”

Whereas your Print Book is for the person who wants to “hold, collect, and cherish the information.”

Translation: It should be 2-3x more expensive.

A lot of times, authors think that by making their Print Book “less expensive,” more people will buy and thus, they’ll make more money. But that’s not what happens. Instead, they sell the same number of copies but make 1/3rd the amount of money—because the people who were going to buy the Print version were ALWAYS going to buy the Print version. You just gave it to them for 1/3rd the price.

Big pricing mistake.

My recommendation to you would be to always price your Print copy at $19.99 or above.

In fact, I see even more benefit in pushing the pricing tier even higher—$24.99 all the way up to $29.99.

The further the gap between the price of your eBook and the price of the Print book, the better.

  • Higher-quality perception

  • More margin

  • More revenue per customer

Which is why, every time I self-publish a book on Amazon, I just default to:

  • Mini-Book = $7.99

  • eBook = $9.99

  • Print = $19.99

records.content:
Hey there!

Welcome to Module 3 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as books, ebooks, and even audiobooks on Amazon (as well as other book publishing platforms).

And in this module, I’m going to show you how to format your collection of newsletters into a ready-to-publish book on Amazon.

Let’s dive in!

Using Reedsy’s Formatting Tool

I think Reedsy is one of the best-kept secrets in the world of self-publishing.

This site is a lot of things.

It’s primarily a marketplace for writers to find editors, designers, and marketers for their book.

But honestly, you don’t need any of that.

It’s greatest tool is its book formatting tool—log in & click on “Books.”

Then select “Create Book” and add your mini-book or book’s title:

The title will then appear in your bookshelf—and you can begin by clicking “Write.”


Reedsy Formatting Walkthrough

This will be easier to show you live opposed to through screenshots, so watch the Loom here for a full walkthrough of how to use Reedy’s formatting tool.


Final Design Recommendations

Now, I want to be transparent:

I am giving you the “lowest-cost, highest-upside” path here for republishing your newsletter content as books on Amazon.

But the truth is, you can invest a lot more money into the quality of your books & book files.

IF YOU WANT.

Actually, making your books look “really professional” isn’t crazy expensive… IF…

  • You have a traffic engine & growing digital audience

  • You have a newsletter & growing (relevant) list of readers

  • You understand this is a lottery model and the more you publish & republish, the more you win (you can’t just “write/publish 1 thing” and expect to make millions of dollars).

For example, I did this for my book The Art & Business of Online Writing because I had achieved the above 3 criteria, and I was game to make a bigger investment (”bet”) into the project for potentially higher upside.

I invested ~$5,000 into the creation of this book:

  • ~$2,500 for the cover design

  • ~$2,500 for a designer to format the interior (so instead of using Reedsy’s free tool, the designer did everything custom in InDesign)

For some people, that’s a big cost (it certainly was for me when I did this back in 2020).

But this book has since made me over $170,000 on Amazon alone—and almost double that including sales directly from my website.

This is the power of this model.

The more you publish, the more “chances” you have to win—and potentially win big.

And the more you win, the more money you have to reinvest into future books.

Why buy real estate when you can build a 1-Person Publishing Empire?

So, if you want to invest more into your books, I’d recommend hiring designs from this really cool website called: I Need A Book Cover.

  • These are all vetted designers who specialize in book design & interior formatting

  • Most of these designers also work (or worked) at one of the Big 5 Traditional Publishers

  • And most of these designers are very affordable—anywhere from $1,000 to $5,000 to bring a really professional book to life

This is now what I do for all of my books.

But in the beginning, I encourage you to keep costs low and start small.

records.content:
Here are the different pieces of information you want to have ready to go before you start uploading to KDP.

Step 1: Price

Just to stay organized, wherever you are compiling all this information, be sure to remember the exact price you set inside Bowker when you created the ISBN for your book.

Price needs to be consistent between Bowker & Amazon.

Step 2: Description Keywords

I would research these first.

KDP allows you to upload 7 (50 character) keywords—so use Publisher Rocket to find the best/most relevant ones to your book & topic.

The reason I would do this FIRST is because you can then weave these keywords into your book’s long-form description.

Step 3: Book Description

Next, write your book’s description and try to organically get as many of those keywords/keyphrases in the description as possible.

If you want to take things to the next level, you can also extend Step 1 and make a list of 10+ keywords/keyphrases, and weave the extras into your book’s description too.

Just more ways for the algorithm to pick up & recommend your book to the right people.

Step 4: Format Your Book Description

Once you’ve written your book’s description, copy/paste it into this tool:

Kindlepreneur Book Description Generator

Then play with the formatting until you like the end result, and copy/paste the code somewhere.

This is what you’ll be uploading to KDP later.

Step 5: Choose 3 Categories (For EACH Format)

Lastly, you’ll want to use Publisher Rocket to find the best categories for your book/eBook/audiobook.

What you’re looking for here is:

  • Most relevant

  • Lowest competition

It doesn’t do you any good to choose low-competition but completely irrelevant categories for your book (Amazon will also ban you for this).

But you also don’t want to pick the most-relevant, highest competition categories either—because then no one will discover your book (and you’ll never become a #1 best-seller!).

*NOTE: Each format you upload to amazon (print, eBook, audiobook) allows you to choose ANOTHER 3 CATEGORIES. And each format actually has different categories & subcategories to choose from, so you want to repeat this step for each format.

Time to publish!

Once you have all the above (I like organizing all of this in a Word Doc beforehand), it’s time to hit publish!

records.content:
Hey there!

Welcome to Module 5 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as books, ebooks, and even audiobooks on Amazon (as well as other book publishing platforms).

And in this module, I’m going to show you how to write a really great description for your book so it sells well on Amazon—and how to subtly incorporate keywords and keyphrases organically into the description to improve its rankings.

Let’s dive in!

Researching Keywords For Your Book

Quick crash course on how “search” works:

  • The more relevant keywords & key phrases you include in your book’s description…

  • The more likely it is to appear in search results…

  • The more likely readers are to discover your book…

  • The more likely you are to sell copies!

Pretty simple, right?

Now, just because you add a few relevant keywords to your book’s description doesn’t magically guarantee you’re going to sell millions of copies.

But it helps more than it hurts so… why not?

(Easy) Finding Relevant Keywords Using Amazon

Here’s an easy way to find relevant keywords and search terms that other people might already be using, that you can easily add to your book’s description:

  • Open an Incognito browser

  • Start typing in a related key phrase to the topic of your book

  • Look at the “related searches” that appear in the drop-down menu

This is an easy way to see what other keywords/keyphrases people are searching for that might be relevant to the topic of your book.

Do this a few times, searching different relevant key phrases, and make a list of the related searches that match your book’s topic.

You’ll be using this list later when you write your book’s description!

(Advanced) Finding Relevant Keywords Using Publisher Rocket

If all this new information is making you really excited about publishing or republishing books on Amazon, and building your 1-Person Publishing Empire, then I’d strongly encourage you to explore this website: https://kindlepreneur.com

Kindlepreneur is the best resource I’ve found specifically for publishing on Amazon’s platform.

Tons here to dig into.

But my favorite tool of theirs is a SaaS tool called Publisher Rocket.

(No affiliate code, I’m just obsessed with this platform.)

This is one of the most fun tools I’ve come across in the self-publishing world, and can give you a tremendous amount of data to make decisions with.

But here, I’m going to walk you through how to use this tool specifically to find relevant keywords & keyphrases for your Amazon book description.


Writing Your Book Description

There’s no “1 right way” to write a book description.

However, there are some pieces you want to make sure you fit in there:

  • What It’s About: State the purpose of your book as CLEARLY, OBJECTIVELY, and TANGIBLY as possible.

  • Who It’s For: List out a couple potential audience archetypes of people who would get the most value out of your book.

  • “Related But Different” Books: An easy ranking trick is to incorporate 2-3 titles of other relevant books in your description, explaining your book is “similar but different.” Getting those titles in your book description will help it rank for similar searches on Amazon.

  • What’s Inside: Some sort of bulleted list “selling” readers on what you explain in the book, what problem(s) you help the target reader solve, and what outcome(s) you help the target reader unlock.

  • Credibility: Any relevant accomplishments or metrics that give readers confidence you are someone they can trust on this topic.

Again, no “1 right way” to write a book description.

Just make sure you get some blend of the above variables in there, and aim for ~300-500 words.

For example, here’s what I wrote for my mini-book, The Perfect Book Title.

The Perfect Book Title 7+ Keyphrases

First, here’s the list of keyphrases I found (using Publisher Rocket) that I plan on attaching to my book in KDP’s backend (and can also weave into the book’s description):

  1. How to write a book title

  2. How to write a book

  3. How to write a book guide

  4. How to write a book beginners

  5. Books about writing well

  6. Writing a book

  7. Books about writing

But here are some other keyphrases & relevant book titles I can ALSO look to incorporate into my book’s description (for extra ranking juice):

  • Writing a book outline

  • Books about writing books

  • Book writing help

  • The Art & Business of Online Writing by Nicolas Cole

  • Bird by Bird by Anne Lamott

  • On Writing by Stephen King

  • On Writing Well by William Zinsser

The Perfect Book Title Description

Now, let’s put this all together—the key pieces of a great book description + as many relevant keyphrases as possible (as long as it sounds organic and not like “keyword-stuffing”).

~

From the best-selling author of The Art & Business of Online Writing.

How do you write a book title?

More specifically: how do you write a book title that makes readers stop, give you their full attention, decide it’s for them, and buy it?

There are thousands of books on how to write, how to write well, and even how to write books for beginners—like Bird by Bird by Anne Lamott, or On Writing Well by William Zinsser. But there are 0 books on the art & science of creating a compelling, memorable, differentiated book title.

Until now!

Nicolas Cole, one of the most-read writers on the Internet with over a billion views on his writing, 10 published books in his library, and millions of dollars generated from his writing programs, is finally revealing his Perfect Book Title Framework.

“Everyone gets this wrong. You don’t write your book and THEN come up with the title. You come up with the title, first… and then you deliver on that promise in the writing,” says Cole.

In this quick read, you will learn:

  • The Perfect Book Title Framework: The fundamental pieces you need in your book’s title, otherwise readers won’t understand what makes it “different” (or why they should read/buy it).

  • The 7 Categories Of Non-Fiction Best-Selling Books: Which types of books typically sell the most copies, what they promise, and why it works.

  • Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility: How to present the right title depending on your level of credibility as an author.

  • Direct vs Indirect Audiences: When to call your target audience out directly, and when to leave the audience more broad to reach a wider number of readers.

  • Timely vs Timeless: How your book title determines the shelf-life and long-term relevance of your book (and whether it will sell for 1 year, or 100 years).

  • The Obvious & Non-Obvious Title Pairing: A little-known secret when it comes to book titles, and how to make sure you are being CLEAR but also intriguing at the same time.

  • Tangible vs Intangible Language: The most underrated copywriting technique out there, and how to immediately make your title more compelling, visceral, and valuable to readers.

This is more than just a book.

This is an Ultimate Guide you should refer back to every time you sit down to write a book.

Publisher Rocket Description Code Tool

Now, one of Amazon’s janky features is that in order for your description to be formatted correctly on your book’s page, you have to add it as “code” and not just plain text.

Luckily, Kindlepreneur also has this great tool for this too!

It has a Book Description Generator that I’ve used dozens of times.

(I sound like an ad but… I’m not! Just giving you the secrets.)


Generate Book Description Code

Copy/Paste the description you wrote for your book into the Description Generator Tool.

Then, start playing with the formatting:

  • Bold

  • Italics

  • Underline

  • Symbols

  • Paragraphs

  • Etc.

Make sure your description is “visually” correct.

Like the video above.

Then click Generate My Code!

The end result should look like this:

Hey there!

Welcome to Module 6 of 1-Person Publishing Empire—a step-by-step walkthrough on how to double and triple monetize your newsletter content as books, ebooks, and even audiobooks on Amazon (as well as other book publishing platforms).

And in this module, I’m going to show you how to use Publisher Rocket to optimize your book, ranking, and searchability on Amazon.

Let’s dive in!

How Categories Work On Amazon

First, let me start with a quick crash course on how Amazon categories work…

Here’s a link again to the tool: Publisher Rocket.

Amazon Category Rankings

Have you ever wondered how some books on Amazon get that little orange “#1 Best Seller” badge?

Well, I hate to be the bearer of bad news… but this is very easy to get.

If you know how to game the system.

So, let me walk you through how this works, so you can “beat the game.”

If you scroll down on any book on Amazon, you can see the Product Details:

Here you can see my book The Art & Business of Online Writing, is currently ranked:

  • #1 in Blogging

  • #1 in Writing Skills in Advertising

  • #3 in Business Writing Skills

Pretty good!

And while I’m my own biggest fan, and think I wrote a pretty great book, the truth is that these “rankings” have very little to do with my quality of writing.

And they have much more to do with how my book is performing (aka: selling) RELATIVE to the competition of these categories.

If I had chosen more competitive categories for my book, my book would have ranked less—and it would have been significantly harder for me to get that “#1 Best Seller” badge.

Which is why, before you hit publish, I’d strongly recommend doing some research:

  • Find relevant categories for your book

  • Then figure out which of the most-relevant categories are the least competitive

How?

By using Publisher Rocket.

Let me show you how this works:

Publisher Rocket Categories Walkthrough

records.content:
Build your design system

🧠 The Mega Prompt

Fill-in-the-blank. The prompt I run on every new brand. Drop it into Claude Design's notes field, attach 3 reference screenshots, and let it bootstrap.

<aside>
⚠️

Claude Design is VERY good at using reference images, so put just as much thought into the pictures you attach as you do the prompt config

</aside>

Start here. A pre-baked design system makes all future

Ship from your design system

🖼️ 10 Asset Prompts for Writers

Once your system exists, prompt for any of 10 surfaces: newsletter header, landing page hero, book cover, LinkedIn carousel, lead magnet cover, podcast art, Mermaid diagram, Remotion animation, HTML email, web component.

Six are visual outputs (run in Claude Design). Four are code- or motion-powered outputs (run in Claude Code with the design system exported).

Includes the Remotion Prompt Builder — a meta-prompt that turns vague animation briefs (“30-second book trailer”) into render-ready prompts with explicit physics, frame ranges, and easing curves. Use it when raw Remotion prompts feel flat.

Reference docs (for max efficiency)

Use these the first time you hit a friction point.

💰 Token Budget Worksheet

How to pace your weekly allowance like ad spend. Tier-sizing decision tree (Pro / Max 5× / Max 20×). Self-tracking template you can fork. The Claude Code bypass when weekly limits become the bottleneck.

🧭 Tool Decision Matrix

When Claude Design wins. When Canva, Figma, Gamma, Claude Code, or Photoshop still win. A 30-second decision tree, the full grid, and 10 memorize-this rules.

“Pitch Anything” Deck Prompt

THE 20-MINUTE PITCH DECK ARCHITECT
A NITAR-structured megaprompt that turns a business idea into a Klaff-style pitch deck brief, ready to paste into Claude Design's Slide Deck mode.

How this is meant to be used:
Run this prompt in regular Claude (or Claude Cowork) to generate a fully-structured slide-by-slide content brief. Then open claude.ai/design, create a new project, select Slide Deck, toggle "Use speaker notes" ON, and paste the generated brief as your first prompt. Your organization's design system is auto-applied. Iterate with inline comments. Export as PDF, PPTX, or Send to Canva.

NAME & IDENTITY
You are the Pitch Deck Architect — a specialized system trained on Oren Klaff's Pitch Anything methodology and on the prompt structure Claude Design responds to best (goal, layout, content, audience).
Your job is not to produce a finished deck. Your job is to produce a paste-ready content brief that Claude Design will use to generate a polished, on-brand deck inside its Slide Deck workspace. You write for two readers at once: a Claude Design instance that needs structured slide content with explicit layout intent, and a human presenter who needs speaker notes that survive the live pitch.
You think like a venture capitalist who has sat through 10,000 bad pitches and exactly 12 great ones. You know the croc brain ignores the boring, fears the complicated, and only pays attention to what's novel and high-stakes. Every slide you brief earns its place by either stimulating the croc brain or satisfying the neocortex — never both, never neither.
You do not write fluff. You do not pad word counts. You hit the time budgets Klaff prescribes because the discipline of the constraint is what makes the pitch land.

INSTRUCTIONS & INTENT
I will give you:

The business/idea I want to pitch: [BUSINESS_OR_IDEA]
Who the pitch is for (audience/investor type): [TARGET_AUDIENCE]
My credibility positioning (top 1-2 wins, not full bio): [MY_RELEVANT_WINS]
What's changed in the world that makes NOW the time: [WHY_NOW_CONTEXT]
The specific ask (deal terms, dollar amount, partnership structure): [THE_ASK]
Anything else relevant — proof, traction, secret sauce: [ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT]

You will give me:
A single, paste-ready content brief formatted for Claude Design's Slide Deck mode. The brief must follow Claude Design's preferred prompt structure (goal, layout, content, audience), be organized slide-by-slide, and include speaker notes blocks for each slide so I can toggle "Use speaker notes" ON in Claude Design and have the detail land in notes instead of cluttering the slide face.
If any of my inputs are weak, vague, or missing — push back before writing. Do not generate a brief on top of weak inputs. A bad pitch wastes the room.

TRAINING COMPONENTS
The brief is organized around Klaff's four phases. Each phase has a strict word budget that translates to slide density. Stay inside the budget.
COMPONENT 1: INTRODUCE YOURSELF AND THE BIG IDEA (5 minutes / ~900 words / 3-4 slides)
Slides to brief:

Cover — Big idea headline, presenter name, one-line positioning.
Why now — Three forces converging: economy, society, technology. One line each. The window must feel open right now and closing.
Who I am — One or two biggest relevant wins. Not a resume. The croc brain averages biographical info; list everything you've done and you become average.
The big idea — Use Geoff Moore's pattern, flipped to lead with the customer:
"For [target customers] who are dissatisfied with [current market]. My [product/category] is a [new category] that provides [key features]. Unlike [competitors], my [product] is [differentiators]."

COMPONENT 2: BUDGET AND SECRET SAUCE (10 minutes / ~1,800 words / 5-6 slides)
Convert croc-brain interest into neocortex belief. Prove it.
Slides to brief:

Market opportunity — Size, shape, growth. Numbers, not adjectives.
Secret sauce — What you have that no one else has. Tech, unfair advantage, IP, distribution, founder-market fit.
Proof — Traction, revenue, signed LOIs, pilot results, user data. If proof is thin, say so and use the strongest analogous proof available.
Competitive landscape — Honest map of who else is in the room and why you win.
Budget / unit economics — Where the money goes and what it produces. CAC, LTV, margins, runway, or non-software equivalents.
Risk and answer — The biggest objection a smart investor will raise, named directly, answered cleanly. Klaff calls this taking the punch before it's thrown.

COMPONENT 3: OFFER THE DEAL (2 minutes / ~360 words / 1 slide)
Slide to brief:

The offer — What they give. What they get. Clean two-column layout: left column give, right column get. Tie the get back to the big idea so the deal feels like the natural payoff of everything before it.

COMPONENT 4: STACK FRAMES FOR HOT COGNITION (3 minutes / ~540 words / 4 slides)
Each frame is its own slide. Short and emotional.
Slides to brief:

Intrigue frame — Short, true, relevant story with no conclusion. Cliffhanger.
Prize frame — Position yourself as the prize. Specific language that signals selectivity.
Time frame — Real, legitimate urgency. Not manufactured "limited time" garbage.
Moral authority frame — Force them to justify themselves to you.

CLOSING SLIDE

Next step — One clear, specific action. End on the action, not a thank-you.

ATTRIBUTES & RULES
These rules are non-negotiable. Apply them to every slide brief.
Voice rules

No corporate hedging. No "we believe," no "we think," no "perhaps."
Active voice. Short sentences.
No buzzwords without numbers attached. "Disruptive" is meaningless. "Replaces a $4B incumbent at 60% lower cost" is a pitch.
No AI tells. Do not write "this isn't about X, it's about Y." Do not write "here's the thing." Do not write "the brutal truth." Rewrite if you catch it.

Slide content rules (what goes ON the slide vs IN speaker notes)

On the slide: headline + max 3 supporting beats. Numbers, not paragraphs. One idea per slide. If two ideas fit, you have two slides.
In speaker notes: the full case, the framing, the transitions, the answers to the obvious follow-ups. This is where the 900/1800/360/540 word budgets actually live. Slide faces stay sparse.
This split is what makes Claude Design's "Use speaker notes" toggle work. Brief accordingly.

Layout intent rules (what to tell Claude Design)
For every slide, specify a layout intent in plain language Claude Design understands. Examples:

"Centered hero layout with oversized headline and one supporting line"
"Two-column split: left = give, right = get"
"Three-column row of equal-weight forces, each with a small numeric anchor"
"Full-bleed quote with attribution in lower-right"
"Data slide: one big number top-left, three supporting metrics in a row below"

Do not specify colors, fonts, or visual style. Claude Design auto-applies the organization's design system. Telling it "use blue" overrides the brand and produces worse output.
Honesty rules

If user input is missing real proof, do not invent it. Use a placeholder line in the brief that names exactly what's missing and what needs to be added before the deck is presentable.
If "why now" is weak, say so. A bad why-now collapses the whole pitch.
If the ask is unclear, do not generate the offer slide. Ask for clarification.

REFERENCE EXAMPLES
Example slide brief (good):
SLIDE 2 — WHY NOW
Layout intent: Three-column row, equal weight. Each column has a small icon
or numeric anchor at the top, a one-word force label, and one line of detail.

On-slide content:
  ECONOMY    | $58B US drone services market. 24% YoY growth.
  SOCIETY    | Skilled-trade labor shortage forcing inspection digitization.
  TECHNOLOGY | DJI ban + open-source PX4 + sub-$3K thermal = US-built finally
               cost-competitive.

Speaker notes:
The window opened in late 2024 when the federal DJI restrictions cleared
the largest competitor out of the US commercial market. At the same time,
PX4 hit production maturity and FLIR Boson sensors dropped under $3K. Three
forces had to align. They have. The pitch isn't "drones are interesting."
The pitch is "the only window in a decade to build a US-manufactured drone
services company is open right now, and it closes when one of the well-funded
defense primes notices the commercial gap."
Example slide brief (bad — do not produce this):
SLIDE 2 — WHY NOW IS THE TIME
In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, drones are becoming
increasingly important across many industries...
(Generic, padded, no numbers, no urgency, no reason to keep listening.)
Example offer slide brief (good):
SLIDE 11 — THE OFFER
Layout intent: Two-column split, equal weight. Left column header "YOU GIVE."
Right column header "YOU GET." Three bullets each. No paragraphs.

On-slide content:
  YOU GIVE                     | YOU GET
  $1.5M for 18% equity         | First-mover position post-DJI
  Board observer seat          | $840K ARR committed (4 pilots signed)
  36-month runway commitment   | Exit-ready ops framework, $50M strategic target Y5

Speaker notes:
This is a priced round, not a SAFE. We've already taken in $200K from
strategic angels at the same valuation. The 18% reflects a $6.8M post.
Comparable deals in defense-adjacent commercial drone services are pricing
at 8-12x ARR; we're priced at 8x committed ARR with the operational
infrastructure already built.

OUTPUT FORMAT
When I provide my inputs, you will:
Step 1 — Audit my inputs
If anything is weak, missing, or self-flattering nonsense, name it before generating. Do not produce a polished brief on a broken foundation.
Step 2 — Generate the Claude Design brief
Output a single, copy-paste-ready block formatted exactly like this:
GOAL: A 14-15 slide investor pitch deck following Oren Klaff's 20-minute
pitch structure. Slides should be sparse on the face (headline + max 3
supporting beats) with detail living in speaker notes. Total presentation
time target: 20 minutes.

AUDIENCE: [pulled from my input]

LAYOUT PRINCIPLES:
- One idea per slide
- Numbers over adjectives wherever possible
- Use the organization's design system as-is; do not override colors or type
- Slide counter visible
- Print-friendly (deck may be exported to PDF and forwarded)

CONTENT — slide by slide:

SLIDE 1 — COVER
  Layout intent: [...]
  On-slide content: [...]
  Speaker notes: [...]

SLIDE 2 — WHY NOW
  Layout intent: [...]
  On-slide content: [...]
  Speaker notes: [...]

[... continues through all ~14-15 slides ...]

EXPORT TARGET: PDF for email forwarding, PPTX for in-room presentation,
Send to Canva for any post-pitch marketing repurposing.
Step 3 — Provide a Claude Design operating kit
After the brief, give me:

Setup checklist — Three lines:

Open claude.ai/design → New project → Slide Deck → toggle "Use speaker notes" ON
Paste the brief above as your first message
Confirm the org design system is applied before iterating

Iteration prompts ready to paste — Five short follow-up prompts I can use as inline comments or chat messages once the first generation lands:

One for tightening slide density
One for strengthening the weakest slide
One for asking Claude Design to show 2-3 layout variations on the offer slide
One for an accessibility/contrast pass
One for requesting a print-optimized variant

Five-line debrief

Strongest slide
Weakest slide and what input would make it stronger
What's missing that a real investor will ask about
Suggested run-of-show timing for the live pitch
One sentence on what to practice first

CONFIRMATION
Before I provide my inputs, confirm you understand by responding with:

The four phases and their word budgets, in order
Why we're NOT specifying colors or typography in the brief
One clarifying question about my pitch context

Then I'll send the inputs and you'll build the brief.
Are you ready?
