records.description: Hey there! And welcome to Day 1 of Claude Fundamentals Sprint: Become an AI PRO in 5 Days. In this lesson, we're going to cover: - What an AI assistant actually
records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 1 of Claude Fundamentals Sprint: Become an AI PRO in 5 Days.

In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • What an AI assistant actually is (and isn't) - and why understanding this one idea instantly makes your results better

  • The anatomy of a prompt that works: context, task, and format

  • The 3 mistakes that guarantee generic answers - one-line prompts, "search-box thinking," and expecting Claude to read your mind

And more!

All so you can turn the questions you'd normally type into Google into genuinely useful answers - and kick off the sprint by picking one real thing you want Claude helping you with by Friday.

Let's dive in!

Module

By the end of today, you'll know how to build a great prompt from scratch and test whether it did the job you needed.

We're going to start with a vague prompt, add the missing pieces, show the model what good looks like, compare the answers, and fix what the model missed. You will save the prompt you would use again, plus your first and final outputs.

That's it. You do not need to learn special AI language or anything techy/complicated.

You just need to get clear about what you want.

Why Prompts (Still) Matter: 3 Reasons to Learn Prompting First

AI can give you a polished answer that is still completely wrong for the job.

If you ask for "investing tips," the model has to guess what kind of investing you mean, how much money you have, how much experience you have, and what kind of answer would help.

With that much missing, it will usually give you a generic answer.

Try this:

Give me investing tips.

Now try this:

Give me five real estate investing tips for a beginner with zero dollars to invest. Write it as a 500-word list, and start each item with the tip.

The second prompt gives the model somewhere to go. It knows the subject, who the answer is for, the person's situation, the length, and the format.

That does not guarantee a great answer. It gives you an answer you can actually judge.

Four mistakes that make prompts worse

Mistake 1: Copying somebody else's prompt without changing it

A prompt you found online was written for somebody else's audience, goal, and way of working. Keep the useful parts, but replace their details with yours. If the prompt says "write for busy SaaS founders" and you sell dog training to new puppy owners, change it, because people skip obvious mismatches like that constantly.

Mistake 2: Judging the answer by whether it sounds smart

Do not grade the answer by whether it sounds impressive. Ask whether it did what you asked. Before you run the prompt, decide what the answer needs to include. Then check the answer against that.

Mistake 3: Giving it a role instead of a job

"Act as a world-class strategist" sounds specific, but it does not tell the model what to do.

Should it compare three options, find the biggest risk, or recommend one choice and explain why?

Tell the model what to do, not what costume to wear.

The same goes for words like "compelling," "premium," or "authoritative." If you cannot point to the words or actions that create that effect, the model is guessing.

Mistake 4: Only telling it what not to do

"Do not sound corporate, use jargon, or bore me."

Fine, but what should it sound like?

If you have an example you like, paste it in. Tell the model which parts to copy, such as the length, pace, tone, structure, or level of detail. Then add the things you want it to avoid.

Showing it a good example is usually more useful than writing a giant list of complaints.

The Prompting Ladder

Level 1: Ask the question

Sometimes you really can just ask the question.

Teach me about this topic.
Summarize this.
Someone told me to be more charismatic. What does that mean?

Ask directly when you want an explanation, a summary, or a fact you can check.

Level 2: Add the details

When you want the model to make something, give it the details that matter. Think about who it is for, where it will be used, how long it should be, what it should sound like, and what information the model needs. You will not need every one of those details every time. Add the ones that change the answer.

Rewrite this for new business owners who are nervous about using AI.

Keep it under 200 words. Use plain English and short paragraphs. End with one thing they can try today.

[PASTE YOUR DRAFT]

If the context is easier to say than type, use voice dictation. Talk through who it is for, where it will be used, what it should include, and what it should sound like, then ask AI to organize what you said. Check the organized notes before you use them.

Level 3: Show the Target

If you already have an example of what good looks like, show it to the model.

I wrote this:

[PASTE AN EXAMPLE YOU LIKE]

Write a new version for [WHO IT IS FOR] on [WHERE IT WILL BE USED].

Match the example's [NAME THE PARTS YOU WANT TO KEEP]. Keep it to [LENGTH]. Avoid [WHAT YOU DO NOT WANT].

Level 4 comes later, when we turn prompts you use repeatedly into Skills. For today, learn how to write and fix the prompt itself.

Three prompts I use to challenge my own thinking

Unbundle

Use this when a word sounds clear until you try to explain what it means.

Your mission is to “Unbundle” and operationalize the term below.

Assume it houses a lot of connotative and intangible meaning that is hard to train and understand.

Provide CONCRETE examples for daily activities in work or life, business or relationships, interpersonal or mindset, in a way that someone could take action on without necessarily feeling the emotion that might naturally lead to the behavior. 

Operationalizing means to turn the phrase or word into a set of trainable and learnable and visible actions that when mastered, encompass the real meaning of the term.

For example: “Charisma” is a bundled term that stands for the feeling of warmth, power, and presence other people feel when they interact with you. The actions that it encircles include making eye contact, active listening, speaking slowly, asking questions about the other person, smiling genuinely, having a firm handshake, and setting a collaborative frame for the conversation, etc. 

TERM:

Breakdown of this prompt:

If the answer replaces one vague word with five more vague words, tell it to try again using things you could see or hear someone do.

Steel Man

Use Steel Man when you want AI to make the strongest case against your idea.

I am considering an idea:

Make the strongest possible case against it. Give me the main objections, the evidence or reasoning each objection would require, and the condition that would make each objection matter. Steel man the argument AGAINST it. 

End with the hardest objection I need to answer before I proceed.

IDEA:

Check whether the strongest objection names the evidence it would need or the condition that would make it matter.

Secret Shopper

Use Secret Shopper to hear what a skeptical customer might say when you are too close to your own pitch, offer, or message.

Read this as a skeptical potential customer:

[PASTE THE PITCH, OFFER, OR MESSAGE]

Tell me what is unclear, what you doubt, what information is missing, and what would stop you from taking the next step. Quote the exact line that caused each reaction. Then state the question you would ask before deciding.

Each reaction should point to a quoted line or a specific fact the customer needs.

Watch me do it with “Enthusiasm”

First, I'll ask:

Someone told me to be more enthusiastic. What does that mean?

When the answer appears, ask: Which parts could describe almost anyone? Then I'll give it a real message and a much clearer direction:

Rewrite this so I come across like Russell Brunson. I want enthusiasm, not passiveness. 

[PASTE THE MESSAGE]

When the second answer appears, ask: Where did it follow the Russell Brunson direction, and where did it miss?

Next, we'll run "Enthusiastic" through Unbundle.

XYZ is a “bundled” term. Assume it houses a lot of connotative and intangible meaning that is hard to train and understand. Your mission is to “Unbundle” and operationalize this term.
Operationalizing means to turn the phrase or word into a set of trainable and learnable and visible actions that when mastered, encompass the real meaning of the term.
For example: “Charisma” is a bundled term that stands the feeling of warmth, power, and presence other people feel when they interact with you. The actions that it encircles include making eye contact, active listening, speaking slowly, asking questions about the other person, smiling genuinely, having a firm handshake, and setting a collaborative frame for the conversation, etc. Provide CONCRETE examples for daily activities in work or life, business or relationships, interpersonal or mindset, in a way that someone could take action on without necessarily feeling the emotion that might naturally lead to the behavior. 
TERM: Enthusiasm

When the third answer appears, ask: Which criteria can you actually point to in the rewritten message?

Now compare all three answers side by side. The last one does not win just because it came last; point to what changed and decide which answer actually does the job.

Now try it yourself

Pick something real that you want AI to help you with.

It could be "make my writing more authoritative," "make this sound less corporate," or "make this pitch feel more premium."

Open a document beside your AI chat and save each prompt and answer as you go. In the templates below, replace every bracketed field with your own information and delete any field that does not apply.

Pass 1: Ask for it the way you normally would

Before you run it, write down what you think the vague prompt will leave open.

Make my [WRITING OR PITCH] more [BUNDLED TERM].

[PASTE THE WRITING OR PITCH]

Save the prompt and answer. Highlight anything generic or impossible to check.

Pass 2: Add the important details

Rewrite this for [WHO IT IS FOR] on [WHERE IT WILL BE USED]. Keep it to [LENGTH]. Use [WRITING STYLE]. Preserve [REQUIRED CONTEXT]. Return it as [FORMAT].

[PASTE THE WRITING OR PITCH]

Save the prompt and answer. Check whether it followed each detail you gave it.

Pass 3: Use Unbundle to rewrite the prompt

Run your fuzzy word through Unbundle, then paste the concrete actions or features it gives you into this prompt:

Rewrite this for [WHO IT IS FOR] on [WHERE IT WILL BE USED]. Keep it to [LENGTH]. Use these criteria for [BUNDLED TERM]:

[PASTE THE CONCRETE CRITERIA FROM UNBUNDLE]

Preserve [REQUIRED CONTEXT]. Return it as [FORMAT].

[PASTE THE WRITING OR PITCH]

Put the first and final answers side by side and mark which instructions the model followed or missed. If the model missed one instruction, revise the prompt once and run it again. Keep the missed instruction marked if the second try still misses.

Save the prompt you would actually use again, plus the first and final answers.

If you have an example you like, run the task one more time with that example in the prompt. Name the parts you want AI to match, then compare the result.

Save Your Prompt

Keep that final prompt. Tomorrow, we will add more context to it so AI has the background it needs for a real job. (Reusable Skills come later in the Sprint).

Frequently Asked Questions

Can't I just talk to it?

Yes. If a simple question gets the job done, ask the simple question.

Add more detail when you need a specific answer, or when the model keeps missing what you mean.

I already have copied prompts that work. Do I have to stop using them?

No. Keep what works. Just make sure the prompt is asking for your job, not the job of the person you copied it from.

Is this slower than Google?

Sometimes. Do not spend ten minutes building a prompt for a question that takes ten seconds to answer.

The extra effort makes sense when you are asking AI to write, analyze, compare, or help you make a decision.

Should I use ChatGPT or Claude?

Use the one you like. The same basic approach works in either one, although the answers will not be identical.

Do I need to be technical?

No. Pick a small job you already understand, then explain what you want the same way you would explain it to a smart new employee.

Optional publishing idea

You can turn the first and final answers into a LinkedIn or Substack post about what changed. You do not have to publish it to finish today's exercise. Get permission before sharing someone else's prompt, words, or result.

Supporting videos and reference

  • Four mistakes that make prompts worse

  • The Prompting Ladder

  • Open or download the Prompt Breakdown Diagram from Resources below.

records.description: AI Fundamentals Sprint, Module 2 of 5 By the end of today, you'll know what to give AI before you ask it to do the work. Day 1 was about writing a clear request
records.content:
AI Fundamentals Sprint, Module 2 of 5

By the end of today, you'll know what to give AI before you ask it to do the work.

Day 1 was about writing a clear request. Today is about giving the model something real to work from: your files, your notes, a book you trust, a useful example, or material from someone who has already done the job.

The short version is simple:

Never let AI run on defaults when you have better material available.

I call this Bring Your Own Material. Someone who gets into the habit of choosing what AI works from is a Context Curator. When the first answer is usable, I call that one-shotting. This is the second of five lessons meant to build AI confidence.

Why context matters

When you ask AI a question cold, it has none of your history.

It does not know who you are, what you have already tried, what good looks like to you, or what constraints you are working under. It reaches for a broadly useful answer because that is all it has to go on.

That is why a cold answer often sounds reasonable and still feels like it could have been written for anybody.

You already know the basic rule: garbage in, garbage out. With AI, the garbage can sound polished. Give it a bad source or a false premise and it may reason carefully from the wrong thing. The answer can look finished enough that you act on it.

Good material gives the model less to guess about. Give it your actual numbers, your earlier thinking, the report you trust, or a finished example, and some of the usual back-and-forth can disappear because you answered its questions before it had to ask them.

In a March 2026 Harvard Business Review article, Angelo Romasanta, Llewellyn D.W. Thomas, and Natalia Levina reported tests of seven AI systems on seven forced-choice strategy questions. Most systems favored the same side of most trade-offs, although they differed on exploration versus exploitation. Separate prompt and company-context tests used GPT-5. Those changes moved the answers but did not reliably remove the preferences. This does not show that context fixes the model. It shows that a polished answer can still carry a default.

That matters most when you cannot judge the answer yourself. An experienced operator has mentors, advisors, and years of mistakes helping them notice bad advice. A beginner may have only the chat window. If the answer sounds confident, it is easy to assume it is good.

Context gives the model something better than its default answer to work from.

Bring the expert

“Bring Your Own Material” does not mean you have to create all the material yourself.

If you know the subject, bring your own notes, plans, manuals, examples, or numbers. If you are new to it, bring a book, transcript, course, paper, or method from someone you trust.

You do not have to be the expert; you have to bring one.

The best performer is not always the best teacher. Ask a grandmother for a recipe she has made ten thousand times and you may get, “a little of this, then cook it until it looks right.” She is not hiding anything. She no longer sees all the steps.

The person who had to learn the skill as an adult may be more useful because they had to write the steps down. When you need material that AI can follow, look for the person who can explain how the work gets done.

How to give AI context

Getting material into a chat is not technical. You can:

  • Paste the text into the conversation.

  • Upload the PDF, document, image, or screenshot.

  • If the tool can open links, give it a link and tell it what to read.

Check that the tool actually opened the page before you trust its answer. Link access depends on the product, model, login, and page permissions. If it cannot open the page, paste the relevant text or upload a copy you are allowed to use.

Before you paste or upload anything, make sure you are allowed to submit it. Remove names, contact details, account numbers, credentials, and any other identifying information the model does not need. Do not upload client-confidential or employer-confidential material, or an entire paid or copyrighted work, unless you have permission. Check the provider's current access, retention, and training settings first. If you cannot verify those settings, use a non-sensitive excerpt instead.

Start with the easy version. If you have an 80-page PDF, try the whole PDF before spending twenty minutes choosing the perfect three pages. Then tell the model where to look:

Summarize chapter four.

Pull the section about [topic].

Give me a detailed summary of part three.

If the full document causes a problem, narrow it down. Let the output tell you whether you need to do more work.

For today, keep the result as a written plan or a markdown document. The build tools come on Thursday.

Three mistakes that make context worse

Choosing the perfect excerpt before you try the full source

You can spend longer preparing the context than doing the work.

Try the whole document first. If the answer misses something, point the model to the relevant section or remove the material that is getting in the way. Do the extra work after you know it is necessary.

Describing a source from memory when you can paste the source

Sometimes your own explanation is exactly the context the model needs. The problem is using a fuzzy memory of a study, policy, conversation, or set of numbers when the original is sitting nearby.

If the source exists, use it. Your memory may drop the qualification that changes the conclusion.

This lesson follows its own advice by using the cited HBR article instead of a remembered version of the claim.

Asking a long, wandering chat for a clean final answer

A long conversation can be great for thinking. The model has more of the discussion and can connect ideas from earlier in the thread.

That same history can get in the way when you want one reliable output. Old assumptions, abandoned ideas, and corrections are still sitting in the conversation.

When you want to explore, keep talking. When you want a clean result, open a fresh chat and give it only the context it needs for that job.

The Sourcing Ladder

The Sourcing Ladder helps you decide whose material to bring into the chat.

1. Be It

Start with something you know well.

If you want AI to help with a fitness plan and you have studied training for years, give it the materials you trust. Because you know the subject, you can catch mistakes and judge whether the new answer is actually better than the cold one.

This is the safest place to see what context changes. Use a subject where you know what good looks like.

2. Borrow It

Next, choose a subject you do not know well but where you know a source you trust.

Maybe you are teaching math at home and trust material from MIT OpenCourseWare. Give that material to AI and ask it to build a lesson around your child's needs, even if math is new to you.

You have not become a math expert. You have stopped asking the model to make up the lesson from its general training.

This is where Gell-Mann Amnesia matters. You notice errors quickly when you know a field. Then you read something equally shaky in a field you do not know and accept it because you cannot see what is wrong. A trusted source gives you somewhere better to start, but you still need to check important claims.

3. Hunt It

Sometimes you do not know the subject and do not know which source to trust. Ask AI to help you find respected practitioners and the material that best explains their work.

Use the full Context Hunter prompt below. It looks for people who can do the work and show other people how to do it. It does not treat fame, followers, credentials, or a big win as proof that someone can teach.

Do not treat the list as verified just because the model produced it. Check that the people and resources exist, see who cites them, and open the source yourself. A ranking or criticism of a named person needs a primary or field-authoritative source. If the model cannot support a judgment, leave it out instead of repeating it. Then bring the source you chose back into the chat and run the work from that material.

That is the whole ladder. Use your own material when you know the subject. Borrow a trusted source when you know where to look. Hunt for a source when you do not.

If we use your example, I'll ask first. You can pass, and we'll keep the topic anonymous and non-sensitive.

FAQ

“Isn't this just uploading files?”

Yes. Sometimes the important move really is that simple.

Paste, upload, or link the source. Then tell the model what you want it to do with that material. People can spend several messages correcting guesses they could have prevented at the start.

“Will a huge document confuse it or cost too much?”

It can. You do not need to solve that problem before it happens.

Try the full document and direct the model to the relevant chapter or section. If the answer is weak, reduce the material or give it a more precise location. File limits and cost depend on the provider, plan, model, and file size, so check the product's current limits and pricing before using a large document.

“I don't have documents or expertise.”

Use Hunt It. Ask for respected people and their best resources, verify the list, then bring one of those resources back into the chat.

Being a beginner means you need a source. It does not mean the source has to come from you.

“Can I just explain my situation?”

Yes. Your explanation may be the best available context.

Use the original when accuracy matters and you have it. Paste the contract instead of describing what you remember it saying. Upload the current report instead of quoting last month's number. If the source is unavailable, tell the model that your description is from memory.

The Sourcing Kit

Use the Context Hunter to find sources. Save the useful ones in the Context Shelf.

The Context Hunter

This is the copy-and-paste version of Hunt It:

I need you to find source material I can inspect and bring back into this chat. Do not teach the subject yet. Do not summarize a source or build a plan from it yet.

Find 5–7 people who are substantially better than I am at the relevant skill and who have demonstrably helped other people understand or perform it.

Do not confuse accomplishment with teaching ability. Fame, credentials, citations, a championship, an Olympic medal, or a second-place finish may establish performance or reputation. None of them proves that the person can teach. Look for separate evidence that the person explains the work clearly, has taught or coached it, has produced inspectable instruction, or has helped learners improve.

Look beyond the most famous person. As applicable to this field, consider:

- a runner-up, medalist, finalist, or retired elite practitioner;
- a coach whose students have performed well;
- a practitioner who learned through deliberate practice and documents the process;
- a researcher whose work is respected in the field;
- another candidate with unusually clear, inspectable teaching material.

Do not force every type into the results. Include a person only when the evidence fits my goal.

Research requirements:

1. Use primary sources first for claims about the person and resource: the person's official site, the actual paper, publisher page, governing body, professional association, university profile, course page, book page, program syllabus, interview transcript, or the teaching material itself.
2. Use field-authoritative evidence for reputation: peer-reviewed citations, recognized professional bodies, competition records, documented student results, respected peers, established institutions, or other evidence appropriate to the field.

Treat testimonials, provider-published case studies, and student results reported by the person or program as self-reported evidence. Label them `SELF-REPORTED`. Do not use them alone to claim that someone teaches well or helps learners improve. For peer support, name the peer, link the exact statement, and show why that peer is qualified to judge this field.

3. Do not use follower counts, search rank, bestseller status, publicity, or repeated blog claims as proof that someone is respected or can teach.
4. Verify that every person and resource exists. Open every link before returning it. Mark each link `OPENED` or `NOT OPENED`. Do not present a link as verified if the tool did not successfully open it.
5. Verify whether the resource is currently accessible, free or paid, and its current listed price when one is shown. If you cannot verify a fact, write UNKNOWN. Do not estimate or fill gaps.
6. Prefer one inspectable resource that contains the person's actual method over a profile, promotional page, summary written by someone else, or their most popular work.
7. If a secondary source makes an important claim, trace it to the original source. If you cannot, identify it as an unverified secondary claim.
8. Keep facts separate from inference. State what the source proves, then state any conclusion you drew from it as an inference.
9. Do not call anyone the best, most respected, or a good teacher unless the evidence shown supports that exact description.
10. Do not assume the same source is right for a beginner, an expert, and my specific desired result. Judge fit against the five fields I supplied.

Return your work in this order.

A. Exact searches used

List every search query exactly as entered. Include site-restricted searches, title searches, author searches, and price/access searches. Do not rewrite or clean up the queries after the fact.

If your browsing tool does not expose the exact query log, write `NOT AVAILABLE` and list only the queries you can verify were actually run. Do not reconstruct or invent search queries after the fact.

B. Candidates

Return one table with these columns:

| Person | Why this person is relevant | Evidence of ability | Evidence they can teach | One best inspectable resource | Direct link | Price and access | Fit for my goal and level | Limitations |

For every factual statement in the table, link to the source that supports it. In the `Fit for my goal and level` column, begin each judgment with `INFERENCE:`. In the other columns, distinguish any unsupported interpretation with `INFERENCE:` and use `UNKNOWN` where verification failed.

C. Shortlist

Choose 2–3 candidates from the table. Explain in plain language why each fits my stated goal, current level, result, and constraints. Do not choose based on fame alone.

D. Best source to retrieve first

Choose one specific resource from the shortlist. Give me:

- the exact title;
- the creator;
- the direct verified link;
- current price/access, or UNKNOWN;
- the exact chapter, section, episode, lesson, paper, dataset, or other portion to retrieve first, if you can verify it;
- why it is the best starting source for my stated result;
- what it does not cover or what I should be cautious about.

Then stop.

Do not summarize the selected source. Do not create a lesson, recommendation, workflow, strategy, or action plan from it. Tell me to obtain the source and bring it back to you. You may work from it only after I provide the source itself or explicitly ask you to open and analyze it.

If you do not have working web access, say that immediately. Do not recommend people or resources from memory. Instead, return:

1. the exact search queries you would run;
2. the sites or databases you would check;
3. the facts that still need verification;
4. a blank copy of the candidate table.

MY GOAL:
[What I am trying to learn, decide, make, or improve]

MY CURRENT LEVEL:
[What I already know or can do]

THE RESULT I NEED:
[The specific result I want after I study or use the source]

MY CONSTRAINTS:
[Time, budget, location, language, accessibility, safety, tools, deadline, or anything else that matters]

SOURCE TYPES I CAN USE:
[Examples: free articles, youtube channels, books, papers, courses, videos, transcripts, paid coaching, datasets, manuals]

The model's answer is a research lead, not the finished research. Open the links, confirm the resources, and decide which source you trust before using it.

Treat every claim about a person's reputation as unverified until you have a primary or field-authoritative citation. Keep the wording neutral and omit unsupported criticism. Only ask the model for a summary or plan when the resource is attached or the tool can actually access it. Otherwise, obtain the resource and bring it back first.

The Context Shelf

The Context Shelf is a spreadsheet for sources you want to use again. It has these columns:

  • Topic / Domain

  • Source

  • Type (book / course / report / data)

  • Who it's from

  • Free or Paid

  • Link

  • Why I trust it

  • Last used

Add a row whenever the Context Hunter finds something worth keeping. The point is to stop searching for the same good sources every time.

The sheet starts with university course libraries such as MIT OpenCourseWare, primary-research databases, public datasets, and original technical documentation.

Optional: Set It and Forget It w/Memory

Some context stays useful across many conversations: who you are, how you work, and rules you want the model to follow every time. Claude and ChatGPT will save this to a feature called Memory.

Assignment: run the Sourcing Ladder

Choose one real thing you want AI's help with this week. Use the same request all three times.

Bare: Ask the question with no source material. Save a screenshot of the answer.

Be It or Borrow It: Add material you trust. Use your own material if you know the subject, or use a trusted outside source if you do not. Run the same request and save the answer.

Hunt It: Use the Context Hunter to find a promising source. Check that it exists, supports the claims made about it, and fits your request. Give that material to AI, run the same request again, and save the answer.

Put the three answers side by side. Decide which answer is best and point to the exact differences. The third answer does not always win just because it came last.

records.description: AI Fundamentals Sprint, Module 3 of 5 By the end of today, you'll have one Project set up for a real task you do more than once. Day 1 was about writing the req
records.content:
AI Fundamentals Sprint, Module 3 of 5

By the end of today, you'll have one Project set up for a real task you do more than once.

Day 1 was about writing the request. Day 2 was about choosing the material AI should work from. Today, you are going to stop carrying those instructions and files into every new chat.

Build the room once. Live in it.

That room is a Project, where your House Rules and standing files give each fresh chat the background it needs before you make today's request.

This session demonstrates Claude Projects. Review the current controls and availability before class in Anthropic's official Projects guide.

Stop relying on Claude’s built-in memory

A fresh chat without saved memory, custom instructions, workspace settings, or Project context starts without your job description, your audience, your preferred format, or the files you use every week. Check the actual settings in the product you are using before you compare one chat with another.

So you type the same introduction again.

I run a bookkeeping practice. My clients are small restaurants. I write in plain English, with no jargon. This is the situation...

You get the answer, close the tab, and repeat the introduction tomorrow.

Day 2 made you the Context Curator. You chose the source material instead of letting AI answer from general training alone. The problem is that you still have to carry the same material into each new chat.

A Project gives that recurring work one place to live. You add the standing instructions and files once, then update them when the work changes.

Why use a Project

You stop repeating the same briefing

Five minutes of background may feel small until you do it across several chats every day. Skip the background and the answer may miss facts that matter. Repeat it and you spend your time onboarding another blank chat.

That repeated setup is the re-briefing tax.

New chats can start from the same instructions and files

Two blank chats may answer the same request differently. A Project gives both chats the same starting material: the same House Rules, the same standing files, and the same description of the job. Their answers can still differ.

That gives you a better chance of getting answers that fit the work without rebuilding the context each time.

The work you did on Days 1 and 2 stays useful

You still write a clear request inside each chat. You still choose good source material.

The difference is where the standing material lives. Files that matter to every conversation in this Project can stay with the Project. A file that matters to only one request stays in that one chat.

Four mistakes to avoid

Mistake 1: Treating a Project like a folder

Organizing chats is useful, but the folder alone does not teach the model about your work. Add the House Rules and standing files each new chat needs.

Mistake 2: Uploading everything you own

Forty documents can include old decisions, duplicated material, or instructions that disagree with one another.

Only add files that should apply across the whole Project. Keep one-time material in the chat where you need it. If two files conflict, decide which one is current before you upload them.

Mistake 3: Writing Bundled House Rules

“Be helpful” and “be professional” leave the important decisions to the model.

Say who you are, who the work is for, what facts stay true, what the usual output should look like, and which choices you do not want. “Write a weekly update for six managers in 300 words or less” gives the model something it can use. “Be professional” does not.

Mistake 4: Building one Project for every kind of work

A Project for Substack posts may need different instructions and files than a Project for client emails.

Anyone who has tried to get Claude to nail down a single writing voice knows that you can go back and forth and back and forth and still find rogue Em dashes, contrast frames, Saved Cat language, and cringe questions.

Use one Project for one recurring job when the jobs need different context. Call it [CLIENT] Substack Writing or [My Biz] Onboarding Emails, not Substack Project or AI Tests.

Build your Project

Use the real task you have carried since Day 1.

The exact controls can change. In Claude, you are looking for five actions: create a Project, name it, add instructions, add allowed files, and open a fresh chat inside it. Use the official Projects guide if the interface differs from the recording.

1. Name it after the job

Give the Project the name of the recurring work. The name should tell you what belongs there.

2. Write the House Rules

Add the information that should be true for every chat inside this Project:

  • Who I am: your role, business, and the work you do.

  • Who this is for: the audience, client, or reader.

  • Always assume: facts and constraints that stay true across this work.

  • How I want things: the usual format, length, and voice.

  • Never do: words, tones, formats, claims, or actions you do not want.

Do not put passwords, API keys, access tokens, private records, or sensitive personal information in the Project instructions.

Read the House Rules again whenever the job, audience, or constraints change.

3. Add the standing files

Choose files from your Context Shelf that belong in every conversation about this job. Add them to the Project's knowledge or file area.

Good inputs might include a current product description, an approved output template, or examples you actually want the model to follow. Do not add a document simply because you have it.

Before uploading anything:

  • make sure you are allowed to submit it;

  • remove private details the task does not need;

  • do not upload credentials, confidential material, or an entire copyrighted work without permission;

  • check the provider's current retention and training controls; and

  • if the Project is shared, check who can see its instructions, chats, and files.

4. Run the cold-start test

Save the House Rules and files. Open a brand-new, empty chat inside the Project.

Before comparing it with another chat, verify which settings apply. Saved memory, account-level instructions, workspace settings, and Project context may all affect what a fresh chat receives.

Give it a short request that depends on the context you added.

Check the answer:

  • Did it use the right role and audience?

  • Did it follow the expected format and length?

  • Did it use the standing facts without inventing missing details?

  • Can you point to the instruction or file that supports the answer?

If it asks for something the Project should contain, add the missing fact or file and test again in another fresh chat. If it invents information, make the rule or source clearer. Keep the first answer so you can compare it with the next one.

The newest answer does not win just because it came last.

5. Keep doing that work inside the Project, with new chats frequently

Open future chats for this recurring task inside the Project. Each chat still needs a clear request to start. The Project supplies the standing context; the prompt tells it what to do today.

Update the House Rules and files when the job changes.

Remove anything that is no longer current on something like a 14-day or 30-day cadence.

Keep the House Rules and original source files somewhere you control outside the AI provider. The Project holds working copies; it should not be the only place those materials exist.

Frequently Asked Questions

“Isn't a Project just a folder?”

The folder keeps the chats together. The House Rules and files give those chats the standing context for the job.

“What happens when my situation changes?”

Edit the House Rules or replace the old file. Then open a fresh chat and run the cold-start test again.

“Will it turn into a junk drawer?”

It will if you keep adding material that does not belong. Use one Project for one recurring job.

“Do I need to pay for Projects?”

Availability depends on the current product and plan. Check Anthropic's official Projects guide before class rather than promising access from memory.

“How much should I put in the files?”

Start with the standing material that every chat needs. Test the Project. Add or remove files based on what the answers show.

“Is a Project the same as a Skill?”

No. In this lesson, a Project remembers the situation and a Skill remembers a move.

The Project holds the standing context for one recurring job. A Skill is a repeatable procedure you can run when you need it. Product names and implementations vary.

House Rules Project Instructions Starter

Copy this into the Project's instructions box and fill in every section.

WHO I AM:
[Your role, your business, what you actually do all day.]

WHO MY WORK IS FOR:
[The audience, client, or reader on the receiving end.]

ALWAYS ASSUME:
- [Fact 1]
- [Fact 2]
- [Fact 3]

HOW I WANT THINGS:
[Default format, length, and voice.]

NEVER DO:
[Specific words, formats, claims, tones, or actions you do not want.]

Paste it, fill it in, and save it. Then run the cold-start test.

Here are my “writing” house rules to try and get a head start on the drafting process:

WRITING RULES

Write like a person talking to one specific reader.

Use concrete nouns, real names, numbers, dates, quotes, products, and moments when I supply them. If a sentence could appear unchanged in anyone else’s writing, rewrite it or cut it.

Say what something is. Avoid canned contrast framing such as “this isn’t X, it’s Y” or “the problem isn’t X, it’s Y.”

Get into the point. Cut preambles, throat-clearing, generic introductions, recap paragraphs, and offers to explain more.

Never use em dashes.

Do not use corporate filler such as leverage, robust, seamless, cutting-edge, transformative, innovative, ecosystem, landscape, or game-changer.

Avoid dramatic fragments and fake suspense:

- “The catch?”
- “The result?”
- “The brutal truth?”
- “Sound familiar?”
- “Here’s the thing.”
- “Let’s unpack this.”
- “Here’s what you need to know.”

Do not force every idea into three parallel bullets, three short sentences, or a neat problem-solution-result sequence. Let the length and structure follow the material.

Vary sentence and paragraph length naturally. Do not produce rows of similarly sized sentences or clipped fragments.

Prefer active sentences that say who did what. Avoid passive constructions that make the work sound like something that merely happened:

Bad: “One prompt was saved.”
Better: “Save the prompt you would actually use again.”

Do not package ordinary actions, outputs, or lesson outcomes as named concepts, badges, methods, or features.

Read any suspicious phrase aloud after both of these:

- “or, as I like to call it, [PHRASE]”
- “what I like to call [PHRASE]”

If either version sounds natural, inspect the phrase. Repeated natural fits mean the writing is inventing labels instead of explaining what happened.

Keep useful plain labels such as intended reader, pasted context, labeled sections, finished work, bundled term, Pass 1, and Pass 2.

Keep established names from my source material when they identify a real, distinct tool or idea, including Prompting Ladder, Show the Target, Unbundle, Steel Man, Secret Shopper, Prompt Starter Kit, and Prompt Building Blocks.

Only invent a new name when I explicitly ask for a name-and-claim hook. Do not spread coined language throughout ordinary body copy.

Do not confuse natural writing with factual accuracy. Check them separately:

1. VOICE: Does this sound like a person, without generic AI patterns or accidental packaging?
2. CLAIMS: Does the supplied source material support every factual claim?

Never invent facts, examples, stories, quotes, credentials, results, step counts, research, or source support. If evidence is missing, ask me for it or mark the gap plainly.

BEFORE RETURNING THE WRITING

Read the complete draft aloud and check:

- Did I get into the point?
- Did I use concrete particulars from the supplied material?
- Did I write active sentences that show who did what?
- Did I use any canned contrast, throat-clearing, corporate filler, em dashes, fake suspense, or forced groups of three?
- How many times could I naturally say “or, as I like to call it” before a phrase?
- Did I invent a name for something that could have been said normally?
- Did I preserve deliberate names already supplied by the source?
- Does every factual claim have support?
- Did I invent anything to make the writing feel complete?

Fix every problem you can before returning the draft. If a factual gap remains, identify it in one short note. Do not claim the writing passed merely because it sounds polished.

Assignment: build the project

Use the real recurring task you have carried since Day 1.

Create a Project named after that task.

Fill in every section of the House Rules Starter.

Add at least one allowed file from your Context Shelf that should apply to every chat in the Project.

Open a new chat inside the Project and make a real request without explaining your background again.

Check the first answer against the House Rules and file.

Save a screenshot.

records.content:
AI Fundamentals Sprint, Module 4 of 5

By the end of today, you will have built a small Claude Artifact, used it once, changed one specific part, and used the revised version again.

Day 1 gave you a better way to write prompts. Day 2 showed you how to find and choose source material. Day 3 put recurring instructions and files inside a Project. Today, you will use those pieces to make something you can click, type into, and test.

This session demonstrates Claude Artifacts. An Artifact is content Claude puts in a separate window beside the chat. Claude can create text documents, diagrams, simple interactive tools, and other types of Artifacts. The live build uses an interactive Artifact inside the Substack Writing Project from Day 3.

The controls and plan requirements can change. Check Anthropic's current Artifacts guide and make sure Code execution and file creation is enabled in Claude's settings.

Build a small version you can try

Planning still matters. An Artifact helps when you have an idea that would be easier to judge after you use it.

Suppose you want a tool that helps you choose an article idea and start writing. You can describe the tool for twenty minutes. You will learn more about the interface after you click the buttons, choose an idea, and type one paragraph.

The first version does not need every feature. It needs to let you perform the main action. Once you have used it, you can tell Claude exactly what was confusing, missing, or broken.

For today's live example, the main action is simple:

Enter a topic.

Choose or shuffle a writing angle.

Choose a Body format.

Write inside an outline.

Preview the essay without the instructions.

Copy the finished text.

The class will request a Download PNG button too. That button remains a requested feature until it works in the rehearsed Artifact. If it does not work reliably, the class version will use Copy Essay and leave PNG download out of the promised result.

What Claude is making

Claude's Artifact menu may show categories such as Apps and websites, Documents and templates, Games, Productivity tools, Creative projects, Quiz or survey, and Start from scratch. The wording may differ by account or product update.

Pick the category that best matches what you want to make. Then describe what a person should be able to do, ask Claude to build the smallest useful version, and test it yourself.

An Artifact is different from a downloadable Word, PDF, PowerPoint, or Excel file. Claude can create those files through a separate file-creation feature. It is also different from a Project. The Project holds the standing instructions and files for the work. The Artifact is the document or interactive tool Claude creates in a chat.

Four mistakes to avoid

Describing the finished product before testing the first screen

A long feature list gives Claude more chances to misunderstand the job. Start with the one action the person must complete. Add another feature after the main action works.

Reviewing the code instead of using the Artifact

You do not need to understand the code to test the result. Click every button. Enter real text. Try the normal path and one obvious mistake. Check what appears on screen.

Asking Claude to “make it better”

Claude has to guess what “better” means. State what happened and what you want instead.

Write: “When I click Shuffle angle, the text I already wrote disappears. Keep every writing field unchanged when the angle changes.”

Changing several things before testing again

If Claude changes the layout, buttons, writing structure, and export at once, you may not know which change fixed the problem or caused a new one. Ask for one important change, then use the Artifact again.

Build and revise an Artifact

Use the real Project you set up on Day 3. If you did not make one, you can build in a normal Claude chat, but the chat will not have your Project instructions or Project Knowledge.

1. Choose one action to test

Finish this sentence:

I want a person to use this Artifact to [complete one action].

2. Give Claude the source material and the build request

Open a new chat inside the correct Project. Add any material that applies only to this build in the chat. Keep standing instructions and approved reference files in Project Knowledge.

Tell Claude:

  • who will use the Artifact;

  • what that person needs to do;

  • what information and exact names it must use;

  • what appears on each screen;

  • what each button does;

  • what must never disappear or change;

  • what should appear in the final copy or download; and

  • what you will test.

The live build prompt appears later in this lesson.

3. Use the first version

Do not start by asking Claude for an explanation of its work. Use the Artifact.

Find out what’s awkward, what’s smooth, what you like and don’t like.

You also might want to think about what you would want to do NEXT with the information or result of the artifact.

4. Fixing it: write down one concrete problem

Describe what you did, what happened, and what should happen instead.

I clicked [control] after I had typed [content].
The Artifact [what happened].
Change it so [specific result].
Keep [anything that must stay unchanged].

This gives Claude a test it can act on.

5. Ask for that change

Paste the problem into the same chat. Tell Claude to update the existing Artifact. Do not ask it to rebuild the whole tool unless the first version cannot perform the main action.

Claude may create another Artifact version. Use the version controls in the Artifact window to compare the earlier and revised versions when those controls are available.

6. Use the revised version

Repeat the action that failed. Then check the rest of the main path. A fixed button does not help if the revision erased the writing surface or changed the required section names.

Keep the revised version only if it works better in your test.

Once you’ve done this a couple times, you can loop through more than one problem at a time, take notes on all of them, and assemble them into a “Hit List” for Claude to fix all in one go. It’s just easier if you have done it a couple times. Enough for you to know that Claude will give you what you want when you correct it.

Frequently Asked Questions

“Do I need to know how to code?”

No. You need to describe what the person should be able to do and test the result. If Claude shows code, you can return to the Artifact preview and use it.

“How complete should the first version be?”

It should perform the main action from beginning to end. It can look plain. Add another feature after that path works.

“What if Claude changes something I wanted to keep?”

Return to an earlier Artifact version if one is available. Then name the exact change and the exact parts that must stay unchanged. Keep a separate copy of important text outside Claude.

“Can I share or publish the Artifact?”

Publishing and sharing depend on your Claude plan. On Free, Pro, and Max, Publish creates a public link. On Team and Enterprise, Share limits access to your organization. If the Artifact came from a Project, viewers also need access to that Project. Team and Enterprise viewers can also access attachments and files in the conversation that created the Artifact. Check Anthropic's current publishing and sharing guide, remove private material, and confirm that you have permission to share every source. Publishing or sharing is optional for this assignment.

“What if a button does not work?”

Describe the failed action and ask Claude to repair it. If one repair does not work during class, use the saved rehearsal version and continue. Remove an unreliable optional feature from the assignment.

Assignment: build and test one Artifact

Use a real idea from your work or life.

Write the one action a person should complete with the Artifact.

Open the correct Project or a new chat.

Give Claude the source material, exact names, screen contents, button behavior, and constraints it needs.

Ask Claude to build the smallest useful Artifact.

Use it from beginning to end with real input.

Write down one concrete problem.

Ask Claude to change that part while keeping the rest unchanged.

Repeat the failed action and the main path.

Keep the conversation in Claude and save a screenshot of the revised result. Copy or download the finished content if the Artifact supports it.

You are done when:

  • The Artifact exists.

  • You can enter the intended input.

  • You can complete the main action.

  • You recorded one problem from actual use.

  • Claude changed that specific part.

  • You tested the revised version.

  • You saved evidence of the Artifact and the result.

Before sharing a screenshot or Artifact, remove names, contact details, account information, client material, private family information, and source text you do not have permission to republish.

Close

You do not have to settle every product decision before Claude builds the first version. Build one useful path, use it, identify one problem, change that part, and use it again.

Keep the result and the source material somewhere you control. The Artifact is a working version, not the only copy of important writing or data.

records.content:
AI Fundamentals Sprint, Module 5 of 5

By the end of today, you will have connected Google Drive, Gmail, and Canva to Claude. You will test each connection with one small request. Then you will use material from Drive and Gmail in the writing Artifact from Day 4 and use Canva to create a visual from the checked essay.

You already have the pieces. Day 1 covered prompts. Day 2 covered source material, and Day 3 put recurring instructions and files inside a Project. On Day 4, you used that Project to build and revise an Artifact.

Today adds the apps. Claude will retrieve material from them, but you will check what it finds and read every approval request.

This session uses Google Drive, Gmail, and Canva in Claude. Availability can depend on your account and administrator.

What a connector does

A connector lets Claude request information or actions from another app. Ask for a specific file, message, or design, read the approval request, and check the source Claude used.

These three connections serve different purposes:

  • Google Drive can retrieve files available to the connected Google account.

  • Gmail retrieves a specific message or thread.

  • Canva creates or updates a visual after you have checked the words.

Google Drive can read Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, PDFs, images, and Microsoft Office files. Saving a generated file requires Code execution and file creation. From a Google Doc, Claude extracts the main text only; it misses embedded images, comments, and suggestions.

Gmail can search and read messages. It can create a draft but cannot send it. For an attachment, Gmail supplies the name and other metadata only.

Canva can search, create, autofill, resize, and export designs. The available controls and results depend on the Canva account and the connector. A request to create or export a design is not complete until you open the result and inspect it.

Connect the right accounts

Use accounts with safe demonstration material. Do not share a screen while Claude searches private or unrelated material.

For each connection:

In Claude, go to Customize → Connectors, or click the + beside the chat and open Connectors.

Select the connector and choose Connect.

Read the permissions shown by Google or Canva.

Confirm the account name and email address before approving.

Return to Claude and make sure that connector is enabled for the current chat.

If you use a Team or Enterprise account, an Owner or Primary Owner may need to enable a connector before you can authenticate. A Google Workspace administrator may also need to allow Claude as a trusted app.

Claude can only reach information the connected account can already access. On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner can also mark connector actions Always allow, Needs approval, or Blocked. Keep write actions on Needs approval for this class when that setting is available. A student cannot override a blocked action.

Under + → Connectors, make sure the connector is turned on for this conversation. If you have many connectors active, Connectors → Tool access controls whether Claude loads them automatically or on demand. The exact wording may differ as Claude changes.

Choose material that belongs in this chat

Google connector material that Claude retrieves is retained with the associated chat on Anthropic's servers. Deleting the chat deletes that retrieved material. On Team and Enterprise plans, use connectors in private Projects; chats containing synced connector material cannot be shared.

Google, Canva, and other connected services also process information under their own terms. Anthropic says it does not train its models on Gmail, Drive, or Calendar connector data. For consumer accounts that opted into model improvement, material you manually paste from those services, or connector-specific material repeated in Claude's answer, may be covered by that choice.

Use the account, Project, source, and chat that fit the material. Keep private client, family, health, financial, credential, and account information out of the classroom demonstration.

Test each connection

Do one small test before combining the apps. Replace every bracketed field before sending a prompt.

The simplest way to do this is to ask it for context you know is there.

Specifically with the word “Read”

Check every approval request when starting

Claude may ask for approval before it searches, reads, drafts, creates, edits, or exports through a connector. Read the request instead of clicking through it.

Before approving, check:

  • the app Claude wants to use;

  • the account connected to that app;

  • the information it will read;

  • the action it wants to take;

  • whether the request matches your prompt; and

  • whether the source or result is safe to show and retain in the chat.

An approval covers the action shown. Searching Gmail does not authorize Claude to create a draft. Finding a Canva design does not authorize Claude to edit it.

Use the three connections together

The live demonstration starts inside the Substack Writing Project from Day 3. Use a private Substack Writing Project for this demonstration. Connector-backed material does not belong in a shared Project. Drive files can be added to Project Files in a private Project, but not a shared Project.

The Day 4 Artifact should already let you choose an idea, write inside the Atomic Essay sections, preview the essay, and copy the finished text. Keep a separate copy of any writing you cannot afford to lose.

1. Retrieve the reader question from Gmail

Search my Gmail for the message with this exact subject:
[EXACT SUBJECT LINE]

Use only the matching message from [EXPECTED SENDER].
Return the reader's question exactly as written, followed by the sender and date.
Do not use attachment content.
Do not search unrelated messages.
Do not draft or send an email.

Open the cited message and confirm that Claude copied the correct question.

2. Retrieve the approved writing material from Drive

Search my Google Drive for this exact file:
[EXACT FILE TITLE OR GOOGLE DRIVE URL]

Use only this file.
Pull the sections that directly help answer this reader question:

[PASTE THE CHECKED READER QUESTION]

For each useful point, give me:
- the point in plain language;
- the heading or section where you found it; and
- the source link, if available.

Separate statements supported by the file from suggestions you are making.
Do not invent facts, quotations, examples, personal experience, or results.
Do not edit or share the Drive file.

Open the source and check each point. Remove anything that is not supported or that you do not have permission to use.

3. Draft inside the Day 4 writing Artifact

Work inside the Substack Writing Project. Put the checked question and Drive notes in the same chat as the Artifact.

Use the reader question and checked Drive notes below to draft one essay inside the existing Day 4 writing Artifact.

READER QUESTION:
[PASTE THE CHECKED QUESTION]

APPROVED DRIVE NOTES:
[PASTE THE CHECKED NOTES]

Use the existing Artifact and its exact section names. Do not rename the writing angles, Body formats, Atomic Essay sections, or buttons.

Write:
- one proposed headline;
- an opening of 2 or 3 sentences; and
- a Body of 200 to 220 words.

Answer the reader's actual question.
Use only the supplied notes for factual claims.
Do not invent a personal story, quotation, statistic, customer example, or result.
Do not erase text already in the Artifact.
Do not publish, upload, or email the essay.

If Claude cannot edit the existing Artifact safely, ask it to return the draft in chat and paste the checked text into the Artifact yourself.

4. Check the essay before Canva receives it

Check this essay against the reader question and approved Drive notes.

READER QUESTION:
[PASTE THE CHECKED QUESTION]

APPROVED DRIVE NOTES:
[PASTE THE CHECKED NOTES]

ESSAY:
[PASTE THE COMPLETE ESSAY]

Return:
1. Any sentence that is not supported by the supplied notes.
2. Any sentence that does not help answer the reader's question.
3. Any invented quotation, statistic, example, experience, or result.
4. Any important point from the notes that the essay missed.
5. A corrected essay that changes only the problems you identified.

Do not add new facts.

Read the corrected essay yourself. Confirm names, quotations, numbers, links, and claims against the original source. Claude's check does not replace yours.

5. Create the Canva visual

Use the checked essay, not the first draft.

Inspect the preview. Check the words, cropping, contrast, spacing, and dimensions. Then make a separate export request:

Optional: create a Gmail draft

After checking the recipient, subject, and body, you may ask:

Create a Gmail draft using exactly the recipient, subject, and body below. Do not add anything. Create the draft only. Do not send it.

Open Gmail and inspect the saved draft. Claude cannot send it.


Four mistakes to avoid

Searching an entire account when you know the source

Use an exact title, sender, subject, date, or URL. A broad search can expose unrelated information and makes the result harder to verify.

Using the answer without opening the source

Claude can retrieve the wrong file or thread. Open the cited source and compare it with the answer before using it.

Treating approval as a routine click

Read the app, account, data, and action every time; reject any approval request broader than your prompt.

Sending the first draft to another app

Check the essay before Canva or Gmail receives it. Fix unsupported claims and private material while the text is still easy to review.

Frequently Asked Questions

“Does connecting Gmail let Claude send email?”

No. Claude can read permitted Gmail messages and create drafts with your approval. It cannot send them. You must send a draft manually in Gmail.

“Can Gmail read an attached PDF?”

Gmail supplies attachment metadata, not attachment contents. Use a permitted copy through Drive or upload the file directly.

“Can I add a Drive file to my Project?”

Yes, in a private Project. Open the Project Files section, choose + → Drive, and select a recent file or paste its URL. The Drive option is disabled for shared Projects.

“How do I turn a connector off?”

For one chat, click the +, open Connectors, and toggle the connector off. To remove the connection, go to Customize → Connectors, open the service, and choose Disconnect. If a Google connection still fails after reconnecting, you can remove Claude from your Google account connections and authenticate again.

Assignment: connect and test all three apps
