records.content:
What is included

Two templates help you set up recurring AI work:

  • Project Setup Template: Creates ready-to-paste Project instructions, a standing-file checklist, a first chat, four starter prompts, and a cold-start test.

  • Prompt Designer: Interviews you for missing facts and returns one reusable prompt with explicit inputs, outputs, evidence rules, and checks.

Three prompts create finished artifacts from source material:

  • Quiz Builder: Builds and tests a source-grounded interactive quiz artifact.

  • Mermaid Diagram Builder: Turns notes or a process into Mermaid code artifact without inventing missing connections.

  • One-Page Visual Builder: Creates a self-contained visual explainer plus a plain-text version and test report.

Downloads

Download the five Markdown files from Resources below. Each file is also copied in full on this page.

Before using the templates

  • Replace the bracketed fields with real information.

  • Remove private information, passwords, API keys, and material you are not allowed to submit.

  • Check every factual claim against the source you supplied.

  • Test the finished quiz, diagram, or visual before giving it to someone else.

  • Product previews and artifact controls vary by plan, device, model, settings, and rollout. Use the returned code or plain-text version when an interactive preview is unavailable.

Current product references:

  • Claude artifacts

  • Claude custom visuals

  • ChatGPT writing and code blocks

  • ChatGPT canvas

Copy the templates

Project Setup Template

# Project Setup Template

Use this when you do the same kind of work more than once and keep explaining the same background to the AI.

Set up one Project for one recurring job. A Project for a weekly client update makes sense. A Project called “All My Work” does not.

## Before you paste the prompt

Have these nearby if they exist:

- a description of your role or business
- examples of past work you want the AI to follow
- current product, service, audience, or client information
- a style guide or a short list of writing preferences
- rules the AI must follow every time

Do not paste passwords, API keys, private credentials, or information you are not allowed to share.

Before adding any file, remove private details the AI does not need and confirm that you are allowed to submit the material. Check the AI provider's current data-retention and model-training controls rather than assuming what happens to an upload. If the Project is shared, verify exactly who can open it and its files.

Keep the canonical copy of your Project instructions and every source file somewhere you control outside the AI provider. The Project holds working copies, not your only copies.

## What to paste

Paste the prompt below into a new chat. Answer its questions. It will give you the instructions and files to put in your Project, plus prompts you can use once the Project is ready.

```text
Help me set up one AI Project for one recurring job.

Do not invent facts about me, my business, my customers, or the work. If something important is missing, ask me for it. Ask only for information you need to finish the setup. Never ask me to paste passwords, API keys, login details, private credentials, or information I am not allowed to share.

We need to keep two kinds of context separate:

1. PROJECT CONTEXT: information that should be true or useful in nearly every new chat for this recurring job. This belongs in the Project instructions or its standing files.
2. ONE-TIME CHAT CONTEXT: information needed for only one piece of work, such as this week's numbers, a single client request, today's notes, or a draft being revised. This should be pasted into the relevant chat, not saved as standing Project context.

Before recommending that I add a file, make sure I:

- remove private details that are not necessary for this recurring job
- verify that I have permission to submit the material
- check the provider's current retention and model-training controls
- verify who can access the Project and its files if the Project is shared
- keep the canonical instructions and source files somewhere I control outside the AI provider

Do not call the Project setup complete until I confirm that I added at least one real standing file that belongs across this recurring job. A file can be an approved example, policy, style guide, product description, or other trusted source that will remain useful across new chats. If I do not have one, mark the setup INCOMPLETE and tell me what real file I need to create or obtain. Do not invent a file or use temporary material just to satisfy this requirement.

Start by asking me only for the missing information from this list:

- The recurring job I want this Project to help with
- My role and what I actually do
- Who receives or uses the work
- What a good result looks like
- Facts and constraints that are true for nearly every instance of the job
- My usual output format, length, and tone
- Words, formats, claims, or behaviors I do not want
- Trusted files or examples I already have and where they came from
- Any approval, privacy, legal, or accuracy rules that apply every time

If I give you a mix of standing information and one-time details, sort them and show me where each belongs. If you are unsure whether something will remain true, ask me instead of guessing.

Once you have enough information, produce all seven sections below.

1. PROJECT NAME

Give me one plain name based on the recurring job, such as “Weekly Client Update” or “New Customer Welcome Emails.” Do not name it after the AI tool. Do not invent a branded name.

2. PROJECT INSTRUCTIONS

Write instructions I can paste directly into the Project's instructions area. Use these headings:

WHO I AM
WHO THIS WORK IS FOR
WHAT THIS PROJECT HELPS ME DO
ALWAYS ASSUME
HOW I WANT THE WORK
NEVER DO
WHEN TO ASK ME

Use only facts I supplied. Make each instruction specific enough to change the answer. Do not include one-time details.

3. STANDING FILE CHECKLIST

Make a table with these columns:

- File or information to add
- Where I should get it
- Why it belongs in the Project
- What should stay out

Recommend only material relevant to nearly every chat for this job. If I do not have a useful file, say “Not available yet”; do not pretend it exists. Exclude passwords, credentials, restricted information, temporary notes, current-week data, and other one-time material.

For every file, tell me to use a working copy with unnecessary private details removed, confirm I am allowed to submit it, and retain the canonical source outside the AI provider. After the table, state one of these:

- SETUP STATUS: COMPLETE — I confirmed that at least one real standing file has been added.
- SETUP STATUS: READY TO FINISH — a real standing file is ready, but I have not confirmed that it was added.
- SETUP STATUS: INCOMPLETE — no real standing file is ready yet, followed by the specific file I need to create or obtain.

4. FIRST CHAT PROMPT

Write one prompt for the first chat in the Project. It should ask the AI to:

- read the Project instructions and available standing files
- state what it understands about the recurring job
- identify missing or conflicting standing context
- help me define a simple process for doing the job well
- produce a short Project brief containing any confirmed information that should be added to the instructions or saved as a standing file

Make clear that a useful conclusion from this chat does not automatically become standing Project context. I must deliberately add it to the instructions or save it as a standing file if I want it available later.

5. FOUR STARTER PROMPTS FOR NEW CHATS

Write four short, reusable prompts tailored to my job:

- Produce the next piece of work using one-time information I paste into that chat
- Review a draft against my usual requirements
- Turn raw notes or source material into the normal output
- Update the Project after a real change to the standing facts or rules

Put obvious placeholders in square brackets. Do not fill those placeholders with invented facts.

6. COLD-START TEST

Give me one deliberately short request to use in a brand-new chat inside the Project. State what the answer should already know from the Project context, what one-time information it may still need, and what would show that my Project instructions or files need work.

7. REVIEW CHECKLIST

Give me a short yes-or-no checklist covering:

- one recurring job only
- job-based name
- instructions use only confirmed facts
- standing and one-time context are separated
- every suggested file has a known source
- at least one real standing file is ready to add
- unnecessary private details have been removed
- I am allowed to submit each file
- I checked the provider's current retention and model-training controls
- I verified who can access the Project if it is shared
- canonical instructions and source files remain somewhere I control outside the AI provider
- no secrets or restricted information
- hard rules are specific
- starter prompts contain clear placeholders
- cold-start test checks the Project instead of testing hidden facts

Write in plain English. Give me material I can copy and use, not an explanation of your process.
```

## Illustrative example

The company and details below are fictional. They show what a completed result can look like; they are not facts about your business.

### Project name

Weekly Client Update

### Project instructions

```text
WHO I AM
I am the account manager at Northstar Studio, a fictional five-person web design agency. I coordinate client work and send the weekly update.

WHO THIS WORK IS FOR
The update goes to small-business clients who are not web developers. They need to understand what changed, what happens next, and whether they owe us anything.

WHAT THIS PROJECT HELPS ME DO
Help me turn the week's project notes into a client update that is accurate, easy to scan, and ready for my review.

ALWAYS ASSUME
- The update covers work completed, work planned next, decisions needed, and risks or delays.
- The source notes may use technical language that clients will not understand.
- I review and approve every update before it is sent.
- Missing dates, decisions, or status details must be called out rather than guessed.

HOW I WANT THE WORK
Use plain English. Keep the update under 300 words unless I ask otherwise. Use four headings: Completed, Next, Decisions Needed, and Risks. Use bullets under each heading. Be direct and calm.

NEVER DO
- Do not claim work is finished unless the notes say it is finished.
- Do not invent dates, owners, results, or reasons for a delay.
- Do not use agency jargon such as “circle back,” “synergy,” or “move the needle.”
- Do not send anything. Draft it for my approval.

WHEN TO ASK ME
Ask when the notes conflict, when a promised date is missing, or when you cannot tell whether an item is safe to share with the client.
```

### Standing file checklist

| File or information to add | Where it should come from | Why it belongs in the Project | What should stay out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approved weekly-update examples | Updates previously approved and sent by the account manager | Shows the normal structure and level of detail | An unusual crisis update that should not become the default |
| Current service description | The agency's approved proposal or service guide | Explains what the agency normally does for clients | Pricing or contract terms that differ by client |
| Writing preferences | The account manager's own notes or an approved style guide | Applies to every weekly update | A one-time request from one client |
| Confidentiality rules | The agency's approved internal policy | Prevents private internal details from entering client drafts | Passwords, credentials, private keys, or access links |
| This week's project notes | Do not add as a standing file; get them from the project manager each week | They are needed for one update only | Keep them in that week's chat instead |

For this fictional example, assume the account manager has an actual approved update file named `Approved-Weekly-Update-Example.md`. A working copy with unnecessary client details removed is ready to add, but the account manager has not confirmed that it was added, so the example's status is:

**SETUP STATUS: READY TO FINISH — one real standing file is ready, but it has not been confirmed as added.**

Before adding it, the account manager still needs to confirm the agency permits the upload, check the provider's current retention and model-training controls, and verify who can access the Project if it is shared. The approved original, the Project instructions, and the other source files stay in the agency's own storage; the Project receives working copies.

### First chat prompt

```text
Read the Project instructions and the standing files available here. Tell me what you understand about the weekly client-update job, then list any missing or conflicting standing information.

Help me define a simple process from receiving the week's notes through my final approval. Do not draft an update yet.

Finish with a short Project brief containing only confirmed information that would be useful in future chats. Label each proposed addition as either “add to Project instructions” or “save as a standing file.” Nothing from this chat becomes standing context unless I deliberately add or save it.
```

### Four starter prompts

**Draft the next update**

```text
Draft this week's client update using the Project instructions and the one-time notes below. Call out anything important that is missing or contradictory. Do not invent details.

CLIENT: [client name]
WEEK ENDING: [date]
THIS WEEK'S NOTES:
[paste notes]
```

**Review a draft**

```text
Review the draft below against the Project instructions. List factual gaps or rule violations first. Then give me a corrected draft. Preserve confirmed facts and do not invent missing information.

[paste draft]
```

**Turn raw notes into the normal format**

```text
Sort these raw notes under Completed, Next, Decisions Needed, and Risks. Mark anything you cannot place confidently. Then draft the update in our normal format.

[paste raw notes]
```

**Update standing context**

```text
One of our standing facts or rules has changed:

[describe the confirmed change and its source]

Show me the exact line or section of the Project instructions that should change. Do not alter unrelated instructions. Tell me whether any standing file also needs to be replaced. I will make the change after reviewing it.
```

### Cold-start test

Open a brand-new chat inside the Project and type:

```text
Turn these notes into this week's client update:

[paste three to five fictional or non-sensitive test notes]
```

The answer should already know the four headings, the intended reader, the length, the plain-English style, and that it must not invent facts or send the update. It may still need the client name, week-ending date, and that week's real notes because those are one-time details.

If it asks what format to use, writes for a technical reader, invents a deadline, or acts as though it can send the update, fix the relevant Project instruction and run the test again in another new chat.

## What to check before you use the Project

- Is this Project responsible for one recurring job?
- Is its name the job, not the name of the AI?
- Does every standing fact come from you or a source you trust?
- Is at least one real standing file ready to add? If not, the setup is still incomplete.
- Did you keep this week's details and other one-time material out of the Project files?
- Did you remove private details the AI does not need and confirm you are allowed to submit every file?
- Did you check the provider's current retention and model-training controls?
- If the Project is shared, did you verify who can open it and its files?
- Are the canonical instructions and source files also stored somewhere you control outside the AI provider?
- Do the instructions say what the output should look like?
- Do the hard rules prevent specific mistakes?
- Do the prompts leave unknown details as placeholders?
- Does the cold-start test prove the AI knows the standing context without expecting it to know this week's facts?
- If something changed, did you update the instructions or standing file instead of assuming one chat changed the Project?

Prompt Designer

# Prompt Designer

Use this when you have a job you expect to give AI more than once and you want one prompt you can save, test, and improve.

Good uses include:

- turning meeting notes into the same kind of follow-up every week;
- reviewing sales calls against the same standards;
- drafting content from your own source material;
- comparing options with the same decision criteria; or
- fixing a copied prompt so it works for your business instead of somebody else's.

You do not need this for every question. If you want a definition, a quick summary, or an answer you can easily check, ask the question directly. Use the Prompt Designer when the output matters enough that you need to specify the inputs, steps, evidence, and checks.

## What to paste

1. Copy the full Prompt Designer prompt below into a new AI chat.
2. Under `MY REQUEST`, describe the job you want the saved prompt to do.
3. Paste any current prompt, real examples, required facts, or rules you already have.
4. Answer only the follow-up questions that the AI asks. If it already has enough information, it should build the prompt without interviewing you.

You can write your request in plain English. For example: “Build me a prompt that turns a customer interview transcript into a one-page research summary. Keep the customer's exact words separate from my conclusions.”

Before pasting anything, remove passwords, API keys, financial details, health information, or other private data the AI does not need. Submit only material you are allowed to use and reuse. Building a prompt does not give the AI permission to publish, send, or share the result.

## The Prompt Designer prompt

```text
You help me turn a recurring task, rough process, or existing prompt into one complete prompt I can save and reuse.

Your job is to make the task executable. Tell the model what work to do, what information it will receive, what it must return, and how the result will be checked. Do not give it an impressive-sounding persona as a substitute for instructions. A plain functional description such as “Review this transcript” is usually enough.

## What I may give you

I may provide any combination of:

- a plain-language description of the job;
- an existing prompt that needs repair;
- source material the prompt will receive;
- rules, constraints, or output requirements;
- real examples of good or bad work; and
- facts about my business, audience, process, or tools.

Use everything I have already supplied in this chat. Do not ask me to repeat it.

## Choose the route

Infer the route from my request. Ask one short routing question only if you genuinely cannot tell which route I want.

### Full Build

Use this when I give you a task, process, or desired result and want a new reusable prompt.

### Audit & Rebuild

Use this when I paste an existing prompt and ask you to review, fix, improve, or rebuild it.

Before changing it:

1. Rate each part of NITAR as `Strong`, `Weak`, or `Missing` in a compact table. Give one evidence-based reason for each rating.
   - N: Job, scope, inputs, and outputs
   - I: Objective, instructions, order, and completion condition
   - T: Necessary areas of work or judgment
   - A: Measurable rules and checks
   - R: Real references, examples, or precise placeholders
2. State exactly what you recommend preserving and exactly what you recommend changing.
3. Ask me to confirm the repair scope before you rebuild anything.
4. After confirmation, ask only for information required to repair the weak or missing parts.
5. Preserve strong wording and working behavior unless a confirmed change is required to keep the prompt coherent.
6. Return the complete rebuilt prompt after running the checks below.

If I refer to a prompt you cannot access, ask me to paste it. Do not claim to have reviewed a file, link, or prompt you could not read.

### Single Block

Use this when I ask you to create or replace only one NITAR block:

- N: Job, name, identity, role, or persona
- I: Instructions, intent, objective, or task
- T: Training, components, skills, modules, or judgment areas
- A: Attributes, rules, criteria, standards, or guardrails
- R: References, examples, samples, or benchmarks

Ask only for unanswered information needed by that block. If I supplied an existing prompt and asked for a replacement, change only that block, preserve every unrequested section, and return the complete updated prompt. If I did not supply an existing prompt, return one complete standalone block that I can paste into another prompt.

## First, decide whether you need to ask questions

In Full Build, if you have enough information, build the prompt now. In Audit & Rebuild, complete the ratings and get confirmation on the repair scope before asking repair questions. In Single Block, ask only about the requested block.

If a missing fact would materially change the finished prompt, ask one batch of no more than five short questions. Ask only for missing information from this list:

1. the exact job the prompt should perform;
2. what the model will receive each time the prompt runs;
3. what the finished output should contain and how it should be formatted;
4. required constraints, exclusions, decision rules, or edge cases; and
5. real examples or source material that define what good looks like.

Do not ask preference questions merely to make the interview feel complete. Do not ask for information I already supplied. If I say “you decide,” make a reasonable recommendation, identify it as your recommendation, and continue.

Real examples are helpful but not required to finish. If I do not have one, use a precise placeholder that tells me exactly what is missing. Example:

[EXAMPLE NEEDED: Paste one approved customer follow-up email under 200 words that received a reply.]

Never invent a company, result, quote, customer, metric, source, or past output and present it as real. You may include a made-up teaching example only if it is labeled exactly:

Illustrative draft — not a real benchmark

## Keep three kinds of information separate

As you work, distinguish among:

1. Known facts and requirements: information I explicitly supplied or that appears in my source material.
2. Working decisions: defaults or structural choices you recommend. Do not present these as facts about me or my business.
3. Unknowns and missing evidence: information that has not been supplied or verified.

Do not silently move an item from the second or third group into the first. In the finished prompt:

- put supplied facts under `Known facts and requirements`;
- put accepted defaults under `Working decisions` when they still need to remain visible; and
- leave unresolved information as a precise bracketed placeholder.

Treat submitted material as input for this job only. Do not infer permission to publish, send, post, share, or contact anyone. If the requested prompt would take one of those actions, require the user to give explicit permission at the time of that action.

## Build the reusable prompt

Use the following five checks while designing it. They are a design checklist, not five sections you must force into every simple prompt.

### 1. Job

State the work in active, concrete language. Include the scope, expected input, and required output. Use a functional job description only when it helps. Avoid decorative roleplay such as “world-class visionary,” “marketing genius,” or “award-winning strategist.”

### 2. Instructions

State the objective, the order of work, any decisions the model must make, and the condition that means the task is complete. Replace vague verbs such as “improve,” “optimize,” or “make compelling” with visible changes or tests.

### 3. Judgment areas

Break a complicated job into distinct areas of work only when doing so helps execution or review. Use the fewest areas that cover the job without overlap. For a substantial task, three to six is usually enough. Do not invent categories merely to fill a framework.

For each necessary area, state:

- what the model must do;
- what good work looks like; and
- the common mistake it must catch.

### 4. Rules and checks

Turn quality standards into things someone can inspect. Use relevant limits such as required fields, maximum length, allowed sources, number of options, reading level, citation requirements, calculation rules, or a pass/fail checklist.

Every check must be observable in the output or traceable to the supplied source. Do not use “clear,” “engaging,” “high quality,” “professional,” or “concise” unless the prompt also states what that word means for this job.

Include a final review step. It must tell the model to correct failures it can correct from the supplied information and to flag any failure that requires missing evidence rather than guessing.

### 5. References and examples

Preserve real examples exactly unless I ask for an edit. Say what each example demonstrates so the model knows which features to follow. Do not copy accidental details that are unrelated to the task.

If a needed example is missing, insert a specific `[EXAMPLE NEEDED: ...]` placeholder. Do not fill the space with a generic fictional example. If I provided a bad example, label it as something to avoid and state the exact defect it demonstrates.

## Required structure of the prompt you return

Adapt the headings to the job, but make sure the finished prompt contains all applicable information below:

1. `Job` — the exact task in active language.
2. `What you will receive` — required inputs and accepted formats.
3. `What you will return` — exact deliverables, order, format, and limits.
4. `Known facts and requirements` — only facts and rules I supplied.
5. `Working decisions` — only recommendations or defaults that still need to be visible. Omit this section if none remain.
6. `Steps` — the execution order and decision points.
7. `Checks` — observable pass/fail criteria and the final review.
8. `References and examples` — real supplied material or precise missing-example placeholders. Omit this section only when examples would not improve the task.
9. `Input for this run` — clear placeholders showing what I should paste each time I reuse the prompt.

Use as much structure as the job needs and no more. A straightforward recurring task may need a short prompt. A task involving several inputs, judgment calls, and examples may need a longer one.

## Before you return it

Check the prompt silently and repair anything you can repair without inventing information:

- The job is explicit and written in active voice.
- Inputs and outputs are unambiguous.
- Steps appear in the order they should be performed.
- Separate areas of work do not duplicate each other.
- Every quality rule can be checked.
- Supplied examples remain intact and are tied to the relevant instruction.
- No invented information is presented as fact or real evidence.
- Every unresolved placeholder says exactly what is missing.
- The model is told what to do when the supplied information is incomplete or contradictory.
- The prompt ends with a clearly marked place for the user to paste the input for each run.

## Delivery

In Full Build, after any necessary questions have been answered, return one complete reusable prompt in one fenced text block.

In Audit & Rebuild, the diagnostic table, preservation list, change list, and repair-scope confirmation come first. After I confirm the scope and answer any necessary questions, return one complete rebuilt prompt in one fenced text block.

In Single Block, return either the complete updated prompt with only the requested block changed or one complete standalone block, depending on my request.

For the final deliverable, do not return an outline, a partial draft, or several alternatives. Do not put an explanation inside the prompt unless that explanation helps the model perform the job.

MY REQUEST:

[DESCRIBE THE JOB YOU WANT THE REUSABLE PROMPT TO DO]

[PASTE AN EXISTING PROMPT, SOURCE MATERIAL, RULES, OR REAL EXAMPLES IF YOU HAVE THEM]
```

## Illustrative example

This example is only here to show how the Prompt Designer works. It is not a real business case or a quality benchmark.

### Example request

```text
Build a reusable prompt that turns a transcript from one customer interview into a one-page research summary. I need the customer's exact words kept separate from the analysis. The summary should include the problem they described, what they have already tried, what happened, and unanswered questions. Do not invent missing answers.
```

Because that request already states the job, input, output, required sections, and evidence rule, the Prompt Designer should not stop to ask generic questions. It can produce the prompt.

### Compact example of the resulting prompt

```text
# Customer Interview Summary

## Job

Turn the supplied customer interview transcript into a one-page research summary. Report what the customer said before drawing conclusions from it.

## What you will receive

One customer interview transcript pasted as text.

## What you will return

Return these sections in order:

1. Problem described
2. What the customer has tried
3. What happened
4. Exact quotes
5. Analysis
6. Unanswered questions

Keep the complete response under 700 words.

## Known facts and requirements

- Treat the transcript as the only source of facts.
- Keep direct quotes separate from your analysis.
- Do not invent an answer when the transcript is silent.

## Steps

1. Read the complete transcript.
2. Extract the customer's statements about the problem, previous attempts, and results.
3. Copy the most useful exact quotes without changing their wording.
4. Write the analysis and label it as analysis rather than customer testimony.
5. List questions the transcript does not answer.

## Checks

- Every factual claim can be traced to the transcript.
- Text in quotation marks appears verbatim in the transcript.
- Analysis is not presented as something the customer said.
- Missing information appears under `Unanswered questions`, not as a guessed answer.
- All six required sections are present and the response is under 700 words.

## References and examples

[EXAMPLE NEEDED: Paste one approved one-page interview summary that cleanly separates direct quotes from analysis.]

## Input for this run

[PASTE THE CUSTOMER INTERVIEW TRANSCRIPT]
```

The length limit in this illustration is a working decision added to make “one page” checkable. In a real build, you could accept it, change it, or remove it.

## What to check before you save the result

- Does the opening sentence tell the AI what to do, rather than who to pretend to be?
- Does it say what you will paste in and what the AI must return?
- Are facts you supplied separated from recommendations and unresolved questions?
- Could you mark every quality check pass or fail by looking at the input and output?
- Did the Prompt Designer preserve your real examples and exact quotes?
- If no real example was available, does the placeholder say exactly what kind of example is needed?
- Does the prompt tell the AI what to do when information is missing or contradictory?
- If you requested an audit, did it show the NITAR ratings and get your approval before changing the prompt?
- If you requested one block, did it leave every other part of your prompt alone?
- Did you remove secrets and private information, and are you allowed to submit and reuse the material you pasted?
- Does the prompt require separate permission before publishing, sending, posting, sharing, or contacting anyone?
- Is every section necessary for this job? Delete anything that only makes the prompt look elaborate.

Save the resulting prompt somewhere you can find it. The next time you use it, replace the fields under `Input for this run`, run it, and compare the output against the checks.

Quiz Builder

# Quiz Builder

Use this prompt when you want Claude or ChatGPT to turn material you provide into a quiz people can complete in the chat's HTML, React, preview, or artifact environment.

It is designed for quizzes that teach as well as test. Every answer gets an explanation, and the learner can review anything they missed at the end.

## What to paste

Paste the lesson, notes, transcript, article, policy, or other source material the quiz should cover. You can also specify:

Only submit material you are allowed to use. Remove unnecessary private details, and do not paste passwords, API keys, credentials, client- or employer-confidential information, or copyrighted material you do not have permission to reuse.

- Who will take the quiz
- The topic or title
- The number of questions
- The kind of feedback you want after each answer

If you leave one of those out, the AI may ask for it. It should not make you answer questions you have already answered.

## Copy-and-paste prompt

```text
Build a self-contained interactive quiz from the material I provide below.

Before building it, check whether you know all five of these things:
1. The intended audience
2. The quiz topic or title
3. The source material the quiz must use
4. The number of questions
5. The feedback style after each answer

Ask only for information from that list that I have not supplied. If I do not choose a question count, use 5 to 15 questions based on the length and complexity of the source. If I do not choose a feedback style, use brief, plain-language feedback that explains why the answer is right or wrong.

SOURCE RULES
- Base every factual question, correct answer, and explanation on the supplied source material.
- Do not use general knowledge to fill gaps in the source.
- If the source does not support a proposed question or answer, omit it. If including an unsupported idea is necessary to satisfy an explicit request, label it clearly as not supported by the supplied source and do not score it as a factual question.
- Do not make ambiguous questions. Each scored question must have a defensible answer in the source.
- Preserve important qualifications from the source. Do not turn "may," "often," or "in this example" into an absolute claim.

QUIZ BEHAVIOR
- Create the number of questions I requested. Otherwise, create 5 to 15.
- By default, use only multiple-choice and true-or-false questions. Use matching, ordering, or short-answer questions only if I explicitly request those formats and the artifact environment supports them reliably.
- If I explicitly request short-answer questions, accept reasonable equivalent wording and show the expected answer after submission.
- Do not use a question format merely for variety if it makes the answer harder to judge or the interface harder to use.
- After each submitted answer, immediately show whether it was correct and explain why, using the supplied source.
- Prevent accidental answer changes after feedback is shown, or make any change update the score and feedback correctly.
- At the end, show the final score and a review of every missed item, including the learner's answer, the correct answer, and the explanation.
- Include a visible button labeled "Check answers" for submitting answers.
- Include a visible restart button labeled "Try again" that clears every answer, feedback message, missed-item review, and score.

ACCESSIBILITY AND PRIVACY
- Use clear labels, readable type, keyboard-accessible controls, visible focus states, and high-contrast colors.
- Do not rely on color alone to indicate right and wrong answers.
- Do not load external packages, fonts, images, scripts, APIs, or other network resources.
- Do not request, collect, store, or transmit names, email addresses, or other personal data.

BUILD AND TEST
- Create a self-contained artifact using the environment's supported HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or React capabilities.
- Put all questions, answer choices, correct answers, and explanations together in one clearly marked quiz-data section so a beginner can replace the quiz without searching through the interface code.
- Divide the code with these exact comments: `QUIZ CONTENT`, `STYLES`, and `BEHAVIOR`.
- Do not claim a feature works merely because the code exists. Test every answer path: correct answers, incorrect answers, unanswered questions, short-answer equivalents if used, completion, missed-item review, and restart.
- Check keyboard navigation and confirm the text remains understandable without color cues.
- Fix any failures you find before returning the result.

RETURN
1. The completed interactive artifact or its complete self-contained code
2. A short test report listing what you tested, what passed, and any limitation that remains
3. Exactly two suggested surgical edits I could make next. Point to the specific quiz text, question, color, or behavior to change; do not propose a rebuild.

Audience:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Quiz topic or title:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Number of questions:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Feedback style:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Source material:
[PASTE SOURCE HERE]
```

## Example request

This tiny example is deliberately simple. The facts needed to write and score the quiz are included in the request.

```text
Audience: Adults attending an introductory astronomy workshop

Quiz topic or title: A Quick Tour of Mars

Number of questions: 5

Feedback style: One or two friendly sentences explaining the answer

Source material:
- Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
- Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
- A Martian day is about 24 hours and 39 minutes long.
- Olympus Mons is a volcano on Mars.
- Liquid water is not stable on most of the present-day Martian surface, but water ice exists at the poles and below parts of the surface.
```

## What to check before you use the quiz

- Can you point to a sentence in your source for every correct answer and explanation?
- Did the AI preserve qualifications instead of making the source sound more certain than it is?
- Does every option lead to accurate feedback?
- Can you complete the quiz with a keyboard?
- Are right and wrong answers identified with words or symbols as well as color?
- Does the final score match the submitted answers?
- Does the missed-question review show the learner's answer, the correct answer, and why?
- Does restart erase the previous answers, score, and feedback?
- Does the test report describe actual checks and disclose anything the AI could not verify?

If any of those checks fail, paste the failure into the same chat and ask the AI to fix it and rerun the entire test list.

Mermaid Diagram Builder

# Mermaid Diagram Builder

Use this prompt when you want Claude or ChatGPT to turn notes, a process, or a description of a system into a Mermaid diagram you can paste into any tool that renders Mermaid.

It is designed to keep the diagram faithful to your source. If your notes leave out a step or do not explain how two parts connect, the AI should say so instead of drawing a plausible-looking connection.

## When to use it

- Map the steps and decision points in a process
- Show how information moves between people or systems
- Explain the order of a conversation, request, or handoff
- Show how something changes from one state to another
- Put dated events on a timeline

A flowchart is the default because it works for most processes and systems. The AI should use a sequence diagram, timeline, or state diagram only when the relationships in your source genuinely require one.

## What to paste

Paste the notes, process, policy, transcript excerpt, or system description you want diagrammed.

Before you paste anything, use only material you are allowed to use and remove private details the diagram does not need. Do not paste passwords, API keys, login credentials, client- or employer-confidential material, or copyrighted material you do not have permission to reuse.

Also provide:

- The point the diagram should make
- Who will read it
- Your preferred direction: left to right or top to bottom
- Any nodes that must appear
- Anything that must not appear

If you leave something out, the AI should ask only for the missing item. It should not ask you to repeat information you already supplied.

## Copy-and-paste prompt

```text
Turn the source material I provide into one valid Mermaid diagram and a plain-language explanation.

Before drawing, check whether you know all five of these things:
1. The diagram's goal
2. The intended audience
3. The source material the diagram must represent
4. The preferred orientation: left to right or top to bottom
5. Any required nodes and forbidden nodes

Ask only for information from that list that I have not supplied. Do not ask unrelated setup questions.

After those five inputs are known, estimate how many nodes the source-supported diagram needs. Use 12 nodes as the default maximum. If representing the goal accurately requires more than 12 nodes, stop and ask whether I want to split the material into smaller diagrams or simplify this diagram's scope. Do not silently omit steps, collapse distinct steps, or shorten away important meaning to stay under the limit. If I choose to split it, ask which section to draw first and return one diagram at a time.

CHOOSE THE DIAGRAM TYPE
- Use a flowchart by default.
- Use a sequence diagram only when the important point is the order of messages or handoffs between participants.
- Use a timeline only when dated or chronological events are the main relationship.
- Use a state diagram only when the source describes an item moving between named states because of events.
- Do not choose a specialized type merely to make the result look sophisticated.
- For a flowchart, use LR for left to right and TD for top to bottom.

SOURCE RULES
- Represent only steps, states, participants, dates, and connections supported by the supplied source.
- Never invent a missing step, decision, participant, date, state, or connection.
- Preserve exact source labels when they are already short and clear. Shorten a long label only when its meaning and qualifications remain intact.
- Preserve words such as "may," "usually," and "only if." Do not turn a possibility into a required step.
- Include every required node if the source supports it. If a required node is not supported by the source, do not invent it; identify the conflict after the diagram.
- Omit every forbidden node.
- If the source names something but does not establish where it belongs or what it connects to, do not guess. List it under "Uncertain or missing from the source" after the diagram.
- If the source explicitly says a relationship is uncertain, label that relationship "uncertain" in the diagram.

MERMAID RULES
- Return exactly one fenced mermaid code block. Do not split the result into several diagrams.
- Use no more than 12 nodes unless I explicitly approve a different limit after the scope question above.
- Keep node text short enough to scan.
- Give nodes simple unique IDs such as n1, n2, and n3. Keep the readable text inside quoted labels, such as n1["Manager reviews request"].
- Escape quotation marks or other punctuation that could break Mermaid syntax. Use safe quoted labels rather than punctuation-heavy IDs.
- Use only syntax supported by the selected Mermaid diagram type.
- Do not use external images, icons, JavaScript, click actions, themes, custom CSS, or experimental styling.
- Do not add decorative colors or classes. The relationships should be understandable from the shapes, labels, and arrows alone.

RETURN
1. One fenced mermaid block containing the complete diagram
2. "Why this diagram type": one or two sentences explaining the choice
3. "Legend": a plain-language explanation of the shapes, arrows, branch labels, participants, or states used
4. "What the diagram says": a brief walkthrough written for the intended audience
5. "Uncertain or missing from the source": every named item or requested connection you could not place without guessing, or "None"
6. "Checks": report the results of both checks below
7. "Plain-text outline": list every node with its Mermaid ID and readable label, followed by every connection with its source node, arrow or relationship label, and destination node. It must contain exactly the same nodes and connections as the Mermaid block and must not add an interpretation, step, or claim.
8. "Two suggested surgical edits": after items 1 through 7, provide exactly two numbered, optional edits that could improve one existing node, label, branch, or connection without rebuilding the diagram. Each suggestion must identify the exact line or node it would change and must be supported by the supplied source or be a presentation-only change such as orientation. Do not suggest a new fact or unsupported connection. If there is no useful source-supported or presentation-only change for one of the two entries, write "No surgical edit suggested" for that numbered entry rather than inventing one.

CHECK BEFORE RETURNING
- Syntax check: inspect every declaration, label, arrow, branch, and diagram-type keyword for valid Mermaid syntax. Correct any problem you find before returning the diagram.
- Coverage check: compare the finished diagram against the source, required nodes, forbidden nodes, and diagram goal. Confirm that no unsupported step or connection was added, and name anything supported by the source that was deliberately left out.
- Outline check: compare the plain-text outline line by line with the Mermaid block. Confirm that its node list and connection list are exact matches and contain no extra claims.
- Do not say the diagram rendered successfully unless you actually rendered it in an available Mermaid environment. If you could only inspect the code, say "syntax inspected" rather than "rendered."

Diagram goal:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Intended audience:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Preferred orientation:
[LEFT TO RIGHT OR TOP TO BOTTOM]

Required nodes:
[PASTE, OR WRITE NONE]

Forbidden nodes:
[PASTE, OR WRITE NONE]

Source material:
[PASTE SOURCE HERE]
```

## Example request

```text
Diagram goal:
Show the two possible paths after a manager reviews a leave request.

Intended audience:
Employees learning how leave requests are handled.

Preferred orientation:
Left to right.

Required nodes:
Manager reviews request; Employee receives confirmation.

Forbidden nodes:
Policy rewrite.

Source material:
- Employee submits request.
- Manager reviews request.
- If approved, payroll schedules paid leave and the employee receives confirmation.
- If declined, the manager sends the reason to the employee.
- HR may review unusual cases, but these notes do not say when that happens or what happens afterward.
```

## Expected diagram from that example

The wording around the code may vary, but the diagram should preserve the two supported branches and should not guess where the HR review belongs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    n1["Employee submits request"] --> n2["Manager reviews request"]
    n2 -->|Approved| n3["Payroll schedules paid leave"]
    n3 --> n4["Employee receives confirmation"]
    n2 -->|Declined| n5["Manager sends reason"]
```

The explanation should say that the arrows show the order of the process and that “Approved” and “Declined” identify the two outcomes of the manager's review. Under “Uncertain or missing from the source,” it should note that HR may review unusual cases, but the source does not say where that review connects. “Policy rewrite” should not appear anywhere in the diagram.

The matching plain-text outline should read:

```text
Nodes:
- n1: Employee submits request
- n2: Manager reviews request
- n3: Payroll schedules paid leave
- n4: Employee receives confirmation
- n5: Manager sends reason

Connections:
- n1 -> n2
- n2 -- Approved --> n3
- n3 -> n4
- n2 -- Declined --> n5
```

The response should then offer exactly two small, optional edits. For example, one could suggest changing the orientation to top to bottom for a narrow page. Another could suggest changing “Manager sends reason” to “Manager sends decline reason,” which remains supported by the supplied source. Neither suggestion should alter the diagram until the user approves it.

## What to check before you use the diagram

- Does the diagram make the point you asked it to make?
- Can you trace every node and connection back to the supplied source?
- Did the AI leave out unsupported steps instead of completing the process from general knowledge?
- Are uncertain relationships identified without being presented as fact?
- Are required nodes present when supported, and are forbidden nodes absent?
- Is the diagram at or below 12 nodes, or did you explicitly approve a larger limit?
- Are the labels short, accurate, and readable?
- Is there exactly one Mermaid code block?
- Does the first line declare the correct diagram type and orientation?
- Does the legend explain what the arrows, branches, participants, or states mean?
- Does the plain-text outline contain exactly the same nodes and connections as the Mermaid block?
- Are there exactly two optional surgical edits, each tied to an existing line and free of invented facts?
- Does the check report distinguish code inspection from an actual render test?

If the diagram fails any check, use one of the revision prompts below in the same chat.

## Revise one branch without redrawing the diagram

Use this when one branch is wrong but the rest of the diagram is accurate:

```text
Revise only the branch that begins at node [PASTE NODE ID OR EXACT LABEL].

Source correction:
[PASTE THE SOURCE THAT SUPPORTS THE CHANGE]

Required change:
[DESCRIBE THE ONE BRANCH TO ADD, REMOVE, OR CORRECT]

Keep every unrelated node ID, label, connection, diagram type, and orientation unchanged. Do not reorganize or restyle the rest of the diagram. Return the complete updated Mermaid block so I can replace the old one, then list the exact lines you changed. Run the syntax and coverage checks again, limited to the revised branch and any line it directly connects to.
```

Use this when new source material resolves an uncertainty:

```text
The source now explains one connection that was previously uncertain.

New source:
[PASTE THE NEW SENTENCE OR EXCERPT]

Connect:
[EXISTING NODE OR EXACT LABEL]

To:
[EXISTING OR NEW SOURCE-SUPPORTED NODE]

Update only that connection and any label required to represent it accurately. Preserve all unrelated lines exactly. Do not infer any additional steps from the new source. Return the complete updated Mermaid block, a one-sentence explanation of the resolved connection, and the syntax and coverage results for the changed lines.
```

One-Page Visual Builder

# One-Page Visual Builder

Use this prompt when a list, process, comparison, timeline, or set of related ideas would be easier to understand as one visual page.

It tells the AI to choose a layout from the actual relationships in your material. A sequence can become a flowchart. Two options can sit side by side. A hierarchy can become a tree. The result should fit on one screen or one printed page without shrinking the words until they are difficult to read.

This is also a good Day 4 exercise: create the page, read the finished result, then ask for one specific edit at a time instead of rebuilding the whole thing.

## What to paste

Paste the notes, lesson, process, article, transcript excerpt, or other source the page must explain. Include any of these details you already know:

Submit only material you are allowed to use. Remove unnecessary private details. Do not paste passwords, API keys, credentials, client- or employer-confidential material, or copyrighted material you do not have permission to reuse.

- Who needs to understand it
- What they should understand or do after reading it
- The source material the page must use
- Where the page will be viewed, such as a laptop screen, phone screen, letter-size PDF, or presentation slide
- Brand colors, if they matter
- Anything that must appear or must not appear

You do not need to choose the visual layout. The AI should choose it after reading the source.

## Copy-and-paste prompt

```text
Turn the source material I provide into a self-contained one-page visual explainer.

Before building it, check whether you know these six things:
1. The intended audience
2. The purpose: what the reader should understand or do after reading
3. The source material the page must use
4. The target page or screen size
5. Any brand colors to use, or permission to choose accessible neutral colors
6. Any content that must appear or must not appear

Ask only for items from that list that I have not supplied, with these defaults:
- If I omit the target, produce and validate both a common 1440 x 900 laptop-screen layout and a US Letter page layout. If the source cannot fit both faithfully and legibly, ask which target matters instead of silently dropping or shrinking content.
- If I omit brand colors, choose accessible neutral colors.
- If I omit required or forbidden content, treat each as none.

Do not ask me to choose a layout unless two materially different layouts would communicate the source equally well and the choice would affect the result.

SOURCE RULES
- Use only the supplied source for facts, numbers, quotations, names, and claims.
- Do not invent a statistic, quote, conclusion, step, benefit, label, or relationship.
- Preserve qualifications such as "may," "often," "in this example," and "as of [date]."
- If the source is incomplete or contradictory, show the limitation plainly or ask one focused question. Do not quietly repair it with general knowledge.
- Use short headings and concise copy, but do not shorten a sentence so aggressively that its meaning changes.
- Keep the title, subtitle, and any introductory or setup copy to 40 words total or fewer unless I request more.
- Include every item marked as required and exclude every item marked as forbidden.

CHOOSE THE VISUAL FROM THE MATERIAL
- First identify the relationships the reader must see.
- Use a flowchart for a sequence with decisions or branches.
- Use a timeline when dates or order over time are the point.
- Use a side-by-side comparison or table when the reader needs to compare the same attributes.
- Use a hierarchy or tree when the material contains levels, ownership, or parent-child relationships.
- Use a cycle only when the final step genuinely leads back to the first.
- Use a simple grouped layout when the ideas are related but have no honest sequence or hierarchy.
- Do not force the material into a diagram that implies a relationship the source does not support.
- Use three to five main sections when the source supports that range. If the source needs fewer or more to remain accurate, use the honest number and state the reason in the test report.

BUILD RULES
- Create one self-contained artifact in plain HTML and CSS, with inline SVG only when it materially improves the explanation.
- Do not use external packages, libraries, fonts, images, APIs, or network requests.
- Make it fit the stated target screen or page. Do not hide, scroll, clip, truncate, or conceal overflow to create the appearance of fitting.
- If the source cannot fit legibly, reduce decoration and wording first. If it still cannot fit, explain the conflict and ask what may be removed. Do not make the type unreadably small.
- Use a clear reading order, useful whitespace, and a small number of visual styles.
- Use sensible type sizes for the stated target and readable contrast between text and background.
- Do not rely on color alone to communicate order, categories, status, or meaning.
- Give diagrams and grouped sections text labels. Add an accessible name or text alternative for meaningful SVG content.
- Keep the artifact understandable when printed or viewed without decorative styling.
- Include one explicit next action when the source supports one. If it does not, write exactly: "No next action supplied".

PLAIN-TEXT VERSION
- After the visual, provide a plain-text version containing the same information in the same reading order.
- Express arrows, branches, levels, and comparisons with headings, indentation, and simple characters.
- The plain-text version is a content check and an accessible fallback. It must not introduce or omit claims.

TEST BEFORE RETURNING
1. Content coverage: compare the finished page with the source and confirm every required point is present and every forbidden item is absent.
2. Claim support: list every number and direct quote used, then confirm where it appears in the supplied source. Check the remaining claims for source support as well.
3. Layout: inspect the artifact at the stated target size and check for clipping, hidden overflow, unintended scrolling, collisions, and text that is too small to read.
4. Accessibility: check heading order, reading order, contrast, text alternatives or accessible names for meaningful graphics, and whether meaning survives without color.
5. Plain-text parity: compare the visual and plain-text versions and fix missing or added information.

Fix failures before returning the result. If your environment does not let you render or inspect the artifact at the target size, say exactly which visual checks you could not perform. Do not report an unrun check as passed.

RETURN
1. The completed visual artifact or its complete self-contained code
2. The matching plain-text version
3. A short test report covering content, claims, fit, and accessibility, including any check you could not run
4. Exactly two suggested surgical edits I could request next. Each suggestion must name the part to change and what must remain unchanged.

Audience:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Purpose:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Target page or screen:
[PASTE OR LEAVE BLANK]

Brand colors:
[PASTE OR WRITE "CHOOSE ACCESSIBLE NEUTRAL COLORS"]

Required content:
[PASTE OR WRITE "NONE"]

Forbidden content:
[PASTE OR WRITE "NONE"]

Source material:
[PASTE SOURCE HERE]
```

## Example request

This example gives the AI a process with one decision point, so a short flowchart is a sensible choice.

```text
Audience: New members of a five-person customer support team

Purpose: Help them decide what to do with a new support ticket

Target page or screen: One 1440 x 900 laptop screen

Brand colors: Navy #15324A and teal #138A8A on a light background

Required content: Show who owns each step and include the 30-minute urgent-ticket response target

Forbidden content: Do not include customer names or suggest refunds

Source material:
- New support coordinators should use this process for every new ticket.
- The support coordinator reads each new ticket and checks whether it blocks the customer from using the product.
- If the customer is blocked, mark the ticket urgent and notify the support lead. The support lead sends the first response within 30 minutes.
- If the customer is not blocked, the support coordinator places the ticket in the standard queue.
- A support specialist investigates tickets from either route and records the cause and resolution in the ticket.
- The support lead reviews any ticket that remains open after two business days.
```

### Compact expected structure

- Title and one-sentence purpose
- Start: support coordinator reads the ticket
- Decision: is the customer blocked?
  - Yes: mark urgent → notify support lead → first response within 30 minutes
  - No: place in standard queue
- Both routes join at support specialist investigation
- Final check: support lead reviews tickets still open after two business days
- Next action: apply the flow to the next new support ticket
- Small ownership key using words as well as color
- Matching plain-text flow and a test report

The finished wording and layout may differ, but it should not add escalation rules, refund authority, service guarantees, or other facts that are absent from the source.

## Two targeted edit follow-ups

Use these in the same chat after the first page exists. They follow Day 4's edit-in-place practice: name the exact change and tell the AI what must stay untouched.

```text
Change only the decision labels to full questions a new support coordinator can answer. Keep every step, owner, number, route, color, and all other wording unchanged. Recheck fit and report whether anything clips at 1440 x 900.
```

```text
Change only the ownership key and owner labels so the page remains understandable in grayscale. Do not change the process, order, wording, 30-minute target, or two-business-day review point. Recheck the visual and plain-text versions for matching content.
```

## What to check before you use the page

- Does the layout show relationships that really exist in the source?
- Can you trace every number, quotation, and factual claim back to the material you pasted?
- Did the AI preserve words that limit a claim, such as "may" or "within this example"?
- Is every required point present and every forbidden item absent?
- Is the title, subtitle, and introductory or setup copy no more than 40 words total?
- Does the page use three to five main sections when the source supports that range, or explain why a different count is necessary?
- Does it include one source-supported next action, or the exact line "No next action supplied"?
- Does the complete page fit at the requested size without scrolling, clipping, hidden text, or tiny type?
- Is the reading order obvious without depending on color?
- Do text labels explain meaningful arrows, branches, groups, and status?
- Does the plain-text version contain the same information as the visual?
- Does the test report distinguish checks the AI actually ran from checks it could not run?
- Did the AI return exactly two suggested surgical edits, each with a specific target and a hold-steady instruction?

If something is wrong, identify the exact section and the exact change. Ask the AI to leave everything else unchanged, then have it rerun the affected checks.

records.content:
AI Fundamentals Sprint, standalone bonus module

By the end of this bonus, you will have one reusable Claude Skill built from a real procedure, two different test runs, and the exact instructions you would use again.

The short distinction is:

A Project holds standing context. A Skill holds a reusable procedure.

Stop rebuilding the procedure in old chats

You find a prompt that works. A week later, you need it again.

You search through old chats, copy the longest version you can find, replace a few details, and hope you did not miss the improvement you made three conversations later.

Or you remember the idea and rewrite it from memory. This version asks for five candidates instead of seven. It forgets to label self-reported evidence. It gives you a plan before you have inspected the source.

You have a working procedure, but pieces of it are scattered across old chats. Put those steps in a Skill so you can inspect, test, edit, and run them again.

That does not make the output automatically correct. It makes the procedure visible enough to check.

What a Skill is

Anthropic describes Skills as reusable, filesystem-based resources that give Claude task-specific workflows, context, and optional supporting files. A Skill can contain:

  • a main

    SKILL.md

    instruction file;


  • reference material;

  • examples or templates;

  • scripts when exact, repeatable computation or validation is useful.

Claude does not need to read every installed Skill in full. Anthropic describes a three-stage loading process:

Claude sees the Skill's name and description.

When a request matches, Claude loads the main instructions.

It reads supporting files or runs scripts only when the task needs them.

That is why the description matters. It should say what the Skill does and when Claude should use it.

Project versus Skill

A Project and a Skill solve different problems.

Put this in the Project

Use the Project for facts that remain true across chats in that body of work:

  • who you are;

  • who the work is for;

  • the current offer, product, or goal;

  • standing files;

  • default voice and format;

  • constraints that apply to that Project.

Example: a Course Research Project might hold the course audience, curriculum, approved sources, tone, and current lesson map.

Put this in the Skill

Use the Skill for the procedure you want Claude to follow when a particular job appears:

  • what should trigger the procedure;

  • required inputs;

  • ordered steps;

  • evidence rules;

  • output structure;

  • quality checks;

  • what to do when information is missing.

Example: the Context Hunter Skill tells Claude how to find and verify people and sources, no matter which suitable Project you use it in.

Do not stuff one client's name, this month's campaign, or one Project's private facts into a general research procedure. Let the Project hold the standing situation. Let the Skill hold the reusable steps.

Why use a Skill

You can run the same procedure again

You no longer have to recover the best prompt from a long thread. The current procedure has a name and a file.

You can inspect what Claude was told to do

If the result misses a rule, open the Skill. Find the instruction that should have prevented the miss. Clarify it, then test again.

You can separate procedure from one situation

The same source-finding procedure may help with course research, a buying decision, or learning a new skill. The Project changes. The procedure can remain the same.

You can keep the main instructions short

The main file should guide the work. Long examples, detailed reference material, and templates can live in supporting files that Claude reads when needed.

Do not add a script because a Skill feels more legitimate with code in it. Use plain instructions for work that requires judgment. Use a script when an exact operation or check needs to behave the same way every time.

Four mistakes to avoid

Saving one giant prompt without finding the procedure

A wall of text may contain inputs, background, examples, output rules, and one-time facts mixed together.

Before you make the Skill, separate them. Ask:

  • What job repeats?

  • What changes every run?

  • What stays true only inside this Project?

  • What steps and checks belong every time this job runs?

Mixing standing context into the reusable instructions

“Our customer is a first-time founder named Jordan” may belong in one Project. “Ask for the learner's current level before finding sources” belongs in the procedure.

If a detail changes when you move to another Project, it probably does not belong in the reusable Skill.

Leaving the finish line vague

“Research this well” gives Claude nothing you can check.

The Context Hunter names the required output: exact searches, a candidate table, a shortlist, and one source to retrieve first. It also tells Claude to stop before summarizing the selected source or building a plan.

Calling it finished after one good answer

One lucky run proves very little.

Test the Skill with one normal input and one meaningfully different input. Also test a request that should not trigger it. Save the outputs. Check them against the rules. Fix the instructions when the results expose a miss.

Build a Skill from a real procedure

Use the steps below for the Context Hunter demonstration and for your own assignment.

1. Name the repeated job

Write one sentence with a verb.

“Do research” is too broad. The sentence above tells us where this procedure starts and where it stops.

2. State when Claude should use it

Use words a person would naturally say:

  • “Find me someone I can learn this from.”

  • “Find the best source to retrieve first.”

  • “Research teachers and resources for this skill.”

  • “Use Context Hunter for this topic.”

Also name requests that do not belong:

  • summarizing a source already supplied;

  • writing a lesson from a source;

  • making a plan from material already chosen;

  • recommending people from memory when web access is unavailable.

Put the positive use case in the Skill description so Claude can discover it. Put the detailed boundaries in the instructions.

3. Name the required inputs

The Context Hunter needs five fields:

My goal.

My current level.

The result I need.

My constraints.

Source types I can use.

The procedure should ask for any missing field before researching. Do not make Claude guess the learner's budget, level, deadline, or acceptable source type.

4. Decide whether the Skill needs supporting files

Start with one

SKILL.md

. It should contain the operating procedure:


  • collect the five inputs;

  • confirm web access;

  • search and verify;

  • keep ability separate from evidence of teaching;

  • return the four required sections;

  • run the checks;

  • stop.

The initial Context Hunter example keeps the full research rules and exact output columns in one

SKILL.md

. It is still short enough to inspect as one file, and no extra file is required for v1.0. The walkthrough below shows the one instruction changed after Test 1 and the final v1.1 upload bundle.


If the procedure grows, move long examples, templates, policies, or domain references into supporting files and link them directly from

SKILL.md

. Do not split a short Skill merely to make the folder look more technical.


A simple folder could look like this:

context-hunter/
└── SKILL.md

For a portable starter, use uppercase

SKILL.md

, a lowercase-hyphenated name, and a short description that says what the Skill does and when to use it. Anthropic's current pages disagree on some validation details; the caveat section below explains that conflict.


5. Write the name and description

The opening metadata can be this plain:

---
name: context-hunter
description: Finds verified people and inspectable sources for a learning or research goal. Use when the user asks who to learn from or which source to retrieve first.
---

Do not write

description: Helps with research.

Claude needs enough information to decide when the Skill applies.


6. Write the steps in order

Step by step, with no steps skipped

7. Define the checks and retry behavior

Before Claude presents the result, it should check that everything you ask for has been done.

For example, In the AI Hunter skill, when rewrites are made to a piece of content, it runs the check AFTER the initial hunting to make sure that the regenerated text is not worse than the initial text.

If a check fails, Claude should fix the specific missing field or label and run the checklist again. It should not hide the miss with smoother prose.

8. Build the reusable files

If you are building the skill IN Claude, you can simply prompt claude to

Turn this into a skill

And the model will assemble what you need.

9. To make it portable, ALWAYS use a zip file.

Files that end in a.skill extension are not portable. If you try to click on them in Notion or in another web browser, it'll open a site that looks like absolute gibberish.

Always share and upload your skills as .zip files

That way, even if the person assembling it did something wrong, you can drop the whole zip file into whichever AI chat you are using, and it can rebuild it natively within the harness that you want.

Current Claude caveats

Anthropic's current documentation does not give one perfectly consistent set of instructions. Treat the stable concept as settled and the interface details as recording-day checks.

Filename, name, and description rules conflict

The Platform overview says:

  • use

    SKILL.md

    ;


  • require

    name

    and

    description

    ;


  • use a lowercase-hyphenated name;

  • keep the description within 1,024 characters.

The Help Center creation article currently shows different details, including

skill.md

, a human-friendly name example, and a shorter description limit.


For this starter, use uppercase

SKILL.md

, a lowercase-hyphenated name, and a concrete description under 200 characters. Recheck the live uploader before recording.


Plan and sharing statements conflict

Newer Help Center pages describe Skills on Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise when code execution is enabled, along with Team and Enterprise provisioning or sharing. The Platform overview still describes a narrower claude.ai plan list and individual-only Skills.

Check these pages on the day you teach:

  • What are Skills?

  • Use Skills in Claude

  • Provision and manage Skills for your organization

  • Agent Skills overview

Do not promise a student that their plan includes custom Skills until the current account shows the feature or the current official plan page confirms it.

The upload path can move

Anthropic pages currently mention different paths, including a Skills area under Customize and a Features area under Settings. Demonstrate the buttons visible in the teaching account. If the path has moved, narrate what is on screen rather than forcing the old directions.

Skills do not automatically sync across Claude surfaces

A Skill installed in claude.ai is not automatically available in Claude Code or the API. Follow the install path for the surface you use. See Anthropic's cross-surface availability note.

Skills can execute instructions and code

Treat a downloaded Skill like software. Read the main instructions and every supporting script or file before enabling it. Look for unexpected network calls, shell commands, file access, outside URLs, or actions that do not match the stated job. Never put passwords, API keys, or tokens inside a Skill.

See Anthropic's security considerations.

Frequently Asked Questions

“Isn't a Skill just a saved prompt?”

A simple Skill can begin with a prompt. The useful difference is that the procedure has a name, a discovery description, explicit inputs, steps, boundaries, checks, and supporting files when needed. Claude can load it when a matching job appears.

Do not overbuild a one-line request that already works. Make a Skill when the procedure repeats and the exact steps matter.

“When should I use a Project instead?”

Use a Project for standing context: the job, audience, rules, and files that should apply across chats in that Project.

Use a Skill for the reusable procedure: the steps Claude should follow when a particular move is needed.

“Does the Skill remember my business?”

Put changing business facts in the appropriate Project or another approved source of standing context. Keep the Skill focused on the procedure unless a fact truly belongs every time anyone runs that Skill.

Which instructions and files a Skill can access depends on the Claude surface and current settings. Verify that behavior in the product you use; do not assume the Skill can see every Project file or account instruction.

“Can I use the same Skill in more than one Project?”

Conceptually, yes: a reusable procedure should not depend on one Project's private situation. The actual availability depends on where the Skill is installed and which Claude surface you use. Test it in each intended context before promising that it works there.

“What if the procedure changes?”

Edit the Skill, update the version and date, then rerun the trigger tests and both a normal and different test case. Keep the earlier version until the new one passes.

“Do I need to know how to code?”

No. Scripts and supporting files are optional. Use them only when they make a repeated operation, reference, or check clearer and more reliable.

“Can I install a Skill somebody sent me?”

Only after you inspect it. Read every file, check scripts and outside links, remove secrets, and confirm that its actions match its description. Do not install a Skill from an unknown source into a workspace with sensitive files or powerful tools.

Three built examples to inspect

The local course download contains three finished examples:

  • AI Hunter v3 combines a mega prompt, reference files, and a deterministic scanner. The scanner handles the check that should produce the same result every time.

  • Content Sawdust uses conditional reference files. Claude loads the supporting material only when the job calls for it. It does not need a script.

  • Lisec Method creates detailed outlines for content, tutorials, and lessons.

Assignment: build one new Skill

Close

A Project holds the standing context. A Skill holds the reusable procedure.

Do not save every conversation as a Skill. Save the move you keep repeating, write down what done means, and test it on more than one case.

The proof is not that Claude said it used the Skill. The proof is that you can inspect the instructions, inputs, outputs, checks, and revision, then run the procedure again.

Official references:

  • Agent Skills overview

  • Skill authoring best practices

  • What are Skills?

  • How to create custom Skills

Skill downloads

Download the three Skills ZIP files from Resources below.
