records.content:
Welcome to the Prompt Building Blocks Skill!

This is the megaprompt that builds megaprompts through a guided interview. It uses a 5-block framework to turn any business process or task into a ready-to-deploy prompt — no writing from scratch. It's one of many skills we give you inside the Claude Cowork Bootcamp.

The 5 blocks are:

Name & Identity — Define who the AI is (persona, role, tone)

Instructions & Intent — Define what it will do (overview and component list)

Training Components — Define how it executes (methodology and process)

Attributes & Rules — Define the standards (3–7 measurable rules per component)

Reference Examples — Define the quality benchmark (real examples)

The Prompt

# Megaprompt Builder

You are **Megaprompt Builder**. Turn a user's task, process, or existing prompt into one executable, evidence-grounded megaprompt. Your work must be portable across capable chat AIs: depend on no plugins, slash commands, hidden files, proprietary tools, or platform-specific features. Work entirely in chat unless the user explicitly asks you to use an available file capability.

Success means the finished artifact has an explicit input/output contract, complete and non-overlapping instructions, observable quality standards, honest evidence, and enough context for another capable AI to execute it without guessing.

## 1. Route the request

Infer the mode from the user's input. Ask one short routing question only if the mode is genuinely ambiguous.

- **Full Build:** The user gives you a task, process, or desired outcome. Build a new megaprompt.
- **Audit & Rebuild:** The user gives you an existing prompt as pasted text or an accessible file. Diagnose it with NITAR, preserve strong material, and rebuild only what needs work.
- **Single Block:** The user asks for N, I, T, A, or R—or a common alias. Create or replace only that block. If an existing prompt is supplied, return the full prompt with that block replaced. If no prompt is supplied, return the selected block as a complete standalone module ready to insert.

Recognize these aliases:

- N: Name, Identity, Role, Persona
- I: Instructions, Intent, Objective, Task
- T: Training, Components, Modules, Skills, Judgment Areas
- A: Attributes, Rules, Criteria, Standards, Guardrails
- R: References, Examples, Samples, Benchmarks

## 2. Use the NITAR framework

NITAR is the complete design method. Do not require an external framework or reference.

### N — Name & Identity

Define:

- A functional role name; use a decorative persona name only when it improves clarity.
- The role's primary function and scope.
- Its tone and working style.
- What it receives as input.
- What it delivers as output.

Failure checks: generic expertise, unclear scope, missing inputs or outputs, decorative roleplay that does not change useful behavior.

### I — Instructions & Intent

Define:

- A precise task summary.
- A numbered list of the work's major components.
- Why precision matters and what failure would cost.
- The required input, restated concretely.
- The execution order, decision points, and completion condition.

Failure checks: vague verbs, hidden assumptions, conflicting steps, missing sequence, or no test for completion.

### T — Training Components

Create **3–7** distinct, logically ordered skill or judgment areas. When proposing the structure yourself, default to **4–6**. Each component must have:

- A noun-based title.
- A 1–2 sentence definition that is understandable on its own.
- A clear boundary from every other component.
- An explanation of what good execution looks like.
- Its common failure mode.

Failure checks: overlap, mixed concerns, missing capability, arbitrary ordering, titles that describe activities rather than a stable area of judgment.

### A — Attributes & Rules

For every training component, define **3–7** specific, measurable, bounded, non-overlapping rules. Target **3–5** during the interview; use 6–7 only when the extra rules are genuinely distinct. Include:

- Observable grading criteria.
- A passing threshold.
- What separates good work from great work.
- Relevant limits, prohibitions, edge cases, and expert practices.

Replace vague standards such as “clear,” “high quality,” “engaging,” or “concise” with tests someone could actually apply. For example, define the required reading level, maximum length, included fields, acceptable error rate, evidence standard, or decision rule. Do not repeat the same rule under different components.

Failure checks: subjective adjectives with no test, unbounded requirements, redundancy, internal conflicts, or rules that cannot be verified from the output.

### R — Reference Examples

For every component, target **2–3 real, varied examples** supplied or verified by the user. Each example must visibly satisfy the associated rules. Optional bad examples may be included when they teach a meaningful boundary.

Evidence rules:

- Never invent a company, result, quote, customer, metric, case study, source, or prior output and present it as real.
- Never relabel an AI-generated illustration as a user benchmark.
- If real evidence is unavailable, insert a precise placeholder such as `[EXAMPLE NEEDED: a real approved sales email under 150 words that received a reply]`.
- You may offer an invented teaching example only when it is clearly labeled `Illustrative draft — not a real benchmark` and the user can replace or approve it.
- Tie every example to the rules it demonstrates. If it contradicts a rule, fix the rule or reject the example.

Failure checks: fabricated evidence, generic placeholders, examples unrelated to the rules, or several examples that all test the same easy case.

## 3. Keep facts and recommendations separate

Maintain a private working ledger with three categories:

1. **User fact or requirement** — explicitly supplied by the user or their source text.
2. **Builder recommendation** — your proposed structure, standard, wording, or default.
3. **Unknown or evidence needed** — information that has not been supplied or verified.

During drafts, label recommendations plainly and never silently turn them into user requirements. Ask the user to accept, change, or reject material recommendations. In the final artifact, integrate accepted recommendations without labels; leave unresolved evidence as explicit placeholders. Never infer a business fact merely because it would make the prompt sound complete.

## 4. Interview efficiently

- Begin with one concise batch covering only missing context: the exact task, business or domain, required output format, constraints or avoidances, and important edge cases.
- Do not ask for anything already present in the conversation or source prompt.
- Ask related questions together in batches of no more than five short questions. Use follow-up batches only when the answers materially affect the build.
- Proceed in N → I → T → A → R order, except in Single Block mode, where you ask only for the selected block.
- After each block, show a compact draft and ask for confirmation or refinement before proceeding. Do not put interim drafts in fenced code blocks.
- If the user says “you decide,” propose 4–6 components based on known facts, clearly mark them as recommendations, and let the user add, remove, reorder, or rename them.
- For each component, establish what it is, what good execution looks like, and its common failure mode.
- For each rule set, establish the grading criteria, passing threshold, and difference between good and great.
- Ask for real good examples and, optionally, useful bad examples. Do not block completion when evidence is missing; use precise placeholders.
- If the user has already approved material or explicitly asks you to use your judgment, do not repeatedly seek confirmation for the same decision.

## 5. Mode-specific workflow

### Full Build

1. Collect the missing context in one batch.
2. Draft and confirm N, then I, T, A, and R.
3. Assemble only confirmed or explicitly delegated material.
4. Run the quality gate, repair failures, and deliver the complete megaprompt.

### Audit & Rebuild

1. Read the supplied prompt. If a referenced file is inaccessible, ask the user to paste its text; do not pretend you read it.
2. Rate each NITAR block **Strong**, **Weak**, or **Missing** in a compact table. Give one plain-language, evidence-based reason for each rating.
3. State exactly which blocks you recommend changing and what will be preserved.
4. Get confirmation on the repair scope.
5. Interview only for weak or missing blocks. Preserve strong language and working behavior unless a confirmed change is required for coherence.
6. Draft and confirm repaired blocks, assemble the rebuilt prompt, run the quality gate, and deliver it.
7. If the user asks for a saved remix, leave the original unchanged and suggest a lowercase hyphenated filename ending in `-nitar-remix.md`.

### Single Block

1. Identify the requested block and whether it should replace a section or stand alone.
2. Inspect any supplied prompt only to gather relevant context and boundaries.
3. Ask only the unanswered questions required for that block.
4. Draft and confirm the block.
5. If replacing, preserve every unrequested section and return the complete updated megaprompt. If standalone, return only the complete insertable block.
6. Run the quality checks relevant to that block before delivery.

## 6. Assemble the final artifact

Use the following structure for a complete megaprompt. Adapt labels to the user's task, but preserve the contract, separators, measurable rules, and closing request.

**[Functional Role Name]**

You are [identity paragraph: function, scope, tone, and working style].

~~~

## What I'll Receive & What I'll Deliver

**I will receive:** [explicit required inputs, accepted formats, and minimum information]

**I will deliver:** [exact outputs, order, format, length or bounds, and completion standard]

~~~

## Instructions & Intent

[Precise task summary, why precision matters, execution order, decision points, and completion condition.]

### Components

1. [Component 1]
2. [Component 2]
3. [Continue through all 3–7 components]

### Required Input

[Concrete restatement of what the user must provide.]

~~~

## 1. [Noun-Based Component Title]

**Definition:** [1–2 independently understandable sentences, including the boundary and purpose.]

**What good execution looks like:** [observable result.]

**Common failure mode:** [specific failure.]

### Attributes & Rules

1. [Measurable rule]
2. [Measurable rule]
3. [Continue through 3–7 distinct rules]

**Passing threshold:** [observable minimum]

**Good → great:** [specific differentiator]

### Reference Examples

- **Example 1:** [real, user-supplied example tied to named rules, or a precise `[EXAMPLE NEEDED: ...]` placeholder]
- **Example 2:** [real example or precise placeholder]
- **Example 3:** [optional real example or precise placeholder]

~~~

[Repeat one component section per component, in logical order, separated by `~~~`.]

## Final Output Instructions

- [Delivery format and section order]
- [Formatting and length constraints]
- [Quality, evidence, and acceptance standards]
- [How to handle missing, conflicting, or unsafe input]
- [Final verification steps before responding]

~~~

Are you ready? Please provide [required inputs] to begin.

For a standalone Single Block result, use only the corresponding NITAR section, make it fully insertable, and preserve the same heading and `~~~` separator style. For a replacement, use the complete structure above with the selected section updated.

## 7. Quality gate and silent repair

Before final delivery, inspect the artifact and repair every failure you can without changing confirmed user facts. Do not expose chain-of-thought or a hidden scoring process. Check that:

- Every instruction is actionable or testable; none depends on unexplained context.
- A complete build has 3–7 distinct, logically ordered, non-overlapping components.
- Every component has a noun-based title, definition, good-execution standard, and common failure mode.
- Every component has 3–7 measurable, bounded, non-redundant attributes.
- Every rule has an observable grading criterion; passing and good-to-great standards are explicit.
- Inputs, outputs, format, sequence, boundaries, and completion conditions are explicit.
- Examples comply with the rules and are varied enough to be useful.
- No invented material is represented as real; missing real evidence uses precise placeholders.
- User requirements and accepted recommendations do not conflict.
- Component sections use `~~~` separators.
- The final artifact is instructional rather than chatty, except for the required closing request.
- No unresolved placeholder is hidden. Each one states exactly what user evidence is missing.

If a check fails, revise and check again before delivery. If a failure cannot be repaired without user evidence, keep a precise visible placeholder rather than guessing.

## 8. Delivery contract

- Always display the completed artifact before any optional save action.
- At final delivery, output **exactly one complete requested artifact in one fenced Markdown block**. Put no commentary, audit notes, validation report, or second artifact inside or outside that block.
- In Full Build and Audit & Rebuild modes, that artifact is the entire finished megaprompt.
- In Single Block mode, it is either the entire updated megaprompt or the one complete standalone block, according to the user's request.
- Do not save or edit files unless the user explicitly asks and the environment supports it. If asked, use a lowercase hyphenated task slug; for remixes, use `[original-name]-nitar-remix.md`. Never overwrite the original during a remix.
- If the user asks for a filename but not a save, place the suggested filename as a Markdown comment at the bottom of the single fenced block so the one-block delivery rule remains intact.

Begin by routing the user's request and asking only the first concise batch of unanswered questions.

Open or download the Prompt Building Blocks Diagram from Resources below.

The Context Shelf is a spreadsheet for sources you want to use again. It has these columns:

  • Topic / Domain

  • Source

  • Type (book / course / report / data)

  • Who it’s from

  • Free or Paid

  • Link

  • Why I trust it

  • Last used

Add a row whenever the Context Hunter finds something worth keeping. The point is to stop searching for the same good sources every time.

The sheet starts with university course libraries such as MIT OpenCourseWare, primary-research databases, public datasets, and original technical documentation. Add Mitch’s own trusted sources after he supplies them.

Optional: Set It and Forget It

Some context stays useful across many conversations: who you are, how you work, and rules you want the model to follow every time.

If your tool supports custom instructions or a system prompt, you can put that material there instead of pasting it into every chat. Keep this part short today. The deeper setup is outside this lesson

records.title: Bonus: The Copywriter's Mindset Checklist

records.description: Use this checklist before writing any piece of copy: Before You Write: ☐ Do I understand my target customer's biggest pain point? ☐ Do I know what outcome they
records.content:
Use this checklist before writing any piece of copy:

Before You Write:

☐ Do I understand my target customer's biggest pain point?

☐ Do I know what outcome they desperately want?

☐ Have I identified their main objections to buying?

☐ Do I understand what makes this product/service unique?

☐ Have I researched what competitors are saying?

While You Write:

☐ Am I speaking to ONE specific person, not "everyone"?

☐ Am I focusing on benefits, not just features?

☐ Am I using the customer's language, not industry jargon?

☐ Does every sentence either build desire or overcome an objection?

☐ Have I included a clear, specific call-to-action?

After You Write:

☐ Would this make ME want to buy if I were the customer?

☐ Is it clear exactly what action I want them to take?

☐ Have I removed any unnecessary words or confusing phrases?

☐ Does it sound like a real person wrote it, not a robot?

records.title: Copywriting vs Ghostwriting
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 1 What Is Copywriting/Copywriting vs Ghostwriting - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Now, a common question I get asked all the time is: “But Cole?! What’s the difference between Copywriting and Ghostwriting?” Let’s keep it simple: - Copywriting
records.content:
Now, a common question I get asked all the time is:

“But Cole?! What’s the difference between Copywriting and Ghostwriting?”

Let’s keep it simple:

  • Copywriting = Sales/Incentivizing

  • Ghostwriting = Education

If you’re a founder, or a CEO, or a YouTuber, or a podcaster, etc., and you want to scale yourself online and start publishing more text-based content, you aren’t going to hire a copywriter. You’re going to hire a ghostwriter. Because when it comes to creating social content, or launching a weekly newsletter—where you share your insights, stories, and perspectives on a specific niche or industry—you aren’t really trying to “sell” readers.

At least, not yet.

Ghostwriting usually comes first.

Most of the time, a client is going to hire a ghostwriter to help them scale their personal brand and start “building an audience.”

  • They want to publish more social content

  • Or they want to turn their audio/video content into text content

  • Or they want to start a weekly newsletter.

  • Or they want to create a really high-value opt-in—to incentivize more people to join their newsletter/email list.

  • Etc.

Ghostwriting is usually the service you provide if you want to clients on the educational side.

Copywriting usually comes second.

Then… once a client has an audience, has an email list, or has traffic (from running ads or SEO), THEN they need a copywriter.

They need someone to help them convert all those free readers into paying customers.

  • They need launch emails—for an upcoming product drop

  • They need abandoned cart emails—when someone “almost” purchases, but doesn’t.

  • They need follow-up emails—reminding customers to buy (or buy again).

  • They need upsell emails—encouraging previous customers to buy again.

  • They need to run ads—to reach more new potential customers.

  • They need to record a VSL—to increase the likelihood a customer converts on a landing page.

  • Etc.

Again, these are not (usually) the same writer. The skills involved in ghostwriting are different than the skills involved in copywriting. Yes, there is some cross-over. Yes, I would recommend you become proficient in both (I did). Yes, every single business owner on planet earth ultimately needs help with both of these things. But it’s important to understand: they are not the same.

Ghostwriting = Education

Copywriting = Sales/Incentivizing

records.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 1 What Is Copywriting/Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Now, whenever I introduce writers to the skill of copywriting, I always get the same handful of questions. So, I want to answer them here for you: “But Cole?!
records.content:
Now, whenever I introduce writers to the skill of copywriting, I always get the same handful of questions.

So, I want to answer them here for you:

“But Cole?! Do I need any special qualifications to become a copywriter?

Nope!

That’s one of the best parts of becoming a writer in the digital age:

  • You don’t need a degree to start ghostwriting.

  • You don’t need a degree to start copywriting.

  • And you don’t need a degree to start writing on the Internet.

If you can write things that drive a result—people giving you their attention, or better yet, their hard-earned money—then you will have more opportunity than you will know what to do with.

“But Cole?! Isn’t AI going to replace copywriters?”

Hardly.

AI will help copywriters, absolutely.

AI will make copywriters more efficient, absolutely.

AI will allow copywriters to take on 10x as many clients, absolutely.

But it’s not going to “replace” copywriters.

“But Cole?! How long does it take to become good at copywriting?”

Copywriting is one of those games that is easy to learn but very hard to master.

I first got introduced to the world of copywriting back in 2015. Which means I’ve been practicing copywriting as a skill for over a decade now. And STILL… to this date… I feel like I’m always learning something new. And the best copywriters in the world have been doing it for decades.

Now, with that said, you can become very proficient in just a couple months.

IF…

  • You master the fundamentals (which we’re going to cover here!)…

  • You take the time to educate yourself about the customer you’re trying to “sell” to…

  • And you practice (a lot) by trying to write things that sell.

And if you REALLY want to become a proficient copywriter, ASAP, nothing will teach you more about copywriting than trying to sell something of your own.

Launch your own digital product or service.

And try writing things that get your customers to take action.

I promise, you’ll learn more doing this than you will working with clients for multiple years.

“But Cole?! Do I need to specialize in a specific type of copywriting?”

Yes and no.

If you can incentivize people properly to take action, PERIOD, chances are you can apply your skills to just about any form of copywriting. Translation: if you get good at writing ads, writing emails isn’t that different. Or if you get good at writing landing pages, writing video sales scripts isn’t that different.

Yes, there are some nuances. But it’s nothing you can’t handle.

But the reason I say that, yes, at some point it’s a good idea to specialize is because that’s how you:

  • Achieve pricing power

  • Build efficiencies for yourself

  • And become known for a niche you own

Generalists almost always make less that specialists.

And so, just put yourself in the shoes of a business owner.

If you were looking to create an all-star landing page to sell your upcoming digital product, which copywriter would you hire?

  • The generalist copywriter: “I’ve done all sorts of different copywriting. I can do whatever you need!”

  • The specialist copywriter: “I specialize in copywriting landing pages for digital products. It’s the only thing I do, and I’ve been doing it for years.”

You (the business owner) are going to hire the specialist… every single time.

So, while you don’t have to start out being super specific about what you specialize in, you do want to trend in this direction.

Hey there!

And welcome to Module 1 of Copywriting 101: A Full Crash Course On How To Write Things That Sell.

If you’re brand new to copywriting, then you’re in the right place!

In this module, I am going to give you a crash course on copywriting:

  • What it is

  • Why it’s so important

  • Why businesses need copywriting help

  • And how you can “think” like a 7-figure copywriter.

Let’s dive in!

records.title: The Copywriter's Core Job
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 1 What Is Copywriting/The Copywriter_s Core Job - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: So, what exactly does a copywriter… do? Well, the skill of copywriting is really all about reader psychology. I have had some pretty incredible copywriting ment
records.content:
So, what exactly does a copywriter… do?

Well, the skill of copywriting is really all about reader psychology. I have had some pretty incredible copywriting mentors in my life, and ALL of them spend more time reading about human psychology than they do “copywriting.” That’s because copywriting is really just a vehicle for clear, effective communication.

So, there’s really 3 big things a copywriter does:

  1. Understand the customer deeply. Copywriters obsess over the customers they are trying to talk to. They take the time—whether it’s through research, talking to people, or simply chatting with AI—to get to know them. They figure out what they want, what they care about, what they’re afraid of, what they’ve tried in the past that didn’t work, etc. They get to know these potential customers inside and out… so they can speak DIRECTLY to their biggest pain points, and most visceral motivations.

  2. Understand the product/service. Copywriters also spend a lot of time getting to know the product or service they are selling. They want to know everything about it: how it works, how long it takes, what sorts of results are typical, what questions customers tend to need answered when getting started, etc. In fact, most of the time, the copywriter of a business knows that business’s products/services than anyone else!

  3. Create urgency. Lastly, copywriters become masters of of overcoming objections and creating urgency. They learn how to give people a reason to act NOW rather than "thinking about it" (which usually means never). And more importantly, they learn how to answer and overcome every single possible objection a customer might have—to the point where a customer has no other believable excuse. The only thing that makes sense is for them to get started right away!

Again, no need to overcomplicate it.

Becoming a proficient copywriter is really just about learning how to communicate with people—and more specifically, the certain type of person you are trying to reach in your specific industry.

Because each industry/niche has different customers, who have different problems, and have different ambitions and hopes and dreams, and want different outcomes.

So it’s not enough to just know how to “sell” to people.

Copywriting is about niching down, and learning so much about a particular industry that you can speak to the customers in that industry better and more clearly than anyone else.

records.title: What Is Copywriting?
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 1 What Is Copywriting/What Is Copywriting_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: In the simplest way, copywriting is where you write things that sell. More specifically, copywriting usually refers to the creation of one or multiple of the fo
records.content:
In the simplest way, copywriting is where you write things that sell.

More specifically, copywriting usually refers to the creation of one or multiple of the following assets:

  • Emails: Nudging potential customers on your free email list to become paying customers.

  • Ads: Writing messages that STOP potential customers when scrolling on social platforms and incentivizing them to take action (whether that’s to type in their email to unlock a download, sign-up for a free training, visit a landing page, buy a product, etc.)

  • Sales/Landing Pages: Long-form pages designed to walk potential customers through the entire buying process and convert them into paying customers.

  • Product Descriptions: Compelling descriptions that make products irresistible and answer customer objections.

  • Website Copy: Homepage, about pages, and service pages that clearly communicate what a business does and why customers should choose them.

  • Video Sales Letters: Scripted short, medium, or long-form videos with the sole intention of selling a potential customer on whatever thing you’re presenting to them on that page.

Really, copywriting can be applied to any asset—physical or digital—where the sole intention is to “sell” the customer.

Now, what does it mean to “sell?”

Let’s keep it simple—because a lot of times the concept of “selling” gets made more complicated than it actually is.

Selling = Incentivizing

And how do you incentivize (aka: “sell”) someone to take action on something?

  • You can incentivize them by making them aware of the GOOD things that will happen if they do take action.

  • You can incentivize them by making them aware of the BAD things that will happen if they don’t take action.

That’s really it.

Now, yes… becoming a proficient copywriter also means learning all sorts of little tactics like rewarding customers with bonuses, or bundling bonuses together, or encouraging they take action within a specific time constraint, etc.

But these are all fairly incremental relative to the true art of copywriting.

Copywriting, and “selling,” is just a game of explaining to potential customers:

  • If you take action, these GOOD things will happen.

  • If you don’t take action, these BAD things will happen.

And that’s really it.

records.title: How To Find BIG Ideas
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 2 The BIG Idea/How To Find BIG Ideas - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Over the years, ever since that day in Craig’s kitchen where he told me this story about Claude Hopkins and Pepsodent, I have spent a lot of time thinking about
records.content:
Over the years, ever since that day in Craig’s kitchen where he told me this story about Claude Hopkins and Pepsodent, I have spent a lot of time thinking about how to find (or create) BIG ideas.

And after generating millions and millions of dollars myself—both selling our own products/programs/services, but also copywriting for other brands, publicly traded companies, and Silicon Valley startup—I’ve assembled a few frameworks that I think would be helpful for you.

Here’s how to find BIG ideas.

Framework #1: Think In Opposites

One of the easiest ways to immediately differentiate a product or service is do this simple exercise:

  • Make a list of all the things that are “conventional wisdom” in an existing industry or niche.

  • Make a list of all the benefits of that existing industry or niche.

  • And make a list of all the problems in that existing industry or niche.

…then, find ways to say the opposite.

For example, here’s how we did this within our beginner writing program, Ship 30 for 30.

First, we remind everyone how the writing world is “today.” (Aka: conventional wisdom.)

Then, we just say the opposite—which immediately presents the benefits of our approach as being “different.”

That, in itself, is a BIG idea.

  • Take what everyone currently believes about an industry/niche.

  • Find ways to say the opposite.

Very simple!

Framework #2: Turn an industry’s biggest problem into its biggest benefit.

Let’s take collectable trading cards (like Pokémon) as an example.

  • Biggest Problem = Trading cards are printed on cheap paper, easy to lose, easy to damage, etc.

  • New Biggest Benefit = But (BIG idea here) if we give these trading cards a “grade” based on quality, and then put them inside a protective case, suddenly they become extremely rare & valuable collectables.

Most of the time, a BIG idea is hiding in plain sight.

And it’s really just a matter of taking an industry or product’s biggest problem and finding a way to shine a spotlight on it and make it “its biggest benefit.”

Framework #3: Invent a problem your product or service solves.

This one is a bit more advanced, but here’s a crazy example to show you how this works (and how powerful this can be).

This is how Purdue Pharma differentiated their highly addictive painkiller, OxyContin, in the late 1990s.

To separate OxyContin from other painkillers, Purdue Pharma created a new term in their marketing materials—and invented a problem their product could solve. Instead of saying OxyContin relieved “pain” (which is what every pharmaceutical company said), they gave the specific type of pain OxyContin treated a name—a name they made up themselves. They said OxyContin relieved “breakthrough pain,” which is the pain you feel despite having taken a painkiller. Your pain “breaks through,” regardless.

And what customer wants to experience “breakthrough pain?”

Nobody—exactly.

It’s so subtle, and yet this one term led to billions of dollars of demand (and, sadly, hundreds of thousands of deaths)

Here are some other examples just to give you some more pattern recognition here:

1. Listerine & “Halitosis”

Problem invented: Bad breath as a medical condition.

What happened: People have always had bad breath—but didn’t think of it as a social disease. Listerine coined the term halitosis, gave it clinical weight, and made it embarrassing. Sales exploded from $100K to $4M in 7 years.

2. Deodorant & “Body Odor”

Problem invented: Smelling like a human is shameful.

What happened: In the early 1900s, sweat was normal. Then brands like Odorono and Mum ran ads telling women their armpits could ruin their social lives. They turned natural scent into a source of anxiety.

3. Dandruff & “Grooming Failure”

Problem invented: Flakes = unattractive.

What happened: Dandruff was common but ignored. Then shampoo brands like Head & Shoulders made it a social dealbreaker. One famous line:

“You never get a second chance to make a first impression.”

4. Toothpaste & “Film on Your Teeth”

Problem invented: That feeling = danger.

What happened: People didn’t brush often. Pepsodent ads told them that invisible film was a threat to beauty, and the tingle after brushing meant it was gone. The feeling, not the science, sold the product.

5. Mouthwash for “Tonsil Stones”

Problem invented: You might have white chunks in your throat and not know it.

What happened: New wave of mouthwash brands targeted tonsil stones—harmless but gross—to scare people into rinsing daily. The fear? You smell and don’t know it.

Why You Should Start With The BIG Idea

Almost every great marketing campaign, ever, can be traced back to a very simple BIG idea.

And listen, you might have no interest in becoming a “marketing executive.” That’s fine. I don’t either. But in order to write effective copy, this is where it all starts. Because your copy has to SAY SOMETHING DIFFERENT. And the way you say something different all comes down to the BIG Idea.

So, before you:

  • Write a subject line

  • Write an email

  • Write an ad

  • Write anything

…you need to spend some time getting to know the customer, familiarizing yourself with the product or service you are “selling,” and then doing some good old-fashioned thinking about some potential BIG Ideas.

And little pro tip here:

If you can’t say your BIG Idea in a single sentence, you don’t have enough clarity yet (and neither will your target customer.)

To get you in the mindset of writing copy that converts, we are going to start high-level.

records.title: The BIG Idea
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 2 The BIG Idea/The BIG Idea - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Let me tell you a quick story. Many years ago, when I first moved to Los Angeles, I got introduced to arguably the most successful copywriter on the planet. His
records.content:
Let me tell you a quick story.

Many years ago, when I first moved to Los Angeles, I got introduced to arguably the most successful copywriter on the planet.

His name is Craig Clemens. We bonded over writing. And over the years, we’ve become great friends (and he’s been a terrific mentor to me).

Almost everything meaningful I know about copywriting, I can attribute to him.

Anyways, one day, I go to hang out with him at his house in Hollywood Hills.

To really set the stage, this was his house:

Him and his brothers built one of the most successful direct-response copywriting-driven e-commerce businesses, ever—valued at over a billion dollars.

So we’re hanging out, and obviously I’m trying to learn everything I can about how to “write things that sell” because, well, I want a house like he has.

And he said, “Cole… it all starts with the BIG idea.”

A BIG Idea That Changed The World

What does it mean to have a BIG idea?

Well, let me tell you a quick story, and I bet you’ll recognize it immediately:

In the early 1900s, Claude Hopkins, one of the early pioneers of advertising, had a BIG idea.

Before toothpaste had a tingling or minty sensation, brushing your teeth didn’t feel particularly satisfying. Even though the mechanical act of brushing removed plaque and helped oral health, there was no immediate sensory feedback to signal that your mouth was clean.

That is, until Pepsodent, a toothpaste brand, launched in the 1910s.

Claude Hopkins helped market it. And his BIG idea was that if they added a cooling, minty ingredient into the product (specifically citric acid and later menthol/eucalyptus) that caused a tingling sensation, customers would FEEL the “result” of toothpaste significantly more.

And he was right.

That tingling sensation didn’t actually clean your teeth any better.

And yet, before Pepsodent… toothbrushing was rare.

And after Pepsodent… it became a daily ritual for millions of Americans.

The BIG Idea Matters Most

Craig went on to tell me the above story, along with a dozen others.

He was like a historian for BIG ideas that had changed the world in marketing.

And his point to me was that the best copy in the world doesn’t really “convince” people of anything. All it does it make them aware of something they weren’t aware of before. Sometimes, that means changing the product slightly. Sometimes, not. But irresistible copy isn’t about convincing. It’s about setting the stage so they convince themselves.

records.title: 5 Proven Naming & Claiming Conventions
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 3 Naming & Claiming Your Category/5 Proven Naming & Claiming Conventions - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Now, for the really fun (and more advanced) stuff. When it comes to naming a new category, there is no right or wrong answer. As long as: - It’s Not Clever: The
records.content:
Now, for the really fun (and more advanced) stuff.

When it comes to naming a new category, there is no right or wrong answer.

As long as:

  • It’s Not Clever: The name of your niche, sub-category, or new industry has to be CLEAR.

  • And It’s Not More Than 4 Words: If the name of your niche, sub-category, or new industry is more than 4 words, that’s not a name. That’s a sentence.

Beyond that, it’s largely subjective—and the success or failure of your “category” usually has more to do with failing to stay committed to marketing that new category for a long enough period of time.

So, with the above in mind, here are my favorite naming conventions when creating new categories:

Naming Convention #1: {Noun or Verb Modifier} + Existing Category

One of the most valuable skills to develop as a writer, but especially as a Category Copywriter, is to constantly be thinking in “modifiers.”

Because any modifier, placed in front of almost any word, dramatically changes its meaning—and as a result, the “direction” in which the reader interprets the message and begins thinking thereafter.

Some examples:

  • The word “money” can be modified and its meaning changed drastically by adding “saving money” or “spending money” or “stealing money.”

  • The word “life” can be modified and its meaning changed drastically by adding “saving life” or “taking life” or “sabotaging life.”

  • The word “building” can be modified and its meaning changed drastically by adding “wood building” or “steel building” or “web3 building.”

Notice how one single word, strategically placed in front of the original word, completely changes a) your interpretation of the word, b) the meaning of the word, and c) the “direction” in which you begin to think.

This means coming up with 1, 2, or 3 words that accurately, uniquely, and immediately communicate what makes you “different.” (More than 4 words max and you begin to write a sentence, which is an explanation. The customer doesn’t want an explanation. The customer wants 1, 2, or 3 words they can hold on to and repeat forever.)

Now, the single biggest mistake founders, executives, investors, and accidental Category Copywriters make when trying to Name & Claim a new category is the use of adjectives.

If you take an existing mega-category (“Cars” or “Food” or “Beauty,” etc.) and attempt to modify it with an adjective to achieve differentiation, you accomplish nothing. Adjectives are weak modifiers—because they don’t actually change the meaning of the original word.

Watch:

  • “Car” modified with an adjective becomes a “Better Car.”

  • “Suitcase” modified with an adjective becomes a “Stronger Suitcase.”

  • “Lipstick” modified with an adjective becomes a “Cheaper Lipstick.”

  • “Pillow” modified with an adjective becomes a “Lighter Pillow.”

If you notice, adjective-modified products, services, companies, and marketing messages exist everywhere. This is what the masses believe marketing and advertising to be all about: communicating how you are {insert adjective} compared to the competition—better, smarter, stronger, cheaper, etc.

Instead, the secret is to modify an existing category with a stand-alone Noun or Verb that has its own individual meaning. Because when you combine two stand-alone words with separate meanings, 1 + 1 = 3.

  • “Paper” modified with a noun becomes “Wrapping Paper.” New category.

  • “Coding” modified with a noun/verb becomes “Vibe Coding.” New category.

  • “Water” modified with a noun becomes “Vitamin Water.” New category.

  • “Tape” modified with a verb becomes “Snore Tape.” New category.

  • Etc.

The more the modifier word stands alone—and an easy trick for this is to think in Nouns & Verbs—the more net-new meaning and differentiation it creates when combined within an existing mega-category.

  • NOTE: Grammatically speaking, many nouns & verbs act as adjectives when combined with another word. But that is in the context of a complete sentence. Naming & Claiming a category is not that.

Now, can you achieve categorical differentiation by using an adjective?

Yes, it’s possible:

  • “Urgent Care” modified with an adjective becomes “Holistic Urgent Care.” New category.

  • “Phone” modified with an adjective becomes “Smartphone.” New category.

  • “Food” modified with an adjective becomes “Fast Food.” New category.

  • Etc.

But over the years, I have found that nouns & verbs tend to produce more effectively named categories than adjectives. More importantly, “thinking” in adjectives, tends to lead to lazy comparison messaging: better, faster, stronger, smarter, cheaper, etc.

Naming Convention #2: {Benefit Modifier} + Existing Category

Building on the above (thinking in “modifiers”), there are lots of other ways you can modify existing categories.

And one of those ways is by making the modifier the new benefit you want to lead with.

Some examples:

  • Vitamin Water

  • Smart Watch

  • Fast Food

  • Casper the Friendly Ghost

  • Etc.

Notice how the modifier in each of the above examples is the primary BENEFIT.

A similar but different example that really exemplifies this naming convention happens with food products all the time.

A lot of new innovations that happen in food are the result of taking an individual ingredient and then making “that ingredient” the primary benefit of a new sub-category.

Just look at Milk, and all the various modifiers that have unfolded—each of which have become massive niches and highly profitable markets.

  • Almond Milk

  • Coconut Milk

  • Walnut Milk

  • Soy Milk

  • Oat Milk

  • Hemp Milk

  • Goat Milk

  • Cashew Milk

  • Rice Milk

  • Etc.

It’s the same mega-category (Milk), just modified infinitely with different modifiers. Each modifier is really just an individual ingredient that has been given the spotlight. And in doing so, that ingredient becomes the leading BENEFIT.

Naming Convention #3: {Problem-Free Modifier} + Existing Category

Another great naming convention is really just the opposite of the above.

Instead of leading with the primary benefit of a new category, you lead with the “absent problem” of the old category.

Some examples:

  • Gluten-Free (problem: gluten intolerance, bloating, autoimmune response)

  • Sugar-Free (problem: obesity, diabetes, sugar crashes)

  • Caffeine-Free (problem: jitteriness, insomnia, addiction)

  • Guilt-Free (problem: emotional eating, indulgence regret)

  • Toxin-Free (problem: harmful chemicals, fear of cancer)

  • Smoke-Free (problem: secondhand smoke, lung damage)

  • Cruelty-Free (problem: animal testing, ethical concerns)

  • Odor-Free (problem: body odor, environmental smells)

  • Sulfate-Free (problem: hair dryness, scalp irritation)

  • Additive-Free (problem: artificial chemicals, hyperactivity, general "unnaturalness")

These modifiers don’t add anything—they subtract something people fear, avoid, or feel guilty about.

Naming Convention #4: {Target Audience Modifier} + Existing Category

This naming convention is a bit more unique, but it can work—and when it does, it works really well.

An example I love here is Dude Wipes.

Now, Dude Wipes is interesting because it’s both:

  • The name of the brand

  • And the name of the category

“Wipes” is the mega-category—but wipes are usually made for, and sold to women.

They differentiated themselves (and created a new sub-category within “Wipes”) by naming the target audience directly.

They aren’t selling “Wipes.”

They’re selling Dude Wipes—which are wipes, for men.

Naming Convention #5: Portmanteau

Lastly, you can create new categories by combining two existing categories into one word. This not only makes the name catchy—it also signals the novelty of the combination. Portmanteaus work especially well when you’re merging two familiar ideas into a new hybrid category.

Some examples:

  • Sushirrito – a sushi burrito

  • Romantasy – romance + fantasy genre

  • Brunch – breakfast + lunch

  • Mocktail – mock + cocktail

  • Hangry – hungry + angry

  • Frenemy – friend + enemy

  • Blog – web + log

  • Guesstimate – guess + estimate

  • Motel – motor + hotel

  • Athleisure – athletic + leisure wear

Portmanteaus let customers infer what the product is, without needing a long explanation.

records.title: Becoming Known For A Niche You Own

records.content:
When it comes to writing effective copy—for yourself and your own products/services, or as a hired-hand selling someone else’s products/services—you have to understand the entire name of the game.

  • And the game is not: “Let me make this brand popular.”

  • The game is: “Let’s educate a lot of people on the benefits of this new category.”

Now, what is a “category?”

Categories are how customers organize information in their minds.

And we all think category-first.

For example, let’s pretend I asked you, “Where do you want to go to dinner tonight? Do you want to go to Tony’s? Or do you want to go to Nancy Sue’s?”

What is the IMMEDIATE clarifying question you would ask me back?

“Well, what kind of food do they both serve?”

You can’t make a decision based off BRAND (the names of the restaurants) because it’s not enough information. What you really need to know is the CATEGORIES of food.

  • Is this sushi?

  • Is this pizza?

  • Is this tacos?

  • Is this Mediterranean?

  • Etc.

Category First, Brand Second.

With the above in mind, this means the ENTIRE game of copywriting isn’t to convince people to buy (or buy-into) a specific brand.

(This is something a lot, and I mean a LOT of copywriters don’t understand.)

The game is to educate people (and get them to buy-into) a specific CATEGORY.

Because if you do that successfully, then your “brand” will inherently be the one they choose—because you’re the one who brought them into the category!

As you can see with all our writing programs and products, this is exactly what we do:

  • We don’t promote Ship 30 for 30 (brand). We educate people to “start writing online” (category).

  • We don’t promote Premium Ghostwriting Academy (brand). We educate people on “ghostwriting” (category).

  • We don’t promote Write With AI (brand). We educate people on “writing with AI” (category).

  • Etc.

So often, “copy” is weak because the writer doesn’t understand what game they’re supposed to be playing.

Your copy isn’t about promoting a brand.

Your copy is about getting people excited (and getting them to buy-into) a specific category.

records.title: Whoever Markets The Problem, Owns The Solution
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 3 Naming & Claiming Your Category/Whoever Markets The Problem, Owns The Solution - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: So, if the game is “Category First, Brand Second,” then the next step is to realize that all your efforts are better spent marketing the BENEFITS of that new ca
records.content:
So, if the game is “Category First, Brand Second,” then the next step is to realize that all your efforts are better spent marketing the BENEFITS of that new category (and/or the PROBLEMS of the old/existing category) more so than the brand itself.

Because whoever introduces you to a new category, sub-category, or niche… you fundamentally assume is someone you can trust to help you navigate that category.

Translation: Whoever markets the problem, owns the solution.

For example:

Let’s say you are a local chiropractor that specializes in back-pain.

And let’s say your facility is called Ken Cracks. (Your name is Ken, and you’re a chiropractor. Just roll with it.)

Now, conventional wisdom would say, “We gotta build the brand!” And a novice copywriter, in this case, would encourage you to promote Ken Cracks… everywhere.

  • Run ads telling people all about Ken Cracks

  • Write emails explaining why Ken Cracks is better than everybody else

  • Write a landing page with a picture of you (Ken), smiling, thumbs-up, in front of your building

  • Etc.

And then let’s pretend another chiropractor opened nearby.

What’s their name? Doesn’t matter.

Who started it? Doesn’t matter.

But everywhere you go, you see them promoting the PROBLEM and not their brand.

  • “Back pain?”

  • “Do you have back pain?”

  • “Do you want to get rid of your back pain?”

  • Etc.

Now, just ask yourself…

Which chiropractor are you more likely to pay attention to?

It’s actually the second one.

Because on a subconscious level, whoever markets the problem… you automatically assume is better equipped to provide you the solution.

Brand is almost irrelevant.

records.content:
Now that we’ve covered the 5 types of proven hooks, we should take a moment to chat about mistakes.

Because copywriters make a lot of them.

And I don’t want you to be one of those n00b copywriters who has no idea what they’re doing!

Mistake #1: Clever, not Clear

Nothing, and I mean nothing ruins more advertisements and marketing copy than “clever” writing.

The way this shows up most often is when copywriters “Prioritize The Pun.”

  • They prioritize the joke over the message.

  • They prioritize the “clever saying” over the category.

  • They prioritize the witty play-on-words over the words themselves.

And it’s always a mistake.

IF THE CUSTOMER DOESN’T KNOW EXACTLY WHAT YOU ARE SAYING, THEY ARE NOT GOING TO LISTEN.

They’re not going to sit there and try to figure it out.

They’re not going to stare for 5-10 seconds to “understand the pun.”

They’re just going to move on.

Mistake #2: Vague, Non-Specific Language

Tell me which company this is. This is the biggest header text on their website:

I’ll give you some hints:

  • You know the company.

  • It’s one of the largest companies in the world.

  • It generates more revenue than most small countries.

  • AND, they spend more on marketing than nearly any other company on earth.

Yet, you still have no idea who the company is.

The answer? It’s SalesForce.

This is a mistake just about every huge company makes. Some of it is the copywriter’s fault, but some of it is also the executive’s fault—because as companies grow, they become so “risk averse” that they end up turning all their marketing materials into billboards for vague, non-specific language.

Don’t make this mistake.

Mistake #3: Industry Jargon

Another big mistake copywriters make is using terminology only a small percentage of people in an industry or niche know, let alone understand.

Now, there’s some nuance to this mistake I want to explain:

  • In some cases, using jargon can be a good thing. Jargon weeds out people because either “you understand these words or you don’t.” So for hyper-niche companies/products/etc., speaking with jargon might be OK. (Example: “Want to learn how to write Python code for algo trading?” Only a specific person will know what these terms are.) ****

  • In other cases, using jargon ends up weeding too many people out. Yes, jargon speaks to “existing prospects,” but doesn’t really allow you to speak to people who aren’t prospects yet. This is crucial.

So, as a copywriter, you need to decide who exactly you’re trying to speak to.

Is it ONLY people who are already in this industry? If so, then using jargon might be a easy way to weed everybody else out—and only speak to “those people.”

Or, do you want to reach people OUTSIDE this industry, and bring more net-new people into your niche? If so, then using jargon is a mistake. You’d only be speaking to existing prospects/customers, not people who “don’t know what this is… yet.”

Mistake #4: Mentioning The Competition

Here’s a little marketing secret:

You do not compete Brand v Brand.

You compete Category v Category.

  • Tesla doesn’t say “Ford is bad.” Tesla (the electric car company) says “gas-powered cars are bad.”

  • Coca-Cola doesn’t say, “Pepsi is bad.” Coca-Cola says, “The original soft drink.”

  • And in 2001, back when Sony was the biggest distributor of portable CD players, Apple didn’t say “Sony is bad.” Apple launched the iPod and said, “CD players are bad. Put 1,000 songs in your pocket with a portable music player instead.”

A lot of novice copywriters end up doing their clients a disservice because they think the way they win the sales war is by calling the competition bad.

And most of the time, it has the inverse effect. You spend marketing dollars marketing someone else’s product! (Why would Coca-Cola spend ad dollars mentioning the brand name Pepsi?)

Instead, what you want to do is attack your competition’s CATEGORY.

Mistake #5: No Clear Category

Which leads to the biggest mistake of all, and that’s failing to have any sort of awareness around the category you are marketing.

Because remember:

  • Copywriting is not about building a “brand.”

  • Copywriting is not about “awareness for the sake of awareness.”

  • Copywriting is not about “talking to anyone and everyone.”

Copywriting is a game of 3 things:

  • Category

  • BIG Idea

  • Hooks

The highest-paid copywriters get paid to come up with those 3 things.

Because once you have those 3 decisions made, then you can have an army of entry-level copywriters help you do all the labor of writing ads and emails and landing pages and video scripts based on those 3 strategic decisions.

records.content:
So, let’s stick with our example for a second.

Let’s say…

  • The industry (or mega-category) you’re playing in is Milk.

  • Your unique modifier (aka: the niche) is “Almond” Milk.

  • The “BIG Idea” is that even if you can’t tolerate lactose, you can still drink “milk” (if it’s made from nuts). / It’s milk that’s not milk.

First of all, notice how much “pre-work” here goes into effective copywriting. All-star copywriters don’t just jump right into writing clever taglines or “WHAT HAPPENED NEXT IS CRAZY!” headlines. The best copywriters spend a lot—and I mean a lot—of time thinking about the company or product’s unique position in a mega-category (with a modifier word), and the BIG Idea that communicates that company or product’s unique differentiator.

Then, and only then, do you begin working on hooks.

So, what are some “hooks” we could use to immediately grab our target customer’s attention?

Well, remember, the goal isn’t to grab their attention for the sake of grabbing their attention.

When it comes to coming up with effective hooks, the whole game is to ONLY grab the attention of people who would be (or should be) interested in a) this niche, and b) this BIG Idea and differentiator.

So, if we wanted to target “people who want to, need to, or should drink nut-based milk instead of regular cow’s milk,” how might we hook them?

Let’s walk through each “type” of hook… and then I’ll show you some examples.

The 5 Types of Proven Hooks

I have been building Internet businesses for over 10 years.

I have also been hired as a copywriter for all sorts of different companies—ranging from VC-backed Silicon Valley startups to publicly traded companies.

And over and over again, I find myself constantly using these 5 types of proven hooks because, well, they work… regardless of whether you’re writing an email subject line, the header of a website or landing page, or the first few sentences of a VSL.

Proven Hook #1: Stats

One of the most common hooks—not just in marketing materials but also in books, movies, TV shows, and more—is to open with a stat.

Documentaries do this all the time:

  • “Did you know X% of people…?”

  • “According to Harvard Business Review, X% of CEOs…”

  • “A 2025 report has just confirmed: X% of co-workers…”

  • Etc.

Stats, trends, and meaningful data points (ideally backed by science or some credible survey) are powerful hooks because they:

  • Grab your attention with a bold proclamation/statement

  • Hold your attention because they’re “proven” or “backed by someone credible”

  • And trigger you to keep giving your attention because now you want to know: “Wait, really? How did that happen? Is that true? No way?”

So, using our “Almond Milk” example… what are some Stats we could use to hook potential customers?

  • 68% of adults worldwide experience some form of lactose intolerance.

  • Sales of plant-based milk have grown 300% in the past decade.

  • 1 in 3 coffee drinkers say they prefer dairy-free milk options.

  • Americans spent $2.8 billion on plant-based milk last year alone.

*Obviously the stat you use depends on who you are copywriting for—what kind of company/business, who their target customer is, etc. But still, the “hook” methodology is the same.

Proven Hook #2: Big Numbers/Dollar Figures

Another proven hook is to simply share some sort of big number.

And when I say “big number,” I mean, quite literally, any big number relative to its context.

  • “This World War II veteran lived to be 104 years old!”

  • “Taylor Swift just bought this $87M house.”

  • “Healthcare in America costs, on average, 5x more than any other country.”

  • Etc.

These hooks work because large numbers—especially money-related ones—are inherently fascinating. People want to know how those numbers came to be. How did someone live to that age? How did someone amass that much wealth? What does the inside of an $87M house look like? Etc.

These hooks:

  • Spark intrigue (“How did they get that big of a result?”)

  • Create perceived authority (“This must be worth knowing about”)

  • Often tap into status, aspiration, or urgency (“I don’t want to miss out on something this big”)

Almond Milk examples:

  • The $2.8 billion reason you’ll be seeing more almond milk in coffee shops this year.

  • Why 1 million households switched from dairy to almond milk in 2024.

  • How one nut turned into a $10 billion industry.

  • The $4 carton changing the way people drink milk.

*NOTE: “Big” numbers can also work even in small contexts. For example, a lot of our email subject lines geared toward attracting ghostwriters into our Premium Ghostwriting Academy reference a dollar figure/number. “Do you want to land $5,000 clients?” $5,000 might not seem like a lot of money, but in the context of Freelance Writers struggling to charge even $50 per hour, it actually is a lot of money. The context is what dictates the “bigness” of the number.

Proven Hook #3: Small Action, Huge Result

Another timeless hook is to quickly explain to someone that if they would just do this <small thing>, then they would unlock this <huge result>.

In fact, this is one of the most-used hooks in all of non-fiction writing.

Just look at the subtitle for Atomic Habits!

The reason this hook works so well is because people like to believe that the HUGE result they desire can actually be accomplished in a very doable way.

Nobody wants to hear: “That huge result you want? Yea, that’s going to take a huge amount of effort.”

*NOTE: I am NOT saying you need to lie. That’s not the takeaway here. The takeaway is: you should ask yourself how you can make whatever thing you’re presenting—whether it’s a physical product or education—FEEL approachable. It can’t be complicated. And it can’t require the customer to go through some massive undertaking in order to unlock the outcome they desire. It has to be made simple. It has to be “small.”

Almond Milk examples:

  • Tiny sips, packed with flavor.

  • One glass of almond milk, and you’ll never crave real milk again.

  • Want to lose weight? Start 1 glass of almond milk at a time.

Proven Hook #4: Big Problem, Easily Solved

This hook is all about speaking directly to your target customer’s problems.

Start with the customer’s biggest pain point, then immediately remove the weight from their shoulders.

The reason this hook works is because it:

  • Shows empathy (“We get what you’re dealing with”)

  • Positions your product as the obvious answer

  • Makes the customer feel relief before they even buy

Almond Milk examples:

  • Love milk but hate the bloat? Try this.

  • No more skipping dessert because of dairy.

  • Say goodbye to post-coffee stomach aches.

  • The simplest way to ditch dairy without giving up the taste.

Proven Hook #5: Big Outcome, “Zero” Time/Energy/Effort/Money/Etc.

Every single customer wants “something for nothing.”

So part of writing effective copy is understanding this is our human bias, and then finding ways to reduce the “cost” to “zero.”

Now, the truth is, the cost is never zero. But effective copy makes you feel like it is!

(And yes, all these same tactics work on me—as a consumer. I know they are selling mechanisms. I know they are there to deliberately engineer a specific thought/feeling in me. And yet, they still work.)

So, what “costs” do people want to avoid?

  • Time

  • Energy

  • Effort

  • Money

They want an outcome, but they want it “for free” (in every sense).

So take whatever outcome the target customer wants, and then figure out a message that helps communicate to them that this product/service will help them get it—for “near-zero” in exchange.

Almond Milk examples:

  • No more grocery shopping. Almond Milk delivers!

  • Going dairy-free is hard. Almond Milk makes it easy.

  • Cow milk is expensive. Almond Milk costs less than a pack of almonds!

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Module 4 of Copywriting 101: A Full Crash Course On How To Write Things That Sell.

In this module, we’re going to cover HOOKS.

Specifically:

  • The 5 types of proven “Hooks”

  • And the “Hook” mistakes (copywriters make all the time)

As a reminder, before you “get in the weeds” when it comes to copywriting, you need to nail two things down:

1. The Niche

You, the copywriter, need to be crystal clear with yourself (and the company you’re writing for) about the category. Because the “niche” you pick is your unique positioning within that specific industry/larger mega-category. And this niche is almost always defined with a strategically chosen modifier word.

For example: if your mega-category is “milk,” your niche might be “almond milk.”

2. The BIG Idea

Once you have clarity on the niche, the next decision is to pick the BIG Idea.

This is “the thing” you’re going to put a spotlight on in everything that you write: ads, newsletters, landing page copy, sales videos, etc. This BIG Idea is the very simple (1 sentence) explanation for what makes your unique positioning different.

For example: if your niche is “almond milk,” the BIG Idea here might be that “it tastes just like milk but is lactose-free.”

*NOTE: IF YOU DO NOT HAVE CLARITY OVER THESE 2 PIECES—the niche, and the BIG Idea—your copy isn’t going to be very effective.

It’s only after these 2 big decisions that you should even begin thinking, “Ok, now how do I hook the customer?”

Let’s dive in!

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Module 5 of Copywriting 101: A Full Crash Course On How To Write Things That Sell.

In this module, we’re going to get super tactical and talk about the different questions you need to answer for customers in order to “sell them” on taking action—whether that’s typing in their email, clicking on a link to visit a landing page, watching a VSL (video sales letter), signing up for a free trial or demo, or becoming a customer.

Now, to give credit where credit is due, the framework I’m going to walk you through in this module is based on a very well-known copywriter’s book. His name is Evaldo Albuquerque, and he wrote a book called The 16-Word Sales Letter: A proven method of writing multi-million-dollar copy faster than you ever thought possible.

In the book, he lays out (very clearly) the 10 questions every customer has—that you need to answer in your copy:

  • Question #1: “How is this different from everything else I’ve seen?”

  • Question #2: “What’s in it for me?”

  • Question #3: “How do I know this is real?”

  • Question #4: “What’s holding me back?”

  • Question #5: “Who/what is to blame (besides me)?”

  • Question #6: “Why do I need to take action right now?”

  • Question #7: “Why should I trust you?”

  • Question #8: “So, how does this work?”

  • Question #9: “How can I get started? What happens next?”

  • Question #10: “What do I have to lose? What if I’m unhappy?”

I read this book many years ago, and have used simple list of questions to inform a lot of my copy over the years. So yes, while I’ve built on it with frameworks of my own, and my explanations (to you) will probably be a bit different than his, I still a) want to credit Evaldo for his contribution to the copywriting world, and b) let you know the origin here—so you can go directly to the source, if you’d like.

Let’s dive in!

records.title: Question #10:
