records.description: “What do I have to lose? What if I’m unhappy?” Lastly, the customer needs to know what their downside protection is. And the easiest way to answer this question
records.content:
“What do I have to lose? What if I’m unhappy?”

Lastly, the customer needs to know what their downside protection is.

And the easiest way to answer this question/overcome this objection is to offer some sort of refund policy.

Now, there are all sorts of ways you can structure this:

  • Basic Money-Back Guarantee: "30-day money-back guarantee. If you're not satisfied, we'll refund your purchase." Simple, straightforward, removes the financial risk.

  • Extended Guarantee Period: "Try it risk-free for 90 days." The longer the guarantee period, the more confidence it shows in your product. Plus, paradoxically, longer guarantees often result in fewer refund requests because customers forget about the guarantee deadline.

  • No-Questions-Asked Policy: "If you're unhappy for ANY reason, just send us an email and we'll process your refund immediately. No hoops to jump through, no forms to fill out." This removes the friction and hassle customers often worry about when requesting refunds.

  • Conditional/Performance Guarantees: "If you don't see a 25% increase in website traffic within 60 days, we'll refund your money." This is powerful because you're not just guaranteeing satisfaction—you're guaranteeing specific results.

  • Better-Than-Risk-Free: "If you're not happy, not only will we refund your money, but you can keep all the bonuses as our apology for wasting your time." Now there's literally no downside to trying.

  • Double-Your-Money-Back: "If this doesn't work for you, we'll not only refund your purchase—we'll double it." This is the nuclear option that shows extreme confidence.

  • Partial Guarantees (For Higher-Ticket Items): "Don't love it after 30 days? We'll refund 50% of your purchase price, no questions asked." For expensive products/services, even a partial guarantee can remove enough risk to get people over the finish line.

  • Success-Based Guarantees: "Do the work for 30 days. If you don't get results, I'll personally work with you one-on-one until you do—at no extra charge." This guarantees not just satisfaction, but success.

  • The "Better Deal" Guarantee: "Find a better price somewhere else within 30 days and we'll not only match it—we'll beat it by 10%." This removes price-shopping anxiety.

Now, a couple important notes about guarantees:

First, you need to actually honor them. If you offer a guarantee but make it difficult for customers to get refunds, word will get out and it'll hurt your reputation.

Second, offering a strong guarantee usually REDUCES refund requests. Why? Because it attracts more confident buyers who are genuinely interested in your solution, rather than fence-sitters who are likely to ask for refunds anyway.

Third, the specific type of guarantee you offer should match your business model and customer base. For example, a 90-day guarantee might make sense for a digital course, but not for a consulting service.

The point is this: the stronger your guarantee, the easier it becomes for customers to say "yes." Because in their mind, they're thinking, "What's the worst that could happen? If it doesn't work, I get my money back."

records.title: Question #1:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #1_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “How is this different from everything else I’ve seen?” This is the million-dollar question. And the truth is, as the copywriter, you don’t always have control
records.content:
“How is this different from everything else I’ve seen?”

This is the million-dollar question.

And the truth is, as the copywriter, you don’t always have control over how this question gets answered. For example, if you get hired as a copywriter for a run-of-the-mill SEO agency, how are you going to present this service as “different” from anything else the target customer has ever seen? That’s hard!

So, a couple things to keep in mind with how you answer this question for customers:

First, if you can (or if it’s your own company/product), this is where Copywriting x Product Innovation actually go hand-in-hand. The more you can (or you can “help”) develop a radically new product (and/or category of product), the easier it is to answer this question for the customer. Because what makes it “different” is immediately apparent.

Second, if the product ISN’T actually different (true for the vast majority of businesses), that’s fine.

Here are 3 easy ways to manufacture differentiation:

  • Solves a specific, unique problem: Pluck out a specific problem the customer has and put that in the spotlight. By framing the product as world-class for solving this “specific problem,” it gets separated from the competition—because the competition is probably saying, “We solve ALL these problems.” By picking 1 problem and leading with it, you have differentiation.

  • Solves a specific/known problem in a new & unique way: The same is true on the solution side. Pick 1 specific component of your solution and put that in the spotlight. By leading with a specific type of solution (vs the competition: “We solve EVERYTHING!”) you have differentiation.

  • Solves a specific/known problem but for a different archetype of customer: Lastly, do either of the above FOR a specific type of customer. Again, the competition usually says, “We solve ALL these problems in ALL these ways for EVERYONE.” You achieve differentiation when you say you specialize in serving just 1 specific archetype of person.

*NOTE: Whenever I explain this concept of leading with a specific problem, solution, or audience archetype, I always get the question/objection back… “But Cole?! Won’t I be cutting out tons of prospective customers?!” And actually, the answer is no, you won’t. Because customers who don’t perfectly match the problem, solution, or archetype you’ve put on the spotlight will still assume “it also works for them.” But by leading with 1, you immediately become differentiated from the competition—which increases the likelihood they consider your product/service in the first place.

records.title: Question #2:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #2_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “What’s in it for me?” Every customer wants to know: “If I do this, how will my life be better?” And so there are all sorts of different ways you can answer thi
records.content:
“What’s in it for me?”

Every customer wants to know: “If I do this, how will my life be better?”

And so there are all sorts of different ways you can answer this question:

  • “If you do this, you’ll be happier!”

  • “If you do this, you’ll get richer!”

  • “If you do this, you’ll be less stressed!”

  • “If you do this, you’ll feel more fulfilled!”

  • Etc.

Ultimately, your goal as the copywriter is to help the customer connect with their “ideal end-state.”

Because the customer can’t get excited about the VEHICLE until they first get excited about the DESTINATION.

Here are some simple examples to drive the point home:

  • Before you can sell a gym membership, the customer has to get excited about getting fit for the summer.

  • Before you can sell a luxury sports car, the customer has to get excited about having a status symbol very few people have.

  • Before you can sell a Japanese A5 wagyu steak, the customer has to get excited about having an exclusive dish that doesn’t even taste like steak—it tastes like butter, and melts in your mouth.

  • Before you can sell eco-friendly olive oil, the customer has to get excited about saving the planet.

  • Etc.

So long before you even begin talking about your product or “the solution,” you need to first make sure the customer is viscerally connected to their ideal end-state.

They have to known “what’s in it for them.”

records.title: Question #3:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #3_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “How do I know this is real?” Proof. Proof. Proof. The customer knows what you’re offering is real when they can “see” that it works—for themselves. - If you’re
records.content:
“How do I know this is real?”

Proof. Proof. Proof.

The customer knows what you’re offering is real when they can “see” that it works—for themselves.

  • If you’re selling weight loss, they want to see other people who have lost weight.

  • If you’re selling day-trading strategies, they want to see other people making money.

  • If you’re selling lead generation services, they want to see leads generated for other companies.

  • Etc.

This is an easy enough concept to understand.

However, there are 2 nuances I want to share here—because they’re important.

The first is that if you don’t have “proof,” you can easily answer this question (aka: overcome this objection) by educating the prospect to such a degree that your solution (and your ability to deliver that solution) becomes undeniable. A lot of times, businesses need lots and lots of “proof” because they aren’t actually very good at educating customers on their problems. So “proof” becomes a crutch. In reality, the question “How do I know this is real?” gets answered for the customer when you educate them to such a degree that they completely trust you.

Second, I really like Alex Hormozi’s framework here, which is that “proof” isn’t binary. It’s that when customers are evaluating whatever it is you’re offering them, they are creating an expectation and Perceived Likelihood of Achievement for themselves.

And this exists on a spectrum.

For example, let’s say you’re selling crypto day-trading strategies to college students (lol).

Well, “proof” exists on a spectrum.

  • V1: You could run an ad showing you talking to college students.

  • V2: You could improve the ad by showing a specific type of college student—who matches your ideal target customer.

  • V3: You could improve the ad by showing you, on a college campus, surrounded by 10 college students—all of whom “look like” your ideal target customer.

  • V4: You could improve the ad by showing you, on a college campus, surrounded by 10 college students (who all “look like” your ideal target customer), with each of them holding up a piece of paper saying how much money they’ve made in the past month from day-trading crypto.

  • Etc.

The point is, “proof” is really a game of CONGRUENCE.

Because the more congruent your messaging (whether it be through words, images, videos, cartoons, etc.), the more it speaks directly to a specific type of customer. And the more “specifically” it speaks to that customer, the more they trust and believe what they are seeing is true—because it is speaking DIRECTLY TO THEM.

records.title: Question #4:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #4_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “What’s holding me back?” Oftentimes, the customer isn’t even aware of what’s holding them back. Which is why, again, the best way to “sell” them is to EDUCATE
records.content:
“What’s holding me back?”

Oftentimes, the customer isn’t even aware of what’s holding them back.

Which is why, again, the best way to “sell” them is to EDUCATE them.

Here are the ways customers tend to hold themselves back:

Mindset Deficiency

The vast majority of customers don’t take action, don’t buy products or services, and don’t “bet on themselves” because of some sort of mindset issue.

  • They don’t believe they can do it.

  • They don’t believe it’ll “work for them.”

  • They don’t consider themselves to be “someone who succeeds” (in that way).

  • They don’t think they will hold themselves accountable and/or can’t trust themselves to follow-through.

  • Etc.

Faulty Beliefs

The next most-common reason customers hold themselves back is they believe things that aren’t true.

  • The way “they think is best” is actually the wrong way.

  • The way you’re proposing, they think, “Is a scam.”

  • Etc.

These types of customers CAN be converted, but the only way that happens is if you spend a lot of time (”time” being literal time, or an abundance of resources) dismantling all these faulty beliefs.

Logistical Confusion

The next most-common reason customers hold themselves back is logistical:

  • They don’t know what to do.

  • They don’t know what to prioritize.

  • They don’t know literally how to get started.

  • Etc.

There are some customers (not to be ageist here, but typically on the older & less tech-savvy side) who, quite literally, don’t take action because they don’t know how. They don’t know which buttons to press. They don’t know the right page to visit. They don’t know who to reach out to with questions. Etc.

Don’t underestimate logistical confusion.

Finances

Lastly, a lot of times customers don’t take the next step because of something related to finances:

  • “I don’t have the money.”

  • “I don’t think I can find the money.”

  • “I don’t want to prioritize spending my money this way.”

  • “I think what you’re proposing is too expensive.”

  • Etc.

Now, yes, in some cases the customer simply doesn’t have the money and there’s nothing you can do about that. They have $11 in their checking account. They’re behind on rent. And they work a minimum-wage job. Not much you can do there—no matter how “hard” you sell them.

But I will say, a lot of the time, money in-and-of-itself isn’t the real issue.

Even if they say it is.

Money is usually a smokescreen for some other mindset issue, faulty belief, or logistical confusion.

It’s just easier for them to say, “Nah, that’s too expensive,” than it is for them to open up and say, “Honestly, I’m just afraid of letting myself down and looking like a fool.”

Which is why YOU (the copywriter) needs to spend a lot of time educating them on all the different things holding them back from their ideal end-state.

records.title: Question #5:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #5_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “Who/what is to blame (besides me)?” Here’s the brutal truth: At the end of the day, if we aren’t where we want to be in life—whether it’s with our health, weal
records.content:
“Who/what is to blame (besides me)?”

Here’s the brutal truth:

At the end of the day, if we aren’t where we want to be in life—whether it’s with our health, wealth, relationships, etc.—it’s ultimately our fault.

We are to blame.

  • We gave up.

  • We weren’t disciplined.

  • We didn’t try hard enough.

  • We didn’t do it long enough to really know.

  • We expected overnight success for little-to-no sacrifices in exchange.

  • We got in our own way, and made up a narrative as to why it “wouldn’t work for us.”

  • Etc.

*No judgement. As a consumer, I do this too. This is just what human beings do.

HOWEVER… as a copywriter, you can’t really come right out and say to someone: “Hey, you want to know who’s at fault here? It’s you, you idiot. You don’t do the things you say you’re going to do. You give up too easily. You’re weak!”

That doesn’t work.

People don’t want to be made to feel bad about themselves.

Instead, the way you answer this question is by using a tried-and-true copywriting tactic:

Give the customer someone else to blame.

You want to show them you’re on the same team.

And what’s the fastest way to get someone on your team? Create an enemy!

Watch:

  • “What’s holding you back from writing online? Well, traditional education does a horrible job teaching you how to write in the digital age, let alone believe in yourself and your writing. It’s not your fault!”

  • “What’s holding you back from buying your first house and starting a family? Blackstone. They’ve been buying up all the residential houses and have turned them into rentals. It’s not your fault.”

  • “What’s holding you back from losing weight? America’s food system! It’s riddled with harmful chemicals and additives. It’s not your fault!”

You win the customer’s trust when you can help them blame someone else—and validating for them they aren’t “the only one” at fault.

So, find an enemy.

And then educate the prospect on how that enemy has done them dirty, and your mission is to right that wrong in the world.

records.title: Question #6:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #6_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “Why do I need to take action right now?” You have to create urgency. Now, sometimes urgency is implied in the thing you’re selling. For example, if you’re runn
records.content:
“Why do I need to take action right now?”

You have to create urgency.

Now, sometimes urgency is implied in the thing you’re selling. For example, if you’re running a Christmas promotion, urgency is implied because “Christmas” is a timed event. And it’s reasonable assume the Christmas promotion will no longer be active… after Christmas.

In other cases, urgency is something you need to create.

Here’s a list of different ways you can create urgency, and how each one works:

  • Limited Time Offers: "This offer expires at midnight on Friday." The key here is making sure the deadline is real and you actually follow through. If customers catch you extending "limited time" offers indefinitely, you lose all credibility.

  • Limited Quantity/Availability: "Only 50 spots available" or "While supplies last." This works particularly well for courses, coaching programs, or physical products. Again, authenticity is crucial—if you're going to claim limited spots, you need to actually limit them.

  • Price Increases: "The price goes up next week" or "This is the lowest price we'll ever offer." This creates urgency around getting a better deal now versus later. Just make sure you're honest about future pricing—if you say the price is going up, it needs to actually go up.

  • Bonus Removal: "If you sign up by Friday, you get these 3 bonuses. After Friday, they're gone forever." This creates urgency around getting additional value that won't be available later.

  • Problem Urgency: Sometimes the urgency isn't about your offer—it's about their problem getting worse. "Every day you wait to fix your credit, you're losing money on higher interest rates." This ties urgency to the cost of inaction rather than just the benefit of action.

  • Seasonal/Event-Based Urgency: "Get ready for summer," "Tax season is coming," "Before the new year starts." This leverages natural timing that feels logical to the customer.

The key with urgency is that it has to feel REAL and REASONABLE to the customer. Fake urgency doesn’t work—because any reasonable customer will recognize it. But genuine urgency (tied to real constraints or logical timing) can be the difference between someone taking action now versus "maybe later" (which usually means never).

records.title: Question #7:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #7_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
“Why should I trust you?”

Credibility. Credibility. Credibility.

Now, this can get achieved in 3 ways:

  • First, the customer trusts you based on how well you can articulate their problem(s). The better you can articulate what they’re going through, what they’ve tried in the past (that didn’t work), and what they are feeling while dealing with this problem, the more they are going to assume you can be trusted. Because how else would you know about their experience so intimately?

  • Second, the customer trusts you based on “proof.” The more you can PROVE whatever it is you’re saying/promising, the more likely they are to trust you. Again, “proof” sits on a spectrum, so proof is also the degree to which the customer believes this will work for them.

  • Third, the customer trusts you based on your credibility. Credibility is really just a fancy word for “context.” Your credibility is the surrounding context of whatever it is you’re promising. For example, “I will help you lose weight” becomes a more believable promise when the context of that promise is your own credibility: “I was overweight my whole life. And then, I started training in this way, and lost 80 pounds.”

In an ideal world, you should be able to build trust with every customer in all 3 of these ways.

As for credibility itself, this could be all sorts of things:

  • Media: What other media can you show, and what other credibility can you “borrow” to reinforce your own? (For example: “As seen in Forbes!”)

  • Awards: What meaningful awards have you won in this industry/space? Have you been on any magazines? Have you won any competitions, grants, etc.?

  • Time: How long have you been in this industry? 5 years? 10 years? 25 years? The longer the “time,” the more credibility you have.

  • Money: How much money have you made in this industry? How much money have you made other people? Etc.

  • Status: Who have you worked with? At what exclusive places in the world?

  • Metrics: How many followers do you have? How many views have your accumulated? How many email subscribers have you attracted? Etc.

Literally anything can be used as “credibility” as long as it provides context to the target customer—including things you wouldn’t even consider to be “professional.”

For example, if you were selling a paid newsletter that shared TV & movie recommendations every weekend, by category, what could your “credibility” be?

“Written by someone who has watched over 5,000 shows & movies on Netflix.”

That “credibility” is just context.

records.title: Question #8:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #8_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “So, how does this work?” Once a customer is sufficiently educated, and has decided your product will indeed work for them, the next thing they need to know is
records.content:
“So, how does this work?”

Once a customer is sufficiently educated, and has decided your product will indeed work for them, the next thing they need to know is “how it works.”

Now, this might seem like a simple question… but it’s actually where a LOT of copywriters go wrong.

Here’s the mistake most copywriters make:

They articulate “how it works” in Subjective, Intangible ways.

So let’s say you’re selling a high-ticket group-coaching program for hobbyist designers who want to become Figma Pros and get a high-paying job as a Lead Designer at a tech company.

Here’s how most copywriters would articulate the “how it works” of this program:

  • “You get a coach.”

  • “You also get a really great curriculum showing you everything you need to know.”

  • “You also get a bunch of bonuses.”

  • “And you also get lifetime access.”

Now, it’s not that any of these are WRONG.

It’s just these benefits are framed in Subjective, Intangible ways.

Just observe the questions you probably have looking at the above example.

  • “What kind of coach? How does that work?”

  • “What kind of curriculum? How’s it structured?”

  • “Well, what are the bonuses?”

  • “OK, lifetime access to what? Is it going to change?”

The way it’s presented actually creates more questions.

And that’s a problem.

Instead, here’s how a Pro Copywriter would articulate “how it works.”

The secret is to speak in Objective, Tangible ways.

  • “First, you get added to a private Slack channel with your 1:1 coach, who will immediately introduce themselves with a Welcome Loom and a link to book your first 1:1 call.”

  • “You also will get immediate access to our 8-module text & video curriculum designed to take you from Figma beginner all the way to your first interview call with a major tech company.”

  • “You will also be receiving 3 bonuses to your email in the next hour. These 3 bonuses are a copy of our founder’s book, a private recording of last month’s masterclass on how to create templates inside Figma, and a bundle pack of 10 templates designed by students of the program for you to use right away.”

  • “Lastly, just so you know, you have lifetime access to the Slack community, the curriculum, the masterclass replay hub, and all future recordings and upgrades.”

Which version is better?

Exactly.

The entire name of the game, when articulating “how something works,” is to speak in Objective, Tangible ways.

  • Objective: You want zero subjectivity. There should be no “room for interpretation.” An easy stress-test here is, “If I asked 10 people what this meant, would I get 10 different answers? Or would they all say the same answer?” You want the latter.

  • Tangible: You want to state assets, objects, steps, things you can hold and measure. Customers don’t value “intangible” promises. They value THINGS. They value anything they can hold in their hands, or interact with, or measure in some way.

records.title: Question #9:
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/Question #9_ - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “How can I get started? What happens next?” If you’ve made it this far, congratulations! That means the customer is red-hot and ready to go. All that’s left is
records.content:
“How can I get started? What happens next?”

If you’ve made it this far, congratulations!

That means the customer is red-hot and ready to go.

All that’s left is to tell them the next 3 things that are going to happen:

For example:

  • “From here, you’ll complete your purchase with me on the next page.”

  • “After the purchase has been completed, you will receive an invitation to our private Slack community within the next 5 minutes or less. Click that link, and find your private Slack channel.”

  • “And once you’re inside Slack, your 1:1 coach will introduce themselves and send you a Calendly link to book your first workshop call!”

Step. By. Step.

Now, little pro tip here:

Be as painfully specific as you can.

Don’t just say, “From here, you’ll complete your purchase.”

Say…

  • “From here, you’ll complete your purchase on the next page.

  • Or, even better… “From here, click the big blue button right below this window and you’ll complete your purchase on the next page.”

  • Or, even better… “From here, click the big blue button right below this window and you’ll complete your purchase on the next page—where you’ll type in your credit card number and home address.”

  • Or, even better… “From here, click the big blue button right below this window and you’ll complete your purchase on the next page—where you’ll type in your credit card number and home address. We ask for your home address, so we can send you a welcome basket!”

Etc.

The more SPECIFIC you can be about what, exactly, is going to happen next… the more likely the customer is to do it.

records.title: The 10 Copywriting Questions Framework
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Copywriting 101/Module 5 Every Customer’s 10 Questions/The 10 Copywriting Questions Framework - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Alright, getting in the weeds here. The following are the 10 questions every customer needs answered in order to make an educated purchasing decision: - Questio
records.content:
Alright, getting in the weeds here.

The following are the 10 questions every customer needs answered in order to make an educated purchasing decision:

  • Question #1: “How is this different from everything else I’ve seen?”

  • Question #2: “What’s in it for me?”

  • Question #3: “How do I know this is real?”

  • Question #4: “What’s holding me back?”

  • Question #5: “Who/what is to blame (besides me)?”

  • Question #6: “Why do I need to take action right now?”

  • Question #7: “Why should I trust you?”

  • Question #8: “So, how does this work?”

  • Question #9: “How can I get started? What happens next?”

  • Question #10: “What do I have to lose? What if I’m unhappy?”

Now, you might be wondering, “OK, but Cole… how am I supposed to speak to all of these?”

Good question.

The goal here isn’t to speak to all 10 of these questions the first time they see an ad, or the first time they subscribe to your email list, or the first time you get on the phone with a prospect.

The goal is for potential customers to have ALL these questions answered from first-touch to final-conversion.

So from the time they first discover you/the business/the product, to the moment where they decide whether or not to make a purchasing decision, these 10 questions should be answered for them.

  • You could answer 1-3 of these in an ad.

  • And then another 1-3 in a downloadable resource.

  • And then another 1-3 in follow-up/reminder emails.

  • And then another 1-3 on a live sales call.

  • Etc.

The point is to just make sure the customer gets these 10 questions answered, SOMEWHERE, SOMEHOW, so they have “all the information they need” in order to make an educated purchasing decision.

Got it?

Good—I knew you were smart.

Let’s go question by question.

records.content:
Hey there!

Welcome to Digital Product Upsells, a mini-masterclass associated with Low-Ticket Launchpad.

In this mini-course, we’re going to cover:

  • The 8 Business Models you can use to upsell your low-ticket digital product customers

  • Why some upsells (and business models) are better than others

  • And how you should think about choosing the right upsells for your right stage of business

Let’s dive in!


Digital Product Upsells 101

https://www.loom.com/share/fc401be0cb394faaa99d31f3b413587d?sid=5d187cd1-74b3-4001-9cac-a3e43890dc9b

To first give you some context:

Since 2021, we have launched a lot of different products and tried a lot of different product upsells.

Some have performed very well for us.

And some were massive flops (and cost us a lot of time, energy, and money).

As you can see from the above chart, not every decision and not every month is “the best month ever.” In fact, there were many points along the way where the revenue trend-line of the business looked as if the business was about to die. You can spot these points in the above graph because the line goes down dramatically… and then later, goes up dramatically (again and again).

This is what launching products and building a business “looks like.”

It’s not one clean line up and to the right.

It’s a lot of ups and downs—and you just hope that, when you zoom out, the average trend-line goes up and to the right (which, in our case, it has).

My goal here is to help you avoid experiencing as tumultuous of a journey!

“What Is An Upsell?”

Let’s start with the basics:

An “Upsell” is something else you sell customers.

And this Upsell can be presented in a bunch of different ways:

  • [Sales Funnel] Your Upsell can be added as an “Order Bump” to the front-end sales funnel. Meaning, before the customer finishes purchasing your main Low-Ticket Digital Product, you give them “something else” to buy that is relevant to the product they’re already purchasing.

  • [In The Product] Your Upsell can also be linked to throughout your Low-Ticket Digital Product as an evergreen “it’s-here-if-you-want-it” option.

  • [Post-Product] Your Upsell can also be something you wait to present to the customer until after they’ve completed your Low-Ticket Digital Product. In this case, your Upsell is usually “the next step.”

The 2 Goals Of Upsells

There are 2 big things you’re trying to accomplish here:

  • Increase Average Cart Value: The more Upsells (also known as “Order Bumps”) in your front-end funnel, the more your average cart value goes up. For example, if your Low-Ticket Digital Product is $350 and 10 people buy it, you make $3,500 in revenue. But if you add in a $99 Upsell (Order Bump), and 20% of people buy it, you make $3,700 in revenue. What’s important to note though is this “incremental revenue bump” scales without any additional work from you. (For context: we’re now at a point where a single Upsell in our front-end funnel usually generates an additional $50k-$150k in incremental revenue for us. As you scale, this is not a small amount of revenue!)

  • Increase Customer Lifetime Value: The more Upsells you also have available to customers (in your funnel, linked throughout your product(s), and available as “next steps” after customers complete products), the more products your Superconsumers will buy and the more your average Customer Lifetime Value will go up.

In an ideal world, you actually want to build multiple products—each of which “pick up” where the last one ended—so that existing customers buy more products, opposed to only having 1 product and constantly needing to find “new customers.”

It’s much easier to generate revenue (and build a sustainable business) if more of your existing customers continue spending money with you.

“What Makes For A Great Upsell?”

Good question!

There are 3 things that make for a great Upsell:

  • Relevance: The Upsell you present the customer, at the moment you present it, needs to be relevant to whatever they’re “currently consuming.” For example, it wouldn’t make sense to link to an Upsell about “gardening” inside of your Low-Ticket Digital Product about sales. What would be relevant is linking to a Sales Tracking Dashboard Upsell.

  • More, But Different: The Upsell should be relevant, and should give the customer “more” of the thing they’re already interested in… but it should also be different. It shouldn’t repeat information, for example, that is already in your core product. It should present something new, or present it in some new way, so that it feels like an entirely separate asset.

  • Access: When in doubt, give the customer either “more” access to you… or “more” access to behind-the-scenes information. One of the most valuable Upsells is always the ability to talk to you, the Creator, or the ability to see the raw files of how you do what you do.

8 Business Models To Collect More Revenue From Existing Customers

So, with all of this in mind, here are the 8 types of Upsells we’ve learned work best:

  • Upsell #1: Swipe File ($49-$99)

  • Upsell #2: Crash Course ($99-$149)

  • Upsell #3: “Behind The Scenes” ($149-$199)

  • Upsell #4: Different Low-Ticket Digital Product ($199 - $350)

  • Upsell #5: Paid Newsletter ($9/mo-$99/mo)

  • Upsell #6: Recurring Community ($9/mo-$99/mo)

  • Upsell #7: “Power-Hour” Consulting ($150-$500+)

  • Upsell #8: Services ($3,000/mo+)

Let’s dig into each one so you understand how it works!


Upsell #1: Swipe File ($49-$99)

https://www.loom.com/share/87a0b867492c434ea391d7ff576b101e?sid=11cc99b3-5e58-43d7-affc-dd60b1e9cf1c

This is the easiest (and most beginner) type of Upsell to immediately add into:

  • Your Sales Funnel

  • Linked throughout your product (Evergreen)

  • Or presented for sale at the end of your core product (either inside the product and/or via email a week or two later)

A Swipe File can be lots of different things.

But generally speaking, there are 2 types of Swipe Files:

  • Collection Of Examples + Commentary: A Swipe File should be a compilation of examples of “how to do something really well.” For example: if you are selling a copywriting digital product, it might make sense to have an Upsell where you’ve collected the 50 best landing pages. The key here, though (at least in our opinion) is to not just “collect” valuable or proven resources, but ALSO give some sort of commentary about each one. Don’t just say, “I collected 50 great landing pages for you.” Say, “I collected 50 great landing pages for you, and took the time to break down each one so you know exactly why it works so well.” It’s the additional commentary that’s the real value.

  • Templates: And/or, a Swipe File could be is a compilation of templates, AI Prompts, etc. For example: if you are selling a personal finance digital product, it might make sense to have an Upsell where you share 10 different excel templates you use to get your end-of-year accounting done in a fraction of the time.

Again, the big idea here is that you’re giving the customer “more, but different.”

They want “more” resources to help them do the thing they’re clearly interested in doing (which is why they’re buying your core Digital Product), but these additional resources are “different” enough that they don’t have the objection: “I bet I don’t need these.”

You always want to frame the value of these additional resources as: “…this will help you do the thing you’ve already decided you want to do, better/faster/more efficiently/more effectively.”

And for this type of asset, standard pricing is typically in the $49 to $99 range, one-time payment.

If you are brand new to creating Swipe Files and selling them as Upsells, here’s an example:

This is one of our Swipe Files from 2024.

It’s nothing crazy complicated—just a cleanly organized Notion Document of Viral Hook Templates.

Feel free to use this as an “example” and/or template when building your own!

*NOTE: Bonus points for linking to ANOTHER upsell at the bottom of your Swipe File :)

Viral Hook Vault (Summer 2024 Edition)


Upsell #2: Crash Course ($99-$149)

https://www.loom.com/share/68f0e98fd35542928887e8bbc46709e5?sid=cd120cc7-3ca8-4c3a-ace5-83685f51809e

The second type of upsell is a stand-alone mini-course (or “Crash Course”) on a “more, but different” topic.

*NOTE: If you are going through this mini-course on Upsells right now, chances are… you’re here because this was presented to you as an Upsell in our Low-Ticket Launchpad sales funnel!

The big idea here is… if someone is interested in buying 1 Low-Ticket Digital Product, they’re probably interested in buying a 2nd IF it’s relevant to them. So, why not give them an option? Why not present a “more, but different” offer? (Chances are 10-30% of people will take it, which increases your average cart value & notches up your customer lifetime revenue.)

For example: Category Newsletter Creator

In 2024, for Black Friday, we launched a Low-Ticket Digital Product called Category Newsletter Creator.

It was all about how to create a category-defining newsletter, how to write effectively weekly newsletters, and the different ways to monetize your weekly newsletter.

Newsletter. Newsletter. Newsletter.

So, when thinking about “Upsells”—specifically other mini-courses we could present to customers, all we did was ask ourselves: “What is the customer going to want to do next? Once they know how to build a newsletter, what’s their next problem or next goal/aspiration?”

And then we created mini-courses that solved those “next problems.”

For example, the 2 we came up with were:

  • 0 to $1: A mini-course about how to create and launch your first very small digital download/product and make your first $1 online. Why did we pick this topic? Because once someone has a newsletter, their “next step” is absolutely going to be “Now how do I monetize?”

  • 1-Person Publishing Empire: A mini-course about how to bundle all your newsletters together and republish them as a book on Amazon. Why did we pick this topic? Because another very easy way to start monetizing online is to take everything you’ve already written (especially in the form of a newsletter) and just repackage it into a self-published book.

Notice how both of these topics are “more” of what the core digital product was about (in some way related to, or building off of “newsletter writing”) but also “different” enough that they felt like separate-but-related things.

This is the whole key to creating mini-courses as Upsells.

“More,” but different.


Upsell #3: “Behind The Scenes” ($149-$199)

https://www.loom.com/share/94f21e0518ea4829aa4f9a0db6c2c88f?sid=5936f356-1b4d-41bd-b7fe-52a1dbf52f65

The third Upsell—and this one has really crushed for us, and is now a key part of our Upsell strategy—is giving customers “more access” to:

  • You

  • Your raw files

  • And your “personal” strategy for <insert anything relevant to the core product>

For example, for all our digital product launches now, there are 2 Upsells we always consider adding (and usually end up using 1 or both):

Behind-The-Scenes

Out of all the people who buy your product, some percentage of customers don’t just want “the product itself.”

They also want to know HOW you created the thing they just bought.

They want to know how the sausage gets made!

So now, whenever we’re doing a digital product launch, we add in this $199 Upsell where we give away ALL our raw files from that specific product launch:

  • Our internal project dashboard for managing the project, start to finish

  • Copies of our entire product launch email sequence

  • Our rough drafts of product outlines

  • Our ad & video scripts

  • Etc.

This is what’s known as “selling your sawdust.”

In addition, we also add in a bonus 60-minute Q&A live call for everyone who buys this Behind-The-Scenes product. So not only do they get to see all our “raw files,” but they can also show up and ask us questions about the product launch & anything else they want to know.

We’ve found this to be an extremely effective Upsell.

Our Personal Strategy For XYZ

The other Upsell option here is to sell a “more, but different” mini-course that specifically emphasizes your personal strategy for XYZ.

For example, when we were launching our Low-Ticket Digital Product, Category Newsletter Creator, we knew that a lot of people would go through the product and inevitably want to know, “OK, so I need to write on social platforms to drive traffic to my newsletter… how do YOU do that?”

  • Option A would have been create a stand-alone mini-course about how to write on X & LinkedIn and drive social traffic, sure.

  • But Option B (which is much more compelling) is creating a product saying, “…and if you want to write on social platforms to drive traffic, here is our personal Social Traffic Strategy for 2025.”

It’s still relevant to the core product. But it’s “more, but different.”

And not just “more, but different”… but is also positioned as exclusive.

This is our PERSONAL strategy.


Upsell #4: Another LT Digital Product ($199-$350)

https://www.loom.com/share/f305ab44a0bb4cb5a9421a5223de6b17?sid=fa31c502-b624-4266-bb74-bca64b86e999

The fourth Upsell, and when in doubt, is to just make customers aware that you have “other” stand-alone digital products for sale.

For example, anytime we launch a new Low-Ticket Digital Product, we create segments in our email list. And one of those segments is “anyone who hasn’t purchased Ship 30 for 30 yet.” And if someone hasn’t purchased Ship 30 for 30 yet, then we mention that product and make that product an Upsell option in their sales funnel. Because if someone is interested in newsletter writing, they’re probably also interested in “starting to write online.”

Additionally, we link to Ship 30 for 30 constantly:

  • In various sales funnels (depending on whether the customer has already purchased it or not)

  • Inside every single digital product

  • Inside follow-up emails to customers after they’ve purchased a digital product… but haven’t purchased Ship 30 for 30 yet

  • Etc.

Again, when in doubt, just make new & existing customers aware of your other products for sale.

Over and over and over again.

Now in the beginning, if you only have 1 product created, you won’t have the opportunity yet.

And that’s OK.

But this is the benefit of playing the Internet game over a long time horizon, and building the skill of creating valuable digital products, and creating lots of different products over time.

Because the more products you create:

  • The more “options” your customers have…

  • The more money they will spend with you…

  • The more your average cart value will go up…

  • The more your average customer lifetime value will go up.

The goal isn’t to just create 1 really great product.

The goal is to dominate a niche, and create an ecosystem of “more, but different” products that extend customer LTV over a long time horizon.


Upsell #5: Paid Newsletter ($9/mo-$99/mo)

https://www.loom.com/share/dd4973e0efa845799ec2d200aa90df46?sid=d48302c8-943d-45a0-94b1-fe1c5ebc93fd

Upsells #1-#4 are the easiest to execute.

From here, the Upsell options start getting more advanced.

Another option you have is to Upsell customers of stand-alone products (like a $350 Low-Ticket Digital Product) to something recurring—like a paid newsletter.

Now, here’s what everyone “thinks” is true about recurring products:

  • “Recurring revenue means passive revenue.” Wrong. Everybody wants recurring revenue until they realize that means recurring work. And we’ve found that recurring revenue products tend to consume MORE energy/time/resources than non-recurring stand-alone products.

  • “A less expensive monthly recurring revenue product means more people will buy.” Correct. You’ll probably have more “customers.” But you will also have more customers churn, and more customers who spend less money with you. Just because it’s “cheaper” doesn’t mean you make more money. (In fact, it’s usually the opposite!)

  • “A less expensive monthly recurring revenue product is easier!” Wrong. A funny thing about business and selling products is the cheaper something is, the MORE expectations customers have. Whereas the more expensive something is, weirdly the LESS expectations they have.

In short: recurring products like paid newsletters, Skool communities, etc., are NOT easy.

When they work, they really work—and they can SCALE like crazy.

But don’t get it confused: they are FAR from the “easiest” business model.

You will make more money, especially as a beginner, just selling more stand-alone digital products to more new & existing customers, rather than trying to get them into some sort of recurring revenue business model/vehicle.

Now… THAT SAID…

Paid Newsletters can be an amazing long-term Upsell.

For example, our paid newsletter Write With AI…

Why does this paid newsletter work so well as an Upsell?

  • First, literally any writing-related product we create, in any niche vertical, we can Upsell customers to Write With AI because WWAI can help them “take that skill they just acquired, and now do it… with AI!”

  • And second, because AI as it relates to writing is CONSTANTLY changing. It’s a fast-moving industry. Which means, if you want to stay on the cutting-edge, there is an incentive to stay informed every single day. This is a different benefit than buying information you only need to learn or hear once.

“What makes for a great paid newsletter?”

This is a whole rabbit hole.

But in short, if you want to start a paid newsletter and have it act as an evergreen upsell for your customers:

  • “More, But Different, And Always Changing”: This is the big rule of thumb. It has to be relevant to your niche and/or the suite of digital products you create. But it also has to be “different.” And most of all, it has to be in a niche or centered around some sort of topic where things are constantly changing. Either it has to be in a fast-moving industry/niche, or related to “news.” It’s very hard to make a paid newsletter work that is in an industry or around a topic where there isn’t something “new” to talk about/share, all the time.

  • Shares Tangible Assets (Not Intangible Ideas): Second, you want to find a way to make every issue of your paid newsletter feel like an ASSET—not “an essay” about a bunch of intangible ideas. For example, the core idea behind WWAI (and why we started it) was the realization that in every WWAI paid newsletter issue we could share a different writing framework + AI prompt to automate it. AI prompts are “tangible assets.” So every paid newsletter FEELS like you’re receiving a tangible asset, straight to your inbox. This is what you’re looking for in your own paid newsletter idea.

  • A Book That Never Ends: Lastly, the best way to think about your paid newsletter is to think of it as a “book that never ends” on a niche topic. It has to be a topic you could talk about endlessly—either because the industry/niche is constantly changing (AI is a great example of this right now) and/or because the industry/niche/topic is complex and can be talked about at length. (For example: this is what I did when I was building the paid newsletter, Category Pirates. That paid newsletter wasn’t in a fast-moving industry. But it was about the complex topic of Category Design, which we could talk about endlessly. And I grew that paid newsletter to 6-figures+ in recurring revenue, making it one of Substack’s most successful business paid newsletters.)

If you want to better understand how we combine this paid newsletter model with our Low-Ticket Digital Product model, I recommend checking out this video I made.

This is how we double-monetize our AI-related digital products, and how we use those digital products to incentivize WWAI subscribers to upgrade to our $350/year subscription tier.


Upsell #6: Recurring Community ($9/mo-$99/mo)

https://www.loom.com/share/6f773dbe6ade4ce686711a37a375ecd0?sid=39379abb-3557-4d93-b3f1-abfe409eb4c1

The other recurring option is to Upsell customers on some sort of long-term community.

Now, “community” is a bit of a loaded term at this point, and can mean lots of different things.

So, let’s define it:

Option 1: Upselling “More, But Different” Ongoing Educational Assets.

This is one version.

For example, having a Skool community where each month you unlock a different module or mini-course. It’s basically “more, but different” low-ticket digital products on an ongoing basis.

Now, there’s 2 challenges with this:

  • Recurring Work: Sure, you’re in a “recurring revenue” model, but the entire model is predicated on you continuing to create more new assets, all the time, for customers to unlock. And trust me, this ALWAYS ends up being way more work than you originally anticipated.

  • Churn & Burn Value: The other problem is that the MOMENT someone unlocks a new asset, the value of that asset immediately goes to $0. There’s no long-term value. And so the only way long-term value gets created is if a) more, new things are constantly being created, and b) the library of assets in the recurring community gets to be so large & so valuable that the person doesn’t want to “unsubscribe”/churn because they don’t want to lose access—which takes time to build.

Option 2: Educational Assets + “Live” Experiences

The second option is some combination of the above, plus:

  • Weekly or monthly “mastermind-ish” calls with you

  • Weekly or monthly guest speakers/presentations

  • Weekly or monthly Q&A sessions

  • Etc.

It’s the ongoing creation element + some sort of live access to you and/or other subject matter experts.

Option 3: Educational Assets + “Live” Experiences + Community Interaction

The third option is ALL of the above, plus:

  • Facilitating community members meeting each other

  • Facilitating group exercises and/or “challenges” where people do things together

  • Facilitating networking, collaboration, even in-person live events bringing the online to the offline

This is what I mean when I say RECURRING COMMUNITIES TAKE WORK!

It’s not as simple as throwing a bunch of people in a Skool together and hoping for the best.

The vast majority of digital writers/creators default to this Upsell business model:

Everyone thinks they should start a recurring community.

And, from our experience, this is not only one of the more advanced business models, but it’s also one of the hardest to execute well.

And we would STRONGLY encourage you to try some of these other Upsell business models, first.


Upsell #7: “Power-Hour” Consulting ($150-$500+)

https://www.loom.com/share/120751a3a7074cc09e7061dc6d94d307?sid=cfe9f38a-988a-420e-a0e4-c88d30bf8373

The seventh upsell option, and maybe the easiest Upsell to start with (even easier than creating a Swipe File!) is to simply sell access to you.

My recommendation here would be to sell stand-alone consulting hours.

And the way you can increase the perceived value is to not just say, “I’ll charge you by the hour,” but to NAME this experience something and then charge a premium.

For example:

Whenever I’m using this Upsell, I call it a “Power Hour.”

I don’t say, “You can buy an hour of my time.”

I say, “You can buy a Power Hour with me—where we dig into <whatever thing they want to talk to you about>.”

By naming the experience something, that hour feels:

  • More tangible

  • More exclusive

  • More purposeful

  • And “worth the premium”

My recommendation here would be to aim for charging 2x whatever you typically would charge for an hour of your time.

So if you value your time at $100 per hour, charge $200.

The reason is because these Power Hours ALWAYS consume more time & headspace than just “the hour.” Because you’re going to be thinking about it the hour or two before the call—especially if you need to prepare. And you’re going to be thinking about it the hour or two after the call—especially if you promise any sort of follow-up thoughts.

It ALWAYS consumes more time than you think.

So, account for that “extra time” and charge accordingly.

Note: I am not a big fan of selling consulting time long term.

For what it’s worth, this is a great Upsell to start with but it’s not something that scales very well—for obvious reasons.

The biggest benefit and why I would encourage you to do some “Power Hour” consulting with people who ask for it, in the beginning, is to learn. You’re basically getting paid to talk to your customers, hear about their problems, listen to what questions they ask, and notice where they’re stuck. All of this is TREMENDOUSLY valuable information long-term for creating valuable digital products in your niche, and knowing a) what people need help with, b) where they get stuck/get in their own way, and c) what they care about the most.

So, my POV here is to not view this as an Upsell you want to use forever.

But instead, treat it as an Upsell you can use in the beginning to get paid to learn.


Upsell #8: Services ($3,000/mo+)

https://www.loom.com/share/5d07324d90254520823eeabda19edaf0?sid=9bc0cc8f-405f-4c55-9f13-221ddf44ed72

And the eighth and final upsell option is to sell some sort of service.

Here’s why—and this nuance is something I’ve found a lot of people don’t understand:

  • Do-It-Yourself (DIY): All Low-Ticket Digital Products are, fundamentally, DIY. You’re giving the customer information so they can “do it themselves.” And that’s great! There’s a lot of value in that.

  • Done-For-You (DFW): But a lot of people who experience some sort of problem don’t want to figure out how to “do it themselves.” They’d rather pay a premium to have someone else do it for them. Fundamentally, this is what “services” are: an easier, but more expensive solution to a problem.

Now, most people think…

“If I tell my target customer how to do it themselves, why would they ever pay me to help them?”

Because in LEARNING HOW TO DO SOMETHING, the customer becomes more aware of “how hard it actually is.”

So what happens is you actually double-monetize:

  • First, you monetize the customer buying your Low-Ticket Digital Product. They’re interested in trying to learn how to do it themselves. And in educating them on how to “do it themselves,” they ultimately come to the conclusion that it’s too hard, too time consuming, too difficult, etc.

  • Second, you monetize that same customer again when they realize, “I don’t actually want to do this myself,” and go looking for a different solution. They’ve decided they don’t want a DIY solution. They want a DFY solution—and will gladly pay you a premium to just take care of it and do it for them.

Which creates a flywheel…

  • You make money selling digital products…

  • Some % of your customers realize, “I don’t actually want to do this myself”…

  • Those customers, who you successfully educated, will consider working with you first…

  • Which means you’re getting paid to “nurture” potential customers…

  • Which means you have NEGATIVE customer-acquisition-cost…

  • Which means you double-monetize with services…

  • Which makes your digital products business more defensible…

  • Which also makes your services business more defensible…

  • Etc. etc. etc.

Combining a digital product funnel with a services funnel is INCREDIBLY powerful.

And it’s the reason why I tell every digital writer to also get into ghostwriting.

Because whatever “skill” you are monetizing by creating digital products, you can double-monetize that skill by “renting it” to other people and providing it as a service.

Some examples:

  • If your digital product is about copywriting… you can double-monetize your knowledge by also providing copywriting services to a small number of customers/clients at a premium rate.

  • If your digital product is about accounting for startups… you can double-monetize your knowledge by providing startup accounting services to a small number of customers/clients at a premium rate.

  • If your digital product is about hiring & training product managers… you can double-monetize your knowledge by providing hiring & training services to product managers at a premium rate.

And if you already provide a service, the inverse is also true: you should create DIY digital products explaining to customers/clients how to do the very service you provide.

This will allow you to tap into wider pools of customers (people who can’t afford your services but would still like your help) AND a % of those customers will inevitably go through your product, decide “it’s too much work,” and then want to work with you—creating a flywheel.

Here’s a short podcast excerpt clip where I talk about this concept.


Upsell Order Bump Example

For example, here’s the “Order Bump” page we created for this very product you’re going through right now (inside of our Low-Ticket Launchpad sales funnel).


Notice how, at the top, it says:

“One last question before we complete your order…”.


Upsell Linked-In-Product Example

If you’ve consumed any of our digital products, or been part of any of our writing programs, you’ve probably noticed we do this constantly.

The goal here is to “mention” other products you have for sale organically inside of all your other products.

You aren’t PROMOTING these other products.

You’re simply using them as “an example,” which subtly makes each customer aware of all the other things you have for sale.

Here’s what this looks like (this is a section from our Low-Ticket Launchpad product):

Do you see how, very organically, we’re mentioning (and linking to) both Ship 30 for 30 & Premium Ghostwriting Academy?

And it doesn’t feel like a “promotion” for these products / programs.

It feels like we’re using these other products as “examples,” but just so happen to also be linking to them incase you’re interested.

This is the art of mentioning your Evergreen Upsells all throughout your other products—creating a tight ecosystem your customers can explore & make multiple purchases within.

records.content:
Hey!

And welcome to Ghostwriting As A Career: Crash Course!

This training is designed to give you a high-level overview of:

  • What ghostwriting is (and why it's one of the best ways to monetize your skills as a writer)

  • The different services you can sell as a ghostwriter (and how much you could charge for each of them)

  • How to land your very first high-ticket ghostwriting client (and the 3 skills you need in order to charge a premium for your services)

  • And much more!

"But Dickie... Cole... Why did you add this training here? I thought the goal was to monetize my skills through digital products and/or newsletters, no?"

Great callout!

And yes, that's the goal.

But here's the thing:

When you're just starting out, it might take some time before you can actually make a living or a full-time income from your digital product sales. And for some people, that's completely fine.

However, we always get asked what's the fastest way to make a living as a writer.

And the fastest way to make a living from your skills as a writer is to provide a service (like ghostwriting).

So if you'd like to learn more about the mysterious world of ghostwriting and what it'd look like to make a living as a ghostwriter WHILE you continue to build your audience & your digital product empire, then this crash course is for you!

Enjoy :)

PS: If you’ve already read my book, The Art & Business of Ghostwriting, then a lot of this will be familiar to you. But hearing it a second time (and explained in a slightly different way) will help you internalize all these new ideas & frameworks. I promise!

And if you haven't read it already, you can get a free PDF copy of it here (as an additional Thank You gift for joining Low-Ticket Launchpad)!

Freelance Writing vs Ghostwriting

This point of view will change your life—literally.

When you hear the term “freelance writer,” what do you think of? Better yet, WHO do you think of? Chances are, the person that comes to mind is a young professional, working out of a coffee shop, sporadically bouncing between their phone (scrolling on Instagram) and their laptop, churning through another blog post assignment.

Without even talking to them, you probably assume a few things:

  • They have a small handful of clients (they’ve gotten from referrals).

  • They are earning enough to pay their bills, but not enough to be comfortable (by any means).

  • They are stressed out, overworked, and burned out from writing the same old blog articles over and over again.

Does this sound like someone you know?

(We know tons of people who fit this archetype.)

However… it’s not their fault.

There’s almost no education around how to be a successful, highly profitable freelancer.

Worse, the term “freelancer” has become so commoditized over the years, that when someone says they’re a “freelancer,” they might as well say they drive Uber. It just sounds “indie.”

And yet, millions and millions of writers (and designers, and project managers, and all sorts of other career professionals) willingly call themselves “freelancers.”

We’re here to tell you: this is a mistake.

Do not call yourself a Freelance Writer. It sends the signal you are “just like everyone else.”

Want to immediately unlock higher-tier opportunities? Call yourself a Ghostwriter.

The term “ghostwriter” is still relatively new.

It’s also becoming more and more popular, as more writers realize that “freelance writing” is a race to the bottom, whereas “ghostwriting” allows you to work directly with an industry leader in a highly specialized capacity. Although ghostwriting can end up leading to lots of other different types of work, this is the central difference: “freelance writing” means you’re a hired writer for a business, whereas “ghostwriting” means you’re a hired writer for a business leader/individual.

But let’s talk about some of the differences between Freelance Writing & Ghostwriting.

Freelance Writing

  • More competition: Millions of people call themselves “freelance writers.” When you call yourself the same exact thing, you are making it HARDER for yourself to stand out.

  • Write for businesses: Freelance writers are typically hired by content marketing teams to churn out branded content (blog posts, newsletters, landing pages, etc.). Since these are highly commoditized assets, and there are millions of freelance writers, many of these writers are treated like virtual assistants (and paid accordingly).

  • “Hire me and I’ll write whatever you need”: Most people “fall into” freelance writing. They don’t really know who they’re servicing or why, so they just say, “Hire me to write!” And then they end up in very reactive situations where they’re constantly adjusting to the client’s wants and needs.

  • Race to the bottom in terms of pricing power ($): All of these things, together, are what cause so many freelance writers to struggle financially. They’re undifferentiated (all calling themselves the same thing), they’re “competing” over commoditized jobs, and they don’t have clarity over what they’re offering or their value—which means they’re “reacting” to whatever the client wants, constantly keeping them on their back foot.

Ghostwriting

  • Less competition: Simply by calling yourself something other than a “freelance writer,” you immediately stand out. Yes, that’s literally how it works. Calling yourself a “ghostwriter” is the fastest way to start separating yourself from the competition.

  • Write for business leaders: When you’re a “ghostwriter,” it’s implied that you are not an average freelance writer. You work directly with business leaders, and as a result, unlock a different level of access to opportunities. And once you become friends with a business leader, they will inevitably send more specialized work your way.

  • “Hire me for 1 specific purpose”: Most ghostwriters specialize in 1 thing. As a result, they are seen as “premium,” which gives them much more pricing power. While freelance writers are stuck “reacting” to the client’s wants and needs, ghostwriters set the agenda and make recommendations to the client.

  • Gain pricing power and charge a premium ($$$$$): All of these things together are what allow ghostwriters to earn so much more money than freelance writers. They are seen as “different,” they work directly with decision-makers, and they have complete and total clarity over the 1 specific value they provide—allowing them to charge a premium for their work.

Now, here’s the central mistake you want to avoid…

Most people “fall into” Freelance Writing.

Here’s how it starts:

Maybe they want to quit their 9-5 job. Maybe they already have. Inevitably, their freelance writing career begins when someone—a current or former employer, a friend of a friend, or someone random on social media—asks, “Hey! Can you help me write something?” Fascinated by the idea of being paid to write, the person says, “Sure!” They have no idea what to charge, or how to even think about putting a price tag on their services, so they basically just say “Yes” to whatever the person is offering.

This first client usually leads to a second. A second leads to a third.

And then 1 or 2 years goes by, and all of a sudden, the person has found themselves trapped: writing “lots of different types of things” for “lots of different types of people.”

Sound familiar?

You aren’t just “ghostwriting.” You’re starting a Ghostwriting Business.

This is the big takeaway:

Mentally, you do not want to think of it as you’re “falling into” ghostwriting.

No—you’re starting a business. Even if it’s a 1-person business, you should think of it as “starting a business.” And when you start a business, you don’t just let customers walk through the door and say, “What should I sell here? You tell me!” No, when customers walk through the door, you already know what you sell. And then you sell it to them!

And we’re going to show you exactly what you should be selling—so you skyrocket your monthly earnings as a ghostwriter.

Mistakes Ghostwriters Make

But first, we want to point out the 4 big mistakes new ghostwriters make.

(Steer clear of these!)

Mistake #1: Trying to ghostwrite “anything” for “anyone.”

In our Ghostwriting Intensive, we are going to help you niche down as a ghostwriter.

The reason is because one of the WORST things you can do for yourself & your “business” as a writer is to fall into the trap of writing “anything” for “anyone.” Again, this puts you in a very reactive state—constantly adjusting your work style, your schedule, your processes, and your expertise to fit the client’s wants and needs (and let us tell you: clients are fickle. They don’t know what they want!)

Instead, you want to solve…

  • 1 specific problem

  • For 1 specific type of person

  • In 1 specific type of way

If this sounds “too niche,” guess what? That’s a signal you’re headed in the right direction!

The most successful ghostwriters specialize.

(And inevitably have more opportunity than they know what to do with.)

Mistake #2: Treating every client as a blank canvas.

Ghostwriting is mysterious.

Ghostwriting is sexy.

As a result, a lot of writers think they need to “start from scratch” every time they work with a client. They think they’re producing “art.” Newsflash: you’re not. Sure, you might be creating important work. But you are not writing The Next Great American Novel. You are providing a specialized service, to solve a specific problem, for a very specific type of person.

After ghostwriting for hundreds of people, we can tell you that the idea “everyone’s voice is unique & different” is also a myth.

People like to believe they are different. But the truth is, many of us are the same.

In fact, 99% of clients can be reverse-engineered into 5 different categories.

The 5 Archetypes Of Voices

  • The Storyteller: Here’s the difference. “In 1982.” Moment in time. That’s it. Or, 1 single sentence of description: “They had on a bright blue blazer.” Literally. You would be shocked how many clients will say to you, “This is so vivid!” when all you do is name a date or describe one object.

  • The Opinionater: This is someone who likes to share their opinions on things, usually newsy topics. It’s a sliding scale here. There are 2 types of Opinionaters: on one end of the spectrum, you have Hedgers—the person who hedges everything they say (I’ve had TONS of clients like this). They cannot say a strong opinion without acknowledging the other side. On the other end of the spectrum are the Betters—they will bet the house on any of their opinions. Your job is to figure out which one of these 2 the client is, and cater the writing accordingly. And here’s a very simple rule to live by: Hedgers, just acknowledge both sides of everything. Betters, pretend the other side doesn’t exist. That’s it.

  • The Fact Presenter: Above story, this client just wants stats. Trends. Studies. NYT, WSJ, HBR, and peer-reviewed journal sources. This is the single point of failure—the rest of the writing almost doesn’t matter. When in doubt here, more is better. If you can, put a stat or a trend or a study in every section. They’ll be happy.

  • The Frameworker: Listen close and this person always reveals themselves with a very subtle cue. Steps. Anytime someone puts something into steps, you should immediately realize who you’re working with. This person thinks carefully about how to move from point A to point B, which means what you’re writing better be organized into “steps” or “a guide.” If you don’t give them this format, they are going to be unhappy.

  • The F Bomb Dropper: Any client that says, “Nobody sounds like me” and drops tons of expletives is this archetype. And, newsflash, they aren’t as special as they think. You can create this voice literally by just adding 1 expletive per section, or even per paragraph (you’ll learn “how many” expletives they feel best represents their persona).

Mistake #3: Not practicing on yourself.

One of the most popular questions aspiring ghostwriters ask is:

“How am I supposed to find clients when I can’t talk about my work?”

Simple: you use yourself as the case study.

Here’s the golden rule: Whatever “type” of ghostwriting you’re selling (whatever service you’re providing), you should have a version (or multiple!) of that same asset for yourself:

  • If you’re selling “ghostwriting someone’s Twitter account,” you should be actively writing & proving YOU can build an audience on Twitter.

  • If you’re selling “ghostwriting someone’s LinkedIn account,” you should be actively writing & proving YOU can build an audience on LinkedIn.

  • If you’re selling “ghostwritten educational email courses,” you should have YOUR OWN educational email course actively building your own email list.

  • If you’re selling “ghostwritten eBooks,” you should have YOUR OWN eBook (or eBooks) for sale.

  • If you’re selling “ghostwritten newsletter content,” you should have YOUR OWN newsletter.

  • Etc.

This is such a simple thing, but so many ghostwriters overthink it.

Getting clients isn’t about having a huge audience, fame, or a 10+ year track record.

It’s literally just about demonstrating you can create the thing you are saying you can create.

Mistake #4: Not starting with the Free Work Pitch.

Finally, so many aspiring ghostwriters underestimate the ROI of working for free.

Let us be clear:

  • We are NOT advocating for you to work for free forever.

  • We are NOT saying you shouldn’t care about earning money.

  • We are NOT saying you should run your business like a non-profit.

  • We are NOT saying you should let people take advantage of you.

In fact, the “Free Work Pitch” isn’t even really “free work.”

It’s literally just you taking the time to paint a vivid picture for your prospective client.

Take a look at these two different DM pitches, for example:

Pitch #1: “Want to buy this service?”

Hey John! I was just reaching out to see if you were looking for someone to build you an educational email course?

I create educational email courses for FinTech startups. They are 5 emails long, sent over 5 days, and are very effective at keeping readers engaged.

For this service, I charge $5,000.

Let me know!

Pitch #2: “Don’t you want to build your email list faster?”

Hey John! Quick question.

I was poking around your site, and then I got hit with your pop-up offering me a 10% discount on my first purchase.

And that got me thinking…

I bet the opt-in rate for that is probably pretty low. I’ve seen a lot more success (instead of doing a discount) offering people a free 5-day educational email course—because it demonstrates free value AND educates them before pitching them to buy something.

I feel like this is a giant missed opportunity for you—and I know exactly how to solve it.

No pressure, but if I put together an outline of what a really compelling 5-day educational email course looked like for your target customers, would you take a look?

Which one of these 2 DM pitches do you think is more likely to get someone to say, “Yes!”

The second one—without a doubt.

And here’s the thing: it will probably take you 20 or 30 minutes to create this free “outline” for anyone who says, “Sure.” But if you do a good job, the likelihood the person says, “You know what? You’re hired!” goes up dramatically.

So, are you “working for free?”

Not really.

All you’re doing is front-loading the work, and getting them excited to pay you.

Whereas trying to convert someone cold on your service is much, much harder.

  • Problem #2: There are a lot of cooks in the kitchen. Especially when you’re ghostwriting a book for someone noteworthy, who is also publishing through a traditional publishing house, you don’t just have to make the client happy. You have to make their agent happy. And their editor happy. And their editor’s boss at the publishing house happy. And their significant other (who will somehow end up part of the project) happy. And so on. All of these voices telling you which direction to take the book adds escalating layers of complexity.

  • Problem #3: There are two types of books that get ghostwritten. There are books in the $10,000 to $30,000 range, and there are books in the $100,000 - $500,000 range. There’s very little middle-ground. Every time you say “Yes” to a different form of ghostwriting, you are creating 3 big problems for yourself:

One minute, you have to think about how to perform Service A, and the next, you have to completely pivot your thinking to perform Service B.
