(Pricing verified July 2026. All three platforms change pricing occasionally—always check the current pricing page before you commit.)


When Substack's 10% Starts To Cost You: platform fees vs. monthly paid-subscription revenue

The Decision Framework: Choose Based On Your Goal

Remember the question from the top? "What is my newsletter's #1 job for the next 12 months?"

Here's the framework:

Goal 1: "I need an audience." → Substack

You're starting from zero (or under ~1,000 subscribers) and nobody knows who you are yet.

Choose Substack. It's the only platform where the network actively sends you subscribers while you sleep—through Recommendations, Notes, and Restacks. It costs nothing, it takes an afternoon to set up, and your only job is to write.

The 10% fee on paid subscriptions? Think of it as the cheapest growth marketing you'll ever buy. 10% of revenue you wouldn't have earned anywhere else is a bargain.

This is the right answer for most people in this Sprint. If you're unsure, pick Substack.

Goal 2: "I need a business engine." → Kit

You already have attention somewhere—LinkedIn, X, YouTube, a podcast, a client base—and your newsletter's job is to convert that attention into sales of courses, products, coaching, or services.

Choose Kit. The free plan covers you to 10,000 subscribers, the automations sell for you around the clock, and you own every inch of the pipeline. You don't need Substack's discovery because YOU are the discovery.

Goal 3: "I want to build a media business." → Beehiiv

You think in terms of CPMs, sponsorships, and audience segments. You want to grow aggressively (and are willing to spend to do it), monetize with ads from early on, and eventually run multiple publications.

Choose Beehiiv. The Ad Network and Boosts are unmatched, the analytics tell you exactly what's working, and the 0% cut on paid subscriptions rewards you at scale.

Goal 3.5: "I want serious paid-subscription revenue AND I hate fees."

This is the edge case. Run the math:

  • Below roughly $500/month in subscription revenue, Substack's 10% is cheaper than Beehiiv's $49/month base plan—and you get the discovery network for free.

  • Above roughly $1,000/month, you're paying Substack $100+/month—enough to cover Beehiiv or Kit with money left over.

But (and this is important): don't optimize the fee before you've earned the revenue. A 10% fee on $0 is $0. Grow first. Optimize later. Migration is always available (more on that below).

The Hybrid Play (What We Do)

You don't actually have to choose one forever. Plenty of successful creators (including us) run a hybrid:

  • Substack as the public-facing newsletter—for discovery, community, and paid subscriptions.

  • Kit behind the scenes—for lead magnets, product launches, and automated sales sequences.

But hear me clearly: this is a later problem. In this Sprint, you're picking ONE platform and shipping. Add the second tool when you have a specific job for it—not before.

Common Mistakes To Avoid

  1. Platform shopping as procrastination. Spending 3 weeks comparing platforms is just fear of publishing wearing a productivity costume. All three work. Pick one today.

  2. Choosing on features you won't use for a year. "But Beehiiv has better A/B testing!" You have 40 subscribers. Test subject lines when a 2% difference means something.

  3. Optimizing fees before revenue exists. Don't leave Substack's growth network to save 10% of nothing.

  4. Choosing a platform to match someone else's goal. Your favorite creator is on Beehiiv because ads are THEIR business model. If yours is paid subscriptions from a cold start, their choice is wrong for you.

  5. Believing migration is impossible. It's not (see below). This decision is important, not irreversible. Make it in a day, not a month.

  6. Signing up for two platforms "to test both." You'll run two half-newsletters instead of one real one. One platform. Full commitment. Five days.

What About Switching Later? (Migration Considerations)

Good news: you always own your email list. All three platforms let you export your subscribers as a CSV and import them elsewhere. Beehiiv even offers free white-glove migration from Substack and Kit on paid plans.

What moves easily:

  • Your subscriber list (emails, signup dates)

  • Your post archive (import/republish; Beehiiv and Substack both have import tools)

What does NOT move:

  • Your Substack Recommendations and network position. Leave Substack and you leave the discovery engine, your Notes following, and your restack relationships behind.

  • Paid subscriptions are messy. Stripe subscriptions can be transferred (Substack lets you export your Stripe customer data), but expect friction and some churn during the switch.

  • Automations and tags. Kit funnel logic has to be rebuilt by hand anywhere else.

  • Deliverability reputation. A new sending domain warms up over weeks. Expect a temporary dip in open rates after any migration.

The takeaway: switching costs are real but survivable. Which means the worst thing you can do is stall for a month trying to make the "perfect" choice. Pick with the framework, ship for 6-12 months, and revisit only if your GOAL changes.

Frequently Asked Questions

"Should I use a custom domain?"

Buy it. Don't connect it yet.

Go to Namecheap (or wherever you buy domains) and grab yourdomain.com. It costs $10-20/year. Do this so nobody else takes it. Set up a simple redirect to your newsletter so when you tell people your URL in conversation, it sounds professional.

But (on Substack specifically) don't connect it yet. Substack's domain authority is 92 out of 100. That means Google trusts Substack, and your posts published under the substack.com domain benefit from that trust. A brand new custom domain starts at 1. Connecting a custom domain costs a one-time $50 fee and means your posts index under YOUR domain instead of Substack's. Long-term, good. Short-term, you lose Substack's built-in SEO advantage.

For what it's worth, we still use the Substack domain. It's working fine.

(On Beehiiv and Kit, custom domains are standard practice—connect away.)

"I already have an audience on social. Doesn't that mean Kit automatically?"

Not automatically. Ask what the newsletter's JOB is. If it's "convert my followers into customers," yes—Kit. If it's "build a second audience that isn't rented from an algorithm," Substack's network still adds growth on top of what you bring. Goal first, platform second.

"Can I make money on the free plans?"

Yes. Substack paid subscriptions work from day one (that's the whole model). Kit lets you sell paid newsletter subscriptions and take tips even on the free plan. Beehiiv is the exception—monetization features (Ad Network, Boosts, paid subscriptions) require the Scale plan at $49/month.

"What about Ghost / MailerLite / ActiveCampaign / [other tool]?"

They're fine tools. Ghost is great for developers who want to self-host and pay 0% fees. But this Sprint is built around the three platforms where creator newsletters actually grow in 2026—and adding more options to the menu makes you slower, not smarter. Pick from these three.

"What if I pick wrong?"

You won't—because "wrong" barely exists here. All three platforms have thousands of creators earning real money. And you own your list everywhere. The only truly wrong choice is not picking.

Homework

Shew! We covered A LOT!

Here's your homework—and it has a deadline: before tomorrow's session.

Step 1: Answer the goal question in one sentence.

Write it down: "My newsletter's #1 job for the next 12 months is ." (Audience growth / business engine / media business / subscription revenue.)

Step 2: Pick your platform.

Run your goal through the decision framework. Unsure? Default to Substack. Decision time allowed: 15 minutes. This is a one-way door you can walk back through later—stop treating it like a tattoo.

Step 3: Create your account and lock in your basics.

  • Claim your publication name and URL (use the positioning you built on Day 1)

  • Write your one-line description / tagline

  • Upload a logo or profile photo (a clean headshot works fine—don't let Canva eat your evening)

  • Connect your "About" info: who it's for, what they get, how often

Step 4: Configure your growth switch.

  • Substack: Add 5-10 Recommendations of complementary newsletters (browse substack.com/explore) and message 3 of those writers about a mutual recommendation.

  • Beehiiv: Turn on your recommendations widget and browse Boosts to see what partner newsletters look like in your niche.

  • Kit: Join the Creator Network and set up one landing page with a signup form you can share.

Step 5: Buy your domain (don't connect it).

$10-20. Five minutes. Future you says thanks.

If you walk through these steps, you'll show up tomorrow with a live, configured newsletter—ready to write.

Because tomorrow is Day 3: Newsletter Writing Mastery—where we take your shiny new publication and teach you how to write issues people actually open, read, and share.

See you Wednesday at 3PM ET / Noon PT.

— Justin

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 3 of Start & Scale Your Newsletter: A 5-Day Sprint To Help You Dominate Your Niche, Build An Audience, And Grow An Email List With The Potential To Pay You 6-Figures.

In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • How to write irresistible subject lines & introductions (so you hook the reader before they even open the email)

  • The modular system for outlining and filling in "the perfect newsletter"—headers, sections, CTAs & formatting

  • How to train AI on YOUR unique writing style so a "perfect newsletter" takes you 60 minutes or less

And more!

All so you can write your first newsletter draft today—and have a repeatable system for publishing every single week.

Let's dive in!

Step 1: Write A Subject Line

Before we dive into our first step, I want to share with you a simple idea which will change the way you think about writing.

This is a truth about writing I want every newsletter creator (and writers more generally) to internalize and never forget:

Writing is like playing with Legos.

In other words, you want to see writing as modular. Don't see it as a big, daunting "thing" artists and the inspired do. You don't have to wait around for the Muse to strike before writing your newsletter. Instead, it's actually all about assembling pieces to create a finished piece of writing.

In order to write the perfect newsletter, there are really only 3 frameworks that you need to know to get to 80, 90, 95% proficiency.

Everything else is little stylistic things that maybe you pick up or choose to do later on (which we'll talk about right at the end of this session).

How To Write An Irresistible Subject Line

Before you can start writing the meat of the newsletter, you need to write a subject line.

See your subject line as the North Star of your newsletter. It is the promise of the newsletter. It creates both curiosity in the mind of the reader AND gives them a reason to open (so they can extract some value or insight from it).

To write a compelling and clickable subject line that will drive high open rates, follow these 5 rules:

Rule #1: 5-15 words, max.

A good rule of thumb is your subject line should not exceed 15 words. Ever.

Less is always more here. Why? Because over half of all emails are opened on mobile, which means you want your idea to be communicated before the subject line is cut off.

Rule #2: Subject lines should read like you're talking to a friend.

This comes down to grammar and punctuation more than anything else.

Use sentence-case over a capitalized subject line. You don't want your subject lines to sound stuffy or boring (or like you're lecturing your readers!). Instead, write simply. This is how you reduce the cognitive load on the reader so they quickly understand whether they want to open your email or not.

So, how do you tempt them to open the newsletter?

That's why Rule #3 comes in.

Rule #3: Use 1 of the 4 proven hook frameworks.

There are 4 types of hooks that work over and over again (regardless of industry, niche, or topic):

  1. Here's a ton of value for minimal time. Time is the only resource we cannot get back. Which means, you want your newsletter to save people time (otherwise, why are they even signed up to your list?!). Stating this directly or hinting to this indirectly in the subject line is how you boost the value of your newsletters.

  2. Here's a ton of value for minimal cost. Another resource people care about is, of course, money. So if your newsletters SAVE them money, they're more likely to stay subscribed. And they're also more likely to open your emails. So, again, if you can, directly state this or hint at it in the subject line.

  3. Here's how to solve your problem without much effort. The whole game of newsletter writing (and content more generally) is to help someone overcome a problem they have. And because everybody wants something for nothing, if you can help them solve a problem they have, they're more likely to pay attention.

  4. Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly. What's better than not expending much effort? Not having to put any effort in at all to get something you want! If you can promise this in your subject line (and deliver it in the contents of your newsletter), then you're more likely to get the click from the reader.

(In the live session, I'll share examples where we've used these rules in our own newsletters — see if you can spot which rules or combination of rules we're using!)


A real subject line from one of our own newsletters — see which rules you can spot.

Alright, onto the two final rules.

Rule #4: Use visceral language.

This is how you "Amp up" your subject lines.

By adding in visceral language like: "OUCH!" "Urgent!" "Steal this!" or even using powerful verbs and nouns, you can catch the attention of readers (especially if you're trying to compete for attention in a crowded inbox).

Here are some power words for your email subject lines:

  • Free

  • Binge

  • Harsh

  • Waste

  • Hidden

  • Rapid

  • Terrible

  • Unique

  • Greatest

  • Dreadful

  • Strongest

  • Surprising

  • Dead simple

  • Inconvenient

  • Little-known

Rule #5: Name & Claim ideas (in the subject line)

The ultimate goal is to Name & Claim ideas right there in the subject line.

E.g. "Life Coach Money Manual: 3 easy ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)" — You should be able to feel (in your skin!) how much more you want to click this subject line—because "Life Coach Money Manual" feels like you're receiving a "thing." This makes it feel exponentially more "valuable."

The challenge, of course, is doing all of this WITHOUT exceeding the word count limit for effective subject lines.

So, once you have a subject line it's time to start the actual "writing" of the newsletter.

And for this, I'm going to share a simple framework you can use in any piece of non-fiction content you write.

Step 2: Prep The Page

Before I carry on, I want to make a general observation:

There is no "1 correct way" to write a newsletter.

Sure, there are some best practices (which I'm going through here).

But you will ALWAYS find outliers who defy those best practices.

  • If I say "short newsletters work," you'll find plenty of people crushing it writing long-form newsletters.

  • If I say "long newsletters work," you'll find plenty of people crushing it writing short-form newsletters.

  • If I say "stories work," you'll find plenty of people crushing it who don't tell a single story.

  • If I say "use data," you'll find plenty of people crushing it who don't use a single piece of data, ever, to back up anything they say.

The point is this:

Don't cherry-pick 1 or 2 writers/creators and then extract sweeping conclusions from their individual circumstances.

And don't think, if you don't do it "perfectly," your newsletter is going to fail.

(There are a lot of newsletters I personally think are AWFUL, that are incredibly successful!)

At the end of the day, writing is subjective.

And the ONLY thing that matters is WHETHER OR NOT YOUR READERS ARE HAPPY & RECEIVING VALUE.

If they are, who cares what I or anyone else thinks?

Now, 70% of the newsletter game is formatting. (Only 30% is the actual content.)

This is going to be controversial to some, but everything I've learned over the past 10+ years writing online has proved it to be true.

At a glance, between a giant wall of text and a piece with clear headers, bullets, and white space—which piece are you more likely to read?


The formatted one. Every time.

In fact, in about 3 milliseconds, before you even consciously "decided" which one you wanted to read, I would bet my right arm you unconsciously started skimming the formatted one.

Because it's impossible not to.

I have written well over 5,000 articles and newsletters on the Internet, and this is one of the biggest lessons I've learned: formatting is everything.

The days of people pulling up a wall-of-text piece, clearing their afternoon, and cuddling up by the fireplace to read it start to finish are OVER.

It doesn't happen.

It might "look" more professional. It might "look" more like "real writing" (whatever that means).

But who cares if nobody reads it?

If you want to have a successful newsletter, 70% of the game is formatting:

  • Making it VISUALLY appealing

  • Making it VISUALLY organized

  • Making it VISUALLY easy to skim & read

If you do this, and do it well, the content can be "mediocre" (it's the truth) but readers will still find it easy to skim, read, and thus extract value.

But if you DON'T do this, and you make it HARD for readers to consume your content, then it won't matter how "good" the content is.

Nobody's going to read it.

Which leads us to our second framework: Prepping The Page.

Prepping The Page allows you to create a skimmable newsletter before you even get into the writing.

How?

By giving you a set of headers which your reader can skim when they open the email. And this is important for another writing-craft related reason.

Expanding on the idea that writing is modular, it's important to see everything in writing as a list:

  • Non-fiction is a list of facts, advice, stories, etc.

  • Fiction is a list of descriptions & dialogue that move the plot forward

  • Even poetry is a list of images and ideas

If you can't think in lists, you won't be able to write 800 words, let alone 8,000 for an article or 80,000 for a book.

Yet most writers skip this crucial step and dive straight into writing. This is a huge problem! It's like walking through a forest at midnight with just a flashlight. Without a list of what they're going to cover, they have no clue where they're going.

So, how do we apply this to writing a newsletter?

Well, realize that 80% of your newsletter's value is in the headers. When readers open your email, they don't read—they skim. They scan your headers to decide if the rest is worth their time.

  • If you're sharing tips, each header should be an actionable tip.

  • If you're sharing lessons, each header should be a valuable lesson.

  • If you're writing about mistakes, each header should be a specific mistake.

Because once your reader has opened the email (based on the subject line), the headers serve an important function:

The headers ARE the promise of the newsletter.

When you pick a topic like "inbox zero," that's not what your newsletter is about.

Your newsletter is about the specific thing you're giving readers in service of that topic:

  • 3 TOOLS to achieve inbox zero

  • 3 MISTAKES that prevent inbox zero

  • 3 REASONS you're failing at inbox zero

  • 3 daily HABITS for maintaining inbox zero

Just by changing one word—mistakes to tools to habits to reasons—you create a completely different newsletter.

The topic stays the same, but what you're giving the reader transforms entirely. So, before writing anything, create your containers. List your headers. Bold them.

So, let's say I want to write a newsletter about the 3 mistakes newsletter writers make that are stopping them from earning $10,000/month.

I'd Prep My Page like this:

Subject: 3 mistakes keeping your newsletter from $10k/month

Hey there,

{Intro goes here}

Mistake #1: {Specific mistake, written as a full sentence}

Mistake #2: {Specific mistake, written as a full sentence}

Mistake #3: {Specific mistake, written as a full sentence}

{Conclusion + PS goes here}

Congratulations—you've just completed 50% of the work, and the thinking is done.

The house is built. Now you just need to add furniture.

Step 3: Write Your Introduction

Once your headers are set, you need to write some single sentence openers to HOOK your reader.

Now, at the start of each section you should hook the reader. But you also need to open your email with a sentence that immediately hooks the reader when they open the email (after all, we want to capitalize on the attention we've just captured with our subject line!).

There are 6 ways to hook a reader at the start of any section.

When I sit down to write, I'm not hoping something brilliant appears—I'm choosing from these options:

  1. Strong declarative sentence: "Most writers fail before they even start typing."

  2. Thought-provoking question: "What if everything you learned about writing was wrong?"

  3. Controversial opinion: "Not using outline templates is killing your creativity."

  4. Moment in time: "At 4:47 AM, I discovered the secret to viral newsletters."

  5. Vulnerable statement: "I wasted 3 years writing newsletters nobody read."

  6. Weird unique insight: "The best newsletters are written backwards."

For each section, I quickly run through these 6 options and pick the strongest one.

After doing this 10,000 times, I can do it in seconds. But don't feel "bad" if your first few attempts feel mechanical—that's the point! You're using a reliable system, not relying on inspiration.

Without compelling single-sentence openers, even brilliant content goes unread. If your first line is generic, readers assume the entire newsletter or section is generic. They'll bounce before reading the meat of your newsletter.

Master this framework and readers will actually finish your newsletters instead of skimming and leaving.

Now, for the Introduction of your newsletter, I highly recommend following the following structure.

Here's a template you can use:

Hey there,

{1 Sentence Strong Opinion opener} [Using one of the 6 Proven Ways To Hook The Reader]

{3-5 Sentences Elaborate On Problems and why they should listen to you} [This increases the stakes for the reader. You're telling them exactly why they should read on]

{1 Sentence Transition To "What We're Going To Talk About Today"} [In other words, "Well you're in luck—that's what we're covering today!"]

{3 succinct bullets} [List out the content of the newsletter to give your reader a "lay of the land"]

{Quick segue sentence} [A simple sentence to open the first point: "Let's dive in." "Let's get started." "Let's go!"]

Why this structure?

For a few reasons:

  • The hook re-hooks the reader's attention in a single sentence. By opening with 1 of the 6 proven hook formats, you're re-capturing the reader's attention.

  • The elaboration raises the stakes so the reader can't afford to skim. The 3-5 sentence problem section names the reader's pain, validates it, and reframes it as something solvable—which spurs the reader into consuming the newsletter.

  • The bullets tease the payoff without revealing the mechanism. Listing 3 succinct bullets gives the reader a "lay of the land" so they know the newsletter is worth their time, but withholding the actual fixes creates an open loop they have to close. That tension between knowing what is coming and not knowing how is what pulls them into the body of the newsletter.

Alright, now we have our Introduction written, let's write the rest of the newsletter using one of my favorite writing frameworks:

The 10 Magical Ways.

Step 4: Use The 10 Magical Ways To Expand Any Section

It's time to add the meat of the newsletter, expanding each section with valuable content.

So, what do you put in each section?

Well, what you need to do is deliver on the promise of the header. And you can do this by expanding the idea by 1) giving readers more of what they want and 2) writing content that expands upon the point you're making in the header.

You can do this with the 10 Magical Ways to expand anything:

  • Tips: Actionable advice they can implement immediately

  • Stats: Numbers that prove your point or surprise them

  • Steps: Sequential instructions to achieve a result

  • Lessons: Share wisdom extracted from experience

  • Benefits: Positive outcomes they'll gain

  • Reasons: Logic that supports your argument

  • Mistakes: Common errors to avoid

  • Examples: Real-world applications of your ideas

  • Questions: They can ask these to help them understand a point/achieve an outcome

  • Personal stories: To illustrate the point of the header

See how we're just building up the writing, here?

Once you view writing through this modular lens, you're never stuck.

You simply ask: "What does this section need?" Then pick from your toolbox. This turns writing from a mysterious, almost mystical act to… building with Legos!

To make this actionable for you, let's return to our newsletter.

  • First, I open with a declarative sentence.

  • Second, I expand the point by giving people the steps to niching down

  • Then I deliver on the promise of the sub-headline by explaining the reasons why writing anything for anyone is a mistake.

(And if you're eagle-eyed, you can see how I've expanded each Reason in the list too using the Ways above!)

It's in this section where you can organically introduce a mention of your product or service.

Depending on the topic of the newsletter, you can use a natural aside to link your product or service to what you're writing:

  • "By the way, in my [Product Name], I help people like you solve this problem by giving you the exact tools to [Outcome 1], [Outcome 2], and [Outcome 3]."

  • "This is exactly what I explain in my [Digital Product]. If you want to get your own copy (so you can [Outcome]), click here to get started."

  • "If you want more help [fixing these mistakes]/[achieving this outcome], then book a call with me and I'll explain how I can help."

  • "For example, this is a framework I help you master in [Digital Product/Service]."

What you're doing here is simply explaining how you can help the reader further with your digital product or service.

Even just a mention of your main website is an easy way to plant the seed to help them take the next step.

Step 5: Adding The CTAs, Media, and Formatting

Alright, 95% of the newsletter is done!

The last 5% is achieved by adding in the small (but extremely important!) things:

Adding a PS with a clear Call To Action

This could be adding more value, offering a "next step" to help them (e.g. a product or service), or a TL;DR summary of the email (which creates an open loop for those skimmers to actually read the content!). In every case, I highly recommend adding a CTA to a product or service.

Template:

Adding a Pre-S.

This is a "Pre-Script."

It sits ABOVE your intro (before the "Hey there,") and looks a bit like this:

Pre-S: Want to [achieve outcome from the subject line] even faster? [Product/Service Name] gives you [key benefit]. [Link to check it out].

Again, you're gently reminding the reader that you have something for sale.

And more often than not, when you present the reader with the next logical step (and how it can solve the problem you hint at/achieve the outcome you mentioned in the subject line), they'll take it!

Don't worry, you won't come off as salesy or sleazy! To get people to buy, you need to remind them you have something to sell more than you need to ACTUALLY sell to them!

What media (e.g. pictures) are you including?

Pictures are a great way to break up the content in your email and add more context.

Screenshots, charts, before/afters, and examples all work. One or two well-placed images per newsletter is plenty.

How are you formatting each section?

This is something I cover in more detail in my book, The Art and Business of Online Writing, but here's a quick crash course on Flawless Formatting.

This is MASSIVELY important.

Using bulleted lists and writing rhythms is how you make your newsletter visually appealing, keep it organized, and make it easy to read and skim. If you DON'T do this, and you make it HARD for readers to consume your content, then it won't matter how "good" the content is.

So, to format your newsletter to reduce the friction for the reader, ask yourself these 3 questions:

Question 1: "Can I turn any of these paragraphs into bulleted lists?"

Here's my advice:

  • If you are listing anything, ever, it should become a bulleted list.

  • If you are rambling off a dozen quick examples, it should become a bulleted list.

  • If you are making a series of distinct points to drive home a point, it should become a list.

Here's why:

Your #1 job as a writer is to always be asking, "How do I make this easier for the reader to fly through?"

Which means (contrary to popular belief) abandoning the belief that your reader is supposed to sit there and drool over, appreciate, and gasp at each and every word—as if your adjective choice is as beautiful as Mona Lisa herself. Give it up. Let go of that dream. It doesn't matter. Whether the reader thinks you are "brilliant" or not is the wrong goal.

Your goal is for them to consume your work, and to not waste any of their time.

Period.

If you are successful, they'll come back for more.

If you are not successful, they'll say to themselves, "Wow that writer sure did waste a lot of my time" and never come back.

So, use bulleted lists when you see an opportunity to save them time.

Question 2: "Where are my subheads?"

We already created our main headings, but there's no reason why you can't also split the section up with more subheadings.

Subheads are bolded sentences throughout a piece that help the reader know "where" they are in your line of thinking.

(Just like this session doc!)

As a reader, subheads are a terrific signal that what you're reading has been carefully constructed for your benefit—as opposed to reading a long-winded, poorly formatted opinion article in The New Yorker that was clearly not written for your benefit, but for the benefit of the author: "Look what a professional writer I am!"

The easiest way to use this formatting trick is to split your newsletter sections equally into chunks.

For a few reasons:

  • Splitting the page evenly (visually) creates a sense of symmetry for the reader. It LOOKS easy and fun to read.

  • Splitting the page also gives the reader big, bolded "milestones" they can look forward to each time they scroll. If you split the page/newsletter/section evenly, then the reader won't be able to scroll more than twice without their eye "seeing" the next bolded subhead—encouraging them to keep reading (because they know the next section is "right around the corner").

  • Splitting the page also gives you clarity as to where you are taking the reader. Think of these subheads as the major mile markers helping remind you that you only have 100 words to talk about X, before you take a turn down a different street and have another 100 words to talk about Y, and so on.

Subheads bring clarity.

Question 3: "Am I using writing rhythms?"

The last step to formatting is to go through each section and look for opportunities to use the classic 1/3/1 writing rhythm (or some variation of it):

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/2/5/2/1

  • Etc.

The key to immediately injecting rhythm and skimmability into your writing is to alternate length of sentences and sections—ideally opening and closing each section with a single sentence. These are your "doors," the things that get the reader INTO a given section (so make sure your doors slide open).

Here's an example of the 1/5/1 writing rhythm in action:

"Entrepreneurship is the activity of setting up a business or businesses, taking on financial risks in the hope of profit." But how likely is the reader to remember what you've just told them? More importantly, how likely are they to be impacted and transformed by your words?

Step 6: Train AI On YOUR Writing Style

Alright, you now have every framework you need to write the perfect newsletter by hand.

But here's the thing: the frameworks are only half the unlock.

The other half is teaching AI to write like YOU—so that when you use the prompt at the end of this doc, the first draft that comes out doesn't sound like a robot (or worse, like everyone else using AI). It sounds like you. And that's what turns a 4-hour writing session into a 60-minute one.

Remember: Writing is like playing with Legos. Your voice is just another set of blocks. And just like the other frameworks, it can be systematized.

Here's how to do it in 3 steps:

Voice Training Step 1: Gather your writing samples.

AI can't mimic what it can't see.

So the first step is to collect 3-5 samples of your REAL writing—the stuff that sounds most like you:

  • Past newsletters or blog posts you're proud of

  • Long emails you've sent to friends or colleagues

  • Social posts that performed well (X threads, LinkedIn posts, etc.)

  • Even voice memo transcripts (talking is often the purest version of your voice!)

Pro tip: Choose samples where you were explaining something you care about to one person. That's the exact energy a newsletter needs.

Don't have any writing samples yet? No problem. Pick 1 of the 5 proven voices below and start there—your real voice will emerge as you publish (remember: the more you write, the more you learn).

Voice Training Step 2: Choose (or extract) your voice.

There are 5 proven writing voices. Choose the one that most resonates with you, and copy/paste the name & description inside your prompt:

5 Writing Voices:

  1. The Storyteller - Use personal or curated stories to emphasize each main point.

  2. The Opinionator - Use declarative language to emphasize each main point.

  3. The Fact Presenter - Use relevant stats, studies, or trend data to emphasize each main point.

  4. The Frameworker - Break each main point down into clear steps (listicle).

  5. The F-Bomber - Use declarative, crass, even sarcastic language to emphasize each main point.

Now, to go one level deeper, feed your writing samples to AI and have it extract your unique voice fingerprint. Here's the prompt:

Run this once. Save the output. This is your Voice Template—one of the most valuable assets you'll create in this entire Sprint.

Voice Training Step 3: Plug your Voice Template into every draft.

From now on, every time you generate a newsletter draft with AI, you'll paste your Voice Template into the <VOICE> section of the newsletter prompt (coming up next).

The result: drafts that need light editing instead of total rewrites.

And a quick reality check on quality:

  • The more specific you are with the inputs, the higher quality the output will be. When you insert your Topic, instead of saying something broad like "Real Estate," something more specific like "How to buy your first rental property and start making money in the first 90 days" will yield a SIGNIFICANTLY higher-quality output.

  • Same goes for Audience. Instead of just saying "For entrepreneurs," you'll get a better output if you say something like, "For indie hackers who want to build their first SaaS platform to $10k/mo."

The 60-Minute Newsletter Workflow

Put it all together, and here's how the perfect newsletter gets written in 60 minutes or less:

  • Minutes 0-10: Prep the inputs. Pick your topic (specific!), write or choose your subject line using the 5 rules, and list your 3-5 headers (Prep The Page).

  • Minutes 10-15: Generate the draft. Paste the Weekly Value Newsletter Prompt (below) + your Voice Template into Claude or ChatGPT. Run it.

  • Minutes 15-45: Edit like an editor, not a writer. Punch up the hooks using the 6 openers, inject your personal stories and examples (AI can't fake these—this is where YOU add the magic), fact-check any stats or links, and add your organic product mention.

  • Minutes 45-55: Format. Run the 3 Flawless Formatting questions: bullets, subheads, writing rhythms.

  • Minutes 55-60: Add the CTAs. Pre-S up top, PS at the bottom. Hit schedule.

That's it. The AI does the assembly. You do the taste.

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 4 of Start & Scale Your Newsletter: A 5-Day Sprint To Help You Dominate Your Niche, Build An Audience, And Grow An Email List With The Potential To Pay You 6-Figures.

In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • The 10 Magical Ways—the extraction workflow that turns every newsletter you write into 10+ atomic social posts (so you never have to "create social content" again)

  • The 4-part traffic strategy for X, LinkedIn & Substack Notes (Content, Cadence, Connection & Conversion)

  • The CTAs and autoplugs that turn followers into subscribers—not just "likes" (plus 2 AI prompts that do the heavy lifting for you)

And more!

All so you can drive organic traffic and acquire subscribers for $0—in as little as 20 minutes a day.

Let's dive in!

The $0 Traffic Model: Newsletter First, Social Second

Most creators have this backwards.

They grind out social content every day, hoping something goes viral, and treat their newsletter as an afterthought. You're going to do the opposite:

  1. Write your newsletter first. (You did this on Day 3.) This is your deep, long-form "source of truth."

  2. Extract social posts from it. One newsletter becomes 10+ short-form posts.

  3. Distribute those posts on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes. Each platform is a top-of-funnel traffic arm.

  4. Convert followers into subscribers with deliberate CTAs, autoplugs, and profile optimization.

This solves the two biggest problems every Newsletter Creator faces:

  • "What do I post on social?" — Answered. You post extractions from your newsletter.

  • "How do I get subscribers without paying for ads?" — Answered. Organic social traffic, converted deliberately.

Your library of newsletters becomes an asset that appreciates. Newsletter #1 gives you 10 posts. By newsletter #10, you have a 100-post library you can extract from, remix, and republish forever.

Now, where should you post? Let's look at your three traffic arms.

Your 3 Traffic Arms: X, LinkedIn & Substack Notes

Each platform plays a different role:

  • X (Twitter): 335.7 million users. Fast feedback loops. Ideas spread quickly. Best for testing hooks, one-liners, and contrarian takes before expanding them into newsletters. Rewards provocation, hot takes, and threads.

  • LinkedIn: 1 billion users. Professional audience with high trust. Best for personal stories, frameworks, and "lessons learned" posts. One good LinkedIn post can drive more email subscribers than 10 tweets because the audience actually clicks links.

  • Substack Notes: "Only" 20 million users — and that's exactly why you should be there.

Let's talk about Notes for a second, because most Newsletter Creators are sleeping on it.

Substack Notes is the new kid on the block when it comes to social media. This means there isn't a huge number of users compared to other, more mature social platforms. This is why so many Newsletter Creators tend to keep their focus on growing their newsletter with their existing social media accounts.

But here's what they're missing:

  1. 20 million users is still a lot of readers to tap into!

  2. These 20 million users are a concentrated pool of readers (compared to X where some people are just there for the memes).

  3. Because Substack Notes is so new, it pays to be an early adopter so you can get that early adopter advantage. And this won't last forever!

One final and important note:

Because this is a new platform the rules change rapidly (sometimes daily). So spend time with Substack Notes. Experiment and observe what's happening. Analyze why other posts get more reach and replicate it for yourself. Being a student of the platform will pay off.

But, if you're still not convinced, let's look at some cold, hard data.

Social posting leads to subscriber growth AND creates more paid subscribers.

Two examples from our own newsletters:

  1. Posting on Substack Notes leads to more subscribers. (We've tracked spikes in daily subscriber growth that map directly to Notes we published.)


  1. Posting on Substack Notes leads to paid subs, too. Here's the story of a reader interacting with one of my Notes and then becoming a subscriber (we have a Zap that sends us a message in Slack every time we get a new paid subscriber!).


Magic!

Substack Notes is the perfect attention engine for your Substack newsletter.

Why?

Because everything remains within one platform.

On "traditional" social media platforms, there's a lot of friction to finding your newsletter:

  • They have to read one of your posts on X, LinkedIn, etc.

  • Then they have to go to your profile

  • Then they have to find the link to your newsletter

  • Then they have to subscribe to read it

Whereas, on Substack there is way less friction. If a reader likes your Note, they can subscribe directly from the Note itself.

So the model is: X and LinkedIn for reach, Substack Notes for frictionless conversion. Post on all three from the same newsletter extraction — the content is 90% identical, only the tone and format shift slightly per platform.

But what do you post? Well, let's look at what the algorithms reward!

How The Algorithms Work (And Why Notes Is Rigged In Your Favor)

Before you start posting, it helps to understand what you're working with.

Most social platforms optimize their algorithm for time spent scrolling. More scroll time = more ads seen = more revenue. That's X and LinkedIn: they want to keep readers ON the platform, which is why link posts get suppressed and why we'll use "autoplugs" (more on that below) instead of naked links.

Substack doesn't have ads. They make money when creators make money (Substack takes 10% of paid subscriptions). So the Notes algorithm is optimized for one thing: getting readers to discover, subscribe, and eventually pay.

Mike Cohen, Substack's Head of Machine Learning, said: "The goal is to get people to discover, subscribe, and ideally pay. That's how we built the feed and how we continue to iterate."

This is a big deal.

It means the algorithm is literally on your side. Every other social platform treats you as content that keeps eyeballs glued to a feed. Substack treats you as a creator it wants to connect with paying readers. You win, they win.

Here's what the algorithm looks at when deciding who sees your Notes:

  • Who the reader is (location, language)

  • What they're subscribed to and who they follow

  • What interests they've selected

  • Their engagement behavior (clicks, likes, restacks, comments)

The system converts all of this into a numerical profile for each reader, then matches it against available content. If your Note is a good match for a reader's profile, it gets surfaced. If they engage with it, the algorithm surfaces more of your stuff.

Now here's the part most people don't know about.

In 2025, Substack upgraded from a static matching system to what they call sequential models. The old system treated each reader's preferences as a fixed snapshot. The new system understands reading as a journey unfolding over time. If a reader clicks on a productivity Note, the feed leans into that momentum and surfaces more productivity content in that same session. Your Note doesn't just compete against everything on the platform. It competes within the context of what that specific reader is interested in right now.

Two more things worth knowing:

  • Restacking and replying create recommendation bridges. When you restack or reply to another writer's content, the algorithm traces the full chain of behavior. If your readers also read Writer X, then Writer X's readers might start seeing your Notes. The system uses audience overlap between publications to build these bridges. (The same principle applies on X and LinkedIn: thoughtful replies to bigger accounts put you in front of their audience.)

  • Consistency beats virality. Substack's own data showed that steady, regular posting drove more subscriber growth than occasional viral hits. The sequential model rewards ongoing patterns of engagement over one-off spikes. Show up every day and the algorithm learns who should see your work. Post once a month and it forgets you exist.

In just 3 months (as of October 2025), the Substack app drove 32 million free subscriptions and 500,000 paid subscriptions. The app became the #1 source of subscriber growth for publishers. Notes is the engine inside that app.

OK?

So the algorithms want to distribute your content. Your job is to give them something worth recommending.

Traffic Mistakes To Avoid

Before we get into what works, let's talk about what doesn't.

These are the 5 most common mistakes we see Newsletter Creators make when driving social traffic. If you're doing any of these, fix them first. Then move on to the strategy.

Mistake #1: Speaking The Wrong Language On The Wrong Platform

Notes is not a microblogging platform for hot takes and dunking on people.

The algorithm rewards connection, not controversy. Writers who bring their Twitter habits to Notes get likes, sure. But they don't get subscribers. And there's a massive difference between the two.

The audience on Substack is there to read and learn. They want depth. They want genuine thinking. So if you're posting the same spicy tweets you'd throw onto X, you're speaking the wrong language to the wrong crowd. (The reverse is also true: a long, vulnerable LinkedIn story posted verbatim on X will die. Same idea, adapted format.)

Mistake #2: Only Posting Links To Your Newsletter

"New post! Link in comments."

Sound familiar?

This is the #1 mistake writers make. They treat social platforms as a promotional bulletin board. And nobody clicks those. Readers want to be engaged on the platform they're on. They don't want to be redirected somewhere else every time you show up in their feed.

If every post you write is a link to your newsletter, you're training the algorithm (and readers) to scroll right past you.

Mistake #3: Posting Once And Disappearing

One post a week is not a strategy. It's a lottery ticket.

The algorithm builds a picture of your voice over time. It watches who engages, what they subscribe to, who else they follow. And then it starts showing your writing to new readers who match that profile. But it needs data. Consistency is what trains the algorithm to work for you. Sporadic posting gives it nothing to work with.

Mistake #4: Ignoring The Engagement Side

Social is a two-way street.

The writers who grow fastest are commenting on other writers' posts, restacking/resharing work they admire, and having conversations. If you're posting but never engaging, you're running at half speed.

And here's the thing: algorithms now rank high-signal interactions (replies that add genuine value) above passive hearts and "love this!" comments. So the quality of your engagement matters, too.

Mistake #5: No Conversion Mechanism

You can write great posts, get tons of likes, and still gain zero subscribers.

Why? Because you never gave anyone a reason to subscribe. There's no bridge between "I liked this post" and "I subscribed to this newsletter."

You need a deliberate system for turning social attention into newsletter subscriptions. (Don't worry. That's coming later in this session.)

OK. Now that we know what NOT to do, let's get to the heart of today: the extraction workflow.

The 10 Magical Ways: Extracting 10+ Social Posts From One Newsletter


The 10 Magical Ways: 1 Newsletter In, 10+ Posts Out

Here's the workflow that ends "what should I post today?" forever.

Take your Day 3 newsletter draft. Read through it with a highlighter (literal or digital). Every newsletter you write contains at least 10 extractable social posts hiding inside it. Here are the 10 Magical Ways to pull them out:

  1. The Standalone Insight. Find your single most surprising claim or observation. Distill it into 1-3 punchy sentences. No context needed — it should make someone stop scrolling on its own.

  2. The Personal Story. Find the best story or anecdote in your newsletter. Rewrite it as a short post (under 250 words) that opens with a specific, vivid moment and builds to a single "aha" insight.

  3. The Listicle. Take any section with multiple points and reformat it as a numbered list post. "5 things I learned about [topic]:" — lists are the most shareable format on every platform.

  4. The Framework Breakdown. If your newsletter teaches a process or framework, extract the steps into a "how to" post. Step 1 → Step 2 → Step 3. On X, this becomes a thread. On LinkedIn, a line-break-heavy post. On Notes, a short numbered Note.

  5. The Contrarian Take. Find the place where your newsletter disagrees with conventional wisdom. Extract it as: "Everyone says X. Here's why they're wrong: [your take]."

  6. The Quotable Line. Find 2-3 "quotable" paragraphs — the lines you're proudest of. Post each one verbatim. On Substack, use the Newsletter Quote feature (highlight → post to Notes) so the quote links back to the full edition automatically.

  7. The Proof Post. Extract any number, result, stat, or before/after from your newsletter. "I did X for 30 days. Here's what happened:" Receipts build trust faster than opinions.

  8. The Question Post (Community Invitation). Take your newsletter's core theme and turn it into a specific question for your audience. Make it about THEM, not you. Include a generous offer ("Drop your newsletter below and I'll check it out").

  9. The Teaser (Open Loop). Pull out the most intriguing insight or claim and format it as a standalone post that creates an information gap. End with: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

  10. The Mistake/Lesson Post. Extract what you (or your reader) were doing wrong before the insight in your newsletter. "I spent 2 years doing [wrong thing]. Then I learned [insight]."

That's the whole workflow: 1 newsletter in, 10+ atomic posts out.

A few rules for extraction:

  • Do NOT repost the newsletter. EXTRACT and TRANSFORM the best parts into standalone posts that work even if someone never reads the full edition.

  • Every post must stand alone. If it requires reading the newsletter to make sense, it's not extracted yet.

  • Adapt per platform. Same idea, three flavors: punchy and provocative for X, story-driven and professional for LinkedIn, warm and reader-to-reader for Notes.

  • Keep each post under 280 words. Short paragraphs (1-2 sentences each). Make them sound like a real person, not a content machine.

Do this every time you publish, and after 10 newsletters you'll have a 100+ post library. You'll never stare at a blank compose box again.

Now let's turn those posts into a system.

The Traffic Strategy: Content, Cadence, Connection, Conversion

The Traffic Strategy is a 4-part system for turning social posting into a consistent, compounding subscriber growth machine.

Here are the 4 parts:

  • Part 1: Content: What to post (the 3 content buckets and specific post types that convert)

  • Part 2: Cadence: When and how often to post (the daily rhythm)

  • Part 3: Connection: How to engage strategically (comments, restacks, relationships)

  • Part 4: Conversion: How to turn social readers into newsletter subscribers

Think of these as four gears. When all four are turning, the engine runs itself. Skip one, and the whole thing stalls.

Most writers only do Part 1 (content). They post, hope for the best, and then wonder why social "doesn't work" for them. The secret is that Parts 2, 3, and 4 are where the compounding happens.

Let's break down each part.

1. What To Post (The 3 Content Buckets)

There are 3 "buckets" of content you can post:

  1. Short-form original. Think of this as your typical social media content. Take snippets from your newsletter (via the 10 Magical Ways above) and post them as tweets, LinkedIn posts, or Substack Notes. Or experiment with new ideas by posting and seeing how the idea performs. If it performs well, expand the idea into a newsletter. This is Lean Writing 101: social is your idea lab, the newsletter is your finished product.

  2. Restacks / Reshares. This is exactly like retweets on Twitter. Use this function to restack other Notes you like or other newsletters you found interesting (or quote-tweet on X, reshare with commentary on LinkedIn). Choose to either share without comment or add your own comment (highly-recommended!).

  3. Newsletter Quotes. If you found a section of a newsletter interesting, highlight it then choose to post it to Notes with your own comment. A screenshot of the quote is created alongside a link to the original newsletter. (You can do this with your own newsletter too.) On X and LinkedIn, the equivalent is a clean screenshot of your best paragraph with a one-line setup.

One final note:

As with all social platforms, the algorithm and audience favor certain types of content. And right now, pairing your post with an image gets far more traction than pairing it with a video. But, of course, this might change so I encourage you to keep experimenting.

2. When And How To Post (Cadence)

Right now, there is no way to schedule posts on Substack Notes (X and LinkedIn do have scheduling — use it).

Which means you have to manage your posts with discipline. As with every other social media platform, consistency is key. It helps you to a) publish a lot of ideas over an extended period of time and b) build trust with your audience because they "expect" you to appear in their feed.

So, pick a schedule and stick with it.

I post twice per day at 10am and 4pm ET. Dickie does the same.

And if you need a little rigor, here's a simple weekly content calendar you can follow:

  • Monday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Restack with Commentary (4pm)

  • Tuesday: Personal Story (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Wednesday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Newsletter Teaser (4pm)

  • Thursday: Restack with Commentary (10am) + Newsletter Quote (4pm)

  • Friday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Saturday: Newsletter Teaser (10am) + Restack with Commentary (4pm)

  • Sunday: Personal Story (10am) + Standalone Insight (4pm)

You don't need to follow this exactly. But it gives you a starting point so you never sit down and think "what should I post today?"

Batch your WRITING (not necessarily your posting):

  1. Sunday night: Extract and write 5-7 posts for the week from your latest newsletter. Standalone Insights and Personal Stories are the easiest to batch. Save them in a doc or your notes app, then copy-paste at your posting times throughout the week.

  2. Daily: Write 1-2 reactive posts in real-time. Restacks, Community Invitations, and Newsletter Quotes work best when they're timely and spontaneous.

  3. Post-newsletter day: Pull 1-2 Newsletter Teasers from your latest edition.

Cross-posting rule: write once, adapt twice. Your Sunday batch is drafted once, then given a 60-second platform pass — tighten the hook for X, add line breaks and a story frame for LinkedIn, soften the tone for Notes.

Content and cadence are locked.

3. How To Engage (Connection)

At the end of the day, I encourage you to be a good social citizen.

If you interact with more people, you're more likely to attract new subscribers to your own content. So it pays to be active and engage with other writers you enjoy reading.

OK. With that philosophy in mind, let me show you why engagement matters even more than posting.

When you leave a substantive comment on a popular writer's post, you show up in front of their entire audience. If your comment is good (if it adds genuine value, a personal example, or a thoughtful perspective), people click on your name, visit your profile, and subscribe.

One good comment on the right post can bring more subscribers than 10 posts of your own.

So engagement is not a "nice to have." It's the multiplier that makes everything else work.

Strategy #1: The Value-Add Comment

When you comment on someone else's post, don't say "love this!" or "so true!"

Those comments don't help the algorithm surface your profile. Substantive comments do. Add something. A personal example. A related insight. A "yes, and…" that takes their point further. The rule: every comment you leave should be good enough to be its own post.

When your comments are consistently thoughtful, two things happen.

  • The algorithm surfaces them higher (more people see them).

  • And the writer you're engaging with starts to notice you (which leads to restacks, cross-promotion, and organic relationship-building).

Strategy #2: The Restack (Or Quote-Share)

I talked about Restacking as a content type above.

But I want to call it out again as an engagement strategy because it's that powerful. When you restack someone's Note with your own commentary (or quote-tweet on X, or reshare on LinkedIn), it goes to YOUR audience with your endorsement, and it notifies the original writer.

They see your name.

They check you out.

And if you've been consistently restacking their work with thoughtful takes, they'll often return the favor.

One restack from the right person can bring dozens of new subscribers.

Restack 2-3 posts per week from writers in your niche or adjacent niches. Always add your own take. (Don't just hit the restack button.)

Strategy #3: Build Your "Traffic 15"

Identify 10-15 writers in your niche or adjacent niches with similar-sized audiences.

Write their names down. These are your "Traffic 15."

Engage with their posts consistently. Comment, restack, reply. Over 2-4 weeks, you'll build a relationship. And the algorithm notices overlapping audiences. When your readers and their readers start interacting with both of you, the platform starts showing your work to THEIR followers and vice versa.

This is the organic version of cross-promotion. And it's more powerful because it's earned.

Rotate 1-2 names per month as your audience grows.

Here's a simple checklist. Every day, in addition to posting your 2 posts:

  • Comment substantively on 3-5 posts from writers in your niche

  • Reply to every comment on your own posts within the first hour

  • Restack/reshare 1 post with your own commentary (if you find something worth sharing)

  • Check your "Traffic 15" — have you engaged with at least 2-3 of them today?

This takes 10 minutes.

You're posting great content. You're showing up consistently. You're building relationships. But are those readers actually becoming subscribers?

Let's make sure they do.

4. How To Convert Followers Into Subscribers (Conversion)

Most writers still leave subscribers on the table because they don't have a deliberate conversion system.

Here's how to fix that.

Conversion Tactic #1: Optimize Your Profiles

Your profile (on every platform) must answer one question instantly for your reader: "What will I get if I subscribe?"

And to answer this question…

  • Your newsletter name must clearly state your niche (you built this on Day 1)

  • Your one-line description/bio needs to communicate the value (you built this on Day 1)

  • Your pinned post should sell the subscription — pin your best newsletter teaser or a "start here" post with your subscribe link

  • On X and LinkedIn: put your newsletter link in your bio, not buried in a linktree

Your social strategy will not work without a profile that converts. The profile is the conversion bottleneck.

Conversion Tactic #2: Leave Breadcrumbs

Inside your posts, occasionally reference your newsletter in a way that creates curiosity.

Here's what I mean:

  • "I broke this down in way more detail in last week's edition. The part about [specific intriguing detail] surprised even me."

  • "My subscribers know I've been tracking this for 6 months now. The data is wild."

  • "This is the short version. The 2,000-word deep dive is in my newsletter if you want the full framework."

When you do this, you create an information gap. There's a piece of the story the reader can only get by subscribing or digging into your newsletter. And that gap creates genuine curiosity.

Use this 2-3x per week. Sprinkle it into Personal Story and Standalone Insight posts. Never force it. When you have something genuinely interesting in your newsletter, mention it casually.

Conversion Tactic #3: "For Example…"

(This is one of my favorite tactics. It's so powerful it's worth teaching everywhere.)

If you want to point readers toward your newsletter without being seen as promotional, all you need are two magical words: "For example…"

Whenever you share an insight in a post, follow it with "For example, in my newsletter I…" and describe something specific and tangible that you do or share.

Like this:

Most Newsletter Creators only think about growth on external platforms. But the biggest lever is right inside the platform you're already on.

For example, in my newsletter [Newsletter Name], I share one specific traffic strategy every week that I've tested myself. Last week's strategy brought in 40+ new subscribers from a single post.

Are you furious at me for being "overly promotional?" Of course not. I just used my newsletter as an example. Casually. Organically.

And yet I still introduced it to you.

This is the whole secret. After the words "for example," you can point to any business, any product, any money-making-anything, and it won't come off as promotional. It comes across as a relevant example. The reader appreciates it.

Conversion Tactic #4: The Autoplug

On X and LinkedIn, the algorithm suppresses posts with links. So don't put your newsletter link in the post — put it in the first reply/comment.

Here's the play:

  1. Publish your post (no link).

  2. Immediately reply to your own post: "If you liked this, I go deeper every week in [Newsletter Name]. Subscribe free: [link]"

  3. If a post starts performing, that reply rides along with it. (Tools like Hypefury and Typefully can automate this "autoplug" to fire only when a post crosses an engagement threshold.)

The post does the work of earning attention. The autoplug does the work of converting it. Never let a post take off without a subscribe path attached.

Conversion Tactic #5: The CTA Rotation

Most posts should focus on pure value delivery. Only ~30% of your posts should have any CTA at all.

Here's the rotation:

  • 60-70% of your posts: No CTA. Just deliver value. Build trust. Let the profile do the converting.

  • 1-2x per week: Link to your newsletter. "Full breakdown in this week's [Newsletter Name] 👇" (On X/LinkedIn: link goes in the reply via autoplug.)

  • 1x per week: Soft subscribe prompt. "If this resonated, my newsletter goes deeper on [topic] every [day]. Subscribe free."

  • 2-3x per week: Breadcrumb trail. Just reference your newsletter casually.

The math on this works. Post 14 posts per week per platform. Average reach per post: 500-2,000 impressions (this grows over time). A small percentage click your profile. A percentage of those subscribe (especially if your profile is optimized).

Result: 10-30+ new subscribers per week from organic social alone. Per platform. And it compounds.

5. More Tips And Tricks To Squeeze Extra Juice

Here are some of my current favorite insights and tricks:

  • Notes lifespan. The life of a post is longer on Substack than on X or LinkedIn. Some Notes can get engagement WEEKS after we've posted them. So traction can really pick up over a number of days and weeks. Again, another reason to start posting on Notes.

  • No platform analytics on Notes. At least, not for now. So you will have to track your engagement manually (likes, comments, restacks, etc). Or try using a tool like WriteStack. (X and LinkedIn have built-in analytics — check them weekly, not daily.)

  • Newsletters get pushed to Notes. Your newsletters automatically drop into your Notes feed so you don't have to manually post them to your feed.

  • Create high-quality thumbnails. As newsletters get pushed into the feed automatically, it's important to have an eye-catching thumbnail for the newsletter so it stands out in the feed (this is the main image of your post). You can use this as an opportunity to tease the value or create an open loop for the reader.

  • Promote your best posts inside your newsletter. You can do this in your long-form newsletters by including a snippet of your best-performing post of the week. This is another way in for your audience to find your social content and start engaging with it. The flywheel runs both directions: newsletter → social → newsletter.

  • Winners get recycled. Any post that outperforms your average earns a spot in your "greatest hits" doc. Repost it in 60-90 days (audiences turn over fast), and consider expanding it into its own newsletter edition.

That's it!

The big POV here is that your newsletter library is a traffic asset, and organic social is a growth lever you should be pulling every single day — especially Substack Notes, where the algorithm is literally built to hand you subscribers.

And the best part?

If you start now, you're early to the party. So there's never been a better time to get started.

(Bonus!) The AI Content Extraction Prompts

Below are two simple prompts you can use to generate social content. Copy-paste them into ChatGPT, Claude, or your AI tool of choice. They'll generate posts for you based on the post types we just covered.

Now, what you can do is:

  • Run Prompt #1 to batch a full week of posts in one sitting

  • OR run Prompt #2 to take your latest newsletter (your Day 3 draft!) and extract 5-7 posts from it

  • Review the AI drafts and add YOUR voice, YOUR stories, YOUR specific details

  • Then post throughout the week

So cool!

Prompt #1: The Weekly Batch Generator

Purpose: Generate a full week's worth of posts (10-14) in one sitting.

Prompt #2: The Newsletter-to-Social Repurposer

Purpose: Take any newsletter edition and extract 5-7 posts from it. (Run this on your Day 3 draft tonight.)

Frequently Asked Questions

"How many followers do I need before this starts working?"

Zero.

Posts from writers with 100 followers can outperform those with 10,000+ because the algorithms weight genuine engagement over follower count. If you write something that resonates with even 5 people and they engage, the algorithm starts showing it to similar readers.

Don't wait until you're "big enough." Start now. That's the whole point of the early adopter advantage.

"I'm getting likes but no subscribers. What's wrong?"

Likes and subscribers are two different things. If you're getting likes but no subscribers, you have a conversion problem, not a content problem.

Go back to the Conversion section above. Check your profile. Does it clearly communicate what readers get if they subscribe? Are you using the Breadcrumb Trail? Are you adding soft CTAs 2-3x per week? Is your autoplug firing on X and LinkedIn? Most likely, your posts are good but your profile isn't closing.

"Should I post the same content on Notes, X, and LinkedIn?"

You can.

But the audiences are different. X rewards provocation, hot takes, and threads. Notes rewards vulnerability, stories, and genuine helpfulness. LinkedIn rewards professional stories and frameworks. A post that works on X might not work on Notes, and vice versa.

If you want to cross-post, adapt the tone and format for each platform. (This is a 60-second edit per post, not a rewrite.)

"I don't have time to post 2x per day. Is once a day enough?"

Once a day is better than zero. But 2x per day is where the compounding kicks in.

If you're strapped for time, commit to spend 20 minutes total. Most of these posts are 2-5 sentences. If you can send a text message, you can write a post. Batch 5-7 on Sunday night and you're already ahead for the week.

"What if I run out of things to say?"

You won't.

If you're publishing a newsletter, every single edition contains 5-7 posts waiting to be extracted (use Prompt #2 above — or the 10 Magical Ways if you're extracting by hand). Every conversation you have, every article you read, every question a subscriber asks — those are all posts.

"Should I engage with writers who have way bigger audiences than me?"

Absolutely. This is one of the highest-leverage things you can do.

When you leave a genuinely valuable comment on a big writer's post, their entire audience sees it. If your comment is good, people click on your name.

Don't be sycophantic. "OMG I love everything you write!" doesn't help anyone.

Add value. Share your own experience. Respectfully extend their point. Be the comment that makes the original writer say "damn, good point."

Homework (Before Day 5)

We just walked through the entire Traffic Engine. The 10 Magical Ways. Content. Cadence. Connection. Conversion. You know the post types. You know the daily rhythm. You know how to engage strategically. You know how to convert.

Now it's time to execute.

Here's what I need you to do before tomorrow's session (60-90 minutes):

Step 1: Extract 5-10 Social Posts From Your Day 3 Newsletter Draft. Use the 10 Magical Ways by hand, or run Prompt #2 (paste in your draft), then add your own voice and stories to the AI output. Save all of them in one doc — this is the start of your content library.

Step 2: Publish At Least ONE Post Today. Pick your strongest extraction and post it on X, LinkedIn, or Substack Notes (or all three, adapted). Done is better than perfect. The algorithm can't reward a post that doesn't exist.

Step 3: Audit Your Profiles. Does your newsletter name, bio, and pinned post clearly communicate what subscribers get? Add your newsletter link to every bio. Your profile is the conversion bottleneck. Everything downstream depends on it.

Step 4: Build Your Traffic 15 List. Identify 15 writers in your niche or adjacent niches with similar-sized audiences. Write their names down. These are the writers you'll engage with consistently starting this week.

Step 5: Commit To The 20-Minute Daily Routine For 14 Days. Morning: post 1 + engage for 5 minutes. Afternoon: post 1 + reply to comments. Track your new subscribers for 2 weeks and watch the flywheel start turning.

~

Reminder:

The writers who win at newsletter growth aren't the most talented. They're the most consistent.

And the best part? If you start now, you're early to the party. So there's never been a better time to get started.

See you tomorrow for Day 5: Newsletter Monetization Methods — how to turn the audience you're building into revenue.
