records.description: Hey there! And welcome to Day 5 of Start & Scale Your Newsletter: A 5-Day Sprint To Help You Dominate Your Niche, Build An Audience, And Grow An Email List With
records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 5 of Start & Scale Your Newsletter: A 5-Day Sprint To Help You Dominate Your Niche, Build An Audience, And Grow An Email List With The Potential To Pay You 6-Figures.

In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: how to make money from subscriptions (pricing, paywalls & when to go paid)

  • The Book Model (Self-Publishing): how to make money republishing your newsletter content as books

  • The Digital Product Model: how to turn your email list into a digital product "engine"

And more!

All so you can leave the Sprint with a 90-day monetization plan—and a newsletter that pays you for years to come.

Let's dive in!

A quick note before we start: why ads aren't on the list

Technically, there's another model out there that everyone talks about, which is The Sponsorship Model. But the reason we're not going to cover it is because we don't recommend it. Yes, many newsletters monetize with ads. (Beehiiv has done a good job here, integrating advertisers into their platform and pairing them with newsletters.)

However, you're here to learn from us.

And OUR take is that ads are one of the worst ways to monetize.

Ads require massive scale before they pay anything meaningful, they put someone else's message in front of your readers, and they slowly exhaust the trust you've spent months building. You'd be much better off (and make way more money) monetizing with one of these other business models instead.

Everything we cover today works whether you're on Substack, Kit, or Beehiiv. The mechanics differ slightly by platform, but the models are identical.

Choosing The Right Monetization Model


3 Ways Your Newsletter Pays You (No Ads Required)

To effectively monetize your newsletter, here are your options:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: how you make money from subscriptions

  • The Book Model: how you make money republishing newsletter content as books on Amazon

  • The Digital Product Model: how you make money from selling one-off digital products

Now, the big question everyone asks is, "OK… so which one should I pick?"

The Answer: All of them!

One of the BIGGEST missed opportunities for newsletter writers is thinking that the only way to monetize is through the Paid Newsletter Model.

And this is wrong.

If you decide to turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter… this is the beginning of monetization, not the end!

  • Yes, you should monetize your content via paid subscription.

  • But you can also sell all your paid subscribers (and also your free subscribers, who are maybe looking for something different) on digital products.

  • And you can also sell all your paid subscribers (and also your free subscribers, who are maybe looking for something different) on the same content presented in different formats: eBook, print books, audiobooks, etc.

It's SHOCKING to us how many newsletter writers don't do any of these things.

They fail to realize how much money they're leaving on the table by not also offering digital products, and not also double-monetizing their content in books & audiobooks.

So. Much. Money. Left. On. The. Table.

It kills us!

(So please, don't make this mistake.)

That said — you can't launch everything at once. Today we'll cover all three models, then give you a decision framework for which one to start with. Your homework is to pick one and map your 90-day plan.

Method #1: The Paid Newsletter Model

The primary monetization model for newsletters is to "go paid."

On Substack, this is built in natively. On Kit, you can do this with a paid recommendation or by pairing your list with a payment tool. On Beehiiv, paid subscriptions are built into the platform as well.

This is a relatively easy monetization model to adopt and understand, which is what makes it great for beginners. You don't have to mess around with learning a bunch of different tech platforms. You don't really have to acquire advanced copywriting skills, or learn how to run ads. All you have to do is add a paywall (placed strategically) into your newsletters and publish consistently for a long period of time.

That's about it.

Why The Paid Newsletter Model Is So Great

Well, it's great for a bunch of reasons:

  • First, paid newsletters are subscription revenue. And subscription revenue is king. Since subscriptions "recur" (over and over again), they create a very defensible sort of business. If you have 1,000 paying subscribers, there's essentially a 0% chance all 1,000 of them unsubscribe at the same time. Instead, you might churn maybe 10% of them per month—while also continuing to attract new paying subscribers. All of this is just a fancy way of saying: you have a defensible, predictable business. Great!

  • Second, paid newsletters are very easy/simple to operate. When you turn your newsletter paid, you connect it to Stripe and payments happen directly inside your platform. There's very little, if any "operational infrastructure" you need to build or even manage. It's quite literally one of the simplest business models to execute in the digital age. Also great for beginners!

  • Third, paid newsletters are insanely powerful engines for other monetization models later. Even if you don't monetize in these other ways, it's worth acknowledging that having a paid newsletter as the "nucleus" of your business will pay you dividends for a long, long time. That's because everyone on your paid newsletter list is essentially a customer raising their hand saying, "I'd love to give you more money—if you can help me solve more and more complicated/valuable problems."

We love paid newsletters as a monetization model.

Free-To-Paid Conversion & Paywall Strategy

The mechanics of going paid come down to three decisions:

  1. What stays free vs. what goes paid. Your free content is your growth engine — it's how new readers discover you. Your paid content is the deeper, more actionable, more "do this exactly" version. A common split: free readers get the "what" and "why," paid readers get the "how" (templates, systems, step-by-step breakdowns).

  2. Where you place the paywall. Don't paywall the whole post. Place the paywall after you've delivered real value and right before the most actionable payoff. The free portion has to be good enough that readers feel the pain of not seeing the rest. Learning how to place your paywall strategically to increase conversions is a skill — and it's one of the fundamentals worth "getting good" at early.

  3. Pricing. The standard range is $5–$15/month, with an annual option priced at roughly 10x the monthly price (so annual subscribers effectively get 2 months free). $10/mo or $100/yr is a perfectly good starting point for most niches. Don't agonize over this — you can always adjust. What matters far more is publishing consistently.

When Should You Go Paid?

Sooner than you think. You don't need 10,000 subscribers. A useful signal: once you have a few hundred engaged subscribers who consistently open and reply, turn on paid — even if only a handful convert at first. Industry-wide, expect roughly 2–5% of your free list to convert to paid over time. The bigger and warmer your free list gets, the more that percentage compounds.

Method #2: The Book Model (Self-Publishing)

This next model is a bit more creative.

As a beginner, you should either turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter first, and/or you should start out launching some digital products to your list. These are much easier monetization models to execute.

But once you've gotten in a flow, and especially the longer you stick with your newsletter (content compounds), we would absolutely recommend adding in this monetization model.

Here's how it works:

  • If you write long-form newsletters (5,000+ words), you can actually get a simple eBook cover designed and also publish them on Amazon. (*NOTE: These cannot go inside KDP Select. But they can be published non-exclusively.) These eBooks will get organized into Amazon's "quick reads" eBook categories.

  • Once you have ~15 long-form newsletters (or ~30-ish standard newsletters) all on the same topic, you can "compile" them into larger print books & audiobooks. The "value" of this is that some readers simply like consuming the same content in different ways. This is what we did with books like Snow Leopard (which was 100% reused content from our newsletter), and readers absolutely loved being able to have a print copy on their desks.

  • You can also sell eBook and audiobook versions on your personal website as digital downloads. This requires a bit more infrastructure setup, but remember… sales generated through your website aren't subject to Amazon taking a cut. Which means you make 2x the profit!

But wait… there's more!

Another clever strategy you can leverage is, when you start turning newsletters into mini-books, and mini-books into bigger books… you can also "bundle in" free access to this library of digital assets back into your paid newsletter.

This is what Cole does with his paid fiction newsletter, Commercial Fiction Club. A benefit of upgrading to paid is you get "free access" to his entire library of fiction writing.

Why is this a great tactic?

Because you're essentially trading one-off revenue (customer buys a book) for recurring revenue (they subscribe to your paid newsletter, and stay subscribed to continue getting access to not just the paid newsletter, but your entire library, in perpetuity).

Books = Authority + Revenue

One thing worth calling out: a book isn't just a revenue stream. "Author of [Book]" is one of the fastest credibility unlocks available to a newsletter writer. It boosts free-to-paid conversion, makes your digital products easier to sell, and gets you podcast invites and speaking opportunities that grow the newsletter itself. The revenue is real — but the authority compounds even faster.

And the best part: you don't have to create anything "new." You just have to repackage work you've already done in the past.

Method #3: The Digital Product Model

Whether you have a free newsletter and/or a paid newsletter, we would strongly encourage you to consider adopting the Digital Product Monetization Model as well.

This means selling subscribers:

  • [$9–$99] Template packs, AI prompts, dashboards, cheat sheets, mini-courses, etc.

  • [$99–$350] Text & video asynchronous courses

  • [$350–$1,000] Workshops, cohorts, challenges, bootcamps, etc.

One of the biggest "mental unlocks" is realizing that both your free & paid newsletter lists are lists of potential customers.

For example, Write With AI has over 112,000 free subscribers—and only 1,800 active paying subscribers.


It would be a HUGE mistake to think, "I guess the only way we can make money is by people upgrading to the paid newsletter list." Why?

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list just don't like paid newsletters as a concept (it happens).

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list want more help, or help specifically on a particular topic.

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list want more hands-on help, more direct access to you, etc.

The point is, all those "free" subscribers should have more than 1 way to give you money.

Having a paid newsletter option is great.

But you want to give them other options, too.

Let us show you how "expensive" of a mistake this can be.

A few weeks ago, we ran a Claude Cowork Bootcamp.

This was a 2-week "cohort" experience teaching writers, creators, and entrepreneurs how to use no-code agents inside Claude Cowork. Why did we do this? Because Write With AI readers had been asking us a lot of questions about Claude, Claude Cowork, and no-code agents!

So, we spun up a curriculum and launched it to our entire Write With AI list.

And guess what? Most of the people who bought weren't even active paying subscribers.

They were free subscribers… who just needed to be presented with a different offer.

And look what happened:


Over $167,000 in revenue from one 2-week bootcamp offer — launched to the same list.

Over 200 people took us up on this specific 2-week bootcamp, generating over $167,000 in revenue.

Translation: this 1 "different" offer did 1/3rd of Write With AI's total yearly revenue… in 2 weeks.

And now, knowing this is possible, imagine if we DIDN'T do this. We'd be "missing" $167,000 in additional revenue! OUCH!!!!!

In short: do not underestimate the power of giving free & paid subscribers "other things to buy."

Writers leave a tremendous amount of money on the table when they make this mistake.

Mistakes To Avoid

Before you pick your model, here are the most common (and most expensive) mistakes we see:

  1. Monetizing with ads/sponsorships too early (or at all). You rent out your readers' attention for pennies, exhaust their trust, and cap your upside. Every model we covered today pays more per subscriber than ads ever will at your size.

  2. Thinking paid subscriptions are the ONLY way to monetize. Going paid is the beginning of monetization, not the end. The Write With AI example above is what this mistake costs: $167,000 in 2 weeks, from one "different" offer.

  3. Paywalling everything. Your free content is your growth engine. Kill it and you kill the top of your funnel. Paywall the payoff, not the post.

  4. Waiting until you feel "big enough." You don't need 10,000 subscribers to go paid or launch a product. You need a few hundred engaged readers and one clear offer.

  5. Never asking for the sale. If you know how to solve a reader's problem and never tell them you can help, you're not being polite — you're letting them suffer. (More on this in the FAQ below.)

  6. Launching all three models at once. Stack them over time, one threshold at a time. That's what the decision framework is for.

Frequently Asked Questions

Now, whenever we walk writers through the different ways they can monetize a newsletter, we always get the same handful of questions.

So let's rapid-fire through them here:

"Which monetization model is the best?"

There's no such thing.

The "best one" is the one that interests you the most, and that you'll be willing to stick with (through the growing pains) and not give up on.

Because we could tell you "the best one," but if it's not one you're interested in executing, then it doesn't matter.

"Can I use more than one monetization model?"

Yes! That's the goal!

Your business becomes more and more profitable, and defensible, the more of these different monetization models you stack together.

For example, this is how Category Pirates was built into a multi-6-figure newsletter and multi-6-figure publishing business:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: We wrote long-form paid newsletters (which we called "mini-books") 2x per month, and charged $20/mo (or $200/yr). Our paid newsletter grew to ~$150,000 in annual recurring revenue.

  • The Book Model: Then, to unlock a secondary revenue stream, we took all of our "mini-books" (newsletters), slapped a cover on them, and republished them as "mini-books" on Amazon. And then we monetized again by compiling 12-15 "mini-books" on a topic, and republishing it again as a print book/audiobook. Republishing our content unlocked another $100,000/yr in annual revenue.

  • The Digital Product Model: Later, we added in digital products and cohort-based programs, giving subscribers yet another way to learn the material and gain more access to us. Adding in these digital products and experiences added another $250,000+ in annual revenue.

So yes, the goal is to combine these different business models—and keep giving readers more and more ways to learn from you and work with you.

"But won't readers get upset if I basically take the same content and charge for it again somewhere else?"

No. This is a faulty belief.

Especially if you are changing the content's consumption type—like turning a newsletter into a Kindle eBook or audiobook, or turning newsletter ideas into more in-depth course modules paired with videos—then it's actually a completely different product.

And readers will be THANKFUL that you created an option for them to consume the content they want, in the way they want it.

"But won't readers get upset if I launch so many new offers? Won't I come across like a money-grubbing sleazy salesman?"

No. This is a faulty belief.

If I saw you had a problem that I knew how to solve, which one would make you more upset?

  • Telling you I know how to solve it, and would be happy to help you (for a price, of course)

  • Not telling you at all and letting you suffer

I'm going to go out on a limb and guess you'd be MORE UPSET at me NOT telling you the answer, and NOT being willing to help.

Right?

OK, great. That's all you're doing.

You aren't "selling" anything.

You're simply creating more available options for readers to get your help.

"How much money can I really earn with a newsletter?"

Infinite.

There are some newsletters generating hundreds of thousands of dollars per month in revenue. Obviously this is an outlier outcome, but it's entirely possible.

That said, here's what we think is a "realistic" home-run outcome:

  • $100,000+ per year in annual recurring revenue. This is completely doable for nearly any newsletter in any niche. Will it take work? Yes. Will it take time? Yes. But building a 6-figure paid newsletter is completely within the realm of "achievable" for most people (who stick with it).

  • $50,000+ per year in self-publishing revenue. If you successfully build a 6-figure paid newsletter, then you can absolutely unlock another $50,000 - $100,000 in incremental revenue simply by republishing your content as eBooks, print books, and audiobooks on Amazon. And it's an easy and lucrative model to execute because you don't have to create anything "new." You just have to repackage work you've already done in the past.

  • $150,000+ in digital product revenue. If you successfully build a growing free and/or paid newsletter, there's also zero reason why you can't unlock another 6 figures (or more) in revenue by launching digital products to your list. For us, Write With AI does ~$400,000 per year in subscription revenue, but does another $1,000,000+ in digital product revenue. So, our "digital product business" is actually 2-3x the size of our "paid newsletter business."

If you do all the above, you have a business well north of $300,000 per year — from a newsletter.

That's an insane outcome—and yet, totally achievable.

It will just take a bit more work than you probably think, and take a bit more time than you probably want (which is why so many people give up).

The Decision Framework: Which Method Do You Start With?

Your homework is to pick ONE of these monetization models, and start there.

But if you want a "constraint" for making forward-leaning decisions, here's what we would recommend:

  • First, turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter—and stay focused on this until you reach at least $50,000 in annual revenue. Focus on "getting good" at executing the fundamentals, learning how to place your paywall strategically to increase conversions, and building up a base of paying customers.

  • Once you reach $50,000 in annual subscription revenue from your paid newsletter, start launching digital products to your list. Keep doing this until you 2x the business—crossing $100,000 per year in revenue.

  • Then, once you cross $100,000 per year in revenue, add in the book/self-publishing component. This will be a time investment, but it will compound significantly in your favor as the years go by. This will unlock another tranche of revenue.

A quick gut-check if you're still torn:

Your situation

Start with

You publish consistently and readers reply/engage

Paid Newsletter — turn on subscriptions now

Your readers keep asking you the same "how do I…" question

Digital Product — package the answer and sell it

You have 15+ long-form posts (or 30+ standard posts) on one topic

Books — compile and republish your archive

You're brand new with a small list

Paid Newsletter — it forces the consistency habit and everything else builds on it

This is the order in which we'd think about monetizing.

But please don't feel like you need to rush to figure out how to monetize in all these different ways tomorrow.

Just focus on going one step at a time. And as you cross each new threshold, adjust your strategy and grow into the next tier of monetization.

Homework (Final Assignment)

Tonight, do two things:

  1. Choose your monetization method. Pick ONE of the three models — Paid Newsletter, Books, or Digital Products — using the decision framework above. Write it down. Commit.

  2. Map your 90-day plan. Break it into three 30-day blocks:

  • Days 1–30: Set up the mechanics. (Paid: turn on subscriptions, set pricing, decide your free/paid split. Products: pick ONE product idea from questions your readers already ask. Books: inventory your archive and pick the 15 posts that share a topic.)

  • Days 31–60: Execute. (Paid: publish weekly with a strategically placed paywall. Products: build and pre-sell it to your list. Books: compile, get a cover designed, format for Amazon.)

  • Days 61–90: Launch and learn. (Paid: run your first "upgrade" campaign to free subscribers. Products: launch to your full list — free AND paid. Books: publish, then announce it to your list and bundle it into your paid tier.)

Keep it to one page. A plan you'll actually follow beats a perfect plan you won't.

What's Next: Wrapping Up the Sprint

That's it — 5 days, start to finish. Look at what you built this week:

  • Day 1: You chose your niche and positioning.

  • Day 2: You set up and launched your newsletter.

  • Day 3: You built your growth engine.

  • Day 4: You created your content system.

  • Day 5: You chose your monetization method and mapped your 90-day plan.

Most people spend months "getting ready" to do what you just did in 5 days.

Here's the truth about what happens next: the sprint was the easy part. The next 90 days are where newsletters are actually built — one consistent send at a time. Content compounds. Trust compounds. Revenue compounds. But only if you keep publishing.

So here's our ask:

  1. Execute your 90-day plan. Don't add to it. Don't second-guess it. Just run it.

  2. Don't touch your monetization model for 90 days. The #1 killer of newsletter businesses isn't picking the "wrong" model — it's switching models every 3 weeks and never letting one compound.

  3. When you cross your first threshold, stack the next model. Paid newsletter → digital products → books. One tier at a time.

You now know more about starting, growing, and monetizing a newsletter than 99% of people who ever hit "create publication."

The only thing left to do is write.

Onwards and upwards!

records.content:
Welcome to the Newsletter Hook Writer!

This prompt writes newsletter introductions using a 5-block framework I've been refining for years.

  • Block #1: Greeting

  • Block #2: Opening sentence

  • Block #3: Promise

  • Block #4: Solution

  • Block #5: Transition

Each block has a specific job.

The greeting warms up the reader. The opening sentence hooks them. The promise educates them on why this topic matters. The solution tells them exactly what you're giving them today. And the transition carries them into the body.

Block #2 is your “hook”.

And in this prompt we generate 10 different kinds:

  1. Open Loop (curiosity gap)

  2. Stakes Escalator (loss aversion)

  3. Interrogation (forced self-diagnosis)

  4. Sacred Cow Slaughter (challenge a belief)

  5. Pattern Break (violate expectations)

  6. Diagnosis (name their exact symptom)

  7. Movie Scene (drop them into a moment)

  8. Insider Briefing (share what peers don't know)

  9. Confession (vulnerability that earns trust)

  10. Proof Drop (stack real credibility fast)

So instead of spending 30 minutes staring at a blank screen trying to nail your opener, you get 10 complete intros you can test, rotate, and reuse.

Which means more people reading past the first line, more replies, and more revenue from every single send.

Here’s how it to use it:

Run the prompt.

Then give it your topic, your audience, and some real details about your credibility. It gives you 10 fully written intros, each using a different psychological hook.

Easy.

Newsletter Hook Writer Prompt

Copy / paste the prompt below.

# NEWSLETTER INTRODUCTION WRITER

## ROLE

You are a direct-response copywriter who specializes in newsletter introductions. You've studied Halbert, Bencivenga, Schwartz, and Caples. You write like a sharp friend who always has something interesting to say, not a robot playing it safe. You understand that a newsletter introduction is a structured sequence of blocks, not just a clever opening line.

## PHILOSOPHY

This is a newsletter. The reader already opened your email. They already trust you enough to subscribe. You don't need to grab a stranger's collar. You need to reward a subscriber for opening and pull them into the body fast enough that they don't bounce back to their inbox.

**Newsletter intros vs. social hooks:**
- Social hooks compete with infinite scroll. Newsletter intros compete with "I'll read this later" (they won't).
- Social hooks need to prove who you are. Newsletter intros can skip that. The reader already knows you.
- Social hooks lean on provocation and bold claims. Newsletter intros lean on curiosity, stories, and earned intimacy.
- The tone is warmer. You're writing to someone who chose to hear from you. Talk to them like it.

The reader's default state after opening: "Ok, I'm here. Make it worth my time."

**THE ENERGY RULE:** Write first. Edit second. Your first job is to write something with FORCE, something a little too bold, a little too specific, a little too confident. Your second job is to check it for slop. Never reverse this order. Caution kills copy. You can always sand down something too sharp. You can't inject life into something born flat.

## THE 5-BLOCK INTRODUCTION FRAMEWORK

Every newsletter introduction is built from 5 blocks stacked on top of each other. Don't think of the intro as one giant block of text. Think of it as 5 smaller blocks, each with a specific job.

### Block #1: THE GREETING

Start every newsletter with a simple, warm greeting on its own line.

"Hey there!"

That's it. Keep it short. Keep it human. This is the handshake before the conversation.

### Block #2: THE HOOK (1 sentence)

This is the single opening sentence that grabs the reader's attention. One sentence only. This is where the 10 hook types below come in. Each hook type gives you a different way to write this one critical sentence.

The best opening hooks do one of the following:
- Ask a thought-provoking question
- Open with a strong, declarative sentence
- Reference a meaningful moment in time (a date, a day, a specific moment)
- Present a vulnerable statement
- Offer a controversial opinion
- Share a unique insight

### Block #3: THE PROMISE (3-7 sentences or 3-7 bullets)

This is the substance of the intro. After the hook grabs them, the promise educates the reader on WHY this matters.

The promise takes one of two forms:

**Problem-oriented promise:** Educate the reader on a specific problem (or series of problems), why those problems exist, and the negative outcomes of leaving them unsolved.

**Outcome-oriented promise:** Educate the reader on a desirable outcome (or handful of outcomes), why those outcomes are so valuable, and the negative consequences of not achieving them.

This block is typically 3-7 sentences long. It can also be presented as a bulleted list of 3-7 bullets. The key is that it's tangible, actionable, and niche-specific. The reader should feel the weight of the problem or the pull of the outcome.

### Block #4: THE SOLUTION (1-2 sentences)

After educating the reader on the problem or outcome, complete the promise by telling them that's exactly what you're going to help them with today.

You're either going to help them solve that problem (or series of problems) or achieve that outcome (or handful of outcomes).

This is where the LAST SENTENCE RULE lives:
- Tell the reader exactly what you're giving them. Be specific about the format: "the exact 6-step process" or "a full breakdown with screenshots" or "my 3-part system." Vague promises ("some tips," "my thoughts") don't pull anyone forward.
- Name a specific, tangible outcome. Noun-oriented outcomes the reader can picture: "...to land your first $10K client" / "...to write a newsletter that gets forwarded" / "...to double your open rate in 30 days." NOT adjective-oriented outcomes: "...to be more successful" / "...to feel confident."

Study the difference:

❌ "So today, I'm going to share some thoughts on growing your newsletter."
✅ "So today, I'm going to walk you through the exact 3-step system I used to add 4,000 subscribers in 30 days."

❌ "Today, I'll show you how to be more productive."
✅ "Today, I'll show you the single daily habit that freed up 2 hours every morning."

### Block #5: THE TRANSITION (1 sentence)

A short transition sentence into the first section of the newsletter body. Something like:

- "Let's walk through each one."
- "Let's dive in."
- "Here's how it works."
- "So, with that in mind, let's [solve that problem / achieve that outcome]."

Keep it brief. Its only job is to carry momentum from the intro into the body.

---

## FULL EXAMPLES OF THE 5-BLOCK FRAMEWORK

Study these. Notice how each block does its job and flows into the next.

**Example 1:**

> Hey there!
>
> Do you want to know the secret to landing your first ghostwriting client?
>
> One of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was: how do I actually charge for my work and make money? And the truth is, it's not that hard. It's just that no one tells you how to do it.
>
> So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to structure your next ghostwriting project, and when to use them to get paid a premium.
>
> Let's walk through each one.

Block breakdown:
- Block 1: "Hey there!" (greeting)
- Block 2: "Do you want to know the secret to landing your first ghostwriting client?" (hook: thought-provoking question)
- Block 3: "One of the biggest challenges I faced..." (promise: problem-oriented, names the struggle and normalizes it)
- Block 4: "So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways..." (solution: specific format + tangible outcome)
- Block 5: "Let's walk through each one." (transition)

**Example 2:**

> Hey there!
>
> What do you need to become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter and build a lucrative side hustle?
>
> Do you need:
> - A portfolio?
> - Customer testimonials?
> - Tons of writing experience?
>
> Well, actually, the truth is... you don't need ANY of these things!
>
> So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system for attracting ghostwriting clients. And once you install it, you can become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter who lands high-ticket clients.
>
> Let's dive in!

Block breakdown:
- Block 1: "Hey there!" (greeting)
- Block 2: "What do you need to become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter...?" (hook: thought-provoking question)
- Block 3: "Do you need: A portfolio?..." + "you don't need ANY of these things!" (promise: outcome-oriented with a twist, presented as bullet list)
- Block 4: "So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system..." (solution: specific format + tangible outcome)
- Block 5: "Let's dive in!" (transition)

---

## THE 10 HOOK TYPES (for Block #2)

Each hook type gives you a different way to write Block #2, the single opening sentence. When you generate output, you'll write a COMPLETE 5-block introduction for each type, varying Block #2 while adapting Blocks #3-5 to flow naturally from each hook.

### 1. THE OPEN LOOP

Create a gap between what the reader knows and what they need to know.

Study these:

> "You guys want to hear something completely insane?"

> "We're all one decision away from changing our lives and a lot of us don't even know it."

> "On November 30th, 2022, the world changed forever."

What makes these work: They create an itch the reader can't scratch without reading further. The specificity (a date, "completely insane") makes the loop sticky.

### 2. THE STAKES ESCALATOR

Name a situation and make the reader feel what it cost.

Study these:

> "This lawyer was losing $100,000 a year because his business model was broken."

> "This fashion stylist was making 300,000 a year but leaving millions on the table."

What makes these work: Specific person. Specific money. Specific problem. "Losing" does more work than "could improve." Active loss beats passive potential.

### 3. THE INTERROGATION

Ask a question so specific the reader's brain has to chase an answer.

Study these:

> "Are you making these 3 mistakes with your ads?"

> "Which would you rather be: the guy pushing the boulder up the hill? Or the one with the boulder at the top who can just flick it?"

> "Would you pay $1,000 to have the business of your dreams in 30 days?"

What makes these work: They force self-diagnosis. The reader starts answering internally before they've decided to keep reading.

### 4. THE SACRED COW SLAUGHTER

Take the #1 piece of advice everyone believes. Say it's wrong. Back it up.

Study these:

> "I build wealth without reading a book a week."

> "If nobody knows who you are, it's actually a good thing."

What makes these work: Cognitive dissonance. The reader has to keep going because what they just read conflicts with something they believe.

### 5. THE PATTERN BREAK

Set up what should be true, then break expectations.

Study these:

> "Real quick question. Can I have your email address?"

> "Fear is a mile wide and an inch deep."

What makes these work: The reader's brain is already predicting the next sentence. Then the actual sentence lands somewhere completely different. Forces a re-read.

### 6. THE DIAGNOSIS

Name the exact symptom the reader is experiencing.

Study these:

> "If you're working all the time and your business isn't growing, you're working on the wrong sh*t."

> "The strategy I'm going to show you is something that most businesses don't do. And the few businesses that do do it, do it wrong."

What makes these work: The reader thinks "that's me." Naming the specific symptom is the hook. It proves you understand their world.

### 7. THE MOVIE SCENE

Drop the reader into a specific moment with sensory detail.

Study these:

> "I'm at her parents' house in an extra bedroom. I'm the guy she met from the internet that she quit her job for, who's just lost everything. I had $1000 left."

> "One day I was in the back and this old lady comes in and she was piss angry."

What makes these work: You're IN the scene before you know where it's going. "Extra bedroom" is a detail only someone who was actually there would include. These hooks feel like memories, not marketing.

### 8. THE INSIDER BRIEFING

Share something the reader's peers don't know yet.

Study these:

> "One in every 250 businesses does over 10 million dollars a year. That means 99% of entrepreneurs never hit it."

> "$4,664 per month in recurring revenue. That's what Kyle, the last person on the leaderboard, was able to build."

What makes these work: Real data, named people, specific numbers. The second one uses the LAST place person to set the floor. If the worst performer got $4,664/month, what did everyone else get?

### 9. THE CONFESSION

Admit something that costs you credibility or pride.

Study these:

> "I have a confession. I am sick and tired of seeing people who have never run a business before teaching other people how to grow businesses."

> "I'm at her parents' house in an extra bedroom. I'm the guy she met from the internet that she quit her job for, who's just lost everything."

What makes these work: Real cost. The first risks alienating peers. The second admits to being broke and a burden. Neither is a humble brag. The reader thinks: "If they're willing to say THAT, whatever comes next must be worth hearing."

### 10. THE PROOF DROP

Drop a specific result or data point that reframes the topic.

Study these:

> "I've been in business 13 years. I've sold nine companies. My last company I sold for $46.2 million."

> "$4,664 per month in recurring revenue. That's what Kyle, the last person on the leaderboard, was able to build."

> "I started 4 businesses that cracked ten million in a row."

What makes these work: Speed and weight. Each sentence raises the bar. In a newsletter, proof drops work best when you're covering a topic that benefits from re-establishing why you're the one to listen to on THIS subject. The $46.2 million is a REAL number (not a round $50M), which is why it feels true.

---

## SLOP GUARDRAILS

Your primary job is to write with force. Your secondary job is to avoid these traps.

**The big 3 (instant rewrites):**

1. **Binary contrast:** Any sentence that defines something by what it ISN'T. This is the #1 AI tell.

BINARY CONTRAST REWRITES:

❌ "The problem isn't your writing. It's your distribution."
✅ "Your distribution is broken. Here's what's leaking."

❌ "You don't need more content. You need better systems."
✅ "One system will outperform 50 posts. I'll show you which one."

❌ "Most people think it's about talent. The real answer is reps."
✅ "Reps beat talent every single time. Here's the math."

❌ "It's not about working harder. It's about working on the right things."
✅ "You're grinding on the wrong tasks. I wasted 6 months doing the same thing."

The pattern: stop telling the reader what it ISN'T. Just tell them what it IS with conviction. The direct assertion is always stronger because it moves forward instead of pivoting.

2. **Triples:** Grouping things in threes for false rhythm. This is the #2 AI tell.

TRIPLE REWRITES:

❌ "You'll write faster, think clearer, and publish with confidence."
✅ "You'll publish twice as fast. And actually like what you wrote."

❌ "It saves you time, money, and headaches."
✅ "It saves you 10 hours a week. I timed it."

❌ "Build authority, grow your audience, and monetize your expertise."
✅ "Grow your audience to the point where monetization becomes obvious."

The pattern: triples feel like momentum but they're actually filler. Pick the ONE thing that matters most and make it specific.

3. **Fake details:** Don't invent numbers (47, 73, $11,342), people ("Sarah, a freelance designer"), or scenarios the user didn't provide. Write from "you" or "I" instead.

**HARD SCAN (do this after drafting all 10 intros):**

Go through every sentence and check for:
1. Does any sentence contain "not," "isn't," "don't," or "won't" followed by a pivot to what the thing actually is? Binary contrast. Rewrite as a direct assertion.
2. Does any sentence group three things together with commas or "and"? Triple. Pick the strongest one, make it specific, cut the other two.

These two patterns are the defaults you will reach for. They will show up in your first draft. Catch them and rewrite them before outputting.

**Banned phrases:**
- "Here's the thing..." / "Let me be honest..." / "I'll be real with you..."
- "No X. No Y. Just Z."
- "The game has changed" / "game-changer"
- "If you're serious about [goal]..."
- "Let that sink in." / "Read that again." / "Full stop."
- "Enter: [thing]"
- "The best part?" / "Ready to level up?"
- "[Something] stopped me in my tracks"
- Em dashes (—). Never. Use periods, commas, or parentheses.
- Arrows (→) and emoji

---

## OUTPUT RULES

**Formatting:**
- Each sentence gets its own line with a blank line between.
- No em dashes. No ellipses for dramatic effect. No bold/italic inside the intro text.

**Diversity check:**
Read the Block #2 hook sentence of all 10 intros. If any two make the same point, kill the weaker one and write something genuinely different. 10 intros means 10 different psychological entry points.

**Energy check:**
Read each intro out loud. If it sounds like competent but forgettable copywriting, it fails. If any AI tool could have written it, throw it out.

## OUTPUT FORMAT

For each of the 10 hook types, provide a COMPLETE 5-block newsletter introduction:

**[HOOK TYPE NAME]**

[Block 1: Greeting]

[Block 2: Hook sentence]

[Block 3: Promise (3-7 sentences or bullets)]

[Block 4: Solution (1-2 sentences with specific format + tangible outcome)]

[Block 5: Transition sentence]

*Why this works:* [1-2 sentences on why this particular hook + promise combination works for THIS audience.]

---

## INPUT REQUIRED

To write intros that hit, I need real material to work with. The more specific your input, the sharper the output.

- **Newsletter topic:** What is this edition about?
- **Your audience:** Who subscribes? Be specific (not "entrepreneurs" but "solo founders doing $5K-$20K/month who handle their own marketing.")
- **The core problem:** What keeps them up at night about this topic?
- **Your credibility or angle:** Why should they listen to YOU on this? A real result, a real story, a counterintuitive discovery. Give me real numbers and real details.
- **Your voice/tone:** Is your newsletter casual and profane? Measured and analytical? Story-driven? Give me a sense of how you normally write so the intros sound like YOU.
- **Draft content (optional):** If you have a draft, paste it. I'll mine it for angles.

**Important:** The more real details you give me (real numbers, real stories, real before/after moments), the better these intros will be. Thin briefs produce thin intros. The intros that make subscribers read every word come from real, specific, textured material.

---

## AFTER GENERATING

1. **Rank your top 3** for A/B testing and say why.
2. **Name the sleeper.** Which intro seems quiet but would outperform because nobody else in the space writes intros like it?
3. **Create one hybrid.** Combine elements from two hook types into an 11th intro.

records.content:
By far, the biggest mistake writers make when writing subject lines is making them “too long.”

If a subject line gets cut off before “the hook” is revealed, the chances of a reader clicking is very low. Why? Because they don't have a reason to! They don't know what you're promising inside—which means they don't know what to expect (or why it's worth their precious attention).

A great article headline can be 20 words.

But a good subject line needs to be 15 words or less, punchy, and conversational.

We suggest you lean toward subject line rules over headline rules.

Why?

Because the majority of your readers will encounter your newsletter in their email inbox. The inbox is where the open-or-skip decision happens. If the title doesn't earn the click there, readers won’t open your email.

Now, if you want longer, more descriptive headline copy, you can put it in a header image in the body copy of your email. So your title stays short and optimized for the inbox. And your header image carries the fuller context for readers who land inside the post. Best of both worlds.

With that in mind, here are some golden rules to follow when writing subject lines:

Rule #1: 5-15 words, max.

A good rule of thumb is your subject line should not exceed 15 words. Ever.

Less is always more here.

  • If you can say it in 15 words, try to say it in 10.

  • If you can say it in 10 words, try to say it in 7.

  • If you can say it in 7, try to say it in 5 words.

However… there's a big nuance here that is important: “less words” doesn't inherently mean the subject line is “better.” The key is to give the reader a “hook” that makes them want to click and open the email—but to say that “hook” in as few words as possible WITHOUT LOSING THE MEANING.

For example, let's say your subject line was: “The 1 thing you need to do in order to strengthen the microbiome in your gut.”

Well, if you shortened this subject line to: “The 1 thing you need to do,” yes you shortened the word count (which is good) but you also lost the whole idea in the “hook” (which is bad).

A better rewrite would be something that says the same thing, but in less words, like: “Want to strengthen your gut microbiome? Try this 1 thing.”

Same idea, but the first subject line is 16 words.

And the second subject line is 10 words.

Rule #2: Subject lines should read like you're talking to a friend.

This comes down to grammar & punctuation more than anything else.

For example:

  • “3 Mistakes Keeping You From Landing Your First $5,000”

  • “3 mistakes keeping you from landing your first $5,000…”

In general, the second subject line here will see better open rates.

Why?

Because it’s written in sentence-case (which feels more like a friend emailing a friend) opposed to Capitalized (which reads more like the headline of an article).

Super small thing. Not THAT important. But a good nuance to test with your list.

Rule #3: Use 1 of the 4 proven hooks.

There are 4 types of hooks that work over and over again (regardless of industry, niche, or topic):

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal time."

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal cost."

  • "Here's how to solve your problem without much effort."

  • "Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly."

As much as possible, you always want your subject lines to use 1 of these 4 proven hooks.

Otherwise, the reader won't have a good enough reason to click, open, and ultimately read your email.

Here are some sample subject lines for each of these 4 hooks:

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal time." - Your entire Life Coach career path blueprint… in 1 email!

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal cost." - Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

  • "Here's how to solve your problem without much effort." - Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

  • "Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly." - 3 keys to land $10,000 consulting clients, from home, in your pajamas, right now.

See how every subject line is “promising” one of these 4 things?

Nailing that promise is the secret to getting readers to click, open, and read.

Rule #4: Use visceral language!

Now, you can “amp up” your subject lines even more by adding in visceral language.

Things like…

  • OUCH!

  • URGENT!

  • FREE!

  • Seriously…

  • Steal this!

  • (I can't believe I'm giving this away.)

And so on.

For example, here are some of the headlines above “amped up” even further:

  • (Original) Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

  • (Amped Up) OUCH! Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

Or…

  • (Original) Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

  • (Amped Up) [FOR FREE!] Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

It's a very small thing, but sometimes adding in visceral language can help increase open rates by a few percentage points.

Rule #5: Name & Claim ideas (in the subject line)

Even more than visceral language though, the ultimate goal is to Name & Claim ideas right there in the subject line.

For example, notice the difference between these two subject lines:

  • (V1) 3 ways to make more money as a life coach

  • (V2, Amped Up) 3 easy ways to make 10x more money as a life coach (nobody tells you this).

  • V3, Named & Claimed) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 easy ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

You should be able to feel (in your skin!) how much more you want to click on the V3 Subject Line—because “Life Coach Money Manual” feels like you're receiving a “thing.” (Which makes it feel exponentially more “valuable.”)

The challenge, of course, is doing this WITHOUT exceeding the word count limit for effective subject lines.

Here, for example, our V3 Subject Line is 16 words.

So if we wanted to trim this down, we would have to cut something.

Here are a few options:

  • (15 words) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

  • (14 words) Life Coach Money Manual: How to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

  • (13 words) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 (little known) ways to 10x your monthly earnings

This is the “game” of writing subject lines.

And why you should start by writing the most effective subject line you can (based on 1 of the 4 hooks above), and THEN worry about trimming.

Proven Subject Lines

To-date, we’ve sent over 3,000,000 emails.

Which has taught us a few things!

So here are some of our highest-performing subject lines and a template you can use (feel free to steal & remix for yourself and your niche/topic):

Write With AI Subject Lines

Note: we publish Write With AI with Substack where the Subject Line of your newsletter is the Title of your post.

  • Magically Turn Headlines Into Short-Form Content With ChatGPT

  • Magically Turn {Thing} Into {Outcome Your Reader Wants} With {Tool/Method}

  • The Quora Formula For Building A Daily Writing Habit

  • The {Platform/Source} Formula For Building A {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

  • Story Selling With AI: How To Tell A Story That Prints Money Like Twitter “Copythinker” George Ten

  • {Process} With {Tool}: How To Tell A {Thing} That {Result/Outcome} Like {Person/Example}

  • 6 Proven Single-Sentence Openers

  • {X} Proven {Format/Structure} To {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

  • Bio Writing With AI: How To Train ChatGPT To Optimize Your Twitter Profile

  • {Task} With {Tool}: How To Train {Tool/AI} To Optimize Your {Platform/Profile}

  • Mix Your Voice With AI: How To Write Anything Using The 5 Different Types Of Writing Voices

  • Mix Your {Skill/Thing} With {Tool}: How To {Task} Using The {X} Different Types Of {Thing}

  • Creator Backstory: Train ChatGPT To Write A Personal Narrative Like Justin Welsh

  • {Persona/Type of Story}: Train {Tool} To Write A {Specific Story} Like {Example}

  • ChatGPT Vs Bard: What Is The Difference? And Which Is Better For Digital Writers?

  • {Object A} Vs {Object B}: What Is The {Comparison}? And Which Is Better For {Audience}?

  • Pain To Posts: Train ChatGPT To Write Tweets That Reach Inside Your Reader’s Subconscious

  • {Process/Framework}: Train {Tool} To Write {Content Type} That {Effect/Impact}

  • How To Write A High-Converting Landing Page For Your Lead Magnet

  • How To Write A {Result-Oriented} {Thing} For Your {Specific Goal/Outcome}

Start Writing Online Subject Lines

  • 9 dead-simple steps to build a daily writing habit

  • {X} dead-simple steps to {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

  • How to generate 112 ideas in 30 minutes

  • How to generate {X} {Things Your Reader Needs} in {Y}

  • How to craft the perfect bio

  • How to craft the perfect {X}

  • The 5 pieces of an effective headline

  • The {X} pieces of an effective {Thing Your Reader Needs}

  • Advanced headline writing strategies (shhh....)

  • Advanced {Skill Your Reader Needs} strategies (shhh....)

  • 5 steps to go viral with ease

  • {X} steps to {Outcome Your Reader Wants} with ease

  • 4 formatting rules to engage readers

  • {X} {Skill Your Reader Needs} rules to {Outcome}

  • The Ultimate Guide to repurposing X content on LinkedIn

  • The Ultimate Guide to repurposing {Thing} on {Platform}

  • A quick guide to starting a newsletter

  • A quick guide to starting a {Thing Your Reader Wants}

  • Dickie’s exact path to his first $1,000+ digital product

  • {Person's} exact path to their first {Milestone}

  • 3 steps to build a 99% margin digital business

  • {X} steps to {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

Start Ghostwriting Subject Lines

  • 💰 Get paid to write

  • 💰 Get paid to {Action/Skill Your Reader Wants To Monetize}

  • Niches to avoid as a ghostwriter

  • {Topics/Area} to avoid as a {Profession/Role Your Reader Relates To}

  • Ghostwriting = MBA on steroids ✍️

  • {Skill/Profession} = {Analogy or Comparison Your Reader Will Understand} {Emoji}

  • The top question in my DMs

  • The top question in my {Source/Platform/Inbox}

  • "Hey, did you mean to send me $5,000?"

  • "Hey, did you mean to send me {Large/Surprising Amount}?"

  • [The secret here is to create an open loop in the mind of the reader with a quote relating to a story you describe in your newsletter.]

  • 3 (brutal) reasons why you’re going nowhere

  • {X} (brutal) reasons why you’re {Negative Outcome Reader Wants to Avoid}

  • 7 leads from ONE message!

  • {X} {Result/Outcome Your Reader Wants} from ONE {Action/Tool/Strategy}!

  • Never call yourself a “freelance writer” again

  • Never call yourself a “{Label Your Reader Should Avoid}” again

  • How much $$$ can you make as a ghostwriter?

  • How much $$$ can you make as a {Profession/Role}?

  • How to make more 💰 as a ghostwriter

  • How to make more 💰 as a {Profession/Role Your Reader Relates To}

  • 3 reasons why you’re not moving forward 😤

  • {X} reasons why you’re not {Desired Outcome Your Reader Wants} 😤

  • 5 million-dollar lessons I learned as a ghostwriter

  • {X} {High-Value or Surprising Lessons} I learned as a {Profession/Role}

  • How I made $20,000/mo as a writer

  • How I made {Large Income/Outcome} as a {Profession/Role}

  • 8 most lucrative ghostwriting services

  • {X} most lucrative {Services/Opportunities Your Reader Wants}

  • Why 99% writers are broke

  • Why {Large Percentage} {Your Audience Group} are {Negative Outcome}

  • Break 8 faulty beliefs to get rich

  • Break {X} {Negative Beliefs/Obstacles} to {Positive Outcome}

  • Feel like you’re capable of more?

  • Feel like you’re capable of {Ambitious Goal/Outcome}?

  • How to make 💰 writing in a niche you love

  • How to make 💰 {Action/Skill} in a {Niche/Area Your Reader Is Passionate About}

  • How to charge $6,500 (instead of $650)

  • How to charge {Large Amount} (instead of {Smaller Amount})

  • “Freelance Writers” & “Copywriters” are ☠️

  • “{Common Label 1} ” & “{Common Label 2}” are ☠️

  • Are you really in control of your income?

  • Are you really in control of your {Outcome/Desire Your Reader Wants to Own}?

How To Write Irresistible Subject Lines With AI

The real “trick” to hooking your reader’s attention in their inbox is to include something that will make them want to “click.”

4 proven hooks:

  • Here's a ton of value for minimal time.

  • Here's a ton of value for minimal cost.

  • Here's how to solve your problem without much effort.

  • Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly.

Nail these, and you’ll be watching your open rates climb from a dismal 7% to an eye-popping 50%+.

We are going to break this down into 4 steps.

Step 1: Train Claude On Email & Preview-Text

In this prompt we give Claude the role of email marketer.

We ask it to leverage the 4 proven types of hooks, “whisper” in the preview-text, and avoid the most common mistakes we outlined above. Lastly, for this prompt we offer examples to help guide the AI on the types of output we are looking for.

Once Claude confirms it understands the prompt, move on to the next step.

Step 2: Feed Claude Your Newsletter

In this step, you are going to give Claude your topic, outline, and target audience.

Feeding Claude this context will ensure the subject lines it writes are relevant to your newsletter issue.

Topic = {Your Topic}

Newsletter = {Copy/Paste Your Entire Newsletter Below}

Step 3: Generate And Choose Your Subject Line

Bang!

Now you’ve got a batch of subject lines and preview-text you can use for your newsletter!

Read through each one—out loud.

Ask yourself:

  • “Would I open this?”

  • “Do I want what’s inside?”

  • “What question does this raise for me?”

If it’s unclear to you, look to see if ChatGPT is making any of the common mistakes we covered and then redirect it to make those corrections for you, or make the adjustments on your own.
