How to Position Your Newsletter So It Actually Grows (and Makes You Money)

In today's Start & Scale Your Newsletter Sprint Live Session with Cole, we did some live workshopping and talked about:

  • The "mega category" trap that quietly kills most newsletters before they get read — and why going smaller expands your audience instead of shrinking it.

  • What Cole means when he says credibility is just context (and why you already have it, even if you don't think you do).

  • The four naming conventions Cole uses to turn a general topic into a subtitle a target reader can't scroll past.

And more.

Cole’s Live Session Notes

Marketing

  • Digital marketing

  • Guerilla marketing

  • Email marketing

  • Meta ads marketing

  • Google adwords marketing

  • Direct response copywriting/marketing

Finance

  • how to get out of debt

  • getting grants and loans for college

  • how to buy a house

  • how to buy the right stocks

  • how to set yourself up for retirement

The Reason Niche Newsletters Win

Niching down is the most misunderstood concept in all of writing.

Most people believe:

  • The more niche I get, the less opportunities I will have.

  • The more broad I get, the more opportunities I will have.

It's actually the opposite.

  • The more niche you get, the easier it is for your target reader to discover you. Discovery → growth → tangential niches → more growth.

  • Parenting:

  • How to prepare for having your first child

  • How to help your 18 year old overcome a drug addiction

  • The more broad you get, the harder it is for your target reader to discover you. Slower growth → harder to tap tangential niches.

This is the #1 reason most newsletters fail—before the first issue is even published.

Example: Write With AI

  • #1 paid education newsletter on Substack.

  • We "lead" with writing—but we attract: Writers, Creators, Solopreneurs, Entrepreneurs, VPs & Execs, Consultants, Coaches, Agencies.

When you niche down, you create a Niche Constellation.

  • Your niche is way bigger than you realize. Any niche is bigger than you can deliver on.

  • Your niche isn't the end—it's the beginning. It's the nucleus, the "tip of the spear."

  • Specificity makes people conclude: "If you specialize in THAT… you could probably also help me with THIS."

The more specific your newsletter niche, the more OTHER niches you can tap into.

Mistakes To Avoid When Naming Your Newsletter

WARNING: You'll see "outliers" who make these mistakes and still succeed. They have a huge existing audience, a ton of money, or something else working. Not good models to follow.

Mistake #1: Naming your newsletter after yourself.

  • "The Tony Johnson Newsletter"

  • Your TAM becomes limited to the number of people who know you.

  • Which TAM is bigger: "Lenny's Newsletter" or "The At-Home Stretching Newsletter"?

  • Name your newsletter after the reader's CATEGORY OF INTEREST—not yourself.

Mistake #2: Going Broad (instead of Going Niche)

  • Health & Wellness, Marketing, Finance, Crypto = "umbrella categories," not niches.

  • "Marketing" alone contains: Digital, Print, Meta Ads, YouTube Ads, Email, SMS, Automation…

  • Going Broad says: "I'm an expert in 100+ niches at once." Nobody believes that.

  • Pick ONE niche inside the umbrella.

Mistake #3: Trying to serve multiple different industries at once.

  • Do you follow anyone for health AND finance AND relationships AND stock picks? No.

  • 99.9% of the time, you follow 1 person for 1 specific thing.

Mistake #4: Picking a "clever" name instead of a clear, niche category.

  • "The Mile." "Cooky Foodie Club." "Slick Skater." What are these about?

  • Nobody blocks 15 minutes to decode your newsletter. They jump back to TikTok.

  • Your name should CLEARLY name the niche you're servicing.

Newsletter Naming Principles

The name of your newsletter is not about "building a brand."

If you want to become known for a niche you own, name your newsletter the niche you serve.

Stress test: imagine a competitor named their newsletter your niche exactly. Upset? Threatened? Good—don't let that happen.

The Alex Hormozi "Value Equation"

"Value" is a bundled term. It really means 1 of 4 things (or some combination):

  • Dream Outcome: Help the person achieve their goal

  • Perceived Likelihood of Achievement: Guarantee the person achieves it

  • Time Delay: Help them achieve it in less time

  • Effort & Sacrifice: Help them achieve it easier (without pain)

The reader does not care about your newsletter. They only care about whether you provide them value.

So your name should do 2 things:

  • Clearly state the niche (what industry, and/or who specifically you serve)

  • Clearly state how you provide value (which of the 4 above)

A newsletter is "a book that never ends."

Your Main Title & Subtitle need to communicate 3 things:

  • Your Niche: What industry do you serve (and, if you can, who "specifically")?

  • Your Value: Which of the value equation are you providing?

  • Your Repeatable, Tangible Value: What "tangibly" are you giving the reader?

2 questions to ask before naming anything:

  1. "Is my topic infinitely repeatable?" (Stock tips: yes, daily. Self-publishing trends: maybe twice a year.)

  2. "What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?" Think in objects: prompts, checklists, blueprints, recipes, templates.

Nobody wants to learn. Everyone wants to collect objects that solve a problem faster, easier, more reliably.

Tangible, Repeatable Asset categories (train your brain to think in these):

  • Templates & Fill-in-the-Blank Tools — email, contract, proposal, script, outreach templates

  • Checklists & Cheat Sheets — pre-launch, audit, routine, "before you hit publish"

  • Frameworks & Systems — decision-making, pricing, hiring, positioning

  • Recipes & Formulas — headline formulas, workout programming, financial formulas

  • Swipe Files & Examples — headline/ad/email swipes, case study breakdowns, teardowns

  • Logs & Trackers — habit trackers, financial trackers, content calendars

  • Scripts & Prompts — sales scripts, objection-handling, AI prompts

  • Guides & Playbooks — step-by-step guides, launch playbooks, glossaries

  • Numbers, Data & Research — benchmarks, salary data, survey results, ROI calculators

  • Curated Collections & Lists — tool stacks, resource libraries, "the shortlist"

Write With AI in one breath: "Everyone wants to learn AI. Our niche is writing. Prompts are infinitely repeatable."

The 4 Category Newsletter Naming Conventions

Naming Convention #1: Niche + Dream Outcome

Make a list of outcomes your target reader cares about.

Example niche: Airbnb Rentals. Outcomes: maximize occupancy, increase nightly rate, get 5-star reviews, automate guest communication, scale to multiple properties…

Build it:

  • Your Niche: Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)

  • Your Value: Pick an outcome ("Automate guest communication")

  • Your Repeatable, Tangible Value: Automations!

Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.

"But Cole… what if the target reader in my niche has lots of different outcomes?!"

Naming Convention #2: Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement

What can you give them to nearly-guarantee success? (Think: SAT Prep Questions & Answers. Parents aren't buying tutoring hours—they're buying Increased Likelihood of Achievement.)

2 components that increase Perceived Likelihood of Achievement:

  1. Templates: Anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success.

  2. Credibility: Templates from someone who has already achieved the thing.

3 credibility options:

  • Your Own Credibility: "I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too."

  • Your Student/Customer's Credibility: "It worked for me, then it worked for them. Now you."

  • Someone Else's Credibility: "I researched what worked for this credible person. Here it is."

Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations from the largest family-owned rental property group in Chicago (800 properties & counting!).

Naming Convention #3: Niche + Time Delay

  • Nobody wants 6-pack abs, slow. Everyone wants 6-pack abs, fast.

  • Nobody wants to get rich slow. Everyone wants to get rich quick.

  • Nobody wants 4 years of learning. Everyone wants the skill in a weekend.

Ask: what problem/outcome can you deliver in a fraction of the "normal time"?

Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations that take 1 hour to build and save you 10-100 hours per month.

Naming Convention #4: Niche + Effort & Sacrifice

  • Everyone wants stock market gains. They just don't want to risk losing what they have.

  • Everyone wants a new skill. They just don't want hours of grueling daily practice.

Between your reader and their goal is a quagmire of effort & sacrifice. Your newsletter is the bridge.

Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automation templates to streamline your rental business, pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed).

"But Cole… can my newsletter combine multiple naming conventions?"

Claim Your Category: The Category Claim Check

A repeatable check to run on any name you come up with today.

Step 1: Scout the competition.

  • Search your niche on Substack, Beehiiv, and Google ("your niche + newsletter").

  • List the 3-5 newsletters closest to yours.

  • Don't skip this—you can't differentiate from competition you've never looked at.

Step 2: Run the swap test.

  • Could you swap your newsletter's name with any of theirs and have nobody notice?

  • If yes, neither name is category-defining.

  • A category-defining name should ONLY make sense for your exact niche and your exact reader.

Step 3: Claim the gap.

  • Look at what nobody on your list clearly owns—a specific reader, a specific outcome, a specific way of getting there.

  • Put THAT in your name. That unclaimed gap is your category.

Differentiation = being the only obvious choice for one specific reader.

When you own the niche, the broader industry treats you as the thought leader.

  • You don't become a thought leader by writing about the whole industry.

  • You become the undisputed king of one corner—then your authority radiates outward, niche by niche.

  • Your name does that thought-leadership work every day, before anyone reads a word.

Newsletter Naming Cheat Sheet

  • Main Title = Write With AI

  • Subtitle = The leading paid newsletter for ChatGPT & Claude prompts, and how to turn AI platforms into your own personal Digital Writing Assistant.

Step 1: Is this "a book that never ends?"

  • Is my topic infinitely repeatable?

  • What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?

Step 2: Name it something "clear," "valuable," and "tangibly repeatable."

  • Clear = the niche is literally in the name. Not open to interpretation.

  • Valuable = you deliver 1+ of: Dream Outcome / Likelihood of Achievement / Time Delay / Effort & Sacrifice.

  • Tangibly Repeatable = you're giving assets, not just information.

Step 3: Can you add some sort of credibility?

  • Your own / your student's / someone else's.

Step 4: Can you add copywriting tactics?

Tactic #1: A "Don't Worry" Whisper — answer the reader's biggest objection in a parenthetical at the end of the subtitle.

  • …handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!)

Tactic #2: "More" problems-solved / outcomes-unlocked — when in doubt, give the reader "more."

  • [Very Weak] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations

  • [Better] …automations to handle check-ins

  • [Even Better] …to handle check-ins and answer guest questions

  • [The Best] …to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7

  • [Pro-Grade] …to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!)

Tactic #3: Numbers & objective measures for success.

  • Money saved/made. Hours saved. Years of experience. Clients/students/readers helped.

"But Cole… can I have a clever Main Title but a very clear Subtitle?"

"But Cole… do I need to state the publishing cadence in the Main Title or Subtitle?"

Preferred structure:

  • Main Title = Niche + Topic. Get the name of the niche in the main title.

  • Subtitle = Value Proposition + Tangible, Repeatable Assets. HOW you'll help + WHAT you'll give.

Assignment

I want you to do 3 specific things before Day 2:

  1. Pick your niche. One. Clearly stated.

  2. Write your Main Title & Subtitle. Main Title = Niche + Topic (painfully obvious). Subtitle = Value Proposition + Tangible, Repeatable Assets.

  3. Run the Category Claim Check. Scout 3-5 competitors, run the swap test, confirm you're claiming an unowned gap.

Being clear always beats being clever—no matter how "clever" it is.

Stuck? Use the Newsletter Name Generator prompt below to generate ideas, then pick your favorite.

Bring your niche, Main Title, and Subtitle to tomorrow's session—we'll be setting up publications live on the call.

[BONUS] Newsletter Name Generator

Copy/paste this prompt into your preferred AI model (we recommend Claude, but it works across ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.).

I am going to train you on a handful of newsletter naming conventions. These are the frameworks I use to come up with category-defining newsletter names, specifically broken out as Main Titles & Subtitles.

I would like you to learn and use these naming conventions, specifically. Then, when you're ready, I will give you my niche/topic and I'd like you to generate 5 potential newsletter names (Main Title & Subtitle) organized by each naming convention here. So that means 5 different newsletter names inside of each newsletter naming convention (so 20 total).

# 4 Category Newsletter Naming Conventions

Ready to combine all these pieces together to give your newsletter a category-defining name?

### Naming Convention #1: Niche + Dream Outcome

The first naming convention for your category-defining newsletter is to combine the niche you want to serve with a dream outcome associated with that niche.

Start by making a list of outcomes your target reader cares about.

For example, let's take the Airbnb Rental niche.

Here are 10 Outcomes people with Airbnb Rentals care about:

- **Maximize occupancy rate** — Keep calendars booked as consistently as possible year-round
- **Increase nightly rate** — Charge more per night without losing bookings
- **Generate passive income** — Earn revenue with minimal day-to-day involvement
- **Get 5-star reviews** — Build a reputation that drives more bookings algorithmically
- **Reduce vacancy gaps** — Fill last-minute cancellations and shoulder-season slow periods
- **Lower operating costs** — Cut cleaning, maintenance, and supply expenses without hurting guest experience
- **Automate guest communication** — Handle check-ins, questions, and issues without being on-call 24/7
- **Stand out in search results** — Rank higher on the Airbnb platform to get more visibility
- **Protect the property** — Avoid damage, bad guests, and liability headaches
- **Scale to multiple properties** — Turn one successful rental into a portfolio

Great!

Now, to "name" your newsletter, remember the 3 Pieces you want to hit:

- **Your Niche:** What industry do you serve (and, if you can, who "specifically")?
- **Your Value:** Which 1 (or multiple) of the above "value equation" are you providing?
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** What "tangibly" are you giving the reader?

So, in this example, here's what this might look like:

- **Your Niche:** Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)
- **Your Value:** Pick an outcome from the list above (let's say: "Automate guest communication")
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** With this outcome in mind, what can we repeat? Automations!

(The wheels should be spinning in your head, and even just hearing these bullet points you should be able to "imagine" the newsletter, and immediately understand why it's valuable to its target reader. Good! That means the framework is working!)

So, what could the final newsletter name (Main Title & Subtitle) be?

How about…

**Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.**

Hey! That's pretty good!

### "But Cole?! What if the target reader in my niche has lots of different outcomes?!"

Of course they do.

But, two things:

**First, just because you "lead" with solving 1 outcome doesn't mean you can't speak to other outcomes in your content.** You absolutely can. You just can't "lead" with 10 outcomes—because if you say everything is a priority then nothing is a priority. So Positioning 101 is you lead with ONE clearly stated outcome, which makes it easier to embed yourself into people's minds (making it easier for them to understand how you can help them). But then you can speak to lots of other relevant outcomes in the content itself.

**Second, if you're struggling to choose which outcome to lead with, here's the secret: pick the one most relevant to financial upside or downside.** For example, let's pretend I'm serving the "Airbnb Rental" niche. Which one of these outcomes is more valuable (aka: has higher perceived value)?

- Outcome A: "I want to know how to hire cleaning companies to make my Airbnbs look flawless after a guest leaves."
- Outcome B: "I want to know how to make my rental properties more profitable."

Both of these outcomes are valuable in some way. But it should be obvious that Outcome B is "more valuable" because it's more directly correlated to making more money. And when in doubt, EVERYONE will ALWAYS prioritize giving their attention to things that help them either a) make more money, or b) stop wasting/losing money.

*(*Do not misconstrue what I'm saying, please. I am not saying, "You have to have a financial newsletter giving away stock tips helping people get rich quick or they won't subscribe." That's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is, if you're stuck, or debating between two different outcomes, go with the one the reader can more easily rationalize being "worth their time"—aka: the one where there is some sort of financial upside or downside.)*

### Naming Convention #2: Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement

Next, what is something your target reader is struggling with—and what "tangible, repeatable" asset can you give them to nearly-guarantee their problem will be solved/their goal will be achieved?

Here's an easy example: **SAT Prep Questions & Answers**

Pretend you're 17 years old again. You're a junior in high school. The SAT is around the corner. Your parents are stressing you out—because if you don't do well on the SAT then you won't get into a good school, and if you don't get into a good school you won't get a good job when you graduate, and if you don't get a good job when you graduate then you're destined for failure. (Sound familiar?)

In the above mental state, your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (aka: "doing well on the SAT") is probably low. You're very worried about how you're going to perform.

…but what if someone gave you the answers ahead of time?

…what if you were able to essentially memorize all of the questions before the exam?

Your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement would go up! Dramatically!

This is fundamentally why parents spend so much money on SAT Prep programs & resources for their kids. They aren't buying "tutoring hours" or "books" or "materials." **What they're really buying is Increased Likelihood of Achievement.** "If I buy this for my child, I believe my child's SAT score will probably go up."

### So, what are things that increase a person's Perceived Likelihood of Achievement?

There's 2 big components here:

1. **Templates:** Anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success.
2. **Credibility:** Templates (and/or anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success) *from someone who has already achieved the thing you're trying to achieve.*

That's really the big question to ask yourself. In this niche, what's something you can Tangibly, Repeatedly give the person that they can copy/paste to replicate success? And, how can you signal to them this "template" has successfully been used by you (or someone else) to solve the problem or achieve the outcome your target reader desires for themselves.

And if you're unsure about how to approach the credibility component here, you have 3 options:

- **Your Own Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too."
- **Your Student/Customer's Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too."
- **Someone Else's Credibility:** "I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too."

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

What might this Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement newsletter Main Title & Subtitle look like?

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations from the largest family-owned rental property group in Chicago (800 properties & counting!).**

See how this naming convention leans on credibility—instead of speaking to the customer's dream outcome(s)?

### Naming Convention #3: Niche + Time Delay

The next naming convention is to pair your niche with the removal of "time."

For example:

- Nobody wants 6-pack abs, slow. **Everyone wants 6-pack abs, fast.**
- Nobody wants to get rich slow. **Everyone wants to get rich quick.**
- Nobody wants to spend 4 years learning a new skill. **Everyone wants to learn the skill in a weekend.**
- Nobody wants to wait a lifetime to fall in love. **Everyone wants to fall in love ASAP.**

Pick any category you want, and it should be obvious why the target consumer in that category would want either a problem solved or an outcome achieved FASTER.

So:

- What's a problem your target reader has and/or what's an outcome they desire?
- And how can you help them solve that problem and/or achieve that outcome in a fraction of the "normal time?"

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations that take 1 hour to build and save you 10-100 hours per month.**

There we go!

### Naming Convention #4: Niche + Effort & Sacrifice

The next naming convention is leading with the amount of effort and/or a tangible obstacle you are going to help your target reader avoid.

For example:

- Everyone wants to make money in the stock market. **They just don't want to risk losing the money they have in the process.**
- Everyone wants to learn a new skill (piano, painting, a foreign language, etc.). **They just don't want to have to go through the grueling effort of practicing hours and hours each day.**
- Everyone wants to find their soul mate. **They just don't want to have to give up their established daily routine to go on a bunch of dates that lead nowhere.**

No matter what your target reader's goal is, between them and their goal is some quagmire of effort & sacrifice.

Which means the value of your newsletter is in being a bridge—a nice, sturdy, trusted bridge that can get them from where they are right now, over that murky quagmire, and onto the other side (their goal) in an easy, pain-free way.

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automation templates to streamline your rental business, pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed).**

See how we're "removing all of the effort & sacrifice" with this phrase? *"…pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed)."*

# (Bonus!) Newsletter Naming Cheat Sheet

When naming your newsletter, there are a suite of different "messages" you want to try to cram into your Main Title & Subtitle.

- **Main Title** = Write With AI
- **Subtitle** = The leading paid newsletter for ChatGPT & Claude prompts, and how to turn AI platforms into your own personal Digital Writing Assistant.

So, let's walk through the hierarchy of which "messages" you want to make sure are in your newsletter's name (Main Title & Subtitle).

### Step 1: Is this "a book that never ends?"

The best way to think about how to create a high-value newsletter is to pretend you're signing yourself up to write a book, on a topic, that never ends.

So before you give your newsletter a name, you first want to make sure the focus of your newsletter achieves 2 goals:

1. **"Is my topic infinitely repeatable?"** Some topics are far more repeatable than others. I'll give you two examples. The first is "stock tips." Are stock tips repeatable? Of course. Every day, there's a new hot company to buy (or sell). There's a reason financial newsletters are some of the most popular, and most lucrative, newsletter categories. Now compare that to "Self-Publishing Trends." Is that a repeatable topic? Well, yes… but is there some huge change happening in self-publishing every day? *No. Every week? No. Every month? Not usually. Every 6 months? Maybe. Every year? Maybe.* It might be a helpful topic, but it's not nearly as repeatable because the industry doesn't move as fast. This is a crucial variable to be aware of.
2. **"What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?"** Second, no matter what topic you choose, you want to go a step further and ask yourself what you can TANGIBLY give the reader. Think in objects. Prompts. Checklists. Blueprints. Recipes. Templates. All of these are "tangible objects." (*Pro Tip: I have now trained my brain to think this way, and whenever I see a new "tangible, digital thing" pop up, a little siren goes off in my head: LUCRATIVE OPPORTUNITY, THATAWAY!)

### Step 2: Name your newsletter something "clear," "valuable," and "tangibly repeatable."

Let's unbundle these terms.

- **"Clear" just means you are naming your niche in the name of the newsletter.** It's not open to interpretation. The reader knows exactly what niche you're in because the name of the niche is literally in the name of your newsletter.
- **"Valuable" just means you're delivering on 1 of 4 (or some combination) of things all readers/customers care about:**
    - **Dream Outcome:** Help the person achieve their goal
    - **Perceived Likelihood of Achievement:** Guarantee the person achieves it
    - **Time Delay:** Help them achieve it in less time
    - **Effort & Sacrifice:** Help them achieve it easier (without pain)
- **"Tangibly Repeatable" just means you aren't just giving the reader information.** What you're giving them are tangible assets that help them achieve their desired goal—faster, with a higher perceived likelihood of success, in less time, for less effort.

So, that's your checklist.

Those are the "messages" you're trying to communicate when naming your newsletter.

For example:

- **Your Niche:** Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)
- **Your Value:** Pick an outcome from the list above (let's say: "Automate guest communication")
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** With this outcome in mind, what can we repeat? Automations!

So, what might the name of our category-defining newsletter be?

**Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.**

### Step 3: Can you add some sort of credibility?

This isn't required, but if you have it… it's great!

- **Your Own Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too."
- **Your Student/Customer's Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too."
- **Someone Else's Credibility:** "I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too."

### Step 4: Can you add in any copywriting tactics to make your Main Title & Subtitle even more compelling?

There's really only a handful you need to memorize—because all the best headlines/newsletter names/book titles/etc. use them over and over again.

**Copywriting Tactic #1: A "Don't Worry" Whisper:**

What's your target reader's biggest objection? Speak to why that objection isn't a problem, or how you're going to help them solve it, inside a parenthetical at the end of your subtitle.

Sticking with our Airbnb example, maybe our target reader's biggest objection to using automations inside their Airbnb business is they don't consider themselves to be tech savvy.

Here's how you'd execute this tactic:

- *Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!).*

**Copywriting Tactic #2: "More" problems-solved and/or outcomes-unlocked.**

When in doubt, just give the reader "more."

For example, look at how much weaker this newsletter name is when we remove some of these additional items—and how much stronger it gets the "more" of them we add back in:

- *[Very Weak] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations*
- *[Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins*
- *[Even Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins and answer guest questions*
- *[The Best] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7*
- *[Pro-Grade] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!).*

This is the big secret to naming newsletters (and really any kind of digital product), is finding ways to speak to as many things the reader wants/cares about as possible.

**Copywriting Tactic #3: Numbers & objective measures for success.**

Anytime you can state a "number" or an objective measure for success, the perceived value of your newsletter goes up.

Numbers can be any of the following:

- **Money:** How much money will you help the reader save? How much money will you help the reader make? How much money have *you* made, doing this exact thing?
- **Hours:** How many hours will you help the reader save? How many hours have you saved? Or how many hours have you invested into doing this thing?
- **Years:** How many years have you been doing this? How many years of hard work will you save the reader from having to go through themselves?
- **Clients:** How many clients, or students, or customers (or readers, or listeners, or viewers) have you helped?
- Etc.

This is not a required piece in naming your newsletter. But if you CAN add in an objective number of some kind, it's always a nice addition that makes your newsletter's value proposition even more compelling.

~

Are you ready for my niche/topic?

Video Timestamps

  • 09:37 Substack: The Easiest Platform to Start On

  • 23:12 Beehive: The Media Business Platform

  • 30:00 Kit: The Engine for a Digital Product Business

  • 37:54 The Sideby-Side Decision Matrix

  • 40:20 Custom Domains vs. Subdomains & SEO

  • 46:04 The One Formatting Rule That Instantly Levels Up Your Newsletter

How to Pick the Right Newsletter Platform (Without Getting Stuck in Research Mode)

Date: 1/13/2026

In today's Sprint Live Session with Cole, we did some live workshopping and talked about:

  • Why the "perfect platform" debate is a form of procrastination — and the simple decision matrix that solves it in under 30 minutes.

  • How Substack's built-in community brings you subscribers other platforms make you fight for (and the math on whether that 10% cut is worth it).

  • The one formatting habit that instantly makes any newsletter look more professional — no matter where you send it from.

Cole’s Live Session Notes

The Newsletter Platform Trap

Your tech stack will NOT make your newsletter successful.

What will:

  • Your writing

  • Your consistency

  • Your positioning

  • Your offer stack

The tech just needs to not get in your way.

All three platforms are excellent.

There is no wrong answer—only a wrong match between platform and YOUR goal.

The real question

"What is my newsletter's #1 job for the next 12 months?"

Three honest answers:

  1. "I need an audience." Starting from zero. Priority = getting discovered.

  2. "I need a business engine." You have attention elsewhere. Job = convert it into sales.

  3. "I need subscription revenue." Readers pay you directly, month after month.

Hold your answer. We'll come back to it.

Substack: The Discovery Machine

Free publishing platform + social network of readers and writers.

Best at: growing from zero + paid subscriptions.

The superpower: it's a network

  • 40%+ of all new Substack subscriptions come through Recommendations

  • Lenny Rachitsky: 78% of his 800k+ subscribers came from recommendations

  • Notes, Restacks, leaderboards, Referrals = multiple layers of growth

  • You set it up once and it compounds forever

Pros

  • $0 to start, $0 forever (until you earn)

  • Best built-in discovery of any platform

  • Paid subscriptions in 2 clicks (connect Stripe, set a price, done)

  • Everything in one place: email, website, podcast, Chat

  • Dead simple—your only job is to write

Cons

  • 10% of paid revenue forever (~13-16% all-in with Stripe)

  • Limited automation (Drip Campaigns still in limited beta)

  • Weak segmentation and tagging

  • No custom CSS/HTML

  • You're renting the network (but you always own your list)

Bottom line

Best answer to "I need an audience." Great answer to "I need subscription revenue."

"But Cole… what if I pick wrong?"

Beehiiv: The Growth & Media Machine

Built by early Morning Brew employees.

Best at: aggressive growth tooling + monetizing through ads.

Substack gives you a network. Beehiiv gives you an arsenal:

  • Boosts — recommendations with money attached (earn or spend)

  • Ad Network — Beehiiv sells sponsorships FOR you (~15% cut, $1M+/month paid out)

  • Real referral program — Morning Brew-style, built in

  • Best-in-class analytics — source tracking, A/B testing, funnels

  • Real websites + SEO — your archive can rank on Google

Pros

  • Free up to 2,500 subscribers

  • 0% cut of paid subscriptions (on paid plans)

  • The best ad monetization in the game

  • Serious growth tooling

  • Scales into a media company

Cons

  • The good stuff costs money (Scale plan: $49/mo and up)

  • No true organic network—growth is something you operate, not something that happens to you

  • More complexity (built for operators)

  • Automation is good, not deep

Bottom line

Best answer for "I want to run a media business."

The middle path between Substack's simplicity and Kit's machinery.

Kit: The Creator Business Engine

Email-first operating system for creators.

Best at: ownership, automation, and selling things.

Full transparency: we use Kit alongside Substack in our own businesses.

  • Visual automations — build funnels once, they sell 24/7

  • Tags, segments, subscriber scoring — right message, right person

  • Landing pages, forms, lead magnets — unlimited, even free

  • Commerce built in — sell products directly (3.5% + 30¢)

  • Creator Network — recommendations, but a feature, not a social network

Pros

  • Free up to 10,000 subscribers—most generous free tier of the three

  • The deepest automation and segmentation, period

  • You own the whole pipeline—no algorithm between you and readers

  • 100+ integrations

  • Built to sell

Cons

  • Almost zero built-in discovery—YOU are the growth engine

  • Paid plans get real at scale (Creator from $33-39/mo, climbs with list)

  • No publication website to speak of

  • Steeper learning curve—week one can feel like homework

Bottom line

Best answer to "I need a business engine."

It assumes you bring the audience; it turns that audience into revenue.

"But Cole… I already have an audience on social. Doesn't that mean Kit automatically?"

Side-By-Side + The Decision Framework

Substack

Beehiiv

Kit

Best for

Audience growth + paid subs

Media business + ads

Funnels + selling products

Free tier

Cut of paid subscriptions

0% + Stripe (on paid plans)

0% on subs; 3.5% + 30¢ on products

Discovery

⭐⭐⭐ Recommendations, Notes, Restacks

⭐⭐ Boosts (paid), Ad Network, referrals

⭐ Creator Network

Automation

⭐ Welcome emails; Drip in beta

⭐⭐ Solid (paid plans)

⭐⭐⭐ Visual automations, tags, scoring

Monetization

Paid subs, founding tiers

The framework: choose based on your GOAL

  • "I need an audience." → Substack. The network sends you subscribers while you sleep. The right answer for most people in this Sprint. Unsure? Pick Substack.

  • "I need a business engine." → Kit. You don't need Substack's discovery because YOU are the discovery.

  • "I want a media business." → Beehiiv. CPMs, sponsorships, aggressive growth, multiple publications.

The fee edge case

  • Below ~$500/mo in sub revenue: Substack's 10% is cheaper than Beehiiv's $49/mo—and you get the network free.

  • Above ~$1,000/mo: you're paying Substack $100+/mo—enough to cover Beehiiv or Kit.

  • But: don't optimize the fee before you've earned the revenue. 10% of $0 is $0. Grow first. Optimize later.

The Hybrid Play (what we do)

  • Substack public-facing: discovery, community, paid subs

  • Kit behind the scenes: lead magnets, launches, automated sales sequences

  • This is a later problem. This week: ONE platform. Ship.

"But Cole… should I use a custom domain?"

"But Cole… can I make money on the free plans?"

Mistakes To Avoid

  1. Platform shopping as procrastination. 3 weeks of comparing = fear of publishing wearing a productivity costume.

  2. Choosing on features you won't use for a year. You have 40 subscribers. A/B test later.

  3. Optimizing fees before revenue exists. Don't leave the growth network to save 10% of nothing.

  4. Matching someone else's goal. Your favorite creator's business model isn't yours.

  5. Believing migration is impossible. You always own your list. Important decision, not irreversible.

  6. Signing up for two platforms "to test both." Two half-newsletters instead of one real one.

On switching later

  • Moves easily: subscriber list, post archive

  • Doesn't move: Substack network position, automations/tags, deliverability reputation

  • Switching costs are real but survivable. The worst move is stalling for a month.

Assignment

Deadline: before tomorrow's session.

  1. Answer the goal question in one sentence. "My newsletter's #1 job for the next 12 months is ______."

  2. Audience → Substack. The network sends you subscribers while you sleep. The right answer for most people in this Sprint. Unsure? Pick Substack.

  • Business Engine → Kit. You don't need Substack's discovery because YOU are the discovery.

  • Media Business → Beehiiv. CPMs, sponsorships, aggressive growth, multiple publications.

  1. Pick your platform. Run the framework. Unsure? Default to Substack. 15 minutes max.

  2. Create your account. Claim your name + URL, write your tagline, upload a photo, fill out your About.

  3. Configure your growth switch.

  • Substack: add 5-10 Recommendations + message 3 writers about mutual recs

  • Beehiiv: turn on recommendations widget + browse Boosts

  • Kit: join the Creator Network + build one landing page

  1. Buy your domain (don't connect it). $10-20. Five minutes.

Show up tomorrow with a live, configured newsletter—ready to write.

Tomorrow: Day 3 — Newsletter Writing Mastery. 3PM ET / Noon PT.

  • 06:38 Modular vs. Linear Writing (The Forest Analogy)

  • 27:36 The Listicle Magic Trick (Everything Is a List)

  • 30:44 Hooking the Reader: Avoiding Bad or Achieving Good

  • 34:30 Main Title vs. Subtitle: Working Within Word Count Constraints

  • 40:11 Chicken Scratch: Outlining Before You Write

  • 44:13 The 10 Magical Ways: Lists Within Lists

  • 46:25 Writing Rhythms & Visual Formatting

  • 49:42 Live Writing Demo: Section 5 Walkthrough

  • 58:51 Bonus: The AI Newsletter Prompt & Writing With AI

  • 1:01:16 Wrap Up & What's Coming on Day 4

How to Write Newsletters Faster (and Better) Using a Modular Framework

Date: 1/14/2026

In today's Start & Scale Your Newsletter Sprint session with Cole, we did some live workshopping and talked about:

  • Why writing linearly from top to bottom is the reason your drafts feel impossible — and the modular approach that changes everything.

  • The single most important decision to make before you write a single word (get this wrong and the whole piece falls apart).

  • The "10 Magical Ways" you can plug into any section to make your writing more valuable — plus the visual formatting trick that determines whether people actually read what you wrote.

Cole’s Live Session Notes

Writing Is Modular

Writing is like playing with Legos.

  • Writing is modular. You assemble pieces — you don't wait for the Muse.

  • Only 3 frameworks get you to 80-95% proficiency. Everything else is stylistic polish.

  • There is no "1 correct way" to write a newsletter. Every best practice has successful outliers.

  • The ONLY thing that matters: are your readers happy & receiving value?

70% of the newsletter game is formatting. Only 30% is the actual content.

  • Make it VISUALLY appealing

  • Make it VISUALLY organized

  • Make it VISUALLY easy to skim & read

  • Wall of text = nobody reads it. No matter how "good" the writing is.

Step 1: Irresistible Subject Lines

Your subject line is the North Star of your newsletter. It's the promise — curiosity + a reason to open.

Rule #1: 5-15 words, max.

  • Over half of emails are opened on mobile. Communicate the idea before it gets cut off.

  • Less is always more.

Rule #2: Read like you're talking to a friend.

  • Sentence-case, not Capitalized Case.

  • Write simply → reduce cognitive load. No stuffy, no lecturing.

Rule #3: Use 1 of the 4 proven hook frameworks.

  1. Here's a ton of value for minimal time.

  2. Here's a ton of value for minimal cost.

  3. Here's how to solve your problem without much effort.

  4. Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly.

(Live: real subject lines from our newsletters — spot which rules we're using.)

Rule #4: Use visceral language.

  • "OUCH!" "Urgent!" "Steal this!" + powerful verbs and nouns.

  • Power words: Free, Binge, Harsh, Waste, Hidden, Rapid, Terrible, Unique, Greatest, Dreadful, Strongest, Surprising, Dead simple, Inconvenient, Little-known

Rule #5: Name & Claim ideas (in the subject line).

  • E.g. "Life Coach Money Manual: 3 easy ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)"

  • Naming a "thing" makes it feel exponentially more valuable.

  • The challenge: do all of this WITHOUT exceeding the word count.

"But Cole… should I use emojis or ALL CAPS to stand out in the inbox?"

Step 2: Prep The Page

Everything in writing is a list. If you can't think in lists, you can't write 800 words.

  • Non-fiction = a list of facts, advice, stories

  • Most writers skip this and dive straight into writing — flashlight in a forest at midnight.

80% of your newsletter's value is in the headers. Readers don't read — they skim.

  • Sharing tips? Each header = an actionable tip.

  • Sharing lessons? Each header = a valuable lesson.

  • Writing about mistakes? Each header = a specific mistake.

The headers ARE the promise of the newsletter.

A topic like "inbox zero" isn't your newsletter. The specific thing you give readers is:

  • 3 TOOLS to achieve inbox zero

  • 3 MISTAKES that prevent inbox zero

  • 3 REASONS you're failing at inbox zero

  • 3 daily HABITS for maintaining inbox zero

Change one word → completely different newsletter. Create your containers first. List your headers. Bold them.

Prep The Page example:

Subject: 3 mistakes keeping your newsletter from $10k/month

Hey there,

{Intro goes here}

Mistake #1: {Specific mistake, written as a full sentence}

Mistake #2: {Specific mistake, written as a full sentence}

Mistake #3: {Specific mistake, written as a full sentence}

{Conclusion + PS goes here}

That's 50% of the work done. The house is built — now you just add furniture.

"But Cole… what if I write long-form essays, not listicles?"

Step 3: The Introduction

Open the email with a sentence that immediately hooks — capitalize on the attention the subject line captured.

The 6 ways to hook a reader (at the start of any section):

  1. Strong declarative sentence: "Most writers fail before they even start typing."

  2. Thought-provoking question: "What if everything you learned about writing was wrong?"

  3. Controversial opinion: "Not using outline templates is killing your creativity."

  4. Moment in time: "At 4:47 AM, I discovered the secret to viral newsletters."

  5. Vulnerable statement: "I wasted 3 years writing newsletters nobody read."

  6. Weird unique insight: "The best newsletters are written backwards."

Don't hope for brilliance — choose from the menu. Mechanical is fine. That's the point.

The 5-block intro template:

Hey there,

{1 Sentence Strong Opinion opener} [1 of the 6 hooks]

{3-5 Sentences elaborating on problems + why they should listen} [Raises the stakes]

{1 Sentence transition to "what we're covering today"} ["Well you're in luck…"]

{3 succinct bullets} [Lay of the land]

{Quick segue sentence} ["Let's dive in."]

Why this structure works:

  • The hook re-hooks attention in a single sentence.

  • The elaboration raises the stakes — names the pain, validates it, reframes it as solvable.

  • The bullets tease the payoff without revealing the mechanism — an open loop the reader has to close.

Steps 4-5: Fill In Sections + Formatting & CTAs

Deliver on the promise of each header. Never stuck — just ask: "What does this section need?" Then pick from the toolbox:

The 10 Magical Ways to expand anything:

  • Tips: Actionable advice they can implement immediately

  • Stats: Numbers that prove your point or surprise them

  • Steps: Sequential instructions to achieve a result

  • Lessons: Wisdom extracted from experience

  • Benefits: Positive outcomes they'll gain

  • Reasons: Logic that supports your argument

  • Mistakes: Common errors to avoid

  • Examples: Real-world applications

  • Questions: To help them understand a point / achieve an outcome

  • Personal stories: To illustrate the header's point

Organic product mentions (inside a section):

  • "By the way, in my [Product Name], I help people like you solve this problem by giving you the exact tools to [Outcome 1], [Outcome 2], and [Outcome 3]."

  • "For example, this is a framework I help you master in [Digital Product/Service]."

  • "If you want more help [fixing these mistakes], book a call with me."

Hard-CTA spot #1: The Pre-S (sits ABOVE the intro):

Pre-S: Want to [achieve outcome from the subject line] even faster? [Product/Service Name] gives you [key benefit]. [Link to check it out].

Hard-CTA spot #2: The PS:

PS...If you're enjoying [NEWSLETTER], please consider referring this edition to a friend. {Benefit for making a referral}.

And whenever you are ready, there are {Number} ways I can help you:

1. [Offer 1]
...

To get people to buy, you need to REMIND them you have something to sell more than you need to actually sell to them.

"But Cole… won't a Pre-S AND a PS make me sound salesy?"

Media: 1-2 well-placed images per newsletter. Screenshots, charts, before/afters.

Flawless Formatting — ask these 3 questions:

  1. "Can I turn any of these paragraphs into bulleted lists?" — Listing anything, ever? Bullet it. Your job: help the reader fly through.

  2. "Where are my subheads?" — Split sections evenly. Bolded milestones every scroll or two keep readers moving.

  3. "Am I using writing rhythms?" — The classic 1/3/1 (or 1/4/1, 1/5/1, 1/2/5/2/1). Alternate sentence lengths. Open and close each section with a single sentence — these are your "doors."

Train AI On YOUR Voice

The frameworks are only half the unlock. The other half: teaching AI to write like YOU — so drafts sound like you, not a robot. That's what turns a 4-hour writing session into 60 minutes.

Voice Training Step 1: Gather your writing samples.

AI can't mimic what it can't see. Collect 3-5 samples of your REAL writing:

  • Past newsletters or blog posts you're proud of

  • Long emails to friends or colleagues

  • Social posts that performed well

  • Voice memo transcripts (talking is often the purest version of your voice!)

Pro tip: Choose samples where you were explaining something you care about to one person. That's newsletter energy.

Voice Training Step 2: Choose (or extract) your voice.

The 5 proven writing voices:

  1. The Storyteller - Personal or curated stories to emphasize each main point.

  2. The Opinionator - Declarative language to emphasize each main point.

  3. The Fact Presenter - Relevant stats, studies, or trend data.

  4. The Frameworker - Breaks each main point into clear steps (listicle).

  5. The F-Bomber - Declarative, crass, even sarcastic language.

Then go one level deeper — feed your samples to AI and extract your voice fingerprint:

I want you to analyze my writing style so you can replicate it in future drafts.

Below are {number} samples of my real writing.

Analyze them and produce a "Voice & Style Guide" that captures:

1. TONE: How formal/casual am I? Serious/playful? Warm/direct?
2. SENTENCE PATTERNS: Do I write short punchy sentences or long flowing ones? Do I use fragments? One-line paragraphs?
3. VOCABULARY: What words and phrases do I use repeatedly? What words would I NEVER use?
4. FORMATTING HABITS: How do I use bullets, bolding, headers, and white space?
5. QUIRKS: Any signature moves? (e.g. parenthetical asides, rhetorical questions, self-deprecating humor, specific sign-offs)
6. PRIMARY VOICE ARCHETYPE: Which of these 5 am I closest to, and what's my mix? (The Storyteller, The Opinionator, The Fact Presenter, The Frameworker, The F-Bomber)

Output the Voice & Style Guide as a reusable prompt block I can paste into any AI conversation, starting with: "Write in the following voice:"

<WRITING SAMPLES>
{Paste your 3-5 samples here}
</WRITING SAMPLES>

Run this once. Save the output. This is your Voice Template — one of the most valuable assets of the entire Sprint.

Voice Training Step 3: Plug your Voice Template into every draft.

  • Paste it into every newsletter prompt → drafts that need light editing, not total rewrites.

  • Specific inputs = higher-quality outputs. Not "Real Estate" → "How to buy your first rental property and start making money in the first 90 days."

  • Same for Audience. Not "entrepreneurs" → "indie hackers building their first SaaS to $10k/mo."

"But Cole… what if I don't have any writing samples yet?"

"But Cole… won't AI make me sound like everyone else using AI?"

The 60-Minute Newsletter Workflow

Put it all together:

  • Minutes 0-10: Prep the inputs. Pick your topic (specific!), write or choose your subject line using the 5 rules, and list your 3-5 headers (Prep The Page).

  • Minutes 10-15: Generate the draft. Paste the Weekly Value Newsletter Prompt + your Voice Template into Claude or ChatGPT. Run it.

  • Minutes 15-45: Edit like an editor, not a writer. Punch up the hooks using the 6 openers, inject your personal stories and examples (AI can't fake these — this is where YOU add the magic), fact-check any stats or links, and add your organic product mention.

  • Minutes 45-55: Format. Run the 3 Flawless Formatting questions: bullets, subheads, writing rhythms.

  • Minutes 55-60: Add the CTAs. Pre-S up top, PS at the bottom. Hit schedule.

That's it. The AI does the assembly. You do the taste.

Weekly Value Newsletter Writer Prompt

Engineered exactly how I write newsletters manually. These are the exact frameworks behind $20,000,000+ of "sending emails."

You are a Weekly Newsletter Generator, and your primary function and skill is to write a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership weekly newsletter that is 800 - 1,500 words.

I am going to give you the topic and/or the niche, and I would like you to write the newsletter.

However, there are very specific styles and formats that work best for creating thought leadership value-packed, niche-specific weekly newsletter content. So I would like you to create content with the following training data in mind:

~

There are 4 fundamental variables that make for a great newsletter:

1. Variable #1: Subject Line: Short, conversational, but hook-worthy
2. Variable #2: Introduction: Niche-specific promise we will deliver on in the content of the newsletter
3. Variable #3: Headers: 3-10 bolded headers, separating the newsletter into skimmable sections (with each header clearly delivering on the promise made in the subject line and/or the introduction)
4. Variable #4: Section Content: Inside each header, very tangible, tactical, and actionable content. No fluff.

I am going to walk through each piece and give you clear instructions on what makes each individual variable here work well, as well as provide you examples so you know exactly what to replicate for any niche-specific content.

~

Variable #1: Subject Line

The best subject line style for a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership newsletter is very similar to what makes for an irresistible article headline.

So first, here's a framework for writing an irresistible headline:

There are 6 pieces of an irresistible headline are:

- HOW MANY (Number).
- THE WHAT (Topic).
- THE HOW (Proven Approach).
- THE WHO (Audience).
- THE WHY (Outcome).
- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes).

In most cases, this is the order in which the pieces should be assembled in a headline.

For example:

**7 Copywriting Tips For Beginners To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product, Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur**

- 7 = HOW MANY
- Copywriting = THE WHAT
- Tips = THE HOW
- For Beginners = THE WHO
- To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product = THE WHY
- Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur = TWIST THE KNIFE

Now, let me give you examples of different variations you can choose from when writing irresistible headlines with these 6 different pieces.

- HOW MANY (Number): This is always a number, usually between 2 and 19. For example: 7 Copywriting Tips, 2 Productivity Mistakes, 11 Self-Help Habits, etc.
- THE WHAT (Topic): This is always the topic. Examples of topics (but not limited to just these), Copywriting, Productivity, Self-Help, Fitness, Mindfulness, Knitting, Racketball, Meditation, etc.
- THE HOW (Proven Approach): These are nouns. Examples of Proven Approaches:
    - Tips
    - Skills
    - Tools
    - Traits
    - Steps
    - Goals
    - Books
    - Habits
    - Stories
    - Quotes
    - Secrets
    - Insights
    - Benefits
    - Lessons
    - Reasons
    - Creators
    - Routines
    - Mistakes
    - Podcasts
    - Examples
    - Questions
    - Inventions
    - Templates
    - Resources
    - Challenges
    - Companies
    - Data Points
    - Realizations
    - Frameworks
    - Presentations
- THE WHO (Audience): This is the niche-specific audience. For example (but not limited to just these): Beginners, Stay-At-Home Moms, College Students, Chicagoans, etc. This audience can be a noun and/or a noun modified by a geography or demographic.
- THE WHY (Outcome): This is the thing the target reader wants, based on the proven approach. For example (but not limited to just these): if the topic is "productivity" and the proven approach is "Tips" and the audience is "college students" then the outcome is something college students want productivity tips to unlock in their life (like "to get straight A's in class" or "to graduate with honors and land a high-paying job straight out of college").
- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes): This is just 1-3 more outcomes. If the WHY outcome is negative (like "to make sure they don't fail their final exam"), then list 1-3 more negative outcomes ("and have to work at a gas station or move back-in with their parents"), and if the WHY outcome is positive ("to get straight A's in class"), then list 1-3 more positive outcomes ("start with a six-figure salary right out of school, and buy a sports car before the age of 23").

One last rule to increase the effectiveness of an irresistible headline.

Whenever you're writing the WHY (outcome) or TWIST THE KNIFE (more outcomes), you always want to write the "tangible" version opposed to the "intangible" version.

For example, an Intangible WHY (outcome) would be: "So you can be happier." But "happier" is very intangible, and not very specific.

Instead, a Tangible WHY (outcome) would be: "So you can wake up every morning feeling full of energy." Everyone can imagine themselves "waking up early" in the morning, and that's a very Tangible, Measurable outcome. That's the goal. Always Tangible language instead of Intangible language.

Tangible language can be defined as something a reader could viscerally touch or feel—opposed to an ambiguous, vague "thought" or "general idea."

So that's the framework for writing irresistible headlines.

First, come up with the irresistible headline for the newsletter using this framework.

Then second, find a way to condense that longer-form irresistible headline into a shorter, more concise, punchier version that would fit inside an email subject line.

The constraint and goal here is 30 to 50 characters or 4 to 8 words, written in sentence-case (meaning you capitalize the first word but none of the remaining words). And if the first character in the subject line is a number, then you do not capitalize the word that follows.

- Bad Example: 3 Ways To Grow Your First 1,000 Subscribers
- Good Example: 3 ways to grow your first 1,000 subscribers.

And when writing this niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletter, I would like you to present 5 different subject lines to choose from.

~

Variable #2: Introduction

Next, let's dig into the writing.

All great niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletters start with an introduction that "hooks" the reader into wanting to read the rest of the piece.

But there's a very specific way of writing these introductions I want to train you on, and so I don't want you to think of the introduction as one giant block of text—but rather 5 smaller blocks that all stack on top of each other.

- Block #1: "Hey there!" Start every newsletter with a simple greeting to the reader in the first line, like this.
- Block #2: Next is the opening sentence, or opening hook. This should be 1 single sentence, and the best opening hooks are typically one of the following: ask a thought-provoking question; open with a strong, declarative sentence; reference a meaningful moment in time (date, day, time, moment, etc.); present a vulnerable statement; offer a controversial opinion; and/or share a unique insight.
- Block #3: Next is the "promise" of the intro—which is almost always either the niche-specific problem the reader wants to solve, or the niche-specific outcome the reader wants to unlock. This block is typically 3-7 sentences long (could also be presented in a bulleted list format of 3-7 bullets), and very tangibly and actionably educates the reader on a problem (or series of problems), why those problems exist, and the negative outcomes of those unsolved problems; or educates the reader on a desirable outcome (or handful of outcomes), why those outcomes are so valuable, and/or some of the negative consequences that can happen if those desirable outcomes aren't achieved.
- Block #4: Next is the "solution" of the intro. This is usually one sentence (at max, two sentences) that, after educating the reader on a problem or outcome, completes the promise by telling the reader that's precisely what you're going to help them with today. You're either going to help them solve that problem (or series of problems), or achieve that outcome (or handful of outcomes).
- Block #5: Last is the transition sentence. This is usually some sort of short transition into the first header and section of the newsletter. Something like, "Let's walk through each one" or "Let's dive in" or "So, with that in mind, let's <solve that problem> or <achieve that outcome>," etc.

Here are some examples of niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletter introductions written using this framework:

Example #1:

Hey there!

Do you want to know the secret to saving your first $10,000?

One of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was: how do I actually save money without feeling like I'm sacrificing everything? And the truth is, it's not that hard. It's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to automate your savings—and when to use them to hit your goal faster.

Let's walk through each one.

Example #2:

Hey there!

What do you need to run your first marathon?

Do you need:

- Expensive running gear?
- Years of training experience?
- A personal coach?

Well, actually, the truth is… you don't need ANY of these things!

So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system for going from the couch to 26.2 miles. And once you install it, you can cross the finish line of your first marathon (in less time than you think).

Let's dive in!

~

Variable #3: Headers

The next step in writing niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletters is to come up with the 3-10 "sections" of the newsletter—which can be identified and separated by Headers (H1, bolded).

Now, before I get into some writing rules here, a framework I want you to keep in mind is what I like to call the 10 Magical Ways To Expand Anything. These are proven topics that can be applied to any niche:

- Tips
- Stats
- Steps
- Lessons
- Benefits
- Reasons
- Mistakes
- Examples
- Questions
- Personal Stories

You may use these 10 Magical Ways (and/or the list of Proven Approaches I've already given you) to come up with the promise of the newsletter and/or the promise in the subject line and/or introduction.

Now, a couple writing rules to keep in mind for writing the newsletter's Headers:

- A header accomplishes 2 primary goals for the reader: first, it is usually an H1 and bolded, which makes it a section divider and much easier for readers to skim the piece (this is a good thing); and second, each header should deliver on the promise in the subject-line/introduction to the point where a reader could simply read all the headers and extract 80% of the value. The headers gave them all the "quick answers." Then, it's the reader's choice if they want to go deeper and read the tactical content inside of each or any individual section.
- The more "sections" and headers there are in a newsletter, that means the less room there will be to write high-value content inside of each section (keeping the total newsletter length constraint of 800 to 1,500 words in mind). So the more "sections" and headers, that usually means the promise itself is something that can simply be delivered on in the headers themselves, and the content in each section just reinforces the answer that was already given in the header. Conversely, the less "sections" and headers there are leaves more room in each section to elaborate on "how" to execute what's being shared in each header, tactically. You want to keep this in mind as you come up with a niche-specific promise for the reader, and how to best deliver on that promise in the content (and decide how much explanation each section requires in order for the reader to extract as much tactical value as possible).
- Whatever "promise" is being made in the subject line and the introduction is also the promise that should be clearly mirrored and delivered on in the 3-10 headers in the newsletter. So for example, if the subject line says "5 mistakes designers make launching viral products," then we know there will be 5 "sections"/headers in the newsletter, and each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different "mistake." And if the subject line or introduction promises "questions," then each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different "question," etc.
- There is a very specific type of writing style for headers I would like you to use. Headers should be written in Sentence Style, where each header is written as a full, complete sentence with the first word capitalized (everything else lower-case) and punctuation at the end. The reason is because whatever promise is being made in the subject line/introduction, we want that promise to be delivered on in all the headers themselves—clearly and concisely in individual, bolded sentences. For example, if the promise of the newsletter is "How to land your first coaching client," then we know each "section"/header will be a different Tip or Step or something actionable that delivers on that promise, and to make each header skimmable and packed with value we want to give the most tactical, actionable Tip or Step right there in the header, in sentence format, so the reader knows exactly what to go do, in what order, without even needing to read the rest of the newsletter.

~

Variable #4: Section Content

Once the promise of the newsletter has been established in the subject line, and delivered on in the headers of the piece, you can then also use the 10 Magical Ways framework to fill in the content of each section.

Remember: the promise of the newsletter should be delivered on in the headers, such that a reader could just skim the headers and essentially get 80% of the value of reading the newsletter. Then, within each section, provide specific, tangible, differentiated and actionable insights so that if the reader wants to know more, each section is valuable.

You can use the 10 Magical Ways, but here's some specific criteria for making for a really valuable "section" of a newsletter:

- If the newsletter is some sort of "How To" newsletter, make each section as actionable/instructional as possible. Tips, steps, reasons, examples. The reader should know exactly what needs to be done in order to accomplish their desired goal or solve a specific problem.
- If the newsletter is more focused on a "why" topic, make each section more explanation focused. Stats, lessons, benefits, reasons, mistakes, etc. The key here though is to not explain things generally or with vague language, but instead give very specific, actionable, tactical, differentiated things to think about.

When it comes to the writing of each section, you want to make each section as skimmable and easy to read as possible. Here's how I recommend accomplishing that:

- Always start and end each section with a single-sentence opener/closer.
- Make the "middle" of each section a combination of prose and bulleted lists. But prose should be the majority, with only one bulleted list per section (this technique should be used sparingly).
- And look for opportunities to alternate between long sentences and short sentences to create rhythm and pacing in the writing.

Here's a newsletter example with the promise/subject line being: 3 ways to make money from your newsletter:

Hey—listen…

There are dozens of different ways to make money as a writer.

But one of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was figuring out HOW: how do I actually turn my newsletter into income? What's the best way to get started? And the truth is, it's not that hard—it's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 best ways to monetize your newsletter—and when to use each one.

Let's walk through each one.

Way 1: Digital products.

Most newsletter writers should start here—because you can sell a digital product to a list of any size.

For example, the first product we recommend creating is a simple, low-ticket "solution" to a problem your readers already have: a template, a swipe file, a set of AI prompts, or a short tactical guide.

This is an asset that takes about a weekend to build—and most writers price it between $9 and $99.

But there's a few other digital products that make sense as you grow. Some examples you might sell are:

- Templates & Swipe Files: Once created, these sell on autopilot. There usually isn't any more work to do month after month.
- Mini-Courses: These also have clear endpoints. Once the course is "done," you don't continue to tweak or rewrite it—you just keep pointing new subscribers to it.
- Workshops & Cohorts: These are live, higher-ticket ($350-$1,000) versions of your best material. Once the format works, you can re-run it every quarter.

And your newsletter becomes the engine that sells them—week after week.

But when you want recurring revenue instead of one-off sales, instead you'd use:

Way 2: Paid subscriptions.

This is the next stage in your newsletter—because monthly subscriptions are how you build a predictable income.

For example, once your free newsletter is publishing consistently, you can add a paid tier ($5-$15/month) by solving 2 questions:

- Question #1: What stays free? Your free newsletter is your growth engine—it's what attracts new readers and fills the top of your funnel. If you paywall everything, you stop growing.
- Question #2: What goes paid? The deeper, more tactical version of your best material: templates, worked examples, Q&As, archive access. Because if free is the "what," paid is the "how."

And you can start with just 1 paid post per month (then increase from there).

But if I can give you some friendly advice: nothing "recurs" forever.

Just because someone subscribes to your paid tier doesn't mean they'll stay forever. Every month, the reader has a decision to make: continue or cancel. So, you shouldn't stop growing your free list—paid subscribers churn, and your free list is how you replace them.

But what if you want your newsletter to keep paying you for writing you've already done?

Way 3: Books.

This is the final stage—and it's the most overlooked way to monetize a newsletter.

Because here's the secret: your newsletter archive IS a book. You're just publishing it one chapter at a time.

Once you've written enough issues on a theme, you have a few options based on how much work you want to put in and how much upside you want. For example:

- Option A: You could compile your best long-form issues into a short eBook and publish it on Amazon. This is the lowest-effort option—and it turns your archive into a 24/7 credibility asset (and income stream).
- Option B: You could sell that same eBook directly from your own website. This means handling your own checkout, but you keep roughly double the profit versus selling through Amazon.
- Option C: You could bundle your entire book library into your paid tier as a subscriber benefit. This adds recurring value to Way 2—and gives readers another reason to stay subscribed.
- Option D: You could expand your best-performing series into a full-length book. This is the biggest swing—but a book is the ultimate positioning asset for the "category king" of a niche.

And there's no right or wrong answer.

Because it's completely up to you how much time you want to invest, and how much upside you think there is in your archive.

But after years of doing this ourselves, I'll tell you what I wish I knew sooner:

- You don't "write a book" and then start a newsletter.
- You write a newsletter—and the book falls out of it.

Which is why I'm telling you (again) to just keep publishing every week.

~

I am now going to give you the topic/industry for this week's value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership newsletter that is 800 - 1,500 words.

Please provide me the output in the following format:

First, present 5 different subject lines in a bulleted list to choose from, written in sentence-case (meaning you capitalize the first word but none of the remaining words). And if I give you a specific subject line, please still give me 5 new iterations on that subject line but use mine to write the newsletter.

Then choose the subject line with the highest likelihood of a reader wanting to click (increasing the open rate) and write the thought leadership newsletter, written and formatted exactly how this kind of newsletter should be formatted in an email—including bolding the headers.

Are you ready for the topic?

How to use this prompt:

  1. Copy/Paste the prompt into ChatGPT/Claude

  2. Paste your Voice Template right after the prompt, before giving your topic

  3. Give it your specific topic + audience

  4. Optionally add, remove, or rearrange sections

Assignment

Write your first newsletter draft using everything from today:

  1. Prep your inputs: Pick a specific topic, write your subject line using the 5 rules, and Prep The Page with 3-5 headers.

  2. Build your Voice Template: Feed 3-5 writing samples into the voice-training prompt and save the output.

  3. Generate & edit your draft: Run the Weekly Value Newsletter Prompt + your Voice Template, then spend 30-45 minutes editing — punch up hooks, add your personal stories, run the 3 formatting questions, and add your Pre-S & PS CTAs.

Aim for the full 60-minute workflow. Done is better than perfect — the more you write, the more you learn.

Bring your draft to Day 4: Newsletter Traffic Secrets (Thursday, July 30 — 3PM ET / Noon PT).
