How to Turn Social Content Into a Newsletter Growth Engine

Date: 1/29/2026

In today's Sprint Live Session with Cole, we did some live workshopping and talked about:

  • Why writing a newsletter without a traffic strategy is like publishing a book and hoping people stumble across it — and the one word that ties every piece of a profitable writing business together.

  • The three-step funnel Cole and Dickie have used to generate millions of dollars (it's simpler than you'd guess, and most people skip step one).

  • The 30-minute morning ritual that grew their audiences faster than any single tactic — and why most people's version of it is completely wasted effort.

Cole’s Live Session Notes

The $0 Traffic Model: Newsletter First, Social Second

Most creators have this backwards.

They grind out social content daily, hope for viral, treat the newsletter as an afterthought.

You do the opposite:

  1. Write your newsletter first. (Day 3.) Your deep, long-form "source of truth."

  2. Extract social posts from it. One newsletter = 10+ short-form posts.

  3. Distribute on X, LinkedIn & Substack Notes. Each platform = a top-of-funnel traffic arm.

  4. Convert followers into subscribers with deliberate CTAs, autoplugs, and profile optimization.

This solves the 2 biggest problems:

  • "What do I post on social?" → Extractions from your newsletter.

  • "How do I get subscribers without ads?" → Organic traffic, converted deliberately.

Your newsletter library is an asset that appreciates. 10 newsletters = a 100-post library to extract, remix, and republish forever.

Your 3 Traffic Arms

  • X: 335.7M users. Fast feedback loops. Best for testing hooks, one-liners, contrarian takes. Rewards provocation and threads.

  • LinkedIn: 1B users. High-trust professional audience. Best for stories, frameworks, lessons learned. Audience actually clicks links.

  • Substack Notes: "Only" 20M users — exactly why you should be there.

Why Notes (most creators are sleeping on it)

  • 20M users is still a LOT of readers

  • Concentrated pool of readers (not meme-scrollers)

  • Early adopter advantage — won't last forever

  • Frictionless conversion: readers can subscribe directly from the Note itself

  • On X/LinkedIn: read post → find profile → find link → subscribe. On Notes: like it → subscribe. Done.

The algorithm is rigged in your favor

  • X and LinkedIn optimize for scroll time (ads). Links get suppressed.

  • Substack has no ads. They make money when YOU make money (10% of paid subs).

  • Mike Cohen, Substack's Head of ML: "The goal is to get people to discover, subscribe, and ideally pay."

  • 2025 "sequential models": the feed follows a reader's journey in real time — your Note competes within what that reader is interested in right now.

  • Restacks + replies build recommendation bridges via audience overlap.

  • Consistency beats virality. Steady posting > occasional viral hits. Post daily and the algorithm learns you. Post monthly and it forgets you.

  • In 3 months (Oct 2025): the Substack app drove 32M free subs + 500K paid subs. Notes is the engine.

The model: X and LinkedIn for reach, Substack Notes for frictionless conversion. Same extraction, 3 flavors.

"But Cole… how many followers do I need before this starts working?"

Traffic Mistakes To Avoid

Fix these first. Then run the strategy.

Mistake #1: Speaking The Wrong Language On The Wrong Platform

  • Notes is not for hot takes and dunking. The algorithm rewards connection, not controversy.

  • Twitter habits on Notes get likes — not subscribers. Massive difference.

  • Reverse is true too: a long vulnerable LinkedIn story posted verbatim on X will die.

  • Same idea, adapted format.

Mistake #2: Only Posting Links To Your Newsletter

  • "New post! Link in comments." Nobody clicks those.

  • Readers want to be engaged on the platform they're on.

  • Every-post-is-a-link trains the algorithm (and readers) to scroll past you.

Mistake #3: Posting Once And Disappearing

  • One post a week is not a strategy. It's a lottery ticket.

  • The algorithm needs data. Consistency trains it to work for you.

Mistake #4: Ignoring The Engagement Side

  • Social is a two-way street. Posting without engaging = half speed.

  • Algorithms rank high-signal replies above passive hearts and "love this!" comments.

Mistake #5: No Conversion Mechanism

  • Great posts + tons of likes + zero subscribers = no bridge from "liked this" to "subscribed."

  • You need a deliberate conversion system. (Coming below.)

The 10 Magical Ways: 1 Newsletter In, 10+ Posts Out

This workflow ends "what should I post today?" forever.

Take your Day 3 draft. Read it with a highlighter. Every newsletter contains 10+ extractable posts:

  1. The Standalone Insight. Your most surprising claim, distilled to 1-3 punchy sentences. Must stop the scroll on its own.

  2. The Personal Story. Best anecdote → short post (under 250 words). Open with a vivid moment, build to one "aha."

  3. The Listicle. Any multi-point section → numbered list. "5 things I learned about [topic]:" Most shareable format on every platform.

  4. The Framework Breakdown. Process → "how to" post. Step 1 → 2 → 3. Thread on X, line-break post on LinkedIn, short numbered Note.

  5. The Contrarian Take. Where you disagree with conventional wisdom. "Everyone says X. Here's why they're wrong:"

  6. The Quotable Line. 2-3 paragraphs you're proudest of, posted verbatim. On Substack: highlight → post to Notes (auto-links back to the edition).

  7. The Proof Post. Any number, stat, before/after. "I did X for 30 days. Here's what happened:" Receipts > opinions.

  8. The Question Post (Community Invitation). Core theme → specific question. About THEM, not you. Generous offer: "Drop your newsletter below and I'll check it out."

  9. The Teaser (Open Loop). Most intriguing claim → information gap. End: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

  10. The Mistake/Lesson Post. What you did wrong before the insight. "I spent 2 years doing [wrong thing]. Then I learned [insight]."

Extraction rules

  • Do NOT repost the newsletter. EXTRACT and TRANSFORM.

  • Every post must stand alone.

  • Adapt per platform: punchy for X, story-driven for LinkedIn, warm reader-to-reader for Notes.

  • Under 280 words. Short paragraphs. Sound like a person, not a content machine.

After 10 newsletters → 100+ post library. Never a blank compose box again.

"But Cole… what if I run out of things to say?"

The Traffic Strategy: Content, Cadence, Connection, Conversion

4 gears. All turning = the engine runs itself. Skip one = it stalls.

Most writers only do Content. Parts 2-4 are where the compounding happens.

Part 1: Content (the 3 buckets)

  1. Short-form original. Extractions via the 10 Magical Ways — or test new ideas; winners become newsletters. Social = idea lab, newsletter = finished product.

  2. Restacks / Reshares. Restack Notes, quote-tweet on X, reshare with commentary on LinkedIn. Always add your own comment.

  3. Newsletter Quotes. Highlight a section → post to Notes with your comment (auto screenshot + link). On X/LinkedIn: clean screenshot of your best paragraph + one-line setup.

  • Right now: image posts > video posts. Keep experimenting.

Part 2: Cadence

  • No scheduling on Notes (yet). X and LinkedIn have it — use it.

  • Pick a schedule, stick with it. I post 2x/day: 10am and 4pm ET.

  • Weekly calendar:

  • Monday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Restack w/ Commentary (4pm)

  • Tuesday: Personal Story (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Wednesday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Newsletter Teaser (4pm)

  • Thursday: Restack w/ Commentary (10am) + Newsletter Quote (4pm)

  • Friday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Saturday: Newsletter Teaser (10am) + Restack w/ Commentary (4pm)

  • Sunday: Personal Story (10am) + Standalone Insight (4pm)

  • Batch your WRITING:

  • Sunday night: extract + write 5-7 posts from your latest newsletter.

  • Daily: 1-2 reactive posts (restacks, invitations, quotes — best when timely).

  • Post-newsletter day: pull 1-2 teasers.

  • Cross-posting rule: write once, adapt twice. 60-second platform pass per post.

"But Cole… should I post the same content on Notes, X, and LinkedIn?"

Part 3: Connection

  • One good comment on the right post > 10 posts of your own. Engagement is the multiplier.

  • Strategy #1: The Value-Add Comment. Never "love this!" Add a personal example, a related insight, a "yes, and…" Rule: every comment should be good enough to be its own post.

  • Strategy #2: The Restack (or Quote-Share). Goes to YOUR audience with your endorsement + notifies the writer. 2-3x/week, always with your own take.

  • Strategy #3: Build Your "Traffic 15." 10-15 writers in your niche with similar-sized audiences. Write their names down. Engage consistently for 2-4 weeks. The algorithm notices overlapping audiences and cross-pollinates. Earned cross-promotion. Rotate 1-2 names/month.

  • Daily checklist (10 minutes):

  • Comment substantively on 3-5 posts in your niche

  • Reply to every comment on your posts within the first hour

  • Restack 1 post with commentary

  • Touch 2-3 of your Traffic 15

Part 4: Conversion (5 tactics)

  1. Optimize Your Profiles. Profile must answer: "What will I get if I subscribe?" Niche-clear name + value-driven bio (Day 1) + pinned post that sells the subscription + newsletter link in bio (not buried in a linktree). The profile is the conversion bottleneck.

  2. Leave Breadcrumbs. "I broke this down in way more detail in last week's edition…" / "This is the short version. The 2,000-word deep dive is in my newsletter." Creates an information gap. 2-3x/week, never forced.

  3. "For Example…" The two magical words. Share an insight, then: "For example, in my newsletter [Name], I…" — points to anything without feeling promotional. Reads as a relevant example, not a pitch.

  4. The Autoplug. X/LinkedIn suppress links. So: publish post (no link) → immediately reply with "If you liked this, I go deeper every week in [Name]. Subscribe free: [link]." If the post takes off, the reply rides along. (Hypefury/Typefully can automate this.)

  5. The CTA Rotation. 60-70% of posts: no CTA, pure value. 1-2x/week: newsletter link (via autoplug). 1x/week: soft subscribe prompt. 2-3x/week: breadcrumb.

  • The math: 14 posts/week/platform × 500-2,000 impressions → 10-30+ new subscribers per week, per platform. And it compounds.

"But Cole… I'm getting likes but no subscribers. What's wrong?"

Extra juice

  • Notes have a LONG lifespan — engagement weeks later.

  • No native Notes analytics — track manually or use WriteStack. (Check X/LinkedIn analytics weekly, not daily.)

  • Newsletters auto-push to your Notes feed — make your thumbnails eye-catching.

  • Promote your best post of the week INSIDE your newsletter. The flywheel runs both directions.

  • Winners get recycled: repost top performers in 60-90 days, expand them into editions.

The AI Content Extraction Prompts

Copy-paste into ChatGPT, Claude, or your AI tool of choice.

  • Prompt #1 → batch a full week of posts in one sitting

  • Prompt #2 → extract 5-7 posts from your Day 3 draft

  • Then add YOUR voice, YOUR stories, YOUR specific details

Prompt #1: The Weekly Batch Generator

You are a social content strategist for newsletter creators.

I'm going to give you context about my newsletter, and I need you to generate a batch of 14 posts for the upcoming week (usable on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes).

MY NEWSLETTER:
- Name: [Your newsletter name]
- Niche: [Your niche]
- Who I write for: [Your target reader]
- What I help them do: [The transformation/value]
- My latest newsletter was about: [Topic of most recent edition]
- A personal story I could share this week: [Brief description]

GENERATE 14 POSTS USING THESE TYPES:

Type 1 — Personal Story + Insight (generate 3):
- A short personal story (under 250 words) that builds to a single "aha" moment related to my niche
- Open with a specific, vivid moment
- End with one clear insight
- Optional: close with a question

Type 2 — Standalone Insight (generate 4):
- My best thinking distilled into 1-3 punchy sentences
- A surprising observation about my niche
- Should make someone stop scrolling

Type 3 — Community Invitation (generate 2):
- A post that invites readers to participate
- Ask a specific question (not generic)
- Make it about THEM, not me
- Include a generous offer ("Drop your newsletter and I'll check it out" or similar)

Type 4 — Newsletter Teaser (generate 3):
- Based on my latest newsletter topic above, pull out the most intriguing insight or claim
- Format as a standalone post that creates an information gap
- End with: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

FORMAT: Number each post. Label the type. Keep each post under 280 words. Use short paragraphs (1-2 sentences each). Make them sound like a real person, not a content machine.

Prompt #2: The Newsletter-to-Social Repurposer

Run this on your Day 3 draft tonight.

You are a social content strategist for newsletter creators. I'm going to paste a newsletter edition below, and I need you to extract 5-7 high-performing social posts from it (usable on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes).

MY NEWSLETTER CONTEXT:
- Name: [Your newsletter name]
- Niche: [Your niche]
- Tone: [Describe your voice — conversational, authoritative, vulnerable, etc.]

EXTRACTION RULES:
1. Find the single most surprising claim or insight. Turn it into a Standalone Insight post (1-3 sentences).
2. Find the best story or personal anecdote. Turn it into a Personal Story + Insight post (under 250 words).
3. Find 2-3 "quotable" paragraphs. Turn each into a Standalone Insight post.
4. Write 1 Newsletter Teaser post that creates an information gap and links back to the full edition.
5. Write 1 Community Invitation post inspired by the newsletter topic (ask readers a question related to the theme).

FORMAT: Number each post. Label the type. Keep each under 280 words. Short paragraphs. Make them sound human.

Do NOT repost the newsletter. EXTRACT and TRANSFORM the best parts into standalone posts that work even if someone never reads the full edition.

---

[PASTE YOUR NEWSLETTER EDITION HERE]

Assignment

Before Day 5 (60-90 minutes):

  1. Extract 5-10 social posts from your Day 3 newsletter draft. By hand (10 Magical Ways) or run Prompt #2 — then add your voice. Save them in one doc. This is the start of your content library.

  2. Publish at least ONE post today. Strongest extraction → X, LinkedIn, or Notes (or all 3, adapted). Done > perfect. The algorithm can't reward a post that doesn't exist.

  3. Audit your profiles. Name, bio, pinned post = what subscribers get. Newsletter link in every bio. The profile is the conversion bottleneck.

  4. Build your Traffic 15 list. 15 writers, your niche, similar-sized audiences. Write the names down.

  5. Commit to the 20-minute daily routine for 14 days. Morning: post 1 + engage 5 min. Afternoon: post 1 + reply to comments. Track new subscribers for 2 weeks.

Reminder: the writers who win aren't the most talented. They're the most consistent.

Video Timestamps

  • 03:21 AI Writing School Upgrades & Sprint Recap

  • 27:26 Where to Place Your Paywall (Info vs. Tangible Asset)

  • 32:04 What Readers Actually Buy (It's Not Writing)

  • 40:43 Monetization Method #2: The Self-Publishing Flywheel

  • 49:15 Monetization Method #3: Digital Products

  • 51:07 Why Cole Doesn't Run Ads

  • 54:52 The Stack: Information + Assets + Access

  • 58:16 Sprint Wrap-Up & Biggest Takeaways

3 Simple Ways to Monetize Your Newsletter (Without Running Ads)

Date: 8/01/2026

In today's Substack Starter Sprint Live Session with Cole, we did some live workshopping and talked about:

  • Where to place a paywall so readers actually convert — and why the split between "information" and "tangible asset" is the cleanest line to draw.

  • How to turn a single long-form newsletter into a Substack post, an Amazon short-read ebook, and eventually a print book — using one repeatable publishing flywheel.

  • What readers are really paying for when they buy a digital product (hint: it's not the writing, and it's not the information either).

Cole’s Live Session Notes

Why Ads Aren't On The List

Everyone asks about sponsorships. We don't recommend them.

  • Ads require massive scale before they pay anything meaningful

  • They put someone else's message in front of YOUR readers

  • They slowly exhaust the trust you've spent months building

  • Every model we cover today pays more per subscriber than ads ever will at your size

The 3 models we DO recommend:

  • Paid Newsletter — money from subscriptions

  • Books — money from republishing your content on Amazon

  • Digital Products — money from one-off products sold to your list

"Which one should I pick?"

  • The answer: all of them (eventually)

  • Going paid is the beginning of monetization, not the end

  • Most writers leave SO much money on the table here

  • But you can't launch everything at once — today you pick ONE to start with

Everything works on Substack, Kit, or Beehiiv. Mechanics differ, models are identical.

Method #1: The Paid Newsletter Model

Why it's great for beginners

  • Subscription revenue = recurring = defensible + predictable

  • Dead simple to operate: connect Stripe, payments happen in-platform

  • Becomes the "nucleus" that powers every other model later

  • Every paid subscriber is a hand raised: "I'd love to give you more money"

The 3 decisions of going paid

1. What stays free vs. what goes paid

  • Free = your growth engine. Paid = the deeper, "do this exactly" version

  • Common split: free gets the "what" and "why" — paid gets the "how" (templates, systems, step-by-step)

2. Where you place the paywall

  • Don't paywall the whole post

  • Place it AFTER real value, RIGHT BEFORE the most actionable payoff

  • The free portion must be good enough that readers feel the pain of not seeing the rest

  • Strategic paywall placement is a skill — get good at it early

3. Pricing

  • Standard range: $5–$15/month

  • Annual = ~10x monthly (2 months free)

  • $10/mo or $100/yr is a perfectly good start for most niches

  • Don't agonize. You can always adjust. Consistency matters more.

When should you go paid?

  • Sooner than you think. You do NOT need 10,000 subscribers.

  • Signal: a few hundred engaged subscribers who open and reply → turn it on

  • Benchmark: expect 2–5% of your free list to convert to paid over time

  • Bigger + warmer free list = the percentage compounds

Method #2: The Book Model (Self-Publishing)

The idea: double-monetize content you've ALREADY written

  • Long-form newsletters (5,000+ words) → simple eBook cover → publish on Amazon as "quick reads" (non-exclusive, no KDP Select)

  • ~15 long-form newsletters (or ~30 standard) on one topic → compile into print books & audiobooks

  • Sell eBook/audiobook versions on your own site too — no Amazon cut = 2x the profit

The bundle-back tactic

  • Once you have a library of books, bundle "free access" to it INTO your paid newsletter

  • This is what Cole does with Commercial Fiction Club

  • Why it works: you trade one-off revenue (buy a book) for recurring revenue (subscribe and STAY subscribed for library access)

Books = authority + revenue

  • "Author of [Book]" is one of the fastest credibility unlocks there is

  • Boosts free-to-paid conversion, makes products easier to sell, gets you podcast/speaking invites

  • Revenue is real — authority compounds faster

  • Best part: nothing "new" to create. Just repackage past work.

"But Cole… won't readers get upset if I take the same content and charge for it again somewhere else?"

Method #3: The Digital Product Model

The 3 price tiers

  • $9–$99 — template packs, AI prompts, dashboards, cheat sheets, mini-courses

  • $99–$350 — text & video asynchronous courses

  • $350–$1,000 — workshops, cohorts, challenges, bootcamps

The mental unlock

  • Your free AND paid lists are lists of potential customers

  • Write With AI: 112,000+ free subscribers… only 1,800 paying

  • Some free subscribers just don't like paid newsletters — but they WILL buy a different offer

  • Give every subscriber more than 1 way to give you money

How expensive is this mistake? A live example:

  • Claude Cowork Bootcamp — 2-week cohort, launched to the full Write With AI list

  • Most buyers were NOT paying subscribers. They were free subscribers who needed a different offer.

  • 200+ buyers → $167,000 in revenue → 1/3 of yearly revenue… in 2 weeks

  • Imagine NOT doing it. That's $167K left on the table.

"But Cole… won't I come across like a money-grubbing sleazy salesman if I launch so many offers?"

Mistakes To Avoid

  1. Monetizing with ads/sponsorships — renting readers' attention for pennies

  2. Thinking paid subscriptions are the ONLY way — the $167K lesson

  3. Paywalling everything — kill your free content, kill your funnel. Paywall the payoff, not the post.

  4. Waiting until you feel "big enough" — you need a few hundred engaged readers and one clear offer

  5. Never asking for the sale — if you can solve their problem and don't tell them, you're letting them suffer

  6. Launching all three models at once — stack them one threshold at a time

The Decision Framework

The threshold sequence

  • Step 1: Turn your free newsletter paid → stay focused until $50K/yr

  • Step 2: At $50K/yr, start launching digital products → 2x the business to $100K/yr

  • Step 3: At $100K/yr, add books/self-publishing → unlocks the next tranche

One step at a time. Cross a threshold, then stack the next model.

Gut-check if you're still torn

Your situation

Start with

You publish consistently and readers reply/engage

Paid Newsletter — turn on subscriptions now

Readers keep asking the same "how do I…" question

Digital Product — package the answer and sell it

15+ long-form posts (or 30+ standard) on one topic

Books — compile and republish your archive

Brand new with a small list

Paid Newsletter — forces the consistency habit

"But Cole… which monetization model is the best?"

"But Cole… how much money can I really earn with a newsletter?"

Assignment

Tonight, do two things:

1. Choose your monetization method.

  • Pick ONE: Paid Newsletter, Books, or Digital Products

  • Use the decision framework. Write it down. Commit.

2. Map your 90-day plan — three 30-day blocks:

  • Days 1–30: Set up the mechanics. Paid: subscriptions on, pricing set, free/paid split decided. Products: pick ONE idea from questions readers already ask. Books: inventory your archive, pick the 15 posts that share a topic.

  • Days 31–60: Execute. Paid: publish weekly with a strategic paywall. Products: build + pre-sell to your list. Books: compile, cover, format for Amazon.

  • Days 61–90: Launch and learn. Paid: first "upgrade" campaign to free subs. Products: launch to your FULL list. Books: publish, announce, bundle into your paid tier.

Keep it to one page. A plan you'll follow beats a perfect plan you won't.

Wrapping Up The Sprint

Look at what you built in 5 days:

  • Day 1: Chose your niche and positioning

  • Day 2: Set up and launched your newsletter

  • Day 3: Built your growth engine

  • Day 4: Created your content system

  • Day 5: Chose your monetization method + mapped your 90-day plan

Most people spend MONTHS "getting ready" to do what you just did in 5 days.

The truth: the sprint was the easy part

  • The next 90 days are where newsletters are actually built — one consistent send at a time

  • Content compounds. Trust compounds. Revenue compounds. Only if you keep publishing.

Our ask:

  1. Execute your 90-day plan. Don't add to it. Don't second-guess it. Run it.

  2. Don't touch your model for 90 days. The #1 killer isn't the "wrong" model — it's switching every 3 weeks.

  3. When you cross your first threshold, stack the next model. Paid → products → books.

You now know more than 99% of people who ever hit "create publication."

The only thing left to do is write. Onwards and upwards!

records.description: Hey there! And welcome to Day 1 of the Start Writing Online Sprint! In this lesson, we’re going to cover: - The 5 proven short-form formats that work across X,
records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 1 of the Start Writing Online Sprint!

In this lesson, we’re going to cover:

  • The 5 proven short-form formats that work across X, LinkedIn, Substack, and more

  • How to test your ideas out with your readers using a short-form framework called “Outlines As Content”

  • How to write short-form content manually or with AI

All so you can start publishing your ideas online and start testing which ideas work with your readers and audience.

Let’s dive in!

5 Proven Short-Form Formats

After writing thousands of viral short-form posts on both X (Twitter) and LinkedIn, I have identified 5 formats that typically out-perform the average over and over again.

These formats also make for a great compounding library of content. (For example, you can take your entire short-form content library on X and copy/paste it over to LinkedIn, and then copy/paste it over to Instagram as screenshots/carousels, and then copy/paste it over to Instagram Threads, etc. etc. etc.)

Let’s dive in!

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is where you write a thought-provoking paragraph connected to your core industry/niche/topic.

There’s something about this formatting, especially on a fast-moving platform like X, that immediately makes it “stand out” simply because it’s formatted differently. As a full paragraph, you (as the reader) inherently assume it to be “smart.” (Ironic, I know.)

It works so well for a few reasons:

  • It takes a strong stance instead of hedging.

  • It uses concise, economical language and alternates long and short sentences to create rhythm and emphasis.

  • And it leans on subtle, barely-perceptible literary touches—a bit of alliteration, repetition, or antithesis (an obvious observation followed by a non-obvious one)—to make the writing more “satisfying” than plain prose would.

One of my favorite formats!

Format #2: What, How, Why

This is a very repeatable formula:

  • “What” = The first line is “what” you are trying to say to the reader.

  • “How” = The middle 3-5 bullets is “how” to accomplish the “what.”

  • “Why” = The last sentence is “why” this is so important.

It works well for a few reasons:

  • The first line/hook grabs attention up front.

  • The bullets deliver tangible, differentiated, actionable items—no fluff.

  • And the closing line motivates action or warns of the cost of inaction, so the reader walks away with a push to actually do something.

You can apply this format to literally any topic, in any niche, and it will work well.

Format #3: Listicle

Anything you can list is a great short-form piece of content.

For example:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

The “Listicle” format has a simple opening sentence promising the "what" you're about to give the reader, followed by a skimmable list that delivers exactly that—tips, tools, books, mistakes, etc.

It works so well because it compresses what could be a long article into a few seconds of reading. Instead of making someone consume 1,500 words to get 7 recommendations, you hand them all the answers instantly.

You’re listing tangible, specific items tied to a clear goal, problem, or outcome (which means you’re differentiating yourself from all the fluff content out there!).

Format #4: Old vs New

This is where you compare the “old” way someone did something (in your niche) to the “new” way.

Or, where you compare any sort of archetype.

Some examples might be:

  • Bad vs Good

  • Rich vs Poor

  • Right vs Wrong

  • Productive vs Unproductive

  • Legacy vs Cutting-Edge

  • Etc.

Here are a few reasons why this works so well:

  • The opposing comparison creates tension

  • The "new" side subtly sells the reader on the better way

  • The symmetry is visually appealing and easy to scan—the two halves mirror each other

Giving TANGIBLE examples on both sides leaves no doubt in the mind of the reader if they’re on the “Old” or “New” side of the equation.

Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

This is where you can mix and match any of these styles by using what I like to call the 10 Magical Ways To Expand Anything:

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

These 10 Ways work in any niche and are always valuable to readers in that space.

The key is differentiation—if you promise benefits, list unconventional ones people don't already know. If you promise mistakes, surface the less obvious ones. It consistently gives the reader something fresh and useful.

So, to take this a level deeper, you can take an idea you’ve already written about in the previous 4 and expand it by adding one of the 10 Magical Ways!

For example, let’s take this short form post from Example 1:

There are AT LEAST 20+ more posts buried in this piece of short form!

You could write another post on:

  • Give 5 examples of classic literature every writer should study (then cycle through all the other types of writing here and/or sub-sets of literature, sales copy, etc.)

  • Explain 1 mistake writers make when studying writing to hone their skills

  • List 3 questions every writer should ask of every sentence they read to help them understand how to construct a good sentence

Etc., etc., etc.

Now, this leads me to another idea I want to explain in relation to short form:

How to treat your short form posts as “Outlines As Content.”

Outlines As Content 101

What does it mean to publish “Outlines As Content?”

Well, to fully understand this framework, here’s something I want you to internalize:

Everything Is A List

Every single piece of writing, in some way, is a list.

  • A New Yorker article discussing the benefits of living in a certain city? It’s a descriptive “list” of benefits.

  • A Buzzfeed article curating different kinds of socks to wear depending on the time of year? It’s “listing” socks, and “listing” the different times of year.

  • A novel that spends 3 pages describing a vacant house? Those 3 pages are “listing” qualities of the vacant house.

Listen closely: “The list goes on and on…”

What is the above? It’s a LIST!!!

At the end of the day, all great “writing” is basically just a Jenga tower of ideas stacked on top of each other. And so what’s the easiest way to figure out what “ideas” need to go together?

By listing them out!

Short-Form Content = An “Outline”

This is the first mental shift we want you to experience.

Short-form content doesn’t have to just be “short Tweets” or “short LinkedIn posts.” In fact, thinking about it that way is extremely inefficient—because it requires you to “think” about each idea individually. It also forces you to create 2x or 3x or 5x more content than you need to (you have to create short-form content and THEN different long-form content and THEN different even longer-form content, etc.).

Instead, we want you to think of all your short-form content (Tweets, short LinkedIn posts, even short Atomic Essays) as “Outlines As Content.”

What does that mean?

It means every time you write something “short,” what you should really be doing is testing to see whether or not this batch of ideas (this list) is compelling to readers. Because IF IT IS, then it becomes extremely clear which of those “outlines” is worth expanding into longer-form content.

Which compounds all of your efforts.

Let’s walk through how this works.

Step 1: Pick A Topic

This could be related to your niche, industry, or just an idea that’s been on your mind recently.

Now, let’s run it through a quick sense check to see if we’re clear on who we’re writing this short-form post for.

We’re going to use a framework I call “For Who/So That.”

First, make sure you’re clear on WHO this is for.

For example:

  • V1: “Copywriting”

  • V2 (FOR WHO?): “Copywriting For Beginners”

  • V3 (FOR WHO, SPECIFICALLY?): “Copywriting For Beginners Without College Degrees”

Specificity is the secret.

Second, what “value” are you sharing?

Step 2: What “Value” Do You Want To Share?

What are ALL the possible things you could give that person (the WHO) related to that topic?

This is the “value” of your writing:

  • “Are you giving me tips?”

  • “Or are you giving me steps?”

  • “Or are you giving me questions?”

  • “Or are you giving me reflections?”

  • Etc.

And as a recap, here are all the Proven Approaches you can use:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

Thirdly, make sure you’re clear on the SO THAT part of the FOR WHO/SO THAT framework.

Remember, having clarity on your topic and WHO it’s for is great.

But what takes your writing to the next level is also having clarity over why it matters to the reader. What’s in it for them? Why are you telling them whatever it is you’re telling them? SO THAT they can do… what?

We call these “incentives.”

These are things the reader wants:

  • …To Get Started {Skill}

  • …To Learn {Skill}

  • …To Master {Skill}

  • …To Overcome {Problem}

  • …To Unlock {Outcome}

  • …To Streamline {Process}

  • …To Get Your First {Small Outcome}

  • …To Achieve {Big Outcome}

  • …So You Don’t {Worst Outcome}

  • …To Hire Your First {Employee}

  • …To Buy Your First {Valuable Asset}

  • …To Sell Your First {Valuable Asset}

  • …To Make Your First {$X}

  • …To Build Your First {Product/Company}

  • …To Improve {Task}

  • …To Scale Your {Business}

  • …To Pitch Your {Idea}

  • …To Help You Fix {Problem}

  • …To Teach You {Solution}

  • …To Create The Perfect {Product}

  • …To {Do More} Without {More Work}

  • …To Make Progress On {Goal}

Etc.

And the beauty is, you can turn 1 small piece of “value” into dozens and dozens of topics just by changing the incentive.

Now let’s tie this all together (and you’ll NEVER run out of short-form ideas to write about for this topic).

Here’s your quick checklist:

  • Topic: What do you want to write about? FOR WHO, specifically?

  • Value: What are you giving the reader?

  • Incentive: SO THAT they can do… what? What’s the outcome?

Now watch how easy it is to generate ideas:

Let’s take Ghostwriting:

  • Topic: Ghostwriting FOR beginners

  • Value: Tips

  • Incentive: SO THAT they can do… what?

Check out all these Incentives (and how many short-form post ideas it gives me!):

  • Tips

    • …To Get Started Ghostwriting

    • …To Learn How To Become A Ghostwriter

    • …To Master Ghostwriting For CEOs

    • …To Overcome Critical Feedback From Ghostwriting Clients

    • …To Unlock Financial Success As A Ghostwriter

    • …To Streamline Your Ghostwriting Process

    • …To Get Your First Ghostwriting Client

    • …To Achieve Financial Success As A Ghostwriter

    • …So You Don’t Lose Ghostwriting Clients Due To Grammar Errors

    • …To Hire Your First Ghostwriting Subcontractor

    • …To Buy Your First Ghostwriting Course

    • …To Sell Your First Digital Product As A Ghostwriter

    • …To Make Your First $10,000 Per Month As A Ghostwriter

    • …To Build Your First Ghostwriting Agency

    • …To Improve Ghostwriting For Early-Stage SaaS Founders

    • …To Scale Your Ghostwriting Services

    • …To Pitch Your Ghostwriting Services To Clients

    • …To Help You Fix Over-Editing From Ghostwriting Clients

    • …To Teach You The Fundamentals Of Ghostwriting

    • …To Create The Perfect Ghostwritten Twitter Thread

    • …To Take On Most Ghostwriting Clients Without Working Harder

    • …To Make Progress On Becoming A Highly Paid Ghostwriter

That’s 22 ideas just from combining one of the “value” pieces on our list with a bunch of different incentives!

Step 3: Create “Outlines As Content”

Here’s the big aha we want you to have:

Once you go through the above exercise, do you need to go write 5,000 words in order to see whether or not that Topic + Value + Incentive is what the reader wants?

Of course not!

You can EASILY test the Topic + Value + Incentive by creating & publishing “Outlines As Content.”

Here’s how it works:

Let’s say our Topic is “copywriting,” our Value is “Tips,” and our Incentive is “…to learn” and you have the credibility because you’ve learned copywriting in the last 2 years.

Tips to learn copywriting.

Do you see how even just this sentence is the start of a short-form content idea? And what you’re “testing” is whether or not readers are interested in

  • A) “Tips…”

  • B) “To learn…”

  • C) “Copywriting…”

  • D) From you! (Because you’re applying the 2-Year test backwards)

Those are the 4 variables you are “testing” with readers.

And you can see how you can isolate these variables by creating different versions of this content and scheduling them a week or two apart from each other to see what works:

  • Do readers want Tips or Mistakes?

  • Do they want “to learn” or do they want a different incentive, like “to optimize?”

  • Are they interested in Copywriting, or a different topic?

  • And most of all, do they want to hear it from YOU? Or do they want to hear it from a different expert whose insights you’ve curated?

(Maybe you have the right Topic, Value, and Incentive, but you just need to either use your own credibility or borrow credibility from someone else)

Follow us…

If your Value is “Tips” (that’s what you’re giving the reader), what should you list out in order to “test” whether or not the reader finds those “tips” valuable?

TIPS!

For example:

Tips to learn copywriting:

  • Read Ogilvy On Advertising

  • Re-write sales letters by hand

  • Try to sell your own products online

  • Join a copywriting mastermind group

This is a Tweet. This is a LinkedIn post.

But it’s also an “Outline As Content.”

Which means, if this short-form post performs well, you now know: readers are interested in a) Tips, b) “To Learn,” c) Copywriting, d) From You, and e) these “Tips” you listed, they found helpful.

That’s a bunch of variables you now have a reasonable amount of data telling you are worth experimenting with over and over again! And you can repeat this “stack” of variables infinite times. Or you can take this “stack,” replace 1 or multiple variables, and compare performance again.

This is what makes Digital Writing such a science experiment.

And the more you publish, the more you learn.

Now, ready for your mind to really be blown?

Let’s say you want to execute all of the above, but you don’t want to write about it from YOUR personal experience anymore. You want to curate someone else’s credibility instead.

Look at all that happens:

For example:

Tips to learn copywriting from Craig Clemens, one of the most successful sales copywriters on planet earth:

  • Read Ogilvy On Advertising

  • Re-write sales letters by hand

  • Try to sell your own products online

  • Join a copywriting mastermind group

Literally the only difference (aside from whatever it is you’re “listing,” which will probably change based on whether YOU are coming up with it yourself versus listing other people’s insights) is adding a single sentence of context/credibility.

Is this coming from you? If so, you can add in your own sentence of credibility: “I have been copywriting for 10 years. Here are some tips to learn how.” But you don’t have to since you are the one writing it.

Or, you add a sentence of context/credibility about the person you picked up these tips from. Who are you learning from? Who are they? What have they done? What context clue can you give the reader that will make them trust you, because the person you’re studying has a ton of credibility?

That’s it!

Day 1 Assignment

Alright, we covered a lot!

Your assignment for today is 3 parts:

  1. Create & post your first piece of content

  2. Drop your first piece of content in the comments of Cole's X, LinkedIn, and Substack posts here:

    -- X

    -- LinkedIn

    -- Substack

  3. Comment in the Assignment 1 Skool thread with the link to your piece of content.

Ready, set, WRITE! ✍️

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 2 of the Start Writing Online Sprint!

In this lesson, we’re going to cover:

  • What an Atomic Essay actually is (and why we recommend them)

  • How to write the Perfect Headline for your Atomic Essay (so you can hook attention)

  • Our 5-step process for going from idea to a finished Atomic Essay in less than 10 minutes

And more!

All so you can start fleshing out your proven idea (which you tested in short form) and master the key fundamentals of Digital Writing.

Let’s dive in!

What Is An Atomic Essay?

(And Why Should You Write Them)

An Atomic Essay is a short, compressed essay of 250 words or less.


And the purpose of writing an Atomic Essay is to share 1 clear idea—small enough that you can come up with "something" to write about every day, but not so much that it feels like a burden (causing you to fall out of your daily writing habit).

Here’s an example from Dickie:

The reason we use the Atomic Essay format is because it is the easiest way for writers to learn the fundamentals of Digital Writing:

  • Headlines: In order to get readers to read your writing, you first need to "hook" them with a clear (not clever) headline (more on that in a moment).

  • Introductions: Right away, at the very beginning of your Atomic Essay (or any other kind of writing), you need to tell the reader why they should trust you. What makes your point of view credible, valuable, and worth their time? This needs to happen in the introduction.

  • Main Points: Next, the reader is going to "skim" your writing. If your Main Points (organized and formatted neatly) speak to their wants, needs, questions, and interests, then they will read your writing. If not, they will give your writing a quick skim, decide it's "not for them," and move on.

  • Writing Rhythms: To keep the reader engaged, it's important to give them small milestones to look forward to all the way down the page. Long paragraphs are a no-no.

  • Conclusions: And finally, how do you want the reader to feel at the end of your piece? How can you make sure you've delivered on the promise you made in your headline? The Atomic Essay format allows you to practice all 5 of these foundational pieces of all Digital Writing, every single day.

In other words, if you can write an Atomic Essay, you can write anything:

  • A Twitter Thread

  • A LinkedIn Post

  • A Newsletter

  • A Lead Magnet

  • A Book

Because all of these different “mediums” use the core components we practice with an Atomic Essay.

Ok, so how do you write an Atomic Essay?

Well, that’s the next part!

I’m going to share the 5 simple steps you can follow to write an Atomic Essay:

  • Step 1: Write A Headline

  • Step 2: Prep The Page With Your Main Points

  • Step 3: Add Context To Your Main Points

  • Step 4: Write Your Introduction

  • Step 5: Write Your Conclusion

Let’s dive in!

Step 1: Write A Headline

OK, I’m about to break down my framework for writing the “Perfect Headline.”


But every time I share this with writers, they come back with 3 pushbacks.

I want to get ahead of them now so you can focus on understanding all the components of a headline (and why you need them) without your brain screaming, “This is clickbait! No-one will read this! I’ll never build an audience using headlines like this!”

All wrong. And let me explain why.

  • “That’s clickbait! What if I don’t want to write headlines like this?”: Writers think if there is a number in the headline (7 Ways…), a triggering adjective (”Mind-boggling…”), or any hint at an outcome (”…so you can retire early”) then it’s automatically clickbait. This is not true. It’s only clickbait if you fail to keep your promise. If you promise to tell readers how they can buy their first rental property and retire early, but then don’t actually tell them how, then the reader hates you. But if you make that promise and over-deliver, giving them an entire step-by-step guide on how they can achieve this same outcome, then they love you. They’re going to bookmark your post. Send it to their friends. And likely go on to read everything else you’ve written—because you kept your promise.

  • “That headline is too long! How do I make it shorter?”: If your high school crush mailed you a 987-page book with everything they thought about you back then, how many pages would you read? The answer is: all of it. Length isn’t what matters. Some people think 1 single tweet is too long, and other people will read 987 pages and STILL want more. Which means length, in and of itself, isn’t what matters. What matters is whether you are speaking directly TO the reader. If you are, there’s no such thing as “too long.” And if you’re not, then even a 4-word headline is a waste of their time.

  • “My favorite writers don’t have to do this! Why do I have to?”: Seth Godin doesn’t write long headlines. His headlines are short and quippy. Things like, “Marketing Thoughts” or “Everyone Is Someone.” The problem is: you’re not Seth Godin. And so, first of all, it’s unproductive for you to compare yourself to someone who has been writing for decades (with an “s”). And second, we would ask the question: “But how many more people would read Seth Godin’s work if he used these tried-and-true headline techniques?” Are writers like Seth Godin successful because of their short, quippy, “clever” headlines? Or despite their short, quippy, “clever” headlines? (We would bet the latter—and that they would be 100x more widely read if they wrote clear headlines instead.)

In short: if you want to get people’s attention online, you need to learn how to write headlines that STOP them in their tracks and make them say, “Hmm… This looks like it’s for me. Maybe I should give this a read.”

To write an effective headline, you need 5 parts:

  1. The Number

  2. The What

  3. The Who

  4. The Why

  5. Twisting The Knife

Let’s run through each one.

Part 1: The Number

Before a reader gives you their attention, they do a quick cost-benefit analysis in their brain.

And it happens in a millisecond. We all do it.

But it’s a very simple equation:

How valuable does the reader perceive this piece to be DIVIDED by how long they think it’s going to take them to consume:

Value Divided by Time

And one of the easy ways readers do this cost-benefit analysis is by trying to figure out “how many” things you’re promising you are going to explain to them.

For example, what’s the perceived “time” difference between these 2 headlines?

  • 3 Steps To Brainstorm, Build, And Sell Your First Digital Product

  • 300 Steps To Brainstorm, Build, And Sell Your First Digital Product

Same idea. They both promise the same “value” and end result.

But the first one says, “This will only take 3 steps” a.k.a. “this won’t take you very much time,” whereas the second one says, “This will take 300 steps” a.k.a. “be prepared for this to take you a lot of time.”

Listicles have a bad reputation because everyone associates a number in the headline with BuzzFeed articles, but the reality is listicles are incredibly effective. They make it very easy for you to organize your ideas. But they also make it easy for the reader to quickly evaluate how long it’s going to take them to read your writing.

So, HOW MANY things are you promising the reader? And how can you signal this time investment right away in the headline?

Part 2: The What (The Topic)

Any content topic can be written through various different lenses:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

The key to writing a great headline is to combine one of those proven approaches with a specific topic—and make that as clear as possible right away in the headline.

Because that’s the fundamental question the reader is asking themselves BEFORE they start reading your writing: “What am I going to GET in exchange for reading?”

Here are a handful of examples:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips.”)

  • Informative Bitcoin Podcasts (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment.”)

This way, you’re being CLEAR about the topic. But you’re not just being CLEAR, you’re being SPECIFIC, too.

If you want your writing to resonate, specificity is the secret.

Part 3: Add a WHO

Alright, who’s your audience?

Again, you should have this dialled in from yesterday’s content strategy session.

Here are some examples:

  • …Tips For Project Managers

  • …Mistakes To Avoid As A Founder

  • …Trends For Wall Street Analysts

You want to make it very clear WHO your content is for (and, as a result, WHO it isn’t for).

Pro Tip: When you “name” an audience in your headline (or anywhere in your content), social algorithms actually take note—and this impacts how they distribute content. For example, if you put “Silicon Valley Founders” in your headline, who do you think X (Twitter)/LinkedIn is going to show your content to? People who have any (or all) of those keywords in their bio, in the content they create or consume, people they’re connected to, etc. This is how social algorithms work!

So, here are the same examples from previously, adding a WHO (audience) to each topic:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips for teenagers.”)

  • Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment, Gen-Zers This Is For You (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment, specifically for Gen-Z.”)

Notice how much more powerful the headline gets when you name the audience explicitly!

Part 4: Add a WHY (Or The Outcome)

The WHY in your headline is your opportunity to “sell” the reader on why they should read your writing over every other piece of content competing for their attention on the Internet:

  • IF the reader reads this, what do they get in return?

  • How is their life different in some meaningful way?

  • What will they learn as a result?

So, here are the same examples, adding a WHY (outcome) to each topic:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds To Start Generating $1,000 Per Month In Passive Rental Income Before You Graduate College (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips for teenagers, specifically to help generate $1,000 per month in passive rental income before graduating college.”)

  • Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners That Will Help You ‘Speak Blockchain’ Fluently (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto, so that I can ‘speak blockchain’ fluently.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment: If You Want To Save The Rainforest, Gen-Zers This Is For You (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment, specifically for Gen-Zers who want to save the rainforest.”)

Notice how the headline gets clearer and clearer the more of these pieces we add in.

And how much more powerful the headline gets when you name the outcome explicitly!

Part 5: Twist The Knife

Twist The Knife is just a fancy way of saying: “more.”

  • More problems

  • More benefits

  • More outcomes

Let’s use this headline as an example:

  • (V1) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn”

Not bad!

But watch how much more compelling the headline gets the more we “twist the knife”:

  • (V2) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn And Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List”

  • (V3) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn, Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List, And Start Selling Digital Products”

Notice how the more outcomes you list (and the more you “Twist The Knife”), it really doesn’t matter that your headline is getting longer and longer. As long as these benefits and outcomes speak directly to the wants and needs of your target reader, they’ll keep reading—because you’re talking about them!

Here are a couple more examples, just to give you more pattern recognition:


Step 2: Prep The Page With Your Main Points

Ok, we just spent a TON of time on the headline of your Atomic Essay.

Why?

BECAUSE IT’S THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF YOUR ESSAY.

You should spend 80% of your time on the headline. The headline is what hooks the attention of the reader and gets them to actually engage with your writing. And if you don’t have a headline that captures their attention, they’ll never read the rest of your essay.

Now, we’re going to flesh out the essay.

First, we start by “Prepping The Page.”

Prepping The Page is how you turn a blank Atomic Essay (with just a headline) into an 80% finished Atomic Essay.

All you need to do is list out your main points and make it clear to the reader what they’re getting (after all, they’ll skim these points before they read the rest of your Atomic Essay—this is how we consume all content online).

Here’s how to think about it:

  • If your headline promises “3 Habits”, list out 3 Habits: “Habit #1: [Insert Habit]”, “Habit #2: [Insert Habit]”, “Habit #3: [Insert Habit]”

  • If your headline promises “3 Tips”, list out 3 Tips: “Tip #1: [Insert Tip]”, “Tip #2: [Insert Tip]”, “Tip #3: [Insert Tip]”

  • If your headline promises “3 Reasons”, list out 3 Reasons: “Reason #1: [Insert Reason]”, “Reason #2: [Insert Reason]”, “Reason #3: [Insert Reason]”

It really is that simple!

The key here is to make these subheadlines in your Atomic Essay. The next step is where we add some text to flesh out each point.

Step 3: Add Context To Your Main Points

Ok, now we’re cruising!

Let’s put some meat on the bones of these Main Points.

Remember: we’re not writing the next great American Novel. Or a 60,000-word non-fiction book. We’re writing an Atomic Essay—that’s no more than 250-300 words! So don’t think you need to write a ton here.

For each Main Point, ask yourself:

“What else will the reader find useful here?”

You can share tips, stories, examples, reasons why, stats, insights, etc. You’re just slightly expanding the idea of each Main Point.

(And we’ll dive more into how to expand these points into a full-blown Article in tomorrow’s session!)

Alright, now it’s time to round this Atomic Essay out with an Introduction and Conclusion.

Step 4: Write Your Introduction

Here’s a simple checklist I like to run through when I’m writing my introduction to an Atomic Essay.

I like to include at least one of these points in the introduction:

  • What is this about?

  • Who is this for?

  • Why should they read it? (The promise—what you're going to give them)

  • What credibility do you have to talk about this? (You could have lived it yourself or you can curate other people's credibility, e.g., "I studied people who experienced this")

Here are some examples:

  • “Over the last 5 years, I’ve lost 100 pounds and gotten into the best shape of my life.

    If you want to get in shape but you’re not sure how to start, here are the 3 steps you should take to find the right gym for you.”

  • “I’ve been flipping real estate for the last 2 years—and made $500,000 profit in the process.

    These are the 5 reasons why I think every college graduate should invest in real estate (so they can retire early in their 30s):”

  • “I read 100 X Articles on Claude Design.

    Here are 5 tips to help you design your first lead magnet landing page (even if you have zero design background):”

What you’re doing is strengthening the case you made in your headline.

Alright, onto the final Step.

Step 5: Write Your Conclusion

We’re taught in school to recap all the points in the conclusion of our reports and essays.

But luckily for us, this isn’t school! It’s the real world. So, don't just recap everything for the sake of recapping.

Add something new—a new detail, an extra piece to the story, or a final insight.

This can be just a single sentence that sits at the bottom of the Atomic Essay.

By the way, if you want to write and publish 30 Atomic Essays over 30 days, highly recommend you joining our writing challenge Ship 30 for 30. We dive deeper into all these Digital Writing frameworks (& more!) over 30 days, helping you publish every single day for 1 whole month! Click here to find out more.

Day 2 Assignment

Now, the good part!

For today’s assignment, you’re going to write an Atomic Essay 💣

Full instructions are inside the Skool post below!

Ready, set, write, PUBLISH! ✍️

records.description: Hey there! And welcome to Day 3 of the Start Writing Online Sprint! In this lesson, we’re going to cover: - What a LinkedIn Carousel is & why you should create
records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 3 of the Start Writing Online Sprint!

In this lesson, we’re going to cover:

  • What a LinkedIn Carousel is & why you should create them

  • The best way to write and structure your LinkedIn Carousel

  • How to “build” these Carousels so you can start publishing them to LinkedIn

And more!

All so you can start creating one of LinkedIn’s most popular content formats.

Let’s dive in!

What Is A LinkedIn Carousel?

This is one of the most popular formats on LinkedIn.

You will have seen them. They look a bit like this:

They are a collection of images, packaged up into a PDF, and posted as a “Document” on LinkedIn.

When they are posted, the reader is able to swipe through the Cards to read the post. Readers swipe left or right to move through them, just like a slideshow. If written and created properly, each Card creates a tiny “open loop” that only closes when they swipe. Instead of scrolling past a single block of text or a static image, readers pause, swipe, and stay.

The goal of Slide 1 is to get your reader to click see Slide 2. And so on.

“But Cole… why are they so popular? Why does everyone seem to create them?”

Ah, glad you asked!

And it can be boiled down to 2 reasons:

Reason 1: Carousels a “visual hook” you can use on LinkedIn.

The other types of visual hooks are Photos, Videos, and Infographics. So, let’s talk about why visual hooks are so important on LinkedIn.

It’s for the same reason any hook is important—to stop the scroll. However, our brains prioritize images over text. Shapes, faces, contrast, and colors hit the attention system almost instantly, before language comprehension even kicks in. Pictures are simply faster for us to recognize.

Think about how you actually scroll through LinkedIn:

  • You scan for visuals first (Is this interesting, familiar, or different?)

  • You process words next (What does this mean, and do I care?)

Your eyes jump image to image, face to face, cue to cue. And somewhere in your rapid-fire scanning, something makes you pause.

That “something” is usually visual.

And that’s why it’s worth optimizing not just what you say but how it looks in the LinkedIn feed.

Reason 2: They allow you to create a “snackable” piece of long-form content.

This is actually pretty genius.

Carousels can be as long as you want. But to a reader, they feel easy to consume. Why? Because you’re guiding the reader through each part of your piece in short-form. Which makes consuming this “long-form” piece of content super easy.

(Remember what we said about creating an “open loop” with each Card? That’s what makes these so snackable!)

In other words, it’s a pretty unique Digital Writing formatting technique.

Let’s look at this example from Eddie Shleyner—where he’s taken this technique to the next level.

He’s famous for being up front about the number of words in his writing before you even start writing.

And he translates this to his Carousels, too:

Notice how the number of words decreases as you read the Carousel:

But you don’t have to add “Words Left” like Eddie here.

Because LinkedIn has it’s own built in feature to let the reader know how “far” they have to go to finish the piece.

It tells you how many slides you’ve consumed out of the total number of slides:

Then on mobile, it doesn’t tell you how many are remaining but does give you an idea of how many pages are in the Carousel itself:

Alright, now we know what a Carousel is and why they’re so popular… let’s start creating them!

How To Write & Structure A Carousel

Here’s a recommended structure you can use to create your Carousels:

Step 1: Create Your Cover Card

First, you create the Cover Card.

This is the first Card in the Carousel.

Here’s a checklist I always run down when creating this first part:

  1. Use a strong visual hook (e.g. use relevant images, etc.).

  2. Write a headline on the cover to re-hook the reader. The main hook lives in the LinkedIn post, but this is the second one. Follow the Headline Writing guide in the Atomic Essay module for a complete guide on how to write a hook for this part of the Carousel.

  3. Write a sub-headline to twist the knife with another opportunity or benefit. Or use it to increase tension.

You want to spend around 80% of your writing time on this part as it’s the part that hooks the reader’s attention on the feed.

Step 2: Write Your Body Cards

These are the main parts of the post.

Here’s a checklist you can use to write these Cards:

  1. Try to stick with one idea per card. E.g. a Mistake, Step, Tip, etc.

  2. Make the first line of the card as short as possible. We want to reduce the cognitive load on the reader. In fact, make all lines in the card as short as possible. Don’t be afraid to split out “bulky” ideas into 2 slides.

  3. Clearly label Steps, Tips, Mistakes, etc. You want to make sure you label your card headers so the reader can skim the Carousel if they want (before diving into the meat of the content): e.g. Tip 1, Mistake 1, etc. Make sure to format it in H1 or H2.

  4. Use bulleted lists. Very important! Again, it makes the card easier to read.

  5. Create an open loop between cards (if possible). This is to keep attention all the way through the Carousel. These mini-open loops help keep the reader engaged.

Step 3: Add A Wrap-up Card

This is a short recap of everything you’ve covered in the Carousel.

Step 4: End On A CTA Card

If you’re trying to get your reader to take action, this is where you introduce the “Ask.”

This could be to:

  • Join your newsletter

  • Sign up for a lead magnet

  • Share the post with others

Etc., etc., etc.

Now you know how to write and structure your Carousel, let’s look at creating them.

How To Create A Carousel

When building your carousel, aside from the content INSIDE the Carousel, there are 3 important areas to think about:

  • The platform you use to build the Carousel

  • What you write in the accompanying post

  • How to title the Carousel

Let’s take a look at each one in turn.

How To Build Your Carousel (Pick Your Platform)

There are many different ways to create a Carousel for LinkedIn:

  • If you want a beginner-friendly option to get started, you can create lightweight, text-only Carousels using Typeshare.

  • If you want something slightly more advanced, you can create more branded-looking Carousels using Gamma.

  • And if you want something pro-grade, you can design your own brand kit and design studio inside Claude Design or ChatGPT.

Now, how do you write the post that goes with the Carousel?

How To Write The Accompanying Text Post

You might think that the Carousel is the main event of the Carousel Post.

Well, not quite!

The Text Post you pair with the Carousel is just as important as the Carousel itself. Why? Because what you include here will determine whether the reader will read the full post.

Now, there are 2 schools of thought when it comes to what you should include in this Text Post (aside from writing a strong hook and using the formatting tips we’ve already covered):

  1. Write a short, punchy introduction to encourage people to read the Carousel

  2. Write a high-level summary of the Carousel to tease the value and get people to read it

Both are designed to increase retention on the post (which in turn signals to the algorithm that this content is worth sharing!).

Here’s an example of the first approach:

Notice how the rest of the post is short and sweet (and introduces the Carousel as a way to find out what the 7 small habits are):

Here’s an example of the second approach:

When you click See More, you see some additional context AND an overview of the points covered in the Carousel:

The idea here is that the reader has a “lay of the land” before diving into the content.

Highly recommend you experiment with both approaches in your client’s content!

How To Write The Document Title

Alright, one final pro tip before we wrap up the Carousel section.

The Document Title is VALUABLE real estate on LinkedIn:

This is the Title that appears on the Carousel when you hover over it in the feed (like this):

So you should see this as a secondary headline, and it’s worth spending a few minutes making sure this is short and punchy (and follows all my rules on how to write the perfect headline).

Day 3 Assignment

Alright, your assignment for today is to create your first (or next!) LinkedIn Carousel.

Use either Typeshare or Gamma to do this.

Full instructions are inside the Skool post below!
