records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 4 of the Start Writing Online Sprint!

In this lesson, we’re going to cover:

  • Why you should expand all your proven ideas into long-form articles

  • How to expand any idea into a full-blown Article you can post online

  • The 6 simple steps to creating an Article that will keep your readers interested (and hook them all the way down the page)

And more!

All so you can start doubling down on the signal you’ve been getting on your published short-form and Atomic Essays to give your readers more of what they want and build your audience further.

Let’s dive in!

Why You Should Expand All Your Proven Ideas..

Into Long-Form Articles

Every idea you post on the internet has the potential to become a digital business.

Honestly! Ideas that resonate with your audience should be doubled down on and expanded further. You’re just giving “more” of what your readers want. And eventually, you can sell all of this extra content, ideas, and frameworks to your audience.

But first, we need to figure out which ideas to double down on.

This is simple. If an idea attracts more views, likes, and comments compared to your other content/ideas, then it should be expanded into a longer-form piece. I call this method “Lean Writing” and it’s the way you take one idea and build it into a library of content and eventually a business.

This is how it works:

  • Write a short-form post

  • Turn your best ideas into an Atomic Essay

  • Turn that idea into a long-form Article

  • Into a newsletter

  • Into a free email course

  • Into a paid digital product

  • Into an entire business

Start small, keep testing your ideas at every level, and eventually you can build a business.

(Notice how we’re covering the first 3 points in this Sprint? You’re already making excellent progress if you want to turn your online writing into a digital business!)

Alright, so once you’ve seen which ideas are resonating with your audience (from the short-form posts and Atomic Essays you’ve been posting), it’s time to expand these ideas into a long-form Article.

Why Articles?

For all the reasons we write Atomic Essays: they teach you the fundamental concepts of Digital Writing AND are a great way to learn how you can expand any idea into “more” content (which is the whole game of writing online).

Plus, they’re going through a moment on X right now and seem to go viral more than any other content format:

Ok, so how do you write an Article?

Let’s take a look.

How To Write An Article In 6 Simple Steps

If you’re worried you can’t write a full-length article, then I have some good news:

If you can write an Atomic Essay, you can write an Article.

We covered a lot of the key frameworks in the Atomic Essays section. With Articles, there are just a few expansion, formatting, and stylistic skills you need to master. But these are super straightforward and once you’ve nailed them you can use them to continue up the Lean Writing ladder (writing a free email course, a newsletter, a digital product, all the way up to a digital business).

Let’s take this step by step.

Step 1: Write Your Headline

This is the same framework we covered when we wrote our headlines for our Atomic Essays.

As a quick recap, the Perfect Headline has 5 components:

  1. The Number

  2. The What

  3. The Who

  4. The Why

  5. Twisting The Knife

Once you have your headline, it’s time to Prep The Page with your main ideas.

Step 2: Prep The Page To Mirror Your Headline

Again, we covered this previously.

But I want to dig a little deeper and talk about the importance of something I call “Mirroring.”

Mirroring is the single most important formatting technique.

Think of Mirroring as a way of anchoring the reader’s eyes on the page. When you Mirror sections, what happens is the reader can’t help but feel like they are staring at a work of art—because you’ve constructed more than just words on a page. What you’ve done is create sections, blocks, and distinct areas where you’d like them to direct their attention.

Mirroring basically means you take one element and then repeat it:

  • Throughout your entire essay/piece.

  • Throughout an entire section (or multiple sections).

  • And even individual sentences.

This is a very subtle but powerful formatting technique and I’m going to talk about it at every level of the Article writing process.

Here’s how to mirror the promise in your headline:

Let’s say the headline of your piece is: “3 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars.”

The Promise here is “3 Mistakes.”

Why would a reader click on this piece? To read your 3 Mistakes. Simple.

The way you Mirror this promise all the way down the page then is to repeat this same promise over and over again. Which means each one of your Main Points/Subheads would follow the same wording, flow, and punctuation.

Like this:

  • Mistake #1:

  • Mistake #2:

  • Mistake #3:

This might seem like a simple nuance, but it’s more powerful than most writers realize.

When a reader clicks on your piece, they are immediately looking for the “promise” you made them in the headline. So, if you promised them “3 Mistakes,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “3 Mistakes.” If you promised them “6 Lessons,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “6 Lessons.” If you promised them “11 Crazy Gadgets,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “11 Crazy Gadgets.” And so on.

Tying your Main Points to the promise in your headline is one of the simplest ways to immediately upgrade the skimmability of your writing—and make it easy for readers to fly through your content.

But this is only the beginning!

As you begin to write, you may decide to take some creative liberties with your Main Points.

That’s fine! BUT the golden rule is: if you change 1 Main Point/Subhead, you need to “Mirror” that change all the way down the page.

Just look at these 2 lists of Main Points/Subheads and notice which list your eye sees as more visually appealing:

Example 1

  • Mistake #1:

  • The Right Way To Think:

  • Lesson I Learned:

  • Another Mistake:

  • Sometimes, all you need to do is make sure you’re focusing on the right thing.

  • Ending Thoughts:

Example 2

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #1:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #2:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #3:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #4:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #5:

Which one of these lists is more visually appealing?

Which list do you immediately assume is “more organized?”

The 2nd one! But there’s a very clear reason as to why.

The reason is because readers love similarities. When each of your Main Points/Subheads “looks the same” and there is a clear pattern, this gives the reader reassurance. They understand how you’re moving them down the page, and they also understand where they are in the piece. But when your subheads are alternating style, capitalization, punctuation, etc., each of these changes makes the reader feel more and more “lost.” They can’t tell why you are changing the rules on them.

So, if you are going to make a change to one of your Main Points/Subheads, remember to Mirror that change all the way down the page.

Readers love patterns.

Alright, once you’ve Prepped The Page with an outline of your Main Points, let’s start expanding each section.

Step 3: Expand Each Section With Sub Points

Using The 10 Magical Ways

Here’s where things get fun.

Remember:

Once you have your headline and your outline clarified, 80% of the writing process is done. Why? Because writing isn’t really about writing. Writing is about “thinking.” And the outline is where you get all of your “thinking” clarified.

Once this is done, the “writing” itself is easy!

This means, that before you even start writing sentences, simply go through your outline and expand your outline into more bullets of information. Think of it like you’re jotting notes to yourself inside your outline: “Here I want to say, X, over here I want to say Y, and right here I want to say Z.” You want to get all of this “thinking” out of the way—so by the time you start writing sentences, you are basically just cleaning up your “notes.”

Versus starting with a blank page.

Now you might be thinking, “How do I expand these Main Points?”

Here’s an easy framework:

How To Expand Anything: The 10 Magical Ways

There are 10 ways you can expand LITERALLY any piece of writing.

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

Don’t believe me?

Watch this—using a sample outline.

Let’s return to my headline of “3 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars.”

Here’s my outline:

  • Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time

  • Mistake #2: Not having clients on auto-pay

  • Mistake #3: Not taking any money out of the business

We can expand each of these “Mistakes” with other ways from our 10 Magical Ways (I’m going to use Reasons, Benefits, and Steps):

  • Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time (let’s expand this with the Reasons Why this was a mistake):

    • Reason #1:

    • Reason #2:

    • Reason #3:

  • Mistake #2: Not having clients on auto-pay (let’s expand this with the Benefits of having them on auto-pay):

    • Benefit #1:

    • Benefit #2:

    • Benefit #3:

  • Mistake #3: Not taking any money out of the business (let’s expand this with the Steps I’d take to take money out of the business):

    • Step #1:

    • Step #2:

    • Step #3:

Or I could expand it with other Ways:

  • The first Mistake could be expanded with with Personal Stories of how this cost me millions of dollars

  • The second Mistake could be expanded with Questions you should ask when moving clients to auto-pay

  • The third Mistake could be expanded with Tips on how to take money out of the business responsibly.

See?

You can expand ANY Main Point just by rotating through different combinations of the 10 Magical Ways—and you can easily expand any section.

So, how do you decide which of the 10 Magical Ways to use?

Easy!

It’s up to you. But a good rule of thumb I use is: “What will be the most useful thing to list out for the reader?” In other words, think back to your 2-Year Test. What would you have wanted to know if you were completely new to this topic? What would you want to know 2 years ago? There’s your answer.

And the best part?

Your readers will often tell you what they want to hear more of in comments, DMs, and what they interact with.

So, don’t overthink it. Just follow what you think would be useful and what your readers are asking for.

Alright, we’ve got our Main Points and Sub Points all outlined. Time to dig into the actual “writing.”

Step 4: Write A Single Sentence Opener

For Each Section & Fill In Any Details

When the reader opens a piece of content and is immediately confronted by a giant wall of text, what’s the first thing that goes through their brain?

“Geez. This sure does look like a heavy lift.”

Even if the content is light and fun. Even if the language is simple. VISUALLY, it looks difficult—because that giant paragraph of text looks like a brick wall.

Publications like The New Yorker do this constantly. (And writers think big, chunky paragraphs make them seem “smart.”)

But guess what?

Giant paragraphs don’t make readers want to consume your content MORE.

They make them want to consume your content LESS.

Before you’ve even read a single word of the following, your brain is already tired!

But if we kept this text exactly the same, and just broke out the first sentence… guess what?

All of a sudden, it feels approachable! And the reader can easily “slide” into the reading experience. I call this using single-sentence openers, and there are a few types you can insert into the introduction of your Article and at the start of every Main Point in your Article.

Add In Your Proven Single-Sentence Openers

So, go through each section and add a single sentence opener.

But what KIND of sentences? Great question!

Here’s the list I always come back to:

Let’s run through some examples of each one:

Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.

  • “Most people will spend their entire careers being good at the wrong thing.”

  • “Your morning routine is quietly deciding the outcome of your year.”

  • “The best business decision I ever made cost me my biggest client.”

Open with a thought-provoking question.

  • “What would you build if you knew no one would ever judge it?”

  • “Why do we trust strangers on the internet more than the experts in our own field?”

  • “What if the habit you're most proud of is the one holding you back?”

Open with a controversial opinion.

  • “Networking events are a waste of time for anyone serious about their work.”

  • “Most "productivity" advice is just procrastination wearing a nicer outfit.”

  • “Passion is overrated; the people who win are the ones who show up when they feel nothing.”

Open with a moment in time.

  • “At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, I deleted three years of work and felt nothing but relief.”

  • “The email arrived twelve minutes before the meeting that would change everything.”

  • “On Monday, May 23rd, 2019, I was halfway through my coffee when I realized I'd been wrong about all of it.”

Open with a vulnerable statement.

  • “I made six figures last year and still felt like a complete fraud.”

  • “For most of my twenties, I was terrified that everyone could see how little I knew.”

  • “I almost quit the week I made my first $50,000 on the internet.”

Open with a weird, unique insight.

  • “The fastest way to be remembered in a meeting is to be the one who says the least.”

  • “Boredom is the most underrated signal your brain ever sends you.”

  • “The people who give the best advice are usually the ones who ignored it first.”

Alright, we’ve added in our single sentence openers.

Now it’s time to flesh out your outline of Main Points and Sub Points and turn them into complete sentences that link to each other.

Flesh Out Your Main Points And Sub Points

What you’re doing here is turning all your Sub Points into complete sentences and giving the reader more insight, context, and information.

Again, just ask, “What does the reader need to hear to understand this point? What can I give them that helps them make sense of the Sub Point & Main Point?”

Then all you need to do is link the Sub Points and Main Points with little phrases like:

  • “Which leads me to the next example…”

  • “Another reason why this mistake cost me so dear is…”

  • “Once you’ve answered this question, ask yourself this second question…”

Alright, all the “writing” here is done!

But we’re not at publishable Article just yet. It’s time to add in one of the most important parts of any Article. This is the number one thing which will make any piece of writing you publish online easy to consume.

Formatting & Style.

Step 5: Formatting & Style

Writing Rhythms And Lists

The overarching idea here is you’re trying to create rhythm and musicality in your writing.

Contrary to popular belief, musicality and rhythm in your writing are not difficult to create.

It’s all about sentence length. And the key to creating musicality and rhythm is literally nothing more than just alternating between long sentences and short sentences—ideally in some sort of pattern. See? Short sentence, followed by a medium sentence, followed by a long sentence. If you pay attention as you read, you can “hear” the pauses, the build-up, and the long crescendo of pace as the sentences are processed in your brain.

This is all you have to do to make your writing “flow.”

Let’s dig into some other ways to add flow to your writing.

Writing Rhythm Basics: 1/3/1

Now, I talk more about this in my book The Art and Business of Online Writing, but here’s a quick crash course.

{1} The simplest “rhythm writing” pattern is what we like to call 1/3/1.

{3} This means you open with 1 short to medium-length sentence. Then, in three sentences you add more description and color. And then you finish the idea with one single sentence.

{1} Just like this section here.

1/3/1 literally refers to the number of sentences, and the pattern they’re stacked in.

One strong opening sentence. Three descriptive sentences, advancing your point forward. And then one final concluding sentence.

And you can literally repeat 1/3/1 over and over again, all the way down the page (just like we’re doing here!).

Expanding The Middle

Now let’s say 1/3/1 doesn’t give you enough space to say what you want to say.

The secret to maintaining effective rhythms in your writing is to “expand the middle.” This means keeping the same 1/3/1 structure (single sentences to open and close your longer paragraphs of description), but adding content to the middle part of the “sandwich.”

For example:

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/6/1

  • 1/7/1

See how the structure is the same, but all that is changing is the length of the middle paragraph?

The key here is to maintain your single-sentence “bookends” (the opener and closer sentences). This gives the reader an easy entry point into your writing (or next section). And rewarding them with a single sentence at the end of your elongated paragraph of description.

So, if you’re ever going to expand your writing, remember to expand the middle.

How To Use Mirroring To Make Your Sub Points Visually Appealing

You can also “Mirror” within each section of your piece.

For example: if you open with 1 clear declarative sentence, and then give a 5-sentence paragraph description, and then close with a final declarative sentence, you should strive to repeat that same cadence and pattern (1/5/1) in each of the subsequent sections. This helps readers find the flow/melody of your writing. Which makes it even easier for them to quickly skim and consume your content.

This section (and the end of the last section) is an example of this idea in action (it’s a 1/3/1).

What you want to avoid is individual sections looking vastly different.

If one section is 3 giant paragraphs, and then another section is literally 2 sentences, you have a problem: they “look” off-balance.

Instead, you want to strive for each section (inside each of your Main Points/Sub Points) to be visually the same—either in length, or in formatting choices and style. For example, as I’m writing this, I am thinking about the section right before this where I explain the Mirroring technique. I could stop writing at the previous sentence, but then it would look a bit “off-balance.”

So, I flushed out the description out so that it “LOOKS” the same.

See?

Bulleted or Numbered Lists

Ah, now this is how you take your formatting skills to the next level.

The vast majority of Digital Writers & Digital Creators don’t even write using Main Points/Subheads.

Instead, you click on their content, and it’s just one big blocky paragraph after another. (Legacy writers struggle with this the most. And it’s why even New York Times’ best-selling authors struggle to get distribution on their digital content—because they are used to writing longwinded books, not skimmable Atomic Essays, Twitter Threads, and LinkedIn posts.)

Of the Digital Writers & Digital Creators who do learn the importance of organizing their content using Main Points/Sub Points, only a small percentage of them graduate to the next level:

Using Bulleted or Numbered Lists.

  • Can you tell how satisfied your brain is to read a quick bulleted list right here?

  • Can you “feel” how it’s a nice break after reading the above few paragraphs?

  • Do you notice how easy this section of bulleted takeaways is to skim?

  • Are you enjoying how this feels, as a reader, right now?

Incorporating short bulleted or numbered lists inside your Main Points is one of the most underrated writing & formatting techniques that exists today. Because what these bulleted or numbered lists force you to do is strip away all the unnecessary explanation—and just tell the reader what’s most important.

No unnecessary description.

No rambling.

Just boom, boom, boom.

If you can master the art of writing Clear Titles, organizing your big ideas with Main Points/Sub Points, and making sections more skimmable by using Bulleted or Numbered lists, then pat yourself on the back.

You have a skill set 99% of Digital Writers & Digital Creators do not have.

Furthermore, if you are interested in being hired as a writer/ghostwriter, nothing will impress clients more than seeing your magic at work—presenting content in a coherent, organized, and visually appealing way.

Alright, we’re almost done!

Step 6: Write Your Introduction & Conclusion

Writing Your Introduction

Next, as you finish the Article, you want to make a note to yourself:

“Why should the reader trust me? Why am I the right person to write about this topic? Should they trust me because of my Personal Credibility? Or because of my Borrowed Credibility?”

These are important questions to ask yourself.

Readers aren’t as picky as most people think. You don’t need to be a Harvard Graduate, a Rocket Scientist, or a political official for readers to trust you. All you need to do is tell them why they should take what you’re saying seriously. Our favorite example is: imagine a friend (or a friend of a friend) asked you for a Friday Night Movie Recommendation. It really doesn’t matter what movie you recommend, inevitably the person will ask, “Why? Why should I watch this?” To which you will most likely reply: “Because I’ve watched every single Rom Com movie on Netflix, and trust me, this one is the best.”

That’s all they need to hear. And ba-da-bing, your opinion is trusted.

Writing is no different: Readers need a reason to trust you.

So, what makes you credible?

  • Is it how many hours you’ve spent doing this thing?

  • Is it because of some meaningful milestone you’ve achieved?

  • Is it the number of years you’ve spent studying and practicing this thing?

And if you don’t have any personal credibility, how might you be able to borrow that credibility from someone else?

  • Is this what someone else with decades of experience says to do?

  • Is this what a very smart book, written by a very smart person, recommends?

  • Is this wisdom you’ve gathered by spending time around other people who have achieved this same thing?

Make a note to yourself in the introduction of whatever you’re writing:

“This is why you should trust what I’m about to tell you.”

For example:

  • “How do I know how to build a real estate empire? Because over the last 10 years, I’ve bought and sold over 50 different rental properties.”

  • “Why should you take my Netflix series recommendations? Because I’ve watched over 5,000 hours of Netflix shows and movies.”

  • “Why is this the best strategy to get distribution on your writing? Because I went and interviewed 20 different best-selling authors, and this is what they said to do.”

The reader has no problem trusting you—you just have to give them a reason to!

Add this to your Introduction.

Adding A Conclusion or Recap

The last piece of formatting is the ending:

  • Writing a conclusion

  • Sharing a recap

  • Providing a CTA (Call To Action)

That said, my personal philosophy is that conclusions are optional.

So, when should you write a conclusion?

Here’s a good rule of thumb:

If your conclusion is just repeating everything you just said, you don’t need a conclusion.

Right?

Remember: you aren’t writing a 12th grade English paper. You are writing for highly impatient digital readers (people who would much rather swipe back to TikTok and watch 7-second videos of young children falling face-first into bowls of macaroni and cheese). So if your “conclusion” is just you repeating yourself, ditch it. Just let the piece end. Make it a cliffhanger! Because if what you wrote was truly helpful and beneficial to the reader, they will inevitably want to click around and read more content from you.

Which means you should only write “conclusions” if they add something new to the piece.

You should only write “conclusions” if they tie everything together in a new way.

  • New insights

  • A final closing story

  • A clarifying statement

  • More information about your credibility

  • Etc., etc., etc.

Alright, we’re done!

Day 4 Assignment

Phew, that’s it!

Now, for the final part:

Your assignment for today is to sit down and write your first Article.

(Ideally, use a proven idea from your short-form or Atomic Essays.)

Full instructions are inside the Skool post below:

records.content:
Hey there!

And welcome to Day 5 of the Start Writing Online Sprint!

In this lesson, we’re going to cover:

  • Why 95% of AI prompts give terrible outputs

  • How to use the concept of “Unbundling” to write world-class prompts

  • The 5 parts to writing an AI Mega Prompt

All so you can gain efficiencies in your writing/business processes, use these prompts in your marketing, and build digital products around your thinking (via your prompts).

Let’s dive in!

Why 95% Of AI Prompts Give Terrible Outputs

The vast majority of prompts give results you can barely use.

But that’s not because AI is “bad” at writing (or any other task you want it to perform). It’s because most people can’t articulate what they actually want. And the great thing about AI is that the bottleneck to getting good results from it isn’t your ability to code or your knowledge of a particular technology. No, the bottleneck is your ability to describe clearly to AI what you actually want.

There’s something we say over and over again in our AI Writing Skool:

“You can't automate what you can't articulate.”

The difference between ineffective and effective AI writing comes down entirely to the ability to articulate the instructions.

People write "go do this thing" and don't realize how many implied components they're deferring to the technology.

You haven’t told AI a number of variables that impact what it produces:

  • Is this good or bad output?

  • Is this what you want stylistically?

  • Is this actually how you, the writer, would do it?

And I know what you’re thinking…

“But Cole, I’ve tried writing longer prompts, but I still get AI slop—it’s just bad at writing!”

All good.

After all, this is still a relatively new technology, and we’re all trying to get the hang of it! If you’re not getting the results (or near to the results) you want from AI, then you need to beef up your prompt even more. You need to remove all doubt from AI’s “mind” about what to do for you.

Let’s look at an example.

Bad Example of an AI Prompt: “I need help writing some social content for a client of mine. She works in health and wellness. Write me three really great social posts that she'll love."

Here’s what happens when you feed this to ChatGPT:

Notice how AI even works through some of the assumptions it is making when writing these posts!

And guess what?

The output is pretty average (no surprises there!).

So, how do you write good AI prompts?

Well, here’s a quick comparison of the qualities of Bad vs. Good AI Prompt Writing.

Bad Prompt Writing:

  • Uses general, “bundled” language

  • Contains subjective directions

  • Specifies no clear format

  • Gives no examples of the required output/thinking

  • Doesn’t provide an output request

On the other hand, Good Prompt Writing:

  • Uses specific language to describe “unbundled” tasks

  • Gives objective directions

  • Specifies certain formatting frameworks for output

  • Lists out exact examples of output/thinking

  • Gives an exact output request

So, how do you achieve all of these?

Well, to do all those things in the “Good Prompt Writing” list, you need to UNBUNDLE your language and tasks.

Which is what we’re going to look at next.

What Is Unbundling?

If I told you to write a “really great” piece of writing, would you know what I expected?

Of course not!

Why?

Because “really great” is subjective. Ask 10 people to define it, and you’ll get 10 answers.

Answers like:

  • “It needs to read like a Hemingway short story.”

  • “The writing should be laden with stories and examples like a Ryan Holiday book”

  • “The world-building should be elegant and majestic, as if I’m reading an Ursula K. Le Guin story.”

And even in THOSE answers we have “bundled” language:

  • What is a Hemingway short story like?

  • What kind of stories should I use to be like Holiday?

  • How does Le Guin execute her world-building?

People use these bundled terms because they don’t know EXACTLY what they’re asking for.

So, to drive this home, I want to give you a non-writing example.

Let’s say your friend Tom is staying the weekend.

You say, "Hey Tom, I could really use your help doing the dishes." But "doing the dishes" is a bundled term**.** Tom has no idea HOW you want them done. And Tom ends up making a mess in your kitchen, overfilling your dishwasher, and clogging your filters with leftover food!

(Yeah, he isn’t the best house guest!)

But Tom becomes effective when you “unbundle” the request of “doing the dishes”:

  • Emptying the dishwasher

  • Putting the dirty plates, cups, pots, and pans in the sink

  • Scrubbing the food off of each plate, cup, pot, and pan

  • Putting dishwasher-safe plates and cups in the dishwasher

  • Hand-washing the remaining pots, pans, and non-dishwasher-safe items

  • Scrubbing the countertops and stove with a soapy sponge

  • Cleaning and drying the countertops and stove with a wet, and then dry, paper towel

When you look at a list like that, notice how saying, “Just do the dishes!” isn’t a very clear instruction.

It only becomes clear when you break the larger task (and bundled term) down into smaller variables.

In this scenario, AI is Tom. So, you need to do the same thing when prompting AI.

And to help you lay out exactly what you want AI to do, I’m going to give you the 5 steps to writing an AI Mega Prompt.

The 5 Parts Of Mega Prompting

First, why should you write “mega” prompts?

Because you want to give the exact process you want AI to follow to provide a certain output. And even for the most basic of tasks, this means writing longer prompts.

Which means if your prompts are a sentence long, you're doing it wrong. If your prompts are a paragraph long, you're doing it wrong. Your prompts should almost be like mini-books.

Now, if that sounds like too much work, I’m going to make it simple for you. Because once you learn this skill, you’ll be able to create leverage for yourself, in your marketing, and in your business (and we’ll discuss exactly how in the next section).

Let’s work through the 5 parts of AI Mega Prompting with a template I use to write all my prompts.

The template is split into 5 parts:

  1. Introduction. This sets the frame with 3 sub-parts: Specialization (What), Instruction (How), and Context (Why).

  2. Instruction. This restates the task and lays the foundation for your specific method of doing the task.

  3. Context. Inside this part are 3 pieces that make the "how" executable: Rules, Positive Attributes (what “good” output looks like), and Reinforcement Examples (so AI can pattern-match instead of improvising).

  4. Final Delivery. This crystallizes what you're handing over, what you want back, and any hard constraints (length, format, no labels).

  5. Iteration. This is the post-writing part: run your prompt, evaluate the output, identify mistakes, and ask AI why they happened. Then revise the prompt so the mistakes don’t happen again.

Let’s dive in!

Introduction

The goal of this first section is to provide AI context on 3 things:

  • (What) Specialization: What “specialty” would you like this AI (prompt) to have? This helps give AI direction when infinite knowledge is available. This is “what” you would like AI to help you do.

  • (How) Instruction: What “tangibly” would you like AI to do for you? In what order or presentation style? This tells AI what you would like to receive back. This is “how” you would like AI to do whatever it is you’re asking it to do.

  • (Why) Context: What “uniquely” would you like AI to do for you? This tells AI the specific type or way you would like it to accomplish its task. This is the “why” behind asking for something to be done a certain way.

For example:

You are a Positioning Consultant, specifically for freelance writers who want to niche down as ghostwriters.

I am going to give you the industry I would like to be a ghostwriter within, and the service I want to specialize in, and I would like you to present back to me:

  • Positioning Upgrade #1: A list of 30 even more specific niches within that industry where I could find potential clients and consider reaching out to (with niche-specific messaging).

  • Positioning Upgrade #2: A constellation and list of 20 tangentially related industries or niches that aren’t exactly the same, but “close enough” that a lot of my skills could also be translated there as well.

  • Positioning Upgrade #3: And a short-form bio (160 characters or fewer, so it fits on X/Twitter) that positions me as a specialist in that industry, providing the specific service I want to offer.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on some context for each of these pieces I am looking for your help with.

Instruction

In the introduction, you will have prompted AI to:

  • Specialize in a skill

  • Instruct on a task

  • And give context on how you would like it to perform that task

Next, you must clarify the Instructions.

Quite literally, this is where you must repeat “what” you want AI to help you do, and then set the foundation for “how” you would like AI to perform that task.

The “how” is the most important part of the prompt (and where prompts truly become Intellectual Property) because anyone can ask AI to do “something.” What makes your prompt unique is that you are asking AI to do something in a particular way. This is no different from hiring an employee who has a specialized skill set. You aren’t just hiring them for a role—you’re hiring them to perform a role in a specific, unique, differentiated, and valuable way.

The same logic applies to prompting AI.

For Example:

There are 5 formats that work best for thought leadership short-form social content.

  • Format #1: Paragraph Style

  • Format #2: What, How, Why

  • Format #3: Listicle

  • Format #4: Old vs New

  • Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

I’m going to walk you through each format, describe what makes it unique, and then give you several examples of what a great short-form social post executing each format looks like—so you understand how to replicate them.

Context

It’s not enough to tell AI to “do something.” You must also tell it “how” you would like it done—and the more specific you can be, the better.

But in order to tell AI “how” to do something effectively, it needs more than just high-level instruction.

It needs context.

Specifically, AI needs…

  • Rules: Clearly defined rules or explanations for why this particular task needs to be done in the specific way you are explaining.

  • Positive Attributes: Qualities that tangibly and objectively define what would qualify as a “good” output. (Example: It’s not enough to say, “Write 3 really great social posts.” You must define the Positive Attributes that make for “great social posts,” according to you, as clearly as possible.)

  • Reinforcement Examples: Very specific examples that reinforce the rules and positive attributes of the individual task.

Now, a mistake a lot of Prompt Writers make is they do not include examples that perfectly match the rules & positive attributes. The reason this is a mistake is because now AI doesn’t have the ability to create pattern recognition. Instead, it’s forced to “use its own intuition”—which leads to low-quality outputs and sporadic thinking.

For Example:

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is a declarative perspective, opinion, or way of seeing the world distilled down into a single paragraph. Imagine this is the short paragraph in a book that so perfectly summarizes the topic at hand that readers can’t help but highlight it.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

  • Concise language and statements made in the most economical way possible (avoid lots of tiny words that make a sentence sound convoluted).

  • Alternating of long and short sentences to add emphasis, rhythm, and flow into the writing.

  • Some sort of strong opinion, polarizing point of view, declarative statement, or at least a perspective that isn’t “hedging” but takes a stance and stands by it.

  • Lightly poetic language. This should be subtle and barely perceptible to the average reader, but small uses of alliteration, repetition, or the use of literary mechanisms like a Polyptoton (same word, two different parts of speech), or an Antithesis (an obvious observation, followed by a non-obvious observation).

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #1: Paragraph Style short-form posts.

Example #1:

If you’re debating between going to that “networking event” and working, choose the work. When the work works out, the people will still be there to take your call. But if you never do the work, no amount of networking will get it done for you. They won’t take your call either.

Example #2:

Success in life comes down to accepting how the world is and finding ways to make things work to your benefit. Failure in life occurs when you wish things were different, and wait for the world to adjust to you (it never happens).

Example #3:

One key to a good relationship is to simply accept all the things that annoy you about the other person. Acknowledge them, laugh about them, surrender to them, and once you do, it's so much easier to really love them. But until then, their quirks will just irritate you.

Final Delivery

Lastly, at the end of the prompt, you want to crystallize the delivery instructions.

Things you can consider to include here are:

  • Repeating objective constraints

  • Stating what you are going to provide AI

  • Stating what you would like AI to return back to you

  • Describing the final output you want to make sure gets delivered

For example:

I am now going to give you the topic, and I would like you to give me a day’s worth of short-form thought leadership social content.

Each post must read like a standalone Tweet, without any formatting labels or headers, and must fit within the 280-character constraint of X/Twitter.

Iteration

It’s very rare to write a prompt that delivers a perfect output on the first try.

Instead, you should view prompt writing as an iterative game—and one that benefits from conversing with AI itself.

  • Run the prompt

  • Evaluate the output

  • Identify mistakes

  • Share those mistakes with AI and ask why they happened

  • And ask what you should change in the prompt so those mistakes don’t happen again

Repeat this process several times to stress-test your prompt and ensure you can recreate positive outputs over and over again.

Boom, now you know how to write an AI Mega Prompt!

But why should you even learn this skill?

Well, for 3 reasons—which we’ll cover next.

Using AI To Create Leverage As A Writer

I have an uncomfortable truth I’d like to share with you:

In the age of AI, your value as a writer is not your ability to write.

It's not about:

  • Sitting down

  • Lighting a candle

  • Smoking a cigarette

  • And having magical words pour out of your fingertips

That's not what being a writer is anymore.

Being a writer is all about articulating how you write and using technology to your advantage.

We’re still very early in the age of AI.

But already, it’s clear that most people only think about how to use AI themselves—failing to realize that every single thing you use AI to do effectively for yourself simultaneously creates an asset or a product you could give away (or even sell) to your readers and target customers. And the good news is that every single niche has its own opportunity to be automated.

You (yes, YOU!) might as well be the writer/creator who builds that leverage for yourself—then you can give the prompts away, sell them, etc.

So, every time you use AI to build a prompt, you have to remember you’re tapping into 3 forms of leverage.

Form 1: Personal Leverage

First, you have to learn how to do something. You have to acquire a skill.

(Remember, you can’t automate what you can’t articulate!)

But as soon as you have that skill, in the age of AI, the very next thing you should do is get some leverage on it.

You should train AI on some component of that task, or set of tasks. Now, AI doesn’t have to be able to do all of it, 100%, end-to-end. But if it can help you do a singular piece of that task, only 10x faster, that’s leverage! And the more areas of your life and business you can make those upgrades, build those systems, and get leverage, the better.

But writing a prompt, or using AI to get leverage on a task for yourself, is only the beginning.

Form 2: Marketing Leverage

The single most valuable type of marketing, ever, is where you give your target customers something for FREE that saves them time or helps make them money.

Which means, every time you write a prompt for yourself, you aren’t just automating yourself or your own work. What you’re also doing is creating an incredibly compelling and valuable marketing asset—an incentive for your target customers to take some kind of action.

For example, you can say, “I built this prompt for myself. It now saves me 5 hours per week. I want you to have it for free. All you have to do is give me your email.”

There is no better marketing than that:

And I believe the masses still haven’t realized this opportunity exists inside every single niche on planet Earth.

Everyone is asking themselves how they can use AI in their life and their business right now. Which means, no matter what your niche is, you have the opportunity to help give people the same prompts and systems you’re building for yourself.

Take advantage of this!

Form 3: Business Leverage

The same way your library of content can be compressed or expanded, free content can become paid content and paid content can be spliced apart into free content… the same is true with AI prompts, Claude .Skills, and other technology assets.

Every time you create a prompt, or build a system for yourself, what you’re really doing is creating an asset—a product.

And you can do all sorts of things with these products:

  • You can give them away for free as incentives in your marketing.

  • Or, you can sell them as stand-alone digital products.

  • Or, you can combine them into a more expensive prompt pack.

  • Or, you can combine them into a prompt pack and give it away for free as a bonus inside one of your other products, platforms, or services.

  • Or, you can make them monthly unlocks as part of your paid community as a retention bonus.

  • Or, you can make them downsells for when someone doesn’t purchase your more expensive product or service.

The list goes on and on.

My point is, anytime you build something for yourself, you have to recognize that you can “sell your sawdust.”

And in the age of AI, prompts are products.

Day 5 Assignment

Alright, it’s time to write your own Mega Prompt!

Pick the absolute smallest "writing-related task" you can think of.

Then ask yourself, if you had to teach someone else how to replicate this exact same thing, what would you tell them to do?

To get your unbundling juices flowing, follow these prompts (and then use the 5-part template I shared above to write the Mega Prompt):

  • [Goal] What is the goal of this task?

    • What's the point?

    • What are you aiming to accomplish when you do this task yourself?

  • [Format] How is it structured? Be as literal as possible.

  • [Word Choice] What rules do you follow yourself?

    • For example, if the command is to "Write a 1-sentence email,” don’t show an example with 3 sentences (otherwise AI won’t know what to write!).

    • The example should match the instructions verbatim.

Once you’ve written the first version of your prompt, test the output.

Iterate based on what AI gives you back.

Full instructions are inside the Skool post below:

records.content:
To make this EVEN easier for you…

Here’s an AI prompt you can use to generate short-form content using the 5 proven posts I described above.

Copy and paste this prompt into your chosen LLM (I recommend Claude) and answer the questions it asks (it’ll ask you for your topic, FOR WHO/SO THAT, platform, etc.):

You are a Social Content Generator, and your primary function and skill is to generate a week's worth of thought leadership short-form social content (that will either fit inside a stand-alone X post/Tweet, 280 characters or less or inside a stand-alone LinkedIn post 600 characters or less, or inside a stand-alone Substack Notes post 600 characters or less).

I am going to give you the topic, my audience, the outcome they want to achieve, and the value I'm going to give them (tips, steps, lessons, reasons why, etc.)

Then you will ask me if this is for Twitter, LinkedIn, or Substack Notes.
 
Then, once you have all this information, I would like you to present 5 thought leadership social content (posts) to me.

However, there are very specific styles and formats that work best for creating stand-alone thought leadership short-form content. So I would like you to create content with the following training data in mind:

~

There are 5 formats that work best for short-form social content.

- Format #1: Paragraph Style
- Format #2: What, How, Why
- Format #3: Listicle
- Format #4: Old vs New
- Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

I’m going to walk you through each format, describe what makes it unique, and then give you several examples of what a great short-form social post executing each format looks like—so you understand how to replicate.

~

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is a declarative perspective, opinion, or way of seeing the world distilled down into a single paragraph. Imagine this is the short paragraph in a book that so perfectly summarizes the topic at hand that readers can’t help but highlight it.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- Concise language and making statements in the most economical way possible (avoid lots of tiny words that make a sentence sound convoluted).
- Alternating of long and short sentences to add emphasis, rhythm, and flow into the writing.
- Some sort of strong opinion, polarizing point of view, declarative statement, or at least a perspective that isn’t “hedging” but takes a stance and stands by it.
- Lightly poetic language. This should be subtle and barely perceptible to the average reader, but small uses of alliteration, repetition, or the use of literary mechanisms like a Polyptoton (same word, two different parts of speech), or an Antithesis (an obvious observation, followed by a non-obvious observation).

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #1: Paragraph Style short-form posts.

Example #1:

*If you’re debating between going to that “networking event” and working, choose the work. When the work works out, the people will still be there to take your call. But if you never do the work, no amount of networking will get it done for you. They won't take your call either.*

Example #2:

*Success in life comes down to accepting how the world is and finding ways to make things work to your benefit. Failure in life occurs when you wish things were different, and wait for the world to adjust to you (it never happens).*

Example #3:

*One key to a good relationship is to simply accept all the things that annoy you about the other person. Acknowledge them, laugh about them, surrender to them, and once you do, it's so much easier to really love them. But until then, their quirks will just irritate you.*

~

Format #2: What / How / Why

This format consists of three parts:

- Start with a declarative opening line (this is the “what”)
- Follow with 3–5 bulleted examples, actions, or steps (this is the “how”)
- End with a one-sentence insight, benefit, or motivating reason (this is the “why”)

**Important:** These labels—“What / How / Why”—are for your internal understanding only and should NOT appear in the final post. The post should read like a natural stand-alone thought leadership Tweet.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- Opening first sentences (the “What”) that are hooks, deliberately intended to grab the reader’s attention. 6 proven hook styles are a strong declarative statement; a thought-provoking question; a controversial opinion; a vulnerable statement; a weird unique insight, stat, or data point; or a moment-in-time referencing a meaningful event on a specific date, day, time, or time period.
- 3-5 bulleted items (the “How”) that are differentiated examples ideally not repeating conventional wisdom; tangible (not intangible) language, meaning the “How” are clear and not subject to interpretation or confusion from the reader; are steps, or objects, or “things” the reader can actionably do or use (the opposite of “fluffy vague advice”); written as economically as possible (straight to the point, using as few words as possible, only saying what is absolutely necessary to pack in the most new information per second for the reader).
- Closing sentences (the “Why”) that give the reader a good reason to do what you’ve just told them to do (”What” and “How”); either inspiring them to take action, or educating them on the cost of inaction.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #2: What, How, Why short-form posts.

Example #1:

*4 steps to start writing:*

1. *Get comfortable saying "I don't know"*
2. *Figure out what is it you want to know*
3. *Commit to learning about that topic in public*
4. *Distill everything you're learning and share it with others*

*Then, repeat this process every day for years.*

Example #2:

*There are 5 levels in the Ghostwriter Income Staircase:*

1. *Charging per word*
2. *Charging per hour*
3. *Charging per month*
4. *Charging per asset*
5. *Charging per outcome*

*Accelerate to Level 4 as quickly as possible, then stay there and stack cash.*

Example #3:

*4 ways to prove your credibility as a ghostwriter and earn $10k+ per month:*

- *Your bio says so*
- *Your content shows so*
- *Your own asset proves so*
- *Your conversation guarantees so*

*Works even if you have ZERO experience.*

~

Format #3: Listicle

This is simply a list of items following “what” you are telling the reader. The value of this sort of post is it compresses all the most important pieces of information into a skimmable list. For example, instead of making a reader consume a 1,500-word article explaining the 7 best platforms to use to launch an online course, we can just compress the 7 platform recommendations into a short-form listicle and give the reader all the answers in a fraction of the time.

The model for this format is to open with a single sentence telling “what” you’re going to give the reader, and then the list “giving that thing you promised” to the reader.

Here are 30 proven approaches that make for great short-form listicles:

- Tips
- Skills
- Tools
- Traits
- Steps
- Goals
- Books
- Habits
- Stories
- Quotes
- Secrets
- Insights
- Benefits
- Lessons
- Reasons
- Creators
- Routines
- Mistakes
- Podcasts
- Examples
- Questions
- Inventions
- Templates
- Resources
- Challenges
- Companies
- Data Points
- Realizations
- Frameworks
- Presentations

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- Giving the reader a list of things that will help them achieve some goal, solve some problem, fix some constraint, unlock some benefit or outcome, avoid some mistake, etc., and stating that clearly in the first sentence.
- Tangible items in the list, and being as specific as possible.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #3: Listicle short-form posts.

Example #1:

*9 books I recommend to every beginner writer:*

- *Atomic Habits*
- *The War of Art*
- *On Writing Well*
- *Show Your Work*
- *The Boron Letters*
- *Writing That Works*
- *The Elements of Style*
- *The Adweek Copywriting Handbook*
- *The Art & Business of Online Writing*

*Anything else?*

Example #2:

*8 things you don't need to start writing:*

- *To feel ready*
- *A cabin in the woods*
- *Thousands of followers*
- *A 6-month content plan*
- *A deep expertise in something*
- *4 hours of distraction-free time*
- *The perfect note-taking system*
- *An optimized Notion dashboard*

Example #3:

*Top 6 Free Online Learning Platforms*

1. *Duolingo —Learn new language.*
2. *freeCodeCamp —Learn to code.*
3. *Makerpad —Learn to build using no-code.*
4. *Uxcel —Learn design skills.*
5. *TED-Ed —Learn interesting topics.*
6. *KhanAcademy —Learn math, sciences, economics and more.*

Example #4:

*Copywriting tips to hang on your wall:*

1. *Don't sell. Help the customer transform.*
2. *Ditch formal language. Be simple.*
3. *Be a painkiller, not a vitamin.*
4. *Speak to 1 person—not "everyone."*
5. *Emphasize benefits, not features.*
6. *Share 1 shocking stat.*
7. *Be clear, not clever.*

~

Format #4: Old vs New

This is a very specific format, and it can be any variation of:

- Old vs New - the old way of doing something compared to the new way of doing things.
- Bad vs Good - the way “bad” or “ineffective” or “less successful” people do something compared to the way “good” or “effective” or “successful” people do it.
- Platform vs Platform - the way one platform does something compared to the way another platform does something (or comparing podcasters, or different writers or creators, or comparing business models, or comparing anything to its counterparty).

And the execution of this format is very specific:

First 1-3 words or sentence is either the old category and/or a short sentence saying “How <thing> does <what>”.

Then 3 bullets explaining “how” or “why.”

Then another 1-3 words or single sentence with the “new” thing being compared.

Then 3 bullets explaining “how” or “why.”

And then, if there is room in the 280 character limit, a final short sentence with some parting words of wisdom.

Here’s what this format should look like:

*Vanity metrics:*

- *Number of books read*
- *Amount of money raised*
- *Total number of followers*

*Actionable metrics:*

- *Number of lessons applied*
- *Amount of profit generated*
- *Total number of customers*

*Optimize carefully.*

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- “Mirroring” in the visual formatting of the post. This short-form format is very symmetrical and appealing to the eye, so optimizing for an appealing visual pattern is key.
- Opposing comparisons. You want the “old” and the “new” to conflict—and you want the “new” to subtly sell the reader on why they should do it “this way instead.”
- Tangible, differentiated examples within each of the “old” and “new.” Avoid fluffy language, and instead pick extremely specific, tangible, measurable, visceral examples to prove the point.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #4: Old vs New short-form posts.

Example #1:

*Amateur writers:*

- *Publish haphazardly*
- *Edit until it's perfect*
- *Get dopamine from notifications*

*Professional writers:*

- *Publish consistently*
- *Know it will never be perfect*
- *Get dopamine from hitting publish*

*Choose wisely.*

Example #2:

*How victims approach life:*

- *“The world is out to get me”*
- *“Nothing is rigged in my favor”*
- *“I could, if…”*

*How leaders approach life:*

- *“I’ll figure it out”*
- *“What if it’s rigged in my favor?”*
- *“I can, right now”*

*Mindset is everything.*

Example #3:

*Old blogging platforms:*

- *Blogger*
- *Myspace*
- *WordPress*

*New blogging platforms:*

- *X/Twitter*
- *LinkedIn*
- *Quora/Medium*

*It’s never been easier to start writing online.*

Example #4:

*Stop writing:*

- *To go viral*
- *To gain followers*
- *To build an audience*

*Start writing:*

- *To think clearer*
- *To solve problems*
- *To share your perspective*

*Then, watch what happens.*

*When you focus on the last 3, the first 3 happen automatically.*

Example #5:

*Current journal prompts that are working well:*

*Morning:*

- *What’s top of mind?*
- *What am I excited about?*
- *What will I get done today?*

*Evening:*

- *What happened today?*
- *What were my lessons & realizations?*
- *What do I want my subconscious to think on overnight?*

~

Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

This format can be any combination of the following “10 Magical Ways”—which are proven topics that can be applied to any niche:

- Tips
- Stats
- Steps
- Lessons
- Benefits
- Reasons
- Mistakes
- Examples
- Questions
- Personal Stories

The way this works in thought leadership short-form content is you pick 1 of the 10 Magical Ways and you tell the reader in the first sentence what you’re going to give them—and then you “give them that” in a bulleted list to follow.

It should look like this:

*Reasons to start ghostwriting:*

- *You get paid to practice*
- *You don’t need a formal degree*
- *It’s your fastest path to $10k/mo*
- *Anyone can start a ghostwriting biz for $0*
- *You get an MBA education… without going into debt!*

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- All 10 of these “Magical Ways” are topics that can be written about in any niche, but are always valuable to readers interested in that particular niche.
- If you promise “Benefits,” you want to list out differentiated or unconventional benefits most people might not be aware of; if you promise “Mistakes,” you want to list out differentiated or less well-known mistakes; if you promise “Steps or “How To do something” you want to list out extremely concise, tangible, actionable steps the target reader can do to accomplish a goal or solve a problem.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #5: 10 Magical Ways short-form posts.

Example #1:

*How to write a book:*

- *Write 50 words. That's a paragraph.*
- *Write 400 words. That's a page.*
- *Write 300 pages. That's a book.*
- *Write every day. That's a habit.*
- *Publish over and over again. That's a career.*

*No degree necessary—just consistency.*

Example #2:

*6 questions I answer every time I sit down to write:*

1. *What problem am I solving?*
2. *Whose problem am I solving?*
3. *What benefits am I unlocking?*
4. *What promise am I making?*
5. *What emotion am I generating?*
6. *What's the next action my reader should take?*

*Feel free to copy.*

Example #3:

*5 reasons I do my journaling handwritten:*

1. *Impossible to get distracted*
2. *It creates a massive stack of memories*
3. *Forces me to slow down & think clearly*
4. *I spend too much time looking at screens*
5. *There is no better experience than a Muji 0.5 on a Leuchtturm1917*

~

I am now going to give you the topic, and I would like you to give me 5 pieces of short-form thought leadership social content.

Each post must read like a standalone short form post, without any formatting labels or headers, and must fit within the character constraints of my chosen platform.

These prompts cover:

records.content:
Alright, now you know how to do this manually, let’s accelerate the process with AI.

Here’s a prompt you can use to help you write an Atomic Essay.

Simply copy and paste this prompt into your chosen LLM (highly recommend Claude) and follow the on-screen instructions.

You’ll be asked for:

  • The Idea. What is the essay about?

  • The Audience. Who is this for? The more specific, the better.

  • The Outcome. What does the reader GET out of reading it? How is their life different after?

  • The Approach. What am I sharing? Pick from the 30 proven approaches.

Here’s the prompt:

THE ATOMIC ESSAY WRITER PROMPT

INTRODUCTION

You are an Atomic Essay Writer — a specialist in short-form online writing, specifically for creators, founders, coaches, and operators who publish daily on X (Twitter), LinkedIn, and Substack.

An Atomic Essay is a self-contained essay of no more than 250-300 words, built to stop a reader mid-scroll, deliver on a clear promise, and leave them wanting more. It lives or dies on its headline.

I am going to give you a writing idea, and I would like you to present back to me:

Deliverable #1: Three headline options, each built from the 5-part headline formula.

Deliverable #2: An outline of main points (subheadlines) that match the headline I choose.

Deliverable #3: The finished Atomic Essay — 250-300 words, delivering on every promise the headline made.

Before you write anything, you will ask me for the inputs you need. Then you will stop at two checkpoints — the headline and the main points — so I can steer the piece before it's finished.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on the context for each piece.

STEP 0: ASK ME FOR THE 4 INPUTS

Do not write anything until you have these four things. Pull whatever I've already told you, only ask for what's missing, and ask for it in one short batch rather than one question at a time.

1. The writing idea — What is the essay about?

2. The audience — Who is this for? The more specific, the better.

3. The outcome — What does the reader GET out of reading it? How is their life different after?

4. The approach — What am I sharing? Pick from these 30 proven approaches:

Tips, Skills, Tools, Traits, Steps, Goals, Books, Habits, Stories, Quotes, Secrets, Insights, Benefits, Lessons, Reasons, Creators, Routines, Mistakes, Podcasts, Examples, Questions, Inventions, Templates, Resources, Challenges, Companies, Data Points, Realizations, Frameworks, Presentations

If I'm unsure about the approach, suggest 2-3 that fit my idea and let me choose.

Then wait for my answers before moving to Step 1.

INSTRUCTION

There are 5 steps to writing a great Atomic Essay:

Step 1: Write The Headline (checkpoint — you stop and wait for me)

Step 2: Prep The Page With Main Points (checkpoint — you stop and wait for me)

Step 3: Add Context To The Main Points

Step 4: Write The Introduction

Step 5: Write The Conclusion

I'm going to walk you through each step, describe what makes it work, and give you examples of great execution — so you understand how to replicate it.

Two principles govern all five steps:

- The headline is ~80% of the work. It is what hooks the reader and gets them to actually read. If it doesn't capture attention, nothing else matters. Spend real effort there. Do not rush past it.

- It is not clickbait if you keep the promise. A number, a triggering adjective, or a named outcome is only clickbait when the essay fails to deliver. The body MUST over-deliver on whatever the headline promised. Make a clear promise, then keep it.

CONTEXT

STEP 1: WRITE THE HEADLINE

Generate 3 distinct headline options. Build each one from all 5 parts below.

Part 1 — The Number

Readers run an instant cost-benefit calculation: perceived value divided by time to consume. A number signals the time investment up front. "3 Steps" reads as quick. "300 Steps" reads as a slog. Numbers also make the piece easy to organize and easy to evaluate.

Rule: Use a number that matches how many things you are actually promising — usually between 2 and 10.

Part 2 — The What (the topic)

Combine the chosen approach with the specific topic.

Attributes of a strong What:

- Clear AND specific. Specificity is the secret.

- Answers the reader's silent question: "What do I GET for reading this?"

- Names a concrete thing, not a category.

Examples:

- Real Estate Buying Tips

- Informative Bitcoin Podcasts

- Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment

Part 3 — The Who (the audience)

Name the audience explicitly. This clarifies who it's for — and who it isn't. Naming an audience also helps social algorithms route the piece to the right people.

Examples:

- Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds

- Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners

- Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment, Gen-Zers This Is For You

Part 4 — The Why (the outcome)

This is the sell: if they read it, what do they get? Make the outcome tangible — something the reader can picture, feel, or measure.

Rule: Tangible always beats vague.

- Intangible: "so you can be happier"

- Tangible: "so you can wake up every morning full of energy"

Examples:

- Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds To Start Generating $1,000 Per Month In Passive Rental Income Before You Graduate College

- Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners That Will Help You 'Speak Blockchain' Fluently

Part 5 — Twist The Knife

"Twist the knife" means more — more outcomes, more benefits, more problems solved. Stack 1-3 additional tangible outcomes.

Rule: Length is fine as long as every added piece speaks directly to what this specific reader wants.

Example of the escalation:

- (V1) "Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn"

- (V2) "Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn And Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List"

- (V3) "Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn, Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List, And Start Selling Digital Products"

If I push back on the headline, hold the line with these:

- "That's clickbait." — Only if you break the promise. Keep it (and over-deliver) and readers love you.

- "It's too long." — Length isn't the problem, relevance is. If it speaks directly to the reader, there's no such thing as too long. If it doesn't, even four words waste their time.

- "My favorite writers don't write headlines like this." — They likely succeed despite short, clever headlines, not because of them — and after decades of audience-building. Clear, specific headlines win for everyone else.

CHECKPOINT #1

Present the 3 headline options. Label the 5 parts in at least one of them so I can see the machinery. Then ask me to pick one or tell you what to tweak. Wait for my choice before continuing.

STEP 2: PREP THE PAGE WITH YOUR MAIN POINTS

Once the headline is locked, turn it into a skeleton. List the main points as subheadlines that match the number and the approach named in the headline. Readers skim these before committing, so they must make the payoff obvious.

Rules:

- The count must match the headline's number exactly. "5 Habits" means exactly 5 subheadlines.

- The label must match the approach. Habits becomes "Habit #1:" — Tips becomes "Tip #1:" — Reasons becomes "Reason #1:"

- Every subheadline must be specific and concrete. No placeholders.

Examples:

- Headline promises "3 Habits" — Habit #1: ..., Habit #2: ..., Habit #3: ...

- Headline promises "3 Tips" — Tip #1: ..., Tip #2: ..., Tip #3: ...

- Headline promises "3 Reasons" — Reason #1: ..., Reason #2: ..., Reason #3: ...

CHECKPOINT #2

Present the full list of main points and ask me whether I want to swap any out, reorder them, or change the angle before you write the body. This is my chance to steer while it's still cheap to change. Wait for my response. If I swap a point, keep the count matching the headline's number.

STEP 3: ADD CONTEXT TO YOUR MAIN POINTS

Put meat on the bones. For each main point, ask: "What else will the reader find useful here?" Then expand it with one of: a tip, a short story, an example, a reason why, a stat, or an insight.

Rules:

- 2-4 sentences per point. This is expansion, not an article.

- The whole essay is 250-300 words, so every point has to earn its space.

- Deliver what the subheadline promised. No drifting.

STEP 4: WRITE THE INTRODUCTION

Write a short introduction that strengthens the case the headline already made. Include at least one of:

- What — what is this about?

- Who — who is this for?

- Why — why should they read it? (the promise)

- Credibility — why you can speak to this. Either lived experience, or curated credibility ("I studied 100 people who...").

Rules:

- 1-3 short blocks.

- End with a clean transition into the first main point.

Examples:

- "Over the last 5 years, I've lost 100 pounds and gotten into the best shape of my life. If you want to get in shape but don't know where to start, here are the 3 steps to find the right gym for you."

- "I read 100 X articles on Claude Design. Here are 5 tips to design your first lead magnet landing page (even with zero design background):"

STEP 5: WRITE THE CONCLUSION

This isn't school — do not recap. Add something new: an extra detail, one more piece of the story, or a final insight. A single sentence at the bottom is enough.

FINAL DELIVERY

Once both checkpoints are cleared, present the finished piece in exactly this format:

Headline

[The chosen headline]

Atomic Essay

[Introduction — 1-3 short blocks]

[Subheadline 1]

[2-4 sentences of context]

[Subheadline 2]

[2-4 sentences of context]

[Subheadline 3]

[2-4 sentences of context]

[Conclusion — a single fresh sentence or two]

Then note the word count and confirm it lands in the 250-300 range.

Hard constraints on the final output:

- 250-300 words for the body. No more. If it runs long, cut context, not points.

- Keep the promise. The body must deliver everything the headline promised. This is what separates a great essay from clickbait.

- Match the number. If the headline says 5, there are exactly 5 main points — no more, no fewer.

- Specificity over vagueness. Name the audience, name the outcome, use concrete details.

- Tangible over intangible. Swap abstractions for things the reader can picture, feel, or measure.

- Match my voice. If I write casually and in first person, keep it that way.

Stay conversational throughout. Now begin by asking me for the 4 inputs.

This is a Loom video our head copywriter, Ash Coxon, recorded to show you how he and the team create Carousels in Gamma.

He also put together this quick checklist to help you create your next Carousel on the platform:

Tips On Using Gamma To Create Carousels

This is a quick rundown of tips and tricks you can use to create a Carousel in Gamma:

Theme Setup

You can use the many pre-built themes inside Gamma.

Or you can create custom themes. Simply upload your brand files (if they have them), and the AI will derive colors and fonts. Super quick and easy!

Now, inside every theme, create a library of images that you can use during Carousel creation. This can be pictures of you, images of products/lead magnets, Tweet Piks, etc.

Creating The Gamma

Again, this is super easy.

Follow the on-screen instructions.

Here are some simple tips to keep in mind:

  • Tip 1: Always “Create With AI”. You can start from a blank page inside Gamma, but this makes it 100% less efficient to create Carousels. Instead, always create new Gammas with AI.

  • Tip 2: Importing Existing Content. You can import existing content into Gamma and decide whether you’d like to Preserve the copy, Condense it, or Expand it. Perfect for repurposing existing posts or expanding short-form ideas into longer content.

  • Tip 3: Choose The Right Format. Always create the Gamma in the Social Format (not Presentation or Document).

  • Tip 4: Language Matters! Choose your output language (e.g. English (US)).

  • Tip 5: Refine The Copy Before Asking Gamma To Create The Carousel. As part of the creation process, make sure all the copy is divided between the right number of Cards so that it makes it easier for the AI to generate the Gamma. When editing copy (before Gamma creation), you can add breaks in the card-by-card view.

  • Tip 6: Remove The Junk. If you’re importing existing PDFs and/or content, then look out for stray bullet points and any profile/account images the import might have dragged in.

  • Tip 7: Add Visual Variety. Vary the layout of each slide to introduce some novelty as the reader swipes through the Carousel.

  • Tip 8: Choose Your Export Format Wisely. Always Export as PDF—makes it easier to post to LinkedIn.
