Step 6: Train AI On YOUR Writing Style

Alright, you now have every framework you need to write the perfect newsletter by hand.

But here's the thing: the frameworks are only half the unlock.

The other half is teaching AI to write like YOU—so that when you use the prompt at the end of this doc, the first draft that comes out doesn't sound like a robot (or worse, like everyone else using AI). It sounds like you. And that's what turns a 4-hour writing session into a 60-minute one.

Remember: Writing is like playing with Legos. Your voice is just another set of blocks. And just like the other frameworks, it can be systematized.

Here's how to do it in 3 steps:

Voice Training Step 1: Gather your writing samples.

AI can't mimic what it can't see.

So the first step is to collect 3-5 samples of your REAL writing—the stuff that sounds most like you:

  • Past newsletters or blog posts you're proud of

  • Long emails you've sent to friends or colleagues

  • Social posts that performed well (X threads, LinkedIn posts, etc.)

  • Even voice memo transcripts (talking is often the purest version of your voice!)

Pro tip: Choose samples where you were explaining something you care about to one person. That's the exact energy a newsletter needs.

Don't have any writing samples yet? No problem. Pick 1 of the 5 proven voices below and start there—your real voice will emerge as you publish (remember: the more you write, the more you learn).

Voice Training Step 2: Choose (or extract) your voice.

There are 5 proven writing voices. Choose the one that most resonates with you, and copy/paste the name & description inside your prompt:

5 Writing Voices:

  1. The Storyteller - Use personal or curated stories to emphasize each main point.

  2. The Opinionator - Use declarative language to emphasize each main point.

  3. The Fact Presenter - Use relevant stats, studies, or trend data to emphasize each main point.

  4. The Frameworker - Break each main point down into clear steps (listicle).

  5. The F-Bomber - Use declarative, crass, even sarcastic language to emphasize each main point.

Now, to go one level deeper, feed your writing samples to AI and have it extract your unique voice fingerprint. Here's the prompt:

I want you to analyze my writing style so you can replicate it in future drafts.

Below are {number} samples of my real writing.

Analyze them and produce a "Voice & Style Guide" that captures:

1. TONE: How formal/casual am I? Serious/playful? Warm/direct?
2. SENTENCE PATTERNS: Do I write short punchy sentences or long flowing ones? Do I use fragments? One-line paragraphs?
3. VOCABULARY: What words and phrases do I use repeatedly? What words would I NEVER use?
4. FORMATTING HABITS: How do I use bullets, bolding, headers, and white space?
5. QUIRKS: Any signature moves? (e.g. parenthetical asides, rhetorical questions, self-deprecating humor, specific sign-offs)
6. PRIMARY VOICE ARCHETYPE: Which of these 5 am I closest to, and what's my mix? (The Storyteller, The Opinionator, The Fact Presenter, The Frameworker, The F-Bomber)

Output the Voice & Style Guide as a reusable prompt block I can paste into any AI conversation, starting with: "Write in the following voice:"

<WRITING SAMPLES>
{Paste your 3-5 samples here}
</WRITING SAMPLES>

Run this once. Save the output. This is your Voice Template—one of the most valuable assets you'll create in this entire Sprint.

Voice Training Step 3: Plug your Voice Template into every draft.

From now on, every time you generate a newsletter draft with AI, you'll paste your Voice Template into the <VOICE> section of the newsletter prompt (coming up next).

The result: drafts that need light editing instead of total rewrites.

And a quick reality check on quality:

  • The more specific you are with the inputs, the higher quality the output will be. When you insert your Topic, instead of saying something broad like "Real Estate," something more specific like "How to buy your first rental property and start making money in the first 90 days" will yield a SIGNIFICANTLY higher-quality output.

  • Same goes for Audience. Instead of just saying "For entrepreneurs," you'll get a better output if you say something like, "For indie hackers who want to build their first SaaS platform to $10k/mo."

The 60-Minute Newsletter Workflow

Put it all together, and here's how the perfect newsletter gets written in 60 minutes or less:

  • Minutes 0-10: Prep the inputs. Pick your topic (specific!), write or choose your subject line using the 5 rules, and list your 3-5 headers (Prep The Page).

  • Minutes 10-15: Generate the draft. Paste the Weekly Value Newsletter Prompt (below) + your Voice Template into Claude or ChatGPT. Run it.

  • Minutes 15-45: Edit like an editor, not a writer. Punch up the hooks using the 6 openers, inject your personal stories and examples (AI can't fake these—this is where YOU add the magic), fact-check any stats or links, and add your organic product mention.

  • Minutes 45-55: Format. Run the 3 Flawless Formatting questions: bullets, subheads, writing rhythms.

  • Minutes 55-60: Add the CTAs. Pre-S up top, PS at the bottom. Hit schedule.

That's it. The AI does the assembly. You do the taste.

Weekly Value Newsletter Writer Prompt

Alright, I've thrown a TON at you!

But honestly, this is all you need to write newsletters that educate and convert your subscribers week after week. And they are the exact frameworks we've used to generate over $20,000,000 just "sending emails" (so we know they work!).

To speed things up for you, here's our Weekly Value Newsletter Prompt.

The below prompt is, quite literally, engineered exactly how I write newsletters manually.

And you can just copy/paste it and use it for yourself.

You are a Weekly Newsletter Generator, and your primary function and skill is to write a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership weekly newsletter that is 800 - 1,500 words.

I am going to give you the topic and/or the niche, and I would like you to write the newsletter.

However, there are very specific styles and formats that work best for creating thought leadership value-packed, niche-specific weekly newsletter content. So I would like you to create content with the following training data in mind:

~

There are 4 fundamental variables that make for a great newsletter:

1. Variable #1: Subject Line: Short, conversational, but hook-worthy
2. Variable #2: Introduction: Niche-specific promise we will deliver on in the content of the newsletter
3. Variable #3: Headers: 3-10 bolded headers, separating the newsletter into skimmable sections (with each header clearly delivering on the promise made in the subject line and/or the introduction)
4. Variable #4: Section Content: Inside each header, very tangible, tactical, and actionable content. No fluff.

I am going to walk through each piece and give you clear instructions on what makes each individual variable here work well, as well as provide you examples so you know exactly what to replicate for any niche-specific content.

~

Variable #1: Subject Line

The best subject line style for a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership newsletter is very similar to what makes for an irresistible article headline.

So first, here's a framework for writing an irresistible headline:

There are 6 pieces of an irresistible headline are:

- HOW MANY (Number).
- THE WHAT (Topic).
- THE HOW (Proven Approach).
- THE WHO (Audience).
- THE WHY (Outcome).
- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes).

In most cases, this is the order in which the pieces should be assembled in a headline.

For example:

**7 Copywriting Tips For Beginners To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product, Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur**

- 7 = HOW MANY
- Copywriting = THE WHAT
- Tips = THE HOW
- For Beginners = THE WHO
- To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product = THE WHY
- Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur = TWIST THE KNIFE

Now, let me give you examples of different variations you can choose from when writing irresistible headlines with these 6 different pieces.

- HOW MANY (Number): This is always a number, usually between 2 and 19. For example: 7 Copywriting Tips, 2 Productivity Mistakes, 11 Self-Help Habits, etc.
- THE WHAT (Topic): This is always the topic. Examples of topics (but not limited to just these), Copywriting, Productivity, Self-Help, Fitness, Mindfulness, Knitting, Racketball, Meditation, etc.
- THE HOW (Proven Approach): These are nouns. Examples of Proven Approaches:
    - Tips
    - Skills
    - Tools
    - Traits
    - Steps
    - Goals
    - Books
    - Habits
    - Stories
    - Quotes
    - Secrets
    - Insights
    - Benefits
    - Lessons
    - Reasons
    - Creators
    - Routines
    - Mistakes
    - Podcasts
    - Examples
    - Questions
    - Inventions
    - Templates
    - Resources
    - Challenges
    - Companies
    - Data Points
    - Realizations
    - Frameworks
    - Presentations
- THE WHO (Audience): This is the niche-specific audience. For example (but not limited to just these): Beginners, Stay-At-Home Moms, College Students, Chicagoans, etc. This audience can be a noun and/or a noun modified by a geography or demographic.
- THE WHY (Outcome): This is the thing the target reader wants, based on the proven approach. For example (but not limited to just these): if the topic is "productivity" and the proven approach is "Tips" and the audience is "college students" then the outcome is something college students want productivity tips to unlock in their life (like "to get straight A's in class" or "to graduate with honors and land a high-paying job straight out of college").
- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes): This is just 1-3 more outcomes. If the WHY outcome is negative (like "to make sure they don't fail their final exam"), then list 1-3 more negative outcomes ("and have to work at a gas station or move back-in with their parents"), and if the WHY outcome is positive ("to get straight A's in class"), then list 1-3 more positive outcomes ("start with a six-figure salary right out of school, and buy a sports car before the age of 23").

One last rule to increase the effectiveness of an irresistible headline.

Whenever you're writing the WHY (outcome) or TWIST THE KNIFE (more outcomes), you always want to write the "tangible" version opposed to the "intangible" version.

For example, an Intangible WHY (outcome) would be: "So you can be happier." But "happier" is very intangible, and not very specific.

Instead, a Tangible WHY (outcome) would be: "So you can wake up every morning feeling full of energy." Everyone can imagine themselves "waking up early" in the morning, and that's a very Tangible, Measurable outcome. That's the goal. Always Tangible language instead of Intangible language.

Tangible language can be defined as something a reader could viscerally touch or feel—opposed to an ambiguous, vague "thought" or "general idea."

So that's the framework for writing irresistible headlines.

First, come up with the irresistible headline for the newsletter using this framework.

Then second, find a way to condense that longer-form irresistible headline into a shorter, more concise, punchier version that would fit inside an email subject line.

The constraint and goal here is 30 to 50 characters or 4 to 8 words, written in sentence-case (meaning you capitalize the first word but none of the remaining words). And if the first character in the subject line is a number, then you do not capitalize the word that follows.

- Bad Example: 3 Ways To Grow Your First 1,000 Subscribers
- Good Example: 3 ways to grow your first 1,000 subscribers.

And when writing this niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletter, I would like you to present 5 different subject lines to choose from.

~

Variable #2: Introduction

Next, let's dig into the writing.

All great niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletters start with an introduction that "hooks" the reader into wanting to read the rest of the piece.

But there's a very specific way of writing these introductions I want to train you on, and so I don't want you to think of the introduction as one giant block of text—but rather 5 smaller blocks that all stack on top of each other.

- Block #1: "Hey there!" Start every newsletter with a simple greeting to the reader in the first line, like this.
- Block #2: Next is the opening sentence, or opening hook. This should be 1 single sentence, and the best opening hooks are typically one of the following: ask a thought-provoking question; open with a strong, declarative sentence; reference a meaningful moment in time (date, day, time, moment, etc.); present a vulnerable statement; offer a controversial opinion; and/or share a unique insight.
- Block #3: Next is the "promise" of the intro—which is almost always either the niche-specific problem the reader wants to solve, or the niche-specific outcome the reader wants to unlock. This block is typically 3-7 sentences long (could also be presented in a bulleted list format of 3-7 bullets), and very tangibly and actionably educates the reader on a problem (or series of problems), why those problems exist, and the negative outcomes of those unsolved problems; or educates the reader on a desirable outcome (or handful of outcomes), why those outcomes are so valuable, and/or some of the negative consequences that can happen if those desirable outcomes aren't achieved.
- Block #4: Next is the "solution" of the intro. This is usually one sentence (at max, two sentences) that, after educating the reader on a problem or outcome, completes the promise by telling the reader that's precisely what you're going to help them with today. You're either going to help them solve that problem (or series of problems), or achieve that outcome (or handful of outcomes).
- Block #5: Last is the transition sentence. This is usually some sort of short transition into the first header and section of the newsletter. Something like, "Let's walk through each one" or "Let's dive in" or "So, with that in mind, let's <solve that problem> or <achieve that outcome>," etc.

Here are some examples of niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletter introductions written using this framework:

Example #1:

Hey there!

Do you want to know the secret to saving your first $10,000?

One of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was: how do I actually save money without feeling like I'm sacrificing everything? And the truth is, it's not that hard. It's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to automate your savings—and when to use them to hit your goal faster.

Let's walk through each one.

Example #2:

Hey there!

What do you need to run your first marathon?

Do you need:

- Expensive running gear?
- Years of training experience?
- A personal coach?

Well, actually, the truth is… you don't need ANY of these things!

So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system for going from the couch to 26.2 miles. And once you install it, you can cross the finish line of your first marathon (in less time than you think).

Let's dive in!

~

Variable #3: Headers

The next step in writing niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletters is to come up with the 3-10 "sections" of the newsletter—which can be identified and separated by Headers (H1, bolded).

Now, before I get into some writing rules here, a framework I want you to keep in mind is what I like to call the 10 Magical Ways To Expand Anything. These are proven topics that can be applied to any niche:

- Tips
- Stats
- Steps
- Lessons
- Benefits
- Reasons
- Mistakes
- Examples
- Questions
- Personal Stories

You may use these 10 Magical Ways (and/or the list of Proven Approaches I've already given you) to come up with the promise of the newsletter and/or the promise in the subject line and/or introduction.

Now, a couple writing rules to keep in mind for writing the newsletter's Headers:

- A header accomplishes 2 primary goals for the reader: first, it is usually an H1 and bolded, which makes it a section divider and much easier for readers to skim the piece (this is a good thing); and second, each header should deliver on the promise in the subject-line/introduction to the point where a reader could simply read all the headers and extract 80% of the value. The headers gave them all the "quick answers." Then, it's the reader's choice if they want to go deeper and read the tactical content inside of each or any individual section.
- The more "sections" and headers there are in a newsletter, that means the less room there will be to write high-value content inside of each section (keeping the total newsletter length constraint of 800 to 1,500 words in mind). So the more "sections" and headers, that usually means the promise itself is something that can simply be delivered on in the headers themselves, and the content in each section just reinforces the answer that was already given in the header. Conversely, the less "sections" and headers there are leaves more room in each section to elaborate on "how" to execute what's being shared in each header, tactically. You want to keep this in mind as you come up with a niche-specific promise for the reader, and how to best deliver on that promise in the content (and decide how much explanation each section requires in order for the reader to extract as much tactical value as possible).
- Whatever "promise" is being made in the subject line and the introduction is also the promise that should be clearly mirrored and delivered on in the 3-10 headers in the newsletter. So for example, if the subject line says "5 mistakes designers make launching viral products," then we know there will be 5 "sections"/headers in the newsletter, and each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different "mistake." And if the subject line or introduction promises "questions," then each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different "question," etc.
- There is a very specific type of writing style for headers I would like you to use. Headers should be written in Sentence Style, where each header is written as a full, complete sentence with the first word capitalized (everything else lower-case) and punctuation at the end. The reason is because whatever promise is being made in the subject line/introduction, we want that promise to be delivered on in all the headers themselves—clearly and concisely in individual, bolded sentences. For example, if the promise of the newsletter is "How to land your first coaching client," then we know each "section"/header will be a different Tip or Step or something actionable that delivers on that promise, and to make each header skimmable and packed with value we want to give the most tactical, actionable Tip or Step right there in the header, in sentence format, so the reader knows exactly what to go do, in what order, without even needing to read the rest of the newsletter.

~

Variable #4: Section Content

Once the promise of the newsletter has been established in the subject line, and delivered on in the headers of the piece, you can then also use the 10 Magical Ways framework to fill in the content of each section.

Remember: the promise of the newsletter should be delivered on in the headers, such that a reader could just skim the headers and essentially get 80% of the value of reading the newsletter. Then, within each section, provide specific, tangible, differentiated and actionable insights so that if the reader wants to know more, each section is valuable.

You can use the 10 Magical Ways, but here's some specific criteria for making for a really valuable "section" of a newsletter:

- If the newsletter is some sort of "How To" newsletter, make each section as actionable/instructional as possible. Tips, steps, reasons, examples. The reader should know exactly what needs to be done in order to accomplish their desired goal or solve a specific problem.
- If the newsletter is more focused on a "why" topic, make each section more explanation focused. Stats, lessons, benefits, reasons, mistakes, etc. The key here though is to not explain things generally or with vague language, but instead give very specific, actionable, tactical, differentiated things to think about.

When it comes to the writing of each section, you want to make each section as skimmable and easy to read as possible. Here's how I recommend accomplishing that:

- Always start and end each section with a single-sentence opener/closer.
- Make the "middle" of each section a combination of prose and bulleted lists. But prose should be the majority, with only one bulleted list per section (this technique should be used sparingly).
- And look for opportunities to alternate between long sentences and short sentences to create rhythm and pacing in the writing.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 best ways to monetize your newsletter—and when to use each one.

Way 1: Digital products.

Most newsletter writers should start here—because you can sell a digital product to a list of any size.

But there's a few other digital products that make sense as you grow. Some examples you might sell are:

- Workshops & Cohorts: These are live, higher-ticket ($350-$1,000) versions of your best material. Once the format works, you can re-run it every quarter.

Way 2: Paid subscriptions.

This is the next stage in your newsletter—because monthly subscriptions are how you build a predictable income.

For example, once your free newsletter is publishing consistently, you can add a paid tier ($5-$15/month) by solving 2 questions:

- Question #1: What stays free? Your free newsletter is your growth engine—it's what attracts new readers and fills the top of your funnel. If you paywall everything, you stop growing.
- Question #2: What goes paid? The deeper, more tactical version of your best material: templates, worked examples, Q&As, archive access. Because if free is the "what," paid is the "how."

And you can start with just 1 paid post per month (then increase from there).

But if I can give you some friendly advice: nothing "recurs" forever.

Just because someone subscribes to your paid tier doesn't mean they'll stay forever. Every month, the reader has a decision to make: continue or cancel. So, you shouldn't stop growing your free list—paid subscribers churn, and your free list is how you replace them.

But what if you want your newsletter to keep paying you for writing you've already done?

Way 3: Books.

This is the final stage—and it's the most overlooked way to monetize a newsletter.

Because here's the secret: your newsletter archive IS a book. You're just publishing it one chapter at a time.

Once you've written enough issues on a theme, you have a few options based on how much work you want to put in and how much upside you want. For example:

- Option A: You could compile your best long-form issues into a short eBook and publish it on Amazon. This is the lowest-effort option—and it turns your archive into a 24/7 credibility asset (and income stream).
- Option B: You could sell that same eBook directly from your own website. This means handling your own checkout, but you keep roughly double the profit versus selling through Amazon.
- Option C: You could bundle your entire book library into your paid tier as a subscriber benefit. This adds recurring value to Way 2—and gives readers another reason to stay subscribed.
- Option D: You could expand your best-performing series into a full-length book. This is the biggest swing—but a book is the ultimate positioning asset for the "category king" of a niche.

And there's no right or wrong answer.

Because it's completely up to you how much time you want to invest, and how much upside you think there is in your archive.

But after years of doing this ourselves, I'll tell you what I wish I knew sooner:

- You don't "write a book" and then start a newsletter.
- You write a newsletter—and the book falls out of it.

In this lesson, we're going to cover:

The $0 Traffic Model: Newsletter First, Social Second

Most creators have this backwards.

They grind out social content every day, hoping something goes viral, and treat their newsletter as an afterthought. You're going to do the opposite:

  1. Write your newsletter first. (You did this on Day 3.) This is your deep, long-form "source of truth."

  2. Extract social posts from it. One newsletter becomes 10+ short-form posts.

  3. Distribute those posts on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes. Each platform is a top-of-funnel traffic arm.

  4. Convert followers into subscribers with deliberate CTAs, autoplugs, and profile optimization.

This solves the two biggest problems every Newsletter Creator faces:

  • "What do I post on social?" — Answered. You post extractions from your newsletter.

  • "How do I get subscribers without paying for ads?" — Answered. Organic social traffic, converted deliberately.

Your library of newsletters becomes an asset that appreciates. Newsletter #1 gives you 10 posts. By newsletter #10, you have a 100-post library you can extract from, remix, and republish forever.

Now, where should you post? Let's look at your three traffic arms.

Your 3 Traffic Arms: X, LinkedIn & Substack Notes

Each platform plays a different role:

  • X (Twitter): 335.7 million users. Fast feedback loops. Ideas spread quickly. Best for testing hooks, one-liners, and contrarian takes before expanding them into newsletters. Rewards provocation, hot takes, and threads.

  • LinkedIn: 1 billion users. Professional audience with high trust. Best for personal stories, frameworks, and "lessons learned" posts. One good LinkedIn post can drive more email subscribers than 10 tweets because the audience actually clicks links.

  • Substack Notes: "Only" 20 million users — and that's exactly why you should be there.

Let's talk about Notes for a second, because most Newsletter Creators are sleeping on it.

Substack Notes is the new kid on the block when it comes to social media. This means there isn't a huge number of users compared to other, more mature social platforms. This is why so many Newsletter Creators tend to keep their focus on growing their newsletter with their existing social media accounts.

But here's what they're missing:

  1. 20 million users is still a lot of readers to tap into!

  2. These 20 million users are a concentrated pool of readers (compared to X where some people are just there for the memes).

  3. Because Substack Notes is so new, it pays to be an early adopter so you can get that early adopter advantage. And this won't last forever!

One final and important note:

Because this is a new platform the rules change rapidly (sometimes daily). So spend time with Substack Notes. Experiment and observe what's happening. Analyze why other posts get more reach and replicate it for yourself. Being a student of the platform will pay off.

But, if you're still not convinced, let's look at some cold, hard data.

Social posting leads to subscriber growth AND creates more paid subscribers.

Two examples from our own newsletters:

  1. Posting on Substack Notes leads to more subscribers. (We've tracked spikes in daily subscriber growth that map directly to Notes we published.)

  2. Posting on Substack Notes leads to paid subs, too. Here's the story of a reader interacting with one of my Notes and then becoming a subscriber (we have a Zap that sends us a message in Slack every time we get a new paid subscriber!).

Magic!

Substack Notes is the perfect attention engine for your Substack newsletter.

Why?

Because everything remains within one platform.

On "traditional" social media platforms, there's a lot of friction to finding your newsletter:

  • They have to read one of your posts on X, LinkedIn, etc.

  • Then they have to go to your profile

  • Then they have to find the link to your newsletter

  • Then they have to subscribe to read it

Whereas, on Substack there is way less friction. If a reader likes your Note, they can subscribe directly from the Note itself.

So the model is: X and LinkedIn for reach, Substack Notes for frictionless conversion. Post on all three from the same newsletter extraction — the content is 90% identical, only the tone and format shift slightly per platform.

But what do you post? Well, let's look at what the algorithms reward!

How The Algorithms Work (And Why Notes Is Rigged In Your Favor)

Before you start posting, it helps to understand what you're working with.

Most social platforms optimize their algorithm for time spent scrolling. More scroll time = more ads seen = more revenue. That's X and LinkedIn: they want to keep readers ON the platform, which is why link posts get suppressed and why we'll use "autoplugs" (more on that below) instead of naked links.

Substack doesn't have ads. They make money when creators make money (Substack takes 10% of paid subscriptions). So the Notes algorithm is optimized for one thing: getting readers to discover, subscribe, and eventually pay.

Mike Cohen, Substack's Head of Machine Learning, said: "The goal is to get people to discover, subscribe, and ideally pay. That's how we built the feed and how we continue to iterate."

This is a big deal.

It means the algorithm is literally on your side. Every other social platform treats you as content that keeps eyeballs glued to a feed. Substack treats you as a creator it wants to connect with paying readers. You win, they win.

Here's what the algorithm looks at when deciding who sees your Notes:

  • Who the reader is (location, language)

  • What they're subscribed to and who they follow

  • What interests they've selected

  • Their engagement behavior (clicks, likes, restacks, comments)

The system converts all of this into a numerical profile for each reader, then matches it against available content. If your Note is a good match for a reader's profile, it gets surfaced. If they engage with it, the algorithm surfaces more of your stuff.

Now here's the part most people don't know about.

In 2025, Substack upgraded from a static matching system to what they call sequential models. The old system treated each reader's preferences as a fixed snapshot. The new system understands reading as a journey unfolding over time. If a reader clicks on a productivity Note, the feed leans into that momentum and surfaces more productivity content in that same session. Your Note doesn't just compete against everything on the platform. It competes within the context of what that specific reader is interested in right now.

Two more things worth knowing:

  • Restacking and replying create recommendation bridges. When you restack or reply to another writer's content, the algorithm traces the full chain of behavior. If your readers also read Writer X, then Writer X's readers might start seeing your Notes. The system uses audience overlap between publications to build these bridges. (The same principle applies on X and LinkedIn: thoughtful replies to bigger accounts put you in front of their audience.)

  • Consistency beats virality. Substack's own data showed that steady, regular posting drove more subscriber growth than occasional viral hits. The sequential model rewards ongoing patterns of engagement over one-off spikes. Show up every day and the algorithm learns who should see your work. Post once a month and it forgets you exist.

In just 3 months (as of October 2025), the Substack app drove 32 million free subscriptions and 500,000 paid subscriptions. The app became the #1 source of subscriber growth for publishers. Notes is the engine inside that app.

OK?

So the algorithms want to distribute your content. Your job is to give them something worth recommending.

Traffic Mistakes To Avoid

Before we get into what works, let's talk about what doesn't.

These are the 5 most common mistakes we see Newsletter Creators make when driving social traffic. If you're doing any of these, fix them first. Then move on to the strategy.

Mistake #1: Speaking The Wrong Language On The Wrong Platform

Notes is not a microblogging platform for hot takes and dunking on people.

The algorithm rewards connection, not controversy. Writers who bring their Twitter habits to Notes get likes, sure. But they don't get subscribers. And there's a massive difference between the two.

The audience on Substack is there to read and learn. They want depth. They want genuine thinking. So if you're posting the same spicy tweets you'd throw onto X, you're speaking the wrong language to the wrong crowd. (The reverse is also true: a long, vulnerable LinkedIn story posted verbatim on X will die. Same idea, adapted format.)

Mistake #2: Only Posting Links To Your Newsletter

"New post! Link in comments."

Sound familiar?

This is the #1 mistake writers make. They treat social platforms as a promotional bulletin board. And nobody clicks those. Readers want to be engaged on the platform they're on. They don't want to be redirected somewhere else every time you show up in their feed.

If every post you write is a link to your newsletter, you're training the algorithm (and readers) to scroll right past you.

Mistake #3: Posting Once And Disappearing

One post a week is not a strategy. It's a lottery ticket.

The algorithm builds a picture of your voice over time. It watches who engages, what they subscribe to, who else they follow. And then it starts showing your writing to new readers who match that profile. But it needs data. Consistency is what trains the algorithm to work for you. Sporadic posting gives it nothing to work with.

Mistake #4: Ignoring The Engagement Side

Social is a two-way street.

The writers who grow fastest are commenting on other writers' posts, restacking/resharing work they admire, and having conversations. If you're posting but never engaging, you're running at half speed.

And here's the thing: algorithms now rank high-signal interactions (replies that add genuine value) above passive hearts and "love this!" comments. So the quality of your engagement matters, too.

Mistake #5: No Conversion Mechanism

You can write great posts, get tons of likes, and still gain zero subscribers.

Why? Because you never gave anyone a reason to subscribe. There's no bridge between "I liked this post" and "I subscribed to this newsletter."

You need a deliberate system for turning social attention into newsletter subscriptions. (Don't worry. That's coming later in this session.)

OK. Now that we know what NOT to do, let's get to the heart of today: the extraction workflow.

The 10 Magical Ways: Extracting 10+ Social Posts From One Newsletter

The 10 Magical Ways: 1 Newsletter In, 10+ Posts Out

Here's the workflow that ends "what should I post today?" forever.

Take your Day 3 newsletter draft. Read through it with a highlighter (literal or digital). Every newsletter you write contains at least 10 extractable social posts hiding inside it. Here are the 10 Magical Ways to pull them out:

  1. The Standalone Insight. Find your single most surprising claim or observation. Distill it into 1-3 punchy sentences. No context needed — it should make someone stop scrolling on its own.

  2. The Personal Story. Find the best story or anecdote in your newsletter. Rewrite it as a short post (under 250 words) that opens with a specific, vivid moment and builds to a single "aha" insight.

  3. The Listicle. Take any section with multiple points and reformat it as a numbered list post. "5 things I learned about [topic]:" — lists are the most shareable format on every platform.

  4. The Framework Breakdown. If your newsletter teaches a process or framework, extract the steps into a "how to" post. Step 1 → Step 2 → Step 3. On X, this becomes a thread. On LinkedIn, a line-break-heavy post. On Notes, a short numbered Note.

  5. The Contrarian Take. Find the place where your newsletter disagrees with conventional wisdom. Extract it as: "Everyone says X. Here's why they're wrong: [your take]."

  6. The Quotable Line. Find 2-3 "quotable" paragraphs — the lines you're proudest of. Post each one verbatim. On Substack, use the Newsletter Quote feature (highlight → post to Notes) so the quote links back to the full edition automatically.

  7. The Proof Post. Extract any number, result, stat, or before/after from your newsletter. "I did X for 30 days. Here's what happened:" Receipts build trust faster than opinions.

  8. The Question Post (Community Invitation). Take your newsletter's core theme and turn it into a specific question for your audience. Make it about THEM, not you. Include a generous offer ("Drop your newsletter below and I'll check it out").

  9. The Teaser (Open Loop). Pull out the most intriguing insight or claim and format it as a standalone post that creates an information gap. End with: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

  10. The Mistake/Lesson Post. Extract what you (or your reader) were doing wrong before the insight in your newsletter. "I spent 2 years doing [wrong thing]. Then I learned [insight]."

That's the whole workflow: 1 newsletter in, 10+ atomic posts out.

A few rules for extraction:

  • Do NOT repost the newsletter. EXTRACT and TRANSFORM the best parts into standalone posts that work even if someone never reads the full edition.

  • Every post must stand alone. If it requires reading the newsletter to make sense, it's not extracted yet.

  • Adapt per platform. Same idea, three flavors: punchy and provocative for X, story-driven and professional for LinkedIn, warm and reader-to-reader for Notes.

  • Keep each post under 280 words. Short paragraphs (1-2 sentences each). Make them sound like a real person, not a content machine.

Do this every time you publish, and after 10 newsletters you'll have a 100+ post library. You'll never stare at a blank compose box again.

Now let's turn those posts into a system.

The Traffic Strategy: Content, Cadence, Connection, Conversion

The Traffic Strategy is a 4-part system for turning social posting into a consistent, compounding subscriber growth machine.

Here are the 4 parts:

  • Part 1: Content: What to post (the 3 content buckets and specific post types that convert)

  • Part 2: Cadence: When and how often to post (the daily rhythm)

  • Part 3: Connection: How to engage strategically (comments, restacks, relationships)

  • Part 4: Conversion: How to turn social readers into newsletter subscribers

Think of these as four gears. When all four are turning, the engine runs itself. Skip one, and the whole thing stalls.

Most writers only do Part 1 (content). They post, hope for the best, and then wonder why social "doesn't work" for them. The secret is that Parts 2, 3, and 4 are where the compounding happens.

Let's break down each part.

1. What To Post (The 3 Content Buckets)

There are 3 "buckets" of content you can post:

  1. Short-form original. Think of this as your typical social media content. Take snippets from your newsletter (via the 10 Magical Ways above) and post them as tweets, LinkedIn posts, or Substack Notes. Or experiment with new ideas by posting and seeing how the idea performs. If it performs well, expand the idea into a newsletter. This is Lean Writing 101: social is your idea lab, the newsletter is your finished product.

  2. Restacks / Reshares. This is exactly like retweets on Twitter. Use this function to restack other Notes you like or other newsletters you found interesting (or quote-tweet on X, reshare with commentary on LinkedIn). Choose to either share without comment or add your own comment (highly-recommended!).

  3. Newsletter Quotes. If you found a section of a newsletter interesting, highlight it then choose to post it to Notes with your own comment. A screenshot of the quote is created alongside a link to the original newsletter. (You can do this with your own newsletter too.) On X and LinkedIn, the equivalent is a clean screenshot of your best paragraph with a one-line setup.

One final note:

As with all social platforms, the algorithm and audience favor certain types of content. And right now, pairing your post with an image gets far more traction than pairing it with a video. But, of course, this might change so I encourage you to keep experimenting.

2. When And How To Post (Cadence)

Right now, there is no way to schedule posts on Substack Notes (X and LinkedIn do have scheduling — use it).

Which means you have to manage your posts with discipline. As with every other social media platform, consistency is key. It helps you to a) publish a lot of ideas over an extended period of time and b) build trust with your audience because they "expect" you to appear in their feed.

So, pick a schedule and stick with it.

I post twice per day at 10am and 4pm ET. Dickie does the same.

And if you need a little rigor, here's a simple weekly content calendar you can follow:

  • Monday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Restack with Commentary (4pm)

  • Tuesday: Personal Story (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Wednesday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Newsletter Teaser (4pm)

  • Thursday: Restack with Commentary (10am) + Newsletter Quote (4pm)

  • Friday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Saturday: Newsletter Teaser (10am) + Restack with Commentary (4pm)

  • Sunday: Personal Story (10am) + Standalone Insight (4pm)

You don't need to follow this exactly. But it gives you a starting point so you never sit down and think "what should I post today?"

Batch your WRITING (not necessarily your posting):

  1. Sunday night: Extract and write 5-7 posts for the week from your latest newsletter. Standalone Insights and Personal Stories are the easiest to batch. Save them in a doc or your notes app, then copy-paste at your posting times throughout the week.

  2. Daily: Write 1-2 reactive posts in real-time. Restacks, Community Invitations, and Newsletter Quotes work best when they're timely and spontaneous.

  3. Post-newsletter day: Pull 1-2 Newsletter Teasers from your latest edition.

Cross-posting rule: write once, adapt twice. Your Sunday batch is drafted once, then given a 60-second platform pass — tighten the hook for X, add line breaks and a story frame for LinkedIn, soften the tone for Notes.

Content and cadence are locked.

3. How To Engage (Connection)

At the end of the day, I encourage you to be a good social citizen.

If you interact with more people, you're more likely to attract new subscribers to your own content. So it pays to be active and engage with other writers you enjoy reading.

OK. With that philosophy in mind, let me show you why engagement matters even more than posting.

When you leave a substantive comment on a popular writer's post, you show up in front of their entire audience. If your comment is good (if it adds genuine value, a personal example, or a thoughtful perspective), people click on your name, visit your profile, and subscribe.

One good comment on the right post can bring more subscribers than 10 posts of your own.

So engagement is not a "nice to have." It's the multiplier that makes everything else work.

Strategy #1: The Value-Add Comment

When you comment on someone else's post, don't say "love this!" or "so true!"

Those comments don't help the algorithm surface your profile. Substantive comments do. Add something. A personal example. A related insight. A "yes, and…" that takes their point further. The rule: every comment you leave should be good enough to be its own post.

When your comments are consistently thoughtful, two things happen.

  • The algorithm surfaces them higher (more people see them).

  • And the writer you're engaging with starts to notice you (which leads to restacks, cross-promotion, and organic relationship-building).

Strategy #2: The Restack (Or Quote-Share)

I talked about Restacking as a content type above.

But I want to call it out again as an engagement strategy because it's that powerful. When you restack someone's Note with your own commentary (or quote-tweet on X, or reshare on LinkedIn), it goes to YOUR audience with your endorsement, and it notifies the original writer.

They see your name.

They check you out.

And if you've been consistently restacking their work with thoughtful takes, they'll often return the favor.

One restack from the right person can bring dozens of new subscribers.

Restack 2-3 posts per week from writers in your niche or adjacent niches. Always add your own take. (Don't just hit the restack button.)

Strategy #3: Build Your "Traffic 15"

Identify 10-15 writers in your niche or adjacent niches with similar-sized audiences.

Write their names down. These are your "Traffic 15."

Engage with their posts consistently. Comment, restack, reply. Over 2-4 weeks, you'll build a relationship. And the algorithm notices overlapping audiences. When your readers and their readers start interacting with both of you, the platform starts showing your work to THEIR followers and vice versa.

This is the organic version of cross-promotion. And it's more powerful because it's earned.

Rotate 1-2 names per month as your audience grows.

Here's a simple checklist. Every day, in addition to posting your 2 posts:

  • Comment substantively on 3-5 posts from writers in your niche

  • Reply to every comment on your own posts within the first hour

  • Restack/reshare 1 post with your own commentary (if you find something worth sharing)

  • Check your "Traffic 15" — have you engaged with at least 2-3 of them today?

This takes 10 minutes.

You're posting great content. You're showing up consistently. You're building relationships. But are those readers actually becoming subscribers?

Let's make sure they do.

4. How To Convert Followers Into Subscribers (Conversion)

Most writers still leave subscribers on the table because they don't have a deliberate conversion system.

Here's how to fix that.

Conversion Tactic #1: Optimize Your Profiles

Your profile (on every platform) must answer one question instantly for your reader: "What will I get if I subscribe?"

And to answer this question…

  • Your newsletter name must clearly state your niche (you built this on Day 1)

  • Your one-line description/bio needs to communicate the value (you built this on Day 1)

  • Your pinned post should sell the subscription — pin your best newsletter teaser or a "start here" post with your subscribe link

  • On X and LinkedIn: put your newsletter link in your bio, not buried in a linktree

Your social strategy will not work without a profile that converts. The profile is the conversion bottleneck.

Conversion Tactic #2: Leave Breadcrumbs

Inside your posts, occasionally reference your newsletter in a way that creates curiosity.

Here's what I mean:

  • "I broke this down in way more detail in last week's edition. The part about [specific intriguing detail] surprised even me."

  • "My subscribers know I've been tracking this for 6 months now. The data is wild."

  • "This is the short version. The 2,000-word deep dive is in my newsletter if you want the full framework."

When you do this, you create an information gap. There's a piece of the story the reader can only get by subscribing or digging into your newsletter. And that gap creates genuine curiosity.

Use this 2-3x per week. Sprinkle it into Personal Story and Standalone Insight posts. Never force it. When you have something genuinely interesting in your newsletter, mention it casually.

Conversion Tactic #3: "For Example…"

(This is one of my favorite tactics. It's so powerful it's worth teaching everywhere.)

If you want to point readers toward your newsletter without being seen as promotional, all you need are two magical words: "For example…"

Whenever you share an insight in a post, follow it with "For example, in my newsletter I…" and describe something specific and tangible that you do or share.

Like this:

Most Newsletter Creators only think about growth on external platforms. But the biggest lever is right inside the platform you're already on.

For example, in my newsletter [Newsletter Name], I share one specific traffic strategy every week that I've tested myself. Last week's strategy brought in 40+ new subscribers from a single post.

Are you furious at me for being "overly promotional?" Of course not. I just used my newsletter as an example. Casually. Organically.

And yet I still introduced it to you.

This is the whole secret. After the words "for example," you can point to any business, any product, any money-making-anything, and it won't come off as promotional. It comes across as a relevant example. The reader appreciates it.

Conversion Tactic #4: The Autoplug

On X and LinkedIn, the algorithm suppresses posts with links. So don't put your newsletter link in the post — put it in the first reply/comment.

Here's the play:

  1. Publish your post (no link).

  2. Immediately reply to your own post: "If you liked this, I go deeper every week in [Newsletter Name]. Subscribe free: [link]"

  3. If a post starts performing, that reply rides along with it. (Tools like Hypefury and Typefully can automate this "autoplug" to fire only when a post crosses an engagement threshold.)

The post does the work of earning attention. The autoplug does the work of converting it. Never let a post take off without a subscribe path attached.

Conversion Tactic #5: The CTA Rotation

Most posts should focus on pure value delivery. Only ~30% of your posts should have any CTA at all.

Here's the rotation:

  • 60-70% of your posts: No CTA. Just deliver value. Build trust. Let the profile do the converting.

  • 1-2x per week: Link to your newsletter. "Full breakdown in this week's [Newsletter Name] 👇" (On X/LinkedIn: link goes in the reply via autoplug.)

  • 1x per week: Soft subscribe prompt. "If this resonated, my newsletter goes deeper on [topic] every [day]. Subscribe free."

  • 2-3x per week: Breadcrumb trail. Just reference your newsletter casually.

The math on this works. Post 14 posts per week per platform. Average reach per post: 500-2,000 impressions (this grows over time). A small percentage click your profile. A percentage of those subscribe (especially if your profile is optimized).

Result: 10-30+ new subscribers per week from organic social alone. Per platform. And it compounds.

5. More Tips And Tricks To Squeeze Extra Juice

Here are some of my current favorite insights and tricks:

  • Notes lifespan. The life of a post is longer on Substack than on X or LinkedIn. Some Notes can get engagement WEEKS after we've posted them. So traction can really pick up over a number of days and weeks. Again, another reason to start posting on Notes.

  • No platform analytics on Notes. At least, not for now. So you will have to track your engagement manually (likes, comments, restacks, etc). Or try using a tool like WriteStack. (X and LinkedIn have built-in analytics — check them weekly, not daily.)

  • Newsletters get pushed to Notes. Your newsletters automatically drop into your Notes feed so you don't have to manually post them to your feed.

  • Create high-quality thumbnails. As newsletters get pushed into the feed automatically, it's important to have an eye-catching thumbnail for the newsletter so it stands out in the feed (this is the main image of your post). You can use this as an opportunity to tease the value or create an open loop for the reader.

  • Promote your best posts inside your newsletter. You can do this in your long-form newsletters by including a snippet of your best-performing post of the week. This is another way in for your audience to find your social content and start engaging with it. The flywheel runs both directions: newsletter → social → newsletter.

  • Winners get recycled. Any post that outperforms your average earns a spot in your "greatest hits" doc. Repost it in 60-90 days (audiences turn over fast), and consider expanding it into its own newsletter edition.

That's it!

The big POV here is that your newsletter library is a traffic asset, and organic social is a growth lever you should be pulling every single day — especially Substack Notes, where the algorithm is literally built to hand you subscribers.

And the best part?

If you start now, you're early to the party. So there's never been a better time to get started.

(Bonus!) The AI Content Extraction Prompts

Below are two simple prompts you can use to generate social content. Copy-paste them into ChatGPT, Claude, or your AI tool of choice. They'll generate posts for you based on the post types we just covered.

Now, what you can do is:

  • Run Prompt #1 to batch a full week of posts in one sitting

  • OR run Prompt #2 to take your latest newsletter (your Day 3 draft!) and extract 5-7 posts from it

  • Review the AI drafts and add YOUR voice, YOUR stories, YOUR specific details

  • Then post throughout the week

So cool!

Prompt #1: The Weekly Batch Generator

Purpose: Generate a full week's worth of posts (10-14) in one sitting.

You are a social content strategist for newsletter creators.

I'm going to give you context about my newsletter, and I need you to generate a batch of 14 posts for the upcoming week (usable on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes).

MY NEWSLETTER:
- Name: [Your newsletter name]
- Niche: [Your niche]
- Who I write for: [Your target reader]
- What I help them do: [The transformation/value]
- My latest newsletter was about: [Topic of most recent edition]
- A personal story I could share this week: [Brief description]

GENERATE 14 POSTS USING THESE TYPES:

Type 1 — Personal Story + Insight (generate 3):
- A short personal story (under 250 words) that builds to a single "aha" moment related to my niche
- Open with a specific, vivid moment
- End with one clear insight
- Optional: close with a question

Type 2 — Standalone Insight (generate 4):
- My best thinking distilled into 1-3 punchy sentences
- A surprising observation about my niche
- Should make someone stop scrolling

Type 3 — Community Invitation (generate 2):
- A post that invites readers to participate
- Ask a specific question (not generic)
- Make it about THEM, not me
- Include a generous offer ("Drop your newsletter and I'll check it out" or similar)

Type 4 — Newsletter Teaser (generate 3):
- Based on my latest newsletter topic above, pull out the most intriguing insight or claim
- Format as a standalone post that creates an information gap
- End with: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

FORMAT: Number each post. Label the type. Keep each post under 280 words. Use short paragraphs (1-2 sentences each). Make them sound like a real person, not a content machine.

Prompt #2: The Newsletter-to-Social Repurposer

Purpose: Take any newsletter edition and extract 5-7 posts from it. (Run this on your Day 3 draft tonight.)

3. Find 2-3 "quotable" paragraphs. Turn each into a Standalone Insight post.
4. Write 1 Newsletter Teaser post that creates an information gap and links back to the full edition.
5. Write 1 Community Invitation post inspired by the newsletter topic (ask readers a question related to the theme).

Frequently Asked Questions

"How many followers do I need before this starts working?"

Zero.

Posts from writers with 100 followers can outperform those with 10,000+ because the algorithms weight genuine engagement over follower count. If you write something that resonates with even 5 people and they engage, the algorithm starts showing it to similar readers.

Don't wait until you're "big enough." Start now. That's the whole point of the early adopter advantage.

"I'm getting likes but no subscribers. What's wrong?"

Likes and subscribers are two different things. If you're getting likes but no subscribers, you have a conversion problem, not a content problem.

Go back to the Conversion section above. Check your profile. Does it clearly communicate what readers get if they subscribe? Are you using the Breadcrumb Trail? Are you adding soft CTAs 2-3x per week? Is your autoplug firing on X and LinkedIn? Most likely, your posts are good but your profile isn't closing.

"Should I post the same content on Notes, X, and LinkedIn?"

You can.

But the audiences are different. X rewards provocation, hot takes, and threads. Notes rewards vulnerability, stories, and genuine helpfulness. LinkedIn rewards professional stories and frameworks. A post that works on X might not work on Notes, and vice versa.

If you want to cross-post, adapt the tone and format for each platform. (This is a 60-second edit per post, not a rewrite.)

"I don't have time to post 2x per day. Is once a day enough?"

Once a day is better than zero. But 2x per day is where the compounding kicks in.

If you're strapped for time, commit to spend 20 minutes total. Most of these posts are 2-5 sentences. If you can send a text message, you can write a post. Batch 5-7 on Sunday night and you're already ahead for the week.

"What if I run out of things to say?"

You won't.

If you're publishing a newsletter, every single edition contains 5-7 posts waiting to be extracted (use Prompt #2 above — or the 10 Magical Ways if you're extracting by hand). Every conversation you have, every article you read, every question a subscriber asks — those are all posts.

"Should I engage with writers who have way bigger audiences than me?"

Absolutely. This is one of the highest-leverage things you can do.

When you leave a genuinely valuable comment on a big writer's post, their entire audience sees it. If your comment is good, people click on your name.

Don't be sycophantic. "OMG I love everything you write!" doesn't help anyone.

Add value. Share your own experience. Respectfully extend their point. Be the comment that makes the original writer say "damn, good point."

Reminder:

The writers who win at newsletter growth aren't the most talented. They're the most consistent.

And the best part? If you start now, you're early to the party. So there's never been a better time to get started.

Lesson 5: Newsletter Monetization Methods

In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: how to make money from subscriptions (pricing, paywalls & when to go paid)

  • The Book Model (Self-Publishing): how to make money republishing your newsletter content as books

  • The Digital Product Model: how to turn your email list into a digital product "engine"

And more!

All so you can leave the Sprint with a 90-day monetization plan—and a newsletter that pays you for years to come.

Let's dive in!

A quick note before we start: why ads aren't on the list

Technically, there's another model out there that everyone talks about, which is The Sponsorship Model. But the reason we're not going to cover it is because we don't recommend it. Yes, many newsletters monetize with ads. (Beehiiv has done a good job here, integrating advertisers into their platform and pairing them with newsletters.)

However, you're here to learn from us.

And OUR take is that ads are one of the worst ways to monetize.

Ads require massive scale before they pay anything meaningful, they put someone else's message in front of your readers, and they slowly exhaust the trust you've spent months building. You'd be much better off (and make way more money) monetizing with one of these other business models instead.

Everything we cover today works whether you're on Substack, Kit, or Beehiiv. The mechanics differ slightly by platform, but the models are identical.

Choosing The Right Monetization Model

3 Ways Your Newsletter Pays You (No Ads Required)

To effectively monetize your newsletter, here are your options:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: how you make money from subscriptions

  • The Book Model: how you make money republishing newsletter content as books on Amazon

  • The Digital Product Model: how you make money from selling one-off digital products

Now, the big question everyone asks is, "OK… so which one should I pick?"

The Answer: All of them!

One of the BIGGEST missed opportunities for newsletter writers is thinking that the only way to monetize is through the Paid Newsletter Model.

And this is wrong.

If you decide to turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter… this is the beginning of monetization, not the end!

  • Yes, you should monetize your content via paid subscription.

  • But you can also sell all your paid subscribers (and also your free subscribers, who are maybe looking for something different) on digital products.

  • And you can also sell all your paid subscribers (and also your free subscribers, who are maybe looking for something different) on the same content presented in different formats: eBook, print books, audiobooks, etc.

It's SHOCKING to us how many newsletter writers don't do any of these things.

They fail to realize how much money they're leaving on the table by not also offering digital products, and not also double-monetizing their content in books & audiobooks.

So. Much. Money. Left. On. The. Table.

It kills us!

(So please, don't make this mistake.)

That said — you can't launch everything at once. Today we'll cover all three models, then give you a decision framework for which one to start with. Your homework is to pick one and map your 90-day plan.

Method #1: The Paid Newsletter Model

The primary monetization model for newsletters is to "go paid."

On Substack, this is built in natively. On Kit, you can do this with a paid recommendation or by pairing your list with a payment tool. On Beehiiv, paid subscriptions are built into the platform as well.

This is a relatively easy monetization model to adopt and understand, which is what makes it great for beginners. You don't have to mess around with learning a bunch of different tech platforms. You don't really have to acquire advanced copywriting skills, or learn how to run ads. All you have to do is add a paywall (placed strategically) into your newsletters and publish consistently for a long period of time.

That's about it.

Why The Paid Newsletter Model Is So Great

Well, it's great for a bunch of reasons:

  • First, paid newsletters are subscription revenue. And subscription revenue is king. Since subscriptions "recur" (over and over again), they create a very defensible sort of business. If you have 1,000 paying subscribers, there's essentially a 0% chance all 1,000 of them unsubscribe at the same time. Instead, you might churn maybe 10% of them per month—while also continuing to attract new paying subscribers. All of this is just a fancy way of saying: you have a defensible, predictable business. Great!

  • Second, paid newsletters are very easy/simple to operate. When you turn your newsletter paid, you connect it to Stripe and payments happen directly inside your platform. There's very little, if any "operational infrastructure" you need to build or even manage. It's quite literally one of the simplest business models to execute in the digital age. Also great for beginners!

  • Third, paid newsletters are insanely powerful engines for other monetization models later. Even if you don't monetize in these other ways, it's worth acknowledging that having a paid newsletter as the "nucleus" of your business will pay you dividends for a long, long time. That's because everyone on your paid newsletter list is essentially a customer raising their hand saying, "I'd love to give you more money—if you can help me solve more and more complicated/valuable problems."

We love paid newsletters as a monetization model.

Free-To-Paid Conversion & Paywall Strategy

The mechanics of going paid come down to three decisions:

  1. What stays free vs. what goes paid. Your free content is your growth engine — it's how new readers discover you. Your paid content is the deeper, more actionable, more "do this exactly" version. A common split: free readers get the "what" and "why," paid readers get the "how" (templates, systems, step-by-step breakdowns).

  2. Where you place the paywall. Don't paywall the whole post. Place the paywall after you've delivered real value and right before the most actionable payoff. The free portion has to be good enough that readers feel the pain of not seeing the rest. Learning how to place your paywall strategically to increase conversions is a skill — and it's one of the fundamentals worth "getting good" at early.

  3. Pricing. The standard range is $5–$15/month, with an annual option priced at roughly 10x the monthly price (so annual subscribers effectively get 2 months free). $10/mo or $100/yr is a perfectly good starting point for most niches. Don't agonize over this — you can always adjust. What matters far more is publishing consistently.

When Should You Go Paid?

Sooner than you think. You don't need 10,000 subscribers. A useful signal: once you have a few hundred engaged subscribers who consistently open and reply, turn on paid — even if only a handful convert at first. Industry-wide, expect roughly 2–5% of your free list to convert to paid over time. The bigger and warmer your free list gets, the more that percentage compounds.

Method #2: The Book Model (Self-Publishing)

This next model is a bit more creative.

As a beginner, you should either turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter first, and/or you should start out launching some digital products to your list. These are much easier monetization models to execute.

But once you've gotten in a flow, and especially the longer you stick with your newsletter (content compounds), we would absolutely recommend adding in this monetization model.

Here's how it works:

  • If you write long-form newsletters (5,000+ words), you can actually get a simple eBook cover designed and also publish them on Amazon. (*NOTE: These cannot go inside KDP Select. But they can be published non-exclusively.) These eBooks will get organized into Amazon's "quick reads" eBook categories.

  • Once you have ~15 long-form newsletters (or ~30-ish standard newsletters) all on the same topic, you can "compile" them into larger print books & audiobooks. The "value" of this is that some readers simply like consuming the same content in different ways. This is what we did with books like Snow Leopard (which was 100% reused content from our newsletter), and readers absolutely loved being able to have a print copy on their desks.

  • You can also sell eBook and audiobook versions on your personal website as digital downloads. This requires a bit more infrastructure setup, but remember… sales generated through your website aren't subject to Amazon taking a cut. Which means you make 2x the profit!

But wait… there's more!

Another clever strategy you can leverage is, when you start turning newsletters into mini-books, and mini-books into bigger books… you can also "bundle in" free access to this library of digital assets back into your paid newsletter.

This is what Cole does with his paid fiction newsletter, Commercial Fiction Club. A benefit of upgrading to paid is you get "free access" to his entire library of fiction writing.

Why is this a great tactic?

Because you're essentially trading one-off revenue (customer buys a book) for recurring revenue (they subscribe to your paid newsletter, and stay subscribed to continue getting access to not just the paid newsletter, but your entire library, in perpetuity).

Books = Authority + Revenue

One thing worth calling out: a book isn't just a revenue stream. "Author of [Book]" is one of the fastest credibility unlocks available to a newsletter writer. It boosts free-to-paid conversion, makes your digital products easier to sell, and gets you podcast invites and speaking opportunities that grow the newsletter itself. The revenue is real — but the authority compounds even faster.

And the best part: you don't have to create anything "new." You just have to repackage work you've already done in the past.

Method #3: The Digital Product Model

Whether you have a free newsletter and/or a paid newsletter, we would strongly encourage you to consider adopting the Digital Product Monetization Model as well.

This means selling subscribers:

  • [$9–$99] Template packs, AI prompts, dashboards, cheat sheets, mini-courses, etc.

  • [$99–$350] Text & video asynchronous courses

  • [$350–$1,000] Workshops, cohorts, challenges, bootcamps, etc.

One of the biggest "mental unlocks" is realizing that both your free & paid newsletter lists are lists of potential customers.

For example, Write With AI has over 112,000 free subscribers—and only 1,800 active paying subscribers.

It would be a HUGE mistake to think, "I guess the only way we can make money is by people upgrading to the paid newsletter list." Why?

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list just don't like paid newsletters as a concept (it happens).

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list want more help, or help specifically on a particular topic.

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list want more hands-on help, more direct access to you, etc.

The point is, all those "free" subscribers should have more than 1 way to give you money.

Having a paid newsletter option is great.

But you want to give them other options, too.

Let us show you how "expensive" of a mistake this can be.

A few weeks ago, we ran a Claude Cowork Bootcamp.

This was a 2-week "cohort" experience teaching writers, creators, and entrepreneurs how to use no-code agents inside Claude Cowork. Why did we do this? Because Write With AI readers had been asking us a lot of questions about Claude, Claude Cowork, and no-code agents!

So, we spun up a curriculum and launched it to our entire Write With AI list.

And guess what? Most of the people who bought weren't even active paying subscribers.

They were free subscribers… who just needed to be presented with a different offer.

And look what happened:

Over $167,000 in revenue from one 2-week bootcamp offer — launched to the same list.

Over 200 people took us up on this specific 2-week bootcamp, generating over $167,000 in revenue.

Translation: this 1 "different" offer did 1/3rd of Write With AI's total yearly revenue… in 2 weeks.

And now, knowing this is possible, imagine if we DIDN'T do this. We'd be "missing" $167,000 in additional revenue! OUCH!!!!!

In short: do not underestimate the power of giving free & paid subscribers "other things to buy."

Writers leave a tremendous amount of money on the table when they make this mistake.

Mistakes To Avoid

Before you pick your model, here are the most common (and most expensive) mistakes we see:

  1. Monetizing with ads/sponsorships too early (or at all). You rent out your readers' attention for pennies, exhaust their trust, and cap your upside. Every model we covered today pays more per subscriber than ads ever will at your size.

  2. Thinking paid subscriptions are the ONLY way to monetize. Going paid is the beginning of monetization, not the end. The Write With AI example above is what this mistake costs: $167,000 in 2 weeks, from one "different" offer.

  3. Paywalling everything. Your free content is your growth engine. Kill it and you kill the top of your funnel. Paywall the payoff, not the post.

  4. Waiting until you feel "big enough." You don't need 10,000 subscribers to go paid or launch a product. You need a few hundred engaged readers and one clear offer.

  5. Never asking for the sale. If you know how to solve a reader's problem and never tell them you can help, you're not being polite — you're letting them suffer. (More on this in the FAQ below.)

  6. Launching all three models at once. Stack them over time, one threshold at a time. That's what the decision framework is for.

Frequently Asked Questions

Now, whenever we walk writers through the different ways they can monetize a newsletter, we always get the same handful of questions.

So let's rapid-fire through them here:

"Which monetization model is the best?"

There's no such thing.

The "best one" is the one that interests you the most, and that you'll be willing to stick with (through the growing pains) and not give up on.

Because we could tell you "the best one," but if it's not one you're interested in executing, then it doesn't matter.

"Can I use more than one monetization model?"

Yes! That's the goal!

Your business becomes more and more profitable, and defensible, the more of these different monetization models you stack together.

For example, this is how Category Pirates was built into a multi-6-figure newsletter and multi-6-figure publishing business:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: We wrote long-form paid newsletters (which we called "mini-books") 2x per month, and charged $20/mo (or $200/yr). Our paid newsletter grew to ~$150,000 in annual recurring revenue.

  • The Book Model: Then, to unlock a secondary revenue stream, we took all of our "mini-books" (newsletters), slapped a cover on them, and republished them as "mini-books" on Amazon. And then we monetized again by compiling 12-15 "mini-books" on a topic, and republishing it again as a print book/audiobook. Republishing our content unlocked another $100,000/yr in annual revenue.

  • The Digital Product Model: Later, we added in digital products and cohort-based programs, giving subscribers yet another way to learn the material and gain more access to us. Adding in these digital products and experiences added another $250,000+ in annual revenue.

So yes, the goal is to combine these different business models—and keep giving readers more and more ways to learn from you and work with you.

"But won't readers get upset if I basically take the same content and charge for it again somewhere else?"

No. This is a faulty belief.

Especially if you are changing the content's consumption type—like turning a newsletter into a Kindle eBook or audiobook, or turning newsletter ideas into more in-depth course modules paired with videos—then it's actually a completely different product.

And readers will be THANKFUL that you created an option for them to consume the content they want, in the way they want it.

"But won't readers get upset if I launch so many new offers? Won't I come across like a money-grubbing sleazy salesman?"

No. This is a faulty belief.

If I saw you had a problem that I knew how to solve, which one would make you more upset?

  • Telling you I know how to solve it, and would be happy to help you (for a price, of course)

  • Not telling you at all and letting you suffer

I'm going to go out on a limb and guess you'd be MORE UPSET at me NOT telling you the answer, and NOT being willing to help.

Right?

OK, great. That's all you're doing.

You aren't "selling" anything.

You're simply creating more available options for readers to get your help.

"How much money can I really earn with a newsletter?"

Infinite.

There are some newsletters generating hundreds of thousands of dollars per month in revenue. Obviously this is an outlier outcome, but it's entirely possible.

That said, here's what we think is a "realistic" home-run outcome:

  • $100,000+ per year in annual recurring revenue. This is completely doable for nearly any newsletter in any niche. Will it take work? Yes. Will it take time? Yes. But building a 6-figure paid newsletter is completely within the realm of "achievable" for most people (who stick with it).

  • $50,000+ per year in self-publishing revenue. If you successfully build a 6-figure paid newsletter, then you can absolutely unlock another $50,000 - $100,000 in incremental revenue simply by republishing your content as eBooks, print books, and audiobooks on Amazon. And it's an easy and lucrative model to execute because you don't have to create anything "new." You just have to repackage work you've already done in the past.

  • $150,000+ in digital product revenue. If you successfully build a growing free and/or paid newsletter, there's also zero reason why you can't unlock another 6 figures (or more) in revenue by launching digital products to your list. For us, Write With AI does ~$400,000 per year in subscription revenue, but does another $1,000,000+ in digital product revenue. So, our "digital product business" is actually 2-3x the size of our "paid newsletter business."

If you do all the above, you have a business well north of $300,000 per year — from a newsletter.

That's an insane outcome—and yet, totally achievable.

It will just take a bit more work than you probably think, and take a bit more time than you probably want (which is why so many people give up).

The Decision Framework: Which Method Do You Start With?

Your homework is to pick ONE of these monetization models, and start there.

But if you want a "constraint" for making forward-leaning decisions, here's what we would recommend:

  • First, turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter—and stay focused on this until you reach at least $50,000 in annual revenue. Focus on "getting good" at executing the fundamentals, learning how to place your paywall strategically to increase conversions, and building up a base of paying customers.

  • Once you reach $50,000 in annual subscription revenue from your paid newsletter, start launching digital products to your list. Keep doing this until you 2x the business—crossing $100,000 per year in revenue.

  • Then, once you cross $100,000 per year in revenue, add in the book/self-publishing component. This will be a time investment, but it will compound significantly in your favor as the years go by. This will unlock another tranche of revenue.

A quick gut-check if you're still torn:

This is the order in which we'd think about monetizing.

But please don't feel like you need to rush to figure out how to monetize in all these different ways tomorrow.

Just focus on going one step at a time. And as you cross each new threshold, adjust your strategy and grow into the next tier of monetization.

You now know more about starting, growing, and monetizing a newsletter than 99% of people who ever hit "create publication."

The only thing left to do is write.

Onwards and upwards!
