Niche Content Strategy

Your First 90 Days Of Content Ideas

No matter what niche you pick, your “content strategy” will be the same.

That’s because readers in every single niche all want the same things:

  • They want answers to their questions

  • They want solutions to their problems

  • And they want assets to achieve outcomes

That’s it.

Doesn’t matter if the niche is soccer or knitting or dropshipping or crypto.

All non-fiction writing fundamentally is in service of those 3 things.

Which means, whatever niche you pick, your “strategy” is really to just give readers those 3 things:

  • As clearly as you can

  • As often as you can

  • For as long as you can

Which is why the whole goal is to become known for a niche you own—and for you to become associated with your chosen niche topic.

So, let’s make this extremely prescriptive for you.

If all non-fiction content, in all niches, is in service of answering questions, providing solutions to problems, and providing assets to achieve outcomes, then your first 90 days of content is just 90 different variations of those 3 things.

Your First 30 Days: The 10 Magical Ways

If you’re a beginner and brand new to writing online (and honestly, even if you’ve been writing for a while but haven’t seen any traction), your first 30 days should be focused on experimentation.

The goal is not to write “well.”

The goal is not to pick a niche (yet).

Your #1 goal should just be to write about a handful of topics that are interesting to you and pay attention to two things:

  • What is resonating with readers?

  • What do you enjoy writing the most?

From there, and once you start to narrow down the list of topics you want to write about, you will eventually realize there are only 1-3 topics that a) consistently attract readers who get value from your writing, and b) you enjoy writing about over and over again.

The easiest way to write lots of content in your first 30 days is to oscillate between what I like to call The 10 Magical Ways (To Expand Anything).

Every day, whatever topic you want to write about, pick an “angle” for how you want to write about it from the following list:

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

10 Magical Ways… multiplied by say 3 topics you want to experiment with… equals 30 days of ideas.

Easy!

Days 30-60: 30 Proven Approaches

As you begin to learn “what works” (combined with “what you enjoy”), the next skill to build is to learn how to write about the same topic(s) over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again!

This is how you become known for a niche you own.

For example, just to put this into perspective.

Over the past 10 years, I have:

  • Written over 5,000 articles

  • Written over 3,000 newsletters

  • Written over 10,000 tweets

  • Written over 1,000 LinkedIn posts

  • And filmed over 1,400 YouTube videos

…almost all on the topic of digital writing, writing online, and monetizing your writing.

Learning how to write about the same topic(s) over and over again is a SKILL.

So, for your next 30 days, the goal is to practice that skill!

You can do this by taking any of your chosen topics and combining them with 30 more “Proven Approaches.”

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

These are all “things” you can give the reader that they would want inside your chosen niche, or related to any individual topic you choose to write about.

Days 60-90: MORE

So, where do you go from here?

Are you done? Have you said everything you could possibly say about your chosen topic(s)?

OF COURSE NOT!

How you generate ideas from here is by recognizing that readers will always want MORE.

  • If you’re interested in Stoicism, you will always want MORE Stoicism content.

  • If you’re interested in Writing Online, you will always want MORE Writing Online content.

  • If you’re interested in Day Trading, you will always want MORE Day Trading content.

  • If you’re interested in Romantasy Books, you will always want MORE Romantasy book content.

  • Etc.

So how do you come up with “MORE” to say to your target readers?

  • Step 1: You look back through your first 60 days of content…

  • Step 2: You identity your top 10 highest-performing pieces… (by vVews or by Likes)

  • Step 3: You write about those topics again… but give the reader MORE.

And when I say “MORE,” I quite literally just mean MORE.

If you gave them 3 tips last time, can you give them 7 next time?

If you pointed out 5 mistakes last time, can you point out 10 mistakes next time?

If you showed readers 4 examples last time, can you give them 8 examples next time?

Etc.

The MORE you give readers, in a niche, the happier they will be.

That’s all it takes to become known for a niche you own!

Writing online is a game of 3 things:

  • Building a library of niche content

  • Over a very long time horizon (10+ years)

  • So you can become known for a niche you own

How you do that is by using the above framework to write about the same topic(s) in slightly different ways, always striving to give the reader MORE, for a prolonged period of time.

Writing online isn’t something that produces some massive outcome overnight.

It’s slow. It takes work.

But over months and years, your library of content will become exponentially more valuable. It will compound.

Until eventually, you will own a niche—and be able to make money inside that niche forever.

Niche Bio Checklist


One of the questions we get asked most often is, "How do I write my social bios to get people to want to follow me?"

Let’s start with what people do wrong—and then I’ll walk you through what to do instead:

Mistake #1: Only listing "what you do."

A huge mistake people make when crafting their bio (on any social platform) is treating it as a list of "here's everything I do."

You see this with entrepreneurs, investors, and "business-y" people most often, but it happens in every industry.

Their bio looks like this:

CEO @companyname, Board Member @companyname, Investor @companyname, @companyname, @companyname.

This is a bio that has over-tilted on credibility, and is basically telling the reader, "Hey, I don't need to tell you who I am OR what you can expect from me. You should just know. See all my credibility?"

And this is a giant mistake. Because credibility, by itself, doesn't answer the most important question:

"What sort of content do you create? Why should I pay attention to you?"

Mistake #2: Trying to be Clever, not CLEAR.

The next BIG mistake people make when crafting their bio is (sort of building on the above) assuming the best way to hook the reader's attention is by proving how clever they are.

Their bio looks like this:

Netflix, Pancakes, And Stephen King novels. Don't bother me, I'm writing.

  • Who is this person? No clue.

  • What do they write about? No idea.

  • What can you expect from them? Who knows.

Being clever in your bio is such a wasted opportunity. It's like having 30 seconds in an elevator with someone who has the power to change your life, and instead of pitching them on who you are and your big idea, you decide to start rambling off random movies you love and jokes you've heard on TikTok. So, don't overcomplicate it. More importantly, don't waste the reader's time.

Just be CLEAR and say who you are, what you do, and what sort of content they can expect from you.

Mistake #3: Saying "just sharing what I'm learning."

When you're first starting out, it can feel comfortable to not state anything too directly in your bio—and instead say something like:

"Just sharing what I'm learning along the way."

The problem with this is (whether you realize it or not) you are subtly telling readers, "Hey, just a heads up, I don't really know who I am yet. Or what I do. Or what sort of content you can expect from me. So, if you want to follow me, go ahead. But honestly, I can't promise you anything yet."

Now, does that make you excited to follow them?

Of course not!

They haven't given you a reason to be excited!

Even if you are just starting out, even if you feel like you have a lot of learning to do, even if you feel like you are a complete and total beginner, you do not want to announce that to each and every potential reader & follower who clicks on your profile.

Instead, PLANT YOUR FLAG SOMEWHERE. Claim where you are. Own it.

"I write about parenting tips for moms who just had their first son."

Remember: You can always change what you write about. You can always rewrite and tweak your bio. Everyone does it. Even established writers and creators change their bios as they progress and decide they want to write about different things. It's not marriage decision.

Just own where you are today—and steer your ship moving forward.

Mistake #4: Not updating their profile picture or banner image.

This is a simple thing, but it does make a difference.

Not having a clean profile picture and banner image causes potential readers & followers to come to the following conclusions:

  • “This person isn’t playing the game of digital writing with intention.”

  • “If this person isn’t playing the game with intention, why should I follow them?”

  • “Is this person a bot?”

It’s really simple: people want to FOLLOW people who appear to be moving in a positive and productive direction.

So if you want people to FOLLOW you, you have to signal to them you know where you’re going and it would be in their best interest to FOLLOW you down that path.

*And this is becoming more and more true in the age of AI. People want to follow PEOPLE. Not AI-avatars or lazy human beings who just copy/paste whatever ChatGPT says.

So now, let’s walk through a simple checklist you should follow to position yourself as a leader in your niche.

Step #1: Upload a professional profile picture, and use AI to create a professional header image.

If you don’t have any professional headshots, ask a friend or your significant other to take your picture in front of a white wall using your phone.

From there, you can do some pretty cool stuff with AI these days.

  • You can drop your camera-phone photo into ChatGPT and edit it. You can ask it to remove the background, change the background color, or make your background a specific location. You can also ask it to edit the colors if you want. Then export the final image and upload it to your social platforms.

  • You can take a screenshot of someone else’s header image and ask ChatGPT to replicate it for you. Go find an example of someone’s header banner that you like and then tell ChatGPT, “Can you make me something that looks like this, except…” and then articulate what you want to change, if you want ChatGPT to use a certain picture of yours, etc.

The technology we all have access to today is crazy.

Which means all of these things are table-stakes when it comes to writing on the Internet.

Step #2: Write your short-form bio.

This applies most directly to platforms like:

  • X

  • LinkedIn’s profile bio

  • Instagram / Instagram Threads

  • Even YouTube’s channel bio

All of these social platforms provide minimal space for you to say “who you are and what you do” at the top of your profile.

If you want a few bio templates, here are ones I come back to often (and would recommend you use):

Social Bio Template #1

<Credibility statement.> I talk about <topic> and help people <solve problem>.

Social Bio Template #2

I talk about <topic> and <related topic>. <Credibility statement.> Click below for my free <email course, opt-in, newsletter, etc.>

Social Bio Template #3

I believe <niche point of view>. Follow for <topic> and <related topic>. <Credibility statement.>

~

Either way, don’t overthink this step. Just make sure, in your bio, you say very explicitly what niche/topic you most frequently write about (and ultimately want to become known for and associated with).

Step #3: Write your LinkedIn long-form bio

This is platform-specific, but LinkedIn also allows you to write a long-form bio.

In this bio, you should look to accomplish a handful of things:

  • Point Of View: Tell people why you care about this niche, why you write about it, and why you have the point of view you do.

  • Credibility: Tell people why they should trust you and listen to you on your chosen topic. (Remember, credibility is just “context.” You don’t need to be a world-renowned expert. Just tell the reader how and why you’ve learned all the things you’ve learned—so they understand where your insight is coming from.)

  • CTAs: Tell people where to go next. Give them a high-level tour of your ecosystem. If you’ve written books, where can they find them? If you have a business, what does it do and how can they learn more? If you have a newsletter, what is it and where can people subscribe? Use your bio to give readers a “lay of the land.”

Step 4: Add relevant CTAs to your bio.

The goal of your social bio is to do 2 things as fast as possible:

  • Tell net-new readers what you write about (what they can expect from you)

  • And instruct new readers to some sort of valuable resource—so you can capture their email

However, different social platforms have different constraints when it comes to bio linking and CTAs.

For example, on LinkedIn you can only attach one link to the top of your bio (”Start Writing Online In 5 Days” sends people to our free email course):

Whereas on YouTube, you can add multiple links to the top of your social profile:

If you’re brand new to writing online, just make the link point to your website. (And if you don’t have a website, don’t worry about it. You don’t have to link anywhere, yet.)

But as time goes on, the progression of how to maximize your link-in-bio should look like this:

  • Total Beginner: No link (you might not have anything to point to yet).

  • Beginner: Link to website.

  • Intermediate: Link to weekly newsletter.

  • Expert: Link to free educational email course or valuable opt-in.

Step 5: Pin an asset to the top of your profile.

Lastly, you can further maximize the effectiveness of your social profiles by “pinning” a relevant asset to the top of each profile, like this:


A pinned post could be:

  • A link to a big announcement you’re making, or something you want to actively drive traffic to.

  • A book you’ve written and want to get in front of more readers.

  • Your business, a product you’ve launched, a service you provide, etc.

  • Your weekly newsletter—or some sort of free educational email course.

  • A SaaS platform, or website you’ve created.

  • Etc.

Your pinned post can really be anything you want.

It’s basically just a choice of what you want to prioritize people seeing FIRST when they click through to your profile (so pick something you want to drive traffic to!).

The Complete Niche FAQ

“But Cole?! What if I'm not an expert in the thing I’m most interested in?”

First of all, nobody cares if you’re an “expert” or not.

The only thing any reader/customer cares about is whether or not you can help them.

Second, you might not feel like an expert, but if you have any sort of Information Advantage (even if it’s small), then to all the other people who don’t know what you know, you are an “expert.” In our beginner writing program, Ship 30 for 30, the metaphor we like to use here is: remember when you were in 5th grade, about to enter middle school? Who did you want to learn from? A “middle-school expert?” Your parents? An adult?

No!

You wanted to hear from the 6th graders! The ones who were just a few steps ahead of you.

That same dynamic is how all knowledge transfers work, everywhere in the world, all the time.

  • If you want to learn how to swim, you don’t need Michael Phelps to be your teacher. You literally just need someone who “knows how to swim” and not drown.

  • If you want to learn how to play the violin, you don’t need Itzhak Perlman to be your mentor. You literally just need someone who “knows how to play the violin” to teach you some basic melodies and hand positions to get going.

  • If you want to learn how to make YouTube videos, you don’t need Mr Beast to hand-hold you through setting up your YouTube channel. You literally just need someone who is “a few steps ahead of you,” and has already done “that thing” to give you a hand.

OK?

So get this expectation of “needing to be an expert” out of your head.

It’s not real.

It’s just a clever faulty belief you’re using to avoid getting started.

“But Cole?! What if the thing I’m most interested in isn’t the most lucrative?”

I want you to really take this to heart: you don’t know whether something will be lucrative or not until you try it.

  • When I was studying creative writing in college, my entire family (my father especially) had an intervention with me to try to explain why I was pursuing a dark and dismal career path and was never going to make any money from it.

  • When I quit my job to pursue ghostwriting and working for myself, my former boss’s and my parents and all of my friends tried to tell me it was a “huge risk” and, especially with writing, I was going to have a really hard time providing for myself.

  • When I first started scaling my ghostwriting agency, all of my entrepreneur friends at the time insisted ghostwriting was a horrible career path and it was going to do “reputational damage” to me long term.

  • When I first started Ship 30 for 30 with Dickie, I can’t tell you how many people in my life said, “A writing course? Who is ever going to spend money on something like that?”

  • Etc. etc. etc.

For the past 10+ years, I have LIVED being surrounded by a never-ending stream of negative opinions trying to tell me that writing, and making a career as a writer, was and is impossible.

And I’ve made more money than every single person who told me that, FROM WRITING.

So I share that with you because, in hindsight, NOBODY (I can’t think of a single person) in my early life thought this path and this topic and this “niche” was a good idea. Nobody thought it was lucrative. Nobody thought it was ever going to pan out to much of anything.

And guess what? This is how it goes for a LOT of people.

Until… you prove otherwise. And THEN everyone says, “Oh, that’s because you picked a great niche!”

No, I didn’t.

I picked something a) I had an Information Advantage in, and b) something I am genuinely interested in and WANT to keep learning about.

YOU are the one who makes the niche work.

Niches don’t “work or not-work” on their own.

“But Cole?! What if the thing I know the most about, isn’t the thing I want to be my niche? What if I’m more interested in something else?”

Then do that.

My goal in walking you through that little exercise is to give you OPTIONS.

Just because you have an Information Advantage doesn’t mean you HAVE to do that thing.

For example, in my early 20s, I clearly had an Information Advantage because I was working at an advertising agency as a copywriter. But, I was also obsessed with bodybuilding—and I knew a lot about it. It’s all I did. I ate 6 meals a day. I went to the gym 6-7x per week, for 2-3 hours at a time. All my friends were bodybuilders. I read about it, I watched YouTube videos about it, and I trained with other professional bodybuilders. That wasn’t a “career” of mine, and nobody was paying me to do any of that (I just genuinely loved it), but I knew a lot about it.

So, could I have made my first niche Copywriting? Sure.

But I was more interested, at the time, in bodybuilding.

So that’s what I decided to start with.

And my first digital product ever was… a bodybuilding eBook!

(I’ve since retired this chapter of my life, so please don’t email me asking for a copy. It’s gone to the wind.)

And then 3 years later, when I got injured and realized I was never going to be a professional bodybuilder myself, what did I do?

Did I force myself to stick with something I was no longer in love with?

No.

I moved on. I changed niches (Ghostwriting & Digital Writing). And there’s nothing wrong with that.

These are all just options.

“But Cole?! What if I want my niche to be something I don’t know very much about.”

You shouldn’t.

Or, let me put it this way: sure, you can… but don’t be surprised if it takes you a long time to get any traction.

Because now you have to do 2 things at the same time:

  • You have to acquire all the skills to write well and create compelling offers and hook readers, etc., etc., etc.

  • AND, you have to simultaneously learn about a topic you know nothing about.

Which is why it is much, much easier to start with something you already have an Information Advantage within, because then “the knowledge” comes easily. You already KNOW about it. And you can focus all your time on acquiring and improving the other skills that bring that knowledge to life (and ultimately monetize it).

The other thing—and this is something a lot of people REALLY struggle to keep in mind—is that the niche you pick TODAY doesn’t have to be the niche you pick FOREVER.

It’s not your forever niche.

It’s your FIRST niche.

Just like my FIRST niche was bodybuilding.

But you have to pick a niche so that you can build all the other skills required to bring that niche to life.

If I told you I was going to stop everything I was doing and dedicate 8+ hours per day to helping you build yourself as a writer, and dominate your chosen niche, even if it was a niche I knew nothing about, you would be over-the-moon-excited to have my help. Right?

OK, why is that?

Because it’s obvious I’ve acquired all the other skills that bring a niche, ANY NICHE, to life.

And you assume that because I’ve acquired those skills, the niche actually doesn’t matter, and I’ll still be helpful to you.

And you would be correct.

So why do you think the same won’t happen, for you?

Of course it will.

If you pick a niche, any niche, and you use it as a vehicle to practice and acquire skills, you can then transfer those skills to any FUTURE niche whenever you want.

"But Cole?! My audience isn't big enough yet. What should I do?"

This is a big myth, and we want to address it right away.

Most creators want to "wait" until their audience is "big enough" before they decide what their niche is going to be—as if, one day, they are just going to wake up and some magical answer will reveal itself.

But when is enough, enough?

When you have 1,000 followers?

When you have 10,000 followers?

When you have 100,000 followers?

At what point are you going to commit to serving a particular niche?

There's a bit of irony in this myth, because most creators want to wait until they get "bigger" on social media before they Name & Claim a niche for themselves—and yet, the reason most creators DON'T GROW on social media is because they haven't claimed a niche for themselves.

It's a chicken/egg dilemma.

So, should you wait to decide what your niche is going to be?

No. If anything, you are incentivized to plant your flag in the ground and Name & Claim some sort of niche (literally anything), now.

And then if you want to change your niche later, you can.

It's not a marriage decision.

"But Cole?! I don't feel comfortable Naming & Claiming a niche because I'm not an expert in anything. Shouldn’t I become an expert, first?"

Yes, you are.

Everyone is an "expert" in something.

The mistake people make here is thinking that "expert" is some far-and-distant achievement. Like you become an "expert" when you're a New York Times best-selling author. Or you become an "expert" when someone like Oprah or Tony Robbins gives you that title.

But the truth is, to your 2-years-ago self, you are an expert.

You know things today you didn't know 2 years ago. Or 1 year ago. Or 6 months ago. Or even 6 days ago.

Which makes you a Niche Expert.

The key to building an audience online, and even creating a portfolio of digital products and ultimately monetizing your knowledge, isn't "pretending to be something you're not." The key is to pinpoint what questions you used to have (in any space, field, or topic area), that you no longer have because you went on the journey to discover the answers for yourself. You already did the hard work. You overcame your own obstacles. Which means, to someone standing in your shoes 2-years-ago, you are "a Niche Expert."

All you have to do is own it.

Accept that you are a Niche Expert to someone who is a few steps behind you.

And just throw down a rope, and give them a hand.

"But Cole?! Once I pick a niche, I can't ever change it. Wouldn’t it be better to get perfect clarity on my niche before I begin?"

This might be the biggest myth of all.

Most writers and creators in general tend to think that picking a niche is a "marriage" decision—as in, once you pick a niche, you can't ever change it.

And this couldn't be further from the truth.

If you look closely, some of the biggest writers & creators today are in niches they discovered along the way. For example: Ryan Holiday was originally a marketing writer—not a Stoicism writer. He started with a niche, wrote a few books and launched a few products, and then ultimately decided he wanted to try something different. And that "something different" ended up being even more successful than the niche he originally started with.

Which is why we say: choosing a niche isn't a marriage decision.

It's Step 1.

Then, as your library of content begins to grow, as you gather more data, and as you learn what's resonating most with your readers, you have the freedom to choose whether you want to stick with that niche or pivot and move into a different niche over time.

(And sure, some of the people who "used to" follow you for, say, marketing will no longer be interested in your next niche. But that's OK. Because if you are choosing to create a new niche in the future, it's most likely because you have data that proves this is the right decision—which means for every 1 person you lose, you'll gain dozens more.)

Creating a niche for yourself isn't a destination.

It's a skill.

And once you acquire the skill, you can create new & differentiated categories for yourself over and over again.

records.content:
Alright, I just threw a lot at you!

So, I want to speed up your Article writing with AI (which will make the “writing” feel a lot less daunting!).

All you need to do is copy and paste the prompt below into your chosen LLM (I recommend Claude) and follow the on-screen instructions. You’ll be asked for your headline and main points (if you have them).

AI will then outline your article and write your article for you!

Dive in here:

# AI Prompt: Long-Form Article Outliner & Writer

You are an Article Outlining & Drafting Specialist, specifically for digital writers who want to expand a single proven idea into a fully outlined *and fully written* long-form Article.

I am going to give you my headline (and, if I have them, my Main Points), and I would like you to walk me through two phases:

**Phase 1 — The Outline.** A complete outline: a headline at the top, a set of Main Points beneath it, and a set of Sub Points expanding each Main Point.

**Phase 2 — The Draft.** Once I confirm the outline, the complete, publish-ready Article written out in full.

The reason I want this done a specific way is because 80% of the writing happens in the outline. Writing isn't really about writing — it's about thinking. The outline is where the thinking gets clarified, so that by the time we write actual sentences, we're just cleaning up notes instead of staring at a blank page. Your job is to help me get all of that thinking out of the way first, and *then* turn it into finished prose.

Do not begin Phase 2 until I have explicitly confirmed the outline.

~

## Instruction

There are eight techniques that govern this process. Two govern the outline. Six govern the draft.

**Phase 1 — Outlining**
- Technique #1: Mirroring
- Technique #2: The 10 Magical Ways

**Phase 2 — Drafting**
- Technique #3: Single-Sentence Openers
- Technique #4: Fleshing Out & Linking
- Technique #5: Writing Rhythm (1/3/1 & Expanding The Middle)
- Technique #6: Visual Mirroring & Lists
- Technique #7: The Credibility Note
- Technique #8: The Optional Conclusion

I'm going to walk you through each one, describe what makes it unique, and give you examples of each executed well — so you understand how to replicate.

~

### Technique #1: Mirroring

Mirroring means taking one element and repeating it down the page so the reader feels like they're looking at something organized and intentional.

**Main Points must mirror the promise in the headline.** Whatever the headline promises is what the Main Points must deliver, in the same wording, flow, and punctuation. If the headline promises "3 Mistakes," the Main Points are "Mistake #1, Mistake #2, Mistake #3." If it promises "6 Lessons," the Main Points are "Lesson #1… Lesson #6." The number in the headline sets the number of Main Points.

**If one Main Point changes, all of them change.** The golden rule: never let the labels alternate in style, capitalization, or punctuation. A list that reads "Business-Destroying Mistake #1 / #2 / #3" feels organized. A list that reads "Mistake #1 / The Right Way To Think / A Lesson I Learned" feels lost. Readers love patterns, so keep the pattern identical all the way down.

### Technique #2: The 10 Magical Ways

This is how we expand each Main Point into Sub Points. There are 10 ways to expand literally any point in any piece of writing:

1. **Tips** — practical pieces of advice for doing the thing
2. **Stats** — numbers, data, or figures that prove or frame the point
3. **Steps** — the sequential actions someone takes
4. **Lessons** — what was learned from the experience
5. **Benefits** — the upsides or payoffs of doing it
6. **Reasons** — the "why" behind the point
7. **Mistakes** — the things that go wrong or should be avoided
8. **Examples** — concrete instances that illustrate the point
9. **Questions** — the questions a reader should ask themselves about it
10. **Personal Stories** — a moment from lived experience that makes it real

You do not have to use the same Way for every Main Point. The best outlines rotate through different combinations — one Main Point expanded with Reasons, the next with Benefits, the next with Steps. You choose the Way that will be **the most useful thing to list out for the reader** on that specific Main Point. A good test: "If I were completely new to this topic, what would I most want to know here?"

### Technique #3: Single-Sentence Openers

When a reader opens a piece of content and is immediately confronted by a giant wall of text, the first thought is: *"Geez. This sure does look like a heavy lift."* Even if the content is light and fun. Even if the language is simple. Visually, it looks difficult.

The fix is a single-sentence opener — one sentence, standing alone as its own paragraph, at the top of the Introduction and at the start of every Main Point. It gives the reader an easy place to "slide" into the section.

There are six types:

**Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.**
- "Most people will spend their entire careers being good at the wrong thing."
- "The best business decision I ever made cost me my biggest client."

**Open with a thought-provoking question.**
- "What would you build if you knew no one would ever judge it?"
- "What if the habit you're most proud of is the one holding you back?"

**Open with a controversial opinion.**
- "Networking events are a waste of time for anyone serious about their work."
- "Most 'productivity' advice is just procrastination wearing a nicer outfit."

**Open with a moment in time.**
- "At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, I deleted three years of work and felt nothing but relief."
- "The email arrived twelve minutes before the meeting that would change everything."

**Open with a vulnerable statement.**
- "I made six figures last year and still felt like a complete fraud."
- "I almost quit the week I made my first $50,000 on the internet."

**Open with a weird, unique insight.**
- "The fastest way to be remembered in a meeting is to be the one who says the least."
- "Boredom is the most underrated signal your brain ever sends you."

Rotate the types across sections. Do not open six consecutive Main Points with declarative sentences.

### Technique #4: Fleshing Out & Linking

This is how Sub Points become prose.

For each Sub Point, ask: *"What does the reader need to hear to understand this? What can I give them that helps them make sense of this Sub Point and this Main Point?"* Then write that out in complete sentences.

Then link the Sub Points to each other with short connective phrases:
- "Which leads me to the next example…"
- "Another reason why this mistake cost me so dear is…"
- "Once you've answered this question, ask yourself this second question…"

**Critical rule: outline labels are scaffolding, not headers.** "Reason #1:" and "Step #2:" exist to organize the thinking. In the finished Article they dissolve into the prose. Only the Main Points survive as visible headers. The single exception is when a set of Sub Points genuinely works better as a bulleted or numbered list (see Technique #6).

**Critical rule: end every Main Point section with a callback closer.** The last line of each section returns to the Main Point's own claim — often the exact wording of the header, standing alone as a single sentence. It snaps the section shut.

### Technique #5: Writing Rhythm (1/3/1 & Expanding The Middle)

The overarching idea is to create rhythm and musicality — and rhythm is almost entirely a function of sentence length. Alternate long and short sentences in a pattern. See? Short sentence, followed by a medium sentence, followed by a long sentence that builds and gives the reader a crescendo of pace before it finally resolves.

**The base pattern is 1/3/1:**

{1} One short-to-medium sentence to open.
{3} Three sentences that add description and color and advance the point.
{1} One single sentence to close the idea.

Repeat 1/3/1 down the page.

**When you need more room, expand the middle.** Keep the single-sentence bookends and grow only the middle of the sandwich: 1/4/1, 1/5/1, 1/6/1, 1/7/1. The bookends are what give the reader an entry point and a reward. Never expand the bookends.

### Technique #6: Visual Mirroring & Lists

This is Mirroring applied at the paragraph level.

**Sections should look the same.** If one section is three giant paragraphs and the next is two sentences, they read as off-balance — even if both are well written. Strive for each Main Point section to be visually similar in length and formatting. If you open one section with a declarative sentence, a 5-sentence paragraph, and a closing sentence, aim to repeat that cadence in the next.

**Use bulleted or numbered lists inside Main Points.** Lists are the single most underrated formatting technique available, because they force you to strip away unnecessary explanation and just tell the reader what matters. No rambling. Just boom, boom, boom.

A strong pattern to reach for: a list of parallel constructions, each line built on the same grammatical frame.

> You think you're running "so many ads" until you sit in a room and hear someone explain how they're running 100x more ads than you.
> You think you're hiring "so many people" until you sit in a room and hear someone explain how they're hiring 10x more people, 10x faster than you.
> You think you have "such high standards" until you sit in a room and hear someone explain their standards, and you realize their standards are way higher than yours.

Aim for at least one list in the Article, but not one in every single section.

### Technique #7: The Credibility Note

Readers aren't as picky as most people think. You don't need to be a Harvard graduate or a rocket scientist for readers to trust you. **All you need to do is tell them why they should take what you're saying seriously.**

Imagine a friend asks you for a Friday night movie recommendation. Inevitably they'll ask, "Why? Why should I watch this?" And you'll say: "Because I've watched every Rom Com on Netflix, and trust me, this one is the best." That's all they need to hear.

Every Introduction must answer the question: *"Why should the reader trust me on this?"*

That answer comes from **Personal Credibility** — hours spent, milestones achieved, years of practice:
- *"How do I know how to build a real estate empire? Because over the last 10 years, I've bought and sold over 50 different rental properties."*
- *"Why should you take my Netflix recommendations? Because I've watched over 5,000 hours of Netflix shows and movies."*

Or from **Borrowed Credibility** — someone else's experience, a book, time spent around people who've done it:
- *"Why is this the best strategy to get distribution on your writing? Because I went and interviewed 20 different best-selling authors, and this is what they said to do."*

### Technique #8: The Optional Conclusion

Conclusions are optional. That is the default position.

**If the conclusion just repeats what was already said, do not write one.** The reader isn't grading a 12th-grade English paper — they're a highly impatient digital reader who would rather swipe back to TikTok. If the piece was helpful, they'll click around and read more on their own. Let it end. Make it a cliffhanger.

Only write a conclusion if it adds something *new*:
- A new insight
- A final closing story
- A clarifying statement
- More information about your credibility

Default to no conclusion. Propose one only when there's genuinely new material to land, and tell me why you think it earns its place.

~

## Context

### Rules

**Outline rules**
- The number of Main Points is dictated by the headline's promise, not by a default. Do not assume three. If the headline says "7 Reasons," there are seven Main Points.
- Sub Points are not locked to three. Ask me how many I want per Main Point before expanding.
- Every Main Point must mirror the headline promise in identical wording and punctuation.
- Within a single Main Point, the Sub Point labels must also mirror each other (Reason #1, Reason #2, Reason #3 — not Reason #1, A Reason, Why This Matters).
- For each Main Point, name which of the 10 Magical Ways you're using, so I can see your reasoning and swap it if I disagree.
- Do not write full sentences or paragraphs in the outline. Sub Points are short notes-to-self.

**Drafting rules**
- **Never invent specifics.** Do not fabricate statistics, dollar figures, dates, company names, client stories, or personal anecdotes. Where the writing needs a specific I haven't given you, insert a bracketed placeholder like `[INSERT: specific dollar figure]` or `[INSERT: the story about the client who churned]` and keep moving.
- Write the entire Article in one pass. Do not deliver it section by section.
- Main Points appear as visible headers, mirrored exactly as they were in the approved outline. Sub Point labels do not appear.
- Every section opens with a single-sentence opener standing alone as its own paragraph.
- Every section ends with a callback closer.
- No paragraph runs longer than roughly seven sentences without a single-sentence break.
- Do not use em dashes as a stylistic crutch; the voice uses them, but sparingly.
- Do not add headers, sections, or Main Points that weren't in the approved outline.

### Positive Attributes

**A great outline is:**
- **Skimmable.** A reader could glance at the Main Points alone and instantly understand the shape of the whole Article.
- **Mirrored.** The Main Points are visually identical in structure, and so are the Sub Points within each section.
- **Useful.** Each Sub Point earns its place — not filler added to hit a number.
- **Varied where it helps.** Different Main Points use different Magical Ways when that serves the reader.
- **Faithful to the promise.** Nothing drifts from what the headline promised.

**A great draft is:**
- **Rhythmic.** Sentence lengths alternate. Single sentences stand alone as paragraphs and act as beats.
- **Specific.** Real numbers, real dates, real names, real dollar figures — or clearly marked placeholders where they're missing.
- **Balanced.** Sections are visually similar in length and formatting.
- **Self-implicating.** The writer admits their own mistakes plainly and without hedging ("Whoops." / "And I feel stupid for ever thinking that's what was going to happen.").
- **Direct with the reader.** Uses second person. Talks *to* someone, not *about* a topic.
- **Willing to caveat.** Nuance gets handled in parentheticals or asterisked asides rather than by watering down the main claim.
- **Free of filler.** No "in today's fast-paced world," no throat-clearing, no summarizing what's about to be said.

### Reinforcement Example — The Outline

**Headline:** *3 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars*

The promise is "3 Mistakes," so there are three Main Points, each mirrored as "Mistake #__":

- **Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time** *(expanded with Reasons — why it was a mistake)*
    - Reason #1: Buying capacity before there's work to fill it
    - Reason #2: Full-time hires can't be un-hired quickly
    - Reason #3: Salary anchors your burn rate permanently
- **Mistake #2: Not having clients on auto-pay** *(expanded with Benefits — the upside of auto-pay)*
    - Benefit #1: Predictable cash flow
    - Benefit #2: No collections conversations
    - Benefit #3: Higher effective retention
- **Mistake #3: Not taking any money out of the business** *(expanded with Steps — how to take money out responsibly)*
    - Step #1: Set a fixed owner's draw
    - Step #2: Separate operating cash from reserve
    - Step #3: Review against a rolling 12-month average

Notice three things: the Main Points all mirror the headline's "Mistakes" promise; each Main Point is expanded with a *different* Magical Way chosen for usefulness; and the Sub Point labels mirror each other within their own section.

### Reinforcement Example — The Draft

Here is Mistake #1 from that outline, drafted. Notice the vulnerable-statement opener standing alone, the 1/5/1 rhythm, the Sub Points dissolved into prose rather than labeled, the parallel list, the parenthetical caveat, and the callback closer.

> **Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time**
>
> I hired six full-time employees before I ever hired a single contractor, and it nearly ended the company.
>
> At the time, it felt like the responsible thing to do. Full-time hires signaled that we were a "real" business — to investors, to the team, and mostly to myself. Every founder I looked up to talked about building a team that was all-in, and contractors felt like a half-measure. So I hired ahead of the work, assuming the work would show up to meet the payroll. It did not. And by the time I understood what I'd actually signed up for, I was spending more time managing capacity than selling.
>
> What nobody tells you is how expensive being "all-in" actually is.
>
> The first problem is that you're buying capacity you can't yet fill. A full-time hire shows up on Monday with 40 hours to give you, and if you only have 12 hours of real work, you will invent the other 28. I have watched myself do this. I have created entire projects — dashboards nobody read, processes nobody followed — for no reason other than justifying a salary I had already committed to.
>
> The second problem is that full-time hires can't be un-hired quickly.
>
> - A contractor who isn't working out ends at the end of the month.
> - A full-time hire who isn't working out ends after a performance plan, a documented paper trail, a severance conversation, and about six weeks of dread.
> - And in the meantime, you're still paying them, still managing them, and still avoiding the conversation.
>
> But the third problem is the one that actually cost me millions: salary anchors your burn rate permanently. Revenue moves up and down. Salaries only move up. Once you've set a monthly number you're obligated to pay, every decision downstream of it gets made under pressure — which pricing to accept, which client to keep, which bad deal to say yes to because payroll is on Friday. You stop making decisions from strategy and start making them from fear.
>
> (*To be clear, I'm not anti-hiring. Some roles genuinely require full-time attention and full-time commitment, and trying to run them on contract is its own expensive mistake. What I'm arguing against is defaulting to full-time because it feels more legitimate.*)
>
> If I could do it again, I'd hire every single person as a contractor first, and convert them only once the work was so obviously there that the decision made itself.
>
> Making every new hire full-time was the most expensive mistake I made.

~

## Final Delivery

Now here's exactly how I want you to run our session. Move through these steps one at a time, and wait for my answer before moving on. Do not dump everything at once.

### Phase 1 — The Outline

**Step 1 — Get the headline.** Ask me for my headline. Once I give it, identify the promise inside it (the number + the thing being promised, e.g. "3 Mistakes," "6 Lessons," "7 Reasons"). Tell me how many Main Points that promise implies.

**Step 2 — Get or build the Main Points.** Ask whether I already have my Main Points.
- If I do, take them and check them against the headline promise. Flag anything that isn't mirrored and show me a corrected, mirrored version.
- If I don't, brainstorm a set of Main Points for me — matching the number the headline promised, all mirrored in identical wording and punctuation. Present them and ask if I'd like any edits. **Do not move on to Sub Points until I've approved the Main Points.**

**Step 3 — Ask how many Sub Points.** Once the Main Points are locked, ask how many Sub Points I want under each Main Point. (Let me know it doesn't have to be the same number for every Main Point if I'd prefer to vary them.)

**Step 4 — Expand with the 10 Magical Ways.** For each Main Point, choose the Magical Way that's most useful for that point, name it in parentheses next to the Main Point, and list out the mirrored Sub Points beneath it. Rotate Ways across Main Points where that serves the reader better than repeating one.

**Step 5 — Deliver the full outline.** Present the complete outline in one clean block: headline at the top, mirrored Main Points beneath it, mirrored Sub Points under each — with the chosen Magical Way labeled on each Main Point. Keep everything in outline form (short notes), not full sentences.

Then ask me directly: **"Do you want to adjust anything, or should I write the full Article from this?"**

**Do not proceed to Phase 2 until I confirm.**

### Phase 2 — The Draft

**Step 6 — Gather what you need to write.** Once I confirm the outline, ask me these four things in a single batch:

1. **Credibility.** Why should the reader trust me on this topic? (Personal or borrowed — Technique #7.) If I don't have an answer, offer me 2–3 options based on what you know from my outline.
2. **Raw material.** Do I have specific numbers, dates, dollar figures, names, or stories I want worked into any of the Main Points? Tell me you'll use bracketed placeholders anywhere I leave a gap.
3. **Length.** Roughly how long should each Main Point section run? (Default: 200–350 words per section unless I say otherwise.)
4. **Delivery.** Do I want the finished Article **in the chat** or **as a document I can download?**

**Step 7 — Write the full Article in one pass.** Deliver the complete piece, start to finish, in the format I chose. It must include:

- An **Introduction** with a single-sentence opener, the credibility note, and enough context to frame why this piece exists right now
- Every **Main Point** as a visible header, mirrored exactly as approved in the outline
- A **single-sentence opener** at the top of every Main Point section
- All **Sub Points fleshed out into prose**, linked with connective phrases, with the outline labels dissolved
- **1/3/1 rhythm** (or expanded middles) throughout, with single sentences used as standalone beats
- At least one **bulleted or numbered list**, and **visually balanced sections**
- A **callback closer** ending every Main Point section
- A **conclusion only if it adds something new** — otherwise let the final Main Point end the piece, and tell me you chose not to write one and why

**Step 8 — Hand it off.** After delivering, tell me:
- Which sections contain `[INSERT: …]` placeholders that need my real specifics
- Which single-sentence opener type you used for each section, in a short list, so I can swap any that feel repetitive

Then ask if I'd like any section rewritten.

Let's begin. Ask me for my headline.

records.content:
As Digital Writers we’re in the business of packaging our ideas to make them easy to consume and visually appealing.

And a part of that (especially on X at the moment) is creating an Article Header/Thumbnail for your Article.

Now, if you don’t have design skills… don’t worry! I created an AI prompt you can use to do this.

The prompt has six fields.

All you have to do is fill in a short template and the AI handles the design. Most are optional. If you skip a field, the AI falls back to a built-in default.

The laziest possible prompt works:

"Make me a banner. Title: How to Write a Newsletter."

You'll get a clean two-tone banner with a serif headline.

Banner Image Prompt

Copy everything below the line, fill in the fields you care about, leave the rest blank or delete them.

Here’s the prompt:

Create a newsletter banner image as an inline SVG.

TITLE: [your headline]

SUBTITLE: [optional — leave blank to skip]

STYLE: [minimal / illustrated / editorial / playful — default: minimal]

COLORS: [vibe like "warm earth tones" OR 2-3 hex codes — default: cream #f5efe4 + charcoal #2a2a2a]

FONT: [type like serif/sans/mono OR specific font name like Inter, Playfair Display — default: Fraunces]

IMAGERY: [objects to include, or "none, typography only" — default: typography only]

IMAGE: [optional — filename and placement: background / corner logo / framed element / hero on left / hero on right / centered hero]

MOOD: [one or two words — default: calm]

Design guidance:
- Banner aspect ratio: roughly 1200x400
- Title should be the focal point
- Use the colors and font specified; fall back to defaults if blank
- Keep the composition balanced and readable at small sizes
- If imagery is included, integrate it with the typography rather than placing it separately
- If an IMAGE is uploaded, place it as specified and ensure text remains readable

How To Configure The Banner Prompt

TITLE

The main headline. Keep it under 8 words for best results.

SUBTITLE

Optional smaller line below the title. Use for issue numbers, dates, taglines, or section labels. Skip if not needed.

STYLE

Pick one:

  • minimal — typography-forward, lots of negative space

  • illustrated — includes drawn elements, scenes, objects

  • editorial — magazine-style, refined, serif-heavy

  • playful — bold colors, casual shapes, energetic

  • Or choose your own

Default: minimal

COLORS

Two ways to specify:

  • Vibe: describe it — "warm earth tones", "navy and cream", "muted pastels", "bold monochrome"

  • Hex codes: give 2-3 exact colors — #1a1a1a, #f5efe4, #ff5a36

Default: cream background (#f5efe4) + charcoal text (#2a2a2a)

FONT

Two ways to specify:

  • Type: serif / sans / mono

  • Specific font name: Inter, Playfair Display, JetBrains Mono, Fraunces, Georgia, etc.

Default: Fraunces (a modern serif)

Free fonts that work automatically (Google Fonts):
Inter, Playfair Display, Fraunces, Lora, Merriweather, JetBrains Mono, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, Space Grotesk, Space Mono, DM Sans, DM Serif Display, Work Sans, Manrope, EB Garamond, Libre Baskerville, Bricolage Grotesque

System fonts (always available):
Georgia, Helvetica, Arial, Courier New, Palatino, Garamond

Suggested pairings for title + subtitle:

  • Editorial → Playfair Display + Inter

  • Modern → Space Grotesk + Inter

  • Techy → JetBrains Mono + Inter

  • Literary → Fraunces + Lora

  • Corporate → IBM Plex Sans + IBM Plex Mono

IMAGERY

Describe objects or scenes to include. Examples:

  • "a typewriter and a coffee cup"

  • "a single paper airplane"

  • "abstract geometric shapes"

  • "none — just typography"

Default: typography only

IMAGE

Optional. If you want to use your own logo, photo, or graphic, upload the file first, then reference it.

Placement options:

  • background — fills the banner, text overlays on top

  • corner logo — small mark in a corner (specify which corner)

  • framed element — cropped into a shape as part of the composition

  • hero on left / hero on right — takes up one side of a split layout

  • centered hero — main visual with title above or below

What works:

  • Logos and icons (PNG with transparent background is best)

  • Photos as background, hero, or framed element

  • Simple graphics and SVG files

What doesn't work:

  • Restyling your photo to match an illustration (use Midjourney/Ideogram first)

  • Removing photo backgrounds (use remove.bg first)

  • Color-correcting the image itself

MOOD

One or two words describing the emotional tone. Examples: calm, urgent, nostalgic, energetic, confident, playful, serious, warm, sharp.

Default: calm

Example 1: Lazy mode (minimum effort)

Make me a banner. 

Title: The Friday Five.

Example 2: Medium effort (some direction)

Make me a banner. 

Title: The Cold Email Playbook. 

Style: editorial. Colors: navy and off-white. 

Font: Playfair Display. 

Imagery: a single paper airplane. 

Mood: confident

Example 3: Full control (every field used, with custom image)

Make me a banner. 

Title: Write With AI. 
Subtitle: Issue #47. 
Style: minimal. Colors: #8ae1a2 and #ffffff and #000000 
Font: SF Pro
Imagery: none, typography only. 
IMAGE: wwai-logo.png — use as a corner logo in the top left. 
Mood: sharp.

Advanced Short-Form: Rhetoric

The best book I’ve ever read on the subject of rhetoric, and how this can apply to short-form content on the Internet, is The Elements of Eloquence by Mark Forsyth.

For example, there’s a reason why people remember this iconic phrase from John F. Kennedy’s inaugural address in 1961: “Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.”

That’s a great line.

But it’s memorable because it uses an age-old rhetoric mechanism called an antimetabole—repeating the same words in reverse grammatical order.

Another more modern example would be entrepreneur, Alex Hormozi, who is known for his short-form content on X.

But if you look closely, the vast majority of his tweets are packaged using these timeless rhetoric principles.

For example, this one where he says, “The goal of youth is optionality. The goal of adulthood is commitment.”


There are two different rhetoric mechanisms working here.

  • The primary one is what’s called an Antithesis. This is an obvious observation (the goal of youth is optionality), followed by a non-obvious observation (the goal of adulthood is commitment).

  • And the secondary mechanism is what’s called Parallelism. This is where two sentences use identical grammatical structures, “mirroring” each other.

Short-Form Content-As-Comments

Posting a piece of short-form content is the exact same thing as “commenting” a piece of short-form content on someone else’s content.

Sometimes, you may even find comments outperforming your own posts!

Let’s Write Short-Form Content LIVE!

3 THINGS to Solve Problem or Achieve Outcome

~

4 foods you should eat if you want to lose weight.

  2. I’m afraid of it not being perfect

  3. I hope people don’t disagree with me

So I’m overcoming my fear and posting this!

My 3 favorite short-form content formats:

I started writing online in 2007.

Since then, I have probably written over 5,000 articles and tweets and newsletters on the Internet. But if I had to pick, I can easily say that I have a few favorites when it comes to writing short-form content.

Let me give you my 3 favorite formats, why I love them, and how you can replicate them.

Format #1: Paragraph Style

The REASON I love Paragraph Style is because it allows you to take conventional wisdom and present it as “academic”—simply because it looks like it should have been published in The New Yorker.

Some TIPS for executing Paragraph Style well:

  • Use academic language

  • Make it look as formal as possible

  • Keep it to 3 sentences or less

Format #2: What, How, Why

My second favorite format is what I like to call What, How, Why:

  • WHAT should the reader do

  • HOW do they do it

  • WHY is it important

A MISTAKE writers often make, however, is only telling readers what to do but not how to do it or why it’s important.

So it’s the combination of all 3 variables that is important.

Big Ideas Recap!

  • Day 1 Big Idea: It’s your content library. You can do whatever you want with it—compress it, expand it, copy/paste it across multiple platforms, etc.

  • Day 2 Big Idea: The same piece of content can be turned into multiple different types of media (text, image, video, audio, etc.)

  • Day 4 Big Idea: Articles are the “foundation” of your entire content library—because they are either expanded versions of smaller assets, or longer versions you can pull smaller assets out of.

  • Day 5 Big Idea: Once you know how to do something yourself, you should look for ways to automate it (or pieces of it). And anything you successfully automate for yourself, you can give away (or sell) to your audience.

Prompts Are Products

Ways you can use AI Prompts:

  1. For yourself

  2. Free marketing assets

  3. Paid digital products

  4. Free bonuses inside paid products

  5. Upsells in addition to paid products

~

Look at our Prompt Library for example:

Prompting Crash Course

  1. What are we writing? (Format)

  2. What are the rules? (Good vs Bad)

  3. What’s an example? (Pattern Recognition)

Let’s automate writing this Tweet!

3 mistakes people make when trying to <desired outcome>

  • Mistake #1

  • Mistake #2

  • Mistake #3

You would be much better off <what to do instead>.

Writing the prompt

What Are We Writing?

I want your help creating infinite variations of a specific type of short-form post (tweet).

I will give you the topic I want to write about, and I’d like you to write me a short-form post (280 characters or less) about that topic but using this tweet template verbatim.

The template goes like this:

~

3 mistakes people make when trying to <desired outcome>.

  • Mistake #1

  • Mistake #2

  • Mistake #3

You would be much better off <what to do instead>.

~

What Are The Rules?

When writing this tweet, based on the topic I give you, I want you to follow these rules as closely as you can:

  1. The tweet must be 280 characters or less, so that it can be published on X (Twitter) without truncating the post.

  2. The tweet must follow the above template structure and formatting verbatim, only filling in these pieces:

    1. The desired outcome (related to the topic I give you) at the end of the first sentence

    2. The 3 mistakes (it should not say “Mistake,” it should just say the mistake itself) as 3 bullets

    3. The “what to do instead” at the end of the last sentence.

  3. The 3 mistakes must be as specific and tangible as possible. Do not provide vague, non-specific mistakes. Be as actionable as possible, using visceral language.

~

What’s An Example?

To help you build some pattern recognition, here is an example of a complete short-form post following this framework on the topic of personal finance:

~

3 mistakes people make when trying to build wealth.

  • Sinking their life savings into buying a home

  • Day-trading crypto hoping to get rich

  • Becoming addicted to sports betting & prediction markets

You would be much better off renting and buying the S&P 500.

~

Are you ready to use this template to write short-form posts? I will give you the topic.

records.content:
As a team, we operate with 3 recurring meetings

  • Daily huddle

  • Weekly KPI review

  • Monthly content review

I should say, this is the aspirational operational cadence. Some weeks we hit all of these, other weeks we realize there is another priority and we trade our meeting time for deep work. I share that because I see a lot of stuff out there from “operators” who make it seem so pretty from the outside when the inside is far more chaotic.

Daily huddle

This is a 30-minute sync we do most mornings, just to align for the day ahead. We simply run through all of the open projects, close loops on anything that requires synchronous communications, and agree on timelines/turnaround times for that day’s action items.

Weekly KPI review

Every Sunday, Dickie runs through our Marketing KPIs tracker and films a Loom overview of everything he’s noticing. This data is then viewed through the lens of our current projects, making sure we’re allocating resources in the right way to work on the right bottleneck of the business. The team then watches it before the Monday meeting and shares their takeaways asynchronously.

Monthly Content Review

Throughout the month, we gather data inside our Master Analytics Tracker (one tab for each of the platforms we use, capturing the data I laid out in Module 2). Then, at the end of the month, we study the data to identified what worked well, what we should double down on, what we should repurpose, etc. Like I mentioned in Module 2, this is our “ongoing improvement” system that ensures we are getting “better” on each platform month after month.

We currently have 11 members on our content team.

Please keep in mind, much of this team “structure” is extremely informal. Each person plays a handful of different roles & manages a handful of different responsibilities. This is a messy work in progress, but it works for us right now.

AND, please keep in mind, this team was just 3 people as little as 2 years ago. We have expanded our resources as we have expanded platforms & needed a larger media presence, but you do not need anywhere near the size of the team we have to run an efficient education-based business.

Here’s the rundown of all 11 members:

Dickie

Dickie oversees our paid ad strategy, writes content, and sets the direction of the team based on KPIs.

Cole

Cole creates writes (a ton) + oversees the creation of video content. He works closely with Dickie to review ads, spot trends on various platforms, and edits emails/scripts/newsletters before they go live.

Daniel

Daniel powers the operations + conversion rate optimization for our marketing team. On the ops side, he makes sure projects stay on track, nothing slips through the cracks, and we don’t waste time repeating ourselves or doing things that could be automated. On the CRO side, he oversees our email marketing campaigns, builds all of the automations within our funnels, and integrates all of our software to make sure our campaigns run smoothly.

Ash — Head Copywriter

Ash is our head copywriter, but that’s a dramatic understatement. He writes our PGA and Start Writing Online emails, he writes copy for our ads, he manages the scheduling of our social content, he repurposes videos into newsletters, basically anything we publish has Ash’s hands on it in some way.

Justin — Head of Write With AI

Justin is the lead writer for Write With AI + runs our Substack Notes accounts.

Vitor — IG Lead

Vitor works directly on our Instagram accounts, giving us a dedicated consultant to help with optimizing for content for that platform.

Viggo — Media Buyer

Viggo runs the media buying for our paid ads, making sure our ads are shown to the right people at the right time for the right price, across all platforms.

Mackenzie — Lead Editor

Mackenzie is our lead video editor, primarily responsible for long-form YouTube content + short-form ads.

Terence — Junior Editor

Terence is a junior video editor responsible for creating short form organic videos, whether those are scripted or pulled from podcasts.

Hana & Jamie — Marketing Operations

And last but not least, Hana is our marketing operations assistant, responsible for inputting analytics data, scheduling content, and QCing our accounts when posts go live.

Jamie also works closely with Hana with content uploading, quality control, and is a general swiss army knife to make sure our content operations hums along smoothly.

1. The simplest framework for social media content creation: More, Better, New

(H/t to Alex Hormozi who put together this framework)

When we are looking to iterate & grow one of our social media platforms, we follow this 3-part system:

1. More

The first step on any platform is to ask yourself this question:

How many times can I post on this platform before I start to see negative returns?

Said another way, what’s the number that “maxes out” a platform, such that posting just one more time might lead to:

  • The algorithm punishing you

  • Your audience fatiguing

  • Your quality bar faltering

This answer is different from each platform, and it’s on you to test, experiment, and ask others who are posting there as well.

OR… you can invest in a course like this, and we can give you the “quick and dirty” answer directly, saving you hours and hours of time.

(We’ll cover this for every single platform we post on in the next module.)

As an example Let’s use Instagram, our newest platform.

We both started to post there over the last 3-4 months. To start, we were at 0 posts per day, so clearly the first step was “more.”

But how much more? Good question—we had the same one as well. So we went and looked up some of the biggest “instagram coaches” on IG, bought their course, and parsed through their different recommendations.

The consensus was that posting 2x per day is roughly the ideal amount there, but the type of post mattered as well. Reels are shown mostly to “non-followers,” so posting more of those does not lead to direct audience fatigue. Posts on the other hand, are shown mostly to just your followers, which increases the chance of audience fatigue.

Combining these two insights, we settled on alternating between:

  • 2 reels per day

  • 1 reel, 1 post per day

  • Switching back and forth between this cadence every day

Within one week of being on the platform, we had maxed out “more”—and that should be your goal on any new platform as well.

Once we set this cadence, we stuck to it for 30 days to get a feel for the platform and how it worked. Then, we moved on to the next step:

2. Better

Once you’re doing more and you’ve “maxed out” the number of times you can post, the priority becomes to post the same amount, but “better.”

Here’s how we think about this process:

There are generally 3 ways you can create “better” content:

  1. Refine the idea

  2. Refine the hook

  3. Refine the packaging

In our experience, the one that leads to the best bang for you buck is dialing in the packaging. Every platform has different nuances & subtleties that create the difference between a flop and viral banger. But that’s unique to our experience, because we’ve posted tens of thousands of times on other platforms. This means we have a general sense of what ideas resonate and the best hooks to deliver them.

But no matter which you’re looking to refine, the best way to do this is with a “monthly content review.”

Every 30 days, we sit down as a content team and go platform by platform, studying our last 30 days of posts for both me & Cole.

We put every post into a giant Google Sheet (which we will share with you, of course) along with the analytics, content bucket, and format commentary.

On top of that, we will pick a few people further along than us on that platform and put their posts into another tab, strictly so we can look at packaging and see what’s working.

We will rank them by engagement, then have a conversation about how we can double down on that idea, reuse that hook, reapply that packaging, etc. There’s nothing overly scientific about this, but it forces us to keep asking the question of “what’s working” and apply our takeaways to the next month of content.

Building on our Instagram example, we are currently experimenting with dozens of different post “packaging” methods this month based on our analysis of last month. And we’re doing so by varying the format, but maintaining the cadence we identified as the “maxed out” cadence in the first step.

At this point, we are going to repeat this process every month for AT LEAST 6 MONTHS until we feel 100% certain that we have a process, as a team, for ongoing refinement and iteration. Then, and only then, do we move onto the third step:

3. New

I’m going to repeat the point I just made so you can recognize its importance.

We sit in the “better” stage for AT LEAST 6 MONTHS before we move onto a new platform. During that 6 months, we are looking to build the refinement system such that we know the content on that platform will get “better” over time just through following the system on a monthly basis. And for the rest of the time we post on that platform, we will stay in this “better” stage.

The mistake we’ve made in the past is starting on a new platform, maxing out the volume, improving the quality for one month, then immediately jumping to another new platform without getting a sense for the current one. This meant we had half-baked content on the platform that was not going to improve over time, ultimately hurting our brand & audience rather than helping it grow.

Had we just focused our attention on that platform for an additional 2-3 months, we could have built a system that would compound in our favor, rather than against us.

On top of that, we stuck with ONE PLATFORM (Twitter/X) for over 2 years before we started to post on LinkedIn. And we didn’t move to LinkedIn until we had both a refinement system for posting on Twitter AND we had generated over $1m in revenue.

After that, we stuck with just Twitter & LinkedIn for another year before we started posting anywhere else. And at that point, we had generated over $5m in revenue.

So the main takeaway from this lesson is not that you need to go do “more” and “better” on every platform. Instead, before you think about going to a “new” platform, ask yourself these questions:

  • Am I currently maxed out volume-wise on my current platform?

  • Do I have a system for constant refinement on my current platform?

  • Have I generated $1m in revenue from my product or service from this platform?

If the answer is no to any of those…stick with the current platform you’re on and focus on getting better. Once you can confidently answer yes to all 3 questions, you can move on to a new one.

records.content:
(if you want to make more money)

For my first 18 months of posting content, I tracked literally nothing.

  • I had no clue where my traffic was coming from

  • I had no clue what types of posts were doing well

  • I had no clue what type of content was generating sales

And as a result, I had no clue what was resonating, so I wasn’t improving. I was “spraying and praying” hoping that the words I put out there would somehow get me closer to my goal of monetizing online.

Then, after 18 months, I began to track basic post analytics:

  • Likes

  • Retweets

  • Comments

  • Etc.

This helped me create more content that optimized for these specific metrics. As a result, I started to write things that were more broad and had more viral potential. And because I was analytical about the process, it worked. I began to consistently go viral and rapidly grew my following.

As a BYPRODUCT of this increased reach, the metric I actually cared about (sales) improved. But that was only because the aggregate number of eyeballs that went to our products & pages went up. But on a percentage basis, the number of people who were buying relative to the size of my audience was small. I was casting a wide net, rather than a targeted one.

Once I realized a big following was not the end goal (in fact, I realized fame was literally the opposite of what I wanted), I began to optimize my content for sales & new customers.

However, I had no way to track this. 3 years into my online journey, I couldn’t answer basic questions like:

  • How many students came from LinkedIn last month?

  • How many email subscribers came from Twitter?

  • What was the conversion rate on our checkout page?

So to start the year, we spent 6 months building out this tracking system for basically EVERY ACTION someone takes in our ecosystem. Ironically, we called this project “tracking infrastructure week,” thinking it would happen in about 7 days. Turns out, it took about 7 months, and we’re still working on it today.

But as a result of this tracking, I have hyper clear data on:

  • The type of content that generates SALES from my audience

  • The conversion rate at every single step of the funnel across every funnel in our business

And having that entire picture allows us to optimize the entire system for the true end goal (sales) rather than a proxy goal (followers).

So the lesson here is I should have set up this type of basic tracking from the beginning:

  • Using Fathom analytics on every page

  • Tracking the number of people who visit each page in the funnel DAILY

  • Constantly identifying the bottleneck of the sales process, making a plan to improve it, executing that plan, and repeating on and on and on

Had I done this earlier, I would have made a lot more money.

records.content:
(no matter the algorithm, but the packaging must be “congruent” to the platform)

This year, we posted consistently across 7 platforms:

  1. Twitter

  2. LinkedIn

  3. YouTube

  4. Threads

  5. Instagram

  6. Substack Notes

  7. Medium

The new ones for us were YouTube, Instagram, Threads, and Substack Notes.

Following the more, better, new process I laid out in the first lesson, we maxed out “more” on each platform simply by copy/pasting content that worked on Twitter over to the new platform (or reading it aloud for YouTube).

This worked, in the beginning, to get started gathering data and build the consistent publishing into our operations.

But, we quickly capped out on each platform.

Why?

The packaging of the post was incongruent to the platform.

The ideas & hooks we use follow universal psychological principles, so they work everywhere. But like I said in the first lesson, users engage differently on each platform, and the users themselves are different people on each platform.

I walk through tangible examples of this lesson in the next module, but the takeaway for us is to invest more time in studying packaging of the people who are crushing the platform, then apply that format to our proven ideas & hooks.

records.title: 4. You Need A Vehicle For Repetition
