records.content:
(to create sustainably long-term, you need a vehicle for repetition and a vehicle for novelty)

Having written consistently every day for 4+ years now, I have a decent idea of the topics and delivery methods that work to get people interested, engaged, and taking action within our ecosystem.

Those proven topics create a level of predictability in our business that is comforting.

At this point, I can basically:

  • Reuse the same ideas I’ve talked about in the past

  • Rearrange the hooks & the formatting to generate a bit of novelty

  • Generate millions of views and millions of dollars as a result, given we have conversion mechanisms for all the different attention we generate.

It’s awesome.

But I’d be lying if I said that at certain times, it felt stifling to my own intellectual curiosity.

As we assembled our content calendar, much of what was going out were things I had said multiple times. And the strange part was knowing that doing so would work and continue to grow the business. It was like I had trained an employee to operate the business on the back of my proven ideas, and it no longer required my input.

Strange, existential feeling there.

Anyway, rather than dwell on that fact, I realized this was actually spectrum, not a binary.

It wasn’t that I had to post 100% “new” ideas to feel intellectually stimulated, nor did I need to post 100% “proven” ideas to grow the business.

The balance sat somewhere in the middle, and that’s what I wanted to create this year. I needed to find the right mix of proven content & novel content, whether that’s ideas or formats.

Rather than overthink this, I just relied on the 80/20 Pareto Principle. Now on any platform, I stick with an 80/20 ratio of proven concepts to novel ones.

80% of the posts are ideas that I know work that will predictably grow the business. 20% are new ideas that I currently find interesting & want to refine through my writing and creation. This shows up in different ways on different platforms, and it’s up to our content team to determine the best place for them.

The format that has worked best for me on this is “single-paragraph” tweets that go out once per day. We post 5x per day on Twitter, which means 4 of the ideas are proven concepts, and 1 of them is novel.

That “novel” slot is always written fresh by me, often on a weekly basis. And at the end of every month, during our “better” monthly content review, I will study those paragraph tweets individually to see which new ideas are resonating. Then, I’ll double down or expand on them the next month.

In 2025, I expect to create another vehicle for novelty, this time in the form of YouTube/podcast/IG video shorts. And I’ll likely strike the same 80/20 principle there, talking about proven concepts for 80% of the time and spending 20% of the time on completely novel ones.

records.title: 5. Five Stages of Buyer Awareness
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/The Vortex 1.0/Module 1 Content Lessons from 2024/5. Five Stages of Buyer Awareness - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: There are 5 stages of buyer awareness, and you must make content for all of them. In his legendary book Breakthrough Advertising (which is so rare it costs $300
records.content:
There are 5 stages of buyer awareness, and you must make content for all of them.

In his legendary book Breakthrough Advertising (which is so rare it costs $300 for a hard copy on EBay), Eugene Schwartz lays out a 5-part spectrum for “audience awareness”

  1. Unaware

  2. Problem aware

  3. Solution aware

  4. Product aware

  5. Most aware

And this simple concept has changed the way I think about content creation.

Early on in my content creation journey, I thought only in content “buckets”:

  • Writing

  • Journaling

  • Health & fitness

  • Productivity

  • Digital business

  • Etc. Etc.

What I didn’t realize is that, if the goal of your content is to eventually drive sales to a product or service related to that content bucket, your content must walk someone through each of these stages of awareness.

A few key points on this idea:

  • The higher up the awareness chain, the more likely it is to go viral

  • Social media content works best to bring unaware people into problem aware

  • The CTAs of your social media content bring problem aware people into solution aware people

  • Email marketing content works best to bring solution aware people into product aware people

  • The CTAs of your email marketing bring your product aware people into your most aware people

  • And at that point, the job is marketing is mostly complete. It’s the job of the sales team (or your landing page) to convert the most aware people into customers.

Let’s walk through a hypothetical example.

Let’s say you sell a 30-day journaling course that helps people work through their anxious feelings.

Here’s how you might structure the funnel:

  • Unaware: Content based around bringing awareness to anxious feelings being a problem. These people are going through life without recognizing their anxious feelings are dominating their mental bandwidth and keeping them from enjoying life

  • Problem aware: At the end of a post breaking down the “signs anxious feelings are hurting your wellbeing” you would put a CTA along the lines of “if you’re looking for the best way to combat anxious feelings without medication or therapy, here’s another post I made about the best ways to overcome anxious feelings.”

  • Solution aware: The CTA of the last post turned the from problem aware into solution aware. They now understand they have a problem (their anxious feelings) and there are solutions out there. Now we are going to help them understand all of the potential solutions they have. At the end of that post, we would have another CTA along the lines of “of each of these methods, I’ve found journaling to be the most effective, given it doesn’t require any medication nor any other people to be involved. If you’re looking to learn more about journaling, check out this post breaking down the 5 best prompts I’ve used to combat my anxious feelings”

  • Product aware. At this point, they are aware you have something to offer them that can solve their problem. You could deliver this as a post, a long-form YouTube video, an email course, the vehicle doesn’t matter. But the goal here is to give them a rough idea of how your product will solve their problem (the information) without selling the implementation (your 30-day guided journaling prompt). After going through your email course / video sales letter / whatever you chose, you would make a CTA to go check out your product.

  • Most aware. At this point, you’ve gotten someone who from completely unaware to the final stage of being most aware. Now your content is all about highlighting the specific benefits & features of your product, overcoming potential objections, etc. This is where “sales” comes in if you have a sales team or a landing page if you sell a digital product. Everyone on this page is strictly in a “consideration mode” of whether or not buying your product is worth it.

Now, here’s where the clarity of this buyer journey gets interesting:

Paid marketing.

Trying to engineer this system with just your organic content is a bit likely playing a slot machine. It could work, but it’s going to be unpredictable and require a bit of luck to pull it off.

With paid marketing on the other hand, you are able to “segment” your advertising by levels of buyer awareness, showing only the most relevant content to the most relevant people, based on where they are on your awareness spectrum.

And that leads us into our 6th and final lesson:

records.content:
(are choreographed propaganda engines)

If you want to spook yourself out a little bit, try this exercise.

The next time you buy something, track your click history backward from purchase to the inception of the idea or concept that buying that product solves.

In fact, let’s get a little bit meta with how you purchased our Category Newsletter Creator product.

  • Unaware to Problem Aware. The main “problem” we wanted to make aware in our reader’s minds is that you are making less money than you would like as a writer/creator. Most of our audience “knows that” because by nature of engaging with our content, you are interested in growing your writer/creator business. A level above this would be the highest level of unawareness, that you can even make a living writing/creating on the internet in the first place.

  • Problem Aware to Solution Aware. Once you were aware of the monetization problem, we needed to educate you on the solution. Our method was to explain that, without a newsletter, you will struggle to monetize your products & services effectively. We recognized that most writers & creators actually do not know this is the top 1% make almost all of their money—selling directly to their most engaged audience without any barrier from social media algorithms and their distribution. So we needed to use examples to show you this “solution” in action.

  • Solution Aware to Product Aware. At this stage, you were interested in starting a newsletter as the solution to your monetization problem, but did not know how to do so effectively. So you began to explore solutions, watch YouTube videos, or read some of our content that was explaining the best way to get started. The CTA of those posts directed you to either 1) our newsletter waitlist if it was live or 2) our general email list where we explore tons of digital writing topics, including starting a newsletter.

  • Product Aware to Most Aware. Over the last week, we sent several emails directing you to either the product waiting list page or the product purchase page. Each of those emails educated you on the basics of the product and explained the benefits of purchasing it through stories & examples. But how did you get onto the product launch list?

  • Most Aware to Customer. You checked out the landing page and maybe had one or two questions left after reading our emails or seeing our social media posts. The landing page answered those questions, and you hit purchase.

Now, in the last module I explained that trying to do this with an organic-only content system is difficult. But with a paid marketing engine, it’s straightforward.

Based on your visit history & the pages you’ve clicked on, we can tell exactly where you are in the journey.

  • If you’ve visited the landing page, you are Most Aware

  • If you are on the launch waitlist but haven’t visited the landing page, you are Product Aware

  • If you are on the launch list but haven’t joined the waitlist, you are Solution Aware

And so our paid advertising campaigns honed in on 3 segments, attempting to show only the most relevant information to get you to the next stage of the buying journey

  • If you were Most Aware, our ads were direct offers educating you on the product

  • If you were Product Aware, our ads were targeted at increasing your interest

  • And if you were Solution Aware, our ads were targeted to educate you on the importance of starting a newsletter

At the time of writing this, we do not have any hard data on the results of this. And importantly, it’s the first time we’ve run retargeting for a product launch like this, so I’m sure we could have been better in like 100 different places.

Cracking this retargeting nut with an Organic Content Vortex is our single biggest priority as we head into 2025.

How will we execute that system?

I break it down in the next module.

Throughout 2024, we posted over 5000 times across 7 different channels.

These posts led to roughly 200,000 new followers gained, 100,000 new email subscribers, and millions of dollars of revenue across 4 main product verticals.

In this module, we’ll dig into lessons we learned, both strategically on social media in general, and tactically for each platform.

  1. The simplest framework for social media content creation: More, Better, New

  2. Track EVERYTHING (if you want to make more money)

  3. Good content works no matter the algorithm, but the packaging must be “congruent” to the platform

  4. To create sustainably long-term, you need a vehicle for repetition and a vehicle for novelty

  5. There are 5 stages of buyer awareness, and you must make content for all of them

  6. The best content systems are choreographed propaganda engines

Let’s dive in.

records.content:
On the email side, we are sending emails across 3 newsletters every week: Start Ghostwriting, Start Writing Online, and Write With AI. Each one of those newsletters has a different “goal” so it makes sense to break them up when talking about them.

For Start Ghostwriting, the goal is to get subscribers to book a call to speak with our team and eventually join PGA. All emails are sent through that lens, which guides our content, our CTAs, and our posting frequency.

Number of emails per week: 7

Yes - we send an email every single day to this list, given it is rather direct-response heavy. The goal is to have someone make a decision to book a call and speak with our team or unsubscribe in the first 7 days.

Email send times (ET): 8:30 AM ET

Seeing a pattern yet?

Analytics we are tracking

  • Open rate

  • Click rate

  • Unsubscribe rate

  • Numbers of calls booked rate

3 examples of email formats

  • The Value Email (Public URL: https://vine-perch-730.notion.site/Start-Ghostwriting-Value-Email-Examples-14601b956bb680558362df953260367f?pvs=4)

  • The Indirect Email (Public URL: https://vine-perch-730.notion.site/Start-Ghostwriting-Indirect-Email-Examples-14601b956bb680c29492e0f4b665cc5e?pvs=4)

  • The Direct Email (Public URL: https://vine-perch-730.notion.site/Start-Ghostwriting-Direct-Email-Examples-14601b956bb680039befee65942864cc?pvs=4)

3 Lessons From Daily Direct Response Emails

  • Daily emails = the maxed out “more” for this type of email. There is no reason to send anything less than daily emails for a direct response newsletter. Given we take calls every day, run ads every day, and can enroll someone on any day, we find there should be some email communication sent every day. Now, the types of email we send will depend on the capacity our sales team has as well as the warmth of the prospect. But either way, daily emails win.

  • Test SOMETHING in every email. Subject line, content topic, CTA, email length, sending time, whatever it is, test SOMETHING in every email and document those changes over time. After running 30 “experiments” we have become at least 50% better at sending emails & converting subscribers into booked calls.

  • Email segmentation is how you go from “more” to “better.” If “more” was sending more emails, “better” is sending the right emails. We’re in the early stages of getting this right, but we want to recreate the organic buying journey with our email sequences in the first half of 2025.

Last but not least, we have our “original” Category Newsletter: Start Writing Online.

This newsletter continues to be the engine of Ship 30 for 30’s growth with a send list of 100k+ at the time of writing this. For nearly 3 years straight we’ve delivered consistent digital writing tips into your inbox, and we don’t plan on slowing down any time soon.

Number of emails per week: 1

This is certainly below the maxed out “more” for this newsletter. On our list for 2025 is to test 2x per week sends for this newsletter, potentially even 3x if we can find the right mix of content that isn’t overwhelming.

Email send times (ET): 8:30 AM ET

Yes that is indeed 3 emails + 12 social posts coming out at this exact time, every day. VOLUME WINS.

Analytics we are tracking

  • Open rate

  • Click rate

  • Unsubscribe rate

3 examples of email formats

  • The in-depth educational email

  • The testimonial email

  • The video-value email

2 things we’re noticing with our Start Writing Online newsletter

  • Email + Skool combo = elite nurturing. On the back of our SWO newsletter, we link to our free SWO Skool group that houses all of our content in an educational Skool portal. This allows us to consistently “link back” to a hub of content that is easy to navigate and dive into. Each one of those posts links to one of our paid product, creating an epic flywheel keeping attention in our ecosystem until someone is ready to buy.

  • Email is boring and it will make you gobs of money. Over the last 4 years, this newsletter has stayed basically the same. The landing page, the contents, the posting cadence, very little has changed hold for a little rebrand here and there. The result? A list of 100k+ and $5m+ of direct revenue generated.

records.content:
Our second newsletter is Write With AI, hosted on Substack. This newsletter costs $20 per month or $200 per year and generates roughly $320k in subscription revenue per year at the time of its recording.

Our goal in 2025 is to grow this to a consistent 500k+ through a blend of subscription + digital products. We’ll do so by really pushing the pace on Substack Notes & trying to convert as much of our audience over there to our paid newsletter.

Number of emails per week: 2 paid, 1 free (3 total)

Our paid newsletters go out on Tuesday & Friday. We send a preview of each paid version to our free list every time, with the real “meat” of the prompt hidden behind the “read more” button.

Our free newsletter goes out on Sundays to just the free list, recapping everything we covered that week and encouraging them to subscribe.

Email send times (ET): 8:30 AM ET

If you’re subscribed to all of our stuff, chances are you get a lot of notifications during this time!

Analytics we are tracking

  • Open rate

  • Click rate

  • Likes

  • Comments

  • Free trial upgrade rate

3 examples of email formats

  • The in-depth prompt (paid)

  • The weekly recap (free)

3 Trends We’re Noticing On Write With AI

  • Substack’s built-in referral engine is powerful. We’ve partnered with several other AI newsletters to “recommend” each other after subscribing, which generates roughly 25% of our new subscribers.

  • Substack is lacking in ideal segmentation features to effectively grow a paid newsletter. The only downside to Substack is the inability to segment readers based on their activity/likeliness to churn/length of subscription/etc. However, we find the built-in referral benefits + Substack Notes outweigh the cons here.

  • The maxed out “more” for a paid newsletter is 2x per week. We’ve tested 1x per week and 3x per week. The people wanted more at 1x per week and felt overwhelmed at 3x per week.

records.content:
Instagram is the newest platform we are taking seriously, and the early results are exciting.

This has been on our “should start doing” list for about a year, but we finally gave it attention this year by hiring a contractor specifically to help with our instagram posting.

The audience there is completely different culturally than LinkedIn & Twitter, because most people use that platform for entertainment rather than education. However, there are a few pockets of education-based creators seeing success there, and we’re bullish on it going forward.

Much of what I’m about to explain for IG is “rough draft” mode since our strategy is in its early stages. However, this is exactly what we would recommend someone do who is getting started like we are.

Number of posts per day: 2

There is a bit of nuance to this number. Since the platform treats “Reels” and “Posts” quite differently, we alternate two different days.

  • Day 1: 2 reels

  • Day 2: 1 post, 1 reel

I’ll explain the thought process behind this in the section below around what we’re noticing on the platform.

Post times (ET): 8:30 AM ET, 8:30 PM ET

Fairly standard here, as you can see we are fans of that 8:30 AM slot when most people are commuting/before the workday really kicks off.

Analytics we are tracking

  • Impressions

  • Likes

  • Shares

  • Comments

  • New followers

5 examples of post formats

  1. The Podcast Snippet

    https://www.instagram.com/reel/DCU2vKcKmFI/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==

  2. The Tweet Shot Reel

    https://www.instagram.com/reel/DCjsEywILtI/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==

  3. The Lifestyle Image + Commentary

    https://www.instagram.com/p/DCZYziwShfB/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==

  4. The Scripted Short-Form Video

    https://www.instagram.com/reel/DCm4S7eM9x6/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==

  5. The Carousel

https://www.instagram.com/p/DCW0ASqvpXN/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==

4 Trends We’re Noticing On Instagram

  • Nothing, nothing, nothing, then big acceleration. The quip I’ve been using with IG is “it only takes on viral post.” The second you get a reel take off for 100k+ views, everything accelerates exponentially. I’m not sure why, but there is definitely something with this algorithm where it immediately shows you a ton of someone’s content after you engage with them for the first time. The key lesson is just to keep posting here, because once something hits, all your future posts will see a “step function” increase in views/likes/engagements.

  • Posts are like emails, Reels are like TikTok. Said another way, when you put up a “Post” (static image or carousel), it shows almost exclusively to your own followers without a strong chance to go viral. Reels, on the other hand, show almost exclusively to non-followers (via the Reel feed / Explore page). Try it yourself, scroll through your feed and you’ll see mostly people you know. Scroll through Reels & you’ll see mostly people you don’t.

  • Stories are the best way to build “brand.” I haven’t started taking this part of IG seriously because it’s a mental bandwidth suck, but I plan to in 2025. If you can bring people “behind the scenes” of your life and make your story something people are excited to watch, you can build a seriously strong “parasocial” relationship that will trickle down into your content views, subscribers, and ultimately, customers.

  • Do not CTA in your content, use pinned posts & bio link. The IG funnel, as I see it right now, is to post organically with 100% “give” and no CTA in the content itself, even to “follow you.” People on IG follow a rather choreographed process of seeing something, clicking over to your profile, looking at your pinned posts, and clicking your bio link. You can rely on them to take that action without giving them explicit instructions, and doing so gives your content a better chance to go viral.

records.content:
Linked is the second most important & lucrative platform for our business.

This one delivers consistent, linear growth day in and day out. We haven’t had many things go incredibly viral, but we consistently generate 30-50k views per post and grow by about 1000 followers per week.

Our approach to LinkedIn won’t change very much in the year ahead, as we appreciate its consistent results.

Number of posts per day: 1

The “more” limit on LinkedIn is either 1 or 2, we aren’t 100% sure. We see a few other big writers posting 2x per day, but we’re sticking with 1x per day for now.

Importantly, every single post we have on LinkedIn includes media. There is a clear distribution bump when something 1) has media and 2) has a long “engagement time” on the media/carousel/video itself.

Post times (ET): 8:30 AM ET, 8:30 PM ET (if we begin posting a second time)

Again nothing overly scientific here, just when we are awake and able to engage.

Analytics we are tracking

  • Impressions

  • Likes

  • Reposts

  • Comments

  • New followers

We use a platform called Shield to manage our analytics on LinkedIn.

5 examples of post formats

  1. The Long-Form + Media

    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dickiebush_everyone-should-have-a-digital-business-that-activity-7260645303790235648-jT4b/

  2. The Carousel

    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dickiebush_9-brutal-truths-i-learned-in-my-20s-activity-7264632808789225472-wcRO/

  3. The Tweet Shot

    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dickiebush_everything-clicked-for-me-when-i-realized-activity-7259557212212150273-U42W/

  4. The Short-Form Video + Long-Form Text

    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dickiebush_the-quickest-way-to-find-a-winning-business-activity-7260289073599197184-9fBq/

  5. The Handwritten Infographic

    https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nicolascole_the-most-powerful-habit-you-can-develop-activity-7262094148151791618-ZYA6/

4 Trends We Are Noticing On The Platform

  1. Comments matter more than ever. Similar to Twitter, we are seeing an increased return on commenting / providing insightful comments / having people comment on your posts. LinkedIn does a good job of “ranking” comments by insightfulness and engagement on those comments themselves, meaning you can jump to “the top” of the comment pool by adding something legitimately valuable.

  2. Post → edit the CTA to have a link in the post after one hour. This hack in itself is worth the entire price of this bonus course. We’ve found that after about an hour, if a post is gaining serious traction, you can “edit” the post to add a link right into the meat of the post and it will continue to get the same distribution. The posts that have gotten the most email subscribers for us this year all came from mid-post CTAs about an hour after posting.

  3. Carousels continue to get the best distribution. Of all the content formats, this one goes viral with the most consistency. My hypothesis here is there is so much “engagement” on a post that requires clicking through the carousel that the algorithm decides everyone should see it. The key with carousels, we’ve found, is having a unique / branded design, rather than something generic.

  4. Video beginning to get additional distribution. We have moved to posting 1 video per week there, with an eye of bringing it to 2 if we see initial success. They’ve begun to test a video feed as well, which is a new wave we would want to ride.

Welcome to Module 2 of The Vortex—Dickie & Cole’s 2025 Content Strategy.

In this module, we are going to walk through the nitty-gritty, tactical details around posting on each platform.

Let’s dive in:

As we go into 2025, we will post consistently on the following platforms:

  • Twitter/X

  • LinkedIn

  • Instagram

  • Substack Notes

  • Threads

On top of that, we will send 3 newsletters consistently:

  • Start Writing Online

  • Start Ghostwriting

  • Write With AI

For each platform, we are going to cover:

  • Posting cadence (number per week, times per day, etc.)

  • Analytics we’re tracking to optimize our growth

  • 5 proven content packaging formats we’re using

  • Some trends & lessons we’re noticing on the platform

Let’s get into it.

Similar to Threads, we have an assumption that the “more” of this platform caps out around 5 posts per day. We will run an experiment with the same exact posting cadence as Twitter during the first 3 months of the year.

Post times (ET): 8:30 AM ET, 8:30 PM ET

We will run the same posting cadence of Twitter/X for the first 3 months of 2025.

2 Trends We’re Noticing On Substack Notes

  1. The most “growth mindset”-oriented audience. On the spectrum of intellectual audiences, Substack Notes sits on the far right (most intellectual), then LinkedIn & Twitter in the middle, then Threads on the far left (least intellectual). Almost no one is anonymous and the comments are positive, thoughtful, and supportive.

  2. Congruence between you newsletter & your content is most important on this platform. Given how easy it is to subscribe to a newsletter straight from a Substack Note (an opportunity Twitter absolutely fumbled with Revue…), your newsletter can explode with a few viral Notes. The more you can create hyper-relevant short-form for your ideal newsletter subscriber, the more you can tap into this platform’s flywheel.

records.content:
Twitter remains the most important & lucrative platform for us and our business.

Despite the noise, it still outperforms all others in terms of impressions, subscribers, customers, and it’s the one we enjoy spending time on the most.

As we head into 2025, we are giving Twitter even more attention, closely studying what is working as the algorithm changes more often than other platforms.

Here’s the quick run down of how we’re approaching the platform this year:

Number of posts per day: 5

The “more” of Twitter is likely higher than this, but there is definitely a limit to the amount of media / long-form you can post per day before seeing negative results.

We are posting 4 regular tweets per day (just text) and then one long-form/Atomic Essay/thread that includes media.

We are not posting video on Twitter at the moment, because personally we both scroll Twitter with our sound off and don’t consume videos there like we do on Instagram.

Post times (ET): 6:30 AM, 8:30 AM, 2:30 PM, 5:30 PM, 8:30 PM

  • Nothing overly scientific here, we’re just trying to space them out between the day

  • We are automatically retweeting each post 9 hours later

Analytics we track on this platform:

  • Views

  • Likes

  • Comments

  • Reposts

  • Bookmarks

  • New followers

6 example post formats:

In this section I’ll give a rundown of the 6 types of posts we are seeing work well, along with an example to see it in action.

  1. The Paragraph Tweet

https://x.com/dickiebush/status/1845775743004934578

  1. The What / How / Why Tweet

    https://x.com/dickiebush/status/1855642463740080287

  2. The Atomic Essay

    https://x.com/dickiebush/status/1850154637304676552

  3. The Thread + Media

    https://x.com/dickiebush/status/1828773043306676417

  4. The Long-Form + Media

    https://x.com/dickiebush/status/1843992910070493538

  5. The Handwritten Infographic

    https://x.com/dickiebush/status/1856691146657018168

4 trends we are noticing on this platform

  1. Algorithm is constantly changing. Of any social media platform, this one sees the most frequent algorithm update. This happened so frequently in 2024 that we sort of “gave up” on trying to figure it out and stuck to our regular formats & posting cadence. There was a serious dip in the middle of the year in average views, but our analytics are at all time highs over the last several months.

  2. Followers matter less than they used to. In 2021, tweets would show to basically all of your followers, every time. That is no longer the case. If you spend a bit of time on the “for you” page you’ll notice that ~maybe 3/10 tweets you see are from people you follow. The rest are from people you don’t, meaning that’s how others will find you as well. This creates a nice “idea meritocracy” where it does not matter how big your account is, good content will find its way in front of people.

  3. Comments matter more than they used to. There is a strong correlation between the number of engagements a post gets & its distribution. Elon is clearly making a push to encourage conversation, which is a double-edged sword. It makes controversial things go more viral, but also means you can “borrow” distribution by leaving insightful replies & comments under big creators’ posts.

  4. Post + auto plug “congruence” matters more than it is used to. A few years ago, you could alap any CTA under a tweet with a link to your newsletter and it would convert. But people are used to seeing that now, meaning there needs to be a strong “relationship” between your post and the value proposition of your newsletter.

Welcome to Module 3 of The Vortex—Dickie & Cole’s 2025 Content Strategy.

In this module, we are going to talk through the newest addition to our content strategy—paid ad retargeting.

I don’t want to exaggerate here, but I have not been as excited for a new core piece of our business in the entirety of my entrepreneurial journey. What I am about to share with you is the outline that, in my opinion, will allow us to double our business in 2025 with NO acceleration in growth on any platform—simply converting a larger percentage of our organic eyeballs.

What we’re going to cover:

  • The Basics of Retargeting

  • The 3 Main Platforms We Use For Retargeting

  • The 3 Main Retargeting Campaigns We Are Running

Let’s get into it.

records.title: The 3 Main Platforms We Use For Retargeting

records.description: What’s the goal of our Organic Content Vortex? One word: omnipresence. We want to use organic content to expand our reach, then retarget people across all platf
records.content:
What’s the goal of our Organic Content Vortex?

One word: omnipresence.

We want to use organic content to expand our reach, then retarget people across all platforms such that they can’t help but go down the rabbit hole of our content.

With that in mind, we are currently running retargeting campaigns on 3 platforms:

  1. Meta (Instagram and Facebook)

  2. Twitter/X

  3. LinkedIn

Importantly, we are only running retargeting campaigns for PGA + the CNC product launch. We are not currently running any ads for Ship 30 for 30 or Write With AI, but we plan to in the first few months of 2025.

Meta

Who we’re retargeting. Website visitors, Instagram profile engagers, email subscribers.

Results we’ve seen so far: Strong positive return, given the “omnipresence” it’s created for our Twitter & LinkedIn audiences. Reading a tweet from us, then swiping over to Instagram and immediately seeing a reel creates a strong familiarity bias that makes them more likely to eventually become customers.

Twitter

Who we’re retargeting. Website visitors, tweet engagers, followers, email subscribers.

Results we’ve seen so far. The best of any platform. Given the organic reach we have over there, being able to programmatically put offers back in front of our audience means we are constantly top of mind.

LinkedIn

Who we’re retargeting. Website visitors, LinkedIn post engagers, followers, email subscribers.

Results we’ve seen so far. Mixed so far, but it’s the one we started most recently. The CPM on LinkedIn is the most expensive, meaning we need to spend more than other platforms to show our ad to the entirety of our retargeting list.

records.title: The 3 Main Retargeting Campaigns We Are Running
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/The Vortex 1.0/Module 3 The Organic Content Vortex/The 3 Main Retargeting Campaigns We Are Running - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: We are currently running 3 major retargeting campaigns on each of those platforms for both PGA and the CNC launch, all based around the buyer awareness levels w
records.content:
We are currently running 3 major retargeting campaigns on each of those platforms for both PGA and the CNC launch, all based around the buyer awareness levels we spoke about in the very first module.

  • Unaware/Problem Aware

  • Solution Aware

  • Product Aware

The main goal for each campaign is to move the lead into the next stage of buyer awareness. To do so, we create a series of short-form content videos that either spark curiosity (at the beginning of the buyer journey) or overcome objections (at the end of the buyer journey), and show them ONLY to the people in that stage.

Unaware / Problem Aware

Who do we target with this campaign? Organic post engagers + ad engagers who have not opted in to our email list or visited our landing page.

What’s the goal of this campaign? Get them to follow Cole’s organic content or visit the PGA landing page.

How do we get them to do that? Rather than show them more direct response ads, we look to establish familiarity with Cole + the world of ghostwriting. These include:

  • Shorts introducing Cole with his story

  • Answering basic questions like “what is ghostwriting?” Or “what’s the best way to make a living as a writer?”

  • Basic mindset-related topics around the importance of starting your own business in 2025

Solution Aware

Who do we target with this campaign? Anyone who has visited the PGA website or opted in to become an email subscriber.

What’s the goal of this campaign? To get them to fill out an application and book a call with our team. Basically, we want them to take the next step toward becoming a ghostwriter.

How do we get them to do that? At this point, the viewer knows about ghostwriting & is interested in using it to solve their problem of earning income on the side / growing their freelance business / etc. So this content is all focused around selling the “opportunity” of ghostwriting, answering questions like:

  • What type of business needs a ghostwriter?

  • How do I know what niche to target as a ghostwriter?

  • Etc. Etc.

Once they feel more confident in pursuing ghostwriting, the natural next step is to do more research on PGA & speak with our team. That brings us to the next stage.

Product Aware

Who do we target with this campaign? People who have booked a call to speak with our team, but have not yet enrolled in PGA.

What’s the goal of this campaign? To get them to show up to the call with basic questions answered, excited about the opportunity to ghostwrite.

How do we get them to do that? We create a specific series of videos that “condense” the answering of key questions that happen on a sales call down to 90-second videos. To create these, we asked our sales team for the most common questions & objections they received were, then created an informational piece of content to answer that question (with the right frame) or overcome that objection. Then, we placed all of those videos into one campaign, showing them to the prospect who booked a call in a very tight window of time between call booking and the time of their call.

records.title: The Basics of Retargeting
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/The Vortex 1.0/Module 3 The Organic Content Vortex/The Basics of Retargeting - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Here’s the quick rundown on everything you need to know about retargeting. Please keep in mind, this is our understanding of it from the perspective of 2 guys w
records.content:
Here’s the quick rundown on everything you need to know about retargeting.

Please keep in mind, this is our understanding of it from the perspective of 2 guys who have been running it for about 6 months. We’ve seen awesome results during that time, but there is a high chance we are doing certain things wrong / suboptimally that we we will only discover by spending more time and more money on it.

However, if used correctly, the basic system I am about to explain has the potential to explode your business like it has ours.

We’re going to cover:

  • What is retargeting?

  • How does it work?

  • Who are you retargeting?

  • Why should you use it?

  • When should you use it?

  • How much does retargeting cost?

  • How do you measure return on your retargeting spend?

  • How do you set up retargeting?

Ready? Let’s dive in.

What is retargeting?

Retargeting is using paid advertising platforms like Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and Twitter/X to show your ads to a defined audience of people that have already engaged with your content in some way.

That nuance is important. These platforms allow you to target “cold audiences” that have never seen or heard of you before. You can select things like interests, countries, demographics, languages, etc. and tell the platform to show your ads to them.

However, you can also create a list of people (either through uploading your email subscribers or “pixeling” your pages to have the retargeting list update automatically) that tells the platform to show your ads only to these people, rather than “cold audiences” who have never heard of you.

Put simply, retargeting is showing ads to people who know you.

How does it work?

Ad platforms use what is called a “pixel” to track website visitors off their platform. It’s a little piece of code you install on your landing pages that lets the ad platforms track everyone who goes there.

As people start to visit your page, the pixel keeps track of everyone who has visited and makes a database of their information. Importantly, the origin of that person’s click does not matter. For example, if we put out a tweet with a link to our newsletter and the users clicks over, the Facebook Pixel can recognize the user visit and add their Facebook / Instagram information to the database. Then, when that Twitter user switches over to their Instagram app, we can advertise to them despite them never having engaged with us on Instagram.

This is what lets you crate an “omni-present” Content Vortex. If you can generate an organic click from every platform, you can then programmatically pay to advertise to that person on every other platform they use.

Who are you retargeting?

3 main groups:

  1. Platform engagers. Each platform allows you to retarget anyone who has engaged with your organic content. Whether that’s a view, like, comment, save, video play, you can keep track of everyone who has engaged and programmatically advertise to them in the future.

  2. Website visitors. Similar to platform engagers, but only for people who have visited your website off platform. You can retarget all website visitors, or just those who have visited specific pages, like a checkout page.

  3. Email list subscribers. Lastly, we integrate our email service provider with each ad platform to upload the email of everyone who subscribes. This is how we started with retargeting, given we did not have pixels set up in the past that could have tracked old visitors.

Why should you use it?

If you are generating a large amount of organic traffic, there are quite a few “ups and downs.”

Some days you are going viral, other days you are going nowhere. And that volatility makes it difficult to forecast business growth.

Retargeting reduces that volatility by delivering a consistent number of impressions to your audience, rather than relying on the unpredictable organic audience.

Put simply, if you want to create a more predictable, forecastable business, retargeting is the first step to do that.

When should you use it?

A few guidelines I would recommend:

  1. You should have a product/service for sale that is making consistent sales from organic (at least $1m in revenue lifetime)

  2. You are actively creating content on the platform you are using to advertise

  3. You have the bandwidth (or someone on your team has the bandwidth) to get into the nitty gritty of the ad manager / tech setup / troubleshooting / etc.

We only began to use retargeting ads after generating over $12m in revenue without it. So please, do not jump to this thinking it is the missing piece of your business. It’s only once you want to convert a higher percentage of your organic audience to customers that you should even entertain starting this process.

How much does retargeting cost?

It is purely a function of the 1) the size of your audience and 2) how many times you want the ad to show to the audience.

When you are retargeting, the hierarchy of budget allocation is:

  1. Show to more people within the audience

  2. Show it more times to the people in the audience

So for example, if you have a retargeting list of just 100 people, it would only cost about $2 per day to show the ad to every person in that audience (since CPM (cost per 1k impressions) is about $20). To be clear on the math for that, cost per 1000 views = $20. We are only generating 100 views. 10% of $20 is $2.

If you have a list of 10,000 people, it would cost about $200 per day to show an ad to everyone one of them. CPM is $20. We need to generate 10,000 views. 10,000/1000 =10. 10*$20 =$200

Before the platform will start showing the ad multiple times, it will try to show the ad to everyone in the audience once. But let’s say you have a retargeting list of just 100 people and you spend $100 per day. That might show the ad to them 50 times in a day! But to do that with your 10k person list, you would need to spend 10k per day.

How do you measure the return on your retargeting?

This is a bit beyond the scope of this module and takes quite a bit of time to explain & set up. At some point this year, we will create a full course breaking down the extreme, advance nitty gritty of paid ad retargeting, so keep your eye out for that.

How do you set up retargeting?

Use the prompt to create a Gamma ready carousel

Step 2: Copy The Prompt. Add Your Input. And Run It.

You are an expert at repurposing LinkedIn posts into Gamma.app carousel decks.

INPUT:  
{Paste LinkedIn post here}  

TASK:  
Transform this LinkedIn post into a Gamma deck with the following structure:  

1. **Main Headline** (big, bold promise or question).  
2. **Sub-Headline** (optional — expand on the promise, create curiosity, or add specificity).  
3. **Hook Slide** (use or adapt the LinkedIn hook as Slide 1).  
4. **Mini-Headlines + Body Content**  
   - Break the post into slides.  
   - Each slide has a **mini-headline** (`##` format) and **1–2 sentences of body content**.  
   - Keep text concise and skimmable.  
5. **Separators**  
   - Use `---` between major sections.  
   - Use `#` for main headline, `##` for slide mini-headlines.  
6. **Call-to-Action Slide**  
   - Rewrite the LinkedIn CTA or create a stronger one that fits Gamma style.  

OUTPUT FORMAT (ready to paste into Gamma):  

# [Main Headline]  
[Sub-Headline]

---  

## [Hook Slide]  
[Short hook copy]

---  

## [Mini-Headline 1]  
[Body text]

---  

## [Mini-Headline 2]  
[Body text]

...  

---  

## [Final CTA]  
[Body text / CTA line]  

OUTPUT: 
Markdown, formatted with #, ##, and --- so I can copy / paste into gamma.

records.content:
Hey there!

This is an updated version of the text SOP we shared in our internal training alongside the Gamma Video SOP.

In it, we’ve included the tips & tricks and AI scripts we use when creating these Carousels using Gamma.

Enjoy!

SOP: Creating Carousels using Gamma

1. Context & Objective

We create carousels (multi-slide decks) for LinkedIn and other social platforms using Gamma.app.

The goal of this task is to repurpose existing content (Twitter threads, PDFs from Typeshare, or other sources) into engaging, branded carousels that drive attention, demonstrate authority, and end with a clear CTA.

This process ensures consistent branding across Cole’s and Dickie’s content while making carousels quick to produce and visually engaging.

2. Frequency

  • When: As new content (threads, decks, PDFs) is ready to be repurposed into carousels.

  • How often: Typically weekly, or whenever new long-form content is published.

  • Dependencies:

    • Access to Gamma.app with login credentials.

    • Source material to turn into a deck (PDF, Typeshare link, text thread, newsletter, YouTube transcript, etc.).

    • Brand themes already uploaded to Gamma (Cole’s personal brand, PGA, or Custom Iris theme for Dickie).

    • Notion document in the Master Content Calendar where links back to the Gamma decks are stored for easy retrieval.

3. Checklist

Tools & Resources

  • Gamma.app (with login credentials)

  • Source content (PDF, TypeShare deck, Twitter thread text, or other content)

  • Pre-built themes (Custom Iris for Dickie, Cole’s personal brand, PGA theme)

  • Image sources:

    • Gamma theme’s accent images

      • Cole’s/Dickie’s personal brand image library (loaded into Gamma)

      • Branded website images

    • Unsplash (free stock, inside Gamma)

    • Tweet screenshots (as needed)

  • Notion (for saving Carousel links)

Step-by-Step Process

  1. Start a new deck in Gamma

    • Log into Gamma.app.

    • Click New → With AI.

    • Choose to import a PDF or paste text (from Twitter thread, newsletter, etc.).

    • Always select “Social” as the deck type.

  2. Prepare the content in the Prompt Editor

    • Clean up formatting: remove unnecessary line breaks.

    • Add card breaks by inserting -- between sections.

    • Identify titles and headings (bolded, steps, or colons often indicate slide breaks).

    • Ensure Output Language is English (US).

    • Add this script to the “Additional instructions” prompt box in the top right-hand corner

      • “Every headline should be an h1 markdown headline except for the "Click the link" sentence at the end, which would be an h3 markdown headline. Non-headline text should be /lg large size text. Convert all bullet points into "Large Bullets" with icons that are relevant to the bullet point.”

  3. Apply the correct theme

    • For Dickie: Use the Custom Iris theme.

    • For Cole: Use Cole’s personal brand theme or PGA theme.

  4. Generate the deck

    • Click Continue → Generate.

    • Let Gamma create the draft slides (this may take a minute).

  5. Refine deck formatting

    • Title card

      • Have a strong hook and title to the Carousel.

      • Use Ship 30 frameworks to address the target reader, open a curiosity loop, and promise a benefit/outcome or solve a problem.

    • Go card by card:

      • Adjust text to Large Text instead of Heading if needed (should be handled by the prompt given up, but double-check).

      • Fix bullet points, steps, or layouts (use vertical arrows, numbered lists, etc.).

        • Again, should be handled by the prompt given up, but double-check.

      • Alternate slide layouts: image left, right, bleed-through, etc.

      • Check that titles follow the branding rules.

      • Optional: Experiment with inverted color schemes to stand out in feeds.

    • Replace or edit AI-generated images with:

      • Accent images (loaded in the theme).

      • Branded photos of Cole/Dickie.

      • Unsplash images relevant to the topic.

      • Screenshots of tweets (check formatting after export).

      • Or keep the AI image if it looks good.

  6. Add visual hooks & CTAs

    • Use a strong cover image (often from Cole/Dickie’s personal photo library).

      • This is a “visual hook.” We want this to stand out in the feed.

    • End with a CTA slide (Premium Ghostwriting Blueprint / other landing page).

    • Reuse CTA assets from the theme library if available.

  7. Export & check final output

    • Export as PDF.

    • Open the PDF and check formatting (especially tweet screenshots and images).

    • If formatting is broken: crop/redo the image and re-insert.

  8. Save & document

    • Rename the Gamma deck with the account name at the start (e.g., “Cole – [Deck Name]”).

    • Copy the Gamma link and paste it into the relevant Notion document for easy retrieval.

records.title: Carousels
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Viral Carousels Using AI/Carousels - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Now, you probably already know what carousels are. But just in case you’re not familiar, here’s an example: (Click here to check out the full post.) A carousel
records.content:
Now, you probably already know what carousels are.

But just in case you’re not familiar, here’s an example:

(Click here to check out the full post.)

A carousel is a type of LinkedIn post made up of multiple images packaged as slides.

Readers swipe left or right to move through them, just like a slideshow. Each slide creates a tiny “open loop” that only closes when they swipe. Instead of scrolling past a single block of text or a static image, readers pause, swipe, and stay.

The goal of Slide 1 is to get your reader to click see Slide 2. And so on.

The reason carousels are an excellent growth tool for LinkedIn is because people spend “more time” engaging with them, “clicking” from slide to slide. Each extra second a user spends flipping through a carousel sends a strong signal to LinkedIn’s algorithm: this post is worth paying attention to. Again, the platform is designed to maximize dwell time, and carousels naturally stretch it. The more your reader swipes, the more time they spend on your content, and the more you get rewarded by the algorithm.

Earning the swipe is the game.

Here’s how it breaks down:

  • Slide 1: Hook / title slide. This is your billboard. Big, bold text. Minimal words. The headline should promise exactly what the reader will get if they swipe. Example: “My 3-Step Process To Master Copywriting (This would have saved me thousands of hours as a beginner).” The goal here is simple: earn Slide 2.

  • Slide 2: Re-hook / context. Restate the promise in a slightly different way to lock in interest. Add one or two short lines of context that tease what’s coming. Think of this slide as your chance to convince someone that sticking with the deck will be worth their time.

  • Slides 3 through (X-1): Main points. Each slide should make one clear point only. Use steps, numbered tips, or simple examples. Keep the text scannable: short phrases, bold keywords, and plenty of whitespace. If you’re teaching a framework, this is where you break it down step by step.

  • Final slide: Closing CTA. End with a simple summary and a clear call to action. You can ask a question (“Which step do you struggle with most?”), invite engagement (“Comment ‘copywriting’ and I’ll send you the template”), or point to your newsletter, offer, or product. The goal is to give readers a clear next step once they’ve swiped through to the end.

For example:

Notice how each slide naturally leads to the next.

The title sparks curiosity. The mistake builds tension. Each step delivers on the promise. The example and tip add credibility. And the CTA gives a clear next action, so all that attention you’ve built flows naturally into the rest of your ecosystem.

So how do you actually make a carousel like this?

Option #1: Typeshare

Inside Typeshare, you can make text-based Carousels—which are called Decks.

Whenever we want to put out a Carousel quickly, this is what we do.

Option #2: Gamma

For more advanced / professionally designed Carousels, we use Gamma.app.

Gamma allows you to quickly create really beautiful Carousels using AI.

The next section is a tutorial on how to do that!

records.title: How To Create LinkedIn Posts With Gamma.app
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Exclusive Mini-Courses/Viral Carousels Using AI/How To Create LinkedIn Posts With Gamma.app - Exclusive Mini-Courses · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Gamma.app is the best AI-carousel tool I've come across. - It's very easy to use. - And you can create a carousel in <10 minutes. Now, the only "cost" (which is
records.content:
Gamma.app is the best AI-carousel tool I've come across.

  • It's very easy to use.

  • And you can create a carousel in <10 minutes.

Now, the only "cost" (which is hilarious to say considering it used to take 2-3 hours in Canva) is that you need their Pro plan for the best image model — about $15/month.

Compare that to hiring a designer at $100+ per hour, and it's a no-brainer.

Not to take anything away from designers, because creating beautiful carousels really is an art and great designers produce incredible work…. but as far as "growing on LinkedIn" goes, you just need something to get you going.

And the truth is, now you can create a really great carousel using AI.

Gamma takes away 90% of the carousel design headaches.

All you have to do is paste in your LinkedIn post, pick a design, and in minutes you’ve got a polished deck ready to share in about 30 seconds. This is where Gamma shines compared to ChatGPT's image generation. Instead of waiting 30+ seconds for each individual image to load (and you can only do 2 at a time), Gamma generates dozens of images simultaneously.

Here’s how we use it to create our LinkedIn carousels (in 4 simple steps):

Step 1: Write your content.

The easiest way to think of your carousels is they’re just blog articles.

And if you look at the example above, you’ll see all of the staples of an article:

  • A main headline for Gamma (e.g. “5 Simple Steps To Become A LinkedIn Ghostwriter”).

  • A sub-headling for Gamma (e.g. “Even if you've never written anything for anyone before, suck at sales, and don't have an audience”). This is optional.

  • A hook for his LinkedIn post (e.g. “The easiest way to make money writing on LinkedIn isn’t by:”).

  • Mini-headline for each slide in Gamma (e.g. “Step 1: Say Exactly What You Do In Your Bio”).

  • Body content underneath each mini-heading in Gamma (e.g. “Example: ‘I ghostwrite LinkedIn content for FinTech startup founders.’”.

  • And a Call-to-action at the end of your LinkedIn post (e.g. “Want more help landing high-paying writing clients on LinkedIn?”).

Again, just like a piece of content you’ve probably already written a bunch of times.

Step 2: Create the carousel.

We use a paid Gamma plan because we use the tool a LOT & get a ton of value from some of its advanced features.

But to be perfectly honest, you should just get started with a free plan. Especially if you’re not using a ton of tokens to AI-generate images (we don’t too often, just because we have so many pictures in our backlogs).

Then later, you can see if you like the tool enough to upgrade.

Now, once inside Gamma, click on “Create new.”

This gives you a few options, but we generally use the “Paste in text” mode (don’t worry, AI is not going to edit your writing):

Next, what you’re going to do is:

  1. Click on “Social” so your content is optimized for LinkedIn.

  2. Copy and paste your writing into Gamma.

  3. Click on “Preserve this exact text” (unless you want your writing edited by AI).

  4. And then “Continue to prompt editor →” (don’t worry, you can still edit on the next screen).

Step 3: Format your piece.

This is SUPER simple to do in the “card-by-card” editor:

  • To turn a piece of text into a headline, sub-headline, or mini-headlines → Just type “#” and then add a space at the start of the line of text.

  • To make a piece of text bold → Highlight and then use CMD + B (on Mac) or CTRL + B (on PC).

  • To make a piece of text italic → Highlight and then use CMD + i (on Mac) or CTRL + i (on PC).

And then, use “---” to split each mini-headline into a new card in your LinkedIn carousel.

For example:

Next, select your Theme and then click on “Generate.”

And voila!

Your LinkedIn carousel is now 95% complete.

Step 4: Add the finishing touches to your LinkedIn carousel.

All that’s left is some minor “graphic design” (think: selecting which pictures to add to each card or slide).

Now, you’re more than welcome to use as many images you’d like, but we usually stick to these 2 rules of thumb:

  1. Most cards have ONE picture to visually break up all of the text.

  2. Ideally, the image should be somewhat relevant to the topic of the card (or else it’ll feel really out of place).

For example:

Talking in front of a room of ghostwriters.

And we just go through each slide, making tweaks that we think look nice:

  • Changing text color (like changing “A LinkedIn Ghostwriter” to orange text).

  • Turning blocks of text into colored boxes.

  • Replacing bullet points with icons.

  • Etc.

And that’s it!

See how easy that was?

That’s exactly how we create our LinkedIn carousels every week.

Then, once we’re happy with final output, we:

  1. Export them as a PDF

  2. Head over to LinkedIn and create a new post

  3. Paste our LinkedIn hook and text in the post

  4. Upload the PDF we exported from Gamma

  5. And hit publish

So simple that even a couple of Digital Writers can look like expert graphic designers :)

Here are a few tips we’ve picked up making dozens of these ourselves:

  • Paste, don’t prompt. Gamma lets you generate decks from scratch with AI prompts, but the real power comes from repurposing content you’ve already written (a LinkedIn post, Twitter thread, or even a PDF). Paste it in, then let Gamma split it into slides — much faster and more relevant than starting blank.

  • Control your card breaks. Gamma tries to guess where slides should split, but it’s not perfect. Add three dashes (---) between sections of your text to force clean breaks. This way, each slide gets one idea, and you avoid bloated or confusing layouts.

  • Brand once, use forever. Build a custom theme with your colors, fonts, and logo. Even better, create two or three variations (like a light and dark mode) so your carousels look consistent but don’t feel repetitive. Again, consistent visuals makes your brand instantly recognizable in the feed.

  • Alternate your visuals. If every slide looks the same, readers stop swiping. Rotate between text-heavy slides, accent images, bleed-through backgrounds, and even tweet screenshots. The visual rhythm keeps attention moving through your deck.

  • Reuse visual assets. Once you hit generate, Gamma creates all your carousel slides AND automatically saves every image to your "AI Images" library. This is huge. You don't have to download images one by one. Just go to your dashboard, click "AI Images," and you'll see every image Gamma has ever created for you, organized and ready to download. You can also see the exact prompt Gamma used for each image, so you can replicate successful styles.

  • Create a CTA template. Save a branded “final slide” in your theme (newsletter, course, or lead magnet). That way, every carousel closes strong without you having to reinvent the wheel each time.

  • Always check your PDF before posting. Gamma exports beautifully, but small glitches (like misaligned tweet screenshots or weird formatting) can sneak in. Take 30 seconds to proof the PDF before uploading to LinkedIn. Note: You can also schedule a post directly to LinkedIn if you connect your account, but manual uploads give you more control.

It’s about as simple as it gets.

Take your post, drop it into Gamma, polish a few slides, export, and boom—you’re done.

records.content:
You might think that the Carousel is the main event of the Carousel Post.

Well, not quite!

The Text Post you pair with the Carousel is just as important as the Carousel itself. Why? Because what you include here will determine whether the reader will read the full post.

Now, there are 2 schools of thought when it comes to what you should include in this Text Post (aside from writing a strong hook and using digital formatting tips techniques):

  1. Write a short, punchy introduction to encourage people to read the Carousel

  2. Write a high-level summary of the Carousel to tease the value and get people to read it

Both are designed to increase retention on the post (which in turn signals to the algorithm that this content is worth sharing!).

Here’s an example of the first approach:

Notice how the rest of the post is short and sweet (and introduces the Carousel as a way to find out what the 7 small habits are):

Here’s an example of the second approach:


When you click See More, you see some additional context AND an overview of the points covered in the Carousel:


The idea here is that the reader has a “lay of the land” before diving into the content.

Highly recommend you experiment with both approaches in your content!

How To Write The Document Title

Alright, one final pro tip before we wrap up this Carousel mini-course.

The Document Title is VALUABLE real estate on LinkedIn:

This is the Title that appears on the Carousel when you hover over it in the feed (like this):


So you should see this as a secondary headline, and it’s worth spending a few minutes making sure this is short and punchy (and follows all my rules on how to write an effective headline).

records.description: Hey there! In this module, we’re going to talk about Carousels. Carousels are a type of “visual hook” you can use on LinkedIn. Before we dive in, let’s talk a
records.content:
Hey there!

In this module, we’re going to talk about Carousels.

Carousels are a type of “visual hook” you can use on LinkedIn.

Before we dive in, let’s talk about why visual hooks are so important.

The #1 reason a visual hook is important on LinkedIn is the same reason any hook is important—to stop the scroll. However, our brains prioritize images over text. Shapes, faces, contrast, and colors hit the attention system almost instantly, before language comprehension even kicks in. Pictures are simply faster for us to recognize.

Think about how you actually scroll through LinkedIn:

  • You scan for visuals first (Is this interesting, familiar, or different?)

  • You process words next (What does this mean, and do I care?)

Your eyes jump image to image, face to face, cue to cue. And somewhere in your rapid-fire scanning, something makes you pause.

That “something” is usually visual.

And that’s why it’s worth optimizing not just what you say but how it looks in the LinkedIn feed.

The Biggest Mistake LinkedIn Creators Make With Visual Hooks

This drives me crazy because it's so common and so easily avoidable.

Let’s say you write a post about "5 ways to double your sales with LinkedIn DMs" but your post image is a random motivational quote about persistence. Guess what happens? Your reader's eye catches the image first, processes "motivation," then reads your hook about "sales tactics," and their brain has to work to connect the dots. The little bit of extra cognitive load is enough to make them keep scrolling.

LinkedIn images are NOT decoration.

They are not there to make your post "look pretty" or to fill space. The purpose of the image is to get your reader’s attention! When you treat your visuals like decoration, you end up with generic stock photos of people shaking hands, or random lifestyle shots, or motivational graphics that could apply to any post about anything. This is a mistake.

A bad visual hook is worse than no visual hook at all. At least with no image, people might read your text. With a confusing or irrelevant image, you've created friction before they even start reading.

Every piece of your hook (visuals + text) needs to be congruent.

A selfie of you drinking coffee means nothing. But a selfie of you drinking coffee at 5 AM with your journal on your desk and the hook "A simple practice I do every morning: The 10-minute Tony Robbins "Priming" exercise.” earns the click.

With that in mind, let's dig into Carousels.

records.content:
To maximize the reach of your social post, you have to create something of “value.”

Now, every marketing influencer on your favorite social platform says, “Deliver value!!!!” but what does that actually mean?

A product has value when it hits on these 3 areas:

  1. When it delivers a tangible outcome for the reader (e.g. “How to make your first $1,000 as a course creator”).

  2. When it is a distillation and curation of knowledge they’d struggle to get anywhere else (e.g. when you’ve spent days, months, even years perfecting what’s inside).

  3. When it “feels” like a product because it has a name e.g. “The Digital Course Kit” sounds more like a complete product than “3 checklists”. This could be a Blueprint, an Ultimate Guide, a Dashboard, a Template Pack, etc.

So, how do you decide what kind of asset you want to create?

Step 1: Find Your Viral Drop Idea & Name Your Asset

Before I dive in here, it’s important that to note this is a two-way process.

Deciding on the title of the asset (and the outcome it delivers) will dictate the content you include. But to find the title for your asset, you need to examine your content to see what could be used in a asset. Then once you’ve refined the title again, you might want to include another set of content in the asset.

And so on and so on.

So let’s start by finding come content ideas.

There are two main buckets of content you can use to create your Viral Drop Asset:

  1. Repurposed content. This can found in two sub-buckets:

    a. Expand popular social posts and newsletters. You’re taking proven content, expanding it (using the 10 Magical Ways to expand any piece of writing), and packaging it up into a product.

    b. Repackaged newsletters. Take individual newsletters and package them up into an Ultimate Guide, A Blueprint, A Step-by-Step guide, etc that will drive an outcome for your reader.

    c. Content from your Low-Ticket Digital Product. Yes, you can give away snippets of your product for free. Pick a section that gives a particular outcome for a reader, but make sure to hold something back (like a templates, etc)—you don’t want to give away a full section of your product!

  2. New content. If you have a new framework or set of ideas that you think will be of benefit to your target readers/potential customers, then package them up into an asset. Sprinkle in proven content, too and you’ll bump up the value of the asset even more.

Once you have the content, it’s time to think of the Title and Subtitle of your Viral Drop asset.

These should hit on the 3 following areas:

  1. Has a clear name (e.g. “The Premium Ghostwriting Blueprint”).

  2. Calls out the intended audience (either directly or indirectly).

  3. Feels “tangible” by:

    1. Has a clear promise / outcome (e.g. “5 Steps to Become a Premium Ghostwriter”).

    2. Uses numbers and specifics that the reader can actually hold.

To get your creative juices flowing, here are some of the viral drop assets I’ve created over the last 2 years (that have attracted thousands of subscribers to our newsletters):

  • The Digital Course Kit: 3 Checklists To Package Your Expertise & Make Your First $1,000

  • The Yearly Review: Your In-Depth Reflection Guide for 2024.

  • The Ghostwriter Prompt Vault: 14 Easy-To-Use Prompts To Start And Scale Your 1-Person Ghostwriting Business

You’ve got the name and content.

Now it’s time to build the asset!

Step 2: Write and Build Your Viral Drop Asset

The key to writing and building a high-value Viral Drop Asset is to give it a clear structure and make it easy to navigate.

Remember, you’re giving something good in exchange for a few seconds of your reader’s time, so it’s important to make sure that a) the asset delivers on the promises you make and b) is easy to use.

You want your “free” stuff to feel as a good as your paid stuff:

So, one of the best ways to do this (and make it feel even more like a product), is to make it easy to navigate.

(I build all of my Viral Drop Assets in Notion, but you can use platforms like Skool or Circle if you’d like).

Let’s look at an example from a Viral Drop I performed: The Ultimate Guide To Organic Lead Gen As A Ghostwriter.

Notice how there is a clear roadmap laid out in this asset:

And then within each Step, it’s easy to move to the next stage:

Click here to see the complete Ultimate Guide To Organic Lead Gen As A Ghostwriter.

Alright, now you have your asset complete, it’s time to create the assets you’ll need to promote and distribute the asset.

Step 3: Create The Supporting Assets

There are 6 main assets you need to launch your Viral Drop:

  1. A Landing Page

  2. A Giveaway Post

  3. A Delivery Message

  4. A Follow-Up Post

  5. A Promo Email (Optional but recommended)

  6. An Asset Delivery Sequence

Writing Your Landing Page

This is where your reader will enter their email so they can a) get access to the asset and b) be added to your email list.

Here are some guidelines for writing a high-converting Viral Drop landing page:

  1. Be clear, not clever in all your copy (especially your headline)

  2. Use a Product image (again, this makes the asset feel more “real”).

  3. Include a “Here’s What You’ll Get Inside” section and list out all the benefits the asset delivers

To give you a template to follow, here’s one of our Viral Drop landing pages:

https://ghostwritingleads.com/

Pro Landing Page tips:

  1. Use a dedicated domain for your landing page (again, this makes it feel like a “product”). Use Namecheap.com to find a relevant domain.

  2. Or you can use your Email Service Provider to build a simple landing page like this one we did recently on Kit: https://pga.kit.com/prompt-library

Writing Your Giveaway Post

Your Viral Drop is attract new subscribers through one social post.

Remember, you’re not giving away the asset directly in the post. You will SEND the link to anyone who engages with your post.

This is very important (otherwise it won't go viral).

Let’s look at this example from our Premium Ghostwriting Blueprint Viral Drop:

https://x.com/Nicolascole77/status/1664247744054145026

Let's break down the template of this giveaway post:

  • [Outcome] “Looking to start making $5,000/mo as a Premium Ghostwriter? You should start by doing 2 things: first, speaking to the outcome your target reader/customer wants, and second, naming the target reader directly. So here, you wouldn't just say, “Looking to start making $5,000/mo?” Because that could apply to ANYONE. We want to clarify this outcome by saying who it's for, specifically. (”…as a Premium Ghostwriter.”)

  • [Obstacle] “I spent 100+ hours creating an email course to help you.” Every good story needs an obstacle—and your target reader/customer needs to know that blood, sweat, and tears went into making this! (Otherwise, they won't value it as highly.) This could be:

    • TIME: How long did it take you to make? (Hours, Days, Weeks, Months, Years, Decades?)

    • COST: How much money did you have to spend to put this together? Or to acquire the information you're about to share? ($100? $1,000? $10,000? $100,000? Etc.)

    • ACCESS: Who did you have to talk to in order to create this? Who do you have access to, who has valuable information, that your target reader/customer would also want access to? (A world-class specialist? A famous person? A billionaire? Etc.)

  • [Benefits]: “Craft an irresistible offer. Charge premium prices. Land your first 5k client.” These are the benefits the target reader/customer will receive IF they “pay” with their attention. This is very, very important. In order for the reader/customer to know why they should give you their attention, they need to know what BENEFITS they are going to receive. And remember: tangible benefits (”Land your first 5k client”) are always better than intangible benefits (”Make more money!”). Be as specific as possible here (and refer back to the Title/Subtitle of your asset).

  • [CTA] “Want access?” Notice how this 1 simple sentence is the virtual equivalent of a red velvet rope. It says to readers/customers, “Not everyone can have this.” And what happens when you say, “Not everyone can have this?” EVERYONE WANTS IT!

  • [Directions] “Like, Retweet, and Comment “{emoji}” and I'll send it for FREE!” These are the tactical instructions you need to give readers/customers, telling them exactly what the trade is: “Do X and I'll give you Y.” From what we've found, at a minimum you should ask for a Like + Comment. And we recommend making the Comment something specific (like an emoji, or a specific phrase like “I want to ghostwrite!” in this example). Retweets and Shares are optional.

Using the above, this will become your Viral Drop Giveaway Post Template!

But just to really drive the point home, here it is in template form:

Want to {Desirable Outcome} as a {Target Reader/Customer}?

I spent {COST} creating {ASSET} to help you:

• {Benefit #1}
• {Benefit #2}
• {Benefit #3}

Want access?

Like & reply "{emoji}" and I'll send it for FREE!

And to show you how these kind of posts work on LinkedIn, here’s a recent one Dickie ran on LinkedIn:

https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dickiebush_last-month-i-spent-8-hours-creating-17-activity-7308455406542962691-XhtO/

Here’s the LinkedIn post in template form:

Last month, I spent {X} hours creating {Asset} to help you:

• {Tangible Outcome 1}
• {Tangible Outcome 2}
• {Tangible Outcome 3}

And tons more.

In other words:

All you need to {Big Tangible Outcome}.

Now, full transparency: 

{1-2 Sentences About How You Weren't Going To Share This — give a real reason!}

So, now I'm giving you the chance to get my {ASSET NAME} for FREE.

Want access?

✅ Like this post
✅ Comment “{WORD}”
✅ And send me a connection request if you haven’t yet (so I can DM you)

I’ll send it over via DMs ASAP.

Writing Your Delivery Message

This is the message that will get sent to the reader when they engage with the post.

(Note: how this is sent will vary from platform to platform—see the sections dedicated to LinkedIn and Twitter below).

Hey there!

So excited to hear you're looking to {achieve outcome your asset helps people unlock}!

Here's the link to download my {Asset Name}:

{Asset landing page link}

I've spent weeks working on this resource—and I honestly think you're going to find it super valuable.

Let me know if you have any questions as you go through it and enjoy!

{Link To Landing Page}

-{your name}

Writing Your Follow Up Post

This is the copy you use in a reply to the original Viral Drop Giveaway you use after the post has gone viral.

Alright, my DMs are officially broken 😅

You can download {Asset} for free below.

This is packed with all {Features} to {Outcome}.

Hope you enjoy!

{Link To Landing Page}

Writing Your Promo Email

This is an optional asset, but I highly recommend it.

This is an email to your existing newsletter subscribers to tell them about your asset and how to get access to it.

I send this email for 2 reasons:

  1. This drives more engagement to your social post, causing it go viral faster.

  2. This delivers a valuable asset to your existing subscribers (and gives them another reason to stay subscribed to your list… and become a customer of your digital product!).

Here’s a template:

Subject line: Want {Outcome Your Asset Delivers}?

Preview text: {Name Of Asset}

Copy:

Hey!

Are you looking to {Specific Outcome Your Asset Delivers}?

If so, you're in luck!

I spent the last {Month/Weeks/Days} creating {Asset Name} to help you:

  • {Benefit 1}

  • {Benefit 2}

  • {Benefit 3}

And tons more!

These are the exact frameworks I have used to {Outcome}.

And now, I’m giving them away for FREE!

To get early access, follow me, like the post below, and then reply “{Emoji}”—I'll send you a copy. {Link To Landing Page}

Let me know how you find it!

—Your Name
