Ahoy!

It’s Cole here today.

Welcome to Day 4 of Ship 30 for 30 Onboarding!

In this module, I’m going to help you:

  • Create a Typeshare account (and claim your free 30-day trial)

  • Set up your Digital Brain inside Typeshare

  • And understand how to publish your writing from Typeshare

Don’t skip this Day!

Setting up your Digital Brain and using it during the cohort is how you get the most out of Ship 30 for 30.

Ready?

Let’s go!

What Is a “Digital Brain”?

Before we dive in, I want to give you a quick crash course on what a Digital Brain is and why it matters more than ever that you build one.

A Digital Brain is, at its core, a “library of you.”

More specifically, it's the cumulative collection of everything you've written or said out loud about how you became yourself:

  • Your stories

  • Your opinions

  • Your lessons learned

  • The mistakes you’ve made

It lives on the Internet, where anyone can access it, at any time, from anywhere in the world, without needing your direct involvement.

Before the digital age, your ideas tended to only live in one place: inside your skull. If you wanted to share a story, you had to tell it in person. One story, one person, one coffee meeting. Then the next week, the same story, a different person, another coffee meeting. This is the unscalable real world, and it has a ceiling.

(After all, there are only so many coffees you can drink, right?!)

A Digital Brain is how you break through that ceiling.

You write the story once, and share it with infinite people across infinite "digital coffee meetings." It isn't constrained by geography, time, or the laws of physics. It’s consumed by people while you sleep.

(Which is one of the highest forms of leverage a human being can build.)

Everything you write online belongs in your Digital Brain.

But not everything in your Digital Brain has the same “value.”

Look at these generally accepted pieces of advice:

  • "Count your calories to lose weight"

  • "The key to marketing is knowing your customer"

  • "Prioritize going to the gym to improve your health"

That's Commodity Content, and a Digital Brain filled with Commodity Content is indistinguishable from everyone else's.

What makes your Digital Brain yours are the non-commodity variables:

  • Life Facts: Where you grew up, what you studied, how many siblings you have.

  • Opinions: Which Commodity Ideas you choose to stand behind, and which ones you'd argue against.

  • Insights: The examples and context that give conventional wisdom its color.

  • Stories: What happened, where you were, who you were with, and what you hoped would happen instead.

  • Lessons: What you learned and carried into the next chapter of your life.

No technology on earth has access to these variables unless you document them.

Which is why the Digital Brain matters more now than ever.

AI is a Commodity Content Machine.

It knows everything about everything but nothing about you.

When the average person asks AI to write a newsletter and it hands back something that "doesn't sound like them," that isn't a failure of the machine. It's a failure of the input. They never built the library for it to pull from.

Your Digital Brain is that library. Over time it becomes your Personal Language Model, the one data set AI companies don't have and can't easily create.

Those who build one will get the most leverage out of these new tools. Those who don't will produce AI Slop and sound like everyone else.

Which leads us to today’s first action:

You’re going to add the 3 topics you picked yesterday to your Digital Brain, which we’re going to build together in Typeshare.

These are the 3 topics you’ll write about during the Ship 30 for 30 cohort (and don’t worry, you can switch these at any point!).

Sure, there will be some Commodity Content in there. But we’re also going to help you add some Personality Content with it—and that all began when you picked the topics using the 2-Year Test. Why? Because you are qualified to talk about those topics AND you have stories, lessons learned, and insights, which will form the basis of your Personality Content.

So, let’s get started with building your Digital Brain inside Typeshare.

(By the way, if you want a deeper dive into Commodity Content, Personality Content, Digital Brains, and the right way to write with AI… then check out this Article I wrote on X.)

Build Your Digital Brain Inside Typeshare

If you’re not familiar, Typeshare is the software platform we’ve created to help Digital Writers scale themselves online in the age of AI.

  • It’s a publishing platform

  • It’s the first place on the internet where you can build your Digital Brain

  • It’s a tool that you can use to repurpose and remix ideas from your Digital Brain, publishing to multiple platforms

You can use it to write & publish your posts, track your publishing streak, write with our proven digital writing templates, use & connect digital writing agents, and more.

Let’s get you set up.

Step 1: Accept your Typeshare free trial & create your account

As part of Ship 30 for 30, you get a free, 30-day trial of the tool (well, we give you about 35 days so you’re covered during Onboarding, too!).

Whether you have an existing Typeshare account or not, click the following link to claim your free trial:

Click here to claim your free 30-day trial of Typeshare.

Once you’ve done that, you’ll be asked to log in.

(Highly recommend logging in with either X or LinkedIn if one of them is your primary platform!)

You’ll then be asked to set up your profile.

Your username is specific to your Typeshare account (and we recommend keeping it the same as your LinkedIn/X handle if you can—it just makes life easier, doesn’t it?).

Next, there will be some screens that explain everything you get inside Typeshare and how the Ship 30 for 30 free trial works.

(Remember, this is one of the bonuses you got by enrolling in Ship 30 for 30!)

You will be asked to add your payment details (but don’t worry, we’ll notify you before we renew your subscription—you’ll have the opportunity to cancel if you decide not to stay with us inside Typeshare).

You will then receive a screen like this (the date will vary depending on when you set up your Typeshare account):

Step 2: Connect your platforms

On the Typeshare home screen, you’ll be presented with the Typeshare-specific Onboarding flow.

It will look a bit like this:

For the Ship 30 Onboarding, we’re going to run through the first 3 steps:

  • Connect your platforms

  • Build your Digital Brain

  • Publish your first post

All so you’re ready to use Typeshare during this cohort.

We highly recommend you use Typeshare because it a) makes writing and publishing to your chosen (and other!) platforms easy, and b) helps you get the most out of your Digital Brain.

Note: We’ll be looking at the agent part during the Ship 30 cohort, so keep your eyes peeled for that!

OK, so let’s do the first step:

Connect your platforms

Select all the platforms you are going to use in this cohort of Ship 30 (we recommend connecting your X account, LinkedIn account, and Substack account).

Note: Highly recommend using Chrome to connect all your platforms as you will need to install the Typeshare Connector to make the link between Typeshare and Substack. Once you’re connected, you can use any browser to access Typeshare.

Here are some specific actions you will need to take for each platform:

  • X. Authorize Typeshare to connect to your account (if you’re doing this for the first time).

  • LinkedIn. Add in your LinkedIn profile URL. You can find the URL by following the on-screen instructions (and clicking the “Open my LinkedIn profile” button as shown below). Then just copy the URL of your LinkedIn profile and paste it into Typeshare.


  • Substack. Once you select Substack, you’ll be asked to add the Typeshare Connector to Chrome. Follow the on-screen instructions to do this. Once you’ve added the Connector, it will automatically find your Substack account if you’re already logged in on your account in Chrome.

Now, when you connect your X and LinkedIn accounts, your Digital Brain will begin building using what you’ve already posted (pretty cool, right?!).

Don’t worry—you can add new topics to your Digital Brain if you’re writing about fresh topics during Ship 30 for 30.

So let’s do that now!

Step 3: Build your Digital Brain

First, click “Next” below to move on to the Digital Brain step.

It will then open the second step:

As you can see, it has already synced my existing content to my Digital Brain.

But let’s say you want to add another topic to your Digital Brain (like the topics you chose yesterday).

All you need to do is click the “Add a topic” button as shown above.

This will take you to your Digital Brain where you can add a topic:

Add your chosen topic and then use the top-right button to add your remaining topics (if they weren’t picked up in the import from your social accounts):

Depending on your existing content and what topics you add, you should eventually have a Digital Brain that looks a bit like this:

Now, every time you post from Typeshare (or post content to your connected platforms), your Digital Brain will grow—the social posts will automatically be assigned to a topic or, if the topic doesn’t already exist in your Digital Brain, it will be added.

Step 4: Post to your Primary Platform using Typeshare

We’re almost done.

But first, we just want to say…

There’s nothing quite like public accountability!

So, a fun “challenge” we give Shippers is to make a post committing to writing & publishing for the next 30 days on X/LinkedIn/Substack—and letting people know what, specifically, you plan on writing about.

We call this the “3 Topics, 30 Days” Post.

To help you do this, we’re going to create your “3 Topics, 30 Days” Post and publish it from Typeshare to your primary platform!

Think of this as your practice rep of publishing from Typeshare to help you get used to the platform before we start shipping.

To do this, I’m going to show you:

  • How to write a post on Typeshare

  • How to schedule / publish a post

  • How to create your Typeshare profile (so people can follow your Ship 30 journey!)

Ready?

Let’s go!

To create a new post, click the “Write” button found in the top-left menu:

From here, you can choose a post format.

Because this is a short post, we’ll pick Short Form. But don’t worry—we’ll be talking about the other formats during Ship 30 for 30.

If LinkedIn is your primary platform, then feel free to use the LinkedIn Post option.

To write your post, you can use this template (which you can copy and paste into the writing editor inside Typeshare):

Interested in {Topic 1}, {Topic 2}, or {Topic 3}? 

Over the next 30 days, I'll be writing every day about these topics. 

Follow along on Typeshare: {Your Typeshare Profile URL}

Now, I bet you’re wondering:

“Cole… where do I find my Typeshare Profile URL?!”

First, let me explain what your Typeshare profile is.

Your Typeshare profile is a place where all your social posts (from multiple platforms) will appear in a single feed:

And you can follow other Typeshare profiles, too:

To access your Profile, go to the “Profile” section in the top-left menu:


To edit it, click “Edit Profile”:

Here you can update different fields:

  • Your Name as it appears on Typeshare

  • Your Username as used by your profile URL. Changing this changes your profile URL, so only do this if you really want to!

  • Your Bio which you can use to tell your Typeshare followers a bit about yourself

And you can find your Typeshare Profile URL here (on the Profile page):


Copy and paste this URL and add it to your draft.

Here’s my post draft:

Then, when you’re ready to publish, you can control which platforms you’re publishing to by selecting them using the top Publish Icons.

To do this, click the 3 little dots above the draft:

Then toggle platforms on or off:

Once you’ve done that, use the top-right menu to either add the post to your queue, schedule it for later, or post now (highly recommend you do this!):

When you select Post Now, you will get a screen a bit like this. Click “Post Now”:

Boom, now go to your primary platform and find your nicely published post!

Or you can choose to schedule a post like this using the “Schedule later” option:

Accessing AI Cole inside Typeshare

One final thing before we move to today's Assignment.

You can access our custom-made AI model, "AI Cole," inside Typeshare.

This is a custom AI model trained on nearly everything Cole has ever said on:

  • Building digital products

  • Digital Writing & ghostwriting

  • Starting a paid or free newsletter

  • Monetizing your writing on the internet

  • Marketing & Category Creation frameworks

And tons more.

It's been trained on over 4,000,000 words and 1,000+ hours of video footage.

This custom AI model is like having Cole in your back pocket—which means you can get answers to all of your digital writing-related questions instantly, 24/7.

To access it, simply follow these steps:

Step 1: In the left-hand Typeshare panel, click the "+" icon by "Your Agents" and click "Hire Agent":

Step 2: Click on AI Cole


Step 3: Start chatting with AI Cole

AI Cole will now be available inside the "Your Agents" panel inside Typeshare:


And to help you get started, we've put together 20 prompts you can use with AI Cole during Ship 30 for 30.

Click here to access the AI Cole Prompt Vault.

Day 4 Assignment - Share Your “3 Topics, 30 Days” Post

OK, one final step on today’s Onboarding:

In the comments of the Skool post below, drop a link to the social post (which you will have just published from Typeshare!) where you announced you’ll be writing about 3 topics over the next 30 days.

records.content:
The Anatomy of an Atomic Essay

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 1 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

The theme for this first week is: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

To get your ship sailing in the right direction from the very beginning, we need to introduce you to a new way of thinking. A “digital” way of thinking. Which means the very first thing we need to do is make sure you aren’t holding onto an “old” way of thinking about writing.

Because this is how “most people” think about being a writer:

  • Step 1: Escape to a cabin in the woods.

  • Step 2: Put on a chapeau. Sit by the window. Light your corn cob pipe.

  • Step 3: Wait for inspiration to strike.

  • Step 4: Wait some more (”Inspiration??? Where are you???”).

  • Step 5: Emerge from the woods 7 years later (disheveled—the mark of a “true writer”).

  • Step 6: The morning you are about to run out of money for food, wake up to a letter from a major publisher. “You are the next greatest novelist of our generation. We would love to publish your manuscript.”

  • Step 7: Ride off into the sunset as a famous writer, the applause of one hundred million raving readers in your wake.

We’re not joking.

This is how “most people” think the journey of a writer is supposed to go.

The Mindset Of A Digital Writer

Instead, we want to introduce you to a NEW way of thinking about writing.

And it goes like this:

  • Step 1: Don’t write “for” an audience. Write “WITH” your audience by practicing in public.

  • Step 2: Build your Daily Writing Habit and use quantity as a forcing function for quality.

  • Step 3: Start small. Ship lots of tiny ideas and see “what works.”

  • Step 4: Leverage rapid-fire feedback loops from social platforms. Learn as you go.

  • Step 5: Double-down “what’s working” and expand proven content for your readers.

  • Step 6: Build your timeless library of content (and increase your efficiency over time).

  • Step 7: Turn proven short-form content into longer and longer forms of content.

This is how you become an endless idea generation machine, mitigate your risk of over-investing in the wrong idea (writing something you aren’t sure readers actually care about), and build your audience as you explore and refine your writing style & niche.

This is the path of becoming a prolific Digital Writer.

The Anatomy Of An Atomic Essay

“But where do I start????”

Great question!

Your digital writing journey is going to begin by writing what we like to call Atomic Essays (short pieces of content 300 words or less).

For 3 reasons:

  1. It’s Doable: Not everyone can write an entire book Day 1 of their writing journey. But everyone can write an Atomic Essay.

  2. It’s Still Substantial: Atomic Essays are the perfect length where you still have enough room to “flush an idea out.”

  3. It’s The Best Way To Learn The Fundamentals: But most importantly, an Atomic Essay has all the pieces of ANY type of writing on the Internet.

If you can write Atomic Essays, you can write anything.

And don’t worry, over the next 30 days, not only are you going to become an Atomic Essay pro, but you’re also going to learn all the different mechanisms that make for great writing—which you can apply to ANYTHING you want to write.

Here is the anatomy of an Atomic Essay:

Questions

Now, here are some questions we always get Day 1 from new Shippers:

  • “But what if I don’t know what to write about?” Don’t worry! We’ve got you covered. See below for your Day 1 template.

  • “But what if that’s not what I want to write about for Day 1?” No problem! You’re welcome to write about whatever you’d like—just remember: imperfect and published is better than “perfect” but unpublished. So don’t sit there and talk yourself out of writing just because you “can’t think of the perfect topic.”

  • “But what if I write and publish something I don’t absolutely love. Isn’t that just wasted time?” No, it’s not. You’re practicing. You’re improving. That’s the whole point. And so if you keep sitting there “waiting” until you’re “ready,” guess what? You’re never going to be ready!

  • “But what if I don’t want to write Atomic Essays?” That’s fine too. However, usually the same people who say they don’t want to write Atomic Essays are the ones trying to skip to “the end” and just write something viral as quickly as possible. And honestly, that “shortcut” just ends up being a longer road in disguise. It’s worth taking this first week to learn how to write Atomic Essays because it will give you the foundation to write everything else.

  • “But if everyone is using this same Day 1 template, isn’t everyone going to sound the same?” Nope. Have you ever decorated Christmas cookies? Think of templates as the little shapes that cut everyone’s cookies the same way—but it’s up to you how you want to decorate yours. And if you want to see the diversity of writing in Ship 30, even just on Day 1, click here to look through thousands of people’s Day 1 posts.

No getting in your own way!

Just ship it!

Assignment

So, nothing to it but to do it.

Obviously, over the next 30 days you’re welcome to write about any topic, any way you’d like.

However, if you’d like to stay on track and take things step-by-step the way we have organized Ship 30 for 30, we encourage you to use each assignment as a forcing function to practice all the different frameworks & techniques we cover.

Your Day 1 Assignment is to use the Day 1 template from your 30 Days of Shipping template pack and share (in public) what you plan to write about over the next 30 days!

Your post should look something like this:

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

records.content:
Want to see some of the principles we’ve covered so far in action?

You got it!

We’ve compiled 20 headlines from articles and blog posts we found on the Internet—and we’ve rewritten them (using the same principles we’ve shared with you over the past 2 lessons), so you can actually see the difference between a bad headline and a GREAT one.

Enjoy!

20 Examples Of Headline Rewrites To Show You How To Hook Readers

In order to write compelling headlines, we encourage you to use this simple checklist:

  • Be CLEAR, not Clever

  • Specify the WHO

  • Specify the WHAT

  • Specify the WHY

  • Twist The Knife

If you follow this checklist, you will write headlines your readers can't help but want to click on (seriously).

Not because you "tricked" them, but because you successfully spoke DIRECTLY to their wants, needs, hopes, dreams, and desires.

There really isn't any secret here.

In fact, I'd argue the more writers try to "trick" readers by using phrases like YOU'LL NEVER BELIEVE WHAT HAPPENS NEXT! the more they mislead their own thinking—and forget the true goal here. You have one job, and that job is to tell the reader exactly what they're going to get in return if they read your content.

That's it.

No magic trick. No "use this word and you'll tap into the reader's subconscious" dark arts. Just complete and total clarity, with a healthy serving of specificity.

Remember: specificity is the secret.

So, to give you a sense of all the different ways you can improve weak, unclear, or just downright "clever" headlines, here are 20 rewrite examples.

(All of the examples included here are real headlines found on the Internet, with rewrites showing how to make them better.)

Betting Big on Retail, Live TV, and (maybe) the Metaverse

Problem: Betting Big... but why? What's the outcome? What happens IF you bet big on retail, Live TV, and the Metaverse?Rewrite: If You Believe In The Metaverse, Add These 7 Stocks To Your Portfolio ASAP

2. Things Men Secretly Do

Problem: OK, that's great men "secretly do" these things. Who cares? What HAPPENS when men secretly do these things?Rewrite: Things Men Secretly Do That Cost Them Their Marriage

3. Why I Switched to Writing on Substack

Problem: Who is "I?" Are you Kim Kardashian? Does the entire world know who you are? Probably not. You need to tell the reader what makes you a credible source of information on this topic.Rewrite: I Have Been Writing On Medium For 8 Years. Here's Why I Made The Switch To Substack

4. 4 Things You Should Feel Zero Shame For

Problem: "Things" is broad. Too easy for someone to ignore. There is an opportunity here to lean into a specific "type of thing" people feel shame for, and then tell them why they shouldn't feel shame for doing it.Rewrite: 4 Nighttime Habits You Should Feel Zero Shame For (Like Brushing Your Teeth In The Shower)

5. Screw Marketing. Choose Art. It’s the Safer Long-term Play.

Problem: When you read this headline, you can sort of hear the default response in your head being "OK." There's no curiosity gap, and nothing urging you to "find out more."Rewrite: Why Trading Your Artistic Passion For A Career In Marketing Will Give You Depression

6. Ray Dalio’s Business Advice Is Invaluable — Here’s How to Make the Most of It

Problem: Which advice? All of his advice? Are there certain specific things he has said that are more valuable than all the other things he has said?Rewrite: Ray Dalio Has A Net Worth Of $20 Billion. But These 7 Pieces Of Business Advice From His Book Are Priceless

7. The Wisdom of Thinking for Yourself In An Age of Experts

Problem: Lots of fancy words but do you know what this is going to be about? Do you know what you're going to walk away with after you read this? Nope. We need to double-down on something and get SPECIFIC.Rewrite: In A World Of Gurus And Overnight Experts, Here's An Independent Thinker's Guide To Stress-Test Your Own Beliefs And Think For Yourself

8. The Hidden Advantages of Working for Yourself by Making Money Online

Problem: As a rule of thumb, if your headline is hinting at it being a "list," just make it a list. It's easier for readers to wrap their heads around.Rewrite: 8 Hidden Advantages Of Working For Yourself, From Home, Making Money Online

9. Don’t bother raising a Series A if you don’t crush these 3 metrics

Problem: This is a pretty good headline, but it can be taken to the next level by framing this less as a statement and more as a question (and hinting at how the reader can answer that question by reading).Rewrite: Think You're Ready To Raise Your Series A? Put These 3 Metrics In Your Pitch Deck And Investors Will Come Running (If They're Up To Par)

10. Eight Uncomfortable Truths About Life That Will Wake You Up

Problem: First of all, if you're going to put a number in the headline, always use the number (8) instead of spelling it out. It's easier for the reader's eye to grab. Second, huge opportunity to "twist the knife" here. What does it mean to "Wake Up?" We need to get specific!Rewrite: 8 Uncomfortable Truths About Life That Will Put Things In Perspective And Guarantee You Wake Up Tomorrow Excited To Be Alive

11. Lovely Words That Shaped My Life

Problem: "Lovely Words" is vague. Huge opportunity to get more specific here. Bonus points if we can twist the knife at the end.Rewrite: 15 Quotes From American Literature That Shaped My Life (And Taught Me How To Be A Man)

12. You’re Never Going to Be Happy Being Anyone Other Than Yourself

Problem: It's easy to read this headline and think, "OK," and then move on. We need to frame this in a way where the reader feels motivated to click and keep reading.Rewrite: An Imposter Syndrome Sufferer's Guide To Loving Yourself For Exactly Who You Are

13. Retire Happy With This Much Money

Problem: According to who? Who says that's the number?Rewrite: Harvard Business Review Interviewed 27 Millionaires. Here's How Much They Said You Need To Have Saved To Retire Happy (On Average)

14. Shadow Work

Problem: This is a classic "clever, not CLEAR" headline. We need to tell the reader exactly WHAT this is about, WHO this is for, and WHY they should read it.Rewrite: A Beginner's Guide To Shadow Work: Overcoming Fears, Working Through Insecurities, And Starting To Live As Your True Self

15. If You Fit In, You’re Replaceable

Problem: "OK, but what can I do about it?" We need to answer this question for the reader.Rewrite: If You Fit In, You're Replaceable: 8 Small But Powerful Ways To Stand Out And Go Your Own Way In Life

16. Why Extreme Wellness Is So Popular

Problem: If "Extreme Wellness" is becoming a new term in the zeitgeist, then this headline would benefit from clarifying what it means for the reader.Rewrite: Extreme Wellness: How The Healthy-Eating Trend Turned Into A Global Obsession With Calorie Counting, Caffeine Addiction, And Creepy Wearable Devices

17. You Can’t Fix Education

Problem: If you're going to be a negative Nancy, then go all the way and don't hold back! Huge opportunity to twist the knife here and lean all the way into the opinion.Rewrite: Why The Legacy Education Systems Is Broken, Teachers Are Going To Quit, And The Next Generation Of Children Is Screwed

18. Anti-Racism Is Becoming Troublingly Racist

Problem: This headline teases the conflict, but we can lean into it and really drive the point home. Remember: the reader needs a reason to click and keep reading.Rewrite: The ****Anti-Racism Movement Is Becoming Troublingly Racist: 9 TikTok Videos That Meant To Do Good But Ended Up Being Toxic

19. I Lived Through Collapse. America Is Already There.

Problem: "I lived through collapse" is a decent credibility statement, but which collapse? Let's get specific! We also need to tell the reader what they're going to get if they read this.Rewrite: I Lost Everything In The Mortgage Crisis In 2008. Here's Why America's Economic Position Today Is Worrisome—And I'm Afraid The Next Crisis Will Be Even Worse

20. Unreal Estate

Problem: Classic "clever, not CLEAR."Rewrite: How NFTs And Blockchain Technology Are Going To Create A $20 Trillion Digital Real Estate Market (Out Of Thin Air)

records.content:
Irresistible Headlines, Part III

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 10 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the the theme for this second week is: Headlines & Hooks.

And today, we’re going to build on what we’ve covered the past two days, and add one more variable into your irresistible headlines…

How To Write Irresistible Headlines, Part III: Topic + Audience + Outcome

It’s one thing to say, “Here’s what this piece is about…”.

It’s another to say, “Here’s what this piece is about, and who it’s for specifically…”.

But your headlines will really kick into gear when you clearly communicate to the reader, “Here’s what this piece is about, who it’s for specifically, and what you can expert to get in exchange for reading and giving me your attention.”

Because that’s really what’s happening.

You aren’t just asking the reader to “read.”

You’re asking them to give you 30 seconds or 2 minutes of their LIFE (which they will never, ever get back).

Which means your headline needs to make the trade explicit:

  • They give you their attention, time, energy, mental focus.

  • You give them… what?

Step 3: Add a WHY

The WHY in your headline is your opportunity to “sell” the reader on why they should read your writing over every other piece of content competing for their attention on the Internet:

  • IF the reader reads this, what do they get in return?

  • How is their life different in some meaningful way?

  • What will they learn as a result?

So, here are the same examples from yesterday, adding a WHY (outcome) to each topic:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year Olds To Start Generating $1,000 Per Month In Passive Rental Income Before You Graduate College **(”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips for teenagers, specifically to help generate $1,000 per month in passive rental income before graduating college.”

  • Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners That Will Help You ‘Speak Blockchain’ Fluently (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto, so that I can ‘speak blockchain’ fluently.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment: If You Want To Save The Rainforest, Gen-Zers This Is For You (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment, specifically for Gen-Zers who want to save the rainforest.”)

Notice how the clearer and clearer the headline gets the more of these pieces we add in.

And how much more powerful the headline gets when you name the outcome explicitly!

Questions

Now, here are some of the questions we always get asked when we start talking about “outcomes” in writing (particularly headlines):

  • “What if the reader wants more than one outcome? If I list multiple outcomes, won’t my headline be too long?” Remember, word count is a horrible measure of value. Just because a headline is short doesn’t make it good, and just because a headline is long doesn’t make it bad. What matters is whether or not you are speaking to the reader’s wants, needs, questions, etc. So yes, you can speak to multiple outcomes—just make sure you keep your promise and deliver!

  • “If I’m promising some huge outcome, isn’t that clickbait?” No. It’s only clickbait if you don’t keep your promise. For example, “How To Make $1,000,000 In 30 Days As A Broke Single Mother With No Job.” That’s a pretty audacious promise. And you don’t have control over whether the reader actually uses any of the information you share with them (you don’t have control over the outcome in their life). However, if that’s the promise you’re going to make in the headline, you better deliver in the content and give the reader exactly what they need to know in order to intelligently strive for that outcome. (It’s clickbait if you make that promise in the headline and then the content inside is: “You have to show up. You have to do it. And you have to work hard.”)

  • “Does the outcome always have to be positive?” No! If your headline is talking about mistakes, for example, then the outcomes would be negative. (Mistakes you made that led to XYZ negative outcomes.)

Assignment

Congratulations!

You’re now officially a headline writing pro!

Today’s Day 10 Assignment is to add in this third piece (outcome) to make your headlines even more irresistible! So, for today’s Atomic Essay, pick a specific topic + explicit audience + outcome. (And if it’s a long headline, don’t worry about it! All that matters is that it’s CLEAR to your target reader.)

Write your Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

records.content:
Twist The Knife

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 11 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the the theme for this second week is: Headlines & Hooks.

And today, we’re going to give you the secret to writing headlines that are IMPOSSIBLE to ignore.

It’s an age-old copywriting technique called:

Twist The Knife

Twist The Knife is just a fancy way of saying: “more.”

  • More problems

  • More benefits

  • More outcomes

Let’s use this headline as an example:

  • (V1) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn”

Not bad!

But watch how much more compelling the headline gets the more we “twist the knife”:

  • (V2) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn And Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List”

  • (V3) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn, Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List, And Start Selling Digital Products”

Notice how the more outcomes you list (and the more you “Twist The Knife”), it really doesn’t matter that your headline is getting longer and longer. As long as these benefits and outcomes speak directly to the wants and needs of your target reader, they’ll keep reading—because you’re talking about them!

Here are a couple more examples, just to give you more pattern recognition:

Questions

Now, whenever we introduce writers to the “Twist The Knife” technique, these are some of the most common questions we get asked:

  • “I shouldn’t have to sell readers on my writing. Isn’t this the definition of clickbait?” NO! Why do you think you give your attention to the things you do? Do you think it’s random? Do you think it just “happens?” Of course not. We all give our attention to things that SPEAK to us—which means if you are not SPEAKING DIRECTLY to your target reader’s wants, needs, hopes, dreams, and aspirations in the headline, how are they supposed to know it’s for them? How are they supposed to know what they should expect to get in return for reading? It IS your job to sell readers on your ideas, and clearly communicate to them how you plan on making their life better.

  • “If I Twist The Knife, my headline is going to get too long.” There’s no such thing as headlines that are ‘too long,’ only headlines that are unclear. Don’t focus on word count. Focus on clearly communicating to the reader: “Here’s what this piece is about. Here’s who it’s for. Here’s what outcome I’m going to help you unlock. And here’s more, and more, and more that I know you care about.”

Assignment

Now you’re a REAL Headline Pro!

Your Day 11 Assignment is to add this fourth bonus component to today’s Atomic Essay headline. So again, here are the pieces:

  • Specific Topic

  • Explicit Audience

  • Outcome

  • Twist The Knife (more outcomes!)

This is how you really start pushing the effectiveness of the headlines you write.

So, crank up the volume, write your Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

records.content:
5 Proven Headline Styles

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 12 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the the theme for this second week is: Headlines & Hooks.

And now that you know how to write Irresistible Headlines, it’s time to combine your headline writing skills with proven headline formats.

Let’s dive in!

The 5 Proven Headline Formats

Almost every headline on the Internet can be reverse-engineered into 1 of these 5 categories:

  • The List

  • The Story

  • The Opinion

  • The Question

  • The Framework

Let’s go through each one.

Headline Style #1: The List

Lists are incredible effective (and efficient) ways of organizing lots of information into a small amount of space. (Just look at what you’re reading—this is a list!)

Things you can “list” are:

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Tips

  • Tricks

  • Techniques

  • Strategies

  • Embarrassing Moments

  • Heartwarming Memories

  • Cooking Recipes

  • Podcast Episodes

Headline Style #2: The Story

The mistake writers make when telling a story is they only put the first half in the headline.

Example: “That Time I Was In 7th Grade”

But in order for the reader to care about your story, you also need to hint at the second half (the “end”) of the story in the headline.

What happens? Where is this story going?

If you don’t hint at this for the reader, that’s sort of like asking them to get on an airplane without knowing the destination.

Rewrite Example: “That Time I Was In 7th Grade—And My Best Friend Let Me Down”

Now the reader can decide whether this story is the sort of adventure they’re looking for (and has a reason to click).

The most compelling stories:

  • Started with $0 -> Achieved $X

  • Experienced X -> Mistakes Made

  • Overcame X -> Lessons Learned

  • Weird Stat/Insight -> Here’s How It Happened

  • Conflict -> Unexpected Resolution

Headline Style #3: The Opinion

Opinions are the most popular form of content on the Internet—because anyone can share their opinion.

However, in order for your opinion to “hold weight,” it’s important to tell the reader WHY they should listen to you. Are you speaking from personal experience? Or are you borrowing someone else’s credibility to make your point? (Going back to our Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility framework.)

In addition, having the same opinion as everyone else isn’t interesting. In order for your opinion to stand out, it needs to go against conventional wisdom in some way.

The most compelling opinions:

  • Most People Think X -> I Don’t

  • Everyone Says X -> I Say The Opposite

  • Conventional Wisdom Says -> Here’s Why That’s Wrong

  • When People Are First Starting Out They All Do X -> Do This Instead

  • X Industry -> Here’s What’s Going To Happen Next

Headline Style #4: The Question

A very effective way of tapping into the reader’s subconscious is by putting the question that target reader is already asking themselves in the headline.

  • “Wonder What It’s Like To Make $1 Million Per Year?”

  • “Looking For The Cheapest Places To Live In America?”

  • “Want To Know The Secret To Staying Happily Married?”

The most compelling question headlines:

  • What’s The Answer To X? / Here You Go

  • “How Does This Happen?” / Here’s How

  • Want To Learn X? / Read This

  • Do People Understand X? / Turns Out No

Headline Style #5: The Framework

A framework is just a slowed-down, step-by-step explanation for how you (or someone credible) does something.

Take anything in your life, audit it, break it down into steps, and then give that “thing” a name—and voila! You’ve just invented a framework.

The most compelling frameworks:

  • How To Do X / Without Compromising Y

  • How To Unlock BIG Reward / For Small Effort

  • How To Solve BIG Problem / Easy Templates

Questions

Now, whenever we introduce writers to these 5 proven styles, these are the questions we get asked:

  • “But if everyone uses these same styles, how are my headlines supposed to stand out?” Most houses are built the same: couple bedrooms, couple bathrooms, a garage, a backyard, etc. Does every house look the same? Not even close. These “styles” are just different canvases for you to play on—and you make yours different with your stories, insights, perspectives, etc.

  • “What if I don’t want to write headlines in any of these styles?” Nobody is forcing you! You’re more than welcome to write however you would like to write. Our job, however, is to pass along all the knowledge we’ve acquired over the past 10+ years writing on the Internet, writing over 5,000 articles, 20,000 tweets & threads, thousands of newsletters, etc. And we’re telling you, there’s a reason these 5 styles are “proven.” (Because readers want to read them!)

Assignment

Congratulations! You now know the 5 most effective headline styles on the Internet.

So, your Day 12 Assignment is to take 1 topic and generate 5 headlines—1 for each style. This will show you how much MORE you can write about that topic, and give you a handful of working headlines to play with over the next few days.

For example, 5 headlines we could come up with for the topic of Digital Writing might be:

  • The List: 7 Digital Writing Tips Every Beginner Should Use To Attract Their First 10,000 Followers

  • The Story: How I Became The Most-Read Writer On Quora—And How You Can Too

  • The Opinion: Why Starting A Blog Is A Horrible Idea If You Want To Build An Audience (And What To Do Instead)

  • The Question: Want To Start Writing Online? ****Here’s A Quick Guide With Everything You Need To Know About Going Viral, Building An Audience, And Selling Digital Products

  • The Framework: The Lean Writing Method: A Proven Framework For Turning 1 Topic Into 30+ Pieces Of Content

See? Endless ideas! (And all-star headlines.)

So, take 1 topic you’re enjoying writing about so far, generate 5 headlines (based on these 5 proven styles), and then pick 1 to use for today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Congrats on completing yet another lesson!

And props to you—because you now know more about headlines than 99% of writers out there.

I will give you the WHO (the audience), the WHAT (the specific topic), and the WHY (the outcome), and you will write 1 headline for each of the 5 categories listed above (Tip, Story, Opinion, Question, Framework).

Do you understand? Are you ready for the WHO, the WHAT, and the WHY?

records.content:
How To Write Irresistible Subject Lines

One of the most common questions we always get from Shippers after we share our headline writing frameworks:

“But Cole… Dickie… Do these same principles apply to writing email subject lines?”

And the short answer is yes—for the most part.

But there’s also a whole series of constraints you need to keep in mind when you’re writing subject lines in order to get people to actually open (and read) your emails.And since we know there’s lots of Shippers who’re already planning on launching a newsletter and building an email list, we wanted to give you a quick crash course on how to craft effective subject lines.

So, here’s a lesson from our Full Stack Writer Sales Email Marketing Module where we break down the 4 subject line writing rules we live by.

Enjoy!

How To Write Subject Lines (That Lead To High Open Rates)

As a reminder: If you’d like to learn how to write engaging newsletters (and how to write “sales” emails your readers actually enjoy), you can join Full Stack Writer here.

By far, the biggest mistake writers make when writing subject lines is making them “too long.”

If a subject line gets cut off before “the hook” is revealed, the chances of a reader clicking is very low. Why? Because they don't have a reason to! They don't know what you're promising inside—which means they don't know what to expect (or why it's worth their precious attention).

So, here are some golden rules to follow when writing subject lines for your FOMO emails:

Rule #1: 5-15 words, max.

A good rule of thumb is your subject line should not exceed 15 words. Ever.

Less is always more here. If you can say it in 15 words, try to say it in 10. If you can say it in 10 words, try to say it in 7. If you can say it in 7, try to say it in 5 words.

However… there's a big nuance here that is important: “less words” doesn't inherently mean the subject line is “better.” The key is to give the reader a “hook” that makes them want to click and open the email—but to say that “hook” in as few words as possible WITHOUT LOSING THE MEANING.

For example, let's say your subject line was: “The 1 thing you need to do in order to strengthen the microbiome in your gut.”

Well, if you shortened this subject line to: “The 1 thing you need to do,” yes you shortened the word count (which is good) but you also lost the whole idea in the “hook” (which is bad).

A better rewrite would be something that says the same thing, but in less words, like: “Want to strengthen your gut microbiome? Try this 1 thing.”

Same idea, but the first subject line is 16 words.

And the second subject line is 10 words.

Rule #2: Subject lines should read like you're talking to a friend.

This comes down to grammar & punctuation more than anything else.

For example:

  • “3 Mistakes Keeping You From Landing Your First $5,000”

  • “3 mistakes keeping you from landing your first $5,000…”

In general, the second subject line here will see better open rates.

Why?

Because it’s written in sentence-case (which feels more like a friend emailing a friend) opposed to Capitalized (which reads more like the headline of an article).

Super small thing. Not THAT important. But a good nuance to be aware of.

Rule #3: Use 1 of the 4 proven hooks.

There are 4 types of hooks that work over and over again (regardless of industry, niche, or topic):

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal time."

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal cost."

  • "Here's how to solve your problem without much effort."

  • "Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly."

As much as possible, you always want your subject lines to use 1 of these 4 proven hooks.

Otherwise, the reader won't have a good enough reason to click, open, and ultimately read your email.

Here are some sample subject lines for each of these 4 hooks:

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal time." - Your entire Life Coach career path blueprint… in 1 email!

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal cost." - Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

  • "Here's how to solve your problem without much effort." - Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

  • "Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly." - 3 keys to land $10,000 consulting clients, from home, in your pajamas, right now.

See how every subject line is “promising” one of these 4 things?

Nailing that promise is the secret to getting readers to click, open, and read.

Rule #4: Use visceral language!

Now, you can “amp up” your subject lines even more by adding in visceral language.

Things like…

  • OUCH!

  • URGENT!

  • FREE!

  • Seriously…

  • Steal this!

  • (I can't believe I'm giving this away.)

And so on.

For example, here are some of the headlines above “amped up” even further:

  • (Original) Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

  • (Amped Up) OUCH! Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

Or…

  • (Original) Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

  • (Amped Up) [FOR FREE!] Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

It's a very small thing, but sometimes adding in visceral language can help increase open rates by a few percentage points.

Rule #5: Name & Claim ideas (in the subject line)

Even more than visceral language though, the ultimate goal is to Name & Claim ideas right there in the subject line.

For example, notice the difference between these two subject lines:

  • (V1) 3 ways to make more money as a life coach

  • (V2, Amped Up) 3 easy ways to make 10x more money as a life coach (nobody tells you this).

  • V3, Named & Claimed) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 easy ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

You should be able to feel (in your skin!) how much more you want to click on the V3 Subject Line—because “Life Coach Money Manual” feels like you're receiving a “thing.” (Which makes it feel exponentially more “valuable.”)

The challenge, of course, is doing this WITHOUT exceeding the word count limit for effective subject lines.

Here, for example, our V3 Subject Line is 16 words.

So if we wanted to trim this down, we would have to cut something.

Here are a few options:

  • (15 words) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

  • (14 words) Life Coach Money Manual: How to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

  • (13 words) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 (little known) ways to 10x your monthly earnings

This is the “game” of writing subject lines.

And why you should start by writing the most effective subject line you can (based on 1 of the 4 hooks above), and THEN worry about trimming it down (without losing the essence of the idea) last.

records.content:
Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 13 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the the theme for this second week is: Headlines & Hooks.

And today, we’re going to pivot away from “headlines” and get you up to speed on “hooks.”

Because, in order to become prolific, you need to know how to write both.

What Is A Hook?

Let’s get clear about terminology, first.

  • When we say “Headline,” we are referring to the Title of a piece (an article, a blog post, an Atomic Essay, even the subject line of a newsletter since that’s typically the Title).

  • When we say “Hook,” we are referring to the first few sentences of a piece (an article or blog post sure, but more the first few sentences of an X/Twitter post or a LinkedIn post).

This is a “hook” on LinkedIn:

And this is a “hook” on X/Twitter:

Think of the hook is the elevator pitch, or the 3-second preview for whatever the reader is about to consume.

The same way you might watch a 30-second movie trailer before committing to a 2-hour movie, readers on the Internet want to know (in literally 5 seconds or less) what you’re promising them and what they can expect to get out of spending 30 seconds or 2 minutes of their time reading your work.

Now, the way you’ve probably been using Hooks up to this point has been copy/pasting the “headline” as the social post hook (which is totally fine), like this:

But the next step is to make that “hook” even more of a mini sales pitch for the reader, giving them even MORE of a reason to give you their attention.

(And yes, this would apply to whatever sort of content you’re posting: an Atomic Essay, a video, a Thread, etc., should all have Hooks drawing the reader in.)

How?

By “summarizing” what the reader is going to get!

Here are some of the best X (Twitter) hooks we’ve written:

  • The most creative company of the past 30 years: Pixar

  • Twitter Advanced Search

  • The world’s most valuable skill

  • Reading 500 business books

  • Ghostwriting 101

  • Journaling every morning

And by the way, we’ve turned all of these (and hundreds more) into Typeshare templates, which OTHER Shippers have used to generate millions and millions of views.

So please, feel free to play with them!

  • Nicolas Cole Thread Hooks Template Pack

  • Dickie Bush Thread Hooks Template Pack

  • Viral ChatGPT Hooks Template Pack

  • Justin Welsh Solopreneur Template Pack

LinkedIn Hooks 101

The same hooks that work on X (Twitter) also tend to work on LinkedIn—which is why, if you follow us on either of these platforms, you have probably seen a lot of the same content.

We re-use our most viral hooks on X (Twitter) all the time on LinkedIn, and vice versa.

However, there is a small difference in formatting when it comes to LinkedIn vs X (Twitter).

Look at this:

The top screenshot is a viral hook on X (Twitter).

The bottom screenshot is the same hook reposted on LinkedIn—with a mistake.

See how the last line of the hook got cut off? And see how, in the bottom right-hand corner of the LinkedIn post, it says, “…see more?”

On LinkedIn, the preview text where a hook would go is a bit shorter than X (Twitter). AND, the word count of this preview text changes based on whether the reader is viewing the post on Desktop vs Mobile. So it’s hard to perfectly optimize hooks for LinkedIn.

Which is why, as much as possible, you want your LinkedIn hook to “get to the point” in 2 sentences or less—especially with some sort of strong, controversial, or counter-intuitive idea.

Like this:

The goal is for this first sentence or two to HOOK the reader and get them to click “see more.”

Because the more readers who click “see more,” the more the algorithm is going to think, “Wow, a lot of people seem to be interested in reading this post,” the more the algorithm is going to distribute your content to more and more new people.

This is the whole game of going viral.

It’s not about being clever, or tricking readers into clicking.

It’s about HOOKING their attention with a strong, controversial, or counter-intuitive idea, and then delivering on that idea in the content.

Questions

  • “So you can have both a Headline and a Hook? Or just one or the other.” This language is typically platform-specific. When you’re talking about writing articles, essays, blog posts, etc., those have “headlines.” Whereas when you’re talking about social posts, those have “hooks.” However, technically, even essays have a hook because it’s the first few sentences that “hook” you into the piece. And even social posts can have headlines (especially if you are posting your Atomic Essay in image form on X or LinkedIn).

  • “But if I use the same hook as everyone else, aren’t I just copying them?” The idea isn’t to copy other people’s hooks. The idea is to figure out why a hook performed well, and then figure out how you can make it your own. We have had thousands of Shippers use our viral hooks. Many of them have gone viral, mega-viral, sometimes even more viral than ours did! And that’s amazing—because they made it their own by tailoring the hook to a different topic, or a different audience.

  • “Do I have to use these hooks for my content to perform well?” We would strongly encourage you to practice with the proven hooks in Typeshare to start, just so you can internalize what viral-worthy hooks read like. But no, great hooks are constantly changing and being reinvented—and we hope you give yourself the freedom to experiment and find viral hooks of your own!

  • “Is short-form content, like a Tweet, really just a hook?” Sort of. A short-form post can share a lot of similarities with a hook. But short-form is typically a full idea compressed into a small amount of space, whereas a hook is more geared toward telling the reader what longer thing they’re about to read is about.

Assignment

Alright! Time to play with some hooks!

Your Day 13 Assignment is to write today’s Atomic Essay, and then write a lead-in for your Atomic Essay that “hooks” readers into reading what you’ve written. If you’re brand new to writing hooks, we strongly recommend using one of the hook templates from our Creator Template Packs in Typeshare:

  • Nicolas Cole Thread Hooks Template Pack

  • Dickie Bush Thread Hooks Template Pack

  • Viral ChatGPT Hooks Template Pack

  • Justin Welsh Solopreneur Template Pack

So, write your Atomic Essay, then write your hook, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
The 5 Types Of Proven Hooks

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 14 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the the theme for this second week is: Headlines & Hooks.

Yesterday, we talked about hooks—specifically the subtle differences between LinkedIn & X (Twitter) hooks.

But today, we’re going to talk about the proven hook styles (that work across all platforms).

Let’s dive in!

Proven Hooks

The psychology behind great hooks is universal.

What “works” on X (Twitter) has a good chance of also working on LinkedIn. And what works on X (Twitter) or LinkedIn probably also has a good chance of working on Instagram, YouTube, or TikTok.

That’s because really great hooks are about the READER’S wants, needs, questions, hopes, dreams, and desires.

And these 5 proven hook styles do just that:

Let’s go through each one:

1. Frameworks

A framework is really just a step-by-step way of thinking about something. So whenever you are trying to articulate a big idea to readers, chop it down into bite-sized pieces and present it as a framework they can learn and implement in tiny chunks.

2. Stories

Stories are the hardest “hook” to execute, but they can be done. And the secret is to give the reader BOTH the beginning AND the end of the story in the hook—forcing them to have to click and read to uncover the middle. If you don’t give the reader BOTH the beginning AND the end, they won’t know why you’re telling them this story, what it’s going to lead to, or why they should care.

3. Actionable Tips

Another proven hook is to simply tell the reader you’re going to give them X tips to solve a specific problem or generate a specific outcome. Here, the trade is very explicit: “Give me your time and attention, and I’ll give you tips to solve this problem/unlock this outcome.”

4. (Anything) Lists

The same holds true for lists of any kind. Again, the trade is very explicit: “Give me your time and attention, and I’ll give you a list of books to read, podcasts to listen to, conferences to attend, templates to use, etc., that will help you solve a specific problem or unlock a specific outcome.”

5. Threads Of Threads

Lastly, as your content library grows, you will be able to re-hook readers into going back through your content library. So you can use hooks like, “Over the past 3 months, I have created…” or “Over the past year, I have written…” and then curate your best work for readers to consume again and again. (This hook style works best on Twitter, but you can make it work on LinkedIn too by driving people to an X/Twitter thread or even a blog post where all of your best work is curated.)

Questions

Now, whenever we start getting into the nitty-gritty of LinkedIn hooks, we hear these questions over and over again:

  • “So wait… what is the exact word count for the perfect LinkedIn hook?” Let’s not forget the forest and get lost in the trees. There is no “exact perfect word count” for a LinkedIn hook (especially because the preview text count changes based on Desktop vs Mobile). What matters is that you communicate the most compelling idea you can in the first 1-2 sentences.

  • “OK, this all makes sense. What time of day should I post to maximize virality?” Ask 10 different creators this question and you’ll get 10 different answers. The time of day is almost irrelevant. What matters is that your content is engaging, speaks directly to a target reader, uses all the fundamentals we’re covering here in Ship 30 for 30, and doesn’t waste the reader’s time.

  • “Can I use the same viral hook from X (Twitter) on LinkedIn, word for word?” Yes! It’s your content! But again, because the LinkedIn preview text appears slightly differently, you might want to make some small edits to ensure that first sentence of the LinkedIn hook is as engaging and thought-provoking as possible.

And again, if you’re brand new to writing hooks, we encourage you to start off by using the proven hooks in these Typeshare template packs to practice:

  • Nicolas Cole Thread Hooks Template Pack

  • Dickie Bush Thread Hooks Template Pack

  • Viral ChatGPT Hooks Template Pack

  • Justin Welsh Solopreneur Template Pack

Assignment

Alright, you now have everything you need to pair your Atomic Essays with engaging X (Twitter) and/or LinkedIn hooks!

Your Day 14 Assignment is to write a hook that uses the proven “zero-to-hero” story arc (used in both the Story and the Actionable Tips examples above), and add this to today’s Atomic Essay.

Here’s an example of how this hook works:

~

A few years ago, I {Problem}.

Today, I am {Accomplishment/Problem Solved}.

How?

By doing {something unexpected}.

~

So, your Atomic Essay, then pair it with an engaging hook using this template, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Prep The Page

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 15 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

We’re officially 2 weeks in!

Congratulations on all the progress you’ve made so far. But, we’ve only just begun.

The theme for this next week is: Flawless Formatting.

This week, we’re going to dig into all things formatting, how to keep readers engaged, how to make your writing look visually appealing, and more.

And we’re going to start with one of the easiest upgrades you can make to your writing:

Prep The Page

All the writing advice in the world doesn’t matter if you can’t get the words to come out.

Which is why so many writers struggle with “Writer’s Block.”

Writer’s Block is this feeling where you sit and stare at a blank page, unsure of how to get started. It’s an uncertainty as to where you should begin, how you should structure your thoughts, and how you can assemble this piece of writing in a way that grabs the attention of your readers.

Well, here is the ultimate cure to Writer’s Block.

Some people call this “outlining.” Others call it “creating a skeleton” before you start writing. We like to call it Prepping The Page. And all “Prep The Page” means is giving yourself a roadmap for where the different pieces of your writing are going to go.

Here's how it works:

  • Headline: What is this piece about? Who is it for? What will the reader get in exchange for reading through to the end? AND, why should they trust you (what’s your credibility)?

  • Introduction: (Repeat the information from the headline with slightly more detail.) What is this piece about? Who is it for? What will the reader get in exchange for reading through to the end? AND, why should they trust you (what’s your credibility)?

  • Main Points: What “proven approach” are you using to organize this piece? (Is this piece organized by Steps, Lessons, Mistakes, Tips, etc.?) How many do you plan on including? 3 Steps? 4 Lessons? 5 Mistakes?

  • Conclusion: What’s the final takeaway? What do you want readers to walk away with after reading this piece? What’s the morale of the story?

By “Prepping The Page,” first, it becomes significantly easier to know where to start.

Because nobody likes staring at a blank page.

(And notice how all of the templates in Typeshare have this “structure” already baked in. These pages have already been prepped for you!)

Prep The Page Checklist

So, before you even start writing the actual content of whatever it is you’re writing (an Atomic Essay, an X (Twitter) thread, a LinkedIn post, a blog post, a newsletter, etc.), set yourself up for success and Prep The Page with:

  • ✅ A Working Headline

  • ✅ Notes to yourself as to why the reader should listen to you on this topic in the introduction (Personal Credibility or Borrowed Credibility)

  • ✅ Divide the page into subheads based on whatever you’re planning on giving the reader (Tips, Mistakes, Lessons, etc.)

  • ✅ Quick note to yourself of the final takeaway/concluding sentence you want to leave the reader with

Because if you have all the above decided, FIRST, the writing will be very easy.

All you have to do is fill in the skeleton!

Whereas if you DON’T have these pieces in place, the writing will feel laborious—even confusing.

Why?

Because you don’t know which pieces you need to fill in!

Your goal, before you write a single word of “content,” should be for your page to look something like this:

Questions

Here are some of the most common questions people ask when it comes to Prepping The Page:

  • “What if I don’t know the different sections I want in my piece? Don’t I need to start writing to figure out what I’m trying to say?” This is a common misconception, and also a bad habit writers have—particularly early in their writing journeys. It’s the same mistake that gets made when you write your headline last, not first. If you want clarity in your writing, and you want to make it easy for the reader to know what they’re getting in exchange for reading your work, it’s much more effective to START with the headline, the main points, etc., and map it all out… and THEN begin writing.

  • “What do I do if I prep the page, start writing, but then realize what I’m writing about is different than the outline I’ve prepared?” Happens all the time! If you begin writing and you realize your piece is actually about something different, it’s totally fine to change up your skeleton on the fly. But it’s worth acknowledging that because you STARTED with a skeleton and gave yourself that initial direction is why you were able to get to that conclusion quickly and effectively.

  • “What if I don’t want to format my content this way?” Again, totally fine—you’re on your own writing journey. Our job is simply to share what techniques we have found work the best after spending thousands and thousands of hours writing on the Internet.

Assignment

So, before you start getting into the “writing” today, try to Prep The Page!

Your Day 15 Assignment is to Prep The Page before you begin writing.

Here’s your checklist:

  • Working Title

records.description: Single-Sentence Openers Ahoy! Welcome to Day 16 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer. Remember the theme for this week is:
records.content:
Single-Sentence Openers

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 16 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the theme for this week is: Flawless Formatting.

And today, we’re going to improve the formatting of EVERYTHING you write by at least 50% with 1 simple change:

Single-Sentence Openers

If you look closely, you’ll see it all throughout this text-based curriculum.

Almost every single module, and every single section within each module, starts with a single sentence. In fact, it’s so subtle, you probably didn’t even realize it was happening—and yet, do you notice how quickly you find yourself falling into the writing? This is the power of single-sentence openers.

When the reader opens a piece of content and is immediately confronted by a giant wall of text, what’s the first thing that goes through their brain?

“Geez. This sure does look like a heavy lift.”

Even if the content is light and fun. Even if the language is simple. VISUALLY, it looks difficult—because that giant paragraph of text looks like a brick wall.

Publications like The New Yorker do this constantly. (And writers think big, chunky paragraphs makes them seem “smart.”)

But guess what?

Giant paragraphs don’t make readers want to consume your content MORE.

They make them want to consume your content LESS.

Before you’ve even read a single word of the following, your brain is already tired!

But if we kept this text exactly the same, and just broke out the first sentence… guess what?

All of a sudden, it feels approachable!

And the reader can easily “slide” into the reading experience.

Proven Single-Sentence Openers

So, step 1: open each section with a single sentence.

(Just like we are here!)

But what KIND of sentences? Great question!

  • Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.

  • Open with a thought-provoking question.

  • Open with a controversial opinion.

  • Open with a moment in time.

  • Open with a vulnerable statement.

  • Open with a weird, unique insight.

Let’s run through some examples of each one:

Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.

The key here is to not “hedge.”

The worst way you could possibly open a new section is with something like: “Some people think cutting costs is the best way to save money. Others believe it’s better to just focus on making more. But the truth is, both work.”

Horrible!

The reader already KNOWS both approaches work.

What they want is for YOU to tell THEM which one is correct and why.

Open with a thought-provoking question.

What question is your target reader already asking themselves?

What’s going through their head? What do they want to know more about? Where are they stuck? What keeps them up at night? What have they tried in the past that didn’t work?

When you can open a piece or a new section with a question your target reader is already asking themselves (or, doesn’t know they should be asking themselves), you’re going to meet them exactly where they are—and they’re going to feel understood.

Open with a controversial opinion.

The key here isn’t to be controversial for controversy’s sake.

The key is to figure out what is conventional wisdom in your industry, and say the opposite.

For example, in the world of online writing, what is conventional wisdom? Well, most people will say, “Start a blog.” This has been everyone’s advice for the past 20 years. So it’s “controversial” when we come along and say, “Want to start writing online? DON’T START A BLOG.” Because we are saying the opposite of conventional wisdom.

So, spend some time thinking about what everyone believes to be true in your industry—then find a way to say the opposite.

Open with a moment in time.

This is a creative writing technique that is incredibly effective at getting a reader’s attention.

Instead of just saying what happened, or telling a story, or recalling an insight… put a specific date, time, place, age, or price tag in front of it. There’s a huge difference between a story starting out, “There was a time when I was incredibly insecure,” versus a story starting out, “When I was 16 years old, at the height of my popularity in high school, was when I was incredible insecure.”

The specificity of age and that “moment in time” pulls you in.

Open with a vulnerable statement.

Vulnerability exists on a spectrum.

When we say to be vulnerable, we don’t mean you have to air your dirty laundry or share things on the Internet that would make you uncomfortable. For some people, talking about getting fired is “vulnerable.” For others, talking about a family member struggling with alcoholism doesn’t feel vulnerable at all.

You have to figure out what level of vulnerability works for you.

But regardless, vulnerability of any kind does wonders to pull readers in to your writing.

Open with a weird, unique insight.

Lastly, this is a technique used all the time by viral documentaries.

The best documentaries always open with some weird, unique insight or stat or study that makes you go, “Woah, I didn’t know that.” And then again, 5 minutes later, right as you’re starting to zone out, they’ll do it again. And then 5 minutes later, again. And again. And again. Until 2 hours has passed and you suddenly know more about America’s food industry or the dying coral reefs than you ever thought you needed (or wanted) to know.

Questions

Now, whenever we talk single-sentence openers, here are some of the most common questions we get asked:

  • “Does it matter how long the first sentence is?” Not really. The idea here is to just introduce one singular thought to the reader, first. This makes it easy for them to follow your line of thinking. That said, if you notice your first sentence starting to cross into a second (or third) line, maybe find a way to say the same thing in a more economical way.

  • “Do I have to use one of these six opener styles? Can I use a different style?” Of course you can. Again, our job is to teach you what has worked for us. But the ultimate goal is for you to take these principles and ideas and allow yourself the creative freedom to figure out what works for you.

  • “Should I use these single-sentence openers just once?” No! You should use them all the way down the page. Each new section warrants a new “opener.” So, if you have 3 main points in your piece, how can you use one of these proven openers at the beginning of each main point? This will help re-hook the reader’s attention.

Assignment

You are now a single-sentence ninja!

Your Day 16 Assignment is to pick a topic and then write 1 single-sentence opener using each of the 6 styles—and then use at least 1 of these single-sentence openers (but feel free to use multiple!) in today’s Atomic Essay.

For example, on the topic of Digital Writing, ours might look like this…

  • Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence: “The single best platform to build an audience as a digital writer right now is X (Twitter).”

  • Open with a thought-provoking question: “Have you ever wondered why some people’s writing goes viral, while other people’s writing goes nowhere?”

  • Open with a controversial opinion: “If you want to build an audience as a writer, starting a blog is one of the worst things you can do.”

  • Open with a moment in time: “In 2018, I was the CEO of a multimillion-dollar ghostwriting. agency.”

  • Open with a vulnerable statement: “When I first started writing online, my biggest fear was being misunderstood.”

  • Open with a weird, unique insight: “Studies show that in order to make $100,000+ per year as an author, you need to have at least 8 titles in your library.”

See? Tons of ways to open your writing in an engaging way (and/or keep engaging the reader over and over again down the page)!.

So, take 1 topic and write your 6 single-sentence openers, and then use at least 1 of them in today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

Want to train ChatGPT to write single-sentence openers for you?

You’re in luck…

Because we have a MEGA prompt to help you do that, too!

All you need to do is give ChatGPT the prompt below and then give it a headline.

Based on your headline, ChatGPT will generate 18 different single-sentence openers for you (3 for each “opener style”).

I am going to train you to write effective single-sentence openers.

These are proven ways to "hook" the reader's attention in the very first sentence.

Here are the 6 most proven single-sentence openers:

1. Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.
2. Open with a thought-provoking question.
3. Open with a controversial opinion.
4. Open with a moment in time.
5. Open with a vulnerable statement.
6. Open with a weird, unique insight.

Now, I'm going to give you examples of each so you can learn how each different kind of single-sentence opener should be written:

1. Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.
- Becoming successful doesn’t just “happen.”
- The wealthiest people in the world have the simplest investment portfolios.
- Going to the gym isn’t a hobby, it’s a lifestyle.
- The key to effective project management isn’t a tool or platform—it’s your ability to listen.
- You can’t change the world without first changing yourself.
1. Open with a thought-provoking question.
- Did you know the average Millennial has less than $10,000 in their savings account?
- What’s the difference between someone who goes pro versus someone who remains an amateur?
- Is there such a thing as eternal happiness?
- Is artistic talent innate? Or can it be taught?
- If you’ve been thinking about writing online, was your first impulse to start a blog?
1. Open with a controversial opinion.
- It’s impossible to be both rich and happy.
- The U.S. should not be involved in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
- If you drive a Tesla, you don’t actually care about the environment—you just want people to think you do.
- Men and women should not make the same amount of money (women should make more).
- Intelligence isn’t something you’re born with.
1. Open with a moment in time.
- In 1982, David Ogilvy wrote an internal memo to the employees of his advertising agency titled “How to write.”
- At 5:46 AM Pacific Time, September 11th, 2001, America changed forever.
- My fear of cafeteria trays began in 8th grade.
- When I was 17 years old, I became one of the highest-ranked World of Warcraft players in North America.
1. Open with a vulnerable statement.
- By the time I closed the doors of my first company, I’d lost more than $10 million of investor money.
- I’ve never been a very social person.
- For 27 years, I’ve struggled with alcoholism.
- The night before running my first marathon, I called my ex-girlfriend and told her I still loved her.
- For the first 10 years of my career, I was a terrible employee.
- I don’t know anything about investing (nada, zilch).
1. Open with a weird, unique insight.
- Did you know that 85% of the world’s oxygen comes from phytoplankton?
- California is not the largest state in the US—Alaska is.
- The average Millennial has less than $60,000 saved up in retirement by the time they reach age 40.
- Crows are one of the most intelligent animals on planet earth.
- My wife can boil a dozen eggs in 7 minutes or less.

I am going to give you the headline of a piece, and you are going to write single-sentence openers based on that headline using these 6 proven single-sentence openers—with 5 opening sentences inside each category.

As a reminder:

Here are the 6 most proven single-sentence openers:

1. Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.
2. Open with a thought-provoking question.
3. Open with a controversial opinion.
4. Open with a moment in time.
5. Open with a vulnerable statement.
6. Open with a weird, unique insight.

I will give you the headline, and you will write 3 opening sentences for each of these 6 categories.

Also, as a rule of thumb: please do not use the headline itself in the first sentence.

Do you understand, and are you ready for the headline?
