records.content:
The Art of Subheads

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 17 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this week is: Flawless Formatting.

And today, we’re going to start combining these different formatting techniques to keep elevating the quality of your writing.

And the next formatting technique you need to know is…

The Art of Subheads

Subheads are bolded sentences throughout a piece that help the reader know "where" they are in your line of thinking.

Just like we’re doing all throughout this text-based curriculum.

Because this module is organized subheads, you can now skim and jump around to find the section you're looking for (both during and after). As a reader, this is a terrific signal that what you're reading as been carefully constructed for your benefit—opposed to reading a long-winded, poorly formatted opinion article in The New Yorker that was clearly not written for your benefit, but for the benefit of the author: "Look what a professional writer I am!"

Some writers like to start their writing process by first listing out their Main Points in bolded subheads and then "coloring inside the lines" afterwards. Remember, we call this Prepping The Page. And for reference, you can watch this video tutorial of how it works.

However, if you've already gotten into the writing and want to add subheads after the fact, the easiest way to use this formatting trick is to split your essay or piece equally into chunks. For example, if you are writing an Atomic Essay and it's ~300 words, then every 100 words should be a bolded subhead (splitting the piece equally into thirds).

For a few reasons:

  • Splitting the page evenly (visually) creates a sense of symmetry for the reader. It LOOKS easy and fun to read.

  • Splitting the page also gives the reader big, bolded "milestones" they can look forward to each time they scroll. If you split the page evenly down, then the reader won't be able to scroll more than twice without their eye "seeing" the next bolded subhead—encouraging them to keep reading (because they know the next section is "right around the corner").

  • Splitting the page also gives you clarity as to where you are taking the reader. Think of these subheads as the major mile markers helping remind you that you only have 100 words to talk about X, before you take a turn down a different street and have another 100 words to talk about Y, and so on.

Subheads bring clarity.

No Subheads vs Subheads

Just notice how you perceive these 2 different Atomic Essays:

Both have the exact same content.

But one uses subheads, and one doesn’t.

Which essay do you immediately assume is better, more professional, and worth your time to read?

(The one with the subheads is the answer.)

Questions

Now, whenever we dig into the art of subheads, these are some of the questions people ask:

  • “But if I use subheads won’t that make my essay or content a listicle?” Yes and no. If you add numbers to the subheads, then technically it becomes a listicle (and that’s not a bad thing—listicles are an amazing format for organizing information quickly). But just using bolded subheads doesn’t make it a listicle. However, it does make it 100x easier for readers to skim your work and follow your train of thought.

  • “How many subheads should I use?” It depends on the length of the piece, but a good rule of thumb is to look at any given “page” of what you’re writing and, at a minimum, divide it in half or in thirds. The subheads should help it “look” symmetrical (like the Atomic Essay image above).

  • “What do I make the subhead? What should each subhead say?” Very simple. If your headline says you’re giving the reader “mistakes,” each subhead should be Mistake #1, Mistake #2, etc. If your headline says you’re giving the reader “reasons,” each subhead should be Reason #1, Reason #2, etc. If your headline says you’re giving the reader “tips,” each subhead should be a tip. And so on, and so forth. Your subheads are the fastest and easiest way for the reader to decide whether or not you are delivering on the promise in the headline.

  • “What about platforms like X (Twitter) and LinkedIn where you can’t bold or use H1 subheads? What do you do then?” You get creative! You can use CAPS, $symbols$, even emojis to help the reader understand where one section ends and another section starts. That said, on X (Twitter) you can bold if you are subscribed to the platform’s Premium tier. And on LinkedIn, there are workarounds using third-party tools like LinkedIn Text Formatter.

If you notice, all the templates we share inside Typeshare have subheads built-in.

That’s because using subheads is one of the most effective upgrades you can make to your own writing. So if you’ve been using the templates, great. But if you’ve been starting with a blank page, make sure to start using subheads in everything you write!

Assignment

Alright, time to implement subheads into your writing!

Your Day 17 Assignment is to make the subheads of today’s Atomic Essay perfectly match the promise in your headline.

For example:

  • 3 Mistakes First-Time Entrepreneurs Make = 3 subheads, “Mistake #1, Mistake #2, Mistake #3”

  • 2 Reasons Why Buying Real Estate Is The Secret To Wealth Preservation = 2 subheads, “Reason #1, Reason #2”

  • 6 Hard Decisions All New Parents Will Have To Make Before Having Their First Child = 6 subheads, “Hard Decision #1, Hard Decision #2,” etc.

This is how you make your digital writing skimmable!

So, write today’s Atomic Essay and make sure the promise in your headline is being mirrored in the subheads, then hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.description: 1/3/1 Writing Rhythms Ahoy! Welcome to Day 18 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer. Remember, the theme for this week is: F
records.content:
1/3/1 Writing Rhythms

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 18 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this week is: Flawless Formatting.

And today we’re going to introduce you to one of our favorite (and one of the frameworks Shippers say they love most) formatting techniques.

Writing Rhythm: 1/3/1

(1) What is 1/3/1?

(3) It’s a technique for injecting rhythm into your writing without even needing to think about it. First you open with a single sentence (remember our single-sentence openers). Then, you expand on the idea of that section in three sentences.

(1) And then end with another sentence of conclusion.

Just like we did here, above!

(We’ve tagged each sentence with a number so you can see how the framework “works” in action.)

Notice how, if we didn’t point out to you the 1/3/1 pattern, you probably wouldn’t have noticed it was there. And yet, using 1/3/1 in a section of your writing gives it the feeling of fast and slow, short and long, alternating back and forth—which is what creates the feeling of rhythm.

Now, is 1/3/1 the only writing rhythm out there?

Of course not!

There are many more, such as:

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/6/1

  • 1/2/5/2/1

  • 1/2/3/5/3/2/1

  • Etc.

The important thing to notice is how the most effective rhythms start with a single-sentence opener, crescendo up, and then come back down and end with a single sentence again.

This helps give readers the feeling of starting & stopping individual thoughts/sections before reading the next idea, etc.

And you can use the 1/3/1, 1/4/1, 1/5/1, etc., writing rhythm all the way down the page and the reader won't have any idea what you're doing.

They'll just think, "Wow! This piece is formatted so beautifully! And the writing just flows!"

Only a trained eye (which you now have) will notice what's happening.

1/3/1 + Subhead

How does this work with subheads?

Think of each subhead as the beginning of a new section—and then inside that section is where you would use these writing rhythms.

So the pattern would go like this:

  • Subhead

  • 1/3/1

  • Subhead

  • 1/3/1

  • Etc.

The subhead doesn’t count as the first “1.” It’s simply drawing a line between the last section (1/3/1) and the next section (1/3/1).

Questions

Now, the 1/3/1 framework is always a Shipper favorite—however it does tend to come with a handful of questions:

  • “Do I have to use the same writing rhythm all the way down the page?” Of course not! You can change it up: 1/3/1, subhead, 1/5/1, subhead, 1/2/5/2/1, etc.

  • “How does this work for short-form content like Tweets?” It’s the same idea, but instead of “3” long sentences in the middle of the rhythm, you would use 3 quick bullet points. So the rhythm would be 1/3 bullets/1. Same holds true for 1/4 bullets/1. Or 1/5 bullets/1. We use this technique in our short-form content all the time.

  • “If I use 1/3/1 in my Atomic Essays it makes the essay too long. What do I do?” That’s OK. This writing technique needs to be adjusted to the type of thing you’re writing. So if you’re writing a Tweet, you might only be able to use 1/3 bullets/1. If it’s an Atomic Essay, you might only be able to fit one or two 1/3/1 sequences in there before you run out of space. But if you were to write an 800-word Medium article, or an 8,000 essay for your website, you could use the 1/3/1 writing rhythm (and many others) over and over again, and the reader would have no idea. They would just think to themselves, “Wow! This writing flows so well!”

  • “Can I use this technique in emails and Slack messages?” Of course! We hear from Shippers all the time that once they see how the 1/3/1 technique works, they begin using it everywhere. (You’ll also begin to read differently, and start to notice how painful it is when co-workers send you long emails that don’t use subheads or 1/3/1.)

Assignment

Your Day 18 Assignment is to use 1/3/1 somewhere in today’s Atomic Essay. It could be right away in the introduction, it could be in the first section (after the first subhead), or it could be all the way down the page! Up to you. Just make sure 1/3/1 makes its way somewhere in there.

Write your Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

records.content:
Formatting Short-Form Content

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 19 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

And remember, the theme for this week is: Flawless Formatting.

So today, we’re going to show you how all these fundamental principles apply to short-form content:

  • Tweets

  • LinkedIn Posts

  • LinkedIn/Instagram Carousels

  • Etc.

Let’s dive in!

The Art of Short-Form Content

The 80/20 of short-form content goes like this:

  • Pick 1 specific topic

  • List out 3-5 “things” related to that topic (refer back to the 30 Proven Approaches: mistakes, reasons, lessons, tips, etc.)

  • Write it using the 1/3/1 or 1/4/1 or 1/5/1 writing rhythm, except make it a bulleted list (like the above).

  • If you have room, end with 1 inspirational or thought-provoking concluding sentence.

And once you “see” it, you’ll notice how many other prolific creators do the exact same thing:

The Screenshot Test

Now, there are literally hundreds of different ways you could format short-form posts.

And we have turned many of them into templates you can use inside Typeshare.

So, the goal isn’t really for you to only write 1 type of short-form content.

The goal is to understand what makes ANY type of short-form content perform well.

We call this The Screenshot Test.

Here’s our checklist:

  • ❓Is this post for a specific type of person, in a specific type of industry?

  • ❓Which of the 4As is this post? Actionable, Analytical, Aspirational, or Anthropological?

  • ❓Is it formatted in a way that is easy to read/skim (1/3/1, etc.)?

  • ❓Is this something you could see yourself (or someone else) taking a screenshot of and sharing on Instagram or in a group chat with your friends?

If your short-form content can achieve the above, it will perform better than 99% of short-form posts out there.

Questions

Now, short-form content is a rabbit hole, and we always get the following questions:

  • “How come other people’s short-form content goes viral, but my short-form content goes nowhere?” Welcome to the lottery of the Internet. A lot of it we don’t have control over. What we DO have control over is the writing and the consistency of our own daily writing habit. So, focus on what you can control, and just keep writing & hitting publish. You have NO idea what your most viral post will be.

  • “How many times per day should I be posting short-form content?” There are a lot of different ways to answer this question, but from our experience: more is better. So if you’re posting 1x per week and you’re not growing enough, try 1x per day. If you’re posting 1x per day and you’re not growing enough, try 3x per day. Etc. Volume wins. (The extremes are what you want to avoid: posting 1x per week probably isn’t enough. But posting 1x every hour, 24 hours per day, is overkill.)

  • “What time of day should I post my short-form content?” This is the wrong question to ask. The time of day isn’t what matters. What matters is that your short-form content passes The Screenshot Test. That said, if you must know, we typically post our short-form content at 7am ET and 7pm ET, with other posts sprinkled throughout the day.

  • “I’m having a hard time coming up with short-form ideas to write about. What do I do?” Take your topic and run through the 30 Proven Approaches. There. That’s 30 short-form pieces of content. Then adjust the topic to a different audience and run through the 30 Proven Approaches again. That’s another 30 short-form pieces of content. Then pick a different topic and run through the 30 Proven Approaches. That’s another 30 short-form pieces of content. And so on.

Assignment

Alright! It’s time to get some short-form content out into the world!

At this point, you now know all the fundamental digital writing principles—which means you can continue writing Atomic Essays, or you can experiment with short-form Tweets and LinkedIn posts (or both!).

So your Day 19 Assignment is to write a piece of short-form content (a Tweet or a short LinkedIn post, or both) using the proven format of 1/3 bullets/1 or 1/4 bullets/1—similar to the examples above.

Hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

records.content:
2-Year Test

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 2 of Ship 30 for 30.

And remember, the theme for this first week is: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

It’s not hard to become a prolific writer.

In fact, most people don’t realize that every “prolific writer” they see publishing isn’t waking up every morning asking themselves to be brilliant. Instead, these “prolific writers” have simply built the skill of idea generation—and created systems for themselves to make sure they never run out of things to write about.

Which is what we’re going to show you how you can do, too.

The 2-Year Test

Whenever someone says, “I don’t know what to write about,” or “I don’t think I’m qualified to write about that, it’s not because they don’t have anything meaningful to share or don’t have enough credibility.

It’s because they take for granted everything they’ve learned—not realizing every single thing they know TODAY, they didn’t know at some point in the past. And that “version” of themselves in the past would LOVE to know everything they know now.

So, what’s our solution to the age-old objection, “I don’t know what to write about?”

It’s called The 2-Year Test.

  • What questions were you asking 2 years ago, that you now know the answers to?

  • What hadn’t you experienced 2 years ago, that you’ve since experienced?

  • Where were you at in life 2 years ago, and where are you today?

Through this lens, everyone is an expert in something.

Remember back when you were in middle school, and you were wondering what high school was going to be like? You didn’t want to hear your parents perspective (even though, technically, they were “very qualified” to give you an answer). What you wanted was to learn from the high schoolers. Ideally a kid who was 1 or 2 years ahead of you. Someone who had just gone through what you were about to go through. They didn’t need to be a “professional.” All you cared about was hearing, from them, what the experience was like—in an effort to prepare yourself.

Sometimes we forget this same logic applies to everything in life.

And if you ever feel like you don’t have anything to write about, or aren’t “qualified” to write about a specific topic, it’s because you are trying to write for the wrong audience.

You don’t need to write for “the whole world.”

You just need to write for the version of yourself 2 years ago—before you knew what you know now.

Questions

Now, here are some of the most common questions we get asked on this topic:

  • “But what if everything I’ve done over the past 2 years isn’t what I want to write about?” First, we’d ask why you want to write about something you haven’t done yet. And second, the goal here isn’t for you to pick 1 topic you’re going to write about forever. The goal is for you to START writing, hitting publish, building the habit, and THEN steering your ship as you go. Don’t overthink it.

  • “Can it be something I’ve learned in the past 5 years?” YES! We just coined the term The 2-Year Test to make it easy to remember, but it could be something you learned 5 or 10 years ago, or something you learned just last week. The skill here is becoming aware of all the things you’ve learned, and are continuing to learn—and turning those things into content.

  • “Who is going to be interested in something I learned, especially if it’s a basic skill?” A LOT of people. We take for granted what we know because it seems so familiar to us. But remember… before you “knew what you know now,” you had questions. And you would have loved for someone to not only give you the answers, but share with you their personal experiences.

  • “OK… but I don’t feel qualified to talk about these topics. I’m not an expert.” This is the biggest faulty belief of all. You don’t have to be an expert to share what YOU’VE learned. In fact, you aren’t even saying (and we wouldn’t recommend saying), “I’m an expert.” This is what gives people Imposter Syndrome. Instead, just say something to the effect of, “A year ago, I didn’t know anything about {Topic}. Then, I read a bunch of books on it—and here’s what I learned.”

Assignment

So, let’s keep momentum going.

Your Day 2 Assignment is to use the 2-Year Test to brainstorm 7 things you have done, experienced, accomplished, completed, etc., over the past 2 years (or more, or less!). Then write about 1 of those things in today’s Atomic Essay! (And… now you have ideas for the rest of the week as well!)

And don’t forget, if you REALLY can’t come up with anything to write about, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

records.content:
Formatting X (Twitter) Threads

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 20 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this week is: Flawless Formatting.

And today, we’re going to talk about how to expand short-form content into longer-form content.

Specifically: X (Twitter) Threads!

Let’s dive in.

The Anatomy Of An X (Twitter) Thread

An X (Twitter) Thread is a unique type of content.

It is a series of Tweets (short-form content) strung together.

A lot of times, new digital writers want to jump straight to writing Threads because they see them go viral and think, “If I write a thread then I’ll go viral too!” But that’s not true.

First of all, every type of content can go viral:

  • Short-Form

  • Long-Form

  • Threads

  • Carousels

  • Articles

  • Short-Form Video

  • Long-Form Video

  • Podcasts

  • Etc.

It’s never “the medium” itself that dictates whether or not something goes viral.

It’s the content INSIDE that matters.

Second, think of Threads as a sub-language of Digital Writing.

If you wanted to learn English, you wouldn’t jump straight to learning Brooklyn slang. You would start by learning the fundamentals of the English language, and THEN learn the nuances, the sayings, the different accents, the “trendy” words, etc.

Writing on the Internet is no different.

And because you’ve spent the past 2+ weeks learning the fundamentals, now learning how to write X (Twitter) Threads will be a breeze!

Let’s go through each piece:

The Thread Lead-In

Remember how we talked about hooks?

The Lead-In of your Thread (also known as the “hook”) is the most important part.


Think of the Lead-In as your sales pitch for the rest of the Thread.

  • What are you promising the reader?

  • Why is it worth their time?

  • What should they expect to get out of reading it?

The entire game of Threads going viral comes down to how compelling the Lead-In is.

So, if you’re brand new to writing Threads (and specifically, “hooks”) we STRONGLY encourage you to practice with the hundreds of hooks we have inside Typeshare.

The Main Points (Tweets Inside Thread)

After the Lead-In (which is basically the “movie trailer” for your Thread) is the actual content of the thread.

And the easiest way to think about it is to treat each Tweet inside your Thread as a Main Point.

The goal, even though all the Tweets inside your Thread should be connected/talking about one overarching topic, is for each Tweet to stand on its own.

You do NOT want to write Threads where the reader has to get further and further into reading in order to understand what you’re trying to say.

No, the reader should be able to follow each Main Point—Tweet by Tweet.

Again, don’t forget all your formatting fundamentals:

  • Use 1/3/1 or 1/4/1 writing rhythms

  • Use bulleted lists

  • Speak directly to 1 target reader

Each Tweet in your Thread should follow all the same rules as really great short-form content.

The Recap

At the end of the Thread, we like to do what’s called a TL;DR Tweet (which is Internet slang for: “Too Long, Didn’t Read.”).

This is essentially a Tweet summarizing all the Main Points of your Thread.

There are 2 reasons we like including this TL;DR Tweet:

  • If you write this first, it actually creates the “outline” for your entire Thread (each bullet point is a Main Point).

  • It is something readers can bookmark and save at the end of your Thread.

CTA: Call To Action

The very last Tweet in your Thread should be a CTA.

The idea here is to give readers somewhere else to go.

You could direct them to:

  • Another relevant piece of writing

  • A product you’ve created

  • A service you provide

  • A newsletter

  • A book

  • Etc.

For example, at the end of our Threads, we typically push readers to either download our free Start Writing Online guide, or opt-in to our 5-Day Ghostwriting Email Course.

And this is how we attract people onto our email lists, and eventually pitch them on joining one of our programs (like you did here!).

Questions

Now, X (Twitter) Threads are a very unique sub-language of the Digital Writing world, so here are some of the most common questions people ask:

  • “I feel like Threads are saturated now. Do they still work?” Yes. Everyone says everything is saturated all the time, forever. People have been saying Facebook ads are dead for 10 years, and newsletters are dead for 20 years. Guess what? Both are more popular today than ever before. Again, very rarely is it “the medium” that doesn’t work. All these different digital platforms & mediums work—success just comes down to the content you are putting inside the medium.

  • “I’ve written tons of Threads and none of them are going viral. What am I doing wrong?” 90% of the time, it’s a Lead-In problem. The content could be really valuable, but if you aren’t “hooking” people then nobody is going to click—and if nobody clicks then the algorithm thinks, “Nobody is interested in this” and doesn’t show it to more people. So, focus on practicing the skill of writing viral-worthy Lead-Ins.

  • “What time of day should I publish my Threads?” Again, this is the wrong question. The time of day isn’t what matters. The CONTENT is what matters. That said, if you really want to know, we publish our Threads around 11:00am ET on a weekday.

  • “What if I don’t want to write Twitter threads like everyone else. How do I make mine different?” Look, writing is subjective so you’re welcome to approach it however you want. But we’ve written (and ghostwritten) thousands of Threads, and we can tell you: there’s a reason why the vast majority of creators all approach Threads in a somewhat similar way. The principles work.

Assignment

Alright, that’s everything you need to know in order to write viral-worthy Threads!

Your Day 20 Assignment is to write your first Twitter Thread! (If you’re enjoying writing Atomic Essays, feel free to stick with those. However, if you’d like to expand to the other digital writing formats, we encourage you to try writing your first Thread!)

You can write the Thread on your own using all the principles we covered today, or (especially if you’re brand new to writing Threads) you can use one of the dozens and dozens of proven Thread templates inside Typeshare.

Write your Thread, hit publish, and onto the next!

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Formatting LinkedIn & X (Twitter) Long-Form Posts

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 21 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this week is: Flawless Formatting.

And for the last day of “formatting week,” we are going to talk about the structure of long-form LinkedIn & X (Twitter) long-form posts!

Let’s dive in.

The Anatomy Of A Long-Form LinkedIn & X (Twitter) Post

Long-form posts on LinkedIn (which you can now also publish on X/Twitter if you are a Premium Subscriber) follow all the same rules as an Atomic Essay.

The only difference is… they’re longer!

So, you already know all the fundamentals.

But let’s talk about some of the nuances:

The Lead-In

The same way a Twitter Thread has a Lead-In (a hook), your long-form LinkedIn posts also have a Lead-In.

It’s just a much smaller amount of space.

Note: The appearance of the 'see more' text in a LinkedIn post depends on the post length and the type of content. For text-only posts, the link appears after 400 characters or 5 line breaks. For media posts, it appears after 250 characters or 3 line breaks.

Notice here how, in the feed, only the first sentence (first 2 “lines”) is what the reader sees:

This means your LinkedIn Lead-In needs to be:

  • Similar to a title (Topic, Audience, Outcome)

  • Concise (250 characters or less)

  • Sales Pitch (this is the movie trailer that needs to hook the reader to click “see more” and continue reading)

Again, the content of your long-form post could be amazing… but if you aren’t able to hook readers into clicking “see more,” nobody is ever going to know.

And you can now publish long-form content on X (Twitter) as well, and so the preview looks like this:

LinkedIn Formatting

Unless you use a third-party tool, LinkedIn’s formatting is pretty sparse (whereas X/Twitter’s long-form actually has formatting capabilities like bolding & italics).

Meaning you have to get creative in order to execute all the digital writing fundamentals we’ve been talking about—like subheads, bulleted lists, etc.

The way we typically execute this is by:

  • Using spacing (and breaking sentences apart)

  • Using numbered lists

  • And separating the Main Points (the numbers in the list) with dashes or some sort of visual signifier of where one Main Point ends and the next begins.

LinkedIn CTA

The same way we recommend ending an X (Twitter) Thread by nudging readers to the next thing you want them to read/do, we encourage you to do the same thing on LinkedIn.

Except this gets executed in a slightly different way on each platform—and on LinkedIn, the way most people do this is by linking to “the next thing” as a comment.

So what you would do is:

  • Write & publish your long-form post

  • Comment on your own post (as yourself) with your CTA—driving readers somewhere else (like we do to Start Writing Online here).

The reason you put the CTA in the comments is because typically external links in the main body of the post hurts engagement—because LinkedIn doesn’t want you sending people off-platform.

But when you put the link in the comments, the algorithm doesn’t flag it.

Now, the other way to execute a CTA (which is something we’ve been experimenting with, along with a handful of other big creators) is edit the body of your post ~4 hours later (after the post has had time to perform in the algorithm) and add a link there.

Like this:

From what we’ve found, when you add a link back into the body text, it does impact distribution of the post slightly—but link clicks are higher than the link being in the comments.

So, pro/con.

There’s no one right answer here. Algorithms are constantly changing so just experiment and see what works best for you!

Questions

Now, whenever we talk about LinkedIn, these are the questions people ask most often:

  • “Can I just copy/paste all my Atomic Essays on LinkedIn as long-form posts?” Yup! We do all the time. Just make sure you tweak the formatting so that it’s still easy to read, Main Points are separated, etc.

  • “Can I copy/paste X (Twitter) Threads on LinkedIn as long-form posts?” Yup! The example shown above is an X (Twitter) Thread reposted on LinkedIn with a few small formatting tweaks, word-for-word. Again, if the content performs well on 1 platform, chances are it’ll also perform well on other platforms.

  • “What time of day should I be posting long-form on LinkedIn?” Again, wrong question. Time of day is irrelevant. What matters WAY more is the content itself. That said, if you must know, we typically publish long-form at 8:30am ET.

Assignment

Alright, you now know everything you need to know in order to start writing, publishing, and maximizing LinkedIn!

See how all these digital writing fundamentals start compounding?

Your Day 21 Assignment is to write and publish your first piece of long-form social content!

  • If you wrote a Thread yesterday, you can literally copy/paste the content of the Thread as a long-form post on X (Twitter) or LinkedIn. (Just be sure to double-check the formatting, and/or if it’s a really long Thread you might have to edit it down so it fits on LinkedIn.)

  • If you wrote an Atomic Essay yesterday, you can also copy/paste the content of the Atomic Essay as a long-form post on X (Twitter) or LinkedIn. (Again, just be sure to check the formatting.)

  • Or, you can write something completely new! Up to you. (We just want you to see how valuable it is to build a library of content, and how you can re-publish that content over and over again!).

So, write a new long-form piece (or take an existing piece & re-format and re-post it as long-form content), hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Now that you’ve learned all the fundamentals of writing engaging LinkedIn posts, the next skill you might want to learn is:

Reverse-engineering other creator’s viral posts and turning them into templates.

Luckily, we’ve already created a ChatGPT prompt to help you do this—in a fraction of the time I’d take you to do it manually (and without even having to type!).

Want to learn how it works?

Here you go!

How To Create The Perfect LinkedIn Post Without Typing (And Get 10X Better Results)

This prompt was originally published as an issue of our paid newsletter, Write With AI. If you'd like to unlock dozens of other prompts and frameworks to help you create viral-worthy content (but 10x faster), you can subscribe here.

Or, if you'd like to learn how to write your own prompts (so you can quickly train ChatGPT on whatever framework you'd like), you'll love our Full Stack Writer AI Prompt Writing Module.

Ahoy, Digital Writers!

I am obsessed with learning different AI writing techniques.

And yesterday I got lost in a 3.5-hour rabbit hole. But there was a fruit at the bottom of the tunnel! Because I discovered Matthew Lakajev (The #1 fastest growing LinkedIn creator in Australia).

I walked away with a dead-simple ChatGPT technique that he uses for writing a LinkedIn post like his favorite creators, in less than 60 seconds, without typing, and without editing a single word!

Sounds too good to be true, right?

Let’s check it out.

Matthew Lakejev’s Method To Remix Any LinkedIn Post In Under A Minute

The magic in Matthew's process is in how he reverse engineers a popular post into a set of questions that you, as the creator, can turn around and answer.

  • In your way

  • In your voice

  • For your context

This makes it very easy for you to use ChatGPT to repurpose a proven post's structure into something unique!

Nerding out here for a second: the "technical" description for what we are about to do is called "Rhetorical Structure." A rhetorical structure is a method for describing the logical organization of a text. It's how words and sentences fit together to make your writing clear, convincing, and flow in a neat package that your reader will enjoy, like LEGOs.

Which means you can pick a piece of writing, leverage ChatGPT to unpack why it works (rhetorical structure), and then create something that follows the exact same pattern—remixed in your voice. Amazing! But we don’t stop there.

To make the process “user friendly,” we turn the structure into a set of questions.

Then all you have to is answer each question—like talking to a friend!

The Setup

You are going to need 3 things to follow along here:

  1. ChatGPT (The “Plus” version works best)

  2. A LinkedIn post (We will use this one as an example.)

  3. Speech-to-text enabled on your computer (or install your favorite plug-in)

Voice dictation is only necessary if you want to test the promise “without typing.”

Full transparency: talking is waaaaay easier and faster for giving ChatGPT a laundry list of instructions or answering questions like we are going to do here in a minute.

With all that out of the way, let’s get into the steps.

Step 1: Train ChatGPT To Analyze A Viral LinkedIn Post

Here’s the prompt:

Hey ChatGPT, I am going to give you a text and I want you to analyze the text and then return a list of questions that someone can answer to create their own post that follows the same rhetorical structure of the original text.  I will give you an example of what I want you to do first before we get started.

For example, here is a post that I might ask you to analyze:

"The most overused cold email phrase ever:

"I hope you're doing well."

Stop this for 3 reasons:

1 → It occupies your first lines (super important space)
2 → It sounds like the start of a selfish sales pitch
3 → It doesn’t add value to your pitch 

It’s said by everyone
→ so you sound like everyone 

It's safe to remove it and
→ get to the point "

And here is an example of how you would respond with questions:

"Question 1: What's an overused phrase or concept in your industry?

Guidance: Think about a term or phrase that is frequently used in your field to the point of becoming a cliché.

Question 2: Can you identify three reasons why this phrase should be avoided?

Guidance: List three reasons that explain why using this overused phrase could be detrimental or ineffective.

Question 3: What's a common characteristic of those who frequently use this phrase?

Guidance: Describe a characteristic that those who frequently use this overused phrase might share.

Question 4: What would be a more beneficial action to replace using this phrase?

Guidance: Propose a more effective or impactful action to replace the use of the overused phrase."

Do you understand what I want you to do?

If so, I will give you the text so you can create the questions.

ChatGPT will “process” your request and kindly ask the post you would like to analyze.

Step 2: Turn A LinkedIn Post Into An Interview Script

Head over to LinkedIn, find a post you want to remix from your favorite creator or use the one we linked above.

If you need some help, here are a few creators to start with:

  • Dickie Bush :-)

  • Justin Welsh

  • Charles Miller

Copy/ Paste the original post into the chat box and hit enter!

Wabam!

Now you have an interview script.

Time to do some talking!

Step 3: Conduct A Personal Interview And Dictate Your Response To Each Question

At this point, you are ready to have a conversation with ChatGPT.

Fire up your speech-to-text software. Then tell ChatGPT knows what you’re going to do.

Here’s a sample script to follow:

Thanks ChatGPT! Here’s what we are going to do next. I'm going to answer the questions you provided and then you are going to rewrite the original post using my answers. You will follow the style and layout of the original post. Mirror the spacing, sentence length, number of characters, etc. as close as possible.

After you have primed ChatGPT with your instructions, go right into answering the questions while you are still recording.

You don’t have to repeat each question verbatim, or even answer all of the questions. Pretend you are talking on the phone with a friend and talk. The dictation software will misspell some things and miss words, but that’s ok because ChatGPT is really smart and can discern what you are trying to say.

When you are done it will look something like this:

Once you are done talking, stop the recording and hit enter!

And then…

Step 4: Print It And Publish It!

I would make a few tweaks, but this is pretty darn good.

And I wouldn’t be totally embarrassed to ship it!

So, does Matthew’s method live up to his promise?

  • Like your favorite creator? Yeah!

  • No typing? Check. I don’t count hitting the enter keys.

  • < 60 seconds? Pretty dang close. The longest bit is answering the questions.

  • No editing? Iffy. It’s hard to skip polishing the last 10%.

Clear your throat and give this strategy a shake down.

Let us know what you think.

Chat soon,

Nicolas Cole

Dickie Bush

Co-Creators of Ship 30 for 30.

records.content:
Make Noise, Listen For Signal

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 22 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

And the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

Let’s dive right in!

Make Noise, Listen For Signal

Over the past few weeks, you have:

  • Done the 2-Year Test

  • Mastered the fundamentals of Digital Writing

  • Written different types of digital content (Atomic Essays, short-form, long-form, etc.)

  • Experimented with different topics, for different audiences

  • Started to build your content library

  • Practiced in public

  • And gathered some data from readers

We call this: making noise, and listening for signal.

See, most writers ASSUME they know what readers want to hear about from them.

But this assumption is 100% emotional. It’s based on “intuition.” A feeling. (And there is nothing concrete or objective about it.)

Our goal is to get you out of subjective “I think…” mode and get you into objective “I know… based on data” mode.

For example: if you write 10 tweets, 10 LinkedIn posts, 10 Atomic Essays, etc…

  • Which 1 or 2 received the most Likes?

  • Which posts received the most comments or views?

  • Maybe most importantly, which posts did you enjoy writing the most? And is there any overlap between the posts you enjoyed writing the most & the posts your readers clearly enjoyed the most?

When you make noise and listen for signal, this is what you’re looking for:

The intersection of your own interests & the interests of your readers.

Because if data says, “This topic works,” but you hate writing about that topic, you’re never going to stick with it. And if the data clearly says, “This topic doesn’t work at all,” but you are determined to write about it, that’s fine—just don’t be surprised when no one engages with your work.

The signals you want to pay attention to are…

Internal Signals

  • Ease: “Wow, this was so easy for me to write. It feels natural!”

  • Enjoyment: “I had a list of ideas and this one jumped to the top.”

  • Friction: “This topic was really hard. I thought I wanted to write about this but turns out I don’t.”

External Signals

  • Views: “This is getting a lot of views/impressions.”

  • Likes: “A lot of people Like this one. I wonder why?”

  • Comments: “This essay is sparking more conversation than usual.”

  • Shares: “More people are sharing this than anything else I’ve written.”

And if you do this enough times, and you go through this process consciously, then your niche and all the topics most likely to attract and engage your audience reveal themselves.

So, let’s do a quick audit of where you are now (based on everything you’ve written up to this point):

  • [Internal] Which 3 topics have you enjoyed writing about the most?

  • [External] Which 3 topics have your readers engaged with and enjoyed reading the most?

Great, that’s 6 strong data points (3 internal, 3 external).

Which means your best path forward is to double-down on those 6 data points and write about them a lot more.

Then, after another ~2 weeks, repeat this exercise again. Look for which 3 topics you enjoyed writing about the most, and which 3 topics your readers engaged with and enjoyed reading the most.

Then, after another ~2 weeks, repeat this exercise again.

And again.

And again.

Forever.

This is the path to becoming “prolific”—constantly adding to your content library, testing new ideas, making noise and listening for signal, and then doubling-down on your winning topics (both internally and externally).

Questions

Whenever we start talking about writing as “science,” here are the questions people ask all the time:

  • “What do I do if I’ve been writing consistently but haven’t generated any signal?” You have, you just aren’t noticing it. For example, if you’ve written 20 things, and all of them got 0 Likes but 1 of them got 1 Like, guess what? That’s signal. That 1 post performed 100% better than the other 19. And it might seem insignificant to you, but it’s not. This same process is how every prolific creator iterates on their content—their numbers are just bigger. But it’s the same fundamental process.

  • “What if the topics that are performing well aren’t things I want to continue to write about.” Totally fine. The whole idea is to just put your ideas, perspectives, insights, and stories out into the world, see which ones you enjoy writing about the most AND which ones readers enjoy the most, and then decide where you want to double-down with your effort. But you don’t “have” to do anything you don’t want to do.

  • “What if the things I enjoy writing the most aren’t performing well. Should I give up?” Not necessarily. Over time, you will learn there are some topics that will always outperform others—and you can use those topics to help build your audience. But that doesn’t mean you should stop writing about things you enjoy (the goal isn’t to be a soulless creator!).

Assignment

So, you’ve made a ton of noise over the past few weeks.

Now, it’s time to listen for some signal.

Your Day 22 Assignment is to look at EVERYTHING you’ve written over the past 22 days and ask yourself which topic you have ENJOYED writing about the most. What internal signal are you picking up on within yourself? This isn’t which topic has performed the best (maybe it has 0 Likes and 0 comments!), but which topic you have enjoyed writing about the most.

Take that topic, and double-down on it today.

Feed your soul!

Write whatever you’d like—an Atomic Essay, a Tweet, a Thread, a long-form post, etc.—hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
How Prolific Authors Turn Small Data Points Into Breakout Success Stories

Over the next few lessons, we’re going to walk through what it actually looks like to “listen for signal”—and how to double-down on that signal using the Lean Writing Framework, which we covered earlier in the curriculum.

But in the meantime, we’d love to give you a quick refresher—and share a few “case studies” of prolific authors who followed this exact playbook to write best-selling books.

Enjoy!

The Lean Writing Framework: How Prolific Authors Turn Small Data Points Into Breakout Success Stories

The Lean Writing Framework we teach in Ship 30 for 30 goes like this:

  • A tweet is...

  • An Atomic Essay...

  • Is an Ultimate Guide...

  • Is a free e-mail course...

  • Is a paid digital product...

  • Is an online course...

  • Is a community...

  • Is a business.

What this means is (walking in reverse now) before you start a business, you should understand what community you can create for the customer. But before you bother creating a community for the customer, you should know what asset they find most valuable inside that community and what urgent problem you’re helping them solve for themselves in their life. But before you invest hours and hours into creating a full-fledged online course for this person, you should beta test your idea by selling a more compressed, less expensive version of your course in the form of a digital product. But before you invest the time to even create a $10 or $20 (or $100) digital product, you should see whether or not you are able to solve any of your target reader’s problems for free via an e-mail course. But before you take the time to write out a full e-mail course, you should probably see whether or not they are interested in reading a 2,500-word Ultimate Guide. But before you take the time to write that Ultimate Guide, you it’s in your best interest to validate your topic idea by just writing a 250-word Atomic Essay. And if you really want to micro-test your idea before even taking the time to do that, well, then just fire off a Tweet.

This is how Lean Writing works.

The big idea here is that before you invest time in writing longer-form content (or building longer-form digital products), you should test and validate your ideas in their most Atomic form.

Which is why we believe the Atomic Essay is so foundational.

Writing Atomic Essays is not just about learning the fundamentals of Digital Writing. Atomic Essays are effective because they are just the right amount of words to explore one single idea with a bit of depth (something you can’t always do with just a Tweet) without over-investing in any individual idea before you know whether or not it resonates with readers (like writing an 800-word blog post or a 2,500-word Ultimate Guide).

Then, when you write an Atomic Essay that strikes a chord, all you have to do is expand it.

  • Turn that Atomic Essay into an Ultimate Guide

  • Turn that Ultimate Guide into a free e-mail course

  • Turn that free e-mail course into a Digital Product

  • Turn that Digital Product into a course

Why invest 100 or 1,000 or 10,000 hours into writing or creating something (like a book or a course) before you know, objectively, that topic is something readers are interested in?

You shouldn’t.

Not in the Digital Age.

Lean Writing Success Story #1: Morgan Housel

You have probably heard of the book The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel.

What you probably don’t know is that this book (which has become an international best-seller and has more than 15,000 reviews on Amazon) has been in the making for over a decade, and is a perfect example of how the Lean Writing Framework works—and often hides in plain sight.

For more than a decade (starting in 2008, at the dawn of the financial crisis), Morgan Housel wrote as a contributor to the Wall Street Journal and The Motley Fool.

Morgan Housel says in the introduction of his book, “The more I studied and wrote about the financial crisis, the more I realized that you could understand it better through the lenses of psychology and history, not finance.” Pause: notice this was not something he “just knew.” This was something he discovered by writing about the same topic over, and over, and over again.

Where The Lean Writing Framework came into play was almost 10 years later.

In the introduction of his book, he continues. “In 2018, I wrote a report outlining 20 of the most important flaws, biases, and causes of bad behavior I’ve seen affect people when dealing with money. It was called The Psychology of Money, and over one million people have read it. This book is a deeper dive into the topic. Some short passages from the report appear unaltered in this book.”

Do you see it?

The best-selling, international book, The Psychology of Money, is really just an expanded version of the shorter “free guide” report called The Psychology of Money.

This is arguably the biggest myth in the entire world of writing, publishing, media, and even digital entrepreneurship.

Breakthrough books, products, courses, and businesses are often not “brilliant ideas” that came out of nowhere.

They’re expanded versions of Atomic, free versions crowds of people loved and validated in advance.

Lean Writing Success Story #2: Malcolm Gladwell

One of the best-selling non-fiction books of all time is The Tipping Point by Malcolm Gladwell.

This book gave a name to the familiar idea of word-of-mouth marketing. Once an idea crosses a certain threshold, word-of-mouth takes over and suddenly the idea can no longer be contained. It’s everywhere. When this happens, “a tipping point” has been reached. (Today, you can’t hear anyone say the words “tipping point” without someone else in the conversation shouting, “Malcolm Gladwell!”)

The book was published in 2002 and went on to sell millions of copies.

Genius idea, right? Malcolm Gladwell just sat in his bedroom, put on his chapeau, lit a cigarette, stared out the window, and waited for this brilliant idea and book title to just magically appear, right?

Wrong.

Malcolm Gladwell is another prime example of the Lean Writing Framework.

The Tipping Point started as an article in The New Yorker (where he was a columnist) six years prior, published with the same title. The article became so popular that it attracted the attention of publishers, who then encouraged Gladwell to expand it it into a book. The idea remained the same. Many of the examples remained the same. Even the title remained the same. All he had to do was go into more depth and add more examples.

Nothing magical here.

Lean Writing Success Story #3: E.L. James

We can see the same story again in the rampant rise of E.L. James, the author of Fifty Shades of Grey.

(For context: The series has sold north of 125 million copies around the world. Whether you like the story or not is irrelevant. There’s always something to learn from 125 million copies sold.)

The story, Fifty Shades of Grey, did not start as a book idea. In fact, it didn’t even start in the hands of a formal publisher. It started as short (atomic) Twilight fan-fiction stories a niche website for free online. When these short (atomic) stories started picking up traction, the author compiled them and self-published the stories on Amazon. And when the self-published versions began picking up traction and selling, the rights were eventually acquired by a publisher (Vintage Books) and re-released as the Fifty Shades of Grey we know today.

Which goes against the myth that this book “exploded out of nowhere.”

No, it didn’t.

It caught a tiny bit of attention online, for free, back when it was a handful of short (atomic) fan-fiction stories.

Then it caught more attention when it was self-published.

Then it caught a lot of attention when it was formally published—and distributed in multiple formats such as paperback, hardcover, audiobook, etc.

This is how the Lean Writing Framework works.

Lean Writing Success Story #4: Ryan Holiday

Another favorite example is best-selling author Ryan Holiday, and his breakthrough book, The Obstacle Is The Way.

Again, most people know the book—but most people don’t know how the book came to be.

Ryan Holiday did not start as a “Stoicism” writer. He started as a marketing writer—because he was a marketer. His first book (2012) was Trust Me, I’m Lying, and a mix of a memoir and a How To guide for manipulating the bloggersphere to attract free media attention. Since the book sold reasonably well (especially for a first-time author), he decided to double-down on that data point and write another marketing book, called Growth Hacker Marketing (2013). This book didn’t sell nearly as well, and certainly didn’t move him closer to becoming the mainstream writer he aspired to be (someone like his mentor, Robert Greene, author of Mastery and The 48 Laws of Power).

So, what did Ryan Holiday do?

He went back through his library to see what other data points stood out.

Turns out, back in 2009, he had written a blog post for Tim Ferriss titled Stoicism 101: A Practical Guide for Entrepreneurs. 4 years later, he was still getting emails from people about this article saying how helpful it was for them, how the found the topic interesting, and what follow-up questions they had as a result. So, Ryan took this data point and decided to double-down.

This is Lean Writing 101.

He spent the next year expanding that blog post into a book called The Obstacle Is The Way.

And the rest is history.

Today, nobody thinks of Ryan Holiday as a marketing writer. He abandoned that category when the data told him that wasn’t what readers valued most from him. And despite having authored two books, built a marketing consulting agency, and created a name for himself as a “marketer,” he decided to sail for open waters and leave that old category behind—in search of something new, with even more potential.

Which is how he became Ryan Holiday, the Stoicism writer.

Lean Writing Success Story #5: Mark Manson

Finally, just to drive the point home, is Mark Manson—the author of one of the best-selling non-fiction books of all time, The Subtle Art of Not Giving A Fck*.

This book has sold tens of millions of copies (and most recently, Mark Manson was committed by Will Smith to ghostwrite his memoir, Will).

Everyone knows the bright orange book cover with the F-bomb in the title sitting on every shelf of every airport in America. What most people don’t know is that (in true Lean Writing fashion), the book did not start as a book.

It started as a blog post.

Mark Manson is one of the old school digital writers, and has been writing online since the 2000s. His website, markmanson.com, receives millions of views each month, and for many years he had a loyal audience of digital readers who loved his conversational and expletive-filled rants in the form of online articles. So, in 2014/2015 when publishers started realizing it was better to give book deals to writers who already had digital audiences, they approached Mark Manson about doing a book.

And his response was, “About what?”

He didn’t even have any plans of writing a book.

So, his publisher told him to go through his library of online articles (aka: look at the data), pick out the one that was most popular, and expand it. Can you guess what the title was?

The Subtle Art of Not Giving A F*ck—and you can still read it on his website today.

The Lean Writing Framework removes all guessing from the equation.

  • No sitting there, staring out the window, waiting for the “perfect idea” to arrive

  • No helplessly wondering whether or not people are going to love your idea

  • No investing hundreds or thousands (or tens of thousands) of hours into an idea you aren’t sure will work

  • And no creating things that end up falling on deaf ears.

By the time you write your book, create your digital product, or launch your course or community, it shouldn’t be a question as to whether or not people will want to buy it.

You should already know.

You should have written that same topic as an Atomic Essay, first.

records.content:
The 5 Ways Ghostwriting “Pays” You

As you continue to “make noise and listen for signal,” there’s something we’d love for you to keep in mind:

It might take some time for you to find this sweet spot of things you enjoy writing about that people also love reading from you.

However, there’s a way to quickly start monetizing your skills as a writer—while you continue to work towards this “sweet spot”:

Ghostwriting.

And the best part?

The benefits of becoming a ghostwriter actually go far beyond just the income you’ll be able to generate (although that part is pretty sweet too!).

So today, we’d love to share with you a Deep Dive we created for our Ghostwriters Anonymous free group where Cole explains the 5 different ways ghostwriting “pays you.”

Enjoy!

And as a reminder: If you'd like us to personally train you on how to land your first $5,000 client as a Premium Ghostwriter, you can fill out this quick form to join the waitlist for our Premium Ghostwriting Academy.

Ghostwriting is such a tremendous career path for writers.

From insider knowledge to building a high-value network, the ROI is far beyond just a monthly “paycheck.” Think of every new client like a deposit into your career "savings account." The interest doesn't just accumulate—it multiplies with each new project you tackle.

5 different ways ghostwriting pays you.

While your name may not grace the cover or the by-line, as ghostwriter you get paid so much more than just money. And if you overlook each of these different ways to earn, you’ll miss out on the opportunity to capitalize on everything ghostwriting has to offer.

Let’s dive in!

1. You get paid to learn.

At Digital Press, our first-ever client, whose agency sealed celebrity mega-deals, once casually halted a conversation for a call from "Warren"—as in Warren Buffet.

For 30 minutes, we got to ask this guy any and every question we could think of:

  • How did you first start your agency?

  • What makes an effective branded partnership?

  • What advice would you give to other entrepreneurs?

  • What do you do when a branded partnership goes wrong?

  • How do you find the right celebrity for each brand campaign?”

We learned so much.

This is a guy who would routinely charge brands upwards of $50,000 for an hour of consulting. And instead, at the end of the call, we sent him an invoice.

Ghostwriting is a life hack for getting paid to learn from experts in their fields.

2. You get paid to master your craft.

Part of what makes mastering writing so difficult is that it’s a lonely endeavor.

It’s just you at your desk.

  • Shuffling around sentences

  • Swapping adjectives and adverbs

  • And subjectively trying to decide whether you think it’s better to say, “It wasn’t until I decided” or “Finally, I decided,” and so on.

But with ghostwriting you have a built in, attentive audience.

Everything you write, you aren’t just writing for yourself, you are writing for a specific person. And, more times than not, that person is a smart, sophisticated, highly intelligent individual with strong opinions about “the writing”: how they want to sound, which topics they want to cover, who they want their target reader to be, and so on. And unlike a college writing program or MFA, you don’t have to put yourself into six figures of debt to keep learning and improving.

Ghostwriting is how you can get paid six figures to rack up thousands of hours of practice.

3. You get paid to meet incredible people.

If I lost everything and needed a job tomorrow, I know I could make five phone calls and one of the founders or executives or investors on the other end of the line would hire me.

Why? Because I have connected with so many decision-makers, so many higher-ups at global companies, that I have built enough “relationship equity” to protect my career for decades.

For example:

In 2020, my co-founder and I scaled down our ghostwriting agency just before the COVID-19 pandemic hit, saving our business. Amidst personal financial turmoil, I conceived a tech startup idea. Within a month, I rallied a team of seven and secured over $1 million in commitments. However, I realized the idea stemmed from fear rather than inspiration, so I chose not to proceed, but the experience highlighted the value of all the relationships I had built.

This is the power of ghostwriting (and being great at your craft) for industry leaders.

They are the ones who pull all the strings.

4. You get paid to be at the forefront.

Here’s a wild story for you:

In 2016, I began ghostwriting for a crypto enthusiast and learned about Ethereum. Despite limited knowledge, I invested $15,000 of my savings in Ether, guided by my client's advice. By 2017, that investment surged to over $250,000 as crypto gained widespread attention.

Now, obviously this was a very rare and unique situation.

But this is the power of being surrounded by smart, successful people who know more about emerging industries than you do. Not a bad tangential benefit when you’re the ghostwriter for these in-the-know types of people.

5. You get paid to learn how to write in different voices.

Most writers spend their entire lives trying to “find” their voice.

And what ghostwriting taught me is that you don’t “find” your voice.

You create it.

You can create any voice you’d like by consciously mixing and matching different identifiable attributes together—no different than the way a painter mixes colors on a palette. Which means the power of “voice creation” is in your hands. And it’s a whole lot easier to learn how to create a voice from scratch when it isn’t your own.

Because when it’s someone else’s, you’re less emotionally attached.

That's it!

records.content:
The 5 Big Data Points

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 23 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

So today, we’re going deep on analytics:

The 5 Big Data Points

As we talked about yesterday, your “niche” is whichever topic(s) sit at the intersection of:

  • What you enjoy writing about the most

  • What your readers enjoy reading from you the most

If you want to unlock ANY sort of external outcomes from your writing (whether it’s building an audience, perceived credibility, monetizing, selling digital products, going viral, etc.) then you have to internalize the fact that you are in service of the reader. The READER is who unlocks those outcomes for you. So you need to be giving them something of value!

So, how do you make sure you are delivering value?

By paying attention to the 5 Big Data Points in your writing!

Let’s go through each one:

Data Point #1: Views

Views are the most talked about metric (right up there with follower count), but the truth is, views aren’t really all that important.

(We have accumulated over a billion views on our own content, and we can tell you… views are somewhat overrated).

Still, Views can be a helpful metric in understanding “which way the wind is blowing,” and whether or not readers would be interested in hearing more from you on a given topic.

Data Point #2: Likes

Likes are the next metric, and they’re important because they are the first metric that requires the reader to take some sort of action.

A View can happen passively (just someone scrolling through their feed).

But a Like is a signal of true engagement—and a better indicator of where your reader’s interests lie.

Data Point #3: Comments

Comments are the most important metric, and the strongest signal for what readers want to hear about from you.

Posts that get a lot of comments should be reflected on and analyzed.

  • Why did this topic prompt so much engagement?

  • What are readers commenting?

  • What questions do they have?

  • Etc.

Data Point #4: Shares

Shares are like public bookmarks.

They are a signal of something people want to publicly associate themselves with—which is rare, and doesn’t happen with the vast majority of posts.

So when you see a post get a lot of Shares, it’s worth questioning why (and how you could potentially repeat that topic again and again in the future).

Data Point #5: Peer Approval

Lastly, it’s always worth putting the performance of a post in the context of what people you respect think.

A post might get very little public engagement, but if someone you really respect Likes, comments, or sends you a message separately saying how great/helpful that post was… that’s a strong signal!

(For example: if you had a post that got 37 views and only 1 Like, you might think that post was terrible or that topic wasn’t resonating with readers. But if the 1 Like was from Jeff Bezos, how would that change your perception of the topic?)

All Signal Is Good Signal

The big takeaway here should be that all signal is good signal.

Too often, writers & creators will see 1 or 2 posts get very little engagement and then get discouraged and give up. How sad! We have posts flop every single day. It’s part of writing in the digital age where algorithms rule the world. But that doesn’t mean the writing is bad, or someone out there didn’t find value in what you wrote.

All signal is good signal—and oftentimes you can learn more about what your target readers want from posts that flop than the ones that go viral.

Typeshare Scoring System

Lastly, if you are having trouble interpreting the “data” of your writing, Typeshare has all these data points baked into a proprietary scoring system—helping guide your digital writing journey and show you which of your pieces are resonating the most.

So, you can either do this process manually—or, you can use Typeshare’s scoring system to give you all the answers!

Questions

Now, whenever we start talking about “data” in writing, here are the questions we get asked most often:

  • “Do you have a Notion template or something where you track each piece of content in your library and how it performs?” No, we don’t. Instead, we built this entire scoring & tracking system into Typeshare (which we encourage you to use, opposed to spending dozens and dozens of hours trying to build the perfect Notion dashboard).

  • “How long should I wait before reviewing the analytics of any given post?” With Typeshare, your “score” gets pulled 24 hours later—which is usually enough time to get an early signal of the performance of the post. That said, every once in a while a post will catch fire later, and so it’s always worth looking back at your analytics at the end of each month and just look high-level: what performed well, what didn’t, why, etc.

Assignment

If you take this data-driven approach to your writing, we promise… you will improve 100x faster than 99% of writers & creators.

Again, you don’t have to double-down on EVERY single topic that performs well.

But being conscious of what’s working and what’s not is the real secret to becoming “prolific.”

So, your Day 23 Assignment is now to look back at EVERYTHING you’ve written over the past 23 days, and find your 3 highest-performing topics:

  • Which topic got the most Views?

  • Which topic got the most Likes?

  • Which topic got the most Comments?

Then double-down on 1 of those topics today in whatever you write. (And we encourage you to double-down on the other 2 later on—and to keep doubling-down on your winning topics as they pop up!)

So, write whatever you’d like to write today—Atomic Essay, short-form content, Thread, or long-form content—hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Doubling-Down On Proven Topics

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 24 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

And in the spirit of “doubling down” based on data, today we’re going to talk about what it means to double-down on proven topics.

How To Write About 1 Topic Forever

The ultimate goal of writing online is to become known for 1 topic.

Can you write about other topics? Of course.

But all of the rewards, all the most desirable outcomes (big audience, industry recognition, lucrative business, etc.) come from dominating a niche. And in order to dominate a niche, you have to become “known” for a niche you own—aka: you have to be known for a specific topic.

  • Ryan Holiday: Stoicism

  • Codie Sanchez: Buying boring businesses.

  • Mark Manson: “Not giving a f*ck” life advice.

  • Etc.

So, even if you don’t know the topic you want to become known for writing about yet, that’s OK.

Because the vast majority of the time, you don’t really know which topic you are best suited to become known for—and you certainly won’t figure it out by sitting at your desk “thinking about it.”

The way you discover which topic you are best suited to become known for is by writing and publishing a lot, noticing which topics resonate best with readers (and that you enjoyed creating), and then continuing to double-down on those topics to see a) if you are able to continue delivering value to those readers, and b) you love the topic enough to write about it over the long-term.

For example, look at all the different ways we have repeated the topic of “writing” (and this isn’t even close to all of them!):

  • Freelance Writing 101

  • Writing On Quora 101

  • Self-Publishing 101

  • Creator Economy Jobs 101

  • Writing On Medium 101

  • Languaging 101

  • Paid Newsletter Growth 101

  • Editing vs Rewriting 101

  • Quora Monetization 101

  • Creative Writing 101

  • Original Ideas 101

  • Social Blogging 101

  • How To Become A Prolific Writer 101

  • Writing Differentiation 101

  • How To Be A World-Class Reader 101

  • Lean Writing 101

  • Sales Copywriting 101

  • Productizing Yourself 101

When a topic resonates, ask yourself how you can write about that topic (and tangential topics) 100 more times.

This is the key to becoming prolific.

You aren’t reinventing the wheel every time you sit down to write.

All you’re doing is noticing what’s working and what readers are responding to—and then doing more of that.

Look at any prolific creator on the Internet and this is what they’re doing:

  • Making noise

  • Building their content library

  • Gathering data

  • Listening for signal

  • Doubling-down on winning topics

  • Repeat

This is the way.

Questions

  • “What if I don’t know which topic I want to become known for yet?” That’s part of the journey! Don’t be in such a rush to have it all figured out. A LOT of writers and creators have to go through a period of exploration (sometimes multiple periods of exploration) before that “winning topic” reveals itself. Just keep writing and publishing, gathering data and talking to readers. Eventually, the answer will reveal itself.

  • “Can my niche change?” No, everyone is watching you and once you write about something 1 time on the Internet, you’re stuck forever and you’ll never be able to grow or change your identity ever again. JUST KIDDING. Yes, of course your niche can change. (Again, just pay attention to your favorite writers & creators. Chances are, they’ve changed niches several times.)

  • “What do I do if I’ve run out of ways to write about 1 topic?” First of all, you haven’t. The more you write about 1 topic, the more you will become aware of how much more you could write about. It’s a bottomless pit. Second, if you truly feel you’ve exhausted the topic… start over again and play the hits. How many times do you think Ryan Holiday has written about the basics of Stoicism? An unfathomable amount of times is the answer.

Assignment

You’re well on your way!

Your Day 24 Assignment is to take another proven data point (could be one of the high-performing topics you identified yesterday) and write about it again—except this time, try isolating and changing one key variable.

Some examples:

  • Same topic, different audience

  • Same audience, different topic

  • Same topic, different approach (if you wrote about “tips” before, maybe write about “mistakes” next, etc.)

  • Same topic, different outcome

  • Etc.

This is how you a) can write about the same or tangentially related topics forever, but also b) how you can start to treat your writing like a “science experiment” by forming hypotheses and testing different combinations over and over again.

So, write whatever you’d like—Atomic Essay, short-form content, Thread, or long-form content—and double-down on a proven topic, but change 1 key variable. (There’s no right answer!)

Hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30
