records.content:
5 Simple Steps To Double-Down On Proven Topics

Another common question we always get whenever we share this advice with other writers:

“But Dickie… Cole… How do I actually go about implementing this?”

So, we thought it would be helpful to do a deep dive into how exactly to turn 1 breakout data point into dozens of proven content ideas—by showing you exactly how I (Cole) have done this over the past year.

To really follow the thinking here, and understand how the journey of being a digital writer is really all about small steps compounded over time, I want to walk you through exactly:

  • What happened

  • What I noticed/thought about

  • What action I took

  • And how those actions played out (and repeated themselves) over time

Ready?

Let’s dive in.

Step 1: Make Noise

In December, 2020, I saw a tweet by Jack Butcher that captured by attention. ﻿﻿

I had been following him for quite a while, was really enjoying his content, but honestly was still very much struggling to figure out what niche and what voice I wanted to create for myself on Twitter. (Yes, even someone like me, who has been writing online for 10+ years, has to go through the same learning experience when starting on a new platform. And in 2020, I was making the decision to start writing on Twitter more deliberately. Since I know someone will ask this question (”Why? Is Twitter a better platform?”): the reason was because I was bored by Quora and Medium. I’d climbed to the top of both of those writing communities, written thousands of 800-word articles, accumulated hundreds of millions of views, and was ready for a new format to play with.)

This tweet from Jack Butcher summarized something I had just written about elsewhere, and so I retweeted it with my own riff on what he said.

I called it Category Creation 101

At the time, I got more engagement on this 1 Retweet (riffing on someone else’s content) than I had gotten on almost anything else I’d written on my own on Twitter.

Up to this point, I had written HUNDREDS of tweets, and started experimenting with threads, almost all of which fell flat. I started with a few thousand followers on Twitter (that I’d slowly accumulated over a 10-year period), and yet despite starting to take the platform more seriously, I felt like I was barely growing (and my content was barely getting any engagement). And, just like everyone else, I went through all the classic mental blocks that come with starting on a new platform:

  • “This is stupid.”

  • “Twitter is broken.”

  • “I tweet great stuff. People must just not understand my brilliance.”

  • “It’s the algorithm’s fault.”

  • Etc.

Step 2: Listen For Signal

The moment I saw this breakout data point, I sat there for a long (long) time and thought about it.

  • “Maybe people like short, easy explanations?”

  • “Maybe it was the list that worked? 1, 2, 3?”

  • “Maybe retweeting other people’s viral content with my own thoughts is a growth hack?”

  • “Maybe people find ‘101’ explanations of difficult frameworks and ideas super valuable.”

I had no idea whether any of these conclusions were correct or not. But this is what we stress to new digital writers constantly: your job is to treat your writing like a science experiment and a startup. Try something. See if it works. Think about why it did (or didn’t) work. Form your own hypotheses. Pick a data point to replicate. And try again.

So, that’s what I did.

I took the signal I heard, and I tried to replicate it.

A few weeks later, I tried another tweet: Overcome Any Fear 101

It fell flat. Maybe the tweet wasn’t valuable enough. Maybe “overcoming fear” wasn’t the right topic for a 101 sort of format. Maybe “overcoming fear” wasn’t a problem the people who follow me feel like they have/resonate with. Maybe it would have taken off it I’d expanded it into a thread. Now, I had EVEN MORE hypotheses as to why this method would or wouldn’t work.

So, I tried again.

Online Writing 101

This time, I saw a little more engagement, and it felt like I was starting to trend in the right direction (tweets, threads, and “101” formats specifically in the niche of digital writing advice seemed to be working). And since that first tweet (Category Creation 101) had taken off, I wanted to keep experimenting to see if I could engineer that sort of success again.

So I tried another: Viral Writing 101

About the same.

Then I tried another (Headlines 101) but using a slightly different medium: video.

This one received 2x the engagement! “MAYBE I SHOULD BE A YOUTUBER,” I thought. (Then I remembered I much prefer writing to being “on video.”) So instead of doubling-down on video, I thought, “Clearly the 101 idea is working. I’ve proven that. Now, I should expand it.”

Step 3: Double-down on proven data points.

I want to point something out here: all of the above happened over the course of several months. Once every 2-3 weeks, I would try the “101” framework again. I had no idea (at this point) whether or not it was going to work. But as I sat down every day, deciding what to write about, I kept coming back to it as a format I could potentially repeat. So I did.

Once I had sufficient data that clearly something about this format and approach was working (aka: it was grabbing readers’ attention, no matter how small), I felt comfortable investing more and more time in doubling-down on this format and striving to make my content more and more valuable.

For example: My next “101” tweet I made a thread.

Memorable Writing 101

4x more engagement! Now I knew not only did the “101” idea work, but 101 threads had the potential to perform much better. (Took me about 5 months to realize, if I titled something “101” as if signaling to the reader I would be giving them a full introductory class on X topic, they were probably expecting more than just a few lines in a single tweet. I needed to seriously UP the value I was providing.)

So, I did it again—this time, tackling a more specific niche where I had a ton of personal credibility.

Ghostwriting 101

This is the thread that took off—and confirmed the format was a winner for me.

I want to point out that it took 7 months from the very first “101” tweet (December, 2020) and 7 different attempts (didn’t plan for this, but basically one each month) before I hit with a massively viral thread (June, 2021).

This Ghostwriting thread became one of my most-read Threads ever.

Step 4: Turn 1 breakout data point into dozens of proven content ideas.

There is a framework I write about in my paid business newsletter, Category Pirates, called “A Super Of 1 Is A Super Of 9.”What this means is, if you are a Superconsumer (or “Super”) of 1 specific category of thing, you are likely also a Super of 9 other tangentially related categories. So, for example, if you are a Super of Online Courses (you love, love, love online courses, you buy multiple per year, you are a firm believer in investing in yourself, etc.), you are probably also a Super of (what are tangentially related categories to “Online Courses?”): note-taking apps (to document your learnings from all the courses you take), productivity journals, iPads, self-help books, ergonomic desk chairs, professional cameras for a pro-grade video setup, studio microphones, even sweatpants and athleisure clothes (because you spend so much time at home, taking online courses!).

Whenever you notice a breakout data point, your VERY FIRST THOUGHT should be, “What other tangential categories are my Super-readers interested in?” Aka: what other relevant problems can I help them solve? What other related topics would they want to read about?

So I thought, “What other kinds of 101 writing-related threads can I write?”

That month (June, 2021), I doubled-down hard and wrote the following:

  • Freelance Writing 101

  • Asking For Help 101

  • Writing On Quora 101

  • Self-Publishing 101

  • Creator Economy Jobs 101

  • Writing On Medium 101

All of these threads combined generated more than 2,000,000 views on Twitter (and attracted thousands of new followers).

For the rest of the year, I continued to return back to the “101” thread format over and over again. And universally, the “101” threads that were more closely related to writing advice outperformed the threads that tried to enter other subcategories I was not as much of an expert in, or touched on content my readers weren’t as used to seeing from me. (My rationale here was: “I don’t know if these topics will perform well, but let’s find out.” And, “I want to write about these topics because they matter to me, and I’m fully aware they probably won’t get as much engagement because this isn’t my core competency.”)

Once data (objectively) tells you what’s working, DO IT A LOT.

For the rest of the year, I continued writing “101” writing advice threads over and over again, each time tackling a slightly different problem, topic area, or question I thought writers (my readers) would be interested in (A Super of 1 is a Super of 9):

  • Languaging 101

  • Paid Newsletter Growth 101

  • Editing vs Rewriting 101

  • Asynchronous Entrepreneurship 101

  • Quora Monetization 101

  • Creative Writing 101

  • Original Ideas 101

  • Social Blogging 101

  • How To Become A Prolific Writer 101

  • Writing Differentiation 101

  • How To Be A World-Class Reader 101

  • Lean Writing 101

  • Sales Copywriting 101

  • Productizing Yourself 101

  • Investing 101

Step 5: Repeat this same process again with a different idea & hypothesis.

This is what makes Digital Writing a game.

And to beat the game, all you have to do is:

  • Step 1: Make a bunch of noise

  • Step 2: Listen for signal (no matter how faint)

  • Step 3: Double-down on your most promising data points

  • Step 4: Turn 1 of those breakout data points into dozens of related content ideas (A Super Of 1 Is A Super Of 9)

  • Step 5: Repeat

Your favorite writer? This is what they do. Your favorite YouTuber? This is what they do. Your favorite TikTok creator? This is what they do. They might not know this is what they are doing (consciously), but every time they post a piece of content, somewhere they are comparing the performance of that content to everything else in their library. They then make the decision, “Since X performed better than Y, maybe I should do more of X?” They form a hypothesis. They try again. They test, measure the results, and then make a different decision. And on and on this process goes.

This is what we mean when we say that becoming a digital writer is not a destination.

It’s a process.

You are a writer the moment you hit publish. You did it. You added a new piece of work to your library. You created a data point (or a dozen data points). And the more you publish, the more data points you’ll gather, the faster you’ll learn what works and what doesn’t, the more you’ll create content that resonates, the more people will say, “Hey! You’re a great writer! You know exactly how to speak to me!”

And on and on your flywheel spins.

records.content:
Doubling-Down On Proven Audiences

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 25 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

And today, we’re going to build on what we talked about yesterday (repeating 1 topic forever) and dig into how you can tailor content for 1 specific audience—over and over again.

The Infinite Audience

There are 2 types of audiences on the Internet:

  • Explicit: When you name the audience directly (Accountants, Project Managers, Stay-At-Home Moms, Surgeons, Biotech Entrepreneurs, etc.)

  • Implicit: When the audience isn’t stated directly but is implied based on the topic. (So if you write about “building wealth,” the implied audience is anyone interested in building wealth.)

Writing for an explicit audience is easy.

If you are writing for Project Managers, and Project Managers are engaging with your content, then you should continue to write for Project Managers (and name them directly in your content).

However, oftentimes there are implied audiences hiding in your content you aren’t even aware of:

  • Sub-audiences interested in specific topics.

  • Sub-audiences interested in specific stories/examples/case studies.

  • Even sub-audiences interested in specific “hooks” (meaning they respond to the same hooks over and over again).

For example, one of the implied audiences we’ve discovered for our own content is people who hate the idea of spending a ton of money on a college degree only to emerge terrible writers.

We have used some variation of this hook hundreds and hundreds of times:

“The world’s most valuable skill is writing effectively.

But colleges charge you $120,000 and still do a terrible job teaching it.”

We have used and re-used this hook so many times—because the data says this specific example and hook is something people in our niche respond to.

So, while most people would think, “I already wrote that, I can’t write about it again,” we think the opposite.

When something works, we use it over and over again.

And you should too.

How do you identify infinite audiences?

Infinite audiences are people you could write for… forever.

  • Look for explicit audiences (archetypes like Project Managers, Accountants, College Professors, Real Estate Agents, etc.).

  • Look for implicit audiences.

  • Then look for examples, stories, case studies, and hooks that grab their attention.

And when you find something that “works,” repeat it 100+ more times.

Questions

Now, whenever we start getting into the weeds on how we think about creating content, we always get these questions:

  • “But if readers see me repeat the same stories, insights, hooks, etc., won’t they get upset at me?” Nope. Most of the time, they will react the opposite way: “I love this story! I agree with this point! I needed to hear this insight again!”

  • “Will the algorithm penalize me if I re-use the same hooks or stories multiple times?” Nope. Social platforms treat each piece of content as “new.” So you can repost, re-use, and remix your content library as much as you want—which is why building a content library is so valuable! The bigger your library grows, the more proven material you have to play with.

  • “If I write for the same audience over and over again, won’t they get bored?” Nope. Do you ever want Ryan Holiday to stop talking about Stoicism? Do you ever want Alex Hormozi to stop talking about business? Of course not. When you follow a writer or creator for a specific topic, you want them to share as much as possible on that topic—forever.

Assignment

So, is there an audience you can double-down on?

What implicit signals can you find in your content that might reveal stories, insights, case studies, stats, or hooks you should repeat over and over again?

Give one a try today!

Your Day 25 Assignment is to double-down on a proven audience (something that has performed well so far).

For example:

  • Did you use an explicit audience before? (”Project Managers” or “Real Estate Investors” or “Software Developers,” etc.) Repeat that explicit audience again!

  • Did you use an implied audience before? (Sub-audiences interested in specific stories/examples/case studies.) Repeat that implied audience again!

Write whatever you’d like to write today—an Atomic Essay, short-form piece, Thread, or long-form piece—hit publish, and onto the next.

Dickie & Cole

records.content:
Doubling-Down On Proven Narratives

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 26 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

And today, we’re going to close out this idea of “doubling-down” on proven topics and audiences with one more thing… and it’s one of the most important components of building your personal brand online:

Core Narratives

If you notice, every prolific creator has 3-5 core narratives you associate with them:

  • Gary Vaynerchuk’s Core Narratives: Immigrant family, helped build his dad’s wine store, founder of VaynerMedia, loves (and wants to buy) the New York Jets football team.

  • Alex Hormozi’s Core Narratives: Built a company called GymLaunch, doesn’t like to dress well and prefers no-sleeved shirts, runs Acquisition.com with his wife, Leila, that does <$100M in revenue through ownership stakes in a portfolio of companies.

  • Etc.

How do we know these things about these people?

Well, because they repeat these same stories about themselves over and over again—which eventually become their “core narratives.”

So, what can YOUR core narratives be?

  • Personal Stories: What things have you done or experienced that made you, you? (For example: Dickie played football at Princeton, and Cole studied fiction writing at Columbia College Chicago. These are some of our “core narratives.”)

  • Personal Achievements: What things have you accomplished? What have you built? These could be in your career or your personal life. (For example: Dickie used to be a hedge fund trader at Blackrock, and Cole used to be a professional World of Warcraft player.)

  • Background: Where are you from? Where is your family from? Where did you grow up, and how did that shape who you are today? (For example, Gary Vaynerchuk speaks often about the impact being an immigrant has had on his entrepreneurial journey.)

  • Aspirations: What do you want to achieve in your lifetime? What is a big, audacious goal you have set for yourself? (Gary Vaynerchuk says constantly how he wants to buy the New York Jets, and Alex Hormozi says he wants to become a billionaire.)

  • Fun Facts: What weird things have been part of your journey? What side-quests has life taken you on? What are your hobbies or interests outside of your primary career, your business, or your niche?

The big idea here is realizing that your Core Narratives, and the “things people know about you, at scale,” can be chosen deliberately.

You decide what stories and qualities people associate with you.

And furthermore, when you see certain Core Narratives resonate with readers… it’s worth considering how you can double-down on them, and repeat them as often as possible.

Questions

Now, whenever we talk about Core Narratives, these are always the questions we get asked:

  • “What if I don’t know what my Core Narratives are?” It’s a subjective decision. You decide. And if you can’t decide, then let the market decide for you. Share lots of different types of stories and see which ones resonate the most—then make those your Core Narratives.

  • “But if I repeat my Core Narratives often won’t readers get tired of hearing the same things from me?” Nope. Gary Vaynerchuk has probably created 3,000+ pieces of content telling the story of him and his parents immigrating to the United States from Belarus. And readers (or listeners, or viewers) never get tired of it. It’s a Core Narrative.

  • “What if I don’t want to share anything personal with my audience?” That’s fine. Ryan Holiday doesn’t share very much “personal” with his audience either. But a lot of people do know he owns a bookstore in Texas. Even something like that is enough to be a Core Narrative and help readers get to know you a little bit more deeply.

  • “Should I repeat my Core Narratives in every single thing I write?” Not necessarily. Don’t force it. But wherever it feels applicable, feel free to re-tell those same stories and tidbits about yourself as often or as little as you’d like.

Assignment

Alright, which Core Narrative can you incorporate into your writing today?

Is there a story you’ve already shared in a previous piece of writing that performed well and that you could repeat again?

And if not… then today is a great day to put a story (and potential Core Narrative) out into the world and see how it a) feels to write & share it, and b) how it gets received by readers!

So, your Day 26 Assignment is to either double-down on a proven Core Narrative (something you’ve shared already that either gave you a lot of Internal signal or External signal), OR share a potential Core Narrative for the first time.

Write whatever you’d like—an Atomic Essay, short-form piece, Thread, or long-form piece—hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

records.content:
The 4 Biggest Mistakes People Make In Their Bio

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 27 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

And today, we are going to show you how to rewrite your X (Twitter) Bio to set yourself up for success.

The 4 Biggest Mistakes People Make In Their Bio

One of the questions we get asked most often is, "How do I write a Twitter bio to get people to want to follow me?"

Let’s start with…

Mistake #1: Only listing "what you do."

A huge mistake people make when crafting their Twitter bio (or any bio) is treating it as a list of "here's everything I do."

You see this with entrepreneurs, investors, and "business-y" people most often, but it happens in every industry.

Their bio looks like this:

CEO @companyname, Board Member @companyname, Investor @companyname, @companyname, @companyname. This is a bio that has over-tilted on credibility, and is basically telling the reader, "Hey, I don't need to tell you who I am OR what you can expect from me. You should just know. See all my credibility?"And this is a giant mistake.Because credibility, itself, doesn't answer the question, "Yea but, what sort of content do you create? Why should I pay attention to you?"

Mistake #2: Trying to be Clever, not CLEAR.

The next BIG mistake people make when crafting their bio is (sort of building on the above) assuming the best way to hook the reader's attention is by proving how clever they are.

Their bio looks like this:

Netflix, Pancakes, And Stephen King novels. Don't bother me, I'm writing.Who are they? No clue. What do they do? No idea. What can you expect from them? Who knows. Being clever in your bio is such a wasted opportunity. It's like having 30 seconds in an elevator with someone who has the power to change your life, and instead of pitching them on who you are and your big idea, you decide to start rambling off random movies you love and jokes you've heard on TikTok. So, don't overcomplicate it. More importantly, don't waste the reader's time. Just be CLEAR and say who you are, what you do, and what sort of content they can expect from you.

Mistake #3: Saying "just sharing what I'm learning."

When you're first starting out, it can feel comfortable to not state anything too directly in your bio—and to instead say something like:

"Just sharing what I'm learning along the way."

The problem with this is (whether you realize it or not) you are subtly telling readers, "Hey, just a heads up, I don't really know who I am yet. Or what I do. Or what sort of content you can expect from me. So, if you want to follow me, go ahead. But honestly, I can't promise you anything yet."

Are you excited to follow them?

Of course not!

They haven't given you a reason to be excited!

Even if you are just starting out, even if you feel like you have a lot of learning to do, even if you feel like you are a complete and total beginner, you do not want to announce that to each and every potential reader & follower who clicks on your profile.

Instead, PLANT YOUR FLAG SOMEWHERE. Claim where you are. Own it.

"I write about productivity hacks for total beginners."

Under no circumstances should you show up to the party with a name tag on that says: HELLO, MY NAME IS I Have No Idea What I'm Doing Here.

That's no way to make friends on the Internet, and puts you at a severe disadvantage when trying to capture and keep people's attention.

Remember: You can always change what you write about. You can always rewrite and tweak you bio. Everyone does it. Even established writers and creators change their bios as they progress and decide they want to write about different things. It's not marriage decision.

Just own where you are today—and steer your ship moving forward.

Mistake #4: Not updating their profile picture or banner image.

This is a simple thing, but it does make a difference.

Not having a clean profile picture and banner image causes potential readers & followers to come to the following conclusions:

  • “This person isn’t playing the game of digital writing with intention.”

  • “If this person isn’t playing the game with intention, why should I follow them?”

  • “Is this person a bot?”

It’s really simple: people want to FOLLOW people who appear to be moving in a positive and productive direction.

So if you want people to FOLLOW you, you have to signal to them you know where you’re going and it would be in their best interest to FOLLOW you down that path.

Questions

Now, whenever we dig into bio re-writing, we always get these same questions:

  • “What if I don’t have a huge budget to get professional photos taken & banner images designed?” You don’t need a huge budget to make yourself look presentable on the Internet. Have a friend, co-worker, or family member take a new picture of you on your phone in front of a white wall—there, new profile picture is done! Then grab a high-quality image off Google and add it as your banner image. Wabam, done!

  • “My favorite creator has a clever bio and I really like it—why can’t I use that too?” We always like asking the question: did they build their audience BECAUSE of that? Or DESPITE of that? We would argue they would see even more growth and traction if they followed the rules we’ve outlined here for you.

Assignment

Alright! Are you making any of these bio mistakes?

If so, let’s crystallize the lesson: which mistakes have you been making?

  • Only listing “what you do?”

  • Trying to be clever instead of clear?

  • Saying you’re “just sharing what you’re learning?”

  • Not updating your profile picture and/or banner image?

Your Day 27 Assignment is to pinpoint which mistakes you’re currently making in your bio—so that you know what to fix when you re-write your bio tomorrow!

So today, write whatever you’d like—an Atomic Essay, short-form piece, Thread, or long-form piece—hit publish, and then tomorrow you’re going to re-write your bio.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

Another common question we always get from Shippers when we talk about bio writing & best practices (especially from those looking to monetize through writing services):

“But Cole… Dickie… How can I use my social media profile to attract leads for my business?”

The answer: Social Selling!

We recently created a step-by-step deep dive on how to do “Social Selling” effectively for our Ghostwriters Anonymous Free Group.

But since we thought some of you might find this helpful, we’ve also uploaded here inside our Ship 30 for 30 Skool Classroom as a bonus.

How To Use LinkedIn To Land Your Next High-Ticket Client

As a reminder: If you'd like us to personally train you on how to land your first $5,000 client as a Premium Ghostwriter, you can fill out this quick form to join the waitlist for our Premium Ghostwriting Academy.

Today we want to help you use LinkedIn to land your next client through an approach called “Social Selling.”

Last week, we spoke about how to use X properly to execute a Social Selling strategy to land more clients.

But X isn’t the only place you can find clients online. One of the most popular social media platforms right now is LinkedIn. And it’s easy to see why:

  • It has 950 million+ members from 200 countries

  • The algorithm favors posts sharing expert knowledge

  • It allows you to search for the key players at companies

In other words, it is a perfect platform to search for your next ghostwriting client.

But, just like X, LinkedIn does a terrible job at feeding you the posts you need to engage with to run a Social Selling strategy. On top of that, LinkedIn likes to push its paid option, Sales Navigator, as a better way to network and find clients. And while it is a useful tool, it’s good to master the free version of LinkedIn before advancing to that level.

Before we dive into how to use LinkedIn to find your next client, here’s a recap on Social Selling.

Here’s how it works:

  • Step 1: You comment on a potential client’s posts for a few days or weeks

  • Step 2: You wait for some kind of acknowledgment or response

  • Step 3: You reach out to them with a value-first approach message and connection request

This final step is crucial.

On LinkedIn, if you aren’t connected to a person, you usually can’t message them straight away. You could try sending a connection request as soon as you come across their profile, but most people won’t accept requests from people they don’t know. This is where Social Selling really helps you. Commenting and building rapport with a potential client makes it easier for them to accept your connection request and open up a channel of communication.

Let’s dive into how to use LinkedIn to find and target your ideal clients so you can execute this strategy.

Step 1: Find your list of target clients

There are several ways to find clients on LinkedIn:

  • Search by job title. This is obvious. If you want to work with founders, search for founders. If you want to work with sales coaches, search for sales coaches. As with everything, get as specific as possible with your search terms.

  • Search by keywords in your niche. What are some of the keywords or concepts people use in your niche? Search for them! Then filter your LinkedIn search by post to find the people posting using the same words and language.

  • Search by hashtag. On LinkedIn, hashtags aren’t dead (yet). People still use them to tag their posts. If you find a relevant one, you can follow this hashtag, and it appears in your navigation bar on the left-hand side (which helps you get to those types of posts quickly).

  • Search by company. This is where LinkedIn shines. If you want to target a particular company, but don’t know who to contact about your services, find the Company’s page on LinkedIn and then look under the “People” tab to find all the people who work there. Then find the person in the relevant department. Easy!

Let’s say you are targeting YouTube marketing agencies.

A simple keyword search brings up a ton of contacts which you can start to curate into a list. This search had 100 pages of results! So it pays to get specific on who you’re targeting and using those keywords in your search. You can also use the filtering options LinkedIn provides.

After typing in your keywords, you can filter by the type of result:

  • Posts

  • People

  • Groups

  • Companies

  • Etc, etc, etc

Filtering by People gives us some potential clients we can target:

And, once you’ve carried out your search, you can narrow down even further using the buttons on the navigation bar or “All Filters” to bring up all the relevant filters.

These filters will change depending on what you are searching for (Posts, People, Companies, etc) but there is a lot of crossover between these options. Here’s a quick rundown on the most useful filters:

  • Connections (1st, 2nd, 3rd). If you want to see people who you’re connected to, choose “1st”. If you want to see people who are connected to your connections, select 2nd. For people connected to your 2nd degree connections, choose 3rd. This is extremely useful if you want to see who in your network knows the people or companies you are targeting. You never know, they might be able to give you an introduction.

  • Connections of / Followers of: Let’s say there is a big creator or founder in your niche who posts on LinkedIn. People interested in their work might also be interested in your services. Use this filter to find people who are also following this person.

  • Industry or Current Company. To niche down even further, you can filter by industry and/or company. This helps you get really specific in your targeting.

  • Date Posted (for Posts search only). This helps you find the most recent posts that used these keywords. This is a great way to find people actively posting about your niche or topic.

Alright, now you’ve found a potential client, let’s start setting up a system to engage with them.

Step 2: Follow them (if you can)

Once you find a target client, the first action you should take is to follow them:

At this point, there are two important things to keep in mind:

  • People who have “Creator” mode turned on can accept followers. Dickie is a good example here—you can see his Follow button. Once you hit the Follow button, their posts will start to appear in your feed.

  • If you can’t follow them, they don’t have Creator mode enabled. This is OK. To get their posts in your feed, you would need to connect with them (but don’t, more on this in a second). Not being a connection won’t stop you from commenting on their posts, though.

At this point, you don’t want to send them a connection request (unless you really do know them).

Why? Because you want to save your one shot at sending a personalized connection request message once you’ve built some rapport with them. We will dive into how to do this in Steps 3 and 4.

Pro tip: When you choose to follow someone, you can request to get notified every time they post something on LinkedIn. Don’t! While this might seem like a good idea, it can actually lead to your notifications getting clogged up. With this setup, you quickly become overwhelmed lose track of who you should be engaging with.

Instead, we have a better solution for you.

Step 3: Find their Activity Feed

Now you’re on your target’s page, let’s find a way to engage with them over and over again (without getting lost in the LinkedIn feed).

If you follow them, their posts will appear in your feed. But just like X, you don’t really have much control over what you see in your feed. And if you’re trying to engage with your potential clients, these default settings won’t work for you.

Here’s how you can view your LinkedIn feed (and why they don’t work for Social Selling):

  • Top Posts. This is what the algorithm is choosing to feed you. There will be posts from your connections and people you follow. But there will also be plenty of noise: promoted posts and “Top Posts” that LinkedIn is pushing. This makes finding your client’s posts very tricky.

  • Recent. This is a live feed in the strictest sense. You get to see in real-time the posts coming from those you follow and those you are connected with. Again, there is plenty of noise, and you can’t usefully engage with your target client’s posts (unless you want to spend hours scrolling through the feed!)

Instead, we will put together a shortcut to see your target’s most recent post.

  • Go to your target client’s profile and scroll down to the Activity section:

  • Now click on “Show all posts” and make a note of this URL in a GoogleSheet or Notion Document:

Now you have a direct link to their posts!

So instead of scrolling through the endless feed on LinkedIn, you can go to your target client’s profile and engage on their most recent posts and updates.

But it doesn’t stop there.

Step 4: Find more connections in the comments

You can find other potential clients just by looking at comments.

Here’s a breakdown of where to look:

  • Who’s commenting on their posts? Look for people commenting on their posts and see if they fit the profile you’re targeting with your ghostwriting services. If they do, add them to your target list like you did in Step 4.

  • Who’s posts are they commenting on? If your target client is active on LinkedIn, chances are they will be commenting on other people in their industry—people you might not know about but who could be clients for you. Keep an eye on their “Comments” in their activity feed to keep adding targets to your list of potential clients.

See how this can easily snowball from a handle of accounts to hundreds of potential clients?

There truly is a wealth of opportunity out there—if you know where to look.

Alright, onto the final step.

Step 5: Comment and then Connect

Every day you should sit down and spend 30 minutes going through your target list of clients and commenting on their posts.

After a few days of commenting, you can send a value-first connection request to get the conversation going. If your target has been replying to or liking your comments, then reference them in your request. They are more likely to accept it if they recognize you.

And once you’ve opened up a direct message with them, you can lead with value, offer some “Free Consulting” and get your target client on a call.

Boom, that’s a wrap.

Happy Social Selling on LinkedIn!

records.content:
Rewriting Your X (Twitter) & LinkedIn Bio

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 28 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

And yesterday, we did a re-write on your X (Twitter) Bio, which means today… it’s time to apply the same principles to your LinkedIn bio!

The Perfect Bio

Think of your bio as a “mini sales pitch” to readers.

The reader needs to know 3 things in order to make a decision as to whether they want to follow you (and keep reading your content) or not:

  • [Topic] What do you write about?

  • [Audience] Who is your content for?

  • [Credibility] Why should the reader trust you?

If your bio can answer all 3 of these questions, readers are exponentially more likely to follow you and take the time to explore your library of content—because they know they’re in the right place!

The inverse is also true: if your bio does not answer these 3 questions (if your bio is “clever,” not clear), readers are exponentially less likely to give you their attention. They don’t know if they’re in the right place!

Now, to make this actionable, let’s break this down into steps:

Step 1: “I talk about {Topic}.”

The easiest way to write a bio that will encourage people to follow you is to use this basic template:

  • “I talk about {Topic}”

  • “I talk about {Topic} and {Topic}”

  • “I talk about {Topic} and {Topic} and {Topic}”

Like Dickie here:

The reader literally cannot follow you unless they know what you write about and what they can expect from you. (And no, it doesn’t matter whether you say “I talk about” or “I write about” or “I post about,” etc. All that matters is that you communicate the TOPIC(S).)

Step 2: “I talk about {Topic}” + Audience

The next step is to add in an explicit audience.

  • “I talk about writing online for Project Managers.”

  • “I write about productivity tips for busy parents.”

  • “I post about nutrition advice for people with diabetes.”

If possible, adding an explicit audience to your bio is incredibly effective at attracting THOSE specific types of people (and people who are tangentially related to them.)

Like Brian here, a Ship 30 for 30 alum.

Notice how his bio says, “I write about SQL, Tableau, Excel, & Python to help DATA ANALYSTS.”

Not everyone.

Just data analysts.

(But guess what? He still ends up attracting lots of people who aren’t data analysts too.)

Step 3: “I talk about {Topic}” + Audience + Credibility

Lastly, why should someone want to follow you on that topic?

What’s some sort of credibility you can signal to them in your bio?

Credibility can literally be anything related or even semi-related to the topics you write about. You could put, “Ship 30 for 30 alumni” in your bio as your credibility statement if you wanted to!

Credibility could be:

  • Years you’ve worked in an industry

  • Well-known companies you’ve worked for

  • Companies you’ve started or products you’ve launched

  • Revenue milestones you’ve reached

  • Awards you’ve won

  • Social media metrics: followers you’ve attracted, views you’ve accumulated, posts you’ve written that have gone viral, etc.

  • Books you’ve read on a subject

  • Etc.

Like Michael here, another Ship 30 for 30 alum.

Notice how the credibility in his bio is: “20+ years in Tech, 7+ years in Stoicism.”

That’s all the reader needs to know in order to trust you on a given topic.

Your LinkedIn Bio

LinkedIn also has a short-form bio (underlined in the screenshot above), as well as a long-form bio (which appears inside your profile in the About section, shown below):

While having a long-form bio is nice, it’s the short-form bio that is way more important.

Because your short-form bio:

  • Is what new readers & potential followers see first

  • Gives people on the platform a summary as to “what you’re all about”

  • Tells readers why they should listen to you (aka: follow you) for specific topics

And your short-form LinkedIn bio should follow all of the same rules as your X (Twitter) bio.

The nuance on LinkedIn is the “link” in your bio.

If you have something external you want to drive readers/followers to (your website, an opt-in, a newsletter, etc.) you want to link it right there in your short-form bio.

That link is going to get more clicks than any other component of your LinkedIn page & bio.

Update Your Profile Picture

Couple other upgrades: make sure your Profile Picture on Twitter is up-to-par.

What does this mean?

  • You need a photo! If you currently do not have a profile picture, upload one. If necessary, get your significant other or friend to take a headshot of you on your phone standing in front of a white wall (this is what I’ve done for my profile picture).

  • No blurry photos. If your profile picture is a cropped photo from 11 years ago and is blurry, replace it. Make sure it’s a current (or relatively current) photo of yourself, and is somewhat high quality (again: a phone headshot will do just fine).

  • No “far” photos. If your profile picture is a silhouette of you 100 yards away, in front of a mountain (or some other setting), replace it. Your profile photo needs to be YOU, because it needs to signal to anyone who comes across your profile that you are a real human. (Yes, this seems overly simple, but it’s important.)

Update Your Banner

Lastly, update your banner image.

Most people either don’t have a banner image or, again, upload a blurry image of their favorite city. These are missed opportunities to make your profile look more “professional.”

So, what do you need to do?

  • Make sure your banner is a high-quality photo. At a minimum, at least make sure it’s not pixelated and blurry.

  • Download some sort of “banner” that has to do with the industry you’re ghostwriting in. For example, Visualize Value has dozens of minimalist entrepreneurship-related banners you can upload to your profile (if you’re writing about business, entrepreneurship, productivity, etc.). Or just Google something like “writing Twitter banners” and find something high-quality.

Basically, all you need is a high-quality banner that is related to the industry you’re writing in.

Pick something high quality off Google and move on.

One Final Thought

Do not overthink your bio.

Go through this short checklist, PLANT YOUR FLAG wherever you are today, and remember your bio can (and probably should) change over time. The more you write, the more you learn about what readers want to hear about most from you, the more clarity you will have as to how to tweak your bio to catch their attention.

Remember: your bio isn't supposed to be "something for everyone."

The whole goal is for you bio to speak directly to the SPECIFIC type of reader you want to attract, based on the type of content you are creating (and data is telling you readers are most likely to engage with).

This is the forever journey of writing online.

Questions

Now, whenever we talk about bio re-writing, we always get these questions:

  • “What if I don’t have any relevant credibility?” Don’t force it. Your bio is perfectly fine with just Topic + Audience. As long as that’s made clear, you will attract readers interested in hearing from you on those topics. Credibility can always be added in later.

  • “What if I want to change the topics I want to write about, do I have to announce to my followers I’m changing my bio? Am I allowed to change my bio?” No, you don’t have to make some big grand announcement, and yes you are allowed to change your bio as often as you would like. But you shouldn’t change your bio proactively (aka: before you start writing about a topic). Instead, just start writing about new topics, see how they feel, see if they resonate, etc., and THEN change your bio later when you feel ready to double-down on them.

  • “Can I add in any personal details to my bio to give it more personality?” Of course you can. But our recommendation would be to only add these things at the END, after you’ve established: Topic + Audience + Credibility. Remember, you have limited space in your bio, so each and every thing you “say” matters. Personal details (”I love long walks on the beach”) should never take priority.

  • “What if I don’t have anything to link to in my bio?” No problem. We just want you to know that when the time is right, that’s where you want to put the link to your most valuable asset, resource, business, etc.

Assignment

Alright! Time to update your LinkedIn bio!

Again, don’t overthink it—you can always change it as time goes on.

Your Day 28 Assignment is to rewrite your bio! And if possible, try to get all 3 pieces in there:

  • Topic

  • Audience

  • Credibility

But if you don’t have a clear Audience yet, or anything you’d like to put as a Credibility statement, then at least make sure your bio says: “I talk about {Topic}.”

Got it?

OK! Write whatever you’d like today—an Atomic Essay, short-form piece, Thread, or long-form piece—hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

5 Proven “Bio Approaches” (With Examples)

Want to see a few other bio examples you could draw inspiration from?

No problem!

Here’s a few other compelling Twitter Bios we’ve come across that you can use as templates for crafting your own:

1. The Outcome Bio

This bio makes a bold promise to the reader. “Follow me and my advice, and I guarantee you’ll get your first $50K” Just make sure you can deliver!

2. The Aspirational Brand Bio

Justin Welsh is the model for this bio. “The Diversified Solopreneur” Justin is on a journey to creating a $5M solopreneur business. People follow him because they “aspire” to be like him.

3. The Credible Category Bio

This bio leans less heavily on credibility in a specific category. Cole calls out his target audience with a clear point of view. If you want to learn from a top ghostwriter (and you are freelancer), Cole is an obvious follow.

4. The Credible Talker Bio

This bio is designed specifically for people who want to "learn." And "Formerly @blackrock trader turned digital builder" is a sign of credibility. It's saying: "I used to work for one of the largest financial institutions. Now, I work for myself." That's someone worth following!

5. The Specialist Bio

If you have hyper-specific skill that you can help someone else acquire, this is the bio for you. Name your skill and name your credibility. It’s simple and clear.

records.content:
Pinning Your Best Work

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 29 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this last week is: Analytics & Category Creation.

And so today, we’re going to tie your whole profile together with a pinned asset!

Pinning On X (Twitter)

At the top of your X (Twitter) profile, you have the option to “pin” a Tweet (or a Thread).

It looks like this:

The reason you want to “pin” something to your profile is because, just like your bio, this first Tweet is something every single person who comes to your profile is going to see.

So, you want your “pinned” asset to say something about you.

Things you can pin:

  • The most viral piece you’ve written (which signals social credibility).

  • A Thread on a topic you want to be associated with (which further solidifies your niche).

  • A Thread that tells your story, or links to all your different products/companies (which gives readers a “crash course” on who you are and what you do).

  • A recent business, product, or book launch (which brings more visibility to something you’re promoting).

  • A video, a podcast interview, etc. (which gives readers access to you through a different medium other than text).

  • Etc.

The big idea here is to give new potential followers another way to understand who you are and what you’re all about.

And yes, this pinned asset can (and likely should) change over time.

Pinning On LinkedIn

You can do the same thing on LinkedIn.

Except on X (Twitter) you can only pin 1 thing to your profile, whereas on LinkedIn you can pin multiple.

In the Featured section of your LinkedIn profile, you can add links to websites, opt-in pages, products, etc., allowing you to drive attention to multiple different offers.

For example, our LinkedIn links point to:

  • Start Writing Online (our free ultimate guide)

  • Premium Ghostwriting Blueprint (free email course for ghostwriters)

  • Write With AI (our paid newsletter for AI writing)

  • Ship 30 for 30 (one of our core products)

  • Our individual, personal newsletters

Now, it’s worth noting these links in the featured section of our LinkedIn profiles don’t get clicked on nearly as much as the 1 link in our short-form bios:

This one is similar to X (Twitter), and is still the priority.

Questions

Now, whenever we talk about optimizing X (Twitter) & LinkedIn profiles, and pinning assets, these are the questions we get asked:

  • “What if I want to change the thing I’ve pinned or am promoting? How often can I do that?” As often as you’d like. You might not want to change it every single day (it’s worth keeping something pinned for at least a few weeks), but it’s completely up to you. And remember: the thing you pin to your profile is most likely to get a lot of visibility & link clicks. So, the longer you leave it pinned, the more people who are going to see it!

  • “What is the best type of thing to pin?” There really isn’t anything that is “the best.” What matters is that the pinned asset gives readers more insight into who you are and what you can do for THEM. How you can help THEM.

Assignment

Alright, time to “pin” something to your X (Twitter) and LinkedIn bios!

Your Day 29 Assignment is to pin something (our recommendation would be to pin your most-engaged pieces of content from the past few weeks) to your X (Twitter) and LinkedIn bios.

Then, write whatever you’d like to write about today—an Atomic Essay, short-form piece, Thread, or long-form piece—hit publish, and tomorrow is Day 30!

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 3 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

And remember, the theme for this first week is: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

Today, we are going to introduce you to a framework that will give you INSTANT clarity in your writing.

Framework: FOR WHO/SO THAT

“Who are you writing this for?”

Most writers don’t know how to answer this question—and that’s a huge problem.

What happens is most people just sit down and start writing without even asking themselves:

  • “Wait, who is this for?”

  • “What does that person want?”

  • “What questions does that person have?”

  • “What outcomes is this person trying to unlock?”

As a result, the writing feels hard, taxing, frustrating, even confusing.

(Have you ever said to yourself, while writing: “Gah! I just don’t know what I’m trying to say!”)

The reason is because you don’t know WHO you are writing for.

So, let’s fix that!

Step 1: What do you want to write about?

Most people think in broad topics, first:

  • “I want to write about real estate.”

  • “I want to write about cryptocurrencies.”

  • “I want to write about health and wellness.”

  • “I want to write about the future of education.”

Totally fine.

Except, you don’t want to stop here.

Because these are all HUGE topic areas that could be applied to so many different people, all of whom want different things.

So…

Step 2: FOR WHO

Saying you want to write about “real estate” is sort of like saying you want to write about North America. That’s a giant category, and there are a billion things you could talk about.

But you IMMEDIATELY narrow down the topic by forcing yourself to pick an audience:

  • “I want to write about real estate for beginners.”

  • “I want to write about real estate for teenagers.”

  • “I want to write about real estate for convicted felons.”

  • “I want to write about real estate for billionaires.”

  • Etc.

Notice how each audience forces you to think about the topic differently—AND, by naming the audience, “that” target reader is going to be 100x more likely to read your piece.

Why?

Because you are literally saying: “This is for you!”

But we can go one step further…

Step 3: SO THAT

Great writing comes down to a very simple equation:

Topic + Audience = SO THAT THEY CAN DO WHAT (OUTCOME)?

It’s not enough to say, “I want to write about {Topic}.”

And it’s also not enough to say, “I want to write about {Topic} for {Audience}.”

The way you REALLY hook readers is by helping them achieve or unlock an outcome, and getting specific about that outcome.

  • “I want to write about real estate for beginners who want to build a small portfolio of rental properties generating $10,000+ per month in profit.”

  • “I want to write about real estate for teenagers who don’t want to go to college and want to be entrepreneurial instead.”

  • “I want to write about real estate for convicted felons, how to buy your first property for $0 down and even if you have a history of offenses, to successfully turn your life around.”

  • “I want to write about real estate for billionaires who are looking for unique ways to reduce their tax liabilities.”

Notice how the more specific you get, the easier it is to understand what exactly you want to write about, who it’s for, and why it matters.

And this clarity makes it easier for you to write, and easier for your target audience to know this is “for them.”

So, write this at the top of your page:

  • Topic

  • FOR WHO (Audience)

  • SO THAT (Outcome)

If you know the above BEFORE you start writing, the writing will be 10x easier to execute.

Questions

Now, some questions we get whenever we explain the FOR WHO/SO THAT FRAMEWORK:

  • “What if I don’t know who I’m writing for?” You do know. The problem is, some part of you believes that if you pick “one” audience, you are going to cut out 99% of people and nobody is going to read your writing and that means you’re a failure (inner critic talking). But it’s the opposite. By picking ONE person to write for, in each of your pieces, your writing is going to speak directly to them—increasing the likelihood they give it their attention. Which is a very good thing.

  • “What if I don’t know what my target reader wants?” Well, how can you find out? Is there someone in your life who is this archetype of reader? Go ask them! Can you ask ChatGPT? Can you ask your X (Twitter)/LinkedIn followers? Can you spend 10 minutes thinking about it? (The answer to all of these is: Yes.)

Besides, even if you don’t have perfect clarity over WHO your target reader is, or what they want, who cares?

Hit publish. Get moving. Figure it out as you go.

Assignment

Congrats! You now know more about writing with intention than 99% of people on planet earth!

Your Day 3 Assignment is to come up with 3 “FOR WHO” audiences and 3 “SO THAT” outcomes (1 for each audience) you can write about—and then pick one of those combinations to use in your Atomic Essay today!

For example, for the topic of Digital Writing, ours might be:

  • FOR WHO #1: Ghostwriters

  • FOR WHO #2: Self-Published Authors

  • FOR WHO #3: Serial Entrepreneurs

  • SO THAT #1: To Land High-Ticket Clients

  • SO THAT #2: To Sell Books On Autopilot
