records.content:
And to set you up for success, we are going to give you the first module of Full-Stack Writer for free—and show you how to create an entire 6-month content strategy for yourself based on everything you’ve learned over the past 30 days, writing and publishing online.

CLICK HERE TO ACCESS YOUR “IDEA FILE” NOTION TEMPLATE!

Building Your Idea File

An “Idea File” is a raw text document with tons and tons of things you could write about—just on 1 topic.

Now, if you are debating writing about 3 different topics, then we encourage you to go through this entire exercise for all 3 topics (and create an “Idea File” for each one). Because again, what will most likely happen is you will realize that even though you COULD write about all 3 topics, there’s probably 1 where you have the MOST to say.

Which means that’s the topic you should start with.

The reason we encourage you to do this exercise is because:

  • An “Idea File” will show you, very objectively, just how much you can say about 1 topic.

  • An “Idea File” is a forcing function for you to get all your ideas out into raw text, first.

  • And an “Idea File” is the foundation of the entire Opportunity Flywheel you want to build for yourself (a loyal audience, an email list, a digital product, etc.).

Once you have an “Idea File” created for 1 topic, you will realize HOW MUCH OPPORTUNITY you have as a writer—and how you could create one of these for ANY topic you wanted to write about, and continue to reinvent yourself over and over again anytime you wanted.

Step 1: Choose 1 Topic

In order to create your first “Idea File,” you need to choose a topic.

Just one.

Now, a couple friendly reminders:

  • This is not “your niche.”

  • This is not a “marriage decision.”

  • This is not “the topic you have to write about, every day, forever.”

There’s absolutely nothing to gain putting all these obstacles in front of yourself when you’re first starting out.

Instead, just pick a topic you want to write more about.

Here are 4 good questions to ask yourself when choosing a topic:

  • “Is this a topic I know a lot about?”

  • “Is this a topic that I have personally experienced?”

  • “Is this a topic that I can easily generate ideas around?

  • “Is this a topic I would be excited to talk about with other people?”

Once you determine which topic you’d like to write about, the next step is to see if you can add 1-2 modifiers to the topic to get more specific on the WHO (the audience), and the WHY (the desired outcome).

For example:

  • Topic V1: “Journaling”

  • Topic V2: “Journaling tips for people who have never started a journal before.”

  • Topic V3: “Journaling tips for busy college students who have never started a journal before.”

  • Topic V4: “Journaling tips for busy college students who have never started a journal before, so they can be more grateful and less stressed.”

If you aren’t sure how you want to narrow-down your topic yet, you can just make your topic “journaling” or “productivity” or “cooking,” etc. (big categories). However, it’s worth noting that the more specific you get on the topic, the more helpful ChatGPT and other AI writing tools will be for you—and the easier it will be for you to generate subtopics & proven approaches.

But again, anytime you run into friction, just move on to the next step.

No sense getting in the way of yourself.

Stuck on which of your topics have the most potential? Look at your analytics!

One easy exercise you can do is scroll back through your Twitter or LinkedIn feed and look at how your content is performing.

On X (Twitter) & LinkedIn, you can see all these high-level metrics below each Tweet (from left to right):

  • Comments

  • Retweets

  • Likes

  • Views

It’s worth noting here that you do NOT need to go Analytics Overboard.

Please do not spend 18 hours putting together a perfectly-organized Excel spreadsheet organizing all of your posts alphabetically and stack-ranking them by engagement ratio. There’s no need (and this is more “procrastination” than it is “progress”).

Instead, just give your profiles a quick scroll and ballpark it:

  • Which posts got the most Comments?

  • Which posts got the most Likes?

  • Which posts got the most Views?

See if you can spot any patterns between which topics are prompting the most engagement vs which topics are falling flat.

Then, pick a “winning” topic and get started.

Still stuck on which topic to write about? Use this ChatGPT prompt to get some ideas!

If you’re still stuck, another easy thing you can do is give ChatGPT some background on your life & career (things you’ve experienced: like The 2-Year Test we talk about in Ship 30 for 30, but more like The 10-Year Test) and ask it to generate ideas for you.

For example, here’s the prompt I gave ChatGPT & the “background” on myself I gave it for context:

And look at the amazing topics ChatGPT generated for me to write about!

(I could write about any of these! But the question is: which one do I know the MOST about, right now?)

Here’s the ChatGPT Prompt:

I need some help coming up with topics to write about.

Here is a bit about me:

{5-10 sentences about your life, careers, unique experiences, etc.}

Could you please generate 20 topics I could potentially write about based on what you know about me?
Step 2: Use ChatGPT To Generate 7 Subtopics For 1 Topic

Now that you have a topic chosen, it’s time to generate some subtopics!

Subtopics are the things you can write about “inside” that 1 umbrella topic you’ve chosen.

Where most writers go wrong is they think, “Well, I already wrote about ‘journaling’ and I don’t have anything else to write about on that topic.” But that’s wrong! You have SO many other things you can write about within that topic.

(And the truth is: it doesn’t matter how specific you get, there will always be subtopics to write about inside whatever topic you’ve chosen for yourself.)

What are “Subtopics?”

Here’s an easy way of thinking about it:

Whatever you want to write about, your Subtopics are verbs.

  • Mastering

  • Developing

  • Improving

  • Building

  • Overcoming

  • Achieving

  • Optimizing

…you get the idea.

Subtopics are verbs because whatever it is you want to write about (the Topic) has to be aimed at a reader’s wants, needs, and desires. Which means verbs are “actions” your target reader (the person on the other end consuming your writing on this topic) wants to take. They want to “master” this skill, or “develop” this framework, or “improve” their proficiency, etc.

How To Manually Generate Subtopics

If you want to do this exercise manually, here’s a simple exercise you can do:

Take the 1 topic you want to write about, and then combine it with this extensive list of “verbs” to easily generate a ton of potential Subtopics:

  • Mastering… {Topic}

  • Developing… {Topic}

  • Improving… {Topic}

  • Building… {Topic}

  • Enhancing… {Topic}

  • Overcoming… {Topic}

  • Achieving… {Topic}

  • Optimizing… {Topic}

  • Expanding… {Topic}

  • Creating… {Topic}

  • Exploring… {Topic}

  • Analyzing… {Topic}

  • Understanding… {Topic}

  • Simplifying… {Topic}

  • Strengthening… {Topic}

  • Navigating… {Topic}

  • Innovating… {Topic}

  • Experimenting… {Topic}

  • Refining… {Topic}

  • Adapting… {Topic}

  • Evolving… {Topic}

  • Resolving… {Topic}

  • Uncovering… {Topic}

  • Conquering… {Topic}

  • Growing… {Topic}

  • Maximizing… {Topic}

  • Streamlining… {Topic}

  • Designing… {Topic}

  • Strategizing… {Topic}

  • Reframing… {Topic}

  • Reinventing… {Topic}

  • Establishing… {Topic}

  • Refocusing… {Topic}

  • Customizing… {Topic}

  • Reducing… {Topic}

  • Eliminating… {Topic}

  • Leveraging… {Topic}

  • Focusing… {Topic}

  • Differentiating… {Topic}

  • Aligning… {Topic}

Phew!

That’s a lot of options!

But remember, just as we shared with you in Ship 30 for 30, first it’s important to understand how the framework/exercise works manually—but then, you should use technology (AI) to “do the doing” for you!

So…

Here’s the ChatGPT prompt to do this for you!

Just copy/paste this prompt below into ChatGPT, give it your Topic, and it will give you back 7 Subtopics you can dig into.

I am a digital writer and you are my personal idea generation consultant.

You are an expert in coming up with topics and subtopics that my audience will find useful.

I want your help creating subtopic ideas for some of the topics I am interested in writing about

What are subtopics?

Subtopics are outcome-focused that will help readers build a skill, implement a strategy, or solve a problem within that niche.

Rules when creating subtopics:
- You MUST begin each subtopic with a verb to create a clear action-oriented focus.
- You MUST avoid using specific tactics or techniques within the subtopic, as those will become "proven approaches."

Here are 40 potential subtopic "verbs" you can use:

- Mastering
- Developing
- Improving
- Building
- Enhancing
- Overcoming
- Achieving
- Optimizing
- Expanding
- Creating
- Exploring
- Analyzing
- Understanding
- Simplifying
- Strengthening
- Navigating
- Innovating
- Experimenting
- Refining
- Adapting
- Evolving
- Resolving
- Uncovering
- Conquering
- Growing
- Maximizing
- Streamlining
- Designing
- Strategizing
- Reframing
- Reinventing
- Establishing
- Refocusing
- Customizing
- Reducing
- Eliminating
- Leveraging
- Focusing
- Differentiating
- Aligning

Here is an example:

Topic: Running your first marathon

Subtopics:

- Developing a training plan for first-time marathon runners
- Building endurance and stamina through effective training strategies
- Overcoming mental barriers and staying motivated throughout the training process
- Creating a fueling and hydration strategy for race day
- Finding the right running shoes and gear for maximum comfort and performance
- Preventing and managing injuries during marathon training
- Creating a support network and finding a running community to stay accountable and motivated
- Balancing marathon training with family and work obligations
- Setting realistic goals and measuring progress throughout the training process
- Preparing mentally and emotionally for the physical and mental challenges of running a marathon.

Here is what I want to avoid:

- Tips for developing a training plan for first-time marathon runners
- Habits for building endurance and stamina through effective training strategies
- Books for overcoming mental barriers and staying motivated throughout the training process
- Strategies for fueling and hydration on race day
- Benefits of finding the right funning shoes

The difference between my ideal list and the list of what I want to avoid:

- Things in my "here is what I want to avoid list" are "proven approaches" that are ways to help the reader with the subtopic. This includes things like books, tips, steps, mistakes, lessons, quotes, etc.
- I want to avoid ever providing "proven approaches" as my subtopics.

Now, here is the assignment:
- You are going to help me generate 7 subtopics.
- You will ask me for the topic I want to write about. When I answer, you will reply with 7 subtopics and only that list of 7 subtopics.

Do you understand?

If so, confirm and ask me for the topic
Step 3: Use ChatGPT To Generate Proven Approaches For Each Of The 7 Subtopics (For 1 Topic)

In your Idea File, you should have 1 Topic & 7 Subtopics.

Next, it’s time to start filling in each Subtopic with all the things you could write about!

Generating Proven Approaches (Per Subtopic)

If Subtopics are “verbs,” then Proven Approaches are “nouns.”

They are the things readers want/need IN ORDER TO achieve the outcome/verb.

A few quick examples to show you how this works:

  • Tips (noun) → …to build (verb).

  • Mistakes (noun) → …to avoid (verb).

  • Lessons (noun) → …to achieve (verb).

Etc.

This little equation is the easiest way to start generating an endless amount of ideas on any given topic.

Proven Approaches Framed As Questions

Now, staring at a list of Proven Approaches (nouns) might be a good way to generate ideas, but we’ve found it’s even easier if each Proven Approach is framed as a question.

For example, let’s say our topic is Premium Ghostwriting:

  • V1: Tips to become a premium ghostwriter

  • V2: What are 3 tips you would give someone who wants to become a premium ghostwriter?

As soon as it’s framed as a question, it’s much easier to imagine yourself “writing the answer.”

So, instead of just generating ideas based on a list of Proven Approaches, let’s train ChatGPT to generate ideas in the form of questions.

Here’s the ChatGPT prompt to do this for you!

Copy/paste this prompt into a new window in ChatGPT:

I am a digital writer and you are my personal idea generation consultant. You are an expert in coming up with writing ideas.

I want your help generating 20 quantifiable, proven-approach based questions to help me explore subtopics within a topic I am interested in writing about based on the list of proven-approach based questions I give you below.

What are subtopics?
- Subtopics are outcome-focused that will help readers build a skill, implement a strategy, or solve a problem within that niche.
- They ALWAYS begin with a verb to create a clear action-oriented focus

Here is a list of proven-approach based questions:

Tips: What are 3 tips for mastering this skill effectively?
Skills: What are the top 3 essential skills needed to succeed in this area?
Tools: What are the 3 best tools available for this task?
Prompts: What are 3 ChatGPT prompts someone could use for this prompt?
Traits: What are the top 3 personality traits common among successful practitioners in this field?
Steps: What are the 3 key steps involved in mastering this technique?
Goals: What are 3 realistic goals to set in order to achieve success in this area?
Books: What are the top 3 must-read books on this subject?
Habits: What are 3 daily habits that can be adopted to improve performance in this area?
Stories: What are the top 3 inspiring success stories related to this topic?
Quotes: What are the top 3 motivational quotes that relate to this topic?
Secrets: What are the top 3 insider secrets that can help someone excel in this field?
Insights: What are the top 3 key insights that can help someone understand this topic better?
Benefits: What are the top 3 benefits of mastering this skill?
Lessons: What are the top 3 important lessons that can be learned from past failures in this area?
Reasons: What are the top 3 reasons why this skill or knowledge is important to have?
Creators: Who are the top 3 creators or experts in this field that someone should follow?
Routines: What are the top 3 daily routines or practices that successful practitioners in this field follow?
Mistakes: What are the top 3 common mistakes to avoid in this area?
Podcasts: What are the top 3 podcasts related to this topic?
Examples: What are the top 3 examples of successful applications of this knowledge or skill?
Questions: What are the top 3 key questions that someone should be asking in order to learn more about this area?
Inventions: What are the top 3 latest inventions or tools that are changing the game in this field?
Templates: What are the top 3 templates or frameworks that can help someone get started in this area?
Resources: What are the top 3 best resources available for learning about this topic?
Challenges: What are the top 3 common challenges or obstacles that people face when trying to master this skill?
Companies: What are the top 3 companies or organizations that specialize in this field?
Data Points: What are the top 3 key data points or statistics related to this topic?
Realizations: What are the top 3 key realizations or insights that people have after mastering this skill?
Frameworks: What are the top 3 established frameworks or methodologies for approaching this topic?
Presentations: What are the top 3 presentations or talks related to this topic that someone should watch?

Important rules:
- Quantifiable, proven-approach-based questions ask for a specific number.
- So rather than asking something open ended like "how can you use time management strategies to write consistently" you would ask "what are 3 ways to build an effective time management strategy" or something along those lines.
- This is a very important rule. Only ask questions that ask for a specific list of 3 items.

ALSO: You must only use the 20 proven approaches listed in my list. Do not make up your own.

Here is what we are going to do:
1. You will ask me for the topic I am interested in and the subtopic within that topic I am writing about
2. You will then generate 20 quantifiable, proven approach based question for each of the examples I listed.

Are you ready to help me generate ideas?

If so, ask for my topic and subtopic.

Then give it:

  • Topic = {Your Topic}

  • Subtopic = {1 of the 7 Subtopics from the previous module, copy/pasted}

Voila!

So, go ahead and fill in 20 Proven Approach “Questions” for each of your 7 Subtopics

Once you have gone through the above exercise, copy/paste the 20 Proven Approach “questions” ChatGPT generates for you, based on 1 Subtopic, and bring them into your Idea File.

Click the dropdown on Subtopic #1 and you will see 20 “question” toggles. Replace {Question} with the actual question ChatGPT asked you.

Do this for each of your 7 Subtopics.

(7 Subtopics x 20 Proven Approach questions for each = 140 things you could write about!)

Completing Your Idea File

You’ve done it!

You have successfully created an entire Idea File for 1 topic.

Which means now it’s time to start answering all these questions you have, inside each Subtopic, and turning your answers into “Outlines As Content” (short-form posts… so that you can keep gathering data and learning what readers find most interesting).

But first…

Still not sure if this is the topic you want to write about?

Here’s the beauty of starting with an Idea File.

If you go through this exercise and find it to be WAY more challenging than you thought, chances are, you picked a topic you “thought you wanted to write about” but might not actually enjoy writing about (or be ready to write about). Conversely, if you went through this exercise and found it extremely easy to complete, chances are, this is a great topic for you to start with!

The easier it is to create an Idea File, the more you should consider writing about that topic.

And the harder it is to create an Idea File, the more you should take that as a warning that you might not know as much about this topic as you think—you should start with something you could write about more easily.

With that in mind… start filling in your Idea File by answering each question!

How to create “Outlines As Content” for each question:

1 Topic, 7 Subtopics, 20 Questions per Subtopic.

The final step of completing your Idea File is to actually start answering each question inside the drop-down menus.

For example:

If ChatGPT gives you the question, “What are 3 tips for choosing a profitable niche as a premium ghostwriter?” you can go ahead and just answer that question in that question’s drop-down menu. Like this:

Because guess what…?!

  • Your answer to this question is a Tweet.

  • Your answer to this question is the outline of an Atomic Essay.

  • Your answer to this question is the outline of a Twitter Thread.

  • Your answer to this question is the outline of a long-form LinkedIn post.

That’s 4 different assets you can easily create from 1 Topic, 1 Subtopic, and just 1 Question!

Pretty cool, right?

But wait… we can train ChatGPT to help fill in answers to all these questions too!

Here’s the ChatGPT prompt to do this for you.

Copy/paste this prompt into a new window in ChatGPT:

I am a digital writer and you are my personal idea generation consultant.

You are an expert in helping me fill in a content file of questions related to a topic and subtopic I want to write about.

I need your help answering some of these questions and giving me new potential angles to answer the questions.

Here is what we are going to do:
1. I am going to input a topic, subtopic, and list of 20 questions to you
2. You will then ask if I am ready for the first question.
3. Upon confirmation, you will ask me the first question but you WILL NOT ANSWER IT.

*IMPORTANT* - You will ask the question to me and nothing else, do not answer it or ask more than 1 question at a time.

For example, you will simply repeat the first question back to me. Do not answer it. Do not provide anything else other than the question.

If this was my list of questions:

1. Tips: What are 3 tips for choosing a profitable niche as a premium ghostwriter?
2. Skills: What are the top 3 essential skills needed to become a successful premium ghostwriter in a niche?
3. Tools: What are the 3 best tools available for researching and selecting a niche as a premium ghostwriter?
4. Prompts: What are 3 ChatGPT prompts someone could use to brainstorm their niche as a premium ghostwriter?
5. Traits: What are the top 3 personality traits common among successful premium ghostwriters in a niche?
6. Steps: What are the 3 key steps involved in establishing yourself as a go-to premium ghostwriter in your niche?
7. Goals: What are 3 realistic goals to set in order to establish yourself as a top premium ghostwriter in your niche?
8. Books: What are the top 3 must-read books on selecting and dominating a niche as a premium ghostwriter?
9. Habits: What are 3 daily habits that can be adopted to increase your visibility and authority as a premium ghostwriter in your niche?
10. Stories: What are the top 3 inspiring success stories of premium ghostwriters who have successfully claimed their niche?
11. Quotes: What are the top 3 motivational quotes that relate to the importance of finding and dominating a niche as a premium ghostwriter?
12. Secrets: What are the top 3 insider secrets that can help someone establish themselves as a top premium ghostwriter in a niche?
13. Insights: What are the top 3 key insights that can help someone understand the importance of finding and dominating a niche as a premium ghostwriter?
14. Benefits: What are the top 3 benefits of establishing yourself as a top premium ghostwriter in a niche?
15. Lessons: What are the top 3 important lessons that can be learned from past failures of ghostwriters who did not properly claim their niche?
16. Reasons: What are the top 3 reasons why it is essential to name and claim your niche as a premium ghostwriter?
17. Creators: Who are the top 3 creators or experts in the field of premium ghostwriting who specialize in niches?
18. Routines: What are the top 3 daily routines or practices that successful premium ghostwriters in a niche follow?
19. Mistakes: What are the top 3 common mistakes to avoid when trying to name and claim your niche as a premium ghostwriter?
20. Podcasts: What are the top 3 podcasts related to premium ghostwriting and niches that someone should listen to for tips and insights?

Then your first output back to me will be:

1. Tips: What are 3 tips for using journaling to cultivate a growth mindset and overcome limiting beliefs?

From here, 2 things can happen:
1. If I give you the answer, you will simply repeat the question back to me with the answers as bullet points & ask me if I am ready to move onto the next question
2. If I say I don't know, you will outline the answer in bullet points, then ask me if I am ready to move onto the next question

Upon confirmation, you will ask me the next question.

Are you ready to help me answer questions?

What’s going to happen is:

  • You are going to give ChatGPT your Topic, Subtopic, and the list of 20 questions it gave you for that Subtopic.

  • ChatGPT will then ask if you are ready for the first question.

  • You can then either answer the question (and use ChatGPT as a “pretend audience” as you write your answer). OR, if you don’t know how you would answer that question, you can say, “I don’t know,” and ChatGPT will fill in the answer for you.

Pretty wild, right?

Answer All 20 “Questions” For Each Of Your 7 Subtopics

Here’s how it should look:

First give ChatGPT your Topic, 1 Subtopic, and the 20 Questions it generated for that 1 Subtopic.

Then, ChatGPT will ask you the first question—giving you the opportunity to either answer it yourself, or say “I don’t know” and have ChatGPT help you out.

Voila!

From here, every time you (or ChatGPT) answer a question, copy/paste that answer into that question’s drop-down menu in your Idea File.

Do this for all 7 Subtopics, and all 20 questions inside each Subtopic, and you will have more content than you could ever imagine creating—all for 1 single topic!

records.content:
Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 4 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this first week is: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

And a crucial part of developing the mindset of a Digital Writer is to understand how the game of “credibility” works on the Internet.

So, let’s dive in!

Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility

First of all, what even is “credibility?”

A lot of people think it’s:

  • Winning the Nobel prize

  • Being on the cover of a magazine

  • Writing a New York Times best-selling book

  • Etc.

And yes, while these are certainly trophies that signal “credibility,” they aren’t the ONLY ways to let people know you’re a credible voice on a specific topic—and they certainly aren’t “required” in order to get people to read your writing.

Credibility could also be small achievements.

And not even “achievements,” but life milestones:

  • “I am a new mom” is credibility because you had a kid! (To anyone who DOESN’T have a kid, you are now credible on this topic.)

  • “I have built an audience of 5,000 software developers on LinkedIn” is credible because an audience of 5,000 people is more than 0. (To anyone who DOESN’T have 5,000 followers, you are credible.)

  • “I have overcome cancer” is credible because you beat a life-threatening disease. (To anyone who DOESN’T have cancer, or is in the process of fighting cancer, you are credible.)

So, what’s your credibility?

Well, first you need to understand there are 2 types of credibility:

  • Personal Credibility: Sharing what you know based on your own personal experience.

  • Borrowed Credibility: Sharing what someone else knows based on their experience.

If you struggle with Imposter Syndrome, it’s because you are trying to write about topics in which you have no personal credibility. (Like writing about what it’s like to be a doctor without actually being a doctor.) Which makes sense! You’re trying to be something you’re not.

Instead, here’s an easy framework you can use to get rid of Imposter’s Syndrome forever:

  • If you are writing about something you have personally experienced, then it doesn’t matter if you’re a “guru” or not. Just tell the reader: “I’m just telling you what I experienced here.” That’s all the reader needs to know in order to trust you.

  • And if you are writing about something you don’t have personal experience in, then “borrow” someone else’s credibility and share what THEY have to say about the topic. For example: you don’t have to be a professional copywriter to share David Ogilvy’s rules for successful copywriting. Because “your” credibility doesn’t matter. You are borrowing David Ogilvy’s.

And here are 2 examples (from us) on how these 2 different forms of credibility change the way you approach the writing:

Here, Dickie is BORROWING credibility by writing about his lessons learned from Gray Halbert (a very credible & successful sales copywriter).

And here, Cole is using PERSONAL credibility to write about ghostwriting—a topic he has personally experienced.

So, before you start writing… you need to know:

  • Are you writing this from a place of Personal Credibility?

  • Or is this a topic that would lend itself better to Borrowed Credibility?

Questions

Now, here are some of the most common questions we get asked whenever we talk about Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility:

  • “But what if I don’t have any personal credibility?” Chances are, you do, you just don’t realize it. Again, personal credibility can be something as simple as: “I moved across the country.” Great, you are “credible” to write about YOUR EXPERIENCE moving across the country, lessons you learned, mistakes you made, things you would do differently next time, etc. And if you truly have no credibility on a topic, then a) why are you writing about that topic? And/or b) you should consider writing about that topic with Borrowed Credibility instead.

  • “But what if someone calls me out for not being an expert?” As long as you are writing about your PERSONAL EXPERIENCE, nobody can call you out for “not being an expert.” Because you’re not trying to be! You’re simply sharing what you’ve learned—and that’s going to be very valuable to anyone a few steps “behind you.”

  • “But how do I position myself as a thought leader on a topic if I’m just writing about things I’ve personally experienced that have nothing to do with that topic?” Let’s level-set here: your primary goal, for now, is to build your daily writing habit. You don’t need to “have it all figured out.” We’re just getting reps. And second, if you want to become a “thought leader,” you have to have specialty knowledge. And so if you don’t have specialty knowledge, then you should be Borrowing Credibility to write about the things you’re LEARNING as you acquire that specialty knowledge.

Assignment

Your ship is really starting to sail now!

Your Day 4 Assignment is to write today’s Atomic Essay using Personal Credibility. What is something you can point to that makes you “credible” to talk about a certain topic? And remember… it can be something really simple!

  • If you want to write about running marathons, you can say, “…because I have run a marathon before.”

  • If you want to write about cooking, you can say, “…because I cook our family’s meals every single day.”

  • If you want to write about buying real estate, you can say, “…because I just bought my first rental property.”

  • Etc.

So, use Personal Credibility to write today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish, and just like that… another day of writing is in the books.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
The 4A Framework

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 5 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this first week is: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

And today, we are going to change the way you look at writing (and the things you read) forever.

With…

The 4A Framework

You might not realize it, but almost all writing can be reverse engineered into just 4 paths:

  • Actionable: How To do something.

  • Analytical: Why something happens, according to data or research.

  • Aspirational: Motivation. If I can, you can too.

  • Anthropological: Human nature. Why, according to psychology.

And the beautiful part of the 4A Framework is it makes you realize you can build an entire career around just ONE of these paths.

And we can prove it.

What if we asked you, “What’s your favorite book on the topic of money/finance?”

What would you say? Which book would you think about? Which writer would come to mind?

Check this out:

Notice how all of these books technically fall under the category of “money,” but approach the topic in COMPLETELY different ways.

Furthermore, your favorite “book” here doesn’t actually have as much to do with the author as you might think. It has a LOT more to do with whether you love Actionable content or Analytical content, Aspirational content or Anthropological content.

So, which one of these paths do you read most often?

Which one of these paths have you been gravitating to in your writing?

Which one do you want to explore more?

The more you write online, the more you will start to realize which of these 4As you are best at.

(For example: we have learned we are very good at writing Actionable and Aspirational content. And we don’t write about Analytical or Anthropological content very much. Not because they aren’t good paths, but because we’ve learned where our strengths are!)

Questions

Now, here are some of the most common questions we get asked whenever we explain the 4A Framework:

  • “Can you combine these paths?” Yes! You might write something that is both Actionable and Aspirational, or Analytical and Aspirational, etc. However, it’s important to recognize that usually ONE of the 4A paths takes the spotlight. Your readers (especially the longer you write online) will begin to associate you with a given “type” of writing—and that’s a good thing.

  • “What if I want to change my 4A path later? Is that OK?” Absolutely. It’s just worth recognizing that the goal is to figure out what your readers value hearing about from you most, and giving them that thing. For example, you probably love a certain author because of how “Analytical” they are, or how “Aspirational” they are, etc. And if you love that about them, and then they suddenly drop something Anthropological, that doesn’t mean you’re never going to read their work again. But you might not give their Anthropological work much attention because that’s not what you go to them for.

  • “Do I have to pick my 4A path before I start writing?” In the long-term, no. It’s very hard to know which of the 4A’s is your strength BEFORE you start writing (but over time, it will become clear to you). However, in the short term, before you write anything, it’s worth asking which of the 4A’s it is. For example, when you write your Atomic Essay for the day today, are you going to write something Actionable? Analytical? Aspirational? Anthropological? In everything you write, you should know which one it is—so that you can deliver for that type of reader.

Assignment

Just like that… Day 5 is done!

Your Day 5 Assignment is to take 1 topic you’re excited to write about (doesn’t have to be your “forever” topic, this isn’t a marriage decision!) and run it through the 4A Framework. This will show you the different ways you can approach writing about that 1 topic—and give you more ideas of things to write about over the coming days.

For example, for the topic of Digital Writing, ours might be:

  • Actionable: How To Write Your First Viral Post On LinkedIn

  • Analytical: Why This Thread Hook Performed 4x Better Than All Our Previous Hooks…. Combined!

  • Aspirational: How I Went From Being A Broke Freelance Writer To One Of The Highest-Paid Ghostwriters On The Planet

  • Anthropological: The 3 Faulty Beliefs That Hold People Back From Starting To Write On The Internet (And How To Solve Them)

So, use the 4A Framework, and then pick 1 of the ideas you generate to write today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 6 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember, the theme for this first week is: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

Today, we are going to obliterate Writer’s Block once and for all.

The Endless Idea Generator

Over the past few days, we have walked you through:

  • The 2-Year Test

  • Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility

  • The 4A Framework

And we wanted to separate each of these ideas because they are important to understand in and of themselves.

However… when you put them all together… you get The Endless Idea Generator!

So, every time you sit down to write, or every time you’re brainstorming new ideas, put all these different frameworks together:

  • The 2-Year Test: Start by asking yourself what you want to write about based on things you’ve learned or experienced over the past 2 years. (And try to get as specific as you can about the topic.)

  • Personal Credibility vs Borrowed Credibility: Once you have your topic, is this something you feel comfortable writing about based on your own personal experience? Or would it be better to leverage someone else’s experience/expertise and borrow their credibility?

  • The 4A Paths: How do you want to approach this topic? Do you want to teach the reader How To do it (Actionable)? Do you want to explain why something works the way it does using data (Analytical)? Do you want to motivate or inspire the reader (Aspirational)? Or do you want to dig into the psychology of the topic (Anthropological)?

This = endless ideas.

Oh, and if you want AI to help, we built the EIG right into Typeshare.

Click here to start generating endless ideas with AI!

Questions

  • “How does the EIG work for really advanced topics, like medicine?” It doesn’t matter what you want to write about, all topics follow the same fundamental rules. So, if you are writing about “medicine,” OK… FOR WHO? Doctors? What kind of doctors? First-year doctors or doctors who have been practicing for 30+ years? OK… SO THAT they can do what? What are you going to help them do? Is it Actionable? Is it Analytical? Is it Aspirational? Is it Anthropological?

  • “I don’t think AI is very good at helping generate high-quality ideas.” Play with the Idea Generator in Typeshare and you’ll be pleasantly surprised!

  • “It’s taking me a long time to come up with ideas using the EIG. Any suggestions?” Yes. Keep at it. You’re building a new skill. But the more you use these frameworks, the faster you will get. We promise. (We use the EIG every single day, and at this point for us we can run through it in seconds. Just practice!)

Assignment

Alright, ideas are one thing… but what REALLY matters is hitting publish!

Today’s Day 6 Assignment is to use the EIG (either manually, or the AI-powered EIG inside Typeshare) to generate 5+ ideas. And remember: you can take the same topic/idea and change it by:

  • Making it more specific (different FOR WHO, and/or different SO THAT)

  • Changing the credibility (personal vs borrowed)

  • Choosing a different 4A path (Actionable, Analytical, Aspirational, Anthropological)

Endless ideas!

Then use 1 of your new ideas to write today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

And just like that, you now have everything you need to generate more ideas you can possibly write about.

However, as you’ve probably noticed already, we like to be efficient here.

Why waste time doing things we could outsource to our robot writing intern, right?

So, we’ve put together a mega-prompt to help you train ChatGPT on the Endless Idea Generator—and become an absolute idea machine (quite literally).

All you need to make it work is:

  • A topic

  • A “FOR WHO”

  • And a “SO THAT”

Once you have those 3 puzzle pieces, you can use the prompt below to start generating content ideas on autopilot:

I am going to train you to become an Endless Idea Generation Machine.

Here's how it works: there are 4 types of ideas we can generate.

The 4 primary types of ideas are:

- Actionable
- Analytical
- Aspirational
- Anthropological

Then there are sub-topics within each of these buckets:

Actionable (here's how)

- Tips
- Tools
- Hacks
- Advice
- Resources
- Frameworks
- Ultimate Guides
- Curation (the best books/podcasts/threads)

Analytical (here's a breakdown)

- Trends
- Numbers
- Reasons
- Examples
- Teardowns
- Swipe files

Aspirational (yes, you can)

- Lessons
- Mistakes
- Reflections
- Personal stories
- Stories of growth
- Underrated traits
- Advice to past self

Anthropological (here’s why)

- Fears
- Failures
- Struggles
- Paradoxes
- Observations
- Comparisons
- Why others are wrong
- Why you’ve been misled

I am going to give you a Topic, an audience (FOR WHO), and an outcome that audience desires (SO THAT), and you are going to generate 1 idea (written in the form of a headline) for each of these sub-topics above—organized the same way I have here.

Do you understand?

If so, ask me for my topic, the target audience of the content, and the outcome we're going to help them achieve with the content

records.content:
Another common question we always get from Shippers whenever we explain how the EIG works:

“But Dickie… Cole… Can I also use the EIG to generate newsletter ideas?”

And the answer is, OF COURSE!

However, there’s another framework we really like using when we’re writing a newsletter:

Pinpoint Writing.

And since we know there’s many Shippers who’re looking to eventually launch a newsletter and start building an email list, we thought you could find this framework helpful.

So, here’s a lesson from our Full Stack Writer Newsletter Writing Module where we break down how we use our Pinpoint Writing framework (and ChatGPT) to write newsletters our readers love—in less than 15 minutes.

Enjoy!

Pinpoint Writing: How To Go From Idea To Newsletter In 11 Minutes

As a reminder: If you’d like to learn how to master the art of crafting newsletters your readers love (as well as the 6 other skills you need to build a 7-figure writing business), click here to join Full Stack Writer.

Pinpoint Writing means using specificity to gain clarity as to who exactly your target reader is (by answering the following questions):

  • What problem am I solving?

  • Whose problem am I solving?

  • What emotion am I creating?

  • What action am I encouraging?

  • What benefit am I unlocking?

From here, writing is simple.

Write directly to one person to solve one problem. And solve their problem by generating one emotion, to get them to take one action, so they can unlock one specific benefit. But here's the most important thing to keep in mind.

You're not actually writing for one person— you're writing for the hundreds, thousands, or millions of other people who have this exact problem.

And if you think you're being too specific, you're failing to recognize the scale of the internet.

Because if you can solve one person's problem, the sheer size of the internet guarantees there are countless others just like them.

Let’s dive in!

Enter ChatGPT: Newsletter Writing Assistant

Most people ignore ChatGPT’s ability to ask clarifying questions—diving head first into commanding AI to do everything for you while forgetting it knows nothing about you.

But a good intern always asks questions to understand what YOU, the boss, want and think. It’s one of the most powerful functions of a Digital Intern. And as a writer, that's pure gold. Because if you can pinpoint what you're thinking, you have clarity in what you're saying.

And with a little guidance, ChatGPT can help you clarify your thinking.

Here’s how it works:

Step 1: Pick a topic

It can be a rough idea or even a fleeting thought.

  • “Scenic roadside photos on I-70 westbound”

  • “I forgot to eat breakfast. It ruined my morning.”

  • “How to turn ChatGPT into your personal thinking assistant”

Choose 1 thing on your mind you want to write about, but that you haven’t spent the necessary time to think through yet.

Let’s move on to the next step.

Step 2: Run the “Pinpoint Writing” prompt.

Give ChatGPT your topic and it will:

  • Ask you questions

  • Challenge your biases

  • And even offer a new perspective

In essence, it’s like having a mentor on speed dial.

Hello, ChatGPT!

Today, we are going to do an exercise I call “Pinpoint Writing.”

I want you to help me:

  • Pinpont my point of view

  • Refine my point of view

  • And help me think clearly about a topic

Ultimately, I want to get clarity on 5 things:

  1. What problem am I solving?

  2. Whose problem am I solving?

  3. What benefit am I unlocking?

  4. What emotion am I creating?

  5. What action am I encouraging?

You will help me test the strength of my topic, identify underlying assumptions, examples, values, influences, etc. Feel free to play devil's advocate. Follow the direction of the conversation naturally. You can ask a variety of surface level, straightforward, and challenging questions to push my thinking. Point out inconsistencies or contradictions you find along the way. We don't need to dive too deep into psychology.

I will respond in brief or in depth.

I only want 1 question at a time, so that I can focus. You can ask follow up questions after each answer. I may ask you to pause along they way to summarize. We will continue until I say stop.

To start, I will give you the topic I want to focus on.

Are you ready?

Step 3: Think WITH ChatGPT.

Treat the conversation like one you would have with a curious friend or a mentor.

We’ve trained ChatGPT on the types of questions we want it to ask. The questions are designed to make your writing sharper, more defined, and resonate better with your target audience. But just like the real world, you have a role to play too.

You have to work with AI.

  • If a question is irrelevant, give ChatGPT the feedback and it will adjust.

  • If a question makes you uncomfortable, tell it you want to avoid sensitive topics.

  • If you want to explore an angle further, guide ChatGPT in that direction.

You might be surprised at how a simple back and forth chat can unearth layers of depth in your thinking just from the seed of an idea.

Step 4: Ask ChatGPT to sum up your thoughts.

When you are done “thinking,” ask ChatGPT to summarize everything for you.

And once you’ve done the thinking, you can hire ChatGPT to turn your thinking into anything you want!

Step 5: Transform your thinking into a newsletter.

Remember, after you’ve done the thinking, writing is simple.

And with AI it’s even easier. Because you can turn your thinking into a list of headlines, a LinkedIn post, an “X” post, a newsletter, etc. with a few simple prompts and a good template.

For example:

Ask ChatGPT to brainstorm a list of “Irresistible Headlines” with the following prompt:

Great, now using the summary of the "Pinpoint Writing" exercise I want you to write 10 “Irresistible Headlines”

An “Irresistible Headline” has these 5 fundamental pieces.

Beside each piece, I am going to give you some examples so you can learn:

  • HOW MANY (a number): 6 tips, 7 reasons, 11 mistakes, etc.

  • THE WHO (an audience): for project managers, for therapists, for founders, etc.

  • THE WHAT (a noun): tips, reasons, mistakes, lessons, examples, templates, case studies, etc.

  • THE WHY (a reason/outcome): to get promoted, to not lose your job, to buy your first house, etc.

  • “TWIST THE KNIFE” (2-3 additional benefits/outcomes): to attract your first 5 high-ticket clients and move into your dream office.

And then turn a headline into a newsletter (or article) using a template.

Here’s the prompt you can use to write an article based on Hudson Rennie’s $100 Article Template. But you can replace the template in the prompt with any template you like. (There are hundreds of templates inside Typeshare.co that you can leverage with this prompt.)

Great, now I want you to write a newsletter post about:

{Your Headline}

Use the following template to write the newsletter post:

Headline

Summarize the newsletter in one sentence.

Write an introduction that answers these 3 questions and makes a promise:

  • What’s it about?

  • Why should readers care?

  • What question needs answering?

— Promise the answer to a tantalizing question.

Sub-head

  • Provide history/background

  • Paint a picture — show don’t tell

  • Expand on the “what” or “why” to create intrigue

Sub-head

Lead up to the answer:

  • “Now, you’re probably thinking this.”

  • “Here’s the thing about this answer.”

  • “Let’s talk about why this is important.”

Introduce the answer but don’t give it away just yet.

Sub-head

Give the reader what they want:

  • Provide the answer readers came for

  • Tell the story you promised in your introduction

Don’t skimp out or withhold information:

  • If you promised 5 tips on ______, give the best 5 tips

  • If your headline reads “How To Do ______”, teach them exactly how

  • If your story is about the rise and fall of ______, cover the rise, fall, and everything in between

Sub-head

If there’s more to the story, add it here:

  • What it means to you

  • What or why it’s important

  • How it differed from original perspectives

Conclusion

You’ve told your story and given your gift. Now, tie a bow on it:

  • Offer key takeaways

  • Summarize what was learned

  • Help solidify into memory with a bullet list

Boom!

And just like that, you’ve gone from the inkling of an idea to a well thought out newsletter in a matter of minutes. Because you, my dear Digital Writer, have learned to leverage the power of AI to accelerate your writing AND your thinking!

records.description: The Lean Writing Framework Ahoy! Welcome to Day 7 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer. This is the last day we’ll spend on
records.content:
The Lean Writing Framework

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 7 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

This is the last day we’ll spend on the theme of: Adopting The Mindset Of A Digital Writer.

And what better way to end this first week than introduce you to…

The Lean Writing Framework

The Lean Writing Framework goes like this:

  • A tweet is...

  • An Atomic Essay...

  • Is an Ultimate Guide...

  • Is a free e-mail course...

  • Is a paid digital product...

  • Is an online course...

  • Is a community...

  • Is a business.

What this means is (walking in reverse now)…

Before you start a business, you should understand what community you can create for the customer.

But before you bother creating a community for the customer, you should know what asset they find most valuable inside that community and what urgent problem you’re helping them solve for themselves in their life.

But before you invest hours and hours into creating a full-fledged online course for this person, you should beta test your idea by selling a more compressed, less expensive version of your course in the form of a digital product.

But before you invest the time to even create a $10 or $20 (or $100) digital product, you should see whether or not you are able to solve any of your target reader’s problems for free via an e-mail course.

But before you take the time to write out a full e-mail course, you should probably see whether or not they are interested in reading a 2,500-word Ultimate Guide.

But before you take the time to write that Ultimate Guide, you it’s in your best interest to validate your topic idea by just writing a 250-word Atomic Essay.

And if you really want to micro-test your idea before even taking the time to do that, well, then just fire off a Tweet.

This is how Lean Writing works.

The big idea here is that before you invest time in writing longer-form content (or building longer-form digital products), you should test and validate your ideas in their most Atomic form.

Which is why we believe the Atomic Essay is so foundational.

Writing Atomic Essays is not just about learning the fundamentals of Digital Writing. Atomic Essays are effective because they are just the right amount of words to explore one single idea with a bit of depth (something you can’t always do with just a Tweet) without over-investing in any individual idea before you know whether or not it resonates with readers (like writing an 800-word blog post or a 2,500-word Ultimate Guide).

Then, when you write an Atomic Essay that strikes a chord, all you have to do is expand it.

  • Turn that Atomic Essay into an Ultimate Guide

  • Turn that Ultimate Guide into a free e-mail course

  • Turn that free e-mail course into a Digital Product

  • Turn that Digital Product into a course

Why invest 100 or 1,000 or 10,000 hours into writing or creating something (like a book or a course) before you know, objectively, that topic is something readers are interested in?

You shouldn’t.

Not in the Digital Age.

The Lean Writing Framework removes all guessing from the equation.

  • No sitting there, staring out the window, waiting for the “perfect idea” to arrive.

  • No helplessly wondering whether or not people are going to love your idea.

  • No investing hundreds or thousands (or tens of thousands) of hours into an idea you aren’t sure will work.

  • And no creating things that end up falling on deaf ears.

By the time you write your book, create your digital product, or launch your course or community, it shouldn’t be a question as to whether or not people will want to buy it.

You should already know.

30 Proven Approaches (How To Write About The Same Topic Over & Over Again)

Now, with the Lean Writing Framework in mind, how are you supposed to test lots of little ideas AND double-down on the ideas that appear to be working?

Very simple!

At the end of the day, ALL readers (regardless of industry, niche, topic, or audience) are interested in the same things.

You could write about ANY topic in all the following ways:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

This is how you can write about 1 topic for a very, very, very long time (and it’ll never stop being valuable to your target reader).

Questions

Now, here are some of the most common questions we get asked about The Lean Writing Framework:

  • “I wrote an Atomic Essay about a topic and it didn’t perform well. Does that mean I should never write about that topic again?” Not necessarily. Notice the data point, but it’s worth giving any topic you care about a good amount of effort before calling it quits.

  • “How many times should I write about a topic before I decide whether it’s worth expanding or not?” You should write about any topic you care about at LEAST 5 times, ideally 10 times in order to gather enough data to make a decision.

  • “What do I do if a topic performs well, but I don’t want to keep writing about it?” You don’t have to! All we’re trying to do is make you more conscious of the opportunities in front of you based on how readers respond to your writing.

  • “Won’t my readers get bored if I keep writing about the same topic over and over again?” No, actually readers love it. We typically don’t get ALL of our education or information or entertainment from just one person. We go to 1 creator for something, and we go to another writer for something else, and another person for something else, etc. So you leaning into 1 topic over and over again is only going to attract MORE people interested in that topic.

That’s It!

Alrighty—less reading, more writing!

Your Day 7 Assignment is to use the Lean Writing method (and the 30 Proven Approaches) to generate 30 more ideas for yourself! Yes, this is a heftier assignment, but we promise this will show you how much you can say about any given topic—and give you TONS of ideas to keep writing about over the coming weeks.

So, take 1 topic and run it through the 30 Proven Approaches.

Then, pick just 1 and write today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish and onto Week 2!

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.description: Irresistible Headlines, Part I Ahoy! Welcome to Day 8 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer. The theme for this second week
records.content:
Irresistible Headlines, Part I

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 8 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

The theme for this second week is: Headlines & Hooks!

By the end of this week, you’ll never write headlines the same way ever again—and your writing, copywriting, and storytelling skills will skyrocket.

Are you ready?

Let’s dive in!

Questions (Headline Pushbacks)

But first, there are 3 pushbacks we hear time and time again whenever we first introduce this way of thinking to new writers (and all 3 are incorrect):

  • “That’s clickbait! What if I don’t want to write headlines like this?”: Writers think if there is a number in the headline (7 Ways…), a triggering adjective (”Mind-boggling…”), or any hint at an outcome (”…so you can retire early”) then it’s automatically clickbait. This is not true. It’s only clickbait if you fail to keep your promise. If you promise to tell readers how they can buy their first rental property and retire early, but then don’t actually tell them how, then the reader hates you. But if you make that promise and over-deliver, giving them an entire step-by-step guide on how they can achieve this same outcome, then they love you. They’re going to bookmark your post. Send it to their friends. And likely go on to read everything else you’ve written—because you kept your promise.

  • “That headline is too long! How do I make it shorter?”: If your high school crush mailed you a 987 page book with everything they thought about you back then, how many pages would you read? The answer is: all of it. Length isn’t what matters. Some people think 1 single tweet is too long, and other people will read 987 pages and STILL want more. Which means length, in and of itself, isn’t what matters. What matters is whether you are speaking directly TO the reader. If you are, there’s no such thing as “too long.” And if you’re not, then even a 4-word headline is a waste of their time.

  • “My favorite writers don’t have to do this! Why do I have to?”: Seth Godin doesn’t write long headlines. His headlines are short and quippy. Things like, “Marketing Thoughts” or “Everyone Is Someone.” The problem is: you’re not Seth Godin. And so, first of all, it’s unproductive for you to compare yourself to someone who has been writing for decades (with an “s”). And second, we would ask the question: “But how many more people would read Seth Godin’s work if he used these tried-and-true headline techniques?” Are writers like Seth Godin successful because of their short, quippy, “clever” headlines? Or despite their short, quippy, “clever” headlines? (We would bet the latter—and that they would be 100x more widely read if they wrote clear headlines instead.)

In short: if you want to get people’s attention online, you need to learn how to write headlines that STOP them in their tracks and make them say, “Hmm… This looks like it’s for me. Maybe I should give this a read.”

How To Write Irresistible Headlines, Part I: Topic

Most writers think of their headline as an afterthought.

They sit down. They write. They work, and work, and work through “the writing.” And then, at the very end, they come up with a headline: something clever, almost like a bow on top.

In reality, this entire process should be reversed.

Of all the things to spend your time on, the headline should be your #1 priority.

  • Your headline is what gets readers to click.

  • Your headline is the “mini sales pitch” telling readers why they should read.

  • And if you don’t have a clear and compelling headline, then it doesn’t matter how great the content of your piece is—no one is going to read it.

Writing irresistible headlines is an art.

However, there’s a BIG mistake almost every writer makes, and we want to make you aware of it…

Don’t Be “Clever.” Be CLEAR!

Your headline should say exactly they can expect (before they click and start reading).

For example, readers don’t know what these headlines mean:

  • “The Dream Brigade”

  • “Nothingness”

  • “How to solve the world’s problems one pixel at a time”

  • “Double Or Nothing”

When writers write “clever” headlines, what they think is happening is that the reader is pausing, giving this headline their full attention, and then whilst hypnotized by the writer’s (obviously genius) creativity, reading each and every word of what they’ve written.

In reality, the opposite happens: a reader glances at a clever headline, doesn’t immediately understand what it’s about (or why they should care), and moves on.

Here are a few Clever → Clear rewrites:

  • How To Lose Time And Money → How To Lose Time And Money: A 30-Day Self-Care Calendar To Reclaim Your Hobbies

  • The Power Of Knowing The Odds → The Power Of Knowing The Odds: 4 Keys To Buying Your First Stock

  • Scenes From A Half-Quarantine → A Vaccinated Civilian’s Guide To Being Social (Again) Without Feeling Guilty About It

See how much more compelling clear headlines are when placed side-by-side clever ones?

Don’t make this mistake!

Now, with this in mind, let’s get you up to speed on how to write irresistible, CLEAR headlines.

Step 1: Make The Topic Clear In The Headline

Today, all we’re going to focus on is the topic (WHAT you are writing about) in the headline.

And then, over the next few days, we’re going to build on this clarity and show you how you can make your headlines stronger and stronger.

So, remember the 30 Proven Approaches from yesterday’s Lean Writing framework?

The key to writing a great headline is to combine one of those proven approaches with a specific topic—and make that as clear as possible right away in the headline. Because that’s the fundamental question the reader is asking themselves BEFORE they start reading your writing: “What am I going to GET in exchange for reading?”

Here are a handful of examples:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips.”)

  • Informative Bitcoin Podcasts (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment.”)

Do you see how important it is to be CLEAR about the topic?

And not just CLEAR, but SPECIFIC.

If you want your writing to resonate, specificity is the secret.

Assignment

OK… no overthinking!

Your Day 8 Assignment is to take the “Clear, Not Clever” pledge (write this down for yourself somewhere… maybe a notecard on your desk) and to write today’s Atomic Essay headline as CLEARLY as possible: 1 specific topic + one of the 30 Proven Approaches.

Some examples:

  • First-Time Parent Sleep-Training Tips

  • Retirement Mistakes You Can Start Avoiding In Your 30s

  • A Simple Workout Routine For Anyone Struggling With A Herniated Disc

  • Etc.

So, take the “Clever, Not Clever” pledge, write your Atomic Essay for the day, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

Dickie & Cole

Co-Founders, Ship 30 for 30

records.content:
Irresistible Headlines Part II

Ahoy!

Welcome to Day 9 of Ship 30 for 30—your 30-day roadmap to become a prolific Digital Writer.

Remember the theme for this first week is: Headlines & Hooks.

And today, we’re going to build on what we covered yesterday and add another variable into your irresistible headlines…

How To Write Irresistible Headlines, Part II: Topic + Audience

We talked about this same idea in the Endless Idea Generator, but it should also make it’s way into the headline.

It’s one thing to say, “This is what my piece is about” and make the topic clear to the reader.

But if you REALLY want to connect with a target reader, you should name their archetype right there in the headline. (Because they will literally think to themselves: “Oh wow… this is written for me!”)

Step 2: Add a WHO

  • …Tips For Project Managers

  • …Mistakes To Avoid As A Founder

  • …Trends For Wall Street Analysts

You want to make it very clear WHO your content is for (and, as a result, WHO it isn’t for).

Pro Tip: When you “name” an audience in your headline (or anywhere in your content), social algorithms actually take note—and this impacts how they distribute their content. For example, if you put “Silicon Valley Founders” in your headline, who do you think X (Twitter)/LinkedIn is going to show your content to? People who have any (or all) of those keywords in their bio, in the content they create or consume, people they’re connected to, etc. This is how social algorithms work!

So, here are the same examples from yesterday, adding a WHO (audience) to each topic:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year Olds (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips for teenagers.”

  • Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment, Gen-Zers This Is For You (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment, specifically for Gen-Z.”)

Notice how much more powerful the headline gets when you name the audience explicitly!

Questions

Now, whenever we start digging deeper into headlines, we always get the following questions:

  • “If I name an audience specifically in the headline, doesn’t that mean I’m going to cut out other potential readers?” Yes, and no. Yes, you will cut out other potential readers, but no, you won’t prohibit yourself from reaching other types of people. For example: “7 Insider Tips For Wealthy Real Estate Investors To Save Money On Taxes.” The named audience here is “Wealthy Real Estate Investors,” but even if you don’t consider yourself to be a “Wealthy Real Estate Investor,” are you still going to click and read that headline? If you’re interested in money, finance, or reducing your tax liability, yes, you will. But the fact that “an audience” is named still helps give you clarity over who this is for (primarily) and what it’s about.

  • “Can I list multiple audiences in the headline?” Of course! Just be careful not to start over-rotating to try to include “everyone.” Remember, if you try to write something for “everyone,” you end up writing something for no one. Here’s what multiple audiences in a headline might look like: “5 Mistakes New Moms & Dads Make 6 Months After Having Their First Kid.” There are actually 2 named audiences in this headline: both moms AND dads.

Assignment

OK… time to implement this second piece into your next headline!

Your Day 9 Assignment is to make today’s headline even more irresistible by adding in an explicit audience (FOR WHO).

Some examples:

  • How To Make Your First $1,000 As A Broke College Student

  • How To Make Your First $1,000 As A Millennial

  • How To Make Your First $1,000 As An Investor

  • How To Make Your First $1,000 As A Writer Online

  • Etc.

Notice how much clearer the headline gets when we make the audience explicit (and notice how you can write about the same topic over and over again by tailoring it to different audiences!).

So, pick an explicit audience, add it into the headline, and write today’s Atomic Essay, hit publish, and onto the next.

And don’t forget, you also have 30 Days Of Shipping templates in Typeshare you can use at any time. Click here to go to the template pack (make sure you’re logged in!).

See you tomorrow,

records.content:
Landing Page Copywriting Mistakes

Another common question we always get from Shippers whenever we start digging into the art of writing Irresistible Headlines:

“But Cole… Dickie… Do these frameworks also work for writing landing page headlines?”

And the answer is, for the most part!

However, there’s some nuances you need to keep in mind whenever you’re writing landing page copy. And since we know there’s plenty of Shippers who’re eager to eventually start launching their own digital products, we thought you could benefit from getting a quick landing page copywriting crash course.

So, here’s a lesson from our Full Stack Writer Sales Landing Page Copywriting Module where we explain the 7 biggest landing page copywriting mistakes beginners make (and how to avoid them).

Enjoy!

7 Landing Page Copywriting Mistakes That Could Cost You $100,000+ In Digital Product Sales

As a reminder: If you’d like to get our exact Ship 30 Landing Page Template (and learn the art of crafting Irresistible Offers so you can start monetizing your audience), check out Full Stack Writer.

We are not trying to be “clever” when we say this.

Seriously.

The mistakes we’re going to break down in this module will cost you money—likely hundreds of thousands of dollars. How do we know? Because over the past year, we have rewritten sections of the Ship 30 for 30 landing page dozens and dozens of times, and seen a clear increase in sales every time we fixed one of these problems.

The good news is: they’re easy tweaks.

You just have to know what to look for—and how to make changes that inspire the customer to take action.

Let’s dive in!

Mistake #1: “Learn how to...”

No! No! No!

The brutal truth is: nobody wants to learn.

Anyone who buys a digital product or online course wants the OUTCOME.

So on your landing page, don't promise customers: "Here's what you're going to learn!"

Instead, promise all the things they're going to:

  • Do

  • Experience

  • Unlock

Mistake #2: “Here’s what you get!”

Customers don't care how much work you've put into your course (features).

They only care about what your course can do for them (benefits).

  • In your landing page headlines, state the benefits.

  • In your product/course descriptions, describe the outcomes.

Too often, creators make their landing pages all about “them.” They want to tell prospective customers about all the hard work they’ve put into their product or course, how much it means to them, who they are, their story, etc. None of it matters. At least, it doesn’t matter nearly as much as the story you need to tell the reader/customer, about themselves:

  • Here’s what you’re struggling with

  • Here’s a unique solution to get rid of that problem

  • Here’s how your life is going to be different after you’ve solved this problem once and for all

  • Ready to get rid of this problem (forever)? Sign up here.

Mistake #3: Not giving templates

The value of your product or course is NOT in how many hours it is.

And it’s NOT how many modules are included.

The value = the Tangibility, specificity & effectiveness of your action steps.

And action steps are usually best shared in templates.

"I do X -> I unlock Y."

All digital products/courses should come with templates of some kind:

  • If you are selling a course teaching people how to master the art of email marketing, give them 10 email marketing templates they can use to immediately 10x their open rates.

  • If you are selling a product helping people get started in real estate, give them an email template for reaching out to home owners, and an excel template for tracking their investment property income.

  • If you are selling a product teaching people how to get hired as a graphic designer, give them Photoshop and Sketch templates to get them from “zero to competent” as fast as possible.

Templates help customers demolish the fear of getting started.

Mistake #4: Not including any bonuses

To increase the level of perceived value of your course, don't just "sell a product."

Sell your product, PLUS:

  • Bonus modules

  • Bonus templates

  • Bonus Q&As

  • Etc.

The more bonuses you add, the more the potential customer feels like they’re getting.

This is also why creating a portfolio of small bets is so valuable over the long term. Because the more eBooks, courses, and other digital products you build, the more “bonuses” you have to include and increase the perceived value of your offers. You can say things like, “Buy this product now and I’ll include these 2 other bonus products for free.”

It doesn’t cost you anything—they’re digital products! But it makes the customer feel like they’re getting “more.”

Mistake #5: Not enough testimonials

So many products/courses settle for 2-3 testimonials on their landing page.

Giant mistake.

You don't just want 2-3 people talking about your product/course.

You want HUNDREDS of testimonials:

  • Text

  • Video

  • Long-form blog post success stories

If you are struggling to gather testimonials, or if you are about to launch your very first digital product/course and don’t have any testimonials yet, consider giving away free access to a beta group of users—in exchange for a testimonial. It doesn’t really “cost” you anything (this is the beauty of digital products), and even though you sacrifice a little bit of revenue in the beginning, you will make all of it back and then some by leveraging those free testimonials to attract future customers.

Mistake #6: Listing solutions before educating on problems

The customer can't care about the solution until they care about the problem.

So, first thing on your landing page:

  • State the 10 biggest problems your target customer is facing

  • Emphasize the top 3

  • And show you understand them

Since your product is the “solution,” you need to make sure the potential customer understands what problem your product is actually going to solve for them, in their life.

Don’t assume they know.

Tell the customer, point blank: “You are experiencing X. It is painful. Here’s why it’s so painful. And here are the negative things that pain is leading to in your life. Great, now that we have established this is an unwelcome problem, let’s solve it, shall we?”

Mistake #7: Not giving away enough “free” material

This is the most important one of all:

The more you give away for free, the more likely people are to sign up and pay.

It’s counterintuitive.

For example: we took almost all our core frameworks from Ship 30 and put them into a free eBook for beginner writers. Someone could easily read the entire eBook and feel like they learned so much they don’t even need to take Ship 30 for 30. Awesome. That is our goal.

Because…

  • A) the person who signs up for Ship 30 for 30 doesn’t just want the information—they also want the accountability, the community support, the live sessions, and the full curriculum.

  • B) Even if they don’t take Ship 30 for 30, they will likely tell someone else about everything they learned (because that eBook is so jam-packed full of free, valuable information), which means someone else learns about Ship 30 for 30 and is likely to sign up.

Free material is your word-of-mouth marketing flywheel.


Want to dig deeper into the art of crafting money-making landing pages (and get our exact plug-and-play template)? Click here to grab a copy of Full Stack Writer!
