🔹[READ ME] Overview

Welcome to Become Known For A Niche You Own!

After completing Ship 30 and building a daily writing habit, most Shippers struggle with at least 1 of these 2 problems:

  • They’re not quite sure what their niche is going to be

  • Or they have an idea of what their niche could be, but don’t know what to name it or how to double down on it

If either of these problems sound familiar, you’re not alone. The truth is, niching down is the single BIGGEST problem Shippers face (even after writing every day for months!).

Which is why we’ve created Become Known For A Niche You Own.

This mini-course is a step-by-step blueprint designed to help you…

  • Overcome the "mental myths" of niching down.

  • Develop the mindset of a Category Creator.

  • And give you a proven framework to Name & Claim your very own unique, lucrative niche.

So, ready to set sail?

Let's go!

🔹Module 1: Overcome The 3 Myths Of Niching Down

Ahoy!

Welcome to the Become Known For A Niche You Own In 7 Steps challenge!

Over the next few days, we are going to show you how to:

Think like a Category Creator

Name & Claim your niche

And write your Category POV (so you never lose sight of your new North Star)

But before we get started, we want to debunk a few myths when it comes to creating your niche.

(This will be helpful for you to keep in mind as you begin your journey.)

Myth #1: "My audience isn't big enough yet. I don't know what my niche is."

This is a big myth, and we want to address it right away.

Most creators want to "wait" until their audience is "big enough" before they decide what their niche is going to be—as if, one day, they are just going to wake up and some magical answer will reveal itself.

But when is enough, enough?

When you have 1,000 followers?

When you have 10,000 followers?

When you have 100,000 followers?

At what point are you going to commit to serving a particular niche?

There's a bit of irony in this myth, because most creators want to wait until they get "bigger" on social media before they Name & Claim a niche for themselves—and yet, the reason most creators DON'T GROW on social media is because they haven't claimed a niche for themselves.

It's a chicken/egg dilemma.

So, should you wait to decide what your niche is going to be?

No. If anything, you are incentivized to plant your flag in the ground and Name & Claim some sort of niche (literally anything), now.

And then if you want to change your niche later, you can.

It's not a marriage decision.

Myth #2: "I don't feel comfortable Naming & Claiming a niche because I'm not an expert in anything."

Yes, you are.

Everyone is an "expert" in something.

The mistake people make here is thinking that "expert" is some far-and-distant achievement. Like you become an "expert" when you're a New York Times best-selling author. Or you become an "expert" when someone like Oprah or Tony Robbins gives you that title.

But the truth is, to your 2-years-ago self, you are an expert.

You know things today you didn't know 2 years ago. Or 1 year ago. Or 6 months ago. Or even 6 days ago.

Which makes you a Niche Expert.

The key to building an audience online, and even creating a portfolio of digital products and ultimately monetizing your knowledge, isn't "pretending to be something you're not." The key is to pinpoint what questions you used to have (in any space, field, or topic area), that you no longer have because you went on the journey to discover the answers for yourself. You already did the hard work. You overcame your own obstacles. Which means, to someone standing in your shoes 2-years-ago, you are "a Niche Expert."

All you have to do is own it.

Accept that you are a Niche Expert to someone who is a few steps behind you.

And just throw down a rope, and give them a hand.

Myth #3: "Once I pick a niche, I can't ever change it."

This might be the biggest myth of all.

Most writers and creators in general tend to think that picking a niche is a "marriage" decision—as in, once you pick a niche, you can't ever change it.

And this couldn't be further from the truth.

If you look closely, some of the biggest writers & creators today are in niches they discovered along the way. For example: Ryan Holiday was originally a marketing writer—not a Stoicism writer. He started with a niche, wrote a few books and launched a few products, and then ultimately decided he wanted to try something different. And that "something different" ended up being even more successful than the niche he originally started with.

Which is why we say: choosing a niche isn't a marriage decision.

It's Step 1.

Then, as your library of content begins to grow, as you gather more data, and as you learn what's resonating most with your readers, you have the freedom to choose whether you want to stick with that niche or pivot and move into a different niche over time.

(And sure, some of the people who "used to" follow you for, say, marketing will no longer be interested in your next niche. But that's OK. Because if you are choosing to create a new niche in the future, it's most likely because you have data that proves this is the right decision—which means for every 1 person you lose, you'll gain dozens more.)

Creating a niche for yourself isn't a destination.

It's a skill.

And once you acquire the skill, you can create new & differentiated categories for yourself over and over again.


🔹Module 2: Think Like A Category Creator

Ahoy!

Now that we’ve gotten the myths out of the way, let’s dig into how to THINK like a Category Creator.

Whether you’ve been writing online and creating digital products for a long time, or are just getting started, you might still be asking yourself, “What in the swashbuckling seahorse is my niche?”

First of all, this is something everyone struggles with.

If you think about the Top 10 biggest questions people have when it comes to creating content, launching products, and building businesses, up there in the Top 10, if not the Top 5, if not #1 is:

“What makes me different?”

And so when people ask the question, “How do I create a niche for myself?” that’s a very powerful and valuable question to have answered.

Right?

Because if you can figure out what makes you different—and you have gained the skill of being able to CREATE what makes you different over and over again—then you possess a superpower not very many people have.

Which you will know how to do by the end of this 7-day challenge.

Let’s dig in:

Better vs Different

The first big idea you need to internalize when it comes to creating a niche for yourself is this:

You do not want to be “better.”

Think about what that word means for a second.

“Better” implies you are similar to what already exists. “Better” means there actually isn’t very much separating you from the next person. And even if you are “a ton better,” you are still existing within the context of someone else.

For example, let’s say someone else came along who was “better” at writing about Stoicism than Ryan Holiday.

Is that “better” writer going to crush Ryan Holiday’s dominance? Is that “better” writer, all of a sudden, going to steal Ryan Holiday’s sunshine? Is that “better” writer going to erase Ryan Holiday’s reputation?

Of course not.

If anything, nobody is even going to notice!

And despite being “better,” that writer & creator is going to forever live in Ryan Holiday’s shadow as the Category King of Stoicism.

Because Ryan created it for himself—and nobody is going to be able to steal it away.

Instead, what you want is to be DIFFERENT.

Remove “better” from your vocabulary.

Get rid of it. If you find yourself writing “better” anywhere to describe who you are and what you do, that’s a neon signal you haven’t yet pinpointed what makes you different.

You are still rooted to “what exists.”

And you haven’t pioneered new ground… yet.

However, when you DO achieve “different,” you move yourself out of a comparison conversation (”Which one is better?”) and into a Creation Decision. When you are different, you force readers, followers, and customers to have to make a choice:

“Do I want the old thing? Or do I want this new and different thing?”

And the bigger you can make that gap, the easier it is for the person to decide: “Yes this is 100% what I’m looking for” or “No this is 100% NOT what I’m looking for.”

And that’s good news for you.

“OK this makes sense. But how do I stop being ‘Better,’ and how can I actually start being ‘DIFFERENT?’”

Great question—let’s break it down.

What are all the ways you can be “different?”

  • You can speak to a different problem. Instead of talking to the same audience about the same old problem(s) “better” than all the other people who talk to that audience about the same old problem(s), choose a different problem. For example: if a conventional problem in personal finance is, “I don’t know how to invest money,” don’t pick that problem. Pick something different!

  • You can speak to a different solution. Instead of talking to the same audience about the same old solution(s) “better” than all the other people who talk to that audience about the same old solution(s), choose a different solution. For example, if a conventional solution in health & wellness is to “eat healthy,” then don't waste your effort running around trying to evangelize the same obvious solution. Recommend something different!

  • You can speak to a different audience. Instead of talking to college graduates “better” than all the other people who talk to college graduates, talk to a different (more specific) audience: high-school graduates, middle-school graduates, grad school graduates, etc. These are DIFFERENT audiences.

The big idea here is that whenever you see lots of people all speaking to the same audience, about the same problem, recommending the same solution, within the same time horizon, in the same context, go do the opposite.

Most people understand this in theory, but when push comes to shove, they chase acceptance.

They can’t do it.

They would rather “fight” to fit in, than go their own way and easily stand out.

Our goal is to help you do the latter.

Start Broad, Niche Down

So, let’s get you started on your path.

In today’s module, our only goal is to get you headed in the right direction.

(Then, over the next few days, we will help you clarify your niche further and further.)

Step: What do you want to write about… generally?

If you want to take a data-driven approach, look through your analytics of everything you’ve published up to this point.

  • What topics perform the best?

  • Which of these topics do you enjoy writing about the most?

  • Choose the 1 that fits both: what’s working for readers, and what genuinely interests you.

Boom. Easy.

If you don’t have as much data yet, then just pick something. Anything. Literally. It’s better to have “a niche” than to have no niche at all.

  • “I want to write about education.” Great.

  • “I want to write about yoga.” Awesome.

  • “I want to write about sales.” OK, perfect.

Just pick something so that you can walk through the exercise with us—and learn how to create a niche for yourself.

That way, you can always change it later in the future if you’d like (but at least you know the steps).


🔹Module 3: Frame The Problem

Ahoy!

In the previous module, we talked about:

  • Better vs Different (and why you should delete the word “better” from your vocabulary)

  • 5 easy ways you can niche down: Audience, Problem, Solution, Time, Geography.

  • And why you should start by choosing a broad topic (anything is better than nothing!)

Now, we are going to begin the process of “niching down.”

Which starts with 2 very important questions.

Who Is Your Content NOT For?

This is the first big question you should ask yourself.

When most people try to create their niche, they ask themselves, “How can I make something for everyone?” They try to think of ALL the different types of people they can attract. And as a result, they keep making their niche broader, and broader, and broader—until eventually, it’s no longer a niche. It’s just… a blob of white noise.

This is what they don’t teach you in creative writing school: that when you try to write something for everyone, you end up writing something for no one.

Instead, an easier way of thinking about what makes your niche “different” is to consider who your niche is NOT for.

  • Who would see your niche and think, “Nope, that’s definitely not what I’m looking for?”

  • Who would see your niche and be repulsed? (”Oh my gosh, someone writes about that? Seriously?”)

  • Who would see your niche and share it with other people, mocking it, condemning it, or (best case scenario) calling it “fake?”

Contrary to popular belief, this is what you want.

You WANT your niche to not be for everyone.

That’s what makes the people who LOVE your niche, and what you write about, feel like it’s “100% for them.”

To be clear: we are not advocating for you to be controversial, dramatic, flagrant, or offensive.

All we’re saying is that some people really love horror movies, and other people hate horror movies. And it’s that “binary” response that is GOOD for both parties: it makes the people who love horror movies feel like they’re part of something special, just for them. And it makes life very easy for the people who hate horror movies, because now they can steer clear from this thing they really don’t like.

Your niche should NOT be for “everyone.”

Are You Building A Category Or A Personal Brand?

The second big question you need to ask yourself is, “Am I building a category or a personal brand?”

Because the two are not the same thing.

A personal brand is a personality. It’s a flavor. It’s a style. Just like how a company’s “brand” is a logo, a font type, a color palette, a specific voice, etc. A “brand” is made up of the symbols you use to represent who you are and what you do (the word comes from a cow literally being “branded” to mark who owns it). But let’s be clear: your “brand” or your “personal brand” is not your value, and it’s certainly not your niche.

To be blunt: most people who aspire to build personal brands aren’t really interested in being known for any meaningful contribution they make to the world, or their industry. They’re just interested in being known, period. (Sort of like a reality TV star—famous for being famous.) As a result, they want (and chase) lots of followers and high social media engagement, and are willing to do just about anything in order to achieve those outcomes. If that means upping their energy level, screaming into the camera, posting inspirational quotes or funny memes 15x per day, or performing outrageous stunts, then so be it. They just want to be “known.”

We would encourage you to think long and hard about whether this is the path you really want to take for yourself as a digital writer & creator.

Building a niche is something completely different.

A niche isn’t about you (whereas a “personal brand” is all about you).

A niche is about a thing, an idea, bigger than yourself. And you are “creating” that niche not with the goal of becoming known for being known, but instead with the goal of creating and evangelizing something you believe matters in the world—and, more importantly, hope to see others join you in building as well.

This is the crucial differentiator. You are successful in creating a niche when you see other people start creating inside that niche too. (Ryan Holiday is successful because other people want to read and write about Stoicism too. And the more people who read and write about Stoicism, and evangelize the category, the more successful Ryan Holiday becomes—because he was the one who turned it into a niche.)

A lot of times, people approach building themselves with a scarcity mentality. They think, “I want to become known for something NO ONE ELSE is known for. Period.” In reality, it’s a GOOD thing when other people hop into your niche. Their presence, and their support, further validates your niche. And if you’re the one who created it, and is out in the world pioneering it, then their involvement only gives you more authority.

So, ask yourself:

Do you want to be known for the sake of being known? Then you might want to consider being a YouTuber who eats Tide Pods.

Or do you want to become known for a niche you own? And if so, then put yourself in the backseat and give the “idea” the spotlight. And furthermore, consider how you can create leaders (not followers) who ALSO want to create within this new niche as well.

Frame The Problem

Alright, now with all of that rumbling around in your head, let’s think about the first way you can make your niche more specific (who is your niche NOT for?).

Step 1: Take your general topic and make a list of the Top 10 problems people experience related to this topic.

For example, maybe you want to write about effective communication (broadly).

Here are 10 problems people who want to effectively communicate might experience:

  • Problem #1: Disorganized thinking

  • Problem #2: Fear of public speaking

  • Problem #3: Not a good listener

  • Problem #4: Rude communication style

  • Problem #5: Afraid of conflict

  • Problem #6: Language barriers & cultural differences

  • Problem #7: Lack of trust (fear of being honest)

  • Problem #8: Not emotionally invested

  • Problem #9: Weak vocabulary

  • Problem #10: Addicted to jargon

(Literally a 5-minute Google search revealed these 10 problems—so if you are sitting there saying, “How am I supposed to figure out what problems people face?” then get to work.)

Most people say they have trouble niching down, but in reality, they can’t even name the Top 10 problems someone faces in their broad topic category. So that’s Step 1.

Do a little research. Talk to some people.

The answers should reveal themselves very quickly.

Step 2: Choose 1 problem to solve.

Now, here’s where things get interesting.

When you make your list of 10 problems, your takeaway shouldn’t be, “Now I have to create a ton of content to solve all these problems.”

Instead, it’s the opposite.

  • You could build an entire career around helping people solve their “disorganized thinking” when it comes to effective communication.

  • You could also build an entire career around helping people overcome their fear of “public speaking” when it comes to effective communication.

  • You could also build an entire career helping people master the art of close listening and improve their weak skill of “not being a good listener” when it comes to effective communication.

And so on.

The big mistake people make when trying to create their niche is they think, “Well people have all these problems, and so I need to solve all of them.” Which, by definition, makes it very hard to know what your niche is! Trying to solve 10 problems at once inherently means you need to “be more broad.” Which is what keeps you up in the “effective community” category.

But if you choose just 1 problem, all of a sudden, you have a niche.

See? Easy.

Now, surely you’re asking yourself, “Well how am I supposed to know which problem to pick?”

There are 3 things to consider.

  • First, which problem is most “weird?”

The weirder the problem, the more opportunity. Right? When you make your list of 10 problems, you will inevitably see 2 or 3 that is “popular.” Everyone knows those are problems. And as a result, there are a LOT of people providing a LOT of solutions to those problems already in the world. And so what most people think to do in this situation is say, “OK then, I’m going to set out into the world and prove I can solve those same problems… but better!”

And as we already discussed, that’s a giant mistake.

Instead, it’s 100x easier (and you will be 100x more successful) if you pick a “weird,” unconventional, ignored problem to solve. And while it might seem small, or insignificant at the start, the opportunity you have is to educate the world on why this is actually a much bigger problem than people realize.

Until 1 year goes by…

3 years goes by…

5 years goes by…

And all of a sudden, you’ve become “known” for that niche—which you now own.

  • Second, which problem is most valuable to solve?

The next stress-test question you need to ask yourself is which problem on your Top 10 list can be directly correlated to some sort of monetary benefit.

And if none of the problems seem correlated to some sort of monetary benefit, how can you make the argument that they are?

For example, on the surface, “Not being a good listener” isn’t really tied to any monetary benefit. Solving that problem isn’t the same as solving a problem like, “I’ll tell you which high-growth stocks to buy—that will get you at least a 20% return in your investment portfolio.” The monetary benefit there is clear.

However, we can make the argument that “not being a good listener” is costing someone money.

Here’s how: “Quick question: how many times have you said to yourself, ‘Why didn’t I think of that?’ Well, the reason you keep saying that to yourself isn’t because you aren’t smart. And it’s not because great ideas aren’t floating around you, all the time. It’s because you haven’t built the skill of being able to recognize a great idea the moment it presents itself. Said more specifically: you haven’t built the skill of being a great listener. And so, just consider for a moment: how much is that costing you? How many life-changing opportunities have you missed because you failed to recognize them when they appeared?”

When you can tie the problem to a very clear monetary cost or benefit, the person on the other side of the screen immediately contextualizes the “value” you are providing in a different way. A $20 per month newsletter (or a $200 course, or a $2,000 coaching product) might seem expensive at first glance. But it seems very, very cheap in the context of the question: “How much is this lacking skill costing you in life-changing opportunities?”

So, when choosing which problem to laser-in on, also consider which one you can make the best argument for being directly correlated to a monetary cost or benefit.

  • Third, which problem are you most passionate about solving?

Finally, the above questions are important, but the most important question is what interests you the most.

Because choosing a “weird,” opportunity-rich problem to solve, and choosing a problem that is monetarily valuable, doesn’t matter if it’s something you aren’t passionate about. And if you really want to make a difference in the world, if you want to create a new category and become known for a niche you own, then you are embarking on a life-long quest. And you are going to give up on that quest (very quickly) if the problem you choose to solve is based on extrinsic rewards vs intrinsic desires.

So, pick something that gets you going—and you’ll keep going for decades.

The magic happens when all 3 of these align.

You know you have a powerful niche (which will lead to life-changing opportunities for you) when you solve a:

  • Weird, unpopular, neglected problem

  • That can be directly tied to a monetary cost or benefit

  • That also aligns with who you are as a person, what you value, and what you feel inspired to solve in the world.

When you get all 3, you won.

And you’ll spend the rest of your life creating assets, education, content, and products you love, helping people you deeply understand and appreciate, doing what aligns with you and your core values. (And you’ll make more money than you ever would working for someone else in the process.)

That is the magic of creating a niche for yourself.

Example: Ship 30 For 30

Here it is in action (just to drive the point home):

Step 1: What are the Top 10 problems in “writing?”

  • Distractions

  • Over-editing

  • Perfectionism

  • Procrastination

  • Self-confidence

  • Generating ideas

  • Impostor syndrome

  • Writing consistently

  • Choosing a platform

  • Finding time to write

Step 2: Which 1 does Ship 30 for 30 really laser-in on?

Writing consistently.

Step 3: What are the 3 reasons why we chose this problem?

  • It’s weird and unpopular. Lots of “writing” courses. Not very many (if any) “writing accountability” courses.

  • We tie it to monetary outcomes: “Writing consistently on the Internet unlocks life-changing outcomes like building a loyal audience, being able to create and sell frictionless, infinitely scalable digital products, connects you with likeminded people, puts ‘networking’ on autopilot to the point where opportunities come to you,” etc.

  • We are insanely passionate about this. Both of us built daily writing habits, and both of us experienced life-changing outcomes. We know it works. And we can’t help but pound the pavement to tell other people about how insanely valuable, rewarding, and fun writing consistently on the Internet can be—if you commit to the process.

See? Easy.


🔹Module 4: Name The Solution

Ahoy!

In the last module, we talked about how you can niche down by getting more and more specific about the problem you are solving.

But there is another way you can niche down, and that’s by getting more and more specific about the new & different solution you are offering.

(And magic happens when you can do both: solve a weird, unpopular problem—and solve it with an unconventional, “How come I didn’t think of that?” solution.)

Obvious Solutions vs Non-Obvious Solutions

If you want to go fully down this rabbit hole, we encourage you to read this mini-book, The Art of Fresh Thinking.

But here’s the nutshell for you:

Most people who want to create a niche for themselves try to solve too many problems. They think they need readers, followers, listeners, users, or customers who have “all of these problems,” when in reality, even just 1 problem will yield you more than enough readers/customers, and it will take you years to solve that problem effectively (and even then, you’ll likely only help 1% of the people in the world who have that problem).

Of those who are able to make it past the first step and actually laser-in on 1 problem, they then sell themselves short by making a giant mistake:

They provide the same solution as everyone else.

Imagine you decide the problem you want to solve is: “I want to help people lose weight.” And you educate people on the amount not-losing-weight is costing them: costing them confidence, which is costing them an intimate relationship, which is costing them emotional support, which is costing them not living the life they really desire for themselves, etc. And you choose this problem because you were once severely overweight and very insecure, and it wasn’t until you turned the corner and got your health in check that your entire life changed. And so you are passionate about helping other people experience this same transformation in their own lives, too.

What someone in this scenario typically does then is announce to the world:

[Problem]: “I’m going to help you lose weight!”

And then…

[Solution]: “And I’m going to do that by helping you exercise and eat healthy!”

OK—now ask yourself.

How many people in the world are solving this exact same problem, with this exact same solution?

(If you guessed 87 gazillion, you’re right.)

The whole key to becoming known for a niche you own isn’t just solving 1 specific problem, but solving it in a new and different way. A way people haven’t seen before, or thought to do. Take Ship 30 for 30, for example. Where does a writer solve their problem called, “I struggle to stay consistent. I can’t build a daily writing habit because I keep falling off.”

  • Maybe they take out $120,000 in loans and go study creative writing in college for 4 years. That’s a solution.

  • Or maybe they ask one of their friends to be their accountability buddy. That’s a solution.

  • Or maybe they buy 25 different productivity, note-taking, and time management apps to try to discipline themselves. That’s a solution.

But then this cohort-based course comes along and says, “Do you really want to take out $120k in debt just to have a little help staying consistent with your writing? How many times have you tried to find an accountability buddy, only for them to fall off? Are any of those productivity, note-taking, time management apps really keeping you on track—or are you just finding new ways to procrastinate? How about instead of any of those solutions, you join a community of likeminded writers on the Internet who are all focused on building a daily writing habit together. How about that solution?”

Notice: there is nothing about the above that is trying to persuade someone why Ship 30 for 30 is “better” than any of those other solutions. It’s very clearly explaining why Ship 30 for 30 is DIFFERENT. And by offering a NEW and DIFFERENT solution, it “stands out.”

So, let’s walk through how you can do this for yourself.

Step 1: Take the 1 problem you are setting out to solve and make a list of the Top 10 solutions people already provide to solve this problem.

This is the easiest place to start.

For example, if the problem you want to solve is, “I want to help you find the job of your dreams,” what solutions already exist to solve this problem?

  • Solution #1: Interview Coaching (”I will help you learn how to answer questions like a pro during the interview process”)

  • Solution #2: Peer Mentoring (”I will connect you with someone who already has your dream job at another company, so you can hear directly from them what’s required to get promoted”)

  • Solution #3: Career Strategy (”I will give you frameworks that reveal unconventional ways other people have climbed the ladder in your industry—so you can too”)

  • Solution #4: Resume Writing (”I will give you templates you can use to spice up your resume and make sure it doesn’t get ignored”)

  • Solution #5: Management Training (”I will train you to be a pro-level manager so that your higher-ups can’t help but see you as VP or C-level material”)

And so on.

Similar to the “problem,” make a list of the Top 10 solutions that already exist to solve the 1 problem you’ve chosen to laser-in on—and go through the same process:

A) Which one of these solutions is the weirdest one? The most unpopular? The most ignored?

B) Which one of these solutions is the easiest to rationalize from a monetary perspective? Which one of these solutions is the “most valuable?”

C) Which one of these solutions am I most aligned with? Which one am I most qualified to execute? And if not qualified, which one am I most excited to learn, master, and share with people for a long time?

Again: as much as possible, you want to avoid creating a niche that solves a popular problem with a popular solution. That’s where all the competition is.

To avoid competition, pick problems that are weird and commonly ignored, and solve those weird problems with unconventional, unpopular solutions.

Step 2: If no “weird,” opportunistic solutions exist for the 1 problem you want to solve, create one.

This is where “creating your niche” starts to get really fun.

If, after a bunch of research and lots of talking to your ideal readers/customers, you don’t find a weird, unconventional solution you can leverage to solve the 1 problem you’ve decided you want to solve, then create one!

Literally. Invent one—out of thin air.

For example, in Ship 30 for 30 we noticed writers were really struggling to keep writing after the first few days of the program. They’d get all excited. They’d hop aboard. They’d ship their first Atomic Essay. And then 2 or 3 days later, they’d say, “I’ve run out of things to write about.” And we’d already given them the Endless Idea Generator. We’d given them group accountability. We’d given them brainstorming sessions during our live calls. We’d given them a ton of “Obvious” solutions—and none of them were working.

So, what did we do?

We invented a solution—called templates.

Instead of going out into the world and finding something that already existed to solve the problem we had, we decided to take it upon ourselves to create our own solution. We gave ourselves this permission. And the more templates we created, and the more people used them, the more we started to realize we’d just created a whole new niche for Typeshare: Digital Writing Templates.

Too often, people look at the world as something that is “fixed,” and their job is to “find” themselves in it. That’s why people use the phrase, “I’m trying to find my niche.” This language implies the world is one way, and your job is to figure out how to “fit” inside of the way it already is.

In reality, all the exponential potential, and all of the fun, is in CREATING things that don’t exist yet.

So if a weird, unconventional solution doesn’t exist for the problem you want to solve, then don’t throw your hands in the air and say, “Oh well.” Take that as a neon sign your creativity is being called into action. Invent a solution from scratch.

This is yet another step forward in you becoming known for a niche you own.

Step 3: Make your solution even more different by changing the WHO, WHEN, and WHERE it gets delivered.

Ah, but finding a weird, unique solution to leverage, or even inventing something 100% new is no easy feat!

So, what are some other ways you can make sure people understand what makes your solution new and different?

  • [WHO]: You can specify the audience. You might not be the only person solving this 1 problem. And you might not be the only person using this weird, unconventional solution to solve this 1 problem. But you can be one of the only people to solve this 1 problem, with this 1 unconventional solution, for this particular audience.

  • [WHEN]: You can change the amount of time. If most people who solve this problem, with this same solution (or solutions like it), solve it in 3 years, how can you solve it in 30 days? Or, even better, is there a way you can solve it (or part of it) in 3 hours? You can massively differentiate yourself by creating new, unique ways of solving problems and exponentially shortening the amount of time it takes for someone to experience a “transformation” (no matter how small).

  • [WHERE]: You can specify the geography. You might not be the only person solving this 1 problem, with this 1 solution. But maybe you can be one of the few who solve this 1 problem with this 1 solution in Chicago. Or in Portland. Or on LinkedIn. Or on Twitter. Sometimes all you have to do is change where you “do what you do,” and suddenly you stand out. (For example: there are tons of heathy restaurants and juice shops in California. Not so many in Arkansas.)


🔹Module 5: Claim The Category

Ahoy!

You’re almost done creating your niche! (Can you feel the level of clarity difference between now and just a few modules ago?)

Choosing 1 specific problem to solve, and finding or inventing an unconventional, “Woah I never thought of that” solution is the key to niching down. Because the more specific the problem, and the more specific (and “new”) the solution, the more you are going to stand out.

But there is one more step to becoming known for a niche you own.

Languaging: Name & Claim Your Category

In order to become known for a niche you own, you have to call it something!

Here’s the difference—watch closely:

  • “I help people overcome their feelings of fear and jealousy in their writing.”

vs…

  • “I help people overcome Writer’s Envy.”

Which one stands out to you more? Which one grabs your attention? Which one are you more likely to remember? Which one sounds like a “thing,” so much so that you might go and Google it afterwards (”Wow, I didn’t even know that was a thing! I want to learn more about that.”).

Writer’s Envy. Obviously.

There are tons of smart, capable, even brilliant writers and creators in the world. But do you notice how it’s really only the ones who are “called” something, or call their ideas “something,” that stand out? Everyone else is talented, but just sort of… forgettable.

Which means the question you need to ask yourself is:

“What do I call this niche of mine?”

Let’s walk through the steps.

Step 1: What 1 problem do you want to solve?

OK—now give that problem a name.

Let’s run through a few examples:

Example #1:

  • Problem = “I want to help people overcome the fear of launching their first online course.”

  • Name = “Do you have Course Launch Anxiety?”

Example #2:

  • Problem = “I want to help people who suffer from low confidence.”

  • Name = “Did you catch Low Confidence Disease?”

Example #3:

  • Problem = “I want to help people stop going into credit card debt.”

  • Name = “Are you stuck in Credit Card Quicksand?”

Let’s not overcomplicate things. All you’re doing is giving a name to the problem you want to solve. (Pro tip: capitalize the name you are giving the problem to help the reader/customer see this as a unique “thing,” and as a forcing function for you to be clear about what problem you’re really solving.)

When naming your problem, here are the qualities you want to aim for:

  • Be clear, not clever. Make sure the problem itself is in the name. Don’t say, “I want to help people stop going into credit card debt” and then name the problem, “Are you stuck in a Money Matrix?” Because notice: this name doesn’t accurately tell the person what problem you’re solving.

  • Aim for 2-3 words. Don’t name the problem you’re solving, “I help people Overcome Fear Of Credit Card Debt And Financial Illiteracy.” That’s not a name. That’s a complete sentence. Think about how to Name & Claim the problem you’re solving in 1, 2, or 3 words—max.

  • Combine words to create a new word. This is called a “portmanteau,” where you combine two words to create a new word. So instead of saying, “I help people go from casual writer to writing entrepreneur,” could you say, “I help people become Writerpreneurs.”

Similar to the way you want the niche you create to be something OTHER PEOPLE would want to be part of (and become creators within along with you), the language you use to Name & Claim what you do should be done with the aspiration of OTHER PEOPLE wanting to use that language too. So again, try to avoid Naming & Claiming things because YOU think it’s “cool.” And instead, strive to invent new language you could imagine other creators wanting to adopt and use too (because it makes so much sense).

Step 2: What’s the 1 surprising solution you want to offer people to solve this 1 problem?

OK—now do the same thing, and give the solution its own name too.

Let’s run through a few examples:

Example #1:

  • Problem = “I want to help people overcome the fear of launching their first online course.”

  • Name = “Do you have Course Launch Anxiety?”

  • Solution = “I want to help people overcome Course Launch Anxiety by giving them a checklist of 10 action items that will ensure their course launch runs smoothly.”

  • Name = “The way I solve your Course Launch Anxiety is by giving you what I like to call The Power Launch List. If you do everything on this checklist, you will be successful.”

Example #2:

  • Problem = “I want to help people who suffer from low confidence.”

  • Name = “Did you catch Low Confidence Disease?”

  • Solution = “I want to help people cure themselves of Low Confidence Disease by working with them 1:1, coaching style.”

  • Name = “To cure your Low Confidence Disease, I am going to work with you 1:1 using a coaching technique I invented called Confidence Mirroring.”

Example #3:

  • Problem = “I want to help people stop going into credit card debt.”

  • Name = “Are you stuck in Credit Card Quicksand?”

  • Solution = “I want to help people get out of Credit Card Quicksand by doing a 30-minute spending audit with them, and then giving them a budgeting template to fill in together.”

  • Name = “To get you out of Credit Card Quicksand, I am going to do a Money Faucet Audit to help you pinpoint where you are spending money unnecessarily, and then I will give you my proven Money Rescue Budget Template to help you rescue all of that wasted money—and put it right back into your pocket.”

Notice how the Naming & Claiming of both the Problem and the Solution makes you so much more interested in the “thing.” It makes it feel real. It makes it seem like this is something the creator has worked hard to put together. It gives you the impression that it’s “proven.” Simply because it has a name.

And again, same rules apply:

  • Clear, not clever.

  • Aim for less than 5 words (it’s a name, not a description).

  • Combine words to create new words.

Name It & Claim It Recap

Your takeaways here should be the following:

  • Name & Claim your niche. This will help people understand that what you are creating is a new universe, a new topic, a new intersection, a new “space.” And if you are successful, other people should want to become creators within your niche too. (We created the niche Digital Writing. Nobody was using those words together before we came along. And now, lots and lots of people call themselves “Digital Writers.” This is great news!)

  • Name & Claim the problem you’re solving. This will help people connect to it, and prioritize it in their life. Fun fact: pharmaceutical companies “invent” new problems all the time. Because how do you sell a drug or a medicine to someone? It needs to solve a problem. And in order for that problem to be a “thing,” it needs a name. When used for evil, this is of course a very manipulative thing to do. But when used for good, this is how you change the world.

  • Name & Claim the solution you’re providing. This will help people trust you. When the solution you are giving them sounds like something they have spent years refining, improving, and ultimately “naming,” your belief “it works” goes up. For example: which marketing agency do you trust more? The one that says, “We will teach you how to improve your Facebook ads” or the one that says, “We will put you through our Facebook Opportunity Optimization bootcamp?” The second one, obviously. Because it has a name. It sounds like “a thing.”

  • Bonus: Name & Claim the transformation. The last thing you can do is Name & Claim the final transformation. Where does someone end up? When they consume your content, buy your product, take your course, use your service, etc., how do they change? What’s life like on the other side? How are they different? Give that thing a name, and voila. You are no longer trying to convince people to pay attention to what you “do.” You’re painting a picture of who they are going to become—on the other side.


🔹Module 6: Write Your Category POV

Ahoy! Now that you're created your niche, and Named & Claimed the 1 problem you're going to laser-in on and the unique, unconventional solution you're going to leverage to solve that 1 problem, now it's time to write your Category POV.

Remember: this is not a marriage decision.

Chances are, your niche and Category POV will change many times throughout your career. This is normal, if not expected. The more you write and create online, the larger your library of content grows. The larger your library grows, the more data you will gather and the easier it will be to spot patterns of “what works” and what doesn’t. The more patterns you notice, the more new content & product ideas you will have—and the more you will discover new opportunities to differentiate yourself further by creating more new categories for yourself.

Which is why we say: learning how to create your niche isn’t a destination.

It’s a skill (and a powerful one that will serve you for years to come).

Write Your Category POV

Think of your Category POV as a short “manifesto.”

This is a public Rally Cry for anyone interested in your category.

The purpose of writing out your Category POV is to give yourself clarity as to why you are writing what you’re writing about. Here’s a little secret: the more you can make your category (and your POV on the category) in service of someone else and having a positive impact, the easier it will be for you to discover “what works.”

Here are some questions to consider when brainstorming your Category POV:

  1. Why does this subject matter to you so much? Is it personal?

  2. Why, right now in the world, is it necessary for people to be educated about this topic?

  3. Why are you choosing to prioritize writing about this in your life?

  4. What positive impact will this information have on the reader’s life? How will they change as a result?

  5. What will the world look like when this topic becomes mainstream knowledge?

Your goal here is to be a “visitor from the future” and help people understand why they need to follow you forward.

Below is a template you can use to write out your Category POV (this template is also in Typeshare).

Category POV Template

In your chosen category, share one commonly held belief most people think is true (but is actually false/wrong/outdated/misunderstood/etc.).

Next, describe the problem in detail. Explain to the reader why this commonly held belief is so prevalent in society, or how it became a commonly held belief in the first place. And finally, tell the reader what this commonly held belief has resulted in.

List off a few examples:

  • Example #1

  • Example #2

  • Example #3

Now, in this subhead, tell the reader the reason this belief is flawed.

And in this first sentence, give the reader a concrete reason.

In this paragraph, expand on your argument. Share a personal story, or a study or stat that gives credibility and context to your perspective. And finally, tell the reader what new and different result they can expect if and when they abandon this old, commonly held belief and adopt this new perspective you're providing instead.

Now, tell them how:

In this subhead, tell them how to shift their mindset from "old" to "new."

This first sentence is an actionable step they can take, right away.

Next, explain what they can expect as a result from shifting their mindset. What new advantages or benefits will they experience in their own life? Be specific, and paint a clear picture of the future.

Finally, in this subhead, tell the reader why the "old" is going away for good.

Bring them back to the beginning of the article, and drive home your point.

Give a few quick reasons why the "old" is on its way out, and this "new" way of thinking is the future. And to send them off, give them one final reminder/example of what this new future will look like—and why it will be so valuable for them to be part of it.

Rewrite Your Bio

Now it’s time to tie it all together.

With your new category Named & Claimed, and your “manifesto” and mission written out in your Category POV, you have everything you need to launch yourself online as a distinct, differentiated digital writer & creator.

Step 1: Copy/paste the Naming & Claiming language from your category.

  • “I write about online course creation for digitally-challenged legacy educators who want to learn how to build an audience online, launch their first product, and monetize their knowledge in the digital world.”

Step 2: Add a sprinkle of credibility.

Use whatever you have in your arsenal today.

Here are a handful of different examples:

  • “Former Professor, Now Creator. I write about online course creation for digitally-challenged legacy educators who want to learn how to build an audience online, launch their first product, and monetize their knowledge in the digital world.”

  • “Teacher for 15 years. I write about online course creation for digitally-challenged legacy educators who want to learn how to build an audience online, launch their first product, and monetize their knowledge in the digital world.”

  • “I write about online course creation for digitally-challenged legacy educators who want to learn how to build an audience online, launch their first product, and monetize their knowledge in the digital world. Student of learning for 10+ years.”

  • “I write about online course creation for digitally-challenged legacy educators who want to learn how to build an audience online, launch their first product, and monetize their knowledge in the digital world. Mark Cuban liked my essay on education.”

Credibility is a great “nice to have” in your bio, however what’s much more important is getting the Naming & Claiming right and being highly specific. Then, over time, as you write more online, launch products, and inevitably “accomplish” more and more things, your credibility bullet points can (and will) change.

That’s it!

records.content:
[READ ME] Overview


Welcome to Build Your Audience On Autopilot!

This is exactly how we have built our own audiences (of hundreds of thousands of readers/followers)...

The steps we are going to walk you through, and the systems we are going to help you build are literally the same we use every single week.

We have done the hard work of removing as many decisions, time-consuming tasks, and unnecessary To Dos from your list—so that all you have to do is focus on following this blueprint to get yourself up and running.

Build Your Audience On Autopilot is designed to:

  • Give you endless content ideas by analyzing your analytics

  • Give you templates to effectively create Reach content to build the size of your audience

  • Give you templates to effectively create Resonance content to engage your growing audience

  • Give you templates to effectively curate content (to both build & engage your audience in different ways)

  • Show you our proven "commenting" strategy to build bridges that connect the audiences of other creators to your content

  • Help you leverage your library of content over time, allowing you to collect dividends from your work

  • And build systems & processes that put your content strategy on autopilot—ensuring you continue growing (no matter what) long into the future!

So pack your bags, because this ship is ready to set sail!


🔹Module 1: Discover Proven Ideas In Analytics

Ahoy! And welcome to Module 1 of the Build Your Audience On Autopilot In 7 Steps Captain's Table challenge! Let's get right into the good stuff.

What is a "Content Strategy?"

Before we give you today's action step, let's just make sure we're on the same page. We notice a lot of creators make the term "content strategy" seem fancy and complicated—when the truth is, it's actually pretty simple. Your content strategy doesn't need to be some massive 200-page document about how you are going to become the greatest creator on earth, and it also doesn't need to be a 6-month exercise where you sit down with a team of "brand consultants" who help you brainstorm your "brand image." Here's an easier way of thinking about it:

  • Your content strategy tells the algorithms you're an active player in the game of Digital Online (the more you write & publish, the more the algorithm learns you are a Creator).

  • Your content strategy is the consistency with which you publish valuable content (Quality Volume)

  • Your content strategy is how you use free content on social media to drive people to your more valuable content & digital assets elsewhere (newsletters, eBooks, courses, services, etc.)

That's it. So, if you already have a business, a book, an eBook, a course, or even a free/paid newsletter, the very first step is making a short list of the digital assets you want to drive people to. Right? Because again, let's not make it complicated:

  • If you want people to sign up for your newsletter, they need to know you have a newsletter.

  • If you want people to buy your book/eBook, they need to know you have a book/eBook for sale.

  • If you want people to buy your course, they need to know you even have a course to begin with—and what problem it solves for them.

Your free content on social media is the "engine" that introduces people to these more valuable assets.

For example, here's our list of Digital Assets we want our social content to drive people to:

  • Typeshare: We want more Digital Writers using templates on Typeshare.

  • Newsletter: We want more Digital Writers learning our frameworks, mental models, and distribution/monetization strategies through our newsletter, The Digital Writing Compass.

  • Ship 30 for 30: We want more Digital Writers to learn about Ship 30, and we want them to see the success stories of alumni who have gone through the program.

  • Podcast: We take the time to interview other prolific creators in our community live sessions, and so we want more Digital Writers to not only learn from those creators but also see how valuable our live sessions & community are.

So, Step 1: Create your list of digital assets you want to drive people to.

It's helpful to start with this list, first, so that you can build your content strategy around these digital assets. If you don't have any digital assets yet (you don't have an eBook, a course, or even a free newsletter, etc.) then don't worry!  You will soon.

Step 2: Open your analytics.

If you have a short list of digital assets you want to drive people to, then great. If you don't, haven't gotten there yet, or just simply want to focus on building the size of your social audience, then no worries. The following steps are the same. Step 2 is going into your analytics and looking for content ideas. This is why we say, "The more you write, the more you write." Your content strategy is basically just the conscious act of doubling-down on things that are clearly working for your readers. That's all. Which is why it's pointless to sit down for 6 months and try to brainstorm your "perfect content strategy." You are making assumptions! And you don't know what's working (and what's not) objectively out in the world. So, let's work from data instead. Open your analytics in Typeshare. (You can also use Ilo.so for analytics as well.)

Set the timeline to "All Time" and in the upper right-hand corner you can select how you want to view the data:

  • Most Recent

  • Engagement Rate

  • Views

  • Likes

  • Shares

  • Replies

  • Link Clicks

  • Profile views

We recommend organizing the data either by Engagement Rate, Views, or Comments—for the following reasons:

  • Engagement Rate: This will almost never be your "most popular" content, but will reveal unique and interesting opportunities where your audience was clearly engaged and may want more content "like this" from you. 

  • Views: Organizing your analytics by Views is a good way to get a sense for what's working at a high level. What's popular, what's not, etc.

  • Comments: Content with a lot of comments are neon signs trying to tell you there is opportunity hiding here. Anytime a piece of content prompts people to comment, you should consider doubling-down there.

Now, look at the data!

Step 3: Put your Idea Generation on autopilot!

Sitting down and expecting yourself to be prolific every morning is asking a lot. (It's also unreasonable.) None of the "prolific creators" you see on social media take this approach with their content. Instead, they create systems that allow them to easily double-down on proven content ideas—and then put those systems on autopilot. So, looking at your most-popular content (organized by Engagement Rate, Views, or Comments), what do you notice?

  • What topics are readers resonating with?

  • What topics did you not expect to see rise to the top? (What topics did you "think" weren't working, but the data is actually telling you they are?)

  • What topics did you expect to see here, that didn't make the cut? (What topics is the data trying to tell you aren't working?)

Action Step: Pull 1 topic that is clearly already working.

This 1 topic is going to become one of the "templates" you use to easily create your content for the week. This is how you double-down on what's working and accelerate your audience growth.

Step 4: Double-down on that 1 idea!

For example, sorted by Engagement Rate, one topic that stands out here is "How To Write A Top 1% Business Newsletter."

So, what are other topics we can create related to this (since our audience is clearly interested in this topic)?

  • How To Write A Top 1% Business Book?

  • How To Start Your First Newsletter As A Busy Business Professional?

  • Why Every Business Should Start A Newsletter On Substack?

  • How To Turn Your Newsletter Into A Book?

  • The 7 Best Business Newsletters On Substack You Should Be Subscribed To?

All of these ideas "make sense" because they're tangentially related to that 1 "proven idea" we see is clearly working in our analytics. This is what removes the pressure of having to sit down and "be brilliant" every single day with your content. No. Just look at your analytics. And double-down on what's working.

Unlock Your Badge!

OK! Let's put your Idea Generation on autopilot and unlock your Idea Gatherer badge. Go through your analytics and pull 3 proven topics that audiences are clearly interested in hearing about from you. For example:

  • How to write a newsletter

  • Copywriting tips

  • Book recommendations

Then, come up with 5 new ideas related to each of these 3 "proven topics." This becomes your content strategy for the week! For example:

  • How To Write A Newsletter

    • How To Start Your First Newsletter As A Busy Business Professional

    • Why Every Business Should Start A Newsletter On Substack

    • How To Turn Your Newsletter Into A Book

  • Copywriting Tips

    • How To Write The Perfect Landing Page

    • 5 Simple Copywriting Tips That Will 10x Your Landing Page Conversion Rate

    • David Ogilvy's Favorite Copywriting Tip

  • Book Recommendations

    • 7 Books Every Writer Should Read Before They Die

    • The Best-Selling Non-Fiction Books Of 2022

    • 3 Business Books Creative Professionals Need To Read To Charge More ($$$)

Look at that! Your "content strategy" for the week took 15 minutes—and, it's 100% based on data (which increases the likelihood that it's going to "work" and resonate with readers on social media). Commenting vs Creating

Most people who want to start creating content online think their job is to create and share content from their own profile.

And yes, that's true.

You create a profile. You get handed your Digital Megaphone. And then you start talking into your Digital Megaphone with the hopes of people hearing what you have to say and deciding to stick around to hear more.

This is content creation 101.

But what most people don't consider are the other ways they can introduce people to their content. The most powerful one being: commenting.

When you "comment" on someone else's content online, you aren't just responding. What you're really doing is you're publishing content—just within the context of someone else's content. It's the same thing as hitting "publish" from your own profile, except here, your content is much more likely to be seen by "the right people."

For example:

Let's say you want to write, Tweet, or post on LinkedIn about what it's like to work for yourself, be a solopreneur, etc.

What most people think to do is create and publish this content from their profile. Right? That's content creation 101 (as we said above). But that's not the ONLY way for you to get eyeballs on your content, your stories, your insights, your lessons learned, your perspectives, etc.

Another option is to go find someone else—a Creator who has a much larger following than you do—and find one of their recent posts on that same topic. Then, instead of publishing your story, or your insights from your own profile, share what you want to share as a Comment on their post. 

Here are a few of the benefits of this strategy:

  1.  If you have a small audience, this is an easy way to ensure people actually see your content (because you're riding another Creator's wave).

  2. You essentially guarantee that your content is going to be seen by "the right readers"—since you are publishing it within the context of a topic those readers have already engaged with.

  3. You can test ideas as comments, first. And then if a particular comment attracts engagement, you can take that as signal to double-down and create something similar again from your own profile.

  4. The more you engage with Creators bigger than you, the more they see your name & content, the more they inherently start engaging with you, the more your content gets seen & shared, the more you become "Internet friends" with them, etc.

  5. And maybe most importantly, every time you comment thoughtfully on a tangentially related Creator's content, you are building a bridge between their content and yours.

Think about this for a second:

Imagine you did this a few times every day for 5 minutes in the morning. 

You make a list of Creators who publish content similar (or tangentially related) to you.

You thoughtfully comment on some of their more popular posts with ideas, stories, perspectives of your own.

And each one of those comments taps into their much larger audience, introducing a handful of people to you and your library of content (which you know they are going to be interested in because you and that Creator both create "similar" types of things!).

Think of how much faster you would grow!

We call this The Bridge Content Strategy.

This is not content you publish from your own profile.

It's content you publish "inside" other Creators' content—building bridges between them and you.

Your Weekly Content Cadence

Some of the questions we get asked all the time are:

  • How often should I be publishing content to build an audience?

  • When in the day should I publish my content?

  • How often should I publish short-form content vs long-form content?

  • How often should I "market" my digital products, courses, services, etc., without being "salesy" or spammy to my audience?

So, we're going to make this super easy for you.

Here is our exact Weekly Content Cadence (so you can see how we do this ourselves):﻿

Feel free to use this as an outline for yourself.

But, to make this even more actionable, let's walk through each one of these questions and create a Weekly Content Cadence you can put on autopilot.

"How often should I be publishing content to build an audience?"

Here's an easy way to remember the answer to this question:

Less is more, until the point where more becomes less.

The truth is, you actually don't need to publish a TON of content to build an audience. Most top-tier creators only post 1-2x per day, and some only post a few times per week.

The key here is to produce Quality Volume: enough content so that you are consistent, and readers can look forward to what you're going to create and publish next, but not so much that you start to sacrifice quality. ("More" doesn't automatically = better or faster.)

Our recommendation: You should aim for publishing 2x short-form pieces of content per day. And if you've walked through the steps up to this point, coming up with enough ideas and things to write about & create 2x per day should be no problem.

"When in the day should I publish my content?"

8:00am and 8:00pm Eastern Time.

There is no correct answer here, and we know creators who post at radically different times than us and are just as successful. But as a rule of thumb: once in the morning, and once in the evening.

7am / 7pm works.

9am / 5pm works.

10am / 4pm works.

Twice a day—ideally not back-to-back (like: 10am / 11am).

Use this 2x/day framework for your short-form content. In addition, use this as a forcing function to alternate between Reach & Resonance content. (Reach content in the morning, Resonance content in the evening, or vice versa.)

For example, we both publish our short-form content (stand-alone Tweets & LinkedIn posts) at 8:30am and 8:30pm. And it takes us roughly an hour to create our week's worth of 2x/day content and schedule it out in advance (which we'll show you how to do tomorrow).

This also allows you to publish any long-form content you want to share between these 2 times.

For example: 

8:30am - short-form

11:00am - long-form

8:30pm - short-form See? Easy.

How often should I publish short-form content vs long-form content?

Long-form content (Threads, Long LinkedIn posts, Ultimate Guide articles, etc.) take longer.

Which means you will produce less "quality" long-form content each week.

The whole purpose of creating and sharing short-form content is basically to keep your audience engaged (and growing) between the moments you publish your really valuable long-form content. The long-form stuff is where you're likely going to see the most engagement, and most growth in your audience. So the short-form stuff is just a "tide-me-over" for audience members until your next long-form post.

If you can publish 1-2 really valuable long-form pieces each week, you'll be in great shape.

For example, on Tuesdays and Wednesdays we typically publish our long-form Threads. And our Threads are the things that tend to drive the majority of our growth—but, they take longer to create. So we can't publish 1-2x really valuable Threads every single day. 

2x per week is plenty.

How often should I "market" my digital products, courses, services, etc., without being "salesy" or spammy to my audience?

Finally, it's important to put your audience-building efforts to good use. Remind people what else you have for them to check out!

  • Do you have a newsletter?

  • Do you have a book/eBook for sale?

  • Do you have a course?

  • Do you have a business?

  • Do you provide a service?

Etc.

Basically, after you have your 2x/day short-form content scheduled, and your 1-2x/week long-form content scheduled, any other time is fair game to drive audience members to your digital assets.

Now, the mistake people make here is they just tell their audience, "Go buy my book!" or "Go sign up for my newsletter!"

You don't want to do that.

You want to find ways to make your "promo" content still valuable for the reader. 

  • Can you give them something for free?

  • Can you provide a summary of the longer thing you are asking them to read?

  • Can you curate interesting, relevant information for them—and then direct them to your resource for a "deeper dive?"

For example, instead of just telling people, "Hey! Go check out Typeshare," here's a Tweet that gives away a mini-template for free—and THEN encourages them to go check out Typeshare "for more templates."

As long as you take a value-first approach, you can literally link to your own digital assets as much as you want.

And readers don't see it as "salesy" or overly promotional because all you're doing is saying: "Hey, I want you to have this... oh and by the way, if you want more stuff like this it, here's a longer resource you should check out."

It's an option, not a sales pitch.

Now let's create your own Weekly Content Cadence!

(We recommend doing this in Notion, Notes, a Google Doc, or even right inside Hypefury for scheduling. Just document it somewhere so you can use this as an outline—and so you can come back to it over and over again.)

Step 1: What is your 2x/day short-form cadence?

What time are you going to publish Reach content each morning? And what time are you going to publish Resonance content each afternoon/evening? Write those 2 times down.

Step 2: What is your 1-2x/week long-form cadence?

What day(s) are you going to publish high-value, long-form content (Threads, long LinkedIn posts, Ultimate Guide articles, etc).

And on that day, choose a time that is halfway between your morning short-form content and your afternoon/evening short-form content.

Write it down.

Step 3: What digital assets do you want to drive attention to?

Take your list of digital assets (book/ebook, course, newsletter, etc.).

And look for open times in your schedule where you can promote 1 of these each day. (Try to avoid promoting more than 1 thing per day.)

Write it down.

Step 4: When in the day are you going to comment and engage with other Creators?

Finally, when are you going to "build bridges" from their content to your content for 10 minutes?

This is more of a habits question.

Do you want to engage for 10 minutes first thing in the morning? 10 minutes during lunch? 10 minutes at night, before bed? Pick a time and put it on the calendar. Consider it a meeting with yourself. (And don't cancel!)

Write it down.


🔹Module 7: Put Your Content Strategy On Autopilot

Ahoy!

You've made it to the very end.

It's time to put your Content Strategy, and Weekly Content Cadence, on autopilot.

All you have to do is block ~2 hours per week to create your content, and schedule it out in advance.

Are you ready to streamline your audience-building efforts for the rest of your life?

Let's do it.

Step 1: Create Your Content Cadence Inside Typeshare or Hypefury.

Both Typeshare and Hypefury have scheduling capabilities.

And both allow you to publish to Twitter and LinkedIn simultaneously (and Typeshare allows you to also cross-post to Medium as well).

What you want to do is set yourself up for success and take the Weekly Content Cadence you created for yourself in the last module, and make it concrete by building it out inside Typeshare or Hypefury.

For example, Hypefury has a nice calendar view that we like to use for scheduling all our content out in advance.

Login to your account, and on the left-hand side click Account and Settings. Scroll down and you'll see a Weekly calendar view like this:

To remove a time from your Weekly Cadence, just click it and it'll disappear. And to add a new time/recurring time, just select the day/time and click "Add Slot."

Building this Weekly calendar view, first, makes it easy for you to just fill in the blanks and create your content each week.

Step 2: Fill-in Your Queue

Once you have your Weekly calendar view setup, now all you have to do is color inside the lines.

In Hypefury, on the left-hand side of the screen, scroll up and find Queue.

Your Weekly calendar view will create slots in your Queue for you to fill in. Which means all you have to do is go down the list!

  • Short-form Reach content in the AM

  • Short-form Resonance content in the PM

  • Long-form Reach/Resonance content 1-2x/week between your short-form content

  • Promo content 1x per day between all your organic content

This process might take you a bit longer the first few times you do it.

But eventually, you'll get it down to a science—and your content for the week should take 2 hours or less! (Long-form content pending. These more valuable pieces might take you a bit longer.)

Step 3: Use Typeshare Templates To Accelerate Your Idea Generation & Writing Process

As you fill in your Queue, if you notice yourself getting stuck, or even if you just want to make sure you are doing everything you can to create effective content, you always have Typeshare templates at your disposal. (There are dozens of free templates you can use.)

In addition...

Click here to access the Reach Template Pack.

Click here to access the Resonance Template Pack.

Step 4: Use Twemex To Find Creators & Proven Approaches

If you don't know about it, Twemex is an amazing Chrome extension that pulls any Creator's most-popular content for you.

(Right-hand side of the screen.)

While you are creating your content for the week, use Twemex to look up Creators relevant to your niche to see a) what their most popular content is and what ideas it gives you, and b) for inspiration on hooks and templates you can use yourself. 

Twemex is the ultimate hack for seeing what's working for other Creators, so that you can adopt similar strategies for yourself.

Step 5: Build your TweetDeck and Twitter Engagement Lists

To streamline your daily "bridge building" efforts, it's worth taking 30 minutes to set up your TweetDeck and creating a list of Creators you want to engage with on a daily basis.

This takes a little bit of time to setup, but it will save you hours and hours of painstaking work in the future.

If you aren't sure how to setup your TweetDeck or lists inside Twitter, read this ultimate guide we put together that walks you through exactly how, step-by-step.

Congrats! Your Content Strategy is now on autopilot!

By taking the time to set all of this up, you have now created the system (and the constraints) that allow you to spend 100% of your "content" time focused on the ideas themselves.

  • You know when you are posting.

  • You know what days you are posting which types of content.

  • You know how often you need to post in order to build an audience.

  • You know when you are creating Reach content, and when you are creating Resonance content.

  • You have dozens of templates at your disposal to use whenever you feel stuck (or if you just want to use proven hooks and formats that you know are more likely to work).

  • AND, you have created a foolproof system to ensure you create content consistently and continue to build your audience long into the future.

Which means all YOU have to do is sit down once per week for ~2 hours and create your content for the week.

Fill in your queue.

And then sit back as your content starts to work for you.

This is how all prolific creators approach content creation online—and now, you can consider yourself part of that crew.
