records.content:
🔹[READ ME] Overview

Welcome to Endless Idea Generation Mastery, a 5-day mini-course designed to:

  • Help you never run out of ideas to write about

  • Leverage Personal Credibility to share your expertise

  • Quickly generate compelling ideas relevant to your niche

  • Find “winning” ideas and reuse them over and over again

  • Leverage Borrowed Credibility to share other people’s expertise

  • And more!

So pack your bags, because this ship is ready to set sail!

After completing this mini-course, you are going to become an Idea Generation Master.

The Idea Generation frameworks we teach in Ship 30 for 30 are only the beginning!

The truth is: idea generation is a skill. And if you want to become a prolific writer, then you need to practice the skill of coming up with ideas quickly, efficiently, and effectively. (You need to increase the rate at which you can not only generate ideas, but generate quality ideas.)

So, that’s what you’re going to do throughout this challenge:

  • Module 1: How To Generate Personal Story Ideas & Curated Story Ideas

  • Module 2: How To Generate Actionable Ideas & “Fun” Ideas

  • Module 3: How To Generate Timely Ideas

  • Module 4: How To Generate Timeless Ideas

  • Module 5: Your Endless Idea Generator Content Strategy Blueprint

Ready to become an Idea Generation Master?

Then let’s set sail!


🔹Module 1: How To Generate Story Ideas

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 1 of Idea Generation Mastery!

Let's get right into the good stuff.

How To Create Your Content Strategy

The number one mistake new Digital Writers & Digital Creators make is thinking they need to “have it all figured out” before they begin.

They think they need some big, fancy, perfectly constructed content strategy—before their ship can set sail.

(And by now we hope you know… that’s not true at all!)

In reality, your content strategy is something that evolves over time.

  • The more you write, the more data you gather.

  • The more data you gather, the more you learn “what works” (and what doesn’t).

  • The more you learn “what works,” the more you can repeat your winners (and cut your losers).

  • The more you repeat your winners, the more likely your content is to perform well (since you already know this content is what readers want to read about).

  • The more your content performs well, the more new readers you attract and the bigger your audience grows.

  • And so on, and so on.

As a result, it’s really not worth overthinking what your “content strategy” should be.

All you need to focus on is writing, gathering data, listening and learning, and repeating “what works” (and cutting what doesn’t).

Your Endless Idea Generator Content Strategy

That said, there is a method to the madness—and we want to give you the method.

All prolific Digital Writers & Digital Creators end up creating (usually “intuitively”) a content strategy for themselves.

And all great content strategies have 4 major components:

  • Story Ideas

  • “Fun” Ideas

  • Timely Ideas

  • Timeless Ideas

Over the next days, you’re going to create content in all 4 of these buckets—and start creating your perfect content strategy over time.

But today, let’s just start with Stories.

Curated Stories

Every single Digital Writer & Digital Creator would benefit from curating success stories from other relevant writers & creators.

  • If you write about Architectural Design, what famous architects could you write about?

  • If you write about Data Science, what famous Data Scientists could you write about?

  • If you write about Nutrition, what famous Nutritionists (or Nutrition Brands) could you write about?

  • If you write about Real Estate, what famous Real Estate Moguls (or Real Estate Companies) could you write about?

The reason is because these “famous” examples are the ones most likely to attract attention. People already know them. They recognize their names. They understand the value of consuming their stories. Which means you can leverage their “interest” in these topics to your advantage.

For example: Here’s a curated story about New York Times’ best-selling author, Ryan Holiday.﻿

“But I don’t want to promote my competitors!”

Most Digital Writers & Digital Creators hesitate to curate other people’s stories (especially related to their niche) because they think they are “promoting” them.

But this is a very short-sighted way of thinking about it.

Instead, consider this frameworks: A Superconsumer of 1 category is a Superconsumer of 9+ other categories.

This means that your target reader isn’t necessarily picking “you” vs “them.” If a reader is interested in Real Estate (for example), then they will want to read a wide variety of writers/creators talking about that same topic. Your “competition” isn’t really your competition. In reality, they are your greatest collaborators.

And so, when you’re first starting out, the fastest way for you to grow is to borrow someone else’s credibility.

  • Write about their successes

  • Write about their frameworks

  • Write about their tips & tricks

  • Write about their “zero to hero” story

Use their credibility to your advantage.

Personal Stories

You can begin to share Personal Stories from the very beginning, if you’d like.

However, if you are focused on growing your audience, then we recommend starting with Curating Stories from other more established and well-known creators & thought leaders, first. Why? Because in the beginning, nobody knows who you are—but readers know who “they” are. So, reduce all friction and curate stories of more well-known people in your industry, market, category, or niche.

Then, once your audience begins to grow, add in Personal Stories of your own.

Personal Credibility

The key to telling Personal Stories is this:

You have to remember it’s not really about you.

We say this all the time in Ship 30 for 30: You are not the main character of your story. The reader is.

If you want your Personal Stories to be successful, to resonate with readers and impact them in some meaningful way, then you need to have clarity around why the Personal Story you are telling is interesting to the READER (not just interesting to you).

  • What’s the takeaway you want the reader to understand by the end?

  • What’s the obstacle you want to help the reader overcome?

  • What’s the realization you want the reader to have?

  • What’s the problem you want the reader to solve?

You have to know “what’s in it for the reader.”

For example:

Imagine you are at a dinner party, and someone overhears you talking to a few friends about how you want to buy your first rental property.

This person walks over (they’re wearing white pants and a blue button down and a dark green chapeau), interjects, and says, “I’ve bought over $10 million worth of rental properties over the past 10 years.” Your eyes light up! Wow! This person has all the experience you don’t have yet! You think, “This person could be a terrific resource.”

But every time you ask them a question, they just keep going on and on about their story. How they grew up in a small town in Arkansas. About how their dad wasn’t around much—he worked construction. About how, for many years, he wanted to be an architect, not a real estate developer. And the whole time you're thinking to yourself, “Great story, but… none of this is really relevant to what I’m interested in.”

Finally, you blurt out: “Can you just tell me how to buy my first rental property?”

The real estate developer looks at you, pauses, and then says: “That’s a great question. You know, when I was trying to buy my first rental property…” and then goes into another 7-minute story about how he bought his first property.

But still doesn't answer your question.

Now, is that a good story?

No, it’s not.

Because you, as the audience member, aren’t being given the thing you want or need. It might be an entertaining story. It might be told wonderfully, full of description and memorable phrases. But at the end of it, you’re left unsatisfied.

That’s not a “good story.” That’s a waste of time.

So, when telling a Personal Story, make sure you know (and make it clear to the reader):

Here’s what’s in it for you!

Why You Should Have Both Curated & Personal Stories In Your Library

Both Curated & Personal Stories play a crucial role in your ability to build an engaged audience.

  • Curated Stories are what appeal to new readers, and make it easy to tap into “the masses” and generate attention.

  • Personal Stories are what appeal to existing readers, and make it easy to deepen the relationship you have with your readers (especially within a certain niche).

In short: you want (and need) both.

How To Generate Curated Story Ideas

So, how do you come up with effective Curated Story ideas?

Here are some questions you can ask yourself to get the creative juices flowing!

  • Who are the people who helped build the industry you’re interested in today? (Who are the pioneers?)

  • Who are the brands/companies who helped build the industry you’re interested in today? (Who helped scale “this thing” all over the country, or the world?)

  • What are some of the biggest success stories in your industry?

  • What are some of the biggest failure stories in your industry?

  • What are some of the little-known weird “woah-I-never-knew-that” stories in your industry?

  • What are the biggest moments of change in your industry? (What were the pivotal moments that “changed everything?”)

  • What are the craziest facts, trends, stats, etc., in your industry?

  • Who are some of the other up-and-coming creators in your industry? (What frameworks, mental models, tips, etc., have you learned from them? How can you share their expertise too?)

All of these questions reveal an abundance of things for you to write about—and all of which not only establish your niche, but tap into the wants, needs, and interests of the very people you want to reach.


🔹Module 2: Generate Actionable Ideas & “Fun” Ideas

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 2 of Idea Generation Mastery!

Digital Writing is a game—and 50% of playing games is learning “How To” play, and the other 50% is about having fun!

Why Every Content Library Needs Actionable Content

Actionable Content is the foundation of every effective content strategy.

On the Internet, people want to learn.

  • Do people want to watch cat videos on YouTube? Sure.

  • Do people want to watch little kids get hit in the face by bouncy balls? Of course.

  • Do people want to watch standup comedy routines? You bet.

But contrary to popular belief, the primary function of the Internet is education. (What is Google? It’s a giant “Question” machine you use dozens and dozens of times per day!)

As a result, one of the easiest ways to build yourself into a reliable, engaging, and valuable Digital Writer & Digital Creator is to become known for a niche you own where you help other people solve specific problems in their lives.

And Actionable Content is how you do that.

How To Come Up With Actionable Content Ideas

The giveaway for Actionable Content is the phrase “How To.”

  • How To Drive A Car

  • How To Cook Eggs Benedict

  • How To Clean A Penthouse Apartment In 2 Hours Or Less

  • How To Build An Audience, Write Your First eBook, And Start Earning $10,000 Per Month

Furthermore, Actionable Content usually gives readers steps, tips, tricks, mental models, etc., helping walk them through the ideas in sequential order. For example: let’s say you buy a new refrigerator.  What do you do? You open the instruction manual that comes with it.

“Step 1: Plug it in.”

This is Actionable Content—and it’s essential.

Anything where you are explaining “How To” do something is Actionable.

So, how do you come up with Actionable Content ideas?

This is where The 2-Year Test is extremely helpful.

  • Step 1: Ask yourself what you know today that you didn’t know 2 years ago.

  • Step 2: List out all the pivotal moments of change (what were the inflection points where you learned whatever it is you learned).

  • Step 3: Turn each “moment of change” into a tip for the reader—if you were in their shoes, what would you suggest they do?

  • Step 4: Tie it all together, and help that person make the transformation you made—but in a fraction of the time!

Just like we did here.

See how this takes an idea and breaks it down into steps?

That’s all you have to do.

Why Every Content Library Also Needs Fun Content

Now, the flipside to Actionable Content is what we call “Fun” Content.

Fun Content is “nostalgic” stuff.

This is content that isn’t necessarily super actionable, but it’s also not “trying” to be entertaining. Its value is that it takes readers for a trip down memory lane. (Buzzfeed does this masterfully: If You're Between 26-32, Then This List Is Your Entire Childhood.)

The reason this content is so valuable is because once you start allowing yourself to think of “fun” things related to your niche, you realize how many random ideas would actually be extremely compelling to your target readers (and engage them in a way most other creators, brands, and media companies oftentimes ignore).

For example:

Let’s say you are are interested in “video games.” Or, more specifically, you’re interested in the video game “World of Warcraft.”

Actionable content would be things like:

  • How To Hit Level 60 In The New World of Warcraft Expansion

  • How To Level Your Herb Gathering Skill To 300

  • How To Maximize Your Hit Points As A Warrior

  • How To Make Money On The Auction House

  • Etc.

And all of this content would be valuable to World of Warcraft players—and that’s great.

However, there are other types of content that aren’t as “actionable,” but just as interesting and engaging—simply because they’re “fun.”

  • World of Warcraft: 25 Best Moments in the Game’s History

  • The 10 Most Popular World of Warcraft Videos of All Time

  • The Very First Screenshots Of World Of Warcraft

  • 10 Secret Locations In World Of Warcraft

  • Etc.

Notice how, as a gamer, you wouldn’t really read any of these pieces to “learn” anything—but that doesn’t mean these aren’t interesting & relevant topics! (In fact, these weird, random, “fun” pieces probably drive more attention than most of the Actionable “How To” Content.)

“Did You Know?” Content Is Fun!

So, how do you come up with Fun Content ideas?

Ask yourself what cool things exist in your industry/niche that most people either don’t know about, or might want to know about—but no one has taken the time to curate.

  • What are some of the “best moments” that have happened in the history of your industry?

  • What are some of the “most popular” things: creators, products, videos, podcasts, pictures, etc.?

  • What are some of the “early days” nostalgic things: first inventions, original copies, first drafts, first pitch decks, first speeches, first awards, etc.?

  • What are some of the “secrets” in your industry?

  • Etc.

All of this content is fun and interesting to your target readers—so long as it is still relevant to your niche.

That’s the key.

🔹Module 3: How To Generate Timely Ideas

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 3 of Idea Generation Mastery!

Let’s talk about when it’s good to be timely.

Why Every Content Library Needs Timely Content

The Internet is divided into two sections:

  • Timely Content: What’s relevant right now.

  • Timeless Content: What will be relevant beyond right now.

What this means for you, as a Digital Writer & Digital Creator, is you need to find a balance between these two extremes.

If all you do is create “timely” content, you will quickly find yourself on a hamster wheel—always fighting to capitalize on the trend of the day.

But conversely, if all you do is create “timeless” content, you will struggle to capture people’s attention in the moment.

Which is why all great Digital Writers & Digital Creators do some element of both.

(And your job is to figure out what that right blend looks like for you.)

Types Of Timely Content

Timely Content would be:

  • News

  • Trending Topics

  • Big Industry Changes

  • Recent Research, Studies, or Reports

  • “This-Just-Happened” Headlines & Current Events

  • Etc.

Timely = You need to know about this ASAP.

Why Timely Content Is So Beneficial

Here’s the short answer:

When something is “happening” in the world (especially when it’s being amplified by the Internet), it’s exponentially easier to ride an existing wave (in the short term) instead of creating a whole new wave of momentum.

Typically, what you see Digital Writers & Digital Creators do is create “content about the content.”

  • Step 1: Something happens (in the world, in an industry, in your niche, etc.)

  • Step 2: Mainstream media sets the agency with a few overarching narratives.

  • Step 3: Writers & Creators create “content about the content,” sharing their own views, personal experiences, insights, stories, analyses, etc.

Which means: when something is happening that is relevant (or you can make relevant) to your niche, capitalizing on “the news” can be a very effective way of generating short-term attention.

Why Timely Content Is So Ineffective

What goes up must come down.

The pro of Timely Content is that it’s much easier to generate short-term attention.

The con, however, is that things that generate short-term attention typically have a very short shelf life. So even though you captured a bunch of attention today, that doesn’t mean any of the attention you gathered is going to last tomorrow. This is why websites like Buzzfeed churn out as much content as they can. Because they live and die by “timely” content—and they only stay relevant as long as they are commenting on what’s happening NOW.

10-20% Of Your Content Can Be Timely

That said, Timely Content still can be beneficial in helping you generate attention and build your audience.

So, how much is the ideal amount?

10-20% of your content—max.

The rest of the content you create should be Timeless (which we’ll get into tomorrow). The strategy then is to create a little bit of Timely Content to generate short-term attention, but to spend the vast majority of your time creating Timeless Content so your library compounds over time.

You don’t want to be the hamster stuck on a content-creation-hamster-wheel!

How To Come Up With Timely Content Ideas

Timely Content ideas are floating around everywhere around you, online.

On Twitter, the #Explore section will show you dozens of trending topics for that day (or that hour):﻿

﻿And on the right-hand sidebar of LinkedIn, you’ll see LinkedIn News:﻿

﻿But you can also find “newsy” topics just by looking through:

  • The front page of your favorite news publication

  • Scrolling through your News Feed on Facebook, Twitter, TikTok, YouTube, etc.—and seeing what “recent” posts have been made.

  • Google News

  • Etc.

Whenever you see something “trending,” or you see a topic grab the masses by the horns and yank their attention away from anything and everything else, it’s worth pausing and asking yourself, “How could I use this to my advantage?” Now, not every topic is going to be relevant to you or your niche (so don’t try to force it). But with a little creativity, you could make a handful of trending topics work in your favor.

For example, take this LinkedIn News topic: “Zuckerberg’s wealth takes $71B hit.”

Here’s how to make that trending topic relevant to a wide variety of niches:

  • “Zuck Just Lost $71B. To Put That In Perspective, Here’s What $1B Of Books Looks Like, All Stacked On Top Of Each Other.”

  • “Zuck Just Lost $71B. Have You Recently Lost A Bunch Of Money? Here Are 5 Yoga Poses To Help You Destress.”

  • “Zuck Just Lost $71B. Here’s Why He Should Have Invested That Into Real Estate 2 Years Ago.”

  • Etc.

Here’s the magic equation: take the trending topic, connect it to your niche, and voila.

Now you’re capitalizing on the trend!


🔹Module 4: How To Generate Timeless Ideas

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 4 of Idea Generation Mastery!

If Timely Content is how you capitalize on short-term waves of attention, then Timeless Content is how you build a library of digital assets that pay you dividends long into the future.

Why Every Content Library Needs Timeless Content

Timeless Content exists on a spectrum.

  • Sometimes, what you write is relevant for 1-5 years.

  • Sometimes, what you write is relevant for 5-25 years.

  • And sometimes, what you write remains relevant for generations.

Regardless, any content you create that has a shelf life beyond 1 year is considered “Timeless” when compared to minute-to-minute Timely Content. And so, if you want to unlock compounding effects in your library, your goal should be to write things that remain relevant, longer.

The reason is because: think of Timeless Content as “Digital Real Estate.”

The more Timeless Content you write, the longer your library remains relevant for readers. The longer your library remains relevant, the more attention your work will naturally accumulate. The more attention your work naturally accumulates, the more likely new readers are to continue engaging with and sharing work you created historically.

And all of this creates a flywheel.

If you successfully build a digital library of Timeless Content, you will eventually reach a Tipping Point.

You won’t need to write as much net-new content to continue attracting attention, building your following, or selling digital products.

(The same way owning a ton of real estate continues to pay you passively long into the future.)

  • Your work will continue to be read, engaged with, and shared online.

  • Your work will continue to attract new readers, followers, and subscribers.

  • You work will continue to bring in net-new opportunities.

  • Your work will continue to sell your products & services.

  • Etc.

This is the long-term goal of writing online.

You build a library of content that eventually works for you.

Types Of Timeless Content

So, what is Timeless Content?

  • Frameworks

  • Breakdowns

  • Mental Models

  • Strategies

  • Lessons

  • Mistakes

  • Insights

  • Etc.

For example, look at this Twitter Thread:﻿

You could read this Twitter Thread in 2022, or 2032, or 2042, or 2052, and it would still be “valuable.”

Why? Because it’s Timeless.

  • It is about one of the most legendary marketers of all time, David Ogilvy (who people will want to learn from for decades).

  • And it is about his “timeless” advice for writing effectively.

Nothing about this Thread has anything to do with what’s happening in the world today. It’s not a response to “the news.” It’s about ways of thinking about the craft of writing that will likely be relevant for many more decades.

Which means the shelf-life of this Thread isn’t 1 day.

It’s 1 year. Or 10 years. Or maybe even 100 years!

Timeless = This will still be true long into the future.

Why Timeless Content Is So Beneficial

When you write something Timely, readers basically have a few hours, or a few days, or maybe a few weeks to consume it.

But do you have any interest in reading the newspaper from 1 year ago?

Of course not.

This is what makes Timely Content such a grind—and why it should only make up 10-20% of your total content library.

Timeless Content, on the other hand, benefits from time. In fact, it may even perform better with time. Instead of getting less valuable, it gets MORE valuable. (The book Think & Grow Rich sells more copies today than when it first came out in 1937.) So, when you invest time, energy, and effort in writing Timeless Content, your library actually improves as time goes on—whereas, if you only write Timely Content, your library is deteriorating by the day.

80%+ Of Your Content Can Be Timely

This should be your goal.

Is there a time and place for Timely Content? Sure.

But the vast majority of your time should be INVESTED in writing & creating assets that will stand the test of time. You want people to read something you wrote 5 years ago and think, “Wow! This was written 5 years ago? It’s still relevant today!” If you can achieve that goal, you will unlock compounding effects in your Digital Writing most Buzzfeed writers could only dream of.

The Secret To Writing Timeless Content

Here it is:

Avoid writing about things that are only relevant “today.”

For example: business books struggle to stand the test of time because they oftentimes use case studies of companies that are successful “today.” But imagine reading a business book written in 1999 about the “dominance of Blockbuster.” If you read that today, your response would be: “What a waste of time! Blockbuster went bankrupt—and Netflix ate their lunch!”

Instead, you want to focus on writing things that aren’t dependent upon the world as it is today (when possible).

For example:

  • How To Have A Happy Marriage

  • How To Start Your Own Home Garden

  • How To Master The Art Of Negotiation

  • How To Build The Habit Of Saving Money

  • Etc.

Will there be new innovations in each of these topic areas? Of course. But notice how “Timeless” these topics feel. Why? Because the fundamentals of having a happy marriage have been true for thousands of years. The fundamentals of starting a home garden have been true since humans became farmers. The fundamentals of negotiation have been true, and will remain true, for decades into the future. This is why books like How To Win Friends & Influence People only get more popular with time.

So, whenever you sit down to write, ask yourself: “How can I make this more timeless?”

  • What are the tips, strategies, or frameworks that will remain true forever?

  • Who are the legendary leaders who will stand the test of time?

  • What are the keys to success that will remain true forever?

  • What are the BIG IDEAS that will remain true forever?

  • What are the mistakes that will remain true forever?

  • What are the lessons that will remain true forever?

Not every topic can be made “Timeless.”

But that should be your goal.


🔹Module 5: Execute Your EIG Content Strategy

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 5 of Idea Generation Mastery!

Now that you understand the 4 different “buckets” of content you can create, let’s put this together into a strategy you can iterate on over time.

Your Endless Idea Generator Content Strategy Blueprint

There are 4 “buckets” of content you can create:

  • Personal Stories & Curated Stories

  • Actionable Ideas & “Fun” Ideas

  • Timely Content

  • Timeless Content

So that you fully understand how to execute this yourself, let’s recap each one of these buckets—and run through a handful of examples.

Personal Stories

Stories you share based on your own personal experience & expertise.

Use The 2-Year Test to discover where you have opportunities here—and always remember to tie the story back to the reader’s wants, needs, hopes, dreams, questions, aspirations, and desired outcomes. It’s not enough to just “share yourself personal story.” The key is to use your personal story as context for the larger point you want the reader to take away from your writing.

Examples:

  • “I Have Been Writing Online For 10 Years. Here Are The 10 Biggest Mistakes I’ve Made—So You Don’t Waste As Much Time As I Did.”

  • “Bored Of Life? I Almost Died In A Car Crash When I Was 17. Here Are 7 Realizations I Had After My Near-Death Experience That Will Make You Cherish Every Day.”

  • “If You Want To Get Into Real Estate, Here’s The Best Piece Of Advice My Grandfather Ever Gave Me (He Owned $100M Of Rental Properties When He Died).”

Curated Stories

Stories you share based on other people’s experience & expertise.

Where you have gaps in your own knowledge and credibility, leverage other (well-known) people your audience is likely to recognize and trust in order to bring more attention to your writing.

Examples:

  • “David Ogilvy Is The Greatest Advertising Mind In History. If You Want To Learn Sales Copywriting, Read This Memo He Wrote In 1982.”

  • “According To Harvard Business Review, There Is A Scientific Reason Men Are Harder To Live With Than Women.”

  • “These 5 NBA Stars Have Made More Money From Investing Than From Basketball.”

Actionable Ideas

“How To” content.

To save yourself hours and hours of repeating the same tips, frameworks, problem-solving strategies, etc., over and over again, you want to build a library of content that answers your target readers’ questions, at scale. This way, whenever someone asks you a question, you can just link them to something you’ve written.

Examples:

  • “How To Rewrite Your Landing Page Copy To 2x Your Customer Conversions.”

  • “How To Buy The Right Running Shoes Based On The Shape Of Your Foot.”

  • “How To Hire A House Manager So You Never Have To Do Your Own Grocery Shopping Again (It’s Not As Expensive As You Think).”

“Fun” Ideas

Nostalgic, entertaining, “Wow-I-didn’t-know-that” content.

You can also create or curate “fun” content as a way of engaging your target readers in a form beyond just education. This “fun” content is more likely to attract a wider range of relevant readers, capturing attention and introducing them to your deeper library of Actionable content.

Examples:

  • “Are You A Writer? Then Your Life Goal Should Be To Write In These 7 Historic Libraries Around The World.”

  • “11 Porsche Designs That Never Became Reality—But Should Have.”

  • “The Greatest Moments In Basketball Ranked In Order Of Fan Amazement.”

Timely Content

News-driven content.

This is content designed to capitalize on a “moment,” generating short-term attention—and should only be 10-20% of your library. The benefit of creating Timely Content is its ability to ride existing momentum and introduce those readers to your broader, deeper library of content. (But the con is that the Timely Content you create likely won’t generate much attention, if any at all, beyond a few days/weeks.)

Examples:

  • “The Fed Just Announced Another Rate Hike. Here’s What That Means For Retail Investors.”

  • “America’s Supply Chain Crisis Means Delays In Car Arrivals. Luckily, Here Are 7 Dealerships That Have More Inventory Than They Know What To Do With.”

  • “Justin Bieber Just Cancelled His Upcoming Tour: 5 Reasons Why.”

Timeless Content

Content that will remain relevant for years into the future.

Timeless Content should be 80%+ of your library, and as a result will unlock compounding effects on your journey as a Digital Writer. The more “timeless” your content is, the more likely it will be to continue capturing readers, followers, and subscribers for years—not just a few days/weeks.

Examples:

  • “7 Reasons Why So Many Millionaires End Up Going Broke.”

  • “About To Have Your First Kid? Here Are 15 Mistakes New Parents Make—And How To Fix Them.”

  • “Business Writing 101: The Fundamentals Of Persuasion, Trust, Credibility, And Effective Communication.”

Let The Data Dictate Your Content Strategy

If you consistently create content in each of the above buckets, consider yourself part of the top 1% of Digital Writers & Digital Creators on the Internet.

Because the truth is, most people have no idea how to think about writing & creating content. They just sit down, ask themselves, “Hmmm… what should I write today?” And then throw paint at the wall. 

And that’s fine to get yourself started. But the key to being a successful Digital Writer & Digital Creator is to understand why you’re creating what you’re creating, the role it plays in your broader library, and how you can learn (over time) which types of content are performing best with your target readers—and then doubling down on your winners.

So, don’t overthink it.

And certainly don’t sit at your desk “waiting” to construct the “perfect” strategy before you get started.

Just start, and let the data be your guide.


🔹Module 6: Claim Your Graduation Badge!

Ahoy!

Congratulations on completing the Idea Generation 5-Step Mastery Captain’s Table challenge!

To recap, over the past 5 days you have:

  • Generated Personal & Curated Story Ideas

  • Generated Actionable & “Fun” Ideas

  • Generated Timely Ideas

  • Generated Timeless Ideas

  • And created your own Endless Idea Generator Content Strategy Blueprint

You now have a bulletproof idea generation system that will be extremely helpful as you clarify your niche, build your audience, and start launching your first digital products!

records.content:
🔹[READ ME] Overview

Welcome to Formatting & Writing Rhythm Mastery, a 5-day mini-course designed to:

  • Help you master the fundamentals of formatting your digital writing.

  • Use “mirroring” to make your digital writing beautiful, organized, and easy to skim.

  • Incorporate writing rhythms to make your digital writing musical and effortless to read.

  • And more!

A few days from now, your writing is going to “look” radically different.

After completing this mini-course, you are going to become a Formatting Master.

You see, formatting is a skill. And if you want to become a prolific writer, then you need to practice the skill of visually organizing and presenting your ideas on the page.

So, that’s what you’re going to do over the next days:

  • Module 1: The 5 Pieces Of Effective Formatting

  • Module 2: Making Your Writing Visually Appealing

  • Module 3: Writing Rhythms

  • Module 4: Formatting Mistakes

  • Module 5: Your Ultimate Formatting Checklist

Ready to become a Formatting Master?

Then let’s set sail!

🔹Module 1: The 5 Pieces Of Effective Formatting


Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 1 of Formatting Mastery!

Let's get right into the good stuff.

Clear Title

Most Digital Writers & Digital Creators write their title last.

This is a mistake.

When you dive right into the writing, without starting with some sort of “working” title, that’s the equivalent of getting on a plane and nobody telling you what city it’s flying to! Your title is your North Star. It’s literally the “goal” of everything you’re about to write. So, if you don’t have a goal in mind, how can you expect to achieve it?

Worse, when Digital Writers & Digital Creators write their title last, they (inevitably) end up steering more in the direction of “clever”—not CLEAR. After two, three, fifty hours of writing, they can’t possibly come up with a CLEAR title that summarizes everything they’ve just written. So instead, they opt for something like this:

  • The World Was Never The Same

  • Midnight In The Morning

  • Broken Glass

They choose this “clever” title because it’s the only way they can wrap their arms around all the different things they just wrote down.

As a result, they don’t have clarity around what their writing is actually trying to say—which means the reader doesn’t either.

And when the reader doesn’t have clarity, what do they do?

They go back to YouTube (to watch cats hang from ceiling fans).

Start With A Working (CLEAR) Title

It doesn’t matter if it’s not perfect.

It doesn’t matter if you end up changing it later.

But it’s important to start with a (CLEAR) title so that you at least understand where you’re headed in the writing. Then, as you move along, if you want to change the promise of your headline, go for it. But that process should be happening WITH the writing—not as an afterthought.

Credible Intro

Next, as you begin to Prep The Page, you want to make a note to yourself:

“Why should the reader trust me? Why am I the right person to write about this topic? Should they trust me because of my Personal Credibility? Or because of my Borrowed Credibility?”

These are important questions to ask yourself.

Readers aren’t as picky as most people think. You don’t need to be a Harvard Graduate, a Rocket Scientist, or a political official for readers to trust you. All you need to do is tell them why they should take what you’re saying seriously. Our favorite example is: imagine a friend (or a friend of a friend) asked you for a Friday Night Movie Recommendation. It really doesn’t matter what movie you recommend, inevitably the person will ask, “Why? Why should I watch this?” To which you will most likely reply: “Because I’ve watched every single Rom Com movie on Netflix, and trust me, this one is the best.”

That’s all they need to hear. And ba-da-bing, your opinion is trusted.

Writing is no different: Readers need a reason to trust you.

So, what makes you credible?

  • Is it how many hours you’ve spent doing this thing?

  • Is it because of some meaningful milestone you’ve achieved?

  • Is it the amount of years you’ve spent studying and practicing this thing?

And if you don’t have any personal credibility, how might you be able to borrow that credibility from someone else?

  • Is this what someone else with decades of experience says to do?

  • Is this what a very smart book, written by a very smart person, recommends?

  • Is this wisdom you’ve gathered by spending time around other people who have achieved this same thing?

Make a note to yourself in the introduction of whatever you’re writing:

“This is why you should trust what I’m about to tell you.”

For example:

  • “How do I know how to build a real estate empire? Because of the last 10 years, I’ve bought and sold over 50 different rental properties.”

  • “Why should you take my Netflix series recommendations? Because I’ve watched over 5,000 hours of Netflix shows and movies.”

  • “Why is this the best strategy to get distribution on your writing? Because I went and interviewed 20 different best-selling authors, and this is what they said to do.”

The reader has no problem trusting you—you just have to give them a reason to!

Main Points

The Main Points of your writing are, well… the Main Points.

These are, at the absolute core, the things you’re trying to say.

For example, look at the way this course module is structured.

What are the Main Points?

  • Clear Title

  • Credible Intro

  • Main Points

  • Bulleted or Numbered Lists

  • Conclusion, Recap, or CTA

Before you even start writing, you should take a moment and list out all the Main Points you want to be sure you cover—in an Atomic Essay, in a Twitter Thread, in a long-form LinkedIn post, or even in a single Tweet. Because when you start with these Main Points in mind, you no longer have to “figure out” what you’re trying to say as you go along. You simply go, section by section, and fill in reasons, mistakes, stories, examples, case studies, trends, tips, etc. (Which is exactly how we wrote this, by the way.)

Furthermore, when you start with a short list of just the Main Points, you can assess whether or not your Main Points (aka: the things you’re trying to say) are valuable enough. You might look at your list of Main Points and think, “Eh, actually, all these things have been said before,” causing you to want to push further and make a new list of Main Points. That’s good! That means you are improving the thinking of your writing—before you begin whacking away at writing sentences and obsessing over adjectives.

Bulleted or Numbered Lists

Ah, now this is how you take your formatting skills to the next level.

The vast majority of Digital Writers & Digital Creators don’t even write using Main Points/Subheads. 

Instead, you click on their content, and it’s just one big blocky paragraph after another. (Legacy writers struggle with this the most. And it’s why even New York Times’ best-selling authors struggle to get distribution on their digital content—because they are used to writing longwinded books, not skimmable Atomic Essays, Twitter Threads, and LinkedIn posts.)

Of the Digital Writers & Digital Creators who do learn the importance of organizing their content using Main Points/Subheads, only a small percentage of them graduate to the next level:

Using Bulleted or Numbered Lists.

  • Can you tell how satisfied your brain is to read a quick bulleted list right here?

  • Can you “feel” how it’s a nice break after reading the above few paragraphs?

  • Do you notice how easy this section of bulleted takeaways is to skim?

  • Are you enjoying how this feels, as a reader, right now?

Incorporating short bulleted or numbered lists inside your Main Points is one of the most underrated writing & formatting techniques that exists today. Because what these bulleted or numbered lists force you to do is strip away all the unnecessary explanation—and just tell the reader what’s most important.

No unnecessary description.

No rambling.

Just boom, boom, boom.

If you can master the art of writing Clear Titles, organizing your big ideas with Main Points/Subheads, and making sections more skimmable by using Bulleted or Numbered, lists, then pat yourself on the back.

You have a skill set 99% of Digital Writers & Digital Creators do not have.

Furthermore, if you are interested in being hired as a writer/ghostwriter, nothing will impress clients more than seeing your magic at work—presenting content in a coherent, organized, and visually appealing way.

Conclusion, Recap, or CTA

The last piece of formatting is the ending:

  • Writing a conclusion

  • Sharing a recap

  • Providing a CTA (Call To Action)

That said, our personal philosophy is that conclusions are optional.

When should you write a conclusion?

Here’s a good rule of thumb:

If your conclusion is just repeating everything you just said, you don’t need a conclusion.

Right?

Remember: you aren’t writing a 12th grade English paper. You are writing for highly impatient digital readers(people who would much rather swipe back to TikTok and watch 7-second videos of young children falling face-first into bowls of macaroni and cheese). So if your “conclusion” is just you repeating yourself, ditch it. Just let the piece end. Make it a cliffhanger! Because if what you wrote was truly helpful and beneficial to the reader, they will inevitably want to click around and read more content from you.

Which means you should only write “conclusions” if they add something new to the piece.

You should only write “conclusions” if they tie everything together in a new way.

When should you write a recap?

Think of “recaps” as mini-conclusions.

Recaps are great endings to short-form content—particularly lists, where readers appreciate you repeating the big ideas/Main Points one more time for them.

For example, this is a recap:

TL;DR is “internet-speak” for “Too Long, Didn’t Read” (which is a quippy way of saying, “Let me recap everything important—incase you didn’t actually read everything that came before this).

For Twitter Threads, LinkedIn posts, and even Medium articles/Quora answers, ending with a short, fast-paced recap list of some sort can be very helpful for readers.

  • It is easy to share.

  • It reminds the readers of “what’s most important.”

  • It is the most compressed version of the longer asset you just published.

In some cases, it may actually be helpful for YOU to write your “recap” Tweet/short list first, because this short list can actually act as the outline for whatever it is you’re writing.

Pretty cool, right?

When should you write a CTA?

CTA stands for “Call To Action.”

Any reader who makes it to the end of anything you’ve written is most likely to be interested in something ELSE you’ve written—especially if it’s on a similar or tangential topic. Think of this as your best opportunity to move readers further into your ecosystem.

CTAs can be everything from:

  • Encouraging readers to follow you directly if they enjoyed your content.

  • Directing readers to another relevant piece of content in your library (”If you liked this, you’ll also like this!”).

  • Driving readers to subscribe to your newsletter or download your free Ultimate Guide.

  • Reminding readers to buy your eBook, book, online course, etc.

Here’s an example of a CTA we use—which is how we drive free readers on Twitter over to our email newsletter:﻿

﻿These are the fundamentals of formatting!

  • Clear Title

  • Credible Intro

  • Main Points

  • Bulleted or Numbered Lists

  • Conclusion, Recap, and/or CTA

And simply understanding these 5 things are the core parts of highly effective Digital Writing puts you leagues ahead of every other person writing (or thinking about writing) online.


🔹Module 2: Making Your Writing Visually Appealing


Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 2 of Formatting Mastery!

Are you ready to learn the secret to crafting “visually appealing” writing?

Let’s dig in!

The Importance Of “Mirroring”

Mirroring is the single most important formatting technique.

Think of Mirroring as a way of anchoring the reader’s eyes on the page. When you Mirror sections, what happens is the reader can’t help but feel like they are staring at a work of art—because you’ve constructed more than just words on a page. What you’ve done is create sections, blocks, and distinct areas where you’d like them to direct their attention.

This is a very subtle but powerful formatting technique.

So let’s get into some examples:

How To Mirror The Promise In Your Headline (All The Way Down The Page)

Mirroring basically means you take one element and then repeat it:

  • Throughout your entire essay/piece.

  • Throughout an entire section (or multiple sections).

  • And even individual sentences.

Here’s how to mirror the promise in your headline:

Let’s say the headline of your piece is: “7 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars.”

The Promise here is “7 Mistakes.”

Why would a reader click on this piece? To read your 7 Mistakes. Simple.

The way you Mirror this promise all the way down the page then is to repeat this same promise over and over again. Which means each one of your Main Points/Subheads would follow the same wording, flow, and punctuation. Like this:

  • Mistake #1:

  • Mistake #2:

  • Mistake #3:

  • Mistake #4:

  • Mistake #5:

  • Mistake #6:

  • Mistake #7:

This might seem like a simple nuance, but it’s more powerful than most writers realize.

When a reader clicks on your piece, they are immediately looking for the “promise” you made them in the headline. So, if you promised them “7 Mistakes,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “7 Mistakes. If you promised them “6 Lessons,” then your Main Points/Subheads needs to be “6 Lessons.” If you promised them “11 Crazy Gadgets,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “11 Crazy Gadgets.” And so on.

Tying your Main Points to the promise in your headline is one of the simplest ways to immediately upgrade the skimmability of your writing—and make it easy for readers to fly through your content.

How To Mirror Main Points

But this is only the beginning!

As you begin to write, you may decide to take some creative liberties with your Main Points. That’s fine! BUT the golden rule is: if you change 1 Main Point/Subhead, you need to “Mirror” that change all the way down the page.

Just look at these 2 lists of Main Points/Subheads and notice which list your eye sees as more visually appealing:

Example 1

  • Mistake #1:

  • The Right Way To Think:

  • Lesson I Learned:

  • Another Mistake:

  • Sometimes, all you need to do is make sure you’re focusing on the right thing.

  • Ending Thoughts:

Example 2

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #1:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #2:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #3:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #4:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #5:

Which one of these lists is more visually appealing?

Which list do you immediately assume is “more organized?”

The 2nd one! But there’s a very clear reason as to why.

The reason is because readers love similarities. When each of your Main Points/Subheads “looks the same” and there is a clear pattern, this gives the reader reassurance. They understand how you’re moving them down the page, and they also understand where they are in the piece. But when your subheads are alternating style, capitalization, punctuation, etc., each of these changes makes the reader feel more and more “lost.” They can’t tell why you are changing the rules on them.

So, if you are going to make a change to one of your Main Points/Subheads, remember to Mirror that change all the way down the page.

Readers love patterns.

How To Mirror Small Sections

This same rule applies to every aspect of your writing.

Mirroring can (and should) also happen within each of the sections of your piece. For example: if you open with 1 clear declarative sentence, and then give a 5-sentence paragraph description, and then close with a final declarative sentence, you should strive to repeat that same cadence and pattern (1/5/1) in each of the subsequent sections. This helps readers find the flow/melody of your writing. 

Which makes it even easier for them to quickly skim and consume your content. (And it’s better for them to quickly skim & consume your content than for them to open your essay, feel lost/overwhelmed, and decide not to read it at all.)

This section is an example of this idea in action (it’s a 1/5/1).

What you want to avoid is individual sections looking vastly different:

If one section is 3 giant paragraphs, and then another section is literally 2 sentences, you have a problem. (They “look” off-balance.)

Instead, you want to strive for each section (inside each of your Main Points/Subheads) to be visually the same—either in length, or in formatting choices and style. For example, as we’re writing this, we are thinking about the section right before this where we explain the 1/5/1 pattern. We could stop writing here, but then it would look a bit “off-balance.” So, we’re going to keep flushing this description out so that it “LOOKS” the same. We’re even going to aim for the same 1/5/1 pattern.

See how the above section, and this section, share visual similarities?

How To Mirror Sentences

Mirroring can also happen on the individual sentence level.

This is an underrated formatting technique we notice most writers ignore. They don’t consider how they can use individual sentences as anchors for the reader’s visual experience. Instead, we find writers just sort of bold random sentences and words with no real rationale for how these bolded elements can help the reader understand what they’re reading. (Bolding doesn’t have to be used for emphasis. It can also be used to anchor the readers attention.)

Here’s how it works:

Instead of burying the pattern inside the writing itself, move the pattern to the beginning or the end of each paragraph.

Mirroring can look like this. You bold the first sentence, and then explain what you need to explain in the same paragraph. This helps the reader understand that the bolded first sentence is the “idea,” and then the words that follow (in that same paragraph) are still related to that same idea.

Mirroring can also look like this. Ah, now you are moving into a new idea, but because you are keeping the visual pattern the same (bolding just the first sentence), the reader can start to see/hear the pattern. They understand what you’re doing—which makes it easier for them to stay engaged and keep giving you their attention.

Mirroring can also look like this. And then you do it one more time, for good measure. You are repeating the pattern. And the repetition of the pattern is what gives the reader confidence that you are taking them on a journey. You aren’t wasting their time. You’ve engineered this experience for them, and all they have to do is sit back and enjoy it.

See? Pretty cool, right?

You can bold and mirror the first sentence of sequential paragraphs. Or, you can bold and mirror the last sentence of sequential paragraphs (emphasizing the takeaways). Or, you can bold and mirror a sentence in the middle of sequential paragraphs (emphasizing the nuanced points). It doesn’t really matter where you choose to execute this bolding/mirroring effect, so long as you’re consistent. DO NOT CHANGE THE PATTERN. The whole key, and what makes this technique work, is repeating the same pattern over and over again in one particular section.

And if you’re going to change the pattern, make sure it’s in a different section altogether (and whatever you change the pattern to, be sure to repeat it!).

Repetition is key.

🔹Module 3: Writing Rhythms

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 3 of Formatting Mastery!

Let’s talk about how to make your writing more musical.

How To Create Rhythm & Musicality In Your Writing

Contrary to popular belief, musicality and rhythm in your writing is not difficult to create.

Watch. It’s all about sentence length. And the key to creating musicality and rhythm is literally nothing more than just alternating between long sentences and short sentences—ideally in some sort of pattern. See? Short sentence, followed by a medium sentence, followed by a long sentence. If you pay attention as you read, you can “hear” the pauses, the build-up, and the long crescendo of pace as the sentences are processed in your brain.

This is all you have to do to make your writing “flow.”

The Basics: 1/3/1

{1} The simplest “rhythm writing” pattern is what we like to call 1/3/1.

{3} This means you open with 1 short to medium-length sentence. Then, in three sentences you add more description and color. And then you finish the idea with one single sentence.

{1} Just like this section here.

1/3/1 literally refers to the number of sentences, and the pattern they’re stacked in.

One strong opening sentence. Three descriptive sentences, advancing your point forward. And then one final concluding sentence.

And you can literally repeat 1/3/1 over and over again, all the way down the page (just like we’re doing here!).

Expanding The Middle

Now let’s say 1/3/1 doesn’t give you enough space to say what you want to say.

The secret to maintaining effective rhythms in your writing is to “expand the middle.” This means keeping the same 1/3/1 structure (single sentences to open and close your longer paragraphs of description), but adding content to the middle part of the “sandwich.”

For example:

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/6/1

  • 1/7/1

See how the structure is the same, but all that is changing is the length of the middle paragraph? The key here is to maintain your single-sentence “bookends” (the opener and closer sentences), which gives the reader an easy entry point into your writing (or next section), and rewarding them with a single sentence at the end of your elongated paragraph of description.

So, if you’re ever going to expand your writing, remember to expand the middle.

Creating Rhythm Pyramids

But this is only the beginning!

The advanced level of “expanding the middle” is creating what we like to call Rhythm Pyramids! This means elongating your writing even more by creating new patterns to repeat—up to your big paragraph of description, and then back down again.

The reason this works so well is because each sentence (and each stack of sentences) builds on the one before it. A single-sentence opener is what makes it feel “easy” to read the next two sentences.  And those two sentences make it easy to want to dig into 5 sentences of description. But then once you get through that big paragraph of 5 sentences, you (as the reader) will be a bit tired from “climbing up the hill” and will want to feel some downhill momentum. So then you need to bring things back down again to two sentences.

Just like we’re doing here. Can you feel the “up & down” pattern?

Ah, a final single sentence—so relieving.

Here are some Rhythm Pyramids that work well:

  • 1/2/5/2/1

  • 1/2/7/2/1

  • 1/2/3/7/3/2/1

Notice how, in all of these, the middle paragraph is the longest, and then the “up” path and the “down” path (both sides) mirror each other.

Remember: the whole secret to formatting, and creating effective writing rhythms, is creating & repeating patterns.

Creating Punchy Rhythms

Finally, the last type of writing rhythm is creating those “punchy” sections.

Boom. Boom. Boom.

  • 1/1/1

  • 2/2/1

  • 3/2/1

These “punchy” rhythms work best at the beginnings of sections—they create an immediate sense of momentum. Or, at the ends of sections—where they create a feeling of strong conclusion).

Either way, the whole key here is to always end on 1 single sentence. Ending a section with 2 or 3 sentences feels a bit like you stopped with no final resolution.

Just like this section here!


🔹Module 4: Formatting Mistakes

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 4 of Formatting Mastery!

Now, if formatting is the easiest upgrade you can make to your writing, then the challenge here is that formatting is also quite easy to mess up.

So, let’s break down some of the big mistakes writers make.

Writing Rhythm Mistakes

First, just so you really understand what makes writing rhythms work, let’s talk briefly about where writing rhythms go wrong.

  • 2/2/2/2/2

  • 3/3/3/3/3

  • 4/4/4/4/4

  • 1/2/2/3/3/2/1

  • 1/3/3/3/3/1

  • Etc.

Notice any patterns here?

The worst writing rhythms are ones where there is minimal change in section length. Even worse, is when multiple sections in a row are the exact same length. (Nothing makes your writing sound more “monotone” than having multiple two or three sentence paragraphs in a row.)

Avoid these like the plague.

Instead, what you want is to think in opposites.

Small numbers to big numbers, back to small numbers:

  • 1/3/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/7/1

The more dramatic the jump (between single-sentence paragraphs and multi-sentence paragraphs), the more your writing will “sound” like it’s moving. (Think of paragraphs like waves in the ocean. What makes them “fun” is when there are some small waves, followed by a BIG wave, followed by some small waves again.)

This is the easiest upgrade you can make to your writing—and the effects it will have on the reader will be immediate.

Your writing will “sound” lovely.

Bolding & Italics

What do you think of this section?

Ask yourself if this is confusing to read. What do you notice about the way you read this paragraph?

Where is your attention being drawn? Do you know what to pay attention to? Chances are, probably not—and the reason is because bolding & italics are very easy to overdo. In small doses, they can be nice ways of reminding readers of what’s most important. But bolding & italics are a bit like truffles in cooking. A little bit goes a long way, but too much can very quickly ruin a delicious meal.

Instead, the best way to use bolding & italics is to think of them as mini-subheadings:

If you’re going to use bolding, use them like this. Create a repeatable cadence & pattern the reader can immediately spot and hold onto. Bolding individual words inside sentences or paragraphs, while it can work, is usually less effective. Similarly, if you really want to use italics, here’s a great technique: italicize the last sentence of a paragraph/section to drive home the emphasis.

Also, if you’re going to use bolding, repeat the pattern. If there’s no pattern to be repeated, chances are, you don’t need to bold anything. Trust the reader. They will likely be able to spot the “important point” you’re trying to make in your writing whether you bold it or not (you don’t need to shout for them to hear you). The same goes for italics: if you can, repeat the pattern.

Also, if you’re going to use bolding, only pick 1 word or phrase. If you absolutely must, force yourself to pick only 1 word or 1 small phrase in a given paragraph/section to bold. Remember, if you bold multiple words/phrases, then what you’re telling the reader is “everything is important.” And if “everything” is important, then nothing is important.

Study the above section to see how bolding & italics are being used intentionally!

Punctuation

This is an extremely overlooked and undervalued aspect of formatting.

The golden rule of Creative Writing is: punctuation doesn’t really “matter.” For proof, just go spend 15-20 minutes reading Reddit, and what you’ll find is that you are (as a reader) very willing to forgive grammar and punctuation errors if the content is good enough. If someone is telling you a fascinating story, answering an important question of yours, or simply being wildly entertaining, you (as a reader) really don’t care if they “mess up” here and there. So, from that perspective, punctuation isn’t nearly as important as your 12th grade English teacher said it was.

However…

There is one important “rule” when it comes to punctuation in your own writing.

You must (as best you can) be consistent.

Remember: writing is an art, which means, technically, there aren’t really any rules (and any rules that “exist” were made up by someone else, no different from you). And so, if there aren’t any rules, then what matters most is that you just don’t lose the reader. That’s all that matters. As long as the reader is engaged and giving you their attention, you are succeeding as a writer.

And the way you keep readers engaged comes down to consistency.

  • This is consistency.

  • Every bulleted item is the same.

  • You, as the reader, know what to expect.

  • Full sentences, followed by a period at the end.

Here’s what consistency is NOT:

  • This is not consistency.

  • Because each sentence has small nuanced differences

  • Can You See It?

  • readers hate this. hate it beyond belief.

99% of writers spend too much time trying to memorize the infinite number of old English rules to writing—when the reality is, none of them REALLY matter.

What does matter (to your readers) is that, whatever style you pick, you stick with it all the way down the page. You could literally write an entire Atomic Essay, Twitter Thread, LinkedIn post, or eBook and not capitalize a single word, and the reader wouldn’t think anything of it. They might even call you a genius! (”Wow! What is this unique style where nothing is capitalized?!”) But if even 1 single word is capitalized (or several), then suddenly the whole style is thrown off. You’ve ruined the magic. And now the reader can’t tell, “Was this a style? Or do you just not know how to write?”

There are no rules in writing.

You are the one who determines the rules.

All that matters, however, is that you stay consistent within whichever rules you set.

🔹Module 5: Your Ultimate Formatting Checklist

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 5 of Formatting Mastery!

We’ve covered a LOT over the past few days. Now, let’s tie it all together.

Here’s a recap of what we’ve covered—and a checklist you can use to check your own formatting going forward:

The 5 Pieces Of Effective Formatting

  • Clear Title

  • Credible Intro

  • Main Points/Subheads

  • Bulleted or Numbered Lists

  • Conclusion, Recap, and/or CTA

Mirroring

  • Mirror the promise in the headline in your Main Points/Subheads

  • Mirror the style & formatting of each Main Point (to be the same).

  • Mirror sections or paragraphs within sections, to “look” the same.

  • Mirror individual sentences at the beginnings or ends of paragraphs/sections.

Proven Writing Rhythms

  • (Basic) 1/3/1

  • (Basic) 1/4/1

  • (Basic) 1/5/1

  • (Basic) 1/6/1

  • (Basic) 1/7/1

  • (Pyramid) 1/2/5/2/1

  • (Pyramid) 1/2/7/2/1

  • (Pyramid) 1/2/3/7/3/2/1

  • (Punchy) 1/1/1

  • (Punchy) 2/2/1

  • (Punchy) 3/2/1

If you can incorporate all of the above into everything you write, you will outperform 99% of Digital Writers & Digital Creators.

We cannot stress this enough.

There are hundreds of thousands (maybe millions) of hired writers, all over the world, in every industry, that do not understand the above. There are writers who get paid $100,000+ per year working inside the content marketing departments of billion-dollar companies that do not understand the above. There are even writers who have hundreds of thousands of followers online who do not understand the above.

Mastering the art of formatting, especially in the Digital World, is a giant unfair advantage.

And now, you have it.
