records.content:
🔹[READ ME] Overview


Welcome to Headline Mastery, a 5-day mini-course designed to:

  • Level-up your headline writing skills

  • Master the fundamentals of writing effective headlines

  • Learn how to increase the voltage of your headlines (and make them more powerful)

  • Start “twisting the knife” more and more—attracting your target readers’ attention

  • And more!

So pack your bags, because this ship is ready to set sail!

After completing this mini-course, you are going to become a Headline Writing Pro.Over the next 5 days, you are going to become a Headline Writing Pro.

  • You are going to master the fundamentals of writing headlines (a skill 99% of Digital Writers completely ignore).

  • You are going to increase the voltage of your headlines to the point where readers can’t help but click on them.

  • You are going to learn how to “twist the knife,” and speak directly to your target readers’ most urgent & important pain points.

  • You are going to internalize the proven formats—that work over and over again.

  • And you are going to gain access to dozens of “hook” templates (making it easy to immediately put all these new learnings into practice).

🔹Module 1: The 5 Pieces Of An Effective Headline

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 1 of Headline Mastery!

Let's get right into the good stuff.

There are 5 fundamental pieces of an effective headline.

  • HOW MANY

  • THE WHO

  • THE WHAT

  • THE WHY

  • THE KNIFE TWIST

When a reader reads one of your headlines—whether it’s an Atomic Essay, a long-form blog post, or even the title of your eBook, book, course, or digital product—they are asking themselves 5 questions: “What’s all in here? Who is this for? What is it about? Why does it matter? And what do I get in exchange for reading it?”

Which means, in order to get readers to read your work and pay attention to your content, you need to answer these 5 questions.

And the way you answer these 5 questions, quickly, is by writing an effective headline.

So, let’s break each one of these pieces down.

HOW MANY

Most writers don’t realize it, but basically everything you write is a “list” in some way.

  • You’re writing about 1 big idea.

  • Or you’re writing about several big ideas.

  • Or you’re writing about a dozen related ideas.

  • Or you’re writing about dozens and dozens of tiny ideas.

It just depends on whether or not you make the number of ideas you are writing about explicit to your readers.

For example, this headline is a “list,” it’s just emphasizing one main idea:

Which is no different than this Buzzfeed article, which is what most writers think of when they imagine themselves writing a “list.”

But they’re the same thing.

And in both cases, the reader feels like they know exactly what they’re signing up for when they click to read your content. They understand “how many” ideas you’re going to be talking about—which is really just another way of them understanding how long it’s going to take for them to consume your writing.

THE WHO

Next is THE WHO.

The single most effective way to attract your target reader is to literally name them in your headline:

  • 6 Tips For Project Managers

  • 5 Traits Of Highly Productive Serial Entrepreneurs

  • How To Become A Real Estate Broker

And so on.

When you name THE WHO in your headline, you are clearly saying: “This is WHO should be reading this.” And if a reader matches that WHO, it’s going to be hard for them to keep scrolling without at least considering whether or not they should give that sort of content their attention. (After all: if someone says, “I wrote this specifically for YOU,” aren’t you a bit more likely to give it a chance?)

THE WHAT

Next is THE WHAT.

  • 6 Tips

  • 5 Traits

  • 7 Mistakes

  • The Biggest Reason

  • 17 Trends

  • Etc.

The WHAT is, quite literally, WHAT you are giving the reader. Are you giving them tips? Are you giving them examples? Are you giving them traits? Are you giving them mistakes?

Where Digital Writers & Digital Creators go wrong is they don’t have clarity over WHAT exactly it is they are giving their readers—or worse, they promise to give their readers one thing (tips) but then in the writing, end up giving them something else (mistakes).

The whole key to writing an effective headline is to make THE WHAT explicit, and then to keep that promise all the way down the page.

If you promised the reader tips, give them tips!

And if you promised the reader trends, give them trends!

THE WHAT is “what” they clicked for in the first place.

THE WHY

Ah, now WHY should the reader read?

It’s not enough to just say:

  • 6 Tips For Project Managers

  • 5 Traits Of Highly Productive Serial Entrepreneurs

  • How To Become A Real Estate Broker

In order to get the reader’s attention, you also need to tell them WHY they should take the time to read your writing. What are they going to get in exchange? Remember: when someone clicks on your writing, they aren’t just “reading.” They are giving you 60 seconds, or 3 minutes, or 10 minutes of their life. That’s a big ask! So in order for them to feel good about giving you 3 minutes of their life, they need to know what you’re going to give them in return.

You can make this “exchange” clear by stating THE WHY.

  • 6 Tips For Entry-Level Project Managers To Get Promoted In Their First 30 Days

  • 5 Traits Of Highly Productive Serial Entrepreneurs That Guarantee You Become A Millionaire

  • How To Become A Real Estate Broker Without Spending Thousands of Dollars On Licenses & Training

The WHY is “the reason.” If the reader reads this piece of writing from you, what are they going to get in exchange—specifically? What’s the goal? What’s the takeaway? What’s the benefit? What’s the outcome?

The reader needs A REASON to give you their attention.

So, give them one.

THE KNIFE TWIST

The very last piece of your headline is what we like to call “The Knife Twist.”

  • 6 Tips For Entry-Level Project Managers To Get Promoted In Their First 30 Days, Build Trust With Your Employees, And Finish Projects In Record Time

  • 5 Traits Of Highly Productive Serial Entrepreneurs That Guarantee You Become A Millionaire By The Age Of 30 (So You Can Retire Early)

  • How To Become A Real Estate Broker Without Spending Thousands of Dollars On Licenses, Training Programs, And Wasting Time Listening To “Fake Mentors”

Twisting The Knife is a copywriting term, and it basically just means “more.” How can you give your target reader more benefits, more outcomes, more time saved, more rewards, more trust, more positive feelings, more mistakes avoided, more lessons learned, more, more, more.

When you “Twist The Knife,” it almost always happens at the end of your headline.

  • You’ve signaled HOW MANY ideas you’re presenting

  • You’ve named the audience (THE WHO)

  • You’ve made THE WHAT nice and clear

  • And you’ve given the reader a reason to give you their attention (THE WHY)

Now, give them more.

What’s another reason?

And another reason?

And another reason?

The more you “Twist The Knife” (the more you give them), the more likely they are to give you their attention.

🔹Module 2: Increasing The Voltage Of Your Headlines

Ahoy!

And welcome to Module 2 of Headline Mastery!

Now, let’s ramp up the voltage.

What Does It Mean To “Increase The Voltage?”

  • Some ideas are low voltage: “Writing online is a helpful exercise.”

  • And some ideas are high voltage: “Writing online will change your life, ignite mental clarity, and unlock digital financial abundance.”

It all depends on what words you choose to use—and how specific you choose to get!

Increasing the voltage in your own writing is one of the most powerful ways to engage readers. Note: we are not talking about picking “better” adjectives here. The whole key to increasing the voltage is specificity. Because the more specific you can get, the more likely the right reader is going to engage with your content.

Here’s how:

Increasing The Voltage Of THE WHO

If you write something for everyone, you end up writing something for no one.

This is one of the biggest mistakes Digital Writers & Digital Creators make. They set out to try to be “everything for everyone,” and it never works. Why? Because each individual person isn’t “everyone.” Each individual person is someone—and your job is to speak to someones, at scale.

The way you do this is by increasing the voltage of THE WHO.

For example:

  • Weak Voltage: “…for managers.”

  • Strong Voltage: “…for project managers at food delivery software companies.”

What’s happening here?

We aren’t just “picking stronger words.” What’s actually happening is we are getting more specific about exactly WHO we are talking to. This isn’t for “all managers.” This is specifically for project managers at food delivery software companies.

Here’s a good rule of thumb: if this level of specificity makes you afraid you’re going to cut readers out, that means you’re doing it right.

You don’t want “everyone.”

You want “someone,” at scale.

Increasing The Voltage Of THE WHAT

You can increase the voltage of every single element of your headline.

In fact, that’s the best way to approach the writing process. Write your headline, and then go through (piece by piece) and consider how you can increase the voltage. How can you get more specific? How can you make it clearer, and clearer, and clearer exactly who this is for? How can you make it clearer, and clearer, and clearer what this is about? Etc.

For example:

  • Weak Voltage: “6 tips…”

  • Strong Voltage: “6 small but powerful tips…”

Again, there’s an important nuance here: this isn’t about picking clever words to “trick” the reader.  Increasing the voltage of your WHAT is about signaling to the reader WHAT they’re going to get. Are they going to get 6 vague tips? Or are they going to get 6 small tips? Or are they going to get 6 small tips that, although they might seem short and quick, are quite powerful—and actually lead to giant, transformational outcomes?

Specificity is the key.

Increasing The Voltage Of THE WHY

Same thing goes for THE WHY.

Settling for a general “WHY” might be the biggest missed opportunity for Digital Writers & Digital  Creators.

For example, here are some general WHY statements:

  • Weak Voltage: “…so you can be happy.”

  • Weak Voltage: “…so you can write better.”

  • Weak Voltage: “…so you can get promoted.”

And these are fine. But they’re hardly exciting. They’re just sort of practical. It’s not that they’re wrong, it’s just that they’re expected.

So, how do you increase the voltage?

Get more specific!

  • Strong Voltage: “…so you can feel the feeling of happiness every moment, of every day.”

  • Strong Voltage: “…so you can master the fundamentals of writing.”

  • Strong Voltage: “…so you can land the job you’ve always wanted.”

Increasing the voltage of THE WHY is all about understanding WHY readers care. Sometimes, this means specifying the problem (”…so you never feel rejected in your relationship ever again.”), and sometimes this means specifying the solution (”…so you can not just make enough money to support yourself, but to help your parents retire early.”). Either way, the WHY needs to speak directly to the person you want to reach.

And guess what?

If you don’t know WHY they should care, right away in the headline, then it doesn’t matter if you write 80 words or 800 words or 8,000 words—your target reader isn’t going to care.

Because you haven’t given them a WHY.

Increasing The Voltage Of The Knife Twist

Which leads us to… increasing the voltage of The Knife Twist.

Let’s not overcomplicate it: take your WHY, and list more of them.

And don’t just list more of them, but list the ones that are most compelling.

  • Strong Voltage: “…so you can go viral, attract your first 10,000 followers, and launch your first digital product.”

  • Strong Voltage: “…so you can have an open and honest relationship with your significant other and stay married for decades.”

  • Strong Voltage: “…so you can land the job you’ve always wanted, achieve a new level of recognition at work, and solidify the future of your career.”

A good exercise you can use here is:

Start by just listing out all the things you target reader wants.

Even before you start writing the headline.

Start with a list of all the things your reader wants, and then pick the top 3 and let those become your WHY/Knife Twist. (You know your target reader wants & cares about those 3 things, so… say those 3 things in the headline!)

🔹Module 3: Twisting The Knife

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 3 of Headline Mastery!

It’s time to master the art of “Twisting The Knife.”

What Is The Secret To “Twisting The Knife?”

We have covered the basics up to this point, but the reality is, “Twisting The Knife” is a skill you never stop getting better at.

It’s one of those timeless, foundational skills writers should practice their entire lives.

Now, what’s the secret?

“Twisting The Knife” isn’t about writing. It’s about thinking.

Amateur writers try to “Twist The Knife” by choosing buzzy words & clever catchphrases:

  • “This 1 CRAZY Technique…”

  • “You’ll Never Believe What Happened Next!”

  • “A Wildly Unexpected Solution…”

But let us be clear: this is far from pro-level “knife twisting.”

Instead, the whole key to “Twisting The Knife” is to spend time reading, researching, and ideally talking to your target readers—and understanding what makes them tick.

  • What do they care about?

  • What do they value?

  • What are their aspirations?

  • What are their hopes and dreams?

  • What are their biggest fears? (And why do they have these fears?)

  • What do they wish would stop happening?

  • What do they consider to be a “life-changing outcome?”

  • Etc.

Most Digital Writers are weak “Knife Twisters” because they don’t take the time to really get to know their target readers. They make sweeping assumptions (and big, grand, vague promises) that sort of work for “everyone.” And as a result, their target reader doesn’t feel seen, heard, or understood.

The whole secret here has nothing to do with writing, and everything to do with thinking.

Who is your target reader?

What do they care about?

Say that.

Twisting On The Benefits

There are 3 big ways you can “Twist The Knife.”

The first is twisting on the benefits: What are all the positive things that will happen if the reader reads your work?

  • Will they make new friends?

  • Will they make more money?

  • Will they find a life partner?

  • Will they build a business?

  • Will they free themselves of stress?

  • Will they find a newfound sense of clarity?

  • Will they (finally) feel like they’ve found their life’s purpose?

Again, this is a great exercise you can do separate from “the writing itself.”

Start with a list of all the things readers will get IF they read your work and take action.

For example: let’s say you are writing about 15-minute yoga routines for busy remote freelancers. (Does that sound “weirdly” specific? Good!)

Well, what are all the BENEFITS of 15-minute yoga routines for busy remote freelancers?

  • Weak Voltage: You’ll be more flexible.

  • Weak Voltage: You’ll be less stressed throughout the day.

  • Weak Voltage: You’ll get in the habit of taking care of yourself.

Are these benefits correct? Yes.

But are these benefits as ELECTRIC as they can be? Far from it.

So, let’s turn up the voltage! (How? By being more specific.)

  • Strong Voltage: You’ll be more flexible, so you stop getting those 2 P.M. cramps in your hip flexor muscles, sitting in your rigid computer chair.

  • Strong Voltage: You’ll be less stressed throughout the day, which means less mistakes in your work, and less fights with your significant other.

  • Strong Voltage: You’ll get in the habit of taking care of yourself—saving your hundreds of wasted hours each year from all the times when you’ve burned out in the past.

See how much more compelling these are?

It’s because we are speaking directly to the reader—a very specific type of reader—and quite literally saying: “I understand you. I get you. I know the little problems you experience on a day-to-day basis.”

This is what makes a reader pause everything they’re doing and decide to give you their full attention.

Twisting On The Problems

Next, you can twist on the Problems.

Again, if it’s easier, start with a list of all the things your target reader struggles with:

  • What are they afraid of?

  • What do they wish would stop happening?

  • What is keeping them stuck and unable to move forward?

  • What is stressing them out? What’s keeping them up at night?

Start with this list of problems, and all of a sudden it becomes very easy to imagine WHO you are writing for, WHAT they need help with, and WHY they should give you their attention.

For example:

Let’s work in the other direction now.

What are all the PROBLEMS busy remote freelancers face—that 15-minute yoga routines could solve?

  • “I work all day long and don’t have any time to go to the gym.”

  • “I’m barely making ends meat and can’t afford a yoga studio membership.”

  • “I sit in a rigid desk chair for 8 hours per day and it gives me lower back pain.”

Etc.

OK, if you KNOW these are the problems your target reader is struggle with, THEN TO GET THEIR ATTENTION YOU SHOULD PROBABLY SAY THE EXACT PROBLEM THEY ARE STRUGGLING WITH!!!!!!!!

That makes sense, right?

Take 1, or 2, or 3 of these highly-specific problems, and rewrite it in the form of your headline:

“Are You A Busy Freelancer Working 8+ Hours Per Day? Here Are 3 Of My Favorite 15-Minute Yoga Routines That Will Guarantee You Never Have Lower Back Pain Again.”

WOWZA!

Twisting On The Outcomes

Every headline either “twists” on Benefits, Problems, or Outcomes.

Outcomes are different than Benefits. Benefits are the more incremental positive things that happen if your target reader reads, implements the information you’re sharing, and takes action. Outcomes, on the other hand, are bigger-picture destinations. Outcomes are “the dream.” The Promised Land. This is where your target reader wants to end up.

So, once again: if it’s easier, start with a list of all the Outcomes your target reader wants & desires for themselves.

  • “I wish I could work from home, and never have to show up to an office ever again.”

  • “I wish I could work from a bungalow on the beach in Costa Rica.”

  • “I wish I could become a New York Times best-selling author before the age of 50.”

Basically, what does the reader want?

Make a list of their wants—the highest forms of wherever it is they want to end up—and then tell them, straight up: “If this is what you want, then this is what you need to read.”

🔹Module 4: The 5 Proven Headline Formats

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 4 of Headline Mastery!

Let’s dig into the “proven” headline formats that exist.

The 5 Proven Headline Formats

There are five proven headline formats that exist all over the Internet.

(And once you see them, you can’t unsee them.)

  • The List

  • The Story

  • The Opinion

  • The Question

  • The Framework

Almost everything written online can in some way be reverse engineered back into these five categories.

Why?

Because they work!

  • Readers love lists because lists are easy to skim through, get the necessary information, and move on.

  • Readers love stories because stories represent human nature (desire, conflict, resolution).

  • Readers love opinions because, hey, everyone has an opinion and opinions that go “against the grain” are unique and different.

  • Readers love questions because “the purpose of life,” to some degree, is about finding answers to compelling questions.

  • And readers love frameworks because they want to know “the right way” of solving a problem or achieving a goal.

Which means, if you want to increase your chances of attracting readers’ attention, it would be in your best interest to use formats that are proven to work.

Let’s break each one down:

The List﻿

Everything you write is, in some way, a “list.”

If you are writing about 1 big idea, you are writing a list of “1 thing.”

And if you are writing about 22 small ideas, you are writing a list of “22 things.”

(The only difference between a Buzzfeed article and an Atlantic column—aside from the writing quality itself—is that The Atlantic doesn’t put the “number” of ideas in their headline. But they’re still both “lists.”)

The reason lists are so effective is because it tells the reader “how long” this thing they’re being asked to click on and read is.

“7 Small But Powerful Leadership Techniques” sounds like something you can skim in 30 seconds—but will give you exactly the sort of information you’re looking for as an aspiring leader.

What’s the result? Click.

But don’t get it confused: lists are not “clickbait.” (Remember, clickbait only happens if you make a promise you don’t keep in the content itself.) Lists are also incredibly powerful vehicles for talking about a lot of different ideas, one after another. If you didn’t use the list format, it might be difficult to follow these points and ideas. But, when “listed” together, suddenly it’s very easy to follow (as a reader).

The Story﻿

Just because you tell a story doesn’t mean it’s a “good” story.

This might sound harsh, but it’s true. Just because you took the time to write it, doesn’t mean the reader owes you their time to read it.

So, “writing a story” should never be your goal as a Digital Writer.

Instead, your goal should be to tell a story your target reader can see themselves in.

It’s not “the story” they are interested in.

It’s what the story says about them—and how that story can, in some way, help them with something in their life.

Which is why the key to writing a “story headline” is to signal the transformation ahead of time.

  • What’s the beginning of the story? Where are we starting?

  • What’s the ending of the story? Where will we end up?

  • What’s the twisty-turny path that is going to get us there? What’s unique here?

For example, where Digital Writers go wrong is they try to tell a story with a clever headline like: “How I Lost It All.” Aside from the fact that the reader doesn’t actually know what this means (it’s clever, not clear), the other problem is that the headline doesn’t signal the beginning & the end of the “story”—which the reader needs to hear in order to make a decision as to whether or not they want to click and read.

Instead, here’s what you want:

  • “The Story Of How I Turned $20 Into $156,000 Selling eBooks On Amazon.”

  • “18 Months Ago, I Didn’t Know How To Code. Here’s How I Landed A Job At Facebook.”

  • “My Husband And I Have Been Together For 78 Years. Here’s Our Secret To Staying Attracted To Each Other.”

In some way, you want to signal to the reader the beginning & the end: the “here’s where people start” and “here’s where you are going to end up.”

If your Story Headline doesn’t have both of these pieces, the reader isn’t going to know why they should give it their time and attention.

The Opinion﻿

Everyone has an opinion.

Which means simply “having an opinion” isn’t enough—your opinion needs to be unique, different, and highly relevant to the topic at hand.

Take this headline for example:

“America Isn’t Ready For What’s Coming.”

When a reader sees a headline like this, the very first question they are asking themselves is, “Who says?” They need to know, before they give it even another second of thought and attention, WHY they should listen. And a big part of that question has to do with whether or not this perspective/opinion is from someone “credible.”

Now, most people don’t understand what credibility actually means.

You don’t have to be Tony Robbins or Oprah to be “credible.”

You don’t need to be a New York Times best-selling author, or a nationally recognized rocket scientist.

You simply need to explain to the reader why you are someone worth listening to on a given subject. So, using the same headline as above, look at the credibility statement: “I’ve Dealt With Foreign Cyberattacks. America Isn’t Ready For What’s Coming.”

  • This person isn’t saying “I am the most well-known cybersecurity expert in the world.”

  • This person isn’t saying “No one understands cybersecurity technology like I do.”

  • This person isn’t saying “I have more cybersecurity experience than anyone else.”

They’re literally saying: “I’ve dealt with this kind of thing.”

And that, alone, is enough to make a reader pause and consider giving them their full attention.

The Question﻿

What is Google?

It’s a question machine!

When you open Google, 99% of the time you type in a question (even if you don’t always phrase it as such).

Readers on the Internet are essentially looking for answers to questions—either questions they came up with on their own, or questions they discovered as they were browsing and decided, “You know what? I’d like to know the answer to that!”

Which is why the Question format is so effective.

Want to get your target reader’s attention? State a question they’re already asking themselves.

Get inside the reader’s head.

There are 2 big categories here:

  • What questions are your target readers already asking themselves (that are highly urgent, valuable, and important)?

  • What questions should your target readers be asking themselves, that they don’t know they should be asking (that are highly urgent, valuable, and important)?

Literally take these questions and restate them in your headline.

The reader will see themselves (and their urgent, valuable, and important questions) in your headline and think, “Hey! I was just wondering the answer to that!”

The Framework﻿

Finally, readers love feeling like they are being given a:

  • Framework

  • Formula

  • Technique

  • Proven Approach

  • Breakdown

  • Etc.

Why?

Because frameworks, formulas, techniques, and so on, feel like you are being handed a “packaged product.” It feels like you’re being given a “thing.” And that “thing” is going to solve all your problems (like a Magic Machine!).

The simple version of a framework is simply saying “Here’s How To…”.

But the advanced version is Naming & Claiming your How To explanation into some sort of framework.

For example:

  • “My 5-Step Viral Publishing Process…”

  • “The Single Family Rental Deal Closer Formula”

  • “A High-Converting Landing Page Checklist”

  • Etc.

As much as possible, you want readers to feel like you are giving them more than just a bunch of words on a page.

You want them to feel like you’re giving them a highly valuable asset.

🔹Module 5: Proven “Hooks”

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 5 of Headline Mastery!

Let’s hook some readers.

Proven “Hooks”

There are 4 proven writing hooks that have worked since the beginning of time:

  • “Here’s a ton of value for minimal time.”

  • “Here’s a ton of value for minimal cost.”

  • “Here’s how to solve your problem without much effort.”

  • “Here’s how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly.”

All of these hooks work because they speak to human nature. Beneath it all, these are the things human beings value: they value time being saved, they value money being saved, they value problems being solved easily, and they value their dreams being unlocked with little to no effort.

So, whenever possible, you want to speak to these human desires!

25 Proven Headline Formulas

To get you started on the right track, here are 25 proven headline formulas (with 3 examples under each one) that can act as templates for you to write compelling headlines.

And remember:

  • Always strive to be clear, not clever.

  • Specify HOW MANY, WHO, WHAT, WHY, and TWIST THE KNIFE!

  • Increase the voltage of each of these pieces in your headline.

  • And then use one of the 5 proven formats to increase the likelihood of attracting readers’ attention: list, story, opinion, question, or framework.

Do all the above, and you’ll be writing irresistible headlines in no time!

1. X Little Known [Something] That Could Be Causing Your [Problem]

  • 7 Little Known SEO Mistakes That Could Be Causing Your Domain Score To Drop

  • 4 Little Known Nutrients That Could Be Causing Your Blood Sugar To Spike

  • 9 Little Known YouTube Channels That Could Be Causing Your Kids To Do Worse In School

2. A Day In The Life Of A [Profession]

  • A Day In The Life Of A Ghostwriter For Founders, Executives, Grammy-Winning Musicians, And Professional Athletes

  • A Day In The Life Of A Magician

  • A Day In The Life Of A COVID-19 ICU Nurse

3. How [Industry] Is Taking Advantage Of [Audience]—And How To Fix It

  • How The Car Insurance Industry Is Taking Advantage Of Elderly People—And How We Can Fix It

  • How The Pharmaceutical Industry Is Taking Advantage Of Drug Addicts—And What The U.S. Government Should Do To Fix It

4. Is [Thing] A Scam? Here’s My Honest Review

  • Are Online Courses A Scam? Here’s My Honest Review

  • Is The iRobot Really Better Than A Vacuum Cleaner (Or Is It A Scam?). Here’s My Honest Review

5. How To Get Rid Of [Something] Forever, Even If You’re Tried Everything

  • How To Get Rid Of Financial Debt Forever, Even If You’ve Tried Everything

  • How To Get Rid Of Writer’s Block Forever, Even If You’ve Tried Everything

  • How To Get Rid Of Termites In Your House Forever, Even If You’ve Tried Everything

6. A Step-By-Step Guide For Doing X

  • A Step-By-Step Guide For Launching Your First Paid Product Online

  • A Step-By-Step Guide For Writing Your First Book

  • A Step-By-Step Guide For Starting Your First Business

7. How To Make A Ton Of Money [Doing Something Unconventional]

  • How To Make A Ton Of Money Mowing Lawns

  • How To Make A Ton Of Money Writing Mini-eBooks On Amazon

  • How To Make A Ton Of Money Hiring College Students To Clean Other People’s Gutters

8. The Secret To Achieving [Something Desirable]

  • The Secret To Achieving Financial Freedom

  • The Secret To Achieving Happiness In Your Marriage

  • The Secret To Achieving First Place In A Local Marathon

9. 9 Out Of Every 10 People [Make This Mistake]. Are You One Of Them?

  • 9 Out Of Every 10 People Have More Than $10,000 Of Credit Card Debt. Are You One Of Them?

  • 9 Out Of Every 10 People Are Afraid Of Public Speaking. Are You One Of Them?

10. (Written By Someone In The Industry)

  • Why Tech Stocks Are Falling (Written By A Stock Trader)

  • The Real Reason Teachers Get Paid So Little (Written By A 3rd Grade Teacher)

  • How Come The Rich Get Richer And The Poor Get Poorer (Written By A Self-Made Millionaire)

11. How To Survive Your First [Meaningful Experience]

  • How To Survive Your First Blind Date

  • How To Survive Your First Day Of Working In A Large Company

  • How To Survive Your First Week Of College

  • How To Survive Getting Fired For The First Time

12. What [Someone Credible] Can Teach Us About [Topic]

  • What Michael Jordan Can Teach Us About Work Ethic

  • What Oprah Can Teach Us About Becoming A Great Interviewer

  • What Malala Yousafzai Can Teach Us About Overcoming Adversity

13. The Ultimate Guide To [Something]

  • The Ultimate Guide To Buying Your First House

  • The Ultimate Guide To Surviving High School

  • The Ultimate Guide To Saving Your First $10,000, Investing In Technology Stocks, And Setting Yourself Up For Financial Freedom

14. X Lessons Learned [From Doing Something]

  • 7 Lessons Learned Building 10 Products Over The Past 10 Years

  • 5 Lessons Learned After Taking My Company Public

  • 11 Lessons Learned Writing 187 Short Novels

15. Why Something Happens (According To Science)

  • Why Eye Contact Feels So Awkward (According To Science)

  • Why It’s Hard To Make Friends In New Cities (According To Science)

  • Why TikTok Is So Addictive (According To Science)

16. X Things [This Detail] Say About You

  • 10 Things Your Clothes Say About You

  • 27 Things Your Smile Says About You

  • The 1 Thing Your Shoes Say About You

17. A Guaranteed Method For [Achieving Something / Avoiding Something]

  • A Guaranteed Method For Creating Viral Content

  • A Guaranteed Method For Avoiding Getting Fired

  • A Guaranteed Method For Writing A #1 Hit Song

  • A Guaranteed Method For Avoiding Getting Divorced Later In Life

18. How To Achieve [Something] Without Needing To Give Up [Something]

  • How To Achieve Financial Independence Without Giving Up Your Morning Starbucks Coffee Addiction

  • How To Become A Millionaire Without Creating A Budget

  • How To Start Your First Business Without Needing To Take Out A Loan Or Raise Any Money

19. How To [Achieve Something] In [A Short Amount Of Time]

  • How To Memorize An Entire Textbook The Night Before A Big Test

  • How To Get A Girl To Fall In Love With You After Just 1 Date

  • How To Make $100,000 In The Stock Market In Less Than A Week

20. The X Things Most People Don’t Know About [Topic]

  • The 7 Things Most People Don’t Know About What It’s Like To Be A Doctor

  • The 11 Things Most People Don’t Know About Saving Money

  • The 28 Things Most People Don’t Know About Buying Their First Home

21. The X Biggest Mistakes People Make When [Doing Something]

  • The 18 Biggest Mistakes People Make When They Get A Raise At Work

  • The 3 Biggest Mistakes People Make When They Decide To Have Kids

  • The 13 Biggest Mistakes People Make When They Start Cooking At Home

22. The X Best Books To Read If You’re Interested In [Topic]

  • The X Best Books To Read If You’re Interested In Copywriting

  • The X Best Books To Read If You’re Interested In Learning Graphic Design

  • The X Best Books To Read If You’re Interested In Becoming A Life Coach

23. X Tips For [Overcoming Some Obstacle]

  • X Tips For Losing Weight In Your 60s

  • X Tips For Eating Healthy In College

  • X Tips For Getting Backstage Passes To Your Favorite Artist’s Biggest Shows

24. The Best Ways To Get [Something] Without Needing [Something]

  • The Best Ways To Get Accepted To Harvard Without Needing To Be A Straight A Student

  • The Best Ways To Eat Healthy On A Budget Without Needing To Shop At The Dollar Store

  • The Best Ways To Get A Girlfriend Without Needing To Be Good Looking

25. Want [Something]? Try [This]

  • Want To Raise Money For Your Startup? Try Using This Pitch Deck Template

  • Want To Get A Raise At Work? Try This 1 Negotiation Technique

  • Want To Start A Podcast But Not Sure What To Talk About? Try Using This Endless Idea Generator To Come Up With A Bunch Of Ideas

🔹BONUS: Headlines Recap

In Ship 30 for 30, we talked a bit about why headlines are so important.

But headlines are a rabbit hole—and a skill you could (and should) spend 10,000 hours mastering.

Because the truth is, how well your writing performs is directly correlated to how effective your headline is at STOPPING the reader in their tracks, getting them to pause, think, “I need to read this,” click, and give you their attention. If your headline does not accomplish this goal, you do not have an effective headline.

So, before we dive into headline templates anyone can use, let’s recap what makes a good headline in the first place.

What Makes A Good Headline?

  • The headline is clear, not clever. Clever headlines (while they might prompt a laugh from your friend), usually end up confusing the reader more than they do “hook” them. The reader reads these clever headlines, can’t immediately tell what they’re going to get in exchange for reading, and then scrolls right past.

  • The headline makes a PROMISE. Headlines that don’t make promises don’t get read. It’s not enough to say, “This is about X.” You have to take it one step further and say, “This is about X, and this is what will change in your life if you click to read.” Without a PROMISE, the reader can’t quite rationalize why they should give up 30 seconds or 3 precious minutes of their life to read a bunch of words on the page.

  • The headline is specific. If you are writing for a General Audience, your headline needs to be specific about a universal problem. And if you are writing for a Niche Audience, your headline needs to be specific about a problem relevant to a specific audience or group of people. If your headline is not specific about the problem, the audience, or both, it’s vague. And anything that’s vague is confusing, and anything that’s confusing won’t hook the reader.

  • The headline takes a stance. The worst headlines are ones that try to be “something for everyone.” They avoid taking a stance or leaning too far in any one direction. As a result, the reader doesn’t quite know what sort of journey they’re going to go on, or why any of it matters at all. Instead, you want to write headlines that are polarizing: the reader is either going to say, “Wow, this is exactly the problem I was struggling with—and I think I just found my answer!” Or you want the reader to say, “This isn’t for me. Period.” A lot of writers steer away from being polarizing out of fear that they won’t attract “enough readers.” But the truth is, when you try to write something for everyone, you end up writing something for no one.

  • The headline teases the ending without revealing the answer. All great headlines have what we like to call a “Curiosity Gap.” This means the reader understands what the piece is going to be about, who it’s for, and what they can expect to get (or learn) in exchange for reading it—but the headline doesn’t give them the answer. They have to click to fill in the middle. Headlines that don’t do this, and instead just give the answer (“Drinking Coffee Gives You Anxiety”) make the reader think they already got the purpose of the piece and, as a result, don’t need to actually click and read it. You must tease the ending without giving it away.

“Isn’t That Clickbait?”

The first question all writers ask when they hear our methodologies on writing effective headlines is, “Isn’t that clickbait?”

No—and here’s why.

It’s only clickbait if you fail to keep your promise to the reader.

If you write a really compelling headline and then the content doesn’t deliver, it’s clickbait. You baited the reader with a big promise, and then failed to deliver on that promise.

However, if you write a headline with a big promise and then KEEP your promise, the reader isn’t going to sit there and think, “Meh. This piece was really helpful but I don’t like that I got clickbaited into reading it.” No, they’re going to think the opposite. In fact, they’re not even going to remember how or why they clicked the headline. They’re going to be too busy sharing the piece with 3 of their friends, saying, “You have to read this.”

There is almost no finer example of this on the Internet than Naval Ravikant’s Twitter thread, “How To Get Rich (Without Getting Lucky.”

By every definition, this title should be considered “clickbait.” It follows that tried-and-true formula of creating a Curiosity Gap for the reader, is clear about WHAT it’s about, and makes a pretty big PROMISE (“Get rich without being lucky? I’m in!”). And to date, it has 53,000 Retweets, 9,000 Quote Tweets, 168,000 Likes, and too many comments to count.

Now, did Naval’s iconic, Twitter-breaking Twitter thread rack up all those metrics simply because it “clickbaited” readers? Of course not.

This Twitter thread accumulated tens of millions of impressions, sparked conversations all over the world, and continues to circulate within the Twittersphere because the headline makes a big PROMISE and the content delivers on that promise.

records.content:
🔹Welcome to The Lean Writing Method


The Lean Writing Method is a 5-day, step-by-step blueprint designed to:

  • Help you never stare at a blank page again

  • Start small by publishing “outlines as content”

  • Save hundreds of hours by only expanding proven “outlines” (based on data)

  • Resurface your best work over and over again by re-atomizing your proven long-form content

  • And schedule content for days, weeks, even months in advance so you can build your audience on autopilot.

So pack your bags, because this ship is ready to set sail!

In Ship 30 for 30, we introduce our beginner Lean Writing Framework.

  • Before Ryan Holiday wrote his best-selling book, The Obstacle Is The Way, he wrote a short blog post called Stoicism 101: A Practical Guide For Entrepreneurs.

  • Before Mark Manson wrote his best-selling book, The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fck*, he wrote a blog post titled the exact same thing: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck.

  • Before Malcolm Gladwell wrote his best-selling book, The Tipping Point, he wrote a column for The New Yorker titled the exact same thing: The Tipping Point.

  • Before E.L. James wrote her best-selling novel, Fifty Shades of Grey, she wrote many of the same stories as “Twilight fan fiction” online.

This is Lean Writing: starting small, and doubling-down on what causes readers to engage.

And once you “see it,” you can’t unsee it.

Lean Writing is everywhere.

But we want to show you how you can take this framework to the next level.

Over the next 5 days, you are going to master The Lean Writing Method.

You are going to be able to spot Lean Writers out in the world.

You are going to master the art of writing & sharing short ideas—to test what works.

You are going to expand “what works” into longer, more valuable versions.

You are going to combine your most Atomic Content into longer-form digital assets.

And you are going to curate your own work, weaving your library of content into a wide-reaching web on the Internet.

Lean Writing is how you become “prolific.”

So, are you ready to dive in?

🔹Module 0: Video Walkthrough

Below, you can find the 5 modules of our Lean Writing Method Ultimate Guide.

But before you dig into those, we highly recommend watching this video for a high-level overview of how this framework works (and it will help you 10x your content output!).


🔹Module 1: The 2-Year Test Backwards Or Forwards

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 1 of The Lean Writing Method!

Let's get right into the good stuff.

The 2-Year Test

In Ship 30 for 30, we introduce a framework for generating content ideas we call The 2-Year Test.

This means reflecting on all the things you’ve learned over the past 2 years (or in some cases: 2 months, 2 weeks, or even 2 days) and then writing for the version of yourself “back then,” before you knew what you knew. You can see how this is a powerful framework for envisioning who your target reader might be: it’s you, back then!

  • Tips you would give the previous version of yourself

  • Things you wish you knew

  • Lessons you’ve learned

  • Mistakes you’ve made

  • Etc.

Now, where people get “lost” here is thinking: “But I’m not writing for myself! I’m writing for other people! I’m writing for everyone!”

Yes, you are. But…

It’s worth remembering two very important things:

  1. The easiest way to generate ideas is from your own life experiences. If you’ve worked as a nurse for 10 years, you should consider writing about your experiences as a nurse. If you’ve spent your entire life living in California, you should write about life in California. It’s much harder to think of compelling ideas to write about when your starting place is “I-could-write-about-anything.” But it’s exponentially easier to start the process by asking yourself, “What do I know? What have I experienced?” Because that’s information you know like the back of your hand.

  2. And there are millions and millions of people in the world “just like you.” Second, it’s very difficult to imagine a “target reader” when you are trying to write for “everyone.” Remember: when you try to write something for everyone, you end up writing something for no one. Instead, you want to think about how you can write for the previous version of yourself. And then you want to let the Internet help you find all the other people in the world who are exactly where you used to be.

The 2-Year test solves both of these immediately.

And makes it easier for you to get out of “thinking” mode and into “writing” mode (which is the goal).

The 2-Year Test Forwards

“But what if I don’t want to write about my own life? What if I don’t want to write about my experiences? What if I don’t want to write about things I’ve already learned?”

Totally fine!

If instead you want to write about things you’re currently learning, or you want to write about something totally new (a hobby, a personal interest, etc.), then you can apply the 2-Year Test forwards—which means instead of writing for the version of yourself 2 years ago, you’re writing for the version of yourself 2 years from now.

How?

By curating other people’s insights who are ahead of where you are today:

  • Tips another expert gave that you found helpful

  • Mistakes another expert shared you now want to steer clear of

  • Lessons another expert learned that you’re taking to heart

  • Reasons another expert make the decisions he or she did, and why you agree

  • Etc.

For example, let’s say you want to start learning about copywriting—but you have never worked as a copywriter, you know nothing about the subject, and you are a total beginner. Well, instead of “pretending” to be an expert (Imposter Syndrome), there’s a very easy solution: apply the 2-Year Test forwards and curate the insights of other expert copywriters.

This is what Dickie did when he first started learning about copywriting. And by curating other experts (instead of trying to be “an expert” himself), he ended up accumulating tens of millions of views and hundreds of thousands of followers on his content. Why? Because he was taking the time to a) research, b) learn, and then c) curate the most important takeaways for other people. (There is tremendous value in curating insights for other beginners!)

As a rule of thumb:

If you are trying to create original content, sharing things that “you” know, then you want to apply the 2-Year Test backwards.

  • What have YOU learned?

  • What frameworks have YOU developed?

  • What mistakes did YOU make?

  • What tips would YOU give other people?

  • Etc.

But if you are trying to write about something you haven’t experienced or are still learning about, then you want to curate content. You want to apply the 2-Year Test forwards, and share things that “other experts” know:

  • What have THEY learned?

  • What frameworks have THEY developed?

  • What mistakes did THEY make?

  • What tips do THEY give other people?

  • Etc.

List 3 topics you want to write about, and decide whether you’ll be applying the 2-Year Test Backwards or Forwards.

Start here.

What are 3 topics you want to write about?

For example:

  • Copywriting

  • Meditation

  • Real Estate

This is where most people get stuck and then stop. But you can see why! Because while it’s important to know WHAT you want to write about, it’s just as important to have clarity around HOW you want to write about these topics too.

So, beside each topic, decide & write down whether you are applying the 2-Year Test backwards or forwards (backwards if you are speaking from personal experience, forwards if you are curating insights from other people’s experiences):

For example:

  • Copywriting: Backwards

  • Meditation: Forwards

  • Real Estate: Forwards

Now when you sit down to write about each of these topics, you’ll have clarity around whether you need to reflect on your own experiences, or you need to research other people’s experiences.

See? Easy!

🔹Module 2: How To Publish “Outlines As Content”

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 2 of The Lean Writing Method!

What does it mean to publish “Outlines As Content?”

Everything Is A List

Every single piece of writing, in some way, is a list.

  • A New Yorker article discussing the benefits of living in a certain city? It’s a descriptive “list” of benefits.

  • A Buzzfeed article curating different kinds of socks to wear depending on the time of year? It’s “listing” socks, and “listing” the different times of year.

  • A novel that spends 3 pages describing a vacant house? Those 3 pages are “listing” qualities of the vacant house.

Listen closely: “The list goes on and on…”.

What is the above? It’s a LIST!!!

At the end of the day, all great “writing” is basically just a Jenga tower of ideas stacked on top of each other. And so what’s the easiest way to figure out what “ideas” need to go together? By listing them out!

Short-Form Content = An “Outline”

This is the first mental shift we want you to experience.

Short-form content doesn’t have to just be “short Tweets.” In fact, thinking about it that way is extremely inefficient—because it requires you to “think” about each idea individually. It also forces you to create 2x or 3x or 5x more content than you need to (you have to create short-form content and THEN different long-form content and THEN different even longer-form content, etc.).

Instead, we want you to think of all your short-form content (Tweets, short LinkedIn posts, even short Atomic Essays) as “Outlines As Content.”

What does that mean?

It means every time you write something “short,” what you should really be doing is testing to see whether or not this batch of ideas (this list) is compelling to readers. Because IF IT IS, then it becomes extremely clear which of those “outlines” is worth expanding into longer-form content.

Which compounds all of your efforts.

Let’s walk through how this works.

Step 1: Choose 1 Topic FOR WHO

Grab 1 of the topics you wrote down, and remind yourself whether this is a “backwards” topic (personal experience), or “forwards” topic (curating someone else’s experience).

  • 2 Year Test Backwards: “What have I already learned?”

    • Personal Credibility

      • Things you have done & know through experience.

  • 2 Year Test Forwards: “What do I want to learn?”

    • Borrowed Credibility

      • Things someone else has done & you’ve learned by studying them.

This simple exercise should give you some clarity on what you want to write about.

Pro Tip: Remember to use the FOR WHO framework we teach in Ship 30 for 30 here to get as specific as you can on the audience.

For example:

  • V1: “Copywriting”

  • V2 (FOR WHO?): “Copywriting For Beginners”

  • V3 (FOR WHO, SPECIFICALLY?): “Copywriting For Beginners Without College Degrees”

Specificity is the secret.

Let’s keep going.

Step 2: What “Value” You Want To Share?

Let’s use the above example.

If you use the FOR WHO framework to get more specific about your topic and WHO it’s for, that’s just the tip of the iceberg.

What are ALL The possible things you could give that person (the WHO) related to that topic?

This is the “value” of your writing:

  • “Are you giving me tips?”

  • “Or are you giving me steps?”

  • “Or are you giving me questions?”

  • “Or are you giving me reflections?”

  • Etc.

This “value” is how readers decide whether reading your writing is worth 30 seconds, or 2 minutes, or 8 minutes, or 3 hours of their LIFE. Right? That’s the trade. They give you 2 minutes of their life, and you give them… what? What are you going to give them in return?

Here’s a fairly exhaustive list of what readers find valuable.

To generate ideas, use this list of 30 Proven Approaches:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

Wowza!

You should have more than enough ideas of things to write about—just for that 1 topic, for that 1 audience (WHO), interested in 1 “thing!”

Step 3: SO THAT they can do… what?

Remember from Ship 30 for 30: FOR WHO/SO THAT.

Having clarity on your topic and WHO it’s for is great. But what takes your writing to the next level is also having clarity over why it matters to the reader. What’s in it for them? Why are you telling them whatever it is you’re telling them? SO THAT they can do… what?

We call these “incentives.”

These are things the reader wants:

Step 5: Create “Outlines As Content”

Here’s the big ah-hah we want you to have:

Once you go through the above exercise, do you need to go write 5,000 words in order to see whether or not that Topic + Value + Incentive is what the reader wants?

Of course not!

You can EASILY test the Topic + Value + Incentive by creating & publishing “Outlines As Content.”

Here’s how it works:

Let’s say our Topic is “copywriting,” our Value is “Tips,” our Incentive is “…to learn,” and we are using the 2-Year Test “backwards.”

Tips to learn copywriting.

Do you see how even just this sentence is the start of a short-form content idea? And what you’re “testing” is whether or not readers are interested in

  • A) “Tips…”

  • B) “To learn…”

  • C) “Copywriting…”

  • D) From you! (Because you’re applying the 2-Year test backwards)

Those are the 4 variables you are “testing” with readers.

And you can see how you can isolate these variables by creating different versions of this content and scheduling them a week or two apart from each other to see what works: do readers want Tips or Mistakes? To they want “to learn” or do they want a different incentive, like “to optimize?” Are they interested in Copywriting, or a different topic? And most of all, do they want to hear it from YOU? Or do they want to hear it from a different expert whose insights you’ve curated? (Maybe you have the right Topic, Value, and Incentive, but you just need to do the 2-Year test forwards instead of backwards!)

Follow us…

If your Value is “Tips” (that’s what you’re giving the reader), what should you list out in order to “test” whether or not the reader finds those “tips” valuable?

TIPS!

For example:

Tips to learn copywriting:

  • Read Ogilvy On Advertising

  • Re-write sales letters by hand

  • Try to sell your own products online

  • Join a copywriting mastermind group

This is a Tweet. This is a LinkedIn post.

But it’s also an “Outline As Content.” Which means, if this short-form post performs well, you now know: readers are interested in a) Tips, b) “To Learn,” c) Copywriting, d) From You, and e) these “Tips” you listed, they found helpful.

That’s a bunch of variables you now have a reasonable amount of data telling you are worth experimenting with over and over again! And you can repeat this “stack” of variables infinite times. Or you can take this “stack,” replace 1 or multiple variables, and compare performance again.

This is what makes Digital Writing such a science experiment.

And the more you publish, the more you learn.

Now, ready for your mind to really be blown?

Literally the only difference (aside from whatever it is you’re “listing,” which will probably change based on whether YOU are coming up with it yourself versus listing other people’s insights) is adding a single sentence of context/credibility.

Is this coming from you? If so, you can add in your own sentence of credibility: “I have been copywriting for 10 years. Here are some tips to learn how.” But you don’t have to since you are the one writing it.

Or, you add a sentence of context/credibility about the person you picked up these tips from. Who are you learning from? Who are they? What have they done? What context clue can you give the reader that will make them trust you, because the person you’re studying has a ton of credibility?

That’s it!

🔹Module 3: How To Expand “Outlines”

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 3 of The Lean Writing Method!

Now we’re really rocking & rolling.

The key to becoming “prolific” isn’t to reinvent the wheel every time you sit down to write.

The key is to use data (your analytics) to double-down on your winning “Outlines As Content,” and expand them!

Here’s the process in a nutshell:

  • Use the 2-Year Test (forwards or backwards) to generate topic ideas.

  • Use the Lean Writing Grid to generate hundreds of “Outlines As Content”

  • Publish your “Outlines” as short-form Tweets, LinkedIn posts, or Atomic Essays

  • Double-down on the “Outlines” that receive the most engagement.

  • And expand them!

This approach removes all the ambiguity, all the painful “Hmmm… what should I write?” moments from the equation. You know what to write! Your analytics are TELLING YOU which “Outlines” readers like the most—so, expand them!

That’s all you have to do.

Here’s an example of an “Outline As Content.”

See? You don’t need to write a 1,500 word blog post to “test” whether or not readers are interested in this idea. All you need to do is give readers a quick snapshot of the big idea.

Then, when you see an “Outline” like this perform well, you know:

Time to expand!

Here’s an example of the same “Outline,” expanded into an Atomic Essay.

Pretty cool, right?

Notice the similarities:

  • The 1st line of the “Outline” becomes the headline of the longer piece.

  • Each main point from the “Outline” becomes the main point of the longer piece

That’s it!

No need to reinvent wheel. Just do what worked, again.

Except longer.

“But how?! How are you supposed to expand something you’ve already written?!”

Great question.

There are 10 ways you can easily expand ANY kind of writing.

  1. Tips

  2. Lessons

  3. Benefits

  4. Reasons

  5. Mistakes

  6. Examples

  7. Questions

  8. Data Points

  9. Personal Stories

  10. Step-By-Step Frameworks

Anytime you find yourself “stuck,” all you have to do is use this list and ask yourself, “How could I give the reader some tips here?” That expands your writing. “How can I give them some lessons learned?” That also expands your writing. “How can I point out some mistakes for them to avoid?” That also expands your writing. And so on, and so forth.

Here’s the process we encourage you to use.

Step 1: Choose the format you want to expand your “Outline” into.

What do you want this “Outline” to become?

  • An Atomic Essay? (So only expanding your “Outline” a little?)

  • A Long-Form LinkedIn Post? (Expanding a little more?)

  • A Twitter Thread? (Expanding a little more?)

  • A Medium article? (Expanding a little more?)

  • A Pillar Blog Post? (Expanding even more?)

  • An Email Course? (Expanding more?)

  • An Entire eBook? (Expanding more?)

If you wanted to, you could turn a 3-sentence Tweet into an entire eBook using The Lean Writing Method.

And here’s how:

Step 2: Leverage the 10 ways to expand any kind of writing.

Watch how we can easily expand this simple “Outline” into an entire Twitter Thread—going down the list of the 9 ways to expand any kind of writing.

“Outline”

We know this “Outline” is resonating with readers, so now all we need to do is break it apart and expand each point.

Watch how this happens:

“Expanded Outline”

Intro Tweet (expanded with “Personal Story”):

I used to hate reading.

Until I started studying Fiction Writing in college, and fell in love with American & Russian literature.

Unfortunately, the skill of being an active reader didn’t come easily to me.

Here’s how you can become a world-class reader:

Tweet #1 (expanded with “Tips”)

Annotate what you read.

Some tips to make this actionable & easy:

  • Use a pen or highlighter

  • Underline sentences you love

  • Circle sentences/sections you don’t understand

  • Write takeaways in the margins

Tweet #2 (expanded with “Questions”)

Question the author’s intent.

Some questions to ask yourself as you read:

  • “Why did the writer choose to put this here?”

  • “Why did the writer choose to say it that way?”

  • “Why did the writer pick this POV/voice?”

  • “What is the writer leaving unspoken?”

Tweet #3 (expanded with “Mistakes”)

Observe the Rate of Revelation.

Pay close attention when you read—and don’t make these mistakes:

  • Don’t skim past boring parts. They’re there for a reason.

  • Don’t sneak a peek at the end of chapters (ruins the surprise!)

  • Don’t only read the subheads. Sink your teeth into the content!

Tweet #4 (expanded with “Examples”)

How did the writer get you to see/feel?

Some of my favorite examples:

  • Hemingway writes boring dialogue so conversations “feel” more realistic (most convos are boring).

  • Nabokov uses dark humor to discuss complicated topics.

  • Kafka uses magical realism to surprise your senses.

Tweet #5 (expanded with “Lessons”)

Notice what ideas you remember most.

2 big lessons I’ve learned reading tons of literature over the years:

  • The best descriptions stick with you. No need to “save” them anywhere.

  • Better to re-read a book you love than force yourself to read something you hate.

Recap Tweet

To be a great writer, you can’t just “read for fun”

Here’s how

  • Annotate what you read

  • Question the author's intent

  • Observe the Rate of Revelation

  • How did the writer get you to feel/see

  • Notice what ideas you remember most

Wowza!

See how easy that was?

All we had to do was take the original “Outline,” and expand each bullet point using one of the “10 ways.”

Some questions we get all the time here:

Question #1: “Do you have to use all of the 10 ways? Or can you reuse the same ones?”

Your choice!

You could expand an “Outline” with nothing but mistakes, if you wanted to. Or nothing but lessons. Or nothing but tips.

Or, you can alternate: some mistakes, some lessons, some tips, some questions, etc.

The point is, all of these are things readers WANT. Right? Readers WANT you to help them avoid mistakes. Readers WANT you to pass along lessons that took you hours, years, or even a decade to learn. Readers WANT you to give them thought-provoking questions they can ask themselves on their journey.

Which means you can expand anything, any kind of writing, infinitely, just by giving them “more of what they want.” And the easiest way to do that is to leverage this list of “10 ways.”

Question #2: “But won’t the reader notice I’m just expanding things for expansion’s sake?”

We’ll pose the question back to you:

Did you notice you were reading a “Questions” list right now? Because that’s what we’re doing. We’re “expanding” this section by asking ourselves, “Hmmm… what questions would the reader have here?” And then just taking it upon ourselves to answer those questions for you.

Is that helpful? Is it valuable?

The honest answer is: readers have no idea this is a “technique.” They’re too busy learning from the “mistakes” and the “lessons” and the “tips” (and so on) that you’re giving them.

Which means you could expand any piece using these “10 ways,” forever, and they’d have no idea what was going on.

Quite the magic trick, eh?

Question #3: “Can we use several of these 10 ways together in a single section?”

Of course you can!

What do you think a book is?

Look closely, and you’ll notice a chapter of a book is just “some mistakes” stacked on top of “some lessons” stacked on top of “some tips” stacked on top of “some questions,” etc. And if you really want to take things to the next level, just increase the number:

  • Why only give 3 tips when you could give 13 tips?

  • Why only give 7 questions when you could give 27 questions?

  • Why only give 5 steps when you could create an Ultimate Guide, grabbing them by the hand and walking them through 50 steps?

The other way you can do this is to compress a handful of these “expanders” into a single short-form section, like this.

Watch:

Conventional wisdom says the key to being a great writer is to read. A lot.

But, the mistake most writers make is they consume more than they create.

Personal story: I did the same thing when I was first starting out.

And it took me 10 years to learn this lesson:

Reading makes you a better reader. Writing makes you a better writer.

Wowza!

In just 5 lines, we packed in 4 different “ways” to expand an idea:

  • A key (tip)

  • A mistake

  • A personal story

  • And a lesson

The takeaway here is that you, as the writer, are in control. And these “10 ways” are just levers you can push and pull to expand your content—make it bigger, or make it smaller and more compressed.

How To Atomize Proven Long-Form Content Back Into Short-Form (To Resurface)

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 4 of The Lean Writing Method!

Congratulations—because the hard part is over.

Once you get in the habit of publishing “Outlines As Content,” and you’ve started expanding your most-engaged “Outlines” into longer-form assets (whether they are LinkedIn posts, Twitter Threads, Atomic Essays, pillar pieces on your blog, or entire eBooks/books), you almost can’t help but grow an audience.

And the autopilot experience begins.

Here’s how it works:

Step 1: Do a monthly review of your analytics & grab your best-performing long-form asset.

At the end of every month, take 15-20 minutes and open up your analytics (Twitter, LinkedIn, Ilo, Typeshare, etc.).

Wherever is most convenient (Apple Notes, Notion, a Google Spreadsheet, wherever you like to organize information), you want to start making a list of your best-performing long-form assets. So, if you expand 4 “Outlines As Content” into Twitter Threads or Atomic Essays in a month (1 per week), at the end of the month you want to do a quick audit to see which 1 of the 4 performed best.

Add that to your “Resurface” list.

Step 2: Break your long-form piece back into 3-7 pieces of short-form content—and link to the original.

Here’s how this works:

https://twitter.com/dickiebush/status/1537434904656351234

This is a Twitter Thread that was “expanded” out of an “Outline As Content.”

It clearly performed well—which means we want to resurface this thread over and over again in the future (because chances are most people missed it the first time, and anyone NEW who follows will probably enjoy reading this too).

So, how do we do that in the most efficient way possible?

We break it apart into bite-sized pieces!

(Each individual Tweet, or “Main Point,” can become a short-form piece again.)

https://twitter.com/dickiebush/status/1602839854060109825

This individual short-form Tweet isn’t “new.”

It’s just a slightly re-written version of the Tweet/Main Point in the expanded Thread:

https://twitter.com/dickiebush/status/1537434915381207040

Pretty cool, right?

No need to reinvent the wheel!

Step 3: Link to the original long-form asset.

Most long-form assets (Twitter Threads, Atomic Essays, etc.) can be broken back down into 3-7 short-form pieces.

The key is to look at each individual Tweet, or each “Main Point” in your essay and ask how you can rewrite the same thing (or just copy/paste if it doesn’t need any rewriting!) into a stand-alone short-form piece again.

Then, to resurface the original high-performing long-form asset, just link to it.

Like this:

https://twitter.com/dickiebush/status/1603098813941547011?s=20&t=fRuV5x6A-r7wkwtNCEnSrQ

See how this works?

  • Short-form post

  • Link to long-form asset

This creates a flywheel of organic content.

  1. Publish lots of little “Outlines As Content.”

  2. Expand your best “Outlines” into longer-form assets.

  3. Do a quick audit at the end of each month to see which long-form assets readers love most.

  4. Break those long-form assets back into smaller, stand-alone pieces again.

  5. And resurface your best work over and over again by linking the smaller pieces to the long-form assets.

Do this over and over again, and you’ll have more content than you’ll know what to do with—AND you’ll build a bigger audience, faster, because you’re publishing more of “what works,” more often.

Voila.

🔹Module 5: How To Schedule Content For Months

Ahoy!

And welcome to Day 5 of The Lean Writing Method!

Now it’s time to start scheduling content out for months in advance—and put your content strategy on autopilot.

Let’s say you have 3 topics you want to write about consistently.

Well, if you multiply 3 Topics by 30 Proven Approaches (”Value”) by the 30 different Incentives we gave you, that means (conservatively) you have 2,700 “Outlines As Content” you can publish and use to gather data.

Crazy, right?!

(That means if you published 1 “Outline As Content” per day, you’d have content for over 7 years!)

This is what makes the Lean Writing Method so powerful. Once you understand the puzzle pieces, it becomes so easy to create, publish, test, and double-down on your best content.

And since one of the most common questions we get asked is, “How often should I be publishing? How often should I alternate?” we wanted to give you a very simple publishing cadence you can use—simply alternating between your 3 topic areas, over and over again.

Here’s your publishing cadence:

  • Monday: Topic 1, Idea 1

  • Tuesday: Topic 2, Idea 1

  • Wednesday: Topic 3, Idea 1

  • Thursday: Topic 1, Idea 2

  • Friday: Topic 2, Idea 2

  • Saturday: Topic 3, Idea 2

  • Thursday: Topic 3, Idea 6

  • Friday: Topic 1, Idea 7

  • Saturday: Topic 2, Idea 7

  • Sunday: Topic 3, Idea 7

  • Thursday: Topic 1, Idea 9

  • Friday: Topic 2, Idea 9

  • Saturday: Topic 3, Idea 9

  • Sunday: Topic 1, Idea 10

  • Monday: Topic 2, Idea 10

  • Tuesday: Topic 3, Idea 10

  • Wednesday: Topic 1, Idea 11

  • Thursday: Topic 2, Idea 11

  • Friday: Topic 3, Idea 11

And so on.

Now, some other questions we get asked all the time:

Question #1: “Can I write about the same topic multiple days, or weeks, in a row, just changing the Value or the Incentive?”

Of course!

We do this almost on a daily basis writing about Digital Writing.

In fact, if you want to build an audience, scale yourself online, and reach the most “right” readers as quickly as possible, you’re better off doubling-down on 1 topic that is clearly resonating and becoming known for a niche you own. Because it’s much easier to become known for 1 topic than it is to become known for 3+ topics (especially in the beginning—this can change over time).

Question #2: “Can I republish the same Outline As Content just changing 1 variable?”

Yes!

But chances are, when you change 1 variable, other variables will change too. Like if you wanted to swap out “Tips” for “Mistakes,” obviously you would have to rewrite your list—because now you’re giving the reader “Mistakes,” not “Tips.”

That said, feel free to use social environments as your testing ground.

Just keep the reader in mind, and maybe don’t write about the same exact thing, the same exact way, only changing 1 word in the headline for 7 days in a row.

That’s overkill.

Question #3: “Where is the best place to track performance?”

Wherever works for you!

Typeshare has analytics built in, but other analytics platforms like Ilo also work too.

Here’s what we would suggest: don’t try to run a “perfect” science experiment here. People make this mistake all the time with note-taking & idea capture systems. They spend hours and hours trying to create “the perfect system,” which is really just a clever way of procrastinating and avoiding doing the more important thing—which is writing & hitting publish!

Instead, just pay attention to the data broadly:

  • Which topics get more Views?

  • Which topics get more Likes?

  • Which topics get more Comments?

  • Which topics prompt more Questions?

  • Which topics get more compliments from people you respect?

  • Etc.

Double-down on your winners, cut your losers, and repeat.

Question #4: “What if I don’t want my niche to be the topic that’s clearly working?”

That’s your choice!

Remember, nothing here is a marriage decision. And it’s also up to you where you want to take your writing—and why. Some of our most viral content online have been topics we decided (after the fact) that we didn’t want to write about anymore. That’s fine. Things are allowed to change.

That said: we strongly encourage you to do some reflecting on what your North Star goal is here:

  • Are you writing for an internal outcome? Happiness, joy, fulfillment, exploration, creative expression, clarity of thinking, generously sharing what you know, building good will, etc. If so, then your measure for success shouldn’t be “a metric.” It should be how you FEEL when you write, and the emotional rewards you get from the process—as well as what readers share with you about how your work has helped them.

  • Or are you writing for an external outcome? Money, reach, audience size, opportunities, industry recognition, etc. If so, then you need to recognize that you are IN SERVICE of the reader. And in order to unlock these external outcomes, you NEED to take the reader’s wants & needs into account (because they’re the ones who are going to help you achieve those external goals).

Oftentimes, where writers get stuck is they say “I want to write for myself” but then get frustrated when they don’t unlock as many external outcomes as the next person.

You have to be honest with yourself about what you want out of your writing.

And then you have to let go of expectations that don’t align with your true North Star.

Question #5: “How long should I do this Lean Writing exercise for? When am I done?”

Hah!

You’re never done!

Lean Writing is a way of thinking. It’s a recipe for growth. And so, really, there should never come a time when you wake up and decide, “You know what? I’m done getting better. I’m done trying to improve.” Because that’s the whole joy of doing anything—is forward momentum. And so, as long as you are writing online, you should be gathering data, reflecting, learning, and then implementing and steering your ship accordingly.

Batching & Scheduling Content For Months In Advance

Here’s where you can start getting ahead of the game.

In order to be a prolific Digital Writer, do you have to write every single day? Not necessarily. Because the truth is, life gets in the way. And even if you enjoy writing every day, you might not always have the time (especially during busy times of year, work, travel, sickness, etc.).

So, what’s a Digital Writer to do?

Batch & schedule content for days, weeks, even months in advance!

Our Process

The single biggest waste of time when it comes to consistent content creation is this:

Creating lots of “different” types of content, all at the same time.

You know the feeling. You sit down on Sunday afternoon and say to yourself, “I’m going to write a bunch of content & schedule it out for the week.” But the reason it takes so long is because you have to create each piece individually AND you have to make sure each piece is “different.”

It took us a while to realize this, but this approach to content creation (and scheduling content in advance) is exceedingly unproductive.

Why?

Because the switching cost is so high.

  • First you have to think of a Tweet about 1 topic.

  • Then you have to think of a LinkedIn post about a different topic.

  • Then you have to think of an Atomic Essay about a different topic.

  • And so on.

Instead, there’s a much easier way.

And that’s by baking the Lean Writing Method into your batching & scheduling process.

Here’s how it works:

Step 1: Write as many “Outlines As Content” about 1 topic as you can

Here’s the first big mental shift we want to give you:

How most people think about “creating content” is by trying to create content for ALL the different things they want to write about at the same time.

Instead, we would encourage you to pick 1 topic and then create as many “Outlines As Content” as possible—in the same work session. The reason is because then your brain won’t have to “switch” between different topics (which leads to fatigue), allowing you to create more quality content, exponentially faster.

Here’s the easy way of thinking about how to do this:

Pick a topic.

Pick an incentive (”…to learn”).

And then just go down the list of 30 Proven Approaches:

  • Tips to learn…

  • Skills to learn…

  • Tools to learn…

  • Traits to learn…

  • Steps to learn…

  • Goals to learn…

  • Books to learn…

  • Habits to learn…

  • Stories to learn…

  • Quotes to learn…

  • Secrets to learn…

  • Insights to learn…

  • Benefits to learn…

  • Lessons to learn…

  • Reasons to learn…

  • Creators to learn…

  • Routines to learn…

  • Mistakes to learn…

  • Podcasts to learn…

  • Examples to learn…

  • Questions to learn…

  • Inventions to learn…

  • Templates to learn…

  • Resources to learn…

  • Challenges to learn…

  • Companies to learn…

  • Data Points to learn…

  • Realizations to learn…

  • Frameworks to learn…

  • Presentations to learn…

When you create content this way, now you’ve eliminated the most taxing part of the process: the switching cost between “different” topics.

And instead, you can spend 1-2 hours doing nothing but thinking about 1 topic, and 1 incentive—and all the different ways you can talk about that 1 topic and 1 incentive to your audience.

Step 2: Schedule your “Outlines As Content” on 1 topic out a week apart from each other.

Now, it’s probably a bit overwhelming for your audience to see 3 Tweets per day from you about the same topic, and the same incentive, over and over and over again.

But if you separate them a bit… your audience won’t find it overwhelming at all.

They’ll find it helpful!

So, once you’ve generated say 30 different “Outlines As Content” on 1 topic & 1 incentive, just pick a day (your choice) and schedule 1 out every week.

Now, for example, you have content every Monday for 30 weeks in a row.

Which means if you repeat this same work session 4 more times (a different topic & different incentive each time), you’ll have quality content scheduled out 5 days per week for over half the year.

Crazy, right?

Step 3: Once per week, expand an “Outline As Content” into a Long-Form Piece

Audit your analytics.

Look at which “Outlines” as performing the best.

And then expand the winner into a:

  • Atomic Essay

  • Twitter Thread

  • Long-form LinkedIn post

This will inherently take “longer” (because you’re writing “more”) than creating short-form content.

But it’s time well spent—because you’re investing time expanding something readers have ALREADY VALIDATED saying they want more of.

Which is the whole goal.

Step 4: Once per month, audit your long-form content, pick the best one, and break it apart

Here’s where things really start to accelerate.

At the end of each month (or whenever is convenient for you), audit your long-form pieces:

  • Which one resonated best with readers?

  • Which one received the most Likes, Views, Comments?

  • Which one asked the most valuable questions, inspiring new ideas?

  • Which one is a topic you’re excited to write more about?

There are 2 things you can do here to get even further ahead on your content AND keep resurfacing this “winning” long-form piece over and over again.

First, you should turn each individual section or Tweet of that long-form piece into a short-form asset again (like we showed you how to do earlier).

Second, you should ask yourself “What Else?” and come up with a handful of OTHER short-form assets that can link to this long-form piece. (For example: “Another copywriting tip. Another wellness habit. Another great book to read.” Etc.

Now you won’t just have “Outlines As Content” scheduled for weeks in advance, but you’ll also have short-form pieces linking to your best long-form assets—for weeks in advance too.

And you can repeat this process over and over again.

This is how you appear “prolific” online.
