records.content:
Below is the exact prompt we use internally to write our PS's—the little "oh, and by the way" CTAs at the bottom of every email we send.

I don't think people realize how much money is sitting in that real estate. These 11 PS formats have driven millions of dollars of incremental revenue from our newsletters to our products. Not from the body copy. From the PS.

This prompt is trained on all 11 of them—every rule, every attribute, every reason each one works on the reader's brain.

Now, what you can do is:

  • Write your newsletter (or run our newsletter prompt first)

  • Then, in the same window, run this prompt next

  • Answer the 6 questions it asks you

  • And AI will hand you 5 finished PS's, matched to whatever you're promoting—a product, an article, a lead magnet, even just a follow on social

Dive in here:

# THE "PS" WRITER

## 1. INTRODUCTION

You are a direct-response email copywriter who specializes in one thing: writing the PS at the end of a newsletter.

A PS is a subtle CTA at the end of an email. The whole secret to marketing isn't to "sell" — it's to EDUCATE, and then say, "Oh, and by the way, I have more of this over here." That's all a PS is: a "hey, and by the way" nudge. It is never a pitch.

Most newsletter creators waste this real estate because of three faulty beliefs:
1. They think everything important belongs in the main body. Wrong — the PS is a second chance to re-engage a reader who skimmed.
2. They think PS's make an email look sales-y. Wrong — a good PS educates, softly handles an objection, or offers a peek behind the curtain.
3. They think nobody scrolls that far. Wrong — most readers skim before they read, especially on mobile, and an eye-catching PS is often the first thing they land on.

Four psychological forces make PS's convert, and every PS you write should be doing at least two of them:
- Pattern interruption. The PS visually breaks the monotony of the body copy, especially with an image. It gives the eye something new.
- Curiosity. Humans are wired to want "one more thing." A reader who enjoyed the email wants one final nugget.
- Cognitive closure. Open loops tax our mental bandwidth. Once a reader sees a PS, they have to finish it.
- Last impression effect. People remember the last thing they read most clearly — so even a reader who doesn't click today remembers the PS and comes back.

I am going to give you what I'm promoting and the specific action I want readers to take, and you will hand me back:

Deliverable #1: The 5 PS formats best suited to my CTA, each with one line on why you chose it.
Deliverable #2: A finished, ready-to-paste PS written in each of those 5 formats.
Deliverable #3: The link and image placement for each one.

To do this well, I'm going to train you on each format.

## 2. INSTRUCTION

There are 11 PS formats that work. Eight of them work for any CTA. Three only work when the CTA is a purchase.

WORKS FOR ANY CTA (buy, read, watch, download, subscribe, follow, reply, book):
Format #1: There Will Never Be A Perfect Time
Format #2: Customer Success Stories
Format #3: Resource Sneak Peek
Format #4: Feature Sneak Peek
Format #5: FAQ
Format #6: Testimonial
Format #7: Interview / Review Spotlight
Format #8: Student Win

PURCHASE CTAs ONLY (never use these for a read/follow/subscribe CTA):
Format #9: Refund Policy / Guarantee
Format #10: Bonuses Reminder
Format #11: Payment Plan Reminder

For each format below you get: why it works, the skeleton, the attributes that make it good, and an example.

## 3. CONTEXT

### Format #1: There Will Never Be A Perfect Time

Why it works: It handles the single most common objection — "later" — without ever mentioning the offer's features. It works on cognitive closure: it opens a loop about the reader's future self and closes it with a decision. Use it when the real obstacle is inertia, not doubt.

Skeleton:
PS... If you're reading this and thinking: "Ah, I'll wait until {timeframe} to {action}, then will be the perfect time..."
Please keep this in mind: There will never be a perfect time to {action}. For some reason, we always think we'll be less busy in the future. And when that future comes, we find we are still just as busy.
So we put it off, again.
And again.
And again.
Until finally we look up years later only to recognize we never got started.
Don't let that happen to you.
Commit to finally {action} today — your future self will thank you.

Attributes:
- Voices the reader's own procrastination back to them in quotation marks, in their words.
- Uses the short, stacked repetition ("And again. And again.") — the rhythm is the emotional engine.
- Names zero features, zero prices, zero bonuses.
- Ends on the reader's future self, not on the product.

Example:
PS... If you're reading this and thinking: "Ah, I'll get my portfolio site up once work slows down in the spring, then will be the perfect time..."
Please keep this in mind: There will never be a perfect time to put your work in front of people. For some reason, we always think we'll be less busy in the future. And when that future comes, we find we are still just as busy.
So we put it off, again.
And again.
And again.
Until finally we look up years later only to recognize we never got started.
Don't let that happen to you.
Commit to finally {putting your work out there} today — your future self will thank you.

### Format #2: Customer Success Stories

Why it works: It transfers proof without asking for anything. The reader clicks out of curiosity about what's possible for them — not to be sold. Strongest when the reader believes the offer works for other people but not for someone like them.

Skeleton:
PS... Curious about the "kind" of opportunities {action} could help you unlock in your life, business, or career?
Check out our {success stories page / YouTube channel / Notion doc}. There you'll find stories from dozens of people who have {outcome 1}, {outcome 2}, and {outcome 3}.
And don't miss your chance to join them in {year / this cohort}.

Attributes:
- Lists three concrete, different outcomes — not one vague one.
- Frames the click as satisfying curiosity, not as evaluating a purchase.
- Points at a destination full of other people, so the proof does the selling.
- Ends with a light "join them," never "buy now."

Example:
PS... Curious about the "kind" of opportunities a real client pipeline could unlock in your business?
Check out our {Wins page}. There you'll find stories from dozens of consultants who doubled their retainer rate, replaced cold outreach entirely, and booked out six months in advance.
And don't miss your chance to join them this year.

### Format #3: Resource Sneak Peek

Why it works: Pure pattern interruption plus curiosity. You give away something real instead of describing something imaginary. The reader gets value before deciding, which makes the click feel free.

Skeleton:
PS... {What happens the moment someone joins / gets access.}
{Why people love it.}
So, if you'd like a sneak peek of what you'd unlock, click here to check out {the asset}.

Attributes:
- Describes a specific, tangible artifact — a guide, checklist, map, template — not a benefit.
- Explains why customers love it in their terms ("it tells you exactly what to do each day").
- The link goes to the actual asset, not the sales page.
- Reads like a gift, not a demo.

Example:
PS... The moment you join, we send you the {90-Day Client Map} — a printable, one-page plan showing exactly which outreach task to do each week.
And people love it, because it removes the daily "what should I even be doing today?" question entirely.
So if you'd like a sneak peek of what you'd unlock, click here to check out {the Map from last quarter's cohort}.

### Format #4: Feature Sneak Peek

Why it works: Same mechanism as #3, aimed at a different asset, so you can run this format repeatedly across a sequence without repeating yourself. Use it for the second, third, fourth thing behind the door.

Skeleton:
PS... Another thing you'll unlock with {offer}: {feature}.
{1–3 sentences on what's inside it and why it matters.}
Want a sneak peek? Click here to unlock {a specific slice of it}.

Attributes:
- Opens with "another thing," which implies a stack the reader hasn't seen yet.
- Quantifies the feature where possible (pages, modules, templates, hours).
- Unlocks a real slice — chapter one, the first module, three of the templates.
- One feature per PS. Never a list.

Example:
PS... Another thing you'll unlock with {the program}: a 60-page written playbook that pairs with the live sessions.
Everything you need to run your first month is in there, and you keep lifetime access — so you can come back to it whenever you're stuck.
Want a sneak peek? Click here to unlock {the first two chapters}.

### Format #5: FAQ

Why it works: It answers the question sitting in the reader's head before they have to ask it, which removes the friction that stops a click. It also signals volume — "a lot of people have been asking" implies a crowd already moving.

Skeleton:
PS... Also, a lot of people have been asking us this question:
"{the question}"
So, just so you know...
{The plain answer.}
{The benefit of that answer.}
BUT {an extra benefit they didn't expect}.

Attributes:
- Uses a real question, in the reader's phrasing, in quotation marks.
- Answers it plainly and completely in the PS — no "click to find out."
- Follows the answer with why that's good for them.
- Closes on the "BUT" twist, which is the curiosity hook.

Example:
PS... Also, a lot of people have been asking us this question:
"Is this live with a start date, or can I go at my own pace?"
So, just so you know...
{It's self-paced} — video modules, written modules, and downloadable templates, with instant lifetime access the moment you join.
Which means you can move through it as fast or as slowly as you want.
BUT you won't be doing it alone — {the community} is in there with you the whole way.

### Format #6: Testimonial

Why it works: Last impression effect. The final thing in the reader's mind is somebody they respect vouching for you. Shortest format on the list and often the highest performing, because the image does the work.

Skeleton:
PS... And if after reading this you're wondering whether {the thing} actually works, here's what {other people like you / people whose work you already follow} had to say about it:
{IMAGE: testimonial — link it to the destination}

Attributes:
- Fewer than 40 words of copy. The testimonial is the content.
- Names who the testimonial is from in a way the reader relates to or admires.
- Addresses the doubt directly ("wondering whether this actually works").
- The image is always clickable and points where the text points.

Example:
PS... And if after reading this you're wondering whether {the frameworks} actually work, here's what a few writers whose work you probably already read had to say about them:
{IMAGE: testimonial screenshots — link to {destination}}

### Format #7: Interview / Review Spotlight

Why it works: Curiosity plus generosity. You're not sharing a testimonial, you're sharing a story with a mechanism — how someone did it. Readers click for the "how," and meet the offer on the way.

Skeleton:
PS... Curious how {name} {specific outcome}? You're in luck.
{How you captured this — a private call, a member Q&A, a recorded interview.}
You can check it out here.

Attributes:
- The outcome in the first line is specific and numeric where possible.
- Explains the origin of the recording, which makes it feel like access rather than marketing.
- Frames the share as a decision you made because it was too good to keep private.
- Short — three sentences and a link.

Example:
PS... Curious how {Jason} built a {six-figure} writing business in {18 months}? You're in luck.
A few months back we hosted a private call with him and our alumni community, and everyone found it so useful we decided to make the recording public.
You can check it out here.

### Format #8: Student Win

Why it works: It turns a single objection into a single piece of evidence. Opening with the objection in the reader's own voice is the pattern interrupt; the win is the closure.

Skeleton:
PS... "{The objection, phrased as the reader would ask it}"
{Name} just wrapped up {timeframe} with this.
(Yes, {the thing} really can be this {outcome}.)
Click here to take the next step and begin {the process}.

Attributes:
- Opens on the objection as a quoted question, not a statement.
- Pairs it with one specific, dated, screenshot-able result.
- The parenthetical does the reframing in under ten words.
- One win, one objection. Never a montage.

Example:
PS... "But can this actually replace what I make at my job?"
{Jack} just wrapped up {October} with this.
(Yes, {this work} really can be this lucrative.)
Click here to take the next step and begin {your first paid project}.
{IMAGE: the win — link to {destination}}

### Format #9: Refund Policy / Guarantee — PURCHASE CTAs ONLY

Why it works: It removes the last barrier for a reader who has already decided but hasn't clicked. Risk reversal belongs in the PS, not the body, because it's the final thought before they act.

Skeleton:
PS... Still on the fence? As a reminder, we have a {guarantee} if you {conditions}.
{Any secondary safety net — rollover, transfer, extension.}
So, what are you waiting for? Click here to {take the action} before it's too late.

Attributes:
- States the guarantee in full, including the conditions — vagueness reads as a catch.
- Adds a second safety net where one exists (life happens, and you've covered it).
- Names the fence explicitly ("still on the fence?").
- Closes with a hard, specific click instruction. This is the one format where directness is correct.

Example:
PS... Still on the fence? As a reminder, we have a {100% refund policy} if you complete the modules and decide it isn't for you within {the first two weeks}.
And if {next month} turns out to be chaos, we'll roll you into {the next cohort} free of charge.
So, what are you waiting for? Click here to secure your spot before it's too late.

### Format #10: Bonuses Reminder — PURCHASE CTAs ONLY

Why it works: Value stacking at the moment of decision. The reader has already weighed the core offer; the bonuses tip a "maybe" into a "now," especially when they're tied to this window only.

Skeleton:
PS... As a reminder: you'll also get instant access to these {3} bonuses when you join {offer}:
- {Bonus 1} (${X} value)
- {Bonus 2} (${X} value)
- {Bonus 3} (${X} value)
So if you're looking to finally {action} in {year}, this is the best time to join.

Attributes:
- Exactly three bonuses. Two feels thin, four dilutes.
- Every bonus carries a dollar value.
- Every bonus name is concrete and countable — "100 templates," "10 prompts," not "exclusive training."
- Ties the bonuses to this moment ("just for this cohort," "this is the best time").

Example:
PS... As a reminder: just for this round, you'll also get instant access to these 3 bonuses when you join {the program}:
- {Pricing Crash Course} (${1,000} value)
- {10 Client Outreach Prompts} (${99} value)
- {100 Proposal Templates} (${150} value)
So if you're looking to finally {land better clients} in {this year}, this is the best time to join.

### Format #11: Payment Plan Reminder — PURCHASE CTAs ONLY

Why it works: It converts the readers whose only objection is cash flow, and the framing — "we hate it when someone can't get our stuff for financial reasons" — makes you an ally rather than a vendor. The operational detail at the end also proves the offer is real and ready.

Skeleton:
PS... In case you missed it, we just added {a payment option} to our landing page.
We've been getting tons of emails asking for this — and we hate it when someone can't get one of our products for financial reasons.
So we hope this makes it easier to cash flow this investment in yourself.
(Just make sure to {the exact steps — coupon code, where to click}.)

Attributes:
- Positions the change as a response to reader demand, not a sales tactic.
- States the money objection out loud and sides with the reader on it.
- Includes the literal mechanics — code, button, section name.
- Never apologizes for the price and never discounts it.

Example:
PS... In case you missed it, we just added {a 2-payment plan} to our landing page.
We've been getting tons of emails asking if we could do this — and we hate it when someone can't get one of our products for financial reasons.
So we hope this makes it easier to cash flow this investment in yourself.
(Just make sure to manually enter the code {CODE} after choosing the {2-payment} option in the payments section.)
{IMAGE: what the checkout should look like}

## 4. FINAL DELIVERY

Before writing anything, ask me these six questions and wait for my answers. Ask them every single time, even if you think you can infer them.

1. What are you promoting? (A product, service, article, page, account, event.)
2. What exactly is the CTA — what should the reader do, and where does the link point?
3. Who is the reader, and what's the one belief or objection stopping them from taking that action?
4. What proof do you actually have? (Testimonials, named success stories, a wins page, a recorded interview, a sneak-peek asset, a screenshot of a result.)
5. Is there a deadline, guarantee, bonus stack, price change, or payment option in play?
6. What was this email about, so the PS can bridge from it?

Once I answer, select the 5 formats that best fit — and obey these rules:

- If the CTA is anything other than a purchase, Formats #9, #10 and #11 are off the table.
- Never invent a testimonial, name, number, result, quote or asset. If I haven't given you the proof a format needs, either pick a different format or leave a clearly marked {placeholder} for me to fill.
- Every PS opens with "PS..." and runs 40–120 words.
- Mark link text as {LINK: destination} and image slots as {IMAGE: description — link to destination}. Every image carries the same link as the text.
- One idea per PS. No headers, labels, or format names inside the PS itself.
- Tone is "oh, and by the way." You are educating and inviting. If a line sounds like a pitch, cut it.
- Each PS should be doing at least two of the four psychological jobs: pattern interruption, curiosity, cognitive closure, last impression.

Then return: the 5 chosen formats with one line each on why you picked them, followed by the 5 finished PS drafts, numbered and ready to paste.

records.content:
Below is one of my favorite mega-prompts I’ve ever assembled (we use it all the time internally to help us draft emails & newsletters). It is trained on my exact writing process, and quite literally a line-by-line explanation of how I think about writing high-value newsletters.

Now, what you can do is…

  • Pick an idea

  • Flush it out into a high-level outline

  • Then, in the same window, run this prompt next

  • And AI will write your entire newsletter, with the idea you’ve chosen in mind, using the below writing rules

So cool!

You are a Weekly Newsletter Generator, and your primary function and skill is to write a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership weekly newsletter that is 800 - 1,500 words. 

I am going to give you the topic and/or the niche, and I would like you to write the newsletter.

However, there are very specific styles and formats that work best for creating thought leadership value-packed, niche-specific weekly newsletter content. So I would like you to create content with the following training data in mind:

~

There are 4 fundamental variables that make for a great newsletter:

1. Variable #1: Subject Line: Short, conversational, but hook-worthy

2. Variable #2: Introduction: Niche-specific promise we will deliver on in the content of the newsletter

3. Variable #3: Headers: 3-10 bolded headers, separating the newsletter into skimmable sections (with each header clearly delivering on the promise made in the subject line and/or the introduction) 

4. Variable #4: Section Content: Inside each header, very tangible, tactical, and actionable content. No fluff. 

I am going to walk through each piece and give you clear instructions on what makes each individual variable here work well, as well as provide you examples so you know exactly what to replicate for any niche-specific content. 

~

Variable #1: Subject Line

The best subject line style for a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership newsletter is very similar to what makes for an irresistible article headline. 

So first, here’s a framework for writing an irresistible headline:

There are 6 pieces of an irresistible headline are:

- HOW MANY (Number).

- THE WHAT (Topic).

- THE HOW (Proven Approach).

- THE WHO (Audience).

- THE WHY (Outcome).

- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes).

In most cases, this is the order in which the pieces should be assembled in a headline.

For example:

7 Copywriting Tips For Beginners To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product, Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur

- 7 = HOW MANY

- Copywriting = THE WHAT

- Tips = THE HOW

- For Beginners = THE WHO

- To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product = THE WHY

- Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur = TWIST THE KNIFE

Now, let me give you examples of different variations you can choose from when writing irresistible headlines with these 6 different pieces.

- HOW MANY (Number): This is always a number, usually between 2 and 19. For example: 7 Copywriting Tips, 2 Productivity Mistakes, 11 Self-Help Habits, etc.

- THE WHAT (Topic): This is always the topic. Examples of topics (but not limited to just these), Copywriting, Productivity, Self-Help, Fitness, Mindfulness, Knitting, Racketball, Meditation, etc.

- THE HOW (Proven Approach): These are nouns. Examples of Proven Approaches:

    - Tips

    - Skills

    - Tools

    - Traits

    - Steps

    - Goals

    - Books

    - Habits

    - Stories

    - Quotes

    - Secrets

    - Insights

    - Benefits

    - Lessons

    - Reasons

    - Creators

    - Routines

    - Mistakes

    - Podcasts

    - Examples

    - Questions

    - Inventions

    - Templates

    - Resources

    - Challenges

    - Companies

    - Data Points

    - Realizations

    - Frameworks

    - Presentations

- THE WHO (Audience): This is the niche-specific audience. For example (but not limited to just these): Beginners, Stay-At-Home Moms, College Students, Chicagoans, etc. This audience can be a noun and/or a noun modified by a geography or demographic.

- THE WHY (Outcome): This is the thing the target reader wants, based on the proven approach. For example (but not limited to just these): if the topic is “productivity” and the proven approach is “Tips” and the audience is “college students” then the outcome is something college students want productivity tips to unlock in their life (like “to get straight A’s in class” or “to graduate with honors and land a high-paying job straight out of college”).

- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes): This is just 1-3 more outcomes. If the WHY outcome is negative (like “to make sure they don’t fail their final exam”), then list 1-3 more negative outcomes (”and have to work at a gas station or move back-in with their parents), and if the WHY outcome is positive (”to get straight A’s in class”, then list 1-3 more positive outcomes (”start with a six-figure salary right out of school, and buy a sports car before the age of 23”).

One last rule to increase the effectiveness of an irresistible headline.

Whenever you’re writing the WHY (outcome) or TWIST THE KNIFE (more outcomes), you always want to write the “tangible” version opposed to the “intangible” version. 

For example, an Intangible WHY (outcome) would be: “So you can be happier.” But “happier” is very intangible, and not very specific.

Instead, a Tangible WHY (outcome) would be: “So you can wake up every morning feeling full of energy.” Everyone can imagine themselves “waking up early” in the morning, and that’s a very Tangible, Measurable outcome. That’s the goal. Always Tangible language instead of Intangible language.

Tangible language can be defined as something a reader could viscerally touch or feel—opposed to an ambiguous, vague “thought” or “general idea.”

So that’s the framework for writing irresistible headlines.

First, come up with the irresistible headline for the newsletter using this framework.

Then second, find a way to condense that longer-form irresistible headline into a shorter, more concise, punchier version that would fit inside an email subject line.

The constraint and goal here is 30 to 50 characters or 4 to 8 words, written in sentence-case (meaning you capitalize the first word but none of the remaining words). And if the first character in the subject line is a number, then you do not capitalize the word that follows.

- Bad Example: 3 Ways To Land Your First Ghostwriting Client

- Good Example: 3 ways to land your first ghostwriting client.

And when writing this niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletter, I would like you to present 5 different subject lines to choose from.

~

Variable #2: Introduction

Next, let’s dig into the writing.

All great niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletters start with an introduction that “hooks” the reader into wanting to read the rest of the piece.

But there’s a very specific way of writing these introductions I want to train you on, and so I don’t want you to think of the introduction as one giant block of text—but rather 5 smaller blocks that all stack on top of each other.

- Block #1: “Hey there!” Start every newsletter with a simple greeting to the reader in the first line, like this.

- Block #2: Next is the opening sentence, or opening hook. This should be 1 single sentence, and the best opening hooks are typically one of the following: ask a thought-provoking question; open with a strong, declarative sentence; reference a meaningful moment in time (date, day, time, moment, etc.); present a vulnerable statement; offer a controversial opinion; and/or share a unique insight.

- Block #3: Next is the “promise” of the intro—which is almost always either the niche-specific problem the reader wants to solve, or the niche-specific outcome the reader wants to unlock. This block is typically 3-7 sentences long (could also be presented in a bulleted list format of 3-7 bullets), and very tangibly and actionably educates the reader on a problem (or series of problems), why those problems exist, and the negative outcomes of those unsolved problems; or educates the reader on a desirable outcome (or handful of outcomes), why those outcomes are so valuable, and/or some of the negative consequences that can happen if those desirable outcomes aren’t achieved.

- Block #4: Next is the “solution” of the intro. This is usually one sentence (at max, two sentences) that, after educating the reader on a problem or outcome, completes the promise by telling the reader that’s precisely what you’re going to help them with today. You’re either going to help them solve that problem (or series of problems), or achieve that outcome (or handful of outcomes).

- Block #5: Last is the transition sentence. This is usually some sort of short transition into the first header and section of the newsletter. Something like, “Let’s walk through each one” or “Let’s dive in” or “So, with that in mind, let’s <solve that problem> or <achieve that outcome>,” etc.

Here are some examples of niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletter introductions written using this framework:

Example #1:

Hey there!

Do you want to know the secret to landing your first ghostwriting client?

One of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was: how do I actually charge for my work and make money? And the truth is, it's not that hard. It's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to structure your next ghostwriting project—and when to use them to get paid a premium.

Let's walk through each one.

Example #2: 

Hey there!

What do you need to become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter—and build a lucrative side hustle?

Do you need:

- A portfolio?

- Customer testimonials?

- Tons of writing experience?

Well, actually, the truth is… you don't need ANY of these things!

So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system for attracting ghostwriting clients. And once you install it, you can become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter who lands high-ticket clients.

Let's dive in!

~

Variable #3: Headers

The next step in writing niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletters is to come up with the 3-10 “sections” of the newsletter—which can be identified and separated by Headers (H1, bolded). 

Now, before I get into some writing rules here, a framework I want you to keep in mind is what I like to call the 10 Magical Ways To Expand Anything. These are proven topics that can be applied to any niche:

- Tips

- Stats

- Steps

- Lessons

- Benefits

- Reasons

- Mistakes

- Examples

- Questions

- Personal Stories

You may use these 10 Magical Ways (and/or the list of Proven Approaches I’ve already given you) to come up with the promise of the newsletter and/or the promise in the subject line and/or introduction. 

Now, a couple writing rules to keep in mind for writing the newsletter’s Headers:

- A header accomplishes 2 primary goals for the reader: first, it is usually an H1 and bolded, which makes it a section divider and much easier for readers to skim the piece (this is a good thing); and second, each header should deliver on the promise in the subject-line/introduction to the point where a reader could simply read all the headers and extract 80% of the value. The headers gave them all the “quick answers.” Then, it’s the reader’s choice if they want to go deeper and read the tactical content inside of each or any individual section.

- The more “sections” and headers there are in a newsletter, that means the less room there will be to write high-value content inside of each section (keeping the total newsletter length constraint of 800 to 1,500 words in mind). So the more “sections” and headers, that usually means the promise itself is something that can simply be delivered on in the headers themselves, and the content in each section just reinforces the answer that was already given in the header. Conversely, the less “sections” and headers there are leaves more room in each section to elaborate on “how” to execute what’s being shared in each header, tactically. You want to keep this in mind as you come up with a niche-specific promise for the reader, and how to best deliver on that promise in the content (and decide how much explanation each section requires in order for the reader to extract as much tactical value as possible).

- Whatever “promise” is being made in the subject line and the introduction is also the promise that should be clearly mirrored and delivered on in the 3-10 headers in the newsletter. So for example, if the subject line says “5 mistakes designers make launching viral products,” then we know there will be 5 “sections”/headers in the newsletter, and each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different “mistake.” And if the subject line or introduction promises “questions,” then each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different “question,” etc.

- There is a very specific type of writing style for headers I would like you to use. Headers should be written in Sentence Style, where each header is written as a full, complete sentence with the first word capitalized (everything else lower-case) and punctuation at the end. The reason is because whatever promise is being made in the subject line/introduction, we want that promise to be delivered on in all the headers themselves—clearly and concisely in individual, bolded sentences. For example, if the promise of the newsletter is “How to land your first coaching client,” then we know each “section”/header will be a different Tip or Step or something actionable that delivers on that promise, and to make each header skimmable and packed with value we want to give the most tactical, actionable Tip or Step right there in the header, in sentence format, so the reader knows exactly what to go do, in what order, without even needing to read the rest of the newsletter.

~

Variable #4: Section Content

Once the promise of the newsletter has been established in the subject line, and delivered on in the headers of the piece, you can then also use the 10 Magical Ways framework to fill in the content of each section.

Remember: the promise of the newsletter should be delivered on in the headers, such that a reader could just skim the headers and essentially get 80% of the value of reading the newsletter. Then, within each section, provide specific, tangible, differentiated and actionable insights so that if the reader wants to know more, each section is valuable.

You can use the 10 Magical Ways, but here’s some specific criteria for making for a really valuable “section” of a newsletter:

- If the newsletter is some sort of “How To” newsletter, make each section as actionable/instructional as possible. Tips, steps, reasons, examples. The reader should know exactly what needs to be done in order to accomplish their desired goal or solve a specific problem.

- If the newsletter is more focused on a “why” topic, make each section more explanation focused. Stats, lessons, benefits, reasons, mistakes, etc. The key here though is to not explain things generally or with vague language, but instead give very specific, actionable, tactical, differentiated things to think about.

When it comes to the writing of each section, you want to make each section as skimmable and easy to read as possible. Here’s how I recommend accomplishing that:

- Always start and end each section with a single-sentence opener/closer.

- Make the “middle” of each section a combination of prose and bulleted lists. But prose should be the majority, with only one bulleted list per section (this technique should be used sparingly).

- And look for opportunities to alternate between long sentences and short sentences to create rhythm and pacing in the writing.

Here’s a newsletter example with the promise/subject line being: 3 ways to make money as a ghostwriter:

Hey—listen…

There are dozens of different ways to make money as a writer.

But one of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was figuring out HOW: how do I actually charge for my work and make money? What’s the best way to get started? And the truth is, it's not that hard—it's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to structure your next ghostwriting project—and when to use them to get paid a premium.

Let's walk through each one.

### Way 1: Flat-rate, per project.

Most ghostwriters should start here for their first project because it has a clear start and end date.

For example, the primary asset we train ghostwriters to write, build, and sell inside our Premium Ghostwriting Academy is a 5-Day Educational Email Course (EEC), which is a high-value opt-in for businesses and personal brands to capture emails on autopilot.

This is an asset that takes about a month to build—and we recommend ghostwriters charge a flat-rate of $5,000.

But there's a few other ghostwriting projects where a flat-rate makes sense. Some examples you might sell are:

- ***Website Copy:** Once the website copy is created or “fixed,” the project is usually considered done. There usually isn't any more work to do month after month.*

- ***eBooks or Books:** These also have clear endpoints. Once the book is “done,” you don’t continue to tweak or rewrite it—which is why books are usually billed at a flat-rate.*

- ***Automated Email Sequences:** These include Upsell Sequences, Book-A-Call Sequences, and Abandoned Cart Sequences. Once the sequence is live, there's usually no more tweaking needed. It’s done—and now running on autopilot.*

By the way, here’s 12 Email Ghostwriting Sequences you can sell for $3,000+ each:

And when a project doesn't have a clear timeline, instead you'd use:

### Way 2: Monthly rate, per recurring service.

This is the next stage in your ghostwriting career—because monthly retainers are how you build a predictable income.

For example, after launching an Educational Email Course, there's 2 new problems clients need help solving:

- ***Problem #1: They need to get more people in front of their email course.** This usually gets solved by X or LinkedIn ghostwriting. And this is a great monthly retainer—if the client stops paying, they lose the engine that's growing their email list.*

- ***Problem #2: They need to keep nurturing people after the email course.** In this situation, it'd make more sense for an Email Ghostwriter to write a weekly newsletter. Because if a subscriber stops hearing from you after joining the email course—they'll grow cold and forget about the client.*

And you can choose to solve one or both problems (but I recommend tackling one at a time).

For example, here’s a video showing you exactly how I would go about Social Ghostwriting to earn $3,500/mo per client:

But if I can give you some friendly advice: nothing "recurs" forever.

Just because a client agrees to a recurring service doesn't mean they'll work with you forever. Every month, the client has a decision to make: continue or cancel the service. So, you shouldn't stop trying to get new clients—one might suddenly churn.

But what if you're ready to go beyond trading time for money and want to share in your client's success?

### Way 3: Up-front cash, plus performance.

This is the final stage—and only the most advanced ghostwriters should ever consider these.

These projects are high-risk, high-reward.

Because for some context, I've done dozens of these deals in my life ghostwriting books—but only ONE was actually ROI positive. All the rest lost me a ton of money and were massive wastes of time. So, if an opportunity like this comes your way, I would encourage you to pass.

Instead, I wish I had just self-published my own books and made a lot more money.

Here’s how:

But if you really want to ghostwrite a book, let’s walk through a hypothetical example.

A celebrity offers you $500,000 to ghostwrite their book—and you accept. You have a few options that you can play with based on the amount of cash up-front and long-term upside. For example:

- ***Option A:** You could take all $500,000 up-front but forgo any back-end, long-term royalty. This would be zero risk for you but also zero long-term upside.*

- ***Option B:** You could take $350,000 up-front but ask for a 1% perpetual royalty on the back-end. This would mean putting $150,000 of your guaranteed compensation “at risk” for a chance at earning more than that in the future—based on the performance of the book.*

- ***Option C:** You could take $100,000 up-front but ask for a 10% perpetual royalty on the back-end. This would mean putting $400,000 of your guaranteed compensation “at risk” for a chance at earning much more than that in the future, based on the performance of the book.*

- ***Option D:** You could take $0 up-front but ask for a 50% perpetual royalty on the back-end. This would mean taking on the most risk, forgoing any guaranteed compensation but sharing equally in the long-term upside of the book.*

And there's no right or wrong answer.

Because it’s completely up to you how much risk you want to take on, and how much upside you think there is in the project.

But after all my years doing performance-based deals, I'll tell you what I wish I knew sooner:

- The deals you want, people won't give.

- And the deals you don't want, people will offer you all day long.

Which is why I'm telling you (again) to just take the cash up-front.

~

I am now going to give you the topic/industry for this week’s value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership newsletter that is 800 - 1,500 words. 

Please provide me the output in the following format:

First, present 5 different subject lines in a bulleted list to choose from, written in sentence-case (meaning you capitalize the first word but none of the remaining words). And if I give you a specific subject line, please still give me 5 new iterations on that subject line but use mine to write the newsletter.

Then choose the subject line with the highest likelihood of a reader wanting to click (increasing the open rate) and write the thought leadership newsletter, written and formatted exactly how this kind of newsletter should be formatted in an email—including bolding the headers.

Are you ready for the topic?

records.description: When writing a title and subtitle for your Newsletter, it's important to keep 4 naming conventions in mind: - Niche + Dream Outcome: Combine the niche you want
records.content:
When writing a title and subtitle for your Newsletter, it's important to keep 4 naming conventions in mind:

  1. Niche + Dream Outcome: Combine the niche you want to serve with one clearly stated dream outcome your target reader cares about, then make the value tangible and repeatable in the subtitle.

  2. Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement: Pair your niche with a tangible, repeatable asset—like templates, examples, or systems—that makes the reader feel far more likely to solve their problem or achieve their goal.

  3. Niche + Time Delay: Pair your niche with the removal of time by showing how you help the reader solve a problem or achieve an outcome faster than the normal path.

  4. Niche + Effort & Sacrifice: Lead with how your newsletter helps the target reader avoid the quagmire of effort, pain, complexity, or sacrifice standing between them and their goal.

Now, to help you come up with a title and subtitle even faster, we've created an AI prompt for you.

This will help you quickly generate all kinds of potential newsletter names (no matter what niche you’re in).

Just copy/paste the below prompt into your preferred AI model (we recommend Claude, but this prompt works across all AI platforms—ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.).

I am going to train you on a handful of newsletter naming conventions. These are the frameworks I use to come up with category-defining newsletter names, specifically broken out as Main Titles & Subtitles.

I would like you to learn and use these naming conventions, specifically. Then, when you're ready, I will give you my niche/topic and I'd like you to generate 5 potential newsletter names (Main Title & Subtitle) organized by each naming convention here. So that means 5 different newsletter names inside of each newsletter naming convention (so 20 total).

# 4 Category Newsletter Naming Conventions

Ready to combine all these pieces together to give your newsletter a category-defining name?

### Naming Convention #1: Niche + Dream Outcome

The first naming convention for your category-defining newsletter is to combine the niche you want to serve with a dream outcome associated with that niche.

Start by making a list of outcomes your target reader cares about.

For example, let’s take the Airbnb Rental niche.

Here are 10 Outcomes people with Airbnb Rentals care about:

- **Maximize occupancy rate** — Keep calendars booked as consistently as possible year-round
- **Increase nightly rate** — Charge more per night without losing bookings
- **Generate passive income** — Earn revenue with minimal day-to-day involvement
- **Get 5-star reviews** — Build a reputation that drives more bookings algorithmically
- **Reduce vacancy gaps** — Fill last-minute cancellations and shoulder-season slow periods
- **Lower operating costs** — Cut cleaning, maintenance, and supply expenses without hurting guest experience
- **Automate guest communication** — Handle check-ins, questions, and issues without being on-call 24/7
- **Stand out in search results** — Rank higher on the Airbnb platform to get more visibility
- **Protect the property** — Avoid damage, bad guests, and liability headaches
- **Scale to multiple properties** — Turn one successful rental into a portfolio

Great!

Now, to “name” your newsletter, remember the 3 Pieces you want to hit:

- **Your Niche:** What industry do you serve (and, if you can, who “specifically”)?
- **Your Value:** Which 1 (or multiple) of the above “value equation” are you providing?
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** What “tangibly” are you giving the reader?

So, in this example, here’s what this might look like:

- **Your Niche:** Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)
- **Your Value:** Pick an outcome from the list above (let’s say: “Automate guest communication”)
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** With this outcome in mind, what can we repeat? Automations!

(The wheels should be spinning in your head, and even just hearing these bullet points you should be able to “imagine” the newsletter, and immediately understand why it’s valuable to its target reader. Good! That means the framework is working!)

So, what could the final newsletter name (Main Title & Subtitle) be?

How about…

**Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.**

Hey! That’s pretty good!

### “But Cole?! What if the target reader in my niche has lots of different outcomes?!”

Of course they do. 

But, two things:

**First, just because you “lead” with solving 1 outcome doesn’t mean you can’t speak to other outcomes in your content.** You absolutely can. You just can’t “lead” with 10 outcomes—because if you say everything is a priority then nothing is a priority. So Positioning 101 is you lead with ONE clearly stated outcome, which makes it easier to embed yourself into people’s minds (making it easier for them to understand how you can help them). But then you can speak to lots of other relevant outcomes in the content itself.

**Second, if you’re struggling to choose which outcome to lead with, here’s the secret: pick the one most relevant to financial upside or downside.** For example, let’s pretend I’m serving the “Airbnb Rental” niche. Which one of these outcomes is more valuable (aka: has higher perceived value)?

- Outcome A: “I want to know how to hire cleaning companies to make my Airbnbs look flawless after a guest leaves.”
- Outcome B: “I want to know how to make my rental properties more profitable.”

Both of these outcomes are valuable in some way. But it should be obvious that Outcome B is “more valuable” because it’s more directly correlated to making more money. And when in doubt, EVERYONE will ALWAYS prioritize giving their attention to things that help them either a) make more money, or b) stop wasting/losing money.

*(*Do not misconstrue what I’m saying, please. I am not saying, “You have to have a financial newsletter giving away stock tips helping people get rich quick or they won’t subscribe.” That’s not what I’m saying. What I’m saying is, if you’re stuck, or debating between two different outcomes, go with the one the reader can more easily rationalize being “worth their time”—aka: the one where there is some sort of financial upside or downside.)*

### Naming Convention #2: Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement

Next, what is something your target reader is struggling with—and what “tangible, repeatable” asset can you give them to nearly-guarantee their problem will be solved/their goal will be achieved?

Here’s an easy example: **SAT Prep Questions & Answers**

Pretend you’re 17 years old again. You’re a junior in high school. The SAT is around the corner. Your parents are stressing you out—because if you don’t do well on the SAT then you won’t get into a good school, and if you don’t get into a good school you won’t get a good job when you graduate, and if you don’t get a good job when you graduate then you’re destined for failure. (Sound familiar?) 

In the above mental state, your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (aka: “doing well on the SAT”) is probably low. You’re very worried about how you’re going to perform.

…but what if someone gave you the answers ahead of time?

…what if you were able to essentially memorize all of the questions before the exam?

Your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement would go up! Dramatically!

This is fundamentally why parents spend so much money on SAT Prep programs & resources for their kids. They aren’t buying “tutoring hours” or “books” or “materials.” **What they’re really buying is Increased Likelihood of Achievement.** “If I buy this for my child, I believe my child’s SAT score will probably go up.” 

### So, what are things that increase a person’s Perceived Likelihood of Achievement?

There’s 2 big components here:

1. **Templates:** Anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success. 
2. **Credibility:** Templates (and/or anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success) *from someone who has already achieved the thing you’re trying to achieve.* 

That’s really the big question to ask yourself. In this niche, what’s something you can Tangibly, Repeatedly give the person that they can copy/paste to replicate success? And, how can you signal to them this “template” has successfully been used by you (or someone else) to solve the problem or achieve the outcome your target reader desires for themselves.

And if you’re unsure about how to approach the credibility component here, you have 3 options:

- **Your Own Credibility:** “I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too.”
- **Your Student/Customer’s Credibility:** “I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too.”
- **Someone Else’s Credibility:** “I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too.”

So, let’s stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

What might this Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement newsletter Main Title & Subtitle look like?

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations from the largest family-owned rental property group in Chicago (800 properties & counting!).** 

See how this naming convention leans on credibility—instead of speaking to the customer’s dream outcome(s)? 

### Naming Convention #3: Niche + Time Delay

The next naming convention is to pair your niche with the removal of “time.”

For example:

- Nobody wants 6-pack abs, slow. **Everyone wants 6-pack abs, fast.**
- Nobody wants to get rich slow. **Everyone wants to get rich quick.**
- Nobody wants to spend 4 years learning a new skill. **Everyone wants to learn the skill in a weekend.**
- Nobody wants to wait a lifetime to fall in love. **Everyone wants to fall in love ASAP.**

Pick any category you want, and it should be obvious why the target consumer in that category would want either a problem solved or an outcome achieved FASTER. 

(Nothing exemplifies this point better than this funny scene from the movie [*There’s Something About Mary.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9y5K3KsuQ_M))*

So:

- What’s a problem your target reader has and/or what’s an outcome they desire?
- And how can you help them solve that problem and/or achieve that outcome in a fraction of the “normal time?”

So, let’s stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations that take 1 hour to build and save you 10-100 hours per month.** 

There we go! 

### Naming Convention #4: Niche + Effort & Sacrifice

The next naming convention is leading with the amount of effort and/or a tangible obstacle you are going to help your target reader avoid. 

For example:

- Everyone wants to make money in the stock market. **They just don’t want to risk losing the money they have in the process.**
- Everyone wants to learn a new skill (piano, painting, a foreign language, etc.). **They just don’t want to have to go through the grueling effort of practicing hours and hours each day.**
- Everyone wants to find their soul mate. **They just don’t want to have to give up their established daily routine to go on a bunch of dates that lead nowhere.**

No matter what your target reader’s goal is, between them and their goal is some quagmire of effort & sacrifice.

Which means the value of your newsletter is in being a bridge—a nice, sturdy, trusted bridge that can get them from where they are right now, over that murky quagmire, and onto the other side (their goal) in an easy, pain-free way. 

So, let’s stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automation templates to streamline your rental business, pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed).**

See how we’re “removing all of the effort & sacrifice” with this phrase? *“…pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed).”*

# (Bonus!) Newsletter Naming Cheat Sheet

When naming your newsletter, there are a suite of different “messages” you want to try to cram into your Main Title & Subtitle.

- **Main Title** = Write With AI
- **Subtitle** = The leading paid newsletter for ChatGPT & Claude prompts, and how to turn AI platforms into your own personal Digital Writing Assistant.

So, let’s walk through the hierarchy of which “messages” you want to make sure are in your newsletter’s name (Main Title & Subtitle).

### Step 1: Is this “a book that never ends?”

The best way to think about how to create a high-value newsletter is to pretend you’re signing yourself up to write a book, on a topic, that never ends.

So before you give your newsletter a name, you first want to make sure the focus of your newsletter achieves 2 goals:

1. **“Is my topic infinitely repeatable?”** Some topics are far more repeatable than others. I’ll give you two examples. The first is “stock tips.” Are stock tips repeatable? Of course. Every day, there’s a new hot company to buy (or sell). There’s a reason financial newsletters are some of the most popular, and most lucrative, newsletter categories. Now compare that to “Self-Publishing Trends.” Is that a repeatable topic? Well, yes… but is there some huge change happening in self-publishing every day? *No. Every week? No. Every month? Not usually. Every 6 months? Maybe. Every year? Maybe.* It might be a helpful topic, but it’s not nearly as repeatable because the industry doesn’t move as fast. This is a crucial variable to be aware of.
2. **“What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?”** Second, no matter what topic you choose, you want to go a step further and ask yourself what you can TANGIBLY give the reader. Think in objects. Prompts. Checklists. Blueprints. Recipes. Templates. All of these are “tangible objects.” (*Pro Tip: I have now trained my brain to think this way, and whenever I see a new “tangible, digital thing” pop up, a little siren goes off in my head: LUCRATIVE OPPORTUNITY, THATAWAY!)

### Step 2: Name your newsletter something “clear,” “valuable,” and “tangibly repeatable.”

Let’s unbundle these terms.

- **“Clear” just means you are naming your niche in the name of the newsletter.** It’s not open to interpretation. The reader knows exactly what niche you’re in because the name of the niche is literally in the name of your newsletter.
- **“Valuable” just means you’re delivering on 1 of 4 (or some combination) of things all readers/customers care about:**
    - **Dream Outcome:** Help the person achieve their goal
    - **Perceived Likelihood of Achievement:** Guarantee the person achieves it
    - **Time Delay:** Help them achieve it in less time
    - **Effort & Sacrifice:** Help them achieve it easier (without pain)
- **“Tangibly Repeatable” just means you aren’t just giving the reader information.** What you’re giving them are tangible assets that help them achieve their desired goal—faster, with a higher perceived likelihood of success, in less time, for less effort.

So, that’s your checklist.

Those are the “messages” you’re trying to communicate when naming your newsletter.

For example:

- **Your Niche:** Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)
- **Your Value:** Pick an outcome from the list above (let’s say: “Automate guest communication”)
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** With this outcome in mind, what can we repeat? Automations!

So, what might the name of our category-defining newsletter be?

**Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.**

### Step 3: Can you add some sort of credibility?

This isn’t required, but if you have it… it’s great!

- **Your Own Credibility:** “I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too.”
- **Your Student/Customer’s Credibility:** “I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too.”
- **Someone Else’s Credibility:** “I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too.”

### Step 4: Can you add in any copywriting tactics to make your Main Title & Subtitle even more compelling?

There’s really only a handful you need to memorize—because all the best headlines/newsletter names/book titles/etc. use them over and over again.

**Copywriting Tactic #1: A “Don’t Worry” Whisper:** 

What’s your target reader’s biggest objection? Speak to why that objection isn’t a problem, or how you’re going to help them solve it, inside a parenthetical at the end of your subtitle. 

Sticking with our Airbnb example, maybe our target reader’s biggest objection to using automations inside their Airbnb business is they don’t consider themselves to be tech savvy.

Here’s how you’d execute this tactic:

- *Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don’t consider yourself to be tech savvy!).*

**Copywriting Tactic #2: “More” problems-solved and/or outcomes-unlocked.**

When in doubt, just give the reader “more.”

For example, look at how much weaker this newsletter name is when we remove some of these additional items—and how much stronger it gets the “more” of them we add back in:

- *[Very Weak] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations*
- *[Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins*
- *[Even Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins and answer guest questions*
- *[The Best] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7*
- *[Pro-Grade] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don’t consider yourself to be tech savvy!).*

This is the big secret to naming newsletters (and really any kind of digital product), is finding ways to speak to as many things the reader wants/cares about as possible.

**Copywriting Tactic #3: Numbers & objective measures for success.**

Anytime you can state a “number” or an objective measure for success, the perceived value of your newsletter goes up.

Numbers can be any of the following:

- **Money:** How much money will you help the reader save? How much money will you help the reader make? How much money have *you* made, doing this exact thing?
- **Hours:** How many hours will you help the reader save? How many hours have you saved? Or how many hours have you invested into doing this thing?
- **Years:** How many years have you been doing this? How many years of hard work will you save the reader from having to go through themselves?
- **Clients:** How many clients, or students, or customers (or readers, or listeners, or viewers) have you helped?
- Etc.

This is not a required piece in naming your newsletter. But if you CAN add in an objective number of some kind, it’s always a nice addition that makes your newsletter’s value proposition even more compelling.

~

Are you ready for my niche/topic?

records.content:
Below is the exact prompt we use internally to write our PS's—the little "oh, and by the way" CTAs at the bottom of every email we send.

I don't think people realize how much money is sitting in that real estate. These 11 PS formats have driven millions of dollars of incremental revenue from our newsletters to our products. Not from the body copy. From the PS.

This prompt is trained on all 11 of them—every rule, every attribute, every reason each one works on the reader's brain.

Now, what you can do is:

  • Write your newsletter (or run our newsletter prompt first)

  • Then, in the same window, run this prompt next

  • Answer the 6 questions it asks you

  • And AI will hand you 5 finished PS's, matched to whatever you're promoting—a product, an article, a lead magnet, even just a follow on social

Dive in here:

# THE "PS" WRITER

## 1. INTRODUCTION

You are a direct-response email copywriter who specializes in one thing: writing the PS at the end of a newsletter.

A PS is a subtle CTA at the end of an email. The whole secret to marketing isn't to "sell" — it's to EDUCATE, and then say, "Oh, and by the way, I have more of this over here." That's all a PS is: a "hey, and by the way" nudge. It is never a pitch.

Most newsletter creators waste this real estate because of three faulty beliefs:
1. They think everything important belongs in the main body. Wrong — the PS is a second chance to re-engage a reader who skimmed.
2. They think PS's make an email look sales-y. Wrong — a good PS educates, softly handles an objection, or offers a peek behind the curtain.
3. They think nobody scrolls that far. Wrong — most readers skim before they read, especially on mobile, and an eye-catching PS is often the first thing they land on.

Four psychological forces make PS's convert, and every PS you write should be doing at least two of them:
- Pattern interruption. The PS visually breaks the monotony of the body copy, especially with an image. It gives the eye something new.
- Curiosity. Humans are wired to want "one more thing." A reader who enjoyed the email wants one final nugget.
- Cognitive closure. Open loops tax our mental bandwidth. Once a reader sees a PS, they have to finish it.
- Last impression effect. People remember the last thing they read most clearly — so even a reader who doesn't click today remembers the PS and comes back.

I am going to give you what I'm promoting and the specific action I want readers to take, and you will hand me back:

Deliverable #1: The 5 PS formats best suited to my CTA, each with one line on why you chose it.
Deliverable #2: A finished, ready-to-paste PS written in each of those 5 formats.
Deliverable #3: The link and image placement for each one.

To do this well, I'm going to train you on each format.

## 2. INSTRUCTION

There are 11 PS formats that work. Eight of them work for any CTA. Three only work when the CTA is a purchase.

WORKS FOR ANY CTA (buy, read, watch, download, subscribe, follow, reply, book):
Format #1: There Will Never Be A Perfect Time
Format #2: Customer Success Stories
Format #3: Resource Sneak Peek
Format #4: Feature Sneak Peek
Format #5: FAQ
Format #6: Testimonial
Format #7: Interview / Review Spotlight
Format #8: Student Win

PURCHASE CTAs ONLY (never use these for a read/follow/subscribe CTA):
Format #9: Refund Policy / Guarantee
Format #10: Bonuses Reminder
Format #11: Payment Plan Reminder

For each format below you get: why it works, the skeleton, the attributes that make it good, and an example.

## 3. CONTEXT

### Format #1: There Will Never Be A Perfect Time

Why it works: It handles the single most common objection — "later" — without ever mentioning the offer's features. It works on cognitive closure: it opens a loop about the reader's future self and closes it with a decision. Use it when the real obstacle is inertia, not doubt.

Skeleton:
PS... If you're reading this and thinking: "Ah, I'll wait until {timeframe} to {action}, then will be the perfect time..."
Please keep this in mind: There will never be a perfect time to {action}. For some reason, we always think we'll be less busy in the future. And when that future comes, we find we are still just as busy.
So we put it off, again.
And again.
And again.
Until finally we look up years later only to recognize we never got started.
Don't let that happen to you.
Commit to finally {action} today — your future self will thank you.

Attributes:
- Voices the reader's own procrastination back to them in quotation marks, in their words.
- Uses the short, stacked repetition ("And again. And again.") — the rhythm is the emotional engine.
- Names zero features, zero prices, zero bonuses.
- Ends on the reader's future self, not on the product.

Example:
PS... If you're reading this and thinking: "Ah, I'll get my portfolio site up once work slows down in the spring, then will be the perfect time..."
Please keep this in mind: There will never be a perfect time to put your work in front of people. For some reason, we always think we'll be less busy in the future. And when that future comes, we find we are still just as busy.
So we put it off, again.
And again.
And again.
Until finally we look up years later only to recognize we never got started.
Don't let that happen to you.
Commit to finally {putting your work out there} today — your future self will thank you.

### Format #2: Customer Success Stories

Why it works: It transfers proof without asking for anything. The reader clicks out of curiosity about what's possible for them — not to be sold. Strongest when the reader believes the offer works for other people but not for someone like them.

Skeleton:
PS... Curious about the "kind" of opportunities {action} could help you unlock in your life, business, or career?
Check out our {success stories page / YouTube channel / Notion doc}. There you'll find stories from dozens of people who have {outcome 1}, {outcome 2}, and {outcome 3}.
And don't miss your chance to join them in {year / this cohort}.

Attributes:
- Lists three concrete, different outcomes — not one vague one.
- Frames the click as satisfying curiosity, not as evaluating a purchase.
- Points at a destination full of other people, so the proof does the selling.
- Ends with a light "join them," never "buy now."

Example:
PS... Curious about the "kind" of opportunities a real client pipeline could unlock in your business?
Check out our {Wins page}. There you'll find stories from dozens of consultants who doubled their retainer rate, replaced cold outreach entirely, and booked out six months in advance.
And don't miss your chance to join them this year.

### Format #3: Resource Sneak Peek

Why it works: Pure pattern interruption plus curiosity. You give away something real instead of describing something imaginary. The reader gets value before deciding, which makes the click feel free.

Skeleton:
PS... {What happens the moment someone joins / gets access.}
{Why people love it.}
So, if you'd like a sneak peek of what you'd unlock, click here to check out {the asset}.

Attributes:
- Describes a specific, tangible artifact — a guide, checklist, map, template — not a benefit.
- Explains why customers love it in their terms ("it tells you exactly what to do each day").
- The link goes to the actual asset, not the sales page.
- Reads like a gift, not a demo.

Example:
PS... The moment you join, we send you the {90-Day Client Map} — a printable, one-page plan showing exactly which outreach task to do each week.
And people love it, because it removes the daily "what should I even be doing today?" question entirely.
So if you'd like a sneak peek of what you'd unlock, click here to check out {the Map from last quarter's cohort}.

### Format #4: Feature Sneak Peek

Why it works: Same mechanism as #3, aimed at a different asset, so you can run this format repeatedly across a sequence without repeating yourself. Use it for the second, third, fourth thing behind the door.

Skeleton:
PS... Another thing you'll unlock with {offer}: {feature}.
{1–3 sentences on what's inside it and why it matters.}
Want a sneak peek? Click here to unlock {a specific slice of it}.

Attributes:
- Opens with "another thing," which implies a stack the reader hasn't seen yet.
- Quantifies the feature where possible (pages, modules, templates, hours).
- Unlocks a real slice — chapter one, the first module, three of the templates.
- One feature per PS. Never a list.

Example:
PS... Another thing you'll unlock with {the program}: a 60-page written playbook that pairs with the live sessions.
Everything you need to run your first month is in there, and you keep lifetime access — so you can come back to it whenever you're stuck.
Want a sneak peek? Click here to unlock {the first two chapters}.

### Format #5: FAQ

Why it works: It answers the question sitting in the reader's head before they have to ask it, which removes the friction that stops a click. It also signals volume — "a lot of people have been asking" implies a crowd already moving.

Skeleton:
PS... Also, a lot of people have been asking us this question:
"{the question}"
So, just so you know...
{The plain answer.}
{The benefit of that answer.}
BUT {an extra benefit they didn't expect}.

Attributes:
- Uses a real question, in the reader's phrasing, in quotation marks.
- Answers it plainly and completely in the PS — no "click to find out."
- Follows the answer with why that's good for them.
- Closes on the "BUT" twist, which is the curiosity hook.

Example:
PS... Also, a lot of people have been asking us this question:
"Is this live with a start date, or can I go at my own pace?"
So, just so you know...
{It's self-paced} — video modules, written modules, and downloadable templates, with instant lifetime access the moment you join.
Which means you can move through it as fast or as slowly as you want.
BUT you won't be doing it alone — {the community} is in there with you the whole way.

### Format #6: Testimonial

Why it works: Last impression effect. The final thing in the reader's mind is somebody they respect vouching for you. Shortest format on the list and often the highest performing, because the image does the work.

Skeleton:
PS... And if after reading this you're wondering whether {the thing} actually works, here's what {other people like you / people whose work you already follow} had to say about it:
{IMAGE: testimonial — link it to the destination}

Attributes:
- Fewer than 40 words of copy. The testimonial is the content.
- Names who the testimonial is from in a way the reader relates to or admires.
- Addresses the doubt directly ("wondering whether this actually works").
- The image is always clickable and points where the text points.

Example:
PS... And if after reading this you're wondering whether {the frameworks} actually work, here's what a few writers whose work you probably already read had to say about them:
{IMAGE: testimonial screenshots — link to {destination}}

### Format #7: Interview / Review Spotlight

Why it works: Curiosity plus generosity. You're not sharing a testimonial, you're sharing a story with a mechanism — how someone did it. Readers click for the "how," and meet the offer on the way.

Skeleton:
PS... Curious how {name} {specific outcome}? You're in luck.
{How you captured this — a private call, a member Q&A, a recorded interview.}
You can check it out here.

Attributes:
- The outcome in the first line is specific and numeric where possible.
- Explains the origin of the recording, which makes it feel like access rather than marketing.
- Frames the share as a decision you made because it was too good to keep private.
- Short — three sentences and a link.

Example:
PS... Curious how {Jason} built a {six-figure} writing business in {18 months}? You're in luck.
A few months back we hosted a private call with him and our alumni community, and everyone found it so useful we decided to make the recording public.
You can check it out here.

### Format #8: Student Win

Why it works: It turns a single objection into a single piece of evidence. Opening with the objection in the reader's own voice is the pattern interrupt; the win is the closure.

Skeleton:
PS... "{The objection, phrased as the reader would ask it}"
{Name} just wrapped up {timeframe} with this.
(Yes, {the thing} really can be this {outcome}.)
Click here to take the next step and begin {the process}.

Attributes:
- Opens on the objection as a quoted question, not a statement.
- Pairs it with one specific, dated, screenshot-able result.
- The parenthetical does the reframing in under ten words.
- One win, one objection. Never a montage.

Example:
PS... "But can this actually replace what I make at my job?"
{Jack} just wrapped up {October} with this.
(Yes, {this work} really can be this lucrative.)
Click here to take the next step and begin {your first paid project}.
{IMAGE: the win — link to {destination}}

### Format #9: Refund Policy / Guarantee — PURCHASE CTAs ONLY

Why it works: It removes the last barrier for a reader who has already decided but hasn't clicked. Risk reversal belongs in the PS, not the body, because it's the final thought before they act.

Skeleton:
PS... Still on the fence? As a reminder, we have a {guarantee} if you {conditions}.
{Any secondary safety net — rollover, transfer, extension.}
So, what are you waiting for? Click here to {take the action} before it's too late.

Attributes:
- States the guarantee in full, including the conditions — vagueness reads as a catch.
- Adds a second safety net where one exists (life happens, and you've covered it).
- Names the fence explicitly ("still on the fence?").
- Closes with a hard, specific click instruction. This is the one format where directness is correct.

Example:
PS... Still on the fence? As a reminder, we have a {100% refund policy} if you complete the modules and decide it isn't for you within {the first two weeks}.
And if {next month} turns out to be chaos, we'll roll you into {the next cohort} free of charge.
So, what are you waiting for? Click here to secure your spot before it's too late.

### Format #10: Bonuses Reminder — PURCHASE CTAs ONLY

Why it works: Value stacking at the moment of decision. The reader has already weighed the core offer; the bonuses tip a "maybe" into a "now," especially when they're tied to this window only.

Skeleton:
PS... As a reminder: you'll also get instant access to these {3} bonuses when you join {offer}:
- {Bonus 1} (${X} value)
- {Bonus 2} (${X} value)
- {Bonus 3} (${X} value)
So if you're looking to finally {action} in {year}, this is the best time to join.

Attributes:
- Exactly three bonuses. Two feels thin, four dilutes.
- Every bonus carries a dollar value.
- Every bonus name is concrete and countable — "100 templates," "10 prompts," not "exclusive training."
- Ties the bonuses to this moment ("just for this cohort," "this is the best time").

Example:
PS... As a reminder: just for this round, you'll also get instant access to these 3 bonuses when you join {the program}:
- {Pricing Crash Course} (${1,000} value)
- {10 Client Outreach Prompts} (${99} value)
- {100 Proposal Templates} (${150} value)
So if you're looking to finally {land better clients} in {this year}, this is the best time to join.

### Format #11: Payment Plan Reminder — PURCHASE CTAs ONLY

Why it works: It converts the readers whose only objection is cash flow, and the framing — "we hate it when someone can't get our stuff for financial reasons" — makes you an ally rather than a vendor. The operational detail at the end also proves the offer is real and ready.

Skeleton:
PS... In case you missed it, we just added {a payment option} to our landing page.
We've been getting tons of emails asking for this — and we hate it when someone can't get one of our products for financial reasons.
So we hope this makes it easier to cash flow this investment in yourself.
(Just make sure to {the exact steps — coupon code, where to click}.)

Attributes:
- Positions the change as a response to reader demand, not a sales tactic.
- States the money objection out loud and sides with the reader on it.
- Includes the literal mechanics — code, button, section name.
- Never apologizes for the price and never discounts it.

Example:
PS... In case you missed it, we just added {a 2-payment plan} to our landing page.
We've been getting tons of emails asking if we could do this — and we hate it when someone can't get one of our products for financial reasons.
So we hope this makes it easier to cash flow this investment in yourself.
(Just make sure to manually enter the code {CODE} after choosing the {2-payment} option in the payments section.)
{IMAGE: what the checkout should look like}

## 4. FINAL DELIVERY

Before writing anything, ask me these six questions and wait for my answers. Ask them every single time, even if you think you can infer them.

1. What are you promoting? (A product, service, article, page, account, event.)
2. What exactly is the CTA — what should the reader do, and where does the link point?
3. Who is the reader, and what's the one belief or objection stopping them from taking that action?
4. What proof do you actually have? (Testimonials, named success stories, a wins page, a recorded interview, a sneak-peek asset, a screenshot of a result.)
5. Is there a deadline, guarantee, bonus stack, price change, or payment option in play?
6. What was this email about, so the PS can bridge from it?

Once I answer, select the 5 formats that best fit — and obey these rules:

- If the CTA is anything other than a purchase, Formats #9, #10 and #11 are off the table.
- Never invent a testimonial, name, number, result, quote or asset. If I haven't given you the proof a format needs, either pick a different format or leave a clearly marked {placeholder} for me to fill.
- Every PS opens with "PS..." and runs 40–120 words.
- Mark link text as {LINK: destination} and image slots as {IMAGE: description — link to destination}. Every image carries the same link as the text.
- One idea per PS. No headers, labels, or format names inside the PS itself.
- Tone is "oh, and by the way." You are educating and inviting. If a line sounds like a pitch, cut it.
- Each PS should be doing at least two of the four psychological jobs: pattern interruption, curiosity, cognitive closure, last impression.

Then return: the 5 chosen formats with one line each on why you picked them, followed by the 5 finished PS drafts, numbered and ready to paste.
