How to Monetize, Stack Revenue Layers, and Build Digital Products That People Actually Want

Date: 3/23/2026

In today’s DWS Masterclass with Cole, we did some live workshopping and talked about:

  • Monetization isn't about selling more information — it's about pairing your expertise with tangible, repeatable assets like templates, prompts, and pre-built skills that compress hours of learning into seconds of doing, because in the age of AI, people don't want to understand the thing, they want the Betty Crocker box that gets them the result in 20 minutes.

  • Stack your monetization layers instead of picking just one — a paid newsletter, digital products, bootcamps, and coaching aren't competing options but complementary tiers where each level simply adds more assets, more access, and more ways to consume and apply what you teach.

  • If you're debating Substack vs. Kit, it's not either/or — Substack's 10% commission gives you access to a 30-million-person discovery ecosystem (which drove 82% of Write With AI's subscribers), so use Substack as your primary newsletter engine and build your additional monetization layers around it through Kit and other tools.

Click here for Cole's Hot Seat notes!

records.content:
Before we let you dive into the curriculum, there's one quick framework we'd like to share with you (to make sure you actually go through the course and take action):

Your Sacred Hours: How to Make Time For Work That Matters

Your Sacred Hours are blocked off chunks of time that are—you guessed it—sacred.

No distractions, no responsibilities, nothing else to check up on.

Just you and your work for at least two hours.

But your Sacred Hours are not something you just stumble upon. They're planned in advanced, blocked on your calendar, and defended ruthlessly from anyone and anything that tries to interfere with them.

And once you start completing these work blocks day in and day out, the compounding results will shock you.

How to find your own Sacred Hours

Now, the big question is:

How do you find your own Sacred Hours?

There are 2 key questions you need answer:

  • What time of day am I most productive?

  • What time of day can I be least responsive?

Your Sacred Hours lay in the intersection between these two times.

Keep in mind that there's no right or wrong answer. This will be different for everyone in every circumstance. And finding the time that works best for you can require some thinking and experimentation. (Practicing interstitial journaling or keeping a Habit Scorecard for a few days can help.)

For example, Dickie's Sacred Hours differ by time of the week:

  • 5 to 7 am on weekdays

  • 6 to 11 am on weekends

  • Noon to 5 pm on Fridays

Once you've found your optimal intersection, choose a two-hour chunk and block it out.

How to get the most out of your Sacred Hours

Remember: we call them Sacred Hours for a reason—they're sacred!

It's on you to defend them ruthlessly and to proactively avoid anything that could take you out of a deep state of flow.

A few tips to get the most out of your Sacred Hours:

  • Clean and organize your workspace

  • Use a website blocker or turn off the Wi-Fi

  • Leave your phone on airplane mode in a different room

  • Wear sound-cancelling headphones with your go-to flow playlist

A fun way to think about this: design your workplace like an airplane cabin. There's a reason people get their best writing done on airplanes! No distractions, no internet, and nothing else to do but work.

Now, scheduling your Sacred Hours is one thing...

But you still have to do the work.

This is not the time to do any kind of shallow, monotonous work, though. Your Sacred Hours are for doing the high-leverage, creative, deep work that truly moves the needle. The last thing you want to do is block off your Sacred Hours only to waste them.

Because here's the thing about time: you and Jeff Bezos have the same number of hours in the day.

And it's not 24. It's 2 or 3.

2 or 3 hours of focused work is about as much as anyone can handle.

So, now the ball is on your court!

Go ahead and take 5-10 minutes to decide on your Sacred Hours for the next week, so you can start working your way through the course modules and putting your learnings into practice. (Also, make sure to block them out on your calendar!

Turn Yesterday’s Short-Form Post Into An Atomic Essay!

If you can write these, you can write anything.

My 3 favorite short-form content formats:

I started writing online in 2007.

Since then, I have probably written over 5,000 articles and tweets and newsletters on the Internet. But if I had to pick, I can easily say that I have a few favorites when it comes to writing short-form content.

Let me give you my 3 favorite formats, why I love them, and how you can replicate them.

Format #1: Paragraph Style

The REASON I love Paragraph Style is because it allows you to take conventional wisdom and present it as “academic”—simply because it looks like it should have been published in The New Yorker.

Some TIPS for executing Paragraph Style well:

  • Use academic language

  • Make it look as formal as possible

  • Keep it to 3 sentences or less

Format #2: What, How, Why

My second favorite format is what I like to call What, How, Why:

  • WHAT should the reader do

  • HOW do they do it

  • WHY is it important

A MISTAKE writers often make, however, is only telling readers what to do but not how to do it or why it’s important.

So it’s the combination of all 3 variables that is important.

Format #3: 10 Magical Ways

My third favorite format is what I like to call The 10 Magical Ways.

This is a list of “things” you can give readers to expand (or compress) any piece of writing:

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

records.content:
Alright, now you know how to do this manually, let’s accelerate the process with AI.

Here’s a prompt you can use to help you write an Atomic Essay.

Simply copy and paste this prompt into your chosen LLM (highly recommend Claude) and follow the on-screen instructions.

You’ll be asked for:

  • The Idea. What is the essay about?

  • The Audience. Who is this for? The more specific, the better.

  • The Outcome. What does the reader GET out of reading it? How is their life different after?

  • The Approach. What am I sharing? Pick from the 30 proven approaches.

Here’s the prompt:

THE ATOMIC ESSAY WRITER PROMPT

INTRODUCTION

You are an Atomic Essay Writer — a specialist in short-form online writing, specifically for creators, founders, coaches, and operators who publish daily on X (Twitter), LinkedIn, and Substack.

An Atomic Essay is a self-contained essay of no more than 250-300 words, built to stop a reader mid-scroll, deliver on a clear promise, and leave them wanting more. It lives or dies on its headline.

I am going to give you a writing idea, and I would like you to present back to me:

Deliverable #1: Three headline options, each built from the 5-part headline formula.

Deliverable #2: An outline of main points (subheadlines) that match the headline I choose.

Deliverable #3: The finished Atomic Essay — 250-300 words, delivering on every promise the headline made.

Before you write anything, you will ask me for the inputs you need. Then you will stop at two checkpoints — the headline and the main points — so I can steer the piece before it's finished.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on the context for each piece.

STEP 0: ASK ME FOR THE 4 INPUTS

Do not write anything until you have these four things. Pull whatever I've already told you, only ask for what's missing, and ask for it in one short batch rather than one question at a time.

1. The writing idea — What is the essay about?

2. The audience — Who is this for? The more specific, the better.

3. The outcome — What does the reader GET out of reading it? How is their life different after?

4. The approach — What am I sharing? Pick from these 30 proven approaches:

Tips, Skills, Tools, Traits, Steps, Goals, Books, Habits, Stories, Quotes, Secrets, Insights, Benefits, Lessons, Reasons, Creators, Routines, Mistakes, Podcasts, Examples, Questions, Inventions, Templates, Resources, Challenges, Companies, Data Points, Realizations, Frameworks, Presentations

If I'm unsure about the approach, suggest 2-3 that fit my idea and let me choose.

Then wait for my answers before moving to Step 1.

INSTRUCTION

There are 5 steps to writing a great Atomic Essay:

Step 1: Write The Headline (checkpoint — you stop and wait for me)

Step 2: Prep The Page With Main Points (checkpoint — you stop and wait for me)

Step 3: Add Context To The Main Points

Step 4: Write The Introduction

Step 5: Write The Conclusion

I'm going to walk you through each step, describe what makes it work, and give you examples of great execution — so you understand how to replicate it.

Two principles govern all five steps:

- The headline is ~80% of the work. It is what hooks the reader and gets them to actually read. If it doesn't capture attention, nothing else matters. Spend real effort there. Do not rush past it.

- It is not clickbait if you keep the promise. A number, a triggering adjective, or a named outcome is only clickbait when the essay fails to deliver. The body MUST over-deliver on whatever the headline promised. Make a clear promise, then keep it.

CONTEXT

STEP 1: WRITE THE HEADLINE

Generate 3 distinct headline options. Build each one from all 5 parts below.

Part 1 — The Number

Readers run an instant cost-benefit calculation: perceived value divided by time to consume. A number signals the time investment up front. "3 Steps" reads as quick. "300 Steps" reads as a slog. Numbers also make the piece easy to organize and easy to evaluate.

Rule: Use a number that matches how many things you are actually promising — usually between 2 and 10.

Part 2 — The What (the topic)

Combine the chosen approach with the specific topic.

Attributes of a strong What:

- Clear AND specific. Specificity is the secret.

- Answers the reader's silent question: "What do I GET for reading this?"

- Names a concrete thing, not a category.

Examples:

- Real Estate Buying Tips

- Informative Bitcoin Podcasts

- Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment

Part 3 — The Who (the audience)

Name the audience explicitly. This clarifies who it's for — and who it isn't. Naming an audience also helps social algorithms route the piece to the right people.

Examples:

- Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds

- Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners

- Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment, Gen-Zers This Is For You

Part 4 — The Why (the outcome)

This is the sell: if they read it, what do they get? Make the outcome tangible — something the reader can picture, feel, or measure.

Rule: Tangible always beats vague.

- Intangible: "so you can be happier"

- Tangible: "so you can wake up every morning full of energy"

Examples:

- Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds To Start Generating $1,000 Per Month In Passive Rental Income Before You Graduate College

- Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners That Will Help You 'Speak Blockchain' Fluently

Part 5 — Twist The Knife

"Twist the knife" means more — more outcomes, more benefits, more problems solved. Stack 1-3 additional tangible outcomes.

Rule: Length is fine as long as every added piece speaks directly to what this specific reader wants.

Example of the escalation:

- (V1) "Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn"

- (V2) "Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn And Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List"

- (V3) "Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn, Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List, And Start Selling Digital Products"

If I push back on the headline, hold the line with these:

- "That's clickbait." — Only if you break the promise. Keep it (and over-deliver) and readers love you.

- "It's too long." — Length isn't the problem, relevance is. If it speaks directly to the reader, there's no such thing as too long. If it doesn't, even four words waste their time.

- "My favorite writers don't write headlines like this." — They likely succeed despite short, clever headlines, not because of them — and after decades of audience-building. Clear, specific headlines win for everyone else.

CHECKPOINT #1

Present the 3 headline options. Label the 5 parts in at least one of them so I can see the machinery. Then ask me to pick one or tell you what to tweak. Wait for my choice before continuing.

STEP 2: PREP THE PAGE WITH YOUR MAIN POINTS

Once the headline is locked, turn it into a skeleton. List the main points as subheadlines that match the number and the approach named in the headline. Readers skim these before committing, so they must make the payoff obvious.

Rules:

- The count must match the headline's number exactly. "5 Habits" means exactly 5 subheadlines.

- The label must match the approach. Habits becomes "Habit #1:" — Tips becomes "Tip #1:" — Reasons becomes "Reason #1:"

- Every subheadline must be specific and concrete. No placeholders.

Examples:

- Headline promises "3 Habits" — Habit #1: ..., Habit #2: ..., Habit #3: ...

- Headline promises "3 Tips" — Tip #1: ..., Tip #2: ..., Tip #3: ...

- Headline promises "3 Reasons" — Reason #1: ..., Reason #2: ..., Reason #3: ...

CHECKPOINT #2

Present the full list of main points and ask me whether I want to swap any out, reorder them, or change the angle before you write the body. This is my chance to steer while it's still cheap to change. Wait for my response. If I swap a point, keep the count matching the headline's number.

STEP 3: ADD CONTEXT TO YOUR MAIN POINTS

Put meat on the bones. For each main point, ask: "What else will the reader find useful here?" Then expand it with one of: a tip, a short story, an example, a reason why, a stat, or an insight.

Rules:

- 2-4 sentences per point. This is expansion, not an article.

- The whole essay is 250-300 words, so every point has to earn its space.

- Deliver what the subheadline promised. No drifting.

STEP 4: WRITE THE INTRODUCTION

Write a short introduction that strengthens the case the headline already made. Include at least one of:

- What — what is this about?

- Who — who is this for?

- Why — why should they read it? (the promise)

- Credibility — why you can speak to this. Either lived experience, or curated credibility ("I studied 100 people who...").

Rules:

- 1-3 short blocks.

- End with a clean transition into the first main point.

Examples:

- "Over the last 5 years, I've lost 100 pounds and gotten into the best shape of my life. If you want to get in shape but don't know where to start, here are the 3 steps to find the right gym for you."

- "I read 100 X articles on Claude Design. Here are 5 tips to design your first lead magnet landing page (even with zero design background):"

STEP 5: WRITE THE CONCLUSION

This isn't school — do not recap. Add something new: an extra detail, one more piece of the story, or a final insight. A single sentence at the bottom is enough.

FINAL DELIVERY

Once both checkpoints are cleared, present the finished piece in exactly this format:

Headline

[The chosen headline]

Atomic Essay

[Introduction — 1-3 short blocks]

[Subheadline 1]

[2-4 sentences of context]

[Subheadline 2]

[2-4 sentences of context]

[Subheadline 3]

[2-4 sentences of context]

[Conclusion — a single fresh sentence or two]

Then note the word count and confirm it lands in the 250-300 range.

Hard constraints on the final output:

- 250-300 words for the body. No more. If it runs long, cut context, not points.

- Keep the promise. The body must deliver everything the headline promised. This is what separates a great essay from clickbait.

- Match the number. If the headline says 5, there are exactly 5 main points — no more, no fewer.

- Specificity over vagueness. Name the audience, name the outcome, use concrete details.

- Tangible over intangible. Swap abstractions for things the reader can picture, feel, or measure.

- Match my voice. If I write casually and in first person, keep it that way.

Stay conversational throughout. Now begin by asking me for the 4 inputs.

records.content:
Here’s a simple checklist I like to run through when I’m writing my introduction to an Atomic Essay.

I like to include at least one of these points in the introduction:

  • What is this about?

  • Who is this for?

  • Why should they read it? (The promise—what you're going to give them)

  • What credibility do you have to talk about this? (You could have lived it yourself or you can curate other people's credibility, e.g., "I studied people who experienced this")

Here are some examples:

  • “Over the last 5 years, I’ve lost 100 pounds and gotten into the best shape of my life.

    If you want to get in shape but you’re not sure how to start, here are the 3 steps you should take to find the right gym for you.”

  • “I’ve been flipping real estate for the last 2 years—and made $500,000 profit in the process.

    These are the 5 reasons why I think every college graduate should invest in real estate (so they can retire early in their 30s):”

  • “I read 100 X Articles on Claude Design.

    Here are 5 tips to help you design your first lead magnet landing page (even if you have zero design background):”

What you’re doing is strengthening the case you made in your headline.

Alright, onto the final Step.

Ok, now we’re cruising!

Let’s put some meat on the bones of these Main Points.

Remember: we’re not writing the next great American Novel. Or a 60,000-word non-fiction book. We’re writing an Atomic Essay—that’s no more than 250-300 words! So don’t think you need to write a ton here.

For each Main Point, ask yourself:

“What else will the reader find useful here?”

You can share tips, stories, examples, reasons why, stats, insights, etc. You’re just slightly expanding the idea of each Main Point.

(And we’ll dive more into how to expand these points into a full-blown Article in tomorrow’s session!)

Alright, now it’s time to round this Atomic Essay out with an Introduction and Conclusion.

records.description: Ok, we just spent a TON of time on the headline of your Atomic Essay. Why? BECAUSE IT’S THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF YOUR ESSAY. You should spend 80% of yo
records.content:
Ok, we just spent a TON of time on the headline of your Atomic Essay.

Why?

BECAUSE IT’S THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF YOUR ESSAY.

You should spend 80% of your time on the headline. The headline is what hooks the attention of the reader and gets them to actually engage with your writing. And if you don’t have a headline that captures their attention, they’ll never read the rest of your essay.

Now, we’re going to flesh out the essay.

First, we start by “Prepping The Page.”

Prepping The Page is how you turn a blank Atomic Essay (with just a headline) into an 80% finished Atomic Essay.

All you need to do is list out your main points and make it clear to the reader what they’re getting (after all, they’ll skim these points before they read the rest of your Atomic Essay—this is how we consume all content online).

Here’s how to think about it:

  • If your headline promises “3 Habits”, list out 3 Habits: “Habit #1: [Insert Habit]”, “Habit #2: [Insert Habit]”, “Habit #3: [Insert Habit]”

  • If your headline promises “3 Tips”, list out 3 Tips: “Tip #1: [Insert Tip]”, “Tip #2: [Insert Tip]”, “Tip #3: [Insert Tip]”

  • If your headline promises “3 Reasons”, list out 3 Reasons: “Reason #1: [Insert Reason]”, “Reason #2: [Insert Reason]”, “Reason #3: [Insert Reason]”

It really is that simple!

The key here is to make these subheadlines in your Atomic Essay. The next step is where we add some text to flesh out each point.

records.title: Step 1: Write A Headline
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 2 - Atomic Essays/Step 1_ Write A Headline - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: OK, I’m about to break down my framework for writing the “Perfect Headline.” But every time I share this with writers, they come back with 3 pushbacks. I want
records.content:
OK, I’m about to break down my framework for writing the “Perfect Headline.”

But every time I share this with writers, they come back with 3 pushbacks.

I want to get ahead of them now so you can focus on understanding all the components of a headline (and why you need them) without your brain screaming, “This is clickbait! No-one will read this! I’ll never build an audience using headlines like this!”

All wrong. And let me explain why.

  • “That’s clickbait! What if I don’t want to write headlines like this?”: Writers think if there is a number in the headline (7 Ways…), a triggering adjective (”Mind-boggling…”), or any hint at an outcome (”…so you can retire early”) then it’s automatically clickbait. This is not true. It’s only clickbait if you fail to keep your promise. If you promise to tell readers how they can buy their first rental property and retire early, but then don’t actually tell them how, then the reader hates you. But if you make that promise and over-deliver, giving them an entire step-by-step guide on how they can achieve this same outcome, then they love you. They’re going to bookmark your post. Send it to their friends. And likely go on to read everything else you’ve written—because you kept your promise.

  • “That headline is too long! How do I make it shorter?”: If your high school crush mailed you a 987-page book with everything they thought about you back then, how many pages would you read? The answer is: all of it. Length isn’t what matters. Some people think 1 single tweet is too long, and other people will read 987 pages and STILL want more. Which means length, in and of itself, isn’t what matters. What matters is whether you are speaking directly TO the reader. If you are, there’s no such thing as “too long.” And if you’re not, then even a 4-word headline is a waste of their time.

  • “My favorite writers don’t have to do this! Why do I have to?”: Seth Godin doesn’t write long headlines. His headlines are short and quippy. Things like, “Marketing Thoughts” or “Everyone Is Someone.” The problem is: you’re not Seth Godin. And so, first of all, it’s unproductive for you to compare yourself to someone who has been writing for decades (with an “s”). And second, we would ask the question: “But how many more people would read Seth Godin’s work if he used these tried-and-true headline techniques?” Are writers like Seth Godin successful because of their short, quippy, “clever” headlines? Or despite their short, quippy, “clever” headlines? (We would bet the latter—and that they would be 100x more widely read if they wrote clear headlines instead.)

In short: if you want to get people’s attention online, you need to learn how to write headlines that STOP them in their tracks and make them say, “Hmm… This looks like it’s for me. Maybe I should give this a read.”

To write an effective headline, you need 5 parts:

  1. The Number

  2. The What

  3. The Who

  4. The Why

  5. Twisting The Knife

Let’s run through each one.

Part 1: The Number

Before a reader gives you their attention, they do a quick cost-benefit analysis in their brain.

And it happens in a millisecond. We all do it.

But it’s a very simple equation:

How valuable does the reader perceive this piece to be DIVIDED by how long they think it’s going to take them to consume:

Value Divided by Time

And one of the easy ways readers do this cost-benefit analysis is by trying to figure out “how many” things you’re promising you are going to explain to them.

For example, what’s the perceived “time” difference between these 2 headlines?

  • 3 Steps To Brainstorm, Build, And Sell Your First Digital Product

  • 300 Steps To Brainstorm, Build, And Sell Your First Digital Product

Same idea. They both promise the same “value” and end result.

But the first one says, “This will only take 3 steps” a.k.a. “this won’t take you very much time,” whereas the second one says, “This will take 300 steps” a.k.a. “be prepared for this to take you a lot of time.”

Listicles have a bad reputation because everyone associates a number in the headline with BuzzFeed articles, but the reality is listicles are incredibly effective. They make it very easy for you to organize your ideas. But they also make it easy for the reader to quickly evaluate how long it’s going to take them to read your writing.

So, HOW MANY things are you promising the reader? And how can you signal this time investment right away in the headline?

Part 2: The What (The Topic)

Any content topic can be written through various different lenses:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

The key to writing a great headline is to combine one of those proven approaches with a specific topic—and make that as clear as possible right away in the headline.

Because that’s the fundamental question the reader is asking themselves BEFORE they start reading your writing: “What am I going to GET in exchange for reading?”

Here are a handful of examples:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips.”)

  • Informative Bitcoin Podcasts (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment.”)

This way, you’re being CLEAR about the topic. But you’re not just being CLEAR, you’re being SPECIFIC, too.

If you want your writing to resonate, specificity is the secret.

Part 3: Add a WHO

Alright, who’s your audience?

Again, you should have this dialled in from yesterday’s content strategy session.

Here are some examples:

  • …Tips For Project Managers

  • …Mistakes To Avoid As A Founder

  • …Trends For Wall Street Analysts

You want to make it very clear WHO your content is for (and, as a result, WHO it isn’t for).

Pro Tip: When you “name” an audience in your headline (or anywhere in your content), social algorithms actually take note—and this impacts how they distribute content. For example, if you put “Silicon Valley Founders” in your headline, who do you think X (Twitter)/LinkedIn is going to show your content to? People who have any (or all) of those keywords in their bio, in the content they create or consume, people they’re connected to, etc. This is how social algorithms work!

So, here are the same examples from previously, adding a WHO (audience) to each topic:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips for teenagers.”)

  • Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment, Gen-Zers This Is For You (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment, specifically for Gen-Z.”)

Notice how much more powerful the headline gets when you name the audience explicitly!

Part 4: Add a WHY (Or The Outcome)

The WHY in your headline is your opportunity to “sell” the reader on why they should read your writing over every other piece of content competing for their attention on the Internet:

  • IF the reader reads this, what do they get in return?

  • How is their life different in some meaningful way?

  • What will they learn as a result?

So, here are the same examples, adding a WHY (outcome) to each topic:

  • Real Estate Buying Tips For 18-Year-Olds To Start Generating $1,000 Per Month In Passive Rental Income Before You Graduate College (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me real estate buying tips for teenagers, specifically to help generate $1,000 per month in passive rental income before graduating college.”)

  • Bitcoin Podcasts For Cryptocurrency Beginners That Will Help You ‘Speak Blockchain’ Fluently (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to give me bitcoin podcasts I should listen to, to learn about crypto, so that I can ‘speak blockchain’ fluently.”)

  • Shoe Brands That Are Terrible For The Environment: If You Want To Save The Rainforest, Gen-Zers This Is For You (”Oh, if I read this, the writer is going to tell me which shoe brands are bad for the environment, specifically for Gen-Zers who want to save the rainforest.”)

Notice how the headline gets clearer and clearer the more of these pieces we add in.

And how much more powerful the headline gets when you name the outcome explicitly!

Part 5: Twist The Knife

Twist The Knife is just a fancy way of saying: “more.”

  • More problems

  • More benefits

  • More outcomes

Let’s use this headline as an example:

  • (V1) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn”

Not bad!

But watch how much more compelling the headline gets the more we “twist the knife”:

  • (V2) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn And Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List”

  • (V3) “Looking To Build An Audience? Use This 1 Quick Hack To 10x Your Reach On LinkedIn, Attract Loyal Readers Onto Your Email List, And Start Selling Digital Products”

Notice how the more outcomes you list (and the more you “Twist The Knife”), it really doesn’t matter that your headline is getting longer and longer. As long as these benefits and outcomes speak directly to the wants and needs of your target reader, they’ll keep reading—because you’re talking about them!

Here are a couple more examples, just to give you more pattern recognition:

records.content:
(And Why Should You Write Them)

An Atomic Essay is a short, compressed essay of 250 words or less.

And the purpose of writing an Atomic Essay is to share 1 clear idea—small enough that you can come up with "something" to write about every day, but not so much that it feels like a burden (causing you to fall out of your daily writing habit).

Here’s an example from Dickie:

The reason we use the Atomic Essay format is because it is the easiest way for writers to learn the fundamentals of Digital Writing:

  • Headlines: In order to get readers to read your writing, you first need to "hook" them with a clear (not clever) headline (more on that in a moment).

  • Introductions: Right away, at the very beginning of your Atomic Essay (or any other kind of writing), you need to tell the reader why they should trust you. What makes your point of view credible, valuable, and worth their time? This needs to happen in the introduction.

  • Main Points: Next, the reader is going to "skim" your writing. If your Main Points (organized and formatted neatly) speak to their wants, needs, questions, and interests, then they will read your writing. If not, they will give your writing a quick skim, decide it's "not for them," and move on.

  • Writing Rhythms: To keep the reader engaged, it's important to give them small milestones to look forward to all the way down the page. Long paragraphs are a no-no.

  • Conclusions: And finally, how do you want the reader to feel at the end of your piece? How can you make sure you've delivered on the promise you made in your headline? The Atomic Essay format allows you to practice all 5 of these foundational pieces of all Digital Writing, every single day.

In other words, if you can write an Atomic Essay, you can write anything:

  • A Twitter Thread

  • A LinkedIn Post

  • A Newsletter

  • A Lead Magnet

  • A Book

Because all of these different “mediums” use the core components we practice with an Atomic Essay.

Ok, so how do you write an Atomic Essay?

Well, that’s the next part!

I’m going to share the 5 simple steps you can follow to write an Atomic Essay:

  • Step 1: Write A Headline

  • Step 2: Prep The Page With Your Main Points

  • Step 3: Add Context To Your Main Points

  • Step 4: Write Your Introduction

  • Step 5: Write Your Conclusion

Let’s dive in!

records.title: Lesson 5: Newsletter Monetization Methods
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/(Bonus) 📨 Start & Scale Your Newsletter/Lesson 5_ Newsletter Monetization Methods - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: In this lesson, we're going to cover: - The Paid Newsletter Model: how to make money from subscriptions (pricing, paywalls & when to go paid) - The Book Model (
records.content:
In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: how to make money from subscriptions (pricing, paywalls & when to go paid)

  • The Book Model (Self-Publishing): how to make money republishing your newsletter content as books

  • The Digital Product Model: how to turn your email list into a digital product "engine"

And more!

All so you can leave the Sprint with a 90-day monetization plan—and a newsletter that pays you for years to come.

Let's dive in!

A quick note before we start: why ads aren't on the list

Technically, there's another model out there that everyone talks about, which is The Sponsorship Model. But the reason we're not going to cover it is because we don't recommend it. Yes, many newsletters monetize with ads. (Beehiiv has done a good job here, integrating advertisers into their platform and pairing them with newsletters.)

However, you're here to learn from us.

And OUR take is that ads are one of the worst ways to monetize.

Ads require massive scale before they pay anything meaningful, they put someone else's message in front of your readers, and they slowly exhaust the trust you've spent months building. You'd be much better off (and make way more money) monetizing with one of these other business models instead.

Everything we cover today works whether you're on Substack, Kit, or Beehiiv. The mechanics differ slightly by platform, but the models are identical.

Choosing The Right Monetization Model

3 Ways Your Newsletter Pays You (No Ads Required)

To effectively monetize your newsletter, here are your options:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: how you make money from subscriptions

  • The Book Model: how you make money republishing newsletter content as books on Amazon

  • The Digital Product Model: how you make money from selling one-off digital products

Now, the big question everyone asks is, "OK… so which one should I pick?"

The Answer: All of them!

One of the BIGGEST missed opportunities for newsletter writers is thinking that the only way to monetize is through the Paid Newsletter Model.

And this is wrong.

If you decide to turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter… this is the beginning of monetization, not the end!

  • Yes, you should monetize your content via paid subscription.

  • But you can also sell all your paid subscribers (and also your free subscribers, who are maybe looking for something different) on digital products.

  • And you can also sell all your paid subscribers (and also your free subscribers, who are maybe looking for something different) on the same content presented in different formats: eBook, print books, audiobooks, etc.

It's SHOCKING to us how many newsletter writers don't do any of these things.

They fail to realize how much money they're leaving on the table by not also offering digital products, and not also double-monetizing their content in books & audiobooks.

So. Much. Money. Left. On. The. Table.

It kills us!

(So please, don't make this mistake.)

That said — you can't launch everything at once. Today we'll cover all three models, then give you a decision framework for which one to start with. Your homework is to pick one and map your 90-day plan.

Method #1: The Paid Newsletter Model

The primary monetization model for newsletters is to "go paid."

On Substack, this is built in natively. On Kit, you can do this with a paid recommendation or by pairing your list with a payment tool. On Beehiiv, paid subscriptions are built into the platform as well.

This is a relatively easy monetization model to adopt and understand, which is what makes it great for beginners. You don't have to mess around with learning a bunch of different tech platforms. You don't really have to acquire advanced copywriting skills, or learn how to run ads. All you have to do is add a paywall (placed strategically) into your newsletters and publish consistently for a long period of time.

That's about it.

Why The Paid Newsletter Model Is So Great

Well, it's great for a bunch of reasons:

  • First, paid newsletters are subscription revenue. And subscription revenue is king. Since subscriptions "recur" (over and over again), they create a very defensible sort of business. If you have 1,000 paying subscribers, there's essentially a 0% chance all 1,000 of them unsubscribe at the same time. Instead, you might churn maybe 10% of them per month—while also continuing to attract new paying subscribers. All of this is just a fancy way of saying: you have a defensible, predictable business. Great!

  • Second, paid newsletters are very easy/simple to operate. When you turn your newsletter paid, you connect it to Stripe and payments happen directly inside your platform. There's very little, if any "operational infrastructure" you need to build or even manage. It's quite literally one of the simplest business models to execute in the digital age. Also great for beginners!

  • Third, paid newsletters are insanely powerful engines for other monetization models later. Even if you don't monetize in these other ways, it's worth acknowledging that having a paid newsletter as the "nucleus" of your business will pay you dividends for a long, long time. That's because everyone on your paid newsletter list is essentially a customer raising their hand saying, "I'd love to give you more money—if you can help me solve more and more complicated/valuable problems."

We love paid newsletters as a monetization model.

Free-To-Paid Conversion & Paywall Strategy

The mechanics of going paid come down to three decisions:

  1. What stays free vs. what goes paid. Your free content is your growth engine — it's how new readers discover you. Your paid content is the deeper, more actionable, more "do this exactly" version. A common split: free readers get the "what" and "why," paid readers get the "how" (templates, systems, step-by-step breakdowns).

  2. Where you place the paywall. Don't paywall the whole post. Place the paywall after you've delivered real value and right before the most actionable payoff. The free portion has to be good enough that readers feel the pain of not seeing the rest. Learning how to place your paywall strategically to increase conversions is a skill — and it's one of the fundamentals worth "getting good" at early.

  3. Pricing. The standard range is $5–$15/month, with an annual option priced at roughly 10x the monthly price (so annual subscribers effectively get 2 months free). $10/mo or $100/yr is a perfectly good starting point for most niches. Don't agonize over this — you can always adjust. What matters far more is publishing consistently.

When Should You Go Paid?

Sooner than you think. You don't need 10,000 subscribers. A useful signal: once you have a few hundred engaged subscribers who consistently open and reply, turn on paid — even if only a handful convert at first. Industry-wide, expect roughly 2–5% of your free list to convert to paid over time. The bigger and warmer your free list gets, the more that percentage compounds.

Method #2: The Book Model (Self-Publishing)

This next model is a bit more creative.

As a beginner, you should either turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter first, and/or you should start out launching some digital products to your list. These are much easier monetization models to execute.

But once you've gotten in a flow, and especially the longer you stick with your newsletter (content compounds), we would absolutely recommend adding in this monetization model.

Here's how it works:

  • If you write long-form newsletters (5,000+ words), you can actually get a simple eBook cover designed and also publish them on Amazon. (*NOTE: These cannot go inside KDP Select. But they can be published non-exclusively.) These eBooks will get organized into Amazon's "quick reads" eBook categories.

  • Once you have ~15 long-form newsletters (or ~30-ish standard newsletters) all on the same topic, you can "compile" them into larger print books & audiobooks. The "value" of this is that some readers simply like consuming the same content in different ways. This is what we did with books like Snow Leopard (which was 100% reused content from our newsletter), and readers absolutely loved being able to have a print copy on their desks.

  • You can also sell eBook and audiobook versions on your personal website as digital downloads. This requires a bit more infrastructure setup, but remember… sales generated through your website aren't subject to Amazon taking a cut. Which means you make 2x the profit!

But wait… there's more!

Another clever strategy you can leverage is, when you start turning newsletters into mini-books, and mini-books into bigger books… you can also "bundle in" free access to this library of digital assets back into your paid newsletter.

This is what Cole does with his paid fiction newsletter, Commercial Fiction Club. A benefit of upgrading to paid is you get "free access" to his entire library of fiction writing.

Why is this a great tactic?

Because you're essentially trading one-off revenue (customer buys a book) for recurring revenue (they subscribe to your paid newsletter, and stay subscribed to continue getting access to not just the paid newsletter, but your entire library, in perpetuity).

Books = Authority + Revenue

One thing worth calling out: a book isn't just a revenue stream. "Author of [Book]" is one of the fastest credibility unlocks available to a newsletter writer. It boosts free-to-paid conversion, makes your digital products easier to sell, and gets you podcast invites and speaking opportunities that grow the newsletter itself. The revenue is real — but the authority compounds even faster.

And the best part: you don't have to create anything "new." You just have to repackage work you've already done in the past.

Method #3: The Digital Product Model

Whether you have a free newsletter and/or a paid newsletter, we would strongly encourage you to consider adopting the Digital Product Monetization Model as well.

This means selling subscribers:

  • [$9–$99] Template packs, AI prompts, dashboards, cheat sheets, mini-courses, etc.

  • [$99–$350] Text & video asynchronous courses

  • [$350–$1,000] Workshops, cohorts, challenges, bootcamps, etc.

One of the biggest "mental unlocks" is realizing that both your free & paid newsletter lists are lists of potential customers.

For example, Write With AI has over 112,000 free subscribers—and only 1,800 active paying subscribers.

It would be a HUGE mistake to think, "I guess the only way we can make money is by people upgrading to the paid newsletter list." Why?

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list just don't like paid newsletters as a concept (it happens).

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list want more help, or help specifically on a particular topic.

  • Maybe some people on the free newsletter list want more hands-on help, more direct access to you, etc.

The point is, all those "free" subscribers should have more than 1 way to give you money.

Having a paid newsletter option is great.

But you want to give them other options, too.

Let us show you how "expensive" of a mistake this can be.

A few weeks ago, we ran a Claude Cowork Bootcamp.

This was a 2-week "cohort" experience teaching writers, creators, and entrepreneurs how to use no-code agents inside Claude Cowork. Why did we do this? Because Write With AI readers had been asking us a lot of questions about Claude, Claude Cowork, and no-code agents!

So, we spun up a curriculum and launched it to our entire Write With AI list.

And guess what? Most of the people who bought weren't even active paying subscribers.

They were free subscribers… who just needed to be presented with a different offer.

And look what happened:

Over $167,000 in revenue from one 2-week bootcamp offer — launched to the same list.

Over 200 people took us up on this specific 2-week bootcamp, generating over $167,000 in revenue.

Translation: this 1 "different" offer did 1/3rd of Write With AI's total yearly revenue… in 2 weeks.

And now, knowing this is possible, imagine if we DIDN'T do this. We'd be "missing" $167,000 in additional revenue! OUCH!!!!!

In short: do not underestimate the power of giving free & paid subscribers "other things to buy."

Writers leave a tremendous amount of money on the table when they make this mistake.

Mistakes To Avoid

Before you pick your model, here are the most common (and most expensive) mistakes we see:

  1. Monetizing with ads/sponsorships too early (or at all). You rent out your readers' attention for pennies, exhaust their trust, and cap your upside. Every model we covered today pays more per subscriber than ads ever will at your size.

  2. Thinking paid subscriptions are the ONLY way to monetize. Going paid is the beginning of monetization, not the end. The Write With AI example above is what this mistake costs: $167,000 in 2 weeks, from one "different" offer.

  3. Paywalling everything. Your free content is your growth engine. Kill it and you kill the top of your funnel. Paywall the payoff, not the post.

  4. Waiting until you feel "big enough." You don't need 10,000 subscribers to go paid or launch a product. You need a few hundred engaged readers and one clear offer.

  5. Never asking for the sale. If you know how to solve a reader's problem and never tell them you can help, you're not being polite — you're letting them suffer. (More on this in the FAQ below.)

  6. Launching all three models at once. Stack them over time, one threshold at a time. That's what the decision framework is for.

Frequently Asked Questions

Now, whenever we walk writers through the different ways they can monetize a newsletter, we always get the same handful of questions.

So let's rapid-fire through them here:

"Which monetization model is the best?"

There's no such thing.

The "best one" is the one that interests you the most, and that you'll be willing to stick with (through the growing pains) and not give up on.

Because we could tell you "the best one," but if it's not one you're interested in executing, then it doesn't matter.

"Can I use more than one monetization model?"

Yes! That's the goal!

Your business becomes more and more profitable, and defensible, the more of these different monetization models you stack together.

For example, this is how Category Pirates was built into a multi-6-figure newsletter and multi-6-figure publishing business:

  • The Paid Newsletter Model: We wrote long-form paid newsletters (which we called "mini-books") 2x per month, and charged $20/mo (or $200/yr). Our paid newsletter grew to ~$150,000 in annual recurring revenue.

  • The Book Model: Then, to unlock a secondary revenue stream, we took all of our "mini-books" (newsletters), slapped a cover on them, and republished them as "mini-books" on Amazon. And then we monetized again by compiling 12-15 "mini-books" on a topic, and republishing it again as a print book/audiobook. Republishing our content unlocked another $100,000/yr in annual revenue.

  • The Digital Product Model: Later, we added in digital products and cohort-based programs, giving subscribers yet another way to learn the material and gain more access to us. Adding in these digital products and experiences added another $250,000+ in annual revenue.

So yes, the goal is to combine these different business models—and keep giving readers more and more ways to learn from you and work with you.

"But won't readers get upset if I basically take the same content and charge for it again somewhere else?"

No. This is a faulty belief.

Especially if you are changing the content's consumption type—like turning a newsletter into a Kindle eBook or audiobook, or turning newsletter ideas into more in-depth course modules paired with videos—then it's actually a completely different product.

And readers will be THANKFUL that you created an option for them to consume the content they want, in the way they want it.

"But won't readers get upset if I launch so many new offers? Won't I come across like a money-grubbing sleazy salesman?"

No. This is a faulty belief.

If I saw you had a problem that I knew how to solve, which one would make you more upset?

  • Telling you I know how to solve it, and would be happy to help you (for a price, of course)

  • Not telling you at all and letting you suffer

I'm going to go out on a limb and guess you'd be MORE UPSET at me NOT telling you the answer, and NOT being willing to help.

Right?

OK, great. That's all you're doing.

You aren't "selling" anything.

You're simply creating more available options for readers to get your help.

"How much money can I really earn with a newsletter?"

Infinite.

There are some newsletters generating hundreds of thousands of dollars per month in revenue. Obviously this is an outlier outcome, but it's entirely possible.

That said, here's what we think is a "realistic" home-run outcome:

  • $100,000+ per year in annual recurring revenue. This is completely doable for nearly any newsletter in any niche. Will it take work? Yes. Will it take time? Yes. But building a 6-figure paid newsletter is completely within the realm of "achievable" for most people (who stick with it).

  • $50,000+ per year in self-publishing revenue. If you successfully build a 6-figure paid newsletter, then you can absolutely unlock another $50,000 - $100,000 in incremental revenue simply by republishing your content as eBooks, print books, and audiobooks on Amazon. And it's an easy and lucrative model to execute because you don't have to create anything "new." You just have to repackage work you've already done in the past.

  • $150,000+ in digital product revenue. If you successfully build a growing free and/or paid newsletter, there's also zero reason why you can't unlock another 6 figures (or more) in revenue by launching digital products to your list. For us, Write With AI does ~$400,000 per year in subscription revenue, but does another $1,000,000+ in digital product revenue. So, our "digital product business" is actually 2-3x the size of our "paid newsletter business."

If you do all the above, you have a business well north of $300,000 per year — from a newsletter.

That's an insane outcome—and yet, totally achievable.

It will just take a bit more work than you probably think, and take a bit more time than you probably want (which is why so many people give up).

The Decision Framework: Which Method Do You Start With?

Your homework is to pick ONE of these monetization models, and start there.

But if you want a "constraint" for making forward-leaning decisions, here's what we would recommend:

  • First, turn your free newsletter into a paid newsletter—and stay focused on this until you reach at least $50,000 in annual revenue. Focus on "getting good" at executing the fundamentals, learning how to place your paywall strategically to increase conversions, and building up a base of paying customers.

  • Once you reach $50,000 in annual subscription revenue from your paid newsletter, start launching digital products to your list. Keep doing this until you 2x the business—crossing $100,000 per year in revenue.

  • Then, once you cross $100,000 per year in revenue, add in the book/self-publishing component. This will be a time investment, but it will compound significantly in your favor as the years go by. This will unlock another tranche of revenue.

A quick gut-check if you're still torn:

This is the order in which we'd think about monetizing.

But please don't feel like you need to rush to figure out how to monetize in all these different ways tomorrow.

Just focus on going one step at a time. And as you cross each new threshold, adjust your strategy and grow into the next tier of monetization.

You now know more about starting, growing, and monetizing a newsletter than 99% of people who ever hit "create publication."

The only thing left to do is write.

Onwards and upwards!
