Variable #1: Subject Line

The best subject line style for a value-packed, niche-specific, thought leadership newsletter is very similar to what makes for an irresistible article headline.

So first, here's a framework for writing an irresistible headline:

There are 6 pieces of an irresistible headline are:

- HOW MANY (Number).
- THE WHAT (Topic).
- THE HOW (Proven Approach).
- THE WHO (Audience).
- THE WHY (Outcome).
- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes).

In most cases, this is the order in which the pieces should be assembled in a headline.

For example:

**7 Copywriting Tips For Beginners To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product, Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur**

- 7 = HOW MANY
- Copywriting = THE WHAT
- Tips = THE HOW
- For Beginners = THE WHO
- To Sell Your First $100 Digital Product = THE WHY
- Start Making Money Online, And Eventually Quit Your Job And Become A Full-Time Internet Entrepreneur = TWIST THE KNIFE

Now, let me give you examples of different variations you can choose from when writing irresistible headlines with these 6 different pieces.

- HOW MANY (Number): This is always a number, usually between 2 and 19. For example: 7 Copywriting Tips, 2 Productivity Mistakes, 11 Self-Help Habits, etc.
- THE WHAT (Topic): This is always the topic. Examples of topics (but not limited to just these), Copywriting, Productivity, Self-Help, Fitness, Mindfulness, Knitting, Racketball, Meditation, etc.
- THE HOW (Proven Approach): These are nouns. Examples of Proven Approaches:
    - Tips
    - Skills
    - Tools
    - Traits
    - Steps
    - Goals
    - Books
    - Habits
    - Stories
    - Quotes
    - Secrets
    - Insights
    - Benefits
    - Lessons
    - Reasons
    - Creators
    - Routines
    - Mistakes
    - Podcasts
    - Examples
    - Questions
    - Inventions
    - Templates
    - Resources
    - Challenges
    - Companies
    - Data Points
    - Realizations
    - Frameworks
    - Presentations
- THE WHO (Audience): This is the niche-specific audience. For example (but not limited to just these): Beginners, Stay-At-Home Moms, College Students, Chicagoans, etc. This audience can be a noun and/or a noun modified by a geography or demographic.
- THE WHY (Outcome): This is the thing the target reader wants, based on the proven approach. For example (but not limited to just these): if the topic is "productivity" and the proven approach is "Tips" and the audience is "college students" then the outcome is something college students want productivity tips to unlock in their life (like "to get straight A's in class" or "to graduate with honors and land a high-paying job straight out of college").
- TWIST THE KNIFE (More Outcomes): This is just 1-3 more outcomes. If the WHY outcome is negative (like "to make sure they don't fail their final exam"), then list 1-3 more negative outcomes ("and have to work at a gas station or move back-in with their parents"), and if the WHY outcome is positive ("to get straight A's in class"), then list 1-3 more positive outcomes ("start with a six-figure salary right out of school, and buy a sports car before the age of 23").

One last rule to increase the effectiveness of an irresistible headline.

Whenever you're writing the WHY (outcome) or TWIST THE KNIFE (more outcomes), you always want to write the "tangible" version opposed to the "intangible" version.

For example, an Intangible WHY (outcome) would be: "So you can be happier." But "happier" is very intangible, and not very specific.

Instead, a Tangible WHY (outcome) would be: "So you can wake up every morning feeling full of energy." Everyone can imagine themselves "waking up early" in the morning, and that's a very Tangible, Measurable outcome. That's the goal. Always Tangible language instead of Intangible language.

Tangible language can be defined as something a reader could viscerally touch or feel—opposed to an ambiguous, vague "thought" or "general idea."

So that's the framework for writing irresistible headlines.

First, come up with the irresistible headline for the newsletter using this framework.

Then second, find a way to condense that longer-form irresistible headline into a shorter, more concise, punchier version that would fit inside an email subject line.

The constraint and goal here is 30 to 50 characters or 4 to 8 words, written in sentence-case (meaning you capitalize the first word but none of the remaining words). And if the first character in the subject line is a number, then you do not capitalize the word that follows.

- Bad Example: 3 Ways To Grow Your First 1,000 Subscribers
- Good Example: 3 ways to grow your first 1,000 subscribers.

And when writing this niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletter, I would like you to present 5 different subject lines to choose from.

~

Variable #2: Introduction

Next, let's dig into the writing.

All great niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletters start with an introduction that "hooks" the reader into wanting to read the rest of the piece.

But there's a very specific way of writing these introductions I want to train you on, and so I don't want you to think of the introduction as one giant block of text—but rather 5 smaller blocks that all stack on top of each other.

- Block #1: "Hey there!" Start every newsletter with a simple greeting to the reader in the first line, like this.
- Block #2: Next is the opening sentence, or opening hook. This should be 1 single sentence, and the best opening hooks are typically one of the following: ask a thought-provoking question; open with a strong, declarative sentence; reference a meaningful moment in time (date, day, time, moment, etc.); present a vulnerable statement; offer a controversial opinion; and/or share a unique insight.
- Block #3: Next is the "promise" of the intro—which is almost always either the niche-specific problem the reader wants to solve, or the niche-specific outcome the reader wants to unlock. This block is typically 3-7 sentences long (could also be presented in a bulleted list format of 3-7 bullets), and very tangibly and actionably educates the reader on a problem (or series of problems), why those problems exist, and the negative outcomes of those unsolved problems; or educates the reader on a desirable outcome (or handful of outcomes), why those outcomes are so valuable, and/or some of the negative consequences that can happen if those desirable outcomes aren't achieved.
- Block #4: Next is the "solution" of the intro. This is usually one sentence (at max, two sentences) that, after educating the reader on a problem or outcome, completes the promise by telling the reader that's precisely what you're going to help them with today. You're either going to help them solve that problem (or series of problems), or achieve that outcome (or handful of outcomes).
- Block #5: Last is the transition sentence. This is usually some sort of short transition into the first header and section of the newsletter. Something like, "Let's walk through each one" or "Let's dive in" or "So, with that in mind, let's <solve that problem> or <achieve that outcome>," etc.

Here are some examples of niche-specific, value-packed, thought leadership newsletter introductions written using this framework:

Example #1:

Hey there!

Do you want to know the secret to saving your first $10,000?

One of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was: how do I actually save money without feeling like I'm sacrificing everything? And the truth is, it's not that hard. It's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to automate your savings—and when to use them to hit your goal faster.

Let's walk through each one.

Example #2:

Hey there!

What do you need to run your first marathon?

Do you need:

- Expensive running gear?
- Years of training experience?
- A personal coach?

Well, actually, the truth is… you don't need ANY of these things!

So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system for going from the couch to 26.2 miles. And once you install it, you can cross the finish line of your first marathon (in less time than you think).

Let's dive in!

~

Variable #3: Headers

The next step in writing niche-specific, value-packed thought leadership newsletters is to come up with the 3-10 "sections" of the newsletter—which can be identified and separated by Headers (H1, bolded).

Now, before I get into some writing rules here, a framework I want you to keep in mind is what I like to call the 10 Magical Ways To Expand Anything. These are proven topics that can be applied to any niche:

- Tips
- Stats
- Steps
- Lessons
- Benefits
- Reasons
- Mistakes
- Examples
- Questions
- Personal Stories

You may use these 10 Magical Ways (and/or the list of Proven Approaches I've already given you) to come up with the promise of the newsletter and/or the promise in the subject line and/or introduction.

Now, a couple writing rules to keep in mind for writing the newsletter's Headers:

- A header accomplishes 2 primary goals for the reader: first, it is usually an H1 and bolded, which makes it a section divider and much easier for readers to skim the piece (this is a good thing); and second, each header should deliver on the promise in the subject-line/introduction to the point where a reader could simply read all the headers and extract 80% of the value. The headers gave them all the "quick answers." Then, it's the reader's choice if they want to go deeper and read the tactical content inside of each or any individual section.
- The more "sections" and headers there are in a newsletter, that means the less room there will be to write high-value content inside of each section (keeping the total newsletter length constraint of 800 to 1,500 words in mind). So the more "sections" and headers, that usually means the promise itself is something that can simply be delivered on in the headers themselves, and the content in each section just reinforces the answer that was already given in the header. Conversely, the less "sections" and headers there are leaves more room in each section to elaborate on "how" to execute what's being shared in each header, tactically. You want to keep this in mind as you come up with a niche-specific promise for the reader, and how to best deliver on that promise in the content (and decide how much explanation each section requires in order for the reader to extract as much tactical value as possible).
- Whatever "promise" is being made in the subject line and the introduction is also the promise that should be clearly mirrored and delivered on in the 3-10 headers in the newsletter. So for example, if the subject line says "5 mistakes designers make launching viral products," then we know there will be 5 "sections"/headers in the newsletter, and each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different "mistake." And if the subject line or introduction promises "questions," then each header will deliver on that promise by sharing a different "question," etc.
- There is a very specific type of writing style for headers I would like you to use. Headers should be written in Sentence Style, where each header is written as a full, complete sentence with the first word capitalized (everything else lower-case) and punctuation at the end. The reason is because whatever promise is being made in the subject line/introduction, we want that promise to be delivered on in all the headers themselves—clearly and concisely in individual, bolded sentences. For example, if the promise of the newsletter is "How to land your first coaching client," then we know each "section"/header will be a different Tip or Step or something actionable that delivers on that promise, and to make each header skimmable and packed with value we want to give the most tactical, actionable Tip or Step right there in the header, in sentence format, so the reader knows exactly what to go do, in what order, without even needing to read the rest of the newsletter.

~

Variable #4: Section Content

Once the promise of the newsletter has been established in the subject line, and delivered on in the headers of the piece, you can then also use the 10 Magical Ways framework to fill in the content of each section.

Remember: the promise of the newsletter should be delivered on in the headers, such that a reader could just skim the headers and essentially get 80% of the value of reading the newsletter. Then, within each section, provide specific, tangible, differentiated and actionable insights so that if the reader wants to know more, each section is valuable.

You can use the 10 Magical Ways, but here's some specific criteria for making for a really valuable "section" of a newsletter:

- If the newsletter is some sort of "How To" newsletter, make each section as actionable/instructional as possible. Tips, steps, reasons, examples. The reader should know exactly what needs to be done in order to accomplish their desired goal or solve a specific problem.
- If the newsletter is more focused on a "why" topic, make each section more explanation focused. Stats, lessons, benefits, reasons, mistakes, etc. The key here though is to not explain things generally or with vague language, but instead give very specific, actionable, tactical, differentiated things to think about.

When it comes to the writing of each section, you want to make each section as skimmable and easy to read as possible. Here's how I recommend accomplishing that:

- Always start and end each section with a single-sentence opener/closer.
- Make the "middle" of each section a combination of prose and bulleted lists. But prose should be the majority, with only one bulleted list per section (this technique should be used sparingly).
- And look for opportunities to alternate between long sentences and short sentences to create rhythm and pacing in the writing.

Here's a newsletter example with the promise/subject line being: 3 ways to make money from your newsletter:

Hey—listen…

There are dozens of different ways to make money as a writer.

But one of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was figuring out HOW: how do I actually turn my newsletter into income? What's the best way to get started? And the truth is, it's not that hard—it's just that no one tells you how to do it.

So today, I'm going to share the 3 best ways to monetize your newsletter—and when to use each one.

Let's walk through each one.

Way 1: Digital products.

Most newsletter writers should start here—because you can sell a digital product to a list of any size.

For example, the first product we recommend creating is a simple, low-ticket "solution" to a problem your readers already have: a template, a swipe file, a set of AI prompts, or a short tactical guide.

This is an asset that takes about a weekend to build—and most writers price it between $9 and $99.

But there's a few other digital products that make sense as you grow. Some examples you might sell are:

- Templates & Swipe Files: Once created, these sell on autopilot. There usually isn't any more work to do month after month.
- Mini-Courses: These also have clear endpoints. Once the course is "done," you don't continue to tweak or rewrite it—you just keep pointing new subscribers to it.
- Workshops & Cohorts: These are live, higher-ticket ($350-$1,000) versions of your best material. Once the format works, you can re-run it every quarter.

And your newsletter becomes the engine that sells them—week after week.

But when you want recurring revenue instead of one-off sales, instead you'd use:

Way 2: Paid subscriptions.

This is the next stage in your newsletter—because monthly subscriptions are how you build a predictable income.

For example, once your free newsletter is publishing consistently, you can add a paid tier ($5-$15/month) by solving 2 questions:

- Question #1: What stays free? Your free newsletter is your growth engine—it's what attracts new readers and fills the top of your funnel. If you paywall everything, you stop growing.
- Question #2: What goes paid? The deeper, more tactical version of your best material: templates, worked examples, Q&As, archive access. Because if free is the "what," paid is the "how."

And you can start with just 1 paid post per month (then increase from there).

But if I can give you some friendly advice: nothing "recurs" forever.

Just because someone subscribes to your paid tier doesn't mean they'll stay forever. Every month, the reader has a decision to make: continue or cancel. So, you shouldn't stop growing your free list—paid subscribers churn, and your free list is how you replace them.

But what if you want your newsletter to keep paying you for writing you've already done?

Way 3: Books.

This is the final stage—and it's the most overlooked way to monetize a newsletter.

Because here's the secret: your newsletter archive IS a book. You're just publishing it one chapter at a time.

Once you've written enough issues on a theme, you have a few options based on how much work you want to put in and how much upside you want. For example:

- Option A: You could compile your best long-form issues into a short eBook and publish it on Amazon. This is the lowest-effort option—and it turns your archive into a 24/7 credibility asset (and income stream).
- Option B: You could sell that same eBook directly from your own website. This means handling your own checkout, but you keep roughly double the profit versus selling through Amazon.
- Option C: You could bundle your entire book library into your paid tier as a subscriber benefit. This adds recurring value to Way 2—and gives readers another reason to stay subscribed.
- Option D: You could expand your best-performing series into a full-length book. This is the biggest swing—but a book is the ultimate positioning asset for the "category king" of a niche.

And there's no right or wrong answer.

Because it's completely up to you how much time you want to invest, and how much upside you think there is in your archive.

But after years of doing this ourselves, I'll tell you what I wish I knew sooner:

- You don't "write a book" and then start a newsletter.
- You write a newsletter—and the book falls out of it.

Which is why I'm telling you (again) to just keep publishing every week.

records.description: In this lesson, we're going to cover: - The one question that makes choosing a platform 10X easier (hint: it's about your goal, not the features) - The pros & c
records.content:
In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • The one question that makes choosing a platform 10X easier (hint: it's about your goal, not the features)

  • The pros & cons of Substack, Beehiiv, and Kit—what each platform is genuinely best at, the real pricing math, and how each "discovery engine" works

  • A simple decision framework so you can pick your platform TODAY and never think about it again

And more!

All so you can give the category-defining name you created on Day 1 a home—and get your newsletter set up and ready to publish.

Let's dive in!

The Newsletter Platform Trap

Before we compare anything, I need to save you from the biggest trap I see writers and creators fall for:

Thinking your tech stack is what's going to make your newsletter successful.

It's not.

  • Your writing is what's going to make your newsletter successful.

  • Your consistency is what's going to make your newsletter successful.

  • Your positioning is what's going to make your newsletter successful.

  • Your offer stack is what's going to make your newsletter successful.

The tech just needs to not get in your way.

I bring this up because I see it ALL the time (especially with new writers). They join a Facebook group or a Reddit thread and someone posts: "What tools do you use to run your newsletter?" And the replies are a mile long. This person uses Zapier. That person uses Beehiiv. Someone else has a 14-step automation that sends a personalized GIF whenever a subscriber opens an email on a Tuesday.

(I'm exaggerating. But barely.)

And what happens? New writers see all of that and think: "Oh no, I'm behind. I need all of those things too."

  • Do you really need "3D analytics" to know if your newsletter is performing?

  • Do you really need 20 automation triggers when you have 100 subscribers?

  • Do you really need behavioral segmentation when you haven't even figured out what to write about yet?

No. You don't.

Here's the truth: all three of these platforms are excellent. Kit, Beehiiv, and Substack have each helped creators build 6- and 7-figure newsletter businesses. There is no wrong answer here—only a wrong match between the platform and YOUR goal.

So the real question isn't "which platform is best?"

The real question is: "What is my newsletter's #1 job for the next 12 months?"

There are three honest answers:

  1. "I need an audience." You're starting from (or near) zero and your top priority is getting discovered by new readers.

  2. "I need a business engine." You already have (or are building) an audience somewhere—social, YouTube, a podcast, clients—and your newsletter's job is to convert that attention into sales of products, courses, and services.

  3. "I need subscription revenue." You want readers to pay you directly for your writing, month after month.

Hold your answer in your head. We'll come back to it.

Now let's meet the three contenders.

Platform #1: Substack — The Discovery Machine

What it is: A free publishing platform where your newsletter, website, podcast, and community all live in one place—wrapped inside a social network of readers and writers.

What it's best at: Growing an audience from zero and monetizing through paid subscriptions.

Substack's superpower is that it's not just a tool—it's a network.

Over 40% of all new Substack subscriptions come through Recommendations. Lenny Rachitsky, who has 800,000+ subscribers, has shared that 78% of his came from other newsletters recommending his. Almost 1/3 of Write With AI subscribers came from recommendations.

Here's how it works: You recommend other Substack publications. Other writers recommend you. When someone subscribes to a newsletter, they're shown that writer's recommendations and offered one-click subscribes to all of them.

It's automatic. You set it up once and it compounds forever.

On top of Recommendations, you get:

  • Notes — Substack's version of Twitter. A built-in social feed where your short posts get surfaced to readers who've never heard of you.

  • Restacks — when another writer shares your post with their audience.

  • Substack Reads & leaderboards — digest emails and category rankings Substack uses to promote your content. You don't configure these—they happen automatically when you're publishing and engaging on the platform.

  • Referrals — a built-in reader-to-reader rewards program with automatic tracking and a leaderboard.

That's multiple layers of growth—and you only need to write.

Substack Pros

  • $0 to start, $0 forever (until you earn). No monthly fee at any list size. Unlimited free subscribers.

  • The best built-in discovery of any platform. Recommendations, Notes, Restacks, leaderboards. No other platform sends you this many free subscribers.

  • Paid subscriptions in 2 clicks. Connect Stripe, set a price, done. No sales page to build, no checkout to configure.

  • Everything in one place. Email, website, podcast hosting, video, private Chat community—no duct tape required.

  • Dead simple. You literally cannot break anything. Your only job is to write.

Substack Cons

  • 10% of paid revenue, forever. Plus Stripe processing fees (~2.9% + $0.30 and a 0.7% recurring billing fee), the real cost lands around 13-16% of gross. At $500/month that's trivial. At $10,000/month that's real money.

  • Limited automation. Substack launched Drip Campaigns in beta in October 2025—but as of right now they're still limited to select writers. If you don't see "Drip Campaigns" in your Email settings, you don't have access yet. Everyone gets welcome emails; almost nobody gets full sequences.

  • Weak segmentation and tagging. You can't (easily) send different emails to different behavioral segments, score subscribers, or build funnel logic.

  • No custom CSS/HTML. What you see in the editor is what you get. Great for simplicity, limiting for brand control.

  • You're renting the network. The discovery engine belongs to Substack. If their algorithm or terms change, your growth channel changes with it. (You always own your email list, though—you can export it any time.)

Bottom line: Substack is the best answer to "I need an audience" and a great answer to "I need subscription revenue"—especially when you're starting from zero.

Platform #2: Beehiiv — The Growth & Media Machine

What it is: A newsletter platform built by early Morning Brew employees, designed for people who want to run their newsletter like a media business.

What it's best at: Aggressive audience growth tooling and monetizing through advertising.

Where Substack gives you a network, Beehiiv gives you an arsenal:

  • Boosts — other Beehiiv newsletters PAY to be recommended to your subscribers (and you can pay to be recommended to theirs). It's Substack Recommendations with money attached. You can earn from day one by recommending newsletters you genuinely like—or spend to buy growth.

  • The Beehiiv Ad Network — Beehiiv sells sponsorships on your behalf (brands like Netflix and Nike buy through it) and takes roughly a 15% cut. The network now pays out over $1 million per month to publishers, from newsletters with 1,000 subscribers up to 1M+.

  • A real referral program — Milestone-based rewards, like Morning Brew's famous program, built in.

  • Best-in-class analytics — 3D analytics, acquisition source tracking, A/B testing, funnels. You'll know exactly where every subscriber came from.

  • Websites & SEO — Beehiiv publications are real websites with proper SEO tooling, so your archive can rank on Google.

Beehiiv Pros

  • Free up to 2,500 subscribers. The Launch plan includes unlimited sends and core newsletter + website tools.

  • 0% cut of paid subscriptions. On paid plans, Beehiiv takes nothing from your subscription revenue (you still pay Stripe fees). If you're doing serious paid-subscription volume, this is the single biggest math difference vs. Substack.

  • The best ad monetization in the game. No other platform will actively sell sponsorships for you.

  • Serious growth tooling. Boosts, referral program, subscribe forms, magic links, recommendation widgets.

  • Scales into a media company. Multiple publications, team seats, segmentation—it grows with you.

Beehiiv Cons

  • The good stuff costs money. Monetization (Ad Network, Boosts, paid subscriptions), automations, and A/B testing live on the Scale plan—$49/month and up (price climbs with list size, roughly $99+/month at 10k subscribers). Max starts around $109/month for branding removal and more publications.

  • No true organic network. Boosts move money, not goodwill. There's no Notes-style feed where strangers stumble onto your writing for free. Growth on Beehiiv is something you operate, not something that happens to you.

  • More complexity. Dashboards, toggles, settings. It's built for operators. If you just want to write, it can feel like flying a 747 to the grocery store.

  • Automation is good, not deep. Better than Substack, lighter than Kit for complex funnel logic.

Bottom line: Beehiiv is the best answer for "I want to run a media business"—ad-monetized, growth-operated, analytics-driven. It's the middle path between Substack's simplicity and Kit's business machinery.

Platform #3: Kit — The Creator Business Engine

What it is: Kit (formerly ConvertKit) is an email-first operating system for creators. Less "publishing platform," more "the marketing engine behind your business."

What it's best at: Ownership, automation, and selling things.

Full transparency: we use Kit alongside Substack in our own businesses. Here's why.

Kit is where email marketing gets serious:

  • Visual automations — "If someone clicks this link, tag them, wait 2 days, send this sequence, then pitch this product." Build funnels once, and they sell for you 24/7.

  • Tags, segments & subscriber scoring — Send the right message to the right person. Your buyers, your hot leads, and your cold subscribers all get treated differently.

  • Landing pages, forms & lead magnets — Unlimited, even on the free plan. Kit is built for the "free download → email sequence → product sale" playbook.

  • Commerce built in — Sell digital products and paid newsletter subscriptions directly (Kit takes 3.5% + 30¢ on product transactions, plus Stripe fees).

  • The Creator Network — Kit's version of recommendations. You cross-recommend with other Kit creators for free, or use paid recommendations to buy/sell growth (paid recs carry a ~23.5% revenue share to Kit). Useful—but it's a feature, not a social network. There's no feed, no Notes, no readers browsing for their next subscribe.

Kit Pros

  • Free up to 10,000 subscribers. The most generous free tier of the three—with unlimited sends, landing pages, and forms. (Limited to one automation and one sequence until you upgrade.)

  • The deepest automation and segmentation. Nothing else here comes close. This is the platform for funnels.

  • You own the whole pipeline. Your list, your tags, your data, your funnel logic. No algorithm between you and your readers.

  • 100+ integrations. Kit plugs into your store, your course platform, your webinar tool, everything.

  • Built to sell. If your newsletter's job is to convert readers into customers, Kit was designed for exactly that.

Kit Cons

  • Almost zero built-in discovery. The Creator Network helps, but there's no organic network effect. On Kit, YOU are the growth engine—via social media, SEO, collaborations, and lead magnets. If you have no audience anywhere, Kit won't hand you one.

  • Paid plans get real at scale. Creator starts at $33-39/month for 1,000 subscribers and climbs with your list ($59/mo at 3k, $89/mo at 5k). Pro (advanced reporting, subscriber scoring, referral system) starts around $79/month.

  • No publication website to speak of. Landing pages, yes. A beautiful browsable archive like Substack or Beehiiv? Not really. Kit assumes you have a home base elsewhere.

  • Steeper learning curve. Tags, rules, sequences, visual automations—powerful, but week one can feel like homework.

Bottom line: Kit is the best answer to "I need a business engine." It assumes you bring the audience; it turns that audience into revenue.

The Side-by-Side (2026)

(Pricing verified July 2026. All three platforms change pricing occasionally—always check the current pricing page before you commit.)


When Substack's 10% Starts To Cost You: platform fees vs. monthly paid-subscription revenue

The Decision Framework: Choose Based On Your Goal

Remember the question from the top? "What is my newsletter's #1 job for the next 12 months?"

Here's the framework:

Goal 1: "I need an audience." → Substack

You're starting from zero (or under ~1,000 subscribers) and nobody knows who you are yet.

Choose Substack. It's the only platform where the network actively sends you subscribers while you sleep—through Recommendations, Notes, and Restacks. It costs nothing, it takes an afternoon to set up, and your only job is to write.

The 10% fee on paid subscriptions? Think of it as the cheapest growth marketing you'll ever buy. 10% of revenue you wouldn't have earned anywhere else is a bargain.

This is the right answer for most people in this Sprint. If you're unsure, pick Substack.

Goal 2: "I need a business engine." → Kit

You already have attention somewhere—LinkedIn, X, YouTube, a podcast, a client base—and your newsletter's job is to convert that attention into sales of courses, products, coaching, or services.

Choose Kit. The free plan covers you to 10,000 subscribers, the automations sell for you around the clock, and you own every inch of the pipeline. You don't need Substack's discovery because YOU are the discovery.

Goal 3: "I want to build a media business." → Beehiiv

You think in terms of CPMs, sponsorships, and audience segments. You want to grow aggressively (and are willing to spend to do it), monetize with ads from early on, and eventually run multiple publications.

Choose Beehiiv. The Ad Network and Boosts are unmatched, the analytics tell you exactly what's working, and the 0% cut on paid subscriptions rewards you at scale.

Goal 3.5: "I want serious paid-subscription revenue AND I hate fees."

This is the edge case. Run the math:

  • Below roughly $500/month in subscription revenue, Substack's 10% is cheaper than Beehiiv's $49/month base plan—and you get the discovery network for free.

  • Above roughly $1,000/month, you're paying Substack $100+/month—enough to cover Beehiiv or Kit with money left over.

But (and this is important): don't optimize the fee before you've earned the revenue. A 10% fee on $0 is $0. Grow first. Optimize later. Migration is always available (more on that below).

The Hybrid Play (What We Do)

You don't actually have to choose one forever. Plenty of successful creators (including us) run a hybrid:

  • Substack as the public-facing newsletter—for discovery, community, and paid subscriptions.

  • Kit behind the scenes—for lead magnets, product launches, and automated sales sequences.

But hear me clearly: this is a later problem. In this Sprint, you're picking ONE platform and shipping. Add the second tool when you have a specific job for it—not before.

Common Mistakes To Avoid

  1. Platform shopping as procrastination. Spending 3 weeks comparing platforms is just fear of publishing wearing a productivity costume. All three work. Pick one today.

  2. Choosing on features you won't use for a year. "But Beehiiv has better A/B testing!" You have 40 subscribers. Test subject lines when a 2% difference means something.

  3. Optimizing fees before revenue exists. Don't leave Substack's growth network to save 10% of nothing.

  4. Choosing a platform to match someone else's goal. Your favorite creator is on Beehiiv because ads are THEIR business model. If yours is paid subscriptions from a cold start, their choice is wrong for you.

  5. Believing migration is impossible. It's not (see below). This decision is important, not irreversible. Make it in a day, not a month.

  6. Signing up for two platforms "to test both." You'll run two half-newsletters instead of one real one. One platform. Full commitment. Five days.

What About Switching Later? (Migration Considerations)

Good news: you always own your email list. All three platforms let you export your subscribers as a CSV and import them elsewhere. Beehiiv even offers free white-glove migration from Substack and Kit on paid plans.

What moves easily:

  • Your subscriber list (emails, signup dates)

  • Your post archive (import/republish; Beehiiv and Substack both have import tools)

What does NOT move:

  • Your Substack Recommendations and network position. Leave Substack and you leave the discovery engine, your Notes following, and your restack relationships behind.

  • Paid subscriptions are messy. Stripe subscriptions can be transferred (Substack lets you export your Stripe customer data), but expect friction and some churn during the switch.

  • Automations and tags. Kit funnel logic has to be rebuilt by hand anywhere else.

  • Deliverability reputation. A new sending domain warms up over weeks. Expect a temporary dip in open rates after any migration.

The takeaway: switching costs are real but survivable. Which means the worst thing you can do is stall for a month trying to make the "perfect" choice. Pick with the framework, ship for 6-12 months, and revisit only if your GOAL changes.

Frequently Asked Questions

"Should I use a custom domain?"

Buy it. Don't connect it yet.

Go to Namecheap (or wherever you buy domains) and grab yourdomain.com. It costs $10-20/year. Do this so nobody else takes it. Set up a simple redirect to your newsletter so when you tell people your URL in conversation, it sounds professional.

But (on Substack specifically) don't connect it yet. Substack's domain authority is 92 out of 100. That means Google trusts Substack, and your posts published under the substack.com domain benefit from that trust. A brand new custom domain starts at 1. Connecting a custom domain costs a one-time $50 fee and means your posts index under YOUR domain instead of Substack's. Long-term, good. Short-term, you lose Substack's built-in SEO advantage.

For what it's worth, we still use the Substack domain. It's working fine.

(On Beehiiv and Kit, custom domains are standard practice—connect away.)

"I already have an audience on social. Doesn't that mean Kit automatically?"

Not automatically. Ask what the newsletter's JOB is. If it's "convert my followers into customers," yes—Kit. If it's "build a second audience that isn't rented from an algorithm," Substack's network still adds growth on top of what you bring. Goal first, platform second.

"Can I make money on the free plans?"

Yes. Substack paid subscriptions work from day one (that's the whole model). Kit lets you sell paid newsletter subscriptions and take tips even on the free plan. Beehiiv is the exception—monetization features (Ad Network, Boosts, paid subscriptions) require the Scale plan at $49/month.

"What about Ghost / MailerLite / ActiveCampaign / [other tool]?"

They're fine tools. Ghost is great for developers who want to self-host and pay 0% fees. But this Sprint is built around the three platforms where creator newsletters actually grow in 2026—and adding more options to the menu makes you slower, not smarter. Pick from these three.

"What if I pick wrong?"

You won't—because "wrong" barely exists here. All three platforms have thousands of creators earning real money. And you own your list everywhere. The only truly wrong choice is not picking.

records.content:
In this lesson, we're going to cover:

  • The biggest mistakes people make when naming their newsletter (and why "niche newsletters" win every time)

  • The 4 Category Newsletter Naming Conventions for naming your newsletter after the niche you want to own

  • How to stress-test your name against the competition using the Category Claim Check (plus an AI prompt that generates category-defining names for you)

And more!

All so you can walk away with your niche picked, your newsletter named, and your positioning locked as the "category king" of your niche—before you've published a single word.

Let's dive in!

The Reason "Niche Newsletters" Win

Niching down is one of the most misunderstood concepts in all of writing.

See, most people believe:

  • The more niche I get, the less opportunities I will have.

  • The more broad I get, the more opportunities I will have.

And this is wrong.

It's actually the opposite.

  • The more niche you get, the easier it is for your target reader to discover you. The easier it is for target readers to discover you, the more you grow. The more you grow, the easier it is to tap into tangential niches and attract other likeminded readers. And so on.

  • The less niche (or more broad) you get, the harder it is for your target reader to discover you. The harder it is for target readers to discover you, the slower you grow. The slower you grow, the harder it becomes to tap into tangential niches and attract other likeminded readers. And so on.

This is an extremely important concept for you to understand.

It's the #1 reason why most people's newsletters fail—even before they've written & published their first issue!

Let's look at Write With AI, for example.

Write With AI is our paid newsletter—and is currently the #1 paid education newsletter on all of Substack.

Write With AI — the #1 paid education newsletter on all of Substack.

Now, is our paid newsletter "limited" to "only" be for "writers?"

Of course not!

We "lead" with writing, but we know (because we survey our subscribers frequently) that we attract all sorts of other tangential archetypes/niches:

  • Writers

  • Creators/Influencers

  • Digital Builders

  • Solopreneurs

  • Entrepreneurs

  • VPs & Executives

  • Consultants

  • Coaches

  • Ad Agencies

  • Etc.

This happens because of a very simple rule.

When you niche down, you inevitably create a Niche Constellation.

Again, the faulty belief people have is that by "getting more specific," they are limiting their opportunity.

But this is wrong.

First of all, your niche is way bigger than you realize. Pick any niche on planet earth. I promise, it's bigger than you, individually, can deliver on. So thinking "my niche won't work because it's too small" is already incorrect.

But second, your niche isn't the end—it's the beginning. Your niche actually acts as the nucleus, the "tip of the spear" to a much larger Niche Constellation. And your specificity is what allows this constellation to come to the conclusion, "Well, if you specialize in THAT… you could probably also help me with THIS."

Here's a visual to drive home the point:

The more specific your newsletter niche, the more OTHER niches you can tap into.

The inverse is also true:

The more broad your newsletter, the FEWER tangential niches you can tap into.

See how this works?

Mistakes To Avoid When Naming Your Newsletter

Alright, now let's talk mistakes.

There are a handful of big mistakes people make time and time again—and they ruin your newsletter's chances for success before it's even off the ground.

WARNING: You may come across "outliers" who make these mistakes and still have very successful newsletters.

Let me tell you why that happens.

  • They have a huge existing audience (meaning they can "get away" with being less disciplined/thoughtful). But I'd still argue they would be 10x-100x more successful if they didn't make these mistakes.

  • They have a ton of money (meaning they can "get away" with these mistakes and mask the problem by over-spending on distribution, ads, partnerships, etc.). But I'd still argue they would be significantly more successful & profitable if they didn't make these mistakes.

  • They have "some other component" of their newsletter working well (meaning readers are willing to overlook these mistakes because of some other incentive). But I'd still argue they would be way more successful if they didn't make these mistakes.

OK?

So just because you see someone else being successful despite these mistakes, doesn't mean you should "do what they're doing." A lot of people make these mistakes with their newsletters. That doesn't mean they're good models to follow.

Let's dive in.

Mistake #1: Naming your newsletter after yourself.

(No shade to Lenny, we actually love his stuff. But…)

The single biggest mistake people make is naming their newsletter something like:

  • The Tony Johnson Newsletter

  • The Amy Adams Newsletter

  • The Peter Piper Picked A Pickled Pepper Newsletter

Why is this a mistake?

Because when you name your newsletter after yourself, that means the TAM—the Total Addressable Market—of people who understand what your newsletter is about is limited to the number of people who know you.

Your "name" becomes the category.

And that's a problem.

For example, which TAM is bigger?

  • Lenny's Newsletter

  • The At-Home Stretching Newsletter

The answer should be obvious.

There are more people in the world who are interested in "at-home stretching" than there are people in the world who a) know who Lenny is, and b) understand at a glance what Lenny writes about and why it's valuable to them.

You want to name your newsletter after the reader's CATEGORY OF INTEREST.

Not after "yourself."

Mistake #2: Going Broad (instead of Going Niche)

When people think about "what to write," they tend to think in big categories:

  • Health & Wellness

  • Relationships

  • Marketing

  • Finance

  • Sports

  • Crypto

  • Etc.

But these are what we like to call "umbrella categories."

Each one of these categories is not a niche. It's actually an umbrella encompassing many (sometimes hundreds) of niches.

For example, let's take Marketing:

  • Digital Marketing

  • Print Marketing

  • Billboard Marketing

  • Meta Ads Marketing

  • YouTube Ads Marketing

  • Email Marketing

  • SMS Marketing

  • Marketing Automation

  • Marketing SaaS Platforms

  • Etc.

So when you "Go Broad," what you're effectively saying to readers is: "I am an expert in this umbrella category, which means I am also an expert in all of the niches inside this umbrella category."

And is that true? Of course not.

It's very hard to specialize in a single niche—let alone an umbrella encompassing 100+ niches!

And you would be much more successful if you picked ONE of these niches, and just talked about that.

Mistake #3: Trying to serve multiple different industries at once.

The above mistake compounds on itself when you also try to do this for multiple industries at once.

Meaning: they don't just "Go Broad" and pick one umbrella category (which we've already explained is a mistake). But they take it one step further and pick MULTIPLE umbrella categories.

Now, I want you to think about the people whose content you read, follow, subscribe to, etc.

Do you follow any of them for ALL of these different umbrella topics?

  • You want their health & wellness advice

  • But you also look to them for financial advice

  • But you also look to them for relationship advice

  • But you also look to them for cutting-edge stock picks

  • But you also look to them for meditation routines & mental health guidance

  • But you also look to them for…

Of course not.

99.9% of the time, you follow 1 person for 1 specific thing—and you follow a different person for a different specific thing.

And the reason is because it is VERY, VERY HARD (if not impossible) to deliver exceptional content across multiple umbrella categories.

Mistake #4: Picking a "clever" newsletter name—instead of a clear, niche category.

Lastly, almost nothing hurts your chances of building a successful niche newsletter as trying to impress readers with your clever newsletter name.

Please, tell me, what are any of these newsletters about?

  • The Mile

  • Cooky Foodie Club

  • Slick Skater

  • Etc.

Sure, you might be able to guess the industry the newsletter is in (I'm guessing the "Cooky Foodie Club" has something to do with food), but that isn't enough.

Do you really think people are going to block 15 minutes to try to figure out what your newsletter is about, who it's for, and how it can help them?

No. They don't. (They're going to immediately jump back to TikTok or IG Reels.)

Instead, you want the name of your newsletter to CLEARLY name the niche in which you are servicing.

(Which I'll show you how to do here in a second!)

Newsletter Naming Principles

OK, so now that you know:

  • Why niche newsletters win

  • And what mistakes to avoid when naming your newsletter

…now let's arm you with some frameworks to come up with a category-defining newsletter name.

That's the secret.

The name of your newsletter is not about "building a brand." Your brand is the relationship people have with you and your content over time—which means your brand sits in the context of the category you serve. So, if you want to "become known for a niche you own," then the whole game is to name your newsletter the niche you serve.

(Here's a fun mental exercise to stress-test how important this is: take your niche, and imagine a competitor just named their newsletter your niche exactly. Would you be upset? Would you feel threatened? Great… make sure that doesn't happen, and name your newsletter after your niche!)

Claim Your Category (Before Someone Else Does)

Now, let's take that mental exercise one step further—and turn it into a repeatable check you can run on any name you come up with today.

I call this The Category Claim Check, and it has 3 steps:

  • Step 1: Scout the competition. Search your niche on Substack, Beehiiv, and Google ("your niche + newsletter"). List the 3-5 newsletters closest to yours. Don't skip this—you can't differentiate from competition you've never looked at.

  • Step 2: Run the swap test. Could you swap your newsletter's name with any of theirs and have nobody notice? If yes, neither name is category-defining. A category-defining name should ONLY make sense for your exact niche and your exact reader.

  • Step 3: Claim the gap. Look at what nobody on your list clearly owns—a specific reader, a specific outcome, a specific way of getting there—and put THAT in your name. That unclaimed gap is your category.

Here's why this matters beyond "standing out":

Differentiation isn't about being different for different's sake. It's about being the only obvious choice for one specific reader. When someone in your niche sees your newsletter name next to 5 others, yours should be the only one that sounds like it was written specifically for them.

And here's the compounding payoff: when you own the niche, the broader industry starts treating you as the thought leader.

Remember the Niche Constellation from earlier? This is where it pays off. You don't become a thought leader in your industry by writing about the whole industry. You become the thought leader by being the undisputed king of one specific corner of it—and then letting your authority radiate outward, niche by niche.

Your newsletter's name is doing that thought-leadership work for you, every single day, before anyone reads a word.

But first, before I give you the specific naming conventions, I want to give you a high-level understanding of why these naming conventions work.

The Alex Hormozi "Value Equation"

This is one of my favorite explanations for what "value" truly means—by Alex Hormozi.

When someone says, "You should provide value," they fail to realize that the word "value" is a bundled term. And that word actually represents a handful of different ideas, all at once.

Value really means 1 of 4 things (or some combination):

  • Dream Outcome: Help the person achieve their goal

  • Perceived Likelihood of Achievement: Guarantee the person achieves it

  • Time Delay: Help them achieve it in less time

  • Effort & Sacrifice: Help them achieve it easier (without pain)

If you do 1 or 2 or 3 or all 4 of the above, you have "provided someone value."

This is what so many people misunderstand about building newsletters on the Internet. The reader literally does not care about your newsletter. In fact, they don't even care that they're reading a newsletter to begin with. They could be reading a piece of parchment hand-delivered by a carrier pigeon. It. Does. Not. Matter. The ONLY thing the reader cares about is whether or not you are "providing them value."

And as you can see above, "providing value" is a bundled term—and when we unbundle it, all that means is that your newsletter is:

  • Helping the person achieve their goal

  • Guaranteeing (in some way) they achieve it

  • Helping them achieve it in less time

  • Helping them achieve it easier (without pain)

  • And/or some combination of any of the above

OK?

So when you are thinking about what kind of newsletter you want to write, AND WHAT YOU SHOULD CALL YOUR NEWSLETTER, the way you make this decision is by first anchoring yourself in the above.

Your goal is to provide the reader value—in a niche.

Which means the name of your newsletter should do 2 very important things:

  • Clearly state the niche (what industry are you in, and/or who specifically do you serve?)

  • And clearly state how you provide value (which of the above do you help the reader with?)

If you do that, congratulations… you have a category-defining newsletter.

And if you don't, then you've just made the same mistake 99% of people make—which is why their newsletters fail.

A Newsletter Is A "Book That Never Ends"

So, here's what's happening (under the hood) when you're trying to come up with a category-defining name for your newsletter.

There are 3 pieces you're juggling.

In your newsletter's Main Title & Subtitle, you're trying to communicate 3 different things:

  • Your Niche: What industry do you serve (and, if you can, who "specifically")?

  • Your Value: Which 1 (or multiple) of the above "value equation" are you providing?

  • Your Repeatable, Tangible Value: What "tangibly" are you giving the reader?

Before we get into the naming conventions, this is the last big idea I want to share with you—and it's an important one to understand BEFORE coming up with the name of your newsletter.

The easiest way to think of the value of a newsletter is to think of it as "a book that never ends."

For example, think of the last non-fiction book you read that you really loved. Remember how it felt to reach the end? I bet some part of you was like, "Aw man… I'm not ready for this to be over! I have more questions! I have more I want to learn! I would love for them to explain XYZ in more detail!"

OK. That's all a newsletter is.

It's a book, on a topic, that gives you something tangible, that you never want to end.

What Is "Infinitely Repeatable?"

If you're going to start a newsletter, and a prerequisite for your newsletter's success is long-term consistency, then from the very beginning you want to make sure you're choosing something you not only enjoy… but can repeatedly provide value to readers for a sustained period of time.

So there's two big questions to ask yourself here:

  1. "Is my topic infinitely repeatable?" Some topics are far more repeatable than others. I'll give you two examples. The first is "stock tips." Are stock tips repeatable? Of course. Every day, there's a new hot company to buy (or sell). There's a reason financial newsletters are some of the most popular, and most lucrative, newsletter categories. Now compare that to "Self-Publishing Trends." Is that a repeatable topic? Well, yes… but is there some huge change happening in self-publishing every day? No. Every week? No. Every month? Not usually. Every 6 months? Maybe. Every year? Maybe. It might be a helpful topic, but it's not nearly as repeatable because the industry doesn't move as fast. This is a crucial variable to be aware of.

  2. "What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?" Second, no matter what topic you choose, you want to go a step further and ask yourself what you can TANGIBLY give the reader. Think in objects. Prompts. Checklists. Blueprints. Recipes. Templates. All of these are "tangible objects." 4 Category Newsletter Naming Conventions

Ready to combine all these pieces together to give your newsletter a category-defining name?

Naming Convention #1: Niche + Dream Outcome

The first naming convention for your category-defining newsletter is to combine the niche you want to serve with a dream outcome associated with that niche.

Start by making a list of outcomes your target reader cares about.

For example, let's take the Airbnb Rental niche.

Here are 10 Outcomes people with Airbnb Rentals care about:

  • Maximize occupancy rate — Keep calendars booked as consistently as possible year-round

  • Increase nightly rate — Charge more per night without losing bookings

  • Generate passive income — Earn revenue with minimal day-to-day involvement

  • Get 5-star reviews — Build a reputation that drives more bookings algorithmically

  • Reduce vacancy gaps — Fill last-minute cancellations and shoulder-season slow periods

  • Lower operating costs — Cut cleaning, maintenance, and supply expenses without hurting guest experience

  • Automate guest communication — Handle check-ins, questions, and issues without being on-call 24/7

  • Stand out in search results — Rank higher on the Airbnb platform to get more visibility

  • Protect the property — Avoid damage, bad guests, and liability headaches

  • Scale to multiple properties — Turn one successful rental into a portfolio

Great!

Now, to "name" your newsletter, remember the 3 Pieces you want to hit:

  • Your Niche: What industry do you serve (and, if you can, who "specifically")?

  • Your Value: Which 1 (or multiple) of the above "value equation" are you providing?

  • Your Repeatable, Tangible Value: What "tangibly" are you giving the reader?

So, in this example, here's what this might look like:

  • Your Niche: Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)

  • Your Value: Pick an outcome from the list above (let's say: "Automate guest communication")

  • Your Repeatable, Tangible Value: With this outcome in mind, what can we repeat? Automations!

(The wheels should be spinning in your head, and even just hearing these bullet points you should be able to "imagine" the newsletter, and immediately understand why it's valuable to its target reader. Good! That means the framework is working!)

So, what could the final newsletter name (Main Title & Subtitle) be?

How about…

Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.

Hey! That's pretty good!

"But Cole?! What if the target reader in my niche has lots of different outcomes?!"

Of course they do.

But, two things:

First, just because you "lead" with solving 1 outcome doesn't mean you can't speak to other outcomes in your content. You absolutely can. You just can't "lead" with 10 outcomes—because if you say everything is a priority then nothing is a priority. So Positioning 101 is you lead with ONE clearly stated outcome, which makes it easier to embed yourself into people's minds (making it easier for them to understand how you can help them). But then you can speak to lots of other relevant outcomes in the content itself.

Second, if you're struggling to choose which outcome to lead with, here's the secret: pick the one most relevant to financial upside or downside. For example, let's pretend I'm serving the "Airbnb Rental" niche. Which one of these outcomes is more valuable (aka: has higher perceived value)?

  • Outcome A: "I want to know how to hire cleaning companies to make my Airbnbs look flawless after a guest leaves."

  • Outcome B: "I want to know how to make my rental properties more profitable."

Both of these outcomes are valuable in some way. But it should be obvious that Outcome B is "more valuable" because it's more directly correlated to making more money. And when in doubt, EVERYONE will ALWAYS prioritize giving their attention to things that help them either a) make more money, or b) stop wasting/losing money.

*(\Do not misconstrue what I'm saying, please. I am not saying, "You have to have a financial newsletter giving away stock tips helping people get rich quick or they won't subscribe." That's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is, if you're stuck, or debating between two different outcomes, go with the one the reader can more easily rationalize being "worth their time"—aka: the one where there is some sort of financial upside or downside.)

Naming Convention #2: Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement

Next, what is something your target reader is struggling with—and what "tangible, repeatable" asset can you give them to nearly-guarantee their problem will be solved/their goal will be achieved?

Here's an easy example: SAT Prep Questions & Answers

Pretend you're 17 years old again. You're a junior in high school. The SAT is around the corner. Your parents are stressing you out—because if you don't do well on the SAT then you won't get into a good school, and if you don't get into a good school you won't get a good job when you graduate, and if you don't get a good job when you graduate then you're destined for failure. (Sound familiar?)

In the above mental state, your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (aka: "doing well on the SAT") is probably low. You're very worried about how you're going to perform.

…but what if someone gave you the answers ahead of time?

…what if you were able to essentially memorize all of the questions before the exam?

Your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement would go up! Dramatically!

This is fundamentally why parents spend so much money on SAT Prep programs & resources for their kids. They aren't buying "tutoring hours" or "books" or "materials." What they're really buying is Increased Likelihood of Achievement. "If I buy this for my child, I believe my child's SAT score will probably go up."

So, what are things that increase a person's Perceived Likelihood of Achievement?

There's 2 big components here:

  1. Templates: Anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success.

  2. Credibility: Templates (and/or anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success) from someone who has already achieved the thing you're trying to achieve.

That's really the big question to ask yourself. In this niche, what's something you can Tangibly, Repeatedly give the person that they can copy/paste to replicate success? And, how can you signal to them this "template" has successfully been used by you (or someone else) to solve the problem or achieve the outcome your target reader desires for themselves.

And if you're unsure about how to approach the credibility component here, you have 3 options:

  • Your Own Credibility: "I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too."

  • Your Student/Customer's Credibility: "I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too."

  • Someone Else's Credibility: "I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too."

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

What might this Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement newsletter Main Title & Subtitle look like?

How about…

Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations from the largest family-owned rental property group in Chicago (800 properties & counting!).

See how this naming convention leans on credibility—instead of speaking to the customer's dream outcome(s)?

Naming Convention #3: Niche + Time Delay

The next naming convention is to pair your niche with the removal of "time."

For example:

  • Nobody wants 6-pack abs, slow. Everyone wants 6-pack abs, fast.

  • Nobody wants to get rich slow. Everyone wants to get rich quick.

  • Nobody wants to spend 4 years learning a new skill. Everyone wants to learn the skill in a weekend.

  • Nobody wants to wait a lifetime to fall in love. Everyone wants to fall in love ASAP.

Pick any category you want, and it should be obvious why the target consumer in that category would want either a problem solved or an outcome achieved FASTER.

(Nothing exemplifies this point better than this funny scene from the movie There's Something About Mary.)

So:

  • What's a problem your target reader has and/or what's an outcome they desire?

  • And how can you help them solve that problem and/or achieve that outcome in a fraction of the "normal time?"

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations that take 1 hour to build and save you 10-100 hours per month.

There we go!

Naming Convention #4: Niche + Effort & Sacrifice

The next naming convention is leading with the amount of effort and/or a tangible obstacle you are going to help your target reader avoid.

For example:

  • Everyone wants to make money in the stock market. They just don't want to risk losing the money they have in the process.

  • Everyone wants to learn a new skill (piano, painting, a foreign language, etc.). They just don't want to have to go through the grueling effort of practicing hours and hours each day.

  • Everyone wants to find their soul mate. They just don't want to have to give up their established daily routine to go on a bunch of dates that lead nowhere.

No matter what your target reader's goal is, between them and their goal is some quagmire of effort & sacrifice.

Which means the value of your newsletter is in being a bridge—a nice, sturdy, trusted bridge that can get them from where they are right now, over that murky quagmire, and onto the other side (their goal) in an easy, pain-free way.

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automation templates to streamline your rental business, pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed).

See how we're "removing all of the effort & sacrifice" with this phrase? "…pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed)."

So before you give your newsletter a name, you first want to make sure the focus of your newsletter achieves 2 goals:

Now compare that to "Self-Publishing Trends." Is that a repeatable topic? Well, yes… but is there some huge change happening in self-publishing every day? No. Every week? No. Every month? Not usually. Every 6 months? Maybe. Every year? Maybe. It might be a helpful topic, but it's not nearly as repeatable because the industry doesn't move as fast. This is a crucial variable to be aware of.

  2. "What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?" Second, no matter what topic you choose, you want to go a step further and ask yourself what you can TANGIBLY give the reader. Think in objects. Prompts. Checklists. Blueprints. Recipes. Templates. All of these are "tangible objects." (*Pro Tip: I have now trained my brain to think this way, and whenever I see a new "tangible, digital thing" pop up, a little siren goes off in my head: LUCRATIVE OPPORTUNITY, THATAWAY!)

Step 2: Name your newsletter something "clear," "valuable," and "tangibly repeatable."

Let's unbundle these terms.

  • "Clear" just means you are naming your niche in the name of the newsletter. It's not open to interpretation. The reader knows exactly what niche you're in because the name of the niche is literally in the name of your newsletter.

  • "Valuable" just means you're delivering on 1 of 4 (or some combination) of things all readers/customers care about:

    • Dream Outcome: Help the person achieve their goal

    • Perceived Likelihood of Achievement: Guarantee the person achieves it

    • Time Delay: Help them achieve it in less time

    • Effort & Sacrifice: Help them achieve it easier (without pain)

  • "Tangibly Repeatable" just means you aren't just giving the reader information. What you're giving them are tangible assets that help them achieve their desired goal—faster, with a higher perceived likelihood of success, in less time, for less effort.

So, that's your checklist.

Those are the "messages" you're trying to communicate when naming your newsletter.

For example:

  • Your Niche: Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)

  • Your Value: Pick an outcome from the list above (let's say: "Automate guest communication")

  • Someone Else's Credibility: "I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too."

Step 4: Can you add in any copywriting tactics to make your Main Title & Subtitle even more compelling?

There's really only a handful you need to memorize—because all the best headlines/newsletter names/book titles/etc. use them over and over again.

Copywriting Tactic #1: A "Don't Worry" Whisper:

What's your target reader's biggest objection? Speak to why that objection isn't a problem, or how you're going to help them solve it, inside a parenthetical at the end of your subtitle.

Sticking with our Airbnb example, maybe our target reader's biggest objection to using automations inside their Airbnb business is they don't consider themselves to be tech savvy.

Here's how you'd execute this tactic:

  • Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!).

Copywriting Tactic #2: "More" problems-solved and/or outcomes-unlocked.

When in doubt, just give the reader "more."

For example, look at how much weaker this newsletter name is when we remove some of these additional items—and how much stronger it gets the "more" of them we add back in:

  • [Very Weak] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations

  • [Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins

  • [Even Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins and answer guest questions

  • [The Best] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7

  • [Pro-Grade] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!).

This is the big secret to naming newsletters (and really any kind of digital product), is finding ways to speak to as many things the reader wants/cares about as possible.

Copywriting Tactic #3: Numbers & objective measures for success.

Anytime you can state a "number" or an objective measure for success, the perceived value of your newsletter goes up.

Numbers can be any of the following:

  • Money: How much money will you help the reader save? How much money will you help the reader make? How much money have you made, doing this exact thing?

  • Hours: How many hours will you help the reader save? How many hours have you saved? Or how many hours have you invested into doing this thing?

  • Years: How many years have you been doing this? How many years of hard work will you save the reader from having to go through themselves?

  • Clients: How many clients, or students, or customers (or readers, or listeners, or viewers) have you helped?

  • Etc.

This is not a required piece in naming your newsletter. But if you CAN add in an objective number of some kind, it's always a nice addition that makes your newsletter's value proposition even more compelling.
