**First, just because you "lead" with solving 1 outcome doesn't mean you can't speak to other outcomes in your content.** You absolutely can. You just can't "lead" with 10 outcomes—because if you say everything is a priority then nothing is a priority. So Positioning 101 is you lead with ONE clearly stated outcome, which makes it easier to embed yourself into people's minds (making it easier for them to understand how you can help them). But then you can speak to lots of other relevant outcomes in the content itself.

**Second, if you're struggling to choose which outcome to lead with, here's the secret: pick the one most relevant to financial upside or downside.** For example, let's pretend I'm serving the "Airbnb Rental" niche. Which one of these outcomes is more valuable (aka: has higher perceived value)?

- Outcome A: "I want to know how to hire cleaning companies to make my Airbnbs look flawless after a guest leaves."
- Outcome B: "I want to know how to make my rental properties more profitable."

Both of these outcomes are valuable in some way. But it should be obvious that Outcome B is "more valuable" because it's more directly correlated to making more money. And when in doubt, EVERYONE will ALWAYS prioritize giving their attention to things that help them either a) make more money, or b) stop wasting/losing money.

*(*Do not misconstrue what I'm saying, please. I am not saying, "You have to have a financial newsletter giving away stock tips helping people get rich quick or they won't subscribe." That's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is, if you're stuck, or debating between two different outcomes, go with the one the reader can more easily rationalize being "worth their time"—aka: the one where there is some sort of financial upside or downside.)*

### Naming Convention #2: Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement

Next, what is something your target reader is struggling with—and what "tangible, repeatable" asset can you give them to nearly-guarantee their problem will be solved/their goal will be achieved?

Here's an easy example: **SAT Prep Questions & Answers**

Pretend you're 17 years old again. You're a junior in high school. The SAT is around the corner. Your parents are stressing you out—because if you don't do well on the SAT then you won't get into a good school, and if you don't get into a good school you won't get a good job when you graduate, and if you don't get a good job when you graduate then you're destined for failure. (Sound familiar?) 

In the above mental state, your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (aka: "doing well on the SAT") is probably low. You're very worried about how you're going to perform.

…but what if someone gave you the answers ahead of time?

…what if you were able to essentially memorize all of the questions before the exam?

Your Perceived Likelihood of Achievement would go up! Dramatically!

This is fundamentally why parents spend so much money on SAT Prep programs & resources for their kids. They aren't buying "tutoring hours" or "books" or "materials." **What they're really buying is Increased Likelihood of Achievement.** "If I buy this for my child, I believe my child's SAT score will probably go up." 

### So, what are things that increase a person's Perceived Likelihood of Achievement?

There's 2 big components here:

1. **Templates:** Anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success. 
2. **Credibility:** Templates (and/or anything the person can copy/paste to replicate success) *from someone who has already achieved the thing you're trying to achieve.* 

That's really the big question to ask yourself. In this niche, what's something you can Tangibly, Repeatedly give the person that they can copy/paste to replicate success? And, how can you signal to them this "template" has successfully been used by you (or someone else) to solve the problem or achieve the outcome your target reader desires for themselves.

And if you're unsure about how to approach the credibility component here, you have 3 options:

- **Your Own Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too."
- **Your Student/Customer's Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too."
- **Someone Else's Credibility:** "I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too."

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

What might this Niche + Perceived Likelihood of Achievement newsletter Main Title & Subtitle look like?

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations from the largest family-owned rental property group in Chicago (800 properties & counting!).** 

See how this naming convention leans on credibility—instead of speaking to the customer's dream outcome(s)? 

### Naming Convention #3: Niche + Time Delay

The next naming convention is to pair your niche with the removal of "time."

For example:

- Nobody wants 6-pack abs, slow. **Everyone wants 6-pack abs, fast.**
- Nobody wants to get rich slow. **Everyone wants to get rich quick.**
- Nobody wants to spend 4 years learning a new skill. **Everyone wants to learn the skill in a weekend.**
- Nobody wants to wait a lifetime to fall in love. **Everyone wants to fall in love ASAP.**

Pick any category you want, and it should be obvious why the target consumer in that category would want either a problem solved or an outcome achieved FASTER. 

So:

- What's a problem your target reader has and/or what's an outcome they desire?
- And how can you help them solve that problem and/or achieve that outcome in a fraction of the "normal time?"

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations that take 1 hour to build and save you 10-100 hours per month.** 

There we go! 

### Naming Convention #4: Niche + Effort & Sacrifice

The next naming convention is leading with the amount of effort and/or a tangible obstacle you are going to help your target reader avoid. 

For example:

- Everyone wants to make money in the stock market. **They just don't want to risk losing the money they have in the process.**
- Everyone wants to learn a new skill (piano, painting, a foreign language, etc.). **They just don't want to have to go through the grueling effort of practicing hours and hours each day.**
- Everyone wants to find their soul mate. **They just don't want to have to give up their established daily routine to go on a bunch of dates that lead nowhere.**

No matter what your target reader's goal is, between them and their goal is some quagmire of effort & sacrifice.

Which means the value of your newsletter is in being a bridge—a nice, sturdy, trusted bridge that can get them from where they are right now, over that murky quagmire, and onto the other side (their goal) in an easy, pain-free way. 

So, let's stick with our Airbnb Rental Properties In Chicago niche.

How about…

**Gold Coast Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automation templates to streamline your rental business, pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed).**

See how we're "removing all of the effort & sacrifice" with this phrase? *"…pre-packaged to install with 1 click (no tech expertise needed)."*

# (Bonus!) Newsletter Naming Cheat Sheet

When naming your newsletter, there are a suite of different "messages" you want to try to cram into your Main Title & Subtitle.

- **Main Title** = Write With AI
- **Subtitle** = The leading paid newsletter for ChatGPT & Claude prompts, and how to turn AI platforms into your own personal Digital Writing Assistant.

So, let's walk through the hierarchy of which "messages" you want to make sure are in your newsletter's name (Main Title & Subtitle).

### Step 1: Is this "a book that never ends?"

The best way to think about how to create a high-value newsletter is to pretend you're signing yourself up to write a book, on a topic, that never ends.

So before you give your newsletter a name, you first want to make sure the focus of your newsletter achieves 2 goals:

1. **"Is my topic infinitely repeatable?"** Some topics are far more repeatable than others. I'll give you two examples. The first is "stock tips." Are stock tips repeatable? Of course. Every day, there's a new hot company to buy (or sell). There's a reason financial newsletters are some of the most popular, and most lucrative, newsletter categories. Now compare that to "Self-Publishing Trends." Is that a repeatable topic? Well, yes… but is there some huge change happening in self-publishing every day? *No. Every week? No. Every month? Not usually. Every 6 months? Maybe. Every year? Maybe.* It might be a helpful topic, but it's not nearly as repeatable because the industry doesn't move as fast. This is a crucial variable to be aware of.
2. **"What is the tangible object I can repeatedly give the reader?"** Second, no matter what topic you choose, you want to go a step further and ask yourself what you can TANGIBLY give the reader. Think in objects. Prompts. Checklists. Blueprints. Recipes. Templates. All of these are "tangible objects." (*Pro Tip: I have now trained my brain to think this way, and whenever I see a new "tangible, digital thing" pop up, a little siren goes off in my head: LUCRATIVE OPPORTUNITY, THATAWAY!)

### Step 2: Name your newsletter something "clear," "valuable," and "tangibly repeatable."

Let's unbundle these terms.

- **"Clear" just means you are naming your niche in the name of the newsletter.** It's not open to interpretation. The reader knows exactly what niche you're in because the name of the niche is literally in the name of your newsletter.
- **"Valuable" just means you're delivering on 1 of 4 (or some combination) of things all readers/customers care about:**
    - **Dream Outcome:** Help the person achieve their goal
    - **Perceived Likelihood of Achievement:** Guarantee the person achieves it
    - **Time Delay:** Help them achieve it in less time
    - **Effort & Sacrifice:** Help them achieve it easier (without pain)
- **"Tangibly Repeatable" just means you aren't just giving the reader information.** What you're giving them are tangible assets that help them achieve their desired goal—faster, with a higher perceived likelihood of success, in less time, for less effort.

So, that's your checklist.

Those are the "messages" you're trying to communicate when naming your newsletter.

For example:

- **Your Niche:** Airbnb Rentals (or, more specifically… Airbnb Rentals In Chicago)
- **Your Value:** Pick an outcome from the list above (let's say: "Automate guest communication")
- **Your Repeatable, Tangible Value:** With this outcome in mind, what can we repeat? Automations!

So, what might the name of our category-defining newsletter be?

**Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7.**

### Step 3: Can you add some sort of credibility?

This isn't required, but if you have it… it's great!

- **Your Own Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Here, you can use it too."
- **Your Student/Customer's Credibility:** "I did this. It worked. Then I showed them how to do it. And it worked for them too. Here, now you can use it too."
- **Someone Else's Credibility:** "I did a bunch of research. This is what worked for this other credible person. Here, I compiled everything so you can use it too."

### Step 4: Can you add in any copywriting tactics to make your Main Title & Subtitle even more compelling?

There's really only a handful you need to memorize—because all the best headlines/newsletter names/book titles/etc. use them over and over again.

**Copywriting Tactic #1: A "Don't Worry" Whisper:** 

What's your target reader's biggest objection? Speak to why that objection isn't a problem, or how you're going to help them solve it, inside a parenthetical at the end of your subtitle. 

Sticking with our Airbnb example, maybe our target reader's biggest objection to using automations inside their Airbnb business is they don't consider themselves to be tech savvy.

Here's how you'd execute this tactic:

- *Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!).*

**Copywriting Tactic #2: "More" problems-solved and/or outcomes-unlocked.**

When in doubt, just give the reader "more."

For example, look at how much weaker this newsletter name is when we remove some of these additional items—and how much stronger it gets the "more" of them we add back in:

- *[Very Weak] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations*
- *[Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins*
- *[Even Better] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins and answer guest questions*
- *[The Best] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7*
- *[Pro-Grade] Chicago Airbnbs On Autopilot: Weekly Zapier automations to handle check-ins, answer guest questions, and handle issues 24/7 (even if you don't consider yourself to be tech savvy!).*

This is the big secret to naming newsletters (and really any kind of digital product), is finding ways to speak to as many things the reader wants/cares about as possible.

**Copywriting Tactic #3: Numbers & objective measures for success.**

Anytime you can state a "number" or an objective measure for success, the perceived value of your newsletter goes up.

Numbers can be any of the following:

- **Money:** How much money will you help the reader save? How much money will you help the reader make? How much money have *you* made, doing this exact thing?
- **Hours:** How many hours will you help the reader save? How many hours have you saved? Or how many hours have you invested into doing this thing?
- **Years:** How many years have you been doing this? How many years of hard work will you save the reader from having to go through themselves?
- **Clients:** How many clients, or students, or customers (or readers, or listeners, or viewers) have you helped?
- Etc.

This is not a required piece in naming your newsletter. But if you CAN add in an objective number of some kind, it's always a nice addition that makes your newsletter's value proposition even more compelling.

~

Are you ready for my niche/topic?

records.content:
Alright, I just threw a lot at you!

So, I want to speed up your Article writing with AI (which will make the “writing” feel a lot less daunting!).

All you need to do is copy and paste the prompt below into your chosen LLM (I recommend Claude) and follow the on-screen instructions. You’ll be asked for your headline and main points (if you have them).

AI will then outline your article and write your article for you!

Dive in here:

# AI Prompt: Long-Form Article Outliner & Writer

You are an Article Outlining & Drafting Specialist, specifically for digital writers who want to expand a single proven idea into a fully outlined *and fully written* long-form Article.

I am going to give you my headline (and, if I have them, my Main Points), and I would like you to walk me through two phases:

**Phase 1 — The Outline.** A complete outline: a headline at the top, a set of Main Points beneath it, and a set of Sub Points expanding each Main Point.

**Phase 2 — The Draft.** Once I confirm the outline, the complete, publish-ready Article written out in full.

The reason I want this done a specific way is because 80% of the writing happens in the outline. Writing isn't really about writing — it's about thinking. The outline is where the thinking gets clarified, so that by the time we write actual sentences, we're just cleaning up notes instead of staring at a blank page. Your job is to help me get all of that thinking out of the way first, and *then* turn it into finished prose.

Do not begin Phase 2 until I have explicitly confirmed the outline.

~

## Instruction

There are eight techniques that govern this process. Two govern the outline. Six govern the draft.

**Phase 1 — Outlining**
- Technique #1: Mirroring
- Technique #2: The 10 Magical Ways

**Phase 2 — Drafting**
- Technique #3: Single-Sentence Openers
- Technique #4: Fleshing Out & Linking
- Technique #5: Writing Rhythm (1/3/1 & Expanding The Middle)
- Technique #6: Visual Mirroring & Lists
- Technique #7: The Credibility Note
- Technique #8: The Optional Conclusion

I'm going to walk you through each one, describe what makes it unique, and give you examples of each executed well — so you understand how to replicate.

~

### Technique #1: Mirroring

Mirroring means taking one element and repeating it down the page so the reader feels like they're looking at something organized and intentional.

**Main Points must mirror the promise in the headline.** Whatever the headline promises is what the Main Points must deliver, in the same wording, flow, and punctuation. If the headline promises "3 Mistakes," the Main Points are "Mistake #1, Mistake #2, Mistake #3." If it promises "6 Lessons," the Main Points are "Lesson #1… Lesson #6." The number in the headline sets the number of Main Points.

**If one Main Point changes, all of them change.** The golden rule: never let the labels alternate in style, capitalization, or punctuation. A list that reads "Business-Destroying Mistake #1 / #2 / #3" feels organized. A list that reads "Mistake #1 / The Right Way To Think / A Lesson I Learned" feels lost. Readers love patterns, so keep the pattern identical all the way down.

### Technique #2: The 10 Magical Ways

This is how we expand each Main Point into Sub Points. There are 10 ways to expand literally any point in any piece of writing:

1. **Tips** — practical pieces of advice for doing the thing
2. **Stats** — numbers, data, or figures that prove or frame the point
3. **Steps** — the sequential actions someone takes
4. **Lessons** — what was learned from the experience
5. **Benefits** — the upsides or payoffs of doing it
6. **Reasons** — the "why" behind the point
7. **Mistakes** — the things that go wrong or should be avoided
8. **Examples** — concrete instances that illustrate the point
9. **Questions** — the questions a reader should ask themselves about it
10. **Personal Stories** — a moment from lived experience that makes it real

You do not have to use the same Way for every Main Point. The best outlines rotate through different combinations — one Main Point expanded with Reasons, the next with Benefits, the next with Steps. You choose the Way that will be **the most useful thing to list out for the reader** on that specific Main Point. A good test: "If I were completely new to this topic, what would I most want to know here?"

### Technique #3: Single-Sentence Openers

When a reader opens a piece of content and is immediately confronted by a giant wall of text, the first thought is: *"Geez. This sure does look like a heavy lift."* Even if the content is light and fun. Even if the language is simple. Visually, it looks difficult.

The fix is a single-sentence opener — one sentence, standing alone as its own paragraph, at the top of the Introduction and at the start of every Main Point. It gives the reader an easy place to "slide" into the section.

There are six types:

**Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.**
- "Most people will spend their entire careers being good at the wrong thing."
- "The best business decision I ever made cost me my biggest client."

**Open with a thought-provoking question.**
- "What would you build if you knew no one would ever judge it?"
- "What if the habit you're most proud of is the one holding you back?"

**Open with a controversial opinion.**
- "Networking events are a waste of time for anyone serious about their work."
- "Most 'productivity' advice is just procrastination wearing a nicer outfit."

**Open with a moment in time.**
- "At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, I deleted three years of work and felt nothing but relief."
- "The email arrived twelve minutes before the meeting that would change everything."

**Open with a vulnerable statement.**
- "I made six figures last year and still felt like a complete fraud."
- "I almost quit the week I made my first $50,000 on the internet."

**Open with a weird, unique insight.**
- "The fastest way to be remembered in a meeting is to be the one who says the least."
- "Boredom is the most underrated signal your brain ever sends you."

Rotate the types across sections. Do not open six consecutive Main Points with declarative sentences.

### Technique #4: Fleshing Out & Linking

This is how Sub Points become prose.

For each Sub Point, ask: *"What does the reader need to hear to understand this? What can I give them that helps them make sense of this Sub Point and this Main Point?"* Then write that out in complete sentences.

Then link the Sub Points to each other with short connective phrases:
- "Which leads me to the next example…"
- "Another reason why this mistake cost me so dear is…"
- "Once you've answered this question, ask yourself this second question…"

**Critical rule: outline labels are scaffolding, not headers.** "Reason #1:" and "Step #2:" exist to organize the thinking. In the finished Article they dissolve into the prose. Only the Main Points survive as visible headers. The single exception is when a set of Sub Points genuinely works better as a bulleted or numbered list (see Technique #6).

**Critical rule: end every Main Point section with a callback closer.** The last line of each section returns to the Main Point's own claim — often the exact wording of the header, standing alone as a single sentence. It snaps the section shut.

### Technique #5: Writing Rhythm (1/3/1 & Expanding The Middle)

The overarching idea is to create rhythm and musicality — and rhythm is almost entirely a function of sentence length. Alternate long and short sentences in a pattern. See? Short sentence, followed by a medium sentence, followed by a long sentence that builds and gives the reader a crescendo of pace before it finally resolves.

**The base pattern is 1/3/1:**

{1} One short-to-medium sentence to open.
{3} Three sentences that add description and color and advance the point.
{1} One single sentence to close the idea.

Repeat 1/3/1 down the page.

**When you need more room, expand the middle.** Keep the single-sentence bookends and grow only the middle of the sandwich: 1/4/1, 1/5/1, 1/6/1, 1/7/1. The bookends are what give the reader an entry point and a reward. Never expand the bookends.

### Technique #6: Visual Mirroring & Lists

This is Mirroring applied at the paragraph level.

**Sections should look the same.** If one section is three giant paragraphs and the next is two sentences, they read as off-balance — even if both are well written. Strive for each Main Point section to be visually similar in length and formatting. If you open one section with a declarative sentence, a 5-sentence paragraph, and a closing sentence, aim to repeat that cadence in the next.

**Use bulleted or numbered lists inside Main Points.** Lists are the single most underrated formatting technique available, because they force you to strip away unnecessary explanation and just tell the reader what matters. No rambling. Just boom, boom, boom.

A strong pattern to reach for: a list of parallel constructions, each line built on the same grammatical frame.

> You think you're running "so many ads" until you sit in a room and hear someone explain how they're running 100x more ads than you.
> You think you're hiring "so many people" until you sit in a room and hear someone explain how they're hiring 10x more people, 10x faster than you.
> You think you have "such high standards" until you sit in a room and hear someone explain their standards, and you realize their standards are way higher than yours.

Aim for at least one list in the Article, but not one in every single section.

### Technique #7: The Credibility Note

Readers aren't as picky as most people think. You don't need to be a Harvard graduate or a rocket scientist for readers to trust you. **All you need to do is tell them why they should take what you're saying seriously.**

Imagine a friend asks you for a Friday night movie recommendation. Inevitably they'll ask, "Why? Why should I watch this?" And you'll say: "Because I've watched every Rom Com on Netflix, and trust me, this one is the best." That's all they need to hear.

Every Introduction must answer the question: *"Why should the reader trust me on this?"*

That answer comes from **Personal Credibility** — hours spent, milestones achieved, years of practice:
- *"How do I know how to build a real estate empire? Because over the last 10 years, I've bought and sold over 50 different rental properties."*
- *"Why should you take my Netflix recommendations? Because I've watched over 5,000 hours of Netflix shows and movies."*

Or from **Borrowed Credibility** — someone else's experience, a book, time spent around people who've done it:
- *"Why is this the best strategy to get distribution on your writing? Because I went and interviewed 20 different best-selling authors, and this is what they said to do."*

### Technique #8: The Optional Conclusion

Conclusions are optional. That is the default position.

**If the conclusion just repeats what was already said, do not write one.** The reader isn't grading a 12th-grade English paper — they're a highly impatient digital reader who would rather swipe back to TikTok. If the piece was helpful, they'll click around and read more on their own. Let it end. Make it a cliffhanger.

Only write a conclusion if it adds something *new*:
- A new insight
- A final closing story
- A clarifying statement
- More information about your credibility

Default to no conclusion. Propose one only when there's genuinely new material to land, and tell me why you think it earns its place.

~

## Context

### Rules

**Outline rules**
- The number of Main Points is dictated by the headline's promise, not by a default. Do not assume three. If the headline says "7 Reasons," there are seven Main Points.
- Sub Points are not locked to three. Ask me how many I want per Main Point before expanding.
- Every Main Point must mirror the headline promise in identical wording and punctuation.
- Within a single Main Point, the Sub Point labels must also mirror each other (Reason #1, Reason #2, Reason #3 — not Reason #1, A Reason, Why This Matters).
- For each Main Point, name which of the 10 Magical Ways you're using, so I can see your reasoning and swap it if I disagree.
- Do not write full sentences or paragraphs in the outline. Sub Points are short notes-to-self.

**Drafting rules**
- **Never invent specifics.** Do not fabricate statistics, dollar figures, dates, company names, client stories, or personal anecdotes. Where the writing needs a specific I haven't given you, insert a bracketed placeholder like `[INSERT: specific dollar figure]` or `[INSERT: the story about the client who churned]` and keep moving.
- Write the entire Article in one pass. Do not deliver it section by section.
- Main Points appear as visible headers, mirrored exactly as they were in the approved outline. Sub Point labels do not appear.
- Every section opens with a single-sentence opener standing alone as its own paragraph.
- Every section ends with a callback closer.
- No paragraph runs longer than roughly seven sentences without a single-sentence break.
- Do not use em dashes as a stylistic crutch; the voice uses them, but sparingly.
- Do not add headers, sections, or Main Points that weren't in the approved outline.

### Positive Attributes

**A great outline is:**
- **Skimmable.** A reader could glance at the Main Points alone and instantly understand the shape of the whole Article.
- **Mirrored.** The Main Points are visually identical in structure, and so are the Sub Points within each section.
- **Useful.** Each Sub Point earns its place — not filler added to hit a number.
- **Varied where it helps.** Different Main Points use different Magical Ways when that serves the reader.
- **Faithful to the promise.** Nothing drifts from what the headline promised.

**A great draft is:**
- **Rhythmic.** Sentence lengths alternate. Single sentences stand alone as paragraphs and act as beats.
- **Specific.** Real numbers, real dates, real names, real dollar figures — or clearly marked placeholders where they're missing.
- **Balanced.** Sections are visually similar in length and formatting.
- **Self-implicating.** The writer admits their own mistakes plainly and without hedging ("Whoops." / "And I feel stupid for ever thinking that's what was going to happen.").
- **Direct with the reader.** Uses second person. Talks *to* someone, not *about* a topic.
- **Willing to caveat.** Nuance gets handled in parentheticals or asterisked asides rather than by watering down the main claim.
- **Free of filler.** No "in today's fast-paced world," no throat-clearing, no summarizing what's about to be said.

### Reinforcement Example — The Outline

**Headline:** *3 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars*

The promise is "3 Mistakes," so there are three Main Points, each mirrored as "Mistake #__":

- **Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time** *(expanded with Reasons — why it was a mistake)*
    - Reason #1: Buying capacity before there's work to fill it
    - Reason #2: Full-time hires can't be un-hired quickly
    - Reason #3: Salary anchors your burn rate permanently
- **Mistake #2: Not having clients on auto-pay** *(expanded with Benefits — the upside of auto-pay)*
    - Benefit #1: Predictable cash flow
    - Benefit #2: No collections conversations
    - Benefit #3: Higher effective retention
- **Mistake #3: Not taking any money out of the business** *(expanded with Steps — how to take money out responsibly)*
    - Step #1: Set a fixed owner's draw
    - Step #2: Separate operating cash from reserve
    - Step #3: Review against a rolling 12-month average

Notice three things: the Main Points all mirror the headline's "Mistakes" promise; each Main Point is expanded with a *different* Magical Way chosen for usefulness; and the Sub Point labels mirror each other within their own section.

### Reinforcement Example — The Draft

Here is Mistake #1 from that outline, drafted. Notice the vulnerable-statement opener standing alone, the 1/5/1 rhythm, the Sub Points dissolved into prose rather than labeled, the parallel list, the parenthetical caveat, and the callback closer.

> **Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time**
>
> I hired six full-time employees before I ever hired a single contractor, and it nearly ended the company.
>
> At the time, it felt like the responsible thing to do. Full-time hires signaled that we were a "real" business — to investors, to the team, and mostly to myself. Every founder I looked up to talked about building a team that was all-in, and contractors felt like a half-measure. So I hired ahead of the work, assuming the work would show up to meet the payroll. It did not. And by the time I understood what I'd actually signed up for, I was spending more time managing capacity than selling.
>
> What nobody tells you is how expensive being "all-in" actually is.
>
> The first problem is that you're buying capacity you can't yet fill. A full-time hire shows up on Monday with 40 hours to give you, and if you only have 12 hours of real work, you will invent the other 28. I have watched myself do this. I have created entire projects — dashboards nobody read, processes nobody followed — for no reason other than justifying a salary I had already committed to.
>
> The second problem is that full-time hires can't be un-hired quickly.
>
> - A contractor who isn't working out ends at the end of the month.
> - A full-time hire who isn't working out ends after a performance plan, a documented paper trail, a severance conversation, and about six weeks of dread.
> - And in the meantime, you're still paying them, still managing them, and still avoiding the conversation.
>
> But the third problem is the one that actually cost me millions: salary anchors your burn rate permanently. Revenue moves up and down. Salaries only move up. Once you've set a monthly number you're obligated to pay, every decision downstream of it gets made under pressure — which pricing to accept, which client to keep, which bad deal to say yes to because payroll is on Friday. You stop making decisions from strategy and start making them from fear.
>
> (*To be clear, I'm not anti-hiring. Some roles genuinely require full-time attention and full-time commitment, and trying to run them on contract is its own expensive mistake. What I'm arguing against is defaulting to full-time because it feels more legitimate.*)
>
> If I could do it again, I'd hire every single person as a contractor first, and convert them only once the work was so obviously there that the decision made itself.
>
> Making every new hire full-time was the most expensive mistake I made.

~

## Final Delivery

Now here's exactly how I want you to run our session. Move through these steps one at a time, and wait for my answer before moving on. Do not dump everything at once.

### Phase 1 — The Outline

**Step 1 — Get the headline.** Ask me for my headline. Once I give it, identify the promise inside it (the number + the thing being promised, e.g. "3 Mistakes," "6 Lessons," "7 Reasons"). Tell me how many Main Points that promise implies.

**Step 2 — Get or build the Main Points.** Ask whether I already have my Main Points.
- If I do, take them and check them against the headline promise. Flag anything that isn't mirrored and show me a corrected, mirrored version.
- If I don't, brainstorm a set of Main Points for me — matching the number the headline promised, all mirrored in identical wording and punctuation. Present them and ask if I'd like any edits. **Do not move on to Sub Points until I've approved the Main Points.**

**Step 3 — Ask how many Sub Points.** Once the Main Points are locked, ask how many Sub Points I want under each Main Point. (Let me know it doesn't have to be the same number for every Main Point if I'd prefer to vary them.)

**Step 4 — Expand with the 10 Magical Ways.** For each Main Point, choose the Magical Way that's most useful for that point, name it in parentheses next to the Main Point, and list out the mirrored Sub Points beneath it. Rotate Ways across Main Points where that serves the reader better than repeating one.

**Step 5 — Deliver the full outline.** Present the complete outline in one clean block: headline at the top, mirrored Main Points beneath it, mirrored Sub Points under each — with the chosen Magical Way labeled on each Main Point. Keep everything in outline form (short notes), not full sentences.

Then ask me directly: **"Do you want to adjust anything, or should I write the full Article from this?"**

**Do not proceed to Phase 2 until I confirm.**

### Phase 2 — The Draft

**Step 6 — Gather what you need to write.** Once I confirm the outline, ask me these four things in a single batch:

1. **Credibility.** Why should the reader trust me on this topic? (Personal or borrowed — Technique #7.) If I don't have an answer, offer me 2–3 options based on what you know from my outline.
2. **Raw material.** Do I have specific numbers, dates, dollar figures, names, or stories I want worked into any of the Main Points? Tell me you'll use bracketed placeholders anywhere I leave a gap.
3. **Length.** Roughly how long should each Main Point section run? (Default: 200–350 words per section unless I say otherwise.)
4. **Delivery.** Do I want the finished Article **in the chat** or **as a document I can download?**

**Step 7 — Write the full Article in one pass.** Deliver the complete piece, start to finish, in the format I chose. It must include:

- An **Introduction** with a single-sentence opener, the credibility note, and enough context to frame why this piece exists right now
- Every **Main Point** as a visible header, mirrored exactly as approved in the outline
- A **single-sentence opener** at the top of every Main Point section
- All **Sub Points fleshed out into prose**, linked with connective phrases, with the outline labels dissolved
- **1/3/1 rhythm** (or expanded middles) throughout, with single sentences used as standalone beats
- At least one **bulleted or numbered list**, and **visually balanced sections**
- A **callback closer** ending every Main Point section
- A **conclusion only if it adds something new** — otherwise let the final Main Point end the piece, and tell me you chose not to write one and why

**Step 8 — Hand it off.** After delivering, tell me:
- Which sections contain `[INSERT: …]` placeholders that need my real specifics
- Which single-sentence opener type you used for each section, in a short list, so I can swap any that feel repetitive

Then ask if I'd like any section rewritten.

Let's begin. Ask me for my headline.

records.content:
As Digital Writers we’re in the business of packaging our ideas to make them easy to consume and visually appealing.

And a part of that (especially on X at the moment) is creating an Article Header/Thumbnail for your Article.

Now, if you don’t have design skills… don’t worry! I created an AI prompt you can use to do this.

The prompt has six fields.

All you have to do is fill in a short template and the AI handles the design. Most are optional. If you skip a field, the AI falls back to a built-in default.

The laziest possible prompt works:

"Make me a banner. Title: How to Write a Newsletter."

You'll get a clean two-tone banner with a serif headline.

Banner Image Prompt

Copy everything below the line, fill in the fields you care about, leave the rest blank or delete them.

Here’s the prompt:

Create a newsletter banner image as an inline SVG.

TITLE: [your headline]

SUBTITLE: [optional — leave blank to skip]

STYLE: [minimal / illustrated / editorial / playful — default: minimal]

COLORS: [vibe like "warm earth tones" OR 2-3 hex codes — default: cream #f5efe4 + charcoal #2a2a2a]

FONT: [type like serif/sans/mono OR specific font name like Inter, Playfair Display — default: Fraunces]

IMAGERY: [objects to include, or "none, typography only" — default: typography only]

IMAGE: [optional — filename and placement: background / corner logo / framed element / hero on left / hero on right / centered hero]

MOOD: [one or two words — default: calm]

Design guidance:
- Banner aspect ratio: roughly 1200x400
- Title should be the focal point
- Use the colors and font specified; fall back to defaults if blank
- Keep the composition balanced and readable at small sizes
- If imagery is included, integrate it with the typography rather than placing it separately
- If an IMAGE is uploaded, place it as specified and ensure text remains readable

How To Configure The Banner Prompt

TITLE

The main headline. Keep it under 8 words for best results.

SUBTITLE

Optional smaller line below the title. Use for issue numbers, dates, taglines, or section labels. Skip if not needed.

STYLE

Pick one:

  • minimal — typography-forward, lots of negative space

  • illustrated — includes drawn elements, scenes, objects

  • editorial — magazine-style, refined, serif-heavy

  • playful — bold colors, casual shapes, energetic

  • Or choose your own

Default: minimal

COLORS

Two ways to specify:

  • Vibe: describe it — "warm earth tones", "navy and cream", "muted pastels", "bold monochrome"

  • Hex codes: give 2-3 exact colors — #1a1a1a, #f5efe4, #ff5a36

Default: cream background (#f5efe4) + charcoal text (#2a2a2a)

FONT

Two ways to specify:

  • Type: serif / sans / mono

  • Specific font name: Inter, Playfair Display, JetBrains Mono, Fraunces, Georgia, etc.

Default: Fraunces (a modern serif)

Free fonts that work automatically (Google Fonts):
Inter, Playfair Display, Fraunces, Lora, Merriweather, JetBrains Mono, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, Space Grotesk, Space Mono, DM Sans, DM Serif Display, Work Sans, Manrope, EB Garamond, Libre Baskerville, Bricolage Grotesque

System fonts (always available):
Georgia, Helvetica, Arial, Courier New, Palatino, Garamond

Suggested pairings for title + subtitle:

  • Editorial → Playfair Display + Inter

  • Modern → Space Grotesk + Inter

  • Techy → JetBrains Mono + Inter

  • Literary → Fraunces + Lora

  • Corporate → IBM Plex Sans + IBM Plex Mono

IMAGERY

Describe objects or scenes to include. Examples:

  • "a typewriter and a coffee cup"

  • "a single paper airplane"

  • "abstract geometric shapes"

  • "none — just typography"

Default: typography only

IMAGE

Optional. If you want to use your own logo, photo, or graphic, upload the file first, then reference it.

Placement options:

  • background — fills the banner, text overlays on top

  • corner logo — small mark in a corner (specify which corner)

  • framed element — cropped into a shape as part of the composition

  • hero on left / hero on right — takes up one side of a split layout

  • centered hero — main visual with title above or below

What works:

  • Logos and icons (PNG with transparent background is best)

  • Photos as background, hero, or framed element

  • Simple graphics and SVG files

What doesn't work:

  • Restyling your photo to match an illustration (use Midjourney/Ideogram first)

  • Removing photo backgrounds (use remove.bg first)

  • Color-correcting the image itself

MOOD

One or two words describing the emotional tone. Examples: calm, urgent, nostalgic, energetic, confident, playful, serious, warm, sharp.

Default: calm

Example 1: Lazy mode (minimum effort)

Make me a banner. 

Title: The Friday Five.

Example 2: Medium effort (some direction)

Make me a banner. 

Title: The Cold Email Playbook. 

Style: editorial. Colors: navy and off-white. 

Font: Playfair Display. 

Imagery: a single paper airplane. 

Mood: confident

Example 3: Full control (every field used, with custom image)

Make me a banner. 

Title: Write With AI. 
Subtitle: Issue #47. 
Style: minimal. Colors: #8ae1a2 and #ffffff and #000000 
Font: SF Pro
Imagery: none, typography only. 
IMAGE: wwai-logo.png — use as a corner logo in the top left. 
Mood: sharp.

records.title: Step 6: Write Your Introduction & Conclusion
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 4 - Articles/Step 6_ Write Your Introduction & Conclusion - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Writing Your Introduction Next, as you finish the Article, you want to make a note to yourself: “Why should the reader trust me? Why am I the right person to wr
records.content:
Writing Your Introduction

Next, as you finish the Article, you want to make a note to yourself:

“Why should the reader trust me? Why am I the right person to write about this topic? Should they trust me because of my Personal Credibility? Or because of my Borrowed Credibility?”

These are important questions to ask yourself.

Readers aren’t as picky as most people think. You don’t need to be a Harvard Graduate, a Rocket Scientist, or a political official for readers to trust you. All you need to do is tell them why they should take what you’re saying seriously. Our favorite example is: imagine a friend (or a friend of a friend) asked you for a Friday Night Movie Recommendation. It really doesn’t matter what movie you recommend, inevitably the person will ask, “Why? Why should I watch this?” To which you will most likely reply: “Because I’ve watched every single Rom Com movie on Netflix, and trust me, this one is the best.”

That’s all they need to hear. And ba-da-bing, your opinion is trusted.

Writing is no different: Readers need a reason to trust you.

So, what makes you credible?

  • Is it how many hours you’ve spent doing this thing?

  • Is it because of some meaningful milestone you’ve achieved?

  • Is it the number of years you’ve spent studying and practicing this thing?

And if you don’t have any personal credibility, how might you be able to borrow that credibility from someone else?

  • Is this what someone else with decades of experience says to do?

  • Is this what a very smart book, written by a very smart person, recommends?

  • Is this wisdom you’ve gathered by spending time around other people who have achieved this same thing?

Make a note to yourself in the introduction of whatever you’re writing:

“This is why you should trust what I’m about to tell you.”

For example:

  • “How do I know how to build a real estate empire? Because over the last 10 years, I’ve bought and sold over 50 different rental properties.”

  • “Why should you take my Netflix series recommendations? Because I’ve watched over 5,000 hours of Netflix shows and movies.”

  • “Why is this the best strategy to get distribution on your writing? Because I went and interviewed 20 different best-selling authors, and this is what they said to do.”

The reader has no problem trusting you—you just have to give them a reason to!

Add this to your Introduction.

Adding A Conclusion or Recap

The last piece of formatting is the ending:

  • Writing a conclusion

  • Sharing a recap

  • Providing a CTA (Call To Action)

That said, my personal philosophy is that conclusions are optional.

So, when should you write a conclusion?

Here’s a good rule of thumb:

If your conclusion is just repeating everything you just said, you don’t need a conclusion.

Right?

Remember: you aren’t writing a 12th grade English paper. You are writing for highly impatient digital readers (people who would much rather swipe back to TikTok and watch 7-second videos of young children falling face-first into bowls of macaroni and cheese). So if your “conclusion” is just you repeating yourself, ditch it. Just let the piece end. Make it a cliffhanger! Because if what you wrote was truly helpful and beneficial to the reader, they will inevitably want to click around and read more content from you.

Which means you should only write “conclusions” if they add something new to the piece.

You should only write “conclusions” if they tie everything together in a new way.

  • New insights

  • A final closing story

  • A clarifying statement

  • More information about your credibility

  • Etc., etc., etc.

Alright, we’re done!

records.title: Step 5: Formatting & Style
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 4 - Articles/Step 5_ Formatting & Style - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
Writing Rhythms And Lists

The overarching idea here is you’re trying to create rhythm and musicality in your writing.

Contrary to popular belief, musicality and rhythm in your writing are not difficult to create.

It’s all about sentence length. And the key to creating musicality and rhythm is literally nothing more than just alternating between long sentences and short sentences—ideally in some sort of pattern. See? Short sentence, followed by a medium sentence, followed by a long sentence. If you pay attention as you read, you can “hear” the pauses, the build-up, and the long crescendo of pace as the sentences are processed in your brain.

This is all you have to do to make your writing “flow.”

Let’s dig into some other ways to add flow to your writing.

Writing Rhythm Basics: 1/3/1

Now, I talk more about this in my book The Art and Business of Online Writing, but here’s a quick crash course.

{1} The simplest “rhythm writing” pattern is what we like to call 1/3/1.

{3} This means you open with 1 short to medium-length sentence. Then, in three sentences you add more description and color. And then you finish the idea with one single sentence.

{1} Just like this section here.

1/3/1 literally refers to the number of sentences, and the pattern they’re stacked in.

One strong opening sentence. Three descriptive sentences, advancing your point forward. And then one final concluding sentence.

And you can literally repeat 1/3/1 over and over again, all the way down the page (just like we’re doing here!).

Expanding The Middle

Now let’s say 1/3/1 doesn’t give you enough space to say what you want to say.

The secret to maintaining effective rhythms in your writing is to “expand the middle.” This means keeping the same 1/3/1 structure (single sentences to open and close your longer paragraphs of description), but adding content to the middle part of the “sandwich.”

For example:

  • 1/4/1

  • 1/5/1

  • 1/6/1

  • 1/7/1

See how the structure is the same, but all that is changing is the length of the middle paragraph?

The key here is to maintain your single-sentence “bookends” (the opener and closer sentences). This gives the reader an easy entry point into your writing (or next section). And rewarding them with a single sentence at the end of your elongated paragraph of description.

So, if you’re ever going to expand your writing, remember to expand the middle.

How To Use Mirroring To Make Your Sub Points Visually Appealing

You can also “Mirror” within each section of your piece.

For example: if you open with 1 clear declarative sentence, and then give a 5-sentence paragraph description, and then close with a final declarative sentence, you should strive to repeat that same cadence and pattern (1/5/1) in each of the subsequent sections. This helps readers find the flow/melody of your writing. Which makes it even easier for them to quickly skim and consume your content.

This section (and the end of the last section) is an example of this idea in action (it’s a 1/3/1).

What you want to avoid is individual sections looking vastly different.

If one section is 3 giant paragraphs, and then another section is literally 2 sentences, you have a problem: they “look” off-balance.

Instead, you want to strive for each section (inside each of your Main Points/Sub Points) to be visually the same—either in length, or in formatting choices and style. For example, as I’m writing this, I am thinking about the section right before this where I explain the Mirroring technique. I could stop writing at the previous sentence, but then it would look a bit “off-balance.”

So, I flushed out the description out so that it “LOOKS” the same.

See?

Bulleted or Numbered Lists

Ah, now this is how you take your formatting skills to the next level.

The vast majority of Digital Writers & Digital Creators don’t even write using Main Points/Subheads.

Instead, you click on their content, and it’s just one big blocky paragraph after another. (Legacy writers struggle with this the most. And it’s why even New York Times’ best-selling authors struggle to get distribution on their digital content—because they are used to writing longwinded books, not skimmable Atomic Essays, Twitter Threads, and LinkedIn posts.)

Of the Digital Writers & Digital Creators who do learn the importance of organizing their content using Main Points/Sub Points, only a small percentage of them graduate to the next level:

Using Bulleted or Numbered Lists.

  • Can you tell how satisfied your brain is to read a quick bulleted list right here?

  • Can you “feel” how it’s a nice break after reading the above few paragraphs?

  • Do you notice how easy this section of bulleted takeaways is to skim?

  • Are you enjoying how this feels, as a reader, right now?

Incorporating short bulleted or numbered lists inside your Main Points is one of the most underrated writing & formatting techniques that exists today. Because what these bulleted or numbered lists force you to do is strip away all the unnecessary explanation—and just tell the reader what’s most important.

No unnecessary description.

No rambling.

Just boom, boom, boom.

If you can master the art of writing Clear Titles, organizing your big ideas with Main Points/Sub Points, and making sections more skimmable by using Bulleted or Numbered lists, then pat yourself on the back.

You have a skill set 99% of Digital Writers & Digital Creators do not have.

Furthermore, if you are interested in being hired as a writer/ghostwriter, nothing will impress clients more than seeing your magic at work—presenting content in a coherent, organized, and visually appealing way.

Alright, we’re almost done!

records.title: Step 4: Write A Single Sentence Opener
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 4 - Articles/Step 4_ Write A Single Sentence Opener - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: For Each Section & Fill In Any Details When the reader opens a piece of content and is immediately confronted by a giant wall of text, what’s the first thing th
records.content:
For Each Section & Fill In Any Details

When the reader opens a piece of content and is immediately confronted by a giant wall of text, what’s the first thing that goes through their brain?

“Geez. This sure does look like a heavy lift.”

Even if the content is light and fun. Even if the language is simple. VISUALLY, it looks difficult—because that giant paragraph of text looks like a brick wall.

Publications like The New Yorker do this constantly. (And writers think big, chunky paragraphs make them seem “smart.”)

But guess what?

Giant paragraphs don’t make readers want to consume your content MORE.

They make them want to consume your content LESS.

Before you’ve even read a single word of the following, your brain is already tired!

But if we kept this text exactly the same, and just broke out the first sentence… guess what?

All of a sudden, it feels approachable! And the reader can easily “slide” into the reading experience. I call this using single-sentence openers, and there are a few types you can insert into the introduction of your Article and at the start of every Main Point in your Article.

Add In Your Proven Single-Sentence Openers

So, go through each section and add a single sentence opener.

But what KIND of sentences? Great question!

Here’s the list I always come back to:

Let’s run through some examples of each one:

Open with 1 strong, declarative sentence.

  • “Most people will spend their entire careers being good at the wrong thing.”

  • “Your morning routine is quietly deciding the outcome of your year.”

  • “The best business decision I ever made cost me my biggest client.”

Open with a thought-provoking question.

  • “What would you build if you knew no one would ever judge it?”

  • “Why do we trust strangers on the internet more than the experts in our own field?”

  • “What if the habit you're most proud of is the one holding you back?”

Open with a controversial opinion.

  • “Networking events are a waste of time for anyone serious about their work.”

  • “Most "productivity" advice is just procrastination wearing a nicer outfit.”

  • “Passion is overrated; the people who win are the ones who show up when they feel nothing.”

Open with a moment in time.

  • “At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, I deleted three years of work and felt nothing but relief.”

  • “The email arrived twelve minutes before the meeting that would change everything.”

  • “On Monday, May 23rd, 2019, I was halfway through my coffee when I realized I'd been wrong about all of it.”

Open with a vulnerable statement.

  • “I made six figures last year and still felt like a complete fraud.”

  • “For most of my twenties, I was terrified that everyone could see how little I knew.”

  • “I almost quit the week I made my first $50,000 on the internet.”

Open with a weird, unique insight.

  • “The fastest way to be remembered in a meeting is to be the one who says the least.”

  • “Boredom is the most underrated signal your brain ever sends you.”

  • “The people who give the best advice are usually the ones who ignored it first.”

Alright, we’ve added in our single sentence openers.

Now it’s time to flesh out your outline of Main Points and Sub Points and turn them into complete sentences that link to each other.

Flesh Out Your Main Points And Sub Points

What you’re doing here is turning all your Sub Points into complete sentences and giving the reader more insight, context, and information.

Again, just ask, “What does the reader need to hear to understand this point? What can I give them that helps them make sense of the Sub Point & Main Point?”

Then all you need to do is link the Sub Points and Main Points with little phrases like:

  • “Which leads me to the next example…”

  • “Another reason why this mistake cost me so dear is…”

  • “Once you’ve answered this question, ask yourself this second question…”

Alright, all the “writing” here is done!

But we’re not at publishable Article just yet. It’s time to add in one of the most important parts of any Article. This is the number one thing which will make any piece of writing you publish online easy to consume.

Formatting & Style.

records.title: Step 3: Expand Each Section With Sub Points
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 4 - Articles/Step 3_ Expand Each Section With Sub Points - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Using The 10 Magical Ways Here’s where things get fun. Remember: Once you have your headline and your outline clarified, 80% of the writing process is done. Why
records.content:
Using The 10 Magical Ways

Here’s where things get fun.

Remember:

Once you have your headline and your outline clarified, 80% of the writing process is done. Why? Because writing isn’t really about writing. Writing is about “thinking.” And the outline is where you get all of your “thinking” clarified.

Once this is done, the “writing” itself is easy!

This means, that before you even start writing sentences, simply go through your outline and expand your outline into more bullets of information. Think of it like you’re jotting notes to yourself inside your outline: “Here I want to say, X, over here I want to say Y, and right here I want to say Z.” You want to get all of this “thinking” out of the way—so by the time you start writing sentences, you are basically just cleaning up your “notes.”

Versus starting with a blank page.

Now you might be thinking, “How do I expand these Main Points?”

Here’s an easy framework:

How To Expand Anything: The 10 Magical Ways

There are 10 ways you can expand LITERALLY any piece of writing.

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

Don’t believe me?

Watch this—using a sample outline.

Let’s return to my headline of “3 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars.”

Here’s my outline:

  • Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time

  • Mistake #2: Not having clients on auto-pay

  • Mistake #3: Not taking any money out of the business

We can expand each of these “Mistakes” with other ways from our 10 Magical Ways (I’m going to use Reasons, Benefits, and Steps):

  • Mistake #1: Making every new hire full-time (let’s expand this with the Reasons Why this was a mistake):

    • Reason #1:

    • Reason #2:

    • Reason #3:

  • Mistake #2: Not having clients on auto-pay (let’s expand this with the Benefits of having them on auto-pay):

    • Benefit #1:

    • Benefit #2:

    • Benefit #3:

  • Mistake #3: Not taking any money out of the business (let’s expand this with the Steps I’d take to take money out of the business):

    • Step #1:

    • Step #2:

    • Step #3:

Or I could expand it with other Ways:

  • The first Mistake could be expanded with with Personal Stories of how this cost me millions of dollars

  • The second Mistake could be expanded with Questions you should ask when moving clients to auto-pay

  • The third Mistake could be expanded with Tips on how to take money out of the business responsibly.

See?

You can expand ANY Main Point just by rotating through different combinations of the 10 Magical Ways—and you can easily expand any section.

So, how do you decide which of the 10 Magical Ways to use?

Easy!

It’s up to you. But a good rule of thumb I use is: “What will be the most useful thing to list out for the reader?” In other words, think back to your 2-Year Test. What would you have wanted to know if you were completely new to this topic? What would you want to know 2 years ago? There’s your answer.

And the best part?

Your readers will often tell you what they want to hear more of in comments, DMs, and what they interact with.

So, don’t overthink it. Just follow what you think would be useful and what your readers are asking for.

Alright, we’ve got our Main Points and Sub Points all outlined. Time to dig into the actual “writing.”

records.description: Again, we covered this previously. But I want to dig a little deeper and talk about the importance of something I call “Mirroring.” Mirroring is the single most
records.content:
Again, we covered this previously.

But I want to dig a little deeper and talk about the importance of something I call “Mirroring.”

Mirroring is the single most important formatting technique.

Think of Mirroring as a way of anchoring the reader’s eyes on the page. When you Mirror sections, what happens is the reader can’t help but feel like they are staring at a work of art—because you’ve constructed more than just words on a page. What you’ve done is create sections, blocks, and distinct areas where you’d like them to direct their attention.

Mirroring basically means you take one element and then repeat it:

  • Throughout your entire essay/piece.

  • Throughout an entire section (or multiple sections).

  • And even individual sentences.

This is a very subtle but powerful formatting technique and I’m going to talk about it at every level of the Article writing process.

Here’s how to mirror the promise in your headline:

Let’s say the headline of your piece is: “3 Mistakes I Made As A First-Time Startup Founder That Cost Me Millions Of Dollars.”

The Promise here is “3 Mistakes.”

Why would a reader click on this piece? To read your 3 Mistakes. Simple.

The way you Mirror this promise all the way down the page then is to repeat this same promise over and over again. Which means each one of your Main Points/Subheads would follow the same wording, flow, and punctuation.

Like this:

  • Mistake #1:

  • Mistake #2:

  • Mistake #3:

This might seem like a simple nuance, but it’s more powerful than most writers realize.

When a reader clicks on your piece, they are immediately looking for the “promise” you made them in the headline. So, if you promised them “3 Mistakes,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “3 Mistakes.” If you promised them “6 Lessons,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “6 Lessons.” If you promised them “11 Crazy Gadgets,” then your Main Points/Subheads need to be “11 Crazy Gadgets.” And so on.

Tying your Main Points to the promise in your headline is one of the simplest ways to immediately upgrade the skimmability of your writing—and make it easy for readers to fly through your content.

But this is only the beginning!

As you begin to write, you may decide to take some creative liberties with your Main Points.

That’s fine! BUT the golden rule is: if you change 1 Main Point/Subhead, you need to “Mirror” that change all the way down the page.

Just look at these 2 lists of Main Points/Subheads and notice which list your eye sees as more visually appealing:

Example 1

  • Mistake #1:

  • The Right Way To Think:

  • Lesson I Learned:

  • Another Mistake:

  • Sometimes, all you need to do is make sure you’re focusing on the right thing.

  • Ending Thoughts:

Example 2

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #1:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #2:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #3:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #4:

  • Business-Destroying Mistake #5:

Which one of these lists is more visually appealing?

Which list do you immediately assume is “more organized?”

The 2nd one! But there’s a very clear reason as to why.

The reason is because readers love similarities. When each of your Main Points/Subheads “looks the same” and there is a clear pattern, this gives the reader reassurance. They understand how you’re moving them down the page, and they also understand where they are in the piece. But when your subheads are alternating style, capitalization, punctuation, etc., each of these changes makes the reader feel more and more “lost.” They can’t tell why you are changing the rules on them.

So, if you are going to make a change to one of your Main Points/Subheads, remember to Mirror that change all the way down the page.

Readers love patterns.

Alright, once you’ve Prepped The Page with an outline of your Main Points, let’s start expanding each section.

records.content:
If you’re worried you can’t write a full-length article, then I have some good news:

If you can write an Atomic Essay, you can write an Article.

We covered a lot of the key frameworks in the Atomic Essays section. With Articles, there are just a few expansion, formatting, and stylistic skills you need to master. But these are super straightforward and once you’ve nailed them you can use them to continue up the Lean Writing ladder (writing a free email course, a newsletter, a digital product, all the way up to a digital business).

Let’s take this step by step.

records.title: Why You Should Expand All Your Proven Ideas..
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 4 - Articles/Why You Should Expand All Your Proven Ideas.. - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
Into Long-Form Articles

Every idea you post on the internet has the potential to become a digital business.

Honestly! Ideas that resonate with your audience should be doubled down on and expanded further. You’re just giving “more” of what your readers want. And eventually, you can sell all of this extra content, ideas, and frameworks to your audience.

But first, we need to figure out which ideas to double down on.

This is simple. If an idea attracts more views, likes, and comments compared to your other content/ideas, then it should be expanded into a longer-form piece. I call this method “Lean Writing” and it’s the way you take one idea and build it into a library of content and eventually a business.

This is how it works:

  • Write a short-form post

  • Turn your best ideas into an Atomic Essay

  • Turn that idea into a long-form Article

  • Into a newsletter

  • Into a free email course

  • Into a paid digital product

  • Into an entire business

Start small, keep testing your ideas at every level, and eventually you can build a business.

(Notice how we’re covering the first 3 points in this Sprint? You’re already making excellent progress if you want to turn your online writing into a digital business!)

Alright, so once you’ve seen which ideas are resonating with your audience (from the short-form posts and Atomic Essays you’ve been posting), it’s time to expand these ideas into a long-form Article.

Why Articles?

For all the reasons we write Atomic Essays: they teach you the fundamental concepts of Digital Writing AND are a great way to learn how you can expand any idea into “more” content (which is the whole game of writing online).

Plus, they’re going through a moment on X right now and seem to go viral more than any other content format:

Ok, so how do you write an Article?

Let’s take a look.
