records.title: The Complete Niche FAQ
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/(Bonus) 🎉 The Niche Famous Playbook/The Complete Niche FAQ - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: “But Cole?! What if I'm not an expert in the thing I’m most interested in?” First of all, nobody cares if you’re an “expert” or not. The only thing any reader/c
records.content:
“But Cole?! What if I'm not an expert in the thing I’m most interested in?”

First of all, nobody cares if you’re an “expert” or not.

The only thing any reader/customer cares about is whether or not you can help them.

Second, you might not feel like an expert, but if you have any sort of Information Advantage (even if it’s small), then to all the other people who don’t know what you know, you are an “expert.” In our beginner writing program, Ship 30 for 30, the metaphor we like to use here is: remember when you were in 5th grade, about to enter middle school? Who did you want to learn from? A “middle-school expert?” Your parents? An adult?

No!

You wanted to hear from the 6th graders! The ones who were just a few steps ahead of you.

That same dynamic is how all knowledge transfers work, everywhere in the world, all the time.

  • If you want to learn how to swim, you don’t need Michael Phelps to be your teacher. You literally just need someone who “knows how to swim” and not drown.

  • If you want to learn how to play the violin, you don’t need Itzhak Perlman to be your mentor. You literally just need someone who “knows how to play the violin” to teach you some basic melodies and hand positions to get going.

  • If you want to learn how to make YouTube videos, you don’t need Mr Beast to hand-hold you through setting up your YouTube channel. You literally just need someone who is “a few steps ahead of you,” and has already done “that thing” to give you a hand.

OK?

So get this expectation of “needing to be an expert” out of your head.

It’s not real.

It’s just a clever faulty belief you’re using to avoid getting started.

“But Cole?! What if the thing I’m most interested in isn’t the most lucrative?”

I want you to really take this to heart: you don’t know whether something will be lucrative or not until you try it.

  • When I was studying creative writing in college, my entire family (my father especially) had an intervention with me to try to explain why I was pursuing a dark and dismal career path and was never going to make any money from it.

  • When I quit my job to pursue ghostwriting and working for myself, my former boss’s and my parents and all of my friends tried to tell me it was a “huge risk” and, especially with writing, I was going to have a really hard time providing for myself.

  • When I first started scaling my ghostwriting agency, all of my entrepreneur friends at the time insisted ghostwriting was a horrible career path and it was going to do “reputational damage” to me long term.

  • When I first started Ship 30 for 30 with Dickie, I can’t tell you how many people in my life said, “A writing course? Who is ever going to spend money on something like that?”

  • Etc. etc. etc.

For the past 10+ years, I have LIVED being surrounded by a never-ending stream of negative opinions trying to tell me that writing, and making a career as a writer, was and is impossible.

And I’ve made more money than every single person who told me that, FROM WRITING.

So I share that with you because, in hindsight, NOBODY (I can’t think of a single person) in my early life thought this path and this topic and this “niche” was a good idea. Nobody thought it was lucrative. Nobody thought it was ever going to pan out to much of anything.

And guess what? This is how it goes for a LOT of people.

Until… you prove otherwise. And THEN everyone says, “Oh, that’s because you picked a great niche!”

No, I didn’t.

I picked something a) I had an Information Advantage in, and b) something I am genuinely interested in and WANT to keep learning about.

YOU are the one who makes the niche work.

Niches don’t “work or not-work” on their own.

“But Cole?! What if the thing I know the most about, isn’t the thing I want to be my niche? What if I’m more interested in something else?”

Then do that.

My goal in walking you through that little exercise is to give you OPTIONS.

Just because you have an Information Advantage doesn’t mean you HAVE to do that thing.

For example, in my early 20s, I clearly had an Information Advantage because I was working at an advertising agency as a copywriter. But, I was also obsessed with bodybuilding—and I knew a lot about it. It’s all I did. I ate 6 meals a day. I went to the gym 6-7x per week, for 2-3 hours at a time. All my friends were bodybuilders. I read about it, I watched YouTube videos about it, and I trained with other professional bodybuilders. That wasn’t a “career” of mine, and nobody was paying me to do any of that (I just genuinely loved it), but I knew a lot about it.

So, could I have made my first niche Copywriting? Sure.

But I was more interested, at the time, in bodybuilding.

So that’s what I decided to start with.

And my first digital product ever was… a bodybuilding eBook!

(I’ve since retired this chapter of my life, so please don’t email me asking for a copy. It’s gone to the wind.)

And then 3 years later, when I got injured and realized I was never going to be a professional bodybuilder myself, what did I do?

Did I force myself to stick with something I was no longer in love with?

No.

I moved on. I changed niches (Ghostwriting & Digital Writing). And there’s nothing wrong with that.

These are all just options.

“But Cole?! What if I want my niche to be something I don’t know very much about.”

You shouldn’t.

Or, let me put it this way: sure, you can… but don’t be surprised if it takes you a long time to get any traction.

Because now you have to do 2 things at the same time:

  • You have to acquire all the skills to write well and create compelling offers and hook readers, etc., etc., etc.

  • AND, you have to simultaneously learn about a topic you know nothing about.

Which is why it is much, much easier to start with something you already have an Information Advantage within, because then “the knowledge” comes easily. You already KNOW about it. And you can focus all your time on acquiring and improving the other skills that bring that knowledge to life (and ultimately monetize it).

The other thing—and this is something a lot of people REALLY struggle to keep in mind—is that the niche you pick TODAY doesn’t have to be the niche you pick FOREVER.

It’s not your forever niche.

It’s your FIRST niche.

Just like my FIRST niche was bodybuilding.

But you have to pick a niche so that you can build all the other skills required to bring that niche to life.

If I told you I was going to stop everything I was doing and dedicate 8+ hours per day to helping you build yourself as a writer, and dominate your chosen niche, even if it was a niche I knew nothing about, you would be over-the-moon-excited to have my help. Right?

OK, why is that?

Because it’s obvious I’ve acquired all the other skills that bring a niche, ANY NICHE, to life.

And you assume that because I’ve acquired those skills, the niche actually doesn’t matter, and I’ll still be helpful to you.

And you would be correct.

So why do you think the same won’t happen, for you?

Of course it will.

If you pick a niche, any niche, and you use it as a vehicle to practice and acquire skills, you can then transfer those skills to any FUTURE niche whenever you want.

"But Cole?! My audience isn't big enough yet. What should I do?"

This is a big myth, and we want to address it right away.

Most creators want to "wait" until their audience is "big enough" before they decide what their niche is going to be—as if, one day, they are just going to wake up and some magical answer will reveal itself.

But when is enough, enough?

When you have 1,000 followers?

When you have 10,000 followers?

When you have 100,000 followers?

At what point are you going to commit to serving a particular niche?

There's a bit of irony in this myth, because most creators want to wait until they get "bigger" on social media before they Name & Claim a niche for themselves—and yet, the reason most creators DON'T GROW on social media is because they haven't claimed a niche for themselves.

It's a chicken/egg dilemma.

So, should you wait to decide what your niche is going to be?

No. If anything, you are incentivized to plant your flag in the ground and Name & Claim some sort of niche (literally anything), now.

And then if you want to change your niche later, you can.

It's not a marriage decision.

"But Cole?! I don't feel comfortable Naming & Claiming a niche because I'm not an expert in anything. Shouldn’t I become an expert, first?"

Yes, you are.

Everyone is an "expert" in something.

The mistake people make here is thinking that "expert" is some far-and-distant achievement. Like you become an "expert" when you're a New York Times best-selling author. Or you become an "expert" when someone like Oprah or Tony Robbins gives you that title.

But the truth is, to your 2-years-ago self, you are an expert.

You know things today you didn't know 2 years ago. Or 1 year ago. Or 6 months ago. Or even 6 days ago.

Which makes you a Niche Expert.

The key to building an audience online, and even creating a portfolio of digital products and ultimately monetizing your knowledge, isn't "pretending to be something you're not." The key is to pinpoint what questions you used to have (in any space, field, or topic area), that you no longer have because you went on the journey to discover the answers for yourself. You already did the hard work. You overcame your own obstacles. Which means, to someone standing in your shoes 2-years-ago, you are "a Niche Expert."

All you have to do is own it.

Accept that you are a Niche Expert to someone who is a few steps behind you.

And just throw down a rope, and give them a hand.

"But Cole?! Once I pick a niche, I can't ever change it. Wouldn’t it be better to get perfect clarity on my niche before I begin?"

This might be the biggest myth of all.

Most writers and creators in general tend to think that picking a niche is a "marriage" decision—as in, once you pick a niche, you can't ever change it.

And this couldn't be further from the truth.

If you look closely, some of the biggest writers & creators today are in niches they discovered along the way. For example: Ryan Holiday was originally a marketing writer—not a Stoicism writer. He started with a niche, wrote a few books and launched a few products, and then ultimately decided he wanted to try something different. And that "something different" ended up being even more successful than the niche he originally started with.

Which is why we say: choosing a niche isn't a marriage decision.

It's Step 1.

Then, as your library of content begins to grow, as you gather more data, and as you learn what's resonating most with your readers, you have the freedom to choose whether you want to stick with that niche or pivot and move into a different niche over time.

(And sure, some of the people who "used to" follow you for, say, marketing will no longer be interested in your next niche. But that's OK. Because if you are choosing to create a new niche in the future, it's most likely because you have data that proves this is the right decision—which means for every 1 person you lose, you'll gain dozens more.)

Creating a niche for yourself isn't a destination.

It's a skill.

And once you acquire the skill, you can create new & differentiated categories for yourself over and over again.

records.title: Niche Bio Checklist
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/(Bonus) 🎉 The Niche Famous Playbook/Niche Bio Checklist - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: One of the questions we get asked most often is, "How do I write my social bios to get people to want to follow me?" Let’s start with what people do wrong—and t
records.content:
One of the questions we get asked most often is, "How do I write my social bios to get people to want to follow me?"

Let’s start with what people do wrong—and then I’ll walk you through what to do instead:

Mistake #1: Only listing "what you do."

A huge mistake people make when crafting their bio (on any social platform) is treating it as a list of "here's everything I do."

You see this with entrepreneurs, investors, and "business-y" people most often, but it happens in every industry.

Their bio looks like this:

CEO @companyname, Board Member @companyname, Investor @companyname, @companyname, @companyname.

This is a bio that has over-tilted on credibility, and is basically telling the reader, "Hey, I don't need to tell you who I am OR what you can expect from me. You should just know. See all my credibility?"

And this is a giant mistake. Because credibility, by itself, doesn't answer the most important question:

"What sort of content do you create? Why should I pay attention to you?"

Mistake #2: Trying to be Clever, not CLEAR.

The next BIG mistake people make when crafting their bio is (sort of building on the above) assuming the best way to hook the reader's attention is by proving how clever they are.

Their bio looks like this:

Netflix, Pancakes, And Stephen King novels. Don't bother me, I'm writing.

  • Who is this person? No clue.

  • What do they write about? No idea.

  • What can you expect from them? Who knows.

Being clever in your bio is such a wasted opportunity. It's like having 30 seconds in an elevator with someone who has the power to change your life, and instead of pitching them on who you are and your big idea, you decide to start rambling off random movies you love and jokes you've heard on TikTok. So, don't overcomplicate it. More importantly, don't waste the reader's time.

Just be CLEAR and say who you are, what you do, and what sort of content they can expect from you.

Mistake #3: Saying "just sharing what I'm learning."

When you're first starting out, it can feel comfortable to not state anything too directly in your bio—and instead say something like:

"Just sharing what I'm learning along the way."

The problem with this is (whether you realize it or not) you are subtly telling readers, "Hey, just a heads up, I don't really know who I am yet. Or what I do. Or what sort of content you can expect from me. So, if you want to follow me, go ahead. But honestly, I can't promise you anything yet."

Now, does that make you excited to follow them?

Of course not!

They haven't given you a reason to be excited!

Even if you are just starting out, even if you feel like you have a lot of learning to do, even if you feel like you are a complete and total beginner, you do not want to announce that to each and every potential reader & follower who clicks on your profile.

Instead, PLANT YOUR FLAG SOMEWHERE. Claim where you are. Own it.

"I write about parenting tips for moms who just had their first son."

Remember: You can always change what you write about. You can always rewrite and tweak your bio. Everyone does it. Even established writers and creators change their bios as they progress and decide they want to write about different things. It's not marriage decision.

Just own where you are today—and steer your ship moving forward.

Mistake #4: Not updating their profile picture or banner image.

This is a simple thing, but it does make a difference.

Not having a clean profile picture and banner image causes potential readers & followers to come to the following conclusions:

  • “This person isn’t playing the game of digital writing with intention.”

  • “If this person isn’t playing the game with intention, why should I follow them?”

  • “Is this person a bot?”

It’s really simple: people want to FOLLOW people who appear to be moving in a positive and productive direction.

So if you want people to FOLLOW you, you have to signal to them you know where you’re going and it would be in their best interest to FOLLOW you down that path.

*And this is becoming more and more true in the age of AI. People want to follow PEOPLE. Not AI-avatars or lazy human beings who just copy/paste whatever ChatGPT says.

So now, let’s walk through a simple checklist you should follow to position yourself as a leader in your niche.

Step #1: Upload a professional profile picture, and use AI to create a professional header image.

If you don’t have any professional headshots, ask a friend or your significant other to take your picture in front of a white wall using your phone.

From there, you can do some pretty cool stuff with AI these days.

  • You can drop your camera-phone photo into ChatGPT and edit it. You can ask it to remove the background, change the background color, or make your background a specific location. You can also ask it to edit the colors if you want. Then export the final image and upload it to your social platforms.

  • You can take a screenshot of someone else’s header image and ask ChatGPT to replicate it for you. Go find an example of someone’s header banner that you like and then tell ChatGPT, “Can you make me something that looks like this, except…” and then articulate what you want to change, if you want ChatGPT to use a certain picture of yours, etc.

The technology we all have access to today is crazy.

Which means all of these things are table-stakes when it comes to writing on the Internet.

Step #2: Write your short-form bio.

This applies most directly to platforms like:

  • X

  • LinkedIn’s profile bio

  • Instagram / Instagram Threads

  • Even YouTube’s channel bio

All of these social platforms provide minimal space for you to say “who you are and what you do” at the top of your profile.

If you want a few bio templates, here are ones I come back to often (and would recommend you use):

Social Bio Template #1

<Credibility statement.> I talk about <topic> and help people <solve problem>.

Social Bio Template #2

I talk about <topic> and <related topic>. <Credibility statement.> Click below for my free <email course, opt-in, newsletter, etc.>

Social Bio Template #3

I believe <niche point of view>. Follow for <topic> and <related topic>. <Credibility statement.>

~

Either way, don’t overthink this step. Just make sure, in your bio, you say very explicitly what niche/topic you most frequently write about (and ultimately want to become known for and associated with).

Step #3: Write your LinkedIn long-form bio

This is platform-specific, but LinkedIn also allows you to write a long-form bio.

In this bio, you should look to accomplish a handful of things:

  • Point Of View: Tell people why you care about this niche, why you write about it, and why you have the point of view you do.

  • Credibility: Tell people why they should trust you and listen to you on your chosen topic. (Remember, credibility is just “context.” You don’t need to be a world-renowned expert. Just tell the reader how and why you’ve learned all the things you’ve learned—so they understand where your insight is coming from.)

  • CTAs: Tell people where to go next. Give them a high-level tour of your ecosystem. If you’ve written books, where can they find them? If you have a business, what does it do and how can they learn more? If you have a newsletter, what is it and where can people subscribe? Use your bio to give readers a “lay of the land.”

Step 4: Add relevant CTAs to your bio.

The goal of your social bio is to do 2 things as fast as possible:

  • Tell net-new readers what you write about (what they can expect from you)

  • And instruct new readers to some sort of valuable resource—so you can capture their email

However, different social platforms have different constraints when it comes to bio linking and CTAs.

For example, on LinkedIn you can only attach one link to the top of your bio (”Start Writing Online In 5 Days” sends people to our free email course):

Whereas on YouTube, you can add multiple links to the top of your social profile:

If you’re brand new to writing online, just make the link point to your website. (And if you don’t have a website, don’t worry about it. You don’t have to link anywhere, yet.)

But as time goes on, the progression of how to maximize your link-in-bio should look like this:

  • Total Beginner: No link (you might not have anything to point to yet).

  • Beginner: Link to website.

  • Intermediate: Link to weekly newsletter.

  • Expert: Link to free educational email course or valuable opt-in.

Step 5: Pin an asset to the top of your profile.

Lastly, you can further maximize the effectiveness of your social profiles by “pinning” a relevant asset to the top of each profile, like this:


A pinned post could be:

  • A link to a big announcement you’re making, or something you want to actively drive traffic to.

  • A book you’ve written and want to get in front of more readers.

  • Your business, a product you’ve launched, a service you provide, etc.

  • Your weekly newsletter—or some sort of free educational email course.

  • A SaaS platform, or website you’ve created.

  • Etc.

Your pinned post can really be anything you want.

It’s basically just a choice of what you want to prioritize people seeing FIRST when they click through to your profile (so pick something you want to drive traffic to!).

records.content:
Your First 90 Days Of Content Ideas

No matter what niche you pick, your “content strategy” will be the same.

That’s because readers in every single niche all want the same things:

  • They want answers to their questions

  • They want solutions to their problems

  • And they want assets to achieve outcomes

That’s it.

Doesn’t matter if the niche is soccer or knitting or dropshipping or crypto.

All non-fiction writing fundamentally is in service of those 3 things.

Which means, whatever niche you pick, your “strategy” is really to just give readers those 3 things:

  • As clearly as you can

  • As often as you can

  • For as long as you can

Which is why the whole goal is to become known for a niche you own—and for you to become associated with your chosen niche topic.

So, let’s make this extremely prescriptive for you.

If all non-fiction content, in all niches, is in service of answering questions, providing solutions to problems, and providing assets to achieve outcomes, then your first 90 days of content is just 90 different variations of those 3 things.

Your First 30 Days: The 10 Magical Ways

If you’re a beginner and brand new to writing online (and honestly, even if you’ve been writing for a while but haven’t seen any traction), your first 30 days should be focused on experimentation.

The goal is not to write “well.”

The goal is not to pick a niche (yet).

Your #1 goal should just be to write about a handful of topics that are interesting to you and pay attention to two things:

  • What is resonating with readers?

  • What do you enjoy writing the most?

From there, and once you start to narrow down the list of topics you want to write about, you will eventually realize there are only 1-3 topics that a) consistently attract readers who get value from your writing, and b) you enjoy writing about over and over again.

The easiest way to write lots of content in your first 30 days is to oscillate between what I like to call The 10 Magical Ways (To Expand Anything).

Every day, whatever topic you want to write about, pick an “angle” for how you want to write about it from the following list:

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

10 Magical Ways… multiplied by say 3 topics you want to experiment with… equals 30 days of ideas.

Easy!

Days 30-60: 30 Proven Approaches

As you begin to learn “what works” (combined with “what you enjoy”), the next skill to build is to learn how to write about the same topic(s) over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again!

This is how you become known for a niche you own.

For example, just to put this into perspective.

Over the past 10 years, I have:

  • Written over 5,000 articles

  • Written over 3,000 newsletters

  • Written over 10,000 tweets

  • Written over 1,000 LinkedIn posts

  • And filmed over 1,400 YouTube videos

…almost all on the topic of digital writing, writing online, and monetizing your writing.

Learning how to write about the same topic(s) over and over again is a SKILL.

So, for your next 30 days, the goal is to practice that skill!

You can do this by taking any of your chosen topics and combining them with 30 more “Proven Approaches.”

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

These are all “things” you can give the reader that they would want inside your chosen niche, or related to any individual topic you choose to write about.

Days 60-90: MORE

So, where do you go from here?

Are you done? Have you said everything you could possibly say about your chosen topic(s)?

OF COURSE NOT!

How you generate ideas from here is by recognizing that readers will always want MORE.

  • If you’re interested in Stoicism, you will always want MORE Stoicism content.

  • If you’re interested in Writing Online, you will always want MORE Writing Online content.

  • If you’re interested in Day Trading, you will always want MORE Day Trading content.

  • If you’re interested in Romantasy Books, you will always want MORE Romantasy book content.

  • Etc.

So how do you come up with “MORE” to say to your target readers?

  • Step 1: You look back through your first 60 days of content…

  • Step 2: You identity your top 10 highest-performing pieces… (by vVews or by Likes)

  • Step 3: You write about those topics again… but give the reader MORE.

And when I say “MORE,” I quite literally just mean MORE.

If you gave them 3 tips last time, can you give them 7 next time?

If you pointed out 5 mistakes last time, can you point out 10 mistakes next time?

If you showed readers 4 examples last time, can you give them 8 examples next time?

Etc.

The MORE you give readers, in a niche, the happier they will be.

That’s all it takes to become known for a niche you own!

Writing online is a game of 3 things:

  • Building a library of niche content

  • Over a very long time horizon (10+ years)

  • So you can become known for a niche you own

How you do that is by using the above framework to write about the same topic(s) in slightly different ways, always striving to give the reader MORE, for a prolonged period of time.

Writing online isn’t something that produces some massive outcome overnight.

It’s slow. It takes work.

But over months and years, your library of content will become exponentially more valuable. It will compound.

Until eventually, you will own a niche—and be able to make money inside that niche forever.

records.content:
If you want to identify another 50 even more specific, lucrative niches, just pick any growing industry from the above list and combine it with this prompt.

This will show you how, inside any of these growing industries, are dozens and dozens and dozens of smaller, also-growing, also-lucrative niches.

You are a Positioning Consultant, specifically for writers who want to niche down and write about a specific industry, positioning themselves as a thought leader and leading voice within that industry and specific niche..

I am going to give you the industry I would like to be a writer within, and I would like you to present back to me:

- Positioning Upgrade #1: A list of 30 even more specific niches within that industry where I could find potential clients and customers.
- Positioning Upgrade #2: A constellation and list of 30 tangentially related industries or niches that aren’t exactly the same, but “close enough” that a lot of my skills could also be translated there as well.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on some context for each of these pieces I am looking for your help with.

~

Positioning Upgrade #1: Identify 30 more specific niches.

For example, if I say the industry I want to write about is “fitness,” there are actually all sorts of smaller niches (and niche opportunities) within that industry you might not be aware of until someone points it out!

- Big box gyms
- Small boutique gyms
- Cycling studios
- Yoga studios
- Personal training
- CrossFit
- Etc.

But there are almost so many opportunities it can be overwhelming.

So here’s a framework I’d like you to use, and when identifying these 30 more specific niches I’d like you to present the information in a very specific way, using this framework.

There are 6 different ways you can niche down:

1. By Sub-Industry (for example: broad industry = health & fitness, sub-industry = physical therapy)
2. By Demographic (for example: broad industry = healthcare, niche down by demographic = healthcare for veterans, or healthcare for moms on disability)
3. By Experience Level (for example: broad industry = watch collecting, niche down by experience level = watch collecting for beginners, or watch collecting for high-net worth individuals)
4. By Price Point (for example: broad industry = business consulting, niche down by price point = business consulting for Series A startups, or business consulting for $100M companies looking to go public)
5. By Problem (for example: broad industry = Airbnb rentals, niche down by problem = luxury Airbnb rentals that aren’t getting booked, or Airbnb rentals that are losing money because of maintenance costs)
6. By Location (for example: broad industry = therapy, niche down by location = therapists in Chicago, or therapists in Denver Colorado)

So I would like you to generate 30 more specific niche ideas, but organize them into these 6 ways (so there are 5 ideas inside each way).

~

Positioning Upgrade #2: Build a constellation of 30 tangentially related niches/industries.

I call this building your Niche Constellation.

For example, if I say “I write about residential real estate,” yes I’m getting more specific and niching down in the industry of real estate, but there’s no reason why I couldn’t also translate my writing skills into other tangentially related niches.

Such as:

- Mortgage lenders
- Airbnb entrepreneurs
- Commercial real estate entrepreneurs
- Home remodeling services
- Plumbers
- Carpenters
- Interior designers
- Etc.

All of these other industries/niches are still related to “real estate,” which is what creates a Niche Constellation.

So I would like you to build a constellation of 30 related industries/niches to the main industry I give you, showing how much more potential there is for me to leverage my skills in other related spaces.

~

Are you ready for the broad industry I want to write about?

records.title: How To Find Profitable, Lucrative Niches
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/(Bonus) 🎉 The Niche Famous Playbook/How To Find Profitable, Lucrative Niches - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml

records.content:
Now, let’s pretend you understand everything I’ve explained thus far, but still find yourself sitting there going:

“Cole… this all makes sense… and I hear what you’re saying… but I just want to know which niche is going to make me the most money. Can you just give me the answer?”

Sigh.

Sure.

But before I give you the answer, I want to point out a couple things—because I genuinely want you to succeed, and sometimes that means telling you what you NEED to hear before telling you what you WANT to hear.

There are a couple reasons why this question of, “What’s the most lucrative niche?” is fundamentally flawed.

Reason #1: Even if it’s a lucrative niche, if you aren’t passionate about it, readers are going to be able to tell.

Let me give you an extremely obvious example.

There’s a My First Million podcast episode with Kevin Van Trump about paid newsletters. If you don’t know who Kevin is, he runs a company called FARMCON and publishes a newsletter called The Van Trump Report. And on the podcast, he reveals he makes over $20,000,000 per year from his newsletter.

Watch it here.

What’s the niche?

Agriculture Marketing.

Now, if I told you, “Agriculture Marketing is a hot niche and will make you tons of money,” first of all you probably wouldn’t believe me… but second, unless you actually care about Agriculture and Ag Marketing, it doesn’t matter how “hot” the niche is—you’re never going to stick with it.

You’re going to get all excited about it.

You’re going to do it for a few days, maybe a few weeks.

And then you’re going to stop—because the real bottleneck to growth was never “whether or not the niche was profitable.”

The real bottleneck was your own personal interest in the niche.

Which is WHY I stress the importance of a) starting with topics where you have an Information Advantage, and b) picking the one you are most GENUINELY interested in.

Long-term consistency beats all.

Reason #2: Most people reject “profitable niche ideas” if they don’t appear to be “already successful.”

I have mentored thousands of writers, and have heard this faulty belief probably 10,000 times at this point (I’m not exaggerating).

The reason people reject the “profitable niche ideas” I give them (which is why I tend to stay away from trying to prescribe good niches vs bad niches in the first place) is because they want 2 opposing things to be true at the same time:

  • They want a niche that’s different, high-potential, and completely novel and new

  • AND, they want a niche that’s proven and already popular with 0 risk

And fundamentally, those 2 things are not the same.

The REASON a niche has risk IS BECAUSE it’s “different.” And it’s different because… nobody else is doing it (or doing it well).

And the REASON a niche doesn’t have risk IS because it’s “already popular.” Which means it’s NOT DIFFERENT because… everyone else is already doing it!

The richest people in the world are the ones who pursue ideas BEFORE they become conventional—not after. You don’t get rich buying Apple stock in 2024, AFTER everyone has already agreed it’s one of the world’s most valuable companies. You get rich buying Apple stock in 1999 BEFORE everyone has agreed it has the potential to become one of the world’s most valuable companies.

So you can’t say, “I want a new & different & lucrative niche” AND “I want a niche that is already proven, that everyone already likes and accepts and has 0 risk” at the same time.

Reason #3: Even if I give you a high-potential, highly profitable niche idea on a silver platter, chances are, you’re going to say, “No way… that’s too niche! It’ll never work!”

Let me tell you a little story to prove how real this is.

One of our most successful students (who has enrolled in all our writing programs and executed on all our advice) is Jason Strimpel.

Back when he was taking Ship 30 for 30 a few years ago, he started writing about how to write Python Code for people in Quant Finance.

A niche within a niche.

At the time, EVERYONE told him, “That’s too small. That’ll never work. Who would even be interested in that?” Well, we told him the complete opposite. We said, “That’s absolutely brilliant. You should double-down on it. You should make this the only thing you write about, and dominate this niche.”

And being a great student of ours, he listened.

He made Python Code for Quant Finance the niche of his newsletter.

He made Python Code for Quant Finance the niche of his website.

He made Python Code for Quant Finance the niche of his online course.

He made Python Code for Quant Finance the niche of the book he wrote.

For 2+ years, all he did, was dig into Python Code for Quant Finance.

And here’s how he’s doing:

2022: Just 8 months after entering our ecosystem, joining Ship 30 for 30, paying for premium access to Dickie and I, and implementing everything we told him to do (which we’re now sharing with you, here!), over 85,000 followers, 9k email subscribers, and over $50,000 in revenue generated.

2023: Crossed $100k in digital product revenue.

2023, Mid-Year: Crossed $200k.

2023, End Of Summer: About to cross $300k.

2024 Goals: Planning on doing $1M+. And write a book. (Both of which he did.)

Now imagine if you asked, “What’s a niche where I’ll make tons of money?” and I told you, “Writing Python Code for Quant Finance.”

I can guarantee you that you would say back to me:

  • “That’s too niche.”

  • “Nobody is going to be interested in that.”

  • “I don’t think that niche is going to be able to generate a profit.”

  • Etc.

And I know because I’ve run into this with THOUSANDS of other writers, who had the exact same opportunity Jason did, but chose to ignore me—and write about something “popular” and “proven,” but completely undifferentiated instead (like Productivity or Leadership or Personal Development).

Do you understand?

If this feels like tough love, that’s because it is. I’m not in the business of telling you what you want to hear, and validating your faulty beliefs. What you’ve bought is HONESTY, and I feel it’s my duty to tell you the truth regardless of whether or not it’s what you want to hear. My goal is not to make you comfortable. My goal is to help you embrace the discomfort required in order to grow.

And that’s real.

records.description: So, with all of that in mind… Where’s the easiest place to start when coming up with what your niche should be? And where are there opportunities for you to cre
records.content:
So, with all of that in mind…

Where’s the easiest place to start when coming up with what your niche should be? And where are there opportunities for you to create a niche newsletter?

(Regardless of whether you want to write for passion, or profit, or some combination of both.)

In our AI Writing Skool, one of the frameworks we coach our students on is called “Finding Your Information Advantage.”

You see, we all take the knowledge we have for granted:

  • If we move across the country, we take the knowledge of “how to move across the country” for granted.

  • If we buy our first house, we take the knowledge of “how to buy your first house” for granted.

  • If we adopt a dog, we take the knowledge of “how to adopt a dog” for granted.

  • If we remodel our kitchen, we take the knowledge of “how to remodel a kitchen” for granted.

  • If we get promoted, we take the knowledge of “how to get promoted” for granted.

  • Etc.

Every single thing we experience in our lives, we tend to take for granted. And the reason we take it for granted is because we’re in it. We can’t see the forest from the trees—we can’t see “the value of the value.” To us, it’s just something we did, or something we experienced. But the irony is, if a friend were to ask us what we learned or if we had any tips for them, we would happily share (some of us, over-share!) everything we’ve learned and now-know.

And yet, when trying to decide what to write about online, what to build products around, or what to start a newsletter on, nothing comes to mind.

That’s because you take your knowledge for granted!

So, how do you pinpoint your Information Advantage?

Step 1: List All Your Careers & Personal Interests

Now, just because you’ve moved across the country or cooked eggs for the first time doesn’t necessarily mean you should make that thing “your niche.”

A better place to start—particularly when you’re trying to find something at the intersection of Passion & Profit—is to make 2 lists:

  • First, list out all the jobs you’ve ever had. Doesn’t matter if it’s being a barista in college (like me!), or being a doctor for 5 years and then deciding medicine wasn’t for you. Just list them all out. The reason is because any “job” you’ve ever had INHERENTLY MEANS YOU HAVE AN INFORMATION ADVANTAGE… otherwise you wouldn’t have had the job! (Even if it was for a small amount of time.)

  • Second, list out all of your personal interests. I don’t care if it’s Video Games or Pokémon Cards or Knitting or Pottery. Just list out the things you care about and are GENUINELY interested in (as in: you make it a priority in your life to keep learning about it). Why? Because anything you’re genuinely interested in means you spend more time than the average person learning about it… WHICH MEANS YOU HAVE AN INFORMATION ADVANTAGE!

Both of these lists are your lowest-hanging fruit opportunities.

Step 2: Stack-Rank each list by “what you know most about” to “what you know least about.”

Now, within each list is inherently a hierarchy.

Some jobs you’ve held for longer than others. Or had a mentor. Or had more traditional training. Etc. And some jobs you’ve held for less time. Or didn’t have a great manager. Or realized you didn’t like that job as much as you thought you would. Etc.

Great.

Take your Careers list and stack-rank it from “what you know most about” to “what you know least about” depending on whatever your experience level is/was.

Easy example: if you were a Project Manager at a SaaS company for 8 years, and a landscaper one summer when you were 16 years old, those two jobs should sit at opposite ends of the hierarchy. (I’m guessing you know a whole lot more about Project Management for SaaS than you do landscaping.)

Then, repeat the process for your Personal Interests lists.

Some interests maybe you’ve had for 15 years. Others, maybe you just became obsessed with 6 months ago. Chances are, those sit at opposite ends of the spectrum too.

For example: If you’ve been playing classical piano since you were 8 years old, but this year you’ve gotten really into buying watches, those are both interests—but I’m guessing you know a lot more about playing classical piano than you do watches (right now).

Step 3: Ask Yourself, “What Do I Want To Keep Learning About?”

Now, with both of these lists in front of you, here’s the most important question of all.

Do you know the biggest reason people’s digital writing, newsletters, and digital products fail?

  • It’s not because of the niche.

  • It’s not because of the person’s credibility.

  • It’s not because the topic isn’t popular, or they can’t go viral.

It’s none of those things.

The #1 reason why people fail is because they stop.

Here’s a fascinating stat we found, and recently wrote about in our Write With AI paid newsletter.

If you want to enter the top 10% of writers on Substack, literally all you have to do is publish 1x per week for 3 months in a row.

Think about that.

On top of that, 35% of newsletters never make it to 2 issues.

Which means if you can piece together even the slightest bit of patience, discipline, and consistency, you have a Top 1% newsletter.

It’s not hard.

So, the most important question isn’t actually, “What’s going to work? What’s most popular? What’s most profitable? What’s the best niche?” Because none of those things matter if you aren’t able to stick with it. And guess what? If you pick a niche you aren’t genuinely interested in, you’re not going to stick with it.

So…

  • Step 1: Look at your Careers list and your Personal Interests list.

  • Step 2: Look at the hierarchy of each list (what do you know most about vs what do you know least about?).

  • Step 3: Look at the Top 3 in both lists and ask yourself, “Now which of these am I most interested in? Which one do I want to keep writing about?”

Your Niche = the topic where you have the largest Information Advantage x most genuine interest.

Because wherever you are most likely to be consistent is where you are most likely to succeed.

records.title: How To Find The Right Niche For You
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/(Bonus) 🎉 The Niche Famous Playbook/How To Find The Right Niche For You - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Everyone’s biggest question—whenever they start writing online, whenever they want to build their first digital product, or whenever they want to launch a newsl
records.content:
Everyone’s biggest question—whenever they start writing online, whenever they want to build their first digital product, or whenever they want to launch a newsletter—is…

“BUT COLE?! WHAT’S MY NICHEEEEEEEEEEEE!1!?!?!?!11!?!?!!”

(Chances are, if you’re reading this right now, you’re probably here because this is a big question for you as well!)

And the follow-up question everyone has, in some way or another, is usually:

“Oh, and by the way… what is the most lucrative niche? How can I make the most money, the fastest?”

These questions are so simple… that we overcomplicate it.

So, let me start by giving you my overarching framework for writing and monetizing writing in general.

  • Some niches you pick for fun/pleasure/enjoyment/passion/purpose.

  • And some niches you pick for profit.

Period. Full stop. End of story.

For example, most people don’t know that I’m actually a very hardcore literary writer at heart. I really don’t read very many pop-mainstream books. I study genre fiction as a mega-category, but I very rarely read it (and have never been one of those readers who reads 30 mystery books per year, etc.). I can’t stand self-help books. And so on.

When I want to read, I am far more likely to pick up Nabokov, Dostoyevsky, Chekhov, Hemingway, Faulkner, Woolf, Bukowski, Morrison, Baldwin, etc.

Why?

Because I love it. It makes my brain hurt. It feels like mental exercise.

Now, imagine if I came to you and said, “Look… I love hardcore literature. That’s what I want my niche to be..”

And then 2 seconds later, I also said, “Oh and by the way… how do I make a ton of money as a writer? What’s the most lucrative niche?”

I can 100000% guarantee you the answer to both of those questions is not the same.

…and yet, writers everywhere expect them to be.

My Personal POV

Here’s my Personal POV on this topic—do with it what you want.

I think it is exceedingly difficult to try to make “what you love to write about” and “what makes you the most money” the same topic/niche.

Sometimes, it happens. I think James Patterson genuinely loves writing thrillers, and it just so happens that thrillers are one of the largest and most lucrative genre fiction categories in the world. (Although, in his memoir, he even admits to his first love being literature, but realizing in college that literature was never going to make him very much money is why he decided to start writing thrillers. So, there you go.)

But in general, what you “love” isn’t always what makes you the most money.

And what makes you the most money isn’t always what you “love.”

Now, full transparency, I have learned-to-love the sort of writing you’re reading right now.

I actually do love building digital products and writing “how to” content for other writers. I’m very passionate about it, because I genuinely want to see other writers succeed—and I wish, desperately, someone had told me all of these things earlier in my own writing career.

But also, full transparency, my dream was not to become a digital-product-creator. I didn’t graduate from college thinking, “I want to sell online courses and launch digital products.”

The reason I’ve decided to dedicate a DECADE of my life to mastering these skills—through ghostwriting, through creating digital products, through writing-about-writing online, etc.—is because these skills are what allow me to monetize my writing (and “get paid to practice”) and not be a broke aspiring writer working at a coffee shop while pursuing my novel-in-progress.

Said differently: these skills, which are directly correlated to “making more money” as a writer, are what ALLOW me to do the other kinds of writing (literature) on my own terms AND write without the constant stress of needing to figure out how it makes me a ton of money.

SO…

My Personal POV here (again, keep the parts you like and ignore what you don’t) is:

  • If you want to pick a niche and start a newsletter because you love that topic and writing about that topic makes you happy, go for it. Just don’t simultaneously expect that niche to be “your fastest path to making the most money.”

  • And if you want to pick a niche solely to make the most money possible, great. Go for it. Just don’t simultaneously expect that money-making niche to fill the same void in you called “I want to do what I ‘love’ and live my passion.”

They don’t have to be the same.

They might be. They can be.

But they don’t have to be.

And in many ways, there’s tremendous benefit in them being separate.

records.title: Why Niching Down Is So Important
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/(Bonus) 🎉 The Niche Famous Playbook/Why Niching Down Is So Important - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: If you refuse to commit to a niche, what you’re really doing is saying: “I believe I can provide better content, in multiple different industries, than anyone
records.content:
If you refuse to commit to a niche, what you’re really doing is saying:

“I believe I can provide better content, in multiple different industries, than anyone else.”

So, just ask yourself… do you really think that’s true?

Better yet, just do a quick audit of who you follow online and whose content you consume.

Do you only follow 1 person—for everything?

Does that 1 person give you:

  • Financial advice

  • And health & fitness advice

  • And book recommendations

  • And movie reviews

  • And cooking recipes

  • And productivity hacks

  • And interior design tips

  • And, and, and, and, and…?

OF COURSE NOT!

You do not follow 1 person for “everything.”

Instead, you follow:

  • 1 person for financial advice

  • And another person for health & fitness advice

  • And another person for books recommendations

  • And another person for movie reviews

  • And another person for cooking recipes

  • And another person for productivity tips

  • And another person for interior design tips

  • Etc.

Why? Why do you do this? Why do we all do this?

Because it’s impossible for 1 person to be an “expert in everything.”

In fact, what you will find is that writing really great content in ONE niche, on ONE topic, is very hard.

One of my favorite examples is Ryan Holiday.

Ryan Holiday does not write about “everything.”

He writes about 1 thing: Stoicism.

  • He writes Tweets about Stoicism

  • He writes LinkedIn posts about Stoicism

  • He writes Medium articles about Stoicism

  • He writes newsletters about Stoicism

  • He writes books about Stoicism

  • He sells products related to Stoicism

Ryan Holiday would not be “Ryan Holiday,” and would not command 7-figure book advances, if he was constantly jumping around different topics—providing surface-level information across “lots of niches.”

Ryan Holiday is “Ryan Holiday” because he has committed to providing the best content in the world to people interested in Stoicism.

It’s his commitment to a niche that has made him successful.

So, why do so many people struggle to “niche down?”

I have mentored over 15,000 writers across our various writing programs, and the reason so many people struggle here is because of 3 faulty beliefs:

  1. You think you can write “great content” about everything. And you can’t. None of us can. You only think this because you haven’t yet written about any of these things—they’re all just topics floating around in your head. But as soon as you start writing, you will very quickly realize a) some topics are easier to write about than others, b) you enjoy writing about some topics more than others, and c) your readers find value in some topics more than others. But thinking you can write “great content” is the epitome of “ignorance is bliss.”

  2. You think niching down limits your opportunity. Yes, it does—but in a good way. When you say you write about “everything” for “everyone,” you end up writing for no one. Because no one knows whether you’re speaking to them or not. But when you commit to writing to a specific target reader, in a specific niche, that specificity is what ALLOWS you to write about lots of of different things. For example, my niche is Digital Writing and writing online. But can I also write about self-publishing? Yes. Can I also write about fiction? Yes. Can I also write about corporate thought leadership? Yes. But I still need to pick specific as my niche to help people understand who I am, what I do, and how I can help them—as a way of getting their foot in the door.

  3. You think your niche needs to be a topic that encapsulates all of who you are. And this is a recipe for a disaster. Your niche is not some magical box that represents every single thing that makes you “you.” I get it—you’re a multi-dimensional human being with lots of different interests. That’s fine. So am I! But I’d bet you aren’t here right now because you want to hear my opinions on rare tequila, or stories about my beautiful & hilarious dog named Meredith. You’re here because you want help writing online. That’s my niche. Digital Writing. And I’m not confused about the fact that the value I’m providing sits in the context of that niche—which are related to my interests, yes (I like talking about this topic), but more importantly, related to YOUR interests. The niche is how I can help YOU. Not how I can summarize all the things that make me “me.”

In summary: people love to overcomplicate their niche.

And you shouldn’t.

Here’s a simple exercise to find the right niche for you:

(And remember… this is not a marriage decision! You can always change your niche later, if you want to.)

This is a Loom video our head copywriter, Ash Coxon, recorded to show you how he and the team create Carousels in Gamma.

He also put together this quick checklist to help you create your next Carousel on the platform:

Tips On Using Gamma To Create Carousels

This is a quick rundown of tips and tricks you can use to create a Carousel in Gamma:

Theme Setup

You can use the many pre-built themes inside Gamma.

Or you can create custom themes. Simply upload your brand files (if they have them), and the AI will derive colors and fonts. Super quick and easy!

Now, inside every theme, create a library of images that you can use during Carousel creation. This can be pictures of you, images of products/lead magnets, Tweet Piks, etc.

Creating The Gamma

Again, this is super easy.

Follow the on-screen instructions.

Here are some simple tips to keep in mind:

  • Tip 1: Always “Create With AI”. You can start from a blank page inside Gamma, but this makes it 100% less efficient to create Carousels. Instead, always create new Gammas with AI.

  • Tip 2: Importing Existing Content. You can import existing content into Gamma and decide whether you’d like to Preserve the copy, Condense it, or Expand it. Perfect for repurposing existing posts or expanding short-form ideas into longer content.

  • Tip 3: Choose The Right Format. Always create the Gamma in the Social Format (not Presentation or Document).

  • Tip 4: Language Matters! Choose your output language (e.g. English (US)).

  • Tip 5: Refine The Copy Before Asking Gamma To Create The Carousel. As part of the creation process, make sure all the copy is divided between the right number of Cards so that it makes it easier for the AI to generate the Gamma. When editing copy (before Gamma creation), you can add breaks in the card-by-card view.

  • Tip 6: Remove The Junk. If you’re importing existing PDFs and/or content, then look out for stray bullet points and any profile/account images the import might have dragged in.

  • Tip 7: Add Visual Variety. Vary the layout of each slide to introduce some novelty as the reader swipes through the Carousel.

  • Tip 8: Choose Your Export Format Wisely. Always Export as PDF—makes it easier to post to LinkedIn.

records.title: How To Create A Carousel
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 3 - LinkedIn Carousels/How To Create A Carousel - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: When building your carousel, aside from the content INSIDE the Carousel, there are 3 important areas to think about: - The platform you use to build the Carouse
records.content:
When building your carousel, aside from the content INSIDE the Carousel, there are 3 important areas to think about:

  • The platform you use to build the Carousel

  • What you write in the accompanying post

  • How to title the Carousel

Let’s take a look at each one in turn.

How To Build Your Carousel (Pick Your Platform)

There are many different ways to create a Carousel for LinkedIn:

  • If you want a beginner-friendly option to get started, you can create lightweight, text-only Carousels using Typeshare.

  • If you want something slightly more advanced, you can create more branded-looking Carousels using Gamma.

  • And if you want something pro-grade, you can design your own brand kit and design studio inside Claude Design or ChatGPT.

Now, how do you write the post that goes with the Carousel?

How To Write The Accompanying Text Post

You might think that the Carousel is the main event of the Carousel Post.

Well, not quite!

The Text Post you pair with the Carousel is just as important as the Carousel itself. Why? Because what you include here will determine whether the reader will read the full post.

Now, there are 2 schools of thought when it comes to what you should include in this Text Post (aside from writing a strong hook and using the formatting tips we’ve already covered):

  1. Write a short, punchy introduction to encourage people to read the Carousel

  2. Write a high-level summary of the Carousel to tease the value and get people to read it

Both are designed to increase retention on the post (which in turn signals to the algorithm that this content is worth sharing!).

Here’s an example of the first approach:

Notice how the rest of the post is short and sweet (and introduces the Carousel as a way to find out what the 7 small habits are):

Here’s an example of the second approach:

When you click See More, you see some additional context AND an overview of the points covered in the Carousel:

The idea here is that the reader has a “lay of the land” before diving into the content.

Highly recommend you experiment with both approaches in your client’s content!

How To Write The Document Title

Alright, one final pro tip before we wrap up the Carousel section.

The Document Title is VALUABLE real estate on LinkedIn:

This is the Title that appears on the Carousel when you hover over it in the feed (like this):

So you should see this as a secondary headline, and it’s worth spending a few minutes making sure this is short and punchy (and follows all my rules on how to write the perfect headline).

records.title: How To Write & Structure A Carousel
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 3 - LinkedIn Carousels/How To Write & Structure A Carousel - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: Here’s a recommended structure you can use to create your Carousels: Step 1: Create Your Cover Card First, you create the Cover Card. This is the first Card in
records.content:
Here’s a recommended structure you can use to create your Carousels:

Step 1: Create Your Cover Card

First, you create the Cover Card.

This is the first Card in the Carousel.

Here’s a checklist I always run down when creating this first part:

  1. Use a strong visual hook (e.g. use relevant images, etc.).

  2. Write a headline on the cover to re-hook the reader. The main hook lives in the LinkedIn post, but this is the second one. Follow the Headline Writing guide in the Atomic Essay module for a complete guide on how to write a hook for this part of the Carousel.

  3. Write a sub-headline to twist the knife with another opportunity or benefit. Or use it to increase tension.

You want to spend around 80% of your writing time on this part as it’s the part that hooks the reader’s attention on the feed.

Step 2: Write Your Body Cards

These are the main parts of the post.

Here’s a checklist you can use to write these Cards:

  1. Try to stick with one idea per card. E.g. a Mistake, Step, Tip, etc.

  2. Make the first line of the card as short as possible. We want to reduce the cognitive load on the reader. In fact, make all lines in the card as short as possible. Don’t be afraid to split out “bulky” ideas into 2 slides.

  3. Clearly label Steps, Tips, Mistakes, etc. You want to make sure you label your card headers so the reader can skim the Carousel if they want (before diving into the meat of the content): e.g. Tip 1, Mistake 1, etc. Make sure to format it in H1 or H2.

  4. Use bulleted lists. Very important! Again, it makes the card easier to read.

  5. Create an open loop between cards (if possible). This is to keep attention all the way through the Carousel. These mini-open loops help keep the reader engaged.

Step 3: Add A Wrap-up Card

This is a short recap of everything you’ve covered in the Carousel.

Step 4: End On A CTA Card

If you’re trying to get your reader to take action, this is where you introduce the “Ask.”

This could be to:

  • Join your newsletter

  • Sign up for a lead magnet

  • Share the post with others

Etc., etc., etc.

Now you know how to write and structure your Carousel, let’s look at creating them.

records.description: This is one of the most popular formats on LinkedIn. You will have seen them. They look a bit like this: They are a collection of images, packaged up into a PDF
records.content:
This is one of the most popular formats on LinkedIn.

You will have seen them. They look a bit like this:

They are a collection of images, packaged up into a PDF, and posted as a “Document” on LinkedIn.

When they are posted, the reader is able to swipe through the Cards to read the post. Readers swipe left or right to move through them, just like a slideshow. If written and created properly, each Card creates a tiny “open loop” that only closes when they swipe. Instead of scrolling past a single block of text or a static image, readers pause, swipe, and stay.

The goal of Slide 1 is to get your reader to click see Slide 2. And so on.

“But Cole… why are they so popular? Why does everyone seem to create them?”

Ah, glad you asked!

And it can be boiled down to 2 reasons:

Reason 1: Carousels a “visual hook” you can use on LinkedIn.

The other types of visual hooks are Photos, Videos, and Infographics. So, let’s talk about why visual hooks are so important on LinkedIn.

It’s for the same reason any hook is important—to stop the scroll. However, our brains prioritize images over text. Shapes, faces, contrast, and colors hit the attention system almost instantly, before language comprehension even kicks in. Pictures are simply faster for us to recognize.

Think about how you actually scroll through LinkedIn:

  • You scan for visuals first (Is this interesting, familiar, or different?)

  • You process words next (What does this mean, and do I care?)

Your eyes jump image to image, face to face, cue to cue. And somewhere in your rapid-fire scanning, something makes you pause.

That “something” is usually visual.

And that’s why it’s worth optimizing not just what you say but how it looks in the LinkedIn feed.

Reason 2: They allow you to create a “snackable” piece of long-form content.

This is actually pretty genius.

Carousels can be as long as you want. But to a reader, they feel easy to consume. Why? Because you’re guiding the reader through each part of your piece in short-form. Which makes consuming this “long-form” piece of content super easy.

(Remember what we said about creating an “open loop” with each Card? That’s what makes these so snackable!)

In other words, it’s a pretty unique Digital Writing formatting technique.

Let’s look at this example from Eddie Shleyner—where he’s taken this technique to the next level.

He’s famous for being up front about the number of words in his writing before you even start writing.

And he translates this to his Carousels, too:

Notice how the number of words decreases as you read the Carousel:

But you don’t have to add “Words Left” like Eddie here.

Because LinkedIn has it’s own built in feature to let the reader know how “far” they have to go to finish the piece.

It tells you how many slides you’ve consumed out of the total number of slides:

Then on mobile, it doesn’t tell you how many are remaining but does give you an idea of how many pages are in the Carousel itself:

Alright, now we know what a Carousel is and why they’re so popular… let’s start creating them!

3 mistakes people make when trying to <desired outcome>

  • Mistake #1

  • Mistake #2

  • Mistake #3

You would be much better off <what to do instead>.

Writing the prompt

What Are We Writing?

I want your help creating infinite variations of a specific type of short-form post (tweet).

I will give you the topic I want to write about, and I’d like you to write me a short-form post (280 characters or less) about that topic but using this tweet template verbatim.

The template goes like this:

~

3 mistakes people make when trying to <desired outcome>.

  • Mistake #1

  • Mistake #2

  • Mistake #3

You would be much better off <what to do instead>.

~

What Are The Rules?

When writing this tweet, based on the topic I give you, I want you to follow these rules as closely as you can:

  1. The tweet must be 280 characters or less, so that it can be published on X (Twitter) without truncating the post.

  2. The tweet must follow the above template structure and formatting verbatim, only filling in these pieces:

    1. The desired outcome (related to the topic I give you) at the end of the first sentence

    2. The 3 mistakes (it should not say “Mistake,” it should just say the mistake itself) as 3 bullets

    3. The “what to do instead” at the end of the last sentence.

  3. The 3 mistakes must be as specific and tangible as possible. Do not provide vague, non-specific mistakes. Be as actionable as possible, using visceral language.

~

What’s An Example?

To help you build some pattern recognition, here is an example of a complete short-form post following this framework on the topic of personal finance:

~

3 mistakes people make when trying to build wealth.

  • Sinking their life savings into buying a home

  • Day-trading crypto hoping to get rich

  • Becoming addicted to sports betting & prediction markets

You would be much better off renting and buying the S&P 500.

~

Are you ready to use this template to write short-form posts? I will give you the topic.
