records.title: Using AI To Create Leverage As A Writer
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 5 - AI Prompts/Using AI To Create Leverage As A Writer - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: I have an uncomfortable truth I’d like to share with you: In the age of AI, your value as a writer is not your ability to write. It's not about: - Sitting down
records.content:
I have an uncomfortable truth I’d like to share with you:

In the age of AI, your value as a writer is not your ability to write.

It's not about:

  • Sitting down

  • Lighting a candle

  • Smoking a cigarette

  • And having magical words pour out of your fingertips

That's not what being a writer is anymore.

Being a writer is all about articulating how you write and using technology to your advantage.

We’re still very early in the age of AI.

But already, it’s clear that most people only think about how to use AI themselves—failing to realize that every single thing you use AI to do effectively for yourself simultaneously creates an asset or a product you could give away (or even sell) to your readers and target customers. And the good news is that every single niche has its own opportunity to be automated.

You (yes, YOU!) might as well be the writer/creator who builds that leverage for yourself—then you can give the prompts away, sell them, etc.

So, every time you use AI to build a prompt, you have to remember you’re tapping into 3 forms of leverage.

Form 1: Personal Leverage

First, you have to learn how to do something. You have to acquire a skill.

(Remember, you can’t automate what you can’t articulate!)

But as soon as you have that skill, in the age of AI, the very next thing you should do is get some leverage on it.

You should train AI on some component of that task, or set of tasks. Now, AI doesn’t have to be able to do all of it, 100%, end-to-end. But if it can help you do a singular piece of that task, only 10x faster, that’s leverage! And the more areas of your life and business you can make those upgrades, build those systems, and get leverage, the better.

But writing a prompt, or using AI to get leverage on a task for yourself, is only the beginning.

Form 2: Marketing Leverage

The single most valuable type of marketing, ever, is where you give your target customers something for FREE that saves them time or helps make them money.

Which means, every time you write a prompt for yourself, you aren’t just automating yourself or your own work. What you’re also doing is creating an incredibly compelling and valuable marketing asset—an incentive for your target customers to take some kind of action.

For example, you can say, “I built this prompt for myself. It now saves me 5 hours per week. I want you to have it for free. All you have to do is give me your email.”

There is no better marketing than that:

And I believe the masses still haven’t realized this opportunity exists inside every single niche on planet Earth.

Everyone is asking themselves how they can use AI in their life and their business right now. Which means, no matter what your niche is, you have the opportunity to help give people the same prompts and systems you’re building for yourself.

Take advantage of this!

Form 3: Business Leverage

The same way your library of content can be compressed or expanded, free content can become paid content and paid content can be spliced apart into free content… the same is true with AI prompts, Claude .Skills, and other technology assets.

Every time you create a prompt, or build a system for yourself, what you’re really doing is creating an asset—a product.

And you can do all sorts of things with these products:

  • You can give them away for free as incentives in your marketing.

  • Or, you can sell them as stand-alone digital products.

  • Or, you can combine them into a more expensive prompt pack.

  • Or, you can combine them into a prompt pack and give it away for free as a bonus inside one of your other products, platforms, or services.

  • Or, you can make them monthly unlocks as part of your paid community as a retention bonus.

  • Or, you can make them downsells for when someone doesn’t purchase your more expensive product or service.

The list goes on and on.

My point is, anytime you build something for yourself, you have to recognize that you can “sell your sawdust.”

And in the age of AI, prompts are products.

records.title: The 5 Parts Of Mega Prompting
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 5 - AI Prompts/The 5 Parts Of Mega Prompting - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: First, why should you write “mega” prompts? Because you want to give the exact process you want AI to follow to provide a certain output. And even for the most
records.content:
First, why should you write “mega” prompts?

Because you want to give the exact process you want AI to follow to provide a certain output. And even for the most basic of tasks, this means writing longer prompts.

Which means if your prompts are a sentence long, you're doing it wrong. If your prompts are a paragraph long, you're doing it wrong. Your prompts should almost be like mini-books.

Now, if that sounds like too much work, I’m going to make it simple for you. Because once you learn this skill, you’ll be able to create leverage for yourself, in your marketing, and in your business (and we’ll discuss exactly how in the next section).

Let’s work through the 5 parts of AI Mega Prompting with a template I use to write all my prompts.

The template is split into 5 parts:

  1. Introduction. This sets the frame with 3 sub-parts: Specialization (What), Instruction (How), and Context (Why).

  2. Instruction. This restates the task and lays the foundation for your specific method of doing the task.

  3. Context. Inside this part are 3 pieces that make the "how" executable: Rules, Positive Attributes (what “good” output looks like), and Reinforcement Examples (so AI can pattern-match instead of improvising).

  4. Final Delivery. This crystallizes what you're handing over, what you want back, and any hard constraints (length, format, no labels).

  5. Iteration. This is the post-writing part: run your prompt, evaluate the output, identify mistakes, and ask AI why they happened. Then revise the prompt so the mistakes don’t happen again.

Let’s dive in!

Introduction

The goal of this first section is to provide AI context on 3 things:

  • (What) Specialization: What “specialty” would you like this AI (prompt) to have? This helps give AI direction when infinite knowledge is available. This is “what” you would like AI to help you do.

  • (How) Instruction: What “tangibly” would you like AI to do for you? In what order or presentation style? This tells AI what you would like to receive back. This is “how” you would like AI to do whatever it is you’re asking it to do.

  • (Why) Context: What “uniquely” would you like AI to do for you? This tells AI the specific type or way you would like it to accomplish its task. This is the “why” behind asking for something to be done a certain way.

For example:

You are a Positioning Consultant, specifically for freelance writers who want to niche down as ghostwriters.

I am going to give you the industry I would like to be a ghostwriter within, and the service I want to specialize in, and I would like you to present back to me:

  • Positioning Upgrade #1: A list of 30 even more specific niches within that industry where I could find potential clients and consider reaching out to (with niche-specific messaging).

  • Positioning Upgrade #2: A constellation and list of 20 tangentially related industries or niches that aren’t exactly the same, but “close enough” that a lot of my skills could also be translated there as well.

  • Positioning Upgrade #3: And a short-form bio (160 characters or fewer, so it fits on X/Twitter) that positions me as a specialist in that industry, providing the specific service I want to offer.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on some context for each of these pieces I am looking for your help with.

Instruction

In the introduction, you will have prompted AI to:

  • Specialize in a skill

  • Instruct on a task

  • And give context on how you would like it to perform that task

Next, you must clarify the Instructions.

Quite literally, this is where you must repeat “what” you want AI to help you do, and then set the foundation for “how” you would like AI to perform that task.

The “how” is the most important part of the prompt (and where prompts truly become Intellectual Property) because anyone can ask AI to do “something.” What makes your prompt unique is that you are asking AI to do something in a particular way. This is no different from hiring an employee who has a specialized skill set. You aren’t just hiring them for a role—you’re hiring them to perform a role in a specific, unique, differentiated, and valuable way.

The same logic applies to prompting AI.

For Example:

There are 5 formats that work best for thought leadership short-form social content.

  • Format #1: Paragraph Style

  • Format #2: What, How, Why

  • Format #3: Listicle

  • Format #4: Old vs New

  • Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

I’m going to walk you through each format, describe what makes it unique, and then give you several examples of what a great short-form social post executing each format looks like—so you understand how to replicate them.

Context

It’s not enough to tell AI to “do something.” You must also tell it “how” you would like it done—and the more specific you can be, the better.

But in order to tell AI “how” to do something effectively, it needs more than just high-level instruction.

It needs context.

Specifically, AI needs…

  • Rules: Clearly defined rules or explanations for why this particular task needs to be done in the specific way you are explaining.

  • Positive Attributes: Qualities that tangibly and objectively define what would qualify as a “good” output. (Example: It’s not enough to say, “Write 3 really great social posts.” You must define the Positive Attributes that make for “great social posts,” according to you, as clearly as possible.)

  • Reinforcement Examples: Very specific examples that reinforce the rules and positive attributes of the individual task.

Now, a mistake a lot of Prompt Writers make is they do not include examples that perfectly match the rules & positive attributes. The reason this is a mistake is because now AI doesn’t have the ability to create pattern recognition. Instead, it’s forced to “use its own intuition”—which leads to low-quality outputs and sporadic thinking.

For Example:

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is a declarative perspective, opinion, or way of seeing the world distilled down into a single paragraph. Imagine this is the short paragraph in a book that so perfectly summarizes the topic at hand that readers can’t help but highlight it.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

  • Concise language and statements made in the most economical way possible (avoid lots of tiny words that make a sentence sound convoluted).

  • Alternating of long and short sentences to add emphasis, rhythm, and flow into the writing.

  • Some sort of strong opinion, polarizing point of view, declarative statement, or at least a perspective that isn’t “hedging” but takes a stance and stands by it.

  • Lightly poetic language. This should be subtle and barely perceptible to the average reader, but small uses of alliteration, repetition, or the use of literary mechanisms like a Polyptoton (same word, two different parts of speech), or an Antithesis (an obvious observation, followed by a non-obvious observation).

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #1: Paragraph Style short-form posts.

Example #1:

If you’re debating between going to that “networking event” and working, choose the work. When the work works out, the people will still be there to take your call. But if you never do the work, no amount of networking will get it done for you. They won’t take your call either.

Example #2:

Success in life comes down to accepting how the world is and finding ways to make things work to your benefit. Failure in life occurs when you wish things were different, and wait for the world to adjust to you (it never happens).

Example #3:

One key to a good relationship is to simply accept all the things that annoy you about the other person. Acknowledge them, laugh about them, surrender to them, and once you do, it's so much easier to really love them. But until then, their quirks will just irritate you.

Final Delivery

Lastly, at the end of the prompt, you want to crystallize the delivery instructions.

Things you can consider to include here are:

  • Repeating objective constraints

  • Stating what you are going to provide AI

  • Stating what you would like AI to return back to you

  • Describing the final output you want to make sure gets delivered

For example:

I am now going to give you the topic, and I would like you to give me a day’s worth of short-form thought leadership social content.

Each post must read like a standalone Tweet, without any formatting labels or headers, and must fit within the 280-character constraint of X/Twitter.

Iteration

It’s very rare to write a prompt that delivers a perfect output on the first try.

Instead, you should view prompt writing as an iterative game—and one that benefits from conversing with AI itself.

  • Run the prompt

  • Evaluate the output

  • Identify mistakes

  • Share those mistakes with AI and ask why they happened

  • And ask what you should change in the prompt so those mistakes don’t happen again

Repeat this process several times to stress-test your prompt and ensure you can recreate positive outputs over and over again.

Boom, now you know how to write an AI Mega Prompt!

But why should you even learn this skill?

Well, for 3 reasons—which we’ll cover next.

records.description: If I told you to write a “really great” piece of writing, would you know what I expected? Of course not! Why? Because “really great” is subjective. Ask 10 peopl
records.content:
If I told you to write a “really great” piece of writing, would you know what I expected?

Of course not!

Why?

Because “really great” is subjective. Ask 10 people to define it, and you’ll get 10 answers.

Answers like:

  • “It needs to read like a Hemingway short story.”

  • “The writing should be laden with stories and examples like a Ryan Holiday book”

  • “The world-building should be elegant and majestic, as if I’m reading an Ursula K. Le Guin story.”

And even in THOSE answers we have “bundled” language:

  • What is a Hemingway short story like?

  • What kind of stories should I use to be like Holiday?

  • How does Le Guin execute her world-building?

People use these bundled terms because they don’t know EXACTLY what they’re asking for.

So, to drive this home, I want to give you a non-writing example.

Let’s say your friend Tom is staying the weekend.

You say, "Hey Tom, I could really use your help doing the dishes." But "doing the dishes" is a bundled term**.** Tom has no idea HOW you want them done. And Tom ends up making a mess in your kitchen, overfilling your dishwasher, and clogging your filters with leftover food!

(Yeah, he isn’t the best house guest!)

But Tom becomes effective when you “unbundle” the request of “doing the dishes”:

  • Emptying the dishwasher

  • Putting the dirty plates, cups, pots, and pans in the sink

  • Scrubbing the food off of each plate, cup, pot, and pan

  • Putting dishwasher-safe plates and cups in the dishwasher

  • Hand-washing the remaining pots, pans, and non-dishwasher-safe items

  • Scrubbing the countertops and stove with a soapy sponge

  • Cleaning and drying the countertops and stove with a wet, and then dry, paper towel

When you look at a list like that, notice how saying, “Just do the dishes!” isn’t a very clear instruction.

It only becomes clear when you break the larger task (and bundled term) down into smaller variables.

In this scenario, AI is Tom. So, you need to do the same thing when prompting AI.

And to help you lay out exactly what you want AI to do, I’m going to give you the 5 steps to writing an AI Mega Prompt.

records.title: Why 95% Of AI Prompts Give Terrible Outputs
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 5 - AI Prompts/Why 95% Of AI Prompts Give Terrible Outputs - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: The vast majority of prompts give results you can barely use. But that’s not because AI is “bad” at writing (or any other task you want it to perform). It’s bec
records.content:
The vast majority of prompts give results you can barely use.

But that’s not because AI is “bad” at writing (or any other task you want it to perform). It’s because most people can’t articulate what they actually want. And the great thing about AI is that the bottleneck to getting good results from it isn’t your ability to code or your knowledge of a particular technology. No, the bottleneck is your ability to describe clearly to AI what you actually want.

There’s something we say over and over again in our AI Writing Skool:

“You can't automate what you can't articulate.”

The difference between ineffective and effective AI writing comes down entirely to the ability to articulate the instructions.

People write "go do this thing" and don't realize how many implied components they're deferring to the technology.

You haven’t told AI a number of variables that impact what it produces:

  • Is this good or bad output?

  • Is this what you want stylistically?

  • Is this actually how you, the writer, would do it?

And I know what you’re thinking…

“But Cole, I’ve tried writing longer prompts, but I still get AI slop—it’s just bad at writing!”

All good.

After all, this is still a relatively new technology, and we’re all trying to get the hang of it! If you’re not getting the results (or near to the results) you want from AI, then you need to beef up your prompt even more. You need to remove all doubt from AI’s “mind” about what to do for you.

Let’s look at an example.

Bad Example of an AI Prompt: “I need help writing some social content for a client of mine. She works in health and wellness. Write me three really great social posts that she'll love."

Here’s what happens when you feed this to ChatGPT:

Notice how AI even works through some of the assumptions it is making when writing these posts!

And guess what?

The output is pretty average (no surprises there!).

So, how do you write good AI prompts?

Well, here’s a quick comparison of the qualities of Bad vs. Good AI Prompt Writing.

Bad Prompt Writing:

  • Uses general, “bundled” language

  • Contains subjective directions

  • Specifies no clear format

  • Gives no examples of the required output/thinking

  • Doesn’t provide an output request

On the other hand, Good Prompt Writing:

  • Uses specific language to describe “unbundled” tasks

  • Gives objective directions

  • Specifies certain formatting frameworks for output

  • Lists out exact examples of output/thinking

  • Gives an exact output request

So, how do you achieve all of these?

Well, to do all those things in the “Good Prompt Writing” list, you need to UNBUNDLE your language and tasks.

Which is what we’re going to look at next.

records.content:
As with all AI output, edit these to suit your voice, style, and approach.

Your Engagement Prompt

This prompt will help you come up with a response to any LinkedIn post by summarizing the core ideas in the post according to 10 categories:

  1. The big idea

  2. A belief inside it

  3. A surprising connection

  4. An analogy

  5. An insight from an expert

  6. A contrasting viewpoint

  7. A common misconception or mistake

  8. A provocative take

  9. A benefit and its ultimate impact

  10. A problem, its root cause, and its ultimate impact

Then you can pick one of these points and say whether you’d like to Affirm, Disagree, Question, or Reframe.

It will then generate a comment for you (which you can edit before posting!).

To use this prompt:

  1. Copy and paste it into your chosen LLM (we recommend Claude)

  2. Paste in the post you want to react to

  3. Follow the on-screen instructions

You are my commenting assistant. You help me write sharp, human comments on other people's posts — comments that sound like me thinking out loud, not like generic praise.

Here's how we'll work, in two steps. Do NOT skip ahead.

STEP 1 — BREAK DOWN THE POST

When I paste a post, read it and return a NUMBERED list of angles I could react to:

1. The big idea
2. A belief inside it
3. A surprising connection
4. An analogy
5. An insight from an expert
6. A contrasting viewpoint
7. A common misconception or mistake
8. A provocative take
9. A benefit and its ultimate impact
10. A problem, its root cause, and its ultimate impact

Rules for this list:
- Each item is 15 words or less.
- No jargon. Simple and clear.
- Colloquial — write it like you're reflecting to yourself.
- Draw each angle out of the post; if one isn't explicit, infer the most plausible version.

Then stop and ask me: "Which number do you want to react to, and how — Affirm, Disagree, Question, or Reframe?"

Do not write a comment yet.

STEP 2 — WRITE THE COMMENT

Once I give you a number + a stance, write ONE comment in the first person using this five-beat structure:

1. Opener (1 sentence): my reaction, flavored by the stance.
2. My angle (1 declarative sentence, 10 words or less): the core of what I'm saying.
3. Why it matters (1 sentence).
4. The useful bit (1 sentence): a tip, a mistake to avoid, an example, or what makes me ask.
5. Close (1 sentence): land it, or invite a reply.

How each stance shapes beats 1 and 2:

- AFFIRM — Opener agrees and adds weight. Beat 2 sharpens or extends their point (don't just repeat it).
- DISAGREE — Opener pushes back respectfully ("I actually see it differently"). Beat 2 is my counter-claim.
- QUESTION — Opener shows genuine curiosity. Beat 2 is the core question, phrased sharply (and beat 4 is what makes me ask).
- REFRAME — Opener offers another lens ("Here's another way to look at it"). Beat 2 is the reframed idea.

Voice rules for every comment:
- First person, always.
- Short sentences. No jargon. Sound like a real person, not a brand.
- It's a reply to their post — it can nod to what they said, but it stands on its own.

EXAMPLES (post: "The only way to grow on LinkedIn is to post every single day.")

AFFIRM:
Couldn't agree more — consistency beat everything else for me.
Showing up daily compounds faster than any single viral post.
Most people quit right before it starts working.
Pick one format and repeat it for 30 days straight.
Boring and consistent wins.

DISAGREE:
I actually see it differently here.
Daily posting matters less than saying something worth reading.
Frequency without a point just trains people to scroll past you.
I'd post twice a week and make each one count.
Quality earns the follow, not the calendar.

QUESTION:
This made me pause for a second.
Is it really daily posting, or daily showing up?
Plenty of accounts grow on three sharp posts a week.
I'm curious what broke for you when you dropped below daily.
Where's the line actually sit?

REFRAME:
Here's another way to look at it.
Daily posting is a side effect, not the goal.
The real driver is having enough ideas worth sharing.
Build the idea pipeline first and the frequency takes care of itself.
Fix the input, not the output.

START

Confirm you're ready, and I'll paste the first post.

Your CTA Prompt

To use this prompt:

  1. Copy and paste it into your chosen LLM (we recommend Claude)

  2. Paste your post into the chat

  3. Tell AI which option you’d like to use (Share, Follow, Newsletter CTA). If Newsletter CTA, it will ask you for additional details. If you don’t have all of them, just say “Don’t include this”

Enjoy!

You are a Call-To-Action (CTA) strategist and copywriter, specifically for content creators who want to grow their audience on social media (LinkedIn, X, Instagram, and similar platforms).

I am going to give you a social media post I'm about to publish, and tell you which ONE of three growth goals I want the CTA to serve. I would like you to present back to me:

3 Tailored CTAs: three distinct, ready-to-paste calls-to-action written specifically for the content of my post — each one drawing on a DIFFERENT proven CTA style so I get three genuinely different angles to choose from.

To accomplish this, I am going to train you on the context for each of the three goals so you can replicate the style that works, instead of falling back on generic "please share / please follow / please subscribe" copy.

IMPORTANT — follow this conversation flow. When I send you this prompt, do NOT write any CTAs yet:

Step 1: Reply by asking me to paste the post I'm about to publish. Say nothing else.

Step 2: Once I give you the post, read it and identify its core idea, the specific problem or topic it addresses, and who would most benefit from it. Then present me the three options to choose from, exactly like this, and ask me to pick one:

   "Which goal do you want this CTA to serve?
   Option 1 — Share: get readers to share/send/tag your post to people in their network.
   Option 2 — Follow: get readers who don't yet follow you to hit follow.
   Option 3 — Newsletter Opt-in: move readers off social media onto your owned email list.
   Reply 1, 2, or 3."

Step 3: If — and only if — I choose Option 3, ask me for the runtime details you can't get from the post: my newsletter URL, my subscriber count, my publishing cadence, and any credibility stats or outcomes I want to feature. Do not invent these.

Step 4: Write the 3 CTAs for the chosen option, following the rules below.

There are 3 CTA goals that work best for growing a creator's audience:

Option 1: Share CTA — get readers to share/send/tag the post to people in their network.
Option 2: Follow CTA — get readers who don't yet follow me to hit follow.
Option 3: Newsletter Opt-in CTA — move readers off social media onto my owned email list.

I'm going to walk you through each goal, describe what makes a great CTA for it, and give you several proven example templates — so you understand the pattern well enough to write fresh, post-specific versions. For whichever goal I pick, write 3 CTAs, and make each one lean on a DIFFERENT example style from that goal's set.

----- OPTION 1: SHARE CTA -----

Rules (and why):
Frame the share as a favor to the reader's NETWORK, never as a favor to me. People share what makes them look helpful to others and what's easy to act on. A "please share so I can grow" ask gets ignored; an ask that helps a specific person the reader knows feels natural and gets acted on.

Positive attributes of a great Share CTA:
- Frames the share as helping someone else (a friend, colleague, or their wider network), not helping me.
- Points at a specific type of person who needs this — tied to the actual problem or topic in the post.
- Low friction: one clear action (share, send, tag, or repost).
- Short and punchy enough to sit naturally at the end of the post.

Reinforcement example styles (adapt these to the post; don't copy verbatim):
- The Direct: "Found this useful? Share it with someone who needs to hear it today."
- The Specific Person: "Know someone who's [struggling with the problem in the post]? Send this their way — it might save them [time/money/headache]."
- The Tag: "Tag the one person who needs this reminder right now. 👇 (We all have that friend.)"
- The Mission: "My goal is to help [number/audience] people [outcome]. If this resonated, a quick share gets it in front of the next person who needs it."
- The Repost Nudge: "If [core idea of post] hit home, repost it. Someone in your network is dealing with [problem] right now and doesn't know where to start."

----- OPTION 2: FOLLOW CTA -----

Rules (and why):
Give the reader a concrete reason this post won't be the last good one — either trigger FOMO (loss aversion) or make a clear promise of future value. "Follow me" alone is about me; people follow when they believe they'll MISS OUT on more value like what they just consumed.

Positive attributes of a great Follow CTA:
- Anchors to the value they just got ("more posts like this one").
- Either triggers FOMO/loss-aversion (the algorithm, missing out) OR makes a clear promise of what they'll get by following.
- States or implies my topic/lane so the follow feels relevant, not random.
- Short, casual, and low-pressure.

Reinforcement example styles (adapt these to the post; don't copy verbatim):
- The FOMO: "Don't let the algorithm swallow this. Follow me so the next post like this actually shows up in your feed."
- The Promise: "This is one of [number] posts I've written on [topic]. Follow for more on [what you cover] — [cadence]."
- The Credibility: "I've spent [X years] [doing the thing] and [credibility statement]. Follow along if you want [outcome] without the fluff."
- The Niche Clarity: "I post about [topic 1], [topic 2], and [topic 3] — no [thing they don't want]. If that's your kind of thing, hit follow."
- The Casual: "If you made it this far, we'd probably get along. Follow me for more [type of content]. 👋"

----- OPTION 3: NEWSLETTER OPT-IN CTA -----

Rules (and why):
The job is to move attention from a "rented" social audience to an "owned" email list. A generic, intangible CTA ("Sign up for my newsletter updates here") won't cut it, because people are swamped with demands on their attention every hour. You must beef up the copy with credibility, social proof, and benefit-focused language so subscribing feels worth it.

Positive attributes of a great Newsletter Opt-in CTA:
- Mixes in at least one of: credibility, social proof (subscriber count), or a benefit-focused outcome.
- Makes a tangible promise of what they get AND how often (the cadence).
- Ties the newsletter's topic back to the post they just read.
- Ends with a clear action and the link.

Reinforcement example styles (adapt these to the post; don't copy verbatim):
- The Classic: "If you love ideas like this, you'll love my newsletter. Every [cadence], I share [2-3 words on what they get]. Join [subscriber number] here: [URL]"
- The Credibility: "By the way, I have [credibility statement 1]. And [credibility statement 2]. Want to know more about [topic related to post]? Subscribe to my newsletter for [cadence] updates: [URL]"
- The Benefits: "If you're looking to [outcome], then my newsletter is for you. I'll show you how to: [benefit 1] / [benefit 2] / [benefit 3]. Join [X] other subscribers here: [URL]"
- The Pivot: "I love [point related to post]. And over the last [X] years, I've [credibility]. It's how I [outcome]. Subscribe for [cadence] updates on [topic]: [URL]"
- The Proven Path: "The quickest way to [outcome]: [topic related to your newsletter]. This is how I [achievement 1, achievement 2]. Every [cadence], I share [tips/frameworks/guides] on how to [outcome]. Join [X] other subscribers here: [URL]"

Once I've given you my post and picked an option (and, for Option 3, the runtime details), return exactly 3 CTAs for the chosen option.

Requirements for the output:
- Each CTA must be tailored to the actual content of my post — reference its real topic, problem, or idea, not placeholders (except for true runtime values like [URL] or subscriber count that I supply).
- Each of the 3 CTAs must use a DIFFERENT example style from the chosen option's set, so I get three distinct angles.
- Keep them punchy and ready to paste at the end of a post.
- Label each CTA with the style name it's based on (e.g., "The FOMO"), but keep the CTA copy itself clean and free of any other labels.
- Keep them platform-agnostic unless I tell you which platform I'm posting on.

Remember: do not produce any CTAs until you've asked for the post (Step 1) and I've chosen an option (Step 2).

records.content:
Here's the thing about engagement:

One thoughtful comment does almost nothing. A thousand thoughtful comments builds an entire trail of “mini” content all leading back to you.

In other words, thoughtful engagement COMPOUNDS. So the goal here isn't to be brilliant every day. The goal is to make this so simple that you can do it every day and unlock all the benefits of engagement compounding.

Let’s dive in.

Before You Start: The One-Time Setup

You only do this once.

Block off 30 minutes, knock it out, and you never have to think about it again.

  • Write down 9 niches that are 1 degree away from yours. Not your exact niche—the ones sitting right next to it. (Remember: their audiences probably don't follow you yet.)

  • Build your list of 20+ Creators. 2-3 per niche. People who are clearly doing well and posting consistently.

  • Set up your X Pro deck with 3 Columns: your handle mentions, your private X List, and 1-2 keyword searches for your niche.

  • Set up your LinkedIn Google Sheet with each Creator's name and a link to their Recent Activity page (not their profile).

Done?

Good.

Now you never have to hunt for anyone again. Everything lives in one place.

The Daily 30 Minutes

⏱️ Minutes 0-5: Take Care of Your Own House First

Before you go build bridges anywhere else, handle the audience you already have.

  • Open your mentions Column in X Pro. Reply to anyone who tagged you, quoted you, or asked you something.

  • Reply to every comment on your own posts. On LinkedIn, do this within the first hour of posting—it significantly boosts the post in the algorithm.

  • Reply like a human, not a brand. "Thanks!" is a wasted opportunity. Add a sentence. Ask them something back. Every reply is a mini-post.

⏱️ Minutes 5-20: Build Your Bridges

  • Open your X List Column and your LinkedIn Sheet of other creators you want to engage with. Fly down them. Don't get tempted to browse the Home or For You feed—that's where 15 minutes turns into 90.

  • Leave 5-10 thoughtful comments on recent posts. Prioritize posts that are a few hours old and clearly picking up steam—you want to be early on a wave, not late.

  • Comment like you're publishing, not replying. Share a story, an insight, a lesson, a disagreement. Something that stands on its own even if you deleted the original post.

  • Stuck on what to say? Paste the post into the Engagement Prompt (see bonuses below), pick an angle, and choose your stance: Affirm, Disagree, Question, or Reframe. Then edit it so it sounds like you.

  • Skip anything you have nothing real to say about. "Great post 🔥" builds zero bridges. Move on.

⏱️ Minutes 20-25: Restock The Pipeline

Your list of Creators should be growing every single week—so let’s add to it!

  • Open your keyword Column in X Pro and scan what's surfacing in your niche today.

  • Add 1-2 new Creators to your X List or LinkedIn Sheet. New and emerging accounts count—they're often the most receptive to engagement.

  • Screenshot or save anything that sparks an idea. Comments you almost wrote, posts you disagreed with, angles you hadn't considered. This is tomorrow's content, for free.

  • Prune anything dead. If someone hasn't posted in a month, they're not a bridge. Cut them.

⏱️ Minutes 25-30: Close The Loop With a CTA

You wrote the content. Now squeeze the juice out of it.

  • Add a CTA to today's post. Pick one: Share, Follow, or Newsletter.

  • Put it at the bottom of the post for LinkedIn, Articles, and Substack Notes. Put it in the follow-up post for X threads and IG Threads.

  • Don't reuse the same CTA every day. Rotate through the templates so it never reads like a signature block.

  • Short on time? Paste your post into the CTA Prompt (see below) and pick one.

The Weekly Add-On (10 Minutes, Once a Week)

Do this on the same day every week. Sunday works well.

  • Find your best-performing comment from the past 7 days. Sort by likes/replies if you have to.

  • Copy and paste it into your own content queue. If it worked as a comment, it'll work even better as a post.

  • Check who's engaging back with you. Anyone who's replied to you 2-3 times is becoming an Internet friend. Move them to the top of your list.

  • Add 3-5 new Creators to bring your list back up to strength.

Some Rules To Help You Stay Consistent

  1. Same time every day. Morning is easiest, because your energy for thoughtful comments is highest before you get distracted by other demands.

  2. Timer on, timer off. 30 minutes means 30 minutes. If you're still scrolling at minute 45, this means you’ve become a consumer, not a creator.

  3. Never open the home feed. Your Columns and your Sheet are the only two places you're allowed to go in those 30 minutes. That's the entire point of building them.

  4. Quality over volume, always. 5 comments that say something real beat 50 that say "This 👏".

  5. Consistency over intensity. 30 minutes a day for a year beats a 6-hour engagement binge you never repeat.

That's it!

records.description: I’m going to show you how to set up some “Dashboards” to making engaging on X and LinkedIn easy. X: Using “X Pro” To Set Up An Engagement Dashboard X makes it S
records.content:
I’m going to show you how to set up some “Dashboards” to making engaging on X and LinkedIn easy.

X: Using “X Pro” To Set Up An Engagement Dashboard

X makes it SUPER easy to engage with your posts or with other creators using X Pro.

Think of X Pro as a turbo-charged Search Engine that you can use to search X, built directly within the platform.

The best part about it?

You can use it to create your own personalized feeds just like this inside X:

This is a Premium feature… so if you’re writing on X, then make sure they upgrade!

You can use X Pro to create feeds based on certain criteria.

Here are a few useful examples:

  • Show handle mentions

  • Show people from an X List

  • Search for particular keywords

I’m going to walk you through each one, explaining a) when you’d use this and b) how to set it up inside X Pro.

Before we dive in, it’s important to clear up some X Pro terminology:

  • Columns. These are the “feeds” you create within X Pro that contain all the results from the search. You specify the specific search criteria within a column’s settings.

  • Decks. This is a collection of Columns. You can create multiple Decks and add different Columns to them (using the symbol below):

Then, once you’re in one of these Columns, you can post replies to any of these posts inside the personalized feeds.

Pretty cool, right?

Alright, let’s get started on how to set all of this up!

Method 1: Show handle mentions

You can use this Method to search for mentions of your username across X so you can a) respond to any engagement and b) keep tabs on what people are asking you.

Here’s how to set it up:

  • Add a new Column and select the “Search” option. You could use the Profile option but it will essentially just show a chosen Profile in the Column. Useful, but not ideal if you want to find all mentions of a handle—which is what we want to do here.

  • Add the handle you want to monitor. You can edit all the different search criteria to filter to your heart's content! Worth playing around with this depending on exactly what you want to see (maybe you only want to see posts with a certain number of likes, etc.).

  • Click “Search”. The new Column is added and you can interact directly with the posts.

Method 2: Show people from an X List

If you don’t know already, X has a feature called “Lists.”

These Lists are a way of keeping track of different accounts at once. You can use this to keep track of the people you’re going to be engaging with. So, instead of navigating to each profile, you can use Lists and X Pro to rapid-fire your engagement all in one place (saving you HOURS!).

Let’s look at how to get this started.

Step 1: How to create an X List

To create your X list, go to https://x.com/i/lists/create.

Type in a name for your list, a short description, and make it private.

(I recommend making it private because if you don’t every user you add will get a notification that you’ve added them to your list. It saves them a notification and gives you some privacy!)


Step 2: Add people to your List.

Now, populate the List with relevant accounts.

To do this, click on “Suggested” and search for people. When you find someone you’d like on your list, click Add.

Step 3: Add your List to X Pro

X’s default way of using Lists isn’t very good.

You can either let the algorithm choose which tweets to show you from the List (the same way the home feed does in an unpredictable fashion), or you can show tweets chronologically (which floods your feed with irrelevant replies and makes it hard to manage).

Neither of these will help you—so we need an alternative.

This is where we put the list inside X Pro:

This involves a few steps, so follow along closely.

  • Add a new Column. Click the “Add column” button, then click “Search”

  • Navigate to your X list and copy the “number” at the end of the URL. Remember that list we created in the previous section? We are going to navigate to that List on your Desktop. From there, you need to look at the URL bar and copy the number that comes after /lists in the URL, like the image below. To find the list, go here: https://x.com/<insert your handle>/lists


  • Create an Advanced Search query in X Pro using that list number. Back in X, create an Advanced Search query of the form “list:yourlistnumber” This will now show all tweets from people in this List, which is X’s default setting.


  • Add Advanced Search queries to make the List nothing but pure signal. Now, if we were to leave this Search setting just like it is now, we would get the same noisy timeline that comes via the default X settings. So instead, we are going to add some advanced search queries to take out the noise.‍

  • -filter:replies. Adding this snippet will remove all replies from people on this List, so you only see their main posts (instead of seeing everything they reply to every person).‍

  • min_faves:50. Adding this snippet will show you only tweets from this list that get 50 or more likes. You can dial this number up or down based on how popular you want the posts to be.

Boom, you’re done!

Now you can fly down this list and do your engagement in a fraction of the time.

Method 3: Search for particular keywords

If you want to keep track of keywords related to your niche (which is a good way of expanding the audiences you can borrow from by keeping tabs on new and emerging accounts in the niche), then you can search for them inside X Pro.

The same principle applies from the last 2 methods:

  • Use the “Search” option when creating the Column

  • Type in the Keyword you’d like to track

  • Alter the filters as required

  • Click the Search icon—and you’re done!


How To Setup A LinkedIn Engagement Dashboard

You could use LinkedIn Sales Navigator to keep track of all the accounts you want to engage with in your niche.

But honestly?

It’s overkill and doesn’t make commenting any easier:

Which is totally fine—it’s geared more towards Sales Teams.

So, in order to a) respond to comments and b) engage with others, we’re going to use a simpler system.

First, keep track of comments on your LI posts.

This is easy.

Just respond to the comments within the first hour after posting to significantly boost the post inside the LI algorithm.

Second, create a list of other creators/professionals whose audience you want to “borrow.”

Don’t track this in Sales Navigator. Instead, you’re better off just using a Google Sheet to keep track of a list of names and a link to their “Recent Activity”.

Why “Recent Activity” and not the Profile itself?

Well, every time you view someone’s profile on LinkedIn, it sends them a notification. And if you’re clicking through to someone’s profile every day, they’re gonna have a ton of profile notifications (and wonder why you are making so many visits!).

You can easily skip this (and find the profile’s most recent posts) by going to their Recent Activity page.

So, how do you find their “Recent Activity” page?

Simple!

  1. Navigate to their profile

  2. Go to their Activity section and click “Show all”:


  1. Copy and paste the URL of the page into your Google Sheets tracker:


Easy!

Now you can fly through all your engagement in a matter of minutes every morning (and not wrestle with Sales Navigator!).

records.title: Comments-As-Content

records.content:
Most people who want to start creating content online think their job is to create and share content from their own profile.

And yes, that's true.

You create a profile. You get handed your Digital Megaphone. And then you start talking into your Digital Megaphone with the hopes of people hearing what you have to say and deciding to stick around to hear more. Then you reply to people’s comments on your content.

This is content creation 101.

But what most people don't consider are the other ways they can introduce people to their content. The most powerful one being: commenting.

When you "comment" on someone else's content online, you aren't just responding. What you're really doing is you're publishing content—just within the context of someone else's content. It's the same thing as hitting "publish" from your own profile, except here, your content is much more likely to be seen by "the right people."

For example:

Let's say you want to write, Tweet, or post on LinkedIn about what it's like to work for yourself, be a solopreneur, etc.

What most people think to do is create and publish this content from their profile. Right? That's content creation 101. But that's not the ONLY way for you to get eyeballs on your content, your stories, your insights, your lessons learned, your perspectives, etc.

Another option is to go find someone else—a Creator who has a much larger following than you do—and find one of their recent posts on that same topic. Then, instead of publishing your story, or your insights from your own profile, share what you want to share as a Comment on their post.

Here are a few of the benefits of this strategy:

  1. If you have a small audience, this is an easy way to ensure people actually see your content (because you're riding another Creator's wave).

  2. You essentially guarantee that your content is going to be seen by "the right readers"—since you are publishing it within the context of a topic those readers have already engaged with.

  3. You can test ideas as comments, first. And then if a particular comment attracts engagement, you can take that as signal to double-down and create something similar again from your own profile.

  4. The more you engage with Creators bigger than you, the more they see your name & content, the more they inherently start engaging with you, the more your content gets seen & shared, the more you become "Internet friends" with them, etc.

  5. And maybe most importantly, every time you comment thoughtfully on a tangentially related Creator's content, you are building a bridge between their content and yours.

Think about this for a second:

Imagine you did this a few times every day for 5 minutes in the morning.

You make a list of Creators who publish content similar (or tangentially related) to you.

You thoughtfully comment on some of their more popular posts with ideas, stories, perspectives of your own.

And each one of those comments taps into their much larger audience, introducing a handful of people to you and your library of content (which you know they are going to be interested in because you and that Creator both create "similar" types of things!).

Think of how much faster you would grow!

We call this The Bridge Content Strategy.

This is not content you publish from your own profile.

It's content you publish "inside" other Creators' content—building bridges between them and you.

For example:

Here's a Tweet by a similar Creator to us (and a friend of ours), Justin Welsh.

And here is Dickie's thoughtful response/comment.

Now, here's what this achieved:

  • This comment received as much engagement as, if not more than, most things Dickie publishes on Twitter.

  • This comment validated an idea Dickie had been wanting to write about—and now data confirms that readers are interested in this idea.

  • This comment engaged "the right readers," because it was published in an already-working, relevant Thread published by someone else.

  • And this comment successfully built a bridge between Justin's audience and Dickie's audience—introducing people who follow Justin to Dickie.

Now imagine doing this 10x, 100x, 1,000x over the course of a year.

You would have an entire city of bridges built between other Creators and you!

More importantly, what did Dickie do?

He later copy/pasted this comment and used it as content in his weekly cadence—and it performed even better.

So, how do you get started with this Strategy?

Let’s take a look.

Step 1: Make a list of 9 other relevant niches.

Let's build some bridges!

First, think about what other niches are tangentially related to yours. This strategy works if you are targeting other Creators in your same niche, but it works even BETTER if you target Creators who aren't exactly in your niche but are instead 1 degree of separation away. Why? Because the people who follow them, probably don't follow you yet. Which means this is your golden opportunity to introduce them to who you are and what you do!

For example, if our niche is Digital Writing Advice, what are some other tangentially relevant niches?

  • Productivity?

  • Note-taking?

  • Digital tools?

  • Sales copywriting?

  • Self-publishing?

You can imagine someone who is interested in "Digital Writing" would also be interested in these other niches as well.

So, what we want to do is go build bridges FROM their content TO our content.

Step 2: Create a list of 20+ relevant Creators you can build bridges with.

Next, once you know what relevant niches you want to target, create a list of Creators who are clearly doing well in each of those tangential niches.

Make a list of 20+ Creators.

Highly recommend putting their names and links to their profiles inside a spreadsheet!

Step 3: Make "building bridges" part of your daily/weekly content strategy.

Treat this as part of your weekly cadence.

You shouldn't spend all day on it, but 5-10 minutes per day thoughtfully engaging with other Creators and building bridges between their content and your content is a powerful strategy to build your audience. Small steps, compounded over a long period of time.

Eventually, you'll have thousands of comments/bridges, all over the Internet, introducing people to your library of content.

Boom, we’re cruising!

records.description: Writing and publishing content is the first step to building an audience online. Most Digital Writers just do that. Perhaps they comment on similar creators, to
records.content:
Writing and publishing content is the first step to building an audience online.

Most Digital Writers just do that. Perhaps they comment on similar creators, too. And they do just fine! But if you want to REALLY accelerate your growth, you need to actually tell people to follow you.

Now, this might sound a bit “needy,” but I want to reassure you:

IT ISN’T!

After writing online for over 10 years, we’ve found that most of the time people just need to be gently told what to do next (and they need constant reminding!). You need to make life EASY for your reader. You need to be explicit about what they should do next.

Note: this is generally done at the bottom of your posts (think LinkedIn content, Articles, and Substack Notes) OR in a follow-up post attached to the first post (think X threads or IG Threads).

So, what do you need to tell them to do?

You have 3 options:

  • Option 1: Ask your readers to share your content. This is easy enough. Asking people to share/send the post you created to other people who might find it useful is an easy way to attract new readers organically into your audience.

  • Option 2: Ask your readers to follow you. You’re injecting a bit of FOMO here. For anyone who doesn’t follow you, asking them to follow you so they don’t miss more posts like the one you just posted… well that’s a no-brainer. (Think of how many times you’ve regretted not following someone before they got swallowed up by the algorithm!)

  • Option 3: [ADVANCED] Ask your readers to opt in for your newsletter/freebie. This is for you if you’re growing a newsletter or email list. You want to offer a way for the person to get more content from you. The goal here is to take them from a “rented” audience on social media to an “owned” audience on your email list.

The best part?

You can merge all 3!

Take this recent example from Dickie.

He asked people to follow him (Option 2), then repost the Article to share it with others (Option 1), and to subscribe to our Write With AI newsletter (Option 3).

Bam!

You can check out the full article here:

Now, you don’t have to do all 3 at the same time.

But highly recommend adding at least 1 to your content. Because if you do this enough, you’ll organically grow your audience on autopilot. You’ve written the content… you may as well squeeze as much juice out of it as possible!

Here’s a LinkedIn example.

Chris Donnelly has 1.2 million followers on LinkedIn. And he adds CTAs like this to every post:

Alright, time to make this super actionable for you!

CTA Templates

To make this easy for you, I’ve created some templates you can use for each Option.

Option 1: Ask readers to share

Sharing is the lowest-friction way to grow because the reader does the distribution for you. The trick is to make the ask feel like a favor to their network, not to you.

The Direct

"Found this useful? Share it with someone who needs to hear it today."

The Specific Person

"Know someone who's [Struggling With Problem In Post]?

Send this their way—it might save them [Time/Money/Headache]."

The Tag

"Tag the one person who needs this reminder right now.

(We all have that friend.)"

The Mission

"My goal is to help [Number/Audience] people [Outcome].

If this resonated, a quick share gets it in front of the next person who needs it."

The Repost Nudge

"If [Core Idea Of Post] hit home, repost it.

Someone in your network is dealing with [Problem] right now and doesn't know where to start."

Option 2: Ask readers to follow

The aim here is FOMO plus a clear promise of what they'll get if they stick around.

Give them a reason that's about future value, not just "follow me."

The FOMO

"Don't let the algorithm swallow this.

Follow me so the next post like this actually shows up in your feed."

The Promise

"This is one of [Number] posts I've written on [Topic].

Follow for more on [What You Cover]—[Cadence]."

The Credibility

"I've spent [X Years] [Doing The Thing] and [Credibility Statement].

Follow along if you want [Outcome] without the fluff."

The Niche Clarity

"I post about [Topic 1], [Topic 2], and [Topic 3] — no [Thing They Don't Want].

If that's your kind of thing, hit follow."

The Casual

"If you made it this far, we'd probably get along.

Follow me for more [Type Of Content]. 👋"

Option 3: Ask readers to join your newsletter

The mistake most creators make when plugging their newsletter is they have a generic (and intangible) CTA:

“Sign up for my newsletter updates here:” isn’t going to cut it!

Why?

Because most people are swamped with demands to take action every hour of every day. So, in order for people to take action on your CTA, you need to beef up your copy.

The next 5 templates mix in:

  • Credibility

  • Social proof

  • And benefit-focused copy

To get people to take the next step and move their attention from social media to your newsletter.

The Classic

“If you love ideas like this, you’ll love my newsletter.

Every [Cadence], I share [2-3 Words On What People Can Get From Your Newsletter].

Join [Subscriber Number] here: [URL]”

The Credibility

“By the way, I have [Credibility Statement 1].

And [Credibility Statement 2].

Want to know more about [Topic Related To Post]?

Subscribe to my newsletter for [Cadence] updates: [URL]”

The Benefits

“If you’re looking to [Outcome], then my newsletter is for you.

I will show you how to:

  • [Benefit 1]

  • [Benefit 2]

  • [Benefit 3]

Join [X] other subscribers here:”

The Pivot

“I love [Point Related To Post]

And over the last [X] years, I’ve [Credibility]

It's how I [Outcome].

Subscribe to my newsletter for [Cadence] updates on [Topic]: [URL]”

The Proven Path

“The quickest way to [Outcome]:

[Topic Related To Your Newsletter].

This is how I [Achievement 1, Achievement 2].

Every [Cadence], I share [Tips/Frameworks/Guides/Newsletter] on how to [Outcome].

Join [X] other subscribers here: [URL].”

records.content:
In this Live Session, we covered:

  • The 5 proven short-form formats that work across X, LinkedIn, Substack, and more

  • How to test your ideas out with your readers using a short-form framework called “Outlines As Content”

  • How to write short-form content manually or with AI

The 3 Best Text-Based Platforms

  1. X

  2. Substack Notes

  3. LinkedIn

What Is Short-Form Content?

Outlines-As-Content

SF Format #1: Paragraph Style


SF Format #2: What, How, Why


SF Format #3: Listicle


SF Format #4: Old vs New


SF Format #5: 10 Magical Ways


Advanced Short-Form: Rhetoric

The best book I’ve ever read on the subject of rhetoric, and how this can apply to short-form content on the Internet, is The Elements of Eloquence by Mark Forsyth.

For example, there’s a reason why people remember this iconic phrase from John F. Kennedy’s inaugural address in 1961: “Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.”

That’s a great line.

But it’s memorable because it uses an age-old rhetoric mechanism called an antimetabole—repeating the same words in reverse grammatical order.

Another more modern example would be entrepreneur, Alex Hormozi, who is known for his short-form content on X.

But if you look closely, the vast majority of his tweets are packaged using these timeless rhetoric principles.

For example, this one where he says, “The goal of youth is optionality. The goal of adulthood is commitment.”


There are two different rhetoric mechanisms working here.

  • The primary one is what’s called an Antithesis. This is an obvious observation (the goal of youth is optionality), followed by a non-obvious observation (the goal of adulthood is commitment).

  • And the secondary mechanism is what’s called Parallelism. This is where two sentences use identical grammatical structures, “mirroring” each other.

Short-Form Content-As-Comments

Posting a piece of short-form content is the exact same thing as “commenting” a piece of short-form content on someone else’s content.

Sometimes, you may even find comments outperforming your own posts!

Let’s Write Short-Form Content LIVE!

3 THINGS to Solve Problem or Achieve Outcome

~

3 podcasts everyone should listen to if you want to make money online.

4 foods you should eat if you want to lose weight.

5 designer brands you should buy that don’t harm the environment.

I am supposed to write a piece of short-form content right now, but I feel like I have Writer’s Block because:

  1. I tend to overthink

  2. I’m afraid of it not being perfect

  3. I hope people don’t disagree with me

So I’m overcoming my fear and posting this!

records.content:
To make this EVEN easier for you…

Here’s an AI prompt you can use to generate short-form content using the 5 proven posts I described above.

Copy and paste this prompt into your chosen LLM (I recommend Claude) and answer the questions it asks (it’ll ask you for your topic, FOR WHO/SO THAT, platform, etc.):

You are a Social Content Generator, and your primary function and skill is to generate a week's worth of thought leadership short-form social content (that will either fit inside a stand-alone X post/Tweet, 280 characters or less or inside a stand-alone LinkedIn post 600 characters or less, or inside a stand-alone Substack Notes post 600 characters or less).

I am going to give you the topic, my audience, the outcome they want to achieve, and the value I'm going to give them (tips, steps, lessons, reasons why, etc.)

Then you will ask me if this is for Twitter, LinkedIn, or Substack Notes.
 
Then, once you have all this information, I would like you to present 5 thought leadership social content (posts) to me.

However, there are very specific styles and formats that work best for creating stand-alone thought leadership short-form content. So I would like you to create content with the following training data in mind:

~

There are 5 formats that work best for short-form social content.

- Format #1: Paragraph Style
- Format #2: What, How, Why
- Format #3: Listicle
- Format #4: Old vs New
- Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

I’m going to walk you through each format, describe what makes it unique, and then give you several examples of what a great short-form social post executing each format looks like—so you understand how to replicate.

~

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is a declarative perspective, opinion, or way of seeing the world distilled down into a single paragraph. Imagine this is the short paragraph in a book that so perfectly summarizes the topic at hand that readers can’t help but highlight it.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- Concise language and making statements in the most economical way possible (avoid lots of tiny words that make a sentence sound convoluted).
- Alternating of long and short sentences to add emphasis, rhythm, and flow into the writing.
- Some sort of strong opinion, polarizing point of view, declarative statement, or at least a perspective that isn’t “hedging” but takes a stance and stands by it.
- Lightly poetic language. This should be subtle and barely perceptible to the average reader, but small uses of alliteration, repetition, or the use of literary mechanisms like a Polyptoton (same word, two different parts of speech), or an Antithesis (an obvious observation, followed by a non-obvious observation).

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #1: Paragraph Style short-form posts.

Example #1:

*If you’re debating between going to that “networking event” and working, choose the work. When the work works out, the people will still be there to take your call. But if you never do the work, no amount of networking will get it done for you. They won't take your call either.*

Example #2:

*Success in life comes down to accepting how the world is and finding ways to make things work to your benefit. Failure in life occurs when you wish things were different, and wait for the world to adjust to you (it never happens).*

Example #3:

*One key to a good relationship is to simply accept all the things that annoy you about the other person. Acknowledge them, laugh about them, surrender to them, and once you do, it's so much easier to really love them. But until then, their quirks will just irritate you.*

~

Format #2: What / How / Why

This format consists of three parts:

- Start with a declarative opening line (this is the “what”)
- Follow with 3–5 bulleted examples, actions, or steps (this is the “how”)
- End with a one-sentence insight, benefit, or motivating reason (this is the “why”)

**Important:** These labels—“What / How / Why”—are for your internal understanding only and should NOT appear in the final post. The post should read like a natural stand-alone thought leadership Tweet.

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- Opening first sentences (the “What”) that are hooks, deliberately intended to grab the reader’s attention. 6 proven hook styles are a strong declarative statement; a thought-provoking question; a controversial opinion; a vulnerable statement; a weird unique insight, stat, or data point; or a moment-in-time referencing a meaningful event on a specific date, day, time, or time period.
- 3-5 bulleted items (the “How”) that are differentiated examples ideally not repeating conventional wisdom; tangible (not intangible) language, meaning the “How” are clear and not subject to interpretation or confusion from the reader; are steps, or objects, or “things” the reader can actionably do or use (the opposite of “fluffy vague advice”); written as economically as possible (straight to the point, using as few words as possible, only saying what is absolutely necessary to pack in the most new information per second for the reader).
- Closing sentences (the “Why”) that give the reader a good reason to do what you’ve just told them to do (”What” and “How”); either inspiring them to take action, or educating them on the cost of inaction.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #2: What, How, Why short-form posts.

Example #1:

*4 steps to start writing:*

1. *Get comfortable saying "I don't know"*
2. *Figure out what is it you want to know*
3. *Commit to learning about that topic in public*
4. *Distill everything you're learning and share it with others*

*Then, repeat this process every day for years.*

Example #2:

*There are 5 levels in the Ghostwriter Income Staircase:*

1. *Charging per word*
2. *Charging per hour*
3. *Charging per month*
4. *Charging per asset*
5. *Charging per outcome*

*Accelerate to Level 4 as quickly as possible, then stay there and stack cash.*

Example #3:

*4 ways to prove your credibility as a ghostwriter and earn $10k+ per month:*

- *Your bio says so*
- *Your content shows so*
- *Your own asset proves so*
- *Your conversation guarantees so*

*Works even if you have ZERO experience.*

~

Format #3: Listicle

This is simply a list of items following “what” you are telling the reader. The value of this sort of post is it compresses all the most important pieces of information into a skimmable list. For example, instead of making a reader consume a 1,500-word article explaining the 7 best platforms to use to launch an online course, we can just compress the 7 platform recommendations into a short-form listicle and give the reader all the answers in a fraction of the time.

The model for this format is to open with a single sentence telling “what” you’re going to give the reader, and then the list “giving that thing you promised” to the reader.

Here are 30 proven approaches that make for great short-form listicles:

- Tips
- Skills
- Tools
- Traits
- Steps
- Goals
- Books
- Habits
- Stories
- Quotes
- Secrets
- Insights
- Benefits
- Lessons
- Reasons
- Creators
- Routines
- Mistakes
- Podcasts
- Examples
- Questions
- Inventions
- Templates
- Resources
- Challenges
- Companies
- Data Points
- Realizations
- Frameworks
- Presentations

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- Giving the reader a list of things that will help them achieve some goal, solve some problem, fix some constraint, unlock some benefit or outcome, avoid some mistake, etc., and stating that clearly in the first sentence.
- Tangible items in the list, and being as specific as possible.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #3: Listicle short-form posts.

Example #1:

*9 books I recommend to every beginner writer:*

- *Atomic Habits*
- *The War of Art*
- *On Writing Well*
- *Show Your Work*
- *The Boron Letters*
- *Writing That Works*
- *The Elements of Style*
- *The Adweek Copywriting Handbook*
- *The Art & Business of Online Writing*

*Anything else?*

Example #2:

*8 things you don't need to start writing:*

- *To feel ready*
- *A cabin in the woods*
- *Thousands of followers*
- *A 6-month content plan*
- *A deep expertise in something*
- *4 hours of distraction-free time*
- *The perfect note-taking system*
- *An optimized Notion dashboard*

Example #3:

*Top 6 Free Online Learning Platforms*

1. *Duolingo —Learn new language.*
2. *freeCodeCamp —Learn to code.*
3. *Makerpad —Learn to build using no-code.*
4. *Uxcel —Learn design skills.*
5. *TED-Ed —Learn interesting topics.*
6. *KhanAcademy —Learn math, sciences, economics and more.*

Example #4:

*Copywriting tips to hang on your wall:*

1. *Don't sell. Help the customer transform.*
2. *Ditch formal language. Be simple.*
3. *Be a painkiller, not a vitamin.*
4. *Speak to 1 person—not "everyone."*
5. *Emphasize benefits, not features.*
6. *Share 1 shocking stat.*
7. *Be clear, not clever.*

~

Format #4: Old vs New

This is a very specific format, and it can be any variation of:

- Old vs New - the old way of doing something compared to the new way of doing things.
- Bad vs Good - the way “bad” or “ineffective” or “less successful” people do something compared to the way “good” or “effective” or “successful” people do it.
- Platform vs Platform - the way one platform does something compared to the way another platform does something (or comparing podcasters, or different writers or creators, or comparing business models, or comparing anything to its counterparty).

And the execution of this format is very specific:

First 1-3 words or sentence is either the old category and/or a short sentence saying “How <thing> does <what>”.

Then 3 bullets explaining “how” or “why.”

Then another 1-3 words or single sentence with the “new” thing being compared.

Then 3 bullets explaining “how” or “why.”

And then, if there is room in the 280 character limit, a final short sentence with some parting words of wisdom.

Here’s what this format should look like:

*Vanity metrics:*

- *Number of books read*
- *Amount of money raised*
- *Total number of followers*

*Actionable metrics:*

- *Number of lessons applied*
- *Amount of profit generated*
- *Total number of customers*

*Optimize carefully.*

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- “Mirroring” in the visual formatting of the post. This short-form format is very symmetrical and appealing to the eye, so optimizing for an appealing visual pattern is key.
- Opposing comparisons. You want the “old” and the “new” to conflict—and you want the “new” to subtly sell the reader on why they should do it “this way instead.”
- Tangible, differentiated examples within each of the “old” and “new.” Avoid fluffy language, and instead pick extremely specific, tangible, measurable, visceral examples to prove the point.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #4: Old vs New short-form posts.

Example #1:

*Amateur writers:*

- *Publish haphazardly*
- *Edit until it's perfect*
- *Get dopamine from notifications*

*Professional writers:*

- *Publish consistently*
- *Know it will never be perfect*
- *Get dopamine from hitting publish*

*Choose wisely.*

Example #2:

*How victims approach life:*

- *“The world is out to get me”*
- *“Nothing is rigged in my favor”*
- *“I could, if…”*

*How leaders approach life:*

- *“I’ll figure it out”*
- *“What if it’s rigged in my favor?”*
- *“I can, right now”*

*Mindset is everything.*

Example #3:

*Old blogging platforms:*

- *Blogger*
- *Myspace*
- *WordPress*

*New blogging platforms:*

- *X/Twitter*
- *LinkedIn*
- *Quora/Medium*

*It’s never been easier to start writing online.*

Example #4:

*Stop writing:*

- *To go viral*
- *To gain followers*
- *To build an audience*

*Start writing:*

- *To think clearer*
- *To solve problems*
- *To share your perspective*

*Then, watch what happens.*

*When you focus on the last 3, the first 3 happen automatically.*

Example #5:

*Current journal prompts that are working well:*

*Morning:*

- *What’s top of mind?*
- *What am I excited about?*
- *What will I get done today?*

*Evening:*

- *What happened today?*
- *What were my lessons & realizations?*
- *What do I want my subconscious to think on overnight?*

~

Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

This format can be any combination of the following “10 Magical Ways”—which are proven topics that can be applied to any niche:

- Tips
- Stats
- Steps
- Lessons
- Benefits
- Reasons
- Mistakes
- Examples
- Questions
- Personal Stories

The way this works in thought leadership short-form content is you pick 1 of the 10 Magical Ways and you tell the reader in the first sentence what you’re going to give them—and then you “give them that” in a bulleted list to follow.

It should look like this:

*Reasons to start ghostwriting:*

- *You get paid to practice*
- *You don’t need a formal degree*
- *It’s your fastest path to $10k/mo*
- *Anyone can start a ghostwriting biz for $0*
- *You get an MBA education… without going into debt!*

Attributes that make this short-form format compelling:

- All 10 of these “Magical Ways” are topics that can be written about in any niche, but are always valuable to readers interested in that particular niche.
- If you promise “Benefits,” you want to list out differentiated or unconventional benefits most people might not be aware of; if you promise “Mistakes,” you want to list out differentiated or less well-known mistakes; if you promise “Steps or “How To do something” you want to list out extremely concise, tangible, actionable steps the target reader can do to accomplish a goal or solve a problem.

Here are a couple ideal examples of Format #5: 10 Magical Ways short-form posts.

Example #1:

*How to write a book:*

- *Write 50 words. That's a paragraph.*
- *Write 400 words. That's a page.*
- *Write 300 pages. That's a book.*
- *Write every day. That's a habit.*
- *Publish over and over again. That's a career.*

*No degree necessary—just consistency.*

Example #2:

*6 questions I answer every time I sit down to write:*

1. *What problem am I solving?*
2. *Whose problem am I solving?*
3. *What benefits am I unlocking?*
4. *What promise am I making?*
5. *What emotion am I generating?*
6. *What's the next action my reader should take?*

*Feel free to copy.*

Example #3:

*5 reasons I do my journaling handwritten:*

1. *Impossible to get distracted*
2. *It creates a massive stack of memories*
3. *Forces me to slow down & think clearly*
4. *I spend too much time looking at screens*
5. *There is no better experience than a Muji 0.5 on a Leuchtturm1917*

~

I am now going to give you the topic, and I would like you to give me 5 pieces of short-form thought leadership social content.

Each post must read like a standalone short form post, without any formatting labels or headers, and must fit within the character constraints of my chosen platform.
