records.title: Outlines As Content 101
records.archivePath: AI Community Writing/AI writing Community/Start Writing Online Sprint/Day 1 - Tweets/Outlines As Content 101 - Start Writing Online Sprint · AI Writing Skool.mhtml
records.description: What does it mean to publish “Outlines As Content?” Well, to fully understand this framework, here’s something I want you to internalize: Everything Is A List
records.content:
What does it mean to publish “Outlines As Content?”

Well, to fully understand this framework, here’s something I want you to internalize:

Everything Is A List

Every single piece of writing, in some way, is a list.

  • A New Yorker article discussing the benefits of living in a certain city? It’s a descriptive “list” of benefits.

  • A Buzzfeed article curating different kinds of socks to wear depending on the time of year? It’s “listing” socks, and “listing” the different times of year.

  • A novel that spends 3 pages describing a vacant house? Those 3 pages are “listing” qualities of the vacant house.

Listen closely: “The list goes on and on…”

What is the above? It’s a LIST!!!

At the end of the day, all great “writing” is basically just a Jenga tower of ideas stacked on top of each other. And so what’s the easiest way to figure out what “ideas” need to go together?

By listing them out!

Short-Form Content = An “Outline”

This is the first mental shift we want you to experience.

Short-form content doesn’t have to just be “short Tweets” or “short LinkedIn posts.” In fact, thinking about it that way is extremely inefficient—because it requires you to “think” about each idea individually. It also forces you to create 2x or 3x or 5x more content than you need to (you have to create short-form content and THEN different long-form content and THEN different even longer-form content, etc.).

Instead, we want you to think of all your short-form content (Tweets, short LinkedIn posts, even short Atomic Essays) as “Outlines As Content.”

What does that mean?

It means every time you write something “short,” what you should really be doing is testing to see whether or not this batch of ideas (this list) is compelling to readers. Because IF IT IS, then it becomes extremely clear which of those “outlines” is worth expanding into longer-form content.

Which compounds all of your efforts.

Let’s walk through how this works.

Step 1: Pick A Topic

This could be related to your niche, industry, or just an idea that’s been on your mind recently.

Now, let’s run it through a quick sense check to see if we’re clear on who we’re writing this short-form post for.

We’re going to use a framework I call “For Who/So That.”

First, make sure you’re clear on WHO this is for.

For example:

  • V1: “Copywriting”

  • V2 (FOR WHO?): “Copywriting For Beginners”

  • V3 (FOR WHO, SPECIFICALLY?): “Copywriting For Beginners Without College Degrees”

Specificity is the secret.

Second, what “value” are you sharing?

Step 2: What “Value” Do You Want To Share?

What are ALL the possible things you could give that person (the WHO) related to that topic?

This is the “value” of your writing:

  • “Are you giving me tips?”

  • “Or are you giving me steps?”

  • “Or are you giving me questions?”

  • “Or are you giving me reflections?”

  • Etc.

And as a recap, here are all the Proven Approaches you can use:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

Thirdly, make sure you’re clear on the SO THAT part of the FOR WHO/SO THAT framework.

Remember, having clarity on your topic and WHO it’s for is great.

But what takes your writing to the next level is also having clarity over why it matters to the reader. What’s in it for them? Why are you telling them whatever it is you’re telling them? SO THAT they can do… what?

We call these “incentives.”

These are things the reader wants:

  • …To Get Started {Skill}

  • …To Learn {Skill}

  • …To Master {Skill}

  • …To Overcome {Problem}

  • …To Unlock {Outcome}

  • …To Streamline {Process}

  • …To Get Your First {Small Outcome}

  • …To Achieve {Big Outcome}

  • …So You Don’t {Worst Outcome}

  • …To Hire Your First {Employee}

  • …To Buy Your First {Valuable Asset}

  • …To Sell Your First {Valuable Asset}

  • …To Make Your First {$X}

  • …To Build Your First {Product/Company}

  • …To Improve {Task}

  • …To Scale Your {Business}

  • …To Pitch Your {Idea}

  • …To Help You Fix {Problem}

  • …To Teach You {Solution}

  • …To Create The Perfect {Product}

  • …To {Do More} Without {More Work}

  • …To Make Progress On {Goal}

Etc.

And the beauty is, you can turn 1 small piece of “value” into dozens and dozens of topics just by changing the incentive.

Now let’s tie this all together (and you’ll NEVER run out of short-form ideas to write about for this topic).

Here’s your quick checklist:

  • Topic: What do you want to write about? FOR WHO, specifically?

  • Value: What are you giving the reader?

  • Incentive: SO THAT they can do… what? What’s the outcome?

Now watch how easy it is to generate ideas:

Let’s take Ghostwriting:

  • Topic: Ghostwriting FOR beginners

  • Value: Tips

  • Incentive: SO THAT they can do… what?

Check out all these Incentives (and how many short-form post ideas it gives me!):

  • Tips

    • …To Get Started Ghostwriting

    • …To Learn How To Become A Ghostwriter

    • …To Master Ghostwriting For CEOs

    • …To Overcome Critical Feedback From Ghostwriting Clients

    • …To Unlock Financial Success As A Ghostwriter

    • …To Streamline Your Ghostwriting Process

    • …To Get Your First Ghostwriting Client

    • …To Achieve Financial Success As A Ghostwriter

    • …So You Don’t Lose Ghostwriting Clients Due To Grammar Errors

    • …To Hire Your First Ghostwriting Subcontractor

    • …To Buy Your First Ghostwriting Course

    • …To Sell Your First Digital Product As A Ghostwriter

    • …To Make Your First $10,000 Per Month As A Ghostwriter

    • …To Build Your First Ghostwriting Agency

    • …To Improve Ghostwriting For Early-Stage SaaS Founders

    • …To Scale Your Ghostwriting Services

    • …To Pitch Your Ghostwriting Services To Clients

    • …To Help You Fix Over-Editing From Ghostwriting Clients

    • …To Teach You The Fundamentals Of Ghostwriting

    • …To Create The Perfect Ghostwritten Twitter Thread

    • …To Take On Most Ghostwriting Clients Without Working Harder

    • …To Make Progress On Becoming A Highly Paid Ghostwriter

That’s 22 ideas just from combining one of the “value” pieces on our list with a bunch of different incentives!

Step 3: Create “Outlines As Content”

Here’s the big aha we want you to have:

Once you go through the above exercise, do you need to go write 5,000 words in order to see whether or not that Topic + Value + Incentive is what the reader wants?

Of course not!

You can EASILY test the Topic + Value + Incentive by creating & publishing “Outlines As Content.”

Here’s how it works:

Let’s say our Topic is “copywriting,” our Value is “Tips,” and our Incentive is “…to learn” and you have the credibility because you’ve learned copywriting in the last 2 years.

Tips to learn copywriting.

Do you see how even just this sentence is the start of a short-form content idea? And what you’re “testing” is whether or not readers are interested in

  • A) “Tips…”

  • B) “To learn…”

  • C) “Copywriting…”

  • D) From you! (Because you’re applying the 2-Year test backwards)

Those are the 4 variables you are “testing” with readers.

And you can see how you can isolate these variables by creating different versions of this content and scheduling them a week or two apart from each other to see what works:

  • Do readers want Tips or Mistakes?

  • Do they want “to learn” or do they want a different incentive, like “to optimize?”

  • Are they interested in Copywriting, or a different topic?

  • And most of all, do they want to hear it from YOU? Or do they want to hear it from a different expert whose insights you’ve curated?

(Maybe you have the right Topic, Value, and Incentive, but you just need to either use your own credibility or borrow credibility from someone else)

Follow us…

If your Value is “Tips” (that’s what you’re giving the reader), what should you list out in order to “test” whether or not the reader finds those “tips” valuable?

TIPS!

For example:

Tips to learn copywriting:

  • Read Ogilvy On Advertising

  • Re-write sales letters by hand

  • Try to sell your own products online

  • Join a copywriting mastermind group

This is a Tweet. This is a LinkedIn post.

But it’s also an “Outline As Content.”

Which means, if this short-form post performs well, you now know: readers are interested in a) Tips, b) “To Learn,” c) Copywriting, d) From You, and e) these “Tips” you listed, they found helpful.

That’s a bunch of variables you now have a reasonable amount of data telling you are worth experimenting with over and over again! And you can repeat this “stack” of variables infinite times. Or you can take this “stack,” replace 1 or multiple variables, and compare performance again.

This is what makes Digital Writing such a science experiment.

And the more you publish, the more you learn.

Now, ready for your mind to really be blown?

Let’s say you want to execute all of the above, but you don’t want to write about it from YOUR personal experience anymore. You want to curate someone else’s credibility instead.

Look at all that happens:

For example:

Tips to learn copywriting from Craig Clemens, one of the most successful sales copywriters on planet earth:

  • Read Ogilvy On Advertising

  • Re-write sales letters by hand

  • Try to sell your own products online

  • Join a copywriting mastermind group

Literally the only difference (aside from whatever it is you’re “listing,” which will probably change based on whether YOU are coming up with it yourself versus listing other people’s insights) is adding a single sentence of context/credibility.

Is this coming from you? If so, you can add in your own sentence of credibility: “I have been copywriting for 10 years. Here are some tips to learn how.” But you don’t have to since you are the one writing it.

Or, you add a sentence of context/credibility about the person you picked up these tips from. Who are you learning from? Who are they? What have they done? What context clue can you give the reader that will make them trust you, because the person you’re studying has a ton of credibility?

That’s it!

records.content:
After writing thousands of viral short-form posts on both X (Twitter) and LinkedIn, I have identified 5 formats that typically out-perform the average over and over again.

These formats also make for a great compounding library of content. (For example, you can take your entire short-form content library on X and copy/paste it over to LinkedIn, and then copy/paste it over to Instagram as screenshots/carousels, and then copy/paste it over to Instagram Threads, etc. etc. etc.)

Let’s dive in!

Format #1: Paragraph Style

This is where you write a thought-provoking paragraph connected to your core industry/niche/topic.

There’s something about this formatting, especially on a fast-moving platform like X, that immediately makes it “stand out” simply because it’s formatted differently. As a full paragraph, you (as the reader) inherently assume it to be “smart.” (Ironic, I know.)

It works so well for a few reasons:

  • It takes a strong stance instead of hedging.

  • It uses concise, economical language and alternates long and short sentences to create rhythm and emphasis.

  • And it leans on subtle, barely-perceptible literary touches—a bit of alliteration, repetition, or antithesis (an obvious observation followed by a non-obvious one)—to make the writing more “satisfying” than plain prose would.

One of my favorite formats!

Format #2: What, How, Why

This is a very repeatable formula:

  • “What” = The first line is “what” you are trying to say to the reader.

  • “How” = The middle 3-5 bullets is “how” to accomplish the “what.”

  • “Why” = The last sentence is “why” this is so important.

It works well for a few reasons:

  • The first line/hook grabs attention up front.

  • The bullets deliver tangible, differentiated, actionable items—no fluff.

  • And the closing line motivates action or warns of the cost of inaction, so the reader walks away with a push to actually do something.

You can apply this format to literally any topic, in any niche, and it will work well.

Format #3: Listicle

Anything you can list is a great short-form piece of content.

For example:

  • Tips

  • Skills

  • Tools

  • Traits

  • Steps

  • Goals

  • Books

  • Habits

  • Stories

  • Quotes

  • Secrets

  • Insights

  • Benefits

  • Lessons

  • Reasons

  • Creators

  • Routines

  • Mistakes

  • Podcasts

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Inventions

  • Templates

  • Resources

  • Challenges

  • Companies

  • Data Points

  • Realizations

  • Frameworks

  • Presentations

The “Listicle” format has a simple opening sentence promising the "what" you're about to give the reader, followed by a skimmable list that delivers exactly that—tips, tools, books, mistakes, etc.

It works so well because it compresses what could be a long article into a few seconds of reading. Instead of making someone consume 1,500 words to get 7 recommendations, you hand them all the answers instantly.

You’re listing tangible, specific items tied to a clear goal, problem, or outcome (which means you’re differentiating yourself from all the fluff content out there!).

Format #4: Old vs New

This is where you compare the “old” way someone did something (in your niche) to the “new” way.

Or, where you compare any sort of archetype.

Some examples might be:

  • Bad vs Good

  • Rich vs Poor

  • Right vs Wrong

  • Productive vs Unproductive

  • Legacy vs Cutting-Edge

  • Etc.

Here are a few reasons why this works so well:

  • The opposing comparison creates tension

  • The "new" side subtly sells the reader on the better way

  • The symmetry is visually appealing and easy to scan—the two halves mirror each other

Giving TANGIBLE examples on both sides leaves no doubt in the mind of the reader if they’re on the “Old” or “New” side of the equation.

Format #5: 10 Magical Ways

This is where you can mix and match any of these styles by using what I like to call the 10 Magical Ways To Expand Anything:

  • Tips

  • Stats

  • Steps

  • Lessons

  • Benefits

  • Reasons

  • Mistakes

  • Examples

  • Questions

  • Personal Stories

These 10 Ways work in any niche and are always valuable to readers in that space.

The key is differentiation—if you promise benefits, list unconventional ones people don't already know. If you promise mistakes, surface the less obvious ones. It consistently gives the reader something fresh and useful.

So, to take this a level deeper, you can take an idea you’ve already written about in the previous 4 and expand it by adding one of the 10 Magical Ways!

For example, let’s take this short form post from Example 1:

There are AT LEAST 20+ more posts buried in this piece of short form!

You could write another post on:

  • Give 5 examples of classic literature every writer should study (then cycle through all the other types of writing here and/or sub-sets of literature, sales copy, etc.)

  • Explain 1 mistake writers make when studying writing to hone their skills

  • List 3 questions every writer should ask of every sentence they read to help them understand how to construct a good sentence

Etc., etc., etc.

Now, this leads me to another idea I want to explain in relation to short form:

How to treat your short form posts as “Outlines As Content.”

records.content:
Welcome to the Newsletter Hook Writer!

This prompt writes newsletter introductions using a 5-block framework I've been refining for years.

  • Block #1: Greeting

  • Block #2: Opening sentence

  • Block #3: Promise

  • Block #4: Solution

  • Block #5: Transition

Each block has a specific job.

The greeting warms up the reader. The opening sentence hooks them. The promise educates them on why this topic matters. The solution tells them exactly what you're giving them today. And the transition carries them into the body.

Block #2 is your “hook”.

And in this prompt we generate 10 different kinds:

  1. Open Loop (curiosity gap)

  2. Stakes Escalator (loss aversion)

  3. Interrogation (forced self-diagnosis)

  4. Sacred Cow Slaughter (challenge a belief)

  5. Pattern Break (violate expectations)

  6. Diagnosis (name their exact symptom)

  7. Movie Scene (drop them into a moment)

  8. Insider Briefing (share what peers don't know)

  9. Confession (vulnerability that earns trust)

  10. Proof Drop (stack real credibility fast)

So instead of spending 30 minutes staring at a blank screen trying to nail your opener, you get 10 complete intros you can test, rotate, and reuse.

Which means more people reading past the first line, more replies, and more revenue from every single send.

Here’s how it to use it:

Run the prompt.

Then give it your topic, your audience, and some real details about your credibility. It gives you 10 fully written intros, each using a different psychological hook.

Easy.

Newsletter Hook Writer Prompt

Copy / paste the prompt below.

# NEWSLETTER INTRODUCTION WRITER

## ROLE

You are a direct-response copywriter who specializes in newsletter introductions. You've studied Halbert, Bencivenga, Schwartz, and Caples. You write like a sharp friend who always has something interesting to say, not a robot playing it safe. You understand that a newsletter introduction is a structured sequence of blocks, not just a clever opening line.

## PHILOSOPHY

This is a newsletter. The reader already opened your email. They already trust you enough to subscribe. You don't need to grab a stranger's collar. You need to reward a subscriber for opening and pull them into the body fast enough that they don't bounce back to their inbox.

**Newsletter intros vs. social hooks:**
- Social hooks compete with infinite scroll. Newsletter intros compete with "I'll read this later" (they won't).
- Social hooks need to prove who you are. Newsletter intros can skip that. The reader already knows you.
- Social hooks lean on provocation and bold claims. Newsletter intros lean on curiosity, stories, and earned intimacy.
- The tone is warmer. You're writing to someone who chose to hear from you. Talk to them like it.

The reader's default state after opening: "Ok, I'm here. Make it worth my time."

**THE ENERGY RULE:** Write first. Edit second. Your first job is to write something with FORCE, something a little too bold, a little too specific, a little too confident. Your second job is to check it for slop. Never reverse this order. Caution kills copy. You can always sand down something too sharp. You can't inject life into something born flat.

## THE 5-BLOCK INTRODUCTION FRAMEWORK

Every newsletter introduction is built from 5 blocks stacked on top of each other. Don't think of the intro as one giant block of text. Think of it as 5 smaller blocks, each with a specific job.

### Block #1: THE GREETING

Start every newsletter with a simple, warm greeting on its own line.

"Hey there!"

That's it. Keep it short. Keep it human. This is the handshake before the conversation.

### Block #2: THE HOOK (1 sentence)

This is the single opening sentence that grabs the reader's attention. One sentence only. This is where the 10 hook types below come in. Each hook type gives you a different way to write this one critical sentence.

The best opening hooks do one of the following:
- Ask a thought-provoking question
- Open with a strong, declarative sentence
- Reference a meaningful moment in time (a date, a day, a specific moment)
- Present a vulnerable statement
- Offer a controversial opinion
- Share a unique insight

### Block #3: THE PROMISE (3-7 sentences or 3-7 bullets)

This is the substance of the intro. After the hook grabs them, the promise educates the reader on WHY this matters.

The promise takes one of two forms:

**Problem-oriented promise:** Educate the reader on a specific problem (or series of problems), why those problems exist, and the negative outcomes of leaving them unsolved.

**Outcome-oriented promise:** Educate the reader on a desirable outcome (or handful of outcomes), why those outcomes are so valuable, and the negative consequences of not achieving them.

This block is typically 3-7 sentences long. It can also be presented as a bulleted list of 3-7 bullets. The key is that it's tangible, actionable, and niche-specific. The reader should feel the weight of the problem or the pull of the outcome.

### Block #4: THE SOLUTION (1-2 sentences)

After educating the reader on the problem or outcome, complete the promise by telling them that's exactly what you're going to help them with today.

You're either going to help them solve that problem (or series of problems) or achieve that outcome (or handful of outcomes).

This is where the LAST SENTENCE RULE lives:
- Tell the reader exactly what you're giving them. Be specific about the format: "the exact 6-step process" or "a full breakdown with screenshots" or "my 3-part system." Vague promises ("some tips," "my thoughts") don't pull anyone forward.
- Name a specific, tangible outcome. Noun-oriented outcomes the reader can picture: "...to land your first $10K client" / "...to write a newsletter that gets forwarded" / "...to double your open rate in 30 days." NOT adjective-oriented outcomes: "...to be more successful" / "...to feel confident."

Study the difference:

❌ "So today, I'm going to share some thoughts on growing your newsletter."
✅ "So today, I'm going to walk you through the exact 3-step system I used to add 4,000 subscribers in 30 days."

❌ "Today, I'll show you how to be more productive."
✅ "Today, I'll show you the single daily habit that freed up 2 hours every morning."

### Block #5: THE TRANSITION (1 sentence)

A short transition sentence into the first section of the newsletter body. Something like:

- "Let's walk through each one."
- "Let's dive in."
- "Here's how it works."
- "So, with that in mind, let's [solve that problem / achieve that outcome]."

Keep it brief. Its only job is to carry momentum from the intro into the body.

---

## FULL EXAMPLES OF THE 5-BLOCK FRAMEWORK

Study these. Notice how each block does its job and flows into the next.

**Example 1:**

> Hey there!
>
> Do you want to know the secret to landing your first ghostwriting client?
>
> One of the biggest challenges I faced getting started was: how do I actually charge for my work and make money? And the truth is, it's not that hard. It's just that no one tells you how to do it.
>
> So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways to structure your next ghostwriting project, and when to use them to get paid a premium.
>
> Let's walk through each one.

Block breakdown:
- Block 1: "Hey there!" (greeting)
- Block 2: "Do you want to know the secret to landing your first ghostwriting client?" (hook: thought-provoking question)
- Block 3: "One of the biggest challenges I faced..." (promise: problem-oriented, names the struggle and normalizes it)
- Block 4: "So today, I'm going to share the 3 ways..." (solution: specific format + tangible outcome)
- Block 5: "Let's walk through each one." (transition)

**Example 2:**

> Hey there!
>
> What do you need to become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter and build a lucrative side hustle?
>
> Do you need:
> - A portfolio?
> - Customer testimonials?
> - Tons of writing experience?
>
> Well, actually, the truth is... you don't need ANY of these things!
>
> So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system for attracting ghostwriting clients. And once you install it, you can become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter who lands high-ticket clients.
>
> Let's dive in!

Block breakdown:
- Block 1: "Hey there!" (greeting)
- Block 2: "What do you need to become a Premium LinkedIn Ghostwriter...?" (hook: thought-provoking question)
- Block 3: "Do you need: A portfolio?..." + "you don't need ANY of these things!" (promise: outcome-oriented with a twist, presented as bullet list)
- Block 4: "So today, I'm going to show you my 5-step system..." (solution: specific format + tangible outcome)
- Block 5: "Let's dive in!" (transition)

---

## THE 10 HOOK TYPES (for Block #2)

Each hook type gives you a different way to write Block #2, the single opening sentence. When you generate output, you'll write a COMPLETE 5-block introduction for each type, varying Block #2 while adapting Blocks #3-5 to flow naturally from each hook.

### 1. THE OPEN LOOP

Create a gap between what the reader knows and what they need to know.

Study these:

> "You guys want to hear something completely insane?"

> "We're all one decision away from changing our lives and a lot of us don't even know it."

> "On November 30th, 2022, the world changed forever."

What makes these work: They create an itch the reader can't scratch without reading further. The specificity (a date, "completely insane") makes the loop sticky.

### 2. THE STAKES ESCALATOR

Name a situation and make the reader feel what it cost.

Study these:

> "This lawyer was losing $100,000 a year because his business model was broken."

> "This fashion stylist was making 300,000 a year but leaving millions on the table."

What makes these work: Specific person. Specific money. Specific problem. "Losing" does more work than "could improve." Active loss beats passive potential.

### 3. THE INTERROGATION

Ask a question so specific the reader's brain has to chase an answer.

Study these:

> "Are you making these 3 mistakes with your ads?"

> "Which would you rather be: the guy pushing the boulder up the hill? Or the one with the boulder at the top who can just flick it?"

> "Would you pay $1,000 to have the business of your dreams in 30 days?"

What makes these work: They force self-diagnosis. The reader starts answering internally before they've decided to keep reading.

### 4. THE SACRED COW SLAUGHTER

Take the #1 piece of advice everyone believes. Say it's wrong. Back it up.

Study these:

> "I build wealth without reading a book a week."

> "If nobody knows who you are, it's actually a good thing."

What makes these work: Cognitive dissonance. The reader has to keep going because what they just read conflicts with something they believe.

### 5. THE PATTERN BREAK

Set up what should be true, then break expectations.

Study these:

> "Real quick question. Can I have your email address?"

> "Fear is a mile wide and an inch deep."

What makes these work: The reader's brain is already predicting the next sentence. Then the actual sentence lands somewhere completely different. Forces a re-read.

### 6. THE DIAGNOSIS

Name the exact symptom the reader is experiencing.

Study these:

> "If you're working all the time and your business isn't growing, you're working on the wrong sh*t."

> "The strategy I'm going to show you is something that most businesses don't do. And the few businesses that do do it, do it wrong."

What makes these work: The reader thinks "that's me." Naming the specific symptom is the hook. It proves you understand their world.

### 7. THE MOVIE SCENE

Drop the reader into a specific moment with sensory detail.

Study these:

> "I'm at her parents' house in an extra bedroom. I'm the guy she met from the internet that she quit her job for, who's just lost everything. I had $1000 left."

> "One day I was in the back and this old lady comes in and she was piss angry."

What makes these work: You're IN the scene before you know where it's going. "Extra bedroom" is a detail only someone who was actually there would include. These hooks feel like memories, not marketing.

### 8. THE INSIDER BRIEFING

Share something the reader's peers don't know yet.

Study these:

> "One in every 250 businesses does over 10 million dollars a year. That means 99% of entrepreneurs never hit it."

> "$4,664 per month in recurring revenue. That's what Kyle, the last person on the leaderboard, was able to build."

What makes these work: Real data, named people, specific numbers. The second one uses the LAST place person to set the floor. If the worst performer got $4,664/month, what did everyone else get?

### 9. THE CONFESSION

Admit something that costs you credibility or pride.

Study these:

> "I have a confession. I am sick and tired of seeing people who have never run a business before teaching other people how to grow businesses."

> "I'm at her parents' house in an extra bedroom. I'm the guy she met from the internet that she quit her job for, who's just lost everything."

What makes these work: Real cost. The first risks alienating peers. The second admits to being broke and a burden. Neither is a humble brag. The reader thinks: "If they're willing to say THAT, whatever comes next must be worth hearing."

### 10. THE PROOF DROP

Drop a specific result or data point that reframes the topic.

Study these:

> "I've been in business 13 years. I've sold nine companies. My last company I sold for $46.2 million."

> "$4,664 per month in recurring revenue. That's what Kyle, the last person on the leaderboard, was able to build."

> "I started 4 businesses that cracked ten million in a row."

What makes these work: Speed and weight. Each sentence raises the bar. In a newsletter, proof drops work best when you're covering a topic that benefits from re-establishing why you're the one to listen to on THIS subject. The $46.2 million is a REAL number (not a round $50M), which is why it feels true.

---

## SLOP GUARDRAILS

Your primary job is to write with force. Your secondary job is to avoid these traps.

**The big 3 (instant rewrites):**

1. **Binary contrast:** Any sentence that defines something by what it ISN'T. This is the #1 AI tell.

BINARY CONTRAST REWRITES:

❌ "The problem isn't your writing. It's your distribution."
✅ "Your distribution is broken. Here's what's leaking."

❌ "You don't need more content. You need better systems."
✅ "One system will outperform 50 posts. I'll show you which one."

❌ "Most people think it's about talent. The real answer is reps."
✅ "Reps beat talent every single time. Here's the math."

❌ "It's not about working harder. It's about working on the right things."
✅ "You're grinding on the wrong tasks. I wasted 6 months doing the same thing."

The pattern: stop telling the reader what it ISN'T. Just tell them what it IS with conviction. The direct assertion is always stronger because it moves forward instead of pivoting.

2. **Triples:** Grouping things in threes for false rhythm. This is the #2 AI tell.

TRIPLE REWRITES:

❌ "You'll write faster, think clearer, and publish with confidence."
✅ "You'll publish twice as fast. And actually like what you wrote."

❌ "It saves you time, money, and headaches."
✅ "It saves you 10 hours a week. I timed it."

❌ "Build authority, grow your audience, and monetize your expertise."
✅ "Grow your audience to the point where monetization becomes obvious."

The pattern: triples feel like momentum but they're actually filler. Pick the ONE thing that matters most and make it specific.

3. **Fake details:** Don't invent numbers (47, 73, $11,342), people ("Sarah, a freelance designer"), or scenarios the user didn't provide. Write from "you" or "I" instead.

**HARD SCAN (do this after drafting all 10 intros):**

Go through every sentence and check for:
1. Does any sentence contain "not," "isn't," "don't," or "won't" followed by a pivot to what the thing actually is? Binary contrast. Rewrite as a direct assertion.
2. Does any sentence group three things together with commas or "and"? Triple. Pick the strongest one, make it specific, cut the other two.

These two patterns are the defaults you will reach for. They will show up in your first draft. Catch them and rewrite them before outputting.

**Banned phrases:**
- "Here's the thing..." / "Let me be honest..." / "I'll be real with you..."
- "No X. No Y. Just Z."
- "The game has changed" / "game-changer"
- "If you're serious about [goal]..."
- "Let that sink in." / "Read that again." / "Full stop."
- "Enter: [thing]"
- "The best part?" / "Ready to level up?"
- "[Something] stopped me in my tracks"
- Em dashes (—). Never. Use periods, commas, or parentheses.
- Arrows (→) and emoji

---

## OUTPUT RULES

**Formatting:**
- Each sentence gets its own line with a blank line between.
- No em dashes. No ellipses for dramatic effect. No bold/italic inside the intro text.

**Diversity check:**
Read the Block #2 hook sentence of all 10 intros. If any two make the same point, kill the weaker one and write something genuinely different. 10 intros means 10 different psychological entry points.

**Energy check:**
Read each intro out loud. If it sounds like competent but forgettable copywriting, it fails. If any AI tool could have written it, throw it out.

## OUTPUT FORMAT

For each of the 10 hook types, provide a COMPLETE 5-block newsletter introduction:

**[HOOK TYPE NAME]**

[Block 1: Greeting]

[Block 2: Hook sentence]

[Block 3: Promise (3-7 sentences or bullets)]

[Block 4: Solution (1-2 sentences with specific format + tangible outcome)]

[Block 5: Transition sentence]

*Why this works:* [1-2 sentences on why this particular hook + promise combination works for THIS audience.]

---

## INPUT REQUIRED

To write intros that hit, I need real material to work with. The more specific your input, the sharper the output.

- **Newsletter topic:** What is this edition about?
- **Your audience:** Who subscribes? Be specific (not "entrepreneurs" but "solo founders doing $5K-$20K/month who handle their own marketing.")
- **The core problem:** What keeps them up at night about this topic?
- **Your credibility or angle:** Why should they listen to YOU on this? A real result, a real story, a counterintuitive discovery. Give me real numbers and real details.
- **Your voice/tone:** Is your newsletter casual and profane? Measured and analytical? Story-driven? Give me a sense of how you normally write so the intros sound like YOU.
- **Draft content (optional):** If you have a draft, paste it. I'll mine it for angles.

**Important:** The more real details you give me (real numbers, real stories, real before/after moments), the better these intros will be. Thin briefs produce thin intros. The intros that make subscribers read every word come from real, specific, textured material.

---

## AFTER GENERATING

1. **Rank your top 3** for A/B testing and say why.
2. **Name the sleeper.** Which intro seems quiet but would outperform because nobody else in the space writes intros like it?
3. **Create one hybrid.** Combine elements from two hook types into an 11th intro.

records.content:
By far, the biggest mistake writers make when writing subject lines is making them “too long.”

If a subject line gets cut off before “the hook” is revealed, the chances of a reader clicking is very low. Why? Because they don't have a reason to! They don't know what you're promising inside—which means they don't know what to expect (or why it's worth their precious attention).

A great article headline can be 20 words.

But a good subject line needs to be 15 words or less, punchy, and conversational.

We suggest you lean toward subject line rules over headline rules.

Why?

Because the majority of your readers will encounter your newsletter in their email inbox. The inbox is where the open-or-skip decision happens. If the title doesn't earn the click there, readers won’t open your email.

Now, if you want longer, more descriptive headline copy, you can put it in a header image in the body copy of your email. So your title stays short and optimized for the inbox. And your header image carries the fuller context for readers who land inside the post. Best of both worlds.

With that in mind, here are some golden rules to follow when writing subject lines:

Rule #1: 5-15 words, max.

A good rule of thumb is your subject line should not exceed 15 words. Ever.

Less is always more here.

  • If you can say it in 15 words, try to say it in 10.

  • If you can say it in 10 words, try to say it in 7.

  • If you can say it in 7, try to say it in 5 words.

However… there's a big nuance here that is important: “less words” doesn't inherently mean the subject line is “better.” The key is to give the reader a “hook” that makes them want to click and open the email—but to say that “hook” in as few words as possible WITHOUT LOSING THE MEANING.

For example, let's say your subject line was: “The 1 thing you need to do in order to strengthen the microbiome in your gut.”

Well, if you shortened this subject line to: “The 1 thing you need to do,” yes you shortened the word count (which is good) but you also lost the whole idea in the “hook” (which is bad).

A better rewrite would be something that says the same thing, but in less words, like: “Want to strengthen your gut microbiome? Try this 1 thing.”

Same idea, but the first subject line is 16 words.

And the second subject line is 10 words.

Rule #2: Subject lines should read like you're talking to a friend.

This comes down to grammar & punctuation more than anything else.

For example:

  • “3 Mistakes Keeping You From Landing Your First $5,000”

  • “3 mistakes keeping you from landing your first $5,000…”

In general, the second subject line here will see better open rates.

Why?

Because it’s written in sentence-case (which feels more like a friend emailing a friend) opposed to Capitalized (which reads more like the headline of an article).

Super small thing. Not THAT important. But a good nuance to test with your list.

Rule #3: Use 1 of the 4 proven hooks.

There are 4 types of hooks that work over and over again (regardless of industry, niche, or topic):

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal time."

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal cost."

  • "Here's how to solve your problem without much effort."

  • "Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly."

As much as possible, you always want your subject lines to use 1 of these 4 proven hooks.

Otherwise, the reader won't have a good enough reason to click, open, and ultimately read your email.

Here are some sample subject lines for each of these 4 hooks:

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal time." - Your entire Life Coach career path blueprint… in 1 email!

  • "Here's a ton of value for minimal cost." - Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

  • "Here's how to solve your problem without much effort." - Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

  • "Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly." - 3 keys to land $10,000 consulting clients, from home, in your pajamas, right now.

See how every subject line is “promising” one of these 4 things?

Nailing that promise is the secret to getting readers to click, open, and read.

Rule #4: Use visceral language!

Now, you can “amp up” your subject lines even more by adding in visceral language.

Things like…

  • OUCH!

  • URGENT!

  • FREE!

  • Seriously…

  • Steal this!

  • (I can't believe I'm giving this away.)

And so on.

For example, here are some of the headlines above “amped up” even further:

  • (Original) Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

  • (Amped Up) OUCH! Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies.

Or…

  • (Original) Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

  • (Amped Up) [FOR FREE!] Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!

It's a very small thing, but sometimes adding in visceral language can help increase open rates by a few percentage points.

Rule #5: Name & Claim ideas (in the subject line)

Even more than visceral language though, the ultimate goal is to Name & Claim ideas right there in the subject line.

For example, notice the difference between these two subject lines:

  • (V1) 3 ways to make more money as a life coach

  • (V2, Amped Up) 3 easy ways to make 10x more money as a life coach (nobody tells you this).

  • V3, Named & Claimed) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 easy ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

You should be able to feel (in your skin!) how much more you want to click on the V3 Subject Line—because “Life Coach Money Manual” feels like you're receiving a “thing.” (Which makes it feel exponentially more “valuable.”)

The challenge, of course, is doing this WITHOUT exceeding the word count limit for effective subject lines.

Here, for example, our V3 Subject Line is 16 words.

So if we wanted to trim this down, we would have to cut something.

Here are a few options:

  • (15 words) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 ways to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

  • (14 words) Life Coach Money Manual: How to 10x your monthly earnings (nobody tells you this)

  • (13 words) Life Coach Money Manual: 3 (little known) ways to 10x your monthly earnings

This is the “game” of writing subject lines.

And why you should start by writing the most effective subject line you can (based on 1 of the 4 hooks above), and THEN worry about trimming.

Proven Subject Lines

To-date, we’ve sent over 3,000,000 emails.

Which has taught us a few things!

So here are some of our highest-performing subject lines and a template you can use (feel free to steal & remix for yourself and your niche/topic):

Write With AI Subject Lines

Note: we publish Write With AI with Substack where the Subject Line of your newsletter is the Title of your post.

  • Magically Turn Headlines Into Short-Form Content With ChatGPT

  • Magically Turn {Thing} Into {Outcome Your Reader Wants} With {Tool/Method}

  • The Quora Formula For Building A Daily Writing Habit

  • The {Platform/Source} Formula For Building A {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

  • Story Selling With AI: How To Tell A Story That Prints Money Like Twitter “Copythinker” George Ten

  • {Process} With {Tool}: How To Tell A {Thing} That {Result/Outcome} Like {Person/Example}

  • 6 Proven Single-Sentence Openers

  • Bio Writing With AI: How To Train ChatGPT To Optimize Your Twitter Profile

  • {Task} With {Tool}: How To Train {Tool/AI} To Optimize Your {Platform/Profile}

  • Mix Your Voice With AI: How To Write Anything Using The 5 Different Types Of Writing Voices

  • Mix Your {Skill/Thing} With {Tool}: How To {Task} Using The {X} Different Types Of {Thing}

  • Creator Backstory: Train ChatGPT To Write A Personal Narrative Like Justin Welsh

  • {Persona/Type of Story}: Train {Tool} To Write A {Specific Story} Like {Example}

  • ChatGPT Vs Bard: What Is The Difference? And Which Is Better For Digital Writers?

  • {Object A} Vs {Object B}: What Is The {Comparison}? And Which Is Better For {Audience}?

  • Pain To Posts: Train ChatGPT To Write Tweets That Reach Inside Your Reader’s Subconscious

  • {Process/Framework}: Train {Tool} To Write {Content Type} That {Effect/Impact}

  • How To Write A High-Converting Landing Page For Your Lead Magnet

  • How To Write A {Result-Oriented} {Thing} For Your {Specific Goal/Outcome}

Start Writing Online Subject Lines

  • {X} dead-simple steps to {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

  • How to generate 112 ideas in 30 minutes

  • How to generate {X} {Things Your Reader Needs} in {Y}

  • How to craft the perfect {X}

  • The {X} pieces of an effective {Thing Your Reader Needs}

  • Advanced headline writing strategies (shhh....)

  • Advanced {Skill Your Reader Needs} strategies (shhh....)

  • The Ultimate Guide to repurposing {Thing} on {Platform}

  • A quick guide to starting a newsletter

  • A quick guide to starting a {Thing Your Reader Wants}

  • Dickie’s exact path to his first $1,000+ digital product

  • {Person's} exact path to their first {Milestone}

  • 3 steps to build a 99% margin digital business

  • {X} steps to {Outcome Your Reader Wants}

Start Ghostwriting Subject Lines

  • 💰 Get paid to write

  • 💰 Get paid to {Action/Skill Your Reader Wants To Monetize}

  • Niches to avoid as a ghostwriter

  • {Topics/Area} to avoid as a {Profession/Role Your Reader Relates To}

  • Ghostwriting = MBA on steroids ✍️

  • {Skill/Profession} = {Analogy or Comparison Your Reader Will Understand} {Emoji}

  • The top question in my DMs

  • The top question in my {Source/Platform/Inbox}

  • "Hey, did you mean to send me $5,000?"

  • "Hey, did you mean to send me {Large/Surprising Amount}?"

  • [The secret here is to create an open loop in the mind of the reader with a quote relating to a story you describe in your newsletter.]

  • 3 (brutal) reasons why you’re going nowhere

  • {X} (brutal) reasons why you’re {Negative Outcome Reader Wants to Avoid}

  • 7 leads from ONE message!

  • {X} {Result/Outcome Your Reader Wants} from ONE {Action/Tool/Strategy}!

  • Never call yourself a “freelance writer” again

  • Never call yourself a “{Label Your Reader Should Avoid}” again

  • How much $$$ can you make as a ghostwriter?

  • How much $$$ can you make as a {Profession/Role}?

  • How to make more 💰 as a ghostwriter

  • How to make more 💰 as a {Profession/Role Your Reader Relates To}

  • 3 reasons why you’re not moving forward 😤

  • {X} reasons why you’re not {Desired Outcome Your Reader Wants} 😤

  • 5 million-dollar lessons I learned as a ghostwriter

  • {X} {High-Value or Surprising Lessons} I learned as a {Profession/Role}

  • How I made $20,000/mo as a writer

  • How I made {Large Income/Outcome} as a {Profession/Role}

  • 8 most lucrative ghostwriting services

  • {X} most lucrative {Services/Opportunities Your Reader Wants}

  • Why 99% writers are broke

  • Why {Large Percentage} {Your Audience Group} are {Negative Outcome}

  • Break 8 faulty beliefs to get rich

  • Break {X} {Negative Beliefs/Obstacles} to {Positive Outcome}

  • Feel like you’re capable of more?

  • Feel like you’re capable of {Ambitious Goal/Outcome}?

  • How to make 💰 writing in a niche you love

  • How to make 💰 {Action/Skill} in a {Niche/Area Your Reader Is Passionate About}

  • How to charge $6,500 (instead of $650)

  • How to charge {Large Amount} (instead of {Smaller Amount})

  • “Freelance Writers” & “Copywriters” are ☠️

  • “{Common Label 1} ” & “{Common Label 2}” are ☠️

  • Are you really in control of your income?

  • Are you really in control of your {Outcome/Desire Your Reader Wants to Own}?

How To Write Irresistible Subject Lines With AI

The real “trick” to hooking your reader’s attention in their inbox is to include something that will make them want to “click.”

4 proven hooks:

  • Here's a ton of value for minimal time.

  • Here's a ton of value for minimal cost.

  • Here's how to solve your problem without much effort.

  • Here's how to unlock this desirable outcome, instantly.

Nail these, and you’ll be watching your open rates climb from a dismal 7% to an eye-popping 50%+.

We are going to break this down into 4 steps.

Step 1: Train Claude On Email & Preview-Text

In this prompt we give Claude the role of email marketer.

We ask it to leverage the 4 proven types of hooks, “whisper” in the preview-text, and avoid the most common mistakes we outlined above. Lastly, for this prompt we offer examples to help guide the AI on the types of output we are looking for.

Once Claude confirms it understands the prompt, move on to the next step.

Act like an expert email marketer with 10 years of experience.

You are a master at grabbing people's attention in their email inbox.

I want to write an email subject line and subtext to capture my target audience's attention.

The job of the subject line is to hook the reader (in an informal fashion, like a note to a friend)

The job of the subtext is “Whisper.” A “here’s what’s inside” sentence. (think parenthetical in copywriting)

Here's what we are going to do:

I am going to give you a topic and a newsletter.

After I have provided you the topic and newsletter, you will write the subject lines and subtext for the email.

Here are the 4 proven hooks:

1. A ton of value for minimal time.
2. A ton of value for minimal cost.
3. How to solve your problem without much effort.
4. How to unlock a desirable outcome, instantly.

Some good subject line example to follow:

- "Your entire Life Coach career path blueprint… in 1 email!"
- "Here's our entire $1M marketing plan. Steal it!"
- "Losing money in the stock market? Just buy these 3 companies."
- "3 keys to land $10,000 consulting clients, from home, in your pajamas, right now."
- "5 steps to write your first viral Twitter thread as a Digital Creator (even if you have 0 Followers)"

The things you can “whisper” are:

- A “trust me” sentence
- A “without this obstacle” sentence
- A “and with this additional benefit” sentence
- A “and so you can achieve this outcome too” sentence

For example:

- Trust Whisper = "Written By A Twitter Creator With 100k Followers"
- Obstacle Whisper = "Without Spending Any Money On Ads"
- Benefit Whisper = "And How To Solve It"
- Outcome Whisper = "And Start Earning $250,000 Per Year In Your Sweatpants"

Here's is and example of what your output will look like for each subject line and pretext you create:

- "Subject Line 1 (Value for Time): Avoid 3 common Twitter pitfalls in minutes."
- "Subtext (Outcome Whisper): And save months of misguided effort."

A few rules:

- Rule #1: Use 15 words, max.
- Rule #2: The subject line should read like you're talking to a friend. (use sentence case)
- Rule #3: Use visceral TANGIBLE language
- Rule #4: Intrigue the reader
- Rule #5: Use numbers
- Rule #6: Be SUPER SPECIFIC

Remember: DO NOT exceed the word count limit for effective subject lines.

Do you understand?

Let me know when you are ready for topic, the outline and the audience.

Step 2: Feed Claude Your Newsletter

In this step, you are going to give Claude your topic, outline, and target audience.

Feeding Claude this context will ensure the subject lines it writes are relevant to your newsletter issue.

Topic = {Your Topic}

Newsletter = {Copy/Paste Your Entire Newsletter Below}

Step 3: Generate And Choose Your Subject Line

Bang!

Now you’ve got a batch of subject lines and preview-text you can use for your newsletter!

Read through each one—out loud.

Ask yourself:

  • “Would I open this?”

  • “Do I want what’s inside?”

  • “What question does this raise for me?”

If it’s unclear to you, look to see if ChatGPT is making any of the common mistakes we covered and then redirect it to make those corrections for you, or make the adjustments on your own.

We just walked through the entire Traffic Engine. The 10 Magical Ways. Content. Cadence. Connection. Conversion. You know the post types. You know the daily rhythm. You know how to engage strategically. You know how to convert.

Now it's time to execute.

Here's what I need you to do before tomorrow's session (60-90 minutes):

Step 1: Extract 5-10 Social Posts From Your Day 3 Newsletter Draft. Use the 10 Magical Ways by hand, or run Prompt #2 (paste in your draft), then add your own voice and stories to the AI output. Save all of them in one doc — this is the start of your content library.

Step 2: Publish At Least ONE Post Today. Pick your strongest extraction and post it on X, LinkedIn, or Substack Notes (or all three, adapted). Done is better than perfect. The algorithm can't reward a post that doesn't exist.

Step 3: Audit Your Profiles. Does your newsletter name, bio, and pinned post clearly communicate what subscribers get? Add your newsletter link to every bio. Your profile is the conversion bottleneck. Everything downstream depends on it.

Step 4: Build Your Traffic 15 List. Identify 15 writers in your niche or adjacent niches with similar-sized audiences. Write their names down. These are the writers you'll engage with consistently starting this week.

Step 5: Commit To The 20-Minute Daily Routine For 14 Days. Morning: post 1 + engage for 5 minutes. Afternoon: post 1 + reply to comments. Track your new subscribers for 2 weeks and watch the flywheel start turning.

~

Reminder:

The writers who win at newsletter growth aren't the most talented. They're the most consistent.

And the best part? If you start now, you're early to the party. So there's never been a better time to get started.

See you tomorrow for Day 5: Newsletter Monetization Methods — how to turn the audience you're building into revenue.

records.content:
"How many followers do I need before this starts working?"

Zero.

Posts from writers with 100 followers can outperform those with 10,000+ because the algorithms weight genuine engagement over follower count. If you write something that resonates with even 5 people and they engage, the algorithm starts showing it to similar readers.

Don't wait until you're "big enough." Start now. That's the whole point of the early adopter advantage.

"I'm getting likes but no subscribers. What's wrong?"

Likes and subscribers are two different things. If you're getting likes but no subscribers, you have a conversion problem, not a content problem.

Go back to the Conversion section above. Check your profile. Does it clearly communicate what readers get if they subscribe? Are you using the Breadcrumb Trail? Are you adding soft CTAs 2-3x per week? Is your autoplug firing on X and LinkedIn? Most likely, your posts are good but your profile isn't closing.

"Should I post the same content on Notes, X, and LinkedIn?"

You can.

But the audiences are different. X rewards provocation, hot takes, and threads. Notes rewards vulnerability, stories, and genuine helpfulness. LinkedIn rewards professional stories and frameworks. A post that works on X might not work on Notes, and vice versa.

If you want to cross-post, adapt the tone and format for each platform. (This is a 60-second edit per post, not a rewrite.)

"I don't have time to post 2x per day. Is once a day enough?"

Once a day is better than zero. But 2x per day is where the compounding kicks in.

If you're strapped for time, commit to spend 20 minutes total. Most of these posts are 2-5 sentences. If you can send a text message, you can write a post. Batch 5-7 on Sunday night and you're already ahead for the week.

"What if I run out of things to say?"

You won't.

If you're publishing a newsletter, every single edition contains 5-7 posts waiting to be extracted (use Prompt #2 above — or the 10 Magical Ways if you're extracting by hand). Every conversation you have, every article you read, every question a subscriber asks — those are all posts.

"Should I engage with writers who have way bigger audiences than me?"

Absolutely. This is one of the highest-leverage things you can do.

When you leave a genuinely valuable comment on a big writer's post, their entire audience sees it. If your comment is good, people click on your name.

Don't be sycophantic. "OMG I love everything you write!" doesn't help anyone.

Add value. Share your own experience. Respectfully extend their point. Be the comment that makes the original writer say "damn, good point."

records.content:
Below are two simple prompts you can use to generate social content. Copy-paste them into ChatGPT, Claude, or your AI tool of choice. They'll generate posts for you based on the post types we just covered.

Now, what you can do is:

  • Run Prompt #1 to batch a full week of posts in one sitting

  • OR run Prompt #2 to take your latest newsletter (your Day 3 draft!) and extract 5-7 posts from it

  • Review the AI drafts and add YOUR voice, YOUR stories, YOUR specific details

  • Then post throughout the week

So cool!

Prompt #1: The Weekly Batch Generator

Purpose: Generate a full week's worth of posts (10-14) in one sitting.

You are a social content strategist for newsletter creators.

I'm going to give you context about my newsletter, and I need you to generate a batch of 14 posts for the upcoming week (usable on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes).

MY NEWSLETTER:
- Name: [Your newsletter name]
- Niche: [Your niche]
- Who I write for: [Your target reader]
- What I help them do: [The transformation/value]
- My latest newsletter was about: [Topic of most recent edition]
- A personal story I could share this week: [Brief description]

GENERATE 14 POSTS USING THESE TYPES:

Type 1 — Personal Story + Insight (generate 3):
- A short personal story (under 250 words) that builds to a single "aha" moment related to my niche
- Open with a specific, vivid moment
- End with one clear insight
- Optional: close with a question

Type 2 — Standalone Insight (generate 4):
- My best thinking distilled into 1-3 punchy sentences
- A surprising observation about my niche
- Should make someone stop scrolling

Type 3 — Community Invitation (generate 2):
- A post that invites readers to participate
- Ask a specific question (not generic)
- Make it about THEM, not me
- Include a generous offer ("Drop your newsletter and I'll check it out" or similar)

Type 4 — Newsletter Teaser (generate 3):
- Based on my latest newsletter topic above, pull out the most intriguing insight or claim
- Format as a standalone post that creates an information gap
- End with: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

FORMAT: Number each post. Label the type. Keep each post under 280 words. Use short paragraphs (1-2 sentences each). Make them sound like a real person, not a content machine.

Prompt #2: The Newsletter-to-Social Repurposer

Purpose: Take any newsletter edition and extract 5-7 posts from it. (Run this on your Day 3 draft tonight.)

You are a social content strategist for newsletter creators. I'm going to paste a newsletter edition below, and I need you to extract 5-7 high-performing social posts from it (usable on X, LinkedIn, and Substack Notes).

MY NEWSLETTER CONTEXT:
- Name: [Your newsletter name]
- Niche: [Your niche]
- Tone: [Describe your voice — conversational, authoritative, vulnerable, etc.]

EXTRACTION RULES:
1. Find the single most surprising claim or insight. Turn it into a Standalone Insight post (1-3 sentences).
2. Find the best story or personal anecdote. Turn it into a Personal Story + Insight post (under 250 words).
3. Find 2-3 "quotable" paragraphs. Turn each into a Standalone Insight post.
4. Write 1 Newsletter Teaser post that creates an information gap and links back to the full edition.
5. Write 1 Community Invitation post inspired by the newsletter topic (ask readers a question related to the theme).

FORMAT: Number each post. Label the type. Keep each under 280 words. Short paragraphs. Make them sound human.

Do NOT repost the newsletter. EXTRACT and TRANSFORM the best parts into standalone posts that work even if someone never reads the full edition.

records.content:
The Traffic Strategy: Content, Cadence, Connection, Conversion

The Traffic Strategy is a 4-part system for turning social posting into a consistent, compounding subscriber growth machine.

Here are the 4 parts:

  • Part 1: Content: What to post (the 3 content buckets and specific post types that convert)

  • Part 2: Cadence: When and how often to post (the daily rhythm)

  • Part 3: Connection: How to engage strategically (comments, restacks, relationships)

  • Part 4: Conversion: How to turn social readers into newsletter subscribers

Think of these as four gears. When all four are turning, the engine runs itself. Skip one, and the whole thing stalls.

Most writers only do Part 1 (content). They post, hope for the best, and then wonder why social "doesn't work" for them. The secret is that Parts 2, 3, and 4 are where the compounding happens.

Let's break down each part.

1. What To Post (The 3 Content Buckets)

There are 3 "buckets" of content you can post:

  1. Short-form original. Think of this as your typical social media content. Take snippets from your newsletter (via the 10 Magical Ways above) and post them as tweets, LinkedIn posts, or Substack Notes. Or experiment with new ideas by posting and seeing how the idea performs. If it performs well, expand the idea into a newsletter. This is Lean Writing 101: social is your idea lab, the newsletter is your finished product.

  2. Restacks / Reshares. This is exactly like retweets on Twitter. Use this function to restack other Notes you like or other newsletters you found interesting (or quote-tweet on X, reshare with commentary on LinkedIn). Choose to either share without comment or add your own comment (highly-recommended!).

  3. Newsletter Quotes. If you found a section of a newsletter interesting, highlight it then choose to post it to Notes with your own comment. A screenshot of the quote is created alongside a link to the original newsletter. (You can do this with your own newsletter too.) On X and LinkedIn, the equivalent is a clean screenshot of your best paragraph with a one-line setup.

One final note:

As with all social platforms, the algorithm and audience favor certain types of content. And right now, pairing your post with an image gets far more traction than pairing it with a video. But, of course, this might change so I encourage you to keep experimenting.

2. When And How To Post (Cadence)

Right now, there is no way to schedule posts on Substack Notes (X and LinkedIn do have scheduling — use it).

Which means you have to manage your posts with discipline. As with every other social media platform, consistency is key. It helps you to a) publish a lot of ideas over an extended period of time and b) build trust with your audience because they "expect" you to appear in their feed.

So, pick a schedule and stick with it.

I post twice per day at 10am and 4pm ET. Dickie does the same.

And if you need a little rigor, here's a simple weekly content calendar you can follow:

  • Monday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Restack with Commentary (4pm)

  • Tuesday: Personal Story (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Wednesday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Newsletter Teaser (4pm)

  • Thursday: Restack with Commentary (10am) + Newsletter Quote (4pm)

  • Friday: Standalone Insight (10am) + Community Invitation (4pm)

  • Saturday: Newsletter Teaser (10am) + Restack with Commentary (4pm)

  • Sunday: Personal Story (10am) + Standalone Insight (4pm)

You don't need to follow this exactly. But it gives you a starting point so you never sit down and think "what should I post today?"

Batch your WRITING (not necessarily your posting):

  1. Sunday night: Extract and write 5-7 posts for the week from your latest newsletter. Standalone Insights and Personal Stories are the easiest to batch. Save them in a doc or your notes app, then copy-paste at your posting times throughout the week.

  2. Daily: Write 1-2 reactive posts in real-time. Restacks, Community Invitations, and Newsletter Quotes work best when they're timely and spontaneous.

  3. Post-newsletter day: Pull 1-2 Newsletter Teasers from your latest edition.

Cross-posting rule: write once, adapt twice. Your Sunday batch is drafted once, then given a 60-second platform pass — tighten the hook for X, add line breaks and a story frame for LinkedIn, soften the tone for Notes.

Content and cadence are locked.

3. How To Engage (Connection)

At the end of the day, I encourage you to be a good social citizen.

If you interact with more people, you're more likely to attract new subscribers to your own content. So it pays to be active and engage with other writers you enjoy reading.

OK. With that philosophy in mind, let me show you why engagement matters even more than posting.

When you leave a substantive comment on a popular writer's post, you show up in front of their entire audience. If your comment is good (if it adds genuine value, a personal example, or a thoughtful perspective), people click on your name, visit your profile, and subscribe.

One good comment on the right post can bring more subscribers than 10 posts of your own.

So engagement is not a "nice to have." It's the multiplier that makes everything else work.

Strategy #1: The Value-Add Comment

When you comment on someone else's post, don't say "love this!" or "so true!"

Those comments don't help the algorithm surface your profile. Substantive comments do. Add something. A personal example. A related insight. A "yes, and…" that takes their point further. The rule: every comment you leave should be good enough to be its own post.

When your comments are consistently thoughtful, two things happen.

  • The algorithm surfaces them higher (more people see them).

  • And the writer you're engaging with starts to notice you (which leads to restacks, cross-promotion, and organic relationship-building).

Strategy #2: The Restack (Or Quote-Share)

I talked about Restacking as a content type above.

But I want to call it out again as an engagement strategy because it's that powerful. When you restack someone's Note with your own commentary (or quote-tweet on X, or reshare on LinkedIn), it goes to YOUR audience with your endorsement, and it notifies the original writer.

They see your name.

They check you out.

And if you've been consistently restacking their work with thoughtful takes, they'll often return the favor.

One restack from the right person can bring dozens of new subscribers.

Restack 2-3 posts per week from writers in your niche or adjacent niches. Always add your own take. (Don't just hit the restack button.)

Strategy #3: Build Your "Traffic 15"

Identify 10-15 writers in your niche or adjacent niches with similar-sized audiences.

Write their names down. These are your "Traffic 15."

Engage with their posts consistently. Comment, restack, reply. Over 2-4 weeks, you'll build a relationship. And the algorithm notices overlapping audiences. When your readers and their readers start interacting with both of you, the platform starts showing your work to THEIR followers and vice versa.

This is the organic version of cross-promotion. And it's more powerful because it's earned.

Rotate 1-2 names per month as your audience grows.

Here's a simple checklist. Every day, in addition to posting your 2 posts:

  • Comment substantively on 3-5 posts from writers in your niche

  • Reply to every comment on your own posts within the first hour

  • Restack/reshare 1 post with your own commentary (if you find something worth sharing)

  • Check your "Traffic 15" — have you engaged with at least 2-3 of them today?

This takes 10 minutes.

You're posting great content. You're showing up consistently. You're building relationships. But are those readers actually becoming subscribers?

Let's make sure they do.

4. How To Convert Followers Into Subscribers (Conversion)

Most writers still leave subscribers on the table because they don't have a deliberate conversion system.

Here's how to fix that.

Conversion Tactic #1: Optimize Your Profiles

Your profile (on every platform) must answer one question instantly for your reader: "What will I get if I subscribe?"

And to answer this question…

  • Your newsletter name must clearly state your niche (you built this on Day 1)

  • Your one-line description/bio needs to communicate the value (you built this on Day 1)

  • Your pinned post should sell the subscription — pin your best newsletter teaser or a "start here" post with your subscribe link

  • On X and LinkedIn: put your newsletter link in your bio, not buried in a linktree

Your social strategy will not work without a profile that converts. The profile is the conversion bottleneck.

Conversion Tactic #2: Leave Breadcrumbs

Inside your posts, occasionally reference your newsletter in a way that creates curiosity.

Here's what I mean:

  • "I broke this down in way more detail in last week's edition. The part about [specific intriguing detail] surprised even me."

  • "My subscribers know I've been tracking this for 6 months now. The data is wild."

  • "This is the short version. The 2,000-word deep dive is in my newsletter if you want the full framework."

When you do this, you create an information gap. There's a piece of the story the reader can only get by subscribing or digging into your newsletter. And that gap creates genuine curiosity.

Use this 2-3x per week. Sprinkle it into Personal Story and Standalone Insight posts. Never force it. When you have something genuinely interesting in your newsletter, mention it casually.

Conversion Tactic #3: "For Example…"

(This is one of my favorite tactics. It's so powerful it's worth teaching everywhere.)

If you want to point readers toward your newsletter without being seen as promotional, all you need are two magical words: "For example…"

Whenever you share an insight in a post, follow it with "For example, in my newsletter I…" and describe something specific and tangible that you do or share.

Like this:

Most Newsletter Creators only think about growth on external platforms. But the biggest lever is right inside the platform you're already on.

For example, in my newsletter [Newsletter Name], I share one specific traffic strategy every week that I've tested myself. Last week's strategy brought in 40+ new subscribers from a single post.

Are you furious at me for being "overly promotional?" Of course not. I just used my newsletter as an example. Casually. Organically.

And yet I still introduced it to you.

This is the whole secret. After the words "for example," you can point to any business, any product, any money-making-anything, and it won't come off as promotional. It comes across as a relevant example. The reader appreciates it.

Conversion Tactic #4: The Autoplug

On X and LinkedIn, the algorithm suppresses posts with links. So don't put your newsletter link in the post — put it in the first reply/comment.

Here's the play:

  1. Publish your post (no link).

  2. Immediately reply to your own post: "If you liked this, I go deeper every week in [Newsletter Name]. Subscribe free: [link]"

  3. If a post starts performing, that reply rides along with it. (Tools like Hypefury and Typefully can automate this "autoplug" to fire only when a post crosses an engagement threshold.)

The post does the work of earning attention. The autoplug does the work of converting it. Never let a post take off without a subscribe path attached.

Conversion Tactic #5: The CTA Rotation

Most posts should focus on pure value delivery. Only ~30% of your posts should have any CTA at all.

Here's the rotation:

  • 60-70% of your posts: No CTA. Just deliver value. Build trust. Let the profile do the converting.

  • 1-2x per week: Link to your newsletter. "Full breakdown in this week's [Newsletter Name] 👇" (On X/LinkedIn: link goes in the reply via autoplug.)

  • 1x per week: Soft subscribe prompt. "If this resonated, my newsletter goes deeper on [topic] every [day]. Subscribe free."

  • 2-3x per week: Breadcrumb trail. Just reference your newsletter casually.

The math on this works. Post 14 posts per week per platform. Average reach per post: 500-2,000 impressions (this grows over time). A small percentage click your profile. A percentage of those subscribe (especially if your profile is optimized).

Result: 10-30+ new subscribers per week from organic social alone. Per platform. And it compounds.

5. More Tips And Tricks To Squeeze Extra Juice

Here are some of my current favorite insights and tricks:

  • Notes lifespan. The life of a post is longer on Substack than on X or LinkedIn. Some Notes can get engagement WEEKS after we've posted them. So traction can really pick up over a number of days and weeks. Again, another reason to start posting on Notes.

  • No platform analytics on Notes. At least, not for now. So you will have to track your engagement manually (likes, comments, restacks, etc). Or try using a tool like WriteStack. (X and LinkedIn have built-in analytics — check them weekly, not daily.)

  • Newsletters get pushed to Notes. Your newsletters automatically drop into your Notes feed so you don't have to manually post them to your feed.

  • Create high-quality thumbnails. As newsletters get pushed into the feed automatically, it's important to have an eye-catching thumbnail for the newsletter so it stands out in the feed (this is the main image of your post). You can use this as an opportunity to tease the value or create an open loop for the reader.

  • Promote your best posts inside your newsletter. You can do this in your long-form newsletters by including a snippet of your best-performing post of the week. This is another way in for your audience to find your social content and start engaging with it. The flywheel runs both directions: newsletter → social → newsletter.

  • Winners get recycled. Any post that outperforms your average earns a spot in your "greatest hits" doc. Repost it in 60-90 days (audiences turn over fast), and consider expanding it into its own newsletter edition.

That's it!

The big POV here is that your newsletter library is a traffic asset, and organic social is a growth lever you should be pulling every single day — especially Substack Notes, where the algorithm is literally built to hand you subscribers.

And the best part?

If you start now, you're early to the party. So there's never been a better time to get started.

records.content:
The 10 Magical Ways: Extracting 10+ Social Posts From One Newsletter



Here's the workflow that ends "what should I post today?" forever.

Take your Day 3 newsletter draft. Read through it with a highlighter (literal or digital). Every newsletter you write contains at least 10 extractable social posts hiding inside it. Here are the 10 Magical Ways to pull them out:

  1. The Standalone Insight. Find your single most surprising claim or observation. Distill it into 1-3 punchy sentences. No context needed — it should make someone stop scrolling on its own.

  2. The Personal Story. Find the best story or anecdote in your newsletter. Rewrite it as a short post (under 250 words) that opens with a specific, vivid moment and builds to a single "aha" insight.

  3. The Listicle. Take any section with multiple points and reformat it as a numbered list post. "5 things I learned about [topic]:" — lists are the most shareable format on every platform.

  4. The Framework Breakdown. If your newsletter teaches a process or framework, extract the steps into a "how to" post. Step 1 → Step 2 → Step 3. On X, this becomes a thread. On LinkedIn, a line-break-heavy post. On Notes, a short numbered Note.

  5. The Contrarian Take. Find the place where your newsletter disagrees with conventional wisdom. Extract it as: "Everyone says X. Here's why they're wrong: [your take]."

  6. The Quotable Line. Find 2-3 "quotable" paragraphs — the lines you're proudest of. Post each one verbatim. On Substack, use the Newsletter Quote feature (highlight → post to Notes) so the quote links back to the full edition automatically.

  7. The Proof Post. Extract any number, result, stat, or before/after from your newsletter. "I did X for 30 days. Here's what happened:" Receipts build trust faster than opinions.

  8. The Question Post (Community Invitation). Take your newsletter's core theme and turn it into a specific question for your audience. Make it about THEM, not you. Include a generous offer ("Drop your newsletter below and I'll check it out").

  9. The Teaser (Open Loop). Pull out the most intriguing insight or claim and format it as a standalone post that creates an information gap. End with: "Full breakdown in this week's [newsletter name] 👇"

  10. The Mistake/Lesson Post. Extract what you (or your reader) were doing wrong before the insight in your newsletter. "I spent 2 years doing [wrong thing]. Then I learned [insight]."

That's the whole workflow: 1 newsletter in, 10+ atomic posts out.

A few rules for extraction:

  • Do NOT repost the newsletter. EXTRACT and TRANSFORM the best parts into standalone posts that work even if someone never reads the full edition.

  • Every post must stand alone. If it requires reading the newsletter to make sense, it's not extracted yet.

  • Adapt per platform. Same idea, three flavors: punchy and provocative for X, story-driven and professional for LinkedIn, warm and reader-to-reader for Notes.

  • Keep each post under 280 words. Short paragraphs (1-2 sentences each). Make them sound like a real person, not a content machine.

Do this every time you publish, and after 10 newsletters you'll have a 100+ post library. You'll never stare at a blank compose box again.

Now let's turn those posts into a system.

records.content:
Before we get into what works, let's talk about what doesn't.

These are the 5 most common mistakes we see Newsletter Creators make when driving social traffic. If you're doing any of these, fix them first. Then move on to the strategy.

Mistake #1: Speaking The Wrong Language On The Wrong Platform

Notes is not a microblogging platform for hot takes and dunking on people.

The algorithm rewards connection, not controversy. Writers who bring their Twitter habits to Notes get likes, sure. But they don't get subscribers. And there's a massive difference between the two.

The audience on Substack is there to read and learn. They want depth. They want genuine thinking. So if you're posting the same spicy tweets you'd throw onto X, you're speaking the wrong language to the wrong crowd. (The reverse is also true: a long, vulnerable LinkedIn story posted verbatim on X will die. Same idea, adapted format.)

Mistake #2: Only Posting Links To Your Newsletter

"New post! Link in comments."

Sound familiar?

This is the #1 mistake writers make. They treat social platforms as a promotional bulletin board. And nobody clicks those. Readers want to be engaged on the platform they're on. They don't want to be redirected somewhere else every time you show up in their feed.

If every post you write is a link to your newsletter, you're training the algorithm (and readers) to scroll right past you.

Mistake #3: Posting Once And Disappearing

One post a week is not a strategy. It's a lottery ticket.

The algorithm builds a picture of your voice over time. It watches who engages, what they subscribe to, who else they follow. And then it starts showing your writing to new readers who match that profile. But it needs data. Consistency is what trains the algorithm to work for you. Sporadic posting gives it nothing to work with.

Mistake #4: Ignoring The Engagement Side

Social is a two-way street.

The writers who grow fastest are commenting on other writers' posts, restacking/resharing work they admire, and having conversations. If you're posting but never engaging, you're running at half speed.

And here's the thing: algorithms now rank high-signal interactions (replies that add genuine value) above passive hearts and "love this!" comments. So the quality of your engagement matters, too.

Mistake #5: No Conversion Mechanism

You can write great posts, get tons of likes, and still gain zero subscribers.

Why? Because you never gave anyone a reason to subscribe. There's no bridge between "I liked this post" and "I subscribed to this newsletter."

You need a deliberate system for turning social attention into newsletter subscriptions. (Don't worry. That's coming later in this session.)

OK. Now that we know what NOT to do, let's get to the heart of today: the extraction workflow.
